en: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll One; Part One of the First Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra from North India together with Kumārajīva during the Later Qin dynasty.

The First Recitation: The Four Pārājika Dharmas. The First Exposition of the Four Pārājika Dharmas. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī. Not far from the city, there was a village where lived the son of an elder named Sudinna Kalandakaputra. He was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and accomplished in all things. Having taken refuge in the Triple Gem as a disciple of the Buddha, he grew weary of the world and left the household life; he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma-robes, and became a bhikṣu. Departing from his native land, he went to a certain place in the kingdom of Kośala to observe the rains retreat.

At that time, there was a famine and alms were difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of the common people lacked sufficient food and drink, let alone being able to give to those who went begging.

Then, Sudinna thought to himself: "This great famine makes it difficult to obtain anything through begging. My kinsmen and relatives possess abundant wealth; they will surely perform acts of charity and cultivate merit on my account. Now is precisely the right time."

Having formed this thought, when the three-month summer retreat had passed and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was concluded, and having finished making his robes, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and returned to Vaiśālī; traveling through various countries, he arrived at his native village.

When the early morning arrived, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the village to beg for food. Upon reaching the house of a relative, he exhorted the various bhikṣus one by one to offer him various kinds of food and drink; he himself practiced the dhūta ascetic practice of begging for alms.
Having finished his alms-round, he returned to his own dwelling and said:
"I previously promised that I would return; I have now come back.
Having spoken these words, he quickly departed.
A young maidservant of the household, seeing him depart so quickly, immediately ran to inform Sūpananda’s mother:
"Just now, Sūpananda entered the gate and then left.
His mother thought to herself:
“Sudin has entered the gate and departed immediately; perhaps he is distressed and wishes to return home to relinquish the precepts, finding no joy in the holy life?
I shall now go to instruct him to return home, where he may indulge in the five desires, practice generosity, and cultivate merit.”
Having had this thought, he went to where Sūpannaka was and said to him:

"If you are distressed and find no joy in the holy life (brahmacarya), and wish to abandon the precepts, then come back home to enjoy the five sensual pleasures, practice giving, and perform meritorious deeds."
He immediately replied to his mother, saying:

“I have no sorrow or anxiety; I do not wish to forsake the precepts, nor do I weary of the holy life (brahmacarya), nor do I wish to abandon the Dharma of a śramaṇa; my heart delights in the holy life.”
His mother thought to herself:
"Although I have spoken with my own mouth, he does not turn his heart.
I must speak to his wife, saying:"
“When it is time for you to be clean, come and inform me.
He then went and told her, and the wife said, “So be it.”
Having received her mother’s instructions, when the time for purification arrived, she went to inform her mother, saying:
"What should I do now?
Then the mother instructed her, saying:
"Put on all the garments and ornaments that you find pleasing.
Having received these instructions, he returned to his room and put on the clothes and ornaments he liked.
The mother then went to where Sudinna was and spoke these words:
"If you are sorrowful and find no joy in the holy life, and wish to abandon the precepts, you should return home to enjoy the five sensual pleasures, practice giving, and cultivate merit."
"The Buddha-dharma is difficult to accomplish, and leaving the household life involves diligent hardship.
He then replied to his mother, saying:
"I have no sorrow or anxiety; my mind does not waver. I personally delight in practicing the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and I do not delight in the five desires."
The mother said,
"Excellent, Sūdena! Since you delight in the holy life and do not wish to abandon the precepts, now that your wife has reached her time, you should remain to continue the lineage."
"If a family has no heir, all its property shall go to the state.
At that time, before the World-Honored One had yet formulated this precept, Sudinna’s mind was moved, and he replied to his mother, "So be it."
The mother then withdrew, and he took his wife to a secluded place and committed sexual intercourse with her; this occurred two or three times.

Soon thereafter she conceived, and when the months were full, she gave birth to a son of great merit, whom they named *Pratāna* (Continuation of the Lineage). When he grew up, he gained faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, left the household life to study the Path, and through diligent and energetic practice, attained the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and became an Arhat.

At that time, having already committed the sexual act, Sudinna felt doubt and regret in his heart; his countenance changed with sorrow and anxiety, and he was devoid of majestic dignity. He remained silent with his head bowed, his shoulders drooping in dejection, and took no pleasure in conversation.
At that time, a bhikṣu who was a close friend came to inquire after his well-being and sat to one side;
he asked Sūdena, "Previously you possessed majestic virtue, your countenance was serene and joyful, and you delighted in practicing the holy life."
For what reason now are you so sorrowful and your countenance changed, remaining silent with head bowed,
bewildered and unhappy? Is your body ill,
or have you committed some evil deed in private?
Sudinna said, "My body is not ill;
it is because I have committed an evil deed in secret that my mind is filled with sorrow.
Then, as the bhikṣus questioned him more and more insistently, he explained the circumstances in detail, as related above.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus rebuked Sūdena with various reasons and causes, saying:
"You ought to be sorrowful, afflicted, and full of remorse, yet you have committed such a private and evil deed."

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path, and to engage in impure conduct without a mind of desirelessness is something that one who has gone forth ought not to do."

"You do not know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has used various causes and conditions to censure desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; and he has used various causes and conditions to praise the abandonment of desire, the relinquishing of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire."

The Buddha constantly teaches the Dharma to instruct people to leave desire behind; you should not even give rise to such thoughts, let alone commit the impure and evil karma that is the root of the fetters of desire, anger, and delusion.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had rebuked him in various ways, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas:

One may ask with full knowledge; or one may know but not ask; one may ask at the proper time; or one may not ask at the proper time; one may ask regarding matters that are beneficial; or one may not ask regarding matters that are not beneficial; or one may ask when there is a specific cause and condition.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, knowing this, at that time questioned Sūdena with right mindfulness and settled wisdom:
"Did you truly do such a thing?
He replied:
“Yes, World-Honored One, he did indeed do it.
The Buddha then rebuked Sūdena with various causes and conditions, saying:

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path, and to engage in impure conduct without a mind of desirelessness is something that one who has gone forth ought not to do."
"You foolish person!

You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; and that I have, through various causes and conditions, praised the severing of desire, the relinquishing of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire. I constantly preach the Dharma to teach people to leave desire behind; you should not even give rise to such a thought, let alone commit the impure and evil karma that is the root of the fetters of desire, anger, and delusion."
He said to the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man has opened the gates of all outflows; he would rather thrust his own limbs into the mouth of a venomous snake than ever touch that woman's body with them."
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus: for the sake of unifying the Saṃgha; for the sake of perfecting its unity;

for the sake of the Saṃgha’s dwelling in peace and happiness; for the sake of subduing those with arrogant minds; for the sake of providing peace and happiness to those who possess a sense of shame; for the sake of inspiring pure faith in those who lack it; for the sake of increasing the faith of those who already believe; for the sake of warding off afflictions and outflows in this present life; for the sake of severing evil in future lives; and for the sake of the long-term endurance of the Brahma-faring."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having entered the training rules of the bhikṣus, does not relinquish the precepts and engages in sexual conduct, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu named Vāgīśaputra who, though he had not formally renounced the precepts nor returned home because his vows were weak, nevertheless engaged in sexual intercourse.
Later, wishing to go forth again, he thought to himself:
"I should first go and ask the bhikṣus whether it is possible for me to go forth."
"If it cannot be obtained, then stop.
Having formed this thought, he questioned the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus were doubtful and reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If there is a person who does not relinquish the precepts, yet, while his precepts have become weak, he does not leave the order to return home and commit sexual misconduct, he may still go forth and become a bhikṣu again.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

'If a bhikṣu has entered the disciplinary law of the bhikṣus together with others, and without relinquishing the precepts or leaving the order due to weakened precepts, commits the act of sexual intercourse, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with the others.'"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu living alone in a forest in the kingdom of Kośala. A female macaque would frequently come to this bhikṣu’s dwelling; the bhikṣu then enticed her with food and drink, and as the macaque’s mind became softened, they engaged in sexual intercourse together.
This bhikṣu had many acquaintances who came to visit him and sat to one side.

At that time, a monkey approached with the intent to commit sexual misconduct; it looked at the face of each bhikṣu in turn, and finally stopped before the bhikṣu it loved, gazing intently at his face.
At that time, this bhikṣu felt ashamed in his heart and would not look at the monkey; the monkey immediately became angry, tore off his ears and nose, and departed after inflicting the injury.
Then the other bhikṣus urgently asked him the reason for this, and he explained the preceding circumstances in detail as above.
The bhikṣus rebuked him with various reasons, saying:

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path. To engage in impure conduct without a mind of dispassion is something that those who have left the household life ought not to do."

You do not know that the Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions, has rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; and by means of various causes and conditions, he has praised the severing of desire, the relinquishing of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

The Buddha constantly teaches the Dharma to instruct people to leave desire behind; you should not even give rise to such thoughts, let alone commit the impure evil karma that is the root of the fetters of desire, anger, and delusion.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had rebuked him with various reasons, they went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to the Buddha in detail.
Then the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he addressed those bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path. To engage in impure conduct without a mind of desirelessness is something that one who has gone forth ought not to do."
"You foolish person!

You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; and that I have, through various causes and conditions, praised the severing of desire, the relinquishing of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire. I constantly teach the Dharma to instruct people to be free from desire."
"You should not even give rise to such a thought, let alone commit the impure and evil karma that is the root of the fetters of desire, hatred, and delusion.
Having thus rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I have already established this precept previously; now I establish it again accordingly."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, having entered the training of the bhikṣus, does not relinquish the precepts, and while his precepts are weak, he commits the act of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and should not live in community."
Regarding "if a bhikṣu," there are four types: first, the bhikṣu by name;
second, the self-proclaimed bhikṣu; [third, the bhikṣu by way of ordination;
fourth, the bhikṣu by way of breaking out of the shell.]
Third, the bhikṣu who begs for alms;
fourth, the bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions.
As for the "bhikṣu by name," he is so designated by his name alone.
One who calls himself a bhikṣu is one who has received full ordination through the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Furthermore, there is the "thief-dwelling" bhikṣu, who shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and says of himself: "I am a bhikṣu."
This is called a "self-proclaimed bhikṣu.
As for a "bhikṣu by begging," because he begs food from others, just as when a brāhmaṇa begs from others, he also says:
"I am a bhikṣu."
This is what is meant by a "begging bhikṣu.

As for the "bhikṣu who destroys afflictions," he is one who can sever the outflows (āsrava), fetters (saṃyojana), and bonds of affliction that cause sentient beings to receive future bodies and undergo the retribution of feverish suffering, and which serve as the causes and conditions for the continuous succession of birth and death.

If one can know and see, thereby severing such outflows and uprooting them entirely—just as when the crown of a *tāla* tree is cut off so that it never grows again—one is called a bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions.
What is it for a bhikṣu to be complete in the precepts?
What is a bhikṣu who is complete in the precepts?

If the Saṃgha, being in harmony, performs the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and this person receives it with faith, follows it accordingly, and does not oppose, resist, or violate it—this is called a bhikṣu complete in the precepts; this is called a bhikṣu complete in the precepts.
The student has three trainings:
the training in virtuous ethics, the training in virtuous mind, and the training in virtuous wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three trainings:
One should well train in the rules of decorum, well train in the Vinaya, and well train in the Prātimokṣa.
Those who enter this training together should learn in the same manner as a bhikṣu who has been ordained for a hundred years; even a person newly ordained should train in this way.

Just as one who has newly received the precepts trains, so too does a bhikṣu of a hundred years train; herein there is one mind, one precept, one teaching, and one Prātimokṣa. Because they share the same mind, the same precepts, the same teaching, and the same Prātimokṣa, it is called the "Dharma of Training for Bhikṣus Entering Together."
Regarding "not relinquishing the precepts": if a bhikṣu relinquishes the precepts while he is insane, it is not called relinquishing the precepts.

If one discards the precepts while the mind is distracted; when the mind is impaired by illness; when speaking to a madman, a person with a distracted mind, or a person whose mind is impaired by illness; if one discards them alone; if one perceives oneself as not alone when one is alone, or perceives oneself as alone when one is not alone; if one speaks in a central dialect to a person from a frontier region who does not understand it, or speaks in a frontier dialect to a person from a central region who does not understand it; if one speaks to a mute, a deaf person, or a person who is both mute and deaf; if one speaks to someone who lacks understanding; if one speaks to a non-human being, a sleeping person, or a person who has entered meditative absorption; if there is a physical barrier between them; if one is angry oneself, or if one is speaking to an angry person; if it is during a dream; or if one’s own mind is unsettled, or if one is speaking to a person whose mind is unsettled—discarding the precepts under such circumstances is not called "discarding the precepts."

There are cases where one abandons the precepts but does not weaken them; cases where one weakens the precepts but does not abandon them; and cases where one both weakens the precepts and abandons them.
Regarding abandoning the precepts without weakening them: if a bhikṣu says, "I renounce the Buddha."
This is called abandoning the precepts.
If one says:
"I abandon the Dharma, I abandon the Sangha, I abandon the precepts;"
Abandoning one's preceptor; abandoning one's teacher;
abandoning those who share a preceptor or a teacher;
abandoning a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī.
They abandon the śikṣamāṇā;
they abandon the śrāmaṇera and the śrāmaṇerī;
they abandon the upāsaka and the upāsikā.
All these are termed "abandoning the precepts.
If one says:

"You should know that I am a layperson (*avadātavasana*), or perhaps a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya; furthermore, I shall no longer practice as a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) with you."
This is called "abandoning the precepts" (śikṣā-pratyākhyāna), not "the weakening of the precepts" (śīla-daurbalya).

Regarding "the weakening of the precepts" but not "abandoning the precepts": if a bhikṣu is distressed and unhappy, desiring to abandon the precepts and grow weary of the bhikṣu-dharma; desiring to cast off the noble robes and take up white lay garments; needing the way of a layman and not needing the way of a bhikṣu; seeking the affairs of a householder, and further saying:

"I think of my father and mother, brothers and sisters; I think of my sons and daughters. They should quickly teach me the skills for making a living, settle me in a good place, and entrust me to virtuous friends."
To speak such words is called "weakening of the precepts" (śīla-klāmya), not "abandoning the precepts" (śīla-tyāga).

Regarding both weakening of the precepts and abandoning the precepts: if a bhikṣu is sorrowful and unhappy, desiring to abandon the precepts; if he loathes the bhikṣu-dharma and wishes to cast off the noble robes, taking up white garments and seeking the way of a layperson; if he no longer requires the bhikṣu-dharma and seeks the affairs of a householder;

and if he further says: "I think of my father, mother, brothers, and sisters; I think of my sons and daughters. They should quickly teach me the arts of livelihood, establish me in a secure place, and entrust me to virtuous friends."
Having spoken these words, he further said:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, and so forth, even renouncing the upāsakas and upāsikās."
This is called "weakening of the precepts" as well as "abandoning the precepts.
Regarding those who practice the dharma of sexual misconduct: "sexuality" refers to non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*).
"Non-celibacy" refers to the physical union of two bodies.

"Pārājika" means falling into a state of non-conformity; this offense is extremely evil and profound. One who commits such an offense immediately falls into non-conformity; they are no longer called a bhikṣu, nor are they a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya; they have lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.

"Those who do not live together" means that they may not perform the monastic rites together—namely, the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the *poṣadha*, and the *pravāraṇā*—nor may they be included among the fourteen classes of persons; this is called "defeat (*pārājika*) and non-cohabitation."
Regarding the offenses within this, there are four types:
men, women, eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs.
As for "women," these include human women, non-human women, and female animals.
A male may be a human male, a non-human male, or a male animal.
Hermaphrodites and those with dual sexual organs may likewise be humans, non-humans, or animals.
If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse with a human female, he commits a pārājika offense in three locations:
the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth;
it is the same for non-human females, female animals, and those with both sexual organs.
If one commits sexual intercourse with a human male, one incurs a *pārājika* offense in two places:
the anus and the mouth;
the same applies to non-human males, male animals, and eunuchs.

Furthermore, there was the case of engaging in sexual intercourse with the female of a beast; in two instances this constitutes an offense of *pārājika*: namely, with a hen or with something resembling a hen.
This occurred when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who lived on alms, named Nandiya. In the early morning, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

Having finished his meal, he took his sitting mat (niṣīdana), placed it over his left shoulder, and entered the Aṅgana Grove. There, beneath a tree, he spread out his sitting mat and sat upright with his body straight.
There was a celestial spirit of Māra who, wishing to destroy this bhikṣu’s samādhi, manifested the body of a beautiful woman and stood before him.

When the bhikṣu arose from samādhi, he saw the woman’s body and immediately gave rise to a mind of attachment; his worldly meditative concentration could not remain firm, and he soon fell away, desiring to touch the woman’s body.
The woman then gradually retreated and moved further away, whereupon he rose and pursued her, desiring to seize her body.

At that time, there was a dead horse in the forest; when the woman reached the horse, she vanished from sight. Because the bhikṣu’s body was consumed by lustful desire, he then engaged in sexual intercourse with the dead horse.
Having already committed the act of sexual misconduct, his feverish passion subsided slightly, and he immediately felt remorse, saying:
"I have fallen away; I am no longer a bhikṣu, nor am I a scion of the Śākya.
Now the bhikṣus will surely abandon me from afar and will no longer dwell with me."
"I ought not to wear this Dharma robe upon an impure body.
He immediately removed his kāṣāya, placed it into his bag, and carrying it on his shoulder, went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions who paid him respectful homage as he preached the Dharma. Seeing [the man] approaching from afar, the Buddha immediately thought:
"If I do not greet him with gentle words and inquire after his well-being, his heart will surely break and boiling blood will gush forth from his face."
That bhikṣu came to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha said:
"Excellent, Nandi!
Do you wish to further train in what is to be trained in by a bhikṣu?"
Hearing what the Buddha said—
"Excellent, Nandi!"—
his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:
"I shall surely dwell together with the bhikṣus; they will certainly not expel me.
Having reflected thus, he replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"I further wish to learn the Dharma of training for bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Return the Dharma of training to the bhikṣu Nandiya; if there are others like the bhikṣu Nandiya, you should likewise grant them the Dharma of training."
The Saṃgha should be united with one mind; the bhikṣu Nandiya should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel on his right knee, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu Nandi, have not abandoned the precepts, nor have my precepts become weak, nor have I committed the act of sexual intercourse.
I now request from the Saṃgha the restoration of the training rules.
Out of compassion for me, may the Saṃgha restore the training rules to me.
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner.
Then, one bhikṣu proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣu Nandi did not return the precepts, nor were his precepts weakened, yet he committed the act of sexual misconduct.
This bhikṣu Nandi now requests from the Saṃgha the restoration of the training rules; out of compassion, the Saṃgha now restores the training rules to him.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let us restore the training rules to the bhikṣu Nandiya.
This is the formal motion. In this manner, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) is performed.

"Having finished returning the training rules to the bhikṣu Nandiya, the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent; thus this matter is upheld! Regarding the practice of a śrāmaṇera under training: he must observe and practice all the precepts established by the Buddha.

He shall sit in the lower seats among the bhikṣus and should offer food, drink, and medicinal decoctions to the mahābhikṣus. He may receive food and drink from other śrāmaṇeras or laypeople, but he must not stay overnight more than twice in the same room as a mahābhikṣu. He himself must not stay more than two nights with laypeople or śrāmaṇeras. He may perform the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, and the two types of *karmavācanā* together with bhikṣus who have received full ordination. However, he cannot count toward the quorum for the *poṣadha*, *pravāraṇā*, or *karmavācanā* when with a śrāmaṇera under training, nor may he perform any *karmavācanā* whatsoever.
After the matter of sexual misconduct was concluded, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were observing the rains retreat together in one place, but there were few dwellings available. Consequently, the bhikṣus solicited grass and wood from those they knew and each built a small hut for themselves to reside in.
While these bhikṣus were entering the city to beg for food, some wood-gatherers destroyed their huts and carried away the timber.
Upon returning from their alms-round, they saw this and immediately became distressed, saying:
"After we have worked so hard to go begging for food, these young fellows have destroyed our huts and taken the timber away."
"We must go again to our acquaintances to beg for grass and wood to build a hut to live in.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly named Daṇḍaka, who was the son of a potter. Relying on his own skillful ingenuity, he immediately constructed a hut of mud, with doors and windows made of mud; the beams, rafters, ox-heads, ivory-like supports, and clothing racks were all made of mud. He gathered various grasses and woods, fired them with fire, and the resulting color was a brilliant, deep red.
Having completed this construction, he instructed the bhikṣus:
"For two months, go on tour for alms, intending to prepare food and drink for the entry ceremony.
At that time, the Buddha and Ānanda were inspecting the various rooms when they saw from afar that the house was crimson and magnificent. Knowing the reason, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:
“What kind of things are these, so red and magnificent?

Ānanda replied, “At present, many bhikṣus in Rājagṛha are observing the rainy season retreat together in one place. As their dwellings are few, these bhikṣus have sought out grass and wood from those they know and built huts to live in.”
While entering the city to beg for alms, a wood-gatherer destroyed the hut and took the timber away. Upon returning from begging, he saw this and was filled with grief and anxiety, saying:
"We have worked hard to build this, yet while we were briefly away begging for food, these young fellows have destroyed our hut and taken the timber."

In that place there was a bhikṣu named Daṇḍaka, the son of a potter, who, relying on his own skillful ingenuity, constructed this earthen hut by gathering various grasses and wood and burning them with fire until it was thus beautifully finished.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"You must demolish this red clay hut of the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka, lest the non-Buddhists censure and reproach us, saying that while the Buddha dwells in the world, he has produced such a source of outflows and fetters."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went to demolish it.
After two months of wandering, the bhikṣu Dhaniya returned and seeing his house destroyed, he asked the bhikṣu who had been entrusted with the task:
"Who has demolished my house?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"It was the Great Teacher, the Buddha, who commanded that it be broken.
Dhanika thought to himself:
“The teachings of the Dharma King have been destroyed; no words [of opposition] may be spoken.
Now, the carpenters of Rājagṛha are my acquaintances; we can build a wooden dwelling.
When the night had passed, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city for alms. Having finished his almsround, he went to the place where the carpenters were.
"Do you know now?
King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī and ruler of Magadha, has provided me with timber.
The carpenter replied:
"If the King grants it, you may take it as you please.

Among these were large, heavy timbers used for guarding the city, which were difficult to carry in or out and unsuitable for mendicants; he immediately cut them into pieces and stored them in one place.

At that time, the city commander saw that the great timber used for the protection of the city had been cut down and concealed; having seen this, he was struck with terror and his hair stood on end as he thought:
"Could it be that hostile bandits are about to arrive?"
Having already gained entry, he went to ask the carpenter:
"This great timber was used to protect the city; who took it, cut it up, and stored it in one place?"
He replied,
"The bhikṣu Dhanika came and said this:
'King Ajātaśatru has given me timber.'"
I then replied,
"If Your Majesty grants it, you may take it as you please.
Thereupon, I myself took large timbers, cut them to size, and stored them in one place.
The city governor thought to himself:
"How can the King now give such a large piece of timber to this bhikṣu?
He immediately went to the King and said:
"Great King!
There are other timbers; why do you give this great timber used for guarding the city to the bhikṣu?
The king said:
"I will not give it.
The city governor said:
"The King has already given it."
“Who said you gave it? He replied,
“The carpenter said he gave it.”
The king said,
"Bring the carpenter here.
He immediately followed these instructions and went to bring the carpenter.
At that time, the carpenter saw the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka on the road and said to him:
"Because of you, I now have some business.
The bhikṣu said:
"Go now! I shall follow later.
Thereupon, the city prefect led the carpenter to the king's presence and said:
"Great King!
This is the carpenter.
At that time, the bhikṣu Daṇḍakin followed behind; seeing him from afar, the king spoke:
"Release the carpenter and bring the bhikṣu.
The city magistrate immediately released the carpenter and led the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka before the king.
The king asked,
"O Bhikṣu, how is it that you take what is not given according to your dharma?
He replied:
"Great King!
I did not take what was not given; Your Majesty gave it to me first.
The king said:
"I do not recall giving it.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I shall now cause the king to remember."
The king asked, "How so? He replied:
"Your Majesty should reflect upon yourself as when you first ascended the throne and spoke these words:
'If there are grasses, trees, or waters within my realm, let them be taken and used by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who observe the precepts.'"
The king said:
"I made that statement because I thought the grasses and trees were ownerless.
The king said:
"You have now fallen into a great transgression.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am an ordained person living as a guest in the king's realm."
"How can you kill me?
The king said,
"Bhikṣu, go away!"
"Do not take such great timber again.
Then the crowd cried out:
"Rare indeed is this bhikṣu! He was destined to die, yet having been rebuked, he has been released."
That bhikṣu was delivered from that great offense and went among the community of monks; after the meal, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Today I was on the verge of being killed by the king."
He related the aforementioned matters in detail.
The bhikṣus censured him with various reasons, saying:

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path, nor is it the practice of one who has a mind of dispassion and delight; it is an impure conduct that those who have left the household life ought not to perform."

"You do not know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has censured the practice of stealing through various causes and conditions, while praising the practice of not stealing through various causes and conditions.
You should not even give rise to such a thought, nor should you speak of it, let alone actually take it."
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he said: "Bhikṣu Daṇḍakī!"
"Did you actually do this? He replied, "I did."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

“What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path, and you have performed impure practices without a mind of dispassion—things that one who has left the household life ought not to do.”
The Buddha said:
"You foolish person!

You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the practice of stealing and plundering the Dharma, and through various causes and conditions, praised the practice of not stealing."
"You should not even give rise to such a thought, nor should you speak of it with your mouth, let alone actually take it.
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he said to Ānanda:

"Take a junior bhikṣu into the city of Rājagṛha, to the streets, lanes, markets, and places where many people gather, and ask the multitude: whether they are believers or non-believers, whether they are wise or unwise, whether they are great ministers, high officials, generals, or subordinate officers."
"To what extent must one steal for the King of Magadha, Ajātaśatru, to inflict upon them a grave punishment?
Ānanda, having received these instructions, led a junior bhikṣu into the city of Rājagṛha. In the streets, alleys, markets, and crowded public places, he questioned the people:
"To what extent must one steal for the King of Magadha, Ajātaśatru, to inflict upon them a grave punishment?"
The assembly replied:
"Venerable Ānanda!
If one steals five coins, or what is equivalent to five coins in value, it constitutes a grave offense."
Having heard this, Ānanda returned to where the Buddha was, paid his respects, and stood to one side. He then related everything in detail to the Buddha:
"If a theft amounts to five coins, or the equivalent value of five coins, King Ajātaśatru inflicts a severe punishment."
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in an open space, takes by theft an object that was not given to him,
and because of that stolen object, he is seized and bound by a king or a royal minister, or is executed, or banished, or fined,
or if they say to him: "You little child!..."
"You fool! You thief!
A bhikṣu who thus takes what is not given commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with others.
Regarding taking what is not given:
when another person has not given this object—whether it be a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a person with dual sexual organs—and one takes it by theft, this is called taking what is not given.

A "King" (rāja) is one of the Kṣatriya caste who has received the royal office and been consecrated with the auspicious water; he is thus called a king, also called the lord of the realm, and also called the consecrated one.
If a brahmin, a householder, or even a woman receives the office of king, they are likewise called a consecrated sovereign of a kingdom.
"Killing" refers to the taking of life.
"Bound" refers to those who are shackled with manacles, fetters, or neck-irons while in prison; all such cases are termed "bound.
"Banished" means being driven out of the national borders.
"Fined gold" refers to redeeming one's offense by paying gold or other items as a fine.
There are two kinds of robbers:
those who plunder and those who steal.
You, being but a child, do not yet understand the Dharma.
"Deluded" means being without knowledge.
"Pārājika" means falling into a state of non-conformity; this offense is extremely evil and profoundly grave.
One who commits such an offense is no longer called a bhikṣu; he is not a śramaṇa and not a son of the Śākya."

"One who has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu and is no longer in communion" means that one does not participate in the communal performance of bhikṣu rituals—namely, the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*)—and is not included among the fourteen classes of persons; this is called "defeat (*pārājika*) and non-comunion."
Regarding the offenses herein, there are three ways of taking another's valuable property that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
first, taking it oneself; second, instructing another to do so; and third, sending a messenger.
Regarding "taking by oneself": if one takes it with one's own hand, or lifts it with one's own hand and moves it from its original location, it is a *pārājika*.

Regarding "instructing another": if a bhikṣu instructs another person to steal another's property, and that person, following his words, immediately steals and takes it away from its original location, at that moment the bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika*.
Sending a messenger: if a bhikṣu says to someone, "Do you know where such-and-such a person has a heavy object?
and if [the messenger] says:
"Know the location.
He was sent to steal it; as soon as the man followed these words and committed the theft, at the moment the object was taken away from its original place, the bhikṣu incurred a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there are three ways of taking another’s property that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
first, by means of the mind; second, by means of the body; and third, by removing it from its original place.
Regarding "by means of the mind," this refers to giving rise to a thought and intending to steal and seize the object.
"Using the body" means taking another's property with one's hands, feet, head, or other parts of the body.
"Moving it from its original location" means lifting the object from wherever it was situated and placing it elsewhere.
Furthermore, there are three conditions for the *pārājika* offense of taking another’s property:
first, it is not given by the other; second, it is a substantial object; and third, it is moved from its original location.
Regarding "not given by the other": this refers to when a man, a woman, a *paṇḍaka*, or a person with both sexual organs does not give it.
"Valuable property" refers to an object worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*.
"Removing from its original place" means lifting it from wherever it was located and placing it elsewhere.
Furthermore, there are three ways of taking another's valuable property that constitute a *pārājika* offense: [the act of moving it, the act of concealing it, and the act of receiving it].
First, the intention to steal; second, the object being of significant value; third, moving it from its original location.
Regarding the intention to steal: it is taking for oneself what another has not given.
As for the object being of significant value and moving it from its original location, these are also as explained above.
Furthermore, there are three conditions for the *pārājika* offense of taking another's property:
first, that the object belongs to another; second, that it is a substantial object; and third, that it has been moved from its original place.
"Belonging to another" means that the object has an owner—whether a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a person with both sexual organs.
Regarding "heavy objects" and "moving them from their original location," it is as explained above.
Furthermore, there are three conditions for the *pārājika* offense of taking another’s property:
first, the perception that it belongs to another; second, the object being of significant value; and third, its removal from its original location.
Regarding "the perception that it belongs to another," this means knowing that the object has an owner.
Regarding heavy objects being moved from their original location, it is as explained above.
Whether it be a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a person with both sexual organs—
regarding heavy objects being moved from their original location, it is as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four factors that constitute a *pārājika* offense for taking another's property:
first, it was not given by the other; second, it was taken with the intent to steal; third, it is an object of value; and fourth, it has been moved from its original location—all as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four conditions for the *pārājika* offense of taking another's property:
the object belongs to another, one takes it with the intent to steal, it is an item of significant value, and it is moved from its original location; [if these are met], it is a *pārājika*.
Knowing that an object belongs to another, taking it with the intent to steal, the object being of significant value, and its removal from its original location—all these are as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four factors for the *pārājika* offense of taking another’s property of significant value:
first, that it is guarded; second, that it has an owner; third, that it is property of significant value; and fourth, that it is removed from its original location.

There are those who possess guardians, such as people who have elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, wives, children, and servants; whether in their own country or in another country, they are protected by others, yet they harbor the thought of "mine," thinking, "Who belongs to me? and their minds follow after these things.

Furthermore, there are fields—fields of sugarcane, rice, barley, hemp, beans, and grapes—which are guarded by people and possessed of the notion of "mine": "Who belongs to me? and "Whose property does my mind follow?"
Furthermore, there are elephant stables, horse stables, gateways, and kitchens where people may hide objects; this is called "guarding.
When one has the notion of "mine," who is it that acts as "mine," and whose mind follows after which objects?
Regarding heavy objects and their removal from their original location, it is as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four ways of taking another's heavy object that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
the object has no guardian, one possesses the thought "this is mine," it is a heavy object, and it is removed from its original location.

There is no one to guard them, just as when a person possesses elephants, horses, a wife, and children—whether in their own country or in another country—these things remain without anyone to guard them.
There is the mind of "mine," yet who is it that is "mine," and to what object does the mind adhere?

Furthermore, there are fields and threshing floors with grain upon them; these things are unguarded by anyone, yet there is the mind of "mine"—who is it that is "mine," and to what object does the mind adhere?
Furthermore, there may be five kinds of jewels or things resembling them, buried in the earth and left unguarded by anyone.
Yet there arises the thought of "mine. Who is it that possesses this thought of "mine"?
That is to say, when there is a sense of "mine" regarding an object belonging to an owner, it is called "having an owner but being unguarded by anyone.
Regarding heavy objects and their removal from their original location, it is as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four ways of committing a *pārājika* offense by taking another's property belonging to others:
the object has a guardian, there is no sense of "mine" on the part of the owner, it is an object of significant value, and it is removed from its original location.

Regarding those who possess the mind of non-ownership and do not guard their possessions: it is like a band of thieves who, having plundered another city or town and acquired much wealth, are subsequently defeated by the power of the king or the strength of the village. The thieves flee, abandoning their goods. In this case, the owners do not guard the mind of non-ownership because they have already lost [the goods];
nor do the thieves guard the mind of non-ownership because they have already seized them.
There is a guarding of the mind that is free from the notion of "mine. Who guards this mind free from the notion of "mine"?
It is the one who has seized it.
Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu who loses his robes and bowl; a bhikṣu he knows, seeing them in another place, immediately seizes them.
This bhikṣu who has lost his robes and bowl failed to guard the mind of non-possessiveness, because they were already lost;
the thief failed to guard the mind of non-possessiveness, because he had already seized them.
There is the guarding of the mind that is free from the notion of "mine. Who guards the mind that is free from the notion of "mine"?
It is the one who takes it away.
Regarding heavy objects and their removal from their original location, it is as explained above.

"Places" refers to: ground places, upper places, open-air places, riding places, carriage places, boat places, within water, fields, monastery grounds, upon the body, customs houses, meeting places, and those of the legless, the two-legged, the four-legged, and the many-legged.

Regarding the location: if a person has five treasures, or something resembling five treasures, lying on the ground, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal and removes them from their original place, it is a pārājika offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *māṣakas*, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one lifts it with wood, tiles, or stones, even if it falls back to its original place, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one drags it out but has not yet crossed the boundary, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Furthermore, if there are iron or copper jars, or iron or copper vats, and within these vessels are the five precious gems or things resembling them, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes them and removes them from their original place, it is a *pārājika*.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If one takes an object from the bottom of a vessel and moves it toward the mouth [of the vessel], it is a *pārājika*.
If an object near the mouth of a jar rolls down to the bottom of the jar, it is also a *pārājika*.
If one pierces the jar to take property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu has the intention to steal—whether his mind is fixed on the vessel and not the object, or on the object and not the vessel, or on both—and he takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called the ground-level area (*bhūmipradeśa*).

Regarding the upper areas: these include fine-woven cord beds, coarse-woven cord beds, stuffed mattresses, thin mattresses, thick mattresses, mattress covers, multi-colored mattresses with multi-colored cords as borders, thin blankets, thick blankets, woolen blankets, woolen blankets lined on both sides, woolen blankets with fringed borders, floor coverings, places atop trees, and places upon roofs. As for the "fine-woven cord bed area," this refers to the foot-end, the head-end, the rings, the bed-railing, the foot-end of the upper cord bed, and the head-end. If it is woven with cords, different cords are designated as different areas.
If covered by skin or cloth, that which is of a single color is called one place, and that which is of different colors is called different places.

If there are five kinds of jewels or things resembling five kinds of jewels in such places, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal for a value of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *māsakas*, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the phrase "at a coarse wooden bed," if a single plank constitutes a single place.
If it is covered by skin, rope, or cloth, the different ropes constitute different locations; the rest is as explained above.
As for a mat (*śayanīya*), if it consists of one kind of wool, it is called a single location.
The front side and the back side of a single piece of cloth constitute one place; different pieces of cloth constitute different places.

If these various places contain the five kinds of precious gems or things resembling them, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, and they are worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one selects [the items] at that time, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once selected, if one takes items worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*.

Regarding bags, thin mattresses, thick mattresses, multi-colored mattresses, mattresses with multi-colored borders, thin blankets, thick blankets, padded blankets, padded blankets lined and backed, and bordered padded blankets: for floor-coverings, one type of fur counts as one "place," one color counts as one "place," and different colors count as different "places"; the rest is as explained above.

Regarding "places of trees": these are the places of roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and even root-fibers. If there are five kinds of precious gems or things resembling them at these various places, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal for a value of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection has been made and one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*.

Regarding "places on a roof," this refers to the space between doors, windows, door-bolts, door-latches, ox-heads, ivory [carvings], clothing racks, beams, rafters, multi-storied pavilions, and ladder-rungs; each single crossbeam is considered one place, and at a balustrade, each hook is considered one place.

If an unbaked clay house has one brick, it constitutes one place; if a thatched-roofed house has one layer, it constitutes one place; if a wooden-shingled house has one beam, it constitutes one place; if a plastered house has one painted line, it constitutes one place. If these various places contain the five precious gems or things resembling them, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *māṣakas*, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called the "superior case."

Regarding the space-element: suppose there are garments of great value—pāṭali cloth, tūṇīra cloth, or kaurava cloth—suspended from a person’s house, palace, or various railings; if the wind blows them into the air and they have not yet fallen to the ground, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, seizes them, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, it is as if a bhikṣu’s robe, that of his upādhyāya, or that of his ācārya, falls from above to below; before the robe has reached the ground, if the bhikṣu takes hold of it with the intent to steal, it constitutes a pārājika offense.

Furthermore, suppose there are various places such as doorways, courtyards, upper stories, eaves, pavilions, or the spaces between houses and upper chambers, where articles for personal adornment have been placed; and suppose a bird with a master—such as a goose, a swan, a peacock, a parrot, or a myna—carries these items away. If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, seizes these items from the bird, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one waits for the bird, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the bird follows the bhikṣu to wherever he desires to go, it is a *pārājika*.
If it goes to another place, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If there are wild birds, such as hawks or vultures, that have seized this object and flown away, and a bhikṣu, with a mind of theft, seizes it from those birds and takes it for himself, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If he merely waits for the bird [to release it], it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bird follows a bhikṣu to wherever he desires to go, it is a sthūlātyaya offense;
if it goes elsewhere, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Furthermore, if various wild birds carry this object away, [the same applies].
If a bird belonging to another is seized by a wild bird, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, seizes that bird belonging to another, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If he waits for the bird [to be taken], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bird follows a bhikṣu to wherever he desires to go, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If it goes to another place, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bird possessing a master carries away this object and it is seized by a wild bird, and the bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, seizes it from the wild bird, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one waits for the bird, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the bird follows the bhikṣu to wherever he desires to go, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it goes to another place, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called the "place of empty space.
Regarding the "places of vehicles," these refer to elephant-vehicles and horse-vehicles.

As for the "places" of an elephant-vehicle, they are: the feet, the knees, the thighs, the hips, the ribs, the back, the chest, the neck, the head, the ears, the nose, the mouth, the tusks, and the tail. If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes any of these parts—whether they consist of the five precious substances or resemble the five precious substances—he commits a pārājika offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once selected, if one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding the parts of a horse for riding: these refer to the feet, knees, thighs, hips, ribs, back, chest, neck, head, ears, nose, mouth, mane, and tail; the rest is as explained above.
Regarding "places where vehicles are kept," these include bullock carts, deer-drawn carts, roe-deer carts, hand-pulled carts, and palanquins.

Regarding the parts of a bullock cart—namely the spokes, the rim, the shafts, the hub, the box, and the railings—if there are the five precious substances or things resembling them in these various parts, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one makes a selection [of items], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes items worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
The same applies to deer-carts, roe-deer carts, and carts drawn by foot-pullers.
Regarding the locations of a palanquin carriage:
these include the footrests, the heavy rings for the feet, the seating area, the wooden platform, the pillars, and the covering.
Whether covered with ropes or cloth, if it is of a single color, it is designated as one location; if it is of different colors, they are designated as separate locations.
If there are the five kinds of precious objects or things resembling them in these various places, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it is a pārājika offense.
If he examines them [before taking], it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one has chosen and taken property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense.
This is called the case of "by means of.
As for the case of "by boat": [text follows].
There are single-hull boats, barges, house-boats, bottle-shaped boats, air-cushion boats, plank boats, wooden rafts, and grass rafts. Regarding the single-hull boat:

at the two sides, the two ends, the bottom, the two cabins, the place for the mast, and the sternhouse—if there are the five kinds of precious things or things resembling them in these various places, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika* offense.
When selecting [the items], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
once selected and having taken items worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "at a boat station," this refers to a place where cross-beams are used or where ropes are tied; the rest is as explained above.
Regarding "places where boats are moored," this refers to places with wooden walls, places for jars, places for pots, places for the lids of jars and pots, places for pillars, and places for beams.

If it is covered with grass, one layer of grass constitutes one place; if it is covered with wooden branches or planks, one covering constitutes one place. Different colors constitute different places.
In these various places, if there are the five precious substances or things resembling the five precious substances, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it is a pārājika offense.
Regarding "places such as jars and boats": this refers to all jars, all places bound by ropes, and all places bound by leather.
Regarding "the place of the inflated skin-raft," this refers to all places where there are skins and all places where there are bindings.
Regarding "the plank-boat," this refers to all places where there are planks.
Regarding "the wooden raft," this refers to all places where there are pieces of wood.
Regarding "a place of grass rafts": this refers to any place of grass or any place of binding materials.

If there are five kinds of precious objects or things resembling the five kinds of precious objects in these places, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it constitutes a pārājika offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *māsakas*, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called the "ship case."

Regarding "in water": if, for the sake of building a house, a vehicle, or firewood, objects floating in the water come down [to the shore], and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it is a pārājika offense.
If, at the time of selecting [the items], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once selected, if one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* worth [of goods] and moves them from their original place, it is a *pārājika*.
If, after having been seized and detained, the water reaches the front [of the object], it is a *pārājika*.
If [the bird] remains submerged at the bottom of the water, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is lifted out of the water, it is likewise a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding birds belonging to others in a pool that has an owner, if a bhikṣu takes these birds with the intent to steal them, it is a *pārājika*.
If one selects [the items] at that time, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once selected, if one takes items worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If one sinks them to the bottom of the water, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If he lifts it out of the water, it is a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, if there are birds belonging to an owner in a pond that has no owner, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika*.
If one makes a selection [of items], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes items worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If one submerges them at the bottom of the water, it is a *pārājika*.
If one uproots [a plant] from water, it is also a *pārājika* offense;
this is called the "water location.
Regarding the "field location," there are two causes and conditions for seizing another's field:
First, making a claim; second, making a sign.
If a bhikṣu, for the sake of land, claims that another has been defeated, it is a pārājika offense.
If he is not defeated, it is a thullaccaya offense.

If one constructs a boundary marker that exceeds the proper measure and thereby gains superiority, and the value of the ground is five *māṣaka* coins, it is a *pārājika* offense; the same applies to a monastery or dwelling.
This is called "a field site."

Regarding "on the body": suppose a bhikṣu is traveling with his upādhyāya or ācārya carrying a robe. If that bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes this robe-bag from various parts of the person's body—namely, from the foot, the calf, the knee, the thigh, the groin, the hip, the rib, the spine, the abdomen, the chest, the hand, the elbow, the upper arm, the shoulder, the neck, or the head—and moves it from one place to another, he commits a pārājika offense.
This is called a "place on the body.
Regarding a customs station: if a bhikṣu crosses a frontier and fails to pay duty on goods that ought to be taxed—worth five coins or more—it is a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there were merchants who arrived at a customs checkpoint and said to a bhikṣu, "Pass these goods through for us.
The bhikṣu passed them through; the value of the tax was five coins, which constitutes a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there were merchants who arrived at a customs station and said to a bhikṣu, "Pass these goods through for us, and we shall give you half of the tax.
The bhikṣu passed them through; if he received goods worth five *kārsāpaṇas* as the tax, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, there were merchants who, upon arriving at a customs checkpoint, said to a bhikṣu:
"Pass these goods through for us, and we shall give you the full amount of the tax.
If the bhikṣu passes them through and the value of the taxable goods is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, there were merchants who arrived at a customs checkpoint; a bhikṣu showed them an alternative route so that they passed through, causing them to lose goods subject to taxation. If the value of the goods was five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, if there are merchants who have not yet reached the customs station and a bhikṣu shows them an alternative route, causing them to lose goods worth five *kārsāpaṇas* that were subject to taxation, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
However, if there are thieves at the customs station, or wild beasts, or if there is famine, and the bhikṣu shows an alternative route for these reasons, he does not commit an offense.
This is called a customs post. Regarding a place of rendezvous:

if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a thief, and they plunder various villages to obtain goods which they then divide with the bhikṣu, if the value of what is obtained is five coins, it is a pārājika offense.
This is called a designated place.

Regarding "footless sentient beings," this refers to centipedes and millepedes; if someone takes one and places it in a vessel, and a bhikṣu takes it with the intent to steal, it constitutes a pārājika offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If one pierces a vessel and takes insects worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu has the intent to steal directed toward a vessel but not toward the insects, or if his intent is directed toward the insects but not toward the vessel, or if his intent is directed toward both, and he acquires something worth five māsakas with the intent to steal and seize it, he commits a pārājika offense.
This is called the state of being footless.
As for those with two feet, they are such as geese, swans, peacocks, parrots, śāri birds, kokila birds, gibbons, and humans.
If someone takes these objects and places them in a basket, and a bhikṣu takes them with the intent to steal, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If he takes them while they are still being selected, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If, having made a choice, one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If one pierces a cage to take a bird worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣu’s intent to steal is directed toward the cage and not the bird; or if his intent is directed toward the bird and not the cage; or if his intent is directed toward both—provided he acquires property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* with the intent to steal—it is a *pārājika*.
There are two ways of stealing:
first, carrying it away; second, by prior agreement. If a bhikṣu carries a person on his back for more than two strides, it constitutes a pārājika offense.
If one goes beyond two strides from a designated meeting place, it is a *pārājika*.
This is called the case of two-footed beings.

Regarding four-footed beings—such as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, donkeys, or mules—if someone has tied them with a rope in one place and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, unties the rope and leads them away beyond four strides, it is a *pārājika*.
If [the animals] are within a wall or a fence, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, drives them out beyond four paces, it is a pārājika offense.
If there are various four-footed creatures lying together in one place, and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, drives one of them up and out beyond four paces, it is a pārājika offense.
If the animal is grazing outside and a bhikṣu thinks to himself,
"When this herdsman enters the village, I shall steal it," it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one kills [the animal], it is a pāyattika.
Once killed, if the meat taken is worth five kārṣāpaṇas, it is a pārājika.
This is called the case concerning four-footed animals.

Regarding "places with many legs": this refers to centipedes, millipedes, and dung beetles. If someone has placed them in a vessel and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes them, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one makes a selection, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Once the selection is made and one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If one pierces a vessel and takes insects worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.

If the intent to steal is directed toward the vessel and not the insect; or if the intent is directed toward the insect and not the vessel; or if the intent is directed toward both—if one takes with such a thieving mind an object worth five coins, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
This is called the "place of many feet.
Furthermore, there are seven conditions for taking another's heavy property that constitute a *pārājika* offense:

first, the perception that it is not one's own; second, lack of consent; third, not using it temporarily; fourth, knowing there is an owner; fifth, not being insane; sixth, not being mentally deranged; and seventh, not having a mind impaired by illness.
Furthermore, there are seven cases where taking another's personal property does not constitute an offense:

first, perceiving it as one's own; second, with the owner's consent; third, for temporary use; fourth, believing there is no owner; fifth, being insane; sixth, having a disturbed mind; and seventh, having a mind impaired by illness.
Furthermore, there are seven conditions under which taking the heavy property of a non-human constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*:

first, not perceiving it as one's own; second, not perceiving it as consented to; third, not intending temporary use; fourth, knowing it has an owner; fifth, not being insane; sixth, not being mentally deranged; and seventh, not having a mind impaired by illness.
Furthermore, there is no offense in taking seven kinds of heavy property belonging to non-humans:

when one perceives it as one's own, when taking with the consent [of the owner], when using it temporarily, when believing there is no owner, or when one is deranged, mentally disturbed, or has a mind impaired by illness.
Furthermore, there are seven conditions under which taking another's light object constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*:

perceiving it as not one's own, not having given consent, not borrowing it temporarily, knowing it has an owner, not being insane, not being mentally deranged, and not having a mind impaired by illness.
Furthermore, there are seven cases where one takes another's light belongings without committing an offense:

taking with the thought that it is one's own; taking with the consent [of the owner]; taking for temporary use; believing there is no owner; acting with a deranged mind; acting with a distracted mind; or acting with a mind impaired by illness.
Furthermore, there are seven types of taking light objects belonging to non-humans that constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense:

when one does not perceive the object as one's own, has not given consent, does not intend temporary use, knows it has an owner, is not insane, is not mentally deranged, and is not afflicted by a diseased mind.
Furthermore, there are seven cases where taking light objects belonging to non-humans constitutes no offense:

taking with the thought that it is one's own; taking with the consent [of the owner]; taking for temporary use; believing there is no owner; acting with a deranged mind; acting with a distracted mind; or acting with a mind impaired by illness.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Śyāmāvatī who had many acquaintances whom she considered to be people of merit; she delighted in making offerings to them of oil, ghee, honey, and rock sugar.
A certain merchant saw this bhikṣuṇī and, with a heart of faith and joy, spoke these words:
"Noble lady! Whatever ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar you require, please take it from my house."
She replied, “It is so.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī heard these words; several days later, she went to her house and said:
“Give five *śīrṣa* of sesame oil to the bhikṣuṇī Śyāmāvatī.
The merchant asked,
“For what purpose will it be used?”
He replied,
"I shall take this to the nunnery.
The merchant then gave it to him.
The bhikṣuṇī took it to the monastery and consumed it herself.
Several days later, a merchant saw the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīvatī and said to her,
"Noble lady?"
"Why do you seek only sesame oil and not other things?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "Why do you ask this?"
He replied: "A bhikṣuṇī came and said:
'You need sesame oil.'"
"I shall give it to you immediately. Śreṣṭhin said,
"Excellent!"
"If you ask for anything else, you shall give it to you as well.
Sāḷha then went to that bhikṣuṇī and said to her:
"You are a wicked bhikṣuṇī, a lowly bhikṣuṇī; you have committed a pārājika offense."
That bhikṣuṇī asked,
"Why have you done this? Śiveya replied:
"The merchant did not give it; you took his oil by fraud.
That bhikṣuṇī said:
"I did not take it without being given; I took it under your name."
He immediately conceived a doubt within himself:
"Could it be that I have committed a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?
He replied,
"I took it with the intention that it was the name 'Śyāma'."
The Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but by intentionally speaking falsehood, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
From this day forward, you must not take [property] by falsely assuming another's name; if you do so, you commit an offense."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣuṇī from the East who was traveling along the same road with the bhikṣuṇī Pāli.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pāli, who was in front, lost her robe and departed; the bhikṣuṇī from the East, who was behind, found it.
When they had gathered together in one place, a bhikṣuṇī from the east cried out:
"Who has lost this robe?
I have now found it on the ground."
The bhikṣuṇī Pāli said,
"Will you take this robe?
She replied:
"I take it. Pāli said,
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
He asked, "For what reason? He replied:
"Because you took it with a thieving mind.
This bhikṣuṇī felt doubt in her heart:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense.

A certain householder was plowing a field near Jetavana and had laid his clothes aside on one side. At that time, a bhikṣu seeking discarded rags (pāṃsukūla) saw the clothes on the ground; seeing no one around him, he took them and departed. The plowman saw this from afar and spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Do not take my robe.
The bhikṣu did not hear him, so the plowman went over, seized the bhikṣu, and said:
"Does the Dharma of you bhikṣus not prohibit taking what is not given?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I took it because I thought the refuse heap was ownerless.
The farmer said:
"This is my robe.
The bhikṣu said,
"If this is your robe, then take it yourself."
The bhikṣu felt doubt in his mind:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what state of mind did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I took it because I thought there was no owner."
The Buddha said, “There is no offense!
From now on, when taking clothing, you must exercise careful consideration: although these are garments belonging to another and there is no one guarding them, they certainly have an owner.”
*The Ten Recitations Vinaya*, Scroll One, Section Two: Theft.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty. *The Ten Recitations Vinaya*, Scroll Two, First Recitation, Part Two.
The Second of the Four Pārājika Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying at the Bhaṅga River in the country of Vajji. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity yields great fruits and great benefits."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One has taught us to practice the contemplation of impurity to attain great fruits and great benefits; we shall diligently cultivate it."

After the bhikṣus had formed this thought, they diligently practiced the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), deeply conceiving a sense of revulsion and shame toward this body. It was as if a youth, fond of self-adornment, having bathed his body, trimmed his nails, groomed his hair and beard, put on fine clothes, and anointed his body with perfumes, were suddenly bound around the neck with a dead snake, a dead dog, or a rotting, bloated, and livid corpse of a human being, being devoured by birds and beasts, oozing pus and blood, and infested with maggots. He would feel such deep revulsion for the foul-smelling carcass that he would be overcome with profound shame.
Because these bhikṣus had deeply cultivated the contemplation of impurity, their sense of shame, remorse, and revulsion were likewise so intense.

At that time, some bhikṣus resolved to die, praised death, sought out blades to commit suicide, or ingested poison; some bound themselves, or threw themselves from high cliffs; and some bhikṣus even took one another’s lives.

There was a bhikṣu who diligently practiced the contemplation of impurity; having developed a profound sense of revulsion, shame, and remorse toward his foul body, he went to the brahmin Māṭhara and praised him, saying:
"O virtuous man!..."
"If you can kill me, I shall give you my robes and bowl.
At that time, the brahmin immediately took a sharp blade and ended his life.
With the blade stained with blood, he carried it to the banks of the Bahukā River to wash it.
A māra deity emerged from the water and, standing upon the surface of the water, praised the brahmin, saying:
"O virtuous man!
You have gained great merit; this śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, has delivered those not yet delivered and liberated those not yet liberated, and you have furthermore obtained his robe and bowl."
At that time, that brahmin gave rise to a wicked and false view, thinking to himself,
"It is truly so.
He then took up a knife and went from room to room and from walkway to walkway, crying out:
"Whoever has not yet crossed over, I shall cause them to cross over.
Whoever has not yet been liberated, I shall cause them to be liberated.

At that time, because the bhikṣus were diligently practicing the contemplation of impurity, they came to loathe their foul-smelling bodies; leaving their dwellings, they went to where a brahmin was and praised him, saying:
“Good man!
You may take my life.
Then that brahmin immediately took his life; in this manner, two, three, and even up to sixty were killed. Due to these causes and conditions, the Sangha was consequently diminished.
When the time for the recitation of the precepts on the fifteenth day of the month arrived, the assembly of monks was diminished. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Today is the day for the recitation of the precepts; the entire assembly of monks should be gathered. For what reason has it been diminished?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, at one time you taught the bhikṣus to deeply cultivate the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), whereby they attained great fruits and great benefits. Those bhikṣus then diligently practiced the contemplation of impurity and came to loathe this foul-smelling body.
