It is like a youth who takes pride in his adornment—bathing his body, trimming his nails, grooming his hair and beard, wearing fine clothes, and anointing his body with perfumes—if someone were to tie around his neck a dead snake, a dead dog, or a putrid, bloated, and blue-black corpse of a human being, scavenged by birds and beasts, oozing pus and blood with maggots crawling out, that person would feel deep loathing and profound shame.”
These bhikṣus practiced the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), and their revulsion, shame, and remorse were likewise.

At that time, some conceived the desire for death, praised death, or sought out blades to commit suicide; some took poison, some bound themselves, some threw themselves from high cliffs, and some bhikṣus even took one another’s lives.

There was a bhikṣu who, through diligent cultivation of the contemplation of impurity, developed a profound sense of revulsion, shame, and remorse toward his foul body; he then went to the brahmin Māṭhara and praised him, saying:
"O virtuous man!"
"If you can kill me, I will give you my robes and bowl.
At that moment, the brahmin immediately took a sharp knife and ended the bhikṣu’s life.
With the blade stained with blood, he carried it to the banks of the Bahukā River to wash it.
A māra deity emerged from the water and, standing upon the surface of the water, praised the brahmin, saying:
"You have attained great merit!
This śramaṇa, the son of the Śākyas, who upholds the precepts, has delivered those not yet delivered and liberated those not yet liberated, and he has furthermore obtained robes and a bowl."
At that time, the brahmin immediately gave rise to a wicked and false view, thinking to himself:
"It is indeed so.
He then took up a sword and went from room to room and from walking path to walking path, shouting aloud:
"Who has not yet crossed over?
I shall ferry them across.
Who has not yet been liberated?"
"I shall deliver them.

At that time, because those bhikṣus had diligently practiced the contemplation of impurity, they developed a profound sense of revulsion, shame, and remorse toward their foul bodies; they left their dwellings and went to where the brahmin was, praising him, saying:
"O virtuous man!"
"You may take my life.
Then that brahmin immediately took his life; in this manner, two, three, and even up to sixty were killed, whereby the Saṃgha was diminished.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain to the bhikṣus other wholesome paths—the dharmas for dwelling in peace and happiness without weariness—and by which any unwholesome states that arise can be immediately eliminated.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"There is yet another virtuous path, a method of peaceful practice that is free from aversion; as soon as any unwholesome dharmas arise, one is able to eliminate them."
“World-Honored One!
What is the path of goodness, by which one dwells in peace and happiness without weariness, and is able to eliminate all evil dharmas as soon as they arise?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“There is the mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), which is called the ‘wholesome path’ and the ‘dharma of dwelling in peace. Why is this?
Because as soon as unwholesome dharmas arise, one is able to eliminate them, for there is no aversion.”
“World-Honored One!

How is it that the cultivation of mindfulness of ānāpāna is called the ‘good path,’ the ‘dharma for dwelling in peace and happiness,’ and how is it that as soon as any unwholesome dharmas arise, they can be eliminated without any sense of aversion?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a city or village, when morning comes he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, restrains all his sense faculties, and with mindfulness fixed in a single point enters the village to beg for food."

Having finished eating, whether in an open space, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, one spreads out the *niṣīdana*, sits upright with body straightened, and binds mindfulness before oneself. One eliminates worldly greed and envy, remaining free from attachment to the wealth and possessions of others. A practitioner who acts in this way is able to abandon ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-worry, and doubt-and-regret. These hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) afflict the mind, weaken the power of wisdom, and prevent one from reaching *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they must be eliminated.

When the breath enters, one should know with single-mindedness that it enters; when the breath exits, one should know with single-mindedness that it exits. Whether long or short, if the breath enters pervading the entire body, one should know with single-mindedness that it enters from the whole body; if the breath exits pervading the entire body, one should know with single-mindedness that it exits from the whole body.
When abandoning bodily formations, one should unify the mind and attend to the inhalation and exhalation.

When experiencing rapture, when experiencing pleasure, when experiencing mental formations, and when abandoning mental formations, one should unify the mind and attend to the inhalation and exhalation.
When awakening the mind, when gladdening the mind, when concentrating the mind, and when liberating the mind, one should unify the mind and attend to the inhalation and exhalation.

Contemplating impermanence, contemplating disintegration, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment, one should unify the mind and attend to the inhalation and exhalation.
"Ānanda! This is called the Dharma of the Blissful Practice of the Good Path; as soon as any unwholesome dharmas arise, they can be extinguished, and there shall be no aversion.
At that time, the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"One should diligently practice mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing) to obtain great fruit and great benefit.
At that time, the bhikṣus each had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has praised for us the practice of mindfulness of *ānāpāna* as yielding great fruit and great benefit; we shall diligently practice it."

Having formed this thought, he immediately applied himself diligently to the practice of *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and attained the realization of immeasurable and manifold knowledges and insights.

The Buddha, knowing that many bhikṣus had attained the path of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and become arhats, gathered the community of bhikṣus for this reason and rebuked them in various ways:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu seek a blade to commit suicide, praise death, or incite others to death?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being or one who is of human form—whether by wielding a weapon himself, providing a knife, instructing them to die, or praising death, saying:
"What is the use of living this wretched life?"
"It is better to die than to live.

Following his inclination toward death, [the monk] instructs him on various grounds to die and praises death. If he dies, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and should not dwell in communion with the Saṃgha.
"Taking life" means taking it oneself or commanding another to take it.
In this regard, how does one commit an offense?
There are three ways a bhikṣu takes human life that constitute a pārājika offense: [the following three methods].
First, acting by oneself; second, instructing another; third, dispatching a messenger.
Acting by oneself means taking the life of another with one's own hand.
Instructing another means speaking to someone else, saying:
"Seize this man, bind him, and take his life.
He sent a messenger to say to another person:
"Do you know such-and-such a person?"
"Seize this person, bind him, and take his life.
When the messenger takes that person's life according to these instructions, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there are three ways of taking a human life:
First, using one's own internal matter; second, using external matter; third, using both internal and external matter. Regarding internal matter:
a bhikṣu strikes another with his hand, or with his foot, or his head, or any other part of his body, with the thought:
"May this cause his death."
If the person dies because of that [act], the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense.
If he does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of it, he also commits a pārājika offense.
If he does not die immediately, and later does not die as a result of it, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

Regarding "using that which is not internal form": if a bhikṣu, using wood, tiles, stones, swords, spears, bows, arrows, or pieces of wood, white tin, or lead, hurls them from a distance at another person with the thought, "May they die because of this."
If the person dies because of that, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, it is also a *pārājika* offense.
If they do not die immediately, and later do not die because of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding "using internal or non-internal matter": if a bhikṣu takes up wood, tiles, stones, knives, spears, bows, or arrows;
or if he strikes another with a piece of wood, a piece of white tin, or a piece of lead or pewter, thinking:
"May he die because of this."
If the person dies because of that, it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, it is also a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, and later do not die because of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, neither by means of internal matter, nor by means of non-internal matter, nor by means of both internal and non-internal matter, prepares various poisonous drugs for the purpose of killing someone. He places them in the eyes, ears, nose, or mouth;

or he places them in the male or female organs, on the body, or in a wound; or he places them in cakes, meat, soups, rice, or congee; or he places them in bedding, large carts, small carts, bedding-furniture, palanquins, or hand-pulled carriages.
He forms this thought: "May they die because of this."
If the person dies because of that [act], it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, it is also a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, and later do not die because of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, for the purpose of killing a person, does not use internal matter, nor external matter, nor both internal and external matter, nor even poison; yet he employs the *uyuta* method of killing, the *tūta* method of killing, sets traps, lays snares, uses pits, performs *vidyā* (magical) killing, performs *ardha-vidyā* (semi-magical) killing, kills by severing the life-force, kills by causing an abortion, kills by pressing on the abdomen, throws [the victim] into fire, throws [them] into water, or throws [them] into a pit; or he dispatches someone else to go along a path so that they die there, even down to the point of killing by employing the means to terminate the two faculties first received in the womb—the body faculty and the life faculty.
Regarding those with much anxiety: there was a bhikṣu who knew that a certain person would come by this path; he first prepared a pit of smokeless fire therein and covered it over with sand and soil.
If one thinks in the mind or speaks with the mouth,
"Because this person has come along this path, I have made this pit," this is called *saṃvidhāna-utpāda*.
If a person dies because of this, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, he also incurs a pārājika offense.
If the person does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu digs a pit for someone and that person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If a non-human being dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If an animal dies, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one digs a pit for a non-human being and that non-human being dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a human being dies [as a result], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If an animal falls and dies, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu digs a pit for an animal and an animal falls and dies, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a human being falls and dies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a non-human being falls and dies, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu does not intend for a specific individual but causes all those who come to him to fall and die, [it is a *dukkaṭa*].
If a human being dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If a non-human being dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is no one who has died, it is a sthūlātyaya and a duṣkṛta.
This is called *autpāda*.
Regarding *mūrdhā*, there are two kinds:
First is earth, second is wood.

Regarding earth, if there are many [types], a bhikṣu might dig a pit and bury a person up to the ankles, or the knees, or the waist, or the navel, or from the armpits to the neck; having buried them thus, he causes elephants to trample them, or causes horses, camels, oxen, and donkeys to trample them, or causes venomous snakes and centipedes to go and bite them, thinking:
"May they die because of this."
If the person dies because of that [act], the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of it, he also commits a pārājika offense.
If they do not die immediately, and later do not die as a result of it, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called *dhituda*. Regarding *kāṣṭhuda*:

there is a bhikṣu who bores holes in wood to fashion shackles for feet, cuffs for hands, or collars for the neck; having bound [the victim] in this way, he causes elephants, horses, camels, oxen, or donkeys to trample them, or causes venomous snakes and centipedes to bite them, thinking:
"May they die because of this."
If the person dies because of that, it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, but later die as a result of this, it is also a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, and later do not die as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called *mukhata*. Regarding "a snare":

suppose there is a monk who knows that a certain person will come along this path, and he sets a snare therein—relying on a tree, a pillar, a stone, a wall, or a piece of wood, a piece of white tin, or a piece of lead—either with a mental intention or by speaking aloud:
"I am setting this snare because such a person will come along this path."
If the person dies as a result of that [act], the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense.
If he does not die immediately, but later dies because of it, he also commits a pārājika offense.
If he does not die immediately, and later does not die because of it, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one sets a snare for a human being and a human dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If a non-human or an animal dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one sets a snare for a non-human and a non-human dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a human or an animal dies [as a result], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sets a snare for an animal and an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a human or a non-human dies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not restrict [the action] to a single individual, but causes all who come to fall into death—if a human dies, it is a *pārājika*;
if a non-human (*amanuṣya*) dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a sentient animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*; if none die at all, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. This is called a "snare. As for a "net": suppose there is a bhikṣu who knows that a person will come by this path, and he sets a net—whether relying on a tree, a pillar, a stone, a stake, a wall, a log, a piece of white tin, or a piece of lead—either with a mental intention or by verbal declaration: [“When such-and-such a person comes, may they be caught in this net”]. If that person comes and is caught in the net, it is a *pāyattika*. If the person does not come, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. This is called a “net. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and hangs a net from it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net upon it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net below it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net on both sides of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net above it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net in front of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net behind it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net in the middle of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net in the center of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very top of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very bottom of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very side of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very edge of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very corner of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very joint of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very knot of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very seam of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very opening of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very gap of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very fissure of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very crevice of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very hollow of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very depression of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very concavity of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very convexity of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very slope of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very incline of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very descent of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very ascent of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very rise of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very fall of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very turn of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very bend of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very curve of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very loop of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very coil of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very twist of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very knotting of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very binding of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the very fastening of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* and a *duṣkṛta*. If one ties a string to a tree or a pillar and places a net at the
"If one sets a snare for the purpose of causing this person to come along this path,
and that snare succeeds such that the person dies because of it, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense."
If one does not die immediately, but dies later as a result of this [act], it is also a *pārājika*.
If one does not die immediately, and does not die later as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu intentionally sets a snare for a person and that person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If a non-human being dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If an animal dies, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one sets a snare for a non-human being and a non-human being dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a human or an animal dies [as a result], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one sets a snare for an animal and the animal falls and dies, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a human or a non-human dies [as a result], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu sets a snare not for a specific individual, such that all who come across it are caused to fall and die, then if a person dies, it is a pārājika offense.
If a non-human dies, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If an animal dies, it is a pāyattika.
If no one dies at all, it is a sthūlātyaya-duṣkṛta.
This is called "killing by means of a snare.

Regarding "the trigger": if a bhikṣu knows that a person is coming along this path, and [he sets] a trap-trigger within a tree, a pillar, a stake, a stone, a wall, a log of wood, a piece of white tin, or a piece of lead-tin.
If one thinks in the mind or says with the mouth,
"I shall strike this person because they have come along this path," and that act of striking is accomplished such that the person dies as a result, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die immediately, but dies later as a result of this [act], it is also a *pārājika*.
If one does not die immediately, and does not die later as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu intentionally strikes another person with the intent to kill and that person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If a non-human or an animal dies, it is all *sthūlātyaya*.
If one makes a blow against a non-human and that non-human dies, it is *sthūlātyaya*;
if a human or an animal dies, it is *duṣkṛta*.
If one sets a trap for animals and an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a human or a non-human dies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu sets a trap not for a specific individual but for anyone who might come along, and as a result, someone dies—if it is a human, it is a *pārājika*.
If a non-human being dies, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if an animal dies, it is a pāyattika;
if no one dies at all, it is a sthūlātyaya and a duṣkṛta.
This is called "denial" (*apavāda*).

Regarding *vidyā* (sorcery): there was a bhikṣu who, on the twenty-ninth day of the month, sought out a corpse with its limbs intact to summon a spirit through incantations, causing it to rise; he washed it, dressed it in clothes, and placed a sword in its hand.
If one thinks in the mind or speaks with the mouth,
"I am performing a *vidyā* for the sake of such-and-such," and then recites the incantation, this is called the accomplishment of the *vidyā*.

If one intends to kill someone, yet that person has entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); or if there is a powerful mantra-master who protects and delivers them; or if there is a powerful celestial deity (*deva*) providing protection—then it is impossible to harm them.

This bhikṣu who performs the incantation must first prepare a sheep; if he obtains a plantain tree, or if he cannot kill the aforementioned person, he should kill this sheep or kill this tree. To act in this manner is good;
if he does not do so, he shall be killed in return.
Such a bhikṣu is called a vidyādhara.

As for the "half-vidyādhara," there is a bhikṣu who, after twenty-nine days, constructs an iron chariot; having constructed the iron chariot, he constructs an iron man; having constructed the iron man, he summons a spirit and casts a spell to make the iron man rise; he washes him with water, clothes him, and ties a sword in the iron man's hand.
If one thinks in the mind or speaks with the mouth,
"I am performing this *ardha-vidyā* for the sake of such-and-such," and recites this incantation,
it is called the accomplishment of the *ardha-vidyā*.

If one wishes to kill someone, yet that person has entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); or if they are protected and rescued by a powerful mantra-master; or if they are guarded by a powerful deva—then one cannot harm them.

This monk who performs the incantation must first prepare a sheep; or, if he obtains a plantain tree, if he cannot kill the person before him, he should kill this sheep or kill this tree. To act in this manner is good;
if he does not do so, he shall be killed in turn.
Such a bhikṣu is called a half-vetāla.

As for one who takes life: if a bhikṣu, on the twenty-ninth day, smears cow dung upon the ground, places wine and food therein, kindles a fire, and then immediately casts it into water; [he is a killer].
With mental intent and verbal recitation, one utters the mantra:
"Just as fire is extinguished by water, so too shall the life of [Name] be extinguished.
When the fire is extinguished, that person's life follows suit and is extinguished.

Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu who, on the twenty-ninth day of the month, smears cow dung upon the ground and places wine and food therein; he draws the image of the person he intends to kill, and having made this image, he immediately erases it while mentally contemplating and vocally reciting a mantra, saying:
"As this image perishes, so too shall his life perish."
"When the image perishes, his life-force perishes accordingly.

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, on the twenty-ninth day, smears cow dung on the ground, places wine and food upon it, and then pierces the corner of a garment with a needle. He immediately withdraws the needle while mentally focusing and verbally reciting a mantra, saying:
'Just as this needle comes out, so shall his life-force come out.'"
"When this needle is withdrawn, his life departs with it;
this is called taking life. Regarding the abortionist:

there is a bhikṣu who gives a woman carrying a fetus emetic medicine, purgative medicine, nasal medication, or medication for the urinary or anal passages; or if he pierces her blood vessels, or causes her to shed tears, or administers blood-dissolving medicine, he forms this thought:"
"By this cause and condition, one causes a woman to die.
If she dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If she does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this, it is likewise a *pārājika* offense.
If she does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result of this act, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of killing that mother, causes an abortion, and the mother dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If the fetus dies, it is a thullaccaya.
If both [the mother and the fetus] die, it is a pārājika.
If neither dies, it is a thullaccaya.
If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of killing the fetus, performs a method to cause an abortion, and the fetus dies, it is a pārājika offense.
If the mother dies, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If both die, it is a pārājika offense.
If neither dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called causing an abortion.

Regarding "pressing the abdomen": there is a bhikṣu who causes a pregnant woman to perform heavy labor, or carry heavy loads, instructs her to run in front of a vehicle, or makes her ascend a steep bank, with this thought: [she shall miscarry].
"By this cause and condition, she causes a woman to die.
If she dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If she does not die immediately, but later dies because of this [act], it is also a *pārājika*.
If she does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu presses on his mother’s abdomen for her sake and she dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If the fetus dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If both die, it is a *pārājika*.
If neither dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If, for the sake of the fetus, one presses upon the abdomen and the fetus dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If the mother dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If both die, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If neither dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "pressing the belly.
Regarding "pushing into fire": pushing [the fetus] into a wood-fire, a grass-fire, a cow-dung fire, or a bran-fire with such a thought:
"If he causes him to die by this means," and if he dies because of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If he does not die immediately, but later dies because of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If he does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "causing one to fall into fire.

As for pushing someone into water: one pushes them into a large pond, the great ocean, a deep spring, a reservoir, a deep well, or a deep river channel, even to the point of submerging their face in the water, with the following thought:
"If he causes him to die by this means," and the person dies,
it is a *pārājika*. If he does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If he does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "falling into water.
Regarding pushing someone from a height so that they fall: this refers to a high mountain, a high bank, a palace, a wall, or a deep pit; having formed such a thought [to push them]:
"If he causes him to die by this means," and the person dies,
it is a *pārājika*. If he does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If he does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the case of dispatching someone to die on the road: suppose a bhikṣu knows that there are wicked bandits, fierce beasts, or starvation on that path, yet he dispatches him to go into this dangerous place with the thought:
"Let him die in that perilous way."
If the person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, but die later as a result of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If they do not die immediately, and do not die later as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "causing death on the way.
Regarding the phrase "even those who have first acquired two faculties within the womb," these refer to the body faculty (kāyendriya) and the life faculty (jīvitendriya).
If, during the stage of the kalala, one employs a means with the intent to kill so as to cause death, and the person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If he does not die immediately, but dies later as a result of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If he does not die immediately, and does not die later as a result of this, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“There are two ways to seek a knife:
first, to seek it oneself; second, to instruct another to seek it.
There are three kinds of praise:”
"First, those of evil precepts; second, those of good precepts; third, the sick. Regarding those of evil precepts:

they are those who kill oxen, kill sheep, raise chickens, raise pigs, release hawks, catch fish, hunt deer with nets, are thieves, are executioners, are dragon-charmers, or are prison guards. When a bhikṣu goes to where such people of evil precepts are and speaks thus:
"You people of evil precepts, why do you commit these sins for so long?"
"It would be better to die early.
If the person dies because of these words, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense;
if the person does not die immediately, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a person of immoral conduct says,
"I will not follow the words of this bhikṣu," and the person does not die as a result, the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a bhikṣu praises a person so as to cause them to die, and then feels remorse in his heart, thinking:
"Why did I instruct this person to die?
he returns and says to them:

"You wicked people, it may be that through the causal conditions of virtuous friends, you have drawn near to good persons and been able to hear the sublime Dharma; by means of correct reflection, you have been able to distance yourselves from evil offenses—therefore, do not commit suicide."
If this person accepts the words of the bhikṣu and does not die as a result, the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Regarding "those of good precepts," these are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
There is a bhikṣu who goes to those who are virtuous people and speaks to them thus:
"O you who uphold the good precepts and possess merit, upon death you will immediately receive heavenly blessings."
"Why do you not take your own life?
If that person, because of these words, takes their own life, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense;
if they do not take their own life, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a person of virtuous precepts thinks,
"Why should I take my own life based on these words of this bhikṣu?
and does not die as a result, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣu, having instructed another to die, later feels regret and says:
"I was wrong! Why did I instruct this virtuous person to die?"
He returned and said to him:

"O person of virtuous precepts, the more you remain alive for the duration of your lifespan, the greater your merit will increase; because your merit is great, the blessings you receive will also be great. Do not take your own life."
If [the person] does not die because of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding a sick person who experiences various sufferings due to the increase or decrease of the four great elements, a bhikṣu says to that person:
"How can you endure these sufferings for long?"
"Why do you not take your own life?
If a bhikṣu dies as a result of this, he incurs a pārājika offense;
if he does not die, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If the sick person thinks,
"For what reason should I take my own life based on this bhikṣu’s words?
and does not die as a result, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣu feels remorse, thinking: "I was wrong!
Why did I instruct this sick person to commit suicide?"
He returned and spoke to them, saying:
"You who are ill, if you obtain good medicine, a skilled caregiver, and food and drink appropriate to your condition, your illness may be cured; do not take your own lives."
If the patient does not die because of it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
These are called the three kinds of praising death.
Kāḷudāyin constantly entered and left the house of a certain lay devotee; at the time of morning, he would put on his robes, take his bowl, and go to that house.
In that household, there was a woman with an infant who had not yet been weaned; she placed the child upon the bed, covered it with a cloth, and departed.
Kāḷodāyin snapped his fingers at the door, and the woman came out to look and said, "Venerable Sir!"
"Enter and sit upon this bed.
Kāḷodāyin did not look and sat down upon the boy; the boy's intestines protruded, and he cried out loudly.
His wife said:
"There is an infant here.
Because the bhikṣu’s body was heavy, the infant died immediately.
Having done this, he returned to the monastery and said to the other bhikṣus:
"I have done such a thing today.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. Knowing [the situation], the Buddha asked intentionally:
"With what state of mind did you do it?"
He replied,
“I sat down without first looking upon the bed.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From now on, you must first inspect the bed and the seating place before sitting down.
If you do not first inspect them, you shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.”

Furthermore, a father and son who were both bhikṣus were traveling together through the Kosalā country toward Śrāvastī; when they reached a perilous path, the son said to his father, "Travel quickly past this."
The father ran as his son commanded, but died from exhaustion; the son immediately felt doubt:
"Have I perhaps committed a *pārājika* offense and incurred the crime of parricide?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the situation, asked him:
"With what intention did you speak?

The novice bhikṣu replied, "Seeing that it was already dusk, I feared we would not survive the perilous path; out of affection and concern, I spoke those words to urge him to travel quickly, which ultimately caused him to die of exhaustion."
The Buddha said, "There is no offense.
Again, there were father and son bhikṣus traveling together through the Kosalā country toward Śrāvastī. Upon reaching a village where there was no monastery, the son asked his father:
"Where are you staying tonight?
His father replied,
"I am staying in the village."
The son said,
"What difference is there between staying overnight in a village and being a layperson?
His father then spoke to his son:
"Where shall we stay for the night?
The son replied,
"We shall stay in an open space."
The father said, "There are tigers and wolves here that are to be feared; I shall sleep while you remain awake.
The son said:
"So be it," he replied, and lay down immediately. The father then fell into a snoring sleep.

Hearing the sound of the snoring, the tiger came and bit the father; his head was split open and he cried out loudly. The son immediately rose to look and saw that his father’s head was shattered and he had already died.
The boy immediately became suspicious, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense or incurred the crime of parricide?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
One should shout loudly and light a fire to frighten them.
A certain bhikṣu entered a dangerous path at dusk and encountered bandits; the bandits wished to seize the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu fled and fell onto a weaver below the bank; the weaver died immediately.
The bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense of *pārājika*.
From this day forward, do not engage in such bodily conduct.

Because the monastic quarters in the kingdom of Āravī were in ruins, a bhikṣu was working on the roof of a house; he dropped a brick from his hand onto a carpenter, and the carpenter died immediately.
The bhikṣu felt doubt in his mind:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forth, you must perform your work with single-minded concentration.

Furthermore, in the Aravī country, the monks’ dwelling was falling into ruin. While the monks were repairing the building, they saw a scorpion inside a brick. Terrified, he leaped down and fell upon a carpenter, who died immediately.
The bhikṣu felt doubt in his mind:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"No offense.
From now on, do not engage in such bodily conduct.
The matter of killing was concluded.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī during the summer retreat, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a famine and alms were difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of the people lacked sufficient food and drink, let alone what they could give to beggars.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:

"You should know that in this place, food is scarce and alms are difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of the common people lack sufficient food and drink and suffer various afflictions, let alone being able to give to others!"

"O bhikṣus, go to dwell during the rains retreat wherever you have acquaintances, wherever there are kinsmen, or wherever you place your trust; do not remain here and undergo various sufferings for the sake of food and drink."
At that time, the bhikṣus each went to their respective acquaintances to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).
Some bhikṣus went to a certain location in the kingdom of Kośala to observe the retreat;

others went to a village on the banks of the Bhagīrathī River to observe the retreat—a village abounding in many nobles, slaves, wealth, treasures, and an abundance of grain, fully endowed with all kinds of prosperity.
At that time, a bhikṣu observing the rains retreat by the river thought to himself:
"In this world of famine, almsfood is difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of ordinary people lack sufficient food and drink, let alone give it to a beggar!"
"In this village there are many wealthy and noble families, with abundant grain and all things accomplished; we shall go to these houses and praise one another, saying:
'Householder, you should know!'"

"You have gained great and excellent benefit, for this great community of bhikṣus has entered the rains retreat within your village. Now, among this assembly, such-and-such a person is an arhat; such-and-such is one progressing toward arhatship; such-and-such is an anāgāmin;

such-and-such is one progressing toward anāgāminship; such-and-such is a sakṛdāgāmin; such-and-such is one progressing toward sakṛdāgāminship; such-and-such is a srotāpanna; such-and-such is one progressing toward srotāpannaship. Such-and-such has attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna. Such-and-such has attained immeasurable loving-kindness, immeasurable compassion, immeasurable sympathetic joy, and immeasurable equanimity. Such-and-such has attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Such-and-such has attained the contemplation of impurity; such-and-such has attained mindfulness of breathing."
After the bhikṣus had formed this thought, they immediately entered a village and went to a wealthy household, where they praised one another, saying:
"You should know that you have gained a great and wholesome benefit!"
"The Sangha of the Field of Merit has entered the rains retreat in reliance upon your village.
Within this assembly, such-and-such a person is an Arhat, and I too am an Arhat;
such-and-such a person is one who is approaching Arhatship, and I too am one who is approaching Arhatship; such-and-such a person is an Anāgāmin, and I too am..."
"Such-and-such a person is a non-returner (anāgāmin), and I too am heading toward the state of a non-returner;

such-and-such a person has attained the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), and I too have attained the fruit of once-returning; such-and-such a person is heading toward the fruit of once-returning, and I too am heading toward the fruit of once-returning;
such-and-such a person has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), and I too have attained the fruit of stream-entry; such-and-such a person is heading toward the fruit of stream-entry..."
"Ananda, I too am a stream-enterer; so-and-so has attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna;
[so-and-so] has attained immeasurable loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

[so-and-so] has attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; [so-and-so] has attained the contemplation of impurity."
“Regarding mindfulness of *ānāpāna*, I too have attained the first dhyāna up to mindfulness of *ānāpāna*.
Thereupon, those householders immediately conceived pure faith and thought to themselves:
“We have gained a great and wholesome benefit!”
There is a great field of merit, the Saṃgha of monks, who are observing the rains retreat in our village.

Among them, some have attained Arhatship; some are practicing for Arhatship; some have attained Anāgāminship; some are practicing for Anāgāminship; some have attained Sakṛdāgāminship; some are practicing for Sakṛdāgāminship; some have attained Srotāpanna-ship; some are practicing for Srotāpanna-ship; and some have attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; the immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception; as well as the contemplation of impurity and the mindfulness of ānāpāna.

"Since this lay devotee has attained such faith, even now, during this time of famine when alms-food is difficult to obtain, he is able to provide the saṃgha with morning and afternoon meals and *tambūla* just as he did previously when food was abundant and easy to find."

At that time, the bhikṣus observing the rains retreat on the banks of the Bhagurā River consumed this food and drink, whereby their bodies became full, they attained physical vigor, and they grew robust and lustrous.
It is the established practice of the Buddhas dwelling in the world to hold two great assemblies each year: at the end of the last month of spring and at the end of the last month of summer.
In the final month of spring, monks from various regions and countries arrive everywhere and think to themselves:
"We shall practice the Dharma taught by the Buddha during the retreat period so that we may dwell in peace and happiness."
This is called the first great assembly.

Regarding the final month of the summer retreat: when the bhikṣus had completed their three-month summer rains retreat in various places and finished making their robes, they took up their robes and bowls and went to where the Buddha was, thinking:
"We have not seen the Buddha for a long time; we have not seen the World-Honored One for a long time."
This was the second great assembly.

At that time, the bhikṣus who had observed the rains retreat in the kingdom of Kośala completed their robes at the end of the three months of summer. Taking their robes and bowls, they traveled on foot and arrived in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when resident bhikṣus who have been observing the rains retreat with the Buddha encounter visiting bhikṣus arriving, they should go together to welcome them, inquire after their well-being with a single mind, carry their robes and bowls for them, open the rooms, and show them the place for bedding, saying:
"These are your rooms; there are coarse-woven rope beds, fine-woven rope beds, blankets, quilts, pillows, and mats; please occupy them according to the order of seniority."

At that time, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, seeing from afar the bhikṣus of Kośala approaching, went out together to welcome them and inquired after their well-being with single-minded attention. They took up their robes and bowls for them, opened the rooms, and showed them the places for bedding, saying:
"These are your rooms; there are coarse-woven rope beds, fine-woven rope beds, blankets, mattresses, pillows, and mats. Please stay according to the order of seniority."
He inquired after them, saying:
"Are you content and dwelling in peace? Is your alms-seeking not lacking, and are you not fatigued by the journey?
The Kosalaka bhikṣus replied:
"We have dwelt contentedly and in comfort, and we were not fatigued on the road; however, almsfood was difficult to obtain.
The bhikṣus from Vaiśālī said:

"It is true that you have dwelt contentedly and in comfort and were not fatigued on the road; it is because almsfood was difficult to obtain that you have become emaciated and your complexions are haggard."
At that time, the bhikṣus of the Pāṭalaka River, having completed their summer retreat and finished making their robes, traveled to Vaiśālī.

When the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī saw the bhikṣus from the Pāṣāṇaka River approaching from afar, they all went out together to welcome them and greeted them with single-minded attention. They took up their robes and bowls for them, opened the dwellings, and showed them the places for bedding, saying:
"These are your rooms; there are coarse-woven rope beds, fine-woven rope beds, blankets, quilts, pillows, and mats. Please stay according to the order of seniority."
He inquired after them, saying:
"Are you content and dwelling in peace? Is there no lack of almsfood, and are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣus on the banks of the Bhagīrathī River replied:
"We are content and dwelling in peace; we have not lacked for alms, but we are utterly exhausted from the journey.
The monk from Vaiśālī said, "It is true that you are content and dwelling in peace, and that you have not lacked for alms, but you are indeed exhausted from the journey."
"Why is it, venerable ones, that you are so plump and flourishing, with such serene and joyful countenances?
Then the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī gradually pressed him further, asking:
"Venerable elders!"
"In this world, there is famine and scarcity, and alms-food is difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of others lack sufficient food and drink, so how much less could they give it to you!
For what reason do you all have such vigorous strength and a pleasant complexion during the retreat, and why is alms-food not difficult for you to obtain?"
Then the bhikṣu from the Pārāvatika River related the causes and conditions as described above.
The bhikṣus from Vaiśālī asked:
"Venerable elders!..."
"Do those qualities you have praised truly exist?
They replied, "Truly not."
The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, by means of various causes and conditions, rebuked the bhikṣu of the Bhagurārāma River:

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path. To engage in impure conduct without a mind of dispassion is something that those who have gone forth ought not to do."

You do not know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has censured false speech through various causes and conditions and praised non-false speech through various causes and conditions; the Buddha constantly teaches the Dharma to instruct people to abandon false speech.
You should not even give rise to the thought of speaking falsely, let alone for the sake of food and drink, falsely claiming to have attained supramundane noble dharmas that you do not possess.
Having thus rebuked them with these various causes and conditions, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣu Pāṭaliputra:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣus of the Pāṅkadhā River with various causes and conditions:

"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path. To engage in impure conduct without a mind of dispassion is something that those who have gone forth ought not to do."
"You foolish person!
You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, rebuked false speech and praised non-false speech through various causes and conditions.

I constantly teach the Dharma to instruct people to abandon false speech; you should not even give rise to the thought of committing a lie, let alone for the sake of food and drink, falsely claiming to have attained superhuman states when you have none."
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there are three kinds of great thieves:
the first is one who acts as the leader of a hundred men; therefore, he stands before the hundred, and the hundred surround him with reverence."

Whether there be two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred leaders, they stand at the head of those five hundred; surrounded and revered by the five hundred, they enter cities and villages, breach walls, block roads to plunder, destroy cities, and kill people—this is called the first kind of great worldly thief.

Second, there are bhikṣus who take the bamboo, wood, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, wealth, food, or drink belonging to the saṃgha of the four quarters from within its groves and gardens, and either sell them for their own livelihood or give them to lay acquaintances; these are called the second kind of great worldly thief.
Third, there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of food and drink offerings, falsely claims to have attained supramundane noble dharmas when he has none.

Whether surrounded by a hundred people in reverence or five hundred people in reverence, he enters cities and villages to receive from others offerings of morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambala*. This is called the third great thief in the world.

Among them, a leader of a hundred bandits is respectfully surrounded by those hundred; a leader of two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred is respectfully surrounded by those five hundred. They enter cities and villages, breach walls, block roads, plunder and seize, destroy cities, and kill people—these are called minor thieves.

If there is a bhikṣu who uses the bamboo, wood, roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, or property and food belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters from within its groves and gardens, and sells them for his own livelihood or gives them to lay acquaintances, he too is a minor thief.
The Buddha said:
"This is the third thief; among the assembly of devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he is the greatest thief of all."

That is to say, for the sake of food and drink, one falsely claims to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) when in fact they are empty and non-existent, speaking such lies to say that one has attained them.

Even if one is surrounded by the respectful veneration of a hundred or five hundred people, entering cities and villages to receive offerings from others—whether before a meal, after a meal, or as *tambala* (refreshments)—such a person is called a great thief.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"A bhikṣu who has not attained the Path yet claims to have attained it is a great thief among gods and humans,
an exceedingly evil person who violates the precepts."
"This deluded person, when his body perishes, shall fall into hell.
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, not knowing and not seeing the superhuman states that are empty [of self], claims: 'I have attained such knowledge and such vision,' and if at a later time, whether questioned or unasked, out of attachment to gain and honor, he speaks falsely with an empty deception, saying he knows what he does not know and sees what he does not see, that bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a secluded place in the kingdom of Kośala where various bhikṣus resided.

Because those bhikṣus had attained meditative concentration through the contemplation of specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), lust and hatred did not arise within them, and they thought to themselves:
"We have already attained the Path; what was to be done has been accomplished."
These bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and said of themselves:
"We are arhats; our births have been exhausted and we shall no longer receive a body.
Having spoken these words, they later resided in a monastery near a village. Because they frequently saw women, desire and anger arose within them, and these bhikṣus spoke as follows:

"We have undergone much hardship and suffering; previously, while dwelling in secluded places, we attained concentration through the contemplation of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, sensual desire and ill will did not arise, and we thought:
'We have already attained the Path; what was to be done has been accomplished.'"
He went immediately to where the Buddha was and said of himself:
"I am an Arhat; my births are exhausted, and I shall no longer receive a body.
Now, because he dwells near a village and frequently sees women, lust and anger have arisen within him.
"We have lost the Dharma of a bhikṣu and burned the Dharma of a bhikṣu; we are empty and devoid of superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma), yet we claimed to have attained them.
These bhikṣus spoke to other bhikṣus, and when those other bhikṣus heard it, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.

For this reason and on account of these circumstances, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts.
Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu neither knows nor sees the superhuman states that are empty [of self], yet claims, "I have attained such knowledge and such vision," and later—whether questioned or not—speaks thus in order to clear himself of the offense:
"I spoke of knowing what I did not know and saw what I did not see; it was an empty, deceptive, and false speech."
"Except in the case of overweening pride, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.
"Not knowing" means not knowing, not attaining, not seeing, not touching, and not realizing the state of a superhuman being.
"Not seeing" means not seeing the truth of suffering, not seeing the truth of the origin, not seeing the truth of cessation, and not seeing the truth of the path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu claims, "I am an arhat," and it is not true, he commits a pārājika offense.
If one falsely claims to be a candidate for Arhatship, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one falsely claims to be an Anāgāmin, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one falsely claims to be a candidate for Anāgāmin, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one falsely claims to be a Sakṛdāgāmin, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one falsely claims to be a candidate for the state of a Sakṛdāgāmin, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one falsely claims to be a Srotāpanna, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one who has not actually attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* claims to have done so, he commits a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu says:

"I have attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; I have attained the immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the contemplation of impurity; and I have attained mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing)."
If it is untrue, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
Even if one says:
"I am a person who well maintains the precepts; lust does not arise in me."
If it is not true, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu says: "Devas have come to me;
nāgas, yakṣas, piśācas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and rākṣasas have come to me; they questioned me and I answered them, and I questioned them and they answered me."
"If this matter is not true, the bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense...
[and so on] ...until:
'A whirlwind-dust spirit came to my place.'"
"If it is not true, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

At one time, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered the concentration of emptiness of non-existence (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-śūnyatā-samādhi*). He had correctly grasped the signs for entering concentration, but he did not correctly grasp the signs for emerging from concentration.
Emerging from samādhi, having heard the sounds of musical instruments in the city of the asuras, he quickly re-entered meditative concentration and formed this thought:
"While in samādhi, I heard the sounds of musical instruments in the city of the asuras."
Rising from samādhi, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"While I was on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered the formless concentration of the sphere of nothingness, I heard the sounds of musical instruments within the city of the asuras."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"How could such a thing be possible—that one who has entered the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) should see forms and hear sounds?
For what reason?"
"If you have entered the formless attainments, you have destroyed the signs of form and abandoned the signs of sound.
Since you falsely claim to possess superhuman states that you do not actually have, you are guilty of lying; you, Maudgalyāyana, should be expelled, disciplined, and banished."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“You must not say that Maudgalyāyana has committed an offense. Why is this?”
Maudgalyāyana sees only what precedes him, but does not see what follows.

The Tathāgata sees both what precedes and what follows. Thus, while Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless concentration of the sphere of nothingness; he skillfully grasped the signs for entering concentration, but did not skillfully grasp the signs for emerging from concentration.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he hears the sounds of musical instruments within the city of the asuras; having heard them, he quickly re-enters concentration and thinks to himself:
"I heard these sounds while in concentration."
"If one has entered the formless attainments, it is impossible for them to see forms or hear sounds.
Why is this? Because such a person has destroyed the characteristics of form and abandoned the characteristics of sound."

"If it were the case that Maudgalyāyana spoke falsely because he lacked superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*), such a thing would be impossible; rather, Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his perception, and thus there is no offense.
On one occasion, the bhikṣus asked the Elder Maudgalyāyana:
"From where does the water of the Bahudhāraka River come?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“This water comes from Lake Anavatapta.
The bhikṣus said:
“The waters of Lake Anavatapta are sweet and possess the eight meritorious qualities.
How can these waters be boiling hot and salty and bitter?
You, Maudgalyāyana!”
"You have falsely claimed superhuman attainments that you do not possess; therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you must be expelled, disciplined, and driven away.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not say that Maudgalyāyana has committed an offense in this matter."

Why is this? Lake Anavatapta is extremely far from here; this water originally possessed the eight meritorious qualities of sweetness and purity, but having passed through five hundred minor hells on its way upward, it has therefore become salty and hot.
If you were to ask Maudgalyāyana,
"For what reason is this water salty and hot?
he would be able to answer according to his perception.
“Maudgalyāyana spoke the truth; there is no offense.
On one occasion, Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration and saw that the yakṣas of the Vṛji were fighting with the yakṣas of Magadha, and had defeated the yakṣas of Magadha.
Having arisen from meditative concentration, he said to the bhikṣus:
"The people of Vaṅga shall defeat the people of Magadha.
Later, King Ajātaśatru, leading his troops skillfully, defeated the people of Vaṅga.
The bhikṣus said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Previously you said:
'The Vajjis shall defeat the Magadhans.'"
"Now the people of Magadha have defeated the people of Vṛji.
You, Maudgalyāyana, have spoken falsely by claiming to possess superhuman qualities when you are actually empty and devoid of them; you ought to be expelled, disciplined, and driven away."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not say that Maudgalyāyana has committed an offense for this matter. Why is that?"
Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind; the Tathāgata sees both what is before him and what is behind.

At that time, the yakṣa of the Vṛji fought with the yakṣa of Magadha and was victorious; the people of the Vṛji likewise defeated the people of Magadha. Later, King Ajātaśatru assembled his troops again and, fighting together, achieved victory.
"This was spoken by Maudgalyāyana according to his own thoughts; there is no offense.
Later, Maudgalyāyana again entered meditative concentration and saw that the yakṣa of Magadha had fought with the yakṣa of the Vṛji and emerged victorious.
Maudgalyāyana arose from his samādhi and said to the bhikṣus,
"The people of Magadha shall defeat the people of Vṛji.
Later, when they fought together, the people of Vṛji were victorious.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Previously you said:
'The people of Magadha shall defeat the people of Vajji.'"
"Now the people of Vṛji have further defeated the people of Magadha.
You, Maudgalyāyana, have spoken falsely because you lacked any superhuman qualities; you should be expelled, disciplined, and driven away."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not say that Maudgalyāyana has committed an offense in this matter. Why is that?"
Maudgalyāyana saw what was before him but not what was behind; the Tathāgata sees both what is before and what is behind.

At one time, the yakṣa of Magadha fought with the yakṣa of Vṛji and was victorious; at that time, the people of Magadha also defeated the people of Vṛji. Later, the people of Vṛji gathered their troops again and fought, achieving victory.
"Since Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his intention, there is no offense.
On one occasion, when morning had arrived, Maudgalyāyana put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the house of a lay devotee. He sat upon a prepared seat and exchanged greetings with him.
The lay devotee said, "Venerable Maudgalyāyana!"
"Is this pregnant woman about to give birth to a boy or a girl?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"She will give birth to a boy."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Then another brahmin came into the house, and the householder asked him:
"Will this pregnant woman give birth to a son or a daughter?"
He replied,
"A girl will be born.
Later, a girl was indeed born.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Previously you said that the householder’s wife had given birth to a son, yet now she has given birth to a daughter.
Since you falsely claimed to possess superhuman qualities when you have none, you, Maudgalyāyana, should be expelled, disciplined, and driven away."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not say that Maudgalyāyana committed an offense for this matter. Why is that?"
Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind, whereas the Tathāgata sees both what is before and what is behind.
At that time this woman was a man, who later transformed into a woman.
Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his perception of the mind; there is no offense.
Later, he likewise predicted that others would give birth to daughters.

At that time, there was a great drought; Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration and saw that seven days hence the heavens would send down heavy rain, filling the ditches and pits to overflowing.
The people of all the cities and towns heard these words and were all filled with great joy.

The inhabitants of the kingdom abandoned their various affairs, repaired their roofs, and secured their stores; each person counted on their fingers and held up counting-sticks to calculate the number of days.
When the seventh day arrived, there was still no sign of rain, let alone a heavy downpour!

The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana, "You said that for seven days there would be heavy rain until the ditches and pits overflow; yet now there is not even the scent of rain, much less any actual rain."
"You have falsely claimed superhuman attainments when you were actually empty of them; therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should be expelled, disciplined, and driven away.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not say that Maudgalyāyana has committed an offense in this matter."
Why is this? Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind, whereas the Tathāgata sees both what is before and what is behind.
During those seven days, there was indeed a great rain; the Asura King Rāhu caught it with his hand and placed it within the great ocean.
“Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his intention;
there is no offense. On another occasion, the Elder Śākata said to the bhikṣus:
“When I enter meditative concentration, I can cause the fires to fill the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.”
The bhikṣus said:
"How could such a thing be possible?
That a śrāvaka disciple could produce a great fire extending from the Avīci Hell all the way up to the Brahma World?"
"You have falsely claimed superhuman states that you do not possess; therefore, Śākyamuni, you must be expelled, disciplined, and driven away.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not say that Śākyamuni has committed an offense in this matter."

Why is this? If a bhikṣu relies on the first dhyāna to cultivate the bases of psychic power and attains supernormal powers, he can, from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, freely fill the space between them with fire.
It is the same for those who rely on the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

This Śāgata, relying upon the four dhyānas and having well-cultivated the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), attained great supernormal powers; if he so desired, from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, he could freely and at will fill them with fire.
"Śāgata speaks the truth; he has committed no offense.
On another occasion, the Elder Śubhūti said to the bhikṣus:
"In a single thought-moment, I can know the events of five hundred kalpas of my past lives."
The bhikṣus said:
"How could such a thing be possible?

Among the śrāvaka disciples, the most one can know in a single moment is a single lifetime. Since you have falsely claimed superhuman qualities that you do not possess, you are guilty of lying; Subhadda, you should be expelled, disciplined, and driven away."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“Do not say that Śubhadda has committed an offense. Why is this?
This person, in a previous life, passed away from the Heaven of No-Thought and was reborn here; having dwelt in the Heaven of No-Thought for five hundred kalpas, he therefore says of himself:
"In a single thought-moment, I can know the events of five hundred kalpas."
"Since this Śūbhita spoke according to his mental perception, there is no offense.
The four *pārājikas* are concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 20;
*Vinaya*, Scroll 3, Part 1 of the First Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
2. The Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas. Regarding the beginning of the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas:
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin had a private dwelling. In that private dwelling there were fine couches and beds, and a well-made bed for solitary sitting was spread with bedding. Both the interior and exterior were swept and sprinkled until they were entirely clean and pure. A water-jar for purification was filled with cold water, and a jar for constant use was also filled with cold water.
When this Kāḷudāyin’s lust arose, he would emit semen; by thus relieving his urgent distress, he was able to dwell in comfort and ease.
Later, a bhikṣu who was a friend of Kāḷudāyin came, greeted him with inquiries after his well-being, and sat to one side.
He said to Kāḷudāyin, "Are you enduring it?"
Are you well?
Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Are you free from want?
He replied, "I am patient,
contented, dwelling in peace and happiness, and lacking for nothing. He asked:
"What is meant by 'patience, contentment, dwelling in happiness, and lack of deficiency'?
They replied,
"Venerable elders!..."

I have a separate room with fine beds and bedding; my water-pitcher for purification and my regular water-jar are both filled with cold water. Having swept and sprinkled both the interior and exterior until they are entirely clean and pure, I spread out a fine bed for solitary sitting. When lust arises, I discharge my semen of my own accord; because I am free from urgent feverish heat, I dwell in peace and comfort.
"Venerable Elders!
For this reason, you shall be patient, contented, dwell in peace, and not lack for anything.
The bhikṣus said:
“You lack patience and contentment; you falsely regard a life of suffering and affliction as peace and happiness.
Your actions do not conform to the Dharma of a śramaṇa, they do not accord with the Path, and they constitute impure conduct—things that one who has gone forth ought not to do.”

You do not know that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has used various causes and conditions to censure desire and the perception of desire, and has used various causes and conditions to praise the departure from desire and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

The Buddha constantly teaches the Dharma to instruct people to detach from desire; you should not even give rise to such thoughts, let alone commit the fundamentally impure evil karma that constitutes the root of the fetters of desire, anger, and delusion.
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him in various ways, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path and is an impure practice, something that one who has left the household life ought not to do."
"You foolish person!

You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire and the perception of desire, and through various causes and conditions, praised the renunciation of desire and the extinguishing of the fever of desire."

I constantly teach the Dharma to instruct others to abandon desire; you should not even give rise to such a thought, let alone commit the impure and evil karma that is the root of the fetters of desire, hatred, and delusion.
"You foolish man!
With these very hands you receive the offerings and alms of others; how can you again use these same hands to commit an impure act?
Having rebuked him in this way with various words, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"

After the Buddha had established this precept, some bhikṣus emitted semen in their dreams; they felt doubt and remorse and went to Ānanda, where they prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and said to him:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept stating that for one who emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
"Now, while in their dreams, the bhikṣus have emitted semen and have conceived doubts and regrets; we pray that you will ask the Buddha about this matter for our sake.

Ānanda silently accepted the words of the bhikṣus. Knowing that Ānanda had silently accepted their request, the bhikṣus rose from their seats, bowed their heads at his feet in prostration, and departed.
Before long, Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: ‘If one emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.’”
"Although the Buddha has thus established this precept, the bhikṣus now experience the emission of semen in their dreams and feel doubt and remorse.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"Is there mental intention within a dream?"
The Buddha said, "There is the mental intention to act, yet one does not do so.

On this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except in a dream, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

Regarding 'saṃghāvaśeṣa': this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; within the Saṃgha there remains a remnant [of the offense], which is extinguished through repentance before the assembly of monks. This is called saṃghāvaśeṣa."
Within this, there are three types of offenses:
first, the arousal of the intention to emit; second, the movement of the body; and third, the emission of semen.
Furthermore, there are another three types:
First, for the sake of pleasure; second, for the sake of curing illness; third, for the sake of self-testing.
If a bhikṣu internally experiences a form and, for the sake of pleasure, gives rise to a thought, moves his body, and emits semen, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If, for the purpose of curing a disease or for the purpose of testing, one emits semen through mental intent and physical movement by internally receiving a sexual form, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu, without internally receiving a sexual form, for the purpose of experiencing pleasure, for the purpose of curing a disease, or for the purpose of testing, emits semen through mental intent and physical movement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, there are four types:
first, movement in mid-air; second, the arousal of the mind; third, bodily movement; and fourth, the emission of semen.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of experiencing pleasure, moves in mid-air, arouses the mind, makes a bodily movement, or emits semen while internally perceiving forms, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If, for the purpose of treating a disease or for the purpose of testing, one moves in mid-air, arouses the intention, moves the body, and semen is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, there are five factors:
if a bhikṣu scratches the urinary organ, presses the urinary organ, forms the intention, moves the body, and semen is emitted, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
