If a bhikṣu, for the sake of experiencing pleasure, for the sake of treating an illness, or for the sake of testing, rubs or presses his urinary organ with internal tactile sensation, and through the arousal of the mind and the movement of the body, semen is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu, though not desiring external forms, for the sake of pleasure, for the sake of treating a disease, or for the sake of testing, scratches or presses the urinary organ, with the arousal of intention and movement of the body, such that semen is emitted, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Within this, there are five kinds of essence:
first, blue; second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; and fifth, thin.
As for the blue, it belongs to a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) and to the crown prince who has received his office.
The yellow ones are the other sons of the wheel-turning monarch;
the red ones are the supreme ministers of the wheel-turning monarch;
the white ones are those who have already reached adulthood.
"Thin" refers to one whose years have not yet reached maturity.
If a person produces the color blue, they will not produce yellow, red, white, or thin; they can only produce blue.
If a person’s semen is yellow, it does not emit red, white, thin, or blue, but can only emit yellow.
If a person’s semen is red, it does not emit white, thin, blue, or yellow, but can only emit red.
If a person emits white semen, they do not emit thin, blue, yellow, or red; they can only emit white.
If a person emits thin semen, they do not emit blue, yellow, red, or white; they can only emit thin.
If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of discharging semen, rubs or presses his urinary organ, with the intention arising and the body moving, and semen is emitted, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of discharging yellow, red, white, or thin semen, rubs or presses the urinary organ, with the intention arising, the body moving, and semen discharged, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
It is impossible for a single person at one time to emit five kinds of semen.

However, some people may emit various kinds of semen due to excessive indulgence in sexual desire; others may do so because of carrying heavy loads, riding long distances, or the breaking and shifting of tendons and joints.

If a bhikṣu experiences thoughts of desire, the longing for desire, sensual perceptions, or the fever of desire, yet does not give rise to the intent, does not attempt to emit, his body does not move, and the semen is emitted spontaneously, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu has sores, blisters, ringworm, scabies, or itching on his male organ, and he scratches or rubs it for the purpose of treating this ailment, resulting in the emission of semen, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu warms his male organ over a fire and, due to scratching or rubbing from the itch, semen is emitted, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu, while walking, has semen emitted due to the friction of his two thighs, or due to contact with clothing, or while riding, or while being carried in a vehicle, and his body moves [thereby], there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu emits semen because he sees a beautiful form, there is no offense.
If he emits semen because he recalls a form without having seen it, there is no offense.
This first case concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin, having risen early in the morning, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Having finished eating, he returned to his quarters and stood between the doorposts holding the door-bolt, thinking to himself:
"If there is a woman who wishes to come into the monastery to see the rooms and dwellings, I shall show her the locations of all the rooms."
At that time, Kālodāyin saw the group of women from afar and said,
"Sisters, come!
I shall show you the locations of the various rooms."
After showing them a little, he led them to his own quarters and touched their bodies.
Among those women, some remained silent with pleasure, while others who were displeased went outside the room and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Is this the nature of the Dharma?
In this place of peace and security, there is yet further terror.
Thus spoke the bhikṣus.
"How can there still be fear in a place of safety?
The women recounted the aforementioned events in detail, and the bhikṣus said:
"It is as you have described."
"In a place of safety, there is yet further terror.

At that time, the bhikṣus, through various causes and conditions, taught the Dharma to the assembly of women, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; they then prostrated at their feet and departed.
Before long, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] already, he nevertheless asked Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked Kālodayin with various causes and conditions:
"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path, it is an impure practice, and it is something that one who has gone forth ought not to do."

"You fool! You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, censured desire and the perception of desire, and through various causes and conditions, praised the departure from desire and the eradication of the perception of desire."

I constantly teach the Dharma to instruct people to leave desire behind; you should not even give rise to such a thought, let alone commit the impure and evil karma that is the root of the fetters of desire, anger, and delusion.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, out of a mind of lustful transformation, touches a woman’s body—whether by grasping her arms or hair, or by stroking and touching each part of her body from top to bottom—it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
That which is characterized by the intensity of desire is called a "transformed mind," and it is also called a "mind of greed," a "defiled mind," or a "bound mind.

However, there may be a transformed mind that is not characterized by the intensity of desire, nor is it a mind of greed, a defiled mind, or a bound mind—such as the minds of those who are insane, deluded, or whose minds are impaired by illness; these are called transformed minds that are not minds of intense desire, nor defiled or bound minds.
Regarding "women," there are those who are large, medium, or small, as well as virgins and non-virgins, all of whom are capable of engaging in sexual desire.
"Touching the body" means being together in one place.
The hand extends from the wrist to the fingers.
The arm extends from the wrist to the shoulder.
Hair refers to the hair of the head, whether it be cotton wool (*karpāsa*), woolen cloth (*vāla-kambala*), or matted locks (*jaṭā*).
Regarding each individual part of the body, these refer to the eyes, ears, nose, and so forth.
Within this context, there are nine types of offenses:
rubbing upwards, rubbing downwards, embracing, grasping, pulling, pushing, lifting up, lowering down, or rubbing the areas of the anus or the genitals.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful transformation, touches the head of a naked woman by stroking it from above or below, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If he touches her face, throat, chest, abdomen, ribs, spine, navel, waist, the openings for excrement or urine, thighs, knees, or calves, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The same applies to embracing, seizing, pulling, pushing, lifting up, rubbing down, or touching the areas of the anus or the urinary organ.
If a bhikṣu lifts a naked woman from the ground and places her upon a mound of earth;
or if he places her on a mound of earth and then onto a couch; [in all such cases, it constitutes an offense].
He sat cross-legged on a small bed;
from the small bed he moved to a large bed;
from the large bed he moved onto a palanquin.
Those on the carriage were placed upon the chariot;
those on the chariot were placed upon the horse;
and those on the horse were placed upon the elephant.
If one carries a woman from atop an elephant onto a hall;
or from a hall onto a lower place, or from a small height onto a higher place—this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful transformation, lifts a naked woman from atop a hall and places her upon an elephant; [this also constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*].
From atop the elephant, he mounted the horse;
from atop the horse, he mounted the chariot;
from atop the chariot, he mounted the palanquin.
One places it upon a large bed on a carriage;
one places it upon a single-seated bed on the large bed;
one places it upon a squatting bed on the single-seated bed.
If one sits on a bed placed upon a raised earthen mound;
or places the earthen mound upon the ground; or even from a slightly higher place to a slightly lower place, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful transformation, rubs or touches the head of a clothed woman above or below [the collarbone], it is a thullaccaya.
If he rubs her face, throat, chest, shoulders, abdomen, ribs, spine, navel, waist, the private parts, thighs, knees, or calves, it is a thullaccaya.
Likewise, if one embraces, seizes, pulls, pushes, lifts up, or rubs down the areas of the anus or genitals, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful transformation, lifts a clothed woman from the ground and places her upon a mound of earth, or even lifts her from a slightly higher place and places her in a slightly lower place, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a woman, her mind transformed by intense lust, rubs and touches from head to toe a monk who is unclothed, and the monk, possessing a lustful mind, moves his body and experiences the sensation of smoothness, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, rubs his face, throat, chest, abdomen, ribs, spine, navel, waist, the areas of the anus or genitals, thighs, knees, or calves, and experiences the sensation of smoothness through bodily movement, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If, with a lustful mind, a bhikṣu embraces, seizes, pulls, pushes, lifts up, or rubs the areas of the anus or genitals, and his body moves and experiences the sensation of smoothness, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a woman, her mind transformed by intense lust, lifts a naked bhikṣu from the ground and places him upon a mound of earth, or even lifts him from a slightly lower place and places him on a slightly higher place, and the bhikṣu, having a lustful mind, moves his body and experiences this smoothness, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a woman, her lustful desire being intense, changes her mind and lifts a naked bhikṣu from an upper story onto an elephant, or even from a slightly higher place onto a slightly lower place, and the bhikṣu, having a lustful mind, moves his body and experiences the sensation of smoothness, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a woman, her mind transformed by intense lust, rubs or touches the head of a clothed bhikṣu from above or below, and the bhikṣu, with a mind of desire, moves his body and experiences the smoothness [of the touch], it is a sthūlātyaya.

If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, rubs his face, throat, chest, spine, abdomen, ribs, navel, waist, the areas of the anus or penis, or his thighs, knees, or calves, and his body moves to receive the sensation of smoothness, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.

A certain bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this matter; his heart was displeased and he felt shame, and for various reasons he rebuked Kāla:

Having thus rebuked him, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, the Buddha said to Kāla: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,

The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa; it does not accord with the Path, it is an impure practice, and it is something that one who has left the household life ought not to do."
"You foolish person!

You do not know that I have, through various causes and conditions, censured desire and the perception of desire, and through various causes and conditions, praised the renunciation of desire and the extinguishing of the fever of desire."

I constantly teach the Dharma to instruct people to leave desire behind; you should not even give rise to such a thought, let alone commit the impure evil karma that is the very root of the fetters of desire, anger, and delusion.
"You foolish man!

After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:

From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker, conveying a woman’s intent to a man or a man’s intent to a woman—whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit intimacy—even if it is only for a single meeting, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"
Regarding the method of matchmaking: it consists of conveying messages back and forth on behalf of others.
As for "women," there are fourteen kinds of protection:

protection by the father, protection by the mother, protection by both parents, protection by brothers, protection by sisters, protection by maternal uncles, protection by paternal aunts, protection by both maternal uncles and paternal aunts, protection by kinsmen, protection by clan, self-protection, protection by the Dharma, and protection by a husband.
Regarding "carrying a woman's message to a man": there is a woman who says to a bhikṣu, "Can you carry this message to that man?

Regarding "one who conveys a man's intent to a woman":
suppose there is a man who says to a bhikṣu, "Can you take this message and deliver it to that woman?

"If you have had illicit relations with me, or if you give me your daughter or your sister, I will become your son-in-law or your brother-in-law.
This is called a man expressing his intentions to a woman.
"Even unto the time of a single assembly" means meeting together at one time.
There are seven kinds of wives for a man:

one obtained by seeking, one obtained by water, one obtained by breaking [the law], one obtained by coming of her own accord, one obtained through food and clothing, one obtained through cohabitation, and one obtained for a moment.
"Obtained by solicitation" means that one obtains a woman as a wife by means of a small or large amount of wealth; this is called "obtained by solicitation.
"Obtained by water" means that if a person takes her hand and pours water over the palm to give her as a wife; this is called "obtained by water."

"Obtained by conquest" refers to when one conquers another country and seizes women to make them wives, or when one punishes those who have rebelled in one's own country and seizes them; this is called "obtained by conquest.

"Obtained through her own coming" refers to when a woman, out of single-minded attachment and longing for love, comes of her own accord to provide service and become a wife; this is called "obtained through her own coming."

"Obtained through food and clothing" means that if a woman is unable to support herself and comes to provide service as a wife for the sake of food and clothing, this is called "obtained through food and clothing.
"Obtained through the union of birth" means that if a woman says to a man:
"You have wealth and I have wealth; if we bear sons or daughters, they shall support us."
This is called "obtaining through union.
Regarding "obtaining momentarily": because it occurs together with a single act of sexual intercourse, it is called "obtained momentarily.

If he does not speak them, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
2. It is the same for two, three, or four eunuchs or those with both sexual organs.
It is the same for two, three, or four bhikṣus.
While a single bhikṣu was walking on a path, a woman, a man, a eunuch, and one with both sexual organs spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"If you can say to so-and-so:
'Give me your son or daughter,
or your sister,'" and the bhikṣu accepts this message and speaks it to that person, who then returns a reply, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one does not report it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to two, three, or four women, men, eunuchs, or those with both sexual organs.
It is likewise for two, three, or four bhikṣus.

There was a householder couple who were at odds and lived in discord. At that time, a certain bhikṣu frequently visited their home; one morning, he arrived, put on his robes, took his bowl, entered the house, and sat down. After exchanging greetings with them, he instructed the two of them to reconcile.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking:
"Have I not perhaps committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There are three kinds of wives:
first, those obtained through wealth; second, those obtained through water; and third, those obtained by defeating an enemy.
If these three kinds of wives enter into a formal contract, saying:”
"She is not my wife; according to the rites and laws, our ties have not yet been severed, so she still enters and leaves [the house].
He had not yet declared, "She is not my wife."
If one teaches such a reconciliation, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one makes a written contract saying:
"She is not my wife; our ritual relations have been severed and she shall no longer enter or leave [the household]," [it is likewise].
Yet, without declaring,
"She is not my wife," he gave instructions for them to unite; this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one were to draw up a contract stating:
"She is no longer my wife; our marital ties are severed and she shall no longer enter or leave [the household]," and then proclaim:
"She is not my wife.
To reconcile these two [statements] constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
There are three ways of receiving another's words, and six ways of responding to them.
There are three kinds: first, deportment; second, signs; and third, agreement.
Regarding deportment, a bhikṣu says to the host:
"If you see me coming and going, sitting and standing, you should know whether [the robe] has been obtained or not."

Regarding "signs": the bhikṣu says to the host, "If you see me with my hair freshly shaven, or wearing a coarse *saṃghāṭī*, or holding an earthen bowl, you should know whether [the gift] has been obtained or not."
Regarding the "agreement," a bhikṣu says to the host:
"If you see me speaking loudly in the midst of the assembly, or if you see me picking at my robes, you should know whether [the robe] has been obtained or not."
These are called the three ways of receiving speech.
As for the six kinds of responses: first, oral; second, written; third, by hand gesture; fourth, by deportment; fifth, by signs; sixth, by appointment.
If a bhikṣu receives a message with his mouth, speaks it to the other person with his mouth, and returns the report with his mouth, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If he returns the report by means of writing, hand gestures, bodily posture, signs, or a prearranged signal, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If a bhikṣu, having been commissioned as a messenger, conveys a message by speech or by writing, and returns with a written report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If he conveys a message by writing, hand gestures, deportment, signs, or a rendezvous, and returns with a verbal report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu, having been commissioned as a messenger, communicates by means of oral speech, hand gestures, or signs, and receives a reply by means of hand gestures, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If he receives a reply by means of hand gestures, bodily postures, signs, appointments, oral speech, or writing, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted a message to be conveyed by letter, conveys it by letter and receives a reply by letter, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If he receives a reply by letter, hand-sign, gesture, sign, appointment, or word of mouth, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted a message, conveys it by hand-sign, seal, or speech, and receives a reply by hand-sign or seal, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣu, having conveyed a message by hand-sign, deportment, physical appearance, appointment, speech, or writing, and receives a reply by hand-sign, deportment, physical appearance, appointment, speech, or writing, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu, having been sent on an errand, speaks to another person with his own mouth and receives a reply with his own mouth, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu, by means of a written message, a hand gesture, a sign of deportment, a physical mark, or a prearranged signal, conveys a message and receives a reply, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message by means of hand gestures, conveys each word of that message through hand gestures, and returns the report by hand gestures, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If he returns the report by means of hand gestures, bodily postures, signs, appointments, speech, or writing, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message by means of a hand gesture and conveys it orally to the other person, and the other person replies orally, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If he conveys it by means of a written document, a hand gesture, a physical gesture, or a sign, and the other person replies accordingly, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu, having received a message via hand gesture, speech, writing, or by returning a written reply, [conveys it], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If he returns the report by means of hand gesture, deportment, signs, appointment, or speech, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If one receives a message from a person of wealth and status, conveys it to a person of wealth and status, and returns a reply to that person of wealth and status, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one receives a message from a person of lowly station, conveys it to a person of wealth and status, and returns a reply to that person of lowly station, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu receives another’s words and understands their intent, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If he receives the intent but does not receive the words, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one merely accepts the words but does not understand their underlying meaning, there is no offense.
This concludes the five matters.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.
At that time, the Ārāmika bhikṣus were building for themselves a large, long, high, and wide dwelling that was old and difficult to repair.
The bhikṣus repeatedly requested various things from the householders, saying:

"We require bricks, tiles, hoes, mattocks, axes and chisels, cauldrons and jars, basins and bowls, water-pots and urns, hempen ropes, various kinds of grasses and wood, leather thongs, earth-sacks, laborers, ox-carts, and deer-carts."

Because of these circumstances, the bhikṣus were constantly in a state of agitation and took pleasure in engaging in administrative affairs, thereby neglecting their recitation of the sūtras, their seated meditation, and their practice of the Path.

At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, having reached the morning hour, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. When the lay devotees saw Mahākāśyapa approaching from afar, they immediately rebuked him, saying:

"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim to cultivate wholesome merit; yet now they beg for materials themselves to build wide, long, high, and great dwellings that are old and difficult to maintain. They repeatedly come to solicit all manner of necessities, and because of these causes and conditions, they obstruct and cause the abandonment of reciting the sūtras, seated meditation, and the practice of the Path."
"We have lost our benefit by making offerings to such people who are difficult to satisfy, difficult to nourish, and never know contentment.

Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was displeased in his heart. Having finished his almsround, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
In the early morning, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city of Ālavī to beg for food.
From afar, the householders saw me coming and rebuked me, saying:

"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim to cultivate virtuous merit, yet now they beg for materials themselves to build a house that is wide, long, high, and large—a structure so old it is difficult to maintain—which they constantly demand from us: bricks, tiles, hoes and spades, axes and chisels, cauldrons and basins, jars and pots, wood, grass, hides, and ropes, always making them perform labor."
For these reasons, it hinders and causes us to abandon our recitation of the sutras, our seated meditation, and our practice of the Path.
We suffer this loss by making offerings to such people who are difficult to satisfy and difficult to support, who have many desires and are never content.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will establish a limit for the bhikṣus.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Mahākāśyapa, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his words by remaining silent, paid his respects and departed, intentionally doing so to protect the feelings of the elder bhikṣus.
Not long after he had left, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the matter, asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied: “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha, using various causes and conditions, rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who begs for materials to build a wide, long, high, and large dwelling that is difficult to maintain due to its age, and who repeatedly solicits various things from laypeople to engage in such pleasurable works?"
"For these reasons, it hinders and causes one to abandon the recitation of sutras, seated meditation, and the practice of the Path.
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu himself begs for materials to build a dwelling, which has no owner and is for his own use, he must build it according to the prescribed measure.
The measure here is: twelve Sugata-spans in length and seven spans in internal width."
That bhikṣu should ask the other bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus shall point out a location that is free from difficulties and obstacles.

If a bhikṣu himself begs for materials to build a dwelling for his own use, without an owner, and does not consult the bhikṣus, yet builds it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Regarding "if one begs for it oneself," this means that a bhikṣu begs from various people and obtains either a hundred coins, fifty, or even a single coin.
Regarding "a dwelling," this refers to a heated room, a cool room, a hall, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-pillar house, or a multi-leveled residence.
"Without an owner" means that this dwelling has no donor—neither a man, a woman, a eunuch, nor one with dual sexual organs.
"For oneself" means not for the sake of the Sangha, but exclusively for one's own sake; thus it is called "for oneself."
Regarding the measurement, the Buddha said:
"Measured by my hand, it shall be twelve spans in length and seven spans in internal width.
Regarding the inquiry, one should ask the Saṃgha.
Regarding "indicating the location," the Sangha should indicate the place where it will be constructed.
Regarding "difficult locations," these include places containing snake dens, centipedes, millipedes, venomous insects, or even rat holes.
"Free from difficulties" means that within this area there are no snake dens, centipedes, millipedes, venomous insects, or even rat holes.

"Obstructed places" refers to ground within one fathom (vyāma) on all four sides of the dwelling where there is land belonging to a stūpa, or government land, or a layperson’s land, or the land of non-Buddhists, or the land of bhikṣuṇīs; or where there are large rocks, flowing water, ponds, large trees, or deep pits. Where there are such obstructions, the Saṃgha should not designate [the site].

Regarding "an unobstructed site": within a distance of one *vyāma* from the four sides of the proposed dwelling, there must be no land belonging to a stūpa, the government, a layperson, a non-Buddhist, or a bhikṣuṇī; nor should there be large rocks, flowing water, ponds, large trees, or deep pits. Such an unobstructed site is what the Saṃgha should designate.
That bhikṣu should request from the Saṃgha the designation of a place for construction.

As for the procedure for requesting the designation of a place for construction: when the Saṃgha is gathered in harmony with a single mind, that bhikṣu should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel on his right knee with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable sirs, please attend to me with a single mind."

I, bhikṣu [name], am personally begging for materials to build a dwelling for myself; as it is for my own use, without an owner, and in a place free from difficulties and obstructions, I now request the Saṃgha to designate the site for its construction.
“Out of compassion for me, may the Saṃgha show me a place where I may build.
He should beg in this manner a second and a third time.

Regarding this, the Saṃgha should deliberate whether it is appropriate to show him the site or not; if a bhikṣu claims there are no difficulties when, in fact, there are difficulties, the site must not be shown to him.
If one says,
"It is no hindrance," yet it actually is a hindrance, one should likewise not show it.
If one says,
"There is no difficulty and no hindrance," yet in reality there is indeed difficulty and a hindrance, one should not reveal it.
If one says,
"There is no difficulty," and indeed there is no difficulty, one should demonstrate it.
If one says,
"It does not matter," and indeed it does not matter, one should show it.
If one says,
"There is no difficulty and no hindrance," and indeed there is truly no difficulty and no hindrance, one should show it.
Regarding the "indication of the site": the Saṃgha should be united in one mind. A single bhikṣu shall announce within the assembly: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu [Name] wishes to beg for materials to build a dwelling for himself; it is to be built for his own use without an owner, in a place that is free from difficulties and obstructions. Therefore, he requests the Saṃgha to indicate the site for its construction."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, the Saṃgha shall designate a place for the bhikṣu so-and-so to work.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu named [Name] has personally solicited materials to build a dwelling for himself; as it is for his own use, without an owner, and he has requested the Saṃgha to designate a site that is free from difficulties and obstructions, he now asks the Saṃgha to show him the place where he may build.
Out of compassion for the Saṃgha, you should indicate the site where he intends to build.

Which elders among you consent to the Saṃgha indicating that such-and-such a person shall have a dwelling built by his own solicitation—on a site belonging to no one, for his own use, and free from obstacles or encroachments—let those who consent remain silent; if you do not consent, please speak.

“The Saṃgha has authorized monk so-and-so to beg for materials to build a dwelling for himself, as an ownerless structure, in a place free from difficulties and obstructions; it has been completed. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, [it is so].”

"Maintain this matter thus! Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu himself solicits materials to build a dwelling for his own use, without a patron, and it is built improperly, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of the prescribed measure, he commits an offense; if he does not inquire about the site, he commits an offense; if there is a dangerous site, he commits an offense; if there is an obstructed site, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of measure and on an uninquiring site, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of measure and on a dangerous site, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of measure and on an obstructed site, he commits an offense; if he does not inquire about a dangerous site, he commits an offense; if he does not inquire about an obstructed site, he commits an offense; if it is built on a dangerous and obstructed site, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of measure and on an uninquiring dangerous site, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of measure and on an uninquiring obstructed site, he commits an offense; if it is built in excess of measure and on an uninquiring dangerous and obstructed site, he commits an offense.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Build a dwelling for me," and having said this, he departs;

and later, when the dwelling has been completed, if it was built contrary to the Dharma, he commits an offense. This includes: if it was built in excess of the prescribed measure, if he did not inquire about the site, if it was on difficult ground, if it was on obstructed ground; or if it was built in excess of measure and on an uninquiring site, in excess of measure and on difficult ground, in excess of measure and on obstructed ground; or if he did not inquire about the difficulty of the site, did not inquire about the obstruction of the site, or if it was both difficult and obstructed; or if it was in excess of measure and on an uninquiring difficult site, in excess of measure and on an uninquiring obstructed site, or in excess of measure and on an uninquiring difficult-and-obstructed site.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Build a dwelling for me," and having said this,

he departs; later, before it is finished, he returns and it is completed, then that dwelling is an offense for being constructed improperly, an offense for exceeding the prescribed dimensions, an offense for not inquiring about the site, an offense for a difficult site, an offense for an obstructed site, and an offense for exceeding the dimensions without inquiry.

The offense of exceeding the limit in a difficult location; the offense of exceeding the limit in an obstructed location; the offense of not asking about a difficult location; the offense of not asking about an obstructed location; the offense of [building] in both a difficult and obstructed location; the offense of exceeding the limit and not asking about a difficult location; the offense of exceeding the limit and not asking about an obstructed location; and the offense of exceeding the limit and not asking about both a difficult and obstructed location.
If it is for the sake of the Buddha or the Sangha, there is no offense.
If one obtains a pre-existing hut, there is no offense.
The six matters are concluded.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 30;
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 4; the fourth part of the First Recitation, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The remainder of the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas and the two *aniyata* dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the Elder Channa had many acquaintances; because the king, the queen, the prince, the ministers, the generals, and the officials were all his acquaintances, he cut down a sacred tree belonging to others to construct a large dwelling.
This tree was well-known to many people and utilized by many.
The laypeople felt resentment and reproached them, saying:

"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim to cultivate wholesome merit; yet, because they are personally known to kings, queens, princes, ministers, generals, and officials, they have cut down this divine tree—well-known to many and utilized by many—to construct a large dwelling."
"We have suffered a loss, for we have made offerings to such people who are difficult to satisfy and difficult to support—men of great desire who are never content.
A certain bhikṣu, who was of few desires, easily satisfied, and practiced the dhūta austerities, heard this matter and was displeased; he went to the Buddha and related it in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Channa: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, because he is known to kings, queens, princes, ministers, generals, and their officials, cut down a divine tree well-known to many people to construct a large dwelling?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling for himself with a patron providing the materials, that bhikṣu should inquire of the other bhikṣus; the bhikṣus should then point out a location that is free from difficulties and obstructions.
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling for himself with a patron, and does not consult the other bhikṣus regarding difficult or obstructed sites, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

"Great dwellings" refers to heated rooms, cooled rooms, halls, towers, single-pillar houses, multi-storied buildings, and so forth, which can accommodate the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
"Having an owner" means that this dwelling has a donor-owner, whether male, female, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite.
"For oneself" means not for the sake of the Sangha, but specifically for one's own sake; thus it is called "for oneself."
Regarding the questioner, they should ask the Saṃgha.
Regarding the indication of the site, the Saṃgha should indicate the site.
As for difficult sites and obstructed sites, it is as explained above.

This bhikṣu should request from the Saṃgha the indication of the place for construction. As for the method of requesting: when the Saṃgha is united in one mind, this bhikṣu should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable elders, please attend to me with one mind!"
I, the bhikṣu [name], wish to construct a large dwelling for myself; it is to have an owner, to be built for my own sake, and to be in a location free from obstacles and hindrances.

Because I, the bhikṣu [name], am building this for myself with an owner in a location free from obstacles and hindrances, I request the Saṃgha to designate the site for me. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, designate the site for me.
A second and third time, he should likewise request.
In this matter, the Saṃgha should deliberate whether it is appropriate to show [the robe] or not.
If he says:
"There is no difficulty," yet in reality there is a difficulty; it is like saying,
"There is no hindrance."
If there is actually an obstacle or an impediment, yet one says,
"There is no difficulty and no impediment," or if there is actually a difficulty and an impediment, yet one says so, in all such cases one should not reveal it.
"It is indeed not an obstacle; it is truly not an obstacle. It is indeed not a difficulty; it is truly not a difficulty. Thus should it be shown.
As for the demonstration of the Dharma: the Saṃgha, being of one mind and in harmony, one bhikṣu shall proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu named [Name] wishes to construct a large dwelling; it has an owner, is for his own use, and is to be built in a location free from obstacles and hindrances.
For the purpose of constructing this large dwelling, this bhikṣu requests the Saṃgha to designate the site for its construction.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha designate a place for the bhikṣu so-and-so to work.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to construct a large dwelling; as it is for himself with a patron, and because it is in a location free from obstacles and hindrances, he requests the Saṃgha to designate the site for its construction.
Out of compassion for the Saṃgha, you should indicate the site for construction.

Which elders among you consent to this bhikṣu’s building of a large dwelling with an owner for his own use, on a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions—those who consent should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
Thus is the formal motion and the threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

"The Saṃgha has finished its instruction. The bhikṣu so-and-so has constructed a large dwelling; it has an owner, was built for himself, and is a place free from obstacles and hindrances. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld as such!"

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu, for himself and with a patron, constructs a large dwelling that exceeds the prescribed dimensions, he commits an offense; if he does not inquire about the site, he commits an offense; if there is a dangerous location, he commits an offense; if there is an obstructed location, he commits an offense; if he does not inquire whether there is a dangerous location, he commits an offense; if he does not inquire whether there is an obstructed location, he commits an offense; if the location is both dangerous and obstructed, he commits an offense; and if he does not inquire whether the location is both dangerous and obstructed, he commits an offense.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Build a dwelling for me," and having said this,

he departs; and later, when the dwelling has been completed, it is an offense because the dwelling was built in excess of the permitted measure, an offense because the site was not inspected, an offense because it was on difficult ground, an offense because it was on obstructed ground, an offense because the presence of difficult ground was not inquired about, an offense because the presence of obstructed ground was not inquired about, an offense because it was on both difficult and obstructed ground, and an offense because the presence of both difficult and obstructed ground was not inquired about.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Build a dwelling for me," and having said this,

he departs; and later, while the construction is not yet finished, he returns and it is completed— this constitutes an offense for building a dwelling that exceeds the prescribed dimensions, an offense for not inquiring about the site, an offense for a site with difficulties, an offense for a site with obstructions, an offense for not inquiring about a site with difficulties, an offense for not inquiring about a site with obstructions, an offense for a site with both difficulties and obstructions, and an offense for not inquiring about a site with both difficulties and obstructions.
If it was already relinquished beforehand, there is no offense.
The seven matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

Then the Elder Dabba Mallaputta, because he had accomplished five qualities, was appointed by the Saṃgha through *karmavācanā* as the distributor of bedding and furniture: he did not act out of favoritism, nor out of hatred, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion; he knew what had been obtained and what had not. This man distributed according to what was appropriate: those who were forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) with forest-dwellers, those who upheld the Vinaya with those who upheld the Vinaya, those who preached the Dharma with those who preached the Dharma, and those who recited the Sūtras with those who recited the Sūtras—in this way, he shared duties with those of like practice.
This person thought to himself:
"If I give in this manner, whether by speaking or remaining silent, I shall abide in peace and happiness.
When Dabba Mallaputta distributed the bedding, there was no need for lamps or candles; light issued from his left hand as he held and gave [the items] with his right.
There was a bhikṣu who intentionally waited for darkness to come, wishing to witness the supernatural power of Dhānañjāni.
At that time, the Buddha was still in Rājagṛha; because this son of a Malla, Dhānañjāni, had accomplished five qualities, the Saṅgha appointed him as the person to oversee the distribution of meals.
When this person assigns the order of the assembly, they do not act out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion; they know the proper sequence and do not overstep it.
At that time, the bhikṣu Mithila-bhūma was next in the assembly and received coarse food; thus, for a second and a third time, he received coarse food.
At that time, he thought to himself:
"I am deeply distressed.
It is because of this son of the Malla, Dabba Mallaputta, that I am troubled by such coarse food."
"How can I retaliate so as to cause him distress?
He further thought:
"I shall slander him with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense."
That bhikṣu had a sister who was a bhikṣuṇī named Mitrā.
At that time, this bhikṣuṇī went to the place where the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra did not speak with her, nor look at her, nor instruct her to sit.
This bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"What evil have I done, what offense have I committed, that this elder brother does not speak with me?"
Having had this thought, he said:
"What fault have I committed against my elder brother that he does not speak with me nor instruct me to sit?
The bhikṣu replied:
“The bhikṣu Dharmapāla has repeatedly troubled me with coarse food, even up to three times,
yet you did not assist me.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"What may I do to assist you?
the bhikṣu said, "Sister!"
When you reach the Buddha's presence, speak these words:
"World-Honored One!
How can such a dharma exist?"
"The monk Dharmapāla committed an act of sexual intercourse with me; this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "This is a pure and blameless bhikṣu; why do you slander him with a groundless *pārājika* charge?"
That bhikṣu said: "Sister!
Had you not uttered such a slander, I would not have spoken with you nor called upon you to sit."
Out of affection for her elder brother, that bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If I do not follow his word, my brother will neither speak with me nor teach me how to sit."
Having reflected thus, he spoke to his elder brother, saying:
"I shall follow your word. That bhikṣu said:
"Sister, wait a moment!
I shall go first to where the Buddha is; you may follow later, and I shall bear witness for you.
She then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side.
That bhikṣuṇī then followed from behind, prostrated with her head at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
how can such a thing as this exist?”
"The bhikṣu Dharmadatta committed the offense of pārājika by engaging in sexual misconduct with me.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra immediately said this:
"World-Honored One!"
"This is indeed so; I also knew this beforehand, just as this bhikṣuṇī has said.
At that time, Dabba was fanning the Buddha from behind. The Buddha looked back at Dabba and said, "What do you think of this?"
This bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyānī said these words before me:
"World-Honored One!
How can such a thing as this dharma exist?"
"The bhikṣu Dharmadatta committed the offense of pārājika by engaging in sexual misconduct with me.
The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra also spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"This is indeed so; I too knew this previously, as this bhikṣuṇī has stated.
The bhikṣu Dharmapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata knows me.
The Buddha said to Dabba:
“You must not speak such words now.”
"The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata knows me.
If you remember it, then say that you remember it;
if you do not remember it, say that you do not remember it.
“I do not recall it,
World-Honored One!
I do not recall it.”
"Sugata! At that time, the Elder Rāhula was also present in the assembly; he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"What was the Bhikṣu Dharmadatta saying?
This Bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā is now speaking these words before the Buddha:
'World-Honored One!'"
"How can such a thing exist?
The bhikṣu Dharmapāla committed the offense of pārājika by engaging in sexual misconduct with me.
The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra also spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
This is indeed so.
I also knew this beforehand.”
"Such is what the bhikṣuṇī has said.
The Buddha said to Rāhula, "I now ask you; answer according to your own understanding."
"What do you think?
If a bhikṣuṇī were to come and say to me:
'World-Honored One!'"
"How can such a thing exist?
Rāhula has committed an act of sexual intercourse with me, which constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
The bhikṣu Mettiyabhūma also spoke thus:
"This is indeed so.
I also knew this beforehand, just as the bhikṣuṇī has said.
What do you think?
Then Rāhula said, “The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata knows me.
The Buddha said:
“Fool! You are even able to say:
‘The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata knows me.’”
"How much more so for the bhikṣu Dharmapāla, who maintains pure precepts and has well-cultivated the holy life—why would he not say:
'The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata knows me'?"
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"You should record that the bhikṣu Dharmapāla did not remember [the offense], whereas the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyāṇī herself admitted to having committed the offense; therefore, the *nihsargika-karman* (act of reconciliation) should be granted to her."
After the Buddha had thus instructed them, he rose and entered his meditation chamber.
At that time, the bhikṣus questioned the bhikṣu Mettiyabhūmajaka with great urgency and precision, saying:
"How did you see it?"
Where did you see him?
What offense did you see him commit?
For what reason did you go to see him?
When those bhikṣus had questioned him thoroughly and urgently, he replied:
“The bhikṣu Dharmapāla is indeed pure in his holy life; out of desire, hatred, fear, and delusion, I spoke those words to slander him.”
The bhikṣus said:
"How can the bhikṣu Dabba, whose holy life is pure, speak such words of slander out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion?"
He replied:

"Because the bhikṣu Dhāvakya is endowed with five qualities, the Saṃgha of monks in Rājagṛha has appointed him as the distributor of meals; he does not act out of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion, and he proceeds in order without skipping anyone."
At that time, during my next meal, I encountered coarse food; thus I ate it two or three times.
My mind was then filled with distress, and I thought to myself:
"The bhikṣu Dharmapāla has intentionally troubled me with this coarse food; how shall I repay him?"
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"I shall slander him with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense.
For this reason, out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, I have uttered these words of slander.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu defame a bhikṣu of pure brahmacarya with groundless charges of a pārājika offense?"
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him with various reasons, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha emerged from his meditation chamber, assembled the community of bhikṣus, and although he already knew the facts, he deliberately asked the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu slander a bhikṣu of pure brahmacarya with groundless charges of a pārājika offense?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three kinds of people who will certainly fall into hell.
What are these three?"
If a person slanders a bhikṣu of pure brahmacarya with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, this first person falls into hell.
Furthermore, there may be another person with such a wrong view who says:
"There is no fault in sexual desire."
For this reason, such a person deeply indulges in negligence and self-indulgence regarding the five desires; this is the second person who falls into hell.

Furthermore, there is another person who violates the precepts and is foul with evil dharmas; though not a śramaṇa, he calls himself a śramaṇa, and though not practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), he claims to practice the holy life; this is the third person who falls into hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke in verse:
"Lying leads to falling into hell; To claim one has not done what one has done— These two cases are similar in nature, And both will later receive the retribution of their offenses."
When a person dwells in the world, an axe is born within their own mouth;
with this they cut themselves, all because of the evil words they utter.
To praise those who deserve rebuke, and to rebuke those who deserve praise;
Through verbal transgressions one incurs decline; because of decline, one does not experience happiness.
To suddenly lose wealth and profit is a decline that is slight;
but to harbor an evil mind toward a virtuous person is a decline more grievous than that.
In the Nirarbuda hell, there are one hundred thousand;
in the Arbuda hell, three thousand, six, and five.
This is because of an evil mind and evil speech, and because of the slighting and disparaging of the Noble Ones.
"When their lives end, they will inevitably fall into such hells.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, out of malice and anger, slanders a bhikṣu who is free from any pārājika offense by means of a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy that person's holy life."

If, at a later time, whether questioned or not questioned, that bhikṣu knows that the matter was groundless, yet speaks these words because he abides in malice and hatred, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"Malicious anger arises from attachment; when malicious anger increases and intensifies, one fails to see that person's virtues and seeks only their faults and evils.
A bhikṣu who has not committed a pārājika offense is one who has not transgressed any of the four pārājikas."
Regarding "without basis," there are three kinds of bases:
what has been seen, what has been heard, or what has been suspected.
As for "slandering," it means that although the bhikṣu has not committed an offense, one forcibly imposes a charge upon him.
"One who destroys the holy life" refers to one who seeks to destroy that bhikṣu’s dharma in order to cause him to fall away from it.
"Knowing this to be groundless" refers to four types of matters:
matters of dispute, matters of mutual assistance, matters of committing offenses, and matters of ordinary conduct.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu slanders a bhikṣu who is not pure by means of groundless *pārājika* charges, there are eleven types of offenses and five types of non-offenses.

Regarding the eleven types: these are cases where one has not seen, not heard, or not suspected [an offense], yet either falsely claims to have seen, falsely claims to have heard, or falsely claims to have suspected; or hears with faith, hears without faith, speaks of suspicion after hearing, speaks of seeing after suspecting, or speaks of hearing after suspecting. These are called the eleven types of offenses.

Regarding the five kinds of non-offenses: if one has seen, heard, or suspected a matter, and having seen it does not speak falsely, and having heard it does not speak falsely—these are called the five kinds of non-offenses.
As it is with an impure bhikṣu, so it is with one who merely appears to be pure.
If a bhikṣu slanders a pure bhikṣu with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, there are ten cases of transgression and four cases of non-transgression.

The ten kinds are: not seeing, not hearing, not doubting; or hearing what is false, doubting what is false; or hearing with faith, hearing without faith; having heard, saying one doubted; having doubted, saying one saw; and having doubted, saying one heard.

There are four cases where one does not commit an offense: if one suspects, if one hears, if one hears without error, or if one suspects without error—just as it is for a pure bhikṣu, so it is likewise for one who appears to be impure.
The eight matters concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā’s son, Dabba Mallaputra, was alone at the foot of a mountain standing in one place together with two bhikṣuṇīs. At that same time, the bhikṣu Mettiyabhūmajaka was also sitting on a rock at that mountain, mending his robes.
Seeing from afar the bhikṣu Dharmadatta standing alone in one place with two bhikṣuṇīs, he thought to himself:
"Previously, my groundless accusation against him using a *pārājika* offense failed; now there is a minor matter, and I shall use the *pārājika* offense to slander him."
Having had this thought, he then said to the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu Dharmapāla is a man who has committed sexual misconduct; I have seen this matter myself and do not follow the words of others."
At that time, the bhikṣus questioned him earnestly and urgently:
"How did you see it? Where did you see it?"
"What offense did you see?
On account of what matter did you go to see him?
After the bhikṣus had thus questioned him thoroughly and precisely, he said:
"I spoke out of favoritism, out of hatred, out of fear, or out of delusion; this Bhikkhu Dabba Mallaputta is indeed pure in his holy life.
The bhikkhus asked:
"How can you say this?"
"I spoke out of desire, hatred, fear, and delusion, saying that the bhikṣu Dharmapāla’s holy life is pure. He replied:
"While I was sitting on a rock in that mountain sewing my robes, I saw from afar the bhikṣu Dharmapāla standing alone in one place with two bhikṣuṇīs. Having seen this, I thought to myself:"

"Previously, when I slandered him with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, it was not established; now there is a minor matter, and I shall slander him by charging him with a *pārājika* offense.
For this reason, he said:
"I speak thus because of desire, hatred, fear, and delusion."
“The bhikṣu Dabba is indeed pure in himself.
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased and rebuked him, saying:
“How can one call himself a bhikṣu who, on account of a trivial matter, slanders a pure bhikṣu with a charge of a pārājika offense?”
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him with various reasons, they reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally asked the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, on account of a minor matter, slander a pure bhikṣu by means of a pārājika offense?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”

If a bhikṣu, out of malice and anger, takes a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a different category of offense and, by means of the *pārājika* rule, slanders a bhikṣu who is free of *pārājika*, desiring to destroy that person’s holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣu knows it to be a partial or similar matter, yet speaks these words out of malice and anger, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"Regarding 'distinct categories' (nānābhāga): these are the four pārājikas. Why is this?

Because if one commits even a single one of these four pārājika offenses, one is no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya, and has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu; therefore, they are called 'distinct categories.'"

Regarding those that do not constitute a separate category: the thirteen matters, the two indeterminate rules, the thirty rules on forfeiture and confession, the ninety rules on offenses involving forfeiture, the four rules on confession, the numerous rules of training, and the seven rules for settling disputes—these are called those that do not constitute a separate category.
Why is this? If one commits such an act, yet is still called a bhikṣu and a son of the Śākyas, and does not lose the dharma of a bhikṣu, this is called "non-differentiation."

"A fragmentary moment" (*khaṇḍa-muhūrta*): "fragmentary" (*khaṇḍa*) refers to matters occurring within the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*); this is called a "fragment," and it is also called a "fragmentary moment.
Regarding "dispute" (*vivāda*), there are four kinds of disputes:
disputes involving litigation and contention, disputes involving mutual assistance, disputes arising from the commission of offenses, and disputes concerning customary practices.

Regarding the offense herein: if, when the ground has been cleared, a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, and that bhikṣu, being certain within the context of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, forms the perception of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense—without having seen the other commit a pārajika offense—and says, "I saw him commit one," [he incurs an offense].
For each individual statement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

This applies likewise at sunrise, after sunrise, before midday, at midday, after midday, in the afternoon, at sunset, after sunset, during the first watch of the night, the first division of the first watch, the middle division of the first watch, the latter division of the first watch, the first division of the middle watch, the middle division of the middle watch, the latter division of the middle watch, the first division of the last watch, the middle division of the last watch, and the latter division of the last watch.
When a bhikṣu has finished his formal recitation, he sees another bhikṣu committing an offense:
whether it be a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta.
This bhikṣu, regarding a *duṣkṛta* offense as definitely a *duṣkṛta*, does not see another committing a *pārājika* offense, yet says:
"I saw him commit it."
For each individual statement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This applies even up to the final watch of the night.

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, at the conclusion of the day, sees another bhikṣu committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; he may regard it as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or regard it as a *pāyattika*, or regard it as a *pratideśanīya*, or regard it as a *duṣkṛta*.
This bhikṣu, while among the saṃgha, certainly conceived the notion that it was a duṣkṛta offense, yet without seeing another commit a pārājika offense, he said:
"I saw him commit one."
For each individual statement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This remains the case even until the final watch of the night.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu perceives another bhikṣu committing an offense—whether it be a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*—that person may regard it as a *duṣkṛta*, or regard it as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or regard it as a *pāyattika*, or regard it as a *pratideśanīya*.
This person, regarding a *duṣkṛta* offense, definitely conceives the notion that it is a *pratideśanīya*; not seeing another commit a *pārājika*, they say:
"I saw him commit one."
For each individual statement, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; this remains the case even until the final watch of the night.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, at the conclusion of the day, saw another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and felt doubt therein: "Is this a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?"
Is it not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
Later, having removed his doubt and being certain that it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, yet not having seen another commit a *pārājika*, he says:
"I saw him commit one."
For each individual statement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This applies even up to the final watch of the night.

Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu, at the conclusion of the day, sees another bhikṣu commit an offense—whether it be a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*—and therein conceives a doubt: "Is this a *duṣkṛta*?"
Is it not a *duṣkṛta*?
Later, having removed his doubt, while within a *duṣkṛta* offense he definitely forms the perception that it is a *duṣkṛta*, yet seeing no one else commit a *pārājika*, he says:
"I saw him commit it."
For each individual statement, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; this remains the case even until the final watch of the night.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu, at the conclusion of the day, sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceives a doubt therein: "Is this offense a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?"
Is it a pāyattika? Is it a saṃghāvaśeṣa?
Or is it a pratideśanīya?
Is it a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *duṣkṛta*?
Later, having removed his doubt, while within the category of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, he definitively forms the perception that it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, yet not seeing another commit a *pārājika*, he says:
"If I see it, I am guilty"—
in each such utterance, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This remains the same even until the final portion of the last watch of the night.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, at the time of the final watch of the night, sees another commit an offense—whether it be a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta.
If one harbors doubt regarding this matter,
is the offense a *duṣkṛta* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
It is a *duṣkṛta*.
Is it a pāyattika? Is it a duṣkṛta?
Or is it a pratideśanīya?
Later, having removed his doubts, while among the *duṣkṛta* offenses he definitely formed the perception that it was a *duṣkṛta*, yet without seeing another commit a *pārājika*, he said:
"I saw him commit one."
For each individual statement, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This remains the case even until the final watch of the night.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, at dawn, saw another commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and felt doubt therein: "Is this a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?"
Is this a pāyattika? Is it a pratideśanīya?
Or is it a duṣkṛta?

Later, having removed his doubt, he formed the definite perception that it was a *duṣkṛta* offense within the category of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; yet, not having seen another commit a *pārājika* offense, he said:
"I saw him commit one."
For each individual word [spoken], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This remains the case even until the final watch of the night.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, at the time of dawn, sees another bhikṣu commit an offense—whether it be a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*.
In this matter, a doubt arises: is this offense a *duṣkṛta*,
a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*?
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya* offense:
later, having removed his doubt, while among the *duṣkṛta* offenses he definitely conceives the notion that it is a *pāṭidesanīya*, and without seeing another commit a *pārājika*, he says:
"I saw him commit one."
In each and every instance of speaking thus, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This remains the case even until the final watch of the night.
The nine matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta sought to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and undertook the acts of schism. Possessing a mind of envy, he devised a stratagem and thought:
"I alone am unable to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroy his turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
Devadatta had four companions:
the first was named Kokālika, the second Khaṇḍadravya, the third Kāḷudāyin, and the fourth Samudradatta.
Having approached these four men, Devadatta spoke to them as follows:
"You should join me in breaking the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroying his turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
Then those four men said to Devadatta:

"The disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama possess great wisdom and great supernormal powers; they have attained the divine eye and the knowledge of others' thoughts. These people know and see that we wish to break the harmony of the Saṃgha and destroy the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. How then could we possibly break the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroy the turning of the Wheel of Dharma?"

Devadatta said to the four men: "The young disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama have recently entered his Dharma and have not long been ordained. We shall go to them and entice them with five practices, saying to the bhikṣus:

'For as long as life lasts, you should accept and wear the patched robe; for as long as life lasts, you should accept the practice of begging for food; for as long as life lasts, you should accept the practice of eating only one meal a day; for as long as life lasts, you should accept the practice of sitting in the open air; for as long as life lasts, you should accept the practice of abstaining from meat.'"
"If a bhikṣu receives these five dharmas, he will swiftly attain nirvāṇa.
If there are elder or senior bhikṣus who are learned and well-informed, who have long practiced the holy life, and who have tasted the flavor of the Buddha-dharma, you should say to them:
"The Buddha is now aged and decrepit; in his final years, he delights in solitude and enjoys the bliss of the present dharma."
"Whatever you require, I shall provide for you.
By this means, we shall be able to break the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroy his turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
The four bhikṣus said,
"So be it, Devadatta," and they accepted Devadatta’s words.
At a later time, Devadatta went to where the young bhikṣus were and enticed them with five practices, saying to the bhikṣus:

"For as long as life lasts, you shall accept and wear the patched robe; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of begging for food; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of eating only one meal a day; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of sitting in the open air; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of abstaining from meat."
"If you practice these five dharmas, you will swiftly attain nirvana.
He then spoke again to the elder bhikṣus and senior monks:
"The Buddha is now aged and his years are in decline; he delights in solitude and enjoys the bliss of the present dharma. Whatever you require, I shall provide for you."

At that time, Devadatta taught what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma; he taught what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya, and what is the Vinaya as not the Vinaya; he taught what is not an offense as an offense, and what is an offense as not an offense; he taught what is light as heavy, and what is heavy as light; he taught what involves a remainder as being without remainder, and what is without remainder as involving a remainder; he taught what is a customary practice as not a customary practice, and what is not a customary practice as a customary practice; he taught what is not a teaching as a teaching, and what is a teaching as not a teaching.

At that time, the bhikṣus saw that Devadatta intended to split the harmonious Saṃgha and destroy the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Having seen this, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. Once seated, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
This Devadatta wishes to break the harmony of the Saṃgha and maintains the causes and conditions for such schism.
This person speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaks Dharma as not Dharma, speaks what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, and speaks Vinaya as not Vinaya.

To declare what is an offense as not an offense, or what is not an offense as an offense; to declare what is light as heavy, or what is heavy as light; to declare what involves a remainder (sāvaśeṣa) as having no remainder, or what has no remainder as involving a remainder; to declare what is a customary practice (dharmatā) as not a customary practice, or what is not a customary practice as a customary practice; and to declare what is a formal instruction (śikṣāpada) as not an instruction, or what is not an instruction as an instruction.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus,
"You should reprove Devadatta and cause him to abandon these matters that constitute the causes and conditions for schism in the Saṃgha.
Having received the Buddha’s words, those bhikṣus went to where Devadatta was and said to him:
"Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not uphold matters that lead to a schism in the Saṃgha. You should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha.

When the Saṃgha is in harmony, they dwell in joy and without dispute, being of one mind and one training like water and milk mixed together, and thus attain a state of peaceful dwelling. You should abandon these causes and conditions for a schism."
At that time, Devadatta did not relinquish this matter.
Then Devadatta’s four companions rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"You must not speak against this matter concerning Devadatta."

Why is this? Because this person preaches the Dharma and the Vinaya; all that this person says is exactly what we desire. This person knows how to preach and does not preach ignorantly; all that this person says is what we find pleasing and can accept with patience.
In this manner, although the bhikṣus instructed Devadatta thus a second and a third time, they were unable to make him abandon his evil and heterodox views.
They then rose from their seats, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
Having sat down, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We have already exhorted Devadatta, yet he does not abandon his evil and heterodox views."
Four of his fellow partisans spoke again as follows:
"Do not speak of this matter concerning Devadatta. Why is that?
"This person preaches the Dharma and preaches the Vinaya; all that this person says is what we desire.
This person speaks with knowledge, not without knowledge; all that this person says is what we find pleasing and can endure."
After the monks had admonished him twice and thrice, he did not relinquish this matter.
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:

"If this foolish man Devadatta and his four associates should succeed in breaking my harmonious Saṃgha and destroying the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, I shall personally admonish Devadatta and cause him to relinquish this matter."
After the Buddha had formed this thought, he immediately exhorted Devadatta himself:
"Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not accept or uphold matters that serve as the causes and conditions for a schism."

"You should live in harmony with the Saṅgha; for when the Saṅgha is in harmony, it dwells in joy and without dispute, being of one mind and one training like milk mixed with water, and thus attains a state of peaceful dwelling."

Do not speak what is not Dharma as Dharma, or Dharma as what is not Dharma; speak what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, or Vinaya as what is not Vinaya; speak what is not an offense as an offense, or an offense as what is not an offense; speak what is light as heavy, or what is heavy as light; speak what has a remainder as having no remainder, or what has no remainder as having a remainder; speak what is a regularly used rule as not a regularly used rule, or what is not a regularly used rule as a regularly used rule; speak what is not a teaching as a teaching, or a teaching as what is not a teaching.
"You must abandon this matter that causes a schism in the Saṃgha.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s oral instruction, Devadatta temporarily abandoned this matter.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked him with various reasons and circumstances:
“What is it to call a bhikṣu one who seeks to cause a schism in the Saṃgha and upholds the matters that lead to a schism?
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha and diligently seeks out means to uphold the matters that cause such a schism, the other bhikṣus should reprimand him thus:
'Do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha; do not seek out means to uphold the matters that cause a schism; you should instead remain in harmony with the Saṃgha.'"

The Saṃgha is in harmony, joyful and without dispute; with one mind and one training, they are like milk and water mixed together, dwelling in peace and happiness. You should abandon this attempt to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus instruct them in this manner, if they do not relinquish that matter, they should be instructed up to three times to relinquish it.
If they relinquish it after being instructed up to three times, it is well; if they do not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Regarding the offenses therein: among these matters, there are fourteen kinds of offenses for a bhikṣu:
to speak what is not Dharma as Dharma is a sthūlātyaya;
to speak what is Dharma as not Dharma is a sthūlātyaya.
To declare what is not the Vinaya to be the Vinaya is a sthūlātyaya;
to declare what is the Vinaya to be not the Vinaya is a sthūlātyaya;
to declare what is not an offense to be an offense is a sthūlātyaya.
To declare what is an offense to be no offense is a sthūlātyaya;
to declare what is light to be heavy is a sthūlātyaya;
to declare what is heavy to be light is a sthūlātyaya.
To say there is a remainder when there is no remainder is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To say there is no remainder when there is a remainder is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak of what is a standard rule as if it were not a standard rule is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To say that what is a dharma not of the permanent nature is a dharma of the permanent nature is a thullaccaya.
To say that what is not an instruction is an instruction is a thullaccaya.
To say that what is an instruction is not an instruction is a thullaccaya.
First, one should admonish them with gentle words; if they then relinquish [the offense], they must perform the confession and purification for fourteen *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If they do not relinquish it, one should carry out the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish them.
