If she does not bring the robe back, does not go to the place where the robe is, and does not accept another robe, then at the conclusion of the designated time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Regarding clansmen, there is both a common boundary and a distinct boundary; herein, the distinct boundaries for clansmen refer to the gatehouse, the dining hall, the courtyard, the latrine, and the water source.

If a bhikṣu is staying with one clan and his robe-cloth is with another clan, the bhikṣu should have the robe-cloth brought to him; or he should go to where the robe-cloth is; or he should accept another robe-cloth.

If he does not have the robe-cloth brought to him, nor goes to where the robe-cloth is, nor accepts another robe-cloth, then when the time for the end of the [robe] season arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

A household has both a common boundary and distinct boundaries; among these, the distinct boundaries refer to the entrance, the dining area, the central courtyard, the latrine, and the place for drawing water.
If a bhikṣu is staying at one house while his robe is at another house, he should have the robe brought to him, or go to where the robe is, or receive another robe [as a substitute].
If he does not have the robe brought, nor goes to where the robe is, nor receives another robe, then when the time for the end of the day arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

In a multi-storied building, there are both a single boundary and distinct boundaries; among these, the "middle boundary" refers to the middle and lower stories being the boundary of the upper story, because they enter through the same door.
The middle layer and the upper layer constitute the lower layer’s boundary, because they enter through a single opening.
The lower layer constitutes the middle layer’s boundary, because they enter through a single opening.
If a bhikṣu is in one layer and his robe is in another layer, the bhikṣu must take the robe and come [to him], or go to where the robe is, or receive another robe.
If one does not bring the robe back, does not go to the place where the robe is, and does not accept another robe, then at the conclusion of the designated time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If the multi-storied building belongs to a single person, there is no offense.

In the dwellings of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika), there are both common boundaries (sīmā) and distinct boundaries. Those called Āśvini-kaṇḍin, the old disciples, the Brahmins, and so forth—excluding the five groups of the Buddha’s followers—are all termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika). As for other remaining renunciants, they are likewise termed non-Buddhists.
Regarding "the dwellings of non-Buddhists," this refers to gatehouses, dining halls, courtyards, latrines, and water-sheds.

If a bhikṣu is staying in one dwelling of non-Buddhists while his robe is in another dwelling of non-Buddhists, he should have the robe brought to him; or he should go to where the robe is; or he should accept another robe [in exchange].
If he does not have the robe brought to him, nor goes to where the robe is, nor accepts another robe, then when the time for the end of the day arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If various non-Buddhists share the same views and doctrines, there is no offense.

Regarding those who travel by means of wheels, there is one boundary and distinct boundaries. Those who travel by wheel include performers, singers, dancers, acrobats, wrestlers, boxers, and jesters; they carry their goods on large wheels and their wives and children on small wheels, traveling through various countries and making camp as they go.
Regarding the "intermediate boundary" herein: it refers to the gate area, the dining area, the restroom area, and the water-drawing area.
If a bhikṣu is at one house while his robe is at another house, he should have the robe brought to him; or he should go to where the robe is; or he should accept another robe [in exchange].
If he does not have the robe brought to him, nor go to where the robe is, nor accept another robe, then when the time for the end of the day arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If those who travel by wheel belong to the same person, there is no offense.

Within the site, there are both a single boundary and distinct boundaries; among these, the "boundaries" refer to the gate area, the dining area, the central courtyard, the latrine area, and the water-drawing area.

If a bhikṣu is in one *kṣetra* (monastic precinct) and his robe is in another *kṣetra*, he should have the robe brought to him; or he should go to where the robe is; or he should accept another robe [in exchange].

If he does not have the robe brought to him, nor goes to where the robe is, nor accepts another robe, then when the time for the end of the [rainy season] retreat arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

In a single monastery complex, there may be one boundary (*sīmā*) and distinct boundaries; herein, "boundary" refers to the gate area, the dining area, the central courtyard, the latrine area, and the water-drawing area.
If a bhikṣu is in one monastery complex and his robe is in another, he must either bring the robe back, go to where the robe is, or take up another robe.
If he does not bring the robe back, does not go to where the robe is, and does not take up another robe, then at the conclusion of the night, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

A garden has both a common boundary and distinct boundaries; among these, the "boundaries" refer to the gate area, the dining area, the central courtyard, the latrine area, and the water-drawing area.
If a bhikṣu is in one garden while his robe is in another garden, he should have the robe brought to him, or go to where the robe is, or receive another robe [as a substitute].
If he does not have the robe brought to him, nor go to where the robe is, nor receive another robe, then when the time for the end of the day arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

A garden residence may have a single boundary or distinct boundaries. Within it, the "boundaries" refer to the gate area, the dining area, the central courtyard, the latrine area, and the water-drawing area.
If a bhikṣu is staying in one garden residence while his robe is in another, he must either bring the robe back, go to the location of the robe, or accept another robe.
If he does not bring the robe back, does not go to the location of the robe, and does not accept another robe, then at the end of the day, he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

When traveling by carriage, there is one boundary and there are distinct boundaries; therein, the "boundary of the preceding carriage" refers to the area reached by the staff of the carriage heading toward the center.
The "boundary of the central carriage" refers to the area reached by the staffs of both the preceding and the following carriages.
Regarding the "subsequent carriage boundary" (*paścāt-śakaṭa-sīmā*): this refers to the area reached by the carriage's pole as it moves toward the center.
If a bhikṣu is within one carriage boundary and his robe is within another carriage boundary, he must either bring the robe back to him, go to where the robe is, or accept another robe.
If he does not bring the robe back, does not go to where the robe is, and does not accept another robe, then at the conclusion of the day, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

A single boat has both its own boundary and distinct boundaries; therein, the boundary of the single boat refers to the place where the boat is moored—whether it be a pillar, a stake, or a wooden platform.
If a bhikṣu is on one boat and his robe is on another boat, he should have the robe brought to him, or go to where the robe is, or accept another robe;
if he does not have the robe brought to him, nor go to where the robe is, nor accept another robe, then at the time the ground is reached, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same applies to the boundaries of boats.

Regarding trees, there are both single boundaries and distinct boundaries; among these, a tree boundary that is not contiguous refers to the area shaded by its shadow at midday, or the area where falling rain does not reach the branches and leaves.
If a bhikṣu is under one tree while his robe is under another tree, he should have the robe brought to him, or go to where the robe is, or accept another robe;
if he does not have the robe brought, nor go to where it is, nor accept another robe, then at the time the ground becomes dark, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Regarding "trees with contiguous boundaries": if the branches and leaves of these trees touch one another even for the distance of a single *krośa*, then there is no offense when one's clothing reaches the ground within that space.

Regarding the robe-corners within a distance of forty-nine *vyāma*: if a bhikṣu carries his robe while traveling on the road with his *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*, whether he is in front or behind, he must not be separated from it within the range of forty-nine *vyāma*.
If he exceeds forty-nine *vyāma* and reaches the end of the journey, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
There were certain bhikṣus who placed their robes and bowls in one spot and lay down on all four sides of the robes.
If one of these bhikṣus rose and departed, having moved beyond the point where he could return to retrieve them by the time the ground became visible, it was a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu lies down within two boundaries and his robe leaves his body—even by half an inch—and falls into the other boundary, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If even one corner of the robe remains upon his body, there is no offense.
The two matters concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus obtained out-of-season robes and kept them, thinking:
"These are unsuitable for keeping; if we obtain similar ones, we shall make them into finished robes."
If these six groups of bhikṣus first obtain a blue garment and later obtain a yellow garment, they think:

"These are not similar; I shall set them aside. If they first obtain a yellow garment and later obtain a red garment, a white garment, a hemp garment, a wild-hemp garment, a kṣauma garment, a kāśika garment, a kośeya garment, a śāṇa garment, a kambala garment, or a karpāsa garment, [they think the same].
Having obtained them, he thought:
"I will not keep these dissimilar ones; if I obtain similar ones, I shall make them into robes.

Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, his heart was displeased, and for various reasons he rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What is meant by a bhikṣu who, having obtained an out-of-season robe, keeps it because it is not of a matching type; however, if he obtains one that is of a matching type, he should have it made into a finished robe?"
If one first obtains a blue garment and later obtains a yellow garment, one should think:
"They are dissimilar; I shall set them aside.

If one first obtains a yellow garment and later obtains a red garment, a white garment, a linen garment, a wild-hemp garment, a *kṣauma* garment, a *kauśeya* garment, a *kācilinda* garment, a *kambala* garment, or a cotton garment...
Having obtained it, he thought:
"It is not suitable to keep this; if I obtain something similar, I shall make a robe.
After the bhikṣus had thus rebuked him for various reasons, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [what had occurred], he intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One!
The Buddha then rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:

"What is meant by a bhikṣu who, having obtained an out-of-season robe, keeps it because it is not of a matching kind; yet, if he obtains one that is of a matching kind, he should have it made into a finished robe?"
If one first obtains a blue garment and later obtains a yellow garment, one should think:

"These are dissimilar; I shall set them aside. If one first obtains a yellow garment and later obtains a red garment, a white garment, a hemp garment, a wild-hemp garment, a kusa-grass garment, a śāṇa-garment, a kṣauma-garment, a kārpāsa-garment, a cotton-garment, or a woolen garment, [one should think the same].
Having obtained it, he thought:
"I will not keep this as it is; if I obtain something similar, I shall make a robe.
After the Buddha had thus rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu has finished his robe-making and has already relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, and he obtains an out-of-season robe, if the bhikṣu desires it, he may take it with his own hand and quickly have it made into a robe; if it is sufficient, that is well.'"
If it is insufficient, one may set aside this robe for up to one month in the hope of obtaining further cloth to make it complete.
Should one set it aside beyond this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Non-seasonal" refers to any remaining robes other than those for a separate dwelling, those offered by a household, and those for the rainy season retreat; these are called non-seasonal robes.
"Taking them with one's own hand and making them quickly for formal acceptance" means that these robes are made either as a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, or an *antarvāsaka*.
Regarding "further hoping to obtain the robe," this bhikṣu thinks:

"Whether my mother gives it to me, or my father, or my brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, or my former second wife; whether there is a *pañcavārṣika* assembly (a five-year festival), or a *ṣaḍvārṣika* assembly (a six-year festival), or a bi-monthly assembly, or an entry-into-the-household assembly—I shall be able to assemble this robe within this one month."
Regarding "making what is insufficient sufficient": if one lacks a saṃghāṭī, or lacks an uttarāsaṅga, or lacks an antarvāsaka, one should make them complete.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, that bhikṣu, from the day he acquires the [additional] robe, should immediately form this thought:
"That which I have hoped for over these ten days will certainly not be obtained."
"This robe must be made into a garment within ten days; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified (*pariśuddhi*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigraha*).

If one does not make it into a garment, nor give it to another, nor purify it, nor accept it as one's own possession, by the time the eleventh day ends, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has obtained an incomplete robe, while waiting in the hope of obtaining more, reaches the second day and thinks:
"What I have hoped for over these nine days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a garment on the ninth day, or given away, or purified, or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a garment, not given away, not purified, and not formally accepted, by the time the ground is cleared on the eleventh day, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining another, he reaches the third day and thinks:
"What I have been hoping for since the eighth day will certainly not be obtained."
Within eight days, this robe must be made into a garment, or given away, or purified, or formally accepted.
If it is not made into a garment, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, and one reaches the end of the eleventh day at the conclusion of the session, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has obtained an incomplete robe, while waiting in hope of obtaining another, reaches the fourth day and thinks:
"That which I have hoped for during these seven days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a garment within seven days; otherwise, it must be given to another, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.
If one does not make it into a garment, nor give it away, nor purify it, nor accept it as one's own possession, by the time the eleventh day ends, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu receives an incomplete robe and, while waiting for more cloth to be obtained, reaches the fifth day and thinks:
"What I expect to obtain on the sixth day will certainly not be possible."
This robe must be made into a garment within six days; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*).
If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it away, does not purify it, and does not accept it, by the time the end of the eleventh day arrives, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while keeping it with the hope of obtaining more, reaches the sixth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not obtain what I have been hoping for during these five days."
This robe-cloth must be made into a robe within five days, or given away, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a robe, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the ground is cleared on the eleventh day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for the chance to obtain another, reaches the seventh day and thinks:
"What I have been hoping for during these four days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a garment within four days; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted (*dhārayitavya*).
If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it to another, does not purify it, and does not accept it, by the time the eleventh day ends, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu has obtained an incomplete robe and, while waiting for more cloth to be provided, reaches the eighth day and thinks:
"What I have been hoping for these three days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a garment within three days, or given away, or purified, or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a garment, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the ground is cleared on the eleventh day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for further robes to be obtained, reaches the ninth day and thinks:
"What I have been hoping for during these two days will certainly not be obtained."
"These robes should be made into a garment within two days; otherwise, they must be given to another, rendered pure (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make them into a garment, does not give them away, does not render them pure, and does not accept them as one's own possession, then by the time the day ends on the eleventh day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, he reaches the tenth day and reflects:
"That which I hoped for on the first day I shall certainly not obtain."
"This robe must be made into a garment on the same day; otherwise, it must be given away, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it away, does not purify it, and does not accept it, then by the time the ground is cleared on the eleventh day, there is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for the chance to obtain another, reaches the eleventh day and thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have been hoping for during these eleven days."
"This robe must be made into a garment on the eleventh day; otherwise, it must be given to another, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make it into a garment, nor give it to another, nor purify it, nor accept it as one's own possession, and it reaches the twelfth day at the end of the period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for further robes to be obtained, reaches the twelfth day and thinks:
"What I have been hoping for during these twelve days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a finished garment by the twelfth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, or rendered pure (*śuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If one does not make it into a garment, nor give it to another, nor render it pure, nor accept it as one's own possession, and it reaches the thirteenth day at the end of the period, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, because he hopes to obtain another, keeps it until the thirteenth day, at which point he thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have hoped for during these thirteen days."
On the thirteenth day, this robe-cloth must be made into a robe, or given to another, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a robe, nor given to another, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the ground is cleared on the fourteenth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for more cloth to be obtained, reaches the fourteenth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not obtain what I have been hoping for by this fourteenth day."
This robe must be made into a garment by the fourteenth day; otherwise, it must be given away, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it away, does not purify it, and does not accept it as one's own possession, then upon reaching the fifteenth day at the end of the period, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, hoping to obtain another, keeps it until the fifteenth day, at which time he thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I was hoping for on this fifteenth day."
"This robe must be made into a formal robe within fifteen days; it must either be given to another, purified (*viśuddhi*), or formally accepted as one's own.

If one does not make it into a formal robe, does not give it to another, does not purify it, and does not accept it as one's own, then upon the completion of the sixteenth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for the chance to obtain another, reaches the sixteenth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have been hoping for on this sixteenth day."
This robe must be made into a formal robe on the sixteenth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If one does not make it into a robe, nor give it to another, nor purify it, nor accept it as one's own possession, by the time the ground is cleared on the seventeenth day, it constitutes an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for the hope of obtaining another, reaches the seventeenth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have been hoping for during these seventeen days."
This robe must be made into a garment on the seventeenth day, or given to another, or purified, or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a garment, not given to another, not purified, and not formally accepted, then by the time the eighteenth day has ended, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more; when the eighteenth day arrives, he thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have hoped for during these eighteen days."
This robe must be made into a garment on the eighteenth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, or rendered pure (*viśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make it into a garment, nor give it to another, nor render it pure, nor accept it as one's own possession, by the time the ground is cleared on the nineteenth day, there is an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for further robes to be obtained, reaches the nineteenth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not obtain what I have been hoping for during these nineteen days."
This robe must be made into a finished garment on the nineteenth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If it is not made into a garment, not given to another, not purified, and not formally accepted, then upon reaching the twentieth day at the end of the period, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for the chance to obtain another, reaches the twentieth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have been hoping for during these twenty days."
Within twenty days, this robe must be made into a garment, or given away, or purified, or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a garment, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the twenty-first day has ended, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for the hope of obtaining more cloth, reaches the twenty-first day and thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have hoped for during these twenty-one days."
This robe must be made into a garment on the twenty-first day; otherwise, it must be given away, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it away, does not purify it, and does not accept it as one's own possession, by the time the twenty-second day ends, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting in hope of obtaining another, reaches the twenty-second day and thinks:
"I will certainly not be able to obtain what I have been hoping for during these twenty-two days."
This robe must be made into a garment on the twenty-second day, or given away, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a garment, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the ground is cleared on the twenty-third day, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu has obtained an incomplete robe and, while waiting for further robes, reaches the twenty-third day and thinks:
"I shall certainly not obtain what I have been hoping for during these twenty-three days."
This robe-cloth must be made into a robe on the twenty-third day, or given away, or purified, or formally accepted as one's own.

If it is not made into a robe, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted as one's own, by the time the ground is cleared on the twenty-fourth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for further robes to be obtained, reaches the twenty-fourth day and thinks:
"I will certainly not obtain what I have been hoping for during these twenty-four days."
This robe must be made into a garment on the twenty-fourth day; otherwise, it must be given away, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigraha*).

"This robe must be made into a formal robe by the twenty-fourth day; it must either be given to another, rendered pure (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If it is not made into a robe, not given to another, not rendered pure, and not formally accepted, then upon reaching the twenty-fifth day at the end of the period, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more. When the twenty-fifth day arrives, he thinks:
"I will certainly not obtain what I have been hoping for during these six days."
"This robe must be made into a garment on the twenty-fifth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified, or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it to another, does not purify it, and does not accept it as one's own possession, then when the twenty-sixth day arrives at the end of the night, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more; when the twenty-sixth day arrives, he thinks:
"What I have hoped for over these five days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a finished garment on the twenty-sixth day, or given away, or purified (*viśuddhi*), or formally accepted as one's own possession.

If it is not made into a garment, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the twenty-seventh day has ended, it constitutes an offense of forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, intending to wait for further robes to be obtained, reaches the twenty-seventh day and thinks:
"What I have been hoping for during these four days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a garment within twenty-seven days; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it to another, does not purify it, and does not accept it as one's own possession, then upon the arrival of the twenty-eighth day at the end of the period, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while keeping it with the hope of obtaining more, reaches the twenty-eighth day and thinks:
"That which I have hoped for during these three days will certainly not be obtained."

This robe must be made into a finished garment on the twenty-eighth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, or rendered pure (*śuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own possession (*parigraha*).

If one does not make it into a garment, nor give it away, nor render it pure, nor accept it as one's own possession, by the time the ground is cleared on the twenty-ninth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and, while waiting for further robes, reaches the twenty-ninth day and thinks:
"The robes I have expected for two days will certainly not be obtained."
This robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-ninth day; otherwise, it must be given to another, purified (*pariṣkāra*), or formally accepted as personal property (*parigṛhīta*).

If one does not make it into a garment, does not give it to another, does not purify it, and does not accept it as personal property, then upon reaching the thirtieth day at the conclusion of the season, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, reaching the thirtieth day, he thinks:
"What I have hoped for during this one day I will certainly not obtain."
This robe must be made into a formal robe within thirty days, or given away, or purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own.
If it is not made into a robe, nor given away, nor purified, nor formally accepted, by the time the ground is cleared on the thirty-first day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and keeps it with the hope of obtaining more, he does not cease his expectation on the day he actually receives the robe, even if he does not obtain what he hoped for; nor does he cease his expectation when something other than what he hoped for is offered. If he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, that specific hope may cease, yet he may still obtain something else. Such a robe must be made into a finished garment within ten days; if it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it may be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the second day he has not obtained what he hoped for, yet he neither abandons that hope nor is granted anything other than what he hoped for, and he continues to strive diligently for what he hopes for; then if that hope is abandoned and he instead obtains something other than what he hoped for, this robe should be made into a garment within nine days. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it should be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and until the ninth day he does not obtain what he hopes for, yet his expectation has not ceased—neither having been disappointed nor having received what was promised—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his expectation ceases and he instead obtains what he did not expect, this robe should be made into a garment within two days; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it should be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and keeps it with the hope of obtaining more, and until the tenth day he has not obtained what he hoped for—neither having abandoned his hope nor having been promised what was not yet expected—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is finally abandoned and he instead obtains what was not expected, this robe must be made into a finished garment within ten days; if it is sufficient, that is well, but if it is insufficient, it may be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, yet by the eleventh day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor having received anything unexpected—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is abandoned but he instead obtains something unexpected, this robe must be made into a finished garment by the eleventh day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twelfth day he has not obtained what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor having been promised anything else—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for; yet even as that hope is abandoned, he obtains something other than what he hoped for, then on the twelfth day he should immediately make a robe out of it. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, he may keep it.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the thirteenth day he has not obtained what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor having received anything unanticipated—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is finally abandoned and he instead obtains something unanticipated, this robe must be made into a finished garment by the thirteenth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it shall be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, yet by the fourteenth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned his hope nor being granted what was not hoped for—and he continues to diligently seek what he hoped for, such that his hope is abandoned but he instead obtains what was not hoped for, then this robe must be made into a finished garment by the fourteenth day; if it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it may be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, yet by the fifteenth day he does not obtain what he hoped for; if his hope has not ceased, and he has neither renounced the hope nor been granted [a new one], and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope ceases and he instead obtains what he did not hope for—this robe must be made into a finished garment by the fifteenth day. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it shall be kept aside.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, yet by the sixteenth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor having been granted what was not hoped for—and he continues to diligently seek what he hoped for, such that his hope is abandoned and he instead obtains what was not hoped for, this robe should be made into a garment on the sixteenth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it shall be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the seventeenth day he has not obtained what he hoped for—neither having abandoned his hope nor being promised what was not expected—and yet he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is abandoned and he instead obtains what was not expected, this robe must be made into a garment by the seventeenth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and keeps it with the hope of obtaining more, and by the eighteenth day he has not obtained what he hoped for, yet his expectation has not ceased—neither being disappointed nor having received what was not expected—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope ceases and he instead obtains what was not expected, this robe must be made into a garment by the eighteenth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the nineteenth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor having obtained anything else unexpectedly—and yet continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is abandoned and he instead obtains something else, then this robe must be made into a finished garment on the nineteenth day; if it is sufficient, that is well, but if it is insufficient, it shall be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twentieth day he has not obtained what he hoped for—provided that his hope has not been abandoned, nor has he received anything other than what was hoped for, and he continues to diligently seek what he hoped for—then even though this hope has been abandoned and he has instead obtained something other than what was hoped for, he must make a robe out of these materials by the twentieth day. If they are sufficient, that is well; if they are insufficient, he may keep them.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twenty-first day he has not obtained what he hoped for—provided that his expectation has not ceased, nor has he been promised anything other than what he expected, and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for—then even if that expectation ceases and he instead obtains something other than what he hoped for, this robe must be made into a finished garment by the twenty-first day. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it shall be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and keeps it in anticipation of receiving more, and by the twenty-second day he has not obtained what he expected—neither having abandoned that expectation nor being granted anything unexpected—and yet he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is cut off and he instead obtains something unexpected, this robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-second day; if the materials are sufficient, it is well; if they are insufficient, he should set them aside.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twenty-third day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor having obtained anything unexpected, yet continuing to diligently seek what he hoped for—and then that hope is abandoned while something unexpected is obtained, this robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-third day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twenty-fourth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned his hope nor being granted what was not hoped for—and yet continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is abandoned but he instead obtains what was not hoped for, this robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-fourth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in anticipation of obtaining more, yet by the twenty-fifth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned his hope nor having been granted what was not hoped for—and he continues to diligently seek what he hoped for, such that his hope is then abandoned and he instead obtains what was not hoped for, this robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-fifth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in anticipation of obtaining more, yet by the twenty-sixth day he does not obtain what he expected—neither having abandoned that expectation nor being promised what was not expected—and he continues to diligently seek what he expected, such that his expectation is abandoned and he instead obtains what was not expected, then this robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-sixth day; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it must be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twenty-seventh day he has not obtained what he hoped for, yet his expectation has not ceased—neither having been fulfilled nor having been abandoned—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for; if that expectation then ceases and he instead obtains something other than what he hoped for, this robe must be made into a garment within twenty-seven days. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it should be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, and by the twenty-eighth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned that hope nor being granted what was not hoped for—he continues to diligently seek what he hoped for; yet even that hope is abandoned and he instead obtains what was not hoped for, this robe must be made into a garment by the twenty-eighth day. If it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it shall be kept.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in the hope of obtaining more, if by the twenty-ninth day he does not obtain what he hoped for—neither having abandoned his hope nor having received what was not hoped for—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope is abandoned and he instead obtains what was not hoped for, this robe must be made into a finished garment by the twenty-ninth day; if it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, it may be kept.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and keeps it with the hope of obtaining more, and by the thirtieth day he has not obtained what he hoped for, yet his hope has not ceased—neither being abandoned nor having been granted—and he continues to diligently seek what he hopes for, such that his hope ceases and he instead obtains what he did not hope for, this robe must be made into a finished garment within thirty days; if it is sufficient, well and good; if it is insufficient, it may be kept.

If a bhikṣu possesses an article of clothing subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika), and without having relinquished the offense or confessed his transgression, he continues to possess it without interruption and then acquires another garment, he commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense on account of the original garment.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu possesses an article of clothing subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika), and having already forfeited it but not yet confessed his transgression, he continues to possess it without interruption and subsequently acquires another garment, he commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense on account of the original garment.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, and having already relinquished it and confessed his offense, he continues to possess it without interruption and subsequently acquires another robe, he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense due to the circumstances of the original robe.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu possesses an article of clothing subject to *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, and having already relinquished the offense and performed confession, his continuity [of possession] has been severed, he incurs no offense upon obtaining another garment.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, observing the rains retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus were receiving many offerings of robes and storing them. Because the Buddha wished to regulate the excessive accumulation of robes by the bhikṣus, he said to the bhikṣus who were observing the rains retreat:
"I wish to regulate the excessive accumulation of robes by the bhikṣus;
therefore, I shall remain in quiet seclusion for four months."
"Let no bhikṣus come to me, except for one bhikṣu who brings food and those attending the poṣadha.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, the bhikṣus who were observing the rains retreat returned to the assembly and established this regulation:
If a bhikṣu, other than one who has been sent with food or who has come for the poṣadha, goes to the Buddha's presence, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
Having established this rule, he informed the Buddha; the Buddha accepted it by remaining silent.

At that time, the Elder Upasena, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus—all of whom were forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), wearers of rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika), eaters of a single meal (aikāsanika), alms-seekers (piṇḍapātika), and sitters in the open air (ābhyavakāśika)—possessed pure deportment in their coming and going, sitting and lying down, looking and moving; they carried their saṃghāṭī robes and held their bowls with steady composure, traveling through Kośala until they reached the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, many bhikṣus were walking up and down in the gateway of the Jeta Grove.
The Elder Upasena asked the bhikṣus, "Where is the Buddha now? The bhikṣus replied:
“The Buddha is in that great eastern chamber with a single wooden plank for a door inside.
If you wish to go there, do as you please.
Then the Elder Upasena went to the great chamber; having arrived, he cleared his throat and knocked on the door with his finger.
The Buddha opened the door for him, and the Elder Upasena immediately entered the great hall, approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked:
"Your assembly is pure and excellent; by what causes and conditions is your assembly so pure in its deportment?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
If a bhikṣu comes to me seeking to study and recite the sūtras or seeking formal reliance, I say to that bhikṣu:

"If you can remain a forest-dweller for as long as you live—wearing rag-robes, begging for food, eating only one meal a day, and sitting in empty spaces—I shall teach you the scriptures and grant you formal reliance."
"If there are bhikṣus who can practice these dhūta-dharmas, I shall instruct them in the recitation of the sūtras and grant them formal reliance (niśraya).
For this reason, World-Honored One,
the deportment of my followers is pure."
The Buddha asked Upasena:
"Do you know the regulations established by the senior bhikṣus?
He replied:
“I do not know,
World-Honored One!
How did the elder bhikṣus establish that regulation?”
The Buddha said to Upasena:
"I wish to remain in secluded meditation for four months. I tell you, monks:
'You monks must not come to me, except for one who brings food and for the purpose of the *poṣadha*.'"
The bhikṣus accepted my words and, returning to the assembly, established a regulation:
"If a bhikṣu goes to the Buddha's presence for any reason other than receiving food or attending the poṣadha ceremony, he commits a pāyattika offense."
"Since the monks established this regulation, they have informed me;
I immediately gave my silent assent.
Upasena said, "World-Honored One!"
“Does the elder bhikṣu understand this intention?
The Buddha said,
“Why does he not understand?”
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit forest-dwelling bhikṣus who practice the dhūta of wearing rag-robes to come to me as they please—whether food is sent or not sent, and whether there is a poṣadha ceremony or not."

When the senior monks heard that the Elder Upasena had neither brought food nor attended the *poṣadha*, but had gone to the Buddha’s presence because he wished to see him, they gathered the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*). Having assembled, they summoned Upasena.

When the assembly of monks had gathered, the Elder Upasena immediately went into the midst of the Sangha, prostrated with his head at the feet of the senior monk, and sat down according to his rank. An elder bhikṣu then asked Upasena:
"Do you know of the regulations established by the elder bhikṣus?"
He replied, "I do not know.
Then he questioned the senior monk (sthavira), saying:
"What is the established rule of the elder bhikṣus? He replied, "Upasena!"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus observing the rains retreat:
"I wish to remain in solitary meditation for four months; no bhikṣus shall come to me, except for one person to bring food and for the purpose of the poṣadha ceremony."
We have received the Buddha’s instruction and established this regulation:
if a bhikṣu goes to the presence of the Buddha for any reason other than being sent food alone or for the purpose of the uposatha, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
The Buddha remained silent, thereby granting his consent. "O Upavāṇa!
It is not for a single delivery of food, nor for going to the Buddha's presence on the Uposatha day, that one incurs a pāyattika offense."
"You should repent according to the Dharma; you must disclose it;
do not conceal this offense. Upasena said, "Does the Elder know?"
I went to where the Buddha was, prostrated myself at his feet, and sat to one side. Knowing this, the Buddha asked me:
"Upasena, for what reason is the conduct of your assembly so pure?"
I said: "World-Honored One!
If there should be a bhikṣu who comes to me seeking to read and recite the sūtras, or seeking to take formal reliance [niśraya], I would say to that bhikṣu:”

"If you can, for as long as you live, act as a forest-dweller (āraṇyaka), wear rag-robes (pāṃśukūla), beg for food, eat but one meal a day, and sit in open spaces, I shall teach you the sūtras and provide you with a formal preceptor."
"If a bhikṣu is able to practice these dhūta-dharmas, I shall instruct him in the recitation of the sūtras and grant him formal reliance (niśraya).
For this reason, World-Honored One,
the deportment of my assembly is pure."
The Buddha asked me,
"Do you know the regulations established by the senior bhikṣus?
I replied:
"I do not know,
World-Honored One!
How was this regulation established?"
The Buddha said:
"Upasena! I wish to remain in meditative seclusion for four months; I tell the bhikṣus:"
"I shall ensure that the bhikṣus do not come to my presence, except for one who brings food and those attending the poṣadha.
The bhikṣus accepted my words and returned to the assembly to establish this regulation:
"If a bhikṣu goes to the Buddha's presence other than to bring food or for the poṣadha, he commits a pāyattika offense."
I immediately agreed to this. I said,
"World-Honored One!"
“Does that senior bhikṣu know this intention?
The Buddha said,
“Why would he not know it?”
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit forest-dwelling monks who wear rag-robes and practice the dhūta austerities to come to me as they please, whether it be for a single meal offering or not, whether it be for the uposatha or not."
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"Why do we not discard these layperson’s robes and wear rag-robes (pāṃśukūla) instead?
Immediately, the bhikṣus discarded their layperson’s robes and all began wearing rag-robes.

The three matters are concluded. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, scroll five, on the second line of the twenty-sixth leaf of this scroll, regarding the phrase "up to thirty days, as explained above" following the *pāyattika* [offense], the Danben (Dan edition) lacks these nine characters. Instead, it contains a passage of ninety-one lines beginning with: "Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and so forth, up to the end of the thirty-day period, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*," and so on. Since these are absent from both the Guoben (State edition) and the Songben (Song edition), I have now supplemented them by following the Danben.

The thirteenth line on the twenty-seventh sheet of this volume—which corresponds to the thirteenth line on the thirty-first sheet of the current standard edition—reads, following the term *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: "For twelve days up to thirty days, it is also as explained above. In the Danben (Dan-zang) edition, these four characters "twelve days" (*shi-er-ri*) are absent; instead, there is a passage of ninety-two characters beginning with: "Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe and sets it aside in hope of obtaining more, until the end of the thirty-day period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*," and so forth. Since these are not present in either the Guoben (Guo-zang) or Songben editions, I have now supplemented them here according to the Danben.

In the twenty-ninth sheet, fourth line of this volume—which corresponds to the fourth line of the thirty-seventh sheet of the current standard edition—following the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rule, the phrase "twelve days up to thirty days, all as explained above" is absent from the Danben (Dan-zang) edition. Instead, it contains ninety-seven lines of text beginning with "Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe... up to *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*," which are not found in the Guoben (Guozang) or Songben editions. Now, following the Danben, these have been inserted to complete the text.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle Six, Part Six of the First Recitation;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
Clarifying the Second of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, having dressed and taken her bowl at dawn, entered the city to beg for food. After she had finished eating, she went into the Āmrapālī Grove and sat upright with her body straight and her deportment pure beneath a tree.

At that time, a band of five hundred thieves had previously entered the forest. The leader of these thieves was a believer in the Buddha-dharma; seeing the Bhikṣuṇī Huase sitting upright with her body composed and her deportment pure, he conceived a heart of pure faith upon seeing her and thought:
"Why should I not give this bhikṣuṇī a skewer of meat to eat?"
Among the bandits, there was one who knew a small amount of the Dharma and said, "This bhikṣuṇī eats only at the proper time; she does not eat at improper times.
Upon hearing this, the leader of the bandits felt his faith deepen further.
"This bhikṣuṇī sits upright with her body composed and her deportment pure; she eats at the proper time and not at improper times. Why should I not give her a skewer of meat for her meal tomorrow?"
One who had some knowledge of the Dharma said,
"This bhikṣuṇī eats whatever she obtains and does not keep leftover food overnight to eat.
At that time, the leader of the bandits conceived even greater faith in the bhikṣuṇī.

"This bhikṣuṇī sits upright with her body composed and her deportment pure; she eats at the proper time and not at the improper time, eating only what she obtains and never consuming leftover food kept overnight."
"Why do I not wrap a piece of meat on a skewer in a costly cotton cloth and hang it upon a tree for the sake of this bhikṣuṇī?
Having formed this thought:
"If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who take this, I shall give it to them.
Having formed this thought, he immediately wrapped the meat in expensive cotton cloth and hung it upon a tree, saying:
"To whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas it may be needed, I give it as a gift."
When the night had passed, the bhikṣuṇī Puṣpacitrā spoke these words:
"Because of me, the thieves wrapped the meat in cotton cloth and hung it upon a tree, saying:
'If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas require it, let them take it as a gift.'"
"I ought not to eat this meat; I shall take it to the Saṃgha, and you may take the cotton cloth yourself.
He then took the meat to Jetavana, asked for the place where the food was being prepared, gave the meat there, and departed from Jetavana.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus saw the bhikṣuṇī Puṣpacitrā coming out carrying a fine piece of cotton cloth; having seen it, they conceived a covetous mind and said to her, "This cloth of yours is fine and excellent."
The bhikṣuṇī replied,
“It is fine and good.
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"It is fine," they said.
Then the group of six bhikṣus remarked, "It is good;
why not give it to someone who is truly worthy?"
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"He is certainly demanding it.
Why should I not give it to him?"
She then gave the cotton cloth to the group of six bhikṣus.
This bhikṣuṇī was deeply faithful and reverent toward the Buddha, and she thought:
"I ought not to return to the city without having seen the Buddha."
Having formed this thought, she immediately proceeded to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
From afar, the Buddha saw the bhikṣuṇī Huase approaching, her robes tattered and worn.
The Buddha, knowing the answer, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Why are the robes of this bhikṣuṇī Huāshè so tattered?
Is she unable to obtain the gift of robes?"
Ānanda said, "I have just obtained some high-quality cotton cloth.
The Buddha said:
“Where is he now? Ānanda replied,
“The group of six bhikṣus have sought him out and taken him away.”
Knowing the answer, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Did the bhikṣu truly take a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative?
He replied:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha then said to Ānanda:
"Take five robes from among my surplus robes and give them to this bhikṣuṇī.
Ānanda replied, "So be it."
He then took five robes from his extra clothing and gave them to her.
The bhikṣuṇī immediately put on these robes, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha taught her the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening her; having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching that instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her, the bhikṣuṇī Puṣpā prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
Not long after they had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the situation], he asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu take robes from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative?"
A person who is not a relative cannot inquire whether one's robes are sufficient or insufficient,
or whether they are too long;
one simply takes whatever is obtained.
If they are relatives, one should ask whether their clothing is sufficient or not,
and whether it is long enough or not.
Since relatives would still offer them clothing of their own accord, how much more so when taking what is insufficient?
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "not a relative": a relative is defined as one's mother, sister, daughter, or even those connected by kinship up to the seventh generation.

As for garments, they are: hempen garments, red hempen garments, white hempen garments, *śāṇa* (coarse grass) garments, *kṣaumika* (linen) garments, *kārpāsa* (cotton) garments, and *kambala* (woolen blanket) garments.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a single bhikṣu takes a robe from a single bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is one *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a single bhikṣu takes robes from two, three, or four bhikṣuṇīs who are not relatives, there is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for each robe he obtains.
If two bhikṣus receive a robe from two, three, four, or one bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, for each such acquisition, there is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If three bhikṣus receive robes from three, four, one, or two bhikṣuṇīs who are not their relatives, they incur as many *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* as there are robes obtained.
If four bhikṣus take robes from four unrelated bhikṣuṇīs, they incur four *niḥsargika-pāyattikas*.
If four bhikṣus take robes from one, two, or three unrelated bhikṣuṇīs, they incur as many *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* as there are [bhikṣuṇīs] from whom they took them.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kośala, two divisions of the Saṃgha obtained a large quantity of robes and divided them into two portions.
The bhikṣus received robes suitable for bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs received robes suitable for bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus received [the robes], the bhikṣuṇīs said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, give us your robes; we shall give our robes to you."
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Buddha has established a precept that one must not accept robes from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu receives clothing from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, yet perceives her as a relative and receives clothing from her, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one claims that the person from whom the robe was taken is a bhikṣu, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, male renunciant, or female renunciant, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, and he harbors doubt as to whether she is a relative or not, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one suspects that she is a bhikṣuṇī when she is not a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā when she is not a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera when he is not a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī when she is not a śrāmaṇerī, one who has gone forth when they have not gone forth, or a bhikṣuṇī who has gone forth when she has not gone forth, and takes a robe from her, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has a relative who is a bhikṣuṇī, yet he takes a robe from her while perceiving her as a non-relative, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he perceives her as a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, pravrajitā, or pravrajitā-ni, yet takes a robe from her, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, and the bhikṣu, harboring doubt as to whether she is a relative or not, takes a robe from her, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one suspects whether this person is a bhikṣu or not a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā or not a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera or not a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī or not a śrāmaṇerī, one who has gone forth or not one who has gone forth, or a bhikṣuṇī who has gone forth or not one who has gone forth, yet takes the robe from them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one takes [a robe] from a relative or a non-relative, whether out of certainty or doubt, and it is made of impure materials—namely, a mixture of camel hair, cow hair, and black sheep wool—it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

There is no offense if it is for a relative, or if one has been previously invited, or if it is given because [the recipient] is staying in a separate room, or if it is given for the purpose of preaching the Dharma; in these cases, there is no offense.
The four matters concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin had been acquainted with the bhikṣuṇī Guptā for some time; they conversed and frequented one another’s company.
At that time, Kālodāyin was traveling through other countries for two months. The bhikṣuṇī Khemā heard that the Elder Kālodāyin had been traveling abroad for two months.
The bhikṣuṇī Khemā heard that Kālodāyin had completed his two-month journey and had returned to Śrāvastī.

Having heard that Kāḷudāyin had returned from his two-month journey to Śrāvastī, the bhikṣuṇī Guptā bathed her body, adorned her face, anointed her hair with fragrant oil, and put on light dyed robes. She went to where Kāḷudāyin was, prostrated herself at his feet, and sat down before him.
At that time, Kālodāyin gave rise to a mind of defiled attachment and gazed intently at her face; the bhikṣuṇī also gave rise to a mind of defilement and looked at the bhikṣu’s face.
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"He gazes at my face and will surely give rise to defiled attachment; why do I not get up and move forward first?"

At that time, Kāḷodāyin was wearing only his inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī) as he walked back and forth together with [the other monk]. His lustful mind was stirred, yet fearing he would commit an offense against the precepts, he did not dare to touch him. As they gazed intently at each other’s faces, he discharged impurity; once the urgent fever had subsided, he returned to his original seat.
The bhikṣuṇī Khujjuttarā thought to herself,
"If the Elder Kāḷudāyin returns to his original seat, he will surely discharge impurity.
Having put on her upper robe again, she approached Kāḷudāyin and said to him:
"Bring this robe here; I shall wash it for you.
Kāḷudāyin put on another robe, took off this one, and gave it to the bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇī moved aside slightly, wrung out the garment, and applied the liquid to her private parts; immediately, a son of merit arrived to receive a womb from his mother.
As her belly gradually grew larger, the bhikṣuṇīs drove her out of the monastery, saying:
"This is a wicked bhikṣuṇī! A thieving bhikṣuṇī!"
"Have you newly come from outside?
How could an old renunciant woman like you become pregnant?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"I have not committed sexual misconduct.
She related these circumstances to the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You must not reproach this bhikṣuṇī; she has not broken her brahmacarya, nor has she committed sexual misconduct. It was due to such circumstances that she became pregnant."
At that time, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Kālodāyin, "Is it true that you have done such a thing? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
For various reasons, the Buddha rebuked Kāḷodāyin:
“How can a bhikṣu have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash his old robes?
After the Buddha had thus rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.”
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"Non-relatives" refers to those who are not relatives; "relatives" are defined as one's mother, sisters, daughters, and so forth, up to the seventh generation of kinship.
"Old clothing" refers to any garment that has been worn on the body even once; all such items are termed old clothing.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, "Wash this old robe for me, or dye it, or beat it."
If a bhikṣuṇī washes this robe for him, the bhikṣu incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If he dyes it, he incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If one beats it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one washes or dyes it, or washes and beats it, or dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative,
"Wash and beat this robe for me,
but do not dye it," and if the bhikṣuṇī washes it for him, the bhikṣu commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
Whether one beats it, dyes it, washes and dyes it, washes and beats it, dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative,
"Wash and dye this robe for me, but do not beat it," and she washes it for him,
it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she dyes it, beats it, washes and dyes it, washes and beats it, dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative:
"Dye and beat this robe for me,
but do not wash it," and she dyes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one beats it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one washes it, or washes and dyes it, or washes and beats it, or dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative,
"Wash, beat, and dye this robe for me," and she washes it for him,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If she beats it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she dyes it, or washes and dyes it, or washes and beats it, or dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative:
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me," and she washes it for him,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one dyes or beats [the robe], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one washes and dyes, or washes and beats, or dyes and beats, or washes, dyes, and beats, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative,
"Dye, beat, or wash this robe for me," and she dyes it,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one beats it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether one washes it, or washes and dyes it, or washes and beats it, or dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative,
"Wash this robe for me; do not dye it, and do not beat it," and she washes it for him,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one dyes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether one beats it, or washes and dyes it, or washes and beats it, or dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative,
"Dye this robe for me; do not wash it,
and do not beat it," and she dyes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she washes it, beats it, washes and dyes it, washes and beats it, dyes and beats it, or washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative:
"Beat this robe for me; do not wash it, do not dye it," and she beats it for him, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she washes it, dyes it, both washes and dyes it, washes and beats it, dyes and beats it, or both washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, yet he regards her as a relative and says to her:
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me," and she washes,
dyes, and beats it for him, the bhikṣu incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If one says, "This is a bhikṣu; this is a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a pravrajitā, or a bhikṣuṇī," and speaks thus:
"Wash, dye, and beat these robes for me."
If a monk has a non-relative nun wash, dye, or beat [a robe], he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a monk has a nun who is not a relative, yet suspects whether she is a relative or not, and says to her:
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me."
If one has it washed, dyed, or beaten [for these purposes], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one suspects whether a person is a bhikṣu or not a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā or not a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera or not a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī or not a śrāmaṇerī, one who has gone forth or not one who has gone forth, or a bhikṣuṇī or not a bhikṣuṇī, and says:
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me."
If one has them washed, dyed, or beaten, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a monk has a relative who is a nun, yet he speaks to her as if she were not a relative, saying:
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me."
If one has them wash, dye, or beat [the cloth], the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, thinking they are a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a renunciant, or a female renunciant, one says to them:
"Wash, dye, and beat this garment for me."
If she washes, dyes, or beats it for him, that bhikṣu commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu has a relative who is a bhikṣuṇī, and he entertains doubt as to whether she is a relative or not, yet says to her:
"Wash, dye, and beat this robe for me."
If one has them wash, dye, or beat [the garment], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one is uncertain whether the person is a bhikṣu or not a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā or not a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera or not a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī or not a śrāmaṇerī, a renunciant or not a renunciant, or a female renunciant or not a female renunciant, and says:
"Wash, dye, and beat this garment for me," [it is a *duṣkṛta* offense].
If he has them washed, dyed, or beaten, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu—whether the person is a relative or not a relative—whether he knows this or suspects it, has someone wash an impure garment, such as one woven from a mixture of camel hair, cow hair, or black sheep’s wool, the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* in all such cases.
If it is not a relative, there is no offense.
The five matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who, wearing his upper and lower robes, came to the Jetavana; he was an old acquaintance of Upananda, with whom he had conversed and transacted business.
When Bāḷhika saw the householder approaching from afar, he felt a sense of greedy attachment toward his upper and lower robes.
As the householder gradually approached Bāḷhika’s place, he prostrated with his head at the elder’s feet and sat down before him.
Having taught him various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden him, Bāḷhika said:
"Householder!
Your upper and lower robes are excellent; you should make a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, and an antarvāsaka from them for the community of bhikṣus."
"If you give it to me, I shall be able to take and keep it.
Although this householder did not hear [the request], or having heard it, was unwilling to give,
at that time Baddhananda further explained various other teachings to instruct, benefit, and gladden him, and then spoke again:
"You have fine upper and lower robes; let us make a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, and an antarvāsaka for you as a bhikṣu.
If you give these to me, I shall be able to accept and keep them."
The householder did not hear these words, or having heard them, was unwilling to give.
Upananda further explained various other teachings to instruct, benefit, and gladden him; having done so, he spoke again to the householder, saying:
"Give me one robe; it is our rule that we receive robes from householders."
The householder thought to himself, "This bhikṣu makes such a firm request; how could I not give?
He immediately took off one of his garments, folded it up, and handed it to him.
After this householder had given the robe, he felt regret and resentment, unable to endure it, and thought to himself:
"I should not have gone to the monastery of the Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas."
If a householder goes there, they will forcibly seize his robes; it is no different from a perilous path. For this reason, one should not go to where the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, reside.
When this householder entered the city of Śrāvastī, the gatekeeper saw him and asked, "When you went out, you were wearing both upper and lower garments; where is one of them now?"
The householder then related these circumstances as he had spoken them.
As he spoke these words, his mind was filled with redoubled remorse, resentment, and intolerance, and he said:
"One should not go to the monastery of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya; if one goes there, they forcibly seize one's robes, no different from a treacherous road."
In this way, one person told it to two, and the two told it to three; thus they passed the word from one to another, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have forcibly seized people's robes."
A bad reputation spread throughout Śrāvastī.
