Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the Śākya son Upananda:
"Did you truly do this? He replied:
"It was indeed done,
Blessed One!
The Buddha rebuked Upananda with various causes and conditions:
“What is it called, monks, for a monk to agree to solicit [goods] from a person who is not a relative?
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the monks:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the monks.”
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

Regarding "one who is not a relative": a relative is defined as one's father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, or even those connected by kinship up to the seventh generation; anyone other than these is called a non-relative.
A "householder" (gṛhapati) refers to a man;
a "householder's wife" (gṛhapatnī) refers to a woman.
"Clothing" refers to white hempen garments, red hempen garments, kṣauma silk garments, kambala woolen garments, śāṇa hemp garments, and kārpāsa cotton garments.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are three kinds: namely, price, color, and quantity.
As for price, it is when a bhikṣu says to a householder:
"Give me a robe of good price."
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she does not obtain the robe, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Even if someone says, "Give me a robe worth two hundred or three hundred coins," if she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called "price.
Regarding "color," if a bhikṣu says to a householder:
"Give me a dark-blue robe.
If she obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if she does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The same applies to robes that are yellow, red, white, or black; robes of white hempen cloth, red hempen cloth, *kṣauma* (linen) cloth, *cīvara* (woolen) cloth, *śāṇa* (hemp) cloth, or *kārpāsa* (cotton) cloth.
This is called "name and form.
As for the measure: if a bhikṣu says to a householder, "Give me a robe of four cubits."
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if she does not obtain the robe, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
This applies likewise to robes measuring five cubits, six cubits, or even up to eighteen cubits; this is called "measurement."
To request one thing and obtain another constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one requests blue cloth and obtains yellow cloth, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one requests blue and obtains red, white, or black, it is likewise.
If a bhikṣu requests white flaxen cloth and receives red flaxen cloth, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This applies even down to requesting a *kṣaumapaṭa* (linen) garment and receiving a *kārpāsa* (cotton) garment; it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if one requests from a relative, or if it was previously invited, or if the person gives it of their own accord without being asked.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a Bhikṣu from Pāṭaliputra was traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī when he encountered bandits on the road who robbed him of his robes; he proceeded on his way naked.
At that time, he had this thought:
"The Buddha has established a precept:
one must not beg for robes from those who are not relatives."
"My kinsmen are far away; now I shall go to Śrāvastī in the nude.
He then entered the Jetavana and paid homage to the resident bhikṣus. The resident bhikṣus asked him, "Who are you?"
He replied,
“I am a śramaṇa. “What kind of śramaṇa?”
He replied,
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
[The other asked,] "For what reason are you naked?"
He replied, "While on my way, I encountered bandits who robbed me of my robes; thus I have come naked. At that time, I thought to myself:
'The Buddha has established a precept forbidding one from begging from those who are not relatives.'"
"My kinsmen are far away; I shall go to Śrāvastī naked.
For this reason, I am now naked.
Next, he went to the place where the group of six bhikṣus were and paid them homage. The group of six bhikṣus asked him:
"Who are you? He replied, "A śramaṇa."
“Who is this śramaṇa? He replied,
“A śramaṇa who is a son of the Śākyas.”
"Why are you naked?
He replied, "On the road, I encountered bandits who robbed me of my clothes; at that time, I thought to myself:"
"The Buddha has established a precept forbidding us from begging from those who are not our relatives.
Since my relatives live far away, I shall go to Śrāvastī naked.
For this reason, he went naked.
The group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"For this reason, the Buddha will surely permit us to beg from those who are not our relatives; we should therefore associate with such people."
The group of six bhikṣus said to him, "Why have you gone to the Buddha's presence naked?
We shall lend you a robe to go to the Buddha's presence; once you have received the robe, you must return it to us."
He replied, “Yes.
The group of six bhikṣus immediately borrowed the robes and put them on, then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they inquire after them with these words and say to the bhikṣus:
"Are you patient?
Are you satisfied?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is your alms-seeking not lacking?
Are you not utterly exhausted by the journey?"
Immediately, the Buddha used these words to inquire after the bhikṣu Pāla:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of almsfood?
Are you not exhausted from the journey?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
We have been patient, dwelling in peace and comfort, and alms-seeking has not been difficult; it was only that we were utterly exhausted on the road.”
He reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts, praised the upholding of the precepts, and praised the precepts.
Having praised the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this rule should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu begs for clothing from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika, except during the [prescribed] season.'"
"Other times" refers to when one's robes have been seized, lost, burned, or washed away; these are considered "times.
Regarding "seized": it means seized by government officials, or by bandits, or by enemies, or by the factions of enemies.
"Lost" means that if it is lost, one does not know where it is;
or if it has decayed, or been gnawed by insects.
"Burnt" means that it has been consumed by fire or scorched by the sun.
"Carried away by water" means swept by a flood or blown by the wind;
this is what is meant by "time.

When the group of six bhikṣus heard that for these reasons the Buddha had permitted bhikṣus to beg from laypeople who were not their relatives, they concluded the six matters. Thus it was at that time.
Having heard this, he said to the bhikṣus from Pāṭaliputra:
"Because you have little knowledge and little learning, you have no robes; yet we, who have much knowledge and much learning, also have few robes. I am now begging for your sake."
"If your three robes are complete, give all your remaining robes to me.
The bhikṣu Pāla replied, "So be it."
Then the group of six bhikṣus entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the houses of wealthy people, praising them, saying:
"The bhikṣu Pāla is excellent; he is a kinsman of the Buddha, and while traveling on a dangerous road, he was robbed of his robes by bandits."
"You all should give them.

Immediately, those with faith gave various garments—whether cotton cloth (*kārpāsa*), *kṣauma*, or *kambala*. Thus, passing from house to house, they obtained many clothes, which they wrapped upon their shoulders and carried back.
The group of six bhikṣus took the better ones for themselves and gave the inferior ones to the bhikṣu Pāla.

Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who intentionally deprives the bhikṣu Pāla of his robe?"
After the bhikṣus had rebuked them with various reasons, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can those who are called bhikṣus intentionally seize the robe of the bhikṣu Pāla?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost them, had them burned, or had them carried away by water, he may beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative.’”
"If, during the *pravāraṇā*, many robes are offered, that bhikṣu should accept two robes:
one for the upper body and one for the lower body. If he accepts more than this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "the two robes," there are two kinds: [the saṃghāṭī and the antaravāsaka].
There are upper and lower garments for laypeople, and there are upper and lower garments for bhikṣus.
Regarding the upper and lower garments of laypeople, there is one upper garment and one lower garment.
Regarding the upper and lower garments of bhikṣus, these refer to the three robes they employ.
If one obtains layperson’s upper and lower robes, if they are insufficient, one should beg for more; if they are excessive, one should return them to the owner.
If one obtains a bhikṣu’s upper and lower robes, if they are insufficient, one should not beg for more; if they are excessive, one should not return them to the owner.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu already possesses the three robes in full, he should not beg for more; if he begs and obtains them, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he begs but does not obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu loses one robe, and his saṃghāṭī can be disassembled to make another robe, he should disassemble it and not beg for more.
If he begs for it and obtains it, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If he does not obtain [the robe] when begging for it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu has lost two robes, and his *saṃghāṭī* is such that it can be torn down to make [another] robe, he should beg for only one robe; he should not beg for two robes.
If one begs for two robes, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one begs but does not obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu loses his three robes, he should temporarily borrow robes from among the five classes of followers and wear them when entering a village to beg for new robes.

If such things were not available, and if among the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions there were woolen blankets, *kocava* rugs, mattresses, *pañcaka* rugs, or pillows, one may take them and make them into robes to wear.
Having put on these robes, one should go to beg for robes.
If one obtains robes through begging, one should wear the new robes and wash the previous ones; having rinsed, dried, and beaten them to restore them, they should be returned to their original place.
If this monastery is empty and no one is living there, one should take the items and follow them to a nearby place where monks reside.
If the original monastery still has people living there, one should take these items and return them to their original location.
The seven matters concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who had provided the funds for a robe for the Śākya son Upananda. He thought to himself:
"With these funds for a robe, I shall purchase such a robe and give it to the Śākya son Upananda."
When the Śākya son Upananda heard this, he went to the householder’s place and asked him:
“Is it true that you have prepared the price for a robe for me with this thought:
‘With this price for a robe, I shall buy such a robe and give it to the Śākya son Upananda’?”
"Is it so? The householder replied,
"It is indeed so."
“How do you make robes for me? He replied,
“I make robes in this manner.”
The Śākya son Baddhananda said, “Excellent!
We bhikṣus who have left the household life possess few robes; it is difficult to obtain them through alms-seeking.”
"O householders, you are not able to constantly provide the conditions for giving.
If you wish to make robes for me, you should make them for me in such and such a manner."
The householder replied,

“So be it. Thereupon, the householder immediately procured robes of twice, thrice, and even more than that value, according to the original price of the first robes, and gave them to the Śākya son Upananda.
Later, he felt regret and rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know the proper time, they do not know contentment, and they do not know how to exercise restraint.
If the giver does not know the measure, the receiver ought to know it."
"The price for the robes we originally prepared has now increased two or three times over.

This is our own fault, a source of affliction and disadvantage; why did we give alms and offerings to such people who are so difficult to satisfy, so difficult to support, and never know contentment?"
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased, and these bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the Śākya son Upananda:
"Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
For various reasons, the Buddha rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"What is it to call a bhikṣu one who, for a person who is not a relative, consents to a request?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If, for the sake of a bhikṣu, a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative prepares the price for a robe and thinks:
'With this price for a robe, I shall buy such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu.'"
"In this case, a bhikṣu, without having been previously invited to choose for himself, goes to the home of a layman or a laywoman and speaks with them in agreement, saying:
'Prepare such an amount of money for me to buy such and such a robe for me, so that it may be of good quality.'"
"If he should obtain such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This was said with reference to the monk Upananda, the son of the Śākyas.
"Robe" refers to a robe made of white flax, red flax, *kṣauma* (hemp), *kambala* (wool), *śāṇa* (coarse hempen cloth), *kauśeya* (silk), or *kārpāsa* (cotton).
"Value of robes" refers to gold, silver, musaragalva, agate, money, and even rice and grain.
"To prepare" means to set aside these items of value in a separate place.
Such is the robe: of such price, such color, and such dimensions.
It is given to a certain bhikṣu because it is for the sake of the Śākya son Upananda.
"Previously not having been invited to choose for oneself" means that the householder has not previously informed the bhikṣu of what is required for him to come and take.
"Acting with consent" means having confidence that this householder will not become angry regardless of how much one asks from him.
Regarding those who desire excellence, they are difficult to satisfy and difficult to support because they lack contentment.
Within this context, there are three types of transgressions:
namely, price, color, and quantity.
Regarding "price": if a bhikṣu says to a layperson,
"Give me a fine robe," and he obtains a robe [in exchange], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Even if [the donor] says, "Give me a robe worth two or three hundred coins," if he obtains the robe,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called "price.
Regarding "color," a bhikṣu says to a householder:
"Give me a dark-colored robe.
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if she does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one says:
"Give me black, yellow, red, or white garments; garments of white hemp, red hemp, *kaiyila* silk, *kambala* wool, *kṣauma* linen, *kauśeya* silk, or cotton cloth."
If he obtains it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called "color."
Regarding the measure: if a bhikṣu says to a householder, "Give me a robe of four cubits, five cubits, six cubits, or even up to eighteen cubits."
If he obtains [the robe], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called "measuring."
If one requests this [item] and receives that, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one requests blue and receives yellow, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one requests blue and receives red, white, or black, it is likewise.
If one requests white hempen cloth and receives red hempen cloth, or even if one requests a *kṣaumpaka* garment and receives a cotton (*kārpāsa*) garment, it is likewise.
There is no offense if one requests from a relative, or if there was a prior invitation, or if the person gave it of their own accord without being asked.
The eight matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were two laymen and their wives who were not related by kinship to the Śākya son Upananda. They had prepared the price for robes for Upananda the Śākya son and thought to themselves:
"With this price for robes, each of us shall buy such-and-such a robe and give it to Upananda the Śākya son."
Having heard this, the Śākya son Baddhālī went to the layman and the laywoman and said:
"Is it true that you have prepared the price for robes for my sake, thinking:
'With these funds for robes, each of us shall buy such a robe and give it to the Śākya son Baddhālī'?"
"Is this not so? He replied,
"It is indeed so."
“How do you make the robes?
The householder replied,
“I make them like this.”
The Śākya son Baddhananda said:
"Excellent!
We bhikṣus are renunciants who possess few robes; it is difficult for us to obtain food through alms."
"You are unable to always provide the causes and conditions for giving.
Now, because you possess such a virtuous heart, you have prepared such-and-such garments for me;
however, if you cannot each make one individually, let two of you together make a single garment and give it to me."
He replied, "Yes. Then the laymen and their wives,
according to the amount they had prepared for the price of the robes, further contributed two or three times that amount to have robes made and gave them to the Śākya son Upananda.
Later, they felt regret and reproached themselves, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are difficult to satisfy and difficult to support; they have no sense of contentment.
We have suffered decline and loss of profit—why did we give alms and make offerings to such people?"
Among them, there were monks who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased, and these monks reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Upananda: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
"It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
For this reason, the Buddha censured him through various causes and conditions:
"What is it to say that a bhikṣu has agreed to a request made by a person who is not a relative?
Having rebuked them with various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, two unrelated laymen or laywomen each provide the funds for a robe, thinking:
'With these funds for robes, we shall each purchase such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu.'"
"In this case, a bhikṣu, without having been previously invited, goes to the place of a householder or a householder’s wife and speaks with them in agreement, saying:
'Each of you should provide the funds for a robe; together we shall make one robe for me, so that it may be of good quality.'"
"If he should obtain the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This was said with reference to the bhikṣu, the Śākya son Upananda.
Regarding the value of the robe, its procurement, and the fact that he had not been previously invited, it is as explained above.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are three types:
price, color, and measure.
As for price, if a bhikṣu says to a householder:
"If you give me fine cloth, let us two together make one garment.
If she obtains it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she says:
"Give me fine clothes.
Or if he says:
"The two together."
If one says,
"The two shall be made into one robe," and the robe is not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one obtains a robe worth two or three hundred coins from me, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one does not obtain the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called "price."
Regarding "colors," a bhikṣu says to a householder:
"Give me a blue garment, or one that is yellow, red, white, black, made of white hemp, red hemp, kṣauma silk, śāṇa hempen cloth, kambala woolen cloth, or kārpāsa cotton cloth."
If she obtains one, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she says:
"Give me a fine robe."
If one says,
"The two are conjoined," or if one says:
"If one makes a robe,
but does not obtain the cloth [for it],
it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
This is called "measurement.
Regarding the measure, a bhikṣu says to a householder:
"Give me a robe of four cubits, five cubits, or even up to eighteen cubits."
If she obtains it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she says, "Give me a fine robe," [and obtains one, it is likewise].
If one says:
"The two are conjoined," or if one says:
"Make one robe.
If one does not obtain a robe [of that measure], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called "measurement."
If one requests this [item] and receives that, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one requests a blue garment and receives a yellow garment, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one requests blue and receives red, white, or black, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one requests white hempen cloth and receives red hempen cloth, or even if one requests a *kṣaumaka* garment and receives a *kaupīna* garment, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one requests from a relative, or if there was a prior invitation, or if the person gives it of their own accord without being asked.
The nine matters concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who sent a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to the Śākya son Upananda.
The messenger brought these goods and saw the Śākya son Upananda sitting on a bed in a shop together with a merchant’s son. When the messenger arrived, he spoke as follows:
“Venerable sir!
A certain lay devotee has sent me with this money for robes; Venerable sir, please accept it.
When the Śākya son Baddhālī heard this, he said to the merchant’s son:
"Accept this price for the robe-cloth, count it out, and set it aside.
Once I have found a lay attendant (*karmadāna*), I shall come to take it away.
The merchant’s son then counted it out and set it aside.
At that time in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, a great multitude had agreed to assemble at one place, stipulating that anyone who failed to attend would be fined fifty coins.
This son of a merchant was required to go to the assembly; he therefore tied his goods in one place, closed the shop door, adorned himself, and prepared to depart.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda brought a laborer with him and said to the merchant’s son,
"Bring me the price for the robe.
He replied:
"There is a gathering of people in this city of Śrāvastī that I must attend; if I do not arrive in time, I shall be fined fifty coins. Wait a moment; I will give it to you upon my return."
Bhadananda said, "That will not do;
you are a layperson living at home who always seeks your own profit. Give it to me first and then depart; you may not stay even for a moment."

The merchant’s son opened the shop door, took out the value of this garment, counted it, handed it over, and returned home. Hearing that the crowd had already gathered and dispersed, he immediately fined them fifty coins, whereupon the people came to reprimand him.
The merchant’s son felt distress in his heart and rebuked him, saying:

"Śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, you do not know the proper time nor exercise discretion; had you waited but a little longer, my business would not have been interrupted and I would not have been punished."
"Because of this śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, I have lost these goods.

One person told two people, and two people told three; in this manner, word spread by successive transmission until the ill repute of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas pervaded the entire city of Śrāvastī.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally asked the son of Śākya, Upananda: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions, rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"You do not know the proper time and you do not know moderation; why did you not stay a little longer to wait until your business was finished so that the householder would suffer no loss?"
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If, for the sake of a bhikṣu, a king, a royal minister, a brāhmaṇa, or a householder sends a messenger to deliver the value of a robe,
that messenger arrives at the bhikṣu’s place and says:
"Venerable Sir!..."
If a king, a royal minister, a brahmin, or a householder sends the price for such robes, you should accept it.
The bhikṣu should say:
‘According to the dharma of us bhikṣus, we should not accept the price for robes.’”
"When you need robes and obtain pure cloth, you should receive it with your own hands and quickly make them into robes for your possession.
Then the messenger said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable One!..."
"Is there an attendant who can perform services for the bhikṣus?
That bhikṣu should point out an attendant—whether a monastery servant or a lay follower (upāsaka)—and say, "This person can perform services for the bhikṣus."
The messenger went to the person in charge and said:
"Excellent, steward!
Take this price for the robes and have such-and-such robes made, and give them to that bhikṣu."
"When that bhikṣu comes at the time he needs robes, you should give him the robes.
Having spoken thus, the messenger returns and reports to the bhikṣu:
"I have finished delivering the message."
"Venerable sir, when you need robes, go and take them; we shall give you robes.
When that bhikṣu goes to the place of the attendant and requests robes, he says:
"I require robes."
If he repeats this up to three times and likewise succeeds in obtaining the robe, that is well.
If he does not obtain it, he should go before the attendant and stand silently for a fourth, fifth, and even a sixth time.
If he stands silently for four, five, or six times and obtains the robe, it is well.
If he does not obtain the robe, and he seeks to obtain it beyond that number of times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go to the place where the price for the robe was sent, either going himself or sending a messenger, and say:
"The price for the robe you sent, I have not received."
"You yourself must know your own property; do not let it be lost—this is how it ought to be.
This was said for the sake of the bhikṣu, the Śākya son Upananda.
As for "a king," whether he is of the Kṣatriya caste, one who holds the office of king is also called a king, also called a lord of the land, and also called one whose head is anointed with water.

Whether they be brahmins, householders, or even women, if they receive royal office, they are also called kings, also called lords of the land, and also called those whose heads are anointed with water.
The "king's ministers" are those who receive official stipends and emoluments.
The "Brahmins" are those of the Brahmin caste.
As for the "householders," excluding the king, the king's ministers, and those of the Brahmin caste, the rest who are laypeople dressed in white at home are called householders.
The messenger may be a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite.
The garments may be white hempen cloth, red hempen cloth, *kṣauma* cloth, *śāṇa* cloth, *kauśeya* silk cloth, *kambala* woolen cloth, or *kārpāsa* cotton cloth.
"Directly" refers to gold, silver, musaragalva, agate, and coin.
"When the messenger has arrived, he speaks to the bhikṣu" means that the messenger says to the Śākya son Upananda:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"This robe-price has been sent by such-and-such a king, a royal minister, a brahmin, or a householder for the Venerable One;
please accept it now.
The bhikṣu says to the messenger:
"It is not in accordance with my rule as a bhikṣu to accept the price of a robe.
If one obtains a pure robe, one should receive it with one's own hands.
Regarding "making the robe quickly": this refers to making the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, or the antarvāsaka.
To instruct the attendant, saying,
"With this price for cloth, make such and such a robe," means [specifying] such a price, such a color, and such a measurement.
I have already spoken to the steward, whether by speaking with my own mouth or by sending someone to speak.
When a bhikṣu requires a robe, he should go to him and ask for a robe, saying these words up to three times. Upon going, he should say:
"I require a robe."
If, after going and speaking thus three times, he obtains the robe, that is well.

If he does not obtain the robe, he may go as many as six times and stand silently before the person in charge of the work; that is to say, he should stand in front of him at the place where the craft is performed, at his own dwelling place, at the place of industry, or at the marketplace.
Regarding skilled workshops: at a smithy, a carpentry workshop, or a pottery kiln, if a supervisor is present in such a place, a bhikṣu should stand silently before him.
The place of one's own residence refers to one's own home, house, or dwelling.
The place of industry refers to places for plowing and sowing, places for buying and selling, places for lending out capital, and places for accounting and calculation.

Regarding those in marketplaces—such as gold shops, silver shops, shops for hired labor, shops for precious stones, or shops for pearls—if a person in charge is present in such a place, the bhikṣu should stand silently before them four, five, or even six times.
If one does not accept the robe, one should speak to the owner of the robe, either going there in person or sending a messenger, saying:
"I cannot use the price of the robe you have sent; you should take your property back yourself."
After that bhikṣu has spoken to the owner of the robe, he may have other business that leads him to go to that place; if the attendant there asks the bhikṣu, "For what purpose have you come?"
The bhikṣu replies,
“I have come because of other business.
If the official says:
"Take this robe and go.
The bhikṣu said:
"I have already informed the owner of the robe; you should go yourself and settle the matter with him."
If the steward says,

"You need only take this price for the robe and go; I myself shall go and explain the matter to the owner of the robe," and if the bhikṣu at that time accepts the price for the robe and takes it away, there is no offense.
The Ten Matters Concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 60.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 7. Part One of the Second Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Recitation II, 4: The Thirty *Naiḥsargika* Dharmas, Part III.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were making new blankets of *koseyya* (silk). In this country, cotton, thread, cloth, and cocoons were expensive; this was because many silkworms were killed [to produce them].
A bhikṣu repeatedly begs, saying to a householder:
"The bhikṣu requires cotton, requires thread, requires cloth, requires cocoons.

He spends much time and effort on carding, processing, drawing out, and storing [the materials], thereby obstructing and abandoning his recitation of scriptures, sitting in meditation, and practicing the Path.
The laypeople grew weary of them, reproached them, and said:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.'"

They then produced new *kauśeya* (silk) bedding; however, because cotton is expensive, thread is expensive, cloth is expensive, and cocoons are expensive in this country—due to the great slaughter of silkworms—the bhikṣus had to beg for cotton, beg for thread, beg for cloth, and beg for cocoons.
They spent much time and effort on carding, processing, drawing out, and storing them, which hindered and caused the neglect of reciting the sūtras, sitting in meditation, and practicing the Path.
"In this matter, we have lost the benefit of offerings; he is one who is difficult to satisfy, difficult to support, and never free from greed.
When the bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this, they were displeased and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī:
"Did you truly do these things?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu making a new *kauśeya* (silk) bedding?
In this country, cotton is expensive, thread is expensive, clothing is expensive, and cocoons are expensive, because many silkworms are killed [to produce them]."
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding or mat from new *kauśeya* silk, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the bedding must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu takes cotton, carding and processing it to make a new bedding, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he uses thread, or cloth, or silk cocoons, carding and processing them to make a bedding, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
There is no offense if one obtains an already completed bedding;
thus the eleven matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then the group of six bhikṣus made bedding out of pure black wool from rams.
In this country, black sheep’s wool is expensive; black wool thread is expensive; and black wool felt is expensive.
The bhikṣus repeatedly begged for these, saying to the householders:
“The bhikṣus require black sheep’s wool; they require black thread and black felt.”
The laypeople grew weary and reproached them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
He then made a new sitting mat using pure black sheep’s wool.
In this country, black wool is expensive; the thread is expensive and the felt is expensive.

When the bhikṣu takes this black wool, he must sort, tear, spread, and store it, which involves much labor and many tasks, thereby obstructing and causing him to neglect reciting the sūtras, practicing seated meditation, and cultivating the Path.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu make a new bedding out of pure black sheep’s wool?

In this country, black sheep’s wool is expensive; so too are the yarn and the felt. To select, card, spread, and store it involves much labor and many tasks, which obstructs and causes the abandonment of sitting in meditation, reciting the sūtras, and practicing the Path."
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat using pure black wool from a ram, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "black wool from a ram," there are four kinds:
namely, naturally black, dyed blue-black, dyed mud-black, and dyed tree-bark-black; these are called the four kinds of black.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bedding must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu, using black wool from a ram that has grown naturally, sorts, tears, spreads, and stores it to make bedding, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one uses indigo dye, clay dye, or wood-bark dye to select, tear, and store cloth to make bedding or sitting mats, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in all such cases.

If a bhikṣu makes a bedding mat by selecting, carding, spreading, and storing black sheep’s wool, black sheep’s wool thread, or black sheep’s wool felt, it is in every case a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if it is for the sake of building a stūpa or for the sake of the Saṃgha, or if one obtains something already completed; there is no offense.
The twelve matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has established a precept:
'It is not permitted to make bedding from pure black sheep's wool.'"
"I shall now make a bedding using a small amount of white goat wool mixed with black goat wool.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and rebuked him in various ways:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, when the Buddha has not permitted the making of bedding from pure black goat wool, they instead make bedding by mixing it with a small amount of white goat wool?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu think thus:
'The Buddha does not permit the making of bedding from pure black sheep's wool'?"
"And yet you have made bedding by mixing it with a small amount of white wool from a ram?
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways for these reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding mat, he should use two parts black, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior."
If a bhikṣu makes a bedding mat using two parts black, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior color, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
Regarding "black," there are four kinds:
naturally black, dyed black with indigo, dyed black with mud, and dyed black with tree bark.
Regarding "white," this refers to the hair on the back, the hair on the flanks, and the hair on the neck.
The inferior [wool] refers to the hair of the head, the hair of the belly, and the hair of the legs.
If one is to make a *pātra* (alms bowl) cover consisting of forty *pala*, one should use twenty *pala* of pure black sheep’s wool, ten *pala* of white sheep’s wool, and ten *pala* of inferior wool.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the bedding must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu takes black sheep’s wool exceeding twenty *pala*, even down to a single *liang*, and makes it into bedding, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes white wool from a ram exceeding ten *pala* in weight, down to even a single *liang*, and makes it into a bedding mat, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one takes inferior wool weighing less than ten *pala*, down to even a single *liang*, and makes it into a bedding mat, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if one takes a large amount of inferior wool, or if one uses exclusively inferior wool.
One *pala* is equal to four *liang*.
The thirteen matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made many bedding materials and kept them, saying:

"This bedding material is too thick; this bedding material is too thin; this is too light; this is too heavy; this is too large; this is too small; this is torn and damaged; this has broken seams; this bedding material is worn out and useless."
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased and censured him in various ways:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu make many bedding materials and store them, saying:

'This is too thick,' 'this is too thin,' 'this is too light,' 'this is too heavy,' 'this is too large,' 'this is too small,' 'this is torn,' 'this has broken seams,' or 'this bedding material is worn out and useless'?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus accumulate many bedding materials and say:

'This is too thick; this is too thin; this is too light; this is too heavy; this is too large; this is too small; this is torn and damaged; this has broken edges; this bedding material is worn out and useless'?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If a bhikṣu wishes to make a new sitting mat, he must necessarily keep his old sitting mat for a full six years.

If a bhikṣu, before the six years have elapsed, discards his old sitting mat—or even if he does not discard it—makes another sitting mat, except by formal authorization from the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma), it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

Regarding the *saṃgha-karman*: if a bhikṣu’s old bedding—whether it be too thick, too thin, too light, too heavy, too large, too small, torn, or its border broken—and he wishes to make new bedding, that bhikṣu must, with a single mind, before the harmonious Saṃgha, rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
“I, bhikṣu [Name], have an old bedding that is either too thick, too thin, too light, too heavy, too large, too small, torn, or its border broken; I wish to make new bedding.”
"I request of the Saṃgha that [you] grant me permission to make a new bedding.
He should request thus a second and a third time.
At that time, the Saṃgha should deliberate; if they say it is "too thick" when it is actually not thick, they should not perform the *karmavācanā*.

If one says it is "too thin" when it is not actually thin; if one says it is "too heavy" when it is not actually heavy; if one says it is "too light" when it is not actually light; if one says it is "too large" when it is not actually large; if one says it is "too small" when it is not actually small; if one says it is "torn" when it is not actually torn; or if one says the "edges are frayed" when they are not actually frayed—then the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should not be performed.
If a tear can be repaired by cutting and patching, one should not perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā).
If a rip in the edge can be repaired by folding and stitching, one should likewise not perform the formal ritual.
If it is said that [the robe] is "too thick" and it is indeed too thick, a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be performed.

If it is said that it is "too thin" and it is indeed too thin; if it is said that it is "too heavy" and it is indeed heavy; if it is said that it is "too light" and it is indeed light; if it is said that it is "too large" and it is indeed large; if it is said that it is "too small" and it is indeed small; if it is said that it is "torn" and it is indeed torn; if it is said that it "cannot be patched" and it truly cannot be patched; or if it is said that the "border is broken" and it is truly broken and cannot be folded and sewn—then a *karmavācanā* should be performed.
Among them, one bhikṣu should announce in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has bedding and mats that are either too thick, too thin, too light, too heavy, too large, or too small; or they are torn and cannot be mended by cutting and patching, or their borders are frayed and cannot be folded and sewn. He now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for making new bedding and mats."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the formal act (*karmavācanā*) be performed for the sake of the bhikṣu so-and-so to prepare a new sitting mat.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus, the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīyakarman*) is carried out.
"The Sangha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so regarding the making of a new sitting mat; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
This is called a formal act of the Sangha (*saṃghakarma*).
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or matting in the same year that he made a previous one, if he makes it, it is a duṣkṛta;
once it is finished, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
If one makes a bedding mat at any time during its [original] year, and when it has reached two, three, four, five, or six years, one makes a new bedding mat—if one makes it, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, regardless of the year, makes a new bedding or matting, he must discard his old bedding or matting of that same year; if he makes a new one [without discarding the old], it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one makes a bedding or matting at any time during the year, and when it has reached two, three, four, five, or six years of age, one discards the old bedding and makes a new one—if one makes it, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu, in whatever year he makes a new sitting mat, does not discard his old sitting mat in that same year but instead makes another new one—if he makes it, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If, in whatever year one makes a new sitting mat, and upon reaching the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth year, one does not discard the old sitting mat but instead makes another new one—if one makes it, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu makes a bedding or matting in any given year, and in that same year he discards his old bedding or matting—or even if he does not discard it—if he makes a new one, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one makes a bedding mat at any time during its [original] year, and then—whether two, three, four, five, or six years have passed—whether or not the old mat has been discarded, one makes a new bedding mat; if one makes it, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu makes a bedding mat in any given year, and at that same time intends to make a new bedding mat, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
once it is finished, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If one makes bedding at any time during its [original] year, or when it has reached its second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth year, and then wishes to make a new set of bedding, it is all *duṣkṛta*;
once it is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu makes a bedding mat (niṣīdana) in any given year, and in that same year he begins making a new bedding mat which remains unfinished, he must complete it by the second year. When that bhikṣu first began making the bedding mat, he incurred a duṣkṛta;
once it was completed, he incurred a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

If one makes bedding at any point during its [initial] year, and then—upon reaching the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth year—makes a new set of bedding and leaves it unfinished, one must complete it by the seventh year. At the time of first making it, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
once it is completed, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, with regard to a bedding or mat he has previously prepared, should give it to another or perform the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*), [he is at fault].
If a bhikṣu, within six years of a bedding or mat he has already used, whether he has relinquished it or not, makes a new bedding or mat, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The fourteen matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Having returned home, he spent the entire night preparing various pure and abundant, delicious foods. When everything was ready, he prepared seats in the early morning and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; the food is prepared. May the Buddha know the proper time."
The community of bhikṣus went to the house of the lay devotee, while the Buddha remained in his own quarters to await his portion of the food.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when the Saṃgha has accepted an invitation and departed, the Buddha takes the keys and goes from room to room to inspect the various dwellings.

At that time, after the bhikṣus had entered the houses of the lay devotees, the Buddha took his keys and went from room to room to inspect all the quarters. Opening the door of one room, he saw it was filled with discarded bedding and requisites, and the clothes racks were sagging under their weight.

Having seen this, he thought: "There is much of this discarded bedding and requisites no longer in use. Lay brahmins and householders exhaust their own flesh and blood to give as offerings to create merit; it would be well if the bhikṣus were to take only a small amount."
"By what cause and condition can I cause the bhikṣus to use these old sitting cloths, so that the donors who give them may obtain merit?
He further thought:
"I shall now permit the bhikṣus to make new sitting cloths and spread cloths, using one Sugata-span from these old cloths for the border, in order to change their color."
"Because of these causes and conditions, the bedding and mats are put to use, and thus the donors obtain merit.
Having had this thought, the Buddha closed the door, lowered the bolt, and returned to his own room to sit in his original place.

At that time, when the householder saw that the assembly of monks had finished sitting, he personally served water and, having provided them with pure, clean, and abundant delicious food until they were fully satisfied, he knew that the monks had finished washing their hands and putting away their bowls; he then took a small bench and sat before the assembly, desiring to listen to the preaching of the Dharma.

When the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma and departed, the other bhikṣus followed in order and returned to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at his feet and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas, when the community of bhikṣus returns from a meal, to inquire with such words of courtesy:
"Bhikṣus, was the food and drink excellent? Was the Saṃgha satisfied?"
He then greeted them with these words:
"Are the bhikṣus satisfied?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
The food and drink were most delicious, and the assembly of monks was fully satisfied.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"After you, the assembly of monks, have entered the householder's residence, I shall take the keys and inspect all the rooms; upon opening the door of one room, I saw that bedding and mats had been left behind, filling the room, while the clothing racks hung down and were bent."
Having seen this, he thought:

"There are many such discarded bedding materials no longer in use; donors have exhausted their own flesh and blood to give as offerings for the sake of merit. It would be well if the bhikṣus were to take only a small amount."
"How can I cause the bhikṣus to use these old bedding materials so that the donors who give them may obtain merit?
He further thought:
"I shall permit the bhikṣus to make new bedding and sitting mats, using one *śugata-vidattha* (a span of the Sugata) from the old bedding around the perimeter for the purpose of discoloring them."
"Because of these causes and conditions, the donor gains merit by providing bedding and seating that may be used.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must use a portion of an old sitting mat measuring one Sugata-span around its perimeter in order to change its color."

If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat or bedding and does not use a piece from an old mat, measuring one Sugata-span in circumference, to disfigure it for the sake of beauty, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bedding and seating mat must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed. As for the transgression herein:
if a bhikṣu wishes to make a new bedding or seating mat, he should take one Sugata-span from the perimeter of the old bedding or seating mat [to be used] for the purpose of discoloring it.
If one takes [the material] to make it, it is well; if one does not take [the material] to make it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes less than half an inch [of the material], it is an *dukkaṭa*.
If one takes [the old material] to be more than one Sugata-span in length, there is no offense.
If one places an old bedding or sitting mat entirely upon a new bedding or sitting mat, there is no offense.
The fifteenth matter concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling together with merchants through the country of Kośala toward Śrāvastī.
The merchants had loaded their carts to capacity with the wool of rams. Upon reaching a dangerous road, one merchant’s cart axle broke and his oxen’s hooves were wounded.
The merchant said to his companions, "Each of you should carry a small amount of this wool for me; do not let it all be lost.
The merchants replied:
"Our own carts are already fully laden; if we were to carry yours as well, we would surely lose everything.
Thus, all the merchants abandoned them and departed.
The merchants stood to one side, grieving and watching over their carted goods.
The bhikṣus followed after them for two reasons:
first, because their bodies were covered in dust; second, because they did not wish to hear the sound of the carts.
When the merchants saw the bhikṣus approaching from afar, they were delighted and thought to themselves:
"This wool shall certainly not go to waste; I shall use it to make an offering to this community of bhikṣus.
Having formed this thought, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Gather together in one place; I shall offer this wool to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha assembled immediately, and the householder departed after having made his offering.
The bhikṣus each divided the portions; some carried them away on their shoulders, some bore them on their backs, and some held them in their hands as they passed through a large village.
Some merchants who had been traveling ahead saw the bhikṣus carrying the wool approaching; they became envious and rebuked them, saying:
"Where did you buy this wool?"
"To where do you wish to take them for sale?
At what market stall will you sit?
Where do you expect to profit?"
"Is this because they have failed to obtain profit?

Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing these merchants’ reproaches, he was displeased in heart and related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [what had occurred], he intentionally asked the bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“How can a bhikṣu carry wool on his own back for more than three yojanas?
Having thus rebuked them with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu obtains a gift of wool while traveling on a road, and the bhikṣu requires it, he may take it himself and carry it away for up to three yojanas."
If there is no one to carry the burden on his behalf, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If two bhikṣus obtain wool and carry it away, they may go as far as six *yojanas*.
If there are three bhikṣus, they can reach nine yojanas; if there are four bhikṣus, they can reach twelve yojanas; if there are five bhikṣus, they can reach fifteen yojanas.
"In this manner, according to the number of people, one person may [carry] up to three *yojanas*.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the wool must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu carries the wool of a ram himself and travels more than three yojanas, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he causes a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to carry it and they travel more than three yojanas, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu carries the wool of a ram, provided it is placed above the ear, or inside the ear, or below the throat, or made into a felt mat, or placed inside a needle-case or thread-bag while being carried away, there is no offense.
The sixteenth section is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Kālodāyin received his share of previously acquired sheep’s wool; he took it to the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra in Rājaka-ārāma. Having arrived, he had the bhikṣuṇīs assemble in one place and said to them:
"Can you card, comb, wash, and dye this sheep’s wool for me?"
Kāḷudāyin possessed great renown, majesty, power, and influence; because of their reverence and fear of him, the bhikṣuṇīs were unable to oppose him and spoke thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"Just leave it on the ground.
Kāḷudāyin then left it there and departed.
The bhikṣuṇīs took the wool, carded, washed, and dyed it; however, the dye stained their hands.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, departed from the Jeta Grove Monastery and went to where the Buddha was; she prostrated with her head at his feet and stood to one side.
These five hundred bhikṣuṇīs also prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and stood to one side.
Seeing that the hands of the bhikṣuṇīs were stained with dye, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"For what reason do the hands of these bhikṣuṇīs have dye on them?"
Gautamī replied,
“World-Honored One!
What we seek is different, and what we do is different.”
The Buddha said:
"Gautamī, how is it that what you seek is different from what you have done?"
Gautamī related these matters to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said, "What you seek is one thing, but what you do is another.
At that time, the Buddha taught various dharmas to Gautamī and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; having done so, he remained silent.

At that time, the community of Bhikṣuṇīs headed by Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having understood that the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after the Bhikṣuṇīs had left, the Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of Bhikṣus and, though he already knew the answer, deliberately asked Kālodayin:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked Kālodayin with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool?"
Having thus rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "not a relative": a relative refers to one's mother, sisters, daughters, and so forth, up to the seventh generation of kin; anyone other than these is called "not a relative."
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the wool must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu goes and says to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, "Wash, dye, and card wool for me."
If a bhikṣuṇī washes [the robe] for him, the bhikṣu commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If she dyes it, he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If she card it, he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Whether it be washing and dyeing, washing and carding, dyeing and carding, or washing, dyeing, and carding, all constitute an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her:
"Wash, dye, and card for me."
If she washes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she dyes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she beats it, or if she washes and dyes it, or if she washes and beats it, or if she dyes and beats it, or if she washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her,
"Wash, card, and dye this for me," and she washes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she splits it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she washes and dyes it, or washes and splits it, or dyes and splits it, or washes, dyes, and splits it, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her,
"Dye and card this for me,
as if you were washing it," and she washes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one tears it apart, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one dyes it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether one washes and tears it apart, or washes and dyes it, or dyes and tears it apart, or washes, dyes, and tears it apart, in all such cases, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her,
"Wash and dye this for me, but do not card it," and she washes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she dyes it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she splits it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she washes and dyes it, or washes and splits it, or dyes and splits it, or washes, dyes, and splits it, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her:
"Wash and card this for me, but do not dye it," and she washes it for him,
it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If she carded it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she dyed it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she both washed and dyed it, or washed and carded it, or dyed and carded it, or washed, dyed, and carded it, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her,
"Dye and card this for me,
but do not wash it," and the bhikṣuṇī dyes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she tears it apart, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she washes it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she washes and dyes it, or washes and tears it apart, or dyes and tears it apart, or washes, dyes, and tears it apart, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her,
"Wash this for me; do not dye it, and do not card it," and she washes it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether it be dyed, carded, dyed and carded, carded and dyed, or dyed, carded, and washed—all these constitute an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her:
"Dye this for me; do not wash it, and do not card it," and she dyes it for him, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
Whether she washes it, or card it, or washes and dyes it, or washes and cards it, or dyes and cards it, or washes, dyes, and cards it—these all constitute an *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and says to her,
"Split this for me; do not wash it,
do not dye it," and she splits it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether she washes it, dyes it, both washes and dyes it, washes and beats it, dyes and beats it, or both washes, dyes, and beats it, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, yet he considers her to be a relative and instructs her to wash, dye, or card wool;
and if the bhikṣuṇī then washes it, dyes it, or cards it for him, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If there is a nun who is not a relative, and she instructs a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a female renunciant, or a female renunciant nun to wash, dye, or card [her robes].
If one causes [a nun] to wash, dye, or card [wool], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, yet he is uncertain whether she is a relative or not a relative, and he speaks to her, commanding her to wash, dye, or card [the wool].
If one has them washed, dyed, or carded, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one is in doubt as to whether they are a bhikṣu or not a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā or not a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera or not a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī or not a śrāmaṇerī, one who has gone forth or not one who has gone forth, or a bhikṣuṇī or not a bhikṣuṇī, yet speaks to a messenger and tells them to wash, dye, or card [the robe-material].
If one causes [a nun] to wash, dye, or card [wool], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has a relative who is a bhikṣuṇī, yet addresses her as if she were not a relative and instructs her to wash, dye, or card [wool], and she does so for him, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one says that this person is a bhikṣu, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, male renunciant, or female renunciant, and instructs a messenger to wash, dye, or tear [the garment], or if one causes it to be washed, dyed, or torn for them, in all such cases it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, and being uncertain whether she is a relative or not, he tells her to wash, dye, or card [wool] for him;
if she does so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one suspects that a person is a bhikṣu rather than a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā rather than a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera rather than a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī rather than a śrāmaṇerī, an ordained male rather than an ordained male, or an ordained female rather than an ordained female, yet tells a messenger to wash, dye, or card [the robes].
If one causes [a nun] to wash, dye, or card [wool], it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu has a relative or non-relative bhikṣuṇī, and whether he states this or suspects it, he tells her to wash, dye, or card impure wool—namely camel hair, black sheep’s wool, or mixed wool—it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if it concerns a relative.
The seventeen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then the group of six bhikṣus took precious objects with their own hands, and the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, claim for themselves:
‘We are virtuous and of good character.
How is it that they take precious objects with their own hands, like kings or great ministers?”
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu take precious objects with his own hands?
Having thus rebuked him with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu takes treasure with his own hand, or causes another to take it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
"Jewels" refers to gold and silver; these two types may be fashioned or unfashioned, marked or unmarked.
There are five ways of taking them:
taking from another's hand with one's own hand; taking from another's garment-pouch with one's own garment-pouch; taking from another's vessel with one's own vessel; or if one says:
"Put it on this. Or if one says:
"Give it to this *śuddhika-puruṣa* (pure person)."
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika. Regarding "naiḥsargika-pāyattika":
this object must be relinquished, and the pāyattika offense must be confessed.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu takes from hand to hand, from robe to robe, or from vessel to vessel, or says:
"Put it on this. Or if one says:
"Give it to this *śuddhika-puruṣa* (pure person)."
In all such cases, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Whether the act has been performed or not, whether there is a sign or no sign, if one takes [the item] from another, it is in every case a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu takes iron coins with his own hand, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he takes copper coins, white tin coins, lead and tin coins, resin coins, leather coins, or wooden coins, all are duṣkṛta offenses.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu takes treasure with his own hand, if it is a small amount, he should discard it.
If it is a large amount, even if he obtains a trustworthy lay attendant (kappiyakāraka), he should say to that person:..."
"I must not take this treasure because it is impure; you should take it.
After the attendant had taken the treasure, he said to the bhikṣu, "This object is for the bhikṣu."
The bhikṣu says:
"This is an impure object; if it were pure, I would accept it.
If he cannot find a fellow practitioner to purify it through shared consent, he should use it as bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions.
That bhikṣu should enter the Saṃgha and say:
"Venerable sirs!
I personally took precious objects with my own hands and thereby incurred a pāyattika offense; I now confess it openly, without concealment, and repent."
The Saṃgha should ask that bhikṣu:
"Have you renounced this treasure?
He should answer:
"Once it has been relinquished," the Sangha should ask:
"Do you see your offense?"
He should reply:
"I see my transgression.
The Saṃgha should then say to him:
"Reveal your transgression and repent; do not commit it again in the future.
If he says, "I have not yet relinquished it," [the procedure continues].
The Saṃgha should issue an injunction ordering him to relinquish it.
If the Saṃgha does not issue such an injunction, all members of the Saṃgha incur a duṣkṛta offense.
If the Saṃgha issues the injunction and he still does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
"If one has deliberated but not yet reached a decision, there is no offense.
The eighteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

Then the group of six bhikṣus took the treasures they had previously relinquished and put them to various uses: they caused dwellings to be built and established gold shops, shops for hired labor, shops for smelting copper, and shops for treating pearls; they maintained herds of elephants, horses, camels, cattle, donkeys, and sheep, as well as male and female slaves, apprentices, and commoners. Among these people, some forcibly seized the fields and property of others and sold them to the bhikṣus.
Those who had lost their livelihoods became angry and reproached him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
They used various kinds of jewels to construct market stalls for buying and selling, no different from those of kings or high ministers.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“What is meant by a bhikṣu using various kinds of precious objects?
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.”

From now on, this precept should be stated as follows: "If a bhikṣu uses various kinds of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. "Various kinds" refers to: using [an object] to exchange for something that can be made; using [it] to exchange for something that cannot be made;

using [it] to exchange for something that can be made but not something that cannot be made; using [it] to exchange for something that cannot be made and cannot be made; using [it] to exchange for something that cannot be made but can be made; using [it] to exchange for something that cannot be made, can be made, and cannot be made; using [it] to exchange a sign for a sign; using [it] to exchange a sign for a non-sign; using [it] to exchange a sign for a sign and a non-sign; using [it] to exchange a non-sign for a non-sign; using [it] to exchange a non-sign for a sign; using [it] to exchange a non-sign for a sign and a non-sign. These are called "various kinds."
There are five kinds of usage:
namely, if one says,
"Take this object," "Take from within this," "Take that much," "Take from this person," or "Bring it here and take it away."
Buying and selling are also like this.
Furthermore, there are five types:
taking that object, taking from among those, taking a certain amount, taking from that person, and carrying it here and there; buying and selling are also like this.
This object refers to gold or silver.
Taking from it means taking either hemp or *koseya* silk.
Taking such an amount means taking either fifty or one hundred [units].
"Taking from such a person" means taking from a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite; the same applies to carrying it away, bringing it back, selling it, or buying it.
"Taking that object" refers to whether it be gold or silver.
Regarding "taking from among them": it means taking either *kuśa* grass or *kusa* grass.
Regarding "taking so much": it means taking either fifty or one hundred.
"Taking from that person" means taking from a man, a woman, a *paṇḍaka*, or a person with both sexual organs; the same applies to bringing it, carrying it away, selling it, or buying it.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this object must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu uses what has been made for exchange with what has been made, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If he uses what has been made for exchange with what has not been made; if he uses what has been made for exchange with what has been made and what has not been made; if he uses what has not been made for exchange with what has not been made; if he uses what has not been made for exchange with what has been made; or if he uses what has not been made for exchange with what has been made and what has not been made—in all these cases, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Whether one exchanges a formal mark for a formal mark, or exchanges a formal mark for a non-formal mark, or exchanges a formal mark for both a formal and a non-formal mark; or whether one exchanges a non-formal mark for a non-formal mark, or exchanges a non-formal mark for a formal mark, or exchanges a non-formal mark for both a formal and a non-formal mark—in all such cases, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one says,
"Take this," it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes from among these, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes that much, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes from this person, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
