The same applies to carrying [something] here or there, or buying and selling it.
If one says: "Take that."
This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says:
"I took it from among those," or "I took that much," or "I took it from that person."
In all such cases, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to carrying [the items] back and forth or buying and selling them.
If a bhikṣu uses iron coins for various purposes, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Using copper coins, white tin coins, lead-tin coins, resin coins, leather coins, or wooden coins for various purposes—all constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If a bhikṣu uses various kinds of precious objects, if they are few, he should discard them; if they are many, even if he obtains a trustworthy lay attendant (śucipuruṣa), he should say to that person:
"Because these are impure, I should not take them; you should take them."
After the attendant had taken these items, he said to the bhikṣu,
"These items are for the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu said:
"This is an impure object; if it were pure, it should be accepted.
If one cannot find a person of like mind to perform the purification, it should be used as bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions.
That bhikṣu should enter the saṃgha and say:
"Venerable sirs!
Regarding various articles of use, I have committed an offense of pāyattika; I now confess it openly, without concealment, and repent."
The Sangha should ask:
"Will you relinquish this object?
He should reply:
"Once it has been relinquished," one should ask:
"Do you see your offense?"
He replied,
"I see my transgression.
The Sangha should say:
"Reveal and repent of your offense; do not commit it again in the future.
If he says, "I have not relinquished it," [the procedure continues].
The Saṃgha should issue a formal admonition to make him relinquish it.
If the Saṃgha does not issue this admonition, all members of the Saṃgha incur a duṣkṛta offense.
If the Saṃgha has issued the admonition and he still does not relinquish it, that bhikṣu incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one has deliberated but not yet reached a decision, there is no offense.
The nineteenth matter is concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a certain brahmin who wore a *kambala* dyed with *cāmīlura* [safflower]; he was an old acquaintance and associate of the Śākya son Upananda.
At that time, Baddhālī saw from afar a brahmin approaching, wearing a *kambala* robe dyed with *cāmīlī* pigment. Upon seeing this garment, he conceived a mind of covetous attachment.
When the brahmin reached Baddhālī’s location, they exchanged greetings and inquiries regarding their well-being, and the brahmin sat down to one side.
Bhadanta said to the brahmin,
"Your *kambala* is beautiful and lovely.
He replied:
"It is indeed excellent," said Upananda. "Give it to me;
I shall take this *kambala* and give it to you."
The brahmin said,
"I myself have need of it.
Upananda spoke again:
"You who follow the dharma of a brahmin are naked and devoid of virtue; what use have you for fine clothing?
The brahmin replied, "I need them for lying down."
Bhadanta again said:

"In the past, when we were laypeople, you were my close friend and we cherished one another deeply. There was nothing of value I possessed that I did not give to you, and there was likewise nothing of value you possessed that you did not give to me."
"Now that you have gone forth as a renunciant, do you harbor thoughts of stinginess and greed, such that you are no better than before?
After Upāli had thus rebuked and censured him with severity, the brahmin immediately took off his saffron-dyed *kambala* cloak and gave it to Upāli.
Bhadrananda returned the *kaṃcilaka* to the brahmin; the brahmin put on the *kaṃcilaka* and went to the brahmin monastery.
When the brahmins saw him, they said:
"Did you go away after dyeing your *kaṃcilaka* Mount Sumeru?"
He replied,
"I traded it away with another.
[The other asked,] "With whom did you trade it?"
He replied,
"I gave it to Baddhananda.
[The other asked,] "What connection do you have with Baddhananda that you would trade with him?"
He replied,
"When I was formerly a layman, because my virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) loved and cherished me deeply,
we traded together. The brahmins said:
“Bānaṃda the Śākya son has teased and deceived you.
The brahmin said,
“Whether he teased me or deceived me, I have already made my exchange with him.”
The brahmins spoke again:
"This dyed *kambala* from Mount Meru is of great value; it cannot be compared to ordinary *kambalas*.
Thus spoke those brahmins.
"Though it was of great value, I have already traded for it.
The Brahmins spoke again:
"Go quickly and fetch those *kṣaumī* saffron-dyed *kārpāsa* cloths; do not let us stand upon wooden planks while we punish you!"
At that moment, the brahmin was struck with fear and thought to himself:
"My fellow students might perhaps set up a wooden board to punish me.
He then went to the place where the Śākya son Upananda was and spoke these words:
"Upananda! Return my cīra-kambala dyed with *cimi-lou*; this kambala shall be returned to you.
Upananda said:
"The exchange is already complete," said the brahmin.
"You have deceived me!"
"Deceive me! Baddhananda replied,
"Even if it were a deception, once the trade is concluded, it is final."
The brahmin spoke again:
"This dyed *kambala* cloth from Mount Meru is of great value; it cannot be compared to your ordinary *kambala*.
He replied:
"Whether the price is high or not, the transaction is already settled.
He spoke again: "Upananda!"
My fellow students said:
"If you do not return the saffron-colored *kambala* cloth from Mount Meru, we shall set up a wooden board to punish you.
You must return it to me; do not let my fellow students set up a wooden board to punish me.
Bhadanta said, "Whether you are punished by having a wooden board placed upon you or subjected to some other form of punishment, what concern is that of mine?
The transaction is already finalized; I will never give it to you."
The brahmin searched urgently but could not find it.
Those who did not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma, hearing of this matter, rebuked him out of envy, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"How excellent and virtuous you are!
[they said]. "How can one who is called a renunciant deceive and provoke other renunciants?
Those who possessed faith likewise rebuked him.
"What is it to call a bhikṣu one who engages in various kinds of buying and selling?
Among them, there was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, his heart was displeased, and he related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Upananda: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can a bhikṣu engage in various kinds of buying and selling?
Having rebuked them in this way, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding "various kinds": it refers to either exchanging similar goods for similar goods, or exchanging dissimilar goods for dissimilar goods.

Regarding "similar": an alms-bowl is similar to an alms-bowl; a robe is similar to a robe; a water vessel is similar to a water vessel; a door-latch is similar to a door-latch; a medicine for the daytime is similar to a medicine for the daytime; a medicine for the night-watch is similar to a medicine for the night-watch; a seven-day medicine is similar to a seven-day medicine; and a lifetime medicine is similar to a lifetime medicine. This is called purchasing the similar with the similar.

Regarding "dissimilar": the bowl is dissimilar to the robe; the bowl is dissimilar to the bathing vessel, the door-bolt, the medicine for the current time, the medicine for the night period, the seven-day medicine, and the lifetime medicine.

The robe is not similar to the washing vessel; nor is it similar to the door-bolt, the *kṣaṇika* (momentary) medicine, the *yāmika* (night-time) medicine, the *saptāhika* (seven-day) medicine, the *yāvajjīvika* (lifetime) medicine, or the bowl.
The washing vessel is not similar to the door-bolt; nor is it similar to the *kṣaṇika* medicine, the *yāmika* medicine, the *saptāhika* medicine, the *yāvajjīvika* medicine, the bowl, or the robe.

The door-hook is not similar to the medicines taken at the proper time; it is not similar to the medicines for the night, the seven-day medicines, the lifetime medicines, nor to the bowl, the robes, or the washing vessel.
The *tatkṣaṇika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the immediate moment) and the *yāmika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the watch of the night), up to the *kuñcikā* (key/door-bolt), are not similar.
The *yāmika-bhaiṣajya* and the *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (seven-day medicines) are not similar, up to the point where they are not similar to the *tatkṣaṇika-bhaiṣajya*.
Seven-day medicines are not similar to lifetime medicines, nor even to night-time medicines.
Lifetime medicines are not similar to alms bowls, nor even to seven-day medicines.
Therefore, it is said that to purchase dissimilar goods with dissimilar means constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the object must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu, for the sake of profit, buys something but does not sell it, it is a duṣkṛta.
If, for the sake of profit, he sells something but does not buy it, it is likewise a duṣkṛta.
If, for the sake of profit, one buys something and then sells it again, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu uses an item that should be relinquished to buy silver with gold, uses silver to buy coins, uses coins to purchase grain, or uses grain to buy goods—if these goods are edible, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for every mouthful consumed.
If these items can be made into clothing, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense upon wearing them.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit that if items are exchanged between people and the former person regrets their mind, they should return them; one may then take back one's own original item."

At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted the mutual exchange of goods, they felt regret and thought they should return the items and take back their own. Having heard this, they continued to wear the clothes of others for half a month or a full month until they became worn and faded in color, and only then did they seek to have them returned.
When he requested a withdrawal of the offense, the other would not grant it; consequently, disputes arose, and they began to argue, revile, and strike one another.
The monks reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"If the request for withdrawal is made within seven days, it should be granted; if more than seven days have passed, it should not be granted."
There was a cloth merchant who was walking about selling clothes. The group of six bhikṣus sought a high-priced garment from him for a small price.
The cloth merchant said, "For what reason do you seek my expensive garment at such a low price?"
"If those who do not know the price of the robe were to undervalue my robe, they would diminish its value.
The Buddha said, "One should not request a costly robe from another by offering a reduced price; if one requests a costly robe from another by offering a reduced price, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If one truly requires these items, one should deliberate carefully and say:
"I will purchase them for such-and-such an amount.
If the other person does not give them, one should speak to them again.
If he still does not give it, one should speak three times.
If, after being asked three times, he still does not give it and the bhikṣu urgently requires this object, he should seek out a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") and have them purchase this object.
If the attendant (kappiyakāraka) does not know the market price, the bhikṣu should first instruct him, saying: "Purchase this item with such-and-such an amount of goods.
He should further instruct him: "Inquire as to how much this item costs, and consider it well."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the selling of robes within the community of monks; before the threefold proclamation has been made, the price may be increased.
At the time of increasing the price, a bhikṣu felt regret.
"Will I not be depriving him of his robe?
The Buddha said:
"If the three proclamations have not yet concluded, it is no offense to increase the price."
If a bhikṣu, for the sake of profit, engages in various kinds of buying and selling using iron coins, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of profit, uses copper coins, white tin coins, lead and tin coins, resin coins, leather coins, or wooden coins for various kinds of buying and selling, in all such cases it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If this bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, he should discard whatever is small in quantity.
If it is large in quantity, even if he finds a trustworthy person (kappiyakāraka), he should say to that person:
"I must not accept these things due to such-and-such causes and conditions; you should take them."
The attendant said to the bhikṣu,
"This object is for the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu said:
"This is an impure object; if it were pure, it should be accepted.
If one cannot find a person of like mind to perform the ritual of purification (*cittavisaṃvādana*), it should be used as bedding for the Saṅgha of the four directions.
That bhikṣu should enter the Saṃgha and say:
"Venerable sirs!
I have committed the pāyattika offense by engaging in various acts of buying and selling."
"I now confess this fault openly and without concealment.
The Sangha should ask:
"Have you relinquished these objects?"
He replies, “I have relinquished it.
The Saṃgha should then ask:
"Do you see your transgression?
He replied,
"I see my transgression."
The Saṃgha should say:
"Now that you have confessed, not concealed, and repented your transgression, do not commit it again. If he says:
"If he has not relinquished it,
the Saṃgha should issue a formal command to make him relinquish it.
If the Saṃgha does not issue such a command, all members of the Saṃgha incur a duṣkṛta offense."
If the Sangha issues a formal injunction and he does not relinquish [the object], that bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he sells it at a low price here and a high price there, even if there is a profit, he does not commit an offense, because his original intention was not for the sake of profit.
The twenty matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then the group of six bhikṣus kept many alms bowls; they accumulated them until they became stained and damaged, yet they did not use them for this reason.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who accumulates many alms bowls, allowing them to become soiled and broken while never using them?"
Having thus rebuked him, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who keeps many alms bowls, accumulating them until they become stained and ruined for no purpose?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl, it may be kept for up to ten days; if he keeps it beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the bowl, there are three types:
superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the "superior bowl": one receives three *pātra* of rice, one *pātra* of soup, and half a *pātra* of other edible food; this is called the superior bowl. Regarding the "inferior bowl":
one receives one *pātra* of rice, half a *pātra* of soup, and half a *pātra* of other edible food; this is called the inferior bowl.
If it is of another size, it is called a medium bowl.
If it is larger than a large bowl or smaller than a small bowl, it is not called a bowl. Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*:
[it refers to the forfeiture and confession required for possessing such an improper bowl].

This bowl must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed. Regarding the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and keeps it for a second day before relinquishing it;

obtains one on the second day and keeps it for a third day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the third day and keeps it for a fourth day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the fourth day and keeps it for a fifth day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the fifth day and keeps it for a sixth day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the sixth day and keeps it for a seventh day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the seventh day and keeps it for an eighth day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the eighth day and keeps it for a ninth day before relinquishing it; obtains one on the ninth day and keeps it for a tenth day before relinquishing it; and obtains one on the tenth day and keeps it—on the tenth day, this bowl should be given to another, or rendered pure (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own. If he does not give it to another, does not render it pure, and does not formally accept it, then when the night of the eleventh day ends, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains another on the second day, he may keep one and discard the other.
If he obtains one on the second day and obtains another on the third day, he may keep one and discard the other.
If one obtains [an item] on the third day and obtains another on the fourth day, one may keep one and discard the other.
If one obtains it on the fourth day and obtains another on the fifth day, one may keep one and discard the other.
If one obtains it on the fifth day and obtains another on the sixth day, one may keep one and discard the other.
If one obtains [an item] on the sixth day and obtains another on the seventh day, one may keep one and discard the other.
If one obtains it on the seventh day and obtains another on the eighth day, one may keep one and discard the other.
If one obtains it on the eighth day and obtains another on the ninth day, one may keep one and discard the other.

If one obtains [a bowl] on the ninth day and obtains another on the tenth day, that bowl must, by the time of the tenth day, be given to another, purified (*pariśuddha*), or formally accepted as one's own (*parigṛhīta*). If it is not given to another, not purified, and not formally accepted, then at the end of the eleventh day, there is an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an alms-bowl on the first day and obtains another on the second day, he keeps the latter and discards the former.
If he obtains one on the second day and obtains another on the third day, he keeps the latter and discards the former.
Having obtained [the robe] on the third day, one obtains it again on the fourth day; one keeps the latter and discards the former.
Having obtained it on the fourth day, one obtains it again on the fifth day; one keeps the latter and discards the former.
Having obtained it on the fifth day, one obtains it again on the sixth day; one keeps the latter and discards the former.
If one obtains [an item] on the sixth day and again obtains one on the seventh day, one retains the latter and discards the former.
If one obtains it on the seventh day and again obtains one on the eighth day, one retains the latter and discards the former.
If one obtains it on the eighth day and again obtains one on the ninth day, one retains the latter and discards the former.

If on the ninth day one obtains a bowl, and on the tenth day obtains another, then at the time of the tenth day, all these bowls must be given away, purified, or formally accepted as one's own. If they are not given away, not purified, and not formally accepted, then by the end of the tenth day, at the conclusion of the day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu obtains an alms-bowl on the first day and obtains another on the second day, he keeps the former and discards the latter.
If he obtains one on the second day and obtains another on the third day, he keeps the former and discards the latter.
If one obtains [an item] on the third day and again on the fourth day, one keeps the former and discards the latter.
If one obtains it on the fourth day and again on the fifth day, one keeps the former and discards the latter.
If one obtains it on the fifth day and again on the sixth day, one keeps the former and discards the latter.
If one obtains [an item] on the sixth day and again obtains one on the seventh day, one may keep the former and discard the latter.
If one obtains it on the seventh day and again obtains one on the eighth day, one may keep the former and discard the latter.
If one obtains it on the eighth day and again obtains one on the ninth day, one may keep the former and discard the latter.

If one obtains a bowl on the ninth day and subsequently obtains another on the tenth day, that bowl must, by the end of the tenth day, be given away, purified, or formally accepted as one's own. If it is not given away, not purified, and not formally accepted, then when the night of the eleventh day ends, there is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu acquires a bowl on the first day and does not acquire one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day, that bowl must, at the end of the tenth day, be given to another, purified, or formally accepted as his own. If he does not give it away, purify it, or accept it as his own, then at the conclusion of the eleventh day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu acquires a bowl on the first day and keeps it, and then acquires another on the second day, and continues to acquire others on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth days, then at the end of those ten days, he must give away all these bowls, perform the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi), or formally take possession of them. If he does not give them away, does not perform the ritual of purification, and does not take formal possession of them, then at the conclusion of the eleventh day, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).

If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that he should have relinquished but has not yet relinquished, and whose offense he has not yet confessed, and while this continuity has not been severed he obtains another bowl, this subsequent bowl constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense due to the circumstances of the original bowl.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has already relinquished his bowl, but the offense has not yet been confessed and the continuity of the transgression has not been severed, and he subsequently obtains another bowl,
that later bowl constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense due to the circumstances of the original bowl.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has already relinquished a bowl that was subject to relinquishment, has already confessed his offense, and subsequently obtains another bowl before the continuity of the transgression has been severed, this later bowl constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense due to the circumstances of the original bowl.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has a bowl that ought to be discarded and has already discarded it, has already confessed his offense, and has already severed the continuity [of the possession], and he subsequently obtains another bowl, there is no offense.
The twenty-one cases are concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Seven.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Eight. Part Two of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Part Four of the Explanation of the Thirty *Niḥsargika* Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was walking along a market street with a young merchant when he saw a fine earthen bowl on a stall—perfectly round, upright, and lovely. Having seen it, he became greedily attached to it and said to the young merchant, "Look at this earthen bowl;
it is perfectly round, upright, and lovely."
He replied, "It is truly so.
The merchant's son said:
"Must you do so? He replied, "I wish to."
He then purchased it and gave it to him.
Having received this bowl, the Śākya son Upananda went out from the city of Śrāvastī into the Jeta Grove and showed it to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable elders!..."
"You all look at this earthen bowl; it is perfectly round and lovely.
The bhikṣus said, "It is indeed excellent!"
“From whom did you obtain it?
Vāḍananda related this matter in detail to the bhikṣus, who asked:
“Did you previously have a bowl that you used?”
He replied,
"It existed previously.
He spoke again:
"What is the use of this bowl?
He replied, "It existed before and it exists now; what harm is there in that?"
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured him for various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu first use an existing bowl and then beg for a new one?"
Having rebuked him in various ways, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the Śākya son Upananda:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, "I indeed did,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu first use an almsbowl he already possesses and then beg for a new one?
Having rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken and has fewer than five mends, yet he begs for a new bowl for the sake of its beauty, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
This bowl should be relinquished among the community of monks; the lowest bowl in this assembly should be given to this bhikṣu, and he should be instructed as follows:
"Bhikṣu, you shall keep this bowl until it breaks; such is the proper course of action."
"As for the bowl used, it is the alms-bowl previously received for use.
There are three types of bowls:
superior, middling, and inferior."

The superior [portion] consists of receiving three *pātra* of rice, one *pātra* of soup, and the remaining edible food equal to half a *pātra* of soup; this is called the superior bowl (*uttama-pātra*).
The inferior bowl consists of receiving one *pātra* of rice, half a *pātra* of soup, and the remaining edible food equal to half a *pātra* of soup; this is called the inferior bowl (*hīna-pātra*).
The remainder is called a medium bowl.
Anything larger than the large or smaller than the small is not designated as a bowl.
"Reduced by five patches" refers to those with four, three, two, or one patch.
One who is fond of such things is a bhikṣu who is difficult to satisfy and difficult to support, because he lacks contentment and has few desires.
This bowl should be relinquished before the community of bhikṣus; it should be filled with water and circulated among the Saṃgha, while this proclamation is made:
"Venerable sirs, assemble!
"Now we wish to prepare a bowl filled with water.
At that time, the bhikṣus should immediately each bring the bowl they have been using and assemble at one place; at this moment, the bhikṣus must not accept any other bowls.
If any bhikṣus at this time should receive another bowl, they incur a duṣkṛta offense.
Once the Saṃgha has reached harmony, one should first perform the *karman* for the person who distributes the bowls filled with water; one bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Who is able to carry out this task of filling the bowl with water?
If a bhikṣu says, "I can."
"If a bhikṣu is possessed of five unwholesome qualities, he should not be appointed as the person who distributes the alms-bowls.
What are these five unwholesome qualities?
Acting out of desire, acting out of hatred, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and not knowing what should or should not be done."

If one has accomplished the five wholesome qualities, they should be appointed as the distributor of alms bowls; being free from desire, hatred, fear, and delusion, and knowing what should and should not be done, such a bhikṣu should be made the distributor of alms bowls.
Thereupon, one bhikṣu immediately proclaimed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so is capable of acting as the person who prepares the bowl of water for the ritual."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the monk so-and-so act as the person who prepares the bowl of water for the procession.
Thus is the motion (*jñapti*) made.
In this manner, the formal procedure of two motions and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is performed.
“The Saṃgha has now authorized monk so-and-so to serve as the water-bowl carrier for the procession; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
If that monk serves as the water-bowl carrier for the procession, he should fill the bowl with water and first go to the foremost senior monk (sthavira), asking:
“Does the Elder require this bowl?”
If the senior monk says,
"I need it," one should give it to the senior monk.
This person should take the bowl of the senior monk and proceed; arriving next at the place of the second senior monk, he asks:
"Do you need this bowl?
If [the monk] says:
“Give it. It should be given.

Furthermore, one should take the bowl of the second senior monk and ask the third senior monk; when asking the third senior monk, if the first senior monk feels regret and seeks his own bowl back, the Buddha said:
"One should not give it.
If the senior monk (upādhyāya) forcibly takes it, one should take it back and instruct the senior monk to perform the *duṣkṛta* confession.
If the foremost senior monk does not take it, it should be distributed in order to everyone.
If the bowl filled with water remains unclaimed by anyone, it should be returned to that bhikṣu.
If someone takes this bowl, one should take that person's bowl and proceed to distribute it in turn throughout the assembly.
If there is no one to take this bowl, then give it to that bhikṣu,
instructing him as follows:
"Keep this bowl until it breaks."

Do not set it on the ground; do not set it on a stone; do not set it in a high place; do not set it where the roof leaks; do not set it on a mound of earth. One should not carry it to places for defecation or urination; one should not carry it into the bathhouse; one should not wash it with sand or cow dung. If the bowl is wet, one should not lift it immediately; one should not let it become too dry. One should not intentionally break it, nor should one use it to wash one's hands or face.
"Guard it well; do not seek after [other things] on account of this broken bowl, thereby obstructing and abandoning your sitting meditation, recitation of the scriptures, and practice of the Path.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bowl should be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense should be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu’s bowl is not yet broken, he should not further beg for a new bowl.
If he begs and obtains one, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he does not obtain one, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken such that it can be mended with a single patch, whether it has been patched or not yet patched, he should not seek another.
If he seeks one and obtains it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he does not obtain one, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken and can be mended two, three, or four times, whether it has already been mended or not yet mended, he should not seek another.
If he seeks one and obtains it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he does not obtain one, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu’s bowl has five cracks that can be mended, whether it has been mended or not, he may request a new bowl; whether he obtains one or not, there is no offense.
The twenty-two matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus begged for thread themselves and took it to the houses of wealthy people, saying:
"O village headmen, have the weavers weave robes for us."
Those nobles then said to the weaver, "Weave a robe for this bhikṣu; we shall give you the payment.
Relying on the residence of these nobles, the weaver was unable to refuse them out of fear and respect.
However, while weaving the robe, he became angry and rebuked him, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas claim for themselves:
'We are good and virtuous. "
"Relying upon this noble person has caused us to labor in vain; we have neither food nor wages, nor do we share in the merit or the kindness.
This is our decline, affliction, and loss of profit, for we have encountered one who is difficult to satisfy and difficult to support—a man of few desires yet lacking in contentment."
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this reproach, his heart was displeased, and he related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu beg for thread and have a weaver who is not a relative weave a robe?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu personally begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Personally begs" means he may obtain fifty *pala*, or a hundred *pala*, or even as much as one *liang*.
"Threads" refers to hemp threads, wool threads, kusha-grass threads, or cotton threads.

"Non-relatives": relatives are defined as parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, and so forth, including those connected by lineage up to the seventh generation; anyone other than these is called a non-relative.
The "weaver" refers to a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a person with dual sexual organs.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this object must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu asks a relative for thread, and then has that relative weave it, weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it.
In this regard, there is no offense in begging from one's own relatives; there is likewise no offense in having a relative weave [the cloth].
However, if one weaves it oneself, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it, in all such cases one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu requests thread from a relative and has a non-relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it.
In this regard, begging from one's own relatives is not an offense.
However, if one causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave [the cloth], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one weaves it oneself, or causes a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to weave it, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu asks a relative for thread and has it woven by a relative or a non-relative, or weaves it himself, or has it woven by a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī.
In this regard, begging from one's own relatives is not an offense; having a relative weave [the cloth] is also not an offense.
Having someone who is not a relative weave it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
To weave it oneself, or to cause a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to weave it, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.

If a bhikṣu asks for thread from one who is not a relative and then has that non-relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or causes a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to weave it [from that thread], [he commits an offense].
In this regard, to beg for thread from one who is not a relative is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To have one who is not a relative weave it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
To weave it oneself, or to have a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all such cases.
If a bhikṣu solicits thread from one who is not a relative and has a relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it.
In this regard, to beg for thread from one who is not a relative is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To have a relative weave it is not an offense.
To weave it oneself, or to have a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it, is in all cases a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu asks for thread from one who is not a relative and has a relative or a non-relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it.
In this regard, to beg for thread from one who is not a relative is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To have someone who is not a relative weave it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
To have someone who is a relative weave it is not an offense.
To weave it oneself, or to have a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it, constitutes a duṣkṛta offense in all cases.

If a bhikṣu requests thread from a relative or a non-relative, and has a relative or a non-relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it.
In this regard, begging from one's own relatives is not an offense;
begging from those who are not relatives is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
Having a relative weave [the cloth] is not an offense.
If one causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave [a robe], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one weaves it oneself, or causes a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to weave it, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu asks for thread from a relative or a non-relative, and has a relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it; [he incurs an offense].
In this regard, if one begs from a relative, there is no offense.
If one begs from a non-relative, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes a relative to weave [the cloth], there is no offense.
To weave it oneself, or to have a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
If a bhikṣu begs for thread from a relative or a non-relative, and then has a non-relative weave it, or weaves it himself, or has a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī weave it.
In this regard, begging from a relative is not an offense;
begging from one who is not a relative is a *duṣkṛta*.
Causing one who is not a relative to weave [a robe] is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
To weave oneself, or to cause a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to weave, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
There is no offense if one weaves a single *pāṭali* (a small cloth), or weaves a meditation belt or a waistband, or weaves only once or twice on the loom.
The twenty-three matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who, for the sake of the Śākya son Upananda, had a weaver weave a robe.
When Bāḷhika heard of this matter, he went to the weaver and said: "Do you know?

This robe is being woven for me; weave it well, weave it wide, weave it most excellently, and weave it with great purity. I shall provide you with some benefit—whether food, or food-like provisions, or the price of food."
The weavers said,
"Venerable Sir!
We study this for the sake of gaining profit."
"If you give me even a small amount of profit, I shall weave for you well, weave extensively, weave most excellently,
and weave with great purity. Upananda said, "Excellent!"
Then the weaver wove it well, wove it broadly, wove it most excellently, and wove it with great purity, using a great deal of warp and woof.
When the householder awoke, he said to the weaver,
"Why have you used so much warp and woof?"
The weaver replied, "I have neither reduced nor stolen anything; once the weaving was finished, we weighed it together.
Because this robe was woven well, woven broadly, woven with great excellence, and woven with such purity, much warp and woof was consumed."
The householder said,
"Who instructed you to weave it in this manner?
The weaver replied:
"Vāḷananda, son of the Śākyas.
The householder said,
"Just weave this well."
The householder took the thread he had previously prepared and used twice or even three times as much before the robe could be completed.
Once it was given to the Śākya son Upananda, the householder rebuked him in anger:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"It is excellent and meritorious.
Why then are you unable to know the proper time and the proper measure?
If the donor does not know the measure, the recipient should know it.
"The thread I previously prepared has had to be used three times over before we could finally complete this robe.
This is our misfortune and loss; how can we offer it to one who is so difficult to satisfy and difficult to nourish, who knows no contentment, and who desires nothing less than much?"
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this layman’s reproach, he was displeased in heart and reported it extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Upāli (Vaddhananda) intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked Upananda with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu agree to act for a person who is not a relative?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, on behalf of a bhikṣu, employs a weaver to weave a robe, and that bhikṣu, having not been previously invited, goes to the weaver and says:'"
"Do you know? This robe has been woven for my sake;
weave it well, weave it very well, weave it wide, and weave it cleanly, and I shall give you some extra compensation."
If that bhikṣu, whether speaking himself or causing another to speak, subsequently provides food or the price for food for the sake of its quality, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"As for 'a bhikṣu,' it refers to Vāḷananda, the son of the Śākyas.

As for 'one who is not a relative,' a relative is defined as one's father, mother, brothers, sisters, sons, or daughters, extending even to the seventh generation of kinship; anyone other than these is called a non-relative."
Regarding "laymen and laywomen": a white-robed man is called a layman (*gṛhapati*), and a white-robed woman is called a laywoman (*gṛhapatnī*).
Regarding "weavers": this includes men, women, eunuchs, and those with both sexual organs.
"Clothing" refers to garments made of white hemp, red hemp, *kṣauma* silk, *kōsama* (flax), *kauśeya* silk, *kambala* wool, and *kārpāsa* cotton.
"Previously uninvited" means that the householder has not previously said,
"If you have anything needed, come and take it.
To act as if one has given consent means to trust that the householder will not be angry with whatever one requires.
To the weaver who is skilled at weaving, he says, "Weave gradually.
To the one who weaves broadly, he says, "Weave as widely as possible.
To the one who weaves with great skill, he says, "Weave with fine, dense texture."
"Purely woven" means having it woven by those who are well-purified and clean.
"Giving food or what resembles food": as for "food," there are five kinds, namely:
boiled rice, parched grain flour, roasted grain flour, fish, and meat.
There are five kinds of food that resemble [actual] food:
namely, rice gruel, millet, parched barley, wild grass seeds, and *kaśa* seeds.
As for the value of the food, it refers to the price required to purchase such foodstuffs.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu goes to a weaver and says, "Weave this robe for my sake;
weave it well, and I shall provide you with some small benefit."
This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Weave it wide; we shall give you more [material]."
This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says,
"Weave it very well, and we shall give you some extra [payment]," [it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*].
This is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he says:
"Weave it cleanly; I shall give you a small amount as an extra."
This is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he says:
"Weave it well and weave it wide; I shall give you a small or large amount of extra [payment]," [it is likewise an offense].
This is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says, "Weave it well;
weave it very well," [it is likewise].
If one says:
"Weave well; weave cleanly.
Or if one says:
"Extensively woven, exquisitely woven.
Or if one says:
"Extensively woven, purely woven."
If one says,
"Weave it very well and weave it cleanly; we shall give you a small amount as a benefit," in all such cases,
it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says:
"It is well-woven, broadly woven, and exquisitely woven.
Or if one says:
“Woven well, woven broadly, and woven cleanly. If he says:
“It is woven broadly, woven excellently, and woven cleanly; I shall give you a certain amount more.”
In all such cases, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Weave it well, weave it wide, weave it very finely, and weave it cleanly; I shall give you some extra [payment]," [it is likewise].
"In all such cases, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu goes to a weaver and says:
'Do you know [this]?'..."
"This robe is being woven for me; do not take pleasure in weaving it, and I shall perhaps give you some small benefit.
If a bhikṣu [speaks thus], he incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu goes to a weaver and says,
"Weave this robe for me; do not weave it wide, or perhaps you will receive a little more," it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says,
"Do not weave it too well; perhaps I will give you a little more," it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says,
"Do not clean the weaving, or I shall give you a small or large amount as a benefit," it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave extensively.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave excessively well.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave cleanly."
If one says:
"Do not weave extensively;
do not weave with extreme excellence."
If one says:
"Do not weave it extensively; do not weave it finely.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave it too finely, nor weave it too cleanly; perhaps this will benefit you slightly.
These are all *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
If one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave extensively; do not weave with extreme care.
Or if one says: "Do not weave well;
do not weave extensively; do not weave cleanly."
If one says:
"Do not weave it extensively; do not weave it with extreme care; do not weave it so cleanly;
[otherwise] you will receive only a small amount of benefit," in each case it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave extensively; do not weave with extreme care; do not weave cleanly;
[rather] give me a little more," it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went to a weaver and said: "Do you know?
This robe is being woven for me; weave it well, and I shall give you no extra payment."
That bhikṣu commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If he says, "Weave it wide," [he commits a duṣkṛta offense].
If one says,
"Weave it very well," or if one says:
“‘O Weaver, this will not benefit you’—
each such statement constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says:”
“Woven well, woven extensively.
Or if one says:
“Woven well, woven exceedingly well.”
If one says:
"Weave it well; weave it cleanly.
If one says:
"Woven broadly, exquisitely woven.
Or if one says:
"Woven broadly, cleanly woven."
If one says,
"It is woven extremely well and cleanly, but it does not benefit you," in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says:
"It is well-woven, broadly woven, and exquisitely woven.
Or if one says:
“Woven well, woven extensively, and woven cleanly.
If one says:
“Woven extensively, woven most excellently, and woven cleanly, it will not benefit you.”
In all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says:
"Weave well, weave broadly, weave most excellently, weave with great purity; it will not benefit you."
All such instances constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to a weaver and says:
"Do you know [this]?"
"If you say, 'This robe is being woven for me; do not weave it well, for I will give you no extra payment,' it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says:
"Do not weave it too wide.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave it too beautifully."
If one says,
"Weave it without making it clean; I will not give you anything extra," in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave extensively.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave too well.
If one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave with great cleanliness."
If one says:
"Do not weave it extensively; do not weave it with extreme excellence.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave it extensively; do not weave it with great refinement.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave it with extreme excellence; do not weave it with purity."
If one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave extensively; do not weave with extreme care.
Or if one says:
"Do not weave well; do not weave extensively;
do not weave cleanly. Or if one says:
"Do not weave extensively; do not weave excellently; do not weave cleanly."
If one says, "Do not weave well;
do not weave extensively; do not weave with extreme care; do not weave cleanly;
it will not benefit you," in each case it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu has property of his own and has a weaver weave it for him, he does not commit an offense.
The twenty-four matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a fellow disciple of the Śākya son Upananda named Dharma, who was virtuous and possessed of good qualities.
At that time, Upāli had temporarily lent his cut-and-sewn robe to Baddhālī.
Then, at the end of the summer retreat, when the month of *pravāraṇā* had concluded, the Buddha intended to travel to another country for two months.
Having heard that the Buddha intended to travel to another country for two months at the end of the summer retreat, the Śākya son Baddhālī spoke to his disciple Dharma:

“The Buddha intends to travel to other lands for two months during the final month of the summer retreat; now, let us travel to other lands together before the Buddha, so that we may obtain abundant clothing, food, and bedding, lacking for nothing.”
Dharma said, "I cannot go. Why is this?"
"I wish to travel to other countries with the Buddha so that I may see the Buddha and the venerable bhikṣus frequently, and through others,
I may hear the Dharma. Baddhananda said:
"Do you not wish to go with me? He replied,
"I will not go."
Bhadanta said, "If you do not leave, give me back my robe.
The disciple replied:
"I have already given you my upper robe.
Baddhalita said, "I did not give it to you for any other reason; I gave it to you for my own sake."
"Do you truly not wish to go?
He replied,
"I truly do not wish to go."
Bhadanta immediately returned, seized the robes, and took them for himself; the disciple stood weeping between the gates of Jetavana.
When the Buddha entered Jetavana and saw Dharma, he knew the situation but asked him nonetheless: "Dharma!"
"Why are you weeping?
He then related the preceding events in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the Śākya son Upananda:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu give a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger and resentment, take it back?”
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger and resentment, either takes it back himself or causes another to take it back, saying:
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you."
"Whoever obtains this robe commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"To take it oneself" means to take it with one's own person.
"To cause another to take it" means to command another person to take it.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger and resentment, seizes it back.
If one succeeds in seizing it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if one does not succeed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes another to seize it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he obtains it by fighting and seizing it through his own strength, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes another to exert effort in a dispute to seize [an object], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if it is not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one temporarily seizes it for the purpose of subduing that person, there is no offense.
The twenty-five matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the elder Vihāra left his saṃghāṭī robe in the Ānanda grove and, wearing only his upper and lower robes, entered the city to beg for food.
Later, he lost his saṃghāṭī robe; unable to find it upon returning, he said to the bhikṣus:
"I left my saṃghāṭī in the Andhavana grove to enter the city for alms, but subsequently lost it. I have searched for it and cannot find it; what shall I do?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the situation] yet asking anyway, he said to Vihāra:

“Is it true that you left your saṃghāṭī in the Ānanda Grove, put on your upper and lower robes to enter the city for alms, and later, having lost the saṃghāṭī, searched for it but could not find it, and then spoke thus to the bhikṣus?”
"Venerable Elders!

I left my saṃghāṭī robe in the Ānanda Grove and entered the city for alms wearing only my upper and lower robes. Later, I lost the saṃghāṭī; when I returned to search for it, I could not find it. What should I do?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha praised, by way of various causes and conditions, the practice of traveling with one’s robes and bowl wherever one goes, saying:

"If a bhikṣu has few desires and is content, using robes merely to cover the body and food merely to sustain life, and travels with his robes and bowl wherever he goes, he will always dwell in peace and happiness."
Just as when a bird flies, its feathers and wings accompany it wherever it goes;
so too is it with a bhikṣu: wherever he goes, he is accompanied by his robes and bowl, dwelling always in peace and happiness.
After the Buddha had praised the practice of keeping one's robes and alms bowl together through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."

From now on, this precept should be stated as follows: If a bhikṣu has completed three months [of the rainy retreat] but the eight months have not yet been reached and the year is not yet full, and if that forest-dwelling bhikṣu, residing in a forest hermitage, experiences doubt or fear, and that bhikṣu wishes to take any one of his three robes outside the boundary to a lay household; [The remainder of the rule follows: he may do so for seven days, provided he intends to return. If he exceeds seven days, it is a *pācittiya* offense. This is the proper formulation of the precept. Thus was this precept spoken by the Blessed One while staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika, concerning a certain bhikṣu who had left his robes outside the boundary and stayed overnight in a village.
