"If this bhikṣu has a reason to go outside the boundary, he may stay apart from his robe for up to six nights.
Should he stay apart beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding those who have not yet completed their year of residence: they shall observe the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*).
An *āraṇyaka* dwelling is five hundred *dhanus* away from a village;
in the kingdom of Magadha this constitutes one *krośa*, whereas in the northern kingdoms it constitutes half a *krośa*.
"Those with doubts" refers to having doubt that something has been lost therein, even down to a single water vessel.
"Those with fear" refers to having dread therein, even down to fearing wicked bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu wishes to take any one of his three robes to wear outside the boundary at a layperson's home—
these three robes being either the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, or the antarvāsaka— [he may do so].
There is no offense regarding being separated from one’s robes for six nights if one is separated from the *saṃghāṭī*, or separated from the *uttarāsaṅga*, or separated from the *antarvāsaka*.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.

Regarding the offense herein: on the sixth night, a bhikṣu should either take back the robe, go to the place where the robe is, or accept another robe. If the bhikṣu does not take the robe back, does not go to the place where the robe is, and does not accept another robe, when the seventh night has ended at dawn, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"Three months having passed" means that although there are four months in the summer season, even though three months have elapsed, the days for those entering the *anvārambhaṇa* (rainy-season retreat) have not yet been completed; therefore, it is said:
"The eight months are not yet full."
The twenty-six matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Then, some merchants from Śrāvastī were traveling through various villages for the sake of trade. Along the way, they saw a monastery that was secluded and remote; entering it, they saw that the community of bhikṣus was small, and they asked the bhikṣus:
"Why are there so few bhikṣus here?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"Do you not know? The merchant said:
"How is that? the bhikṣu replied, "In this place there are no donors to provide robes, food, and medicinal requisites; for this reason, the community of bhikṣus is small."
The merchants said,
"We wish to repair this place and provide it with clothing, food, and medicinal requisites. Thereupon,
these merchants immediately left the value of the clothing, food, and medicine, and departed to travel through various regions.
At the beginning of the summer retreat, the bhikṣus took these goods and went to dwell in other places for their rains retreat.
When these merchants returned from their travels after gaining profit, they saw this monastery and thought to themselves:
"This is the place where we made offerings; we should go inside and see how many people are dwelling there."
"If there be any deficiency regarding food, clothing, or medicine, you should provide these further.
Having entered, he saw that the bhikṣus were even fewer than before, and he asked:
"Why are the bhikṣus here even fewer now?"
The bhikṣu said, "Do you not know?
There is no donor here to provide the value of robes, food, and medicinal requisites; for this reason, they have diminished."
The merchants said,
"Where has the value of the food, clothing, and medicinal decoctions that we previously provided gone?
The bhikṣu replied:
"In the first month of summer, the bhikṣus divided these goods and departed to observe the rains retreat in other places.

The merchants said, "We did not give these to you for the sake of division so that you might go to other places to observe the rains retreat; we gave them to you because you were staying here, so that you might receive our offerings."
Among them, there was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and reprimanded him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who divides the goods for the summer retreat at the very beginning of the month?"
At that time, the Buddha merely rebuked them but had not yet established a formal precept.

Later, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit had a thousand combat generals; five hundred men formed one company. They all wore tattered, filthy clothes that were neither colorful nor dignified, and within their own quarters they possessed no fine couches, beds, or bedding.
The wives of the various generals likewise lacked fine clothing, bracelets, anklets, necklaces, flower garlands, and other articles for adorning the body.
Even when they attained official rank, the provisions and rations supplied to them were insufficient.
These people were fond of food and drink; they enjoyed wine, quarreling, or sometimes weeping, or at other times laughing, leaping about, and shouting loudly.
A bhikṣuṇī named Dharmadinnā lived near this place, and because of the disturbance caused by these loud noises, it hindered the bhikṣuṇī from practicing meditation and reciting the sūtras.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinā went to the wife of the general and asked:
"Why do your husbands wear such tattered, filthy, and colorless garments, lacking both beauty and virtue? Furthermore, why are there no fine beds or bedding within your rooms?"
"You yourselves also lack fine clothing, bracelets, armlets, necklaces, flower garlands, and ornaments.
Even if you were to obtain official positions, your provisions would still be insufficient."

"Your husband delights in food and drink; his guests crave wine and enjoy quarreling, or they weep and laugh, or leap about and shout loudly, thereby obstructing my sitting in meditation and reading the sutras."
"Why do you not restrain him? He replied,
"How could I possibly subdue him?"
If one were to reject it, one would no longer obtain even the remnants of food and drink previously received.
O virtuous one!
If one were to criticize it, one might still be able to make use of it.
Having heard these words, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinna departed to seek food and drink.

From time to time, she invited those among the generals who possessed great strength and influence, providing them with food as an inducement. Once she knew they had faith and were capable of accepting her words, she spoke to them, saying:
"O village chiefs, you should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."
Because he accepted these words with faith, he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, he no longer took pleasure in drinking alcohol, nor did he take pleasure in inviting guests for drink; he no longer took pleasure in quarreling, nor did he take pleasure in weeping, laughing, leaping, or shouting loudly. Within his own dwelling, he possessed fine couches, bedding, clothing, and requisites.
All the wives possessed fine garments, bracelets, anklets, necklaces, flower garlands, and various ornaments for adorning the body.
They received from the government sufficient provisions and rations.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, the generals gradually became very wealthy, possessing abundant gold, silver, treasures, slaves, servants, and subjects, achieving success in every respect.
Because King Prasenajit was surrounded by such wealthy men, the king possessed majesty and virtue, and was revered by the multitude.
At that time, a small kingdom rebelled against King Prasenajit, who addressed his generals:
"Go there and subdue them, then return."
Among these generals, there were some who held the Buddha in deep reverence; they placed water-strainers upon the tips of their bows and thought to themselves:
"If we encounter water containing insects, we shall strain it before drinking."
Among them, there were those who did not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma; conceiving a mind of jealousy, they went to King Prasenajit and said:
“There is a certain commander among these men who carries a water-strainer at the head of his bow and thinks to himself:
‘If I encounter water containing insects, I shall strain it and drink.’”
"These people have deceived Your Majesty.
The King said,
"If these beings possess such a heart of compassion even toward tiny insects, how much more so toward human beings?"
The king said,
"Summon him. They immediately went to summon him.
The King said:
"Do you truly fasten water-strainers to the heads of your bows?
Do you entertain such a thought?"
"Is it true that 'when encountering water with insects,
one should strain it before drinking'? He replied:
"It is indeed so," the king said.
"You have deceived me."
The general said,
"How can you deceive the King?
The King replied:
"You even have a heart of compassion for small insects, how much more so for human beings?
The general said,
"What fault do insects have?"
"If there should be anyone who commits an offense against the King, you should know that we shall punish them on the King's behalf.
The King thought to himself:
"Perhaps there are some who, out of a fondness for cleanliness, might not necessarily fear killing insects?"
The king said,
"Bring him before the front lines of the battle.
They were then brought before the front lines of the battle.
Among these generals, some had attained the *maitrī-citta-samādhi*; by the power of entering this samādhi of loving-kindness, they shattered the enemy ranks and immediately subdued them.
When the king heard that the enemy had been defeated, his heart was filled with great joy.
At that time, once the various generals had defeated the enemy, they returned to the king’s presence, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and said:
"May Your Majesty always be victorious.
Having spoken these words, they stood before the king.
The king immediately repaid them with wealth, villages, fields, houses, and subjects, providing them with twice as much as before.
At that time, the power and prosperity of the generals increased further; their gold, silver, treasures, slaves, servants, and subjects all grew manifold.
Because the king was surrounded by these people, his majestic virtue became even more preeminent, and the multitude revered him with double the intensity.
The generals thought to themselves:
"That we possess such wealth and honor is entirely due to the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinna; why should we not invite this bhikṣuṇī to come?"
During the three-month summer retreat in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, these military commanders went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said,
"Venerable ladies!
Please come to our kingdom of Śrāvastī for the summer retreat."
The bhikṣuṇī replied, “I cannot. “Why is that?”

He replied, “Wherever the Buddha dwells during the rains retreat, we shall go there to dwell as well; therein we shall frequently see the Buddha and frequently see the venerable bhikṣus, and through others, we shall be able to hear the Dharma.”
"If you wish for me to observe the rains retreat here, you should first invite the Buddha to spend the summer retreat in this city of Śrāvastī.
The general then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.

Having seen that they were seated, the Buddha taught the Dharma through various causes and conditions, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; having thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma through various causes and conditions, which instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, those generals said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"Please accept our invitation to observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in Śrāvastī.
Out of compassion, the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted their invitation through his silence, the generals prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to their respective homes, they exhorted one another to prepare, according to their means, meals for one day, two days, or three days; in this manner, they successively prepared food for the three months of the retreat. They also provided separate rooms for the Saṃgha, household robes, and robes for the summer retreat.
At that time, ten days remained before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was due; King Prasenajit had another small kingdom in rebellion.
He immediately dispatched his former general to fight, saying:
"Because you previously defeated the rebels, I now send you once again."
Upon hearing this, the generals were filled with grief and anxiety:
"What suffering is this?
We have barely escaped death due to our previous battles; if we go there again now, we may well lose our lives."

"We have already invited the Buddha for a three-month period to provide him with robes, food, and medicinal requisites. If we do not offer these as alms, the Sangha will lose the opportunity for offerings, and we ourselves will lose our merit."

"We previously intended to give material goods; what hardship is there now in giving through almsgiving? We shall ensure that the practice of giving is never interrupted, so that we may constantly cultivate merit within the field of blessings that is the Saṃgha. When the Saṃgha receives these offerings, we too shall obtain merit."
He then brought forth the items he had previously promised for alms, carrying many bundles of robes, and went to the Jeta Grove to strike the *gandī* gong.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Why do you strike it?"
The commander replied,
"Venerable sirs, since you have assembled, I shall give this robe as an offering to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not permitted us to divide the robes for the rainy season retreat before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
The warriors said, "We are officials who belong to others and lack independence; we were nearly perished due to the circumstances of our previous battle, yet we have managed to escape."
"Now we do not know what will happen as we go; we might even lose our lives.
The community of monks should assemble and receive these robes and articles.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"How many days remain until the *pravāraṇā*?"
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One,
ten days remain.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Although ten days have not yet passed until the *pravāraṇā*, I fear that the gift of robes may be lost; you should accept them.

Then the Buddha and the Saṃgha gathered and sat together in one place; because the various generals had already distributed the robes among the monks, they sat before the Buddha to listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
When the Buddha saw that they were seated, he taught them various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden them; having instructed, benefited, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, these generals prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Not long after he had departed, the Buddha, on account of previous causes and conditions as well as this present matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, the Buddha praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts; having thus praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has ten days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, he may accept an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*).
If the bhikṣu requires such a robe, he may take it with his own hand and keep it until the time for the distribution of robes."
"To keep it beyond this time constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Ten days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*" means that one knows there are ten days left until the *pravāraṇā*.

Regarding "urgent gifts of robes": if a king gives, or a queen gives, or a prince gives, or a great minister, a high official, a military commander, an inner court official, or if a woman is about to be married, or if one is ill, or if one is about to slay a bandit—when such persons give robes, if one knows that ten days have not yet passed until the *pravāraṇā*, one should accept them.

Regarding the time for robes: if there is a residence where the kaṭhina has not been spread, it is the final month of the summer retreat; if the kaṭhina has been spread at that residence, it is the final month of the summer retreat and the four months of winter.
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed. As for the transgression herein:

if, at the end of the summer retreat, on the final day of the month, one does not accept the *kaṭhina* robe in that place, then at the first day of the first month of winter, when the season has concluded, if that robe has not been relinquished, nor purified (*pariśuddha*), nor taken into formal possession (*parigraha*), it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If, at a residence where the kaṭhina robe has been spread, it is the final day of the last month of winter, those bhikṣus should relinquish that robe, purify it, or formally take possession of it. If they do not relinquish it, do not purify it, and do not take possession of it, then when the first day of the first month of spring arrives and the ground is cleared, there is an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The twenty-seventh matter concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has permitted us to keep rain-bathing robes."
Consequently, they kept them at all times, throughout both spring and winter.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked them:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, because the Buddha permitted the keeping of a rain-bath robe, one keeps it at all times, throughout both winter and spring?"
"The Buddha has permitted the keeping of three robes; the rain-bath robe is the fourth.
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him in various ways, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he said to the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can it be called being a bhikṣu if I permit you to keep a rain-bath robe, yet you keep it at all times, even during winter and spring?
Having rebuked them with various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
When one month of the spring season remains, a bhikṣu should seek to obtain a rain-bath robe; it should be accepted and kept for the remaining half-month.
"If a bhikṣu seeks to have [a robe] made less than one month before the end of spring, and accepts and keeps it after half a month has passed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
In this context, what constitutes 'seeking'?"
How is it made?
How is it maintained?
To "seek" means to beg this robe from another.
The "maker" refers to one who washes, dyes, cuts, or sews.
The "holder" refers to one who uses the robe.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bath robe in a place where there is an intercalary month, yet goes to a place without an intercalary month to observe the rains retreat, and therein seeks it from outside and brings it back to make one, all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta*.
From the moment it is accepted and held, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If there is a place observing the intercalary month, a bhikṣu sends a messenger to a place not observing the intercalary month, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Wait a moment; let us perform the *pravāraṇā* together.
If a monk from a non-leap-year region accepts this instruction to wait, and that monk from a non-leap-year region subsequently acts upon it, all such individuals commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
From the moment it is accepted and kept, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
However, if a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bathing robe in a place where there is an intercalary month, and he observes the rains retreat in such a place, he does not commit an offense.
Having completed the observance, one must relinquish it three months before the end of the summer retreat.
In a place where there is no intercalary month, since the eighth month has already begun and the heat season has passed, one commits an offense [if not relinquished by then].

In a place where there is an intercalary month—meaning that in this country the heat comes late and the intercalary month falls at the end of spring—one should seek [the robe] within that intercalary month.
If it can be obtained, one should receive and maintain it at the end of the third month.
If it cannot be obtained, one should receive and maintain it on the sixteenth day of the fourth month; once obtained, one must not let it pass beyond the fifteenth day.
The twenty-eighth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who resolved to provide food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as robes for the Saṃgha.

At that time, there was famine in the world and alms were difficult to obtain; this householder’s wealth was not great, and as the summer season had already passed, he felt sorrow in his heart and spoke these words:
"Why is it that my pain, affliction, and distress are now so extreme?"
Originally, my heart’s desire was to provide food and drink for the Buddha and the Sangha, and also to offer robes to the Sangha.

However, at that time, the world was suffering from famine and it was difficult to obtain anything through begging; my wealth was meager, and the summer retreat had already passed. My mind was filled with sorrow and urgent distress, as my wishes remained unfulfilled.
"I shall now request from among the Saṃgha some few bhikṣus to give them food and robes for the Saṃgha, so that my merit may not be in vain.
Having formed this thought, he entered the Jetavana and struck the *gandī* bell.
A bhikṣu asked the householder, "For what reason have you struck the *gandī*?"
The householder replied,
"I wish to invite a certain number of bhikṣus from the Saṃgha to my home for a meal. Thereupon,
the person in charge of the assembly dispatched that many bhikṣus, and they proceeded in order until they reached the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika).

Previously, when the group of six bhikṣus had received an invitation in turn, they would take their robes and bowls and arrive at the donor's house beforehand; while the food and drink were being prepared, they would instruct them to prepare it in such and such a manner.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took their robes and bowls in the early morning and went to the house of this lay devotee. After exchanging greetings, they sat to one side.
The lay devotee paid his respects and sat before them, speaking gently to the group of six bhikṣus:
"It was my original intention to provide food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as robes for the Saṃgha."

"In this world there is famine and scarcity, making it difficult to obtain alms; my wealth and goods are few, and now that the summer retreat has passed, my heart is filled with anxiety and urgent distress.
I thought to myself: 'Why do I not now invite a small number of bhikṣus from the Saṃgha, provide them with food, and give them robes as well, so that I may not lose my merit?'"
"For this reason, we shall give the food to you, but the robes should be given to the Saṃgha.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus heard the word "robes" and their minds were stirred;
they said to the lay devotee, "What are these robes like?"
"Bring it here and show it to me.
The householder said,
"Very well!"
He immediately brought out the robe and showed it to them.
Upon seeing the robe, the group of six bhikṣus felt an even greater sense of greed and said to the householder,
"Do you intend for this robe to be put to use?"
"Do you wish for it to be set aside?
The householder said,
"The reason I give is that I wish for it to be used."
“If you wish for us not to use it, you should give it to the Saṃgha. Why is this?

The Saṃgha possesses many robes that are kept in one place, where they become moldy and are eaten by insects; if you wish for us to use it, you should give it to us, for our robes are few and we shall use whatever is offered.”
The householder said,
"If you know that the Sangha will not use it, but if you yourselves can use it, then I shall give it to you.
Having given the food, the householder then took these robes and gave them to the group of six bhikṣus.
After eating, the group of six bhikṣus took these robes and entered the Jeta Grove, showing them to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"How fine and excellent are these robes!
The bhikṣus said:
“Excellent! From where did you obtain this?
The group of six bhikṣus then related the matter in detail.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires and were content; practicing the dhūta austerities, they were displeased when they heard of this matter and rebuked it for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that property was intended for the Saṃgha, seeks it for himself?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied: “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that property is intended for the Saṃgha, seeks it for himself?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, yet seeks it for himself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Knows" means: either he knows it himself, or he hears it from another, or a donor tells him.

"Objects" refers to items given to the Sangha, such as robes, alms bowls, door-bolts, water jars, medicinal food for the daytime, medicinal food for the night watch, medicinal food for seven days, and medicinal food for life.
"Directed toward the Sangha" means having resolved to give it to the Sangha but not yet having given it.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" means that this robe must be relinquished and the pāyattika offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the community of bhikṣus, yet seeks it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he seeks it for three, two, or one [individual], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that an object is intended for the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, seeks it for herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she seeks it for three, two, or one [individual], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items are intended for three bhikṣus, requests them from other three bhikṣus, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items are intended for three bhikṣus, requests them from two bhikṣus or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two bhikṣuṇīs, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, two śikṣamāṇās, or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two śrāmaṇeras, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two śrāmaṇerīs, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu saṃgha—in all such cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for these two bhikṣus, requests it from other two bhikṣus, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, knowing that an object is intended for two bhikṣus, he requests it from one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two bhikṣuṇīs, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one particular bhikṣu, yet seeks it from another bhikṣu, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If he knows that an object is intended for one bhikṣu, yet seeks it from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, from three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī, from three, two, or one śikṣamāṇā, from three śrāmaṇeras, two, or one śrāmaṇera, from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī, or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, from three, two, or one bhikṣu, in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three bhikṣuṇīs, seeks them from other three bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three bhikṣuṇīs, seeks them from two bhikṣuṇīs or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇera*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇerī*; or from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two bhikṣuṇīs, requests them from other two bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two bhikṣuṇīs, requests them from one bhikṣuṇī, or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*, or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇera*, or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇerī*; or from the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*, or from three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*, or from three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that this object is intended for one bhikṣuṇī, seeks it from another bhikṣuṇī, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that this object is intended for one bhikṣuṇī, seeks it from three, two, or one śikṣamāṇā; from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera; from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, from three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, from three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items are intended for three śikṣamāṇās, requests them from other three śikṣamāṇās, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items are intended for three śikṣamāṇās, requests them from two or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī—in all such cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śikṣamāṇās, requests them from other two śikṣamāṇās, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śikṣamāṇās, requests them from one śikṣamāṇā, or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śikṣamāṇā, yet requests it for another śikṣamāṇā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If he knows that an object is intended for one śikṣamāṇā, yet requests it for three śrāmaṇeras or two or one śrāmaṇera; for three śrāmaṇerīs or two or one śrāmaṇerī; for the bhikṣu-saṃgha, or three, two, or one bhikṣu; for the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, or three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or for three śikṣamāṇās or two or one śikṣamāṇā—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇeras, requests them from other three śrāmaṇeras, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇeras, requests them from two śrāmaṇeras, one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, or two or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, or two or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, or two or one śikṣamāṇā—in all such cases, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object was intended for these two śrāmaṇeras, requests it from other two śrāmaṇeras, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object was intended for two śrāmaṇeras, requests it from one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇera, yet requests it from another śrāmaṇera, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇera, yet requests it from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; from three *śikṣamāṇās*, two or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from other three śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from other two or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from two other śrāmaṇerīs, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from one śrāmaṇerī; or from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇera*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇerī*, in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇerī, yet requests it from another śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇerī, yet requests it from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī—in all these cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for many animals, yet seeks it out for other many animals, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for many animals, yet seeks it out for two animals or one animal, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for these two animals, yet seeks it for other two animals, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for two animals, yet seeks it for one animal or many animals, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one particular animal, yet seeks it for another single animal, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one animal, yet seeks it for many animals or two animals, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the community of bhikṣus, yet requests it for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, yet requests it for the community of bhikṣus, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a monk, when the Sangha has split into two factions of monks, knows that an object belongs to one faction and seeks it from the other faction, he commits a *dukkaṭa*.
If a monk perceives within [the object] the notion that it belongs to [that specific faction], he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one intends [to give] to a person but perceives them as not that person, one incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one intends [to give] to a person but harbors doubt regarding it, one incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one perceives what is not the direction as being the direction, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one entertains doubt regarding what is not the direction, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives what is not the direction as not being the direction, there is no offense.
The twenty-ninth matter concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, observing the rains retreat with a great community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyāni was observing the rains retreat in Rājagṛha; he had many acquaintances and received a great abundance of ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.

Because this elder had obtained so much, he filled one bowl, half a bowl, a kuṇḍaka, half a kuṇḍaka, a large gaṇḍī, and small gaṇḍīs, some of which were placed in net-bags and suspended from ivory pegs.
When taking from it, they instead threw it away, soiling the walls; the bedding became rotten and ruined; the rooms were smeared with filth; and the dwellings became foul-smelling.
These disciples of the Elder Piṅgiyānī ate food that had been kept overnight, handled it improperly, failed to receive it through formal acceptance, and stored food indoors.
During the time that the Buddhas dwell in the world, there are two great assemblies each year: at the end of the last month of spring and at the end of the last month of summer.
Regarding the last month of spring, monks from various regions and lands come to where the Buddha is and think:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha, we shall practice during our period of retreat so as to dwell in peace and happiness."
This was the first great assembly.

At the end of the summer months, when the bhikṣus had completed their three-month summer retreat and finished making their robes, they took up their robes and bowls and went to where the Buddha was, thinking:
"We have not seen the Buddha for a long time; we have not seen the World-Honored One for a long time!"
This was the second great assembly.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed his summer retreat in Rājagṛha and finished making his robes, took up his bowl and robe and traveled to Śrāvastī. He went to where the Buddha was staying, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they inquire after the resident bhikṣus with these words:
"Are you patient?
Are you well-sustained?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of alms-food, and are you not weary from the road?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu with these words of inquiry.
"Are you patient?
Are you content?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Is there no lack of almsfood? Are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣu replied, "World-Honored One!"
"He dwells in contentment and ease; he does not lack for alms; and he is not fatigued on the road.
Having related these matters in detail to the Buddha, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and censured [the offender] through various causes and conditions:
“Out of compassion and for the benefit of sick bhikṣus, I permit the consumption of the four kinds of medicinal substances taken by mouth:
ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
How is it that a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, handled improperly, not formally received, or stored indoors?”
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu is ill, he is permitted to take four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption—
clarified butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar— and may keep them overnight and consume them for up to seven days.
"To consume more than this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Regarding "the sick":
if one suffers from the onset of wind, the onset of heat, or the onset of cold, and these four kinds of medicines can cure it, this is called "being sick."
"Non-illness" refers to being different from these causes and conditions, which is termed "non-illness.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this medicine should be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense should be confessed.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu obtains ghee on the first day and keeps it until the second day before relinquishing it; obtains it on the second day and keeps it until the third day before relinquishing it; obtains it on the third day and keeps it until the fourth day before relinquishing it; obtains it on the fourth day and keeps it until the fifth day before relinquishing it; obtains it on the fifth day and keeps it until the sixth day before relinquishing it; obtains it on the sixth day and keeps it until the seventh day before relinquishing it; and obtains it on the seventh day—on that seventh day, the bhikṣu must give the ghee to another, perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), or consume it. If the bhikṣu does not give it to another, does not perform the ritual of purification, and does not consume it, then at the end of the eighth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu obtains ghee on the first day and obtains it again on the second day, he may keep one portion and must relinquish the other.
If he obtains ghee on the second day and obtains it again on the third day, he may keep one portion and must relinquish the other.
On the third day one obtains ghee; on the fourth day one obtains more, storing one portion and discarding one.
On the fourth day one obtains ghee; on the fifth day one obtains more, storing one portion and discarding one.
On the fifth day one obtains ghee; on the sixth day one obtains more, storing one portion and discarding one.

If on the sixth day one obtains ghee and on the seventh day obtains more, then during that seventh day the bhikṣu must give the ghee to another, perform the ritual of purification (*kappiya-kāraṇa*), or consume it; if he does not give it to another, does not perform the ritual of purification, and does not consume it, then when the eighth day has ended, it constitutes an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu obtains ghee on the first day and stores it, and obtains more on the second day, he should store the latter and discard the former.
If he obtains ghee on the second day and obtains more on the third day, he should store the latter and discard the former.
On the third day one obtains ghee, and on the fourth day one obtains more; one retains the latter and discards the former.
On the fourth day one obtains ghee, and on the fifth day one obtains more; one retains the latter and discards the former.
On the fifth day one obtains ghee, and on the sixth day one obtains more; one retains the latter and discards the former.

If on the sixth day one obtains ghee and on the seventh day obtains more, then at the time of the seventh day, the bhikṣu should give that ghee to others, perform the ritual purification (*pariśuddhi*), or consume it; if he does not give it to others, does not perform the ritual purification, and does not consume it, then when the eighth day arrives at its conclusion, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu obtains ghee on the first day and obtains it again on the second day, he may keep the former and discard the latter.
If he obtains ghee on the second day and obtains it again on the third day, he may keep the former and discard the latter.
On the third day one obtains ghee, and on the fourth day one obtains more; one keeps the former and discards the latter.
On the fourth day one obtains ghee, and on the fifth day one obtains more; one keeps the former and discards the latter.
On the fifth day one obtains ghee, and on the sixth day one obtains more; one keeps the former and discards the latter.

If on the sixth day one obtains ghee and on the seventh day obtains more, then at the time of the seventh day, the bhikṣu should give that ghee to others, perform the ritual of purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*), or consume it; if he does not give it to others, does not perform the ritual of purification, and does not consume it, then when the eighth day arrives at the end of the period, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains ghee on the first day and stores it, but does not obtain any on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, then on the eighth day at the end of the watch, that bhikṣu must give the ghee away, perform the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi), or consume it. If he neither gives it away, performs the ritual of purification, nor consumes it, then at the end of the eighth day, it constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains ghee on the first day and keeps it, and obtains more on the second day, and again on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh days, then on the eighth day at the end of the day, that bhikṣu must give all that ghee to others, perform the *pariśuddhi* (purification) rite, or consume it; if he does not give it to others, does not perform the purification rite, and does not consume it, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense at the conclusion of the eighth day.

If a bhikṣu possesses ghee that ought to be relinquished, and without having relinquished it or confessed his offense, he subsequently obtains more ghee while the continuity of possession has not been severed, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for the later ghee on account of the original ghee.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has already relinquished ghee and that offense remains unconfessed, and he subsequently obtains more ghee while the continuity of his possession has not been severed, he incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for the later ghee on account of the original cause regarding the former ghee.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has already relinquished ghee, confessed his offense, and repented, but subsequently obtains more ghee before the previous period has expired, he incurs a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for that later ghee on account of the original cause regarding the first ghee.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has already relinquished ghee, confessed his offense, and severed his connection to it, he commits no offense if he subsequently obtains ghee again.
The same applies to oil, honey, and rock sugar.
If one is gravely ill, there is no offense.
The thirty matters are concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Eight. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who resolved to provide food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as robes for the Saṃgha.
At that time, there was famine in the world and alms were difficult to obtain; this householder, whose wealth was not great, felt sorrowful once the summer retreat had passed and spoke these words:
"How painful and urgent is my distress now!"

"Originally, my heart’s desire was to provide food and drink for the Buddha and the Sangha, and furthermore to offer robes to the Sangha. However, at this time of famine and scarcity, it is difficult to obtain anything through begging; my wealth is meager, and the summer retreat has already passed. My mind is filled with sorrow and urgent distress, as my wishes remain unfulfilled."
"I shall now request several bhikṣus from among the Saṃgha to give them food and robes, so that my merit may not be in vain.
Having formed this thought, he entered the Jeta Grove and struck the *gandī* gong.
A bhikṣu asked a householder,
"For what reason are you striking the gong?
The householder replied:
"I wish to request from among the Saṃgha that so many bhikṣus come to my house.
At that time, the person in charge of the assembly immediately dispatched that many bhikṣus; next, it was the turn of the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika).

The group of six bhikṣus, having previously received an invitation by turn, took their robes and bowls and arrived at the donor's house ahead of time; while the food and drink were being prepared, they instructed them to do such and such things.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took their robes and bowls in the early morning and went to the house of this lay devotee. After exchanging greetings, they sat to one side.
Once the lay devotee had paid his respects and sat before them, he spoke gently to the group of six bhikṣus:
"It was my original intention to provide food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as well as robes for the Saṃgha."

"In this world, there is famine and scarcity, making it difficult to obtain alms. My wealth and goods are few, and the summer season has already passed; my heart is filled with sorrow and urgent distress. I have thought thus:
'I should now invite a small or large number of bhikṣus from the Saṃgha to provide them with food, and then give robes to the community of monks, so that I do not lose my merit.'"
"For this reason, we shall give the food to you, but the robes should be given to the Saṃgha.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard the word "robes," their minds were moved, and they said to the householder,
"What are these robes like?"
"Bring it here and show it to me.
The householder said,
"Very well."
He immediately brought out the robe and showed it to them.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw the robe, their greed increased all the more, and they said to the householder,
"Do you wish for this robe to be put to use?"
"Do you wish for it to be set aside?
The householder replied,
"The reason I give this is that I wish for it to be used."
“If you wish that it not be used, you should give it to the Saṃgha. Why is this?
The Saṃgha has many robes kept in one place, which become moldy, decay, and are eaten by insects.”
"If you would have us use it, we shall share it with you.
We have few robes; if you obtain alms, we shall use them together.
The householder said:
"You know that this is of no use to the Saṃgha;
if you can make use of it yourselves, we shall give it to you.
After the householder had given the food and they had finished eating, he took these robes and gave them to them.
After the group of six bhikṣus had finished eating, they took these robes with them and entered the Jeta Grove to show them to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"What do these robes look like?
Are they not fine and good?"
The bhikṣus said:
"It is truly excellent.
From where did you obtain it?"
The group of six bhikṣus explained this matter in detail.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu know that property is intended for the Saṃgha, yet seek it for himself?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [what had occurred], he nevertheless asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed, I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, seeks it for himself?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for the Saṃgha, seeks it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Knowing" means: knowing by oneself, hearing from another, or being told by a donor.

"Objects" refers to items given to the Sangha, such as robes, alms bowls, door-bolts, water pitchers, medicinal food for the time, medicinal food for a portion of the day, medicinal food for seven days, or medicinal food for life.
"Directed toward the Saṃgha" means having resolved in one's mind to give it to the Saṃgha, though not yet definitively given.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" means that this robe must be relinquished and the pāyattika offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the community of bhikṣus, yet seeks it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he seeks it for three, two, or one [individual], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that an object is intended for the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, yet seeks it for herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she seeks it for three, two, or one [individual], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for these three bhikṣus, yet requests it from other three bhikṣus, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for three bhikṣus, yet requests it from two bhikṣus and one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two bhikṣuṇīs, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, two śikṣamāṇās, or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two śrāmaṇeras, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two śrāmaṇerīs, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu saṃgha—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two specific bhikṣus, requests them from other two bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, knowing these items were intended for two bhikṣus, he requests them from one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two bhikṣuṇīs, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, two śikṣamāṇās, or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two śrāmaṇeras, or one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two śrāmaṇerīs, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, or from three, two, or one bhikṣu—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for one particular bhikṣu, requests it from another bhikṣu, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, knowing that an object is intended for one bhikṣu, he requests it from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two bhikṣuṇīs, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, two or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two bhikṣus, or one bhikṣu—in all these cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for three bhikṣuṇīs, yet requests it from other three bhikṣuṇīs, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that this object is intended for three bhikṣuṇīs, yet requests it from two bhikṣuṇīs or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇera*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇerī*; or from the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*, or from three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*—in all these cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two specific bhikṣuṇīs, requests them from other two bhikṣuṇīs, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two bhikṣuṇīs, requests them from one bhikṣuṇī; or from three *śikṣamāṇās*, two or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three *śrāmaṇeras*, two or one *śrāmaṇera*; or from three *śrāmaṇerīs*, two or one *śrāmaṇerī*; or from the *bhikṣu-saṃgha*, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from the *bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for one particular bhikṣuṇī, requests it from another bhikṣuṇī, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object is intended for one bhikṣuṇī, requests it from three śikṣamāṇās, two śikṣamāṇās, or one śikṣamāṇā; from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera; from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, from three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, from three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī—in all these cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that this object is intended for these three śikṣamāṇās, yet seeks it from other three śikṣamāṇās, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that this object is intended for three śikṣamāṇās, yet seeks it from two śikṣamāṇās, one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; or from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī—in all such cases, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śikṣamāṇā, yet seeks it from another two śikṣamāṇās, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for two śikṣamāṇās, yet seeks it from one śikṣamāṇā—from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera; from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās—in all such cases, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that this object is intended for one śikṣamāṇā, yet seeks it for another śikṣamāṇā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If he knows that this object is intended for one śikṣamāṇā, yet seeks it for three śrāmaṇeras or two—one śrāmaṇera; for three śrāmaṇerīs or two—one śrāmaṇerī; for the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, or two—one bhikṣu; for the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, or two—one bhikṣuṇī; or for three śikṣamāṇās or two śikṣamāṇās—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇeras, requests them from other three śrāmaṇeras, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇeras, requests them from two śrāmaṇeras or one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*, in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śrāmaṇeras, requests them from other two śrāmaṇeras, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śrāmaṇeras, requests them from one śrāmaṇera; or from three, two, or one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three, two, or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three śrāmaṇeras—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇera, yet seeks it from another śrāmaṇera, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇera, yet seeks it from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī; from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣu; from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three, two, or one bhikṣuṇī; from three *śikṣamāṇās*, two or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera—in all these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from other three śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for three śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from two other śrāmaṇerīs, one śrāmaṇerī; or from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, two or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from two other śrāmaṇerīs, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that these items were intended for two śrāmaṇerīs, requests them from one śrāmaṇerī; or from the bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three *śikṣamāṇās*, two or one *śikṣamāṇā*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇera*; or from three, two, or one *śrāmaṇerī*—in all such cases, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇerī, yet seeks it from another śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one śrāmaṇerī, yet seeks it from a bhikṣu-saṃgha, three bhikṣus, two or one bhikṣu; or from a bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, three bhikṣuṇīs, two or one bhikṣuṇī; or from three śikṣamāṇās, two or one śikṣamāṇā; or from three śrāmaṇeras, two or one śrāmaṇera; or from three śrāmaṇerīs, two or one śrāmaṇerī—in all such cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for many animals, yet seeks it for other many animals, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for many animals, yet seeks it for two animals or one animal, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for these two animals, yet seeks it for other two animals, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for two animals, yet seeks it for one animal or many animals, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one particular animal, yet seeks it for another single animal, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for one particular animal, yet seeks it for many animals or two animals, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the community of bhikṣus, yet requests it for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object is intended for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, yet requests it for the community of bhikṣus, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If the Bhikṣu Saṃgha has split into two factions, and a Bhikṣu knows that this object belongs to one faction but seeks it from the other faction, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a Bhikṣu perceives something within [the Saṃgha] as belonging to that [faction], he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one perceives what is not a direction as being a direction, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one has doubt regarding what is a direction, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one perceives what is not a direction as being a direction, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not give rise to doubt regarding that which is not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
If one regards that which is not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense as not being a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, there is no transgression.
The twenty-nine matters are concluded.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Nine; Second Recitation, Part Three;
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Section Five: The Ninety *Pāyattika* Dharmas; Part One: An Exposition of the First of the Ninety *Pāyattika* Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a master of debate from South India who came to Śrāvastī with his belly bound by copper plates and a torch burning upon his head.
People of the time asked him,
"For what reason are you like this?
He replied:
“I possess great wisdom; I fear my belly might burst.
“Why do you place fire upon your head?
“I wish to illuminate the darkness.”
He said: "Foolish brāhmaṇa!
The sun illuminates the world; why do you say it is dark?"
He replied:
"You do not know that there are two kinds of darkness:
first, the absence of the sun, moon, fire, and lamps; second, the ignorance of lacking the light of wisdom."
The people said,
"Because you have not yet seen the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa, the son of the Śākyas, you dare to speak such words.
If you were to see him and converse with him, day would become dark at sunrise, and night would become bright at sunset."
At that time, the people within the city immediately summoned the Śākya bhikṣu Hāṭaka, wishing to have him engage in debate.
When Hāṭaka heard this, his heart was filled with distress; having no choice, he entered the city streets and saw two rams fighting. Taking this as an omen, he immediately formed this thought:
"One ram is the brāhmaṇa, and one ram is myself."
"Since I am the one who is losing in this fight," he thought, and upon seeing this, his sorrow and anxiety increased even further.
Moving forward, he again saw two oxen fighting together, and he further thought:
"One ox is the brahmin, and the other ox is I."
"Thinking 'This is I' was again not correct.
Furthermore, as he proceeded, he saw two men wrestling and thought to himself:
"One is a brahmin, and one is I."
I, however, am not as fortunate.
As I was about to enter the place of debate, I saw a woman carrying a full jar of water; the water jar immediately broke. Then I thought to myself:
"I have seen these inauspicious omens; will it not turn out that I am not as successful?"

Having no other choice, he proceeded to enter the house; seeing the appearance of the eyes and mouth of this debating Brahmin, he knew for himself that he was not his equal, and his sorrow became even more intense.
After sitting for a short while, the people said,
"We should engage in discussion together. He replied:
"I am currently somewhat unwell and must wait until tomorrow," he said, and having spoken these words, he returned to his lodging; then, during the last watch of the night, he set out for Rājagṛha.
At dawn, the people of the city gathered; waiting for a long time, they did not see him arrive and realized that the time had already passed.
They went to the Jetavana themselves to search for him, and the other bhikṣus said:
"The son of the Śākyas, Hāṭaka, took his robes and bowl and departed during the latter part of the night."
When the people within the various cities heard this, they censured him in many ways, saying, "How can one who is called a bhikṣu deliberately speak falsehoods?
One person told two, and two told three; in this manner, the evil reputation spread by word of mouth until it filled the entire city of Śrāvastī.

Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; having put on his robes and taken up his bowl to enter the city for alms, he heard of this matter and was displeased. After eating, he went to the Buddha and recounted it in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and reprimanded them with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu speak a deliberate lie?
Having reprimanded them in various ways, he said to the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

one was named Lion of Fine Fur, and the other was named Tiger of Fine Teeth. They were good friends to one another, affectionate and caring for each other, greeting one another and closing their eyes while licking each other's fur."
These two beasts constantly obtain and eat soft, high-quality meat.
Not far from them, there was a two-tongued jackal who thought to himself:

"This fine-haired lion and this fine-toothed tiger have become good friends; they are affectionate toward one another, inquire after each other's welfare, and at times close their eyes while licking each other's fur, so that they always get to eat soft, high-quality meat."
"I shall go to these two beasts and become their third companion.
Having formed this thought, he went to where the tiger and the lion were and said:
"I will serve as your third companion; will you allow me to enter?"
The lion and the tiger said, "As you wish.
Because the two-tongued jackal had obtained and eaten the remains of the flesh of the two beasts, his body became fat. Having become fat, he thought to himself:

"This fine-haired lion and this fine-toothed tiger have become good friends; they are affectionate toward one another, inquire after each other's welfare, and at times close their eyes while licking each other's fur. They always obtain choice meat to eat, but should they ever fail to find it, they will surely devour me."
"Why do I not first employ skillful means to cause their minds to become estranged? Once they are estranged, they will all receive my favor.
Having had this thought, he went to speak to Siṃha, saying: "Do you know?"
The tiger "Fine Teeth" harbored ill will toward you and spoke these words:
"Whatever the lion 'Fine Fur' devours is entirely through my power.
He then uttered this verse:
"Though one possesses a fine coat, it is swift and feared by men;
'this fine coat does not surpass me,' so says the one with fine teeth."
The Lion with Fine Fur asked,
"How can this be known?
The Two-Tongued Jackal replied:
"When Good-tooth sees you tomorrow and closes his eyes to lick your fur, you should know it is an ill omen.
Having said this, he went to the tiger and said: "Do you know?"
The fine-furred lion harbored ill will toward you and spoke these words:
"My fine teeth have the power to devour whatever is eaten; all this is by my strength.
He then uttered this verse:
"Though one may have beautiful teeth, they are feared by those who are swift;
'beautiful teeth do not surpass me,' so says one with beautiful fur. Thus spoke the one with beautiful fur.
"How can this be known? He replied,
"When you see him tomorrow with his fine fur, if he closes his eyes and licks your fur, you should know that it is an evil omen."
"Between these two acquaintances, the tiger conceived a sense of fear; therefore, he went first to the lion and said:
'You have conceived an evil intent toward me and have spoken such words as:
"When there are fine teeth for devouring food, it is all due to my power."'"
He further spoke in verse:
“Though one may possess beautiful teeth and a fine complexion, they are feared by those who are swift;
such beautiful teeth do not surpass me.”
“Do you speak these words? Siṃha replied,
“Who would say such a thing?”
He replied,
"A two-tongued jackal.
Sumātra (Good Fur) asked again:
"You conceived an evil mind toward me and spoke these words:
'That the fine hair was devoured is all due to my power.
You further spoke this verse:"
“‘Though one may have a beautiful coat, it is swift and feared by men;
my beautiful coat does not equal mine.
Did you speak these words?”
The tiger said, "No.
The tiger then spoke to the lion, saying:
"If you possess such evil speech, you shall not be able to act as a virtuous friend.
Sumukha said, "Regarding this two-tongued jackal who speaks such words, what do you think?"
"Do you not wish to dwell with me?
He then spoke in verse:
"If you believe me to be an evil person, Then depart quickly and leave me."
Constantly harboring sorrow and anxiety, with resentment never leaving the heart;
one who acts as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) does not cause separation through the words of others;
one who does not believe and wishes to eliminate [afflictions] constantly seeks the appropriate means.
If one believes in causing others' separation, one will be devoured by them;
if one does not believe in double-tongued speech, one will instead bring about reconciliation.
One speaks what is held in the heart toward others, with a pure mind and gentle words.
One should act as a spiritual friend, harmonizing like water and milk.
But this wretched little insect, born with a naturally evil disposition, has but one head and two tongues;
only by killing it can harmony be restored.
At that time, having verified the facts, the tiger and the lion together seized the jackal and tore him into two pieces.
The Buddha said:
"If even animals find no peace and happiness due to the causes and conditions of double-tongued speech, how much more so for human beings?"
The Buddha, having rebuked them for these reasons, addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu engages in divisive speech, it is a pāyattika.
"Pāyattika" means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
Within this, there are eight types of offenses:
namely, lineage, craft, labor, transgression, illness, appearance, affliction, and abuse.
In each of these eight matters, five factors are employed:
Thus is his name, thus his clan, thus his lineage, thus his occupation, thus his physical marks. Regarding "thus is his name":
it refers to such-and-such a person, the name of such-and-such a bhikṣu.
As for clan names: the Vatsa clan, the Kutsa clan, the Śāṇḍilya clan, the Bhāradvāja clan, and the Ātreya clan—these are called clan names.
As for "caste," it refers to the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, the Vaiśya caste, and the Śūdra caste.
As for "occupation," it refers to those who run gold shops, silver shops, hired labor shops, or jewel shops.

Regarding "physical marks" (*lakṣaṇa*): having curled hands, stumps for hands, goiters or swellings, being left-handed, or arms resembling bird wings—these are called physical marks. Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*):
if a bhikṣu goes and says to a son of the Kṣatriya caste who is a bhikṣu, "They say you are of the Kṣatriya lineage;
what is the use of leaving home and receiving the precepts?"
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
“Who is this person named so-and-so?
He replied, “He is of such-and-such a clan.”
"Who is this person of such-and-such a surname?
He replied, "It is the one named Such-and-such."
"Who was that person? He replied, "It was so-and-so."
"Who is this person named 'Something'?
He replied, "It is a mark."
If the other understands, it is a duṣkṛta;
if they do not understand, it is also a duṣkṛta;
if one speaks again after they have already understood, it is also a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu goes and says to a son of a brahmin who is also a bhikṣu:

He replied, "I did.

"Who is the one with the surname 'Some'?
He replied, "The one surnamed 'Some'."
"Who was that person? He replied, "It was so-and-so."
"Who is this person named 'Somebody'?
He replied, "It is the mark."
If he understands it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if he does not understand it, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he speaks further after having already understood it, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the merchant’s son, "He says you are of merchant stock;

you should sit at a gold stall, a silver stall, a laborer's stall, a copper stall, or a pearl stall. You should train in such various merchant affairs—what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
"Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, "I am of such-and-such a clan."
"Who is the one with the surname 'Some'?
He replied, "It is the person surnamed 'Some'."
"Who was that person? He replied, "It was so-and-so."
"Who is this person named 'Something'?
He replied, "It is 'Some Sign'."
If the other understands, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if they do not understand, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one speaks further after they have already understood, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the smith’s son, Bhikṣu Sūta:

“He says you are of a smith’s lineage; you ought to make bracelets, anklets, chains, cauldrons, griddles, plowshares, hoes, mattocks, axes, spears, large swords, small knives, bowls, *kuṇḍikās*, half-*kuṇḍikās*, large ladles, small ladles, razors, needles, hooks, bowl-hooks, locks, and keys. You should perform such various smith’s tasks; what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?”
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is so-and-so.”
“Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, “He is of such-and-such a clan.”
“Who is the one surnamed So-and-so?
He replied, “The one surnamed Such-and-such.”
"Who is that certain person?
He replied, "It was I who did it."
“Who is this person named So-and-so?
He replied, “It is So-and-so.”
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one speaks again after [the offense] has already been understood, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the bhikṣu Kāṣṭha-siṃha:

"He says that you are of the wood-worker caste; you ought to make mechanical wooden figures, chariots, plows, and all such various works of a wood-worker. Why do you go forth and receive the precepts?"
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is so-and-so.”
“Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, “He is of such-and-such a clan.”
"Who is the one surnamed Mou?
He replied,
"The one surnamed Zhong."
“Who is that person?
He replied, “It was made by such-and-such.”
“Who is this person named So-and-so?
He replied, “It is So-and-so the Elder.”
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one speaks again after they have already understood, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the potter’s son, the bhikṣu:

“He says you are of the potter caste; you ought to take earth, prepare the clay, turn the wheel, and make jars, pots, bowls, cauldrons, lids, alms-bowls (*pātra*), *kuṇḍa*, *ardhakuṇḍa*, large *kaṭacchu*, and small *kaṭacchu*. Such are the various potter’s tasks you should perform; what is the use of leaving home to receive the precepts?”
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is so-and-so.”
"Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, "I am of such-and-such a surname."
“Who is this person of such-and-such a surname?
He replied, “It is Mr. Zhong.”
"Who is that certain person?
He replied, "It was someone who acted."
“Who is this person named So-and-so?
He replied, “It is So-and-so the Elder.”
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one speaks again after they have already understood, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the bhikṣu Carmakāra:

"He says you are of the leather-worker caste; you ought to take hides, soak, treat, cut, and sew them together to make boots, *puḍraka* shoes, sandals, saddles, bridles, whips, and straps. You should perform all such various tasks of a leather-worker—what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
"Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, "I am of such-and-such a surname."
"Who is the one with the surname 'Some'?
He replied, "It is the family name 'Some'."
"Who is that certain person?
He replied, "It was made by such-and-such."
"Who is this person named 'Something'?
He replied, "'Something' is a characteristic."
If he understands it, it is a pāyattika;
if he does not understand it, it is a dukkaṭa.
If he speaks again after having already understood it, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
