Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the bamboo-worker’s son, Bhikṣu:

“He says you are of a bamboo-worker lineage; you ought to learn the various crafts of a bamboo-worker—breaking bamboo and reeds, making spears, arrows, fans, umbrellas, boxes, and mats. You should learn to perform such works of a bamboo-worker; what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?”
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
“Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, “He is of such-and-such a clan.”
"Who is the one with the surname 'Some'?
He replied, "It is the one named 'Some'."
"Who was that person? He replied, "It was so-and-so."
"Who is this person named 'Somebody'?
He replied, "It is Some-character."
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one speaks again after [the offense] has already been understood, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went to the barber Śīrṣaka and said to him:

"He says you are of the barber caste; you ought to learn how to leave a topknot on the crown of the head, learn how to shave the hair, shave the beard, shave the hair under the armpits, trim the nails, and pluck out the nose hairs. You should learn these various skills of a barber—what is the use of leaving home to receive the precepts?"
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is so-and-so.”
"Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, "He is of such-and-such a clan."
“Who is the one with the surname ‘Some’?
He replied,
“The one named ‘Some-kind.’”
"Who is that certain person?
He replied, "It was made by such-and-such."
"Who is this person named 'Something'?
He replied, "It is the mark."
If the other understands, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they do not understand, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one speaks again after they have already understood, it is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu went and said to the bhikṣu Caṇḍālaputra: "He says you are of the Caṇḍāla caste;

you ought to perform the work of cutting off people's hands, feet, ears, noses, and heads, placing them upon wooden frames, carrying out corpses, and burning them—such various tasks of a Caṇḍāla you should perform. What is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
“Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, “He is of such-and-such a clan.”
“Who is the one surnamed So-and-so?
He replied, “The one surnamed Such-and-such.”
"Who is that person? He replied, "It was I who did it."
"Who is this person named So-and-so?
He replied, "It is So-and-so the Elder."
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one speaks again after they have already understood, it is a pāyattika and a duṣkṛta.
This is called "making [a formal accusation].
Regarding the offense: if a bhikṣu goes to another bhikṣu and says, "That person says you are a transgressor;
what is the use of your going forth and receiving the precepts?"
"You have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa; you have committed a pāyattika; you have committed a pratideśanīya;
you have committed a duṣkṛta. "Who is that person?"
He replied, “My name is so-and-so.
“Who is the person named so-and-so?”
He replied, “My surname is such-and-such.
[The other asked,] “Who is that person with such-and-such a surname?”
He replied, “Cūḍapanthaka.
“Who is Cūḍapanthaka?”
He replied, “I did.
[The other asked,] “Who is this ‘I’ that did it?”
He replied, "It is such-and-such a mark.
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika offense.
If the listener does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, after they have understood, one speaks further, it is a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
Regarding "the sick": if a bhikṣu goes to another bhikṣu and says, "That person calls you a sick man with an evil disease;
what is the use of your leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?
You have leprosy, abscesses, consumption, epilepsy, or possession by spirits."
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
“Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, “He is of such-and-such a surname.”
"Who is this person of such-and-such a surname?
He replied, "It is Mr. Zhong."
"Who was that person? He replied, "It was so-and-so."
"Who is this person named 'Something'?
He replied, "It is the mark."
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one speaks again after they have already understood, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
This is called "affliction.
As for its characteristics: if a bhikṣu goes to another bhikṣu and says, "That person speaks ill of you;
what is the use of your leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
"You have contracted hands, stumps for hands, goiters, scrofula, left-handedness, and arms like bird wings.
"Who is he? He replied:
"His name is so-and-so.
"Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied:
“[He is] of such-and-such a surname.
“Who is this person of such-and-such a surname? He replied:
"Something. "What is this 'something'?
He replied:
"Someone made it. "Who is this 'someone'?
He replied:
"Such-and-such a mark.
If the other understands it, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand it, it is a dukkaṭa.
If, after having understood [the offense], one speaks further, it is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
This is called the characteristic mark (*nimitta*).
As for the affliction (*kleśa*): if a bhikṣu goes and says to another bhikṣu:
"He says that you are a person of heavy afflictions; what is the use of your going forth and receiving the precepts?
You have much desire, much hatred, and much delusion, and you delight in grief and distress."
“Who is he? He replied, “His name is So-and-so.”
"Who is the one named so-and-so?
He replied, "I am of such-and-such a surname."
"Who is the one surnamed Mou?
He replied, "It is Mounde."
"Who is that certain person?
He replied, "It was I who did it."
"Who is this person named 'Somebody'?
He replied, "It is Some-Aspect."
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one speaks again after they have already understood, it is a pāyattika and a dukkaṭa.
This is called "affliction. Regarding "reviling":
if a bhikṣu goes to another bhikṣu and says, "That person says you are fond of reviling others;
what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
"You revile others with two kinds of insults: the insults of a layperson and the insults of one who has gone forth.
"Who is that person? He replied:
"His name is so-and-so.
"Whose name is so-and-so? He replied:
“[He is] of such-and-such a surname.
“Who is this person of such-and-such a surname? He replied:
"Something. "What is this 'something'?
He replied:
"Someone made it. "Who is this 'someone'?
He replied:
"Such-and-such a mark.
If the other understands, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not understand, it is a duṣkṛta.
If, having understood [the meaning], one speaks further, it is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
This is called "reviling.
If a bhikṣu uses these eight kinds of speech toward another bhikṣu with the intent to cause division, it is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Apart from these eight kinds,
if one causes a bhikṣu to be separated by other matters, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Excluding the case of a bhikṣu, if one causes any other person to be separated by these eight kinds of matters, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The three matters concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus delighted in quarreling, speaking abusively, and reviling one another.
These six bhikṣus quarreled, spoke abusively, and reviled other bhikṣus; the Saṃgha had already settled the dispute according to the Dharma.
After the group of six bhikṣus knew that the matter had been settled according to the Dharma, they resumed their agitation and said:
"Venerable sirs! This matter was not properly dealt with;
it was an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta), and it should be done again."
It is not that one abandons evil by abandoning it,
nor that one ceases evil by ceasing it, nor that one extinguishes evil by extinguishing it; rather, there is further abandonment, further cessation, and further extinction.

In this situation, monks who have not yet caused a schism do so, and those who have already caused a schism cannot be reconciled; those who have not yet quarreled begin to quarrel, and those who are already quarreling cannot be pacified.

Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and, for various reasons, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you be called bhikṣus when, after the Saṃgha has settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, you initiate it again and say:
'Venerable sirs!'"
This matter is not a non-action that is further acted upon;
it is not a non-cessation of evil that is further ceased;
it is not a non-stilling of evil that is further stilled.
"Is it not that what has already been extinguished is not extinguished again?

Within this, do those who have not yet broken [the Sangha] break it, and those who have already broken it cannot be reconciled; do those who have not yet quarreled quarrel, and those who have already quarreled cannot be pacified?"
After rebuking them in various ways, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, after the Saṃgha has settled a dispute according to the Dharma, initiates it again and says:
'Venerable elders!'"
This matter is not a case of having committed an evil deed and then committing it again;
nor is it a case of having abandoned an evil and then abandoning it again;
nor is it a case of having ceased an evil and then ceasing it again.
"It is not that the extinction of evil is extinguished, but rather it is further extinguished.

Why is it that among those bhikṣus, some who have not yet split the Saṃgha do so, while those who have already split it cannot be reconciled; and why is it that those who have not yet quarreled begin to quarrel, while those who have already quarreled cannot be pacified?
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a monk, after a dispute has been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, should reopen it again, it is a pāyattika.
"In accordance with the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, the discipline, and as taught in the Buddha's instruction.
There are four kinds of disputes:
disputes concerning verbal altercations, disputes concerning groundless matters, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning customary practices.
To "re-ignite" them means to speak as follows:
"Venerable elders!
This matter is not an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*); it should be performed again.
It is not an abandonment of what should be abandoned; it should be abandoned again."
"It is not that one stops what is already stopped, nor does one stop further;
it is not that one extinguishes what is already extinguished, nor does one extinguish further.
There are five kinds of such persons:
First, the resident; second, the visitor; third, the person who experiences desire; fourth, the person who recites the *karmavācanā*; and fifth, the person who witnesses the *karmavācanā*.
*Pāyattika* means "to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct"; if one does not repent, it can obstruct and hinder the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if an elder *bhikṣu*, regarding a dispute over points of doctrine, perceives it as such a dispute, and after it has been settled according to the Dharma, perceives it as thus settled, yet initiates it again, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
This matter is not a case of committing evil and then committing it again;
nor is it a case of severing evil and then severing it again;
nor is it a case of ceasing evil and then ceasing it again.
"It is not that the evil has been extinguished; it is extinguished again.
This is a *pāyattika*.

In a dispute concerning verbal quarrels, if one perceives a groundless dispute as a dispute over an offense, or perceives a dispute over an offense as a dispute regarding customary conduct, and after it has been settled according to the Dharma, perceives it as being settled according to the Dharma, yet then initiates it again, saying: [it is not settled]. This is a *pāyattika*.
"Venerable elders!
This matter is not a transgression that has been committed and then repeated;
it is not a fault that has been abandoned and then abandoned again."
"To cease what has not yet ceased, and to further cause it to cease;
to extinguish what has not yet been extinguished, and to further cause it to be extinguished"—
this is a *pāyattika* offense.

If an elder bhikṣu, regarding a dispute that has no basis, perceives it as a dispute without basis, and after it has been settled according to the Dharma, perceives it as settled according to the Dharma, should nevertheless initiate it again, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
This matter is not a case of having committed an unwholesome act that should be performed again;
it is not a case of having abandoned what should have been abandoned, which must be abandoned further;
it is not a case of having ceased what should have been ceased, which must be ceased further.

If, after a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma—whether it was a dispute concerning offenses, a dispute concerning habitual conduct, or a dispute concerning mutual verbal abuse—one thinks that it has been settled according to the Dharma and yet further incites it by saying: "It is not settled;

it should be settled again," this is a *pāyattika*. In a dispute concerning nothing at all, if one perceives it as a dispute concerning offenses, or perceives it as a dispute concerning habitual conduct, or perceives it as a dispute concerning mutual verbal abuse, and after it has been settled according to the Dharma, one perceives it as having been settled according to the Dharma, yet further incites it by saying: [it is not settled; it should be settled again], this is a *pāyattika*.
"Venerable elders!
This matter is not a transgression that has been committed and then repeated;
it is not a fault that has been abandoned and then abandoned again."
"To cease what has not yet ceased, or to further cease it;
to extinguish what has not yet been extinguished, or to further extinguish it"—
this is a *pāyattika* offense.

An elder bhikṣu, regarding a dispute over an offense as a dispute over an offense, and having settled it according to the Dharma while perceiving it as settled according to the Dharma, should not again raise the matter, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
This matter is not a non-action that is made, nor is it an evil action that is made again;
it is not a non-cessation of evil that is ceased, nor is it an evil that is ceased again;
it is not a non-stilling of evil that is stilled, nor is it an evil that is stilled again.
"To extinguish what has already been extinguished is a further extinguishing;
this is a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) that has been settled according to the Dharma, if one perceives it as a constant dispute, a dispute involving formal accusation, or a groundless dispute, and having perceived it as settled according to the Dharma, should again initiate it by saying: [it is not settled]. This is a *pāyattika*.
"Venerable elders!
This matter is not a transgression that has been committed and then repeated;
it is not a fault that has been abandoned and then abandoned again."
"To cease what has not yet ceased, and to cause it to cease further;
to extinguish what has not yet been extinguished, and to cause it to be extinguished further—
this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense."

An elder bhikṣu who was habitually engaged in a dispute and who perceived it as a dispute, having settled it in accordance with the Dharma and perceiving it as settled in accordance with the Dharma, again raises the matter, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
This matter is not a case of having committed a misdeed and then committing it again;
nor is it a case of having abandoned a vice and then abandoning it again;
nor is it a case of having ceased a vice and then ceasing it again.
"If one says, 'It is not that the dispute has been settled;
it must be settled again,' it is a *pāyattika*.

While in the midst of a formal legal proceeding (*adhikaraṇa*), if one perceives a dispute over views (*dṛṣṭi-adhikaraṇa*) as a dispute over facts (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*), or perceives a dispute over facts as a dispute over offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*), or perceives a dispute over offenses as a dispute over views, and after the matter has been settled according to the Dharma, perceiving it as settled according to the Dharma, yet initiates it once more, saying:"
"Venerable elders!
This matter is not a transgression that has been committed and then repeated;
it is not a fault that has been abandoned and then abandoned again."
"To cease what has not yet ceased, and to cause it to cease further;
to extinguish what has not yet been extinguished, and to cause it to be extinguished further—
this is a *pāyattika* offense."
The same applies to a visiting bhikṣu, a bhikṣu who has accepted the consent (*chanda*), a bhikṣu performing the formal act (*karmakāraka*), and a bhikṣu witnessing the formal act.

If a bhikṣu, while a dispute is being settled according to the Dharma, perceives it as being settled according to the Dharma, yet subsequently re-ignites that dispute, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If, regarding a dispute settled in accordance with the Dharma, one perceives it as not having been settled in accordance with the Dharma and causes it to be reopened, it is a *pāyattika*.
If, regarding a dispute settled in accordance with the Dharma, one harbors doubt about it and causes it to be reopened, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one perceives that a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma when it was not actually settled according to the Dharma, and then initiates it again, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one harbors doubt regarding whether a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, and then initiates it again, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, regarding a dispute settled in accordance with the Dharma, one perceives it as settled improperly and then causes it to arise again, there is no offense.
The four matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Then, before midday, Kāḷudāyin dressed, took his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished eating, he returned to his own quarters, put away his robe and bowl, took his door-knob, and stood between the doors, thinking thus:
"If there are women who come here to visit, I shall show them the various rooms.
At that time, many women came to enter the monastery to look around. Seeing the women approaching from afar, Kāḷudāyin said:
"Sisters, come; I shall show you the locations of the various rooms."
For this reason, groups of women gather and speak of two kinds of shameful matters.
Regarding the mother of another, they say to a woman:
"Such-and-such marks are found in your mother's private parts."
At that time, the woman thought to herself:
"What this bhikṣu has said must mean he intends to have illicit relations with my mother.
She then told her mother about the matter regarding the woman.
"Your daughter has such-and-such marks in her private parts.
The mother thought to herself:
"What this bhikṣu says must mean that he has had sexual intercourse with my daughter."
Furthermore, she spoke to her mother-in-law regarding the conduct of her daughter-in-law, saying:
"Your daughter-in-law has such-and-such characteristics in her private parts.
The mother-in-law then thought to herself:
"He must have had an affair with my daughter-in-law," she thought,
and she told her daughter-in-law about her mother-in-law's private parts:
"Your mother-in-law has such-and-such marks on her private areas."
The daughter-in-law thought to herself:
"What this bhikṣu has said must mean he has had an affair with my mother-in-law.
When Kāḷudāyin spoke these words, he created doubt regarding both another's body and his own; thus, these women began to suspect one another.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured him with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who speaks of such doubly shameful matters before women?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who speaks of matters that cause shame for both parties in front of a woman?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman and exceeds five or six words, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Except in the presence of a man capable of understanding.
As for "a woman," it refers to a female who is capable of receiving sexual desire.

Regarding "exceeding five or six words": the five words are: "The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is impermanent; feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) aggregates are impermanent."
The six phrases refer to the impermanence of the eye, and the impermanence of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

"Dharma" refers to that which is spoken by the Buddha, spoken by his disciples, spoken by devas, spoken by rishis, and spoken by emanated beings; it reveals generosity, ethical discipline, rebirth in heaven, and nirvana.
"A wise man" refers to one who knows names and is able to discern the excellence or deficiency of speech.
"Pāyattika" means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, in the absence of a man who understands the language, preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six words, or if he speaks in verse, there is a pāyattika for each verse.
If the Sūtra says, it is a *pāyattika* for each individual act;
if it is stated as separate phrases, it is a *pāyattika* for each phrase.

If a bhikṣu sits in his previous seat and there is no man present who understands the language, and another woman comes and he again preaches the Dharma to her beyond five or six words, and the first woman is also sitting there and both hear the Dharma, [the offense is incurred].
If it is spoken in verse, there is a pāyattika for each verse.
If it is spoken in prose, there is a pāyattika for each point.
If it is spoken in individual phrases, there is a pāyattika for each phrase.
If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman in the absence of a man who understands the language, and after speaking more than five or six sentences, he rises from his seat and departs;
yet another woman comes along the path and he again teaches her the Dharma in the absence of a man who understands the language, exceeding five or six sentences.
If a woman arrives later and both listen to the Dharma together,
if it is taught in verse, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each verse;
if it is taught as prose, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each point.
If explained according to individual phrases, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each phrase.

If a bhikṣu, in the absence of a man who understands his speech, preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six phrases, and subsequently enters another house where he again preaches the Dharma to another woman for more than five or six phrases while still in the absence of a man who understands his speech.
Previously, women also came and stood by the walls, or by the screens, or by the fences, or by the moats, and likewise listened to the Dharma.
If it is spoken in verse, there is a *pāyattika* for each verse.
If it is spoken as a sūtra, there is a *pāyattika* for each matter.
If it is spoken as individual phrases, there is a *pāyattika* for each phrase.

There is no offense if the bhikṣu is chanting, or receiving a donation, or explaining the merit of the gift, or conferring the precepts, or answering when a woman asks a question. There is no offense in these cases.
The five matters concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.

Then, the bhikṣus in the kingdom of Ālavī were teaching those who had not yet received full ordination the method of reciting phrases within the monastery. Sometimes they added extra phrases or omitted necessary phrases; sometimes they added extra flavor (*rasa*) or omitted necessary flavor; sometimes they added extra syllables or omitted necessary syllables. For these reasons, a great clamor arose within the monastery—a loud noise, the sound of a large crowd, like the sound of people learning arithmetic, like the sound of Brahmins reciting the Vedas, or like the sound of a fisherman when he has lost his catch; such was the sound produced by those within the monastery teaching the unordained through the method of reciting phrases.
When the Buddha heard this great, loud sound, he knew the cause yet asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is there such a great clamor of many people within this monastery?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!

The bhikṣus of the city of Āravī teach those who have not yet received full ordination within the monastery using the method of phrases; they do so with phrases that are either complete or incomplete, with meanings that are either complete or incomplete, and with words that are either complete or incomplete.”
"For this reason, there was a great, loud clamor from the multitude.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the answer, intentionally asked the bhikṣu Ārāḍa:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
For these various reasons, the Buddha rebuked the bhikṣu Ālavī:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu teach the dharma of phrases to those who have not yet received full ordination?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu teaches the dharma according to the phrasing [of the scriptures] to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
One who has not received full ordination refers to everyone except bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the rules of composition: there are complete phrases and incomplete phrases, complete words and incomplete words, and complete flavors and incomplete flavors.
A complete phrase is one that fully expresses the intended meaning.
"Deficient in phrasing" means not fully explaining the phrasing.
"Complete in flavor" means fully explaining the flavor.
"Deficient in flavor" means not fully explaining the flavor.
"Complete syllables" refers to words that are fully articulated.
"Incomplete syllables" refers to words that are not fully articulated.
If a phrase is complete, it is one in which the flavor and the syllables are complete; it is not a case where the phrase, the flavor, or the syllables are incomplete.
If a phrase is incomplete, it is likewise deficient in flavor and deficient in syllables; it is not a complete phrase, nor is it complete in flavor or syllables.

As for "Dharma," it refers to what is spoken by the Buddha, what is spoken by his disciples, what is spoken by devas, what is spoken by ṛṣis, and what is spoken by emanated beings, which reveals generosity, ethical discipline, rebirth in heaven, and nirvāṇa.
*Pāyattika* means "boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct and hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu teaches a person who has not yet received full ordination using verses or metrical phrases, for each verse, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is stated according to the sūtra, there is a *pāyattika* for each individual matter;
if stated according to individual phrases, there is a *pāyattika* for every phrase.
This is likewise true for the completion of flavors and the completion of syllables.
If a bhikṣu teaches a person who has not yet received full ordination using verses that are incomplete in their phrasing, for each verse taught, it is a pāyattika offense.
If he teaches them by individual lines, for each line, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a sutra states that for each individual item it is a *pāyattika*,
the same applies to what is insufficient in flavor and insufficient in syllables.
There is no offense if one speaks after the recitation has been completed.

There is no offense if it concerns a *uddeśa* (instruction) where both question and answer are recited; therein, one who is himself a *uddeśa*-giver imparts the scripture, and the others who are reciters finish their recitation.
The six matters are concluded. *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya), Scroll Nine.
*Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vinaya*, Scroll Twelve; the fourth recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The second part of the ninety *pāyattika* rules:
When the Buddha was staying at the kingdom of Vaiśālī during the summer retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, there was famine in the world and alms were difficult to obtain.
At that time, even the wives and children of ordinary people lacked sufficient food and drink for themselves, let alone what they could give to beggars.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:

"Do you know? There is currently a famine here and alms-food is difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of the people lack sufficient food and drink for themselves, let alone give it to beggars."

"O bhikṣus, go to dwell in retreat according to whom you know, according to your kinsmen, or according to those in whom you have faith; do not undergo various sufferings and afflictions for the sake of food and drink."
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣus prostrated at his feet and departed according to their acquaintances.
Some went to the country of Kośala to observe the rains retreat; one bhikṣu went to the banks of the Bhagīrathī River and took up residence for the retreat in dependence upon a certain village.

In this village there was a wealthy family, possessing abundant wealth and treasures and an abundance of grain; they had many enterprises, fields, people, slaves, and laborers, and were successful in every respect.
At that time, the bhikṣu Bhagu thought to himself:
"In this world of famine, alms-food is difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of ordinary people lack sufficient food and drink for themselves, let alone give it to a beggar."

In this village there was a wealthy family, possessing abundant riches and treasures with an ample supply of grain; they were fully endowed with various assets, including fields, lands, people, servants, and laborers.
"Why do we not go to his house and say to one another in praise:
'Does the village headman know? You have gained a great and excellent benefit;
you possess a great field of merit, for the Saṃgha relies upon your village to dwell in retreat.'"

In this assembly, such-and-such a person is an arhat; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward arhatship; such-and-such a person is an anāgāmin; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward anāgāminship; such-and-such a person is a sakṛdāgāmin; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward sakṛdāgāminship; such-and-such a person is a srotāpanna; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward srotāpannaship; such-and-such a person has attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna; such-and-such a person has attained [the immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; such-and-such a person has attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; such-and-such a person has attained the contemplation of impurity; such-and-such a person has attained mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
After the bhikṣus had formed this thought, they entered a village and went to the house of a wealthy man, where they said to one another in praise:
"Does the householder know?"
"You have obtained great and excellent benefit and possess a great field of merit, for the Saṃgha relies upon your village for the rains retreat.

Such-and-such a person is an Arhat; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward Arhatship; such-and-such a person is an Anāgāmin; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward Anāgāminship; such-and-such a person is a Sakṛdāgāmin; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward Sakṛdāgāminship; such-and-such a person is a Srotāpanna; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward Srotāpannaship; such-and-such a person has attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; such-and-such a person has attained the immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; such-and-such a person has attained the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; such-and-such a person has attained the contemplation of impurity; such-and-such a person has attained mindfulness of ānāpāna."
Having heard this, the laypeople attained faith and patience, and they thought:
"We have truly gained a great benefit; we have the Sangha, a field of great merit, who rely upon our village for the rains retreat."
"Such-and-such a person is an Arhat; such-and-such a person is one progressing toward Arhatship," and so on, up to "one who practices mindfulness of *ānāpāna*.
Just as he provided the Saṃgha with morning meals, midday meals, and *drākṣāpāna* (grape drinks) during times of plenty and prosperity, he did likewise during times of famine and scarcity.

The bhikṣus who were observing the rainy season retreat at the various Pāṅkramaṇa rivers consumed this food and drink, whereby they attained great physical vigor, becoming robust, flourishing, and lustrous.
It was the custom of the Buddha during his lifetime to hold two great assemblies each year:
at the end of the spring month and at the end of the summer month.
In the final month of spring, monks in various regions and lands everywhere had this thought:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha, we shall practice during our summer retreat so that we may dwell in peace and happiness."
This was the first great assembly.

At the end of the summer months, when the bhikṣus had completed their three-month summer retreat and finished making their robes, they took their robes and bowls and went to where the Buddha was, thinking:
"We have not seen the Buddha for a long time; we have not seen the World-Honored One for a long time."
This was the second great assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣus of the kingdom of Kośala, having completed their summer retreat of three months and finished making their robes, took up their robes and bowls and traveled on to Vaiśālī.

It is the constant practice of the Buddhas that when guest monks arrive while there are monks who have entered the rains retreat with the Buddha, they should go together to welcome them, inquire after their well-being with a single-minded heart, open up the rooms, and point out the places for bedding, saying:
"These are your rooms; here are the beds, stools, individual sitting benches, blankets, quilts, pillows, and mats; please stay according to the order of seniority."

At that time, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī saw the bhikṣus of Kośala approaching from afar; they went out together to welcome them, inquiring after their well-being with single-minded devotion. They assisted them by carrying their robes and bowls, opening their rooms, and showing them where the bedding was.
They spoke thus: "This is your room, bedding, and couch; please stay according to the order of seniority."
He inquired after them, saying:
"Are you not weary from the road? Is your strength light and vigorous? Was it not difficult for you to obtain alms?
They replied:
"We are not weary from the road and our physical strength is light and vigorous; however, almsfood is difficult to obtain.
The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī said:
"It is true that you are not weary from the road and your physical strength is light and vigorous, yet almsfood is difficult to obtain, for you are emaciated and your complexions are haggard."

At that time, the bhikṣus who had been in retreat by the banks of the Bhagurī River completed their robes at the end of the three-month period; taking their robes and bowls, they traveled on and arrived at Vaiśālī.

The bhikṣus who were observing the rainy-season retreat together with the Buddha saw the bhikṣus coming from afar along the Bhagurā River; they all went out together to welcome them and greeted them with single-minded attention. They took up their robes and bowls for them, opened the rooms, and showed them the places for bedding, saying:
"These are your rooms, couches, and bedding; please stay according to the order of seniority."
He inquired after them, saying:
"Are you not weary from the road? Are your physical strength and vigor light and robust? Was it not difficult for you to obtain alms?
They replied:
"We are light and agile in our physical strength; begging for alms is not difficult for us, but we are utterly exhausted from the journey.
The bhikṣus staying in Vaiśālī said, "It is true that you are utterly exhausted from the journey, and that begging for alms is not difficult for you."
"Why is this? You all are plump and flourishing, with serene and joyful countenances.
Then the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī gradually pressed him with questions:
“Venerable elders!
In this present age of famine, alms are difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of ordinary people lack sufficient food and drink for themselves, let alone give to beggars.
For what reason and by what cause do you remain so robust in strength and so serene in countenance during the rains retreat, such that alms are not difficult for you to obtain?”
Then the bhikṣus of the Pāṅkadhā River immediately recounted the causes and conditions as described above.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Are the virtues for which you have offered praise truly possessed by you?"
He replied, "Indeed there are.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased and censured it through various causes and conditions:
“How can a bhikṣu, for the sake of mere food and drink, claim to possess superhuman qualities and speak of them to one who has not yet received full ordination?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [what had occurred], he intentionally asked the bhikṣu Pāpamārga:
"Did you truly do these things?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“What is it to call oneself a bhikṣu who, for the sake of food and drink, falsely claims to possess superhuman qualities and speaks of them to one who has not yet received full ordination?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, possessing a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
"Those who have not received the full ordination" refers to everyone other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
"In reality" means that they have attained these noble dharmas.
*Pāyattika* means that which burns, consumes, and obstructs; if one does not repent for it, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu is actually an arhat and speaks of this to others, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one who is actually a candidate for Arhatship tells others that they are so, it is a pāyattika.

If one who is actually an Anāgāmin tells others that they are an Anāgāmin; if one who is actually a Sakṛdāgāmin tells others that they are a Sakṛdāgāmin; or if one who is actually a Srotāpanna tells others that they are a Srotāpanna—in all such cases, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu truly attains the first dhyāna and speaks of it to others, it is a pāyattika. If he truly attains the second, third, or fourth dhyāna;

the [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the [four formless attainments of] the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; or the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), and speaks of these to others, it is a pāyattika.
If one says, "I am well-versed in maintaining the precepts," to others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu truly sees various devas come to him, or nāgas, yakṣas, pūtana ghosts, piśāca ghosts, or rākṣasa ghosts come to him, and he speaks of this to others, it is a *pāyattika*.
Even if one sees a spirit of the soil (*kṣetrapāla*) come to one's presence and speaks of it to another person, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The seven matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then the group of six bhikṣus delighted in quarreling, speaking abusively, and reviling one another.

At that time, after the group of six bhikṣus had engaged in quarreling, disputing, reviling, and abusing other bhikṣus, they spoke of their evil offenses to those who had not yet received full ordination, saying:
"Such-and-such a bhikṣu has committed a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a prātideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta offense."

In this regard, monks, that which was not yet split becomes split; that which was already split does not become reconciled; matters not yet brought forward are brought forward; and matters already brought forward cannot be settled.

Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and, for various reasons, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who delights in quarreling, mutual accusation, and mutual abuse, and having already fought with others, speaks of their evil offenses to those who have not yet received full ordination?"
"A certain bhikṣu has committed a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a prātideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta.
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported this in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the truth] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"What is meant by a bhikṣu who delights in quarreling, mutual recrimination, and verbal abuse; having engaged in a dispute with another, he reveals his evil offenses to one who has not yet received full ordination, saying:
'A certain bhikṣu has committed a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta offense'?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another has committed a grave offense, speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
"Knows" means: either he knows it himself, or he hears it from another, or the person himself tells him.
"Evil offenses" refers to all violations of the precepts, including *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, which are all termed "evil.
"Those who have not received the full ordination" refers to all persons other than *bhikṣus* and *bhikṣuṇīs*.

Regarding "except for those who have been subjected to a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*)," the term "monastic act" refers to the following: if a bhikṣu commits an evil deed in the house of a layperson or causes another to do so, the Saṃgha present before him should perform a formal act of confessing the offense (*āpatti-deśanā-karman*) against that person.
Regarding the ritual for proclaiming an offense (*āpatti-karman*): first, one should seek out a person capable of proclaiming the offense; it should be performed in this manner.
With a unified and harmonious Sangha, one person should announce:
"Who is able to proclaim the offense of such-and-such bhikṣu?"
"Who among you is able to proclaim the offense of such-and-such a bhikṣu before such-and-such a lay devotee?
If there is a bhikṣu therein who says he is able, the Saṃgha of bhikṣus should deliberate upon that matter.
If there are five qualities, the Saṃgha should not appoint someone as a person to proclaim an offense.
What are these five qualities?
Speaking out of favoritism, speaking out of hatred, speaking out of fear, speaking out of delusion, and not knowing what should or should not be proclaimed.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with five qualities, the Saṃgha should appoint him as a person to proclaim an offense.

What are the five? He does not speak out of favoritism; he does not speak out of hatred; he does not speak out of fear; he does not speak out of delusion; and he knows when to speak and when not to speak.
In this assembly, one bhikṣu proclaims within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [name] is capable of acting as the one who confesses the offense; he is able to proclaim the offense of the bhikṣu [name] before the layperson [name]."

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let it be known that the bhikṣu so-and-so is able to act as the one who confesses the offense, and is able to proclaim the offense of the bhikṣu so-and-so before the layperson so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one subsequent proclamation):
"The Saṃgha has completed the *āpattideśanā-karman* (the formal act of confessing an offense). Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
If a bhikṣu is the one who confesses the offense, he should state that bhikṣu’s offense; other bhikṣus should not speak of it.
If any other bhikṣu speaks [of this], he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu acts as one who confesses his offense, he should speak to that layperson and should not speak to anyone else.
If one speaks of this to others, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies whether one speaks according to households— whether one household or many households—
or according to places of practice— whether one place of practice or many places of practice.
It is spoken with reference to a village—whether it be a single village or many villages—and with reference to streets, lanes, or marketplaces—whether they be one or many.
One should speak of it in this very location; if one speaks of it in another location, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu who has committed an offense, after the Saṃgha has performed the *karma* of proclaiming his offense, continues to trouble the Saṃgha with diligence, at that time the entire Saṃgha should proclaim this person’s offense.
It should be performed in this manner:
within a harmonious Saṃgha gathered with a single mind, one bhikṣu shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, after the Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā* for the confession of his offense, continues to diligently harass the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent: let the entire Saṃgha, according to their will, at the appropriate time and place, proclaim the offense of this bhikṣu.
Thus it is announced.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Saṃgha has completed the *yathā-prajñapti-āpatti-karman*. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
This is called the *saṃghakamma* for removal. Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, scorches, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path. As for the offense herein:

if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pārājika* offense, and he forms the perception that it is a *pārājika*; or sees within [the category of] "seen" the perception of having seen; or sees within "seen" the perception of not having seen; or sees within "seen" doubt; or hears within [the category of] "heard" the perception of having heard; or hears within "heard" the perception of not having heard; or hears within "heard" doubt—if he then speaks of the name [of the offender], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one speaks of the matter itself, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
According to the names spoken of, for each statement regarding the matter, there is a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, he may have the perception that it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the perception of seeing within what is seen, the perception of not seeing within what is seen, the perception of doubt within what is seen; or the perception of hearing within what is heard, the perception of not hearing within what is heard, or the perception of doubt within what is heard.
If one speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*;
if one speaks of the matter [of the offense], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
According to whether one speaks of the name or the matter, for each individual word, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta offense. Regarding that duṣkṛta, he has the perception of it being a duṣkṛta; regarding what was seen, he has the perception that it was seen; regarding what was seen, he has the perception that it was not seen; regarding what was seen, he has doubt; regarding what was heard, he has the perception that it was heard; regarding what was heard, he has the perception that it was not heard; regarding what was heard, he has doubt.
If one speaks of the name, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one speaks of the matter, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
For every word spoken, whether regarding the name or the matter, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, yet perceives it as a pārājika; or perceives it as a saṃghāvaśeṣa; or perceives it as a pāyattika; or perceives it as a pratideśanīya; or perceives it as a duṣkṛta—this bhikṣu, regarding what is a pārājika, forms the notion that it is a duṣkṛta; regarding what he has seen, he forms the notion that he has seen it; regarding what he has seen, he forms the notion that he has not seen it; regarding what he has seen, he is in doubt; regarding what he has heard, he forms the notion that he has heard it; regarding what he has heard, he forms the notion that he has not heard it;
regarding what he has heard, he is in doubt. If he speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a pāyattika; if he speaks of the matter [itself], it is a duṣkṛta.
To speak according to what was said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *pāyattika* or a *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, he may regard it as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or as a *pāyattika*, or as a *pratideśanīya*, or as a *dukkaṭa*, or as a *pārājika*. In this case, regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, that bhikṣu may conceive the notion of a *pārājika*: having seen it, he has the notion that he saw it; having seen it, he has the notion that he did not see it; having seen it, he is in doubt; having heard it, he has the notion that he heard it; having heard it, he has the notion that he did not hear it; or having heard it, he is in doubt.
If one speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*;
if one speaks of the matter [of the offense], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For every word spoken, whether speaking of the name or speaking of the matter, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa* respectively.

Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*. Among these *duṣkṛtas*, he perceives one as a *duṣkṛta*, or as a *pārājika*, or as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or as a *pāyattika*, or as a *pratideśanīya*. This bhikṣu, regarding a *duṣkṛta*, gives rise to the perception that it is a *pratideśanīya*. Regarding what is seen, he has the perception that it was seen; regarding what is seen, he has the perception that it was not seen; regarding what is seen, he has doubt. Regarding what is heard, he has the perception that it was heard; regarding what is heard, he has the perception that it was not heard; regarding what is heard, he has doubt.
If one speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one speaks of the matter [of the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For every word spoken, whether referring to the name or the matter, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense and conceives doubt as to whether it is a pārājika or not a pārājika, and that bhikṣu later resolves his doubt, forming the perception of a pārājika regarding what was a pārājika:

if he perceives what he saw as having been seen, perceives what he saw as not having been seen, perceives what he saw with doubt, perceives what he heard as having been heard, perceives what he heard as not having been heard, or perceives what he heard with doubt—if he speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a pāyattika;
if he speaks of the matter [itself], it is a dukkaṭa.
To speak in accordance with what was said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceives a doubt as to whether it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or not a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:

That bhikṣu subsequently eliminates his doubt; regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, he conceives the perception that it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding what was seen, he has the perception that it was seen; regarding what was seen, he has the perception that it was not seen; regarding what was seen, he has doubt. Regarding what was heard, he has the perception that it was heard; regarding what was heard, he has the perception that it was not heard;
regarding what was heard, he has doubt. If he speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*; if he speaks of the matter [itself], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak in accordance with what has been said is called "speaking of a matter"; for each such utterance, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *dukkaṭa*, and that bhikṣu develops doubt regarding that *dukkaṭa*, wondering whether it is indeed a *dukkaṭa* or not a *dukkaṭa*, [he incurs an offense].

That bhikṣu later resolves his doubts: regarding a *duṣkṛta* offense, he forms the perception that it is a *duṣkṛta*; regarding what was seen, he forms the perception that it was seen; regarding what was seen, he forms the perception that it was not seen; regarding what was seen, he has doubt; regarding what was heard, he forms the perception that it was heard; regarding what was heard, he forms the perception that it was not heard;
regarding what was heard, he has doubt. If he speaks of the name, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if he speaks of the matter, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak according to what was said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pārājika* offense, but has doubts regarding that *pārājika*, wondering whether it is a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
Is it a pārājika? Is it a pāyattika? Is it a pārajika or a pratideśanīya?
Is it a pārājika or a duṣkṛta?

This person has severed their doubts; regarding a *pārājika* offense, they conceive the perception that it is a *pārājika*. Regarding what is seen, they have the perception that it was seen, the perception that it was not seen, or doubt regarding what was seen. Regarding what is heard, they have the perception that it was heard, the perception that it was not heard, or doubt regarding what was heard.
If they speak of the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*; if they speak of the matter itself, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak in accordance with what was said—that is, to speak of the matter word for word—constitutes a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceives a doubt as to whether this offense is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, [he incurs an offense].
Is it a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pratideśanīya*?
Is it a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *duṣkṛta*?
Is it a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pārājika*?

This person has severed their doubts; regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, they conceive the notion that it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Regarding what is seen, they have the notion that it was seen, the notion that it was not seen, or doubt as to whether it was seen. Regarding what is heard, they have the notion that it was heard, the notion that it was not heard, or doubt as to whether it was heard.
If they speak of the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*; if they speak of the matter [itself], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak according to what was said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *dukkaṭa*, and he harbors doubt regarding that *dukkaṭa*, wondering whether it is a *dukkaṭa* or a *pārājika*:
Is it a *duṣkṛta*, or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?
Is it a *duṣkṛta*, or a *pāyattika*?
Is it a *duṣkṛta*, or a *pratideśanīya*?

This person has severed their doubts: regarding a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing), they conceive the thought that it is a *duṣkṛta*; regarding what is seen, they conceive the thought that it was seen, the thought that it was not seen, or doubt; regarding what is heard, they conceive the thought that it was heard, the thought that it was not heard, or doubt.
If one speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*; if one speaks of the matter [itself], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak according to what was said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pārājika* offense and conceives doubt as to whether this offense constitutes a *pārājika*, [he incurs an offense].
Is it a saṃghāvaśeṣa?
Is it a pāyattika? Or is it a pratideśanīya?

Is it a *duṣkṛta*? This person, regarding a *pārājika*, definitely forms the perception of a *duṣkṛta*. Regarding what was seen, there is the perception of having seen; regarding what was seen, there is the perception of not having seen; regarding what was seen, there is doubt. Regarding what was heard, there is the perception of having heard; regarding what was heard, there is the perception of not having heard; regarding what was heard, there is doubt. If one speaks of the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*;
if one speaks of the matter [itself], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak according to what was said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceives a doubt as to whether this offense is indeed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, [he must address it].
Is it a pāyattika? Is it a pāṭidesanīya?
Or is it a duṣkṛta?
Is this a *pārājika* offense?

This person, regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, definitely forms the perception that it is a *pārājika*. If they perceive it as such, perceive it as such, perceive it as not such, or have doubt regarding it; or if they hear it as such, perceive it as such, perceive it as not such, or have doubt regarding it—then if they state the name [of the offense], it is a *pāyattika*;
if they state the matter [itself], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
To speak according to what was said is "speaking of the matter"; for each individual word, there is a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *dukkaṭa*, and that person develops doubt regarding the *dukkaṭa*, wondering: "Is it a *dukkaṭa*?"
Is it a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*,
or a *pāyattika*?
Regarding the *pāṭidesanīya*:

if this person, within what is actually a *duṣkṛta*, definitely forms the perception that it is a *pāṭidesanīya*; or if they perceive what was seen as having been seen, perceive what was seen as not having been seen, or have doubt regarding what was seen; or if they perceive what was heard as having been heard, perceive what was heard as not having been heard, or have doubt regarding what was heard—then if they state the name [of the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if they state the matter [itself], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak according to what has been said is to speak of the matter; for each individual word, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The eight matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then, the Elder Dabba Mallaputta was widely learned and well-informed, capable of procuring offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and other requisites for life.

At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmapāla’s robes were worn out and tattered. Because of the bhikṣu Dharmapāla, the lay devotees provided the community of monks with abundant food, drink, and clothing; these items should now be distributed among the *saṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* (the assembly present).
At that time, the bhikṣu Mettiyabhūma had this thought:

"It is because of this bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta that the Saṅgha has received much offerings of food, drink, robes, bedding, and medicinal requisites; yet the robes of this bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta are worn out."
"Now that the Sangha has obtained property that should be distributed by the present assembly, we shall perform a *karmavācanā* before the assembly to give it to the bhikṣu Dhāva.
Having formed this thought, he immediately performed the *karmavācanā* within the assembly to give it to the bhikṣu Dhāva.
This bhikṣu Mithilābhūma first personally exhorted [the donors] to give, and later spoke these words:
"The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal attachments."
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased and censured it for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who first encourages others to give, and later says:
'The bhikṣus have diverted the property of the Saṃgha and given it away according to their personal attachments'?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the truth, asked the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who first encourages others to give, yet later says:
'The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal friendships'?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu first encourages [others] to give, and later says,
"The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal intimacy," it is a pāyattika.
Regarding those who first encourage giving: having first offered their consent to the Saṃgha, they subsequently say:

"According to [one's] intimacy, according to one's preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya), according to those with the same preceptor and the same teacher, according to one's spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), according to those one holds dear, according to one's colleagues, according to the country, according to the village, according to the household, or according to one's companions."

"Regarding 'property of the Saṃgha': it refers to items obtained through offerings, such as robes, alms bowls, door-bolts, medicines for the current time, medicines for the night period, medicines for seven days, and medicines for life."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is a cooking, a burning, and a covering obstruction; if one does not repent, it can obstruct and hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu has first already encouraged [others] to give their consent (*chanda*), and later says:
"The bhikṣus have distributed the property of the Saṃgha according to their personal intimacy."
One incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If one says:

"I follow my preceptor (*upādhyāya*), I follow my teacher (*ācārya*), I follow those who share a preceptor with me, I follow those who share a teacher with me, I follow my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), I follow those I hold dear, I follow those with whom I work together, I follow the country, and I follow the village."
"To follow one's own household or one's own companions"—in all such cases, it is a *pāyattika*.
The nine matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Elder Channa had committed an offense requiring confession. Then, out of compassion, pity, and a desire for his welfare, the bhikṣus instructed him to confess, saying:
"Channa!..."
"You have committed a certain offense requiring confession; you should reveal it and not conceal it.
Channa said, "What is the use of these minor precepts?"

"When the half-monthly *poṣadha* confession is being recited, it causes the bhikṣus to feel doubt, regret, distress, and feverish agitation; they become sorrowful and unhappy, giving rise to the thought of renouncing the precepts.
Among them, there was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the *dhūta* austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and censured [the speaker] through various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu speak in such a manner?"
"What is the use of these minor precepts?

When they are recited every half-month, they cause the bhikṣus to feel doubt, regret, distress, and feverish agitation; they lead them to sorrow and discontent, giving rise to the thought of abandoning the precepts."
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked Channa intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu disparage what he has studied?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, should speak thus:'"
"What is the use of these minor precepts?

When they are recited every half-month, they cause the bhikṣus to feel doubt, regret, distress, and feverish agitation; they become sorrowful and unhappy, giving rise to the thought of abandoning the precepts."
"To thus disparage and revile the precepts constitutes a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* means "cooking, burning, and obscuring"; if one does not repent, it can obstruct and hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if, when a bhikṣu recites the four pārājikas, he says, "What is the use of these four pārājikas?

When they are recited every half-month, they cause the bhikṣus to feel doubt, regret, and distress; they cause them grief and discontent, leading them to give rise to the thought of abandoning the precepts."

[Pāyattika. If, when a bhikṣu is reciting the thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas, the two aniyata dharmas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika dharmas, the ninety pāyattika dharmas, the four pratideśanīya dharmas, the numerous śaikṣa dharmas, the seven adhikaraṇa-śamatha dharmas, or when reciting the Sūtra on the Concordance with the Vinaya (Vinayānuvartaka-sūtra), he should say:
"What is the use of this Sūtra on the Concordance with the Vinaya? [he commits an offense.]

"When the fortnightly recitation is being performed, it causes the bhikṣus to experience doubt, regret, distress, feverish anxiety, and unhappiness, leading them to give rise to the thought of abandoning the precepts.
Those who speak such words all commit a pāyattika offense.
When teaching other sūtras, excluding those that follow the Vinaya, [he said]:
"What is the use of preaching this sūtra?
It causes the bhikṣus to feel doubt, regret, distress, and feverish agitation; they become sorrowful and unhappy, giving rise to the thought of abandoning the precepts."
One who speaks these words commits a *duṣkṛta*.
For every single word spoken in the place where it was said, one incurs a *pāyattika* and a *duṣkṛta*.
The ten matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Ālavī personally pulled up the grass within the monastery, the grass on the walking paths (*caṅkrama*), and the grass at both ends of the walking paths; they also personally gathered flowers.
At that time, there was a householder who perceived life within grasses and trees; out of a mind of envy and jealousy, he said:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are takers of life; they kill all sentient beings."
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the bhikṣu Ārāḍa:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣu of Ālavī with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu pull grass from within the monastery, grass from the walking path (caṅkrama), grass from both ends of the walking path, or pluck flowers with his own hands?"
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a formal precept.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a certain mahallaka bhikṣu who was by caste a carpenter; he cut down a large piplu tree to build a large dwelling.

Then, during the latter part of the night, this tree deity carried a young boy upon her back and, with her hands, led and embraced both boys and girls as she surrounded them and approached the place where the Buddha was. Having bowed her head at his feet and stood to one side, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How can such a thing exist?
This dwelling, this residence, this support, this refuge, this abode where I stay—there was a certain Mahallaka bhikṣu who cut down my trees to construct a large dwelling for himself."
"My sons are young and numerous; during these eight nights of winter, the cold wind pierces like splitting bamboo and the frost is most severe.
Where shall I find a place of safety and comfort for my children?"
At that time, the Buddha commanded the other spirits, saying,
"You must provide a dwelling place for this one.
Because of the Buddha's words, the spirits immediately granted him a place to stay.
When that night had passed, the Buddha gathered the community of bhikṣus for this matter and said to the bhikṣus:
"Last night, a spirit carrying a small child on its back and holding boys and girls by the hands came to me, surrounding me, and having bowed its head in salutation, stood to one side and said:
'How can such a thing exist?'"
"In the dwelling, residence, shelter, refuge, and abode where I live, a certain mahallaka bhikṣu cut down my trees to construct a large dwelling."
"My sons are young and numerous; during these eight nights of winter, the cold wind pierces like splitting bamboo and the frost is most severe.
Where shall I find a place of safety for my children?"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This matter is contrary to the Dharma, it is not right, and it should not be done.
The lay devotees and the devas all find fault with and rebuke this."

"What is meant by a bhikṣu who, with his own hands, pulls up grass within the monastery, grass on the walking path (*caṅkrama*), grass at both ends of the walking path, or plucks flowers with his own hands?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For the sake of ten benefits, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu cuts or uproots the seeds of a 'ghost village' (bhūtagāma), it is a pāyattika.
A "ghost village" refers to growing grasses and trees upon which sentient beings dwell.

These sentient beings are tree spirits, spring spirits, river spirits, house spirits, crossroads spirits, market spirits, highway spirits, mosquitoes, gadflies, dung beetles, butterflies, hemp-eating insects, scorpions, and ants; these sentient beings take grasses and trees as their dwellings, and they regard them as villages, hamlets, and cities.

"Living beings" refers to those whose roots possess moisture; whether one cuts them oneself or instructs another to cut them, breaks them oneself or instructs another to break them, burns them oneself or instructs another to burn them—this is called "cutting."
There are five kinds of seeds for plants and trees:
root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, self-falling seeds, and fruit-seeds.
As for root-seeds, these refer to lotus roots, radishes, turnips, *śālūka*, and *sthalūka*—such are the various species that grow from roots.
Regarding seeds from stems: these refer to pomegranate, grape, willow, and śāla; such types are those that produce beings from stems.
Regarding seeds from joints: these refer to sugarcane, coarse bamboo, and fine bamboo; such types are those that produce beings from joints.

Regarding those that propagate by dropping their own seeds: these refer to plants such as *śaivāla*, *aśuruka*, *pāsuruka*, *sugara*, and *bodhana*, as well as other similar species that reproduce by shedding their seeds.
"Actual seeds" refers to rice, hemp, wheat, large beans, small beans, and flat beans—such seeds as these produce living beings.
"Pāyattika" means to boil, burn, cover, or obstruct; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, with respect to a root seed, perceives it as a root seed, and with respect to a living plant, perceives it as living, should he himself cut it or instruct another to cut it, himself break it or instruct another to break it, or himself burn it or instruct another to burn it, it is a pāyattika.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu perceives a root seed as a stem seed, a branch seed, a self-falling seed, a fruit seed, or perceives that which is already growing as being further growing, and if he himself cuts it or instructs another to cut it; himself breaks it or instructs another to break it; himself burns it or instructs another to burn it, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, regarding a stem-seed as a stem-seed and regarding what has grown from it as having grown from it, cuts it himself or instructs another to cut it, breaks it himself or instructs another to break it, or burns it himself or instructs another to burn it, it is a pāyattika.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu perceives a stem-seed as a branch-seed, a self-falling seed, a fruit-seed, or a root-seed, or perceives growth within growth, and then cuts it himself or instructs another to cut it, breaks it himself or instructs another to break it, or burns it himself or instructs another to burn it, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, regarding a plant propagated from a cutting as being a plant propagated from a cutting, or regarding what has grown [from it] as being what has grown, cuts it himself or instructs another to cut it, breaks it himself or instructs another to break it, or burns it himself or instructs another to burn it, it is a pāyattika.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu perceives a branch-propagating seed as a self-falling seed, a fruit seed, a root seed, or a stem seed, and conceives the thought that it is a living thing, and then cuts it himself or instructs another to cut it; breaks it himself or instructs another to break it; or burns it himself or instructs another to burn it, it is a pāyattika offense.

If a bhikṣu himself cuts seeds that have fallen of their own accord, perceiving them as such; or if he himself breaks or instructs another to break, himself burns or instructs another to burn seeds that have grown within living organisms, it is a pāyattika.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu himself cuts seeds that have fallen of their own accord—perceiving them as seed-fruits, root-seeds, stem-seeds, branch-seeds, or perceiving what has grown from within as seeds—and either cuts them himself or instructs another to cut them, breaks them himself or instructs another to break them, or burns them himself or instructs another to burn them, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, regarding actual seeds with the perception of actual seeds, or regarding living things with the perception of living things, cuts them himself or instructs another to cut them; breaks them himself or instructs another to break them; burns them himself or instructs another to burn them; it is a pāyattika.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, regarding actual seeds, perceives them as root-seeds, stem-seeds, branch-seeds, self-falling seeds, or sprouts within sprouts, and then cuts them himself or instructs others to cut them; breaks them himself or instructs others to break them; burns them himself or instructs others to burn them—this is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu burns five types of seeds at one time, he commits five pāyattikas simultaneously;
if he burns them one by one, he commits one pāyattika for each.
For as many seeds as he burns, he incurs that many pāyattikas.
If a bhikṣu cuts down a tree himself or instructs another to cut it down, it is a pāyattika offense.
For every tree cut down, he incurs that many pāyattika offenses.
If a bhikṣu cuts down grass himself or instructs another to cut it down, it is a pāyattika offense.
For every blade of grass cut, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
