If one perceives a living being as a living being and cuts it oneself or instructs another to cut it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one perceives a living being as something dry and cuts it oneself or instructs another to cut it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one suspects that what is being cut is dry [wood] rather than living [plant matter], and cuts it oneself or instructs another to cut it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one perceives what is dry as being living, and cuts it oneself or instructs another to cut it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one suspects that what is dry is actually living matter, and one cuts it oneself or instructs another to cut it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives what is dry as dry, and one cuts it oneself or instructs another to cut it, there is no offense.
The eleventh matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta, having accomplished five qualities, was appointed by the Saṃgha through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) as the distributor of meals. When he assigned the various bhikṣus to their seats for the meal, he did not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion; he knew the proper order and assigned them according to their seniority, never skipping anyone in the sequence.
At that time, the bhikṣu Mittavindaka obtained coarse and unpalatable food; while eating this unwholesome meal, he thought to himself:

"This bhikṣu Dabba assigns meals according to his own desires, and out of anger, fear, delusion, or ignorance of the proper order, he bypasses the sequence and does not follow the hierarchy of seniority."
"We shall collectively expel this person and appoint another to serve as the *saṃgha-karman* official.
Among them, there was a bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the *dhūta* austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and rebuked them with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, when the Saṃgha has performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) according to the Dharma to appoint an official, one immediately speaks with anger and derision?"
"‘They sit according to desire, hatred, fear, or delusion; they do not know the proper order, nor do they follow the sequence by skipping over those who should sit above or below.
Having thus rebuked them for various reasons, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣu Mithilābhūta:
"Is it true that you have done this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
For this reason, the Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is it to call a bhikṣu one who reviles and becomes angry when the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, appoints him to a formal assembly?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, reviles those who have been appointed to a committee, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it means boiling, burning, and covering over; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a monk, out of anger, reviles a person appointed by the Saṃgha through a formal legal procedure (*karmavācanā*), it is a *pāyattika*.
If he, out of anger, reviles one of the fourteen persons appointed by the Saṃgha through a formal legal procedure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one reviles these twelve persons while they have not yet relinquished the *karmavācanā*, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one reviles them after they have already relinquished the *karmavācanā*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Among fourteen persons, if one reviles two individuals—whether they have relinquished the formal act (*karmavācanā*) or have not relinquished it—one commits a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
Even down to assigning separate rooms or appointing colleagues for meetings, one who scorns another with anger commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

After the Buddha had established this precept, the bhikṣus no longer scorned others face-to-face, but instead scorned the bhikṣu Dharmabhāṇaka from afar, according to their own desires in appointments and assemblies, and according to anger, fear, delusion, or ignorance of the proper order—skipping turns and failing to follow the sequence of seats according to seniority.
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked him for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu? Since the Buddha has established the precepts, why do you not express your anger and reproach in his presence, but instead express your anger and reproach from afar?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha has duly appointed someone to oversee the assembly, instead harbor resentment and utter insults from afar?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu reviles a person appointed by the Saṃgha to his face, or reviles them from afar, it is a pāyattika.'"

Regarding the offenses herein: if a monk, when the Saṃgha has duly performed a *karmavācanā* (formal act) to appoint a person to attend a meeting, should out of anger revile that person, it is a *pāyattika* if the person hears it;
if they do not hear it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If the Saṃgha has performed a formal act (karmavācanā) according to the Dharma involving fourteen persons, and someone, out of malice, utters words of reproach from afar—if the person hears it, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not hear it, it is a duṣkṛta.
If twelve bhikṣus have not yet relinquished their formal act (karmavācanā), and someone reviles them with anger from afar, those who hear it commit a pāyattika offense;
those who do not hear it commit a duṣkṛta offense.
If, after the *karmavācanā* has been relinquished, one utters angry insults from afar, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for the listener;
it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense for one who does not hear it.
Regarding two persons among the fourteen, whether the *karmavācanā* has been relinquished or not, if they utter angry insults from afar and another person hears them, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not hear it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This applies even to cases involving separate rooms or colleagues who have been appointed to a meeting; if one reviles or mocks from afar, and the person hears it, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
if they do not hear it, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding these two persons: one is the person who instructs the bhikṣuṇīs, and the other is the person appointed by the fourth *karmavācanā* among the four types of expiation to go and receive food.
The twelve matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Channa had committed an offense entailing confession. Out of compassion, pity, and a desire for his welfare, the bhikṣus said to Channa:
"You have committed an offense entailing confession; you should disclose it and not conceal it."
Channa said to the bhikṣus:
"Can you truly say that I have done such a thing?
I do not say that you can claim I have committed this offense."
The bhikṣus said: "Channa! If you have a fault, say so;
if you have none, say so. Why do you employ one matter and rely upon another matter?"
Channa said: "How am I involved in your affairs?
Am I afraid of you?"
"Furthermore, he uses a different matter and relies upon a different matter.
Among them, there was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was not pleased, and for various reasons he rebuked him:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense, uses a different matter and relies upon a different matter?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he said to Channa: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked Channa with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu, having committed an offense, employ a different matter or rely upon a different matter?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he said to the bhikṣus:
"You should remember the case of the bhikṣu Channa for his misconduct; if there should be others like the bhikṣu Channa, you should likewise remember them for their misconduct."
Regarding the recollection of a dharma by means of consciousness: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu shall announce within the assembly of bhikṣus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Channa has committed an offense for which he employs a different pretext."
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha remember and recognize the monk Channa regarding his use of improper matters.
O Channa, according to the improper matters you have used, the Saṃgha shall likewise remember and recognize them.
Thus it is announced.
Thus is the motion followed by a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
"The Sangha has completed its recollection; since the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be upheld as such!"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu annoys another with some pretext, it is a pāyattika. Regarding "pāyattika":
it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent, it can create an obstacle and hindrance to the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if the Saṃgha of bhikṣus has not yet recognized [the matter], and one employs a different matter or relies upon a different matter, at that time employing a different matter constitutes a duṣkṛta.
If the Saṃgha has already taken note of this, yet at that time one employs a different matter or relies upon a different matter, it is a pāyattika offense.
When the Buddha was staying in Kauśāmbī, the bhikṣu Channa committed an offense requiring confession. Out of compassion, pity, and a desire to benefit him, the bhikṣus said to Channa:
"You have committed an offense requiring confession; you should disclose it and not conceal it."
Channa thought to himself:
"If I engage in other matters, the Saṃgha will perform a *smṛtivinaya-karman* against me;
therefore, I shall remain silent. Channa immediately remained silent.
The bhikṣus said to Cchanna:
"If you have committed an offense, say so; if you have not, say so. Why do you remain silent and trouble us?"
Cchanna said: "What am I to you?
I do not fear you."
Having spoken these words, he again became silent.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, his heart was displeased, and for various reasons he rebuked him:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu remain silent after committing an offense and thereby distress others?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he said to Channa: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu remain silent after committing an offense and thereby distress others?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You all should remember the matter of the bhikṣu Channa who silently harassed others.
Regarding the formal act of remembrance (*sativinaya*): with a single mind, the Saṃgha should assemble in harmony, and one bhikṣu within the assembly should declare:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
This bhikṣu Channa has committed an offense and has silently troubled others.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to call Channa to account for his silent troubling of others.
"O Channa, according to your conduct of silently harassing others, the Sangha remembers and recognizes it.
Thus it is announced.
[Then] the second motion (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) is performed.
"Monks, having recollected this, the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, for some other reason, silently harasses another, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the offenses herein: if one silently annoys others while the Saṃgha has not yet become aware of it, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one silently annoys others after the Saṃgha has already become aware of it, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu suffers from an ailment of the mouth, the lips, the teeth, the tongue, the throat, or the heart; or if his face is swollen with gas, or if he is bleeding—in such cases, not speaking does not constitute an offense.
If one does not speak out of reverence for the Buddha, reverence for one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya), or reverence and respect for the elders (sthavira), there is no offense.
If one does not speak because one is unable to do so, there is no offense.
The thirteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was then a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, the householder prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed; returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink that night.
At that time, the bhikṣus spread out the monastic bedding in the open air; taking their robes and bowls, they stayed there until the time for the meal arrived.
Some bhikṣus practiced walking meditation, while others sat.
At that time, the householder rose early, prepared a seat, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The meal is ready; may the Noble One know the proper time."
Immediately, the bhikṣus left the monastic bedding and, taking their own robes and bowls, went to the house of a lay devotee.
The Buddha remained in his dwelling to receive his portion of food.
After the bhikṣus had gone to the lay devotee’s house, rain fell and soaked the monastic bedding.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when the bhikṣus go to the houses of householders, the Buddha himself takes the door-bolt and inspects the various rooms from one chamber to another.

Opening the door of a room, he saw the monastic bedding lying in the open air, dampened by the rain and rotted; he immediately took it up, wrung it out, spread it in the sun, folded it, and placed it in a sheltered spot. He then closed the room door, bolted it from within, and returned to his own quarters, where he sat alone upon his bed in the full lotus posture.
At that time, when the householder knew that the Saṃgha was seated, he personally served water and provided them with abundant, delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied.

When the householder knew that the Saṃgha had finished eating and had withdrawn their bowls, he personally offered them water, took a small seat, and sat before the assembly of monks, desiring to hear the Dharma being preached.
When the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed. The monks followed one after another in order out, returning to where the Buddha was.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when the monks return after their meal, they inquire of them with these words:
"Was the food delicious? Was the Sangha well-satisfied?"
The bhikṣus said:
“World-Honored One!
The food and drink were most delicious, and the Saṃgha was fully satiated.”
The Buddha said:

"Today, after you had entered the householder's residence, I followed behind carrying the door-bolt, inspecting the various rooms from one to another. Upon opening the door of one room, I saw that the monastics' bedding had been left on the open ground and was ruined by the rain."
He said to the bhikṣus:
"This matter is improper, contrary to the Dharma, and not to be done.
How can you use the bedding and furniture belonging to the entire Saṃgha as you please, treading upon them without knowing how to protect or cherish them?"
"The lay devotees' flesh and blood have been exhausted as they give alms and offerings for the sake of merit; you should use [these resources] sparingly. It is well that you protect them.
Having thus rebuked them through various causes and conditions, the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu spreads bedding, fine rope-cots, coarse rope-cots, or mattresses and covers for the Saṃgha in an open space, or causes another to spread them, and then sits or lies down upon them."
"If one leaves [a seat] without lifting it oneself or instructing another to lift it, it is a pāyattika.
There are five kinds of fine corded couches:

those with legs shaped like the hoof of an ass, those with legs shaped like a *po-lang-qu* (a type of animal), those with legs shaped like the horns of a ram, those with pointed legs, and those with curved legs.
There are five types of coarse rope beds:

those with legs shaped like the hoof of an *aśvattha* horse, those with legs shaped like a *pāṅgu* bird’s foot, those with legs shaped like the horns of a ram, those with pointed legs, and those with curved legs.
Regarding stuffed mattresses and covers: there are mattresses stuffed with sugarcane pulp, gourds, long melon stems, wool, *kṣauma* grass, cotton, *muñja* grass, hemp, and aquatic moss.
"Covered" refers to being covered by a woolen blanket, a *kṛmuka* blanket, a fleece blanket, or a cotton blanket.

"In the open air" refers to a place that has no earthen walls, no walls of grass or wood, no walls of bamboo mats, and no coverings of cloth or curtains—any such place that is not shielded by any object.
"To spread oneself" means to spread it with one's own hands.
"To have another spread it" means to instruct another person to spread it.
"To sit" means to sit upon it.
"Lying down" means the body is resting upon a bed.
"Not lifting up" means not lifting it with one's own hands.
"Not instructing another to lift it" means not directing someone else to lift it.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "to cook, burn, cover, or obstruct. If one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, when the ground is prepared, has spread out bedding for the Saṃgha in the open air and then enters a room to sit and rest, and only after the ground has been finished does he lift it and place it under cover, it is a *pāyattika*.

Having finished the work on the ground, during the middle part of the day, the forenoon, midday, the afternoon, or at sunset, if one spreads out the bedding for the Saṃgha in an open space and then enters a room to sit and rest, only picking it up and putting it away under cover when sunset has finally passed, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, having spread out monastic bedding on an open space, goes beyond forty-nine paces from the monastery gate, it is a pāyattika.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, having spread out monastic bedding on an open space, goes beyond the wall or fence by even a small distance after leaving the monastery gate, it is a duṣkṛta at the moment he reaches the ground.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has spread out monastic bedding in an open area and wanders through the various quarters without entrusting it to someone else, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If two bhikṣus have spread out monastic bedding in an open area and both rise from their seats and depart, the one who leaves later should put it away.

Furthermore, if two bhikṣus have spread out monastic bedding in an open space and left their robes and bowls therein, if one bhikṣu takes his robes and bowl and departs first, the one who departs later must pick up the items; if he does not pick them up, he commits an offense.

On one occasion, the community of monks was eating together in the open air. When the bhikṣus had finished eating, they left their bedding in the open and departed. A violent wind and rain arose, and the dust defiled and dampened it. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should lift them up and place them in a covered location."
After the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus finished their meal, and some laypeople (avadātavasana) sat upon the bedding and couches used by the Saṃgha.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"You should wait."
The bhikṣus waited for a long time until they were stifled with heat and suffered from nausea and vomiting. The Buddha said:
"If there is one who is ill, he should leave; whoever sees [the furniture] should lift it.
If two bhikṣus see it, one should lift the large bed and the small bed, and the other should lift the large mat and the small mat.

If one takes bedding from a monastery on the outskirts of a village to a secluded place, or brings it back from a secluded place to a monastery on the outskirts of a village, and encounters rain, there is no offense.
If the door-bolt or the door-key is lost and there is no place to deposit it, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises, there is no offense in not depositing it.
The fourteen matters are concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 10 (end);
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 11, Second Recitation, Part 5.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
The ninety *pāyattika* rules, part three.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, two visiting bhikṣus arrived toward evening; they received rooms in succession and stayed together, one obtaining a bed and the other obtaining a grass mat.
After the two had stayed there overnight, they departed without putting away their bedding.

At that time, insects arose within the straw matting; they ate the grass, the legs of the bed, the bed frame, the crossbars, the bed ropes, and the blankets, quilts, and pillows. Having finished eating these, they entered the wall and dwelt therein.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted through his silence, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed, returning to his own home.
That night, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink; rising early, he arranged the seating and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time."
The bhikṣus went to the house of a lay devotee, while the Buddha remained in his own quarters to receive his portion of food.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when the bhikṣus go to the houses of lay devotees, the Buddha himself takes the door-knob and inspects the various rooms, going from one room to another.

The Buddha then took his door-knob and went from one room to another, opening the door of each room; he saw that upon these grass mats, insects had grown and were devouring the grass, the legs of the beds, the bedposts, the crossbars, the bed-ropes, and the bedding and pillows.

Having seen this, the Buddha entered the house; he slowly lifted the bedding and pillows, gently raised the bed, and gradually removed the straw matting once the insects had been cleared away. Having finished, he swept, sprinkled water, and plastered the floor.
He shakes out his bedding and pillows, strikes the bed to drive away insects, and returns them to their original places.
Having spread his mat for lying down and closed the door and bolted it, he remains in the dwelling, sitting alone upon the bed in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
At that time, having seen that the Saṃgha was seated, the householder personally served water and provided them with abundant and delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied.

Then, knowing that the Saṃgha had finished eating and had put away their bowls, the householder personally offered water, took a small stool, and sat before the assembly of monks, desiring to hear the Dharma.
After the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed. The bhikṣus followed one after another in order out, returning to where the Buddha was.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when the bhikṣus return after their meal, they inquire of them with these words:
"The food and drink were most excellent; was the Saṃgha satiated?"
The Buddha then asked the bhikṣus:
"Was the food and drink very delicious? Were the monks satisfied?
The bhikṣus replied:
"The food and drink were very delicious, and the community of monks was fully satiated. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"After you had entered the householder's home, I took the door-knob and wandered through the various rooms. Opening the door of one room, I saw insects born within the grass matting; these insects were eating the grass, the bed-legs, the bed-frames, the bed-slats, and the bed-ropes, as well as the blankets, bedding, and pillows. Having finished eating, they entered the wall to dwell there, intending to bite people. This matter is improper, contrary to the Dharma, and should not have been so."
Why is it that you take and use the monastic bedding, treading upon it without knowing how to protect or cherish it?
Laypeople have exhausted their own flesh and blood to provide these offerings for the sake of merit; you should use them sparingly, and it would be well if you were to guard them.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"Who among you is the middle-aged one?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
Two guest bhikṣus arrived and stayed together there in succession; one obtained a bed and the other obtained a grass mat. Having stayed the night, they departed once the ground was cleared.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu take the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha and depart without having entrusted it to someone?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha in a bhikṣu’s dwelling—whether he spreads it himself or causes another to spread it—and sits or lies upon it, yet when departing does not put it away nor instruct another to put it away, it is a pāyattika.'"

"A bhikṣu’s dwelling" refers to one belonging either to the community of monks (*saṃgha*) or to a single individual; it is at least as small as to accommodate the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
"Laid out by oneself" means laid out with one's own hands.
"To cause to spread" means to instruct another to spread it.
"To sit" means to sit upon it.
"To lie down" means for the body to lie upon it.
"Not lifting" means not lifting it with one's own hand.
"Not instructing another to lift" means not instructing another person to lift it.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it refers to boiling, burning, covering, or obstructing; if one does not repent for the offense, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a visiting bhikṣu spreads out monastic bedding in a bhikṣu’s cell and then departs beyond the boundary, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a resident bhikṣu spreads out monastic bedding in a bhikṣu’s cell and then departs beyond the boundary, thinking:
"I shall return on this very day."
"If there is an urgent matter and one cannot return immediately, but leaves the boundary until the time for the ground-ritual (dīrgha-karma) has concluded, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to depart after having entrusted the bedding to the Saṃgha."
Regarding "entrusting," there are three kinds of statements:
"This is the key; this is the dwelling; these are the bedding and requisites. If one says:
"This is the key, this is the room, and these are the bedding; to whom should they be entrusted?
They should be entrusted to the one responsible for distributing bedding.
If there is no one to provide bedding and mats, one should entrust them to the keeper of the quarters.
If there is no keeper of the quarters, one should entrust them to those who maintain and repair the dwellings.
If there is no such person, one should entrust them to a senior monk residing there who is virtuous, meritorious, and observant of the precepts.
If such a person is not available, then within this monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma), one should entrust [the matter] to a virtuous and worthy person or to a lay attendant who guards the monastery.
One should not entrust it to a shameless, precept-breaking bhikṣu, nor should one entrust it to a young śrāmaṇera.
If one cannot find a suitable person [to assist], and if there are clothing racks or ivory pegs, one should place the bedding, blankets, and pillows upon them and then depart.

If there are no clothing racks or ivory pegs, and if there are two beds within that space, one should place the bedding, blankets, and pillows on one bed and cover them with the other bed; then, leaving a distance of four inches from the wall, one may depart.
There is no offense in leaving items behind in the dwelling, even including bags for storing footwear (*pūrala*).
The fifteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then the Elder Yaśas, together with five hundred attendants, came toward Śrāvastī, intending to enter the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*).

At that time, the bhikṣus all performed the preliminary tasks for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), namely: filling in holes and crevices in the walls, sealing up pits and fissures in the earth, repairing broken or dilapidated areas, dismantling and mending their rope beds (*śayanāsana*), and shaking out their blankets and pillows.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were indolent and did no work; seeing others working from afar, they thought to themselves:
"We are the senior elders; we must wait until their work is finished and they have received their bedding and seats, so that we may enter later and, following our seniority, drive them out."
Having had this thought, after the other bhikṣus had finished their work and received their bedding, the group of six bhikṣus entered after them.
The bhikṣus asked the group of six bhikṣus,
"Did you come with us to perform the preliminary tasks?"
He replied, "I did not. The bhikṣus said:
"You all come with us without having performed the preliminary duties; we shall complete the preliminary duties first, and I will not rise.
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"As the Buddha has taught:..."
"Rooms are to be received according to seniority among the elders.
If one does not speak or perform the preliminary duties, they shall not be granted [a room].
"I am the senior elder; why should I not rise?"
The group of six bhikṣus were powerful and vigorous, yet lacked great circumspection; they forcibly dragged him out.
This bhikṣu was gentle and fond of comfort, so his head and hands were injured, his bowl broken, and his robes torn.

Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; upon hearing this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and censured it for various reasons, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, when another bhikṣu is angry and displeased within the bhikṣu’s quarters, he forcibly drags him out?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure within a bhikṣu’s cell, forcibly drag another out?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, out of anger or resentment, drags a bhikṣu out of his dwelling himself or causes another to drag him out, saying, "Foolish man, go far away; you should not stay here," except under specific circumstances, it is a pāyattika offense.

"A bhikṣu’s dwelling" refers to a residence belonging either to the Saṃgha or to an individual, being at least as small as to accommodate the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
"Out of resentment" means because [the other] does not comply with one's wishes.
"Disliking" means that one feels anger and does not wish to see [the person].
"Dragging oneself out" means dragging oneself out with one's own hands.
"Causing another to drag [one] out" means instructing another to do so.

If one goes from a bed to the ground, from inside a room to the doorway, from the doorway to a place for walking, from a high place to a low place, or from a raised earthen mound to the ground, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, out of anger or resentment, seizes another bhikṣu against his will—if he succeeds in seizing him, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he fails to seize him, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he causes another to pull [the bedding], if the other is able to do so, it is a *pāyattika*; if the other is unable, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If [he pulls] from a bed or chair, if he is able to pull it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he is unable, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one drags [an object] from a bed, from inside a room, from a walkway outside, from a high place, or from a mound of earth, it is a *pāyattika* offense if it can be moved;
it is a *dukkaṭa* offense if it cannot.
If one drags [an object] by oneself or drags it according to another's instruction, it constitutes a *pāyattika* and a *dukkaṭa*.
If one drags it out because the dwelling is about to collapse, there is no offense.
Section sixteen concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin slept poorly and did not sleep with a single-minded focus; he snored, ground his teeth, talked in his sleep, yawned frequently, clapped his hands, and moved his feet, making loud noises.

When the bhikṣus heard this sound, they were unable to sleep; because they could not sleep, their food was not digested; because their food was not digested, their bodies suffered from itching; thus they became distressed and agitated, feeling nauseated and ill at ease.
The bhikṣus each spread out their bedding in close proximity to one another, thinking:
"Let us not allow Kālodāyin to enter and lie down among us.
At that time, Kālodāyin forcibly entered and spread out his bedding there.
The bhikṣus said:
"Kāḷudāyin, do not force yourself to lie down inside. Why is that?
"You sleep poorly and do not sleep with a single-minded focus; you snore, grind your teeth, talk in your sleep, yawn frequently, clap your hands, move your feet, and make loud noises.

When the bhikṣus hear these sounds, they are unable to sleep; because they cannot sleep, their food does not digest; because their food does not digest, their bodies suffer from itching; they become distressed and nauseated, finding no peace."
Kāḷudāyin said, "I am at ease;
if you are not happy here, then leave of your own accord.
Having spoken these words, he forcibly spread out his bedding.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked it for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that bedding has already been spread in a bhikṣu’s room, comes later and forcibly spreads his own?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked Kālodayin with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that bedding has already been spread in a bhikṣu’s room, later come and forcibly spread his own?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu knows that bedding has already been spread in a bhikṣu’s room, yet later comes and forcibly spreads his own, or causes another to spread it, [the occupant] should leave of their own accord if they are displeased; except for those specific circumstances, this is a pāyattika offense.
"Knowing" means either knowing for oneself, hearing it from another, or being told by that person.
"Forcefully spreading [the bedding]" means not following the other's wishes, but rather spreading it according to one's own will.
"To cause someone to spread [a rug]" means to instruct another person to spread it.

If one causes it to be spread before a sitting bed, or before a sleeping bed, or inside a room, or in a walkway outside the door, or on a high place, or on a raised earthen mound, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing. If one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished spreading bedding in a bhikṣu’s room, comes later and forcibly spreads bedding in front of the sitting platform—if he succeeds in spreading it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he does not succeed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Whether it be before a bed, inside a room, in a place for walking outside, on a high place, or before a raised earthen platform—whether one spreads it oneself or causes another to spread it—if one is capable of spreading it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one is not capable, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
In such cases, whether one spreads out a seat oneself or instructs another to do so, each instance constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; if it is done repeatedly, there are *dukkaṭa* offenses.
If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of annoying others, closes a door and then opens it, or closes a window and then opens it;
or lights a fire and then extinguishes it, or lights a lamp and then extinguishes it; [he commits an offense].

If one performs chanting, reciting prayers of blessing, reading scriptures, preaching the Dharma, or engaging in debate—doing each of these as things that another person does not find pleasing—it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
The seventeenth [chapter] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, two visiting bhikṣus arrived at dusk; these two visiting bhikṣus were assigned a single room by lot, with one obtaining the upper story and the other obtaining the lower story.

Those who occupy the upper pavilion are practitioners of meditation; having entered their rooms early in the morning in a state of tranquility, they spread out their mats and sit cross-legged, for they delight in silence.

Those on the upper pavilion, however, mostly enjoy frolicking and jesting; they chant scriptures, recite incantations, engage in debates, and laugh loudly, uttering all manner of useless talk before entering their rooms to sit forcefully upon beds with pointed legs.
Because of a reed mat, the legs and supports of the bed sank down, injuring the head of a bhikṣu so severely that he was on the verge of death.
That bhikṣu came out of his room and said to the other bhikṣus, "Look at this bhikṣu;
because he did not sit or lie down with a single-minded focus, the bed leg sank down and injured my head, nearly killing me."
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased in heart and censured him with various reasons:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who does not sit or lie down mindfully, but by sitting with such force causes the legs of the bed to sink down and injure another bhikṣu’s head so that he nearly dies?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you actually did this?"
He replied,
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I did."
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu fail to sit or lie down with a single-minded focus, causing the legs of the bed to sink and injure another bhikṣu’s head until he is on the verge of death?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu sits or lies down forcefully on a bed with pointed legs inside a bhikṣu’s room, it is a pāyattika. Regarding "a bhikṣu’s room":
it may belong to the Saṃgha or to an individual; it is at least small enough to accommodate the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
Regarding "pavilion" (*kūṭa*): anything consisting of more than one story is called a pavilion.
Regarding "bed" (*mañca*): it refers to a bed for reclining.
There are five kinds of beds for reclining:
There are five types of legs: legs shaped like the hoof of an ass (*aśvattha*), legs shaped like the hoof of a *palaṅgu*, legs shaped like the horn of a ram, pointed legs, and curved legs.
There are likewise five types of meditation seats:
those with legs shaped like the hoof of an ass, legs shaped like the hoof of a *palaṅgu*, legs shaped like the horn of a ram, pointed legs, and curved legs.
"Sitting" means the body is seated upon it;
"lying down" means the body is lying upon it.
*Pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation) means that it cooks, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent the transgression, it can hinder the Path.

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu uses a bed with one leg pointed and three legs of the *aśvattha* type, or two legs pointed and two legs of the *aśvattha* type, or three legs pointed and one leg of the *aśvattha* type, or four legs all pointed—if he sits or lies down upon it according to his exertion, for each instance, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one lies on a bed with one leg pointed and three legs curved inward (pālaṅgu), or two legs pointed and two legs curved inward, or three legs pointed and one leg curved inward, or all four legs pointed—if one sits or lies upon it according to how much force is applied, for each instance, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If it is a bed, whether it has one leg with a point and three legs like the horns of a ram, or two legs with points and two legs like the horns of a ram, or three legs with points and one leg like the horn of a ram, or four legs with points—if one sits or lies upon it according to its use, for each instance, it is a *pāyattika*.

If it is a bed, and one leg is pointed while three legs are curved; or two legs are pointed while two legs are curved; or three legs are pointed while one leg is curved; or all four legs are pointed—if one sits or lies down upon it using force in any of these cases, for each instance, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to a meditation seat.
If one props up a seat with legs that point upward using a stone, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses a brick, or wood, or white tin, or lead and tin to prop it up, each instance is a *pāyattika*.

If one uses a wooden plank, a board plank, a rafter plank, or thick mud; or if the supporting wood for a bed leg is decayed and rotten; or if it is supported by a bundle of grass, a bundle of cloth, or a bundle of felt—there is no offense. Since the wooden support has rotted and become soft, it cannot injure a person; therefore, it is said there is no offense.
The eighteenth [section] concludes. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Elder Channa used water containing living beings to sprinkle on grass and mix it with mud.
The bhikṣus said to Channa:
"Do not use water containing living beings to sprinkle on grass or mix with mud, for you will kill many small creatures.
Channa replied,
"I use water to mix with the mud, but I do not use the creatures."
The bhikṣus said:
"Knowing that this water contained insects, why did you use it to mix with mud?
You have no heart of compassion for animals."
Among them were monks who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked him with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that water contains living beings, uses it to water grass or mix with mud?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Channa intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu know that water contains living beings and yet use it to sprinkle grass or mix with mud?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living organisms, and he himself uses it to sprinkle grass or mix with mud, or causes another to do so, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing it from another.
"Insects" means those seen with the eye or those filtered out by a water-strainer.
"Pouring on grass" means pouring with one's own hand.
"To cause another to pour" means to instruct another to pour.
"To mix mud oneself" means to mix it with one's own hands.
"To cause another to mix" means to instruct another to mix.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is a burning, scorching, and obstructive offense; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains insects, uses it to sprinkle grass, for every insect that dies, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one causes another to water grass, for every insect that dies as a result, there is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains insects and uses it to mix with mud, for every insect that dies as a result, there is a pāyattika offense.
If he causes them to mix mud, and insects die as a result, for each one there is a *pāyattika*.
If he places cow dung, dry soil, or even bamboo, reed, or leaves into water containing insects, and insects die as a result, for each one there is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu uses water containing living beings while perceiving it as containing living beings, it is a pāyattika.
If he uses water containing living beings while perceiving it as being free of living beings, it is a pāyattika.
If one uses water with insects while suspecting it contains them, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses water that is free of insects while perceiving it to contain insects, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one uses water that is free of insects while suspecting it to be so, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one uses water that is free of insects with the perception that it is free of insects, there is no offense.
Case nineteen concludes. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Elder Channa wished to build a large gabled chamber; this man was by nature indolent and lazy, and he thought to himself:
"Who can oversee this day by day?
Then, on one day, he dug the earth, laid the foundation, and finished stacking the walls; the door was installed and facing toward completion for the second story.
Once the door was set, the walls were plastered and treated, the rafters were placed, and the roof was finished. On that very day the work was done, yet on that very day it collapsed.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured it for various reasons:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu construct a great hall or pavilion using such vast amounts of grass, wood, mud, and clay, only for it to collapse on the very day it was completed?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the truth] yet asking deliberately, he said to Channa: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: “I did indeed do so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked Channa with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu construct a great hall or pavilion using such vast amounts of grass, wood, mud, and clay, only for it to collapse on the very day it was completed?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu wishes to construct a large dwelling, he should pile up the walls, install the beams, set the doorways, and prepare the ground; he should then have it roofed over two or three times.
Should he exceed this number of roofings, it is a pāyattika offense.
"A large hall" refers to a heated bathhouse, a lecture hall, a hall with a central skylight, a high tower, a multi-storied pavilion, or a long, narrow building.
"Walls" refers to the four walls made either of wood or of earth.
The "beam" (liáng) is the place upon which the ridgepole rests.
The "door" (hù) is the place where the panels are installed.
The "window" (xiàng) is the opening facing outward that allows light to pass through.
Regarding the preparation of the ground: it consists of clay soil, coarse mud, and husk-mud.
It is treated by sprinkling red, white, and black lime, and by plastering and painting with black, blue, white, and red pigments.
"Covering two or three times" means one should cover it either twice or thrice.
"Pāyattika" refers to boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knows he has concealed [a fault], he should first conceal one part himself; for the second part, he should expose his head; for the third part, he should give instructions, saying:
"It shall be concealed in this manner."
Having given these instructions, he departed.
If that bhikṣu was present and completed the third layer of covering, then for that house—if it was covered with grass—there is a pāyattika offense for each individual blade of grass used.
If one uses wooden planks for covering, for each plank used, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one uses tiles for covering, for each tile used, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if one covers it with a board, or covers it with bird wings, or covers it with the roots of the *uśīra* plant; there is no offense.
[The twentieth section ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I am utterly exhausted from teaching the fourfold assembly; you bhikṣus should now instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus then proceeded to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs in due order.
When the senior bhikṣu had finished his sequential instruction, it was next the turn of the elder Paṇḍita.
At that time, Ānanda went to Paṇḍita and said to him: "Do you know?"
"Tomorrow it is your turn to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Paṇḍita said to Ānanda, "I am of dull faculties and have heard little; I have not yet attained any realization."
After four months of the summer retreat, I was finally able to recite this single Kumāra verse:

"The wise person, in body, speech, and mind, commits no evil whatsoever; always maintaining mindfulness before them, they abandon all desires and do not undergo the world's useless ascetic practices."
“Ānanda! It is well for one who can surpass this sequence.
Ānanda spoke thus to Paṭṭa three times.
“The elders have already finished their exhortations; now it is your turn.
The bhikṣu Pañcaśikha replied to Ānanda a second and a third time:
“I am of dull faculties and have heard little; I have nothing to know.”
"In the fourth month of summer, you were able to recite one verse of Kumāra; it would be well if you could surpass this next time.
Ānanda spoke again:
"Tomorrow, it is your turn to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
He accepted Ānanda’s words.
When the night had passed, before midday, he dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in sequence.
After his meal, he returned to his own quarters, spread out a seat upon the open ground, and entered the room to practice meditation.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs heard that on this day it was the turn of the bhikṣu Paṇḍita to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, they all conceived a sense of contempt, thinking:
"This man has not heard much of the Dharma and has recited but little of the sūtras."
In the fourth month of summer, while practicing intensive recitation, I mastered a single verse by Kumāralāta:

"The wise person, in body, speech, and mind, commits no evil whatsoever; always maintaining mindfulness before them, they abandon all desires and do not undergo the world’s useless ascetic practices."
"How shall we hear the Dharma that we have not yet heard?
How shall we know the Dharma that we have not yet known?
As for the verses of Kumāra that we recite, we have already recited them before."
"Whatever bhikṣuṇīs had not previously entered the Jeta Grove to listen to the Dharma all came together at that time.
Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs departed from the Bhikṣuṇī Vihāra in Rājagṛha and went to the Jetavana to listen to the Dharma."
He went before the elder Pāṭika’s dwelling and stood there; clearing his throat to make a sound, he knocked on the door and said, "Venerable Pāṭika, come out!
The elder Pāṭika immediately rose from meditation and left his room, proceeding to his solitary seat where he sat upright and composed.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had finished prostrating with their heads at his feet, they all sat down before him.
Then the Elder Pūrṇa addressed them with gentle words: "Sisters!..."
"You should know that I am of dull faculties and have read and recited little; having spent the four months of the summer retreat, I have mastered this single verse:

'The wise person, in body, speech, and mind, Commits no evil whatsoever. Always maintaining mindfulness before them, They abandon all desires, And likewise do not undergo The world's unbeneficial ascetic practices.'"
"Nevertheless, I shall speak according to what I know; you all should practice with a single mind the dharma of non-negligence. Why is this?
Even the Buddhas have all attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of practicing with a single mind and through non-negligence."
"All wholesome dharmas that assist the path have non-heedlessness as their root.

Having spoken these words, he used his supernormal powers to vanish from his seat and appear in the midst of the empty space to the east, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. He entered the Fire-Light Samādhi, and from his body issued flames and various colored lights—blue, yellow, red, and white. From the lower part of his body fire issued forth while water flowed from the upper part; from the lower part of his body water issued forth while fire flowed from the upper part. It was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. After manifesting these various supernatural powers, he returned to sit at his original place.

When the bhikṣuṇīs saw such supernatural power as this displayed by the Elder Panthaka, their sense of contempt vanished; because they gave rise to a mind of faith and reverence, they honored him with a pure heart and subdued their pride.
He then expounded the Dharma according to what the bhikṣuṇīs delighted in and what they were capable of understanding.
Among the assembly, there were those who attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.

There are those who possess the causal conditions for the path of the śrāvaka, those who possess the causal conditions for the path of the pratyekabuddha, and those who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the assembly obtained various great benefits; this was the initial cause and condition for the precepts.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took turns instructing the bhikṣuṇīs. On one occasion, they neglected their duties of instruction, neglected their duties of admonition, and neglected their delivery of the Dharma, instead engaging in two kinds of evil speech: coarse and vulgar speech.

At that time, there was a junior bhikṣuṇī who did not deeply delight in observing the precepts; she engaged in playful banter, light conversation, and loud laughter with the group of six bhikṣus, addressing one another by their nicknames and discussing various kinds of impure matters.

Among them was an elder bhikṣuṇī of high standing who, deeply delighting in the observance of the precepts, practiced walking meditation in another location, or stood waiting, desiring to hear the teaching of the Dharma.

On another occasion, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, departed from the Rājaka Garden Monastery and went to where the Buddha was staying; she prostrated herself at his feet and stood to one side.

Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs also prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Buddha and stood to one side. Having stood to one side, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The Buddha has permitted the instruction of bhikṣuṇīs for our benefit; yet we do not obtain this benefit.
The Buddha asked Gautamī, "In what way have I permitted the instruction of bhikṣuṇīs for our benefit, such that you do not obtain this benefit?"
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī related this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It is indeed so!"
"I permitted you to receive instructions from the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of your benefit, yet you have not actually obtained such benefit.
Then the Buddha, having taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs with various dharmas, remained silent.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, having understood that the Buddha had instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Not long after Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs had left, the Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who instructs bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
"Not appointed by the Saṃgha" means that the Saṃgha has not yet reached a state of unity and harmony to appoint him for the purpose of instruction.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is that which burns, obstructs, and covers; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if there is a single bhikṣu and the Saṃgha has not yet appointed him to instruct a bhikṣuṇī, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one bhikṣu instructs two, three, or four bhikṣuṇīs, there are four pāyattikas.
If two bhikṣus instruct two bhikṣuṇīs, there are two pāyattikas.
If one instructs three, four, or one bhikṣuṇī, it is one pāyattika.
If one instructs three bhikṣuṇīs while being three bhikṣus, it is three pāyattikas.
If one instructs four, one, or two bhikṣuṇīs, there are two pāyattikas.
If one instructs four bhikṣuṇīs while being four bhikṣus, there are four pāyattikas.
If one instructs one, two, or three bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes three pāyattikas.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the Saṃgha had not appointed them to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, went outside the boundary and appointed themselves by mutual consent to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, and only then entered the boundary.
When the bhikṣuṇīs arrived, she said to them:
"The Saṃgha has appointed me to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; since you have come, I shall expound the Dharma."

For these reasons, having assembled the community of bhikṣuṇīs, he set aside matters of admonition, matters of instruction, and matters of preaching the Dharma, thereby committing two kinds of evil deeds.

Among them was a young bhikṣuṇī who did not deeply delight in observing the precepts; she engaged in flirtatious banter with the group of six bhikṣus, laughing loudly and addressing one another by name in various kinds of impure ways.

Among them was an elder bhikṣuṇī of senior standing who, deeply delighting in the observance of the precepts, was walking in meditation or standing still in another location while waiting; at that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs had gathered together in harmony nearby.
The Buddha saw from afar that the community of bhikṣuṇīs was gathered together in harmony and drew near; knowing the reason, he asked Ānanda,
"For what reason has the community of bhikṣuṇīs gathered together in harmony and drawn near?"
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!

These six groups of bhikṣus, knowing that the Saṃgha had not performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to authorize them to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, went outside the boundary and performed a mutual formal act among themselves to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Only after that did they enter the boundary; seeing the bhikṣuṇīs approaching, they spoke as follows:”
"O Saṃgha, with one mind, perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for me to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; come, and I shall proclaim the teachings.

For this reason, he assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, setting aside the matter of instruction, setting aside the matter of admonition, and setting aside the discourse on the Dharma, thereby committing two kinds of faults.

Among them was a young junior bhikṣuṇī who did not deeply delight in observing the precepts; she joined with the group of six bhikṣus in playful banter and light conversation, addressing one another by their personal names.
Among them was a senior elder bhikṣuṇī who, deeply delighting in the observance of the precepts, was walking up and down in another place and standing there waiting.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, the community of bhikṣuṇīs has come together in harmony and drawn near.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu possesses five qualities, he should not be appointed to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs."
What are the five?
First, being less than twenty years of age or not having reached twenty;
second, being unable to uphold the precepts.
Third, they are unable to cultivate extensive learning;
fourth, they are unable to speak the Dharma with correct speech;
fifth, they commit the thirteen offenses and defile the three assemblies in various places.
"One who has not yet reached twenty years of age" refers to one who, since receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), has not yet completed twenty years.

"One who cannot uphold the precepts" refers to one who violates the precepts established by the Buddha, does not follow the instructions within the full ordination, lacks knowledge of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), and does not know what conduct is appropriate or inappropriate; even to the point of violating minor precepts without a sense of dread, such a person is unable to train in the precepts in their proper sequence.
One who has not heard much does not recite or study the two collections of the precepts in accordance with their meaning.
One who cannot correctly speak the Dharma is unable to skillfully understand worldly correct speech and excellent expressions.

Regarding those who have committed the thirteen offenses: if, among these thirteen matters, one has defiled the Śikṣamāṇās, Śrāmaṇeras, or Śrāmaṇerīs in various instances, this constitutes an offense against these three groups; even if such a person repents, they shall not be permitted to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
If a bhikṣu possesses these five qualities, he shall not be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with five qualities, he should be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
What are the five?
Being twenty years of age, or more than twenty;
being able to uphold the precepts;
He is able to hear much;
he is able to speak correctly and preach the Dharma;
he does not transgress the thirteen matters and does not defile the three assemblies.
"Having completed twenty years" means that since receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), twenty years have elapsed or more.

"One who upholds the precepts" means not violating the precepts established by the Buddha, following the instructions of the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*), knowing the proper deportment (*īryāpatha*), and knowing what is appropriate and inappropriate conduct; even regarding the breaking of minor precepts, one gives rise to great fear, and thus knows the sequential training and upholds the precepts.
"One who is learned" refers to one who recites and studies the combined meaning of the two divisions of the Great Precepts (*mahā-śīla*).
"One who can correctly speak and teach the Dharma" refers to one who well understands worldly correct speech and excellent diction.
"Not committing the thirteen matters" means not defiling oneself in any of those thirteen instances.
"The three groups" refers to the *śikṣamāṇā*, the *śrāmaṇera*, and the *śrāmaṇerī*.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with these five qualities, the Saṃgha should appoint him to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

If a bhikṣu is less than twenty years of age, cannot maintain the precepts, cannot be learned, cannot speak correctly or preach the Dharma, and has committed the thirteen matters, thereby defiling the three assemblies in various ways.
If the Sangha appoints such a person to instruct and admonish bhikṣuṇīs, the appointment is not valid; if such a person does instruct and admonish bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika offense.

If one is twenty years of age or older, yet is unable to maintain the precepts, unable to possess great learning, unable to speak correctly or preach the Dharma, and has committed the thirteen offenses thereby defiling the three assemblies—if the Sangha appoints such a person, the appointment is not valid; if they appoint such a person to instruct and admonish bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika offense.

If one is twenty years of age or older, is able to uphold the precepts, but lacks extensive learning, is unable to speak the Dharma with correct speech, and has committed the thirteen offenses thereby defiling the three assemblies—if the Saṃgha appoints such a person, the appointment is not valid; if this person instructs the bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.

If one is twenty years of age or older, capable of observing the precepts and possessing great learning, yet is unable to speak correctly or preach the Dharma, and has committed the thirteen offenses thereby defiling the three assemblies—if the Saṃgha appoints such a person, the appointment is not valid; if this person instructs the bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.

If a person is twenty years of age or older, is able to uphold the precepts, is learned, is able to speak correctly and preach the Dharma, yet has committed one of the thirteen offenses that defile the three assemblies—if the Saṃgha appoints such a person, the appointment is not valid; if this person instructs the bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.

If one who is twenty years of age or older, who is able to maintain the precepts, who is learned, who can correctly speak and preach the Dharma, and who has not committed the thirteen offenses nor defiled the three groups [of monastics], should instruct a bhikṣuṇī before being appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
If one who has been appointed after fulfilling the five requirements instructs and admonishes [the nuns] before being formally appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one who has fulfilled the five requirements and has already been appointed by the Saṃgha instructs and admonishes [the nuns] without first speaking [to them], it is a dukkaṭa offense.

If one who has fulfilled the five qualifications has been appointed, has been appointed by the Saṃgha, has already spoken [to the candidate], but has not yet spoken before the Saṃgha, and then proceeds to instruct and admonish her, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one who has fulfilled the five qualifications has been appointed, has been appointed by the Saṃgha, has already spoken [to the candidate], and has already spoken before the Saṃgha, yet does not ask those who have arrived:
"Sisters, have you all assembled? [it is a *duṣkṛta* offense].
If one instructs and admonishes [the nuns] immediately, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Once the five qualities have been accomplished, she has been appointed; having been appointed within the Saṃgha, she has spoken, she has spoken within the Saṃgha, and she has asked:
"Sisters, have you all assembled?"
If one speaks to a later nun before the Eight Rules of Respect have been proclaimed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Once the five qualifications have been fulfilled, she has been appointed; once she has been appointed by the Saṃgha, she has spoken; once she has spoken in the midst of the Saṃgha, she asks:
"Have all you sisters assembled?"
"Having already explained the Eight Rules of Respect, it is not an offense to speak next to a later bhikṣu.
Section Twenty-one concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Nanda, saying:
“You should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; you should teach the bhikṣuṇīs; you should preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs.
Why is this? If you instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, you will be no different from me.”
Thereupon, the Elder Nanda accepted the instruction in silence.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should appoint Nanda to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs."
If there are other such bhikṣus, they should also be appointed to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs.
It should be done in this manner: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Nanda has been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha appoint Nanda to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs.
The motion is thus made.
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is performed:
"The Saṃgha has finished appointing the bhikṣu Nanda to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is to be upheld in this way."

When that night had passed, the bhikṣu Nanda dressed in his robes and took up his bowl before midday to enter the city for alms. After eating, he returned to his cell, spread out a solitary seat upon the open ground, and entered the room to sit in meditation.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard that Nanda was instructing the bhikṣuṇīs, those who had not previously come to listen to the Dharma all gathered to hear him.

Five hundred bhikṣuṇīs together departed from the Rājakārāma Vihāra, entered the Jeta Grove, and went before Nanda’s cell. Standing there, they cleared their throats, made a sound, and knocked on the door, saying:
“Venerable Nanda!”
"Please preach the Dharma and give us instruction.
Then Nanda arose from meditation, opened the door, and went out to sit upright and cross-legged upon his solitary couch.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs prostrated themselves at Nanda’s feet and all sat down before him.
Nanda immediately taught them various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden them; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs, having tasted the flavor of the wholesome Dharma and feeling deep affection for it, did not wish to rise and leave.
Nanda thought to himself:
"Because these bhikṣuṇīs have attained the flavor of the Dharma, they still desire to hear the teaching."
He then further taught them various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden them until sunset.
He said to the bhikṣuṇīs, "The sun has set; you may depart."
The bhikṣuṇīs immediately rose, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

As they were leaving the Jeta Grove and entering the city, the city gates were already closed; they therefore stayed overnight by the moat at the edge of the city, some beneath trees, some beside wells, and others in secluded or screened places.
At dawn, when the gate was opened, the bhikṣuṇīs entered first.
Then the gatekeeper asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"O virtuous daughters!..."
"From where have you come now?
He replied, "I came from the Jeta Grove to listen to the Dharma; as the sun set, I was returning and found the city gates already closed, so I did not have time to enter."
He asked, "Where did you stay overnight?
Each answered according to where they had stayed.
One who had stayed overnight beneath a city replied,
"Beneath a city.
One who had stayed overnight beneath a tree replied:
"Under a tree.
The one staying by the well replied,
"By the well."
The one staying in a screened place replied,
"In a screened place.
The gatekeeper said:
"How can such a thing exist?
These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have violated the holy life; having engaged in evil acts together at night, they release them in the morning.

It is like thieves who, having stayed the night with a courtesan, release her at the gate in the morning; so too it is with these śākya bhikṣus, who, after staying the night together, release her in the morning."
In this way, one person spoke to two, and two spoke to three; thus, by successive transmission, the evil reputation spread throughout the city of Śrāvastī.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Nanda: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked Nanda with various causes and conditions:
"You do not know the proper time nor the proper measure, yet you delight in preaching the Dharma even until sunset.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, remains until sunset, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing. If one does not repent for the offense, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī from the time the ground is cleared until sunset, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu instructs bhikṣuṇīs at the time when the ground has been prepared, during the forenoon, at midday, in the afternoon, in the late afternoon, or at sunset, it constitutes a pāyattika offense upon the completion of the sunset.
If, when sunset has already occurred, one gives instruction while perceiving that sunset has not yet occurred, it is a *pāyattika*.
If, when sunset has already occurred, one gives instruction while perceiving that sunset has already occurred, it is a *pāyattika*.
If, when the sun has already set, one gives instruction while harboring doubt, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the sun has not yet set, but one gives instruction with the perception that it has set, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the sun has not yet set and one gives instruction while harboring doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the sun has not yet set and one gives instruction while perceiving that it has not yet set, there is no offense.
The twenty-second [section] is finished. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing for themselves that they would no longer be permitted to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, spoke these words out of jealousy and anger:
"The bhikṣus instruct bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of gain and offerings—namely, robes, alms bowls, door-latches, food for the daytime, food for the night-time, food for seven days, and food for life."
"For this profit, the bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; they do not do so for the sake of the wholesome Dharma.

Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, their hearts were displeased, and they censured it through various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu speak thus?"
"Monks, for the sake of material gain, they instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
After rebuking them with various reasons, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu speak in such a manner?”
"Monks, for the sake of material gain, you instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the monks:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the monks."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu should say,
'The bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of material gain.'"
