"A *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* is that which boils, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu says:
"If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī for the sake of a bowl," it is a pāyattika.
If, for the sake of robes, door-hooks,
food to be taken at the proper time, food to be taken during the night, seven-day medicine, or lifetime medicine, he instructs a bhikṣuṇī, in all such cases it is a pāyattika.
For each instance as described, one incurs that many *pāyattika* offenses.
[The twenty-third section is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus conspired with the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta to travel together on the same road, engaging in mockery and loud laughter, uttering coarse and evil speech, and performing various kinds of impure acts.
Among them, there were householders coming against the current of the road and others following behind;
having seen this, they said to one another, "Look at this! Is it a woman?"
"Is this a private liaison?
Surely they have committed acts of sexual desire together.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] yet asking for the sake of instruction, he asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“What is it to call a bhikṣu one who makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together along the same road from one village to another?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together along the same road from one village to another, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Agreed upon" means that either a bhikṣu makes the agreement or a bhikṣuṇī makes the agreement.
"Road" is of two kinds:
land roads and water routes.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together by land from one village to another, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one returns by way of the middle path, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one goes toward an open space or a place without a village, even for a distance of one *krośa* (five hundred *dhanus*), it is a *pāyattika*.
If one returns by the middle path, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same for the water route.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī; having reached a dangerous road, they waited for a large company.
At that same time, there were also various bhikṣus traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī.
Seeing the bhikṣus from afar, the bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"If we go together with the bhikṣus, we shall pass through safely.
As the bhikṣus drew near, the bhikṣuṇīs asked them:
"Venerable sirs!
Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Let us go toward Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"We shall go together with the venerable ones."
The bhikṣus replied:
“The Buddha has established a precept that bhikṣus must not travel along the same path with bhikṣuṇīs by prior appointment.
How then can you go together?”
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "If that is so, Venerable Sir, please go on ahead.
At that time, the bhikṣus were numerous; they passed through the perilous road safely, and the bandits did not dare to attack.
The bhikṣuṇīs followed behind at a slow pace; seeing that the group of women was small, the bandits emerged and seized their robes, leaving them all naked before letting them go.
The bhikṣus traveled on and eventually reached the kingdom of Śrāvastī, where they went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they greet them with these words of inquiry:
"Bhikṣus, are you patient?
Are you content?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking easy for you?
Are the roads not too arduous?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
We are contented and dwelling in peace; almsfood is easily obtained and the roads are not arduous.”
He then related this matter in detail to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī, from one village to another, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding "circumstances" (nidāna): if, while on the road, one must necessarily have many companions because there is doubt or fear regarding the path being traveled, this is called "circumstance.
There are two kinds of doubt:
first, doubt regarding the loss of robes and bowls; second, doubt regarding the loss of provisions.
If there is concern that food and provisions may be lost, a bhikṣu should take and carry away the food and drink of the bhikṣuṇīs.
If there is concern that robes and bowls may be lost, a bhikṣu should take and carry away the robes and bowls of the bhikṣuṇīs.
When they reach a place that is secure, peaceful, and prosperous, at that time they should return the bhikṣuṇīs' robes and food, and should say to them:
"Sisters! You may go as you please; you must not travel together with us."
If, at that time, they travel together along the same path and reach a village, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he returns midway, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If he goes from a village toward an open space for even one *krośa*, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one returns by the central road, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
It is the same for the water route.
There is no offense if one did not intend to go, or if one travels together with the king’s consort.
The twenty-fourth section concludes. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Eleventh.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Twelfth. The Sixth Part of the Second Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
The Fourth of the Ninety Pāyattika Rules:
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus traveled in a single boat with the bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta; they engaged in playful jesting and loud laughter, uttered coarse and evil speech, and committed various kinds of impure acts.
Among them were laypeople on both banks who, having seen this, said to one another:
"Look at this! Is this a wife, or is it an illicit affair?"
"They will certainly engage in sexual misconduct together.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was not pleased, and he went to the Buddha to relate it in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu traveling in the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to board the same boat, it is a pāyattika.
There are two kinds of appointments: [the explicit agreement and the implicit understanding].
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment, or if a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment, it is a pāyattika offense;
for such acts as boiling, burning, covering, or obstructing, if one does not repent, they will be able to obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if one bhikṣu makes an appointment with one bhikṣuṇī to ride in the same boat, it is a pāyattika.
If one bhikṣu makes an appointment with two, three, or four bhikṣuṇīs to ride in the same boat, there are four pāyattikas.
If two bhikṣus agree with two bhikṣuṇīs to board a single boat together, there are two pāyattikas;
if they agree with three, four, or one bhikṣuṇī to board a single boat together, there is one pāyattika.
If three bhikṣus agree with three bhikṣuṇīs to board a single boat together, there are three pāyattikas;
if they agree with four, one, or two bhikṣuṇīs to board a single boat together, there are two pāyattikas.
If four bhikṣus and four bhikṣuṇīs agree to board a single boat together, it constitutes four pāyattikas;
if they agree to board a single boat with one, two, or three bhikṣuṇīs, it constitutes three pāyattikas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, several bhikṣuṇīs were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī; they arrived at the riverbank and stayed there waiting for a boat.
At that time, there were certain bhikṣus who were also traveling from the country of Kośala toward Śrāvastī; having reached the riverbank, they waited for a boat.
When the boat arrived, the bhikṣus quickly boarded it.
The bhikṣuṇīs came again, wishing to board the boat, but the bhikṣus said:
"Do not board! For what reason?"
The Buddha established a precept that bhikṣus must not board the same boat as bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "If that is so,
Venerable Sirs, please cross first."
The boat departed immediately and did not return again.
The bhikṣuṇīs then stayed overnight on the bank; at night, thieves came, stripped them of all their clothes, and sent them away naked.
The bhikṣus were traveling and arrived at Śrāvastī, where they went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they greet them with these words of inquiry: “Are you well?”
Are you well?
Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is almsfood easy to obtain?
"Are you not fatigued by the journey?
The Buddha immediately greeted them with these words:
"Do the bhikṣus endure well?"
"Are you well?
Do you not lack for alms, and are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
You dwell in contentment and ease; alms are easily obtained, and you are not fatigued by the roads.
He then related these matters to the Buddha in detail.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to ride together in a boat, whether going upriver or downriver, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Except for crossing directly.
"Upstream" means against the current;
"downstream" means with the current.
"Crossing directly" means crossing straight to the other shore.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī ride together in one boat upstream from one village to another village, it is a pāyattika;
if they turn back midway, it is a dukkaṭa.
If there is no village, and one travels even as far as one krośa on open ground, it is a pāyattika;
if one returns midway, it is a dukkaṭa.
The same applies to traveling downstream.

There is no offense if there was no prior agreement; or if one crosses directly; or if, while intending to cross directly, one is carried away by the current; or if the bank collapses while crossing directly; or if one loses one's belongings due to being swept away; or if one boards or disembarks from a boat—there is no offense in these cases.
[The twenty-fifth case is finished. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus were dividing robes in a secluded place. There was one bhikṣu who was an old acquaintance of the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā; they had conversed with her frequently and were on intimate and familiar terms.
When that bhikṣu emerged from the place where the robes were being distributed, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā saw him and asked,
"Venerable sir,
where have you come from?"
He replied, "The robe-portion has come from such-and-such a place; what is the portion of robe you have received like?
He answered:
"Excellent," the bhikṣuṇī said after examining it;
"It is indeed excellent."
He asked, "Do you need this robe?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"Even if she were to need it, I am a woman of meager merit; from where could I possibly obtain it?
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This bhikṣuṇī makes such a firm request; how could I not give it to her?"
He then gave the robe to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.
At that time, at the end of the summer retreat, the Buddha was traveling through various countries; while all the other bhikṣus were wearing new robes, this bhikṣu alone was wearing old ones.
The Buddha, having already perceived this, asked him intentionally:
"Why are you alone wearing old robes?
The bhikṣu then related these matters to the Buddha in detail.
Knowing the answer, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Is this bhikṣu now giving a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative?
He replied:
“It is true,
World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and censured [the offender] through various causes and conditions:
"What is it called for a bhikṣu to give clothing to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative? Why is this?
Because a person who is not a relative cannot inquire whether one’s clothing is sufficient or insufficient, or whether there is anything more or less."
If one encounters such a person, one should take directly what can be obtained.
If they are a relative, one may inquire whether they have enough or not, and whether more is available.
If they cannot give it themselves, how much less would they be able to provide it upon request?
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu gives clothing to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika. Regarding "not a relative":
a relative is defined as one's mother, sister, daughter, or even those connected by kinship up to the seventh generation; anyone other than these is called "not a relative."
Regarding "robes": these are robes of hemp, white hemp, red hemp, *kusa* grass, *kāśī* silk, *kauśeya* silk, and cotton.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, when a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative gives him a robe while claiming she is a relative, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one gives a robe to a nun who is not a relative—namely, to a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a female renunciant, or a female renunciant nun—it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, suspecting that a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative is either a relative or not a relative, gives her a robe, it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, suspecting that a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative is either a bhikṣu or not a bhikṣu, a śikṣamāṇā or not a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera or not a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī or not a śrāmaṇerī, one who has gone forth or not one who has gone forth, or a bhikṣuṇī who has gone forth or not one who has gone forth, and gives her a robe, in all such cases it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu, regarding a relative bhikṣuṇī as not being a relative, gives her a robe, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he regards a relative bhikṣuṇī as a bhikṣu, or as a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, one who has gone forth, or a female renunciant, and gives her a robe, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a relative bhikṣuṇī while harboring doubt as to whether she is a relative or not, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a relative bhikṣuṇī while harboring doubt as to whether she is a bhikṣuṇī or not, or whether she is a śikṣamāṇā or not, a śrāmaṇera or not, a śrāmaṇerī or not, one who has gone forth or not, or a bhikṣuṇī who has gone forth or not, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu gives an impure robe—namely, one made of camel hair, cow hair, sheep’s wool, or a mixture of various hairs—to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, whether he considers her so or suspects it; or to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, whether he considers her so or not, or suspects it or does not suspect it, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The twenty-sixth section concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Kāḷodāyin had been acquainted with the bhikṣuṇī Guptā for some time; they frequently conversed together, being close, friendly, and familiar with one another.
The bhikṣuṇī Jotidharā had some cloth that ought to be cut and sewn into a robe; she said to Kālodāyin,
"Venerable Sir,
could you cut and sew this cloth into a robe for me?"
He replied,
"I shall leave it behind.
Having left it, he departed.

Kāḷodāyin immediately took up some cloth, stretched it out, and cut and stitched it; he fashioned an image of a man and woman in union upon the back of the robe, and having finished sewing it, he folded it up and placed it back in its original location.
The bhikṣuṇī Gokulā came and asked:
"Venerable sir,
have you finished cutting and sewing the robe for me?"
He replied, "It has been made;
this is your robe, take it away. Do not spread it out here;
you may spread it out once you have returned to the bhikṣuṇī monastery."
She immediately took it and went away, saying to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Look at this robe my teacher has made for me—is it not good?
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Very well, who made it for you?
He replied,
"The Venerable Kāḷudāyin."
"Unfold it and look.
He immediately unfolded it for him, and in the center of the strip there was an image of a man and woman in union.
Among them was a young bhikṣuṇī who delighted in playful jesting; having seen this, she spoke:
"This robe is excellent; were it not for Kāḷudāyin, who else could have made such a robe for you?
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣuṇī who delighted in observing the precepts, who said:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if he intentionally defiles a bhikṣuṇī's robe?"
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, because of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, addressed Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu intentionally soil a bhikṣuṇī's robe?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Non-relatives": "Relative" refers to one's mother, sister, or daughter, extending even to those connected by kinship up to the seventh generation; anyone other than these is called a non-relative.

"Garments" refers to hempen garments, white hempen garments, red hempen garments, *śāṇa* (coarse hemp) garments, *kṣaumika* (linen) garments, *kauśeya* (silk) garments, and *kārpāsika* (cotton) garments.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking," "burning," and "obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes clothing for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, for each individual act involved, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he washes it, for each individual act, there is a *pāyattika*.
If he dyes it, for each individual drying, there is a *pāyattika*.
If he cuts it, stitches it with pins, or sews it, for every needle-stitch, there is a *pāyattika*.
If one sews directly, for every stitch there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one uses a string to mark the lines, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one uses pins to trim the edges, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes robes for a relative bhikṣuṇī, there is no offense.
[The twenty-seventh case ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Kālodāyin had been an old acquaintance of the bhikṣuṇī Khujjuttarā; they frequently conversed with one another and were intimate and familiar friends.
Kālodayin went to the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇī Khujjuttarā and sat alone with her in a secluded, concealed place.
There was a bhikṣu there who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; having heard of this, he rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu sit alone with a single bhikṣuṇī in a secluded, concealed place?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though already aware of it, intentionally asked Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who sits alone with a single bhikṣuṇī in a secluded and concealed place?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sits alone with a single bhikṣuṇī in a secluded, concealed place, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Alone with a single bhikṣuṇī" means there are exactly two persons, and no third person is present.
"A secluded place" refers to being covered or screened by such things as a wall, a curtain, or a mat; this is what is meant by a secluded place.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, scorching, and obscures; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu sits alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded place, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one rises and then sits back down again, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of rising and sitting back down, one incurs that many *pāyattikas*.
[The twenty-eighth section ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Kālodāyin had been acquainted with the wife of the householder Ghoṣila for some time; they frequently conversed and were close, familiar friends.
On one occasion, Kālodāyin went to the householder’s wife’s residence and sat alone with her on the open ground.
When the laypeople saw this, they said:
"Look at this! Is she the wife of a bhikṣu, or is it an illicit affair?"
"This bhikṣu must certainly have engaged in sexual misconduct.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and rebuked him with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who sits alone with a woman in the open air?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Kāḷudāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu sit alone with a woman in the open air?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sits alone with a single woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"A woman" refers to one who has life, whether she is old or young, married or unmarried, and is capable of engaging in sexual acts.
"Alone with a single woman" means there are exactly two people present, with no third person.
"An open space" means there is no obstruction of walls, no obstruction of cloth canopies, and no obstruction of mats.
"Pāyattika" means that by boiling, burning, covering, or obstructing [the path], if one does not repent, it will be able to hinder the Way.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman on open ground, it is a pāyattika.
If he rises and then sits down again, it is a pāyattika.
If one sits down again after having risen, for every such instance, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits at a distance of half a *vyāma* from another, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits at a distance of one *vyāma* from another, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sits at a distance of one *vyāma* and a half, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one sits at a distance of two *vyāmas* or more than two *vyāmas*.
The twenty-ninth section concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a householder who invited the four great disciples of the Buddha—Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha—for a meal the following day; they all accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the bhikṣus had accepted by remaining silent, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at their feet, circumambulated them to the right, and departed.

He returned to his own home and prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night. Having prepared the abundant and delicious food during that night, he spread out multicolored sitting mats in the early morning and went in person to inform the four great bhikṣus, saying, "The time has come."

The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had previously been frequenting this household. Rising early and putting on her robes, she entered the house of this lay devotee and saw that much delicious food and drink had been prepared and variously colored seats were laid out.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī asked a householder’s wife,
“Have you prepared much delicious food and drink, and spread out variegated seating mats, to invite the bhikṣus?
She replied:
"Please. "Whom do you ask to come? He replied:
"Please invite Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha.
This bhikṣuṇī said to the householder’s wife:
"If you were to ask me, I would invite these minor bhikṣus; rather, you should invite the Great Dragon Bhikṣus."
The householder’s wife asked,
“Who is the great nāga?
He replied:
“Venerable Devadatta, Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Samudradatta, and Kāḷudāyin.
When the bhikṣuṇīs were conversing with the wives of householders, Mahākāśyapa was walking ahead; hearing these words, he thought:
“If we do not enter immediately, these bhikṣuṇīs will commit a grave offense.”
She immediately made a sound.
Upon hearing the sound, the bhikṣuṇī became silent; turning her face, she saw him and said to the householder’s wife, “You have invited this great nāga.”
The householder’s wife asked,
“Who is the Great Dragon?
He replied:
“Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha.
At that time, a lay devotee arrived later and, hearing the bhikṣuṇīs speaking in two ways, said to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
“You are a wicked, evil, and thieving bhikṣuṇī with a double tongue; you have just said:”
"Little bhikṣu," he said, and then again,
"Great Nāga."
"If you enter my house again, I shall punish you according to the law for thieves.
He then spoke further to his wife, saying:
"If you go forward again to meet that bhikṣuṇī, I shall cry out: [and so forth]."
"You are not my wife;
I shall abandon you and depart.
At that time, the householder had the bhikṣus sit upon variegated mats, personally provided them with water, and personally served them abundant, delicious food and drink.
After they had eaten their fill of various delicious foods and drinks to their satisfaction, the householder served water.
Once the bhikṣus had set aside their bowls, they took low seats and sat before the bhikṣus, wishing to hear the Dharma being taught.

After Mahākāśyapa had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat together with the bhikṣus and went to where the Buddha was; there he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and smiled.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Mahākāśyapa,
"For what cause and condition do you smile?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Today we were addressed by the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā with the name ‘little bhikṣus,’ and she further said:”
"O Great Dragon," the Buddha said,
"for what reason is this so?"
Mahākāśyapa related the preceding circumstances in detail to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Are there any bhikṣus who eat food provided by a bhikṣuṇī as a result of her mediation?"
He replied, “It is truly so. For this reason,
the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and censured him with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has acted as an intermediary to obtain food, eats it?
Having rebuked them with various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that he has received food through the cause of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, eats that food, it is a pāyattika.
"Knowing" means either knowing by himself or knowing from another.
If a bhikṣuṇī praises herself, and other bhikṣuṇīs praise her, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Pāyattika" means being boiled, burned, covered, and obstructed; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī goes to a householder’s wife and says,
“You should invite a bhikṣu,” [the wife asks], “Whom shall we invite?”
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so.
The householder’s wife said:
"Yes," the bhikṣuṇī said,
"I shall prepare the rice for you."
If that bhikṣu eats [the food], it is a pāyattika offense.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who went and said to a householder’s wife:
"You should invite a bhikṣu."
"To whom have you invited?
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so."
The householder’s wife said,
“Yes. The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Prepare a soup of ghee and beans for me.
If a bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī goes and says to a householder’s wife:
"One should invite bhikṣus.
[He asked,] "Whom do you mean by 'invite'? He replied:
"Please [call] so-and-so.
The householder’s wife said, "Yes."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I have prepared partridge meat, francolin meat, and quail meat.
If a bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
Even if one instructs [a layperson] to prepare a small amount of ginger and place it in the food, for a bhikṣu who eats it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī goes and says to a householder’s wife:
"You should invite the bhikṣus."
"To whom have you invited?
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so."
The householder’s wife said,
“I have already invited him. He asked:
"What is the rice like?
He replied,
"It is coarse rice."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"I shall prepare rice for you.
If a bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī went and said to a householder’s wife,
“You should invite a bhikṣu.
[The woman asked,] “Whom shall we invite?”
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so.
The householder’s wife said:
"I have already invited him. He asked,
"How is the soup?"
He replied,
“I am making a soup of *puluga* beans.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"If you prepare a soup of ghee and beans for him," [the nun says].
If a bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who went and said to a householder’s wife:
"One should invite a bhikṣu.
"Whom should one invite?
He replied:
"Please [so-and-so].
The householder’s wife said,
"I have already invited him first."
Question:
"What food do you eat?
Answer: [He] replied:
“Beef. [The donor says:
“Do not give him beef; prepare partridge meat, francolin meat, or quail meat for him.
If a bhikṣu eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
Even to the point of instructing [a layperson] to place a small amount of ginger in the food, if a monk within the community eats it, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a householder who had previously intended to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to hold a feast.

At that time, there was a famine in the world and food and drink were difficult to obtain. This householder, who was not particularly wealthy, possessed few fields, houses, or people to serve as his laborers.
As the summer months drew to a close, the householder spoke with sorrow:
"How painful this is! Previously, I had the intention to invite the Buddha and the Sangha to hold a feast."
In this world, there is famine and food and drink are difficult to obtain; I am not very wealthy and possess few fields, houses, people, or servants.
As the end of summer approaches, let me not let my merit and virtue pass in vain.
"If I cannot invite the entire Saṃgha, I should instead invite a small or large number of bhikṣus from among them.
Having formed this thought, he went to the Jetavana and struck the ghaṇṭā.
The bhikṣus asked the householder,
"For what reason did you strike the ghaṇṭā?
He replied:
"I wish to invite such-and-such numbers of bhikṣus from among the Saṃgha to my home for a meal tomorrow.
The bhikṣus said, "So be it."
After this householder had invited the Saṃgha, he then encountered an urgent matter requiring him to leave the city. He instructed his wife, saying:
"I have an urgent business that requires me to go in person; you must invite these many bhikṣus. Are you able to prepare such-and-such food and drink?"
At that time, because the wife had faith and delighted in merit, she replied, "I can do as instructed.
She immediately prepared various kinds of fine food and drink, spread out multicolored seats, and, having no one else to send, went herself to invite the bhikṣu.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who used to go in and out of this family. Rising early and putting on her robes, she went to their house and saw that much fine food and drink had been prepared and variously colored seats were laid out. Having seen this, she asked:
"Are you inviting bhikṣus?"
She replied, "I wish to invite them;
however, although my husband has instructed me to prepare everything as he taught, there is no one who can go to invite the bhikṣus.
If you could go and invite the bhikṣus to come, they may eat here together with us."
He replied, "I can invite them. Thereupon,
the bhikṣus set down their robes and bowls and paced back and forth on the open ground, standing and waiting for the invitation to arrive.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī went out of the city and saw that the bhikṣus had each already finished their preparations.
She said to the bhikṣus, "Those who have accepted the invitation of a certain layperson should know that the food and drink are ready and that it is time."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
“The Buddha has laid down this precept:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī prepares food through a formal arrangement (karaṇīya), it should not be eaten.’”
"Now that the bhikṣuṇī has been sent to fetch us, this bhikṣuṇī must surely have some reason for preparing food.
The bhikṣus did not go, and because they missed this invitation, they went without food that day.
At that time, when the householder returned from his journey, he asked his wife,
"Did you invite the bhikṣus and provide them with a good供养 (offering)?
The wife replied:
"As my husband instructed, I have prepared many kinds of delicious food and drink and spread out variegated seats.
I sent a bhikṣuṇī to summon you, but the bhikṣus have not come; how then shall I make offerings?"
Having heard this, the householder spoke with anger:
"If these bhikṣus do not eat or drink, why did they accept my invitation?

These bhikṣus do not realize that in this present age of famine, food and drink are difficult to obtain; even the wives and children of ordinary people lack sufficient food and drink, so how much less could they be given to beggars?"
Because this layman could not endure his anger, he went to the Jetavana to visit the Buddha and spoke to the bhikṣus.
As the layman was about to enter the Jetavana, he saw the bhikṣus he had invited and said to them:
"If you do not eat and drink, for what purpose did you accept my invitation?"

"Do you not realize that in these times of famine and scarcity, food and drink are difficult to obtain? Even the wives and children of ordinary people lack sufficient food and drink; how much less could they be given to a beggar?
The bhikṣus said, "Householder, do not be distressed.
The Buddha has established a precept for us: we are not permitted to eat food prepared on account of a bhikṣuṇī."
"Because a bhikṣuṇī came today on an errand, we thought this meal was for her sake; therefore, we did not go [to the donor's house], and since morning we have been fasting."
Upon hearing that the bhikṣus had fasted, the householder’s anger was immediately extinguished, and he said to the bhikṣus:
"Previously, I had the intention to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal; however, at present, due to famine, food and drink are difficult to obtain."
"I am not very wealthy; I have few fields, houses, people, or servants.
As the summer months draw to a close, I do not wish for my merit to pass away in vain.

If I cannot invite the entire community, I shall instead invite a small or large number of bhikṣus from among the Saṅgha for tomorrow’s meal. You should know that this is my own resolve and was not prompted by the bhikṣuṇīs; you all should come tomorrow to eat cold food."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts; having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu knowingly eats food obtained through the praise of a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika,
except when previously invited by a donor.'"
Regarding "previously invited": this refers to when a donor first conceives the thought in their mind and intends to invite the community of bhikṣus.
In this case, there is no offense if a bhikṣuṇī goes and says to the householder’s wife, "You should invite the bhikṣus."
"To whom have you invited?
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so."
The householder’s wife said,
“I have already invited her.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"To prepare non-glutinous rice porridge.
If it is prepared for the sake of the family members, there is no offense for a bhikṣu who eats it.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī went and said to a householder’s wife:
"One should invite a bhikṣu.
"Whom should one invite?
He replied:
"Please [someone else].
The householder’s wife said,
"I have already invited him."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"I shall prepare a soup of ghee and beans.
If she prepares it for a lay family and the bhikṣu eats it, he does not commit an offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī went and said to a householder’s wife, “You should invite a bhikṣu. [The woman asked:
“Whom do you intend to invite?”
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so.
The householder’s wife said:
"I have already made my request," the bhikṣuṇī said.
"I shall prepare the meat of pheasants, francolin partridges, and quails."
If it is prepared for the sake of one's family members, a bhikṣu who eats it does not commit an offense.
Even if he is instructed to place a small amount of ginger in the food, if it is prepared for the sake of one's family members, a bhikṣu who eats it does not commit an offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a householder’s wife and says,
“You should invite a bhikṣu,” [the wife asks], “Whom should we invite?”
He replied, "I have invited such-and-such.
The householder’s wife said:
"I have already made a prior request," the bhikṣuṇī said.
"I shall prepare the non-glutinous rice for you."
If it was prepared for a bhikṣu beforehand, there is no offense if the bhikṣu eats it.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī goes to a householder’s wife and says,
“You should invite a bhikṣu,” [there is likewise no offense].
"To whom have you invited?
He replied, "I have invited so-and-so."
The householder’s wife said,
“I have already invited her.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Prepare a soup of ghee and beans.
If she first prepares it for the bhikṣus and the bhikṣu eats it, he commits no offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī goes and says to a householder’s wife:
"One should invite a bhikṣu.
"Whom should one invite?
He replied:
"Please [someone else].
The householder’s wife said,
"I have already invited him first."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I shall prepare partridge meat, francolin meat, and quail meat.
If she first prepared it for a bhikṣu and the bhikṣu ate it, there was no offense.
Even down to instructing [a layperson] to place a small amount of ginger in the food—if it was prepared for a bhikṣu beforehand and the bhikṣu eats it, there is no offense.
Section Thirty concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a householder who, due to the conditions of impermanence, had lost his fields and houses and whose family members had all died, leaving only one son remaining. Having heard it said that those who provide meals for the Buddha and the Sangha are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he immediately made this vow:
"It would be well if I were to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Sangha."
Having made this vow, he further thought:
"I have nothing at present; I must go to work as a laborer.

At that time, there was a wealthy householder in Śrāvastī who possessed many fields, houses, people, gold, silver, and wealth, and was endowed with all kinds of meritorious virtues and majestic marks.
At that time, the boy went to his house and said to the householder,
"I shall work for you as a hired laborer.
The householder asked:
"What are you capable of?

He replied, "I am able to write, I am able to read, I am able to calculate, I am able to examine the marks of gold, silver, and coins; the marks of hair, silk, cotton, and fine cloth; and the marks of pearls. I am able to sit at a gold stall, a silver stall, a pearl stall, a copper stall, or a stall for hired labor."
The householder asked,
"For how much do you seek for one year's work?
He replied:
"A thousand pieces of gold.
The householder said, "You children do not understand;
in these times of famine and scarcity, even food is difficult to obtain, let alone demanding a price."
The boy said, "I possess many skills. Thus, through a mutual deliberation based on superior,
middling, and inferior qualities, it was settled that five hundred gold coins would be paid as wages.

The boy said, "I ought to receive a high price; because I was in haste, I have worked for you until now. We should make an agreement that at the end of the year, you shall pay me my wages all at once."
Having heard this, the householder thought to himself,
"These laborers work for themselves and yet demand wages.
He then spoke to the boy:
"Do not grieve; at the end of the year, I shall give it to you all at once.
The householder then placed it upon his stall.
At that time, the young boy watched over the market stall with great care; whereas previously the householder had not obtained much profit, he now gained two or three times as much.
After one month had passed, this householder inspected his shop and obtained a threefold profit.
The householder thought to himself:
"If I had sat at my stall myself with these goods, I would not have obtained such a profit."
"This hired laborer possesses great merit; that he now obtains this profit is entirely due to the young boy.
He then took him to the field, where the boy worked with clear diligence and guarded it well. The granaries that were previously not full are now all twice as full.
When the year ended and the granary was inspected, those that had previously been less than full were now three times full.
The householder thought again:
"Even though I have this field as my place of labor, I do not obtain such profit from it."
"This boy possesses great merit; that my storehouses are full is entirely due to the boy's power.
At the end of the year, the boy went to the householder’s place and demanded payment all at once.
The householder stepped aside a short distance and thought to himself:
"If this boy obtains the price, he will surely abandon me; that is why I have stepped aside, not because I do not wish to give it to him."
This child came repeatedly to demand a price, so the householder said, "Why do you urgently demand a price? What do you intend to make with it?
He replied:
"Layman! I have heard people say that by providing a meal for the Buddha and the Saṅgha, one is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
For this reason, I have worked as a laborer for one year, desiring to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Saṅgha so that I may be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Upon hearing these words, the householder immediately conceived faith; that boy, for the sake of another, was able to undergo such diligent toil for a full year.
The householder asked, "Where do you wish to work?"
He replied,
"I wish to build it within the Jeta Grove.
Having thought thus, with the expedient means of wishing to cause virtuous people to enter his house, he spoke to the young boy:

“In the Jetavana there is a scarcity of cauldrons, pots, vessels, firewood, grass, and laborers; it is not like my home, which is fully provided with many cauldrons, pots, vessels, firewood, grass, and laborers of every kind. Even if they should be lacking, I shall assist you. You should invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to come to my residence.”
The boy immediately left the householder’s residence and headed toward Jeta’s Grove.

At that time, in the late afternoon, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma. From afar, the boy saw the Buddha within the grove, his faculties well-restrained and having attained the foremost tranquility; from his body issued a radiant glow like a mass of pure gold, so upright and extraordinary that it caused the hearts of men to become pure.

Having seen him, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha taught the Dharma to the boy through various causes and conditions, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he remained silent.
The boy rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One, together with the Sangha, will accept my invitation for tomorrow.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, the boy prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Returning to the householder’s residence, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night.

At that time, during a festival in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, laypeople rose early and brought much dried pork and parched grain to the community of monks. The bhikṣus accepted these, tasted them, and gradually ate until they were full.
After the boy had prepared many kinds of delicious food throughout the night, he rose early, arranged the seating, and went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know the time."
The bhikṣus went to the house of a lay devotee, while the Buddha remained in his own quarters to receive his portion of food.
When the young boy saw that the Saṃgha was seated, he personally served water and, holding food, wished to place it into the bowl of the senior elder.
The Elder said,
"A little. The second Elder said:
"Do not wear it too much," said the third elder.
"Wear half of it."
Thus, as they passed the food around, they gave only a little, not much, but half a portion each; yet all the monks spoke in this same way.

When the child went to look at the place where the rice was served, it had not diminished much; next, looking at the place where the soup was served, that too had not diminished much; looking into the bowls and vessels, they were all full and had not decreased.
At that time, the young boy went before the elder and said,
"Is it because you have compassion for me that you do not eat?
Or is it because of the world's scarcity?"
"Is it because of my year of hard labor as a hired hand?
Or is it because the food is not cooked well, does not smell fragrant, or is not delicious?
The Elder Ṛjuka replied:
"It was not out of compassion, nor out of worldly frugality, nor because of the toil of working as a hired laborer, nor because it was unripe, unscented, or unpalatable.

Today was a festival day in Śrāvastī; rising early, I obtained a great deal of dried pork and parched grain. Initially intending to taste only a little, I gradually became full, and for that reason I ate so little."
Having heard this, the child became sorrowful and regretful, thinking:
"I have not prepared sufficient food; perhaps I shall not be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The child left the layman’s house and, weeping, went to where the Buddha was, reporting that the bhikṣus had received too little food.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly who paid him reverent homage as he preached the Dharma for them. From afar, the Buddha saw a young child coming along crying.
The Buddha asked the child, "Why are you crying?"
He then related these matters in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the child, "Go back quickly;
give [the food] to whichever bhikṣus are able to eat it, and you will surely be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Upon hearing this, the child was greatly delighted and thought to himself, "The Buddha has given no other prediction;
there is no doubt that I shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Then the child took the food and went to where the senior elder was.
"This food is fragrant and delicious; take a little or a lot.
He then gave him another kind, saying:
"This is also very fine; take a little or a lot."
A second and third time he exhorted them in this same manner.

With his own hands, the boy served much delicious food and drink; once the bhikṣus had eaten their fill to their heart's content and knew the Saṃgha had finished taking their bowls, he personally poured water for them, took a small stool, and sat before the assembly of monks, desiring to hear the Dharma being preached.
After the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed; the bhikṣus followed in succession and left as well.

At that time, during the late afternoon in Śrāvastī, a large caravan of merchants arrived. They deposited their treasures outside the city and said to one another, "We shall enter the city to purchase food and drink."
He immediately sent people to search for it, but for two reasons they were unable to find it:
first, because of the world's scarcity; second, because during the heat of the season, food was not kept as leftovers.
At that time, the man who had gone to buy food returned and told the merchants that it was impossible to obtain any food within the city.

The leader of the merchants said, "In the perils of the great ocean, we have never lacked for food; yet now, having arrived at this great city, we cannot find any. You all must go back once more and search thoroughly and diligently, using whatever means necessary to ensure we obtain some."
When this child first cried out toward the Buddha, many people saw and recognized him. These people said to the merchants:
"In such-and-such a house today, much food and drink has been prepared, yet little has been consumed; go to that house to seek alms, and you will surely receive it."
The merchants went to the householder’s residence and said to the gatekeeper:
“Inform your master that there are sea merchants standing at the gate.”
Then the gatekeeper entered and informed his master. The master said, "Let him enter.
He entered immediately and was offered a seat; they exchanged greetings regarding their well-being and comfort. After the householder had remained silent for a short while, he asked:
"Why have you come? He replied,
"I have come for the sake of food."
The householder said, "This is food for children; it does not belong to me.
The merchant spoke to the child, saying:
"We must have food and drink," the children said.
The boy replied, "It can be obtained; no price need be paid."
"Now, how many merchants are there with you?
He replied,
"There are five hundred."
"Call them all in.
The man then went and said to the merchant leader:
"There is food and drink to be had, and no price need be paid."
The caravan leader said, "We are exhausted by hunger;
we would even take it if it were bought at a high price, let alone if we obtain it for free.
We should all go together, leaving someone behind to guard the goods."
The others all went into the householder’s residence.
They seated the child and, with their own hands, served water and provided him with abundant, delicious food and drink until he was fully satisfied.

Having been served abundant and delicious food and having eaten their fill to satiety, the children, knowing the meal was finished, put away their vessels, performed the ritual washing of hands, and sat to one side.
At that time, near the children, there was a large copper bowl from the kingdom of Kośala.
Then the merchant leader said to the boy,
"Bring this bowl here.
The boy replied:
"Why is that? [He replied,] "Just bring it here.
He immediately brought it and placed it before the caravan leader. Then the caravan leader said to the merchants:
"Whoever receives such excellent offerings as these should repay them with fine goods; if you are able to do so, place them in this bowl.
At that time, the merchant leader had a pearl on the corner of his garment worth one hundred thousand gold coins; he untied it and placed it in the bowl.
The second merchant had a pearl worth ninety thousand gold coins.
Likewise, there were those worth eighty thousand, seventy thousand, sixty thousand, fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, and ten thousand, all placed within copper bowls.
He filled a bowl to the brim and gave it to the child, saying:
"I give this to you; use it as you please.
The child said:
"I shall give you food directly; I do not sell it for a price.
The merchants said, "We too shall give it directly; we do not buy food."
"How much do we eat? Each one of these pearls is worth a great deal.
The boy then had another doubt:
"If I take these things, perhaps I will not be able to be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
He said to the caravan leader, "Wait a moment; let me go ask the Buddha and return.
The caravan leader said:
"As you wish," [the boy replied].
He left the city and went to where the Buddha was; prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet, he stood to one side and related these matters to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said, "Take it; you will certainly be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This is the present retribution; the ultimate fruition shall follow later."
Having heard these words, he thought to himself:
"The Buddha does not speak falsely; He has granted me this prediction that I shall certainly be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He then immediately returned to the merchants' place and took those precious goods.

Because this child suddenly attained great wealth and nobility, he was named Sudden Wealth (Huran Jushi). He served as a hired laborer for a family of great wealth and nobility, who was endowed with all manner of merit and majestic signs, and possessed every requisite excellence.
However, he had no sons, only a daughter who was upright, beautiful, and exquisite.
This householder thought to himself:
"This child's lineage is not inferior to mine; it is only that she is destitute of wealth."
"The wealth I have acquired today is beyond my household's capacity; I shall now give it to you as a dowry for your daughter.
He then spoke to his wife, who replied, "As you wish."
The householder then gave his daughter to him, as it is said in the verse:
"That which exists must all perish; that which is high shall also fall.
There is separation from what is joined; for those who are born, there is death."
For this reason, that householder died.
Having heard this, King Prasenajit asked,
"Does this householder have a son?"
He replied, "I have no son.
[The other asked,] "Do you have brothers?"
He replied, "There is none.
[The other asked,] "Who manages this household?"
He replied, "I have a son-in-law who is virtuous and meritorious; he manages our household.
The king said:
"His family wealth and property shall be given to this man, and he shall also be granted the rank of a great householder within the city of Śrāvastī.
Having given these instructions, he was immediately appointed to the office of a great householder.
After the meal, these bhikṣus left the city and went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that when bhikṣus return from a meal, they inquire of them with these words:
"Was the food delicious? Were the members of the Saṃgha well-satisfied?"
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus with these words:
"Was the food and drink abundant and delicious? Were the members of the Saṃgha fully satiated?
The bhikṣus replied:
"The food and drink were most excellent, and the community of monks was fully satiated.
He reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the bhikṣu:
“What is meant by a bhikṣu eating repeatedly?
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a precept.
This occurred while the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.

At that time, there was a powerful great minister in Vaiśālī who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, taught the Dharma to him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, the Buddha remained silent.
Having understood the Buddha’s various demonstrations of instruction, benefit, and encouragement, the powerful Great Minister rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my meal for tomorrow.”
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the minister prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own residence, he prepared various kinds of pure, clean, and delicious food throughout the entire night.
At that time, during a festival in Vaiśālī, the community of monks received a large quantity of dried pork and parched grain.
Having accepted them, the bhikṣus wished to taste a little to see [the quality], and as they did so, they gradually became full.
Having prepared various kinds of pure, clean, and delicious food and drink, he rose early in the morning, arranged the seats, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know the time."
The bhikṣus went to the house of the great minister, while the Buddha remained in his own quarters to receive his portion of food.
When the great minister saw that the Saṃgha was seated, he personally served water and brought the rice with his own hands to give to the elder;
the elder said, "Do not put too much on."
The second senior monk said,
"A small amount.
The third senior monk said:
"Give half. Thus, as they passed it along from one to another, none gave more, none gave less; each gave exactly half, and so it was with everyone.

At that time, the great minister went to inspect the place where the rice was served and saw that the rice had not diminished much; he inspected the place where the soup was served and saw that the soup had not diminished much; he inspected the bowls and vessels and saw that they were all full and had not decreased at all.
At that time, the minister went to the Elder and said,
"Why do you not eat?
Is it out of compassion for me?"
"Is it because the world is in a time of scarcity?
Or is it that the food is not cooked, not fragrant, or not delicious?
The Elder Ṛjusamdhi replied:
"It is not because of compassion, nor because of worldly scarcity, nor because it is unripe, unscented, or unpalatable.
Today being a festival day, I rose early and obtained much dried pork and parched grain; I initially intended to taste only a little, but gradually became full, and for this reason I ate so little."
When the minister heard these words, he spoke with anger:
"Take away this fine food and bring me dried pork and parched grain instead.
Thereupon, the messenger immediately took away the fine food and gave him a bowl filled with dried pork and parched grain; the minister said:
"Eat! Do you think there is no such food in my house?
At these words, the bhikṣus immediately felt ashamed and abstained from eating, remaining silent.
Having seen this, the minister thought:
"If he cannot even eat such fine food, how much less could he eat coarse food!
Let it be taken back."
Then the minister went before the senior monks and said:
"If you cannot even eat fine food, how much less can you eat coarse food?
Dried pork and parched grain are what is appropriate for the world; if you have accepted an invitation from another, you should wait for their meal."
The minister took a fine dish with his own hand and said, "This food is fragrant and delicious; you may eat of it as much as you wish.
He then took another dish and said:
"This food is fragrant and delicious, superior to what you had before; you may accept it and eat.
Having thus exhorted them, the entire assembly of monks was fully satiated.
Then the minister, having freely and abundantly satisfied himself with pure, clean, and exquisite food, personally served water with his own hands.
Knowing that the Sangha had finished collecting their bowls, he took a small seat and sat before the assembly, desiring to listen to the preaching of the Dharma.

When the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed; the bhikṣus followed in succession, rising and departing, and returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves at his feet.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when monks return from their meal, they inquire with these words of courtesy:
"Was the food delicious? Were the monks well-satisfied?
The Buddha asked the monks this very question.
"Was the food and drink abundant and delicious? Were the Sangha satiated?
The bhikṣus replied, "The food and drink were abundant and delicious; the assembly of monks was satiated."
He reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
On account of this matter and its prior circumstances, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the bhikṣus:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu eat repeatedly?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, it is a pāyattika.
"Repeatedly" means eating again after having already finished eating.
"Pāyattika" means being boiled and scorched, covered and obstructed; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense if one does not eat repeatedly.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, during the cold season of autumn, suffered from a severe illness of alternating heat and cold; he could not eat or drink, becoming emaciated and pale.
Seeing the bhikṣu emaciated and pale, the Buddha, though already knowing the cause, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is this bhikṣu emaciated and pale?"
Ānanda replied, “World-Honored One!
This bhikṣu is currently suffering from a severe autumnal illness of cold and heat; he cannot take food or drink, and for this reason he has become emaciated and pale.”
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"From this day forward, out of compassion and for the benefit of sick bhikṣus, I permit the consumption of three kinds of complete meals—namely, those possessing excellent color, fragrance, and flavor."
A sick bhikṣu should accept one invitation; he should not accept two invitations.
If he cannot be satiated at the first invitation, he may accept a second invitation, but he should not accept a third.
If one cannot be fully satisfied at the second invitation, one may accept a third invitation, but one should not accept a fourth.
If one still cannot be satisfied at the third invitation, one should eat gradually after having accepted it, until midday.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, it is a pāyattika offense,
except at the proper time."
"Time" refers to the time of illness; this is called "time.
If a person has an excess of cold-natured humors, an excess of heat-natured humors, or an excess of wind-natured humors, they may eat when they wish to stop.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill eats repeatedly, it is a pāyattika.
If it is actually an illness, there is no offense.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. At that moment, they received an invitation to a meal with robes;
the host said, "Those who accept my food shall be given these robes as a gift."
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat repeatedly for the sake of robes.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, because of the occasion of robes, I permit the bhikṣus to eat repeatedly."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats more than once [in a day], it is a pāyattika offense, except at the proper times.
The 'proper times' are: the time of illness and the time of receiving robes; these are called the proper times."

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu has been invited for food and clothing, and those [invitors] come with food and clothing, it is not an offense to accept the invitation, nor is it an offense to eat.

Furthermore, if a monk has been invited for food and clothing, and another person comes who lacks food and clothing, it is not an offense to accept the invitation; however, if one eats [the food], it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if a monk has been invited for food and clothing, and another person comes who both has food and clothing and lacks food and clothing, it is not an offense to accept the invitation; however, if one eats [the food], it is a *pāyattika*.

If there is an invitation for a monk that provides neither food nor clothing, and he comes without food or clothing, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he eats, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if there is an invitation for a monk that provides neither food nor clothing, and he comes with food or clothing, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, but eating does not constitute an offense.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has been invited for food and clothing, and a person comes who both has food and clothing as well as one who has neither, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he eats, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has been invited for food and clothing, and a person comes who both has food and clothing as well as one who has neither, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; if he eats, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, regarding invitations for a bhikṣu that include provisions or do not include provisions: if he who was invited with provisions comes, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, but eating the food does not constitute an offense.

Again, regarding invitations for a bhikṣu that include provisions or do not include provisions: if he who was invited without provisions comes, accepting the invitation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, but eating the food constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one receives many invitations for food and clothing; if all manner of people come bringing food and clothing—there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, during a festival in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an abundance of food and drink. Various laypeople prepared diverse kinds of food and drink and brought them to the park. Upon entering Jetavana, they struck the *gandī* (wooden gong). The bhikṣus asked:
“Householder!
For what reason and by what cause was the ghaṇṭā struck?
The householders replied:
"I have invited so many bhikṣus from among the assembly for a meal.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat repeatedly at lay gatherings on festival days."

The householder said, "According to the custom of us laypeople, when there are marriages, festivals, or gatherings where we entertain our kinsmen and acquaintances, we hold the bhikṣus in high esteem; there is no deity superior to the Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas. You must certainly accept our meal."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to eat repeatedly on festival days.
He gives it away to others and receives it from among them.
What is it that he gives away?

This refers to food that has been prepared for consumption, food for a fast day, food on the first day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, food for the Sangha as a whole, food for a specific room, invitations to the Sangha as a whole, and private invitations; all of these should be shared with others.
If the five assemblies invite one to a meal, one should not engage in divining the signs of others, such as auspicious or inauspicious omens.
Therefore, those who perform such acts are merely great virtuous bhikṣus providing offerings for others.
The five groups are: bhikṣuṇīs, ṣaḍ-dharma-bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
[Section] Thirty-one ends. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At that time, the householders of the kingdom of Kośala constructed a house of merit. Whenever any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas came to stay there, the householders would go out to meet them, inquire after their well-being, and pay them homage. They provided them with warm water for washing their feet, anointed their feet with ghee and oil, and supplied fine beds, couches, bedding, woolen rugs, blankets, and pillows. On the following day, they gave them fragrant and delicious morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambūla* (refreshments), honoring and making offerings to them with deep respect.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī, arriving at the Puṇyāvasa (House of Merit).

The lay devotees immediately came out to meet them, inquiring after their well-being and prostrating to them; they provided hot water for washing their feet, applied ghee and oil to their feet, and supplied fine beds, bedding, rugs, blankets, and pillows. On the following day, they respectfully made offerings of fragrant and delicious food before and after the meal, as well as *tambūla*.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to one another, "In these degenerate times, food and drink are difficult to obtain; we should stay here for a while and enjoy ourselves.
Having thought this, they remained there and did not depart.
If other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas come there wishing to stay overnight, they are not admitted.
These later-arriving śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas say to the host:
"May we be allowed to stay here overnight?"
The host said,
"Very well," and entered until he reached the place where the group of six bhikṣus wished to stay. The group of six bhikṣus said:
"No. Why is that? I have already been dwelling here first."
The group of six bhikṣus were naturally robust and possessed great strength, so they could not engage in conversation with the visiting guests.
The laypeople became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent and virtuous!
How does one dwell firmly in the house of merit?
Like a king, like a great minister."
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, because of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu stay at a house of merit for more than a single meal?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu stays at a house of merit (puṇya-śālā) for more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the "Dharma of the House of Merit," one should stay there for only one night and take only one meal.
As for the *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation), it is a cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu stays at a house of merit for more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.
If he stays for more than one night without eating, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one stays elsewhere and eats there, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one stays for one night and eats once, there is no offense; however, regarding a "merit-dwelling" (*puṇya-śālā*), one should say it is a place where one stays for one night.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra, having traveled from the country of Kośala, arrived at the Puṇyāvasa in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a wind-related illness flared up, and he thought to himself:
"If I remain here for one night without eating, I will incur a *duṣkṛta* offense; it would be better for me to depart."

Having departed, his illness increased in severity along the way; traveling by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī and went to where the Buddha was, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sitting to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when visiting bhikṣus arrive, they ask the resident bhikṣus with these words:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not weary from the road?
The Buddha asked Śāriputra with these words.
"Are you patient?
Are you satisfied?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Is it not difficult for you to beg for alms? Are you not weary from the road?
Śāriputra replied, "World-Honored One!"
"Alms-food is easy to obtain, but one cannot endure the extreme exhaustion of the road.
He explained this matter in detail to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu who is not ill eats more than one meal in a house of merit, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding 'one who is ill': even traveling from one village to another, or having a wound on the body—even a wound as small as that caused by a bamboo leaf—is all termed being 'ill.'"
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill stays in a merit-house (puṇya-śālā) for more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.
If he stays for more than one night without eating, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one stays overnight in another location and eats there, it is a *pāyattika*.

There is no offense in the following cases: staying for only one night and eating only one meal; being ill; if the merit-house (*puṇya-śālā*) was built by relatives; if one has been previously invited; if one is staying at a merit-house waiting for companions before entering a dangerous road; if there are many merit-houses; or if one knows that the people of the merit-house have requested one to remain. In all these instances, there is no offense.
The Thirty-two [Rules] Concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 12.5.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 13. The Second Recitation, Part Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
The fifth of the ninety *pāyattika* rules.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a brahmin who had a daughter with squinting eyes; she was thus named Kāṇā (the Squint-eyed One).
When the husband’s family sent a messenger to come and fetch her, the girl’s parents, who were Brahmins, said:
“Wait a moment!
We will finish making the fried cakes and send them.”
At that time, there was a famine in the world. This brahmin worked hard to obtain the ingredients for fried cakes and prepared them.
The śramaṇa Upāli, son of the Śākyas, frequently entered and left his house and said to the assembly:
"Whichever house I enter, you all should follow me in."
"If I obtain food, you shall also receive it in succession.

At that time, the Śākya son Upananda dressed in the morning, took his bowl, and entered the house of a brahmin, where he sat together with him and exchanged greetings regarding their mutual well-being.
Once seated, the brahmin, with single-minded reverence, inquired after the welfare of Upananda.
Upananda was a great Dharma master who possessed the eloquence of joyful exposition; he preached various sublime Dharmas for him.
The host, having attained the flavor of the Dharma, spoke these words:
"Venerable Sir!
There is no soup or rice; can you eat this cake?"
He replied,
"If even you eat it, why should I not be able to?
He then gave him the cake and went out with it.
The second and third bhikṣus were treated in the same manner, until the vessels of cakes were all empty.
The husband’s family sent a messenger again to summon the squint-eyed woman, but the brāhmaṇa sent a messenger back with this reply:
"Wait a moment!"
"Once you have finished making the cakes, send them here.
He then sought out the implements for frying cakes.
