At that time, Upananda returned with his followers; after he had preached various Dharmas to them, he took the cakes away again.
The third time, the husband’s family again sent a messenger to summon the squinting woman; the Brahmin replied once more:
"Wait a moment!
I shall finish making the fried cakes and send them."
At that time, the husband, suspecting her and feeling resentment, said:
"She may not come back again.
He took another wife and sent a messenger to say:
"I have already taken a wife; do not come here again.
When the brahmin heard these words, he spoke with sorrow and anger:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas are thus insatiable! The giver does not know moderation, but the receiver ought to know moderation."
"My son-in-law previously cherished me with affection; for this reason, he has now abandoned me and departed.
Filled with resentment and unable to restrain herself, the woman went to the Jetavana Grove to speak to the Buddha regarding the matter of Upananda.
At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions as he preached the Dharma;
as [the man] gradually drew near to the Buddha, his anger was immediately dispelled through the power of the Buddha’s mind of loving-kindness.
He went to where the Buddha was and said:
"World-Honored One!
There is no such thing as a precious possession for a woman; my daughter has already been lost."
The Buddha taught the Dharma through various causes and conditions, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.

Having heard the Buddha teach the Dharma through various causes and conditions, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, the brahmin prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of monks and, though he already knew the matter, intentionally asked Baddhananda:
"Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who does not know the proper time, does not know moderation, and does not know the Dharma?
If the donor does not know moderation, the recipient should know moderation."
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a precept.

At that time, while the Buddha was still residing in Śrāvastī, there was a group of merchants in the city of Śrāvastī who, on an auspicious day under the constellation Puṣya, intended to travel to another country.
There was a merchant who was an acquaintance of the Śākya son Upananda; Upananda frequently entered and left his house.
At one time, before midday, Upananda dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to the merchant's house, where he sat down with him and exchanged greetings concerning their mutual well-being.

Once they were seated, the merchants, with single-minded reverence, greeted Baddhananda; as Baddhananda was a great Dharma master endowed with the eloquence of joyful speech, he preached the sublime Dharma for them.
Having tasted the flavor of the Dharma, this person said:
"Venerable sir!
There is no soup or rice; there is only roasted flour, the provisions for traveling on the Path. Can you eat it?"
He replied, "If you yourselves are able to eat it, why should I not be able to?
He then gave him some flour and went out with it. A second and a third bhikṣu did likewise, until the merchants' flour vessels were all empty.
The merchant went and said to the caravan leader:
"All the provisions for our journey have been taken away entirely by the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.
Wait a moment!"
"I shall prepare provisions for you.
The caravan leader said, "The merchants wish to depart on the auspicious day of the constellation Puṣya; how can we stay?"
“You need only prepare your provisions; follow later at a leisurely pace.
Those merchants who went on ahead were numerous, so the bandits did not dare to attack them.

However, when one merchant had finished preparing his provisions and entered a dangerous pass with only a few companions, the bandits launched an attack, seized their goods, and killed that merchant. Thus, a wicked reputation spread through the various kingdoms, and they spoke these words: [as previously described].
“The Śākya bhikṣus have consumed the provisions for a journey belonging to others; these merchants were killed by bandits on a perilous road.
One person told two people, and two people told three; thus it was passed along from one to another until the ill repute of the śramaṇa Śākyaputrīya bhikṣus spread throughout the city of Śrāvastī.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, because of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Upananda: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who does not know the proper time, does not know moderation, and does not know the Dharma?
If the donor does not know moderation, the recipient should know moderation."
"How could these merchants have been killed by bandits in the midst of this perilous road?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and they freely invite him, offering much cake and parched grain,
the bhikṣus who require them may take two or three bowls."
If one takes more than this, it is a pāyattika offense.
Having taken two or three bowls and gone outside, one may say to other bhikṣus, "Let us divide them together"; this matter should be done in this way.
“House” refers to the households of laypeople.
“Invited to give much” means invited to give repeatedly.
“Bread” (apūpa) refers to those made from wheat flour, barley flour, or rice flour; large *gandhāra* cakes, small *gandhāra* cakes, and other such pure breads.
"Powdered food" refers to rice powder and wheat powder.
"Bowl" has three types:
superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the superior bowl, one receives three *pātra* of rice, one *pātra* of soup, and a half-*pātra* of other edible food.
Regarding the inferior bowl, one receives one *pātra* of rice, a half-*pātra* of soup, and a half-*pātra* of other edible food.
If it is of medium size from top to bottom, it is called a "medium bowl.
Regarding "going outside and speaking to other bhikṣus to share [the food] together," this refers to what is within the range of sight.
As for *pāyattika*, it means "to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct"; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu takes an alms bowl, he should take only one bowl; he should not take two bowls.
To take two bowls constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one takes with a medium bowl, one may take at most two bowls and should not take three.
If one takes three, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one takes with a small bowl, one may take at most three bowls and should not take four.
If one takes four [measures], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one goes outside and sees that the bhikṣus have divided [the items] among themselves, it is well; if they have not divided them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The thirty-third [section] ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, during the darkness of night, amidst falling drizzle, thunder, and flashes of lightning, the Elder Kālodāyin entered the house of a layperson to beg for alms.

At that time, a woman who was washing a vessel came out from the house; seeing Kāḷudāyin from afar in the flash of lightning, she observed that his body was black. Having seen him, she was struck with terror and her hair stood on end;
she cried out loudly, "A ghost has come!"
"A ghost has come!
Out of fear, she immediately miscarried. Kāḷodāyin said:
"Sister! I am a bhikṣu, not a ghost.
I have come here for the sake of alms."
At that time, the woman became enraged and addressed the bhikṣu with malicious speech, coarse speech, impure speech, and bitter words, saying:

"May your father die, may your mother die, and may your entire clan perish! May this śramaṇa’s belly burst! You shaven-headed śramaṇa, you who have cut off your lineage and wear black, tattered robes—why do you not slit open your own belly with a sharp ox-tongue knife instead of begging for alms in the pitch-black darkness of this night amidst thunder and lightning?"
“O śramaṇa, you have committed such great evil that my son has fallen and died, causing me to suffer the ruin of my life.
Because Kālodāyin had brought about such transgressions in this family, he immediately departed.
They reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus recounted it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: "I indeed did,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who enters the homes of laypeople to beg for food at an improper time?
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu enters the home of a layperson at an improper time, he will not only incur such a fault as this, but shall further incur a fault even greater than this.
From now on, all bhikṣus should eat but one meal [a day]."
At that time, because the bhikṣus were eating only one meal a day, they became emaciated, pale, and weak.
Seeing the bhikṣus emaciated, pale, and weak, the Buddha, though already knowing the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are the bhikṣus emaciated, pale, and weak?"
Ānanda replied:
"The World-honored One has established a precept that the bhikṣus should eat but one meal a day.
Because they eat but one meal, the bhikṣus have become emaciated, lack color, and are without strength."

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, I permit you to eat the five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods) at will.”
"The five kinds are: roots, stalks, leaves, tubers, and fruits.
At that time, when the bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food, there was a layperson who gave the bhikṣus various foods mixed with radish leaves, coriander leaves, and basil leaves.
Because the bhikṣus did not eat, they could not be satiated; consequently, they became increasingly emaciated, pale, and weak.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are the bhikṣus so emaciated, pale, and weak?"
Ānanda replied:
“The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of *khādaniya* food as much as they desire.

When the bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, there were laypeople who gave them food mixed with radish leaves, coriander leaves, and basil leaves. The bhikṣus did not eat it; because they could not obtain their fill, they became emaciated, pale, and weak.”
Having heard this, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow you to eat five kinds of *pūjāni* foods—namely, boiled rice, parched grain, parched rice flour, fish, and meat—and to accept these five kinds of food at will."
When these bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, the laypeople gave them food mixed with radish leaves, coriander leaves, and basil leaves.
Because the bhikṣus neither ate nor were satiated, they became emaciated, pale, and weak.
Seeing that the bhikṣus were emaciated, pale, and weak, the Buddha, knowing the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are the bhikṣus emaciated, pale, and weak?"
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!

You have permitted the eating of five kinds of food. When the bhikṣus enter the city to beg for alms, they may receive radish leaves, coriander leaves, and basil leaves mixed with other food and give them to the bhikṣus.”
Because the bhikṣus did not eat and were not satiated, they became emaciated, pale, and weak.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow you to eat five kinds of 'resembling food' (sappi-anna) at will, according to what is mixed with them: namely, gruel, millet, coarse wheat, wild grass seeds, and kāśī-rice."
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a householder who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.

Once the Buddha saw that the householder was seated to one side, he taught him various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden him; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s various causes and conditions that instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, the householder rose from his seat, joined his palms, and said:
“I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my offering of food tomorrow.”
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent. Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by his silence, the householder prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Returning to his own home, he spent the entire night preparing various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink.
Rising at dawn, he prepared his seat and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know the time.
The community of bhikṣus went to the householder's residence, while the Buddha remained in his quarters to receive his portion of the food.

When the householder knew that the community of monks was seated, he personally served water and provided them with various kinds of abundant and delicious food, allowing them to eat to their heart's content until they were fully satisfied.

At that time, many of the bhikṣus in Vaiśālī were ill; there were bhikṣus who attended to the sick, who would first finish eating among the community and then take the portion of food belonging to the sick bhikṣus away.
Among the sick bhikṣus, some have food, some have no food, and some have little food; if the bhikṣu who is attending to them has already eaten, he must not eat again after rising from his seat.
Many sick bhikṣus had leftover food which they discarded within the monastery grounds; at that time, many crows and birds came to devour this food, making a great clamor.
The Buddha heard the many sounds of crows and birds within the monastery;
knowing the reason, he intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason are there so many sounds of crows and birds within the monastic quarters? Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣus here in Vaiśālī are frequently ill. There are bhikṣus who attend to the sick; they first finish eating with the Saṃgha and then bring back a portion of food for the sick bhikṣu.”
Among the sick bhikṣus, some have eaten, some have not eaten, and some have eaten little; the bhikṣu who attends to them has already eaten, and having risen from his seat, he may no longer eat.
Many sick bhikṣus had leftover food which they discarded inside the monastery; because crows and birds came to eat this food, they made a great clamor.

For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, for the sake of two benefits, I permit the practice of receiving leftover food."
First, because of the circumstances involving a bhikṣu who was tending to the sick; second, because there were circumstances in which a bhikṣu’s food was insufficient.
For these ten benefits, he established a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, having finished eating, rises from his seat and departs, and then eats again without having received the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the formal permission for leftover food), it is a *pāyattika* offense."
"Eating" refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods).
"Consuming" refers to the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods) and the five kinds of similar foods.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is like being boiled, burned, covered, or obstructed; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, having finished eating and risen from his seat, departs without having received the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rule for leftover food), and then eats root-food, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats the stalks, leaves, flour, or fruit, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has finished eating and risen to leave, and then eats rice without having received the *śeṣa-bhojana-vidhi* (the formal permission to eat leftovers), it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats parched flour, roasted grain, fish, or meat, it is all a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, having finished eating and risen from his seat, departs without having received the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rule regarding leftover food), and then eats gruel, millet porridge, coarse barley porridge, wild grass seed porridge, or *kaśa* porridge, it is all a *pāyattika*.
From now on, regarding those who wish to receive the *vighasa* (leftover food) practice, the bhikṣus did not know how to receive it.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"Those who wish to receive the *vighasa* practice should place as much food as they can eat into their bowl. Knowing that other bhikṣus have not yet finished eating and have not yet risen, one should stand before such a person, bare the right shoulder, kneel on the right knee, hold the bowl, and say:"
"Venerable sir, please remember!
Grant me the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover food) procedure.
If the preceding bhikṣu does not take a small amount of this food, it is not called performing the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* procedure.
If one uses this method for receiving leftover food (vighasa) and then chews or eats it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one places the bowl on the ground to receive leftover food, it is not considered the method of receiving leftover food.
If one uses this method for receiving leftover food to chew or eat it, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one receives the method for leftover food by placing the bowl upon the knees, it is not considered "receiving."
If one uses this method for receiving leftover food (vighasa), whether by chewing or swallowing, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If the distance between [the giver and receiver] is so great that their hands do not reach each other, it does not count as having received leftover food.
If one employs this method for receiving leftover food (vighasa) and then chews or eats it, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
If one receives the method for leftover food using impure food, it is not called "receiving leftover food."
If one uses this method for receiving leftover food (vighasa) to chew or eat it, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one receives leftover food by means of impure meat, it is not considered to have been received.
If one uses this method for receiving leftover food (vighasa) and then chews or eats it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu wishes to chew the five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods) while using the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods) to perform the formal act of receiving leftover food, it is not considered a valid reception.
If one uses this method for accepting leftover food (*vighasa*) and then chews or eats it, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).

If one wishes to eat the five kinds of soft foods (*bhojaniya*) while using the method for accepting leftover food intended for the five kinds of hard foods (*khādaniya*), it is not considered a valid acceptance.
If one uses this method for receiving leftover food (*vighasa*) to chew or eat it, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

If, when wishing to eat the five kinds of "resembling food" (*pañca khajjakāni*), one employs the method for receiving the five kinds of *pūjānīya* [foods] as the reception of leftover food, it is not considered a valid reception.
If one uses this method of receiving leftover food (vighasa-dharma) to chew or eat it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu has received the method of leftover food and sits down to eat, and then five kinds of food are brought to him, if he chews each one of them, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
In how many places may a bhikṣu perform the *pravāraṇā* while traveling?”
How many times did he stand?
How many times did he sit?
How many times did he lie down?
The Buddha told Upāli:
“There are five instances when a bhikṣu may act according to his own will while walking, and five instances while standing, five while sitting, and five while lying down.
Regarding the five instances while walking: knowing the path, knowing the offerings, knowing the prohibitions regarding food, knowing various kinds of food, and violating the rules of decorum.”
There are five [faults] regarding standing: knowing how to stand, knowing how to offer, knowing how to refuse food, knowing various kinds of food, and violating dignified deportment.
There are five [faults] regarding sitting: knowing how to sit, knowing how to offer, knowing how to refuse food, knowing various kinds of food, and violating dignified deportment.
"There are five ways of lying down: knowing how to lie down, knowing how to offer [food], knowing how to refuse food, knowing various kinds of food, and violating one's dignified deportment.
The Buddha said to Upāli:

"If a bhikṣu is performing the ritual rinsing of the mouth and a donor offers him the five kinds of food, the bhikṣu should eat and consume them; he should perform the rite of receiving leftover food (vighasa-kalpa), and he should not stand, sit, or lie down while doing so."
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, one should know that this violates the rules of dignified deportment; the *khalupaścādbhakti* (residual food) rule should not be accepted.
If it is accepted, it is not considered a valid acceptance.
If one uses this [invalid] acceptance of residual food to chew or eat, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all cases.

If a bhikṣu has finished rinsing his mouth and a donor offers him the five kinds of food, the bhikṣu should eat and consume it; he should perform the ritual for accepting leftover food (vighasa-kalpa), and he should not stand, sit, or lie down while doing so.

Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, one should know that this violates the rules of decorum (*airyāpathika*) and the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rule regarding leftover food) should not be accepted.
If it is accepted, it is not considered a valid acceptance.
If one uses this [invalid] acceptance of leftover food to chew or eat, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If, while that bhikṣu is receiving food, a donor offers the five kinds of food, the bhikṣu should eat and consume them; he should perform the ritual for accepting leftover food (vighāsa-dharmam), and he should not stand, sit, or lie down while doing so.
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, one should know that this violates the rules of decorum; the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the rule regarding leftover food) should not be accepted.
If it is accepted, it is not considered a valid acceptance.
If one uses this method of accepting leftover food to chew or eat, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu has finished eating his meal and a donor offers him the five kinds of food, the bhikṣu should eat and consume it; he should perform the ritual for receiving leftover food (vighasa-kalpa), and he should not stand, sit, or lie down while doing so.
Whether standing, sitting, or lying down, one should know that this violates the rules of decorum (īryāpatha) and the rule for accepting leftover food (vighasa-dharma) should not be observed.
If one does accept it, it is not considered a valid acceptance.
If one uses this method of accepting leftover food to chew or eat, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
"If he stands, it is the same whether he sits or lies down.
There is no offense if the bhikṣu says:
"Wait a moment."
If one says,
"The time is still early," or if one sips congee, or drinks, or first requests food, there is no offense.
The thirty-four matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were two bhikṣus at a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala; one of these bhikṣus had broken the precepts, was full of flaws and leaks, lacked a sense of shame and dread of blame, and did not guard the subtle rules of training.
The second bhikṣu maintains pure precepts and feels great dread even toward minor transgressions.
When this pure bhikṣu sees another commit an offense, he always says to him:
"You have now committed such and such an offense."
A precept-breaking bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"When shall I see this transgression committed so that I may expose it?

At one time, this precept-breaking bhikṣu sees a precept-observing bhikṣu who, having finished his meal and because there was no further invitation to eat, has risen from his seat. He then takes some *pūjānna* (soft food) and *khādaniya* (hard food), calls him over, and eats together with him.
The precept-observing bhikṣu did not recall or assign the food, and they ate it together.
The precept-breaking bhikṣu said: "Elder!..."
"You have committed a pāyattika offense.
He asked, "What kind of pāyattika?"
He replied, "You have already finished eating; you may eat this as an invitation for which there is no formal invitation.
The precept-observing bhikṣu said:
“You know that after I have eaten, there is no invitation for me to eat at will;
why then do you call me to eat? He replied, “Whenever you repeatedly pointed out my faults, I thought to myself:”
"When we see you committing an offense, we shall expel you immediately.
For this reason, seeing that you had finished eating without an invitation to eat more, we urged you to eat in order to trouble you.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured it for various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that another has finished eating and there is no further invitation, urge him to eat for the sake of causing him distress?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, [the monk] reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [what had occurred], he intentionally asked that bhikṣu: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that another has finished eating and there is no further invitation to eat at will, encourages them to eat for the sake of causing annoyance?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished eating and there is no further invitation to eat at will, encourages him to eat *pūrasānīya* or *khādaniya* food for the purpose of causing him distress, and if it is done for no other reason than this, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Knows" means: if a bhikṣu knows it himself, or knows it from another, or if that bhikṣu tells him himself.
"Eats" refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods), the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and the five types of similar foods.
"To urge one to eat" means to earnestly entreat them to eat.
"To annoy" means to bring forth their faults and transgressions with a mind of anger and resentment.
"Pāyattika" (an offense requiring expiation) means that it boils, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, seeing another bhikṣu who has finished eating and for whom there is no further invitation to eat, instructs him to consume root food, stalk-food, leaf-food, ground-food, or fruit-food;
or if he instructs him to eat the five kinds of *pūjāni*—cooked rice, flour, parched grain, fish, or meat;
or if he instructs him to eat the five kinds of similar foods—gruel, millet, coarse barley, wild grass seeds, *kaśa*, or wheat-flour porridge—in all such cases, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to eat at an improper time, and that person eats, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to consume food at an improper time, and that person consumes it, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to steal or seize the property of others, both are guilty of an offense corresponding to the value of the object.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to take a human life, both are guilty of a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to kill grass or trees, and they do so, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to drag someone out of a room, and they do so, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to forcibly spread bedding, or if he spreads it himself, both incur a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to use water containing insects to sprinkle grass or mud, or if he uses it himself, both incur a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to take and drink water containing living organisms, and they do so, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to give food or drink to naked ascetics, whether male or female, and he does so, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to kindle a fire on bare ground, and he does so, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to take gold or silver with his own hand, and he takes it, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to take the life of an animal, and it is taken, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to hide the robes and bowl of this bhikṣu, and they are hidden, both are guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to dig the earth with his own hands, and if he digs it, both are guilty of a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to eat leftover food from the previous night, and if he eats it, both are guilty of a *pāyattika* offense. It is said:
"When a great bhikṣu eats food that has been stored overnight without having received it with his own hand, it is called 'storing within' (*antar-upanidhi*)."
To eat this food constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has received it with one's own hand and kept it overnight, it is called "leftover overnight food.
To eat such food constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The thirty-five matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru’s various ministers and generals placed their faith in Devadatta; these people assisted the bhikṣu Devadatta by providing him with offerings of morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambula*.

To those young bhikṣus who had been ordained for not long, Devadatta used his alms-bowl hook, large bowl, large jar, small jar, robe hook, meditation weight, cord belt, spoon and chopsticks, bowl rest, fan and parasol, and leather sandals—indeed, all such items required by a bhikṣu—to entice and seduce them.

Devadatta himself, surrounded by a respectful retinue of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred bhikṣus, entered the city of Rājagṛha to receive special offerings, including *tambula* before and after meals.

There were certain senior elder bhikṣus who had attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma and long cultivated the holy life; these bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms, sometimes obtaining stale, cold rice, or sometimes obtaining nothing at all;
or they obtained foul-smelling flour, or sometimes obtaining nothing at all.
Such coarse food may be eaten either to satiety or not.
Among them, there was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked them:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, while surrounded by respect by a hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred bhikṣus, he separately accepts offerings of morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambula*?"

There are certain senior elder bhikṣus who have tasted the flavor of the Buddha-dharma and long cultivated the holy life; yet when these bhikṣus enter the city to beg for alms, they may receive stale cold rice or receive nothing at all, or they may receive foul-smelling parched grain or receive nothing at all.
Is it that such coarse food satisfies them or not?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"How can one who is called a bhikṣu, while surrounded by a respectful retinue of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred bhikṣus, separately accept offerings of morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambula*?"

The elder bhikṣus who are senior elders have attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma and have long cultivated the holy life. When these bhikṣus enter the city to beg for food, they may receive stale, cold rice or receive nothing at all; they may receive foul-smelling parched grain or receive nothing at all.
Is it that with such coarse food they are either satiated or not?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, for the sake of two benefits, I prohibit eating in a separate group and permit three people to eat together."

The first benefit is that, out of compassion, one protects the donors; the second benefit is that one overcomes the power and influence of monks who harbor evil desires, so that those with evil desires do not form separate groups or perform separate legal acts to contend with the Sangha.
For ten reasons, he established the precept for bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika offense."
"Eating apart from the assembly" means eating in one place with as few as four bhikṣus.
"Pāyattika" means it is cooked, burned, covered, and obstructed; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if four bhikṣus eat separately from the assembly, it is a pāyattika.
If three bhikṣus eat separately together in one place, and a fourth person takes a portion of the food, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, several sick bhikṣus were suffering from exhaustion and emaciation due to the hardships of seeking alms.
A lay devotee in the city saw them and asked:
"Are you suffering? They replied,
"We are suffering."
"For what reason? They replied, "We have illnesses;
we suffer because of our practice of begging for alms."
The laypeople said, "You who are ill, we now invite you; let all those who are sick come to our house for a meal.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted eating apart from the community for reasons of illness.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit sick bhikṣus to eat separately from the assembly."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika offense, except in cases of special circumstances.
Special circumstances refer to times of illness."
"Regarding 'the sick': if a bhikṣu suffers from an excess of wind, cold, or heat, this is called being sick.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not sick eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika."
There is no offense for one who is ill.

When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, it came time for the monks to make their robes. Those monks rose early in the morning to seek the materials for dyeing—firewood and grass for boiling the dye—and they strained the liquid, set it out to cool, and took out the dyed robes. As the time for the midday meal drew near, they were unable to go out for alms, and because of this, they suffered distress.
In the city there was a householder who, having seen them, asked:
"Are you suffering? They replied:
“It is distressing. “For what reason?

“The time has come for us to make our robes; we must rise early to seek the materials for dyeing, burn wood and grass to boil the dye, strain it out, let it cool, and then take out the dyed robes. Because of this, the time for the midday meal draws near and we are unable to obtain almsfood. It is for this reason that we are distressed.”
The laypeople said, "We now invite you;
let those who are making robes come to our house for a meal.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat separately from the community for the sake of making robes.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of monks. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the monks:
"From now on, I allow monks, when they are engaged in making robes, to go among those making robes and eat separately from the group."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of special circumstances.
Special circumstances are: when one is ill, or when one is making robes."
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu eats separately from the community when the time for making robes has not yet arrived, it is a pāyattika.
If he eats separately from the community when the time for making robes has arrived, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a group of bhikṣus were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī.
The terrain of that country was flat and its villages were far apart; thus, they appeared near when viewed from a distance.

The bhikṣus intended to go for alms from the village ahead, but by the time they reached the village, midday had already arrived; as they were about to beg for food, the day had already passed, and because the bhikṣus had missed their meal, they suffered from distress.
The laypeople of that village, having seen them, asked the bhikṣus,
"Are you suffering? They replied:
“I am distressed.
“By what cause? “I was traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī;
seeing a village in the distance, I thought it was near and intended to go there for alms, but by that time the day had already passed midday. Because I did not obtain food, I am distressed.”
The laypeople said:
"We now invite you all; those who wish to go may come to our home for a meal.
The bhikṣus said:
"Because the Buddha has not yet permitted it for specific reasons,
we eat separately from the assembly. The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit bhikṣus who are traveling to eat separately from the assembly."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of special circumstances.
Special circumstances are: when one is ill, when making robes, and when traveling."
Regarding "walking": it refers to traveling back and forth within a distance of up to half a yojana.
As for the offense therein: if a bhikṣu arrives yesterday and eats today, it is a pāyattika.
If one travels tomorrow but eats today, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one travels that very day for at least half a *yojana*, whether going or returning, or if one eats separately from the community, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, several bhikṣus were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī by boat.
As the boat drew near a village, the bhikṣus spoke to the boatman, saying:
“I shall turn the boat toward the shore, for I wish to beg for food.
He immediately turned the boat toward the shore. The bhikṣus disembarked from the boat and entered the village;

having sought alms from house to house, they left the village to eat. After eating, they washed their hands, rinsed their mouths, and cleaned their bowls. They rolled up their robes and placed them in bags. In this manner, by the time they had finished, the boat had already traveled a great distance away.

The bhikṣus immediately followed along the footpath to pursue the boat, but they encountered the dangers of lions, tigers, and wolves, as well as the dangers of bears and brown bears; thus they departed by a non-path filled with thorns, bamboo splinters, and blades of cut grass, and as they ran after the boat, their feet suffered pain and distress.
On the bank, a layperson saw this and asked the bhikṣu,
"Are you suffering? He replied:
“It is distressing. “For what reason?
“We were previously carrying a ship toward Śrāvastī.”
When the boat drew near the village, we said to the boatman, "Turn the boat toward the shore; we wish to beg for food.
Immediately, it headed for the shore.

We departed from the ship and entered the village; having sought food from house to house, we left the village to eat. After eating, we washed our hands, rinsed our mouths, and cleansed our bowls; then we rolled up our robes and placed them in our bags.
At that time, as the ship had already traveled far away, he followed it along the path, encountering the dangers of lions, the dangers of tigers and wolves, and the dangers of bears and brown bears.
Had he followed a non-path, there would have been thorns, bamboo splinters, and blades of cut grass; running after the ship’s wake, he would have suffered great pain and distress.
The laypeople said, "We now invite you;
let the boatmen come to our house for a meal.
The bhikṣus said:
"Because the Buddha has not yet permitted traveling by boat, we have eaten separately from the community.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit bhikṣus traveling by boat to eat separately from the assembly."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika, except in cases of special circumstances.
Special circumstances are: when one is ill, when making robes, when traveling on a journey, and when traveling by boat."

Regarding the boat traveler: if they travel back and forth within a distance of at most half a yojana, one who violates this rule—such as a bhikṣu who arrives yesterday and eats today—is guilty of a pāyattika offense.
If one travels tomorrow but eats today, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one travels on that very day for at least half a *yojana*, whether going or returning, and eats separately from the community, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a great assembly had gathered within Rājagṛha; the Buddha was there together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Among them, the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for food, but the lay devotees were only able to provide food for two or three bhikṣus and could not provide for any more.
He then closed the door and said, "It is so abundant; who could possibly give it all?
Because he did not obtain alms, the bhikṣu who came later was distressed.
A householder, having seen them, asked the bhikṣus:
"Are you suffering? They replied:
"It is distressing. "For what reason?
the bhikṣus replied.
"Because there is a great assembly gathered in this city of Rājagṛha, only two or three bhikṣus who go for alms early are able to obtain anything.
The laypeople then close their doors and say:
'This is far too many; who could possibly give to you?'"
"We came later and were unable to obtain alms; for this reason, we are distressed.
The householders said, "We now invite you all:
whenever there is an occasion for a large assembly to gather, please come to our home for a meal."
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat in separate groups on account of the causes and conditions for the assembly of the great multitude.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.

On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow the bhikṣus to eat separately from the assembly when there is a specific reason for a large gathering."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika, except for special circumstances.
The special circumstances are: when one is ill, when making robes, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, and when a great assembly has gathered."
Regarding the assembly of the great multitude: it is at least eight people, consisting of four resident bhikṣus and four visiting bhikṣus gathered together.
For this reason, the lay devotees in the village are unable to provide food and drink for the bhikṣus.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu eats separately from the assembly when fewer than eight persons are gathered, it is a pāyattika.
If eight persons or more are gathered, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra’s maternal uncle had gone forth among the Ājīvika non-Buddhists. This uncle thought to himself:
"My nephew, King Bimbisāra, holds the Buddha and his disciples in deep veneration."
"For the sake of this king, I shall invite the Buddha and his disciples for a single meal.
Thereupon, the non-Buddhist entered the city of Rājagṛha and sought rice, flour, sesame, and small beans.
The laypeople asked,
"What do you wish to do? He replied:
"My nephew deeply reveres the Buddha; wishing to bring him joy, I desire to invite the Buddha and his disciples for a single meal.
Because these householders had faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, they gave him much rice and flour.
Having obtained it, he went out of the city and saw a bhikṣu, to whom he immediately said:
"Could you please invite the Buddha and that many disciples for me to a meal at my house tomorrow?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept separate meals for the saṃgha. They said:
"You are all renunciants; why do you not allow it? What is so improper?
I have no particular respect for you, but because my nephew respects the Buddha, I wish to bring him joy and have prepared this food for you."
At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioners thought to themselves:
"We shall prepare food and drink; if the Buddha and his disciples come, we will give it to them, but if they do not come, we shall use it to make wine for ourselves to drink."
"What should this bhikṣu do? Being thus uncertain, he reported the matter to the Buddha.

On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit monks to eat separately from the community for specific reasons.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika offense, except in cases of specific reasons.'"

"Regarding the 'circumstances': these are the time of illness, the time of making robes, the time of traveling on a road, the time of traveling by boat, the time of a great assembly gathering, and the time of being invited by śramaṇas.

As for "śramaṇas," this refers to the old disciples of the Ājīvikas and Nirgranthas; briefly stated, with the exception of the fivefold assembly of the Buddha, all other renunciants are called śramaṇas.
Regarding the offense herein: if a śramaṇa invites a bhikṣu, and a layperson holds food in their hand to give it to him, the bhikṣu incurs no offense by accepting the invitation;
however, if he eats it, it is a pāyattika.
If a layperson invites a bhikṣu and hands food to him with their own hands, because that bhikṣu has accepted the invitation, it is a duṣkṛta offense;
however, there is no offense for the one who eats it.
If a layperson invites a bhikṣu and holds food in their own hand to give it to him,
by accepting the invitation, there is a duṣkṛta offense;
if he eats it, there is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense if a śramaṇa invites another śramaṇa, or if one gives food with their own hand, or if one accepts an invitation, or if one eats; there is no offense.
Section thirty-six concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, when the season had arrived, various lay devotees prepared many kinds of excellent food and drink and went out from the city into the grove.
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus said to one another,
"We should go together to that grove to look around."
They all said, "So be it.
They immediately bathed themselves, adorned their faces, applied fragrant oil to their hair, put on fresh clean garments, and went to a certain spot within the grove to stand and watch.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus were handsome and attractive, and many people loved and respected them.
When the laypeople saw them, they said to one another, "Look at these young renunciants; they are so handsome and attractive."
They all replied,
"It is indeed so.
Because the lay devotees were filled with joy, they brought various kinds of fine wine and food and said to them:
"Can you eat it? He replied,
"If you yourselves can do so, why should I not be able?"

After the seventeen groups of bhikṣus had obtained much food and drink, they became intoxicated, disordered, and bewildered; following their meal, they shook their heads and flailed their arms as they headed toward the Jetavana, saying:
"Today we have experienced supreme joy; possessing merit, we are free from decay and affliction."
At that time, while the bhikṣus were walking in meditation upon the open ground between the gates of the Jetavana, they heard this sound.
The bhikṣus asked, "For what reason do you now say:
'Today we are exceedingly happy; we possess merit and are free from decline or affliction'?"
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus recounted the aforementioned matter in detail.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; upon hearing this, he was displeased and censured them with various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu consume food at an improper time?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though already aware of it, asked the seventeen groups of bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha, having rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus through various causes and conditions, said:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu eat and drink at an improper time?
Having rebuked them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"Improper time" (*akāla*) refers to the period from after midday until the ground has dried; this interval is called improper time.
"Chewing" (*khādya*) refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods).
"Eating" (*bhojana*) refers to the five *pūjaniya* (soft foods) or the five types of similar foods.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu eats root-food at an improper time, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats the stalks, leaves, flour, or fruit, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu eats rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, or meat at an improper time, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu eats five kinds of "resembling food" at an improper time—
namely, gruel, millet, coarse wheat, wild grass seeds, and *kāśa*— it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time while perceiving it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats during the improper time while perceiving it as the proper time, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats during the improper time while doubting whether it is so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats during the proper time while perceiving it as the improper time, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one eats during the improper time while harboring doubt about it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one eats during the proper time while perceiving it as such, there is no offense.
The thirty-seventh [case] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Uttara who practiced the rule of alms-gathering.
Each day he begged for two portions of food:

one portion he ate immediately, and the other he took back to his own quarters, placed upon a stone to dry, and the following day washed his hands and received it from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) to eat.
At that time, the Buddha was walking together with Ānanda through the quarters of the bhikṣus when they arrived at the cell of the bhikṣu Uttara. There he saw rice being dried upon a stone.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Whose rice is this being dried on the stone?"
Ānanda replied:
"World-Honored One!
There is a bhikṣu in this room named Uttara, who observes the practice of begging for food."
He requested two portions of food:

one portion he ate immediately, and the other he took and placed upon a stone to dry. On the following day, having washed his hands, he received it from a *karmadāna* (attendant) and ate it; for this reason, the rice was dried.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Do the bhikṣus eat food that was left over from the previous night?
He replied:
"I truly ate it.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, addressed the bhikṣu Upaśānta: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I indeed did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu eat leftover food kept overnight?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats *khaḍaniya* or *bhojaniya* food that has been kept overnight, it is a *pāyattika* offense.'"
Regarding "storing leftover food": if a *bhikṣu* takes food received by hand on this day and stores it until the following day, it is called storing leftover food.
"Food" refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods), the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and the five types of similar foods.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is like boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu eats stored roots, it is a pāyattika.
If he eats stalks, leaves, tubers, or fruits, it is likewise a pāyattika in all cases.
If one eats stale rice, parched flour, roasted grain, fish, or meat that has been kept overnight, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
If one eats stale gruel, millet, coarse wheat, weeds, or *kāśī* rice that has been kept overnight, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.

If a tree grows in pure ground but its branches hang over impure ground, and its fruit falls onto impure ground, should a bhikṣu stay overnight within [the boundary] and eat this fruit, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If a tree grows in impure ground but hangs over pure ground, and its fruit falls onto pure ground, if a bhikṣu picks up that fruit with grass, bamboo leaves, or a tile, and eats it after having kept it overnight until the next day, it is a pāyattika offense.

If a monk takes fruit from a tree growing on pure or impure ground—whether the fruit has fallen onto bamboo, onto a *vetra* branch, or onto a *māluta* branch—and eats it after having kept it overnight, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; the rule regarding pure ground was already relinquished during the time of the Buddha.
The thirty-eighth [case] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāla observed the practice of accepting all kinds of discarded items (*pāṃśukūla*).
This man carried a discarded *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, an *antarvāsaka*, a discarded alms bowl, a discarded staff, discarded leather sandals, and discarded food.
What is the practice of wearing a *pāṃsukūla-saṃghāṭī*?

If there is a piece of worn-out clothing found in an alleyway, at a place where the dead are disposed of, or among refuse, one takes it and washes and cleans it thoroughly in water; having made it into a *saṃghāṭī*, the same applies to an *uttarāsaṅga* and an *antarvāsaka*.

Regarding the "refuse-bowl" (pāṃśukūla-pātra): if there are discarded, worn-out vessels found in an alleyway, at a place where the dead are disposed of, or among refuse heaps, one may take them, wash and clean them with water, and then use them.

Regarding the "rag-robe staff": if one finds a discarded staff in an alleyway, at a place where the dead are disposed of, or amidst refuse, one may take it, wash it thoroughly with water, and keep it for use.

Regarding "rag-leather sandals": if one finds discarded leather sandals in an alleyway, at a place where the dead are disposed of, or amidst refuse, one may take them, wash them clean with water, repair them by sewing, and keep them for use.

Regarding "scavenger-food" (*pāṃsukūlabhaktika*): if one takes by hand radish leaves, coriander leaves, basil leaves, or foul-smelling parched grain discarded in an alleyway, a cemetery, or among refuse, and having washed and cleaned them thoroughly at a body of water, then eats them—this is called scavenger-food.
This elder has adopted the practice of dwelling in places where the dead reside and delights in dwelling in such places.
When there is an epidemic and deaths occur within the country, he does not enter the city to seek food, but instead eats only the food and drink discarded by the dead.
When there is no epidemic or death, he enters the city to seek food.
This bhikṣu’s body is stout, with abundant fat, blood, and flesh; he is robust and possesses great strength.
Once, as this bhikṣu entered the city to seek alms, a gatekeeper saw him and thought to himself:

"When there is an epidemic and people die, this bhikṣu does not come into the city to seek alms; yet when there is no epidemic, he comes into the city. This bhikṣu’s body is fat, with much adipose tissue, blood, and flesh, and he is strong and powerful; this man must surely eat human flesh."
One person told it to two, and two told it to three; in this manner, the foul reputation spread by word of mouth until it filled the city of Śrāvastī, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat human flesh."
Among them, there was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked him with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if he does not receive food and drink from another and place it in his own mouth?"
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet lay down a formal precept.
This Venerable Mahākāla had attained mundane meditative concentration and practiced the method of dwelling among the dead, taking pleasure in residing among the dead.
At that time, there was a householder in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who was escorting a deceased relative to the charnel ground.
When the other householders saw this bhikṣu, they said:
"This is a man-eating bhikṣu; today we are escorting this dead person, and once our relative has departed, he will surely be devoured by the bhikṣu."
After they had discarded the corpse, the laypeople stood watching from a concealed spot.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Let no crows or birds come to defile whatever leafy vegetables and parched grain are here."
He immediately rose and went to guard it.
The householders said,
"This bhikṣu has already risen, departed, approached, taken, and eaten."
The laypeople became convinced that "the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat human flesh.
One person told two, and two told three; in this way, the foul reputation spread by word of mouth until it filled the entire city of Śrāvastī.
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, truly eat human flesh.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu place food in his mouth without having first received it?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu places food in his mouth that he has not received, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Not receiving food" means not receiving it from a man, a woman, a eunuch, or a person with dual sexual organs.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu receives food or drink and places it in his mouth, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every morsel that enters the mouth while one is eating, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard the Buddha establish this precept, they desired water and tooth-sticks for rinsing their mouths; however, because they had to request them from lay attendants (*kappiyakāraka*), they could not obtain them at the proper time and suffered great hardship.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. He praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts; having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu places food in his mouth that has not been formally received, it is a pāyattika, except for water and tooth-sticks.'"
Regarding the offenses within this [category], there are five types:
if it is at an improper time, if it is not given, if it is not accepted, if it has not been purified, or if it is impure.
As for "at an improper time": from after midday until the ground has not yet cooled, this is called "at an improper time."
"Not given" means that it is not given by a man, a woman, a *paṇḍaka*, or a person with dual sexual organs; this is called "not given.
"Not received" means that it is not received from another—whether from a man, a woman, a *paṇḍaka*, or a person with dual sexual organs—and for this reason it is called "not received."
"Not purified" means not having performed purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by fingernail, or purification by a parrot's beak; this is called "not purified.
"Impure" refers to food and drink that is impure, or that which has been mixed with impure food.
If a bhikṣu eats this food at an improper time, without it being given, without having received it, without it being purified, or when it is not pure, he incurs five kinds of offenses.
If he eats this food at the proper time, without it being given, without having received it, without it being purified, or when it is not pure, he incurs four offenses.
If at the time [of giving], it is given, not received, not made pure (*apariśuddha*), and impure, one who eats this food incurs three offenses.
If at the time [of giving], it is given, received, not made pure, and impure, one who eats this food incurs two offenses.
If at the time of giving, receiving, and performing the ritual purification (pariṇāmanā), it is impure, one who eats this food incurs one offense.
If at the time of giving, receiving, and performing the ritual purification, it is pure, one who eats this food does not commit an offense.
Among impure foods, eating leftover food that has been kept overnight constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Eating human flesh, which is impure, constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a *bhikṣu* touches impure food with his hand and then eats it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Thirty-nine [sections] complete. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him; having thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, exhortation, benefit, and gladdening through various causes and conditions, Mahānāma rose from his seat, joined his palms, and said to the Buddha:
“I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will accept my invitation for tomorrow.”
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he spent the entire night preparing various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink, as well as boiling medicinal herbs with milk.
Having prepared everything, he rose early in the morning, spread out the seats, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time.
The Buddha and the assembly of monks went into his house and sat down upon the seats.
When Mahānāma saw that the Buddha was seated, he personally served water and personally offered him fragrant rice, medicinal milk, and curds.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus poured medicinal milk over the fragrant rice, filling their bowls to the brim and placing them before the Buddha, hoping to receive more.
Mahānāma had this thought:
"Who eats and who does not eat?
Who eats little and who does not?"
Having had this thought, he looked and saw the group of six bhikṣus with their bowls filled to the brim with medicinal milk-juice; they poured it over the rice before them and would not eat.
He asked, "For what reason do you not eat?"
He replied,
"Is there anyone who has given birth to a child? Mahānāman said:
"These medicinal herbs and milk are fragrant and delicious; let us eat them together. Those who have produced milk should give it to one another.
He asked again, "Is there any curd?"
“Is there clarified butter, fresh butter, oil, fish, or dried meat?

He replied, “These are milk products, fragrant and excellent, boiled with medicinal herbs and fit for consumption; if there is curd, clarified butter, fresh butter, oil, fish, or dried meat, I shall give them to you.”
The group of six bhikṣus became angry and said to Mahānāman:
"You have deceived the Buddha and defrauded both the Buddha and the Saṃgha! Since you were unable to provide fine food and drink, why did you invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha?"
"If others invite us, we may give them as much delicious food and drink as they desire; where would we not obtain such matured milk?
This Mahānāma was virtuous by nature, neither angry nor startled, while those who subsist on human flesh were jealous and full of ill-will:
"The Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, say of themselves:"
"Excellent and virtuous!
Thus did Śākya Mahānāma deeply revere the Buddha and the Saṃgha; how could he revile them in their very presence?
When the Buddha saw that the bhikṣus had committed such an evil deed as to be censured by the laypeople, he remained silent upon seeing this.
At that time, Mahānāman provided the community of monks with abundant and delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied.
Seeing that the bowls had been set aside, he personally served water, took a small seat, and sat before the Buddha, desiring to hear the Dharma.

The Buddha taught the Dharma through various causes and conditions, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened them, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, after the meal, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu revile Mahānāma—who deeply reveres the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—with coarse language in their very presence?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”

If a bhikṣu who is not ill, for his own sake, requests such fine foods as milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, fish, or dried meat from a household of laypeople, it is a pāyattika offense.
"House" refers to the residences of laypeople.
"Delicious food and drink" refers to milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, fish, and dried meat.
Regarding the sick person: when wind, cold, or heat flare up, if they consume this food, their illness is cured; setting aside these causal conditions, it is called "not being ill."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill seeks milk for himself and obtains it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one who is not ill requests for oneself curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, fish, or dried meat, it is a *pāyattika* offense if they obtain them;
if they do not obtain them, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one who is not ill seeks out rice, soup, or vegetables for oneself, if they obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if they do not obtain them, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
If one seeks curd-juice, curd-drink, or curd-sediment for oneself, if they obtain them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To fail to do so is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if one is ill, if it is a relative, if one was previously invited, or if the person gave it of their own accord without being asked.
The forty [rules] are concluded; the second recitation is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Ten;
*Triṃśadbhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Fourteen; Part One of the Third Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
Recitation Three, Five: The Sixth of the Ninety *Pāyattika* Offenses.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Elder Channa used water containing living organisms. The monks said to Channa:
"Do not use water containing living beings; many insects will die.
Channa replied, "I use the water, but I do not use the insects."
The bhikṣus asked,
"Do you know that there are insects in the water?
He replied:
“I know. “If you know it, why do you use it?
He replied:
"I myself use water that is free of insects.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and rebuked him with various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu lack a heart of compassion for sentient beings?"
After rebuking him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Channa intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked Channa with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu knowingly take and use water that contains living beings, yet harbor no heart of compassion for those sentient beings?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu knows that water contains insects and uses it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
"Knows" means either knowing by himself or hearing it from another.
"Insects" refers to those seen with the eye or caught in a water-strainer.
*Pāyattika* means that which burns, consumes, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu knows that water contains insects and uses it, for every insect that dies, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each one.
If a bhikṣu uses water containing living organisms to boil rice, soup, gruel, or dye for cloth, for every single organism that dies as a result, he commits one *pāyattika* offense.
If he uses water containing living organisms to wash his hands, feet, mouth, face, or body, for every single organism that dies as a result, he commits one *pāyattika* offense.
If one uses water containing insects with the perception that it contains insects, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses water containing insects with the perception that it contains no insects, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses water containing insects while doubting whether it contains them, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses water that is free of insects with the thought that it contains insects, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one uses water that is free of insects while suspecting that it contains insects, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one uses water that is free of insects with the thought that it is free of insects, there is no offense.
The forty-first section concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda frequently went to and from a certain family.
Once, before midday, Upananda dressed, took his bowl, and went to that family; having sat down, he exchanged greetings with them, asking whether they were well or not.
Not long after this layman had taken a wife, he wished to touch her with his hand, but the wife said:
"Do not do so! A bhikṣu is here."
The householder thought to himself,
"If I remain here, the bhikṣu will never leave.
He said to his wife:
"Give food to the bhikṣus.
He replied, "Yes."
The householder then went out, and his wife said to the bhikṣu,
"Please accept this rice gruel.
Bāḍhananda replied:
"It is early; stay a while, for when the time comes, you shall receive [alms].
The householder thought the bhikṣu had already departed, so he entered with the intention of approaching his wife.
Seeing that the bhikṣu was still there, the householder had this thought:
"If I am here, the bhikṣu will not leave.
He said to his wife,
"Give food to the bhikṣu."
He replied, “Yes.
The householder then went out, and his wife again brought him rice and parched grain; she spoke to the bhikṣu, who accepted them.
Bhadanta said, "Wait a moment;
it is still early. When the time arrives, you shall receive [the meal].
The householder thought again:
“The bhikṣu must have left.
Having entered, he saw that he was indeed gone, and immediately spoke these words of anger:
“What use is this bhikṣu?”
"I do not have the autonomy to do as I wish within my own home.
Having thus distressed the householder, Upananda departed.
After his meal, he went to the bhikṣus and said:
"I intentionally troubled this householder today.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires, contented, and practicing the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and censured him with various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu sit forcibly in a house where food is being prepared?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he said to Upananda: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who sits forcefully in the home of a person providing food?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu sits down forcefully in a house where food is being served, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Regarding 'having food': for women, it refers to the food of men. Regarding 'house':
it refers to the dwellings of laypeople.
Regarding 'pāyattika': it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path."
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu sits forcefully in a household where food is being served, it is a pāyattika.
If he rises and then sits back down, he incurs as many pāyattikas as there were instances of sitting.

There is no offense if it is the home of those who have severed lustful desires, or the home of those observing the fast, or if there is another person of greater respect present in the seat, or if it is a house where many people come and go; in these cases, there is no offense.
The forty-second [case] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Śākya son Upananda frequently visited a certain family. Before midday, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to their house; having closed the door, he sat alone with a young woman of the household in close proximity within the room.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms; rising early, he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Arriving in succession before the gate of this house, he stood there and snapped his fingers.
At that moment, the Śākya son Upananda saw the bhikṣu seeking alms, but the bhikṣu did not see Upananda.
Bhadanta said to the householder’s wife,
“Give food to this bhikṣu.
The woman thought to herself:
