"This must be someone known to Upananda.
She immediately took his bowl, filled it with steamed rice, and poured fine soup over it.
Once the bhikṣu seeking alms had received it and departed, the woman returned inside.
Bhadanta asked,
"Are you giving food to the bhikṣus?
He replied:
"It has already been given," said Upananda.
"Excellent!"
"This is like a true bhikṣu.
After his meal, Bhaṇḍana returned to the Jetavana and saw a bhikṣu who had gone for alms;
he thought to himself, "Let me not labor in vain to bestow my favor upon him."
He said to that bhikṣu,
"Did you go to such-and-such a house today to beg for alms?
He replied:
"Have you arrived?
"Did you obtain good food?
He replied:
“Yes, I have. “Do you know?
I have instructed you.”
The bhikṣu asked,
"Where were you at that time?
He replied:
“[He] begged for alms inside a house.

The bhikṣus reported this matter to the other bhikṣus. Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased and rebuked him in various ways:
“How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu sit forcibly alone with a woman inside a house where food is being served?”
After rebuking him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] already, he nevertheless asked Upananda:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu sit alone with a woman inside a house while there are others present at a meal?"
Having thus rebuked him, the Buddha explained the causal conditions of his past life to the bhikṣus, saying:
"In a past age, there was a dog that left its own home to go to another's house for alms. When it entered the other's house, its body was inside the gate while its tail remained outside."
At that time, the host, a layman, beat him and gave him no food.
The dog went before the officials and said:
"This layman came to my home to beg for food; instead of giving me food, he beat me. I have not broken the laws of dogs."
The officials asked,
"What dharma does the dog possess?
He replied:
"I sit and lie down as I please in my own home; when I go to another's home, my body enters within the doorway while my tail remains outside.
The officials said, "Summon the householder."
At that time, he immediately brought him forward and asked,
"Did you truly beat this dog and refuse it food?
He replied:
"It is indeed so," the officials said.
"A causal condition such as this has never occurred since time immemorial."
He then asked the dog,
"How should this man be punished?
The dog replied:
"Grant him the rank of a great householder within this city of Śrāvastī.
"For what reason? He replied:
"In the past, I was a great householder in this city of Śrāvastī; because I committed evil with my body and speech, I received the body of this wretched dog.

This person’s evil is even greater than mine. If this person were endowed with power and influence, he would commit the utmost evil, causing him to enter hell and undergo extreme suffering. What further punishment could be more severe than this?"
The Buddha said,
"If even animals know that there are limits to the laws of entering another's home, how much more so should humans not be ignorant of the Dharma?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, while in a house where food is being served, sits down forcibly alone with a woman inside a room, it is a pāyattika.'"
"A family where food is being eaten" refers to a place where women are called "men-eaters.
"Alone" means a single bhikṣu and a single woman, with no third person present.
"Sitting in a secluded place" means sitting in a deep, hidden spot that is out of sight of the bhikṣu who went for alms.
*Pāyattika* means "to boil, burn, and obstruct"; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, in a household where food is being prepared, sits alone with a single woman, three conditions are met, constituting one *pāyattika*:
first, it is a household where food is being prepared; second, he is alone with a single woman; third, they sit in a secluded place.
If one rises from one's seat and sits down again, three further offenses arise, each being a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of rising and sitting down again, one incurs that many *pāyattikas*.
If one faces toward a closed door and there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who performs the ritual of purification) outside, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one faces toward an open door and there is a *kappiya-kāraka* outside, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If the door is open and there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) inside, there is no offense.
[The forty-third case ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the kingdom of Virāṭa, there was a Brahmin king named Ajātaśatru. For a certain reason, he traveled toward Śrāvastī and stayed overnight at the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*). He asked that lay devotee:
"In this city of Śrāvastī, are there any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are teachers of great assemblies, revered by many people, and all of whom are called good men?"
"I shall go to visit and attend upon him from time to time, so that my mind may become pure and joyful.
The householder said, "There is!"
The śramaṇa Gautama emerged from among the Śākya clan; out of faith he left the household life, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"You should go to visit and attend upon him from time to time; it may cause your mind to become pure and joyful.
He asked, "Where is the śramaṇa Gautama now?"
"I shall go to see him.
He replied,
"The śramaṇa Gautama is at the Jeta Grove Monastery in the city of Śrāvastī."
Having heard this, he left the householder’s residence and proceeded to the Jetavana.

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings, preaching the Dharma. King Ajātaśatru saw the Buddha from afar in the grove—exceedingly handsome and distinguished, with his sense-faculties stilled and extinguished, and a body emitting immeasurable flames of light like a mass of pure gold. Arriving at the entrance of a small path, he dismounted from his carriage and advanced on foot. Having approached the Buddha and completed his greetings, he sat to one side.

When the Buddha saw that [Ajita] was seated, he taught the Dharma through various causes and conditions, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
Then, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma which instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, Ajita said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation to observe the summer rains retreat for one period in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"I must certainly accept this as the fruition of my deeds in previous lives."
Having formed this thought, he accepted the invitation in silence.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, the brahmin rose from his seat, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

When this Brahmin had finished all his business, he returned to his own home in the kingdom of Vairaṇyā and prepared many delicious foods and drinks for the Buddha and the Saṅgha during the four months of the summer retreat.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to the gatekeeper:
"I wish to remain in seclusion for the four months of summer to enjoy peace and happiness; no matters from outside, whether good or bad, shall be reported to me."
At that time, the gatekeeper received the command and acted accordingly.
Knowing that the time for the rainy season retreat had arrived, the Buddha, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"We shall now proceed to the kingdom of Veḷukaṇṭaka to observe the rains retreat."
The bhikṣus replied,
“We accept your instruction.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One entered that country together with five hundred bhikṣus.

The people of that country believed in heterodox teachings and previously had no monasteries. To the north of the city was a forest of *śāla* trees; the trees were lush and beautiful, and the ground was exceptionally level and vast. The Buddha and the great assembly stayed within this forest.
That town was narrow and its inhabitants few, and there was little faith; it was difficult to obtain alms.
When the night had passed, the Buddha assembled the Sangha, and having assembled them, he instructed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that this town is narrow and its inhabitants few, and there is little faith; it is difficult to obtain alms."
"If you wish to remain for this *varṣā* retreat, you may do so; otherwise, stay as you please.

At that time, Śāriputra went alone to Mount Anavatapta and accepted the invitation of Śacī, the consort of the heavenly king Śakra and daughter of the Asura, to observe the summer retreat for the four months, being provided with celestial food.
At that time, the Buddha was observing the rains retreat with five hundred bhikṣus minus one in the kingdom of Vairaṇyā.
The local householders and brahmins, possessing only slight faith, provided offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha for only five or six days before ceasing.
When the bhikṣus were going on their almsround, they found it extremely difficult to obtain food. The Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
There is a tree named Jambu; because of this tree, the land is called Jambudvīpa. I wish to fetch its fruit to give to the great assembly for them to eat."

Near the Jambu tree, there is a grove of harītakī trees and āmalaka fruits; in Uttarakuru, there is naturally grown non-glutinous rice; and in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is food called sudhā—all of which they wish to bring here to provide for the great assembly.
There is the taste of sweet earth; with one hand I shall lift up all sentient beings and with the other turn over the earth, so that the bhikṣus may take this earth-flavor and eat it.
I pray that you will all grant me your permission.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
“Although you possess great supernormal powers, the maturation of the retribution for the evil deeds of these bhikṣus cannot be shifted; none of them may be permitted [to leave].”
"This kingdom is cool and refreshing, with abundant water and lush grasses.
At that time, there were several horse-herders from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who followed the water and grass until they arrived in this country."
The horse-herders, whose faith in the Buddha was pure, saw that it was extremely difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain food while wandering for alms;
they said to the elders, "Is it not exceedingly arduous?"
He replied,
"It is extremely painful.
They all said:
"We know that it is extremely difficult for you to obtain food through begging; now that our provisions are exhausted, we have only horse-barley. Would you be able to eat it?
The bhikṣus replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat horse-barley."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“As for the horses and the horse-keepers: if the horse-keepers can nourish the horses with good fodder and brine so that they become fat, then this barley may be freely enjoyed.”
"There are five hundred horses, and there are five hundred bhikṣus minus one.
One horse consumes two *dōng* of barley; one *dōng* is given to a bhikṣu, and one *dōng* is given to a horse."
Among them was an excellent horse that ate four *dō* of barley; it gave two *dō* to the Buddha and kept two *dō* for itself.
Ānanda took his own portion of the Buddha’s barley and entered a village, approaching a woman to praise the Buddha’s merits:

“The Buddha possesses such mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; he has great kindness and great compassion, all-encompassing knowledge, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics. His body is of true golden color with a halo around his neck, and he has a Brahma-voice; one never tires of beholding him.”
"If he had not left the household life, he would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, and I and all of you would have been subject to him.

Now that he has left the household life and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he delivers those who have not yet been delivered, liberates those who have not yet been liberated, extinguishes those who have not yet been extinguished, and delivers those who have not yet been delivered from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; for these minor reasons, he remains here in summer retreat."
"You take this barley and prepare a meal for the Buddha.
The woman replied, "My household has many affairs; I am unable to do it."

At that time, there was a woman who, upon hearing of the Buddha’s merits, immediately conceived a heart of reverence, thinking, "Such a person as this has never before existed in the world. She said to Ānanda:
"I shall prepare food for him and for your own portion; furthermore, if there are other virtuous bhikṣus who observe the precepts and have the strength, I shall also provide for them."
The woman then prepared the rice and brought it to Ānanda.
Ānanda, with a heart of deep reverence for the Buddha, thought to himself:
"The Buddha is of royal lineage and is accustomed to refined delicacies; how can this coarse and poor food possibly benefit his body?"
Having formed this thought, he served water and presented the rice; seeing the Buddha eating it, he was choked with grief and his heart was overwhelmed.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, wished to console him and said:
"Can you eat this rice?"
He replied, "I can eat it.
Having accepted it, he ate it;
its flavor was extraordinary, for the devas had indeed infused it with taste. His joy was immeasurable, and his overwhelming grief was immediately dispelled.
When the Buddha had finished eating, Ānanda served water for him to rinse his hands, set aside his robes and bowl, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Just now, when I asked a certain woman to prepare the meal, she was unwilling; however, there was another woman nearby who did not ask for help but prepared it herself."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"One who did not prepare the meal would not have obtained what she ought to have obtained; had she prepared the meal, she would have become the foremost queen of a Wheel-Turning King."
"One who prepares rice for oneself gains immeasurable merit; if one does not perform other meritorious deeds, this virtue shall be so vast as to lead even to liberation.

At that time, because the World-Honored One’s past karmic traces had not yet been eliminated, there was no one at that moment who knew that the Buddha and the Saṃgha were eating horse-gram in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

At that time, the Māra-king transformed himself into various bhikṣus, carrying abundant food and drink toward various kingdoms; those who encountered them on the road asked, "From where have you come?"
He replied,
"I have come from the country of Vairañjā.
The lay devotees said:
"Does the Buddha dwell there, and is there any offering made to him?
He replied, "There is always a great assembly there with abundant food and delicacies; what I have brought here is the remains from that."

At that time, the World-Honored One had completed his prior practices, and it was heard throughout the sixteen great kingdoms that the World-Honored One, together with five hundred bhikṣus, was eating horse barley for three months in the kingdom of Vairaṇyā.

The nobles, elders, householders, and great wealthy merchants of various kingdoms, having prepared a multitude of offerings and various delicacies that filled carts and pack animals, came to welcome the World-Honored One as if a long-lost kinsman had arrived.
At that time, seven days remained before the *pravāraṇā*. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda, "How many days remain until the *pravāraṇā*?
Ānanda replied:
"There are seven days remaining.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go into the city and say to Ajātaśatru:..."
The Buddha said,
"I have completed my rains retreat in your kingdom and wish to travel through various countries. The bhikṣus said:
“World-Honored One!
What kindness or virtue has this brāhmaṇa toward the Buddha and the Saṃgha,
that he departs from us here at the conclusion of the rainy season retreat while we are so impoverished and exhausted?”
The Buddha said,
"Although this brahmin has offered no kindness or virtue, according to the dharma of host and guest, he should be granted leave.
Ānanda received these instructions and, accompanied by a bhikṣu, went to the gate and spoke to the gatekeeper:
"You may inform your king.
While Ānanda was outside, the gatekeeper thought to himself:
"Ānanda’s name is auspicious; hearing it at this clear dawn, if I do not inform the king, it will be an ill omen."
At that time, Ajātaśatru rose early, washed his head, and put on clean white robes, sitting alone in the central hall.
The gatekeeper announced, "Ānanda is outside.
According to the Brahmanic rules of physiognomy, a person named Ānanda is auspicious; thus, the king was pleased and immediately told him to come forward.
"Who is stopping you?
Ānanda immediately entered.
After exchanging greetings with those seated there, he was asked by them:
"Why have you come? He replied,
"The Buddha has sent me to speak to you:"
"I have stayed within your kingdom for the three months of summer; now that my *varṣā* retreat is completed, I shall travel to other countries.
Ajita was startled and said, "Ānanda!"
“Is the Śramaṇa Gautama currently residing for the summer retreat in the country of Vairaṭya?
Ānanda replied,
“Indeed he is.”
The brahmin asked:
"How will you be able to stay?
Who will provide for you?"
Ānanda replied, “We have been impoverished and exhausted;
the Buddha and the community of monks have eaten horse grain for three months.

At that time, Ajātaśatru first realized his error, remembering his previous invitation for the Buddha and the Saṃgha to reside for four months during the summer retreat, for which all provisions had already been prepared.
"How could it be that the Buddha and the Sangha must eat horse fodder for three months?
Such an evil reputation will spread throughout all lands, saying:
'Ajātaśatru has long been wicked and perverse; out of hatred and envy for the Buddha-dharma, he has caused the Buddha and the Sangha to undergo extreme suffering and hardship.'"
He then said to Ānanda:
"Can the śramaṇa Gautama be persuaded to repent and stay?
Ānanda replied:
"No," he replied.

At that moment, Ajātaśatru was filled with shame, grief, and distress; overcome by agitation, he fell prostrate on the ground. His kinsmen then sprinkled water on his face and helped him up, whereupon he regained consciousness.
The kinsmen said by way of analogy:
"Do not grieve; we shall offer our apologies to Gautama on your behalf for his forceful invitation to remain.
If he refuses to stay, we shall bring food and drink to escort him along the way, and should he be in need, we shall provide for his sustenance."
At that time, Ajātaśatru immediately went with his kinsmen to the Buddha’s dwelling to repent and request him to stay. The Buddha thought to himself:
"If I do not accept [his invitation], he will vomit hot blood and die."
Out of compassion, the Buddha accepted the invitation for seven days.
At that time, Ajātaśatru thought to himself:
"How can these provisions for four months be exhausted in only seven days?"

When the Buddha had finished his *pravāraṇā*, he wished to travel through the kingdom of Vaiśālī for two months. Hearing that the Buddha was coming, the people of Vaiśālī each prepared offerings, saying, "I shall provide them today, and you tomorrow," continuing in this manner in succession until the end of the two months.

After the Buddha had finished his *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he departed for Vaiśālī; Ajātaśatru brought various offerings and accompanied the Buddha on his journey, intending to provide them with sustenance should they become scarce.
Upon hearing this, the people of Vaiśālī made a collective agreement:
"If the Buddha comes, each person shall prepare on their own day small meals, midday meals, and post-midday refreshments and drinks, ensuring that nothing is lacking."
"Do not allow others to cause confusion among you.
Ajita, knowing where the Buddha was staying, went there first to prepare the offerings, saying:
"I shall provide the offering today; you may provide it tomorrow."
The people of Vaiśālī did not permit him to do so, and they said to Ajātaśatru:
"You have long been evil and heterodox; you are an enemy of the Buddha, and for that reason you harass both the Buddha and the Saṃgha."
Now, desiring to please others, you have made this statement:
"I shall provide offerings today, or perhaps tomorrow.
What business do you have that you would cause the Buddha and the Saṅgha to eat horse barley for three months, only now seeking the day to provide offerings?
Having heard these words, Ajātaśatru felt ashamed and sorrowful; standing to one side, he wondered what the Saṃgha lacked that was so small, thinking, "I shall provide it."
At that time, as there was no rice gruel, he prepared various kinds of gruel:

ghee-gruel, sesame-gruel, oil-gruel, milk-gruel, mung-bean gruel, mocha-bean gruel, hemp-seed gruel, and clear gruel. Having prepared them, he offered them to the Buddha, who said, "Give them to the community of monks."
The community of monks did not accept it,
saying, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat the eight kinds of gruel.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the eating of eight kinds of gruel.
There are five benefits of gruel for the body:
first, it removes hunger; second, it removes thirst; third, it relieves flatulence; fourth, it removes coldness below the navel; and fifth, it digests food remaining from the previous meal."
At that time, Ajātaśatru thought to himself:

"I have enjoyed myself in peace and comfort during the four months of the summer retreat; if I were to pursue the śramaṇa Gautama for another two months, my single pursuit would cause all state affairs to fall into neglect."

"These offerings are so numerous they cannot be exhausted; let us instead spread them upon the ground for the Buddha and the Sangha to tread upon with their feet, which shall constitute their acceptance and use.
He then addressed the Buddha, requesting that they be accepted and used at that time.
The Buddha told Ajātaśatru:
"It is not as you say; this is food that should be consumed directly from the mouth.
Wishing to dismiss Ajātaśatru, the Buddha spoke these verses of benediction:
"Among all celestial shrines, the worship of fire is supreme;
among the Brahmanical scriptures, the Sāvitrī is supreme;
among all human beings, the sovereign king is supreme."
Of all rivers and streams, the great ocean is the deepest;
Among all the constellations, the moon’s brightness is foremost;
Among all things that illuminate, the light of the sun is supreme.
"Among the devas and humans of the ten directions, the Buddha is the supreme field of merit.
At that time, having finished bestowing blessings upon Ajātaśatru, the Buddha traveled through the Vṛji country toward Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a naked ascetic who followed behind the Buddha; this ascetic’s body was stout and fleshy.
Another ascetic came toward them from the opposite direction and asked the naked ascetic, "What have you gained by practicing in this way?"
He replied,
“I have obtained such and such food.
He asked:
"By what causes and conditions was this obtained? He replied,
"It was obtained because of this shaven-headed householder."
He immediately reviled him, saying:
"You wretched sinner! Having obtained such food and drink through others, how can you utter evil and unwholesome words?
One who reviles others while enjoying whatever fine food they have obtained and dwelling in a place of security cannot be called a human being."
"If the śramaṇa Gautama hears these words, he will surely establish a precept, forbidding his disciples from eating with non-Buddhists.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"These non-Buddhists have long harbored wrong views; they are enemies and thieves of the Dharma, seeking out faults and transgressions."
"If others strike them with knives or clubs, or if they obtain poison, or if there is a killer, they will certainly say it was done by the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas.
At that time, the Buddha merely rebuked them but had not yet established a precept.

The Buddha traveled by stages until he arrived at Śrāvastī; at that time, because the people heard that the Buddha had eaten horse-grams for three months, their offerings remained abundant and did not cease.
There was a woman selling cakes who prepared food and drink for the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
At that time, Ānanda was in charge of the food service; it is the constant rule of all Buddhas not to rise from their seats until they have finished eating all the food.
Why is this? If food were insufficient, the Buddha’s power would make it sufficient.
At that time, while the Buddha was still seated and had not yet risen, two female ascetics from among the non-Buddhist sects came to Ānanda and begged for cakes.
Ānanda did not remember [the number], so the Buddha said,
"Give each person one cake.
At that time, because two cakes were stuck together, one person received one and another person received two.
Having gone a short distance after obtaining them, they asked one another,
"How many cakes did you obtain?
He replied:
“One. “How many more have you obtained?
He replied:
"I have received two.
At that time, the one who had received one said:
"Give me half of the cake; if you do not give it to me, I shall humiliate you."
He replied, "Each person receives according to their own merit; why should I give it to you?
A second time he spoke again:
"Give me half of your cake; if you do not give it to me, I shall humiliate you.
He replied, "Each person should keep what they have obtained; I will not give it to you."
One of them said:
"Ānanda must either be your husband or have had illicit relations with you.
If he is neither your husband nor has had illicit relations with you, then for every one given to you, one should be given to me; as for every two given to you, two should be given to me."
They immediately became angry with one another, pressing each other's heads down and shouting loudly.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are they shouting so loudly?"
He replied,
“A female heterodox practitioner.
[The other asked,] “Why did she cry out so loudly?”
Ānanda related this matter in detail to the Buddha.
Then, after the meal, on account of these circumstances as well as previous ones, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“You should know that these non-Buddhists have long harbored wrong views; they are enemies and thieves of the Dharma who seek out faults and transgressions.”
If they are struck by others with knives or clubs, or if they obtain poison, or if there is a murderer, they will certainly say, "This was done by the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu gives food or drink with his own hand to a naked ascetic or a female naked ascetic, it is a pāyattika.
"Naked" refers to those of the Ājīvika sect or the Nirgrantha sect.
Regarding the *nirgrantha* non-Buddhists, they are Laozi and his disciples.
The Buddha said:
"Briefly stated, with the exception of the fivefold assembly of the Buddha, all other remaining members of the renunciant community are called 'non-Buddhists' (*tīrthika*)."
"Food" refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods), the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and the five kinds of similar foods.
"Pāyattika" means that it boils, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) or a female naked ascetic, it is a pāyattika.

Whether it be roots, stalks, leaves, flour, fruits, cooked rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, meat, porridge, millet, coarse wheat, wild grass seeds, or *kāśa* grass, if he gives these with his own hand to a naked ascetic or a female naked ascetic, it is a pāyattika.
If a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) comes begging for fruit, one should say:
"We do not withhold fruit from you.
If he begs for water, one should likewise say:
"I do not prohibit you from using water.

There is no offense if it is given to a naked ascetic, a female naked ascetic, one who is ill, a relative, or at the time of seeking or undergoing ordination, or during the four-month period of probation; in these cases, there is no offense.
The forty-fourth [chapter] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a small kingdom in rebellion; he mobilized the fourfold army:
the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.
Having assembled the fourfold army, the king went in person to inspect it: "Are the armor and weapons excellent?
Are the soldiers contented?
Is this host of troops capable of defeating the enemy?"
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"Now that the army is about to set out, shall we go together to see it?
They all replied: [Yes.]
"As you wish.
He then went to the location of the army and stood watching from one spot.
The eyes of kings are always accustomed to gazing at a distance; seeing the bhikṣu from afar, the king sent someone to inquire:
"For what reason have you come?
The group of six bhikṣus immediately replied,
"We wish to see the king."
The king had this thought and said to his ministers:
"Was I difficult to see at other times?
Yet now the bhikṣus have seen me in the midst of the army."
"The Buddha, upon hearing of this matter, will surely establish a precept, forbidding bhikṣus from viewing military forces on the march.
The king summoned the bhikṣu, who immediately went to the king's presence.
The king asked,
"By what causes and conditions have you come? He replied:
"I have come wishing to see the King.
The King said,
"Is it that I am difficult to see at other times?"
"He has come to the midst of the army.
When the Buddha hears of this matter, he will surely establish a precept, forbidding bhikṣus from visiting an army on its march.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this, his heart was not pleased, and he censured [the others] through various reasons:
"What is it to call oneself a bhikṣu and yet watch an army set forth?
Having rebuked them with various reasons, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this? He replied,
"I truly did."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu go to watch an army set out on a campaign?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu intentionally goes to see an army setting out on a campaign, it is a pāyattika offense.
"An army setting out on a campaign" refers to the gathering of various soldiers for the purpose of fighting and defeating enemies.
Regarding armies: there are armies consisting of a single type of force and armies consisting of two, three, or four types of forces.
An army of a single type consists of either exclusively elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, or infantry; this is called an army of a single type.
The two types of forces are: elephant forces and cavalry;
elephant forces and chariot forces;
and elephant forces and infantry.
Cavalry and chariot troops; cavalry and infantry;
chariot troops and infantry—these are called the two types of forces.
The three types of forces are: elephant forces, cavalry, and chariot forces;
elephant forces, cavalry, and infantry;
and cavalry, chariot forces, and infantry. These are called the three forces.
The fourfold army consists of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry; these are called the fourfold army. Regarding the *pāyattika*:
it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu intentionally goes to see an army setting out for battle, he commits a pāyattika if he sees it;
if he does not see it, he commits a dukkaṭa.
If one goes from a lower place to a higher place and sees [the person], it is a *pāyattika*;
if one does not see them, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one goes from a higher place to a lower place and sees [the person], it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not look [for the army], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies equally to an army of one soldier, two soldiers, three soldiers, or four soldiers.
There is no offense if one does not go intentionally, or if there is a reason for the path to pass through the midst [of the army].
At that time, the army had gone there and had not yet defeated the enemy after a long time. King Prasenajit had two ministers:

one named Niṣadha and the other named Pūraṇa. They were already stationed with that army and had a relative who was a bhikṣu; having been separated from him for a long time, they were anxious and longing to see the bhikṣu.
These two ministers sent messengers to summon him, wishing to see the bhikṣu within their army.
The bhikṣu sent a messenger back with this reply:
"The Buddha has established a precept that one must not visit an army."
"Do not grieve; for this reason, I am unable to go.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally goes to see an army setting out for deployment, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.'"

Regarding the causal conditions: if a king sends a messenger to summon one, or if the king’s consort, a prince, a minister, a high official, or a general sends a messenger to summon one, there is no offense in going.

[The forty-fifth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to enter military camps when there was a valid reason. However, as the bhikṣus had many relatives, they were invited by those here today and by those there tomorrow; in this manner, they remained in the military camp for a long time.
Among those in the army, there were some who lacked faith; out of jealousy and malice, they said:
"We are here for the sake of our positions as local officials and for the grain rations provided by the people. This bhikṣu is wicked and inauspicious; for what reason has he come here again?"
"If this bhikṣu remains here for a long time, he may act as a spy, and we might, because of this bhikṣu, suffer loss, ruin, or downfall.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was displeased, and he went to the Buddha to relate it in detail.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked those bhikṣus:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu go to stay overnight in an army for more than two nights?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, having a reason, stays overnight in an army for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it burns, consumes, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu goes among an army and stays for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.
If he remains within the army until the third night has ended, it is a pāyattika.
Section Forty-Six concludes. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stayed overnight in an army for two nights; they went there to observe the military formations, to look at weapons, elephant banners, and ensigns, and to watch the two armies engage in battle.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured it for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who stays two nights among an army, going there at the time to watch military formations, observing weapons, banner standards, and the two armies engaged in battle?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who stays in an army for two nights, then goes to view military formations, views weapons, ensigns, banners, and the two armies engaged in combat?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu stays overnight in an army for two nights, and at that time goes to view the military formations, views weapons, tooth-flags, banners, or the two armies engaged in combat, it is a pāyattika.
Those who don armor and weapons do so to adorn themselves for the intent to fight.
An army consists of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry.
A battle array refers to formations such as those shaped like a bow, a half-moon, the sun, or a spearhead.
When two armies are arrayed against each other, to look upon them constitutes a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* means that which cooks, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu goes to view a military array while weapons are being donned, if he sees them, it is a pāyattika;
if he does not see them, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one goes from a lower place to a higher place and sees [the person], it is a pāyattika;
if one does not see them, it is a dukkaṭa.
If one goes from a higher place to a lower place and sees [the person], it is a pāyattika.
If one does not look [at the battle], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies equally to one army, two armies, three armies, or four armies.
It is likewise when watching banners and streamers during a combat between two arrays.

There is no offense if one does not go intentionally, if there is a specific cause or condition, or if the path passes through the middle and one sees [the person] there; in these cases, there is no offense.
The forty-seventh case concludes. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in a quarrel with the group of seventeen bhikṣus; driven by anger and a state of displeasure, they struck the group of seventeen bhikṣus.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus wept, and the other bhikṣus asked,
"Why are you weeping?
They replied:
"The group of six bhikṣus struck me.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and rebuked them for various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu engage in quarreling and disputing with other bhikṣus, giving rise to anger and a displeased mind, and strike another bhikṣu?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu engage in quarreling and disputing with other bhikṣus, giving rise to anger and a displeased mind, and strike another bhikṣu?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and with a mind of displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding "striking," there are two kinds:
either with the hand or with the foot.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation): it is that which burns, obstructs, and covers; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the transgression herein: if one strikes with the hand, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes with the foot, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one strikes with any other part of the body, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one strikes or beats for the sake of incantation, or because of choking on food, there is no offense.
The forty-eighth [case] is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus quarreled with the group of seventeen bhikṣus; incited by anger and harboring a mind of displeasure, the group of six bhikṣus raised their palms toward the group of seventeen bhikṣus.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus thought to themselves, "The group of six bhikṣus are robust and possess great strength; if they were to seize us with their palms, we would die.
Thereupon, they began to cry out.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Why are you crying out?
He replied:
"The group of six bhikṣus are robust and strong; they raised their palms toward me, and because I was terrified, I cried out.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu engage in quarreling and disputing with another bhikṣu, giving rise to anger and a state of displeasure, and raise his palm toward him?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu engage in quarreling and disputing with other bhikṣus, giving rise to anger and a displeased mind, and even raising his hand toward another?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and with a mind of displeasure, raises his palm toward another, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "raising the palm," there are two kinds:
the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, consumes, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu raises his palm, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one lifts the sole of the foot, it is a *pāyattika*.
Except for the hands and feet, if one lifts any other part of the body toward another, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if a bhikṣu lifts his palm to ward off a vicious beast or to ward off a wicked person.
Forty-nine [cases] concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda had an elder brother who was a bhikṣu named Nanda.
Upananda also had a disciple named Dharma, who likewise maintained the precepts well; however, this disciple did not follow his teacher’s conduct.
Nanda thought to himself:
"This is my younger brother's disciple; he does not follow my way, nor does he follow my younger brother's way. I ought to discipline him so that he will follow us."
At that time, Nanda placed the woman in a room and went to speak with Dharmā,
saying, "Come to such-and-such a place. Dharmā said:
"What are you going to do?
He replied, "Just come."
Dharmatrāta thought to himself:
"This is my elder brother in the Dharma; why should I not follow his words?
He then immediately went along with him.
Nandū knew that by standing in this spot he would be able to see the woman, so he instructed her to stand there and wait for him.
Nandū then went to where the woman was; he removed three of her sores, embraced and pressed against the rest of her body so that they were joined and touched one another.
Having done this, he said to Dharmā, "Do you see?"
He replied, “I have seen it.
[The Buddha said: “Do not tell this to anyone else.”
He replied, "I cannot conceal it; I must certainly inform the Buddha of this matter and speak of it to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs. Nanduka said:
“I have also seen your preceptor perform such acts, and I have even seen more severe than this, yet he did not speak of it to anyone;
why then do you speak of it?
He replied, “It is your own intention that you wish not to speak of it, but I cannot conceal it; I must certainly inform the Buddha and speak toward the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.”
At that time, Dharmadatta reported this matter to the bhikṣus.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; upon hearing this, they were displeased and censured him with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, intentionally conceals it and does not report it?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though already aware of it, asked Nanda intentionally:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, conceals it?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense and conceals it for even a single night, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Knows" means: either he knows it himself, or he hears it from another, or that bhikṣu tells him himself.
"A grave offense" refers to a pārājika or a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"One night" means from sunset until the ground has not yet dried.
"Pāyattika" means it boils, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if, at the time of the assembly, a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, and this bhikṣu conceals it throughout the day while maintaining the perception that it is a pārājika offense within the category of pārājikas, he commits a pāyattika upon reaching the time of the assembly.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, to the act of suspension for not confessing an offense, or to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is one whose mind is deranged, whose mind is distracted, or whose mind is impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Saṃgha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, and at that time one conceals another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

Once the day has ended—at sunrise; once sunrise has passed—at before midday; at midday; at afternoon; at sunset; once sunset has passed—at the first watch of the night; at the middle watch of the night; at the last watch of the night; at the first part of the middle watch; at the middle part of the middle watch; at the latter part of the middle watch; at the first part of the last watch; at the middle part of the last watch; at the latter part of the last watch—if one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense at the conclusion of the *poṣadha* ceremony, and perceiving it as a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, conceals it for the entire day until the conclusion of the next *poṣadha* ceremony, he commits a pāyattika offense.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, to the act of non-suspension, or to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views; and if he is of deranged mind, distracted mind, or a mind impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Sangha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, then at the time when one conceals another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

Once the day has ended, at sunrise; once sunrise has passed, during the forenoon, at midday, in the afternoon, at sunset; once sunset has passed, during the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, the last watch of the night; during the first part of the middle watch, the middle part of the middle watch, the latter part of the middle watch; during the first part of the last watch, the middle part of the last watch, or the latter part of the last watch—if one conceals another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta* offense at the conclusion of the *poṣadha*, and that bhikṣu perceives it as a *duṣkṛta* within the category of *duṣkṛta* offenses, yet conceals it throughout the entire day until the conclusion of the *poṣadha*, he commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If this bhikṣu has been subjected by the Saṃgha to a suspension for not seeing [an offense], or to a non-suspension, or to a suspension for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is of deranged mind, distracted mind, or a mind impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Saṃgha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the night, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Once the night has ended, at the time of sunrise; once sunrise has occurred, during the forenoon, at midday, in the afternoon, or at sunset; once sunset has occurred, during the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, or the last watch of the night; during the first part of the middle watch, the middle part of the middle watch, or the latter part of the middle watch; during the first part of the last watch, the middle part of the last watch, or the latter part of the last watch—if one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the night, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense at the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, yet perceives it as a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pāyattika-deśanīya, or a duṣkṛta; and that bhikṣu, while regarding this pārājika offense as a duṣkṛta, conceals it throughout the day until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*, he commits a pāyattika.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, to the act of suspension for not confessing an offense, or to the act of suspension for not abandoning evil views; or if he is one whose mind is deranged, whose mind is distracted, or whose mind is impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Sangha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.
From sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, in all such cases it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense at the conclusion of the *poṣadha*, and within that *saṃghāvaśeṣa* he perceives it as a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or a *pārājika*, yet conceals it for the entire day until the conclusion of the *poṣadha*, he commits a *pāyattika* offense in each case.

If the Saṃgha performs an *adarśana-pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment for not seeing an offense), an *apravāsanīya-karman* (act of not performing banishment), or an *apratinihsṛṣṭāpatti-pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment for not relinquishing evil views) against one who is insane, deranged, or whose mind is impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Saṃgha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.
From sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of the formal assembly (*sīmā*), that bhikṣu regards that *duṣkṛta* as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, or a *pratideśanīya*.

If, while that *duṣkṛta* is occurring, he conceals it for an entire day—conceiving of it as a *pratideśanīya* or a *pārājika*—until the time of the formal assembly, all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta*.

If the Saṃgha carries out an act of suspension for one who has not seen [the offense], does not perform the formal act of suspension, or whose evil and false views have not been removed; or if the person is insane, deranged, or has a mind impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Sangha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
From the time of sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pārajika offense when the ground is clearly visible, and that bhikṣu conceives doubt regarding the pārajika—wondering whether it is a pārajika or not a pārajika?
Later, having severed his doubts, he perceives what is a *pārājika* offense as such; if he conceals it for the entire day until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

If this bhikṣu has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the suspension of one who does not acknowledge [the offense], to the suspension of one who does not undergo [the formal act], or to the suspension of one whose evil views are not abandoned; or if he is of deranged mind, distracted mind, or a mind impaired by illness, he does not commit an offense.
If the Sangha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.
From sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense when the ground is exposed; he then gives rise to doubt: "Is this a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, or is it not a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"

At a later time, having severed his doubts, he perceives a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense as being a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; if he conceals it for the entire day until the end of the watch, it is a *pāyattika*.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been suspended by the Saṃgha for not acknowledging an offense, for not performing a formal act, or for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is deranged, distracted, or his mind is impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Saṃgha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the night, it is a *pāyattika*.
From the time of sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the night, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta offense during the formal determination of the site, that bhikṣu conceives doubt regarding the duṣkṛta: "Is this duṣkṛta actually a duṣkṛta, or is it not a duṣkṛta?"
Later, when his doubts are severed, if he perceives a *duṣkṛta* offense as a *duṣkṛta* offense and conceals it throughout the day until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If this bhikṣu has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense (*adarśana-pratiniḥsarga*), or has not been so suspended, or is suspended for not relinquishing evil views (*apratiniḥsṛṣṭa-pāpaka-dṛṣṭi*), or if he is deranged, distracted, or his mind is impaired by illness, he does not commit an offense.

If the Saṃgha has lifted the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), or if the suffering has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
From sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another's offense until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu having committed an offense of pārājika upon the ground, he conceives a doubt as to whether it is a pārājika, or a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika, or a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?
If that bhikṣu later severs his doubt and perceives what was a pārājika offense as a duṣkṛta, yet conceals it for the entire day until the end of the day, it constitutes a pāyattika.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to a formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, for not undergoing the formal act of suspension, or for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is deranged in mind, distracted in mind, or his mind is impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Sangha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.
From the time of sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu committing an offense against the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, he becomes doubtful as to whether it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *dukkaṭa*, or a *pārājika*.

If that bhikṣu later eliminates his doubt and conceives the notion of a *pārājika* offense regarding what was actually a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and he conceals it throughout the entire day until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, to the act of suspension for not performing an act, or to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is deranged in mind, distracted in mind, or his mind is impaired by illness, there is no offense.
If the Sangha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, yet one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.
From sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one continues to conceal another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta* offense when the ground is clearly visible. That bhikṣu then develops doubt regarding that *duṣkṛta*: "Is this a *duṣkṛta*, or is it a *pārājika*; is it a *duṣkṛta*, or is it a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; is it a *duṣkṛta*, or is it a *pāyattika*; or is it a *duṣkṛta*, or is it a *pratideśanīya*?"

If that bhikṣu later eliminates his doubt and perceives what was a *duṣkṛta* as a *pratideśanīya*, or as a *pārājika*, and conceals it for the entire day until the end of the night, all of these constitute *duṣkṛta*.

If it is a bhikṣu who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, to the act of suspension for not confessing an offense, or to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is deranged in mind, distracted in mind, or his mind is impaired by illness—there is no offense.
If the Saṃgha has lifted the suspension, or if the pain has ceased, or if one conceals another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

From sunrise until the final watch of the night, if one conceals another’s offense until the end of the day, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Upon seeing another’s offense, one should confess it to a single person and then stop; if there is doubt, it is not necessary to speak of it.
The Fifty [Rules] Concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Fourteen.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Fifteen. Part Two of the Third Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
The seventh of the ninety *pāyattika* rules:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda had this thought:
"This disciple of Dharma has insulted my elder brother; we ought to retaliate against him.
At that time, he called out, "Come together to such-and-such a village."
Question: "For what reason? Answer:
"Come," [the voice] said.
Dharmatrāta thought to himself, "This is my upādhyāya; why should I not follow his word?"
As he was leaving the Jetavana,
there were several bhikṣus walking up and down (caṅkrama) at the entrance of the Jetavana. Those bhikṣus said to Dharmadatta,
"Today you will surely obtain much delicious food and drink."
"Why is that? "Because he followed after a bhikṣu who has many acquaintances. Dharmā said:
"Much from little—this you should know today.
Whenever this Śākyan son, Upananda, entered a house, he was invited to take a meal; Upananda said, "Wait a moment;
it is still early. When the time arrives, I shall come to receive it."
Dharma thought to himself:
"My preceptor must surely be accepting invitations to fine meals today; that is why he has not accepted food at any of the places.
A second and a third household also invited him and offered him food.
Bhadanta said, "Wait a moment; it is still early. We shall take [the meal] when the time arrives.

At that time, Bhadanta left the householder's home and looked at the sun; it was already midday. He thought that if he were to enter the village to beg for food, he would not reach the proper time, and if he were to return to Jetavana, he likewise would not reach the proper time. He then spoke to Dharma:
"Go back; I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you, but I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone.

Dharma then looked at the sun and saw that it was already midday; if he were to enter the village for alms, he would miss the proper time, and if he were to return to Jetavana, he would likewise miss the proper time.
Dharmatrāta thought again,
"Where should I go now?
and immediately returned to Jetavana.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Did you obtain much excellent food today?
He replied:
"Do not speak with me; today I shall fast.
He asked, "For what reason?"
He then related this matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and censured him in various ways, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who intentionally cuts off a bhikṣu’s food?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked Bhaṇḍana intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked the Śākya son Upananda with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu intentionally cut off a bhikṣu’s meal?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:"
"Come, let us go together to various households.
Having arrived at the various households, that bhikṣu did not instruct them to give food, but instead spoke these words: "Go away!"
"I find no pleasure sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure sitting and speaking alone.
If, for the purpose of annoying him, one speaks these words based on such causes and conditions, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika), provided there is no other [justifiable] reason.
"House" refers to the household of laypeople.
"To drive out" means to expel oneself or to instruct another to expel one.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense of expiation): it is boiled, burned, covered, and obstructed; if one does not repent, it will hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Come!
Let us go together to another's house."
If one causes [the person] to turn back before entering the city gate, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes [the person] to turn back after having entered the city gate, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes [the person] to turn back before entering the outer gate of a layperson’s house, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes [a person] to turn back after they have entered the outer gate, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same if they have entered the middle gate.
If one causes them to turn back before they have entered the inner gate, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes someone to turn back when they have entered the inner gate but have not yet reached a place where [the sound] can be heard, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes them to turn back once they have reached a place where [the sound] can be heard, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Section fifty-one concludes. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, traveling together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a caravan of five hundred merchants traveling along with the Buddha, who thought to themselves:
"By following the Buddha on his journey, we shall surely obtain abundance, joy, and peace."
The Buddha traveled until he reached a forest where he wished to stay for the night. At that time, the merchants each followed their own fire, gathering wood and grass to kindle it together.
The bhikṣus also followed those they knew, gathering wood and grass together to kindle fires for warmth.

There was a certain mahallaka bhikṣu who dragged a piece of wood from the air and placed it into a fire. Within the wood was a venomous snake that, upon becoming heated, emerged. When the bhikṣu saw it, he cried out in terror and alarm. The merchants, struck with wonder and thinking a thief had arrived, said to one another:
"Each of you take up your spears, swords, shields, bows, and arrows, and gather our goods!"
The merchants immediately rose, seized their weapons, gathered their goods, and asked one another,
"Where are the thieves?
The bhikṣu said:
"There are no thieves, but only venomous snakes.
The merchants said,
"If you knew it was a snake, why did you cry out so loudly?"
"Because of that loud shouting, some among the group of merchants even killed one another; we nearly came to harm each other.

When the Buddha heard this matter and the merchants' reproaches of the bhikṣu, at the end of that night, he assembled the community of bhikṣus for this reason and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the bhikṣu Mahālu:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu kindle a fire in the open air?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, when not ill, kindles a fire in the open air and directs it toward himself—whether burning grass, wood, cow dung, tree bark, or refuse—whether he kindles it himself or causes another to kindle it, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Regarding 'the sick': when cold, heat, or wind are in excess, if one recovers by facing a fire, this is called being sick.
Apart from these conditions, it is called not being sick."
"An open space" refers to a place that is not covered by walls, not covered by mats, and not covered by clothing; such uncovered places are called "open spaces.
"To put on oneself" means to put it on with one's own hands.
"To cause to put on" means to instruct another to put it on.
"Pāyattika" means that which cooks, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu puts grass into a fire of grass, it is a pāyattika.
If one places firewood, cow dung, tree bark, or refuse among the grass fire, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu places wood among a wood fire, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places cow dung, tree bark, refuse, or grass into a fire made of wood, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu places cow dung into a fire of cow dung, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places wood-bark, refuse-rags, grass, or wood into a fire of cow-dung, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu places wood-bark into a fire of wood-bark, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places refuse, grass, wood, or cow dung into a fire made of tree bark, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu places refuse into a fire of refuse, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places grass, wood, cow dung, or tree bark into a fire of discarded refuse, it is a *pāyattika*.
To instruct another to do so is likewise [an offense]. Even to place firewood on an open ground into a fire is a *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense if it is due to illness; or if one is boiling rice, boiling soup, boiling gruel, boiling meat, boiling broth, or boiling dye; or if one is fumigating a bowl, repairing a staff, or repairing a hook—there is no offense.
Fifty-two [cases] concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus wished to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to expel Upananda, but the group of six bhikṣus obstructed it from within the assembly so that the formal act could not be accomplished.
On another occasion, when the group of six bhikṣus had gone elsewhere, the bhikṣus said,
"We shall now perform the formal act of banishment (pravāsanīya-karman) against Upananda."
A certain bhikṣu said,
"The group of six bhikṣus will come and obstruct [the assembly] again.
The other bhikṣus said:
"The group of six bhikṣus has now gone far away to another village; they have many affairs and have not yet returned.
A certain bhikṣu who had assisted the group of six bhikṣus remained there at that time and did not depart.

The group of six bhikṣus were indolent and lazy; when the time came for the recitation of the precepts, the invitation to the *pravāraṇā*, or the formal acts (*saṃghakarma*) of the Saṃgha, they did not come, but merely gave their consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pariśuddhi*).
The other bhikṣus thought:
"Let us not allow those who assist the group of six bhikṣus to come into the assembly to create obstacles; let them simply take the consent and come."
He immediately struck the ghaṇṭā to assemble the community of bhikṣus and sent a messenger to the place where that bhikṣu was to request his consent for coming. That bhikṣu asked:
"What business do you wish to conduct?"
He replied, "There is a matter concerning the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu then gave his consent.
At that time, the Saṃgha, being of one mind and in harmony, performed the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion) against Upananda.
On a subsequent day, he proclaimed loudly:
"The Saṃgha has already performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* against me, Upananda."
That bhikṣu said,
"This formal act (karmavācanā) should not be performed in this manner, for it does not accord with my view.
The other bhikṣus said:
“You have already granted your consent.
That bhikṣu said:
“I did not know that the Saṃgha was performing the formal act of suspension against the Śākya son Upananda; had I known, I would not have granted my consent.”
He himself said, "I am not one who has committed an offense; I should not be granted the *chanda*.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and censured him through various reasons:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who, having given his consent (*chanda*) regarding a legal matter of the Saṃgha, later regrets it?
After rebuking him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to that bhikṣu: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is it called for a bhikṣu to regret after having given his consent?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has already given his consent for a legal matter of the Saṃgha, and later regrets it, saying:
'I should not have given my consent.'"
"A *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding "monastic affairs" (*saṃghakaraṇīya*): it refers to all matters pertaining to the Saṃgha, whether they be a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*); or whether they be the Uposatha, the *Pravāraṇā*, or a formal act involving fourteen persons.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu has already granted his consent (*chanda*) for a legal matter of the Saṃgha, yet later regrets it and says, "I should not have given my consent."
This is a *pāyattika*.

If a monk, regarding a legal matter of the Saṃgha—whether it be a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or a formal act requiring fourteen members—and having already granted his consent (*chanda*), later regrets it and says:
"I should not have granted my consent."
"An *pāyattika*.
For every instance of speaking with a mind of remorse, there is one *pāyattika*.
The fifty-third [rule] is concluded. The Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī."

At that time, the various worthy ones, according to the day of their fast, went to the monastery to receive the precepts for the fast; they sat cross-legged throughout the night with lamps lit, for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus sat in the great assembly during the first watch of the night, and when the middle watch arrived, each entered his own room.

However, the junior bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras remained overnight in the Dharma-preaching hall; they did not lie down with a focused mind, but instead snored, muttered in their sleep, shouted loudly, and tossed their arms about.
The virtuous ones said, "Look at this assembly of elders; they are not sleeping with a unified mind.
Among them was a bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was displeased, and he went to the Buddha to report it in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the bhikṣu Ālavī: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
"It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu staying overnight with one who has not yet received full ordination?
At that time, the Buddha merely rebuked him but had not yet formulated this precept.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera Rāhula was driven out of his room by the bhikṣus and not allowed to stay with them; Rāhula then went and stayed in a small room at the edge.
At that time, a visiting bhikṣu arrived and thought to himself:
"The great hall must be full of senior monks; I shall go to a small room at the edge.
Having had this thought, he went to a small room at the edge. Upon arrival, he cleared his throat, knocked on the door, and asked:
"Who is here? He replied, "I am Rāhula."
The bhikṣu said,
"Go out," and he immediately went out.
Upon entering the second room, he was again driven out;
upon entering the third room, he was again driven out.
Rāhula thought to himself:
"Since I have been driven out of every dwelling I go to, I shall now go to the Buddha’s latrine.
He immediately went to the latrine and lay down, using the wooden planks of the latrine as a pillow.

Beneath the wooden planks there was a snake; having previously emerged, it was not there, but later at night, during a great wind and rain, the snake fell down and suffered distress, whereupon it returned to its burrow.
At that time, the Buddha remembered Rāhula lying there and thought:
"If I do not wake up, he will surely be harmed by the snake right now."
The Buddha immediately entered into samādhi, vanished from within his chamber, and appeared beside the latrine. There, by means of his supernatural power, he produced the sound of a dragon.
Rāhula was awakened by it, and the Buddha, knowing the answer, asked him nonetheless: "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am Rāhula.
"For what reason are you here?"
He replied,
"I am lying down.
He asked:
"Why are you lying down here?
He replied, "I have no other place to stay for the night."
The Buddha said, "Come out.
He immediately came out.
The Buddha stroked Rāhula’s head with his right hand and spoke these verses:
“You are not poor, nor have you lost your wealth and nobility;
But for the sake of seeking the Way, you have left the home life and should endure suffering.”
Having spoken this verse, the Buddha took him by the arm and led him to his own quarters.

At that time, the Buddha sat alone upon a great seat on his bed; throughout the night, he entered into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and remained in noble silence until daybreak. On account of these circumstances, he assembled the community of monks and said to them:
"This śrāmaṇera is pitiable; having no father or mother, if we do not show him compassion, by what means shall he survive?"
