If they encounter a fierce beast and suffer great distress, their kinsmen will surely speak with anger, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are only able to keep śrāmaṇeras, yet they cannot even protect them."
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, for the sake of two benefits, I permit a person who has not yet received the full precepts to stay overnight together with you for two nights:
first, out of compassion for the śrāmaṇeras; second, because there may be laypeople who come to the monastery and should be provided with a room and lodging.”
For ten reasons, he established a precept for the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣu stays overnight in the same dwelling as a person who has not received full ordination (upasampadā), and exceeds two nights, it is a pāyattika."
"Those who have not received the full ordination" refers to all persons other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
There are four types of dwellings:

first, those entirely roofed and entirely enclosed; second, those entirely enclosed but not roofed; third, those entirely roofed and half-enclosed; and fourth, those entirely roofed and partially enclosed.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it refers to boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu stays together with a person who has not received the full ordination in any of the four types of dwellings for more than two nights, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he rises and then lies down again, for each instance of rising and lying down, it is a *pāyattika*.
If he remains seated throughout the night, there is no offense.

At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who had a śrāmaṇera attend to his medical needs; on the third night, that bhikṣu drove the śrāmaṇera away. Because the sick bhikṣu had no one to care for him, he was on the verge of death.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"You should summon the śrāmaṇera to stand beside the sick bhikṣu; do not allow him to lie down."
There was a sick bhikṣu; a śrāmaṇera stood beside him for a short while, then fell to the ground and lay down. The Buddha said:
“The sick bhikṣu commits no offense.
However, any bhikṣu who is not ill must not lie down there.”
Fifty-fourth [Section] concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa conceived a wicked and heterodox view and said:
"As I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, the performance of practices that obstruct the Path does not actually obstruct the Path."
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"You should admonish the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, saying:"
"Do not speak these words:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; though one practices the dharmas that obstruct the path, they cannot obstruct the path.
Do not slander the Buddha, for slandering the Buddha is unwholesome. The Buddha does not speak such words."
"The Buddha has explained through various causes and conditions that the dharmas which obstruct the Path are indeed able to hinder it; you must abandon this evil and false view.
Thus he should instruct him three times to relinquish this matter.
The bhikṣus said: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
He immediately went to reprimand the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, saying:
"Do not speak such words as:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma; even practicing what obstructs the path cannot actually obstruct the path.'"
"Do not slander the Buddha; it is unwholesome to slander the Buddha, for the Buddha does not speak such words.
Through various causes and conditions, the Buddha has taught that obstructive dharmas can indeed obstruct the Path. You must abandon this evil and false view."
Having given this instruction to make him abandon this matter, they instructed him a second and a third time in the same manner.
After the monks had instructed him three times and were unable to make him abandon it, they rose and departed.
They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
We have instructed the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa to abandon this evil and false view, yet we were unable to make him abandon it."
We then immediately rose up.
The Buddha said,
“You should perform a formal act of suspension (*karmavācanā*) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, because he does not relinquish his evil and heterodox views.”
If there are other bhikṣus who do not relinquish their evil and false views, they shall likewise be dealt with according to this rule.
To perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* for one who does not relinquish evil and false views, the Saṃgha must be united in single-minded harmony.
A certain bhikṣu proclaims within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa has given rise to such evil and heterodox views, saying:"
"I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; the practices that obstruct the path cannot actually obstruct the path.
Although the Sangha has already exhorted him to abandon this evil and heterodox view, he is unwilling to do so.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the formal act (*kamma*) of not relinquishing evil and false views be performed against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa; for as long as you do not relinquish your evil and false views, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of banishment (*pabbājana-kamma*) against you for that same duration.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for not relinquishing his evil and heterodox views. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!"
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu should speak thus:

"I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma in this way: that which constitutes an obstacle to the path does not actually obstruct the path," the other bhikṣus should instruct that bhikṣu as follows:
"Do not speak these words:
'I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma in such a way that practicing obstructive dharmas cannot obstruct the Path.
Do not slander the Buddha; slandering the Buddha is unwholesome, for the Buddha does not speak such words."
"The Buddha has taught through various causes and conditions that the dharmas which obstruct the path are indeed able to hinder progress; you should abandon this evil and heterodox view.
When the bhikṣus instruct them in this manner, if they persist in holding their position and refuse to relinquish it, the bhikṣus should instruct them two or three times more to abandon this matter.
"If, after being instructed up to three times, one relinquishes [the offense], it is well; if one does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika*.
A *pāyattika* means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: this bhikṣu should first admonish him with gentle words; if he relinquishes [the matter] through such gentle admonition, he should be made to perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
If he does not relinquish it, the Sangha should issue a formal admonition through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
As for the method of this admonition: within a harmonious assembly of monks, one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to a wicked and heterodox view, saying:
"I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; even those practices that are said to obstruct the Path cannot actually obstruct it."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha issue a formal charge to the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, commanding him to abandon his evil and heterodox views.
This is the motion (jñapti). Thus the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) is performed.
“The Saṃgha has finished exhorting the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa to abandon his evil and false views. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!

In this context, when the Buddha says that the bhikṣu should be exhorted a second and a third time to abandon this matter, this is called “exhortation” (saṃjñapti), this is called “instruction” (anuśāsana), and this is called “exhortation-instruction” (saṃjñapty-anuśāsana).
If one does not relinquish [the position] despite being admonished with gentle words, there is no offense.

If one does not relinquish it when the first statement is unfinished, finished, or both; when the second statement is unfinished, finished, or both; when the third statement is unfinished; or if it is an illegal separate assembly, an illegal harmonious assembly, a semblance-of-dharma separate assembly, a semblance-of-dharma harmonious assembly, a lawful separate assembly, or something different from the Dharma, different from the Vinaya, and different from the Buddha’s teaching—yet one does not relinquish it upon being admonished, there is no offense.

If, after being formally admonished three times in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, the discipline, and the Buddha’s teaching, one does not relinquish [the offense], it is a *pāyattika*. The fifty-fifth rule concludes.

At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. Then the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that a certain person had spoken such words—that he had not expiated his offense according to the Dharma, had not abandoned his evil and heterodox views, and had not been lawfully expelled—nevertheless associated with him in affairs, lived together with him, and shared a room for lodging.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, they were displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, knowing that such a person has spoken these words, he does not purify his offense according to the Dharma, does not abandon his evil and false views, and yet associates with him, dwells with him, and shares a room with him after he has been lawfully expelled?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that such a person has spoken these words, has not repented according to the Dharma, has not abandoned their evil and false views, and yet—after they have been rightfully expelled—still engages in affairs with them, dwells together with them, and shares a room for lodging?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has spoken in such a manner, yet has not repented according to the Dharma and has not abandoned his evil and false views, and if he nevertheless associates with him in affairs, dwells together with him, or sleeps in the same room as him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Knowing" means knowing by oneself, hearing from another, or being told by that person themselves.
One who speaks thus speaks according to what has been seen.
"Not repenting in accordance with the Dharma" means that the mind has not yet been subdued and pride has not yet been broken.
"One who does not abandon evil and false views" refers to one whose evil and false views have not yet been separated from the mind.
"Expelling according to the Dharma" means expelling from within the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
Regarding "engaging in joint activities," there are two kinds of activities:
those concerning the Dharma and those concerning material wealth.
Regarding "living together," it means living with such a person.

Regarding the performance of the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, as well as the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*, or the performance of a *karman* involving fourteen persons:
if one stays overnight together [in a dwelling], there are four types of dwellings:

first, those entirely roofed and entirely enclosed; second, those entirely enclosed but not entirely roofed; third, those entirely roofed and half-enclosed; and fourth, those entirely roofed but with little enclosure.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu performs ritual acts together with a person who has been expelled, whether by teaching the sūtras and the Dharma or by reciting verses, for every verse there is a *pāyattika*.
If one recites from a sūtra, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each chapter;
if one recites from individual verses, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every sentence.
The same applies if one asks a person who has been expelled [from the saṃgha] for instruction and learns it by recitation.
Regarding shared material goods: if a bhikṣu gives a bowl to one who has been suspended, it is a pāyattika.
To give robes, a door-bolt, food for the proper time, food for the night, food for seven days, or food for life—all these are pāyattikas.
If one takes the robe or bowl from a person who has been expelled, it is a *pāyattika*.
This applies even down to taking medicinal substances for lifelong use; all such acts are *pāyattikas*.
If one sleeps together with [an expelled person] within the same fourfold dwelling, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one rises and then lies down again, for each instance of rising and lying down again, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one remains seated throughout the night without lying down, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The fifty-sixth [offense] is concluded. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a novice named Māgadha who conceived such a wicked and heterodox view:
"I understand the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; engaging in sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path."
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported it in detail to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and said:
"You should strictly instruct the śrāmaṇera Māgha:
"Do not speak these words:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path.
Do not slander the Buddha, for slandering the Buddha is unwholesome. The Buddha does not speak such words."
"The Buddha has taught through various causes and conditions that sexual desire can obstruct the Path; you should abandon this evil and false view.
The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
he said, and immediately went to rebuke the śrāmaṇera, saying:
“Do not speak such words.”
"I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; engaging in sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path.
Do not slander the Buddha; to slander the Buddha is unwholesome, for the Buddha does not speak such words.
"The Buddha has explained through various causes and conditions that sexual desire can obstruct the Path; you must abandon this evil and false view.
Although the bhikṣus instructed him thus two or three times, they were unable to make him renounce it.
Immediately rising from his seat, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have exhorted the śrāmaṇera Moga, commanding him to abandon his evil and heterodox views.”
“Since he cannot be made to relinquish [his views] and rise from his seat,” the Buddha said,
“you should perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against the śrāmaṇera Māgha, because he does not abandon his evil and heterodox views.”
If there are other śrāmaṇeras such as this, they should also be dealt with in this same manner.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* for the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), within a harmonious Saṃgha gathered with a single mind, one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This śrāmaṇera Māgha has given rise to evil and heterodox views; although the Saṃgha has already exhorted him to abandon these evil and heterodox views, he is unwilling to do so.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (expulsion) against the śrāmaṇera Māgha.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of suspension for the śrāmaṇera Māka; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that this śrāmaṇera had already been subject to the penalty of parivāsa (exclusion), nevertheless kept him, provided for him, worked together with him, and stayed overnight with him.
Among them were bhikṣus who possessed few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured it for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled, yet keeps him, provides for him, shares tasks with him, and sleeps with him?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled for extinction [of his status], yet continues to keep him, provide for him, work together with him, and sleep together with him?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a śrāmaṇera speaks these words:
"I know the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma; practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path," the bhikṣus should instruct the śrāmaṇera as follows:
"Do not speak these words:
'I know the meaning of the Buddha's Dharma; practicing sexual desire cannot obstruct the Path.
Do not slander the Buddha, for slandering the Buddha is unwholesome. The Buddha does not speak such words."
"You should know that the Buddha, through various causes and conditions, has rebuked sexual desire as being able to obstruct the Path; you should abandon this evil and false view.
If the śrāmaṇera, when the bhikṣus reprove him in this way, persists and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should instruct him two or three times to abandon this matter.
If, after being instructed thus a second and third time, he relinquishes [the claim], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should speak to the śrāmaṇera as follows:
"From this day forward, you must not say:
'The Buddha is my teacher.'"
"Furthermore, you must not follow behind the bhikṣus. While other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay in the same room with a bhikṣu for two nights, you are not.
You fool, get out! You should not remain here."
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled by suspension, nevertheless keeps him, provides for him, works with him, or sleeps with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Knowing" means knowing by oneself, hearing from another, or being told by the śrāmaṇera himself.
Regarding "expulsion" (*pravāsanīya*): according to the Buddha's Dharma, the Saṃgha, being in harmony with a single mind, performs the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*).
Regarding "one who keeps [the expelled person]" (*dhārayati*): one accepts him as a disciple, acting for oneself as either an *upādhyāya* or an *ācārya*.

"Relieving through the scriptures" refers to providing robes, bowls, door-hooks, medicinal food for the daytime, medicinal food for the night watch, medicinal food for seven days, or medicinal food for life.
"Shared affairs" consist of two types of affairs:
affairs concerning the Dharma and affairs concerning material wealth.
"Staying overnight together" means staying overnight within four kinds of dwellings.

A "dwelling" refers to one that is entirely roofed and entirely enclosed; one that is entirely enclosed but not entirely roofed; one that is entirely roofed and half-enclosed; or one that is entirely roofed but only partially enclosed.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu instructs in the method of expelling a śrāmaṇera, whether by prose or by verse, for each verse there is a *pāyattika*.
If one receives a sutra from a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each chapter;
if received from him sentence by sentence, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each sentence.
The same applies to receiving, reading, or reciting [the scriptures].
If one gives a bowl to a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled by the saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.

If one gives him robes, a door-bolt, or any of the medicines—whether those to be taken at the proper time, those for the night, those for seven days, or those for life—it is in every case a pāyattika.

If one takes from a śrāmaṇera who has been expelled the robe, the alms bowl, the door-bolt, the food for the day, the food for the night, the food for seven days, or the lifelong medicine—one for each item, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
Staying overnight in any of the four kinds of dwellings constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one rises and then lies down again, for each instance of rising and lying down, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
To remain sitting through the night without lying down also constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The fifty-seventh [chapter] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, for the sake of almsround, the World-Honored One rose early, donned his robes, and took up his bowl; Ānanda followed behind him as they entered Rājagṛha.
At that time, it rained heavily, and the waters burst forth from the hidden storehouse, revealing many precious objects.
Then the World-Honored One went out for alms, and having finished his meal, returned to Vulture Peak Mountain.
The Buddha saw that this treasury contained many precious objects; he walked ahead while Ānanda followed one pace behind, walking slowly.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"If I draw near to the Buddha, the breath from my mouth or the sound of my footsteps might disturb him."
The Buddha, seeing this storehouse, said to Ānanda:
"O poisonous snake, Ānanda!"
Having spoken these words, he passed straight through and did not go to where the object was.
Seeing this, Ānanda said,
“A venomous snake!”
"World-Honored One!
Having spoken these words, he passed straight on without going to where the goods were.
At the foot of this mountain, there was a poor man reaping wheat who, upon hearing these two kinds of speech, had this thought:
"I have never before seen a venomous snake among the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas; I shall go now to see one.
He went at once and saw that the water had burst forth from its hiding place. Having seen this, he was filled with joy and said:
"The venomous snakes among the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas are all truly excellent things."

He immediately brought his carriages, clothing, and bags into the house; using these treasures to manifest an air of wealth and nobility, he constructed a great residence and established shops for gold, silver, hired labor, copper, and pearls, as well as herds of elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, along with vehicles, litters, retainers, and slaves.
Previously, there was a person who did not get along with him; when the great house was being built, it interfered with that man’s livelihood. Out of envy and jealousy, he said to the king:

“In this place there was formerly a poor and lowly man who has suddenly acquired the appearance of wealth. He has constructed a grand hall and shops for gold, silver, hired labor, copper, and pearls, as well as herds of elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep, and a multitude of people, servants, and slaves. This man must have obtained a great treasure, yet he does not wish to inform the king.”
The king immediately summoned him and asked,
"Did you find the treasure?
He replied:
"No," [the man] replied.
The king thought to himself, "This man has not been subjected to torture; how could he speak the truth?"
He immediately commanded the officials:
"Seize all their wealth and property, bind them to the top of a stake; if anyone discovers a treasure trove and does not inform the King, they shall all be punished in this manner."
Having given these instructions, he immediately seized their property and bound them to the top of a stake, proclaiming:
"Whoever obtains a treasure hoard and does not inform the king shall all be punished in this manner."
That person spoke these words:
"O poisonous snake! Ānanda!"
"O evil venomous snake!
World-Honored One," the people said.
"Do not speak such words:
'A venomous snake,
Ānanda!'"
"A venomous snake,
World-Honored One!
You should speak these words.
"Whoever obtains this treasure-trove need not speak to the king; all have this share.
This person, single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, spoke these words:
"A poisonous snake."
"Ānanda! A venomous snake.
"World-Honored One!"
At that time, the people said to the king:
"This man has marked his head with these words:
'A poisonous snake.'"
"Ānanda! A venomous snake.
"World-Honored One!"
The king immediately summoned him and questioned him:
"It was you who were bound with your head tied to the stake, and it was you who truly spoke these words:
'A venomous snake!'"
"Ānanda! A venomous snake.
"World-Honored One!"
"Is this not so? The man replied,
"Great King!"
"Since you grant me fearlessness, I shall speak the truth.
He replied,
"I grant you fearlessness."
He immediately said, "There is such a treasure store. Formerly, when I was poor and lowly, I was reaping wheat at the foot of the mountain.
Two bhikṣus came together up the mountain; one walked in front, and the other walked behind."
When the bhikṣu who was walking ahead saw this treasure, he said:
"A poisonous snake, Ānanda!"
Having spoken thus, he went straight away without reaching the object and did not take the object.
A monk who was walking behind also saw him and spoke these words again:
"A venomous snake!"
“World-Honored One!
Having spoken these words, he went straight away; he did not go to where the object was, nor did he take the object.
Upon hearing these two statements, I immediately thought to myself:
"I have never seen a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, who is like a venomous snake or a fierce serpent.
He immediately went to look and saw that this treasure store had been submerged by water.

Upon seeing this, he was filled with joy; he immediately took it home in wagons and cloth bags, manifesting the signs of wealth and nobility, and constructed a great hall, shops for gold, shops for silver, shops for hired labor, shops for copper, and shops for pearls, as well as herds of elephants and horses, flocks of cattle and sheep, carriages, palanquins, retainers, and slaves.
Now that I have fallen into this transgression, I recall those words: "What can this evil venomous snake do to my body?
It will surely devour my life.
For the sake of this jewel, the king has confiscated all my wealth and is now on the verge of taking my life.
The king thought to himself:
"This must surely be the Buddha and Ānanda.
The king said:
"Go; you have no fear for your life, and I shall reward you with five hundred gold coins.
Because he had spoken the words of the Buddha and what Ānanda had said during that moment of crisis, he was delivered from death.
At that time, a great minister and high official among the assembly cried out in a loud voice:
"This is a most rare occurrence! By recollecting the Buddha’s words, one has been delivered from death.
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported it in detail to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Taking heavy objects incurs such offenses, as well as those exceeding them, all because of taking precious goods.
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a formal precept.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.

At that time, a group of youths went out of the city to a grove to practice archery; they shot through the holes of a door-panel, shooting upward into the air so that the arrowheads struck one another in succession.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda rose early, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and was about to enter the city for alms. From afar, the young boys saw him and said to one another:

"This Śākya son Upananda delights in committing evil offenses; whether he sees an offense, hears of an offense, or suspects an offense, he has no shame or remorse and knows no satiety. We shall now test him."
He immediately placed a treasure worth one thousand [units of currency] in the middle of the road and stepped back to watch from afar.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda arrived at the place where the treasure was, looked around to ensure no one was there, and tucked it under his arm.
Upon seeing him, the youths immediately surrounded him, seized him, and said:
"Is this the dharma of you bhikṣus, that you steal another's property when it is not given?
He replied:
"I did not steal. "Why then did you take it?
He replied:
"I took it because I thought it was refuse. The youths said,
"How can you take a precious object thinking it is refuse?"
The youths thought,
"This wicked man shall be taken before the officials.
Having had this thought, they took him to the officials.
The officials asked,
"Did you truly steal?
He replied:
"I shall not steal; I take it with the thought that it is refuse.
The officials spoke again:
"There is no such thing as taking something that is not a treasure by thinking it is refuse."
The officials were disciples of the Buddha; because they had faith in and delighted in the Buddha, they spoke these words:
"How could a bhikṣu commit theft?
These young boys must surely be lying."
He immediately said, "Go away;
do not do this again in the future.
Do not take anything from the open grounds that has not been given to you."
At that time, after Vaddhananda had committed this evil deed, he returned and related the matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"Such evils and even greater evils than these all arise from the acceptance of gold, silver, and precious objects."
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, whether it be a jewel or something resembling a jewel, takes it himself or causes it to be taken, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "jewels": money, gold, silver, musāragalva, agate, vaidūrya, and pearls.
"Resembling jewels" refers to copper, iron, white tin, lead, pewter, and counterfeit pearls.
"Taking for oneself" means taking with one's own hand.
"Causing another to take" means instructing another to take it.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu takes up or holds another's money, gold, or silver, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one picks up or handles another's *śukti*, *musāragalva*, *vaidūrya*, or *muktikā* pearls, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu picks up or handles articles resembling jewels—whether they be ornaments for men, ornaments for women, or weapons for combat—it is a *pāyattika*.
To seize and display a counterfeit pearl constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, it happened that a festival day arrived in the city of Śrāvastī; various laypeople prepared all kinds of food and drink and went out into the grove.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātḥ, having adorned her body with ornaments worth five hundred gold coins, went out of the city for recreation and was about to re-enter it.
This mother of Mṛgāra had faith and devotion in the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and she thought:
"Now that I have gone out of the city, I should not return without seeing the Buddha; furthermore, I should not go to the place where the Buddha is while wearing such ornaments."
She immediately removed her ornaments, wrapped them in her garment, and gave them to a young maidservant.
Having given them away, she went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her with various teachings on the Dharma; having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, Mṛgāramātṛ rose from her seat, prostrated with her head at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Because the Buddha had so skillfully taught the Dharma, and because the young maidservant had tasted the flavor of the Buddha’s Dharma, she immediately forgot her ornaments and left.
The Buddha saw this garment wrapped up and said to Ānanda, "Look inside this;
what object is there? Take it out.
Ānanda told the attendant to open it for inspection, and then had him wrap it back up and take it away.

For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, whether it be a jewel or something resembling a jewel, takes it up himself or instructs another to take it up, it is a pāyattika offense, except in cases of necessity.'"

Regarding the causal conditions: if there are jewels or jewel-like objects within a monastery or a dwelling, and one takes them with the thought that "if the owner comes, they shall be returned," [this constitutes the condition].
"This matter should be thus.
Regarding "within the monastery grounds," it refers to objects located within the walls of the monastery, within the fences, within the moats, or within the enclosures.
Regarding "within the dwelling place," it refers to the dwelling place as requested by a layperson.
In this regard, what constitutes non-offense?
If the object is within the monastery and a lay attendant (kappiya-kāraka) can be found, one should instruct them to take it up, examine it, and store it away.
If no lay attendant can be found, one should take it up, examine it, and store it away oneself.
If anyone comes to demand [an item], one should ask:
"What are the characteristics of your object?
If they describe the characteristics correctly, it should be returned to them.
If it is not so, he should reply:
"There is no such thing.
If the owner has not yet arrived and this bhikṣu wishes to go for a valid reason, there is a long-resident, virtuous, and competent bhikṣu among them who should say to him:
"If I obtain an item forgotten by another, you should take it, examine it, and keep it.
Should someone come to search for it, ask them for its description; if it matches, you should return it;
if it does not match, you should reply:"
"There is no such thing.
If more than five or six years have passed and no owner comes to claim it, it should be used from among the goods belonging to the Sangha of the four directions.
If an owner later comes to claim it, one should repay it using goods from the Sangha of the four directions.
Regarding these items being in their place of storage: if a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites) is available, one should instruct them to take, inspect, and store them.
If no *kappiya-kāraka* is available, one should take, inspect, and store them oneself.
If anyone comes to request them, one should ask for identifying characteristics; if they match, they should be returned.
If it is not so, one should reply:
"There is no such thing.
If the bhikṣu has a reason to depart and there is a householder or a virtuous man or woman therein, he should say to them:
"I have found this object belonging to another here; you should take it and examine it.
If anyone comes seeking it, ask for its identifying marks; if it is his, you should return it;
if it is not, you should reply: [as follows]."
"There is no such thing.
If, after five or six years, there is no one to come and take it, then the bedding—whether small seats, large beds, or bed-boards—at that dwelling place should be used for practical purposes.
If someone comes later to request it, one should take this bed or seat and return it to them.
This matter should be handled in this way.
[The fifty-eighth case ends. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, because of the incident involving the dragon and the hail, the people of Rājagṛha held a month-long festival.
On the final day of the festival, as the performers gave their performance, they were entitled to receive a large payment.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us go and see who comes and goes.
They all said:
"As you wish.
They then went together and stood to one side, sending a messenger to say to the performers:
"Whatever is obtained from this [performance], give us an equal share; if you do not, we shall ruin your assembly."
He then went immediately and said to them:
"Share with us an equal portion of what you have obtained; if you do not, we shall destroy your assembly.
Question:
"Who said these words?
He replied, "A śramaṇa."
Question: "What kind of śramaṇa is he?
He replied:
“Śākyaputra śramaṇa! the performers said to one another, “We have now captivated the hearts of the spectators;
our musical performance is already mastered. Even if there were a great master musician, he could not defeat us, let alone a Śākyaputra śramaṇa.”
"I will not share a portion with you.
The messenger immediately returned and reported:
"He is unwilling to share a portion with you."
Having heard that he had not yet been given [permission], he immediately spread out various garments to form a canopy, various garments to form a screen, and various garments to form a seat.
Seated there upon them in the full lotus posture, dressed in white robes, he—adorned with eloquence—praised the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the noble precepts.
Among them, some people rose from the great assembly and went to investigate;
likewise a second and a third time, the gathering place was entirely empty. Those who had come to the bhikṣu to hear the Dharma and attained its flavor did not return; thus, that place became empty.
At that time, the performers were expected to receive a great reward, but they received none at all.
They asked one another, "Who was it in there?"
He replied,
“A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
Thereupon, he rebuked him, saying:
"This destroys the dharma of a śramaṇa and burns away the dharma of a śramaṇa; it completely robs us of the wealth we have obtained.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was displeased, and he went to the Buddha to relate it in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [what had occurred], he intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?
They replied:
"It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu wearing dyed robes that have not been purified?
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a formal precept.
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a group of bhikṣus were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī together with a caravan of merchants, intending to cross a dangerous road.
Then, some bandits came and plundered the merchants' goods, stripping them naked before letting them go; the bhikṣus likewise lost their robes.
Furthermore, there were other renunciants who had also lost their robes in this same place.
At that time, the thieves gathered the robes together in one spot; because these thieves loved the Buddha-dharma, they said to the bhikṣus, "Each of you may go and take back your own robes."
Other renunciants also wear dyed robes; the bhikṣus were in doubt, thinking them to be the garments of others, and did not dare to take them.
Proceeding by stages, they arrived at Śrāvastī and went to where the Buddha was, prostrating with their heads at his feet and sitting to one side.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they address him with words of greeting and inquiry:
"Are you able to endure?
Are you well?"
"Was it not difficult to beg for alms? Were you not weary on the road?
With these words, the Buddha inquired after the bhikṣus:
"Are you able to endure it?"
"Are your feet not weary?
Is begging for alms not difficult? Are you not fatigued by the road?
The bhikṣus replied:
“With patience as my feet, begging for alms is not difficult, and the roads do not weary me.
He related this matter in detail to the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must, from among three types of colors, apply one or another to ruin the color of that robe—either blue, mud-colored, or madder.'"
"If a bhikṣu wears a new robe without treating it with one of the three kinds of dye for disfiguring it, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "a new robe": if a bhikṣu obtains another's old robe, because it is newly acquired by him, it is also termed a "new robe."
The three kinds of dyed colors are blue, mud-color, or madder.
If a bhikṣu obtains a blue robe, it must be purified in two ways:
either with mud-color or with madder.
If one obtains a garment dyed with mud-color, it is purified by two methods:
either by indigo or by madder.
If one obtains a garment dyed with madder, it is likewise purified by two methods.
Whether it be blue or mud-colored;
if one obtains a yellow robe, it should be purified by three methods:
blue, mud, or madder.
One who obtains red cloth should purify it in three ways: with indigo, mud, or madder.
One who obtains white cloth should likewise purify it in three ways:
with indigo, mud, or madder.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it is "cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu wears a garment that has not been purified (*apariśuddha*), it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes a bedding mat, it is a pāyattika.
If one makes a pillow, it is a pāyattika.
Even if one merely tries it on for a short time, it is a duṣkṛta.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe that has already been made pure, he may patch it with impure pieces of cloth; he should then remove the stitches and resew them in a single point to make it pure, or if he sews them directly, each section must be made pure individually.

If a bhikṣu obtains a pure dyed robe, merely stitching it back together constitutes purification; however, if impure materials have been used for patching or trimming, he must return it to the Saṃgha for re-purification through dyeing with the appropriate colors according to the Dharma.
Regarding "impure patches": these are not cloth of a proper color, measuring only one or two chi in length; thus they are called "impure patches.
Because this robe has become worn out, it should be patched with such pieces, and all must be sewn with backstitches.

If it is a robe with a straight seam, when the owner of the robe passes away, one should remove this straight seam and give it to the Saṃgha; then, one should give this robe to the attendant of the sick person, having purified it by making three dots at each point, because its color is impure.
To wash and then remove the pins is what the Buddha permitted as the proper way to store and use [the robe].

As for why one must not simply sew it straight, it is because that is the method for the garments of worldly people; therefore, one uses the removal of pins to distinguish [the monastic] from the laity.
The fifty-ninth [section] concludes. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle Fifteen.
3. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle Sixteen. Third Recitation, Part Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The eighth of the ninety *pāyattika* rules.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra had three kinds of ponds.
In the first pond, the king and his queen bathed; in the second pond, the princes and ministers bathed; in the third pond, the rest of the people bathed.
This king, having attained the Way and possessing deep faith in the Buddha, asked his ministers:
"Have the superiors bathed yet?"
He replied, "I have also washed.
The king said:
"The Superior One should wash in my pond.
At that time, the bhikṣus were constantly washing many times during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night.
Once, King Bimbisāra wished to wash and said to the keeper of the pond:
"I wish to go and bathe after clearing the way for others.
He immediately cleared away the other people so that only the bhikṣus remained.
The person in charge of the pond then thought to himself:
"The king respects the bhikṣus; if you dismiss them, the king may become angry.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"All those others have been dismissed, but the bhikṣus remain."
The king said, "Excellent!
Let the Superior wash first."
During the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night, the bhikṣus finished washing and departed.
The keeper of the pond informed the king,
saying, "The bhikṣus have already left."
The king then went to bathe.
According to royal custom, bathing takes a long time; by the time the king had finished his bath, it was already midday.
Having completed his ablutions, the king thought to himself:
"I ought not to leave the city and return home without seeing the Buddha.
He then proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking for the sake of instruction, the Buddha said:
“Great King! Where have you come from so early this morning?
Then the king related these matters to the Buddha in detail.
At that time, the Buddha taught the King various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden him; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the king rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after the king had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them:

"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu constantly wash himself repeatedly during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, thereby preventing a consecrated Kṣatriya great king from being able to bathe in his own pool?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding a pāyattika: it is a state of being cooked, burned, covered, and obstructed; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu bathes before half a month has passed, it is a pāyattika.
If he bathes when half a month has passed, or after that time, there is no offense.

At that time, during the remaining month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two months and a half being the season of great heat—the bhikṣus were not permitted to bathe; consequently, their bodies became soiled and itchy, causing them distress and nausea.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, saying:
"May the World-Honored One, during such great heat as this, permit the bhikṣus to bathe.
The Buddha said:
“Listen to the rule for bathing.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, it is a pāyattika offense, except when there is a valid cause.’”
Regarding the causal conditions: the remaining one month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two months and a half are called the "Great Heat" season.
Within this context, the offense is as follows: if a bhikṣu bathes before the Great Heat season has arrived, it is a pāyattika.
If one bathes during times of great heat, there is no offense.

When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time some bhikṣus were ill; because they had applied ghee and oil to their bodies and were not permitted to bathe, they suffered from itching, distress, and nausea.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“We pray that you will permit us to bathe for the sake of illness.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I permit bathing for the sake of illness; it is as beneficial to a sick person as food.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, it is a pāyattika offense, except for [valid] causes.’”

Regarding the "circumstances" (*nidāna*): during the final month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two and a half months being the time of great heat—one may bathe, except during times of illness.
As for "illness": if cold, wind, or heat disorders arise, and one can recover through bathing, this is what is meant by "illness."
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill bathes less than once every half-month, it is a pāyattika.
If he is ill, there is no offense.

When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time some bhikṣus put on their robes and took up their bowls before midday to enter the city for alms. Then a violent wind arose, blowing their robes off their bodies and covering them with dust; because they were unable to bathe, they became distressed and vomited.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to bathe for the sake of the wind.
The Buddha said:
“From now on, bathing is permitted due to the cause of wind.
From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, except for a specific cause, it is a pāyattika offense.’”

Regarding the causes and conditions: during the final month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two and a half months being the time of great heat—one may [use fans], except during times of illness or when there is wind.
Regarding the offense herein: if one bathes when there is no cause such as wind, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one bathes when there is a cause such as wind, there is no offense.

While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time some bhikṣus, having put on newly dyed robes, entered the city to beg for food. They encountered rain, and their robes became damp; the sweat from dyeing soaked into their bodies, causing them to break out in scabs. Because they were unable to bathe, they suffered from itching and nausea.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“We pray that the World-Honored One will allow us to bathe on account of the rain.
The Buddha said:
“Because of the circumstance of listening to the rain, bathing was permitted.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, except for a legitimate reason, it is a pāyattika offense.’”

Regarding the conditions: during the final month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two and a half months being the period of great heat—one may [go out] except during times of illness, wind, or rain.
Regarding the offense herein: if one bathes without the causal condition of rain, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one bathes with the causal condition of rain, there is no offense.

When the Buddha was in the country of Āravī, at that time the bhikṣus were constructing a new stūpa. They carried earth, mud, brick, tile, grass, and so forth, and applied coarse plaster, fine plaster, black and white plaster; because they were unable to bathe, their itching and distress caused them nausea and extreme exhaustion that would not subside.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One will permit us to bathe for a specific reason.
The Buddha said:
"Listen: bathing for the sake of a causal occasion is permitted.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, except for a causal occasion, it is a pāyattika.'"

Regarding the causal conditions: during the final month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two and a half months being the time of great heat—one may [use a fan], except during times of illness, wind, rain, or while engaged in work.
"Regarding 'making': even sweeping the ground of the monastic quarters five times is called making.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu bathes without a valid reason for doing so, it is a pāyattika."
If one acts with a valid cause or condition, there is no offense.

When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time a group of bhikṣus were traveling from Kośala toward Śrāvastī. The land was very dusty, and as they walked, the dust covered their bodies. Because they were unable to bathe, their bodies became itchy and oppressed, causing them nausea.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will permit bathing for the sake of the causal conditions of travel.
The Buddha said:
“Because bathing is permitted due to specific causes and conditions,
from this day forward this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu bathes less than once every half-month, except for a specific cause, it is a pāyattika offense.’”

Regarding the causes and conditions: during the final month and a half of spring and the first month of summer—these two and a half months of great heat—one may [use a fan], except during times of illness, wind, rain, manual labor, or while traveling.
"Traveling" means coming or going for even half a yojana.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu bathes today after having arrived yesterday, it is a pāyattika.
If one intends to go away the next day but bathes today, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one bathes while traveling within half a *yojana* distance, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, lacking these six causes and conditions, bathes less than once every half-month, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is a specific reason for bathing, yet one bathes without informing the other bhikṣus, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
[The sixty rules are concluded. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

At that time, the princes of Vaiśālī went out into the groves to practice archery; they shot upward through the keyhole of a gate panel, with the arrowheads of each successive shot meeting the notch of the previous one.

At that time, before the midday meal, Kāḷudāyin dressed in his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Seeing from afar the princes practicing archery in this manner, he smiled upon seeing them.
The princes said,
"For what reason do you smile?
Is our archery not skillful?"
He replied, "It is not good. He asked:
"Are you able? He replied,
"I am able."
"If you can, then shoot. Kāḷudāyin said,
"According to our rules, we ought not to hold bows or arrows."
The princes said,
"We have a wooden bow that can be used.
They then gave him the wooden bow.
At that moment, a flying bird circled in the air; Kāḷodāyin shot an arrow, surrounding it so that it could not escape.
The princes asked, "Why has it not been struck?"
He replied,
"What difficulty is there in hitting the mark?
The princes said:
"No, that will not do.
If you are able to put it on, then you should put it on; do not merely speak empty words.
He then spoke with arrogance:
"Where do you wish for him to hit?
the prince said,
"I wish for him to hit his right eye."
He immediately placed it over his right eye, and the bird died instantly.
At that time, the princes were all filled with shame, envy, and resentment, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas are capable of intentionally depriving an animal of its life."
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured him with various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu intentionally take the life of an animal?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he said to Kālodāyin: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu intentionally take the life of an animal?
Having rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Taking life" means either taking it oneself or instructing another to take it.
"Pāyattika" means that by boiling, burning, covering, or obstructing, if one does not repent, it will be able to obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are three ways of taking the life of an animal that constitute a *pāyattika*:
acting oneself, instructing another, or sending a messenger.
"Acting oneself" means if a bhikṣu himself takes the life of an animal.
As for "instructing," it means saying to another:
"This animal must be seized, bound, beaten, and killed.
If another accepts the instruction and kills it, that bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
Sending a messenger: if a bhikṣu says to someone, "Do you recognize such-and-such an animal?
and the person replies:
"Recognize him.
"Go, seize, bind, beat, and kill him.
If a bhikṣu goes and seizes, binds, beats, or kills the person so commanded, he commits a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, there are three ways in which a bhikṣu takes the life of an animal and incurs a pāyattika:
first, by using that which has been formally accepted; second, by using that which has not been formally accepted; and third, by using that which has both been and has not been formally accepted.

Regarding the offense of inflicting injury: if a bhikṣu strikes an animal with his hand, or with his foot, head, or any other part of his body, intending to cause its death—if it dies, it is a pāyattika;
if it does not die immediately but later dies as a result, it is a pāyattika;
if it does not die immediately nor later die as a result, it is a dukkaṭa.

Regarding "not taking life by means of material objects": if a bhikṣu, using wood, tiles, stones, knives, spears, bows and arrows, or pieces of wood, white tin, lead, or pewter, hurls them from a distance at an animal with the intent to cause its death, it is a *pāyattika* offense if the animal dies;
if it does not die immediately but later dies as a result of this, it is also a *pāyattika* offense;
if it neither dies immediately nor later dies as a result of this, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

Regarding "striking those who have received or not yet received the precepts with physical objects": if one seizes wood, tiles, stones, knives, spears, bows, arrows, wooden blocks, or pieces of tin, lead, or pewter with the hand and strikes them with the intent to cause death, if they die, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they do not die immediately but later die as a result of this, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they do not die immediately nor later die as a result of this, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If a bhikṣu, whether with the intention of taking life or not, or with an intention neither to take nor not to take life, for the purpose of killing, places poison in the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, or in a wound on the body of an animal; or places it in food, drink, bedding, or walking areas, intending that they die—if they die, it is a pāyattika;
if they do not die immediately but later die as a result of this, it is also a pāyattika;
if they do not die immediately and do not die later as a result of this, it is a duṣkṛta.

If a bhikṣu, whether by means of taking life, not taking life, or both taking and not taking life, or by means of poison, for the purpose of killing, commits *uyuta*-killing, *thoda*-killing, killing with snares, nets, or *vidala* traps, *vidalābhāsa*-killing, killing by severing the life-force, killing by causing an abortion, killing by pressing on the abdomen, killing by casting into water or fire, or killing by casting into a pit; or if he sends someone along a path to die;

or even regarding the two faculties first received in the mother’s womb—the body faculty and the life faculty—if he employs a means therein, intending to cause death, then if the person dies, it is a *pāyattika*;
if they do not die immediately but later die because of this, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not die immediately, nor dies later as a result, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[The sixty-first case ends. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus quarreled and reviled the group of seventeen bhikṣus, their minds being in disharmony.

At that time, after the group of six bhikṣus had quarreled and reviled the group of seventeen bhikṣus, the group of six bhikṣus, wishing to cause the group of seventeen bhikṣus to feel doubt and regret, spoke as follows:

"You received full ordination when you were less than twenty years of age; if a person receives full ordination when they are less than twenty years of age, it is not called having obtained full ordination."
"If one does not obtain full ordination, one is neither a bhikṣu, nor a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
Having heard these words, that person became sorrowful, anxious, doubtful, and regretful, and wept.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Why are you weeping?
He replied:
"The group of six bhikṣus caused me to fall into doubt and regret, saying:
'We received full ordination when we were less than twenty years old; if one receives full ordination when less than twenty years old, it is not called having obtained full ordination.'"
"If one does not receive full ordination, one is neither a bhikṣu, nor a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
Hearing these words, we wept out of doubt and regret.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he rebuked them with various reasons:
"How can a bhikṣu intentionally cause another to fall into doubt and regret?
Having rebuked him with various reasons and circumstances, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the situation] already, he asked the group of six bhikṣus:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
“How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu intentionally cause another bhikṣu to feel doubt and regret?”
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu to feel doubt or regret, such that for even a moment his mind is not at peace, for this reason, there is no difference: it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation): it burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Within this, there are six matters concerning the offense:
first, birth; second, receiving full ordination; third, committing an offense; fourth, interrogation; fifth, objects; and sixth, the Dharma.
Regarding "birth": if a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu, "When were you born?
and the other replies:

"He was born during the time of such-and-such a king; he was born during the time of such-and-such a great minister; he was born during a time of abundance and joy, a time of famine and scarcity, a time of peace and security, or a time of illness."
He then spoke again:

"If a person was born during the time of a certain king, or at the time of a certain great minister, or during a period of abundance and joy, famine, peace and security, or pestilence, that person has not yet reached twenty years of age."
If a person is less than twenty years of age, they cannot receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If they do not receive full ordination, they are not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya.
If another bhikṣu becomes doubtful or regretful, whether such doubt or regret actually arises or not, it is a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu:
"When did hair grow beneath your armpits? it is a pāyattika offense.
"When will a beard grow upon your lips?
When will your throat appear?
If one says:
"During the time of such-and-such a king, during the time of such-and-such a minister, or during times of abundance and joy, famine, peace and security, or pestilence, he was born.
He then further said:

"If a person, during the time of such-and-such a king, during the time of such-and-such a minister, or during times of abundance and joy, famine, peace and security, or pestilence, has hair, a beard, or a visible Adam's apple, this person is not yet twenty years of age."
If a person who is not yet twenty years of age receives full ordination, it is not said that they have obtained full ordination.
If they do not obtain full ordination, they are not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya.
Whether doubt and regret arise or do not arise, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
This is called "arising.
Regarding one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), if a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu:
“When did you receive full ordination? He replied, “I received full ordination at the time of such-and-such a king,
at the time of such-and-such a great minister, or during times of abundance and joy, famine, peace and security, or pestilence.”
He then spoke again:

"If a person receives full ordination during the time of a certain king, during the time of a certain great minister, or during times of abundance and joy, famine, security, or epidemic, that person does not obtain full ordination."
"One who does not obtain full ordination is neither a bhikṣu, nor a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
Whether one conceives doubt or regret, or whether one does not, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu asked another bhikṣu:
"Who is your preceptor (upādhyāya) for full ordination?
Who is your teacher (ācārya)?"
"Who acts as the preceptor?
He replied,
"So-and-so acts as the upādhyāya, so-and-so acts as the ācārya, and so-and-so acts as the preceptor."
He then spoke again:
"If such-and-such acts as preceptor, such-and-such acts as ācārya, and such-and-such acts as instructor, that person is not said to have obtained full ordination."
"If one does not obtain full ordination, one is neither a bhikṣu, nor a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
Whether such doubt or regret arises or does not arise, it is all a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu asked another bhikṣu:
"Did you receive full ordination (upasaṃpadā) before a group of ten, or did you receive the complete precepts before a group of five?
He replied:
"In a group of ten," he then said again,
"if one receives full ordination within such a group of ten, that person does not obtain the full precepts."
"If one does not obtain full ordination, one is neither a bhikṣu, nor a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
Whether such doubt or regret arises or does not arise, it is all a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu asked another bhikṣu:
"Did you receive full ordination within the boundary (sīmā) or outside the boundary?
He replied:
"Receive it within the boundary.
He then spoke again:
"If one receives it within the boundary, this person does not obtain full ordination."
"If one does not obtain full ordination, they are not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya.
Whether doubt or regret arises, or whether it does not, it is all a pāyattika offense.
This is called the full ordination (upasampadā).
Regarding offenses: if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "You have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
you have committed a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta offense."
If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, this person is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya.
Whether doubt or regret arises, or does not arise, it is all a *pāyattika*.
This is called an offense.
Regarding "one who asks": if a bhikṣu asks another bhikṣu:

“Did you enter such-and-such a village, walk through such-and-such an alley, go to such-and-such a house, sit in such-and-such a place, converse with such-and-such a woman, go to such-and-such a bhikkhunī’s dwelling, and converse with such-and-such a bhikkhunī?”
He replied:

"I entered a certain village, walked through a certain lane, arrived at a certain house, sat in a certain place, conversed with a certain woman, went to a certain bhikṣuṇī’s quarters, and conversed with a certain bhikṣuṇī."
He then spoke again:

"If a bhikṣu enters a certain village, walks through a certain lane, arrives at a certain house, sits in a certain place, converses with a certain woman, goes to a certain bhikṣuṇī’s quarters, or converses with a certain bhikṣuṇī—this person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya."
Whether one gives rise to doubt and regret or does not, it is all a *pāyattika*.
This is called "inquiring.
Regarding "objects": if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"With whom do you share the same intent regarding the alms bowl?
With whom do you share the same intent regarding the robes, the needle case, the medicine for immediate use, the medicine for the night, the medicine for seven days, and the medicine for life?"
He replied,
“I share in common with him the bowl, robes, door-bolt, food for the time, food for the night, food for seven days, and food for life.”
He then spoke again:

"If a bhikṣu conspires with another to use their robes, bowls, door-latches, medicinal food for the time, medicinal food for the night, medicinal food for seven days, or medicinal food for life, that person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya."
Whether doubt or regret arises, or whether they do not arise, it is all a *pāyattika*.
This is called "the object.
Regarding "the rule": if a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:

"Do not possess many robes; do not eat frequently; do not eat apart from the community; do not enter another's house uninvited; do not enter a village at an improper time; and do not enter a town or village without wearing the saṃghāṭī."
If a bhikṣu replies,
“I have accepted the kaṭhina robe,” and then immediately says again:

"If a bhikṣu, at his own will, keeps many robes, eats repeatedly, eats apart from the community, enters another's house uninvited, enters a village at an improper time, or enters a town or village without wearing his saṃghāṭī—such a person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya."
Whether the doubt or regret arises or does not arise, it is all a *pāyattika*.
This is called the rule (*dharma*).
If a bhikṣu, by means of these six matters, causes another bhikṣu to feel doubt or regret, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If, setting aside these six matters, one causes another bhikṣu to feel doubt or regret by means of other matters, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, setting aside a bhikṣu and these six matters, one causes another person to feel doubt or regret by means of other causes and conditions, it is in all cases a duṣkṛta offense.
The sixty-second [case] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, among the seventeen groups of bhikṣus, there was a young lay child who enjoyed laughing.

Because the child enjoyed laughing, the seventeen groups of bhikṣus tickled him with their fingers; the child laughed so much that he became breathless, his hands and feet could no longer move, and he died.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus became doubtful,
thinking, "Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha asked the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
"With what intention did you do this?
They replied:
“I did it as a joke.
The Buddha said, “If that is so,
you have not committed the offense of killing.”
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu tickles another with his finger, it is a pāyattika.
A *pāyattika* means that which cooks, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu tickles another with one finger, it is one pāyattika.
With two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten fingers, there are ten pāyattikas.
If one strikes or prods another with wood or stone, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
[The sixty-third case ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a bathing pool with embankments built at various points.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus said to one another, "Let us go to the banks of the Ajiravatī River to bathe.

Among the seventeen bhikṣus, there was one who had attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and did not actually wish to go; however, he went for the sake of protecting the feelings of the others.

All the bhikṣus went to the bank of the Ajiravatī River, took off their robes, and entered the river to engage in various sports: some clapped the water with their hands, some submerged themselves upside down, some rolled like fish, some flailed their arms, some scooped up water with both hands, some with one hand, and some floated on their backs.
This bathing place could be seen from afar atop the king’s palace.
At that time, the king and Queen Mallikā were enjoying the pleasures of the five senses within the palace, while female musicians entertained them.
At that time, the king saw from afar the group of seventeen bhikṣus performing various kinds of play in the water, and he said to Queen Mallikā:
"These are those whom you hold in such high esteem, yet they engage in such various coarse frolics in the water."
The lady replied, "Why does Your Majesty say such a thing?
Look at this; he is merely a youth!"
"Why does the King not say:
'Look at Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha'?
At that time, those among them who had attained meditative concentration did not wash, but sat in meditation in a separate place; they heard these two words:
The King spoke and the Queen spoke.
Having heard this, he said to the other bhikṣus:
"Wash your own feet and do not wash them again; you should step onto the bank, put on your robes, fill your water-jars to the brim, place them before you, and sit cross-legged."
Having been thus instructed, they all immediately went up onto the bank, put on their robes, filled their water-jars, and placed them before them, then sat down cross-legged.

At that time, those who had attained meditative concentration used their supernormal powers to cause each of their water-jars to rise into the air in front of them, while the bhikṣus remained seated with eyes closed, following after them as they departed.
At that time, Queen Mallikā, having seen this, said to the king:
"This is one whom I hold in high esteem; he performs such acts even in places where Your Majesty cannot see him."
At that time, the lady immediately dispatched a messenger to the Buddha’s dwelling and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“This king constantly delights in exposing the faults and transgressions of the bhikṣus because of their bathing and playing in this water. I pray that you would cause the bhikṣus not to bathe in this place again.”
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the group of seventeen bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:

"What is meant by a bhikṣu performing various sports in the water—beating the water with his hands and submerging head-first, or rolling like a fish, or grasping the water with both hands, or with one hand, or floating face-upward?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it refers to boiling, burning, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Within this, there are eight types of offenses: first, causing joy; second, causing pleasure;
third, causing laughter; fourth, engaging in play; fifth, playing with water; sixth, causing another to feel joy; seventh, causing another to feel pleasure; eighth, causing another to laugh.
If a bhikṣu, desiring to make sport, strikes the water with his hand, it is a pāyattika.
If he submerges himself upside down in the water, or turns like a fish, or floats on one arm or two arms, or leaps up from the water, or floats face-upward, in all such cases it is a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, desiring to make music, laughter, or playful sport with water, for the sake of causing others to rejoice, to be happy, or to laugh, engages in such various kinds of frivolous play, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If there is water on a tray, or if there is water on a bed, and one draws with a finger upon it, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if one is learning to swim or crossing straight across.
The sixty-fourth [chapter] concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Aniruddha, traveling from Kośala toward Śrāvastī, arrived at a village where there was no monastery and wished to stay the night.
