The Eighty-sixth Matter. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, taught the Dharma to her, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening her; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened her, he remained silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had finished teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them with his Dharma discourse, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for tomorrow.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted through his silence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night.
That night, the Buddha was walking in the open air together with Ānanda. Observing the signs of the constellations, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Suppose someone who knows the signs of the constellations were asked today:
'When will it rain?'"
"He will surely say:
'It shall rain for seven years.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“When the first watch of the night has passed and it is the middle watch, these star-signs vanish and other signs appear.
If at that time someone asks a knower of signs,
‘When will it rain?’”
"He will surely say:
'It shall rain after seven months have passed.
He then spoke again to Ānanda:
"When the middle watch of the night has passed and the latter watch has arrived, these star-signs will vanish and other signs will appear.
If at that time one asks those who know the signs,
'When will it rain?'"
"He will surely say:
'It shall rain for seven days.

When that night had passed and the ground was dry, clouds emerged from the east, shaped like round bowls and filling the sky; these clouds were capable of producing a great rain that filled all the pits and hollows.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Tell the bhikṣus:
'This bowl-cloud rain possesses merit; it can eliminate illness.'"
"If any bhikṣus wish to wash, they should stand in the open air and wash.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, told the bhikṣus:
"This bowl has the merit of the rain-clouds; it can eliminate illness."
"If there are bhikṣus who wish to wash, they are permitted to stand and wash in the open air.
At that time, the bhikṣus stood and washed in the open air as they pleased.
Then, having prepared the food and drink, Visākhā Mṛgāramātā rose early to arrange the seating area and sent a maidservant to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come and the meal is prepared; the Buddha himself knows the proper time.

Having received these instructions, the maidservant went to the Jetavana Monastery. Not seeing any bhikṣus, she peered through a crack in the door and saw them naked, bathing in the open. Upon seeing this, her heart was not pleased, and she thought:
"There are no bhikṣus here at all; they are all naked heretics, shameless people."
Having thought this, he immediately returned and said to Visākhā Mṛgāramātā:
"Not a single bhikṣu is in the Jetavana; they are all naked ascetics."

Vishakha’s mother was wise and of sharp faculties; she knew that it was raining today and that the bhikṣus would surely be bathing naked in the open air. However, this maidservant was dull-witted and ignorant, so she spoke these words:
“There is not a single bhikṣu in the Jeta Grove; they are all naked heretics.”
She immediately called another maidservant to go to the Jeta Grove, knock on the gate, and announce:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared.
Having received these instructions, she departed, went to the Jeta Grove, knocked on the gate, and announced:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared. The Buddha himself knows the proper time.
Thereupon, the Buddha, together with the great assembly, put on his robes and took up his alms bowl, and surrounded by the monks, proceeded to the house.
The Buddha was seated among the Saṃgha. Viśākhā herself served the water for washing and personally offered him many kinds of delicious food and drink.

When he had finished eating, she again personally served the water for rinsing. Knowing that he had set aside his bowl, she took a small stool and sat before the Buddha to listen to the Dharma, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Grant me my wish.
The Buddha said:
"The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot grant you a wish that exceeds [the bounds of reality]."
Viśākhā said, "I wish to receive [this] favor.
The Buddha said:
"I shall grant you a wish; what wish do you desire?
Viśākhā replied, "First, I wish to provide rain-bathing robes for the community of bhikṣus."
Second, to provide bathing robes for the community of bhikṣuṇīs;
third, to provide food for visiting bhikṣus;
fourth, to provide food for bhikṣus traveling on distant journeys.
Fifth, I shall provide food and drink for sick bhikṣus.
Sixth, I shall provide food and drink for bhikṣus who are nursing the sick.
Seventh, I shall constantly provide gruel to the community of bhikṣus.
"Eighth, for bhikṣus who have many acquaintances or few acquaintances, I shall provide them with medicinal broths for the occasion of illness and whatever else they require.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason do you wish to give the saṃgha of bhikṣus rain-bathing robes?"
He replied:
"Venerable Sir!
This morning, after I had prepared the seats, I sent a maidservant to Jetavana to inform the Buddha that it was time."
The maidservant went to the gate and saw the bhikṣus bathing naked in the open air amidst the rain;
she returned and said, "There is not a single bhikṣu in the Jeta Grove, only these shameless followers of other paths."
"Venerable Sir!

A bhikṣu who stands naked before the Buddha, his preceptor (upādhyāya), his teacher (ācārya), and all the senior monks (sthavira) would be considered shameless. Therefore, I wish to provide the community of bhikṣus with rain-bathing robes so that they may bathe freely in the open air during the rains."
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide bathing robes for the community of bhikṣuṇīs?
She replied:
"Venerable Sir!
On one occasion, I went with several householder wives to bathe in the river Ajiravatī; at that time, some bhikṣuṇīs also entered the river and bathed naked."
When the wives of the lay devotees saw them, they were displeased and rebuked them, saying:
"These people have meager merit and are inauspicious; with coarse bodies, large bellies, and sagging breasts, what use is there in practicing the holy life?"
"Venerable Sir!
A woman’s naked form is ugly and loathsome; for this reason, I wish to give her a bathing robe.
"Viśākhā! [the Buddha replied.]
"For what reason do you wish to provide food and drink to the visiting bhikṣus?
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
When visiting bhikṣus arrive, they do not know where it is permissible or impermissible to go,
and they are utterly exhausted from the road without having found rest. Therefore,
after providing them with food and drink, I wish for them to proceed according to their knowledge of where it is permissible or impermissible to go.
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to give food to the bhikṣu who is traveling far?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!

When a bhikṣu traveling on a long journey waits for the time of the *taṭṭaka* meal, if he goes out to beg for alms, his companions may abandon him; or he may enter dangerous paths at night, or travel alone through the wilderness. Because I give him food, he does not lose his companions nor enter dangerous paths; for this reason, I provide him with food and drink.”
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to give food and drink to the sick bhikṣu?
She replied:
"Venerable Sir!

If a sick bhikṣu does not receive food and drink appropriate to his illness, his ailment will be difficult to cure; therefore, I am giving him food and drink appropriate to his illness so that his ailment may be easily cured."
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide food and drink to the monk who is tending to the sick?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!
If the monk who attends to the sick waits for the meal after the community has finished eating, or if he goes out to beg for alms, the duties of caring for that sick monk will be neglected.”

If one cooks rice, makes porridge, prepares soups, boils fish or meat, decocts medicinal broths, or handles the impure vessels for excrement and urine, as well as the vessel for spitting—therefore, I provide food and drink to the attendant bhikṣu so that his care and support are never lacking;
thus he may cook rice, make porridge, prepare soups, boil meat, decoct medicinal broths, and handle the vessels for excrement and urine, as well as the vessel for spitting.
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide rice gruel for the community of bhikṣus constantly?
She replied:
"Venerable Sir!
If a bhikṣu does not eat gruel, he may suffer from hunger and thirst, or wind may arise within his belly; because I constantly provide him with gruel, he is free from such afflictions."
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide medicinal broths and necessary items for the sake of illness to both well-known and little-known bhikṣus?”
He replied:
"The sick bhikṣu certainly required various items for medicinal decoctions; for this reason, I gave them to him.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikṣu has died at such-and-such a residence, and the Buddha has declared that this bhikṣu has severed the three fetters and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, will not fall into the evil realms, and will certainly attain *nirvāṇa* after wandering at most seven times among gods and humans until all suffering is exhausted.
"Venerable sir!
I shall ask:
'Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?'"
"If I hear that this bhikṣu has previously come to Śrāvastī, I reflect:

'This elder may have accepted my rain-bathing robe, or food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, or food and drink for those traveling from afar, or food and drink for those who are ill, or food and drink for those attending the sick, or the daily rice-gruel, or medicinal decoctions and various requisites for a sick bhikṣu.'"
"Venerable sir!
It is for this reason that my mind of awakening is fulfilled.
Venerable sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikṣu has died at such-and-such a residence, and the Buddha has declared that this bhikṣu has exhausted the three fetters, thinned the three poisons, and attained the stage of sakṛdāgāmin—one who returns once more to this world to bring an end to suffering—then [I know he has attained it].
I shall ask:
"Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?
If I hear that this bhikṣu has indeed come to Śrāvastī.
"Venerable Sir!
I have reflected thus:

'This elder may accept my rain-bath robe, or accept food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, or food and drink for those traveling from afar, or food and drink for the sick, or food and drink for those nursing the sick, or the daily rice-gruel, or medicinal decoctions and various requisites for a sick bhikṣu.'"
"Venerable sir!
It is for this reason that my mind of awakening is fulfilled,
venerable sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikṣu has died at such-and-such a residence, and that the Buddha has declared that bhikṣu to have attained the stage of Anāgāmin—having exhausted the five lower fetters—and that he will attain parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms without returning to this world.
"Venerable sir!
I shall ask:
'Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?'"
"If I hear that this bhikṣu has previously come here, I reflect:

'This elder may have accepted my rain-bathing robe, or the food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, or food for those traveling from afar, or food for the sick, or food for those nursing the sick, or perhaps he regularly received rice gruel, medicinal decoctions, and various requisites for sick bhikṣus.'"
"Venerable sir!
It is for this reason that my awakening-mind is fulfilled.
Venerable sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikkhu has died at a particular residence, and the Buddha has declared that bhikkhu to have attained arhatship—knowing for himself: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I have realized it for myself"—[then I am satisfied].
I shall ask:
"Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?
If I hear that this bhikṣu has indeed come here before, I will reflect:

"This elder has either accepted my rain-bathing robe, or he has accepted food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, food and drink for those traveling on distant journeys, food and drink for those according to their illnesses, food and drink for those attending to the sick, or he has constantly provided gruel, medicinal decoctions, and various requisites for sick bhikṣus."
"Because of these causes and conditions, my awakening-mind is fulfilled.
Venerable Sir!
Thus, having accomplished wealth and merit, I gather the merit of the Dharma through these causes and conditions."
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā!”
I have heard these vows of yours:

that you provide rain-bathing robes for the community of bhikṣus, bathing robes for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, food and drink for bhikṣus traveling from afar, food and drink for bhikṣus according to their illnesses, food and drink for bhikṣus attending to the sick, regular rice gruel for the community of bhikṣus, and medicinal decoctions and various requisites for bhikṣus who are well-known or unknown, depending on their illness.
"Viśākhā! This is the accomplishment of wealth and merit; by these causes and conditions, one gathers the merit of the Dharma.
Having taught Viśākhā various causes and conditions, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her, the Buddha rose from his seat and departed.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to keep rain-bathing robes and to wash them at will in the open air."
When those bhikṣus learned that the Buddha had permitted the keeping of rain-bathing robes, they made them wide and long and large.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and censured it for various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that the Buddha has permitted the keeping of rain-bathing robes, make them so wide, long, and large?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, knowing that I have permitted the keeping of a rain-bath robe, makes it wide and long and keeps such a large one?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu wishes to make a rain-bath robe, he must make it according to the prescribed measurements.

As for the measurements: the length shall be six spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width two and a half spans. Should he make it exceeding these dimensions, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking," "burning," and "obstructing"; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe that exceeds the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes it wider than the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes it both longer and wider than the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe that exceeds the prescribed length and width, that robe must be cut down, and he must enter the Saṃgha and speak as follows:
"I have made a rain-bathing robe that exceeds the prescribed measurements for length and width; I have committed a *pāyattika* offense and now confess it without concealment.
The Saṃgha should ask:
"Have you cut it down?"
If he says, "It has been cut," the Saṃgha should ask:
"Do you see your transgression?
If he says, "I see my transgression," [the procedure continues].
One should say to them:
"Repent according to the Dharma; do not commit it again in the future.
If they say:
"If it has not been cut," the Sangha should issue an instruction to have it cut.
If the Sangha does not issue such an instruction, the Sangha incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Saṃgha issues a formal injunction and he does not accept it, that bhikṣu commits a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding the eighty-seventh matter: when the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the soil was salty and damp, and many bhikṣus suffered from boils and sores.
There was a bhikṣu whose wound was discharging pus and blood, which stained his *antarvāsaka* as if it had been soaked in water.
The Buddha saw him from afar; knowing the situation, he nevertheless asked that bhikṣu:
"Why have you stained your *antarvāsaka* with pus and blood?"
The bhikṣu replied, "Venerable sir!
I am suffering from an ulcerous sore; pus and blood are flowing out and defiling my antaravāsaka."

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit you to keep a wound-covering cloth to wear for up to ten days after the wound has healed. If you keep it beyond this period, it is a pāyattika offense."
When the bhikṣus learned that the Buddha had permitted the keeping of wound-covering robes, they made them wide and long and large.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and censured them in various ways:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that the Buddha has permitted the keeping of wound-covering robes, make them wide, long, and large?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that I have permitted the keeping of a wound-covering robe, make it so wide and long?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu wishes to make a garment for covering sores, he must make it according to the prescribed measure.
The measure is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width; if he makes it exceeding these dimensions, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means to boil, burn, cover, and obstruct; if one does not repent for the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores that exceeds the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes it wider than the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes it both wider and longer than the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores wider and longer than the prescribed measure, that garment should be cut down, and he should enter the Saṃgha and speak these words:
"I have made a wound-covering cloth that is excessively large in length and breadth; I have committed a *pāyattika* offense.
I now confess this transgression and do not conceal it.

These are the eighty-eighth matters; at that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the bhikṣus had soiled their bedding with semen; having risen early, they were washing it and drying it in the doorway of the vihāra.
Before midday, the Buddha, having dressed and taken his bowl, entered the city to beg for food, and saw those impure, soiled beddings being washed and dried in the doorway.
After the meal, the Buddha gathered the community of bhikṣus for this matter and said to them:

"Today before noon, I put on my robes, took my bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. I saw that the bedding and mats of the bhikṣus were stained with semen; they had risen early to wash them and were drying them in the gateway of the vihāra."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"This should not be so. The monastic community uses bedding and requisites in excessive amounts without moderation; thus, the flesh and blood of the lay devotees are withered away as they give alms to cultivate merit."
In this regard, it is good to exercise moderation in one's use.
If a bhikṣu sleeps with distracted thoughts and a lack of single-mindedness, there are five faults.
What are these five?

First is the suffering of difficulty falling asleep; second is the suffering of difficulty waking up; third is seeing evil dreams; fourth is the failure of benevolent deities to protect one while sleeping; and fifth is the difficulty of the mind entering into wholesome contemplation when awake.
If a bhikṣu sleeps with undistracted mindfulness and one-pointed concentration, there are five beneficial qualities.
What are these five?

First, he sleeps without difficulty; second, he awakens easily; third, he has no evil dreams; fourth, while sleeping, he is protected by benevolent deities; and fifth, upon waking, his mind readily enters into wholesome contemplation and observation of the Dharma.

If a bhikṣu possesses lust, anger, and delusion and has not yet attained freedom from desire, he does not even lose his vital essence while sleeping with an undistracted and one-pointed mind; how much less so when he is free from desire?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to possess a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), for the sake of protecting the monastic bedding. One must not sit or lie down upon the monastic bedding without having spread a *niṣīdana* over it."
When the bhikṣus learned that the Buddha had permitted the possession of a *niṣīdana*, they made them wide and long, and produced them on a large scale.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the *dhūta* austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked them:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that the Buddha has permitted the possession of a *niṣīdana*, yet make it wide, long, and large, and keep such a one?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he said to the bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu know that I have permitted the possession of a *niṣīdana*, yet nevertheless make it wide and long and keep such a large one?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana*, he should make it according to the prescribed measure. As for the measure:
it is two *vitasti* of the Buddha’s span in length and one and a half *vitasti* in width. Should he make it exceeding these dimensions, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means "cooking, burning, covering, and obstructing"; if one does not repent for the offense, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) that exceeds the prescribed measurement in length, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes it wider than the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one makes it longer than the prescribed measure, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu has made a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) exceeding the prescribed width and length, he should cut it down and then address the Saṃgha, saying:
"I have made a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) exceeding the prescribed measurements in length and breadth, and thus incurred a *pāyattika* offense.
I now confess this transgression and do not conceal it.
The Saṃgha should then ask:
"Has it been cut off yet?
If he says, "It has been cut."
The Saṃgha should ask:
"Do you see your offense? If he says:
"Recognize your offense.
One should instruct them, saying:
"Now you have repented according to the Dharma; do not commit it again hereafter."
If it has not yet been cut, the Saṃgha should issue an instruction to have it cut.
If the Saṃgha does not issue such an instruction, it incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If the Saṃgha issues the instruction and the bhikṣu does not comply, that bhikṣu incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, before the midday meal, the Buddha put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having finished eating, he went into the Andhavana forest, spread out a sitting mat beneath a tree, and sat down.
The Elder Kālodāyin also entered the Andhavana forest and, not far from the Buddha, spread out his *niṣīdana* beneath a tree and sat down.
This elder was tall and large of stature; his two knees touched the ground and he had to grasp his robe with both hands as he made this vow:
"When will the Buddha allow us to make *niṣīdana*s of one span (*vitasti*) according to the Buddha’s measure, so that they may be complete?"
In the afternoon, the Buddha arose from meditation and, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Today at mealtime, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. After eating, I entered the Andhavana forest and spread out my sitting mat beneath a tree to sit."
Kālodāyin returned from his almsround and sat beneath a tree, reflecting thus:
"Where is the Buddha currently practicing the path?
I, too, shall practice the path in that same place."
At that time, I entered the Andhavana forest and spread out my *niṣīdana* beneath a tree to sit; Kālodāyin did likewise.
This son of good family was large of stature, his two knees touching the ground, and he made this vow:
"When will the Buddha allow us to make a *niṣīdana* of one span (*vitasti*) for the sake of a Buddha, so that it may be thus complete?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu wishes to make a niṣīdana, he must make it according to the prescribed measurements.'"
Regarding the measurements: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hand, the width one and a half spans, with an additional span for the seam of the threads.
Should one make it exceeding these dimensions, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the eighty-ninth matter: The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

At that time, there was the Elder Nanda, who was the Buddha’s younger brother, born of his maternal aunt. He resembled the Buddha in physical form and possessed thirty of the marks of a great man; he was only four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha.

At that time, Nanda made robes the same size as those of the Buddha. When the bhikṣus were at their mealtime or attending an assembly, they would see Nanda coming from afar and, thinking he was the Buddha, all rose to greet him, saying:
"Our Great Teacher is coming!"
“World-Honored One, please come.
Only upon his arrival did they realize it was not he.
All the senior elders felt ashamed and reflected thus:
"This is our junior; why should we rise to greet him?
Nanda was also ashamed and said, "This will cause all the senior elders to rise and greet me."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Nanda:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu make robes according to the same measurements as the Buddha’s?
From now on, your robes should be made smaller; this kāṣāya should be used for spreading out and drying."
"O Bhikṣus!
You have spread out and dried Nanda’s robe; there are others like him as well, and the Saṃgha should likewise act with one mind to spread them out and dry them.
He spoke thus to the Bhikṣus.
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to the Buddha’s robe or exceeds that size, he commits a pāyattika offense.'"
As for the measurement of a Buddha’s robe: it is nine spans long and six spans wide; this is the measurement of a Buddha’s robe. Regarding the *pāyattika*:
it is that which boils, burns, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu makes a robe the same size as the Buddha’s robe, it is a pāyattika.
If he makes one exceeding the size of the Buddha’s robe, it is a pāyattika.
For every such act, one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were acts.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe the same size as the Buddha’s robe, that robe must be cut down, and he should go before the Saṃgha and declare:
"I have committed a *pāyattika* offense by making a robe the size of the Buddha’s robe."
"I now confess my transgression and do not conceal it.
The Sangha should ask:
"Have you cut it off?"
If they say, "It has already been cut," one should ask:
"Do you see your fault?
If he says, "I see my fault," [the procedure continues].
The Saṃgha should say:
"You have now repented according to the Dharma; do not commit it again in the future. If he says:
"If it has not been cut," the Sangha should issue an order for it to be cut.
If the Sangha does not issue such an order, the Sangha incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Sangha issues a formal injunction and [the monk] does not accept it, this bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The ninety matters are concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 18.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 19. The sixth section of the Third Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Section 6: The Four Pāṭidesanīya Dharmas. Regarding the Four Pāṭidesanīya Dharmas:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a famine in the world. The bhikṣuṇī Huase was virtuous, possessed of great knowledge and extensive learning, and was able to obtain in abundance clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other necessary items.
This bhikṣuṇī rose early in the morning, donned her robes, took up her alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, she saw the assembly of bhikṣus who had been unable to obtain any food while begging in Śrāvastī, and they were distressed and unhappy.
This bhikṣuṇī looked into the bowls of the bhikṣus; if they had little, she gave them a little; if they had half, she gave them half; if they had nothing at all, she gave them everything.
Whatever this bhikṣuṇī obtained from her almsround in a single day, she gave it all to the bhikṣus.
After two or three days in this manner, because she had obtained no food, she collapsed in the street, fainting from exhaustion.
A merchant saw her and said to his wife, "The bhikṣuṇī Puṣpacitrā has fallen in the street; help her up and bring her here."
The wife immediately went to support him up and bring him into the house; she quickly prepared a gruel of parched grain and gave it to him, whereby he regained consciousness.
She asked him, "What ailment do you suffer from?"
"What illness do you have?
Why have you fallen to the ground in such haste in the street?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"I am without illness, without pain, and without distress.
However, because I have not obtained food, I have become dazed and fallen to the ground in the alleyway.
He asked again:
“Were you unable to obtain alms? He replied, “I did obtain alms;
however, because the great assembly was unable to obtain alms while begging in Śrāvastī, they were distressed and unhappy.”
I observed the alms bowls of the bhikṣus: when there was little, they gave a little; when there was half, they gave half; and when there was nothing at all, they gave nothing at all.
Thus, for two or three days, I went without food; consequently, I became dazed and fell to the ground in the alleyway.
When the laypeople heard of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know the proper time nor the proper measure. If the giver does not know the measure, the receiver should certainly know it."
"The bhikṣuṇī Huāshè has nearly died because she fasted.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them:
"How can those called bhikṣus fail to know the proper time and fail to know moderation?"
"If the donor does not know moderation, the recipient should know moderation.
This Bhikṣuṇī Huase has nearly died because she fasted.
Having rebuked her with various reasons and causes, he said to the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu who is not ill enters a village and receives food with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, that bhikṣu must confess this offense to another bhikṣu.'"
"Elder! I have fallen into a blameworthy state, which is improper; this is a dharma that must be confessed. I now disclose and repent of my transgression.
This is called a *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
As for "the sick," it refers to those with a predominance of wind, heat, or cold; when they eat this food and are cured, this is called "sickness.
Apart from these conditions, it is called "not being sick."

Regarding "those who are not relatives": a relative is defined as one's mother, daughter, sister, or even those connected by kinship up to the seventh generation; these are called relatives. Those other than these are not relatives.
Excluding these is what is called a non-relative.
Regarding "food," there are five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods), five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and five kinds of similar foods.
The five *khādaniya* foods are: roots, stalks, leaves, flour-based preparations, and fruits.
The five *pūjaniya* foods are: cooked rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, and meat.
The five *pratirūpaka* (similar) foods are: congee, millet, wild barley, *yau* seeds, and *kāśa* grass.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu who is not ill enters a village and receives staple food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, he incurs a *pratideśanīya* offense.
Eating the stalks, leaves, flour, or fruits;
eating rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, or meat;
or eating gruel, millet, wild rice, oats, or *kāśa* grass seeds—all constitute a *pāyattika* offense.

There is no offense if it is given to one who is ill, or to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, or if it is given in a temple, or in a place where many people are gathered, or in a dwelling place of śramaṇas, or in a bhikṣuṇī’s quarters outside the village. In these cases, there is no offense.
1. Once, when the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha of the two divisions for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, the householder prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. He returned to his own home and prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink; having spread out seats in the early morning, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha that the time had come, saying:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know the proper time."
The Buddha then entered the householder’s residence with the two divisions of the Saṃgha and sat down.
Once the Buddha and the Saṃgha were seated, the householder personally served water for washing and was about to set down the food.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta; for the sake of the group of six bhikṣus, she instructed the donors, saying:
"This is the foremost elder, this is the second elder, this one is a master of the Vinaya, and this one is a Dharma teacher; give rice to these bhikṣus and give soup to these bhikṣus."
The laypeople said,
"We do not know who is the first elder and who is the second elder."
"Who is the master of the Vinaya?
Who is the Dharma teacher?
There is plenty of food and drink here; you should distribute it to everyone."
"Do not engage in idle chatter; if you do so, you shall go and eat by yourselves while we remain here.
The Buddha saw from afar that the bhikṣuṇīs were engaging in such idle behavior and heard the reproaches of the lay devotees.
After the meal, for this reason, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and, by means of various reasons, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus eat food given at the instigation of a bhikṣuṇī?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
There were some bhikṣus who had been invited to a meal at the home of a layperson. Among them, a bhikṣuṇī pointed out, saying:
"Give rice to this bhikṣu; give soup to that bhikṣu."
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Wait a moment!
Wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If, among all the bhikṣus, not a single bhikṣu says to that bhikṣuṇī, "Wait a moment!
Wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating," then all those bhikṣus should say to another bhikṣu:
"Elder! We have fallen into a censurable state that is improper.
This matter is subject to repentance; we now disclose it and confess our transgression."
"This is called a *pāṭidesanīya* dharma. Regarding the offense herein:
if a bhikṣu accepts food from the instruction of a bhikṣuṇī and receives it, he incurs a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.
According to what she receives [the instruction], she incurs as many *pāṭidesanīya* offenses as there are [instances].
If the two divisions of the Saṃgha are seated together, if even one person among one division speaks to this bhikṣuṇī, the second division is also said to have spoken.
If they enter separately, sit separately, eat separately, and depart separately, the bhikṣu who enters the gate of the donor therein should ask the departing bhikṣu:
"Which bhikṣuṇī instructed the donor here to give food to the bhikṣus?"
He should reply, "I am so-and-so.
Then one should ask:
"Have you given the instructions? He replied,
"I have already given the instructions."
This entry for a bhikṣu is also called "injunction.
When there are bhikṣus exiting through a city gate, if there is a bhikṣu entering, they should question the one who is exiting.
If the one who has gone out has not given instructions, the one who enters should give instructions.
If the one who has gone out has already given instructions, the one who enters is also considered to have given instructions.
These two rules were established by the Buddha while he was at Vaiśālī.

At that time, there was an elephant trainer named Śūra, who was wealthy, noble, and possessed of majestic power; he abounded in riches and treasures, and was fully endowed with people, fields, and houses of every kind.

This person takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Sangha; having seen the Four Noble Truths and attained the initial path, they delight in the giving of donors and cannot measure its value.

This person receives a monthly stipend of one thousand coins from the government treasury; yet, even if he uses it all for almsgiving and other expenditures, his possessions cannot suffice, and his wife and children suffer from hunger and deprivation.
The laypeople rebuked them in anger, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know the proper time and do not know moderation.
If the giver does not know moderation, the receiver ought to know it."

This Śūla, the elephant trainer, was originally very wealthy with abundant possessions; yet, giving without moderation, he could not provide for their needs, leaving his wife and children in extreme hunger and destitution—a truly pitiable sight.
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked those bhikṣus:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu neither know the proper time nor know moderation?"
If the donor does not know the proper measure, the recipient should know it.

This elephant trainer Śūra, because he was fond of giving to donors but could not gauge the amount, gave [the food] away; how then could he provide for the hunger and deprivation of his wife and children?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"You all shall perform the *kula-karman* (formal act concerning a family) against Śūra, the elephant trainer; no bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī shall enter this household and receive food with their own hands."
If there are further such individuals within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should likewise perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of granting training) for them.
Regarding the *śikṣādattaka-karman*: the Saṃgha, being united with a single mind, one bhikṣu shall proclaim within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

When the Śūla elephant trainer’s family is a *śaikṣa-kula* (a family under training), no bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī may enter this family and receive food with their own hands.

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha graciously listen: the Saṃgha shall perform the *karmavācanā* of a "family under training" (*śikṣamāṇa-kula*) for the householder Śūra; no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs shall enter this household to receive food with their own hands.
"Thus it is announced.
Thus is the formal motion with one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
"The Saṃgha has completed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the elephant trainer Śūra. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such!"

When Śūra, the elephant trainer, heard that the Saṃgha had performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* against him, he thought: "No bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs shall enter my house to receive food with their own hands."
Having heard this, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that the Buddha will grant me the revocation of the *karmavācanā* for being a family under restriction.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Perform the ritual for revoking the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the householder Śūra.
If there are others who beg like the householder Śūra, you should likewise revoke it for them."

Regarding the procedure for relinquishing [the offense]: The harmonious Saṃgha being gathered with one mind, the householder Śūra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, joined his palms, and addressed them, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

"I, the householder Śūra, gave alms in measureless abundance, yet I was unable to provide for the hunger and deprivation of my wife and children. For this reason, the Saṃgha has performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (formal act of declaring a family under training) against me; therefore, no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs shall enter my house to receive food with their own hands."

I now beg the Sangha for the revocation of the *karmavācanā* regarding the household under probation, so that the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs may enter my house and receive food with their own hands as they did before.
In this manner, he should request a second and a third time.
The Saṃgha should deliberate on whether it is appropriate to relinquish [the property] or not.
If Śūra, the elephant trainer, suffers a loss of wealth and his resources do not increase, then whether he requests it or not, it should not be relinquished.
If the householder Śūra’s wealth increases, he should give and relinquish it whether asked for or not.
If Śūra the elephant trainer’s wealth neither increases nor decreases, then he should relinquish it if asked, but not if not asked.
Among them, one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This elephant trainer, Śūra, was formerly a donor who gave gifts without moderation, such that he could not provide for the hunger and deprivation of his wife and children."

For this reason, the Saṃgha performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* against him; consequently, no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs may enter this householder's dwelling to receive food with their own hands.

Now this Śūra, the elephant trainer, requests from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *karmavācanā* regarding the household under probation, saying: "Just as it was originally for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, please allow me to receive food with my own hands."

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the *karmavācanā* of relinquishing the household for Śūra the elephant trainer, so that—as previously permitted—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs may enter his house and receive food with their own hands."
"It is announced thus.
This is the formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

"The Saṃgha has completed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the ritual for granting training) for the householder Śūra, suspending his household from its status as a lay supporter. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'There are families who have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act (karmavācanā) of being designated as "families under training" (śaikṣakula). If a bhikṣu, having not been previously invited by such a family, later goes there and receives food with his own hands, that bhikṣu must confess his offense to another bhikṣu.'"
He speaks thus:
"Venerable sir!
I have fallen into a blameworthy state, which is improper; this matter is subject to repentance."
"I now confess and repent my transgression.
This is called the *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
Regarding "a family of noble lineage" (*kula*), it refers to those who have attained the first stage of the Path.
Regarding the *śikṣā-karman* (act of training): it is when the Saṃgha performs the *śikṣā-karman* against this household.

"Previously uninvited" means that after the household had not previously invited them, they later personally received food themselves—namely, the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods), the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and the five kinds of similar foods.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, while in a family home where he has not been previously invited, later arrives and receives food with his own hands, and accepts staple foods, he commits a *pratideśanīya* offense.

Stems, leaves, flour, fruits, cooked rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, meat, porridge, millet, *kaṇa* grain, wheat, *yava* grass seeds, and *kāśī* food—all these constitute *pāṭidesanīya* offenses.
According to how much one receives with one's own hand, one incurs that many *pātideśanīya* offenses.
Regarding the three rules: when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, at the time of the evening meal, the Śākyas saw that the food was fragrant and delicious, and they thought:
"We should not consume such excellent food and drink alone; why do we not set aside portions for the Buddha and the Saṃgha?"
Having formed this thought, she set aside her portion of the evening meal for the sake of the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

When the day had ended, the women of the Śākya clan adorned themselves with fine jewels and, carrying excellent food and drink, approached the monastery with loud voices and boisterous laughter, saying:
"The Buddha shall first eat my food."
He also said, "May the Buddha first partake of my food, so that I may obtain benefit and peace for a long night.
At that time, there was a thief in the Nyagrodha Grove who, having previously committed an offense, had been expelled and entered this forest; he carried weapons and lay there surrounded by them.
However, the bandit leader did not lie down; hearing the sound of people's voices, he said to the bandits, "All of you, rise!
Take up your swords, shields, bows, and arrows. Gather your property in one place, lest we be surrounded by the power of the king and the power of the village and suffer great distress."
All these people rose and, as they had been instructed, took up their swords, shields, bows, and arrows, and gathered their wealth and goods in one place.
The bandit leader said:
"Wait a moment!"
"I shall go to see who this person is.
He then stood among the trees and heard the voices of people on the road; hearing them speak with the voices of śramaṇas, he asked, "Who are you?"
They replied, “We are women of the Śākya clan;

having adorned our bodies with fine jewels and carrying excellent food and drink, we have come toward the monastery and entered the Nyagrodha grove. The Buddha shall now first eat our food, and through this, we shall obtain benefit and peace for a long night.”
The leader of the bandits immediately returned and said to the other bandits, "Now we have succeeded; let us simply rise and take them.
They asked:
"What is it? He replied:
"The women of the Śākya clan, their bodies adorned with exquisite jewels, carrying fine food and drink, have entered the Nyagrodha Grove."
Immediately, the bandits all rose up; having stripped them of their clothing until they were naked, they released them.

Thus the report spread through the cities and villages that wicked bandits had stripped the women of the Śākyas, leaving them naked and gone. Thereupon, by means of official power and the strength of the local communities, they surrounded and captured the bandits.
At that time, the women were standing there naked. The group of six bhikṣus went to them and said:
"This food is fragrant and delicious; give some to us. This food is even more excellent; give some to us as well."
At that time, the women rebuked them in anger, saying, "It is not that you do not care for us at all;
you simply have no concern for our being naked, but only think of obtaining this food.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Take the robes from among them and give one robe to each of the women.
Ānanda replied:
"So be it," she replied.
She then took the garments from her bundle and gave one to each of the women.

Once the women had put them on, she took the food into the monastery and struck the *gandī* bell to provide the monks with their portion of food; she then sat before the Buddha to listen to his teaching of the Dharma.

When the Buddha saw that the women were seated, he instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them through various causes and conditions. Having thus instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, he remained silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, the women prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after the women had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can those who are called bhikṣus receive food with their own hands inside the monastery when they have not received a formal instruction from the Saṃgha not to do so outside the monastery?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
There is a community of monks dwelling in a forest hermitage who experience doubt, fear, and apprehension.

If a monk knows that this forest hermitage is subject to such danger and has not been designated by the Saṃgha as a place where one may receive food outside the monastery precincts, yet he receives food within the monastery precincts with his own hands, that monk should confess his offense to another monk, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state that is not appropriate; this matter is subject to confession.
I now disclose and repent of my transgression.
This is called the *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.
Regarding the "forest hermitage" (*āraṇyaka-sthāna*): it is five hundred *dhanus* from a village, which is one *krośa* in the kingdom of Magadha, but half a *krośa* in northern countries.
"Doubt" refers even to doubting the loss of a single water vessel.
"Fear" refers herein even to the fear of wicked bhikṣus.
"The Saṃgha has not yet appointed" means that the Saṃgha has not yet unanimously appointed this person.
"Outside the monastery grounds" refers to the area outside the walls of the monastery, or outside its fences, or outside its moats.
"Inside the monastery grounds" refers to the area within the walls of the monastery, or within its fences, or within its moats.
Regarding "food," there are five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods), five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and five kinds of similar foods.

Among these, as for the offense: if a monk has not yet been appointed by the Sangha [as a distributor], and that person receives root-food with their own hands outside the monastery precincts but then consumes it inside the monastery precincts, they incur a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.

Regarding stems, leaves, flour, fruit, cooked rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, meat, gruel, millet, wild rice, oats, weeds, and *kāśa* grass—[if one eats these as food], it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
One incurs as many *pāṭidesanīya* offenses as there are morsels received with one's own hand.
From now on, the Saṃgha should perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint a person to oversee the food. With the Saṃgha in harmony and of one mind, one bhikṣu should ask:
"Who is able to serve as the overseer of food for the Saṃgha?"
If someone says, "I am able," yet possesses five qualities,
they should not be appointed as the person in charge of food:
If one follows desire, follows hatred, follows fear, follows delusion, or lacks knowledge of what exists and what does not exist—
if these five qualities are present— one should not be appointed as a supervisor of food. However, if one possesses five qualities— namely, not following desire,
not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what exists and what does not exist— one should be appointed as a supervisor of food.
Among them, one bhikṣu announces in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so is capable of acting as the distributor of food."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let monk so-and-so serve as the distributor of food.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Thus the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) is performed.
“Bhikṣu so-and-so has finished acting as the distributor of food; the Saṃgha consents, for it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld!

Once a bhikṣu has received the formal authorization (*karmavācanā*) of the Saṃgha, if that bhikṣu perceives that a thief has entered among them, he should bring a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and stand in their midst.
If, while inside, one sees someone who resembles a thief, one should take this food and say to those carrying the food:
"Do not come in; there is someone here who resembles a thief."
"If it is a person carrying food who comes by force, there is no offense.

The four rules are concluded. 7. Explaining the One Hundred and Seven Rules of Training (Śaikṣa-dharmas). Regarding the initial explanation of the One Hundred and Seven Rules of Training: At one time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarments) extremely high, extremely low, unevenly, or without them being properly aligned.
Having seen this, the Buddha thought:
"I should observe how the Buddhas of the past wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*."
The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven in the sky said:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddhas of the past all wore the nivāsana robes with even hems; the Buddha himself also remembers that the Buddhas of the past all wore the nivāsana robes with even hems.”
The Buddha again thought:
"I should observe how the Buddhas of the future put on their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
Then, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven spoke from mid-air:
“World-Honored One!

The Buddhas of the future will all wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes with even hems; the Buddha also perceives and knows that the Buddhas of the future shall likewise wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes with even hems.”
The Buddha again had this thought:
"I shall look upon the Śuddhāvāsa devas; how should I put on my inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī)?
A deity in the sky said:
“The Śuddhāvāsa devas were all wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes.
The Buddha also knew for himself that the Śuddhāvāsa devas were all wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the bhikṣus:
"What is meant by a bhikṣu wearing his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) too high, too low, unevenly, or not level?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) too high.
If a bhikṣu wears it too high, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he does not wear it too high, there is no offense.
First, one should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) too low.
If one wears the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* too low, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not wear it too low, there is no offense.
One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* unevenly.
To wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* unevenly is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* unevenly is not an offense.
Third: One should train oneself to wear the nivāsana (undergarment) like the head of a wood-chisel.
To wear the nivāsana unlike the head of a wood-chisel is a duṣkṛta offense.
Not wearing it like the head of a wood-chisel does not constitute an offense.
Fourth: One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) like an elephant’s trunk.
To wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* like an elephant’s trunk is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not wearing it like an elephant’s trunk does not constitute an offense.
One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* like a palm leaf;
to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* like a palm leaf is a *duṣkṛta*.
It is not as good as wearing a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) with many *tāla*-leaves; one does not commit an offense.
One should train thus:
it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) to wear a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with a ball of roasted grain (*saktu-piṇḍa*).
It is better to wear it like a ball of flour; thus one does not commit an offense.
Seventh: One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with fine pleats at the front.
If one wears the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with fine pleats at the front, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one wears the inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī) without fine pleats, there is no offense.
One should train not to wear the inner robe with a loose hem;
to wear the inner robe with a loose hem is a duṣkṛta offense.
One must not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) with the edges tucked in;
there is no offense [if one does so]. Ninth: One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with both edges tucked together.
If one wears the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with both edges tucked together, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
One should train oneself not to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with both edges pleated together; this is one of the ten rules for not wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with fine thread.
If one wears the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with fine thread, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not wear a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) with fine thread;
there is no offense [if it is coarse]. One should train oneself to wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with its hems even all around.
To wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with uneven hems is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
The robes were uneven and not symmetrical; this was not an offense.
At that time, the twelve Buddhas were in Rājagṛha.
Then, the bhikṣus wore their robes extremely high, extremely low, unevenly draped, and asymmetrical.
Having seen this, the Buddha thought to himself:
"I should observe how the Buddhas of the past donned their robes.
Then, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven spoke from mid-air:
"The Buddhas of the past all wore their robes with even hems.
The Buddha himself also recalled that the Buddhas of the past all wore their robes with even hems.
The Buddha then reflected further:
"I shall observe how the Buddhas of the future put on their robes.
A deity in the sky said,
"The Buddhas of the future will wear their robes evenly and symmetrically."
The Buddha also knew for himself that the Buddhas of the future would all wear their robes in the same manner.
The Buddha then reflected:
"How do the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens wear their robes?"
The devas in the sky said,
"The devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens are all wearing their robes in a uniform manner.
The Buddha also saw for himself that the devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens were all wearing their robes in a uniform manner.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus wear their robes with the hems excessively high, excessively low, uneven, or not properly aligned?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
From now on, you should train yourselves not to wear your robes excessively high."
To wear the upper robe excessively high is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not wearing the upper robe excessively high is not an offense.
Thirteenth: One should train oneself not to wear the upper robe excessively low.
To wear the outer robe too low is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not wearing the outer robe too low is not an offense.
Fourteenth: One should train oneself not to wear the outer robe unevenly.
To wear the robe unevenly is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Not wearing the robe unevenly is not an offense.
One should train in wearing the robe with its fifteen folds even and level.
If one wears the robe unevenly or untidily, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one wears the robe evenly and tidily, there is no offense.
(16) The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day. The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted through his silence, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night. In the early morning, he arranged the seating and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; the food is ready. May the Buddha know the proper time."
Before midday, the Buddha dressed and entered the householder’s residence.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered this house without properly covering their bodies; they gazed at their own shoulders and arms, and looked at their chests.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and possessed of merit.'"
“They do not properly cover their bodies when entering the houses of laypeople; they look at their own shoulders, arms, and chests like kings or great ministers.

The Buddha saw the group of six bhikṣus entering the dwellings of householders without properly covering their bodies and heard the householder’s reproach that they were like kings or great ministers.
After the meal, the Buddha gathered the community of bhikṣus for this matter and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus enter the homes of others without properly covering their bodies, looking about at their own shoulders, arms, and chests?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus: from this day forward, you should train yourselves to enter the interior of a house with your body properly covered."
To enter a house without properly covering one's body is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To enter a house while properly covering one's body is not an offense.

Seventeenth: At one time, although the group of six bhikṣus entered a house while properly covering their bodies, they did not remain properly covered while sitting; they looked at their own shoulders and arms, and looked at their chests.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"One should not sit inside a house with one's body uncovered, looking at one's shoulders and arms or looking at one's chest, like a king or a high minister.
The Buddha saw that some bhikṣus were sitting inside houses with their bodies uncovered, looking at their own shoulders, arms, and chests.
After the meal, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them:
"How can those called bhikṣus sit inside a house without properly covering their bodies, looking at their own shoulders, arms, and chests?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, you must train yourselves to sit properly covered within the houses of laypeople."
"To sit inside a house without properly covering one's body is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To sit while properly covering one's body is not an offense.

18. At one time, the group of six bhikṣus entered houses without properly restraining their bodies; they kicked large carts, small carts, calf-carts, and palanquins, causing wheels, trees, pillars, walls, jars, and pots to fall to the ground."
The householders rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"One who does not properly restrain the body when entering another's home may kick things so that they fall to the ground like a blind person.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should train yourselves thus: 'We shall enter houses with the body well-restrained.'"
If one enters a house with the body uncontrolled, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters a house with the body well-controlled, there is no offense.

(19) Furthermore, although the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with their bodies well-controlled, they sat with their bodies uncontrolled; they kicked large carts, small carts, calf-carts, and palanquins, and [knocked over] wheels, trees, pillars, walls, jars, pots, beds, and stools until they fell to the ground like blind men.
The Buddha, knowing this matter, addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself thus: 'When sitting inside a house, one must maintain proper control over the body.
To sit inside a house without maintaining proper control over the body is a duṣkṛta offense."
If one sits with the body properly composed, there is no offense.
At that time, when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
the World-Honored One dressed himself before midday and entered the city of Śrāvastī together with the bhikṣus.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they enter cities or villages by means of their supernormal powers, they manifest such rare wonders as these: elephants trumpet, horses neigh plaintively, and the lords of oxen bellow; geese, swans, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kokaṇadas, and other birds such as the orang-utan emit harmonious and elegant sounds.
Large drums, small drums, harps, zithers, flutes, lutes, pipes, and gongs and cymbals resounded spontaneously without being struck.
All the golden vessels and various ornamental furnishings within and without the mansions of the nobles produced sounds naturally, even those kept inside chests and boxes.
The blind regain their sight; the deaf regain their hearing; the mute are able to speak; those who are bound or crippled regain the ability to stretch;
the lame and deformed regain their hands and feet; those with squinting eyes have them set straight; the sickly and emaciated are cured;
those in pain attain happiness; poison is neutralized; the insane regain their composure; and the murderous turn away from killing.
Thieves abandon theft; those who engage in sexual misconduct refrain from sexual misconduct; those who speak falsehoods refrain from falsehoods;
those who engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, or idle chatter refrain from such speech; the greedy refrain from greed; the angry refrain from anger;
those with wrong views abandon wrong views; and all those imprisoned, confined, shackled, or bound in fetters shall be completely released.

Those in liberation and those in noisy, crowded places all obtain seclusion; those who have not yet planted roots of goodness plant them, those who have already planted them cause them to grow, and those who have already grown them attain liberation.
Hidden treasures spontaneously emerge, and through such rare occurrences, all sentient beings receive benefit.
At that time, the Buddha gradually proceeded toward the city; as he placed his right foot upon the threshold of the gate, various such rare and wondrous events manifested.

Then the people, from atop their houses, halls, walls, and towers, gazed upon the Buddha and the Sangha. Among them were those who had never before seen the Buddha and those who had. Those who had seen him before pointed and said: "This is the Buddha;
this is Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandiya, Kapphiṇa, and these are the group of six bhikṣus."
Having heard this, the group of six bhikṣus looked up at her and said:

"Such-and-such a woman is blind; such-and-such has squinting eyes; such-and-such has red eyes; such-and-such has a short nose; such-and-such has a goiter; such-and-such has a hunched back; such-and-such is lame; such-and-such is pale; such-and-such is dark; such-and-such lacks majesty."
Having heard this, the women said to the group of six bhikṣus, "We are not your wives, nor have we had illicit relations with you; why should our beauty or ugliness concern you?"
The group addressed them by their names.
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We entered the city with the Buddha and the Saṃgha; what business is that of yours?"
They pointed at us, saying,
"These are the group of six bhikṣus," treating us as if we were transgressing criminals.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to look upward while entering a house.
To enter a house looking upward is a duṣkṛta offense.
Entering a house without looking up high does not constitute an offense.

(21) At that time, the Buddha and the Saṃgha were sitting and eating on an open ground, while various people were on the roofs of halls, atop walls, and in watchtowers, watching the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Among them were some who had never seen the Buddha, while others who had seen him before pointed them out, saying:
"This is the Buddha; this is Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kapphiṇa; these are the group of six bhikṣus."
Having heard this, the group of six bhikṣus looked up and spoke thus:

"Such-and-such a woman is blind; such-and-such has squinting eyes; such-and-such has bloodshot eyes; such-and-such has a short nose; such-and-such has a goiter; such-and-such has a hunched back; such-and-such is lame; such-and-such is black; such-and-such is white; such-and-such lacks majesty."
Having heard this, the women said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"We are not your wives, nor do we have relations with you; why should our beauty or ugliness concern you?"
"But we are the ones who have received the names.
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We have accepted an invitation from the Buddha and the Saṃgha to eat while seated; what business is that of yours?"
Yet he points to us and says,
"These are the group of six bhikṣus," treating us as if we were transgressing criminals.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit inside a house while looking around with a high gaze.
To sit inside a house while looking around with a high gaze is a duṣkṛta offense.
Sitting inside a house without looking up does not constitute an offense.
(22) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, resentful of the offerings received upon entering a house, spoke thus:
"Yesterday the food and drink were fragrant, delicious, and well-prepared; we were provided with seats in proper order and excellent bedding."
"Today's [food] may not be as fragrant, delicious, or well-ripened as yesterday's, or it may not be served in the proper order.
The householders rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are not virtuous; they neither sow nor reap, but merely consume food and expose the faults and transgressions of others."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall not enter a house while scolding the offerings.
To enter a house while scolding the offerings is a duṣkṛta offense.”

They did not reprove [the donors] when they entered for the meal, yet they did not refrain from violating the twenty-three rules. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus did not reprove [the donors] when they entered for the meal, but once they were seated, they immediately reproved them, saying:
"Yesterday the food and drink were fragrant, delicious, and well-prepared, and you provided excellent seating in an orderly fashion;
today it may not be as fragrant, delicious, and well-prepared as yesterday, nor may you provide it in an orderly fashion."
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are unskillful; they neither sow nor reap, but merely consume food and expose the faults and transgressions of others."
Having heard this matter, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall not scold one who is receiving offerings while seated inside a house.
To scold one who is receiving offerings is a duṣkṛta offense."

Not rebuking while receiving offerings and sitting [inappropriately] constitutes the twenty-fourth offense. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with loud voices, whereupon the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"Entering a house with a loud voice, like a brahmin.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves to enter a house in silence."
If one enters a house without remaining silent, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one enters while remaining silent, there is no offense.
Twenty-fifth: furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not enter the house with loud voices, sat with loud voices like brahmins.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
“Sitting in the houses of others with a loud voice, like a brahmin.
Having heard this, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you should train yourselves to sit silently within the house.”
"If one sits inside a house without remaining silent, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sits silently, there is no offense.
(26) Furthermore, when the group of six bhikṣus entered a house walking in a squatting posture, the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
‘We are virtuous and possessed of merit.
Yet they enter the houses of others while squatting, appearing as if their legs have been severed.”
Having heard this, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house while squatting.
To enter a house while squatting is a duṣkṛta offense."
Entering while squatting does not constitute an offense.
Twenty-seventh: Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not enter a house while squatting, then sat down squatting inside the house.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, squat inside houses just like the non-Buddhists.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to squat while inside a house.
If one squats inside a house, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Not squatting, there is no offense.
28. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with their heads covered by their robes.
The laypeople became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent and virtuous one! [He said.
Then, covering his head with his robe, he entered the house as if he were a spy or a hunter.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to enter a house with the head covered.
If one enters a house with the head covered, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one enters without the head covered, there is no offense.

Twenty-ninth: Furthermore, although the group of six bhikṣus did not enter the houses with their heads covered, they sat inside the houses with their heads covered. The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
