"The bhikṣus claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
“Sitting inside a house with one’s head covered is like acting as a lookout for a hunter.
The Buddha said:
“From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit inside a house with your head covered.”
If one sits with the head covered, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sits without the head covered, there is no offense.
Furthermore, thirty-six bhikṣus of the group of six entered a house with their heads wrapped in turbans; the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
Yet they wrap their heads in turbans and enter households like kings or like great ministers."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter the interior of a house with your head wrapped in a cloth.
If one enters with the head wrapped, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
Entering with one's head uncovered is not an offense.
Thirty-one: Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not enter a house with their heads uncovered, sat inside the house with their heads covered.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.'"
"Wrapping his head-cloth (*pōtóu*) while sitting inside a house, as if he were a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit inside a house with your head-cloth wrapped."
If one sits with the head-wrap (bandhana) wrapped around the head, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sits without the head-wrap wrapped around the head, there is no offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with their elbows tucked against their shoulders.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"Entering a house with one's elbow hidden behind the shoulder, like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house with your elbow hidden behind your shoulder."
If one enters a house with the elbow tucked against the shoulder, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters without tucking the elbow against the shoulder, there is no offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not enter with their elbows tucked against their shoulders, then sat inside the house with their elbows tucked against their shoulders.
The laypeople rebuked them in anger, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.'"
“Sitting inside a house with one’s elbow hidden against another’s shoulder is like the manner of a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit inside a house with your elbow hidden against another’s shoulder.”
To sit with one’s elbow resting on another’s shoulder is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not sitting with one’s elbow resting on another’s shoulder does not constitute an offense.
Thirty-fourth: Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with their hands crossed over their hips.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Entering a house with hands on hips, like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house with hands on hips."
Entering with hands on the hips is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
entering without hands on the hips is not an offense.
(35) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not enter the interior of a house with hands on their hips, proceeded to sit inside the house with hands on their hips.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Sitting inside a house with hands on hips, like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself not to sit inside a house with hands on hips."
To sit with hands on the hips is an *dukkaṭa* offense;
not to sit with hands on the hips is not an offense.
(36) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered lay dwellings with their robes tucked up over both shoulders.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Entering a house with the robes tucked up on both sides, like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house with the robes tucked up on both sides."
If one enters a house with the robes tucked up on both sides, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not enter with the robes tucked up on both sides, there is no offense.
(37) At that time, although the group of six bhikṣus did not enter a house with their robes tucked up on both sides, they nevertheless sat inside the house with their robes tucked up on both sides.
The laypeople rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu sit inside a house with his robe tucked up on both sides, like a king or a high minister?"
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself not to sit inside a house with one's robe tucked up on both sides.
To sit inside a house with one's robe tucked up on both sides is a duṣkṛta offense."
It is not an offense to sit with one’s robe tucked up on either side.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus tucked up their robes while entering the interior of a house.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
Yet they enter private homes with their robes tucked up on one side, like kings or great ministers."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house with one shoulder bared.
If one enters with one shoulder bared, it is a duṣkṛta offense.”
Entering with one shoulder bared does not constitute an offense.
(39) Furthermore, although the group of six bhikṣus did not enter a house with one shoulder bared, they sat inside the house with one shoulder bared.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
“[He] sits inside a house with his robe tucked up on one side, like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“One should train oneself not to sit inside a house with the robe tucked up on one side.”
If one sits inside a house with the robe partially tucked up, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not sit with the robe partially tucked up, there is no offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with their right shoulders covered by the robe and their left shoulders fully exposed.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Covering the right shoulder with the robe and fully raising the left shoulder over it while entering a house is like the manner of a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house covering the right shoulder with the robe and fully raising the left shoulder over it."
If one enters a house with the right shoulder covered by the robe and the left shoulder fully raised, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one enters without covering the right shoulder and without fully raising the left shoulder, there is no offense.

41. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they had entered a house without covering the right shoulder with their robe and with the left shoulder fully bared, then covered the right shoulder with their robe and fully bared the left shoulder while sitting inside the house.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Covering the right shoulder with the robe and fully lifting the left shoulder, one sits within a house like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit within a house covering the right shoulder with the robe and fully lifting the left shoulder; this is how you should practice."
If one covers the right shoulder with the robe and sits while fully raising the left shoulder, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not cover the right shoulder and sits without fully raising the left shoulder, there is no offense.
42. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with their arms swinging.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent! You are virtuous!
he said, swinging his arms as he entered the house like a man sowing grain.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to enter a house with swinging arms.
If one enters with swinging arms, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters without swinging arms, there is no offense.
43. At that time, although the bhikṣus did not swing their arms while entering a house, they would swing their arms while sitting inside.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent! This is meritorious!
he said, as he sat inside the house with his arms dangling like a man sowing grain.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to sit with arms dangling while inside a house.
If one sits with arms dangling, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one does not sit with arms dangling while inside a house, there is no offense.
44. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house shaking their shoulders.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent! You are virtuous.
Shaking his shoulders, he entered the house like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to shake the shoulders when entering a house.
If one enters a house shaking the shoulders, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters without shaking the shoulders, there is no offense.
45. At that time, although the group of six bhikṣus did not shake their shoulders when entering a house, they nevertheless shook their shoulders while sitting there.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent! You are virtuous.
Shaking his shoulders, he sat within the house like a king or a great minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself: 'I shall not sit with my shoulders shaking while inside a house.
If one sits with the shoulders shaking, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sits without shaking the shoulders, there is no offense."
46. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered lay households shaking their heads.
The householders rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent! You are virtuous!
he said, shaking his head as he entered the house, appearing as if possessed by a ghost.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to enter a house shaking the head.
If one enters a house shaking the head, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters without shaking the head, there is no offense.
47. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not shake their heads while entering a house, nevertheless sat inside the house shaking their heads.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent! You are virtuous!
he said, shaking his head as he sat within the house, appearing as if possessed by a ghost.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to sit with the head shaking while inside a house.
To sit with the head shaking is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
to sit without shaking the head is not an offense.
48. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus swayed their bodies as they entered a house.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:..."
"How excellent and virtuous!
he said, shaking his body as he entered the house like a dancer.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to sway the body when entering a house.
If one enters swaying the body, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one enters without swaying the body, there is no offense.
49. At that time, although the group of six bhikṣus did not sway their bodies upon entering a house, they swayed their bodies while sitting inside.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying, "These śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas sit in houses swaying their bodies like dancers."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you must train yourselves thus: do not sit with swaying bodies inside a house.
To sit with a swaying body inside a house is a duṣkṛta offense.
It is not an offense to sit inside a house without swaying the body.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house holding hands, kicking over jars, pots, and other vessels so that they fell to the ground.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Entering a house hand-in-hand, as if one were a king or a high minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should train yourselves not to enter a house hand-in-hand."
If they enter a house holding hands, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If they enter a house without holding hands, there is no offense.
(51) Furthermore, although the group of six bhikṣus did not enter a house holding hands, they sat down inside the house while holding hands.
The laypeople said, "Venerable elders!
Sit down close together; there are many bhikṣus invited here."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"What other business do you have?
Why do you not spread out your seats more widely so that we may sit close together?"
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit with hands clasped inside a house.
If one sits with hands clasped inside a house, it is a duṣkṛta offense.”
Sitting without holding hands does not constitute an offense.
(52) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus entered a house with one foot raised.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas claims for himself:
'I am virtuous and excellent.
Yet he enters a house with one foot raised, like a king or a great minister."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to enter a house with one foot raised.
If one enters with one foot raised, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
It is not an offense if one does not enter a house with one leg raised.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, although they did not enter a house with one leg raised, nevertheless sat inside a house with one leg raised.
The householders said, "Venerable elders!
Sit down nearby; I have invited many bhikṣus."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"What other matters do you have?
Why do you not spread out your seats more widely so that we may sit near you?"
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should not sit with one foot raised while inside a house; you should train yourselves accordingly.
To sit with one foot raised inside a house is a duṣkṛta offense.
Sitting with one leg raised does not constitute an offense.
(54) At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat with their thighs crossed inside a house, exposing their bodies below.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character,' yet they sit with their thighs crossed inside houses, exposing their bodies below."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit with your thighs crossed inside a house.
If one sits with the thighs crossed inside a house, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
Not to sit with one hip resting upon the other is not an offense.
(55) At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat with their feet crossed.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
Yet they sit inside houses with their legs crossed, like kings or great ministers."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit with legs crossed.
To sit with legs crossed is a duṣkṛta offense."
Sitting without crossing one's legs does not constitute an offense.
Fifty-six Buddhas were in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus rose early, put on their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
A certain householder was sitting alone on a bed in front of his middle gate, propping his cheek with his palm, sorrowful and unhappy.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to one another, "This man is grieving; we can make him laugh."
The group of six bhikṣus went before the householder and stood there with their hands cupping their cheeks, filled with sorrow and anxiety.
The householder smiled and asked them,
"Why are you so urgently distressed together, standing here with your hands cupping your cheeks?"
The group of six bhikṣus looked back and said to the other bhikṣus,
"We have already finished speaking and laughing.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are excellent and virtuous.
Yet they rest their cheeks upon their palms to provoke the speech and laughter of laypeople, acting like jesters."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to sit with your chin resting on your hand inside a house, lest it cause laughter among laypeople."
If one sits with the palm of the hand supporting the cheek, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not sit with the palm of the hand supporting the cheek, there is no offense.
(57) When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, at that time a certain householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink throughout the entire night, and in the early morning, he arranged the seating area.
He sent a messenger to inform the Buddha that the time had come, saying:
"The meal is prepared; may the Buddha himself know the proper time.
The Buddha and the Sangha entered the householder's home and took their seats.
When the householder knew that the Buddha and the Sangha were seated, he personally offered water for washing and prepared to serve the food and drink.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus placed their bowls before them and looked around in the four directions; once the householder had served the rice into the bowls, he passed by.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"Why is no rice given here?
The householder replied:
"I have already given it.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"You have not given it."
The householder said,
"Look into the bowl.
Having looked, he called to the householder and said:
"Give me your bowls.
The laypeople said,
"Where was your mind just now?"
"Now he is about to call out to offer the bowl.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you should train yourselves to receive the food with a single-minded focus."
If one receives the rice without a single-minded focus, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one receives it with single-minded focus, there is no offense.
Furthermore, when the group of six bhikṣus filled their bowls with rice and looked toward another place, the laypeople had already passed the soup over the bowls.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"Why was no soup given here?
They replied:
"It has already been given.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"It has not been given."
The householder said,
"Why do you not look into the bowl?
Having looked, he spoke, saying:
"Give me your bowl.
The laypeople said,
"Where was your mind just now?"
"Now I am about to call for the bowl to be given.
When the Buddha heard this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves to receive the soup with a single-minded focus."
If one receives soup without a single-minded focus, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one receives soup with a single-minded focus, there is no offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus received food and drink until their bowls overflowed, such that rice and soup spilled out from within them.
The laypeople said, "The rice should have been replenished, and the soup should also have been replenished; why did you take it until your bowls overflowed and then discard it?
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to accept food that overflows the bowl.
If one accepts food that overflows the bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one accepts food without it overflowing the bowl, there is no offense.
Furthermore, sixty-six groups of bhikṣus poured soup and vegetables over their rice and ate only from the places where the soup and vegetables had been placed.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"Why do you pour food over it like children?"
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves to eat by mixing the soup and the rice together.
If you do not eat with the soup and rice mixed, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
If it concerns food such as soup or rice, there is no offense.
(61) Furthermore, when the six groups of bhikṣus encountered ghee, curd, or soup upon their rice, they ate from the center of the bowl as if from a well.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying,
"Do the bhikṣus eat like brahmins?
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should not eat from the center [of the bowl] like a well; this is how you should train.
Eating from the center [of the bowl] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not eating from the center is not an offense.
62. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus ate their rice by forming it into balls.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus eat their rice in balls like children."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to eat by forming balls of rice.
If one eats by forming balls of rice, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
Eating without forming the food into balls is not an offense.
(63) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus ate by forming large balls of food.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus are eating rice in large mouthfuls, as if someone were trying to seize them and drive them away.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to eat rice in large mouthfuls."
If one takes food in large mouthfuls, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one does not take food in large mouthfuls, there is no offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus ate with their hands grasping the food.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus hold food in their hands like farmers sowing seeds.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one should train oneself not to hold food with the hands.
To hold food with the hands is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not holding food with the hands is not an offense.
65. Furthermore, at one time, while the bhikṣus were sitting in order to eat, there was one bhikṣu who opened his mouth wide before the food had even arrived.
The group of six bhikṣus, sitting beside him, for the sake of a joke, took a clod of earth and placed it in his mouth.
At that time, there was such an impure matter among the assembly, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to stand with the mouth wide open in anticipation of food."
If one opens the mouth in anticipation before the food has arrived to wait for it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not open the mouth in anticipation to wait, there is no offense.

(66) At one time, the group of six bhikṣus spoke while chewing their food; the soup and rice flowed out from their mouths, and when the bhikṣus sitting nearby saw this, they were overcome with nausea and vomited.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to speak while chewing food.
If one speaks while chewing food, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There is no offense for speaking while chewing food.
(67) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus chewed their food in half, with one half remaining in their mouths and the other half in their hands.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel of food.
If one bites off half a morsel, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Biting into food halfway through a mouthful does not constitute an offense.
Sixty-eight Buddhas were in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, he rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of fine food and drink throughout the entire night. Rising early in the morning, he arranged the seating area and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha, saying:
"The time has come!"
"The meal is prepared; the Buddha himself knows the proper time.
The Buddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the Saṃgha, entered the house of Mahānāma and sat down.
Having seen that the Buddha was seated, Mahānāma personally served water for washing.
When the meal of milk-rice was prepared, he personally served the rice and milk with his own hands. As the bhikṣus sucked at it, they made a sucking sound.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had previously been an actor; hearing this sound, he immediately began to dance.
The bhikṣus laughed loudly; as they laughed, grains of rice came out from their mouths, and some even came out through their nostrils. The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"How can you cause others to laugh like acrobats?
When the Buddha saw that the bhikṣus were doing these things and heard the lay devotees (gṛhapati) reproaching them, he remained silent.
After the meal, he assembled the community of bhikṣus regarding this matter.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked the dancing bhikṣu, "With what intention did you dance? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to expel those bhikṣus who have committed the offense of slurping while eating, as well as those who engage in frivolous laughter.
The Buddha said:
“From now on, one should train oneself not to make a sound while inhaling [air].
If one makes a sound while inhaling air while eating, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not make a sound while inhaling air, there is no offense.
69. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus made smacking sounds while chewing their food.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent, virtuous one!
he said, making a smacking sound as he chewed his food, like a pig eating.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to make sounds while chewing food.
To eat while making sounds while chewing constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not making sounds while chewing does not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, there were seventy-six groups of bhikṣus who put food into their mouths and swallowed it bit by bit.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying,
"They eat like monkeys."
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to eat food until it has been swallowed.
To eat food before it has been swallowed is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If one has already swallowed it before eating, there is no offense.
(71) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus ate with their tongues protruding, saying:

The laypeople rebuked them, saying,
"The bhikṣus stick out their tongues while eating like small children.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to eat with the tongue protruding.
To eat with the tongue protruding is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Not to do so is not an offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus ate with their noses scrunched up.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"You should properly discard your mucus; are you cold?"
"Is it because you have eaten garlic?
The Buddha said,
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to eat with a wrinkled nose."
Eating with the nose wrinkled is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Eating without wrinkling the nose is not an offense.
(73) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus licked their hands while eating.
The laypeople rebuked him, saying, "When the soup and rice are finished, they should be replenished; why are you licking your hands?
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to lick the hands while eating.
If one licks the hands while eating, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not lick the hands while eating, there is no offense.
74. Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus wiped their bowls with their fingers while eating.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The soup and rice should be replenished when they are exhausted; why do you wipe your bowls with your fingers?"
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must train yourselves not to wipe the bowl with the fingers while eating.
If one wipes the bowl with the fingers while eating, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If one does not wipe the bowl with the fingers while eating, there is no offense.
(75) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus ate with their hands soiled and shook them off.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
“The bhikṣus eat like kings or high ministers, shaking their hands as they eat and dropping food.

To eat while shaking the hand is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
To eat without shaking the hand is not an offense.
(76) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus threw away the rice remaining on their hands.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are not good; they neither sow nor reap, but merely consume and then discard [the food].
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself not to discard food from the hand.
To discard food from the hand is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Not to discard it is not an offense."
77. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took hold of their drinking vessels with greasy hands; when the bhikṣus sitting nearby saw this, they were made to vomit.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you should train yourselves not to take hold of drinking vessels with greasy hands."
If one grasps a drinking vessel with greasy hands, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one grasps it with hands that are not greasy, there is no offense.
Furthermore, [regarding] the sixty bhikṣus of the group of six, they sought rice and soup for themselves when they were not ill.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one should train oneself thus: 'When not ill, I shall not seek out rice or soup for myself.
To seek out rice or soup for oneself when not ill is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If it is for the sake of illness, there is no offense.

(81) Furthermore, while a certain bhikṣu was looking elsewhere during the midday meal in the midst of the Saṃgha, the group of six bhikṣus (Ṣaḍvargika), for the sake of a joke, placed a bone into his bowl.

(82) Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus received much food; without eating it all in due order, they left the remainder in the bowl, poured water over it to discard it, and filled the washbasin until the vessels for leftover food were all full.

The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself to eat until it is finished in successive order.
To eat until it is finished without eating in successive order constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To eat until it is finished in successive order does not constitute an offense.
83. When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day. The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted through his silence, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night. "The time has come!
The meal is prepared; the Buddha himself knows the proper time.
The Buddha and the Sangha arrived at the house of the lay devotee, where the floor of the new hall was made of crystal.
When the various bhikṣus washed their bowls, there was leftover food in the water; they discarded it upon the hall floor as if it were vomit.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus are not well-behaved. There are private places where this water could be discarded; why did you discard it upon this hall floor?"
The Buddha said:
"If there is rice in the water used for washing the bowl, one should not discard it inside [the dwelling] without asking the owner; this is how you should train.
If one discards it inside without asking the owner, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Question: If one discards it for the owner, there is no offense.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit established this rule:

When the king heard that the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, he immediately commanded his charioteer to prepare the carriage.
Having received these instructions, the charioteer prepared the carriage and reported, "Great King!
The carriage is ready; Your Majesty may know the time."
The king immediately mounted his carriage and departed from the city toward the Jeta Grove.
While the king was still upon the carriage, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma for him, saying: “Great King!
"Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; seeing this matter, his heart was not pleased, and for various reasons he rebuked him:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if a person is seated upon a vehicle while he walks and preaches the Dharma to them?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “One should train oneself thus:
‘If a person is not ill and is riding in a vehicle, one should not preach the Dharma to them.’”
"If one preaches the Dharma for someone who is not ill while they are riding in a vehicle, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Preaching the Dharma for a sick person is not an offense.
(85) Furthermore, at one time the King was walking in front, and the group of six bhikṣus followed behind him, preaching the Dharma as they went, saying:
"Great King!
Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus.
"One should train thus: 'One must not preach the Dharma to a person who is not ill while walking ahead of oneself, nor to one following behind.
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is not ill while walking ahead of oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
It is not an offense to preach the Dharma for the sake of a sick person.
Furthermore, on another occasion, while the King was traveling along a road, the group of six bhikṣus stood outside the road and preached the Dharma to the King, saying:
"Great King!"
"Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If a person who is not ill walks upon the Path while a bhikṣu walks outside the Path, one should not preach the Dharma to them; this is how you should train."
If one preaches the Dharma for a person who is not ill while they are walking on a path outside the royal precincts, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma for a person who is ill, there is no offense.

Regarding the eighty-seventh rule concerning the conduct of kings: when kings travel, they carry their couches with them; the king sits upon a high couch, yet the group of six bhikṣus stands and preaches the Dharma for him.
"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one should train oneself thus: 'If a person who is not ill is seated and a bhikṣu is standing, he shall not preach the Dharma to them.
If one stands while preaching the Dharma to a person who is not ill and is seated, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
It is not an offense to preach the Dharma for the sake of a sick person.
Regarding the eighty-eight kings and the group of six bhikṣus, the kings lacked great reverence.
When the group of six bhikṣus obtained a lowly or small seat while the king sat on a high seat—the bhikṣus being in a position lower than the king—they preached the Dharma to the king, saying:
"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus.
"One should train oneself thus: 'If a person is healthy and situated on high ground, one must not preach the Dharma to them while remaining in a lower position.
If one remains in a lower position and preaches the Dharma to a healthy person situated on high ground, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There is no offense in preaching the Dharma for the sake of a sick person.
Eighty-nine: At one time, when the King’s body was large and he had been sitting for a long time, he lay down while the group of six bhikṣus remained seated, preaching the Dharma to him, saying:
"Great King!"
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself thus: 'When a person is lying down ill and I am sitting as a bhikṣu, I shall not preach the Dharma to them.'"
If one sits while the listener lies down and preaches the Dharma to them when they are not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is ill, there is no offense.
On another occasion, when a king had covered his head, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to the king, saying:
"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.

If one preaches the Dharma to a person whose head is covered who is not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
It is not an offense to preach the Dharma to a sick person.
Ninety-first: On one occasion, when a king had wrapped his head, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to him, saying:
"Great King!"
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.

If one preaches the Dharma to a person who has wrapped their head to avoid illness, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma to a sick person, there is no offense.

"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.

"One should not teach the Dharma to one who hides their shoulder with their elbow, except in the case of illness; this is how you should train.
If one teaches the Dharma to someone who hides their shoulder with their elbow and is not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma for the sake of a sick person, there is no offense.
Ninety-three: On one occasion, when the King stood with his hands on his hips, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to him, saying:
"Great King!"
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not teach the Dharma to a person with hands crossed behind the back.'"
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is not ill and has their hands clasped around their waist, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is ill, there is no offense.
Ninety-fourth: At one time, King [Aśoka] had his attendants pull up his robes; the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to him, saying:
"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has tucked up their robe on either side, except when they are ill.
If one preaches the Dharma to someone who has tucked up their robe on either side and is not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
It is not an offense to preach the Dharma for the sake of a sick person.
Once, when King Paiṅgiya was adjusting his robe, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Except in the case of illness, you should train yourselves not to preach the Dharma to one who has tucked up their robe on one side."
If one preaches the Dharma for someone who is not ill while they have partially tucked up their robe, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
To preach the Dharma for one who is ill is not an offense.
At one time, when King Kālāśoka had covered his right shoulder with his robe and fully raised his left shoulder, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma for the king, saying:
"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to a person who has covered their right shoulder with a robe and fully raised the left shoulder over it, except in cases of illness.
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is not ill and who has covered their right shoulder with a robe and fully raised the left shoulder over it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There is no offense in preaching the Dharma to a sick person.
Ninety-seven: On one occasion, when a king was wearing leather sandals, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Except when ill, you should train yourselves not to preach the Dharma to those wearing leather sandals."
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is not ill while they are wearing leather sandals, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma to a person who is ill, there is no offense.
At one time, when a king was wearing sandals, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to the king, saying:
"Great King!
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
Thus the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus.
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to a person wearing wooden clogs, except in cases of illness.
If one preaches the Dharma to a person wearing wooden clogs who is not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."

There was once a time when the Buddha was preaching the Dharma while surrounded with great reverence by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings.

Among King Prasenajit’s retinue were those carrying staves, those carrying parasols, those carrying swords, those carrying shields, and those carrying bows and arrows; yet the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma separately to them.

Among this assembly, there were those capable of attaining the Path; however, because the assembly had been divided into two factions, their minds became distracted and they could not attain the Path.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that they do not preach the Dharma to sentient beings who are not single-minded. The Buddha then preached various teachings to the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.

When the king knew that the Buddha had taught the Dharma in various ways to instruct, benefit, and gladden him, he rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after the king had left, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu preach the Dharma to someone carrying a staff who is not ill?"
"If one preaches the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, a large sword, a small knife, a shield, a bow, an arrow,
or various other weapons," having thus rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Except in the case of illness, you should train yourselves not to preach the Dharma to those holding staffs."
If one preaches the Dharma to someone holding a staff who is not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma to someone who is ill, there is no offense.
One hundred: One should train oneself not to preach the Dharma to someone holding a parasol, except when they are ill.
If one preaches the Dharma to someone holding a parasol who is not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one preaches the Dharma to someone who is ill, there is no offense.
One hundred and one: unless the person is ill, one should train oneself not to preach the Dharma to someone holding a knife.
If one preaches the Dharma for a person holding a blade, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not preach the Dharma for a person holding a blade, there is no offense.
102. One should train oneself: except in cases of illness, one must not preach the Dharma for a person holding a shield or a bow and arrows.
If one preaches the Dharma for those who carry shields, bows, or arrows, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does not preach the Dharma for those who carry shields, bows, or arrows, there is no offense.
(103) When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus went to speak to the gardeners, saying:
"Give us some vegetables," they said. He asked,
"Will you pay for them?"
He replied, "I am begging for it; it has no price.
The vegetable guard said:
“Those who give us vegetables for nothing— how shall we survive?
The group of six bhikṣus said,
“Are you not giving them to us?”
He replied, "I will not give it. At another time,
the group of six bhikṣus defecated, urinated, spat, and drooled upon the vegetables, which became putrid, rotten, and decayed.
The vegetable guard asked,
"By whom was this made?
The group of six bhikṣus went to speak to the vegetable guard, saying:
“Do you know who defiled your vegetables?
He replied, “I do not know.”
The group of six bhikṣus said, "Whatever we have done was simply because you demanded vegetables and refused to give them; we intentionally acted in this manner.
The group of six bhikṣus were bold and possessed great strength; they did not greatly fear the offense, and the vegetable guards could do nothing against them.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
“[One should not] defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon leafy vegetables, as one would do for a king or a high minister.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon leafy vegetables, except in cases of illness; you should train yourselves accordingly.”
If one voids excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or spittle upon vegetables when not ill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one is ill, there is no offense.
(104) The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to a laundryman and said,
"Wash our robes for us. He asked:
"Will you give it to me for a price? He replied,
"It has no price."
The laundryman said, "If there are those who have clothes washed but do not pay the price, we will have washed them for nothing; how shall we survive?
The group of six bhikṣus said:
“Did you not wash it for me?
She replied,
“I did not wash it for you.”
The group of six bhikṣus went to a place of clean water for washing clothes and voided excrement, urine, mucus, and spittle there.
The laundrymen, believing beforehand that the water was pure, soaked their clothes in it; the water immediately became foul-smelling and lost its color.
The washerman thought, "Who has done this?
At another time, the group of six bhikṣus went to him and asked:
"Do you know? Who has defiled this water?
They replied:
"I do not know.
The group of six bhikṣus said, "What we have done was because you did not wash our robes for us; that is why we acted in this way."
The group of six bhikṣus were bold, vigorous, and possessed great strength; they did not stand much in awe of the precepts, and the laundrymen could do nothing with them.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"It is excellent and virtuous to use pure water for defecation, urination, spitting, and salivating.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu defile pure water with excrement, urine, snot, or spittle?"
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a formal precept.
Furthermore, while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
there was at that time a large pond in the city of Śrāvastī named Sumana, which was used by many people.
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another,

They all agreed.
"As you wish.
They then went together to look at the pond,
whereupon they defecated, urinated, spat, and drooled into the water.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are not virtuous; is there no other place for defecation and urination?
You have gone so far as to defecate, urinate, spit, and expectorate into this pure water used for drinking."
Among them, there was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu defile pure water with excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva into pure water, except in cases of illness; this is how you should train."
"If one is not ill and uses water that has been purified for defecation, urination, nasal mucus, or spitting, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
For one who is ill, there is no offense.
[Section 105] While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the group of six bhikṣus stood while defecating and urinating.
Upon hearing of this matter, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One must not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is how you should train.
To defecate or urinate while standing when not ill constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If one is ill, there is no offense.
[Case 106: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, a certain householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. He returned to his own home and prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night.
Having risen early and prepared the seating area, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come!
The meal is ready; may the Buddha know the proper time."
The group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were constantly at odds with one another, quarreling and contending.
At that time, it was the turn of the group of seventeen bhikṣus to guard the monastery, while it was the turn of the group of six bhikṣus to go out to receive food.
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"Today we shall intentionally deprive the group of seventeen bhikṣus of their food.
Another said:
"How is it severed? He replied,
"Simply come and you shall know."
The group of six bhikṣus went to where the group of seventeen bhikṣus were and asked for their bowls, saying, "We shall bring back your share of the food.

They then followed the Buddha and the Saṃgha to the house where they had been invited; once the group of six bhikṣus had finished eating first, they took the share of the food for the group of seventeen bhikṣus and departed.

Having emerged, he then attends to other matters and passes through the homes of various acquaintances in other places; having seen them, he dwells in places where many people gather—such as outside the city, or beneath trees, or on riverbanks, at wells, or by ponds.
At that time, the seventeen groups of young bhikṣus were hungry and distressed, and they said to one another,
"Why is the food so late?
They spoke to each other again:
"Can you see him from atop the great tree outside the gate of Jeta’s Grove?
At that time, a certain bhikṣu climbed the tree, looked, and said:
"He is staying among a great multitude of people on the shore below a well under a certain tree."
When the sun was nearly at its zenith, his forehead was dripping with sweat as he came and called out,
"Take your portion of food. He asked:
"Why are you late?
They replied,
"We left as soon as we received our food."
He asked, "Are you not staying with a great multitude of people under that tree by the riverbank?
Yet you say:"
"Once you have received food, you must leave.
The group of six bhikṣus asked, "Who said that?"
The group of seventeen bhikṣus said, "We saw it while up in the tree.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and rebuked them, saying:
"How can it be that a bhikṣu climbs a tree when the Buddha has not yet permitted it?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus through various causes and conditions:
“How can one be called a bhikṣu who climbs a tree when I have not permitted it?”
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should train oneself: except in cases of urgent necessity, one must not climb trees that exceed a person's height."
If a bhikṣu climbs a tree higher than a human’s reach without a pressing cause, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If there is a pressing cause, there is no offense.

The one hundred and seven rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) are concluded. 8. The seven methods for settling disputes (adhikaraṇa-samatha). Regarding the first of the seven methods for settling disputes: At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then, the group of six bhikṣus encouraged donors to prepare a bath, and the bathing requisites had already been prepared.

There was a visiting bhikṣu who arrived at night, took off his robes and placed them upon the other garments, and entered the bathhouse to wash. Due to certain circumstances, the clothes became mixed up.
After the visiting bhikṣu had finished washing and emerged, he went to his original place to retrieve his robe; seeing outside that it was another's robe, he thought to himself:
"I shall return this robe to its original place and search for my own."

They returned to the place where the robes were kept; the group of six bhikṣus, who were constantly at odds with the virtuous bhikṣus, saw the visiting bhikṣu enter and said to him, "You have already left;
for what reason have you come back?"
He replied, "I arrived later;
having taken off my clothes and put them upon the other garments, I entered the bathhouse to wash. Due to certain circumstances, the clothes became mixed up."
Having first bathed and emerged to take his robe, he went outside and saw that it was not his own. He thought to himself:
"This robe should be returned to its original place; I must seek my own robe."
"For this reason, we have returned.
The group of six bhikṣus said, "It is not as you say;
you took it with a thieving mind, and having taken it, you felt regret and wished to place it back where it was. Do you see your offense?"
He replied, "I did not see them.
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"How can he simply not speak for himself regarding his offense? We must carry out an *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) against him for failure to acknowledge it.
The group of six bhikṣus then carried out the *ukkhepanīyakamma* against that visiting bhikṣu.
The visiting bhikṣu thought to himself:

"The group of six bhikṣus have carried out a formal act of suspension against me for not acknowledging an offense, yet they lack any basis, cause, or context for it. Since I have not myself confessed my fault, why do I not now go to Śrāvastī to visit the Buddha?"
Having stayed in Rājagṛha as long as he wished, that bhikṣu took his robes and bowl and traveled toward Śrāvastī to visit the Buddha.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with these words of inquiry: "Are you well?"
"Are you well?
Do you not lack for alms, and are you not weary from the road?
At that time, the Buddha asked the visiting bhikṣu:
“Are you patient?
Are you well?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not weary from the road?”
The visiting bhikṣu said, “I have been content with my needs;
begging for alms was not difficult, and I am not weary from the road.
He then related the aforementioned matters in detail to the Buddha.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha asked that bhikṣu:
"For what reason have the group of six bhikṣus performed an *ajñāpya-niḥsaraṇa* (act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense) against you?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Since there is no cause or condition from beginning to end, I did not say I was guilty myself; yet you have forcibly performed an *ajñapti* (formal act of suspension) against me for not acknowledging my fault.
The Buddha said:

“If the group of six bhikṣus, without any basis or reason, does not allow you to speak for yourself regarding your offense but instead forcibly carries out a formal act of suspension against you for refusal to see your fault, do not be distressed.
I shall act as your companion in the Dharma and assist you.”
The Buddha said:

"From now on, I authorize the method of settling disputes through one's own statement (*svavāda*). By means of this settlement through one's own statement, various matters that arise within the Saṃgha should be settled."
Regarding the settling of disputes through confession (*patisāraṇīya*), there are ten kinds that are contrary to the Dharma and ten kinds that are in accordance with the Dharma.
As for the ten kinds that are contrary to the Dharma: if a bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense, he says of himself, "I have not committed it."
The community of monks asked, "Do you yourself admit to having committed an offense? He replied: "I do."
"It is not an offense.
This is called an illegal [proceeding].
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, he says of himself:
"I have not committed an offense.
The community of monks asked him,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense?"
If he says of himself,
"I have not committed an offense," this is called illegal.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense but says of himself,
"I have committed one," and the community of monks asks him:
"Do you yourself say that you have committed a pārājika offense?
He replied, "I admit that I have committed a pārājika offense."
This is called unrighteous.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, he says of himself:
"I have committed one."
The assembly of monks asked, "Do you yourself admit that you have committed an offense? He replied: "I do."
"I have committed [an offense].
These are called the ten illegal [proceedings].
Regarding the ten types of legal [proceedings]: suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense and says to himself:
"I have committed a *pārājika* offense.
The community of monks asks him:
"Do you yourself say that you have committed it?"
If he says of himself,
"I have committed it," this is called acting according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense, and says of himself:
"I have committed [this offense]."
The assembly of monks asked,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense? He replied:
"I have committed it.
This is called acting in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense, he says of himself:
"I have not committed a pārājika offense.
The community of monks asked him,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed one?"
If he says himself,
"I have not committed an offense," this is called being in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta offense declares:
"I have not committed one."
The assembly of monks asked,
"Do you yourself say that you have committed an offense? He replied:
"I have not committed an offense.
This is called the tenth formal admission according to the Dharma.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard of this matter:

“We have performed the act of *ajñapti-karma* (formal condemnation) against a bhikṣu in Rājagṛha; yet he has gone to Śrāvastī and is living and working together with the bhikṣus there. We shall go to Śrāvastī.”
After the group of six bhikṣus had stayed in Rājagṛha as they pleased, they took their robes and bowls and went to Śrāvastī to visit the Buddha.
At that time, many bhikṣus were walking up and down in the open space near the gate of the Jetavana. When the group of six saw them, they asked:
"We, having been expelled from Rājagṛha for not recognizing [the offense], have come to Śrāvastī; do you bhikṣus associate with us and dwell together?"
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Buddha has settled this matter by means of his own declaration.
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"This matter has not been settled, yet the evil has been extinguished; it is because we are not present that this occurred.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having heard from the Buddha that the method for settling disputes through self-accusation was permitted, opposed it and refused to accept it, slandering the Buddha’s insight into the truth.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, their hearts were not pleased, and they spoke thus:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, when the World-Honored One permits the method for settling disputes through self-accusation, refuses to comply and instead slanders the Buddha’s vision of reality?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, [the monks] reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"How can those called bhikṣus, when I have authorized the method for settling disputes through their own confession (pratijñākāraka), reject it in opposition and slander the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From now on, I authorize the method of settling disputes in the presence [of the parties]. By means of this settlement in the presence, whatever various matters arise within the Saṃgha should be settled through the method of settlement in the presence."
There are two kinds of what is contrary to the Dharma and two kinds of what is in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding the two kinds that are contrary to the Dharma: there is a Saṃgha that acts contrary to the Dharma; one should issue a formal injunction to that Saṃgha to subdue them, thereby effecting the settlement of the dispute through the presence of the assembly.

Furthermore, an illegitimate Saṃgha may issue a formal charge against three individuals who act contrary to the Dharma, commanding them to submit and thereby effecting the settlement of a dispute before the assembly.

Likewise, an illegitimate Saṃgha may issue a formal charge against two or one individuals who act contrary to the Dharma, commanding them to submit and thereby effecting the settlement of a dispute before the assembly.

Furthermore, three persons who act contrary to the Dharma may direct three other persons who act contrary to the Dharma to subdue [the offender] and grant them the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).

Likewise, three persons who act contrary to the Dharma may direct two persons, one person, or the entire *saṃgha* who act contrary to the Dharma to subdue [the offender] and grant them the *saṃmukhavinaya*.

Furthermore, two persons who act contrary to the Dharma may instruct two other persons who act contrary to the Dharma—a single person, a group, or three persons—to subdue them by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).

Furthermore, when one person who acts contrary to the Dharma instructs another person who acts contrary to the Dharma, or a *saṃgha*, or three persons, or two persons, to subdue them by means of the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face legal procedure), this is called the "one illegal *pratyakṣa-vinaya* rule."
Furthermore, an unrighteous Saṃgha may command a righteous Saṃgha to perform a *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) for the purpose of subduing [the latter].
Likewise, an unrighteous Saṃgha may command three, two, or one person who is righteous to perform a *saṃmukhavinaya* for the purpose of subduing [them].

Furthermore, three persons who act contrary to the Dharma may direct three, two, one, or the entire Saṃgha who act in accordance with the Dharma, commanding them to subdue [the offender] by means of the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).

Furthermore, two persons who act contrary to the Dharma may instruct two persons who act according to the Dharma—one person, a *saṃgha*, or three persons—to subdue [the former] by means of the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (settlement before the assembly).

Furthermore, one person who is not in accordance with the Dharma may command another person who is in accordance with the Dharma—whether it be a Saṃgha, three persons, or two persons—to subdue [the former] by means of the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (disciplinary procedure in the presence of the accused).
These are called the two *adharma-abhimukha-vinaya* (unlawful procedures before the assembly).

Regarding the two types of *dharma-abhimukha-vinaya* (lawful procedures before the assembly): there is a community that acts lawfully, and it issues an injunction to that lawful community, commanding them to subdue [the offender] and grant the *abhimukha-vinaya*.

Furthermore, as with the Dharma and the Saṃgha, three, two, or one person who acts according to the Dharma may be instructed to subdue [the offender] by means of the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Likewise, three persons who act according to the Dharma may instruct three, two, one, or the entire Saṃgha who act according to the Dharma to subdue [the offender] by means of the *saṃmukha-vinaya*.

Furthermore, as when two persons acting according to the Dharma commission two persons, one person, a *saṃgha*, or three persons to subdue [the offender] by means of the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (settlement before the eyes).

Furthermore, when one person who acts according to the Dharma instructs another person who acts according to the Dharma, or a group of monks consisting of three or two persons, to subdue [the offender] and grant the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (face-to-face discipline), this is called the first method of *pratyakṣa-vinaya* according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, as when a legitimate Saṃgha instructs an illegitimate Saṃgha, commanding them to submit and granting them the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Likewise, as when a legitimate Saṃgha instructs three, two, or one person who is illegitimate, commanding them to submit and granting them the *saṃmukha-vinaya*.

Furthermore, as with three persons who act according to the Dharma, they may instruct three, two, one, or the entire Saṃgha who do not act according to the Dharma, commanding them to subdue [the offender] through the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).

Furthermore, as when two persons who act according to the Dharma instruct two, one, or three persons who do not act according to the Dharma, commanding them to be subdued through the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).

Furthermore, for example, one person who acts according to the Dharma may instruct another person who does not act according to the Dharma, or a group of monks consisting of three or two persons, to subdue them and grant them the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (face-to-face discipline).
This is called the two kinds of *yathādharma-pratyakṣa-vinaya* (settlement by presence according to the Dharma). Regarding the second method:

when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the Elder Dabba Mallaputta was constantly accused of this matter by the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā—whether before the Saṃgha, or by three, two, or even one person—on account of a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, Dabba Mallaputta spoke to the bhikṣus regarding this matter:

"Since the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā has slandered me with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense, and since the Saṃgha, or three people, two people, or even one person constantly speak of this matter, what should I do?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked Dabba Mallaputta:

"Is it true that you have constantly reported this matter to the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā—whether to a saṃgha, or to three people, two people, or one person—on account of her groundless charge of a pārājika offense?"
"You previously said to the bhikṣus:
'What should I do? Was it not indeed so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"From now on, I authorize the practice of the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection). By means of this *smṛtivinaya*, various matters that arise within the Saṃgha should be extinguished."
There are three kinds of *adharma-smṛtivinaya* (unlawful settling by recollection) and three kinds of *dharma-smṛtivinaya* (lawful settling by recollection).

As for the three kinds that are unlawful: there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense without remainder (*anavaśeṣa-āpatti*), yet he says of himself, "I have committed an offense with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa-āpatti*)."
If this bhikṣu requests the *saṃgha* for the *smṛti-vinaya*,
and the *saṃgha* grants him the *smṛti-vinaya*, this is called illegal. Why is that?
This person should be subject to expulsion (pravrājana).

Furthermore, it was like the case of the bhikṣu Śreṇika, who, because his mind was deranged and perverted, frequently committed acts that were impure, contrary to the Dharma, inconsistent with the Path, and not the way of a śramaṇa.

When this person has recovered their original mind, if they have previously committed offenses against a *saṃgha*, three people, two people, or one person, and constantly speak of these matters, and this person requests the *saṃgha* for the *smṛtivinaya* (the discipline of recollection), yet the *saṃgha* grants this person the *smṛtivinaya*, this is called an illegal act.
Why is this? Because such a person should be granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not deluded).

Furthermore, it is like the bhikṣu Hāta, who was shameless and lacked a sense of propriety, having broken the precepts and incurred charges based on what was seen, heard, or suspected; this person spoke of himself as follows:
"I have this fault," he says;
later, he says,
"I do not have this fault."
If this person requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha,
and the Saṃgha grants this person the *smṛtivinaya*, it is called illegal. Why is that?
Because this person should be granted the *yadbhūyaḥ-pratijñā-vinaya*, this is called the third *adharma-smṛti-vinaya*. Regarding the three *dharma* [cases]:

furthermore, as in the case of the bhikṣu Dharmapāla, who was falsely accused by the bhikṣuṇī Mettānī with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, if the Saṃgha—whether consisting of three, two, or one person—constantly speaks of this matter, that bhikṣu should request the *smṛti-vinaya* from the Saṃgha.
If the Saṃgha grants this person the *bhiṣaṇīya-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure of calling to mind), it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because this person ought to be granted the *bhiṣaṇīya-vinaya*.

Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu has committed an offense, and having already confessed it, he has eliminated it through repentance in accordance with the Dharma. If the Saṃgha, or three, two, or one person, still speaks of this matter, that bhikṣu should request from the Saṃgha the *smṛti-vinaya* (the legal procedure for restoration of mindfulness).
If the Sangha grants this person the *bhiṣaṇīya-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure of calling to mind), it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because this person ought to be granted the *bhiṣaṇīya-vinaya*.

Furthermore, suppose a bhikṣu has not yet committed a particular offense, but it is certain that he will do so; for this reason, if a saṃgha, or three, two, or one person, declares that he has committed this offense, that bhikṣu requests from the saṃgha the *smṛti-vinaya* (the legal procedure based on mindfulness).
If the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣu the *smṛtivinaya*, it is called "in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because this person is one to whom the *smṛtivinaya* ought to be granted.
"This is called the third *yathādharma-smṛtivinaya*.
After the Buddha had spoken thus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should grant the *smṛtivinaya* to the bhikṣu Dharmadatta."
If there should be another person such as this, they too should be granted the *smṛti-vinaya*.

As for the procedure for the *smṛti-vinaya*, the monk Dabba should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."

I, the bhikṣu Dharmapāla, because the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā slandered me with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, have constantly spoken of this matter before the Saṅgha, or before three, two, or one person.
I now request from the Saṃgha the *smṛti-vinaya*. May the Saṃgha—whether it be three persons, two persons, or one person—not speak of this matter again.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant me the *smṛti-vinaya*.
Thus he requested a second and a third time.
At that moment, a certain bhikṣu proclaimed among the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Because the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta was slandered by the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, the Saṅgha, groups of three, two, and one person constantly spoke of this matter.
Now, the bhikṣu Dabba has requested from the Saṃgha the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection); let neither the Saṃgha, nor three, two, or one person, speak further on this matter.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: let the Saṃgha grant the *buddhānusmṛti-vinaya* (the Vinaya of recollection) to the bhikṣu Dharmapada; let neither the Saṃgha, nor three persons, nor two persons, nor a single person speak of this matter again.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has completed the bestowing of the *dharmabhāṇaka*’s *smṛti-vinaya*. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!"

Regarding the practice of a bhikṣu who has obtained the *smṛtivinaya*: other bhikṣus should not point out his faults or offenses; they should not cause him to be reminded [of them]; they should not request permission from him, nor should they accept requests for permission from other bhikṣus.
If one solicits permission from another and receives it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one receives permission from another, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the other does not grant permission, or if one causes them to exceed the limit of the offense, or if one causes them to recall [the offense], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The Three Dharmas. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Śreṇika who, because his mind was deluded and inverted, frequently committed impure acts, unrighteous deeds, and actions contrary to the Path and inconsistent with the Dharma of a śramaṇa.

This person regains his original mind; regarding the transgressions he previously committed—whether before a Saṃgha, three people, two people, or a single person—they constantly speak of these matters.
Śīva speaks to the bhikṣus:

"Because my mind was originally deranged, deluded, and inverted, I committed many impure acts, unrighteous deeds, things not in accordance with the Path, and practices that are not the Dharma of a śramaṇa."
Now that I have regained my original mind, if the Saṃgha, or three people, two people, or even a single person were to constantly speak of the offenses I originally committed, what should I do now?
The bhikṣus related this matter in detail to the Buddha.
Knowing [the situation], the Buddha nevertheless asked Śreṇika:
"Is it true that, because your mind was deranged and inverted, you committed many impure acts, unrighteous acts, acts not in accordance with the Path, and acts not befitting a śramaṇa?"
Once you have recovered your original mind, whether it be a Saṃgha, three persons, two persons, or a single person who speaks to you regarding the offenses you originally committed,
you should say to those bhikṣus: "What should I do?"
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
