“From now on, I authorize the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict for one who was not insane). By means of this *amūḍha-vinaya*, various matters that arise within the Saṃgha should be extinguished.”
Regarding the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane), there are four kinds that are contrary to the Dharma and four kinds that are in accordance with the Dharma.
As for the four kinds that are contrary to the Dharma: suppose there is a bhikṣu who is not actually insane or deluded, yet manifests the appearance of being insane.
When the community of bhikṣus asks him, "Do you remember what you did while you were insane and deluded? [he responds accordingly].
He replied:
"Venerable sir!

I recall acting out of delusion; I recall being instructed by another to do so; I recall acting while dreaming; I recall running about naked to the east and west, or standing while passing urine or excrement."
If this person requests the *amūḍhavinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants this person the *amūḍhavinaya*, these are called the four illegal [procedures].
Regarding the four legal [procedures]: there is a bhikṣu who is actually insane, whose mind is deluded and inverted, and who manifests the appearance of insanity. The other bhikṣus ask him:
"Do you remember what you did while insane?"
He replied:
"I do not recall being instructed by others to perform any actions; I do not recall anything done in dreams; nor do I recall running or standing about naked, or defecating or urinating."
If this person requests the *amūḍha-vinaya* from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants this person the *amūḍha-vinaya*, this is called the fourth *amūḍha-vinaya* that is in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, I authorize the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict of sanity). By means of this *amūḍha-vinaya*, various matters that arise within the Saṃgha should be settled.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should grant the *amūḍhavinaya* (the verdict of sanity) to the bhikṣu Śīva.
If there are others like him, the Saṃgha should likewise grant them the *amūḍhavinaya*.
As for the procedure, the bhikṣu Śīva should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:”
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu Yue, was originally deranged, deluded, and mentally inverted, whereby I committed many impure acts, unrighteous deeds, actions contrary to the Path, and practices not befitting a śramaṇa."
I have now regained my original mind; may the Saṃgha, or three persons, or two persons, or one person, speak of the transgressions I previously committed.
I now request from the Saṃgha the *amūḍhavinaya* (the discipline for one no longer insane). May the Saṃgha, or three persons, or two persons, or one person, not speak of this matter again.
"Out of compassion for me, may the Saṃgha grant me the *amūḷhavinaya*.
Thus he requested a second and a third time.
At that moment, a certain bhikṣu proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Śreṇika was formerly deranged and mentally inverted; he committed many impure acts, unrighteous deeds, actions contrary to the Path, and conduct unworthy of a śramaṇa."
Having now recovered his original mind, if there are four monks, three, two, or even one, he shall confess the offenses previously committed.
Now, the monk Citta begs the Sangha for the *amūḷhavinaya* (the verdict of sanity); if there are four monks, three, two, or even one, let them no longer speak further of this matter.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: let the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of non-insanity) be granted to the bhikṣu Śiveyyaka; let neither the Saṃgha, nor three, two, or one person, speak of this matter again.
"Thus it is announced.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the threefold proclamation (*karma*).
"The Saṃgha has finished granting the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane) to the bhikṣu Śreṇika. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

Regarding those who have attained the *amūḷhavinaya* (the discipline of being no longer deluded) through the practice of the Dharma, other bhikṣus should not point out their faults or transgressions, should not cause them to be reminded [of them], should not request their confession, nor should they accept a confession from another bhikṣu.
If one solicits permission from another and receives it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one receives permission from another on behalf of someone else, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the other person does not grant permission, one incurs a transgression; if one causes them to remember [the offense], one incurs a *pāyattika*.

Regarding the four dharmas: when the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, there was at that time a bhikṣu named Khadira who was shameless, lacked a sense of moral dread, and possessed evil desires. Having committed an offense—whether seen, heard, or suspected—that bhikṣu first said of himself: "I did it."
Later, he said, "I did not do it.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:

"From now on, I allow you to settle disputes through the search for truth (*yathābhūta-vijñapti*). By means of this *yathābhūta-vijñapti* vinaya, the various matters that arise within the Saṃgha should be settled."
In seeking the Vinaya according to reality, there are five kinds that are contrary to the Dharma and five kinds that are in accordance with the Dharma.
As for the five contrary to the Dharma: suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense, yet he first says, "I have not committed it."
If he later says,
"I have committed it," and the Saṃgha proceeds to search for the *vinaya* (disciplinary rules) with this person in reality, this is called an illegal [proceeding].
Why is this? Because such a person ought to be subjected to the penalty of banishment (*pravāsanīya*).
There are monks who have committed offenses of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *dukkaṭa*.
First one says,
"I have not committed an offense," and later says:
"Guilty. If the Saṃgha grants this person a *yadbhūya-vinaya* (verdict according to what was actually found), it is called illegal. Why is that?
Because this person must be disciplined according to the offense they have committed.
Fifth, regarding "acting in accordance with the Dharma": suppose there is a bhikṣu who commits a pārājika offense and first says, "I have committed it."
If he later says,
"I have not committed an offense," and the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣu a *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (seeking according to what has actually occurred) *bi-ni*, this is called acting in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this? Because such a person should be dealt with according to the *vinaya* of searching for the truth (*yathābhūta-vijñapti-vinaya*).
If a bhikṣu has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* offense, yet first says:
"Having committed it," he later said,
"I have not committed it."
If the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣu the *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya* (the legal procedure of searching for the truth), it is called a proceeding in accordance with the Dharma. Why?
Because this person deserves to be granted the *yadbhūyaḥparyeṣaṇā-vinaya*.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should grant the *yathābhūta-paryeṣaṇā-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure of searching for the truth) to the bhikṣu Hāṭaka.
If there are other bhikṣus such as this, the Saṃgha should likewise grant them the *yathābhūta-paryeṣaṇā-vinaya*."
Regarding the granting of the *dharma*: with a single mind, the Saṃgha is in harmony, and one bhikṣu proclaims within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Kakuda is shameless and lacks remorse; he possesses faults regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."
First he says himself,
"I have committed an offense," and later he says:
"He has not committed an offense.
For this reason, the Saṃgha shall grant the *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya* (the disciplinary procedure for one who seeks the truth) to Śikhaṇḍin.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha grant the *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya* to the bhikṣu Śikhaṇḍin.
"Thus it is announced.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*) followed by three proclamations (*karmavācanā*).
"The Saṃgha has completed the *yadbhūyasikī-vinaya* for the bhikṣu Hāṭaka. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

Regarding those who have obtained the Vinaya and practice its rules: such a bhikṣu should not confer the full ordination (upasampadā) upon others, should not receive dependence (niśraya) from others, should not keep śrāmaṇeras, and should not accept the duty of instructing bhikṣuṇīs.
If the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (karmavācanā) of instructing bhikṣuṇīs, one should not instruct others.
Regarding the offense for which the Saṃgha has granted one a *śuddhaka-vicaya* (investigation of purity), one must not commit it again.
If an action appears to be a transgression or exceeds what constitutes a transgression, one should not perform it.
One should not criticize the *saṃgha*’s formal act (*karmavācanā*), nor should one criticize the person who performs the formal act.

One should not accuse a pure bhikṣu; one should not cause others to recall [his faults]; one should not engage in mutual recrimination; one should not beg from others for the formal hearing of a desire to expose another’s offense, nor should one accept such a request from others; one should not obstruct the recitation of the *Poṣadha*; one should not obstruct the reception of the precepts; one should not obstruct the *Pravāraṇā*; one should not expose the transgressions or offenses of a pure bhikṣu; one should always remain humble, subdue one’s own mind and conduct, and act in accordance with the will of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.
"If one does not practice the Dharma in this manner, one shall not be released from this *karmavācanā* for as long as one lives.
These five rules were established while the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the monks of Kauśāmbī took pleasure in quarreling and engaging in various disputes over matters of great and small importance, and they thought to themselves:
"If the Elder Śāriputra were to act as the presiding judge in legal matters, we would obtain a definitive resolution.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Is there a bhikṣu named Tāla who is capable of being appointed as the presiding judge for legal cases?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
There is one capable of serving as the presiding judge for legal cases.
The Buddha then assembled the community of bhikṣus on this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:

“From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣu Tāla to act as the presiding judge for settling disputes; he shall receive these rules for settling disputes in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, thereby resolving them through the presence of the parties concerned.”
There are three types of *tālaṭṭha*:
those whose bodies are virtuous but whose speech is not; those whose speech is virtuous but whose bodies are not; and those whose bodies are virtuous and whose speech is virtuous.
Regarding one whose body is virtuous but whose speech is not: such a *tālaṭṭha* does not personally go to the place of the accuser or the accused, nor does he himself utter these words:
"Regarding this matter, whether it be favorable or unfavorable, it should arise in such a way and not in another;
if you are victorious and the other is defeated, or if the other is victorious and you are defeated."
Although this person does not go there himself to speak, he dispatches a messenger to say:
"Regarding this matter, whether it be favorable or unfavorable, you ought to rise [in debate] in such a way or not so; if you defeat him, you shall win, and if he defeats you, you shall lose."
This is called being good in body but not good in speech.
As for being good in speech but not good in body: having gone in person to the place where the matter is being raised or where the parties involved are, one does not say these words:
"Regarding this matter, whether it be favorable or unfavorable, it should have arisen thus and should not have arisen thus; you have won and he has lost, or he has won and you have lost."
If one does not send a messenger to the person who has raised the matter, that person who has the matter may say this:

"Regarding this matter, whether it be good or bad, it should have been raised in such a way or not so raised; if you were victorious and he was defeated, or if he were victorious and you were defeated."
This is called being virtuous in speech but non-virtuous in body.
As for being virtuous in both speech and body: one does not go in person to the place of the accuser or the accused, nor does one speak such words as:
"Regarding this matter, whether it be favorable or unfavorable, it should be raised thus or it should not be raised thus; you have won and he has lost, or he has won and you have lost."
Furthermore, he does not dispatch a messenger to the one who has brought the charge or the one who is the subject of the charge to say:

"Regarding this matter, whether it be favorable or unfavorable, it should have arisen thus and not otherwise; if you were victorious and they defeated, or if they were victorious and you were defeated."
This is called excellence of body and excellence of speech.

From now on, those who act as *karmadāna* (stewards) should train themselves in this way: they should not travel along the same path as those who have been formally charged with a case or those involved in a dispute; nor should they separately travel along the same path with a single individual; nor should they make appointments together.

If one has previously established an appointment based on various causes and conditions—whether it be before noon or after noon, by day or by night, in a forest hermitage or near a village monastery—one should cancel that appointment. "Appointment" refers to such a scheduled engagement.

This *talaṭṭha* (one who has been suspended) shall undergo the resolution of this matter to be abandoned in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, by means of its manifestation and cessation.
This employs a *kamma-vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
What is meant by "presence"?
There are two kinds of presence:
presence of persons and presence of the *vinaya*.
"Presence of persons" means that those who assist in the formal act of accusation and the person against whom the charge is brought are assembled together in one place.

"Presence of the Vinaya" means that this matter is settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; this is called the presence of the Vinaya.
If a *talaṭṭha* (a committee of two) is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, it should be relinquished to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should accept this matter and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Saṃgha can settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the parties).
Regarding *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*. As for the presence of the Saṃgha:

all those monks who are eligible to participate in the *karmavācanā* (formal act) together must assemble in one place with harmonious minds; those entitled to convey their consent (*chanda*) must bring that consent; and those present among the monks who are capable of obstructing [the act] must not do so. This is called the presence of the Saṃgha.

"Presence of the person" means that the person who is the subject of the legal action and the persons who assist in bringing the case forward assemble together in one place; this is called "presence of the person.

"Presence of the Vinaya" means that the matter is settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; this is called "presence of the Vinaya."

If the Saṃgha is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, then one should nominate a *kukkula* (crow-feeder) within the Saṃgha; one should perform the *karmavācanā* for that *kukkula* to have him settle this matter.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* procedure: with the Saṃgha gathered in harmony and of one mind, one bhikṣu asks within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as the *āvāsika* (resident) to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha's teaching?"
If among the Saṃgha there should be one who says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, he should not be appointed as an *avavādaka* (instructor).
What are the five?
Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and not knowing whether [the offense] has been abandoned or not.
One who possesses these five qualities should be appointed as an *avavādaka* (instructor).
Not acting out of attachment, not acting out of aversion, not acting out of fear, and not acting out of delusion, he is able to know whether [the offense] has been abandoned or not.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu should announce in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣu so-and-so, so-and-so, is capable of acting as an *avakāśaka* (a mediator), resolving matters according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, in accordance with the affairs of the Saṃgha.

If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so shall act as *āvāsika* (resident stewards), capable of adjudicating matters according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).

"The Saṃgha appoints such-and-such and such-and-such bhikṣus as *āvāsika* (resident) to conclude the affairs within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
"If this Uvāra-guḷa is a senior elder (*sthavira*), the junior monks (*navaka bhikṣu*) should give him their consent (*chanda*) and then depart to a distance.

If this Uvāra-guḷa is a junior monk, he should take the consent from the elders and then move a short distance away; then, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha's teaching, this matter shall be settled."

If the Kukkula can resolve this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called resolving by means of a single *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (resolution through presence).
Regarding *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"Presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "presence of the person" and "presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.

If the *ubhatovibhaṅga* (the dual code) is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, another *ubhatovibhaṅga* should be established.
Regarding the establishment of the rule: when the Saṃgha is united in one mind, a single bhikṣu shall ask within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as the *karmakāraka* (executor of duties) to carry out the affairs of the Saṃgha?"
If he says, "I am able," one bhikṣu shall announce within the saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so are capable of acting as *āvāsika* (resident mediators), being able to adjudicate matters according to the Dharma as they arise within the Saṃgha.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so shall act as *āvāsikas*, being able to adjudicate matters according to the Dharma as they arise within the Saṃgha."
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act with one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).

"The Saṃgha appoints such-and-such a person and such-and-such a bhikṣu to serve as the *āvāsika* (resident) to conclude the business of the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held thus!"
“If this Uvāḷī is the senior monk (*sthavira*), the junior monks (*navaka bhikṣu*) should give their consent (*chanda*) and then move a short distance away.

If Uvāḷī is a junior monk, he should receive the consent from the senior monks and then move a short distance away; in this manner, the matter should be settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.”

If Kūṭadanta is able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling through the application of one *vinaya*—namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of others).
Regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"The presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "the presence of the person" and "the presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.
If the *āvāsika* and *kappiya-kāraka* are unable to settle the matter according to the Dharma, it shall be returned to the original *āvāsika* and *kappiya-kāraka*.
The original *āvāsika* and *kappiya-kāraka* should then settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching.
If one can resolve this matter in accordance with the Dharma, it is called resolving through the application of a single *vinaya* method, namely, the *sammukhavinaya* (resolution in the presence).
As for *sammukhavinaya*, it consists of the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as described above; the presence of the person and the presence of the Vinaya are also as described above.

If this former *āvāsa-kula* (monastic community) is likewise unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, it should be relinquished and entrusted to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should accept this matter and resolve it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Saṃgha accepts this matter and is able to resolve it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called resolving by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the parties).
Regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

If the Sangha is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, the Sangha should dispatch a messenger to a neighboring Sangha and say:

"This matter arose through such and such causes and conditions; it could not be settled by the *talaṭṭha*, nor could it be settled by the assembly of monks, nor could it be settled by the former *ukkhujjā*, nor could it be settled by the latter *ukkhujjā*. It is now returned to the former *ukkhujjā*."
"Previously, Ukha-kula was unable to resolve this matter, so he returned it to the Saṃgha.
You, venerable ones!
Come together in harmony for the sake of resolving this matter."
"Immediately that assembly should act in harmony. If the Saṃgha has already entered the rains retreat, one should depart after receiving a seven-day pass.
If the seven days have expired, one should break the rains retreat before departing."
For the sake of reconciliation, the resident Saṃgha should accept this matter and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the resident Saṃgha is able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the parties).
Regarding the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

If the local community of monks is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, then at that time one should perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) within the assembly to appoint an *āvāsika* (resident monk) to resolve it.
Regarding the *karmavācanā*: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu asks within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as the *āvāsika* (resident) to settle this matter according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching?"
In this regard, if one says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, one should not be appointed as an *avakāśika* (a monk who provides lodging).
What are the five?
Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and not knowing whether one has desisted or not.
If one possesses these five qualities, one should be appointed as an *avakāśika* (a monk who provides space for confession).
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, and not following delusion, he knows what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned.
Immediately, one bhikṣu proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"Venerable sirs, the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so are capable of acting as *karmakāraka* (the official who conducts the formal act) and are able to adjudicate matters according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and authorize the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to act as *karmakāraka* and adjudicate matters according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha."
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act of motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*):

'The Saṃgha appoints such-and-such a person and such-and-such a bhikṣu to serve as the *āvāsika* (resident) to conclude the affairs within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held thus! "
"If this Kūṭadanta is a senior elder (*sthavira*), the junior monks (*navaka bhikṣu*) should come to him, convey their consent (*chanda*), and then depart to a distance.
If he is a junior monk, he should receive the consent from the senior monks and then move a short distance away."
This matter should be settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If this matter can be settled by Auvākuḷa in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it is called settling through the application of one *vinaya*, namely, the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of others).
Regarding *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"The presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "the presence of the person" and "the presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.
If the *ukkhittaka* (one suspended) cannot settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, another *ukkhittaka* should be appointed.
Regarding the establishment of the legal procedure: when the Saṃgha is unified in one mind, a single bhikṣu shall ask within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as the *karmakāraka* (executor of the formal act) to resolve the matter according to the Dharma in accordance with the Saṃgha?"
If he says, "I am able," one bhikṣu shall announce within the saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so are capable of acting as *karmakāraka* (officials) to adjudicate matters according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so act as *karmakārakas* to adjudicate matters within the Saṃgha."
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation):

'Let such-and-such a person and such-and-such a bhikṣu be established as an *āvāsika* (resident) to conclude the affairs within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!'"
If this monk Uvāra is the senior (*sthavira*), the junior monks (*navaka*) should give him their consent (*chanda*) and then move a short distance away.
If Uvāra is a junior monk, he should take the consent from the seniors and then move a short distance away.
This matter should be settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the *ukkhujāta* (the "crooked one") is able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of a single *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
Regarding *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.
If that *āvāsika* monk is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, it should be returned to the previous *āvāsika* monk.
First, the *āvāsika* (resident monk) Kūṭa should accept this matter; he shall settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching.

If this *āvāsika* Kūṭa can settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, it is called "settling by means of one *vinaya*," namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Regarding the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"Presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "presence of the person" and "presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.

If the *pūrva-āvāsika* and *āgantuka* bhikṣus are unable to settle the matter according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, they should hand it over to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should accept this matter and settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Saṃgha accepts this matter and is able to settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling through the application of one *vinaya*—namely, the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Regarding *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

If the monks of the nearby residence are unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, they should hear that at a certain residence there is a great assembly of virtuous elders who know the Prātimokṣa, and that among those monks there are many bhikṣus who uphold the Sūtras, who uphold the Vinaya, and who uphold the Mātṛkā; then the monks of the nearby residence should dispatch a messenger to that residence regarding this matter.
Within the Saṃgha, one should first appoint a person to carry the matter. If they are outside the boundary, one should ensure the full number of monks is present.
As for the procedure for appointing them, the harmonious Saṃgha, with a single mind, should ask:
"Who is able to act as the bearer of the matter, taking this matter from this place to that place, provided it is well done even if interrupted along the way?"
In this regard, if someone should say,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, they should not be appointed as a messenger.
One who follows desire, follows hatred, follows fear, follows delusion, and does not know what has been extinguished and what has not been extinguished—
should these five qualities be present, one should be appointed as a messenger: one who does not follow desire,
does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, does not follow delusion, and knows what has been extinguished and what has not been extinguished.
At that time, the messenger shall take this matter with him.

If, while on the way, it can be settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called "settling by means of one *vinaya*," namely, the *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*).
Regarding *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as described above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as described above.

"If the person conveying the matter is unable to settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, or according to the Buddha's teaching while on the way, they should carry it to that assembly of monks.
If there is an elder (*sthavira*) among those monks who is highly learned and widely renowned, one should say to that person:

'This matter arose from such and such causes and conditions; the *talaṭṭha* could not settle it, the community of monks could not settle it, the *pūrvāvavādaka* could not settle it, and the *paścimāvavādaka* also could not settle it; therefore, it is returned to the *pūrvāvavādaka*.'"
The former Uvāḍa-Kūla was unable to resolve it, so he returned it to the Saṃgha.

The Saṃgha was also unable to resolve it; the Saṃgha of the neighboring residence was likewise unable to resolve it; the Uvāḍa-Kūla of the neighboring residence was unable to resolve it; and the latter Uvāḍa-Kūla was also unable to resolve it, so he returned it to the former Uvāḍa-Kūla.

Furthermore, they were unable to resolve it; returning to the community at their place of residence, the community was also unable to resolve it; and as the matter was transmitted through the path of people, it could not be resolved along the way. Having come here, Elder, are you able to accept this matter and resolve it?
If he says, "I can sever it," one should make an appointment with him.
If no time limit is set, it is not permitted;
however, if one sets a time limit with you, it may extend up to nine months.
There are five kinds of matters that are difficult to resolve:
First is stubbornness, second is rigidity, third is perversity, fourth is coming and going, and fifth is doubt and fear.
As for stubbornness, it refers to being obstinately attached to one's own views.
The "strong" refers to those who undertake tasks and are courageous, robust, and powerful.
The "obstinate and perverse" refers to those who undertake tasks and possess an evil nature, prone to anger and resentment.
The "coming and going" refers to these matters proceeding from one dwelling place to another dwelling place.
Regarding those who harbor doubts and fears: it is because the bhikṣus fear that during the formal act of adjudication, the unified and harmonious Saṃgha will be split into two factions.
First, a person to distribute the voting tallies (*śalākā*) should be appointed.
He should be appointed as follows: the unified and harmonious Saṃgha should ask him:
"Who can serve as the person to distribute the voting sticks? Among them, someone said, "I can."
There are five qualities by which one should not be appointed as a person to distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*):
being swayed by affection, being swayed by hatred, being swayed by fear, being swayed by delusion, and not knowing when to distribute the voting sticks and when not to distribute them.
If one possesses five qualities, they should be appointed as the person who distributes the voting sticks (*śalākā*):
they do not follow favoritism, they do not follow hatred, they do not follow fear, they do not follow delusion, and they know when the voting sticks have been distributed and when they have not.
Among them, one bhikṣu proclaims:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of acting as the distributor of voting sticks."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let monk so-and-so act as the distributor of voting tallies for the Saṃgha.
This is called the *jñapti*.
Thus is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement).
"The Sangha has completed the appointment of such-and-such a bhikṣu as the distributor of voting sticks. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
If a bhikṣu has already been appointed as the distributor of voting sticks, he should, according to the number of monks, prepare two kinds of sticks:
one portion long and one portion short; one portion white and one portion black.
For those who speak according to the Dharma, long tally-sticks are made; for those who speak contrary to the Dharma, short tally-sticks are made.
For those who speak according to the Dharma, white tally-sticks are made; for those who speak contrary to the Dharma, black tally-sticks are made.
When announcing a tally that accords with the Dharma, one should hold it with the right hand; when announcing a tally that does not accord with the Dharma, one should hold it with the left hand.
When announcing a tally that accords with the Dharma, one should hold it loosely; when announcing a tally that does not accord with the Dharma, one should hold it tightly.
First, the tally for those who speak according to the Dharma is presented; subsequently, the tally for those who speak contrary to the Dharma is presented.
The person distributing the tallies should say:
"This is the tally for those who speak according to the Dharma; this is the tally for those who speak contrary to the Dharma."

If, after the voting sticks have been distributed, even one more stick than those declared to be in accordance with the Dharma is found, this matter is called "settlement by means of two *vinayas*," namely: the *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhavinaya*) and the *vinaya* of majority decision (*yadbhūyasikīya-vinaya*).

Regarding the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): if, within this matter, the person who has raised the issue and the person against whom it is raised are together in one place in their presence, and the matter is settled through a procedure that is in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called *sammukhavinaya*.

Regarding the *yadbhūyaḥ-pratijñā-vinaya* (the legal procedure of majority decision): herein, one seeks [the truth] through repeated inquiry and response to resolve matters according to the Dharma. If someone speaks what is contrary to the Dharma, even by a single vote, this matter is also termed "resolution" (*vinīta*) by means of two legal procedures: the *sammukha-vinaya* (legal procedure of presence) and the *yadbhūyaḥ-pratijñā-vinaya*.

Regarding the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): herein, if there are both those who assist in the formal accusation and the person against whom the charge is brought, and they are all assembled together in one place in the presence of one another, yet [the matter] is settled through what is not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it is [an invalid settlement].
There are four types of persons who distribute voting tallies (*śalākā*):

first, those who conceal the distribution; second, those who distribute them in reverse order; third, those who distribute them according to a fixed schedule; and fourth, those who distribute them to everyone.

Regarding "concealed voting" (*saṃvṛta-śalākā-cāra*): if someone distributes voting sticks while walking in the dark, or distributes them where there are walls or obstructions, this is called concealed voting. Regarding "inverted voting" (*viparyasta-śalākā-cāra*):

if a bhikṣu distributes voting sticks in an inverted manner—giving the voting stick for those who speak according to the Dharma to one who speaks contrary to the Dharma, and giving the voting stick for those who speak contrary to the Dharma to one who speaks according to the Dharma—this is called inversion.

Regarding "agreements": if various bhikṣus, following their preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya), follow those with the same preceptor or the same instructor, follow those who are acquainted, follow those who converse together, follow spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), follow those of like mind, or follow [the customs of] a country, a village, or a household, they make an agreement together, saying:
"We shall take such tally-sticks; you must not distance yourselves from our side, nor be separate or different, nor fail to converse with one another, but perform our duties together."
This is called the "appointment.
When the entire Saṃgha takes the voting sticks (*śalākā*), at that time the entire Saṃgha should assemble together in one place; they must not take their consent (*chanda*) by proxy. Why is this?
Because many bhikṣus speak what is not the Dharma,
this is called "the entire Saṃgha taking voting tickets.

If the great elder of that assembly knows the Prātimokṣa and is able to resolve this matter, it is then said that the matter is resolved by means of a single Vinaya procedure, namely, the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Among these, "settling through confrontation" (*sammukhavinaya*) consists of the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.
If a great senior elder (sthavira) knows that the community of bhikṣus, through the prātimokṣa, cannot resolve this matter, he should hand it back to the official who transmits the matter.
That official should take up the matter and, while on the road, resolve it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the person conveying the matter is able to settle this issue on the path in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the assembly).
The *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) is as explained above.

If the person conveying the matter is unable to settle this issue in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, then while that bhikṣu is on his way, if he hears that within the monastic quarters of that place there are three, two, or even one bhikṣu who can uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā, and who are revered and respected by the fourfold assembly; [he should go there].
The messenger shall go to that dwelling place and say to one of the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sir, such-and-such a matter has arisen here; the *talaṭṭha* was unable to settle it, nor did the Saṃgha..."
He was able to resolve it, yet the Pūrva-āvāsika monks were unable to resolve it;
the Apara-āvāsika monks were unable to resolve it, so he returned it to the Pūrva-āvāsika monks, who again were unable to resolve it;
the Saṃgha was unable to resolve it, the local resident Saṃgha was also unable to resolve it, and the Pūrva-āvāsika monks were unable to resolve it, as was the Apara-... [the latter].
The *āvāsika* monks were unable to resolve it; returning to the original *āvāsika* monks, they were again unable to resolve it.
Returning to the resident community (*saṃgha*) at their dwelling place, they were again unable to resolve it.

It was also not resolved through the person conveying the matter along the way, nor by the community of great senior monks who uphold the Vinaya. The person conveying the matter was likewise unable to resolve it while on the road.
"Venerable Sir! Three bhikṣus or two bhikṣus are unable to resolve this matter.
Regarding this matter, please act in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching to resolve it."
Regarding this bhikṣu who is honored, respected, and praised by the fourfold assembly, one should say:
"It is impossible for two people to claim victory over each other; between them, there must be one winner and one loser."
If one speaks in such a manner, it is called speaking according to the Dharma;
if one does not speak in such a manner, it is called speaking contrary to the Dharma.
Regarding these various signs, if a bhikṣu, after a matter has been settled according to the Dharma, raises it again, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one merely rebukes them by saying,
"This act of severing is not in accordance with the Dharma," one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the six dharmas: the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī delighted in quarreling and engaging in mutual recrimination. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, the *tṛṇastāraka* (covering with grass) procedure is permitted. By means of this *tṛṇastāraka* procedure, whatever various matters arise within the Saṃgha should be extinguished.
What is the *tṛṇastāraka* procedure?..."
By means of this *tṛṇa-prastāra* (spreading of grass) *vinaya* rule, one extinguishes the various matters that arise within the Saṃgha.
Suppose there is a certain residence where the monks take pleasure in quarreling and speaking abusively to one another; those monks should assemble together in one place and reflect as follows:
"Venerable Elders!..."
We have suffered a great loss and not gained anything; we have met with great decline and not benefit; it is a great evil and unwholesome.

We have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma out of faith, yet now we delight in quarreling and speaking ill of one another. If we continue to pursue the root of such matters, there may be those within the Saṃgha who cause disputes that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen cannot be extinguished.
Having formed this thought, he informs the Saṃgha:

"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; this matter shall be settled by the *bhūtagrāma-vinaya* (the legal procedure of 'covering over as with grass'). This is called the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Immediately, these bhikṣus should divide themselves into two groups, each staying in a separate place.
If among them there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense, he should address the senior elder (sthavira) in this way:
"We have suffered a great loss and not a gain; we have met with great decline and not benefit; it is a great evil and unwholesome."

Out of faith, we have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma; yet now we delight in quarreling and speaking ill of one another. If we were to seek the root of this matter, there would be those among the Sangha who might initiate disputes that have not yet arisen, and those already arisen could not be extinguished.

Now we shall humble ourselves; regarding the transgressions we have committed—excluding those that constitute *sthūlātyaya* offenses and excluding those associated with laypeople—we now confess and repent before the Elder in his presence, without concealment.
"If not even one bhikṣu among them objects to this matter, they should go to where the second group of the community is.
If there is an elder or senior monk there, they should say to him:
'We have suffered a great loss and not a gain; a great decline and not a benefit; a great evil and what is unwholesome.'"

"Out of faith, we have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma; yet now we delight in strife and mutual recrimination. If we were to seek the root of this matter, there might be those within the Saṃgha who would initiate disputes that have not yet arisen, and those already arisen could not be extinguished."

Now we shall humble ourselves; regarding the transgressions we have committed—excluding those of the *sthūlātyaya* class and those associated with laypeople—we shall now, for our own sake and for the sake of others, openly confess and repent before you without concealment.
The bhikṣus said,
"Do you yourself see your fault?
He replied:
“I see my fault.
“Repent according to the Dharma; do not commit it again.
The second group of the assembly speaks in this same manner; this is called the *tṛṇastāraka* (grass-spreading) *vinaya* method.
The third recitation of the Seven Dharmas is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle Twenty.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle Twenty-one. The first of the fourth recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The Four Recitations, Part 9: The Seven Dharmas, Chapter 1: The Method for Receiving Full Ordination. Regarding the first of the seven dharmas, the method for receiving full ordination:

When the Buddha, the Bhagavān, was residing outside the city of Rājagṛha, at that time it had not yet been permitted for bhikṣus to act as upādhyāyas or ācāryas, nor was there the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) for receiving full ordination.

At that time, because the bhikṣus had as yet no preceptors (upādhyāya) or instructors (ācārya), they made their monastic robes (kāṣāya) improperly, wore their robes improperly, and their physical deportment was entirely improper.

Furthermore, when these bhikṣus travel from village to village, from city to city, and from country to country; while wandering on their alms-rounds, they beg for rice, they beg for soup, and they beg for *khādaniya* (solid food).

When invited by others to eat, they demand rice, demand soup, and demand *khādaniya*. They take the leftovers of others—the remnants of rice in the bowl, the remnants of soup, the remnants of *khādaniya*, and the remnants of drinks.
They eat with loud voices and great clamor, just like the Brahmins when they eat.
There was a bhikṣu named Mahālu who was suffering from painful illness; he had no companion and no one to look after him.
When those of external paths and other sects saw this situation, they criticized and reviled him, saying:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, have no good teaching; they are not taught, they lack discipline, and they lack the methods of self-mastery. They make their kāṣāya robes improperly, they wear their robes improperly, and even their bodily deportment is entirely improper."
When traveling from village to village, city to city, and country to country; when wandering on almsround, begging for rice, begging for soup, and begging for solid food (*khādaniya*);
when invited by others to eat, requesting rice, requesting soup, and requesting solid food;
or taking the leftovers of others—namely, the remnants of rice in the bowl, remnants of soup, remnants of solid food, and remnants of drink.
"Eating with loud voices and making great noise, just like the various brahmins when they eat.
When certain bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this matter, they felt shame and remorse; they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, for this reason, assembled the Saṃgha.

Once the assembly was gathered, it is the constant law of all Buddhas to inquire with knowledge, not to inquire despite knowing, to inquire when the time is right, not to inquire when the time is not right, to inquire when it is beneficial, not to inquire when it is not beneficial, and to inquire when there is a specific cause and condition.
Now the Buddha, knowing [the truth], asked.
The Buddha questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who has no upādhyāya or ācārya, yet makes his kāṣāya robes improperly, wears his robes improperly, and whose bodily deportment is entirely improper;
as he travels from village to village, city to city, and country to country, when wandering and when going on alms-rounds, begging for rice, begging for soup, and begging for khādaniya food?"
When invited to eat, one asks for rice, asks for soup, or asks for solid food (*khādaniya*);
one takes the leftovers of others—leftover rice from the bowl, leftover soup, leftover solid food, or leftover drinks;
and one eats with a loud voice and great noise, like the various Brahmins when they eat?
Various followers of external paths and heterodox sects, out of jealousy, reviled and censured him, saying:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no good instruction; they are not disciplined, lack the methods of training and self-mastery, and their making of the kāṣāya robes is contrary to the Dharma, as is their wearing of the robes; even their bodily deportment is entirely contrary to the Dharma.
As they travel from village to village, city to city, and kingdom to kingdom, when wandering and begging for alms—whether seeking rice, soup, or solid food (khādaniya)—[their conduct is improper]."
When invited to eat, they ask for rice, ask for soup, and ask for solid food (*khādaniya*);
they take the leftovers of others—leftover rice in the bowl, leftover soup, leftover solid food, and leftover drinks;
they eat with loud voices and great noise, just like the various Brahmins when they eat.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I authorize the appointment of upādhyāyas and ācāryas, and I authorize the conferral of full ordination through the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* in the presence of a quorum of ten monks."
What is the full ordination through the white-four-fold *karmavācanā*?
The community of monks, being united with one mind, has one monk proclaim within the assembly:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, has received the full ordination from such-and-one.
This person, so-and-so, requests the full ordination from the Saṃgha, with such-and-one as preceptor.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant the full ordination to so-and-so, with such-and-one as preceptor.
Thus it was announced. This is the formal motion followed by the threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

From now on, it is permitted for a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) to attend to his co-practicing disciple (*sahacaryā-śrāvaka*): if he is ill, he should be nursed; if he is about to die, he should be saved. If he is ill, one should provide him with food and drink suited to his illness, medicine suited to his illness, and all necessary provisions suited to his illness.
If the disciple has no wealth, the preceptor should provide it for him.
If the preceptor has none, he should seek it from others and give it.
If he has few acquaintances and cannot obtain it through seeking, he should give whatever fine food he receives from almsround.
If the preceptor is ill, the disciple should likewise attend to him.
It is the same for an ācārya looking after his resident disciple, and for a resident disciple looking after his ācārya.

From now on, all preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya), when looking after their co-resident disciples (sahavāsika) and resident disciples (antevāsika), shall cherish and support them as they would their own children.
Co-resident disciples and resident disciples, in turn, shall look upon their preceptors and instructors as they would their own fathers.
"In this way, you all shall dwell supporting one another in succession, increasing wholesome qualities within my Dharma.
While the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha,
the bhikṣus thought to themselves:

“The Buddha has already permitted us to act as preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*), and has permitted the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*) through the formal procedure of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) in the presence of ten monks.
Thus, those young bhikṣus acted as preceptors—even if they were one, two, three, four, or five years senior—while the elder bhikṣus served as their teachers.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; they rebuked the other bhikṣus, saying: "How can one be called a bhikṣu?

The Buddha has already permitted us to have upādhyāyas and ācāryas, and permitted the conferral of full ordination through the formal procedure of a jñapti-caturtha-karman before a quorum of ten monks. Yet these young bhikṣus act as upādhyāyas—some with only one year, two years, three years, four years, or five years of seniority—acting as elders to those who are junior?"
After those bhikṣus had rebuked him in various ways, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Once the assembly was gathered, the Buddha, knowing the reason, questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣus with various causes and conditions: "Why are you called bhikṣus?

The Buddha has already permitted us to have upādhyāyas and ācāryas, and has permitted the reception of full ordination through the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* before an assembly of ten monks. Yet these young bhikṣus act as upādhyāyas—some only one year, two years, three years, four years, or five years senior—to elder bhikṣus?"
Although the Buddha rebuked him, he had not yet established a formal precept.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the Elder Upasena Vaṇḍaputra conferred full ordination upon a co-resident disciple who had been with him for one year; both the preceptor and the disciple had been together for one year. They went [together] without [the disciple] having completed his full term.
He observed the summer retreat in a certain location in the kingdom of Kośala. It is the constant custom of the Buddhas to hold two great assemblies:
at the end of spring and at the end of summer.
When it was time for the retreat at the end of spring, bhikṣus from various regions and countries came to hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, thinking to themselves:
"This Dharma is pleasant for the summer retreat.
This was the first great assembly.
At the end of the summer, having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and finished making their robes, they took up their bowls and robes and went to where the Buddha was, reflecting thus:
"I have not seen the Bhagavān for a long time; I have not seen the Sugata for a long time.
This was the second great assembly.

At that time, the Elder Upasena was observing the rains retreat at that dwelling place. Having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and finished making his robes, he took up his bowl and robes and, together with his disciple—who had been ordained for one year—set out on a journey, both having been ordained for two years, toward Śrāvastī.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas to inquire of an incoming bhikṣu:
“Was your summer retreat endured?”
Are you well?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of alms-food, and are you not fatigued by the journey?
Now the Buddha likewise asked:
“Upasena! Was the summer retreat endured and was it sufficient?”
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of alms-food, and are you not weary from the road? Upasena replied:
"You truly possess sufficient patience, you dwell in peace and happiness, you do not lack for alms, and you are not fatigued by the roads.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked: "Upasena!"
"Who is this son of good family?
He replied, "It is I."
The Buddha asked, "What is this that you are doing?
They replied:
"This is my co-resident disciple.
The Buddha asked,
"How many years of seniority do you have?"
He replied, "Two years.
[The Buddha asked,] "How old is this son of good family?"
He replied, "One year.
Thereupon, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha censured Upasena with various causes and conditions:
"You foolish man!

Why did you previously contemplate only desiring to maintain a following? How can one who has been a bhikṣu for only two years maintain a disciple who has been ordained for only one year as a co-resident?

For what reason is he called a 'bhikṣu,' when the Buddha permitted us to act as upādhyāyas and ācāryas, and permitted the conferral of full ordination through the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* before an assembly of ten monks?"
Is this young bhikṣu one who has conferred full ordination upon a co-resident disciple after [only] one year, two years, three years, four years, or five years as a senior elder bhikṣu?
After the Buddha had finished his reprimand through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one who has not yet reached ten years [of seniority] shall not confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple."
"If one confers full ordination [in such a manner], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"The Buddha has permitted us to receive full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) performed in the presence of ten monks, with our preceptors and teachers having been authorized."
"One who has not reached ten years [of seniority] shall not confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.
These bhikṣus, having reached ten years [of seniority], all conferred full ordination upon their co-resident disciples.
Whether one knows the Dharma or not, they bestow it; whether one is virtuous or not, they keep them; whether one abides in the precepts or not, they ordain them.

In this regard, if one sees that the preceptor does not know the Dharma and the disciple also does not know the Dharma, that the preceptor is unvirtuous and the disciple is also unvirtuous, and that the preceptor does not abide in the precepts and the disciple also does not abide in the precepts.

At that time, certain bhikṣus, being themselves ignorant of the Dharma, unskilled in the wholesome, and not abiding in the precepts, gave others the going-forth and the full ordination, acted as preceptors for them, and maintained śrāmaṇeras.

There was a bhikṣu named Mahālu who did not know the Dharma, was not virtuous, and did not abide in the precepts; though he had completed ten full years [of seniority], he conferred full ordination upon a co-resident disciple. Because of a minor matter, he quarreled with his disciple, and the disciple then renounced the precepts and returned to lay life.
The bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities rebuked him, saying: "How can one be called a bhikṣu?

The Buddha permitted the preceptor, permitted the ācārya, and permitted the formal conferral of full ordination before a quorum of ten monks through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. One who has not completed ten years [of standing] is not permitted to confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple."

These bhikṣus, having completed ten years [of standing], all conferred full ordination upon their co-resident disciples; they conferred it whether they themselves knew the Dharma or not, they kept them whether they were virtuous or not, and they ordained them whether they abided in the precepts or not.

In this regard, if one sees that the preceptor does not know the Dharma, is not virtuous, and does not abide in the precepts—and if the disciple is likewise—and yet they ordain another, confer full ordination upon them, act as their preceptor for dependence (*niśrayācārya*), and keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*)?
After those bhikṣus had finished censuring him in various ways, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the situation], questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu? The Buddha has permitted preceptors, permitted ācāryas, and permitted ten monks to confer full ordination through the presence of the assembly and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. One who has not completed ten years [of standing] is not permitted to grant full ordination to a co-resident disciple."
These bhikṣus, having completed ten years [of standing], all conferred full ordination upon their co-resident disciples.

They conferred it whether they knew the Dharma or did not know the Dharma; they kept those who were virtuous and also kept those who were not virtuous; they ordained those who dwelt in the precepts and also ordained those who did not dwell in the precepts.

In this regard, if one sees that the preceptor does not know the Dharma, is not virtuous, and does not abide in the precepts—and the disciple is likewise—would they still ordain others, grant them full ordination, act as a teacher of dependence, and keep śrāmaṇeras?
After the Buddha had finished his reprimand through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, it is permitted that one who has fulfilled five dharmas and has been ordained for ten years or more should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple."

What are the five? First, having completed ten years or more; second, maintaining the precepts without violation; third, being learned; fourth, possessing the power to eliminate a disciple’s distress and remorse in accordance with the Dharma; and fifth, being able to uproot a disciple’s evil and deviant views.
Furthermore, there are five qualities that must be perfected; having completed ten years [of standing], one should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.

What are these five? First, perfection of faith; second, perfection of ethical discipline; third, perfection of learning; fourth, perfection of relinquishment; and fifth, perfection of wisdom. Such a person is able to praise and instruct the disciple, causing them to properly enter and abide in faith, ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom.
Furthermore, when one has accomplished five qualities and completed ten years [of seniority], one should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.

What are these five? First, accomplishment in the aggregate of unlearned ethical discipline; second, accomplishment in the aggregate of unlearned concentration; third, accomplishment in the aggregate of unlearned wisdom; fourth, accomplishment in the aggregate of unlearned liberation; and fifth, accomplishment in the aggregate of unlearned knowledge and vision of liberation. Such a person is able to praise and instruct the disciple, and is skilled in causing them to enter and abide in the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, there are five qualities that must be fulfilled; having completed ten years [of standing], one should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.

What are these five? First, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense; third, knowing when an offense is light; fourth, knowing when an offense is heavy; and fifth, knowing how to recite the *Prātimokṣa* and provide a detailed exposition of its training rules.
Furthermore, there are five qualities that must be fulfilled; having reached ten years [of standing], one should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.

What are these five? First, knowing the dharma of renunciation; second, being able to act as a preceptor (ācārya); third, being able to act as a preceptor for the precepts (śīlācārya); fourth, being able to know the dharma regarding the teacher of dependence (niśrayācārya); and fifth, being able to know the dharmas that obstruct the path and those that do not obstruct the path.
Furthermore, there are five qualities that must be fulfilled; having reached ten years [of standing], one should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.
What are these five?
First, being able to teach the disciple pure precepts.
Second, he is able to teach the Abhidharma;
third, he is able to teach the Vinaya;

fourth, when a disciple is in another region and is distressed, suffering, and unhappy, he is able to cause that person to come, either by his own power or, if he himself is unable, through the power of others.
If the five disciples are able to provide for one when ill, or if one is unable to do so oneself, one can cause others to provide for them;
having thus accomplished these five qualities and reached ten years or more [of seniority], one should confer full ordination upon a co-resident disciple.
If one does not possess the aforementioned five qualities and has completed ten years or more, yet confers full ordination upon a co-resident disciple, one incurs an offense.
"If a bhikṣu possesses the aforementioned five qualities and has completed ten years, he should grant dependence to others."
How should it be granted?

The bhikṣu who seeks to obtain formal reliance (niśraya) should rise from his seat, adjust his robe to bare one shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with both hands clasping the feet of the elder, and speak as follows:
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], beg for reliance from the elder."
"Venerable sir, please grant me formal reliance; I shall dwell in reliance upon you, venerable sir.
He should request a second and a third time in this same manner.
The elder should then say:
"It is as you have said.
If one possesses the five qualities and has completed ten years [of seniority], one may receive dependence from others.
If one lacks the five qualities, even if ten years have been completed, one commits an offense by receiving dependence from others.
“If a bhikṣu possesses the aforementioned five qualities and has been ordained for ten years, he should take a śrāmaṇera into his care.
How should he take him into care?
If the boy has not yet had his hair shaved, at that time he should have his hair shaved.”

If he has his own *kāṣāya*, he should wear it; if not, the preceptor should provide him with a robe to wear. He should be instructed to kneel on his right knee with palms joined, and the preceptor should instruct him:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha."
The second:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. The third:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha.
"I, [Name], have already taken refuge in the Buddha, have already taken refuge in the Dharma, and have already taken refuge in the Saṃgha."
"From this day forth for as long as life lasts, may you remember me as a lay follower (upāsaka) of the Buddha. Second:
"I, [name], have taken refuge in the Buddha, have taken refuge in the Dharma, and have taken refuge in the Saṃgha."
"From this day forth for as long as life lasts, may you remember me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of the Buddha. Third:
"I, [name], have taken refuge in the Buddha, have taken refuge in the Dharma, and have taken refuge in the Saṃgha."
"From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall remember myself as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) of this Buddha.

"Listen, [Name], to these five precepts for lay followers spoken by the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, who possesses knowledge and vision; all lay followers must protect and uphold them for as long as life lasts."
What are the five?
To abstain from taking life for as long as one lives is the precept of an upāsaka.
Among these, it is to abstain from taking life for as long as one lives.
If one is able to uphold this, one should say:
"I am able.
To refrain from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts is the precept of an upāsaka.
Regarding this, one should abstain from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts.
If you are able to maintain this, you should say:
"I am able."
"Abstaining from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts is a lay follower's precept (*upāsaka-śīla*).
Regarding this, one must abstain from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts.
If you are able to uphold it, you should say: "
“I can. To abstain from false speech for as long as life lasts is a precept of the upāsaka.
Within this, it is to abstain from false speech for as long as life lasts.
If one is able to uphold it, one should say: "I can.
To abstain from drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts is a lay follower's precept (*upāsaka-śīla*); herein, one abstains from drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts.
Grain liquor, grape wine, sugarcane wine, and intoxicants that lead to heedlessness.
If one is able to observe them, one should say:
"I am able."

"I, [Name], having already taken refuge in the Buddha, having already taken refuge in the Dharma, and having already taken refuge in the Saṅgha, have gone forth as a renunciant under this Blessed One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I too have gone forth following the Buddha, with [Name] as my preceptor."

Second: "I, [Name], having already taken refuge in the Buddha, having already taken refuge in the Dharma, and having already taken refuge in the Saṃgha, have gone forth; I have gone forth under this Blessed One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. I too follow the Buddha in going forth, with [Name] as my preceptor."
The third [recitation]:

"I, [Name], having already taken refuge in the Buddha, having already taken refuge in the Dharma, and having already taken refuge in the Saṃgha, have gone forth. I have gone forth under this Buddha Bhagavān Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I also follow the Buddha in going forth, with [Name] as my preceptor."

"I, [Name], have already taken refuge in the Buddha, have already taken refuge in the Dharma, and have already taken refuge in the Saṃgha; I have gone forth as a renunciant under this Blessed One, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. I too have completed going forth following the Buddha, with [Name] as my preceptor."
At that time, one should ask:
"How old are you?
He should answer according to his age.
"When did you leave the household life?
Was it in winter, spring, or summer? Was there an intercalary month or not?
One should answer according to these questions.
"Remember this for as long as you live.
The Preceptor should say:

"Listen, [Name], this is what the Buddha Bhagavān, the Śākya-muni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, who possesses knowledge and vision, has proclaimed as the ten precepts for renunciation for śrāmaṇeras; all śrāmaṇeras must protect and uphold them for as long as they live."
What are the ten?
To abstain from taking life for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Among these, "abstaining from taking life for as long as one lives" means:
If one can say,
"So be it," and for as long as life lasts abstains from taking what is not given, this is the śrāmaṇera precept.
In this regard, one should abstain from taking what is not given for as long as life lasts;
if one can say, "So be it."
"To abstain from unchaste conduct for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Regarding this, one must abstain from unchaste conduct for as long as life lasts.
If one is able, one should say:"
"Yes. To abstain from false speech for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, one abstains from false speech for as long as life lasts.
If one can say,
"So be it," and for as long as life lasts abstain from drinking intoxicants, this is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Among these, one should abstain from drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts:
rice wine, grape wine, sugarcane wine, and any other liquor that can cause heedlessness.
One should be able to say:
"Yes. To abstain from high and large beds for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, "for as long as one lives" means abstaining from high and large beds for the duration of one's life.
If one can say,
"So be it," and for as long as life lasts abstain from wearing flower garlands, jeweled necklaces, scented ointments on the body, or perfumed clothing, this is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Among these, for as long as life lasts, one should abstain from attaching oneself to flower garlands, necklaces, perfumes for anointing the body, and perfumed clothing.
One should be able to say: "I can."
To refrain for the duration of one’s life from performing music, singing, or dancing, and from going to watch or listen to various musical instruments—this is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Within this, one refrains for the duration of one’s life from performing music, singing, or dancing, and from going to watch or listen to various forms of adornment.
If one can say,
"So be it," and for as long as life lasts abstain from receiving, keeping, or accumulating gold, silver, coins, or treasures, this is the śrāmaṇera precept.
In this regard, one should renounce the acceptance and possession of gold, silver, money, and treasures for as long as life lasts.
If one is able to say: "So be it."
"Abstaining from eating at improper times for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
Regarding this abstention from eating at improper times for as long as life lasts, if one is able to say: "
"Yes. If one has accomplished these five qualities and completed ten years of seniority, one may keep a śrāmaṇera.
