If one has not accomplished these five qualities, yet keeps a śrāmaṇera after completing ten years, one incurs an offense.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
The Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana conferred full ordination upon seventeen young musicians from Rājagṛha, including Cūḍapanthaka.
At the hour of *pradoṣa*, these people were so overcome by hunger that they wailed loudly within the monastery, crying out like infants.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Why is there the sound of infant crying within the monastery?"
Ānanda replied,
“World-Honored One!
The Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana has conferred full ordination upon seventeen young musicians from Rājagṛha, including Upatiṣya.”
"These people, being extremely hungry at the hour of *pradoṣa*, are crying out loudly within the monastery, making sounds like the wailing of infants.

At that time, the Buddha, for this reason, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the situation, asked intentionally, addressing Maudgalyāyana: "Did you truly do this?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked Maudgalyāyana with various causes and conditions:
"You do not know the proper time, you do not know the measure, and you do not know the limit.

You wish to save others, yet when there are fewer than twenty people, they cannot endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, snakes, vipers, and venomous stings; nor can they endure the harsh words of others or the painful afflictions within their own bodies."

A person who has reached twenty years of age is able to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, lice, snakes, and venomous stings; they are able to endure the harsh words of others as well as all physical suffering within their own bodies.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one who is less than twenty years of age should not be granted full ordination."
"If one grants them the full ordination, they shall incur a *pāyattika* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a follower of another path, having faith in the True Dharma, desires to go forth, this person should be granted the *parivāsa* probation for four months."
If, after four months have passed, he has won the favor of the bhikṣus, he should be granted ordination.
Likewise, he should be granted the *parivāsa* (probation).

With a single-minded focus, the Saṃgha should assemble. This former follower of another path should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, put on his robe, remove his leather sandals, enter the midst of the Saṃgha, prostrate at the feet of the monks, kneel with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable elders, please bear it in mind: I, [Name], was formerly a follower of another path; now, having faith in the True Dharma, I desire to go forth.
I, [Name], who was formerly a follower of another path, now request from the Saṃgha a four-month period of parivāsa."

The Sangha has granted me, [Name], who was originally of another sect, the four-month *parivāsa* penance; having obtained the consent of the bhikṣus, the Sangha shall now grant me the going-forth and the full ordination.
A second and a third time, he should likewise request.
At that time, one bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This person, [Name], was originally of a different sect; having faith in the wholesome Dharma, he desires to go forth.
Now this person, [Name], who was originally of a different sect, requests from the Saṃgha a four-month *parivāsa*. He speaks thus:

"The Saṃgha has granted me, [Name], who was originally of a different sect, the four-month *parivāsa*. Having obtained the consent of the bhikṣus, the Saṃgha should now grant me the going forth and the full ordination."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha grant a four-month *parivāsa* to the monk so-and-so, who formerly belonged to another sect.
Thus is the motion (*jñapti*). [Followed by] the formal act of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Sangha has granted so-and-so, who originally belonged to another sect, the four-month *parivāsa* penance; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld!
How is the meaning to be understood here?
What is meant by "not gaining favor"?
It refers to those who originally belonged to other paths; when the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts are praised in their presence, they should be censured.

If, while the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts are truly being praised, these followers of other paths do not give rise to joy or delight, and even for a moment feel sorrow, anger, or contention when the other paths are truly censured, this is called "not gaining favor."

If, when the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts are being praised, those who originally belonged to other paths feel joy and delight; and when those other paths are criticized, they do not become sorrowful or engage in anger and contention at the truth—this is called "attaining the meaning."
In this manner, one should grant them the going-forth and the full ordination.

As for the legal procedure: the Saṃgha should assemble with a single mind. This person, who formerly belonged to another path, should rise from their seat, bare one shoulder, put on their robe, remove their leather sandals, enter the midst of the Saṃgha, prostrate at the feet of the monks, kneel with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please attend to me!"
I, [Name], was formerly of another path; having faith in the wholesome Dharma, I desire to go forth.
I have already requested from the Saṃgha a four-month *parivāsa* (probation), and the Saṃgha has already granted me a four-month *parivāsa*.

I, [Name], was originally of another path; I have already completed the four-month *parivāsa* probation within the Saṃgha. I now request from the Saṃgha the going-forth and the reception of full ordination.

The Sangha has granted me, [Name], who was formerly of another sect, the four-month *parivāsa* probation; it has been completed, and I have already obtained the consent of the bhikṣus. May the Sangha now grant me the going-forth and the full ordination.
A second and third time, he should likewise request.
Therein, one bhikṣu within the saṃgha should announce:
"Venerable saṃgha, listen!..."
This person, so-and-so, was originally of another path; having faith in the true Dharma and desiring to go forth, he requested from the Saṃgha a four-month *parivāsa*.
The Saṃgha has already granted him a four-month *parivāsa*, and he has already performed that four-month *parivāsa* among the Saṃgha.
Having completed the *parivāsa* probation, he now seeks from the Saṃgha to go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: this person, so-and-so, was originally of another religious path; he has already completed the four-month *parivāsa* probation within the Saṃgha and has won the favor of the bhikṣus. The Saṃgha shall now grant him the going forth and the full ordination.
Thus it is announced.
This is the motion followed by the threefold formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*):

"The Saṃgha has completed the ordination by full admission for this person of such-and-such a name, who was previously of another sect. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha; having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he wished to travel for two months through the lands of the Southern Mountains.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Tell the bhikṣus: [this is what you should say]."
“The Buddha has finished the *pravāraṇā* ceremony in Rājagṛha and wishes to travel for two months through the southern regions. Who wishes to follow the Buddha?
Those who wish to go should assemble and wait for him.”
Ānanda said, “I shall obey the instruction,” and immediately went out and spoke to the bhikṣus:
“The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha; having completed the *pravāraṇā*, he intended to travel for two months through the southern mountain regions.
Who wishes to follow the Buddha?
Those who wish to go, assemble and wait for him.”
At that time, there were many young bhikṣus in Rājagṛha—bhikṣus who had been ordained for one, two, three, four, or five years—who thought to themselves:

"If we depart from the Buddha, we will not remain long in any one place; we will receive various offerings and benefits, repeatedly take formal reliance upon teachers, and return again with great speed."
“If our preceptor and ācārya do not go, why should we go?
Thus, not all the junior bhikṣus followed the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha traveled with a small number of bhikṣus and returned to Rājagṛha.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Why are there so few bhikṣus following the Buddha?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
In this city of Rājagṛha, there are many young bhikṣus and few elder bhikṣus.
These bhikṣus have been reflecting as follows:”

"If one follows the Buddha's practice, one does not dwell long in any single place; through various offerings and benefits, one repeatedly receives formal reliance upon a teacher, yet returns again with great speed."
“If our preceptor and ācārya do not go, why should we go?
For this reason, many did not follow the Buddha.

On account of these circumstances, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, it is permitted for a bhikṣu who has accomplished five qualities and completed five years of seniority to not receive formal dependence (*niśraya*).
What are these five?

First, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense; third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy; and fifth, having recited the *Prātimokṣa* with its detailed explanations.”
"Even if one has received the precepts for many years, if they do not know the five dharmas, they should remain in dependence upon another for as long as they live.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Should a senior bhikṣu receive dependence and dwell under a junior bhikṣu?"
The Buddha said,
"It should be accepted.
Upāli asked again:
"Should a great bhikṣu serve and make offerings to a junior bhikṣu?
The Buddha said:
"Except for prostrating at his feet, he should perform all other duties."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a householder in the city of Śrāvastī who encountered death; his wealth, wife, children, kinsmen, servants, and all else had perished, leaving only three people: himself, his son, and his daughter.
The layperson thought to himself:

"Among all paths, only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, obtain the joy of offerings and are free from all sorrows and sufferings; there is nothing improper about leaving the household life among them."
Having reflected thus, he took his two sons to the Jeta Grove to seek ordination; the bhikṣus, unaware of his intention, granted them the going forth.

After several days had passed, when it was time for the alms-round, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and led his two sons into the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. They went to the stalls selling cooked food, cakes, parched grain, fried cakes, stuffed cakes, and sweetmeat balls.
These two children were hungry; seeing the various cakes and foods, they spoke to their father, Mahālu, saying: "Father!
Give us food; give us cakes."
The father said to his sons,
"If you demand an immeasurable price, who would ever give it to you?
The two boys wept as they followed their father.
The laypeople rebuked and reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have not severed their desires; they have cohabited with bhikṣuṇīs within the monastery and fathered children.
One person told two, and two told three, until this foul reputation spread throughout the city of Śrāvastī.
There were some bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse, and reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked the bhikṣu Mahālu:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways and by many causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who allows a person less than fifteen years of age to become a śrāmaṇera?
Having finished his rebuke through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, one who is less than fifteen years of age should not become a śrāmaṇera.
If one does so, they incur the offense of duṣkṛta.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, the foolish men of Vaiśālī killed the Śākyas of Kapilavastu.
Then two young children, relatives of the Elder Ānanda, fled to him; Ānanda sustained them by feeding them with his leftover food.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Whose child is this? He replied:
"He is my close relative.
The Buddha said,
"Why has he not gone forth [into homelessness]?"
Ānanda replied, "The Buddha has established a precept:
one who is not yet fifteen years of age should not become a śrāmaṇera."
"These two boys are not yet fifteen years of age.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Are these two boys able to drive away the crows from the food served to the Saṃgha?"
He replied, “I can. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit those capable of driving away crows to become *śrāmaṇeras*, provided they are at least seven years of age.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
there were two *śrāmaṇeras* belonging to the Śākya son Upananda.
One was named Bhadra and the other was named Māgadha; they engaged in sexual intercourse together within the monastery.
When some lay devotees came and saw them, they said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, have no pure conduct; they engage in sexual intercourse together."
One person told it to two, and the two told it to three; thus the ill repute spread throughout Śrāvastī.
Those bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this matter and felt shame and remorse. They reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why do you, who are called a bhikṣu, keep two śrāmaṇeras?
After the Buddha had finished rebuking him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to keep two śrāmaṇeras."
If one keeps [a novice], one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one keeps one or two novices with the intention that they will receive full ordination before long, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
The Śākya son Upananda had taken a slave into the religious life against the wishes of his master.
Not long after he had gone forth, the time for alms-round arrived; he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
When the head of the household saw him being seized, that bhikṣu cried out loudly.
A great crowd gathered and asked, "Why are you doing this?"
The master said, "This is my slave;
I will not allow him to leave home and become a renunciant.
The crowd said:
"In which path have you gone forth?
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa."
“Who is a śramaṇa? He replied,
“The son of the Śākyas is a śramaṇa.”
The people said, "Do not do so!
King Bimbisāra has issued a decree: if a master does not release his slave, no one shall obstruct him from going forth among the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya."
"Why is this? Because it is difficult for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, to practice asceticism and perform austerities; it is difficult to renounce worldly affairs and head toward nirvāṇa.
Thus the householders spoke with anger and reproach.
“The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are a place of fearlessness; though their masters have not released this slave, he has gone forth among the sons of the Śākyas and must not speak [of this].
One person told two, and two told three, until the evil reputation spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha.

There were certain bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse in their hearts and reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, though already knowing the truth, asked Bāḷhika (Bhadanta) intentionally:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if his master has not released his slave before allowing him to go forth?
Having finished rebuking him with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, if a master does not release his slave, he should not be allowed to go forth.
If one allows him to go forth, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
The Śākya son Upananda gave ordination to a man who was burdened by debt and would not be released from his creditors.
After he had been ordained for several days, the time for alms-round arrived; he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
The creditor caught hold of him and cried out at the top of his voice.
A crowd gathered and asked, "Why are you doing this?"
He replied,
“This man owes me a debt, yet he has gone forth as a monk without repaying it.
The crowd said:
“What kind of path have you left home for?
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa.”
"Who is a śramaṇa? He replied,
"The son of the Śākyas is a śramaṇa."
The crowd said, "Do not do so!
King Bimbisāra has issued a decree:
creditors shall not detain anyone, and no one may obstruct those who have gone forth among the sons of the Śākya."
"Why is this? Because it is difficult for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, to practice the holy life; it is difficult to renounce worldly affairs and head toward nirvāṇa.
Thus the lay devotees rebuked them with anger.
“The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are a place where one cannot remain in debt; if a debtor goes forth among the sons of the Śākyas, the creditors will not release him.
One person told it to two, and two told it to three, until this evil reputation spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha.

There were certain bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse in their hearts and reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, questioned Upāli’s brother, Upananda:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can you be called a bhikṣu if creditors will not release him, yet you allow him to go forth?
Having finished his rebuke through various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, if a debtor is not released by their creditor, they should not be granted ordination.
If one grants them ordination, they shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha."
There was a young goldsmith’s apprentice who came into the bamboo grove monastery and approached the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I wish to go forth; please grant me the going forth."
The bhikṣus did not reflect upon this and granted him the going-forth.
The child’s parents and kinsmen searched everywhere until they reached the Bamboo Grove, where they went to the bhikṣus and asked:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Have you ever seen or heard of such a small child?

Among them, those monks who had not seen him said they had not seen him, and those who had not heard of him said they had not heard of him. The relatives, having searched for him long without success, then gave up and departed.
Not long after this boy became a bhikṣu, the time for alms-round arrived; he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
When his kinsmen saw him, they asked, "Have you gone forth into homelessness?"
He replied,
"I have left the household life.
[The other asked,] "In what path have you gone forth?"
He replied, "A śramaṇa. [The other asked,] "What kind of śramaṇa?"
He replied,
“A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
He asked:
"Is it near or far?
He replied,
"It is within the Bamboo Grove."

The kinsmen reviled him in anger, saying, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, deliberately speak falsehoods; they say they have not seen what they have seen, and they say they have not heard what they have heard.
One person told it to two, and two told it to three, until his ill repute spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha.
There were some bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse, and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, those seeking to leave the household life should report two matters to the Saṃgha: [the name of the candidate and the name of the preceptor]."
First, the going forth; second, the shaving of the hair.
Whether the Sangha is assembled or not, these two matters should be announced.
One should speak as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth and have his hair shaved.
I inform the Sangha of this matter."
If he has already shaved his hair and comes before the Saṃgha—whether the Saṃgha is assembled or not—one matter should be announced as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person named so-and-so seeks to go forth."
"The Sangha should remember this.
If the Sangha has not assembled, one should go from room to room to announce it, saying:
"Elder! This person named so-and-so seeks to go forth.
Please bear this in mind."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the physician Jīvaka treated two kinds of people:
first, King Bimbisāra; second, the Buddha and his community of bhikṣus.
Why did you punish King Bimbisāra?
For the sake of food and clothing.
Why did you punish the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus?
Because of self-confidence, self-desire, self-love, and self-purification. At that time,
there were some householders suffering from severe and malignant diseases—
leprosy, carbuncles, epilepsy, and consumption— who went to Jīvaka’s place and offered him a hundred gold coins to cure their illnesses, but he refused.
In this manner, even up to five hundred people, none were willing.
The householder became deeply distressed and worried, thinking:
"Jīvaka treats only two kinds of people:..."
First, he governs King Bimbisāra for the sake of food and clothing;
second, he governs the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus out of self-confidence, self-desire, self-love, and self-purification.
"Now we have offered them a hundred gold coins, even up to five hundred, yet they are unwilling.
These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are people who have accomplished great merit; if Jīvaka were to go forth among them, he would surely treat us."
These sick people went to the bhikṣus and requested to go forth.
The bhikṣus immediately granted them the going forth and the full ordination.

For the sake of these sick people, the bhikṣus boiled rice, prepared soups, made gruel, boiled broth, boiled meat, and decocted medicines; they treated them with medicinal baths and removed their vessels for excrement and urine, as well as their spittoons.
Coming and going amidst many affairs and numerous entanglements, he neglects and abandons reciting the sutras and sitting in meditation, thinking only of his business.
Such patients are so many that even Jīvaka cannot treat them all, and he thus neglects the urgent matters of King Bimbisāra.
When that patient had recovered, regained his composure, and attained a healthy complexion, strength, and plumpness, he abandoned the precepts and returned home.
There were certain bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; they rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:

"How can you be called bhikṣus? You have granted the going-forth and full ordination to these various evil and grievous patients—those with leprosy, abscesses, epilepsy, and consumption—and for them you cook rice, prepare soups, prepare gruels, boil broth, boil meat, decoct medicines, and treat them by soaking them in medicinal baths; you even provide receptacles for their excrement and urine, and spit-pots."
He was constantly occupied with many affairs and numerous entanglements, neglecting his recitation of the sutras and his seated meditation; he thought only of attending to his tasks.
Illnesses were so numerous that Jīvaka could not treat them all, and he neglected the urgent matters of King Bimbisāra.
"Once these patients have recovered, their complexion, strength, and vigor restored, they will abandon the precepts and return home.
Having finished this various rebuke, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Sangha. Having assembled the Sangha, the Buddha, knowing the matter, questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so?
They replied: [It is so.]
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"Why is he called a bhikṣu? He has allowed himself to be ordained and receive full ordination for the sake of various sick people who are evil; he cooks rice, prepares soups, boils broth, cooks meat, decocts medicines, and treats them by soaking them in liquid; he empties their vessels for excrement and urine, as well as their spittoons."
With much coming and going and many affairs and conditions, he neglected his recitation of the sutras and his seated meditation, thinking only of worldly tasks.
There were so many patients that Jīvaka could not treat them all, and he had to neglect the urgent matters of King Bimbisāra.
"When that patient has recovered, with his complexion, strength, and vigor restored and his health fully regained, he shall relinquish the precepts and return home.
After the Buddha had finished censuring them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, in the event of such a grave illness as this:"
Those suffering from leprosy, carbuncles, epilepsy, or diabetes should not be granted ordination or the full precepts.
If one grants them ordination or the full precepts, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, King Śuddhodana went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
“O Virtuous One!
"Grant me my wish.
The Buddha said,
"Kauṇḍinya!"
"The Buddha will not grant you an excessive boon.
The king said,
"May you grant me a boon that I may obtain."
The Buddha said,
“I shall grant whatever you wish.
What boon do you seek now?”
The king said, “When the Buddha left the household life, my heart was filled with sorrow, distress, and displeasure.
When my sons Nanda and Rāhula later left the household life, my heart was likewise filled with sorrow, distress, and displeasure.”
Now the Buddha has granted my wish, yet my parents will not release me so that I may go forth into homelessness.
Why is this? Because my parents rely upon their son for their honor.
The Buddha said, "Kauṇḍinya!
This was my original thought: "
"I also wish to establish a precept for the bhikṣus:
'If one has not been granted permission by one's parents, one shall not be allowed to go forth into homelessness.
At that time, after the Buddha had taught the Dharma to King Śuddhodana in various ways, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, he remained silent.
Having heard the Dharma, the king rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.
Not long after the king had left, the Buddha, on account of these circumstances, assembled the Saṃgha. When the assembly was complete, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, no one shall be granted the going forth unless their parents have given permission.”
"If you grant them ordination, you will incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
at that time, various bhikṣuṇīs were traveling from Kośala toward Śrāvastī.

In the Sāla Grove, there were bandits who destroyed the Dharma; they plundered bhikṣuṇīs and committed acts of humiliation, causing their evil reputation to spread throughout the cities, kingdoms, and towns.

Whether by the power of the king or the power of the local communities, they surrounded and captured all the bandits, except for one bandit who fled to the kingdom of Vākīḍa. Arriving at the place where the bhikṣus were, he spoke to them, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!..."
"Allow me to go forth.
The bhikṣus, without reflecting, allowed him to go forth.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that there are two great assemblies at fixed times:
The last month of spring and the last month of summer.
When it was time for the retreat during the last month of spring, bhikṣus from various regions and countries came to hear the Buddha preach the Dharma, thinking to themselves:
"It is pleasant to observe the summer retreat in this Dharma."
This was the first great assembly.
At the end of the summer retreat, having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and finished making their robes, they took their bowls and robes and went to where the Buddha was, thinking thus:
"It has been a long time since we last saw the Buddha; it has been a long time since we last saw the Sugata."
This was the second great assembly.
After the bhikṣus from the country of Vajji had completed their *pravāraṇā* ceremony and finished making their robes, they took up their robes and bowls, intending to travel to Śrāvastī.
The young bhikṣu said,
"I wish to travel together with you.
The bhikṣus replied:
"Go as you please.
They then departed together.
On the way, the bhikṣus saw the Sāla grove and recalled it, saying:
“In this Sāla grove, there was originally a wicked bandit who destroyed the Dharma; he robbed the bhikṣuṇīs and committed acts of humiliation.
The junior bhikṣus said, “Venerable elders!...”
"The evil thieves were my karmic companions and friends; I too committed these evil deeds.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They gradually traveled on until they reached the kingdom of Śrāvastī and went to where the Buddha was. They bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet in salutation and withdrew to sit to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas to inquire of an incoming bhikṣu with these words:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of alms-food, and are you not weary from the road?
Now the Buddha likewise spoke these words to inquire after the visiting bhikṣu:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Is there no lack of almsfood? Are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we have been content, dwelling in peace and happiness; there has been no lack of almsfood, nor are we weary from the road."
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“In this Sāla grove, there were wicked bandits who committed great crimes; they plundered bhikṣuṇīs and committed acts of impurity. These bandits have incurred a grave offense.”
Why is this? Because most of these bhikṣuṇīs are arhats; one who defiles bhikṣuṇīs should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination.
If one grants them ordination and bestows the full precepts, they should be expelled. Why?
Because those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī do not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. In that city of Śrāvastī, there was a householder who met with death; his wealth, family, wife, children, servants, and all else perished. This householder thought to himself:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are those who have accomplished merit and happiness. I shall emulate these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, by making a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, an antarvāsaka, an alms bowl, a water filter, a mendicant’s staff, a leather bag for ghee, leather sandals, and a needle case. What hardship could there be in doing so?"
"He is then like one who dwells as a thief.

He immediately imitated the making of a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, an antarvāsaka, an alms bowl, a water-strainer, a mendicant’s staff, a leather bag for holding ghee, leather sandals, and a needle-case; having done so, he secretly entered among the monks and stayed there.
Whether the bhikṣus have gathered or not, one should ask them gently:
"Venerable sir, how many years of seniority do you have?"
"What is the current season?
Is there an intercalary month or not?
This thief, unaware of the seasons, pressed him further with gentle words.
He said, "I have stolen [the robes] and am living like a thief.
There were some bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities, who rebuked him:

"For what reason is he called a bhikṣu who has fully obtained a preceptor (upādhyāya), fully obtained a teacher (ācārya), and fully obtained an instructor (śāstṛ), and who has attained the subtle and excellent Dharma and Vinaya?"
"Why have you falsely claimed to be bhikṣus and lived like thieves?
After the various bhikṣus had finished their reprimands, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked them; the Buddha said:
“Is it truly so? He replied,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“One may obtain a complete and perfect preceptor, a complete and perfect ācārya, and a complete and perfect instructor; one may obtain the subtle and wondrous *vinaya* of the wholesome Dharma.”
"Why do you falsely claim to be bhikṣus while living like thieves?
After the Buddha had finished rebuking them with various causes and conditions, he said to the bhikṣus,
"This is called 'living like a thief' (caura-vāsa)."
Such a person should not be granted ordination or the full precepts; if they have been granted ordination or the full precepts, they should be expelled. Why is this?
Because one who dwells as a thief does not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda gave ordination to a eunuch, who would grope the bhikṣus at night.

The bhikṣus drove them out; they went to the side of the bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, and they all groped and touched the bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, so they were all driven out.
Various laypeople stayed overnight inside the monastery and groped among the laypeople.
The laypeople said,
"Among the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, there is one who has gone forth and received full ordination while being a paṇḍaka."
One person told two people, and two people told three; thus his ill repute spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha.

There were certain bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse, and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
For these reasons, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked Baddhālī with various causes and conditions:
"Why do you allow a *paṇḍaka* (one who is impotent) to go forth as a bhikṣu?
After the Buddha had finished rebuking them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, a *paṇḍaka* should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination."
"If one grants them the going-forth and confers full ordination, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha said,
"There are five kinds of impotent persons (*paṇḍaka*)."

What are the five? First, one who is impotent from birth; second, one who is impotent for half the month; third, one who is impotent through jealousy; fourth, one who is impotent regarding semen; and fifth, one who is impotent due to illness.
What is one who is impotent from birth?
One who is incapable of sexual intercourse from birth is one who is impotent from birth.
What is one who is impotent for half a month?
One who is capable of sexual intercourse for half the month and incapable for the other half is called a "half-month impotent" (pandaka).
What is the "jealous impotent"?
One whose sexual organs become functional through jealousy upon seeing others engaged in sexual intercourse; this is the jealous impotent.
What is one who is impotent by nature?
One whose bodily functions for sexual intercourse depend upon another person is one who is impotent by nature.
What is one who is impotent due to illness?
If one is decayed, or has fallen away, or is infested by worms, such a person is a "diseased impotent.
These are the five kinds of impotents.
As for the four kinds of impotents—the congenital, the semi-monthly, the jealous, and the seminal—these four kinds of impotents should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination.
If one grants him the going-forth and confers full ordination, he should be expelled. Why?
Because a paṇḍaka does not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.
If one who is a eunuch has already left the household life and received full ordination, even if [the organ] falls off, decays, is eaten by worms, or does not function, he is permitted to remain.

Although he has not moved [from his status], if he renounces the precepts and wishes to go forth again to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), he should not be granted going-forth or full ordination.
If he is granted going-forth and full ordination, he should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*).
"Why is this? Because one who is diseased and impotent does not give rise to my *saddharma-vinaya*.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

There was a bhikṣu who had previously been a renunciant of another sect. On account of a minor cause, he quarreled with his teacher, and without relinquishing the precepts, he returned to his original sect.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Sangha. Having assembled the Sangha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there is a dog, hungry and emaciated, who is given delicious food but refuses to eat it, instead eating filth."
"This foolish person is just like that; having abandoned the wholesome Dharma, they have returned to their original heterodox path.
After the Buddha had finished his reprimand through various causes and conditions, he said to the bhikṣus:
"This person who has crossed over [to the heterodox] should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination."
If one grants him ordination and bestows the full precepts, he should be expelled. Why?
Because this person who has transgressed cannot give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin who took his mother’s life. He then thought to himself:
“I have committed a great crime by taking my mother’s life; where can I find a way to eliminate this evil transgression?”
"I have heard that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are able to remove it.
He then went to where the bhikṣus were and said,
"Venerable sirs!"
“Let us go forth [into homelessness] with you. The bhikṣus said:
“You brahmins are faithless and arrogant, long steeped in evil and heterodoxy, and enemies of the Buddha’s Dharma; by what means could you possibly gain faith and wish to go forth?”
The brāhmaṇa said:
"Venerable Sir!
I previously took my mother's life, and I reflected to myself:..."
"I have committed an extremely grave offense; where can it be expiated?
"I have heard that the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are able to expiate great offenses; for this reason, I wish to go forth."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This person has committed the offense of killing his mother; he should not be granted ordination."
If one grants them ordination and the full precepts, they should be expelled.
Why? Because they have committed the crime of killing their mother, and thus the *vinaya* of my wholesome dharmas cannot arise within them.
"Killing one's father is likewise so.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A group of bhikṣus, traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī, arrived at the Sāla Grove.
In a forest there were bandits who violated the Dharma, plundered, and took the lives of various bhikṣus; their evil reputation spread throughout the cities, kingdoms, and towns.
By the power of the king or the local community, they surrounded and captured all the bandits, with the exception of one bandit who fled to the Jeta Grove and went before the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Allow us to go forth [into the religious life].
Without reflecting, the bhikṣus granted them ordination.
When the king issued the command for these thieves to be executed, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us together observe the retribution for sins in the world.
The junior bhikṣu said,
"I also wish to go."
He replied,
"As you wish," and they immediately went together.
As he stood watching from one side, the bandits were severing heads and shedding blood; at that time, the young bhikṣu reflected to himself:
"If I had not left the household life, I too would have been like this."
He immediately fell to the ground in terror.
The bhikṣus sprinkled water on his face; he revived and recovered, and they asked him, "What ailment or suffering do you have?"
"Did you not also commit evil deeds therein, nor contemplate such evil deeds?
The bhikṣus questioned him earnestly with gentle words, and he replied:
"The bandits in the Sāla forest who plundered and killed the bhikṣus were my karmic companions and close friends; I too committed these evils together with them, and I thought thus:"
"The bandits have severed their heads and shed blood; had I not gone forth into homelessness, I too would have been like this.
For this reason, I was terrified and fell to the ground.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They went together to where the Buddha was and informed him of these matters.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"The bandits in the Sāla forest, through negligence and perversion, have taken the lives of many bhikṣus and committed much evil karma."
Those bhikṣus were for the most part arhats; this person who killed an arhat should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination.
If he has been granted the going forth and the full ordination, he should be expelled.
"Why is this? Because by killing an Arhat, one does not give rise to my *saddharma-vinaya* (the discipline of the true Dharma).
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a dragon whose faith was pure and clear; loathing his own dragon body, he emerged from his palace, transformed himself into human form, and went to where the bhikṣus were, saying:
"Virtuous ones!..."
“Allow me to go forth.
Without reflecting, the bhikṣus granted him the going-forth.
This nāga was assigned to a junior bhikṣu and shared a small room with him for lodging.
The next day, he went out to beg for alms; because this dragon possessed merit, he obtained alms quickly.
At times, he would return to his palace to eat; having finished eating, he would first return to his room, close the door, and sit there.
At that time, the Naga Dharmasupta, being fond of sleep during the heat, suddenly lay down.
There are five circumstances under which a naga’s body does not change:
first, at birth; second, at death; third, at the time of sexual desire; fourth, at the time of anger; and fifth, at the time of sleep.
At that time, the dragon was asleep, its body filling the entire room. A bhikṣu who shared the same quarters arrived later and saw it; struck with fear, he let out a cry.
Hearing this sound, the dragon quickly woke up and resumed sitting in the full lotus posture.
The bhikṣus gathered in great numbers and asked,
"Why did you cry out so loudly?
He replied:
"This is a snake.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It is not a snake; it is a dragon.
The Buddha said:
"Call him here!

When the dragon arrived at the Buddha’s location, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma through various causes and conditions, he immediately sent him away.
The Buddha said to the dragon, "Return to your own palace.

Having heard this teaching of the Dharma, the dragon wept; wiping away his tears with his hands, he rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
After the dragon had departed, the Buddha, for this reason, assembled the community of monks. Having assembled them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, a dragon should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination."
If one grants them the going forth and the full ordination, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same for all non-humans as well.
The Buddha was staying at the Campaka Garden in Śrāvastī.
There was a son of an elder who had left home and suffered from a chronic illness; at that time, his kinsmen sent a messenger to summon him, saying:
"Virtuous one!
Come here to treat this illness."
The sick person then went there.
This man had many kinsmen, each of whom invited him, saying:
"I [will take you] today; I [will take you] tomorrow; I [will take you] the day after."
For the sake of the sick bhikṣu, people gave him great wealth; however, his illness was incurable, and he eventually passed away.
This sick bhikṣu was named Bharadvāja, and during this interval, there was a śrāmaṇera who received full ordination.
In that assembly were six groups of bhikṣus, and the six groups of bhikṣus said:
"A bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts should not receive a portion equal to that of a senior bhikṣu; he should receive a portion equal to that of a śrāmaṇera."
The teacher asked,
"For what reason? He replied:
"Because the formal ritual for receiving the precepts was incomplete.
The teacher, not knowing what to do,
reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You should ask the bhikṣu who was present during the *karmavācanā* whether that *karma* was complete or not.
He then questioned the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus said,
"Although we were present during the formal procedure (karmavācanā), we do not recall it and do not know it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "From now on, when the bhikṣus perform a *karmavācanā*, they should listen with a single mind; they must not have other perceptions or other thoughts. They should concentrate their minds, be diligent, be respectful, and reflect; with every thought they should maintain the same mindfulness. It is in this manner that they should listen to the *karmavācanā*."
The one performing the *karmavācanā* (formal act) should speak with clear distinction, saying:
"This is the first *karmavācanā*, this is the second *karmavācanā*, this is the third *karmavācanā*.
If one does not speak with such distinction, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is anyone who, with an evil mind, draws blood from the body of a Buddha, they should not be granted ordination."
If one were to grant him ordination and confer the full precepts, he should be expelled. Why?
Because this person who, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha, does not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.
If there is one who perceives what is not the Dharma as not the Dharma, and having caused a schism in the Saṃgha, subsequently holds the view that it is not the Dharma, he incurs an offense.
If there is one who perceives what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and having caused a schism in the Saṃgha, subsequently holds the view that it is not the Dharma, he incurs an offense.
If one perceives what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and after having caused a schism in the Saṃgha, subsequently harbors doubt, this person incurs an offense.
Such a person should not be granted ordination or the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
If they have been granted ordination or the full precepts, they should be expelled.
Why is this? Because one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha does not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.
If there is a person who, at the time of their original renunciation, committed sexual misconduct—even with an animal—this person should not be granted renunciation or full ordination.
If one grants him ordination and confers the full precepts, he should be expelled. Why?
Because a person who has fundamentally violated the precepts does not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.

If there is a person who, at the time of their original renunciation, committed theft—up to five coins or an object worth five coins—that person should not be granted renunciation and full ordination.
If one were to grant them ordination and confer the full precepts, they should be expelled.
Why? Because those who have fundamentally violated the precepts do not give rise to my *śīla* (virtue) and *vinaya* (discipline).

If there is a person who, at the time of originally leaving the household life, intentionally took the life of another with their own hands, without any other intention or any other means, this person should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination.
If one grants him ordination and the full precepts, he should be expelled. Why?
Because a person who has fundamentally violated the precepts does not give rise to my wholesome Dharma-vinaya.
There may be someone who, at the time of his original ordination, was empty of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) yet praised himself, saying:
"If one says, 'I possess superhuman qualities,' this person should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination.
If they have been granted the going-forth or the full ordination, they should be expelled."
"Why is this? Because for one who has fundamentally violated the precepts, my *śīla-dharma-vinaya* does not arise.
There was a person who had been expelled for not seeing [his offense] who, having renounced the precepts, wished to return to the homeless life and went to where the bhikṣus were:
“Venerable Sir!
Grant me the going forth; once I have gone forth, I shall acknowledge my transgression.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha:
"Should this person be granted ordination?
The Buddha said,
"He should be granted ordination."
Having gone forth, he said:
"Venerable Sir, I do not see this as an offense."
"Grant me full ordination; once I have received full ordination, I shall acknowledge this offense.
"Should it be granted?
The Buddha said:
"One should grant this person full ordination.
After having received full ordination, he further says:
"I do not see this offense."
“Should he be expelled again?
The Buddha said,
“If a harmonious Saṃgha is attained, he should be expelled again.”
"If the Saṃgha cannot reach a consensus, then the original act of banishment shall stand.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the wives of various generals had long been away with their husbands on campaign; they consorted with non-human beings (*amanuṣya*). These non-human beings were deformed in body: some had elephant heads, horse heads, ox heads, monkey heads, deer heads, warts on their heads, or flat heads; even when seven parts of their heads were visible, the children born from them were likewise so.

Because their mothers loved them, they were raised and brought up until they were unable to perform manual labor; consequently, their parents cast them out, and they went forth into homelessness from the temples and debating halls.
Wandering through various places in search of food and drink, they eventually arrived at the Bamboo Grove.
Among them, the group of six bhikṣus delighted in committing transgressions; good people were unwilling to stay near them, and if any did stay, the other bhikṣus would mock them, saying:
"This person is so evil; why do you associate with him?"
These disciples, having seen with their own eyes their teacher committing an unwholesome deed, would abandon him and depart.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw such people, they thought to themselves:
"If we keep excellent disciples, other bhikṣus will mock us and instruct them to abandon us and leave."
"We shall support this person; there is no one who would instruct us to abandon him.
Even if someone wished to instruct us, who would take pleasure in this person's ugliness?"
Having reflected thus, he spoke, saying:
"Why do you not go forth into homelessness?
He replied:
"We are so unsightly; who would ordain us and let us go forth?

The group of six bhikṣus said, "If you can take turns guarding our rooms for us, if you can bring food for those guarding the rooms on our behalf, and if you can carry our robes and bowls for us, we will ordain you."
He replied, "So be it.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus immediately granted him the going forth.

At that time, someone invited the Buddha and the Sangha. For two reasons, the group of six bhikṣus sent their disciples ahead to carry their robes and bowls: first, because one group was traveling slowly; second, because they were ashamed to travel together with them.
At that time, the lay devotees had pure faith in the Buddha, but the disciples of various heterodox paths mocked them, saying:
"This is the one you all worship as your field of merit."
When those who were walking ahead and those who had already eaten arrived, the lay devotees heard of this matter and felt ashamed. They reported the incident in full to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Once the assembly was gathered, the Buddha, knowing the reason, questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why are you called a bhikṣu? You have given ordination to those with heads like elephants, horses, oxen, monkeys, deer, goiters, or flat heads—those whose heads are seven parts exposed to view."
After the Buddha had finished reprimanding them through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, those with heads like an elephant's, up to those with flat heads, should not be granted ordination."
"If one grants them ordination and confers the full precepts upon them, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Those with yellow hair, green hair, red hair, white hair, hair resembling red, pig-like hair, horse-like hair, and those who are hairless—none of these should be granted ordination."
If one grants them the going forth and the full ordination, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This also applies to those with bloodshot eyes, deep-set eyes, protruding eyes, crystal-like eyes, small eyes, bulging eyes, one-eyed persons, and those who are blind; such individuals should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination.
If one grants them the going-forth and confers full ordination, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
[This applies to those with] elephant ears, horse ears, ox ears, sheep ears, curled ears, single ears, or no ears;
crooked noses, parrot-beak noses, ox noses, monkey noses, long noses, elephant trunks, flat noses, or no noses;
Large lips, horse-like lips, drooping lips, or no lips;
bristles like those of a pig, ox, or donkey, or no bristles;
tusks like those of an elephant, horse, ox, fish, or dog, or no teeth.
Long-necked, short-necked, crooked-necked, and neckless;
overly tall, overly short, overly dark-skinned, and overly fair-skinned;
pure blue, pure yellow, pure red, pure white, and pure black.
Lame feet with missing toes; having the genitals cut off, or castrated, or suffering from scrotal hernia and impotence;
having an arm severed, or the thigh severed, or a hand severed, or a foot severed, or a finger severed;
fingers that cannot be bent, or having the lips cut off, or the ears cut off, or the nose cut off.
Those afflicted with leprosy, those with deformed genitals, those with club feet, those with withered hands, and those who drag their hips;
those resembling ghosts, the blind, the sightless, those with scaly skin, the crippled, and the lame;
those with goiters, those with hands like sheep-dung, those with short arms, and those who are mute and deaf.
Those who are too young, too old, or physically infirm;
those who cannot walk, sit, lie down, or stand—all such persons who defile the Sangha should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination.
"If one confers the full ordination upon such a person, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"There are three matters regarding the method of receiving full ordination; through these, one may receive full ordination in the presence [of the Saṃgha]."

What are the three? First, there is the Saṃgha; second, there is a person who wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*); third, there is the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*). These are the three.

When the person wishing to receive full ordination first arrives, he should be instructed to perform the sequence of prostrations, touching his head to each member’s feet one by one, as a mark of respect to the Saṃgha.
Having completed the ritual, he should instruct him to receive the robe and ask: "Is this robe yours?"
If he replies,
"It is my robe," one should instruct him as follows:
"You should repeat my words as follows:
'I, [name], receive this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips, whether it be cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe.'"
The second [formula]:
"I, [Name], accept this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of so many strips, whether cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe."
Third: "I, [Name], receive this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of so many patches, whether cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe."
Next, he asks:
"Is this robe yours? He replies:
"Yes. "I, [Name], receive this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe—whether it be cut or uncut—and I shall maintain this robe."
The second [formula]:
"I, [Name], accept this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe—whether it be cut or uncut—and I shall maintain this robe."
Third: "I, [Name], accept this seven-strip *uttarāsaṅga* robe—whether it be cut or uncut—as my possession."
Next, he asks:
"Is this robe yours? He replies:
"Yes. "I, [Name], receive this five-piece lower robe (antarvāsa), whether it is cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe."
The second [formula]:
"I, [Name], accept this five-piece lower robe (antaravāsaka), whether it is cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe."
Third: "I, [Name], accept this five-piece lower robe (antaravāsaka), whether it is cut or uncut; I shall maintain this robe."
Next, he asks:
"Is this *pātra* yours? He replies:
"Yes. "I, [Name], accept this *pātra* of proper measure for the purpose of long-term use. Second:
"I, [Name], accept this bowl, which is of the proper measure, for the purpose of long-term use.
Third: "I, [Name], accept this bowl, which is of the proper measure, for the purpose of long-term use."
"Having received the robe and bowl, one should seek out a preceptor (upādhyāya) and say:
'I, [name], request the Elder to be my preceptor.
May the Elder act as my preceptor; by relying upon the Elder as preceptor, I, [name], shall receive full ordination.'"
The second [request]:
"I, [Name], request the Elder to be my preceptor (upādhyāya).
May the Elder act as my preceptor."
"By virtue of the Elder Preceptor, I, [Name], shall receive full ordination. Third:
"I, [Name], request the Elder to be my preceptor."
"The Elder shall serve as my preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
By relying upon the Elder as my preceptor, I, [Name], shall receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The teacher should then ask:
"Can you, [Name], act as the preceptor for [Name]?
If he says, "I can," [then it is accepted].
Immediately, he should be placed within the boundary and moved from a place where he can hear to a place where he can see.
The preceptor should then announce:
"The Sangha is assembled in harmony; who is able to act as the instructor for [Name]?"
If there is a bhikṣu among the Saṃgha who says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, he should not be appointed as a teacher of instruction (śāstṛ).

One who teaches out of affection, one who teaches out of anger, one who teaches out of fear, one who teaches out of delusion, and one who does not know what has been taught and what has not been taught—
if these five qualities are present, one should not be appointed as a teacher.

One who does not teach out of affection, one who does not teach out of anger, one who does not teach out of fear, one who does not teach out of delusion, and one who knows what has been taught and what has not been taught— if these five qualities are accomplished, one should be established as a teacher.
Next, one should chant as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor [Name]; the bhikṣu [Name] is capable of acting as the instructor."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha authorize that so-and-so shall act as the instructor for the purpose of instructing so-and-so.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, so-and-so; this person, so-and-so, is able to instruct so-and-so.
Therefore, the monk, so-and-so, acts as the instructor to teach so-and-so.
"Whichever elders approve that so-and-so be appointed as the instructor to teach so-and-so, let those elders remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Sangha has already approved that so-and-so be appointed as the instructor to teach so-and-so. Since the Sangha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
Immediately, the instructor shall go to the disciple’s place and instruct him to drape his robe over one shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, and join his palms.

He should ask as follows: “Listen, [Name], this is now the time for sincerity; it is the time for truthful speech. Later, when questioned in the midst of the Saṃgha, you shall likewise speak thus: if it is true, say it is true; if it is not true, say it is not true.”
I now ask you:
Are you a man? Have you reached the age of twenty?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not working as a servant for others?
Were you not purchased?
"Are you not one who has broken [the precepts]?
Are you not a government official?
Have you not been involved in legal disputes with the authorities?"
Have you not conspired against the royal family?
Have you not incurred debts to others?
A man may suffer from such diseases as these:
If one has leprosy, carbuncles, abscesses, scrofula, consumption, or epilepsy—do you have such illnesses?
Are your parents living?
Have your parents given their permission?
"Did you previously become a bhikṣu? If he says, "I did."
"Are you pure in the observance of the precepts?
When relinquishing the precepts, did you restore them with a single-minded focus in accordance with the Dharma?
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?"
"What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor?
One should answer:
"I am named [Name], and my preceptor is named [Name].
Once the instructor has finished questioning him, he should report back to the Saṃgha:
"The questioning of [Name] is finished."
The preceptor says:
"If you are pure, bring it forward.
Once it has been brought forward, he instructs them to pay homage to the Sangha.
Having paid homage to the Saṃgha, he requests full ordination from them:
"I, [Name], shall receive full ordination from the Upādhyāya [Name].
I now request full ordination within the Saṃgha; [Name] is my Upādhyāya."
"The Sangha has delivered me; the Sangha has granted me full ordination out of compassion. Second:
"I, [Name], receive full ordination from the preceptor [Name]."
I now request the full ordination within the Saṃgha; so-and-so is my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha deliver me; may the Saṃgha grant me the full ordination out of compassion.
The third [statement]:
"I, [Name], have received full ordination from my preceptor [Name].
I now request the Sangha to grant me full ordination; [Name] is my preceptor."
"The Saṃgha has delivered me; the Saṃgha has granted me full ordination out of compassion.
At that moment, the Preceptor should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], has received full ordination from the preceptor, [Name].
This person, [Name], with [Name] as preceptor, requests full ordination from the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; I shall now inquire of [Name] within the Saṃgha regarding the obstructing dharmas.
Thus he makes the formal announcement:

"Listen, [Name], this is the time for sincerity; this is the time for truthful speech. Now the Saṃgha questions you: if it is true, you should say it is true; if it is not true, you should say it is not true."
Are you a man? Are you twenty years of age?
Are you not a slave?
Did you not work as a hired laborer for others?
Did you not obtain it by purchase?
Did you not obtain it by means of theft?
Are you not a government official?
Have you not committed offenses against the state?
Have you not conspired against the royal house?
"Have you not incurred debts to others?
A man may suffer from such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, abscesses, scrofula, consumption, or epilepsy; do you have any such diseases?"
Are your parents still living?
Have they given their permission?
Have you not previously become a bhikṣu?
If he says, "I have," [ask]:
"Do you maintain the precepts purely?"
When you relinquished the precepts, did you restore them according to the Dharma with a single-minded focus?
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
What is your name?
"What is the preceptor’s name?
One should reply:
"My name is [Name], and my preceptor's name is [Name]."
He addressed the Saṃgha:
"Is there anyone who has not yet asked?
If there is anyone who has not yet asked, they should ask; if you have already asked, remain silent."
The Preceptor should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, wishes to receive full ordination from the Upādhyāya, so-and-so."
This person, [Name], requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination, with [Name] as preceptor.
This person declares themselves to be pure and free from obstructing dharmas; they possess the three robes and the alms bowl. Their preceptor is [Name].
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
This is the formal motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This person, [Name], receives full ordination from the preceptor, [Name].
This person, [Name], requests full ordination from the Sangha, with [Name] as preceptor.
So-and-so declares himself pure and free from obstructing dharmas; he possesses the three robes and alms bowl; his preceptor is So-and-so.
The Sangha now confers full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as his preceptor.
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha conferring full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor—if you consent, remain silent; if you do not consent, speak."
This concludes the first *karmavācanā*.
The second [motion] is stated again as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This person, [Name], receives full ordination from the preceptor, [Name].
This person, [Name], requests full ordination from the Saṃgha, with [Name] as preceptor.
So-and-so declares himself pure and free from obstructing dharmas; he possesses the three robes and the alms bowl; his preceptor is So-and-so.
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as preceptor.
"Whichever elders approve that the Sangha grant full ordination to so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor—let those elders remain silent; if you do not approve, please speak."
"This is the conclusion of the second *karmavācanā*.
For the third time, this matter is stated again:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
This person, [Name], receives full ordination from the preceptor [Name].
This person, [Name], requests full ordination from the Sangha, with [Name] as preceptor.
So-and-so declares himself pure and free from obstructing dharmas; he possesses the three robes and the alms bowl; his preceptor is So-and-so.
The Saṃgha now confers full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as preceptor.
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha conferring full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor—those elders who approve should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak."
"This third *karmavācanā* has been completed.
The Sangha has granted full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"If asked, 'How old are you? one should say:"
"Has the year not yet begun?
"When [does it begin]?
"Whether it be winter, spring, or summer—whether there is an intercalary month or not—these seasons are what you should keep in mind for as long as you live."
Immediately, one should recite the Four Reliances: "Listen, [Name]!
These four reliances were taught by the Buddha Bhagavān, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of those receiving full ordination."
Relying on these four dharmas, a bhikṣu goes forth, receives full ordination, and becomes established in the dharma of a bhikṣu.
What are the four reliances?
Relying on rag-robes, a bhikṣu goes forth, receives full ordination, and becomes established in the dharma of a bhikṣu.

If one further obtains white hempen garments, red hempen garments, coarse woolen garments, *kauseya* (silk) garments, *kāśika* (fine cotton) garments, *kambala* (woolen blanket) garments, *karpāsa* (cotton) garments, or any other such pure garments, all of these may be kept as surplus.
Regarding this, can you accept and use the paṃsukūla (rag-robe) for as long as life lasts?
If you can, you should say: "I can."
"Relying on alms-food, a bhikṣu goes forth and receives full ordination, thereby establishing the dharma of a bhikṣu.

If he further obtains food prepared for him, monthly food, food on the eighth, twenty-third, fourteenth, twenty-ninth, fifteenth, thirtieth, first, or sixteenth day of the month; communal meals, meals for individual rooms, or invited meals—whether from the Saṃgha or privately—all such other pure foods may be accepted as surplus."
Regarding this, can you rely on alms-gathering for as long as you live?
If you can, you should say: "I can."
"By relying on dwelling under a tree, a bhikṣu who has gone forth and received full ordination fulfills the dharma of a bhikṣu.

Furthermore, if he obtains a warm bathhouse, a lecture hall, a palace, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, a gabled house, a flat-roofed house, an earthen cave, a mountain cave, a *mañca* (bed) with a canopy, a *mañca* without a canopy, a *khaṭvā* (couch), or even a bed of grass or leaves—whatever such other pure dwellings and bedding there may be—all of these are obtained as surplus."
Regarding this, can you, for as long as life lasts, make use of dwelling under a tree?
If you can, you should say: "I can."
"Based on the discarded medicine, a bhikṣu goes forth and receives full ordination, thereby accomplishing the dharma of a bhikṣu.
If he further obtains the four kinds of 'stored' medicines—
ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar;"
The four kinds of purified fats:
bear fat, donkey fat, pig fat, and sturgeon fat;
the five kinds of root medicines:
Ginger, galangal, red aconite, *pāṭhā*, and kusha root;
the five medicinal fruits:
*harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, black pepper, and *pippalī*.
The five kinds of salt:
black salt, white salt, purple salt, red salt, and halite;
the five kinds of broth:
Root decoctions, stem decoctions, leaf decoctions, flower decoctions, and fruit decoctions;
five kinds of resinous medicines:
hiṅgu, sārjarasa, yaṣṭī, yaṣṭikā, and yaṣṭimadhu—these and other such pure medicines may all be obtained in abundance.
Regarding the medicine to be discarded after use (caturtha-paryuṣita-bhaiṣajya), can it be used for the remainder of one's life?
If so, one should say: "I can."

“Listen, [Name]! The Buddha Bhagavān, the Śākya-muni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—who possesses knowledge and vision—has proclaimed for the sake of bhikṣus who have received full ordination the four *pārājika* dharmas.”
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these four offenses involving defeat, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Just as the head of a tāla tree, once severed, does not grow again, nor turn green, nor increase, nor expand;
so too it is with a bhikṣu: if he commits any one of the four pārājika offenses, he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.
The Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire;
he praised the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

If a bhikṣu, while remaining among the community of bhikṣus within the framework of the precepts, does not renounce the precepts nor withdraw due to weakness in his observance, and commits the act of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—he is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; he has lost the status of a bhikṣu.
"You must not do this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold this matter?
If you can, you should say:
“Yes,” [the monk replied].

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked taking what is not given and praised refraining from theft, even down to the measure of a single thread, a single needle, or a single drop of oil, or five *kārsāpaṇas* or the equivalent of five *kārsāpaṇas*. If a bhikṣu takes what is not given, for that reason, whether a king or one equal to a king seizes him, or kills him, or binds him, or drives him out, they will speak thus:
“You are small, you are foolish, you are a thief, you are a stealer.”
"Thus, a bhikṣu who takes what is not given is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya; he has fallen from the dharma of a bhikṣu.
You must, for as long as life lasts, refrain from doing so."
"Can you uphold this matter?
If you can, you should say: 'I can.'"

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the taking of life and praised the abstention from it; one should not intentionally take the life of even an ant, let alone that of a human being.

If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, intentionally takes the life of a human being; or if he dispatches another person to kill with a sword; or if he instructs someone to die; or if he praises death; or if he speaks these words: "Ho!..."
"Sir, what is the use of living such a wretched life?
Death is better than life.

Thus, following his own inclinations and thoughts, he taught death through various causes and conditions and praised it—whether by killing in a pit, or by killing with a snare, or by killing with a mechanical trap, or by killing by trampling, or by killing with a *bhedara* (a type of weapon), or by killing with a *pāribhedara*, or by killing by severing the life-force, or by causing an abortion, or by pressing the abdomen to induce an abortion, or by casting into fire, or by casting into water, or by throwing from a height to the ground, or by sending a messenger on a road to kill—even down to [killing] one who has just acquired the two faculties within the mother’s womb.

Regarding the body-faculty and the life-faculty: if, while first in the womb, one gives rise to anger and desires to kill, and dies as a result of these causes and conditions, one is no longer a bhikṣu, no longer a śramaṇa, and no longer a son of the Śākya; one has lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Among these, one must not do anything for as long as life lasts. Can you uphold this?
If you can, you should say:
"Yes. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked false speech and praised truthful speech; he taught that one should not speak falsely even in jest, let alone intentionally.
If a bhikṣu, knowing for himself that he possesses no superhuman qualities or states of realization, yet praises himself, saying:

"I have realized the fruit of arhatship, or I am one who is progressing toward arhatship; I have realized the fruit of anāgāmin, or I am one who is progressing toward anāgāmin; I have realized the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, or I am one who is progressing toward sakṛdāgāmin; I have realized the fruit of srotāpanna, or I am one who is progressing toward srotāpanna;
I have attained the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyānas."

I have attained the meditations of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling; as well as the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing.

Devas come to me, and likewise nāgas, yakṣas, bhūta-demons, piśāca-demons, kumbhāṇḍa-demons, and rākṣasa-demons—such classes of spirits question me and I question them; they answer me and I answer them.
"This matter is empty and devoid of falsehood; such a person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, and not a son of the Śākya; they have lost the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Within this, one must not act for as long as life lasts."
"Can you uphold this matter?
If you can, you should say: 'I can.'"
“Listen, [Name]! Regarding the first offense, the Saṃgha cannot lift it.
As for the second offense, although the Saṃgha may lift it, for how long was it concealed?”
One should perform the *pārivāsika* penance for as long as required.
