Having performed this, one should then perform the *pravāraṇā*; one must not create an obstacle to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed by means of a single proclamation.
"What is the danger of bandits?

It is when bandits, driven by malice, issue orders to capture Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas—killing them, binding them, or driving them out; taking their blood to smear on doorways, ear-holes, and windows; making banners and inscriptions; or using the gates, door-latches, bull-heads, ivory pegs, beams, rafters, purlins, clothing racks, monastic cells, private rooms, walls, dining areas, spaces between doors, meditation caves, latrines, urinals, multi-storied buildings, walking paths, and the base of trees to make banners and inscriptions with their blood."

The bhikṣus reflected thus: "In this dwelling place, the enraged bandits have issued orders to capture, kill, bind, and drive out the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; they have taken the blood from their heads and smeared it upon the doors, windows, and eaves, forming characters and making banners. They have used it on the gates, door-bolts, door-levers, bull-heads, ivory stakes, beams, rafters, purlins, and clothing racks; in the monastic quarters, private rooms, walls, dining areas, and between the doors; in the meditation caves, the places for defecation and urination, the multi-storied pavilions, the walking paths, and beneath the trees—all of these they have marked with characters and banners made of blood."
"If we were to perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting three times, there might be loss of life or violation of the precepts.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting once."

Having made this announcement, one should then perform the *pravāraṇā*. One must not create an obstacle to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed with a single proclamation.
"What is the danger of fire?

Suppose monks construct a monastery within a grove of trees, and then a celestial fire or a great fire comes forth. This fire burns the grove of trees, the walking paths, the multi-storied pavilions, the individual cells of the monastery, the walls, the dining areas, the gateways, the places for excrement and urine, and it burns the dwellings of the householders' oxen, sheep, donkeys, horses, camels, and threshing floors, as well as their servants."
The bhikṣus reflected:

"If we build a vihāra within this grove, a celestial fire or a great conflagration will come and burn the grove, the walking paths, and even the layperson’s sugarcane fields, rice fields, wheat fields, sesame fields, and grapevines; it will burn the cattle, sheep, donkeys, horses, camels, and threshing floors, and it will burn all the laborers."
"We have performed the *pravāraṇā* three times, yet some have lost their lives or broken the precepts.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once."
"Thus one should announce.
Having completed this, one should perform the *pravāraṇā*; do not create obstacles to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed with a single proclamation.
"What is the danger of water?

If bhikṣus construct a monastery in a bend of a river, there may be nāgas dwelling there who rely on the Snowy Mountains; as their bodies grow and they gain strength, they enter great rivers and return to the great ocean, causing the river waters to swell so greatly that they sweep away forests, walking paths, multi-storied monasteries, private rooms, dining areas, gateways, and places for excrement and urine. They likewise sweep away the sugar cane fields, rice paddies, and even the threshing floors and the people of the lay householders."
Thereupon, the bhikṣus reflected: "This river bends around the monastery;
various nāgas and mahānāgas dwell there, relying on the Snowy Mountains, and have even gone so far as to flood the people."
"We have performed the *pravāraṇā* three times, yet some have taken life or broken the precepts.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once."

Having made this announcement, one should then perform the *pravāraṇā*; one must not create obstacles to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed with a single proclamation.
"What is the difficulty of wild beasts?

If bhikṣus construct a monastery in a place inhabited by wild beasts, and the junior bhikṣus therein do not know the proper rules—such as voiding excrement or urine in improper places or washing and drying their soiled robes there—the wild beasts become enraged."
"Wild beasts" refers to lions, tigers, leopards, bears, wolves, and brown bears.

These wild beasts may enter the monastery’s individual quarters, the walls, the dining area, meditation caves, doorways, places for defecation and urination, the bathhouse, multi-storied pavilions, walking paths, or beneath the trees.
The bhikṣus reflected:

"We have built a monastery in this place inhabited by fierce beasts. The junior bhikṣus here do not know the proper rules; they void excrement and urine in improper places, wash their soiled clothes, and hang them out to dry. Consequently, the fierce beasts become enraged and enter the monastery, even coming as far as the trees at the head of the walking paths."
"We have performed the *pravāraṇā* three times, yet some have lost their lives or broken the precepts.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once."

Having made this announcement in this manner, one should perform the *pravāraṇā*; one must not create an obstacle to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed with a single proclamation.
"What is the difficulty regarding the belly-crawling insects?

Suppose there are bhikṣus who construct a monastery in a place inhabited by nāgas. Among them, some junior bhikṣus do not know the proper rules of conduct; they void excrement and urine in improper places and wash their soiled clothes there to dry them. Consequently, the nāgas there become enraged and release venomous snakes and centipedes, which enter beneath the beds, upon the beds, beneath the couches, upon the couches, beneath the solitary seats, into the door-sockets and windows, between the doors, onto the door-latches, on the ox-heads, ivory, stakes, beams, rafters, and clothing racks, as well as into the monasteries, private rooms, walls, dining areas, gateways, meditation caves, bathhouses, multi-storied pavilions, latrines, urinals, walking paths, and beneath the trees at the head of the walkways."
Thereupon, the bhikṣus there reflected:
"This nāga’s dwelling has been made into a monastery; the junior bhikṣus do not know the proper rules of conduct, even regarding [the use of] places under trees."
"We have performed the *pravāraṇā* three times, yet some have lost their lives or broken the precepts.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once."

Having made this announcement in this manner, one should perform the *pravāraṇā*; one must not create an obstacle to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed with a single proclamation.
"What is the 'difficulty regarding persons'?

It is when monks reside in dependence upon a city or village, yet those monks do not know the appropriate conduct; thus, when noblewomen address them with either gentle words or insults, they seek to bring them into submission."

Therein, the people, acting out of anger and issuing strict commands, captured various śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas, killing some, binding others, and driving them out; they did not permit them to enter cities, towns, villages, streets, or marketplaces, nor did they allow them to enter houses; they would not let them sit down, beg for alms, or receive offerings.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus there reflected:

"These bhikṣus do not know the proper way; they think that by using either gentle words or insults, they can cause noblewomen to submit. Yet these people respond with anger and reprimands, arresting them, killing them, and even forbidding them from receiving offerings."
"We have performed the *pravāraṇā* three times, yet some have lost their lives or broken the precepts.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* by reciting it once."

Having made this announcement in this manner, one should then perform the *pravāraṇā*. One must not create obstacles to the *pravāraṇā*; thus, in such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed with a single proclamation.
"What is the difficulty caused by non-humans (*amanuṣya*)?

There are monks who build monasteries in places inhabited by non-humans; these monks, not knowing the proper rules, void excrement and urine in improper places, wash their soiled clothes, and hang them out to dry. Thereupon, the non-humans become angry and terrify the monks, seizing them and placing them upon or beneath beds, upon or beneath solitary sitting benches, in doorways, windows, or between doors, on door-bolts, ox-heads, ivory, stakes, beams, rafters, clothing racks, in common rooms, private rooms, walls, dining areas, gateways, meditation caves, bathhouses, multi-storied buildings, latrines, urinals, walking paths, or at the foot of trees; or they may seize a monk and suspend him upside down."
Thereupon, the bhikṣus there reflected:
"These bhikṣus do not know the proper dharma, even to the point of seizing a bhikṣu and hanging him upside down.
We shall recite the *pravāraṇā* three times, lest they take our lives or cause us to break the precepts."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha perform the *pravāraṇā* by a single recitation.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having performed this, one should then perform the *pravāraṇā*; one must not create obstacles to the *pravāraṇā*. In such a residence, the *pravāraṇā* should be performed by a single recitation.
"In a certain residence, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, if a bhikṣu says,
'Let us set aside matters concerning offenses and perform the *pravāraṇā* together with others,' the Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu:"
"Elder! One must not perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony with others while harboring a matter of offense; if there is a matter to be addressed, speak of it now.
For what purpose?"
"We have requested that the Buddha permit us to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together, but this matter is not permitted.
Another bhikṣu said:
"Setting aside the person and setting aside the offense, let the rest of the assembly perform the *pravāraṇā* together."
The Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu: "Venerable one!
You may not set aside a person or set aside an offense; you must perform the *pravāraṇā* together with the others. If there is any matter to be mentioned, mention it now."
"For what reason?
We have been granted the *pravāraṇā* by the Buddha, yet this matter is not permitted.
Another bhikṣu said:
"Having set aside the offense, having set aside the person, and having set aside his faction, the remaining monks shall perform the *pravāraṇā* together.
The Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!..."

One must not harbor resentment toward another person or their faction; one may perform the *pravāraṇā* together with the remaining members of the community. If there is anything to be said, say it now.
For what purpose?
We have been permitted by the Buddha to perform the *pravāraṇā*, yet this matter is not permissible.

"In a certain residence, at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, one recognizes the offense but does not recognize the person [who committed it]. The Saṃgha should request a confession after the *pravāraṇā* has passed; they should not request it during the *pravāraṇā* itself."
If one requests a formal confession (*pārivāsika*) at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

At a certain residence during the *pravāraṇā*, there were those who recognized the person but did not recognize the offense; the Saṃgha should have requested the confession after the *pravāraṇā* rather than requesting it during the *pravāraṇā*.
If one requests a formal confession at the time of the *pravāraṇā*, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

At a certain residence during the *pravāraṇā*, if the offense is recognized and the person is identified, the Saṃgha should request the confession at the time of the *pravāraṇā*; one should not request it after the *pravāraṇā* has passed.
If one seeks to confess after the *pravāraṇā* has passed, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.

At a certain residence, during the time of *pravāraṇā*, there was a case where the offense was not recognized and the person [who committed it] was not recognized; in such a case, the Saṃgha should seek confession after the *pravāraṇā* has passed, rather than seeking confession at the very time of *pravāraṇā*.
If one requests a formal confession (*pravāraṇā*) at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
At a certain residence during the *pravāraṇā*, the bhikṣus established this restriction:
"Venerable Elders!..."

"We do not perform the *pravāraṇā* after three months; rather, we perform the *pravāraṇā* during the fourth month of the eight-month rainy season. If we receive much alms-giving at the end of the summer retreat, we use this to perform the *pravāraṇā*, for the purpose of receiving and managing those offerings."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not originally consented to go—whether sent by his parents as a messenger, or by his brothers, sisters, children, or his former wife—and he did not go of his own accord but was forced to do so. This bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"Venerable Elders!..."
Originally, I did not desire to be sent by my parents as a messenger, nor by my brothers, sisters, children, or even a second relative; it was against my will that I was compelled to go.
"You have all assembled; I now wish to perform the *pravāraṇā*, I wish to suspend the *pravāraṇā*, or I wish to suspend the *pravāraṇā* of a certain bhikṣu.
The Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!"

One may not perform the *pravāraṇā* today, nor may one obstruct another bhikṣu from performing the *pravāraṇā*. If there is any matter to be mentioned, it should be mentioned now; because one’s own person is pure, the Buddha has permitted the *pravāraṇā*.
That bhikṣu said: "Venerable elders, assemble!
Today I shall perform the *pravāraṇā*; when you have arrived later, you must then obstruct this one bhikṣu’s *pravāraṇā*."
The Saṃgha should say: "Venerable one!
You may not perform the *pravāraṇā* today; later, another bhikṣu was already obstructed from performing the *pravāraṇā*."
"If there is anything to be said regarding the matter at hand, speak now; because one's own person is pure, the Buddha permits the *pravāraṇā*.
If that bhikṣu says: "Venerable elders, assemble!
Today is the *pravāraṇā*; those who arrive later shall no longer obstruct other bhikṣus from their *pravāraṇā*."
The Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should act in harmony and grant this bhikṣu the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā). Why is this?
"Because it would violate the restrictions regarding the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*).

"One should not go at the time of the invitation ceremony if there is a monk in one's own residence, a monk in that [other] residence, a monk who has no residence there, or a monk who has both a residence and no residence there, and if the monks between those places do not live together."

"One should not go at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if there is a residence where monks reside and another residence where non-monks reside, or if there is a residence where non-monks reside and no residence where monks reside, or if there is a residence where non-monks reside and a residence where monks reside, yet the monks in between do not live together."
The rest is as explained in detail in the *Poṣadha* [Karmavācanā]. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: "One should not perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) in the presence of laypeople;

nor before śrāmaṇeras; nor before those who are not bhikṣus, such as followers of other paths; nor before those who have been suspended for not seeing an offense, those who have been suspended for not making amends, or those who have been suspended for not relinquishing evil views; nor before those who do not live in communion, those who live in various forms of non-communion, those who have committed a pārājika offense, those who were originally laypeople, eunuchs, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, those who have gone over to another sect, those who have killed their father, mother, or an arhat, those who have caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or those who have shed the blood of a Buddha with malicious intent. In all such cases, one should not perform the *pravāraṇā* in their presence."
When all preliminary matters have been completed, the Saṃgha should perform the *pravāraṇā*.
If it is appropriate to grant the *saṃmukha-vinaya*, it should be granted; if it is appropriate to grant the *smṛti-vinaya*, it should be granted;

if it is appropriate to grant the *amūḍha-vinaya*, it should be granted; if it is appropriate to grant the *pratijñā-vinaya*, it should be granted; if it is appropriate to grant the *tattvika-vinaya*...
If one has already performed the *mānāpya* (probation) and the *āvarhana* (reinstatement), one should perform the *mānāpya* and *āvarhana* again;

likewise, if that bhikṣu should have the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) performed upon him, or the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) performed, or the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) performed, or the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) performed, or... [if it should be performed].

If one has performed the *ajñapti-karman* (formal act of notification) for the *adarśana-pratiniḥsarga-kaṛman* (act of suspension for not seeing an offense), but should have instead performed the *pratinisargaka-kaṛman* (act of suspension);

or if one has performed the *ajñapti-karman* for the *apratiniḥsṛṣṭa-pāpaka-dṛṣṭi-pratiniḥsarga-kaṛman* (act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views), but should have instead performed the *pratiniḥsargaka-kaṛman*;

or if one has performed the *ajñapti-karman* for the *parivāsa-kaṛman* (act of probation), but should have instead performed the *mānatva-kaṛman* (act of penance); or if one should have performed the *mūlāpakarṣa-kaṛman* (act of resetting the probation to the beginning).

When the *karmavācanā* has been performed— whether it be the *karmavācanā* for the granting of absolution from an offense (*āpattivyutthāna*) that ought to be granted— and the Saṃgha is ready to perform the *pravāraṇā*,
if a monk has accepted the *pravāraṇā* invitation in advance, the Saṃgha should not perform the *pravāraṇā* together with him.

If the Saṃgha has not yet risen in this manner, and the time for the *pravāraṇā* has not yet arrived, one should not perform the *pravāraṇā*; however, this is excepted in the case of a divided Saṃgha that has returned to harmony and listens with a single mind to the *pravāraṇā*.
The third section on the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) within the seven dharmas is concluded.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 23 [and] Fascicle 24; the fourth recitation, part four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
4. The Dharma of the Rains Retreat (*Varṣā*). This is the fourth of the seven dharmas.
When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, various bhikṣus were wandering through various countries during the summer retreat, treading upon living grass and depriving many insects of their lives.
At that time, various non-Buddhist renunciants criticized, disparaged, and censured them, saying:

"The śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of other paths remain in secluded retreats during the summer rains retreat, just as birds seek out their nests and burrows to avoid the heat when the sun is at its zenith."
While the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of other paths remain in secluded retreat during the summer rains retreat, the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya constantly harbor such thoughts as these:
they claim to possess virtue, yet they wander about during the summer, treading upon living grass and harming the lives of sentient beings.

There were certain bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse in their hearts and reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, questioned the bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, while traveling during the summer retreat, treads upon living grass and deprives living creatures of their lives?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should observe the summer retreat (varṣā).
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Who should observe the rains retreat?
The Buddha said,
"The fivefold assembly should observe the rains retreat."
What are the five? First, bhikṣus; second, bhikṣuṇīs; third, śikṣamāṇās; fourth, śrāmaṇeras; and fifth, śrāmaṇerikās.
"How should one undertake the rains retreat?
The Buddha said:

"If the senior monk wishes to undertake the rains retreat, he should rise from his seat, drape his robe over one shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:"
"Venerable sir, please remember!

I, bhikṣu [Name], am observing the summer retreat at this residence during the first three months, relying upon the village of [Name] which is suitable for practice, in order to repair the holes and cracks in the [Name] monastery."
The second [formula]:
"Venerable sir, please remember!

I, bhikṣu so-and-so, am observing the summer rains retreat in this residence during the first three months, depending upon the village of such-and-such—a place fit for practice—and the monastic dwelling of such-and-such, for the purpose of repairing its holes and cracks."
Third: "Venerable sir, please remember!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am observing the summer retreat at this residence during the first three months, relying upon the village of [Name] which is fit for travel, for the purpose of repairing holes and cracks in the [Name] monastery."
The junior monk replied,
"Do not be negligent.
The senior monk said:
"Receive and uphold it.

If one of lower rank receives the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) from one of higher rank, he should rise from his seat, expose one shoulder, adjust his robe, kneel with both knees on the ground, and grasp the two feet of the superior with both hands, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir, please take note!"

I, Bhikṣu [Name], am observing the summer retreat at this residence during the first three months, depending upon the village of [Name] which is fit for travel, in order to repair the holes and cracks in the [Name] monastery.
The second [formula]:
"Venerable sir, remember!

I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, am observing the summer retreat at this residence during the first three months, relying upon the village of so-and-so which is suitable for practice, in order to repair the holes and cracks in the so-and-so monastery."
Third: "Venerable sir, please remember!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am observing the summer rains retreat at this residence during the first three months, relying upon the village of [Name] which is suitable for practice, in order to repair the holes and cracks in the [Name] monastery."
The senior monk said,
"Do not be negligent.
The junior monk said:
"Accept and uphold it.
The same applies during the subsequent three months.
If one does not observe the *anavasa* (rainy season retreat), one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a village in the kingdom of Kāśi named Hastibala.
In it lived a householder named Uttara, who was immensely wealthy, with vast agricultural estates and an abundance of precious goods.

Having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and having seen the truths and attained the fruits of the Path, he established a monastery for the Sangha and sent a messenger with this message:

"There is an abundance of fine food, drink, and various robes here; may the Elders come to receive my offerings of food and drink, while the bedding and furnishings of the monastery are given to the Sangha of the four quarters."
Then the bhikṣus sent back a messenger to inform the householder, saying:
"The Buddha has established a precept for the bhikṣus that they must not travel through various countries during the summer retreat; do not be distressed or troubled by this."
The householder thought to himself:
"My wish has not been fulfilled; I am filled with grief, suffering, and distress. I built this monastery for the sake of the Saṃgha, yet the Saṃgha is unwilling to come—what should I do?"
"Let us invite as many resident bhikṣus as possible from the nearby area to assemble for a meal, and offer bedding and furniture for the monastic quarters to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
It is the constant rule of all Buddhas to hold two great assemblies each year: at the end of the spring month and at the end of the summer month.
In the final month of spring, bhikṣus from various regions and lands went to where the Buddha was to hear his teaching on the joy of the summer rains retreat.
This was the first great assembly, as the bhikṣus proceeded to the place where the Buddha resided.

At the end of the summer, when the bhikṣus had completed their three-month *varṣā* retreat and finished making their robes, they set out gradually with their robes and bowls on a journey to visit the Buddha. Having not seen the Bhagavān for a long time, and not seen the Sugata for a long time, this was the second great assembly of bhikṣus going to visit the Buddha.

There were other bhikṣus who, having completed their rains retreat in Rājagṛha and finished making robes after the three months had passed, traveled by stages together with their robes and bowls until they arrived at the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they inquire with these words:
"Are you patient?
Are you well?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Do you have no lack of alms-food, and are you not weary from the road?
Now the Buddha likewise asked the visiting bhikṣu in this manner:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Is there no lack of alms-food? Are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣus replied, "We have sufficient food, we dwell in peace and happiness; there is no lack of alms-food, and we are not weary from the road."
He reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, when there is a need, you are permitted to receive the seven-night rule."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Regarding the matter of being permitted to depart for seven nights, for whose sake should one go?
The Buddha said:
"One should go for the sake of the seven assemblies.
Which seven? First, bhikṣus; second, bhikṣuṇīs; third, śikṣamāṇās; fourth, śrāmaṇeras; fifth, śrāmaṇerīs; sixth, upāsakas; and seventh, upāsikās."
What is meant by "one should go for the sake of an upāsikā"?
It is as when an upāsikā builds a dwelling and sends a messenger to the place where a bhikṣu is, saying:
"I am building a dwelling; may the Venerable One come to enter the dwelling and receive my offerings."
"If such circumstances arise, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.
For example, if a laywoman (*upāsikā*) has constructed elephant stables, horse stables, gatehouses, or dining halls, she may send a messenger to the place where a bhikṣu resides and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I have constructed elephant stables, horse stables, gatehouses, and dining halls; may the Venerable One come to receive the hospitality of entering these dwellings.
In such a case, it is permitted to depart for seven nights.

Suppose a laywoman, for the sake of the Saṃgha, has built a dwelling—whether it be a warm hall, a cool hall, a hall with a covered roof, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house—and sends a messenger to a bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."

"For the sake of the Saṃgha, I have constructed dwellings, heated halls, cool halls, halls with joined eaves, multi-storied pavilions, single-story houses, and flat-roofed houses; may the Venerable Ones come to enter these houses and receive offerings."
"If such a situation arises, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.
This applies when a laywoman (*upāsikā*) serves many bhikṣus—two or one;
or when she serves many bhikṣuṇīs—two or one."
For many śikṣamāṇās, two or one;
for many śrāmaṇeras, two or one;
for many śrāmaṇerīs, two or one.
For the sake of many renunciants, two or one;
for the sake of many renunciant nuns, two or one.

If, for the sake of a single renunciant nun, one constructs a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a unified roof, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house, and sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu, saying:
“Venerable sir, come!
For the sake of a single ordained nun, I have constructed a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a unified roof, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, and a flat-roofed house.”
"Venerable sir, please come to receive offerings at my home.
If such a situation arises, he may be permitted to go for seven nights.
Suppose a certain laywoman is seized by a king, or a thief, or an enemy, or an enemy's ally, or an ally of an enemy; she then sends a messenger to the bhikṣu’s location and says:
"Venerable sir!
Whether it be a king, a thief, an enemy, an enemy's ally, or an ally of an enemy who has seized me, come, Venerable sir;
they wish to see the bhikṣu."

"If such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights: if one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, see a bhikṣu, practice giving, listen to the Dharma, and practice giving; or if one wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, and practice giving—if such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights."
Just as when a female lay follower was suffering from extreme illness, she sent a messenger to where a bhikṣu was staying and said:
"I am suffering from extreme illness; Venerable Sir, please come, for I wish to see the bhikṣu."

"If such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights: if one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one is permitted to go for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one is permitted to go for seven nights.

If one wishes to see a bhikṣu and listen to the Dharma, or wishes to see a bhikṣu and practice giving, or wishes to both listen to the Dharma and practice giving while seeing a bhikṣu, or wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, and practice giving—if such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights."
For example, when a female lay follower’s suffering from illness became extreme, she sent a messenger to a bhikṣu and said:
"Venerable Sir!
My suffering from illness has become extreme."
"Venerable sir, come and instruct me on food according to my illness.

If such a situation arises, he may leave for seven nights. "Instruct me on medicine according to my illness"—he may leave for seven nights. "Instruct me on how to provide a full supply of utensils for the attendant who cares for me according to my illness"—he may leave for seven nights. For the sake of food according to the illness, medicine according to the illness, utensils for the attendant who cares for one according to the illness, medicine for the attendant who cares for one according to the illness, or food and medicine for the attendant who cares for one according to the illness—if such a situation arises, he may leave for seven nights.

For example, there was a laywoman (*upāsikā*) who was widely learned and possessed great knowledge of many sūtras, such as: the *Ekavyūha-sūtra* (translated into Chinese as the "One-Purity Sūtra"); the *Bhañjati-śastra* (translated into Chinese as the "Samādhi Sūtra");
the *Manaśrāmaṇa* (translated into Chinese as the "Transformation Sūtra"); the *Parasudhāra* (translated into Chinese as the "Brahma Sūtra");
the *Aṭanāṭiya* (translated into Chinese as the "Sūtra on the Accomplishment of Ghosts and Spirits"); and the *Mahāmāyūrī*.
*The Sword*, translated into Chinese as *The Scripture on the Great Assembly*;

The *Yajus-tru-lo* (in the Jin language, the *Sūtra on All Virtues*), and the *Satyadṛśa-tru-lo* (in the Jin language,
the *Sūtra on True Vision*). If one has not yet studied them and wishes to study them,
or if one has previously studied them but has forgotten them and wishes to recite them, one should send a messenger to a bhikṣu and say:
"Venerable Sir!
These are the many renowned and widely known great sūtras, from the *Pārāyaṇa* up to the *Sarghātasaṃyukta-sūtra*."

"If one has not yet studied and wishes to study, or has previously studied but forgotten it and wishes to recite it, [one may say]: 'Venerable sir, please come and teach me so that I may receive instruction, read, recite, and inquire about the meaning.
In such circumstances, permission is granted to depart for seven nights."
As it is for a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) that one should go, so it is for a male lay follower (*upāsaka*).
"How is it that one should go for the sake of a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*)?

For example, if a female novice, for the sake of the Saṃgha, has built a dwelling—a room, a warm hall, a cool hall, a hall with a covered roof, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house—and sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu, saying:"
"For the sake of the Saṃgha, I have constructed dwellings, heated halls, cooled halls, halls with converging eaves, multi-storied pavilions, single-story houses, and flat-roofed houses."
"Venerable sir, please come to partake in the offering at my home.
In such a case, it is permitted to go for seven nights.
If it is for the sake of many bhikṣus, one may go for two or even one [night].
Many bhikṣuṇīs, two or one;
many śikṣamāṇās, two or one;
many śrāmaṇeras, two or one:
Many śrāmaṇerikās, two or one;
many pravrajitas, two or one;
many pravrajitās, two or one.

If, for the sake of a single ordained nun, one constructs a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a unified roof, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house, and sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu to say:
"Venerable Sir!..."
For the sake of a single ordained nun, I have built a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a sloping roof, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, and a flat-roofed house.
"Venerable sir, please come to receive offerings at our home.
If such a situation arises, he may be permitted to go for seven nights.

Suppose a śrāmaṇerikā is seized by a king, or by a thief, or by an enemy, or by an associate of an enemy, or by an associate of an associate of an enemy; they capture her and subject her to punishment, and then send a messenger to the bhikṣu’s location, saying:
"Venerable sir! Whether I am seized by a king,
or by a thief, or by an enemy, or by an enemy’s faction, or by a faction of an enemy’s faction,
and am being punished— come, Venerable sir, for I wish to see the bhikṣu."

"If there is such a matter, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, see a bhikṣu practice giving, listen to the Dharma and practice giving, or see a bhikṣu listening to the Dharma and practicing giving—if there is such a matter, one is permitted to go away for seven nights."
Suppose a śrāmaṇerī, suffering from extreme illness, sends a messenger to a bhikṣu and says:
"I am suffering from extreme illness; Venerable Sir, please come, for I wish to see the bhikṣu."

"If such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights: if one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, or practice giving; or if one wishes to see a bhikṣu who is listening to the Dharma and practicing giving—if such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights."
For example, if a śrāmaṇerī suffers from illness, she sends a messenger to a bhikṣu, saying:
"I am suffering from illness; Venerable Sir, please come and instruct me on what food to eat according to my condition."

"If such circumstances exist, permission is granted to depart for seven nights: if one is instructed to provide medicine according to the illness, permission is granted to depart for seven nights; if one is instructed to provide a full complement of caregivers, permission is granted to depart for seven nights; whether it be for providing food according to the illness and medicine according to the illness, or for providing food according to the illness and a full complement of caregivers, or for providing medicine according to the illness and a full complement of caregivers, or for providing food according to the illness, medicine according to the illness, and a full complement of caregivers—if such circumstances exist, permission is granted to depart for seven nights."
For example, when a śrāmaṇerī was suffering from illness, she sent a messenger to the place where a bhikṣu was, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I am suffering from illness. May the Venerable Sir come here; or, if it is appropriate, take me from this place to that place; or, if it is appropriate, take me from that place to this place."
When such a situation arises, permission is granted for her to depart for seven nights.
For example, if a śrāmaṇerikā becomes distressed and wishes to renounce the precepts, she sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I am filled with anxiety and wish to renounce the precepts; Venerable Sir, please come and preach the Dharma to me.
In such a case, one may be granted leave for seven nights.
If a śrāmaṇerikā gives rise to evil and heterodox views, she may send a messenger to the bhikṣu and say:
"I have a wicked and erroneous thought arisen; Venerable Sir, please come and remove this wickedness for me.
In such a case, it is permitted to go away for seven nights.
If a śrāmaṇerikā feels doubt or regret, she may send a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and say:
"I have doubts and regrets in my heart; Venerable Sir, please come and remove them for me according to the Dharma.
In such circumstances, it is permitted to go away for seven nights.
If a female novice (śrāmaṇerī) who has been in her husband's household for ten full years, or a maiden who has reached eighteen years of age, sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and says:
"If one says, 'I have been in my husband's household for ten years, and I am a maiden of eighteen;
Venerable Sir, please come and receive the training rules for me,' such a case permits her departure for seven nights."

Suppose a śrāmaṇerī, who is well-versed and knowledgeable in many great sūtras, such as the *Pārāyaṇa* up to the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, should wish to study them if she has not yet studied them, or wish to recite them if she has previously studied them but forgotten them; she sends a messenger to where a bhikṣu is and says:
"Venerable Sir!..."
I am one who has studied much and possesses great knowledge of the various great sūtras, from the *Pāramitā-saṃgraha* up to the *Sarvadharmavaipulya-sūtra*.
If there are those I have not yet studied that I wish to study, or those I have studied that I have forgotten and wish to recite.
“Venerable sir, please come and teach me how to receive instruction and recite the scriptures.
For such a matter, one may grant leave for seven nights.
As it is for a śrāmaṇerikā, so it is for a śrāmaṇera as well.
The rest should be understood according to what is appropriate. "What is meant by 'one should go for the sake of a śikṣamāṇā'? It is as follows:

if a śikṣamāṇā, for the sake of the Saṃgha, has constructed a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a joined roof, a multi-storied building, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house, she sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and says:"
"Venerable Sir!
For the sake of the Saṃgha, I have constructed dwellings, heated halls, cooled halls, halls with joined eaves, multi-storied pavilions, single-story houses, and flat-roofed houses."
"Venerable sir, please come to partake in the offering at my home.
In such a case, it is permitted to go for seven nights.
If it is for the sake of many bhikṣus, one may go for two or three nights.
Many bhikṣuṇīs, two or one;
many śikṣamāṇās, two or one;
many śrāmaṇeras, two or one:
Many śrāmaṇerikās, two or one;
many pravrajitas, two or one;
many pravrajitās, two or one.

If, for the sake of a single nun who has gone forth, one constructs a dwelling, a warm hall, a cool hall, a hall with a covered eaves, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house, and sends a messenger to a bhikṣu to say:
"Venerable Sir!..."

For the sake of a single ordained nun, I have constructed dwellings: chambers, heated halls, cooled halls, halls with converging eaves, multi-storied pavilions, single-story houses, and flat-roofed houses.
"Venerable sir, please come to receive offerings at my home.
If such a situation arises, he may be permitted to go for seven nights.

As with a *śikṣamāṇā*, if she is seized by a king, or by a thief, or by an enemy, or by a partisan of an enemy, or by a partisan of a partisan, and they dispatch a messenger to the place of the bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

Whether I am seized by the king, or by bandits, or by enemies, or by the enemy's partisans, or by the partisans of the enemy's partisans, and am brought before them for punishment—Venerable Sir, please come;
I wish to see the bhikṣu."

"If such circumstances exist, one may be granted leave for seven nights: if one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one may be granted leave for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one may be granted leave for seven nights; if one wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, see a bhikṣu, practice giving, listen to the Dharma while practicing giving, or see a bhikṣu while listening to the Dharma and practicing giving—if such circumstances exist, one may be granted leave for seven nights."
For example, if a śikṣamāṇā is suffering from illness, she sends a messenger to a bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable sir!
I am suffering from illness."
"Venerable sir, come; we wish to see the bhikṣus.

If such a matter arises, one may be permitted to go for seven nights. If one wishes to hear the Dharma, one may be permitted to go for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one may be permitted to go for seven nights. Whether it be to see the bhikṣus and hear the Dharma, to hear the Dharma and practice giving, or to see the bhikṣus, hear the Dharma, and practice giving—if such matters arise, one may be permitted to go for seven nights.
For example, if a śikṣamāṇā is suffering from illness, she sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable Sir!
I am suffering from illness."
"Venerable sir, come and teach me how to eat according to my illness.

In such a case, one may go away for seven nights. "Teach me the medicine according to my illness"—one may go away for seven nights. "Teach me a complete attendant for my illness"—one may go away for seven nights. Whether it be for the sake of food according to the illness, medicine according to the illness, a complete attendant for the illness, food and medicine according to the illness, or a complete attendant for both food and medicine according to the illness—in such cases, one is permitted to go away for seven nights.
For example, if a śikṣamāṇā suffers from illness, she sends a messenger to the bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable Sir!
I am suffering from illness."

"Venerable sir, come; if it is lawful to take me from this place to that place, or if it is lawful to take me from that place to this place, then for such a matter, I authorize you to go for seven nights."
Suppose a śikṣamāṇā, being distressed and desiring to renounce the precepts, sends a messenger to a bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable sir!
I am distressed and wish to renounce the precepts."
"Venerable sir, please come and preach the Dharma for me.
If such a situation arises, one may go for seven nights.
If a śikṣamāṇā develops evil and heterodox views, she may send a messenger to where a bhikṣu is and say:
"Venerable Sir!
Evil and heterodox views have arisen within me.
Venerable Sir, please come and remove this evil and heterodoxy for me."
"If such a situation arises, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.
Should a śikṣamāṇā feel doubt or regret, she may send a messenger to where a bhikṣu is and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"My mind is filled with doubt and regret.
Venerable Sir, please come and dispel it for me.
In such a case, one may be granted leave to go away for seven nights.
If a śikṣamāṇā violates either of the latter two precepts, she shall send a messenger to where a bhikṣu is and say:
"Venerable Sir!
I have violated one of the latter two precepts."
"Venerable sir, please come and receive the precepts for me once more.
In such a case, it is permitted to go away for seven nights.
If a *śikṣamāṇā* who has been married for twelve years, or a maiden of twenty years of age, sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and says:
“Venerable Sir!
I have already been married for twelve full years; I am a girl who has reached twenty full years of age. Venerable Sir, please come and grant me the full ordination.”
"If such a situation arises, she may be granted leave for seven nights.

If a *śikṣamāṇā* is well-versed and knowledgeable in the great sūtras, from the *Pārājika* down to the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa-sūtra*, and if she has not yet studied them and wishes to study, or has studied them but forgotten them and wishes to recite them, she may send a messenger to where the bhikṣus are and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"
I am well-versed in and knowledgeable of many great sūtras, from the *Pārāyaṇa* up to the *Sarghāvaśeṣa-sūtra*.

Whether I have not yet studied them and wish to do so, or have studied them but forgotten them and wish to recite them, may the Venerable One come and teach me, instruct me in their reception and recitation, and explain their meaning.
"If such a situation arises, you are permitted to depart for seven nights.
What constitutes 'departing for the sake of a śikṣamāṇā śrāmaṇerī'?

For example, if for the sake of a śikṣamāṇā śrāmaṇerī, one is building a dwelling for the Saṃgha—a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a gabled roof, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house—and sends a messenger to the place where the bhikṣus are to say:"
"Venerable Sir!

For the sake of the Saṃgha, I have constructed a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a unified roof, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, and a flat-roofed house. Venerable Sir, please come to enter these dwellings and accept my offerings."
"If such a situation arises, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.
This applies whether it is for many bhikṣus, two or one;
or for many bhikṣuṇīs, two or one."
Many śikṣamāṇās, two or one;
many śrāmaṇeras, two or one;
many śrāmaṇerīs, two or one.
If many renunciants, or two or one;
or many renunciant nuns, or two or one;

or for the sake of a single renunciant nun, one constructs a dwelling, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a covered roof, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, or a flat-roofed house, and sends a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu to say:
"Venerable Sir!

For the sake of a single ordained nun, I have constructed a dwelling—a room, a heated hall, a cool hall, a hall with a unified roof, a multi-storied pavilion, a single-story house, and a flat-roofed house. Venerable Sir, please come to enter this house and accept my offerings."
"If such a situation arises, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.

This applies as it does when a trainee śrāmaṇerī is seized by a king, or by a thief, or by an enemy, or by an enemy’s faction, or by a faction of that faction, and they are arrested and punished; she then sends a messenger to the bhikṣu and says:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"If I am seized by the king, or by bandits, or by enemies, or by the enemies' partisans, or by the partisans of the enemies' partisans, and they arrest and punish me—Venerable Sir, please come;
I wish to see the bhikṣu."
"If such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights.

If one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one is permitted to go away for seven nights. If one wishes to see a bhikṣu and listen to the Dharma, or wishes to see a bhikṣu and practice giving, or wishes to listen to the Dharma and practice giving, or wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, and practice giving—if such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights."
For example, if a trainee śrāmaṇerikā is suffering from illness, she sends a messenger to where a bhikṣu is staying and says:
"I am suffering from illness.
Venerable sir, please come; I wish to see the bhikṣu."
"If such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights.

If one wishes to listen to the Dharma, one is permitted to go away for seven nights; if one wishes to practice giving, one is permitted to go away for seven nights. If one wishes to see a bhikṣu and listen to the Dharma, or wishes to see a bhikṣu and practice giving, or wishes to listen to the Dharma and practice giving, or wishes to see a bhikṣu, listen to the Dharma, and practice giving—if such circumstances exist, one is permitted to go away for seven nights."
For example, if a trainee śrāmaṇerī is suffering from illness, she sends a messenger to where a bhikṣu is and says:
"Venerable sir!
I am suffering from illness."
"Venerable sir, come and instruct me on food according to my illness"—in such a case, one may go away for seven nights.

"Instruct me on medicine according to my illness"—one may go away for seven nights. "Instruct me on how to provide full care for the patient"—one may go away for seven nights. "Instruct me on food according to my illness and medicine according to my illness"—one may go away for seven nights. "Instruct me on food according to my illness and how to provide full care for the patient"—one may go away for seven nights. "Instruct me on medicine according to my illness and how to provide full care for the patient"—one may go away for seven nights. "Instruct me on food according to my illness, medicine according to my illness, and how to provide full care for the patient"—in such a case, one may go away for seven nights.
Suppose a trainee śrāmaṇerikā is suffering from illness and sends a messenger to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!
I am suffering from illness."

"Venerable sir, come! If it is lawful to take me from this place to that place, or if it is lawful to bring me back from that place to this place—since such a matter exists, you may go for seven nights."
For example, if a trainee śrāmaṇerī, being distressed and desiring to renounce the precepts, sends a messenger to a bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable sir!
I am distressed and wish to renounce the precepts."
"Venerable sir, please come and preach the Dharma to me.
If such a situation arises, he may be permitted to go for seven nights.
If a śikṣamāṇā who is under training develops wrong views, she may dispatch a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and say:
"Venerable Sir!
A wicked and perverse state has arisen within me.
Venerable Sir, please come and remove this wickedness for me."
"If such a situation arises, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.
If a trainee śrāmaṇerī feels doubt or regret, she may send a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I have doubts and regrets in my heart.
Venerable Sir, please come and dispel these doubts and regrets for me in accordance with the Dharma.
For such a matter, he may be granted leave to go for seven nights.

If a nun under training (śikṣamāṇā) or a female novice (śrāmaṇerī) wishes for the Saṃgha to perform a *karmavācanā* of censure, or a *karmavācanā* of strict admonition, or a *karmavācanā* of dependence, or a *karmavācanā* of expulsion, or a *karmavācanā* of humbling, she shall send a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu and say:
"Venerable One!..."

The Sangha intends to perform for me the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), or the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), or the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), or the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), or the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of subordination).
"Venerable sir, please come and assist me according to the Dharma.
In such circumstances, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.

This applies when a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī has been subjected to the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), or the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of requiring an apology). Once these acts have been completed, she sends a messenger to the place where the bhikṣu is and says:
"Venerable Sir!
The Saṃgha has finished performing the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* against me, as well as the *tarjanīya-karman*, the *niśraya-karman*, the *pravāsanīya-karman*, and the *pratisāraṇīya-karman*. "
"Venerable sir, please come; let him do what is light and not let him do what is heavy.
When such a situation arises, he may be permitted to go for seven nights.

Just as with a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, if the Saṃgha intends to apply the *smṛti-vinaya* (the verdict of mindfulness) or the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict of sanity), they send a messenger to the place of a bhikṣu, who speaks thus:
"Venerable Sirs!
The Saṃgha wishes to grant me the *smṛti-vinaya* (the discipline of recollection) and the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who is not insane).
Venerable Sirs, please come and grant me the *smṛti-vinaya* and the *amūḍha-vinaya*."
"Since such a situation exists, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.

Just as with a śikṣamāṇā śrāmaṇerī, if the Saṃgha intends to perform the *bhūtaparyeṣaṇā-karman* (the formal act of seeking the truth) against her, they shall send a messenger to the place of the bhikṣus and say:
'Venerable Sirs!'"
"The Sangha wishes to perform the *yathābhūta-mṛgīya-karman* against me; Venerable Sirs, please come and assist me in accordance with the Dharma.
In such a case, it is permitted to depart for seven nights.
Just as with a śrāmaṇerikā under training, once the Sangha has completed the *yathābhūta-mṛgīya-karman* against her, they dispatch a messenger to the bhikṣu's location to say:
"Venerable Sir!
The Sangha has completed the formal act of searching for the truth (*yathābhūta-mṛga-karman*) on my behalf.
Venerable Sir, please come so that what was light may not be made heavy."
"Since such a situation exists, I permit you to depart for seven nights.

Just as with a śikṣamāṇā śrāmaṇerī, if the Saṃgha intends to carry out a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), or a *pravrājaniya-karman* (act of banishment for not abandoning evil views), they shall send a messenger to the place of the bhikṣu and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"

The Saṃgha intends to carry out against me the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense, the formal act of suspension for not making amends, and the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views.
Venerable sirs, please come; I do not see what I should see, I do not make what I should make, and I do not relinquish what I should relinquish.
"If such a situation arises, she may be granted leave for seven nights.
If a śikṣamāṇā has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and it is necessary to grant her a mānatva, or a mūlāpakarṣa, or a pratyosāraka-karman, a messenger shall be sent to the bhikṣus to announce:
'Venerable Sirs!'"
I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; the Saṃgha intends to grant me *mānāpya*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, or rehabilitation from the offense.
Venerable sirs, please come and grant me either *mānāpya*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, or rehabilitation from the offense.
"In such a case, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.

Just as with a śikṣamāṇā śrāmaṇerī, regarding the distinctions of the two sets of Prātimokṣa: if she has not yet studied them and wishes to study, or if she has studied them but has forgotten them and wishes to recite them, she may send a messenger to where the bhikṣus are and say:
'Venerable Sirs!'"
I shall distinguish the two divisions of the Prātimokṣa: for those who have not yet studied it and wish to study it, or for those who have studied it but have forgotten it and wish to recite it.
Venerable sirs, please come and teach me how to receive, study, recite, and inquire about its meaning.
"If such a situation arises, permission is granted to depart for seven nights.

For instance, if a śikṣamāṇā śrāmaṇerī who has studied much and possesses great knowledge of the various great sūtras—from the *Pārājika* down to the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa-sūtra*—wishes to study what she has not yet studied, or wishes to recite what she has forgotten after having studied it, she may send a messenger to where the bhikṣus are and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"
I am one of great learning and vast knowledge regarding the various great sūtras, from the *Pāṭikā* up to the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*.
Whether there are things I have not yet studied that I wish to study, or things I have studied that I have forgotten and wish to recite.
"Venerable Sir, please come and teach me how to receive instruction, recite, and inquire about the meaning.
If such a situation arises, one may go for seven nights.
Just as it is when going to provide instruction to a śrāmaṇerikā, it is likewise when providing instruction to a śrāmaṇera.
Except as may be appropriate; as it is for a bhikṣu that he should go, so it is for a bhikṣuṇī.
As it is when he should go for the sake of another's business, so it is when he should go for his own business.
It is the same whether one sends a messenger or does not send a messenger when one ought to go.
Whether it be a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, they should go for their own sake or for the sake of another, whether they send a messenger or do not send a messenger.
"One week and seven nights is permitted, but two weeks and seven nights is not permitted.
If a bhikṣu observing the summer retreat falls ill and cannot obtain food suited to his condition, he may leave due to this difficult circumstance without incurring any offense."
"If a sick bhikṣu observes the summer rains retreat (varṣā), and because he cannot obtain medicine suitable for his illness, he leaves due to this difficulty, there is no offense.
"If a sick bhikṣu observes the summer rains retreat, and because he cannot obtain a full-time attendant to care for him, he leaves due to this difficulty, there is no offense."

"If a sick bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat (varṣā), and if he cannot obtain food appropriate for his illness or medicine appropriate for his illness; or if the attendant does not have sufficient food appropriate for his illness; or if the attendant does not have sufficient medicine appropriate for his illness; or if the attendant does not have sufficient food and medicine appropriate for his illness—if, due to such difficulties, he departs, there is no offense."
"There was a bhikṣu observing the summer retreat. During this time, a woman spoke to him improperly, saying:
'Venerable Sir!
I am like a daughter or a sister to you; please act as my son-in-law or act as the husband for my sister.'"
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"In this matter, a woman has spoken words that are not in accordance with the Dharma, saying:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I am like a sister to your daughter; you should act as my son-in-law and my sister's husband.
If I were to remain in this place, I might lose my life or lose my holy life (*brahmacarya*).
"If there is such a difficulty, one may leave and there is no offense.
Suppose a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat, and a man therein speaks to him in an improper manner, saying:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I am like a sister to your daughter; you may become my son-in-law and my sister's husband.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"The man here speaks words that are not in accordance with the Dharma."
"Venerable Sir!
Your daughter and I are like sisters; you would be my son-in-law and my sister's husband.
If I were to dwell in such a place, I would lose either my life or my holy life."
"If there is such a difficult circumstance as this, he may go out without fault.

There was a bhikṣu who, during the summer retreat, engaged in improper reflection and focused his thoughts on the marks of a woman—whether she was coming or going, standing or sitting, laughing or speaking, weeping or singing, performing music or dancing, whether she was naked or wearing many or few garments, or whether she was adorned or unadorned."
A bhikṣu reflects thus:

"While I am dwelling here, there is improper reflection and reflection on signs: [the thought] of a woman coming or going, sitting or standing, speaking or laughing, or weeping; dancing, singing, or performing as a courtesan; being naked, or wearing few or many garments; or being adorned or unadorned."
"If I remain in this place, I may lose my life or lose my holy life (brahmacarya).
Because of such dangers, he departs; there is no offense.
"There was a bhikṣu who, while observing the summer retreat (varṣā), saw a hidden treasure of great value and precious jewels. The bhikṣu thought to himself:"
"If I see a great treasure of priceless jewels as a hidden store within this [place], and if I remain here, I may lose my life or lose my holy life (brahmacarya)," thinking thus,
there is no offense in departing due to such difficulties.
“Suppose there is a bhikṣu observing the summer retreat (varṣā), and his parents, brothers, sisters, children, daughters, or former second wives come to visit him.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
‘If my parents, brothers, children, sisters, or former second wives should come to me during this time.’”
"If I remain in this place, I may lose my life or lose my holy life.
Because of such dangers, he departs; there is no offense.
"There was a bhikṣu who was observing the summer retreat when he saw the Sangha split into two factions. The bhikṣu reflected thus:"

"In this matter, the Sangha is split into two factions; if I were to dwell therein, I might give rise to an evil mind or utter evil speech, whereby I would suffer long-term diminution and fall into the evil realms."
Because there is this difficulty, one may leave; there is no offense.
Suppose a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat and sees that the Saṃgha is striving to cause a schism. That bhikṣu reflects thus:

"In this dwelling place, the Saṃgha is striving to cause a schism. If I remain here, I might give rise to evil thoughts or utter evil words, and for a long night I would suffer diminution and fall into the evil realms."
If one leaves because of such difficulties, there is no offense.
[The same applies to] seeing many bhikṣus (two cases), one bhikṣu (one case);
many bhikṣuṇīs (two cases), one bhikṣuṇī (one case).
Many śikṣamāṇās: two, one; many śrāmaṇeras: two, one; many śrāmaṇerīs: two, one.
There are many renunciants, two or one;
there are many renunciant nuns, two or one.
Seeing a single renunciant nun who is intent on causing a schism in the Saṃgha, a bhikṣu reflects as follows:

"In this place, the nun who has gone forth is intent on causing a schism in the Saṃgha. If I were to dwell here, I might give rise to evil thoughts or utter evil words; thus, for a long night, I would suffer diminution and fall into the evil realms."
If there is such a difficulty, it is no offense for one to depart.
Suppose a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat, and he hears that at that residence there is a concerted effort to break the Saṃgha through contentious means. The bhikṣu reflects thus:

"At that residence there is a concerted effort to break the Saṃgha through contentious means; I am able to admonish them with gentle words so that their minds may be appeased, and cause them to return to a state of single-minded harmony."
Because there is such a matter, he departs and is without offense.

Suppose a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat, and he hears that in the dwelling place where he intends to stay, there is a community of monks who are striving to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. The bhikṣu reflects thus:

"In that dwelling place, there is a community of monks striving to cause a schism; I am able to admonish them with gentle words so that their minds may be pacified, so that they will not strive to cause a schism, but instead return to being united as one mind."
Because there is such a reason for departing, there is no offense.
"If it is many bhikṣus [and two or one];
or many bhikṣuṇīs [and two or one];"
Many śikṣamāṇās, two or one;
many śrāmaṇeras, two or one;
many śrāmaṇerīs, two or one.
If there are many renunciants and one [lay follower],
or many renunciant nuns and one [lay follower];
or if a single renunciant nun is diligently intent on causing a schism in the Saṃgha, a bhikṣu reflects as follows:

"In that place there is a certain ordained nun who is diligently striving to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; I am able, through such gentle words of admonition, to bring about their reconciliation so that she no longer strives to cause a schism, but instead returns to a state of single-minded harmony."
If one leaves for this reason, there is no offense.

Suppose a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat and hears that at a certain residence there is a gathering of those intent on using skillful means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha. That bhikṣu reflects thus:

"At that residence there is a gathering of those intent on using skillful means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; I am unable to issue such instructions or speak with such gentle words as would cause their minds to be stilled and return to unity in harmony."

I have relatives there in that intermediate state; by the power of those relatives, they will be able to speak gentle words of exhortation, causing the schismatic's stratagems for convening the assembly to cease, so that they may once again become harmoniously united with one mind.
If one leaves for this reason, there is no offense.
Suppose a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat and hears that the Saṃgha in that place intends to strive toward schism and is gathering together to achieve it. The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"The Saṃgha there is striving to cause a schism; my power is insufficient to pacify their minds through gentle words and exhortations so that they might return to a state of single-minded harmony."

I have relatives there in that intermediate state; through the power of those relatives, they can speak gentle words of exhortation, causing that person’s intention to divide the Saṃgha to subside and their minds to reunite in harmony once again.
If one goes out for the sake of such matters, there is no offense.
"The same applies to many bhikṣus [and two or one];
many bhikṣuṇīs [and two or one]."
Many śikṣamāṇās, two or one;
many śrāmaṇeras, two or one;
many śrāmaṇerīs, two or one.
There are many renunciants, or one;
there are many renunciant nuns, or one.
For example, if a renunciant nun diligently seeks the means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha by convening an assembly, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"In that place, there is a nun who has gone forth and is diligently striving to cause a schism in the Saṃgha through various means; my power is insufficient to pacify her mind with gentle words and exhort her so that she might return to a state of single-minded harmony."

I have relatives there in that intermediate state; by the power of those relatives, they can speak gentle words of exhortation to cause those who employ the means of schism to cease their intent and instead return to a state of single-minded harmony.
If one goes out for the sake of such matters, there is no offense.
"If a bhikṣu is observing the summer retreat, and at that time one or another of the eight difficulties arises, and he goes out because of such difficult circumstances, there is no offense."
The full explanation is as given in the *Pravāraṇā* [Karmavācanā].
Suppose a bhikṣu resolves to enter the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) at a certain location, but an urgent matter arises here.
If he reaches that place and is compelled to return, that bhikṣu reflects thus:
"If I have not finished my business here and go to that other place, I must certainly return here.
Only after his business is concluded should he go to that residence; otherwise, that bhikṣu commits an offense by violating his own word by staying at that residence for the three months.

A bhikṣu resolves to observe the summer rains retreat at a certain place; these two residences share the same distribution of offerings but have separate *poṣadha* ceremonies. This bhikṣu reflects thus:
"If I perform the *poṣadha* ceremony here, I shall receive a share of the robes from this location."
"If one performs the *poṣadha* at that other residence, one shall also receive a share of the robes from this place.

If a bhikṣu performs the *poṣadha* at a non-residence during the rainy season retreat and subsequently returns to his actual residence, that bhikṣu should not have spent the first three months at that former residence; by failing to do so, he incurs an offense for violating his own word.

If a bhikṣu intends to go and reside in a certain place, and having gone and completed his residence there, departs for a place outside the boundary without performing the poṣadha, that bhikṣu shall not spend the first three months at that residence; by doing so, he violates his own word and incurs an offense.

If a bhikṣu intends to go to that residence and has indeed gone to that residence, and having completed the poṣadha ceremony, departs beyond the boundary without taking his bedding and furniture, that bhikṣu should not remain at that residence for the preceding three months; by acting contrary to his word, he incurs an offense.

If a bhikṣu intends to go to that residence, and having gone to that residence and finished the *poṣadha* ceremony and the distribution of bedding and seats, he departs beyond the boundary without a valid reason, that bhikṣu should not remain in that residence for the first three months; by acting contrary to his word, he incurs an offense.

If a bhikṣu intends to go to that residence, and having gone to that residence and finished the *poṣadha* ceremony and the distribution of bedding and seats, he departs for beyond the boundary without having received the seven-night permission, that bhikṣu should not remain at that residence during the preceding three months; to do so would be a transgression against his own word.

If a bhikṣu intends to go to that residence, and having gone to that residence, completed the *poṣadha* ceremony and received the bedding and furniture, he then receives a seven-night permit to go beyond the boundary; if he returns from outside the boundary after the full seven nights, that bhikṣu should not remain at that residence for the first three months of the rainy season, as he would incur an offense by violating his own word.

If a bhikṣu wishes to go to that residence, and having gone there, completed the uposatha ceremony and received the bedding and seats, he takes seven nights’ leave to go beyond the boundary and returns before the seven nights have expired.
That bhikṣu should remain at that residence during the first three months; if he does not act contrary to his word, there is no offense.
The same should be explained in detail for the latter three months as well.
On the seventh day, he should perform the *pravāraṇā*; if he accepts an overnight stay and goes outside the boundary, there is no offense.
Whether for six nights, five nights, four nights, three nights, two nights, or one night, if one stays overnight outside the boundary, there is no offense.
The fourth section on the Rules for the Rain Retreat within the Seven Dharmas is concluded.

The fifth part of the Fourth Recitation, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
5. The Leather Rules (Carmavastu), the fifth among the seven rules.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avantī, there was a village named Rājagṛha.
Among them was a wealthy householder whose wealth and treasures were abundant and all things were fully provided; he lacked only one thing:

he had no children. He prayed and entreated various deities—from the spirits of the ponds, the household spirits, the great spirit of the crossroads, the great spirit Pūrṇabhadra, the great spirit Mahābhadra, and the god Maheśvara, down to the god Nārāyaṇa, the god Viṣṇu, and as far as the god Bṛhaspati—for the sake of obtaining a son, yet he could not obtain one.
When the time for conception arrived, the householder’s wife realized she was pregnant; women of sharp faculties possess four unique knowledges.

What are these four? First, knowing when a man desires her; second, knowing when a man does not desire her; third, knowing the time of conception; and fourth, knowing from whom the child was obtained.
When the wife realized she was pregnant, she said to the householder, "I am pregnant.
Upon hearing this, the householder’s heart leaped with joy;

thinking that he might be born a son, he provided her with excellent care, bathing her until she was clean and pure, anointing her body with fragrances, and attending to her needs at all times so that she remained peaceful and comfortable.
Wherever he went, he was escorted by a great retinue so that no one would suffer distress.
When the ninth month had passed, she gave birth to a son; his ears were adorned with golden rings, and the child was so handsome that all who saw him rejoiced.
Upon hearing this, the householder’s heart leaped with joy; he gathered various Brahmins skilled in the signs of men to examine him, and asked:
"What is the power of this child's merit?"
The brahmins said, "Householder!
This boy truly possesses the power of merit."
The householder said, "Should a name be given to him?
At that time, according to the laws of the land, two kinds of names were used: either based on the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or based on auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). The people said:
“Householder!
When was this child born?
He replied:
"It was born on such-and-such a day.
Having calculated this, the brahmins said, "This child was born on the day of Śramaṇa; therefore, his name shall be Śramaṇa."
The householder again assembled brahmins and householders who were skilled in discerning the characteristics of gold and jewels, and showed them the boy’s ear, asking:
"What is the value of this boy’s earring?"
The people said, "Householder!
These earrings of the child were not made by any worldly craftsman and are difficult to appraise; yet, by our estimation, they are worth one hundred million pieces of pure gold."
The boy’s name was Śramaṇa; his earrings were worth one hundred million. Because of this, the people immediately named him Śramaṇa-Īśvara (Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa), and thus he should be known by all.
This householder had him raised and cared for by five kinds of nurses.
What are the five?
First, the nurse who attends to the body; second, the nurse who removes impurities; third, the wet-nurse; fourth, the nurse for auspiciousness; and fifth, the nurse for play and laughter.
What is a mother who treats the body?
One who treats the child’s head, hands, feet, ears, nose, and various fingers is called a mother who treats the body.
What is a mother who removes impurities?
When one bathes and washes the child from time to time, she is called the "mother who removes impurities.
What is the wet-nurse?
When one feeds and nourishes the child with milk and food from time to time, she is called the "wet-nurse."
What is the Mother Auspicious (Śrī)?
When this child travels, she holds a peacock-feather whisk and carries a trident to guard and protect him; she is named the Mother Auspicious.
What is the Mother Laughter (Hāsā)?

To create for her children mechanical wooden figures, elephants, horses, chariots, bows, arrows, and various other playthings to entertain them at all times—this is called the "Mother of Playful Laughter."

By virtue of this boy’s merit and power, he grew up rapidly; the king then taught him writing, arithmetic, calculation, and sealing, so that he became skilled in discerning the value and quality of various goods.
This royal caravan leader’s village was a place where merchants from the four quarters gathered; at that time, merchants arriving from the four directions asked:
"Who here is well-regarded, virtuous, trustworthy, and capable of showing us what is beneficial or harmful?"

The people pointed out the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, saying, "He is virtuous and excellent, worthy of entrustment and trust, and skilled at discerning what is beneficial and harmful. Thereupon, the merchants went to the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and requested him to act as their host.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked the merchants,
"From where have you come?
They replied:
"From such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a country. He then asked,
"What good and what evil are there in that country?"
The merchant gave a full account of all matters, both favorable and unfavorable.
At that time, there were other merchants arriving from the sea who came to the caravan leader’s settlement and asked:
"Who among those here is virtuous and excellent, trustworthy and reliable, such that we may entrust our affairs to him and have him show us what is beneficial and what is harmful?"

The people pointed out the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to them, saying, "He is virtuous and excellent, worthy of being entrusted with and trusted; he can skillfully distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful. Thereupon, the merchants immediately entrusted him as their host.
