The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked the merchants,
"From where have you come?
They replied:
“From within the great ocean.
He asked,
“What good or evil is there within the great ocean?”
The merchant gave a full account of all the matters in the ocean:

"In the great sea, there is the fear of waves, the fear of turtles, the fear of the timi fish, the fear of the timingila fish, the fear of the śiśumāra fish, the fear of swirling currents, the fear of submerged mountains, the fear of black winds, the fear of the abodes of evil nāgas, and the fear of evil rākṣasas."
"Eṣukāri! Of a hundred thousand people who depart, only one may return.
If one succeeds in returning, they may bestow various rare treasures as alms to cultivate merit; this would not be exhausted for seven generations, let alone for their own person."
When those merchants saw that the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa possessed such great power, they thought to themselves:
"If he acts as the caravan leader and enters the sea with many people, we will surely return in safety."
The people said,
"Śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa!
Why do you not enter the great ocean?"
He replied:
"What would I achieve by entering the great ocean?
It is full of many terrors; though hundreds of thousands go there, only one in a while returns."
These merchants exhorted him, saying:
"What kind of person lives by depending on others, even down to a courtesan who lives by depending on others?
If one seeks to perform the merit of giving, that is excellent and good."

Thus did the merchants exhort him; the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviśa, having accepted their words with faith, wished to depart. Upon reaching his parents’ home, he took leave of them, intending to enter the sea.
At that time, his parents recounted various terrifying matters, wishing to cause him to change his mind and desist so as to keep him from leaving:

“People enter the great ocean for the sake of wealth, yet our house contains many treasures. You may use these to practice giving and cultivate merit, which will not be exhausted for seven generations; why must you enter the sea?”
At that time, he did not follow his parents' words. His parents spoke to the various nobles, saying, "Help us to detain Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
Then the high officials, elders, householders, the wealthy lord of a hundred million, and the great and affluent merchants—these nobles likewise tried to detain him, but he would not comply.
The parents, knowing his intention was righteous, granted him permission to depart.
Thereupon, riding an elephant and shaking a bell, he traveled throughout the village to proclaim:
"The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa wishes to enter the great ocean; I am acting as the caravan leader (*sārthavāha*). Who wishes to go with me?"
The merit of this man was such that all five hundred merchants joyfully followed him.

According to the custom of that land, one who acts as a *sārthavāha* (caravan leader) must provide two hundred thousand gold coins: one hundred thousand to procure the ship and one hundred thousand to procure provisions.
Once the adornments were complete, he descended from the ship into the water and fastened it with seven ropes. Day after day, he proclaimed:
"Who is able to renounce father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, and children, as well as the various pleasures of Jambudvīpa and even the pleasure of life?"

Who among you wishes to obtain gold, silver, mani-jewels, lapis lazuli, and various precious objects to provide for seven generations and perform meritorious acts through giving—let them enter the great ocean together?

Thus he proclaimed day after day, severing one rope each day. In this manner, six ropes were severed, and the seventh rope remained, awaiting the *iler* wind—translated in the Jin language as the "Fine-Attendant Wind."
Having obtained the favorable wind and severed the seventh rope, the ship moved faster than an arrow; this was due to the merit and majestic power of the Sārthavāha.
The ship quickly reached the island of jewels, whereupon he commanded the merchants, saying:
"Take up the various treasures and load them until the ship is full, but do not let it become too heavy."
Having finished taking the treasures, he encountered the *ila* wind; at that time, the ship moved with a speed swifter than an arrow as it returned to Jambudvīpa.
Approaching the caravan leader King’s village, there were two routes:
a water route and a land route.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked the merchants,
"Which road shall we take?
The men replied:
"Let us go by land.
At that time, there was a desolate marsh where they stayed during the middle of the night.
He said to the merchants, "I have heard that bandits come to plunder traveling merchants; if they kill the caravan leader first, then the merchants will achieve nothing."
"If we do not kill the caravan leader, then whether by means of money and goods, by our own strength, or by the strength of others, we will certainly capture the thieves.
I shall go to stay elsewhere; you must call for me when the time comes."
The men replied, "Yes.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa drove his donkey to stay elsewhere for the night; when those merchants set out at midnight, they woke one another but did not call for Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa at all.
Later in the night, a great wind and rain fell; Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa woke up and called out to the merchants, but none of the merchants responded.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself: "Why have all these people abandoned me?"
He immediately followed after him.
This road was full of sand and dust; because wind and rain had washed it away, there were no tracks remaining.
The donkey moved forward by sniffing at the traces, and as Aśvajit was exhausted with hunger, he pressed on until he saw a city that was magnificent, beautiful, and pure. He thought to himself:
Thinking that he would obtain food, he stood at the city gate;
following that thought, he cried out in a loud voice, "Food!"
"Food! At that time,
countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of hungry ghosts emerged and all said,
"What kind of food?"
"Who gave it to you?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, "I had no food;
as I walked along, I was so overcome with hunger that I longed for food, and thus I spoke these words."
"I have no food," he thought,
"I shall obtain food at the edge of the city.
For this reason, he uttered the cry for food.
The hungry ghosts said, "This is a city of hungry ghosts;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, we have heard the sound of food being called out today for the first time.
Because we were stingy and failed to practice generosity, we fell into this realm of hungry ghosts."
"Where do you wish to go?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"I wish to go to the village of the merchant leader, Rājagṛha."
The ghost said, "Go by this path.
Thereupon he proceeded forward and again saw another city; thinking thus once more:
"Previously we could not obtain food in this city, but perhaps now we can obtain water.
He went immediately to the gate, stood there, and called out: "Water!"
"Water!
At that moment, hundreds of thousands of hungry ghosts emerged and all cried out, "What water?"
"Who gave it to you?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, "There was no water;
I was so parched with thirst that I thought of obtaining some, and because of that, I uttered this sound."
"I have no water," he thought; thus reflecting,
"I shall find water by the city," he cried out for water.
The hungry ghosts said:
"This is a city of hungry ghosts; for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, we have heard the sound of water only today.
Because we failed to practice generosity and were full of stinginess, we fell among the hungry ghosts."
"Where do you wish to go?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"I wish to go to the village of the merchant leader Rājagṛha."
The ghost said, "Go by this path.

After traveling forward for a short while, they saw another tree named *bala*. They stayed overnight beneath it; shaking the tree, they ate the fine leaves themselves and gave the coarse ones to the donkey.
Thus, from sunset until nightfall, couches appear therein, and men and women emerge—handsome and upright in appearance, wearing celestial jewel crowns—and they enjoy themselves together.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:
"I ought not to have looked thus upon the private affairs of another.
Then, as the night passed and day arrived, the bed immediately vanished and the woman vanished; a pack of dogs came and devoured it, until only the bones of that man remained.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:
"I regret that I did not ask this man previously what practice he had performed to now receive such a retribution—good by night and evil by day.
I should stay here and wait to question him."
When night fell, there were even finer couches; men and women of upright countenance appeared, wearing jeweled celestial crowns, and they enjoyed themselves together.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went at once to question the man:
"What practice did you perform to obtain this retribution—excellent by night and wretched by day?"
The man said,
"Why do you ask? Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied:
"I wish to know this," the man said.
"Do you recognize King Sārthavāha of the country of Aśmaka-Avanti?"
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"I recognize him.
The man said:
“I am a butcher named so-and-so. There is an elder, Kātyāyana, who frequently comes and goes to my home; I have always provided him with food, drink, clothing, and medicinal requisites.”
"Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa!
He would always say this to me:
'Do not commit evil deeds, lest you experience great suffering hereafter.'"
I then replied: "Since past lives this has been my occupation; if I do not practice it now, how shall I support myself?
At that time, Kātyāyana spoke to me again:
"Did you commit this evil more during the day or more at night?
I replied, "More during the day."
He then said to me:
"If you receive the five precepts at night, you may obtain some slight merit.

I immediately accepted them from him, and now I have obtained this retribution. Since both the goodness of the night and the evil of the day arose from my own actions, what benefit would there be in regret?
The man asked Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
"Where do you wish to go?
He replied:
"Go to the merchant town of Rāja.
The man said,
"Go by this path."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then departed.

After traveling forward for a short distance, he saw another tree named *pāla*; he stayed beneath it for the night, shook the tree to bring down the leaves, ate the fine ones himself, and gave the coarse ones to the donkey.

When night passes and day arrives, there again appear couches in that place; men and women emerge, their countenances upright and handsome, wearing jeweled celestial crowns as they enjoy each other’s company.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then thought:
"I ought not to remain here observing the private affairs of others.
Thus it continued until evening, when the bed vanished and the woman vanished; a centipede emerged and devoured the man, until his flesh was gone and only his bones remained.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:
"I regret not having asked:
'What practice did you perform to obtain this retribution—good by day and evil by night?'"
"You should remain here and wait for questions.

When the night had passed and day arrived, another bed emerged, from which men and women appeared—handsome and beautiful in countenance, wearing jeweled celestial crowns, and enjoying themselves together.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went and asked the man:
"What practice did you perform to obtain this retribution now—good by day but evil by night?
The man said:
"Why do you ask? Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"I wish to know."
The man said,
"Do you know King Sārthavāha of the village in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Āpaṇa?
He replied:
"Recognize this:

A certain man here has committed adultery with another's wife. Now, the Elder Kātyāyana frequents my house, and my household regularly provides him with food, drink, clothing, and medicinal decoctions."
"Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa!
At that time, he instructed me, saying:
'Do not commit evil deeds, lest you receive bitter retribution later.'"
I replied, "I cannot restrain myself; what can be done?
He spoke to me again:
"In what matter are you more prevalent? I replied, "At night."
At that time, Kātyāyana spoke to me, saying:
"By observing the five precepts for a day, one may obtain slight merit.
Following his words, I received the five precepts for a day; therefore, I have obtained this retribution—virtuous by day and evil by night.
"Regret comes first; there is no further benefit to be gained.
The man asked Ayiravata:
"Where do you wish to go?"
He replied,
"I wish to go to the village of King Sārthavāha.
The man said:
"Go by this path.
As he proceeded forward, he again saw a grove of trees and a pool of water, pure and clear; there, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa bathed and gave the donkey water to drink.
By the side of the pool was a hall adorned with various jewels; looking up at the hall, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa immediately had this thought:
"I am so hungry and thirsty that I am on the verge of death; where should I go?
He then immediately went up to the hall and recited a verse from the Buddhist sutras:
"Hunger is the foremost illness; craving is the foremost suffering."
"Thus one knows the Dharma-treasure; Nirvana is the supreme bliss.
While ascending the hall, he saw a woman sitting on an ivory couch, with two hungry ghosts tied to its legs. This woman recognized the monk Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa by name and greeted him, asking:
"Was your journey not too arduous? Were you not thirsty or hungry?"
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself, "This woman has never seen me, yet she knows my name; how can this be?
The woman then called for Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa to sit down, and after they had exchanged greetings, he said to her:
“Noble lady!
Please grant me food.
The woman said:
"Give it to them together.
You must simply not give it to these two hungry ghosts.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said:
“Noble lady! I am currently in such urgent hunger that how could I give [food] to a ghost?
The woman immediately gave him water to wash his hands and provided food. Desiring to let Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa know this causal connection, she stepped slightly outside the hall.
At that time, two hungry ghosts reached out their hands and said to the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:
"Give us one mouthful; give us half a mouthful! The hunger within our bellies burns like fire."
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, who had previously been fond of practicing charity and felt compassion for sentient beings, thought to himself:
"I am suffering from the urgency of hunger and exhaustion; how could these hungry ghosts not be in pain?"

Each was given a mouthful; when these two hungry ghosts placed the food in their mouths, it turned into pus and blood. No matter how much they swallowed, they spat it back out, filling the hall with a foul stench.
The woman returned and saw that the hall was filled with a foul odor.
She said, "I told you not to give it to him; why did you give it to him?"
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said,
“Sisters! I did not know this matter, so I gave it to you.”
The woman immediately cleared away the vomit, swept and sprinkled the area, burned incense, and returned to her original seat.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said, “Sister!”
"Give me some food as well.
The woman said, "I do not begrudge the food, but if I give it to you, I fear you will give it to the ghosts; this matter would be improper."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said, “Sisters!
Previously I gave it because I did not know; now I shall no longer do so.”
The woman then washed her hands with water and gave food to Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
At that moment, another woman came and said:
"Noble lady!..."
"Give me some food.
The woman said,
"Eat your usual food."

Having spoken these words, three cauldrons immediately appeared, filled with boiling brine over a blazing fire. This woman stripped off her clothes, placed them to one side, and entered a cauldron; her skin and flesh were completely consumed by the heat, leaving only a skeleton. A cold wind then blew upon her, and she was able to emerge from the cauldron, restored to life. She put on her clothes, devoured her own decomposed flesh, and departed.
While Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was eating, another woman came and said,
"Noble lady!
Give me some food."
The woman said,
"Eat your usual food.
Having finished speaking these words, the woman transformed into a black ewe eating grass.
The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:
"I wonder if I have died among humans and been reborn in this realm of hungry ghosts?
He then spoke to the noble lady:
"What is this matter?
the woman said,
"What is the use of asking?"
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said,
"I wish to know.
The woman said:
"Do you know the country of Aśmaka-Avanti, and the merchant caravan leader of the village there?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"I know it."
“The ghost that bound the foot of the bed at my head is my husband, the householder so-and-so.
The one that bound the foot of the bed at my feet is my son.”
"The elder Kātyāyana comes and goes to my house, accepting from me offerings of robes, medicine, and other necessities.
These two men have spoken angrily to me, saying:
'We toil to produce wealth and give it to others; you merely exhaust yourself in vain, and in a future life you shall receive the retribution of pus and blood.'"

"Because of this stinginess and greed, and because she took no pleasure in giving, she has fallen among the hungry ghosts. Due to the retribution for her evil verbal karma, the food she receives turns into pus and blood.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked, "Why does this woman eat her own flesh?"
The woman said:
"This girl is my daughter-in-law; she took the goods and either ate them herself or gave them to others.
When I questioned her, she spoke thus:"
"I shall not eat it myself nor give it to another; if I were to eat it myself or give it to another, I would be eating my own flesh.
For this reason, he now eats his own flesh.
"What did this second daughter do next to transform herself into a black ewe eating grass?
The noble lady said, "She is my servant;
I employed her to husk and grind grain, and she either ate it herself or gave it to others."
If questioned at that time, one should say:
"I do not eat [meat] myself, nor do I give it to others; were I to eat it myself or give it to others, I would become a sheep to eat grass in future lives."
"By reason of these causes and conditions, I am now a sheep eating grass.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked,
"What practices did you perform?"
The woman said:
"I have committed a slight offense; I shall not remain here for long. When I die in this place, I shall be reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings."
"Can you do a small favor for me?
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied,
"What kind of matter?"
The woman said:
"In the village of King Sārthavāha, I have a daughter who does not yet know how to practice virtue. Return there and speak thus to my daughter, so-and-so:
'I have seen your father, mother, elder brother, brother's wife, and servant; only your mother alone receives merit, while the others receive retribution.'"
"Your mother told you this because of my words: 'Do not commit evil deeds; in future lives you will suffer many painful retributions.

If you do not believe your mother's words, there is a treasure here containing great wealth. Take it and use it to perform meritorious acts by making offerings to the Sangha, and also make offerings to the Elder Kātyāyana; with what remains, you may support yourself."
Having spoken these words, he asked Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
"Do you wish to go? He replied:
"I wish to depart.
The woman said,
"Close your eyes."
He then closed his eyes exactly as he had been told. After a short while, he was placed not far from the village of the royal caravan leader.
Those merchants who had already arrived at the village asked him, "Why do we not see the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa?"
The merchants replied,
"He was lost at sea. At that time,
when the people of the village heard that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had perished, the entire town wept as if they had lost their own parents.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked them,
"Why is it like this?
The people replied:
“The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa has been lost at sea; because of his loss, they weep and console one another.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then thought to himself:
“The news of my death has caused such distress and turmoil in this village; if they were to see me now, they would surely be disturbed once more. Why should I return?”
"That noble lady has entrusted me with a message for her daughter; I shall go there for her sake.
Gradually, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa arrived at the girl's house, exchanged greetings with them, and said to the girl:
"Does so-and-so know?"
I see that your father, mother, elder brother, brother’s wife, and servant are all among the hungry ghosts.
Only your mother alone enjoys blessings; the others undergo suffering.
"Your mother said to you:
'Do not commit evil deeds, lest you suffer the retribution of suffering hereafter.
The girl said:
"Hey! Man, you fool, you madman! My parents gave these as offerings to cultivate merit; they must have been reborn in heaven after death. Why then are they here among the hungry ghosts?"
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then said to the girl, "Your mother said:

'There is a storehouse in such-and-such a place containing vast amounts of wealth; use it to perform meritorious deeds for me by making offerings to the Saṅgha and the Elder Kātyāyana, and live on what remains.'"

Having heard this, the girl went to the place where the treasure was kept; she opened it and obtained a great amount of wealth. Having gained faith through this, she followed her mother’s instructions and immediately made offerings to the assembly of monks.

This śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa planted roots of goodness by making offerings to the Buddhas in previous lives; possessing sharp faculties and being close to the vision of the Truths, through the power of these causal conditions, he was able to attain untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) in this present life.
Pursued by the power of his roots of goodness, he thought to himself:
"What is the use of returning home in such sorrow?
I shall go to where Mahākātyāyana is."
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at [the elder’s] feet and sat to one side.

The śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṣa was weary of his former life and terrified of the world; the Elder Kātyāyana, in accordance with his disposition, preached the Dharma for him. Thereupon, while still seated, he attained the pure and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and purified the Dharma, he transcended doubt and regret, no longer relying on others or following others, and established himself within the fruit of the Path, attaining fearlessness.
Rising from his seat, he bowed his head at the feet of the Elder Kātyāyana and said:
"Venerable Sir!
I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha; I become a lay follower."
"Please remember me: from this day forth for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life, my mind being pure in faith.
Venerable Sir!
I wish to go forth in the well-taught Dharma and receive full ordination to become a bhikṣu; I wish to practice the path within the well-taught Dharma."
Kātyāyana asked, "Śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
have your parents given you permission to leave the household life?
He replied:
“Venerable sir!
My parents have not yet given their permission. Kātyāyana said:
"Our rule is that if one's parents do not give permission, one may not go forth to receive full ordination.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said,
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I seek this matter for myself; if my parents grant permission, I shall come to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
Kātyāyana said, "You should know that now is the time."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa prostrated with his head at the feet of the Elder Kātyāyana and immediately returned home. There he saw his parents; he paid his respects and inquired after their welfare.

Because his parents had previously lost their sight due to grief and suffering, when they heard that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had returned safely from the great ocean, tears of sorrow and joy fell from their eyes, and their vision was restored.
After Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had stayed for five or six days, he said to his parents,
"Please allow me to go forth into the well-taught Dharma.
His parents replied:
“Śroṇa! I have only you;
it was with my original wholehearted aspiration that I sought to obtain you.
Because you did not heed my words and entered the great ocean, and because I have become blind from the grief of hearing news of your death.”
"Now that you have returned safely from the midst of the great ocean, I am filled with great joy and my eyes are opened once more; you have truly been born anew.
If you accept my words, you will be making an offering to us."
"Our lifespans will not last much longer; if we do not go forth into homelessness before our lives come to an end, we shall have no regrets at death.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, "So be it."
He made offerings for twelve full years until the end of his parents' lives, as the verse says:
"Those who are born must die; even the high shall fall.
All things come to an end; nothing is eternal."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa bathed and went to where the Elder Kātyāyana was; he prostrated with his head at the elder’s feet and sat to one side.
“Venerable Sir,” he said, “I have now attained faith in the True Dharma and wish to go forth in the Buddha’s teachings to practice the holy life.”
The Elder Kātyāyana then granted Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa the going-forth.
At that time, there were few bhikṣus in the kingdom of Āśmaka-Avantī, and it was difficult to find a group of ten; this śrāmaṇera had completed his summer retreat and finished the *pravāraṇā*.

The Elder Kātyāyana was visited by his resident disciples and those staying nearby, who had come from various directions to see their teacher and pay their respects. At that time, the assembly of monks numbered ten; it was then that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa received full ordination.
At that time, several bhikṣus wished to travel to the eastern countries; upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, they paid their respects to him.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa asked the bhikṣus, "Venerable ones, where are you going?"
The people said,
"We wish to go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and to pay him our respects in person.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said:
"I also wish to go.
The people said,
"As you please."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said, "Wait a moment;
I shall take leave of my preceptor.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then went to where the Elder Kātyāyana was, prostrated with his head at the elder's feet, sat to one side, and spoke as follows:

“Venerable Upādhyāya, my summer retreat has now concluded, and I wish to travel through the eastern lands to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and pay him homage in person; I pray that you will grant me leave to go.”
Kātyāyana said:
"If you wish to go, do as you please; you should represent me by prostrating with your head at the Buddha’s feet and inquire after him:
‘Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily activities? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?’"
And other bhikṣus questioned him in this way:
"Venerable Mahākātyāyana was my preceptor; in the land of Aśmaka-Avantī, the elder bhikṣus Māmata and Titila saved me."
Then that elder prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and inquired after him:
“Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your movements? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
After he and the other bhikṣus had likewise inquired according to the Dharma, they requested five matters of the Bhagavān.

First, in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avanti, there are few bhikṣus, and it is difficult to assemble the ten-member assembly required for full ordination; we pray that the Buddha will permit the conferral of full ordination in this country with fewer than ten bhikṣus.

Second, in the land of Aśmaka-Avanti, the ground is hard and abounds with broken stones and clods of earth; we pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus of this country to wear single-layered leather sandals.
Third, the people of the country of Āśmaka-Avantī delight in bathing and consider water to be purifying; they pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus of this country to bathe regularly.

Fourth, just as the lands of the eastern countries are covered with mats of hemp, mats of wool, and mats of flowered cloth, we pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus of the country of Aśmaka-Avanti to use mats of leather, sheepskin, deerskin, and goat-skin.
Fifth: Suppose there is a bhikṣu who sends another bhikṣu to give a robe to a third bhikṣu, but that person does not accept the robe and it is lost in the interim; what should we do?
"Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa!
If you go to the eastern lands and see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, approach him and pay him homage, and on my behalf inquire after his well-being.
Report these five matters in detail to the World-Honored One."

At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, having received and mastered the words of the Elder Kātyāyana from memory, rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the Elder Mahākātyāyana, and immediately went to his own quarters to set aside his bedding and requisites before taking up his robes and bowl to travel through various lands.
Gradually arriving at Śrāvastī, he saw the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with these words:
“Are you well? Are you at ease?”
Are your feet sound?
Do you dwell in peace and comfort?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not fatigued by the journey?
At that time, the Buddha asked Ervāvaṇa with these words:
"Are you patient?
Are you satisfied?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking not difficult, and are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣu replied:
"It is truly patient, peaceful, and comfortable; alms-seeking is not difficult, and one does not grow weary on the road.
It is the constant law of the Buddhas that when staying overnight in the same place as a visiting bhikṣu, they instruct their attendant to spread out beds and bedding within the visitor's room.
At that time, the Buddha instructed Ānanda to prepare beds and bedding within the rooms for the visiting bhikṣus.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"As the Buddha has commanded, I shall prepare beds and bedding for the visiting bhikṣus."
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, must surely wish to stay in the same room tonight as the visiting bhikṣus.
He then went to the Buddha’s room, prepared the beds and bedding for the visiting bhikṣus, and returned to report:
"Venerable Sir!"
"Having finished arranging the beds and bedding for the visiting bhikṣus, the Buddha himself knows the proper time.
The Buddha rose from his seat and went toward his own room; upon reaching his place, he spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana) and sat down cross-legged.

Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa went toward the Buddha’s chamber; having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, spread out his *niṣīdana* on the seat, and sat cross-legged. These two men spent much of the night in silent meditation.
When the middle watch of the night had passed and the latter watch arrived, the Buddha said to Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, “Monk, recite a verse.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa produced a subtle voice and completed the recitation of the *Saccakāra-sutta* from the *Pārāyana*. The Buddha praised him, saying:
“Excellent, bhikṣu! You have praised the Dharma well.
You are able to recite it in the Apabhraṃśa dialect; it is distinct, pure, and entirely easy to understand. Bhikṣu, you are well-trained and well-recited.”
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked:
"Why did you enter the Path so late?
Ayiravata replied:
"Venerable Sir!
For a long time I have known the peril of sensual desires; however, because of certain circumstances, I am unable to go forth.
He then spoke this verse:
"Having seen the faults of the world, one sees no delight in the outflows of phenomena;
the noble do not delight in evil, nor do the wicked delight in the good.
Having definitively seen the flavor of the Dharma, the flavor of the Dharma stills all afflictions."
"Removing heat and departing from all evils, one partakes of the flavor of the Dharma and the joy of the Dharma.
Thus Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa reflected:
"The time has come for me; I shall extensively question the World-Honored One on five matters."
Thereupon, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Elder Mahākātyāyana is my preceptor; it was he who, while I was dwelling in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avanti, delivered me at Mamateya and Titibha.”
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and inquired after his well-being, saying:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily activities? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
He also inquired after the other bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma.
He questioned the World-Honored One extensively on five matters.
The Buddha said to Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:
"Cease for a moment; you shall speak when it is my time to ask."
The Buddha, for this reason, assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, he addressed Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa:
"Ask whatever you wish to ask.
At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa said to the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
The Elder Kātyāyana is my preceptor; the elder monks Māmattrāta and Tittira from the land of Āśmaka-Avantī have delivered me.”
This elder prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and inquired after him:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily activities? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
The other bhikṣus also inquired after him in the same manner.
He presented these five matters in detail to the World-Honored One!
What are the five?

First, in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avanti, there are few bhikṣus; it is difficult to obtain a quorum of ten for full ordination. He prayed that the Buddha would permit the conferral of full ordination in this country with fewer than ten bhikṣus.

Second, in the land of Āśmaka-Avantī, the ground is hard, with many broken stones and many clods of earth; we pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus of this land to wear single-layered leather sandals.
Third, the people of the land of Āśmaka-Avantī delight in bathing and consider water to be purifying; we pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus of this land to bathe regularly.
"Fourth, O Virtuous One!

If the kingdoms of the eastern regions use such mats made of hemp, furs, or flowered garments as coverings, we pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus of those kingdoms to use mats made of leather—namely, sheepskin, deerskin, and the skin of wild rams—as coverings."
Fifth, there was a bhikṣu who sent another bhikṣu to give a robe to a third bhikṣu; the latter did not accept it, and the robe was lost in the interim. Regarding this matter, what should we do?

The Buddha praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having thus praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I permit the conferral of full ordination in border regions with a quorum of five who are masters of the Vinaya. Among these, the village of Śvetavatavya in the south is a border region; outside of Śvetavatavya lies the border country."
To the west there is a brahmin village; beyond that brahmin village lies a borderland.
To the north is Mount Uśīra; not far from the mountain is the Puṣkariṇī spring and the Sāla tree; beyond the Sāla tree lies a borderland.
To the east there is a brahmin village named Kālaṅga; outside of Kālaṅga lies a frontier country.
To the northeast there is the Bamboo River; outside of the Bamboo River lies a frontier country.
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus of the country of Aśmaka-Avantī to wear single-layered leather sandals.
If they become worn through, they may be repaired by patching both ends with leather placed in the center. They should not wear thick or heavy leather sandals;
they should not wear fur-lined leather sandals; they should not wear creaking leather sandals; and they should not wear sandals with wrapped heels.
All blue leather sandals; all yellow, all red, all white, and all black;
those with blue leather inlays, yellow leather inlays, red leather inlays, white leather inlays, and black leather inlays;
and those embroidered with blue leather, yellow leather, red leather, white leather, and black leather.
Embroidered shoes of *veṇu* grass, embroidered shoes of lion skin, embroidered shoes of tiger skin,
embroidered shoes of leopard skin, embroidered shoes of otter skin, embroidered shoes of cat skin; sandals of *tūla* cotton, sandals of woolen cloth, sandals of *karpāsa* cotton,
sandals sewn with woolen thread from the hair of a ram, sandals of ram-horn leather, and sandals with broad toes.
One should not wear leather sandals stitched with peacock sinew threads, nor sandals made from a mixture of peacock feathers and leather, nor any kind of leather sandal adorned with various colors,
patterns, or embroidery. If one wears such sandals,
one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
From this day forward, I permit those in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avanti to bathe regularly.

Just as in the eastern regions one covers [the floor] with mats of hemp, mats of wool, or flower-mats, I now permit those in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avanti to cover it likewise with mats made of skins—namely, sheep-skins, deer-skins, and goat-skins.
There was a bhikṣu who sent another bhikṣu to give a robe to someone else, but that other bhikṣu did not accept it; the robe was lost in the interim. The Buddha said:
"If the robe is obtained, that bhikṣu should keep it for ten days; if it exceeds ten days, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was residing in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept large skins: lion skins, tiger skins, leopard skins, otter skins, and marten skins. The Buddha said:
"One should not keep five kinds of skins; if one keeps them, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Furthermore, there are five types of hides that should not be kept:
elephant hide, horse hide, dog hide, jackal hide, and black deer hide.
To keep them constitutes an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Elder Cunda possessed a high and fine bed. The Buddha and Ānanda went to Cunda’s room.
Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, Cunda joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke as follows:
"Venerable sir, please come into the room and look.
When the Buddha saw that Channa had spread out a high and fine bed, he said to Ānanda upon seeing it:
"This foolish man!"
"He spreads out a high and fine bed, which rots within and leaks without.
After the Buddha had finished his reprimand through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one should not possess high and fine beds; if one possesses them, one commits a pāyattika offense."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a wicked upāsaka who had become a disciple of the Śākya son Upananda; they spoke with one another respectfully and cherished each other.
At dawn, the Śākya son Upananda dressed, took up his bowl, and went to that house; the wicked upāsaka provided him with a seat and invited Upananda to sit, and they exchanged greetings.
In that household there was a calf with variegated spots; having seen it, he immediately conceived a greedy desire, thinking, "This is excellent and can be used as a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).
Udāyin said to him, "Your calf has variegated spots; this can be used as a *niṣīdana*."
The upāsaka asked, “Do you need it? He replied:
“Give it. He immediately killed the calf, flayed its skin, and brought it to him; he then took the skin and departed. The mother cow bellowed and pursued him from behind.
At that time, several bhikṣus were walking up and down on an open space between the gates of the monasteries in Vaiśālī when they saw Baddhālaka Nanda approaching from afar.
The bhikṣus said to one another:
"This son of the Śākyas, Upananda, is a shameless man who has seen, heard, or suspected much.
He is a man of evil desires; that lowing cow follows behind him, and he will surely commit an evil deed—whether he intends to do so or has already done it."
Gradually approaching the place where the bhikṣus were, he asked them,
"Venerable sirs!
Why is this ox lowing behind you?"
Bhadananda recounted this in detail to the bhikṣus.
For various reasons, the bhikṣus rebuked Bhadananda:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu intentionally deprive a living being of its life?"
"You lack a heart of compassion.
After he had thus rebuked him with various such reasons, this matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the situation], asked Upananda:
"Is it truly so? He replied,
"It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“How can you be called a bhikṣu while intentionally depriving a living being of its life?”
"You lack a heart of compassion.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should neither accept nor sit or lie upon cowhide in the homes of laypeople."
“Monks, one may accept dried cowhide from a household, but one should neither sit nor lie upon it.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika) transported women on vehicles, engaging in various forms of impure conduct.
The Buddha said:
"A woman should not be carried on a vehicle; if one carries her, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The group of six bhikṣus carried women together, engaging in various forms of impurity. The Buddha said:
"One should not ride in a vehicle together with a woman; if one rides together with a woman, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The group of six bhikṣus rode in a vehicle with a woman in an enclosed space, engaging in various forms of impurity. The Buddha said:
'One should not ride in a vehicle with a woman in an enclosed space; if one so rides, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.'"

The Elder Piṅgiyānī suffered from an eye ailment; his kinsmen sent a messenger with two oxen yoked to a carriage to come and meet the Elder, so that he might ride in the carriage to this place for treatment of his eyes.
He replied,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted riding in a carriage drawn by two oxen.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to ride in a cart drawn by a bull, but another person must drive it; one must not drive it oneself.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus seized the tails of cows to cross a river, which was variously impure. The Buddha said:
"One should not seize the tail of a cow to cross a river; if one does so, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"If a lion, tiger, elephant, horse, or ox is male, there is no offense in grasping its tail to cross a river.
The group of six bhikṣus grasped the hands of young women to cross a river; as this was variously impure, the Buddha said:
"One should not grasp the hand of a young woman to cross a river. If one grasps the hand of a young woman to cross a river, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
There were several housewives who went to the Āciravatī River to bathe; having removed their clothes on the bank and entered the water to wash, the river suddenly swelled and swept them away.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were walking up and down on an open space by the riverbank, some women said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
See and rescue us!"
The bhikṣus said:
"Sisters! The Buddha has established this precept:..."
"One should not intentionally touch the body of a woman. The women said:
"Venerable Sir, you are compassionate and have pity for us. Among all the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, where else could we be caught when we are being swept away by the water?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"They should save him."
When the bhikṣus held them in this manner, lustful thoughts arose and they released them again.
The women said, "Venerable sirs, do not release us for a moment; let us reach the other shore."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Even if lustful thoughts arise, you should merely hold onto one part and not let go; once you have reached the shore, you must not touch her intentionally."
If one touches her again, one incurs an offense.
If she is a woman depicted in embroidery or a wooden woman, one should not touch her intentionally; to touch her constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The Buddha Bhagavān was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.

The bhikṣus of Āloka wore wooden sandals; from time to time they went to their *upādhyāyas* and *ācāryas* to receive, study, and inquire about the sūtras. At that time, within the vihāra, the dragging of their sandals produced a clattering sound.
There was a mahalla bhikṣu who stepped on and killed a long-bodied insect.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is there the sound of sandals dragging within the vihāra?"
Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!

These bhikṣus of Āravī wear wooden sandals; from time to time they go to their preceptors and teachers to receive, study, and inquire about the sūtras. For this reason, the sandals drag along and make a noise.”
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, he, though already aware of the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why is it called a bhikṣu who keeps wooden sandals?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, you must not wear wooden sandals, tāla-leaf sandals, bamboo sandals, bamboo-leaf sandals, muñja-grass sandals, or *pāvi* sandals; if you keep them, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
The Elder Bāṣpa had gone forth from a noble family; when he was formerly a layman, he wore *kambala* sandals, and according to the original rule, he continued to keep *kambala* sandals.
The lay devotees criticized, disparaged, and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves that they are virtuous and excellent, yet they wear *kambala* sandals like kings or high ministers."

There were certain bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they felt shame and remorse, and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"Why do you call yourself a bhikṣu while wearing leather sandals?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not wear *kambala* sandals; if you do, you shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Campā, there was a son of a householder named Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoṭi."

This man abandoned twenty billion pieces of gold and relinquished five hundred villages in the city of Campā; Āniruddha went forth into homelessness and practiced walking meditation on the open ground barefoot. Blood flowed from his feet, spreading across the entire path of his meditation, and as he walked from one end to the other, crows pecked at the blood. The Buddha and Ānanda arrived at that place and witnessed this scene.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked Ānanda:
"Who is it whose blood flows over the ground where they were practicing walking meditation?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!

This son of an elder from the country of Campā, named Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoṭi, has renounced twenty koṭis of gold and abandoned the five hundred villages of the city of Campā to go forth under Āniruddha.”
He walked back and forth on foot until blood flowed from his feet, covering the entire walking path; as he paced from this end to that, crows pecked at the blood.
The Buddha, regarding this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said,
"Śramaṇa! Are you able to wear single-layered leather sandals for walking?"
He replied, "I cannot.
The Buddha said:
"Why is it that they cannot? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
If I should happen to keep the precepts together with others, the bhikṣus will say:

"The son of a householder from the country of Campā, named Śramaṇa Viśākha, having abandoned twenty koṭis of gold and left behind five hundred villages of Campā, went forth under Āniruddha, yet he remains attached to a single layer of leather sandals."
“If the Buddha permits all bhikṣus to wear them, I shall wear them.
After the Buddha had praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“From now on, I permit you to wear single-layered leather sandals for walking meditation. If they become worn, they may be patched at both ends with the repair placed in the center. You should not wear thick or heavy leather sandals; you should not wear fur-lined leather sandals; you should not wear noisy leather sandals; you should not wear sandals with wrapped heels. Furthermore, you must not wear any leather sandals that are entirely blue, entirely yellow, entirely red, entirely white, or entirely black.”

One must not wear sandals made from leather of various colors—namely, blue leather, yellow leather, red leather, white leather, or black leather; nor those embroidered with blue, yellow, red, white, or black patterns; nor those embroidered with lion skins, tiger skins, leopard skins, otter skins, or cat skins; nor sandals made of *tūla* cotton, woolen cloth, or *karpāsa* cotton; nor those sewn with goat’s wool thread; nor those made of goat horn; nor those with wide fronts; nor those sewn with peacock sinews or sewn with peacock feathers. One must not wear any sandals of such variegated colors.
"If you wear it, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

While the Buddha was at the Eastern Garden in the Mākandikā Mother’s Hall in Śrāvastī, he rose from meditation in the late afternoon, descended from the hall, and walked in meditation upon the open ground.
At that time, some bhikṣus were walking up and down with the Buddha while wearing leather sandals. The Buddha looked back and saw the bhikṣus walking with him in leather sandals, so he said to them:

"There are teachers among the non-Buddhist renunciants whose disciples, out of respect and reverence for their teacher, do not wear leather sandals when following their teacher on his walking meditation; how much more so should this be for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? Yet you all wear leather sandals while walking with me."
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, leather sandals must not be worn in the presence of the Buddha.

They must not be worn before one’s upādhyāya, ācārya, or any senior elder; nor within a stūpa of the Buddha, a stūpa of those who have attained the Way, a warm bathhouse, a lecture hall, the entrance to the refectory, a meditation cave, places for defecating or urinating, places for washing after defecating or urinating, bathing areas, or any place frequented by a large assembly."
"If one persists in this, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

The Elder Piṅgiyāni suffered from eye pain; he entered a village barefoot and stepped on a stone, injuring his foot and aggravating his eye pain. He spoke of this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the situation, asked Pilindavatsa:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!

After the Buddha had praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions, and having finished praising the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From now on, I allow you to enter a village wearing single-layered leather sandals; however, you should not wear thick, heavy leather sandals, nor should you wear woolen leather sandals, nor even various multicolored leather sandals sewn with thread."
"If you do so, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, various bhikṣus washed their feet in the open air; they walked on their toes, walked on their heels, or walked by stepping on tree leaves, or hopped across stones, and then entered the rooms and sat upon the beds.
At times they used grass, or cloth, or worn-out rags to wipe their feet.
Consequently, the various grasses, cloths, and rags in the dwelling lay scattered and disheveled on the ground, and the bedding became soiled and foul-smelling.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed. Arriving at his own residence, he prepared a great variety of delicious foods, fragrant and pure in aroma, and having completed the preparations, he spread out seats and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
“The time has come!”
"The meal is prepared; the Buddha himself knows the time.
The bhikṣus went to the householder's residence, while the Buddha remained in his own room to await his portion of the food.

It is the constant practice of all Buddhas to thus go on tour and inspect the rooms of the bhikṣus, taking the door-bolt and visiting the large halls, the separate quarters, and all the rooms throughout.
Upon opening a room, he saw grass, clothing, and tattered rags strewn about on the floor, and the bedding was foul-smelling and filthy.

The Buddha entered the room and, with calm composure, lifted the coverlets and removed the bedsteads. He discarded the grass, clothing, and tattered rags from the floor, swept the interior of the room, and finished plastering the ground.

He returned to his inner quarters, put away his bedding and couch, closed the door, lowered the bolt, and proceeded toward his own room to his seat; there he spread out his *niṣīdana* and sat down cross-legged.

During this interval, having seen that the monks were seated, the householder personally brought water for washing and, with his own hands, served them various kinds of delicious food and drink, fragrant and pure in aroma.
When the Sangha had finished their self-examination (pravāraṇā) and were fully satiated, they took up their individual sitting benches and sat upon them in order to hear the Dharma.
After the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma, they departed in succession and returned to the monastery, where they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when the bhikṣus have returned from their meal, they inquire with joyful and gentle words:
"Have the bhikṣus eaten their fill of fine food?
At that time, when the bhikṣus had returned, the Buddha questioned them in this manner.
“Monks, have you all eaten your fill of fine food?
They replied,
“We have eaten our fill.”
The Buddha said:
"Today I took my key and went from room to room, through the great hall and the private chambers, inspecting all the quarters.
Upon opening the door of one room, I saw grass, robes, and tattered rags strewn about on the floor, and the bedding was filthy and foul-smelling."
This matter is not right.
Why do you all fail to cherish and protect the bedding and requisites of the Sangha?
Laypeople and brahmins exhaust their own blood and flesh to give in charity and cultivate merit; the bhikṣus should receive these offerings sparingly and protect them with care.
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow single-layered leather sandals for washing the feet; if they become worn, they may be repaired by patching both ends and placing the repairs in the center."
One should not wear heavy leather sandals, nor indeed various multicolored leather sandals sewn with thread;
if one wears them, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A certain bhikṣu lost one of his double-layered leather sandals for washing the feet. The bhikṣu went to a householder’s place and requested, saying:
“I have lost one of my double-layered leather sandals for washing the feet; please give it to me.”
The householder instructed the cobbler:
"Make a single-layered leather sandal for this bhikṣu; I will give you the price.
However, because a thick, heavy leather sandal was worth two or three coins, the cobbler was unwilling to make a single-layered one for him.
The bhikṣu went to the tanner’s place and requested [leather], but the tanner did not give it to him nor make it for him.
Not obtaining it, the bhikṣu returned and asked a householder, saying:
“Householder!...”
"Yet this cobbler has ultimately not made a single pair of leather sandals for me.
The householder said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I have already given you strict instructions; since you are unwilling to comply with me, what shall I do?
Can you wear heavy, thick leather sandals?
The bhikṣu reflected thus:
"I shall destroy these thick-soled leather sandals and make single-layered leather sandals to wear.
With this thought, that bhikṣu took his awl and thread and went to the gate of the Jetavana, intending to destroy the thick-soled leather sandals and make single-layered leather sandals.
After the Buddha had finished his meal, he wandered about practicing walking meditation and went to that place, where he saw the bhikṣu sitting beneath the gate.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu: "What are you doing?"
He replied, "World-Honored One!
I have lost a single heavy leather sandal for washing my feet; I am asking a householder for it."
The lay devotee instructed a leather-worker, saying:
"Make a single-layered leather sandal for this bhikṣu; I will give you the payment.
Because the leather-worker considered a thick, heavy sandal worth two or three coins, he was unwilling to make a single-layered sandal for him.
I went to the tanner’s place and requested it again, but the tanner still would not give it to me.
Having no other choice, I went back to the householder and asked him, saying:
"Householder!..."
"The cobbler ultimately did not give me even a single pair of leather sandals.
The householder said, "I have already given my instructions; since he is unwilling to give them to you, what can I do?"
He then said to me:
"Are you able to wear heavy, thick leather sandals?
I reflected thus:
"You should tear it apart and make a single-layered leather sandal for washing the feet.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"Do not tear apart thick, heavy leather sandals."
Why is this? Because it is not firm.
From now on, I permit the practice of destroying attachment to purity.

"If someone offers you thick, heavy leather sandals, you may accept them provided that you cause the donor to wear them themselves and walk in them for at least two or three steps; in this way, they may be kept.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
Because the Buddha had permitted the wearing of leather sandals that were worn-out, dyed, or pure, the group of six bhikṣus sought out and kept various kinds of multicolored leather sandals.
On one occasion, the group of six bhikṣus went to the Śākyas and begged them for leather sandals.
If the owner did not give them up, one bhikṣu would hold them aloft while another would slip off his own sandals to take them.
Because of this matter, the Śākyaputrīyas never dared to go out, fearing that the group of six bhikṣus might slip off their leather sandals and take them.
The laypeople criticized, disparaged, and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves that they are virtuous and of good character, yet they wear various multicolored, ornate leather sandals like kings or high ministers."

There was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; upon hearing this matter, he felt shame and remorse in his heart and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha.
Having assembled the community of monks, the Buddha, knowing the situation, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?
They replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why do you, O bhikṣus, wear various multicolored and ornamented leather sandals?
Having rebuked them with these and other such reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is a single-layered leather sandal, or if there is a broken, dyed, clean, thick, and heavy leather sandal, its possession is permitted; however, one should not wear any leather sandals that are multicolored or ornamented."
"If you wear it, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the end of the summer retreat after the *pravāraṇā*, he traveled through various countries together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There was a bhikṣu who walked with a limp while holding a leather sandal in his hand.
The Buddha saw this bhikṣu and, though he already knew the reason, asked him intentionally: "Bhikṣu!..."
"Why do you walk with a limp while holding leather sandals in your hand?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"The nose of my leather sandals is hard, and the space between my toes is chafed; because of the pain, I walk with a limp.
The Buddha said, "You should make them using soft materials."
The fifth section on Leather within the Seven Dharmas is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 25.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 26. The sixth part of the Fourth Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
6. The Rules on Medicine, the Sixth of the Seven Rules.

When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, during the autumn season, various bhikṣus suffered from cold-fevers, heat-fevers, chronic abdominal ailments, and catarrh; they could not eat their fill, becoming emaciated and lacking in complexion and strength.
The Buddha saw that the bhikṣus were emaciated and lacked physical vigor and color; knowing the reason, he asked Ānanda:
"Why are the bhikṣus so emaciated and lacking in physical vigor and color?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

For these bhikṣus, the cold and heat have flared up in autumn; they suffer from chronic abdominal ailments and indigestion, and cannot eat their fill. For this reason, they are emaciated and lack complexion and strength.”
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"What medicine should be given for him to take so that he may recover his complexion and strength?
If coarse rice, parched grain, or roasted flour cannot benefit his body, I shall allow him to take the four kinds of medicinal electuaries."
Ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to consume the four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption.”
"Ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
At that time, although the bhikṣus took their meals before noon and did not eat after midday, they remained emaciated and lacked physical vigor and complexion.
Having seen this, the Buddha again asked Ānanda,
"For what reason are the bhikṣus so emaciated?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!

Although the World-Honored One has permitted sick bhikṣus to consume the four kinds of medicinal substances for internal use, the bhikṣus do not take them before midday and do not take them after midday; therefore, they remain emaciated.”

For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I allow you to freely consume the four kinds of medicinal substances for internal digestion before noon, at noon, and after noon."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyāśana suffered from eye pain, and a physician said to him:
"Apply a paste of *lāsana* to your eyes."
They replied,
“The Buddha has not yet permitted us to apply *rocanā* ointment to our eyes.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; I shall apply *rocanā* ointment to your eyes.
Thus, the Elder took *rocanā* ointment—half a bowl’s worth of large and small *kañcaka* seeds—and, having placed them in a netted bag, suspended it from a peg made of ivory.
When taking the medicine, it flowed out and soiled the walls and bedding, making the interior of the room foul-smelling and filthy. The Buddha said:
"It should be kept in a casket.
Although it was kept in one, it was not covered, and dust fell into it; when used, this increased the eye pain. The Buddha said:
"One should make a lid for it.
When it was pulled off by simply moving it straight, the Buddha said,
"The opening and the lid should be joined together."
At that time, the bhikṣus used the feathers of birds, the feathers of chickens, or peacock tails to apply eye medicine, which caused their eye pain to increase further. The Buddha said:
"Use a spoon."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"What kind of object should be used to make a spoon?
The Buddha said:
"Whether it be iron, copper, shell, ivory, horn, wood, or clay.

While the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the ground there was salty and damp; the bhikṣus suffered from scabies, and the pus and blood flowed out, staining their *antarvāsas* as if they had been soaked in water.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha intentionally questioned the bhikṣus:
"Why is your antaravāsaka so stained with water as if it had been soaked?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
We have scabies, and the flowing pus and blood soil our *antarvāsas*.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus suffering from scabies to apply bitter medicinal ointments.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"What constitutes a bitter medicinal ointment?"
The Buddha said:
“The *kurañja* tree, the *kubala* tree, the *kurundi* tree, the *sira* tree, the *pāgara* tree, and the *pāṇi-mucilinda* tree.”
The bhikṣus did not know how to pound and grind [the medicine], so the Buddha said,
"I allow a stone mill.
When the medicine ground with the stone mill fell to the ground, the Buddha said:
[The monks] heard the sound of mortars and pestles being used for pounding.
The bhikṣus damaged their hands [with the pestles], so the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make wooden pestles."
When they made a wooden pestle, they did not know how to make it; their hands slipped from the grip at the top and bottom. The Buddha said:
"Make the middle part slender.
When the medicine being pounded was coarse, the Buddha said: [Make the pestle wider at the base.]
"One should sift it to make it fine, apply oil to the wound, and sprinkle the medicine upon it.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
the Elder Śreṇika suffered from insanity and followed the instructions of others:
"Eating raw meat and drinking blood will cure my madness," said Seyya to the bhikṣus.
"I was mad when I accepted his words to eat raw meat and drink blood; what should I do now?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, questioned Śiveyyaka:
"Is it true that you, being deranged, accepted the words of others, ate raw meat, drank blood, and said to the bhikṣus:..."
"What shall I do now?
"Did you truly commit this deed?
He replied:
“It is real, Blessed One!

Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions, and having finished praising the precepts and the observance of the precepts, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if such an illness occurs, I permit you to eat raw meat and drink blood; however, you should do so in a secluded place and not let others see you.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, he observed the summer rains retreat together with the great assembly.
At that time, the Elder Pilindavatsa was observing the summer retreat in Rājagṛha.

This elder was widely learned and well-informed; he obtained much ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar, which he placed in large and small bowls and various vessels. He tied them with cords and hung them from ivory pegs. When he took them out, they leaked, staining the walls and bedding and making the dwelling place foul-smelling and filthy.

There were certain bhikṣus who, together with their co-practitioners and resident disciples, took ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar; they set aside the leftovers, handled them improperly, and consumed them after they had been stored overnight, having placed them all together in a single vessel.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas to hold two great assemblies during the final months of spring and the final month of summer.
In the final month of spring, bhikṣus from various regions come to the Buddha’s dwelling to hear the Buddha preach the Dharma and to rejoice in the summer retreat; this is the first great assembly.

At the end of the summer month, having completed the *varṣā* retreat and finished making robes after the three months had passed, he took his robe and bowl and traveled by stages until he arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, saying:
"I have not seen the Buddha for a long time; I have not seen the Sugata for a long time."
This was the second great assembly.

Having completed their summer retreat in Rājagṛha, and having finished making robes after the three months had passed, the bhikṣus set out on their journey together with their robes and bowls. They gradually traveled until they arrived at the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they ask him:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not weary from the road?
Now, the Buddha is also like this.
The Buddha asked the visiting bhikṣu:
"Are you patient?
Are you content?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Enduring with contentment, dwelling in peace and happiness, alms-seeking is not difficult, and the journey on the road is not weary.
He reported these matters to the Buddha in detail.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the Sangha; having assembled the Sangha, the Buddha censured the bhikṣus through various causes and conditions:
“Out of compassion for the sick bhikṣus, I permit the consumption of four kinds of medicinal substances taken by mouth:
ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar. However, one must not take them from leftover or impure sources, nor receive them from an unclean person, nor store them overnight.”
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, it is permitted for a sick bhikṣu to consume four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption; once accepted, he may take them at will for seven days. If he exceeds seven days, he commits an offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Cūḍapanthaka saw stone honey being prepared by mixing flour, fine bran, burnt earth, or soot and boiling it together; having seen this, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable elders!..."
"This stone honey—whether mixed with flour, fine bran, scorched earth, or soot—and having been boiled together, should not be consumed after midday.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the matter, questioned Cīrāyus:
"Is it true that you saw the making of stone honey, or flour, or fine bran, or parched earth, or soot mixed and boiled together, and told the bhikṣus:
'One should not eat this after midday'?"
"Is this not so? He replied,
"It is indeed so."
"World-Honored One!

The Buddha praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having finished praising the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow you to prepare stone honey, or flour, or fine bran, or parched earth, or soot, by mixing them together and boiling them."
"If it is before noon, one should eat; once noon has passed, one must not eat.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Śāriputra suffered from a wind-cold ailment, and his physician said:
"You should drink *suttirā* gruel.
Śāriputra said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to drink *suttirā* gruel."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow you to drink *sūtila* juice.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what substance is *sūtraka* gruel made?
The Buddha said, "Take barley, remove the coarse husks, do not break the grains, and cook them slightly; place them in a vessel and soak them in hot water until they become sour."
"One should take daytime medicine during the day and nighttime medicine at night; one should not take it outside of its designated time.
The Buddha was then staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra suffered from a disease involving hot blood, and his physician said:
"You should drink śīru-gruel.
Śāriputra said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to drink śīru-gruel."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to drink śīru-juice.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"What substance is used to make śīdhu?
The Buddha said:
"Barley, whether ground or pounded, is mixed with oil in equal parts and combined with water to make it sour; it may be consumed at the proper time, but not at an improper time."
The Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, observing the summer retreat together with a great assembly.

Among them was a female lay follower named Mahāsenā, who was very wealthy and possessed abundant money, grain, fields, houses, and treasures; she had accomplished all manner of merit and, having faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, had realized the Truth and attained the Path. She invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for the four months of the summer retreat to provide the sick with food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and whatever else they required at their own discretion.
There was a bhikṣu who, being ill, had taken a purgative and required meat.
He said to his attendants: "Go to the upāsikā Mahāsena and say these words:
'A bhikṣu is ill; he has taken a purgative and requires meat.'"
The attendant for the sick person then went to the laywoman Mahāsubhaddā and said to her:
"There is a bhikṣu who is ill; he has taken a purgative and requires meat."
The upāsikā then took the goods and gave them to the maidservant, instructing her to buy meat for the attendant of the sick man.
The maidservant went throughout the city of Vārāṇasī seeking meat but was unable to find any, because King Brahmadatta had prohibited the taking of life.
She returned and said to her master, "The King has prohibited killing; though I searched everywhere, I could not find it.
The upāsikā reflected:
"Why do you suffer so much?

I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for the four months of the summer retreat and provided all their necessary provisions. However, a certain bhikṣu who was ill required meat as a purgative medicine, which I have been unable to obtain."
"If I do not obtain meat, my illness will surely increase. Having reflected thus,
she took a sharp knife, entered her room, cut flesh from her own thigh, and gave it to the maidservant, saying,
"Cook this well and give it to the bhikṣu."
When the maidservant had finished cooking it, she gave it to the attendant; the attendant took it away, washed the sick bhikṣu’s hands with water, and presented the meat to the sick bhikṣu.
A sick bhikṣu did not know what kind of meat it was, yet he ate it, and from this his illness was cured.
The upāsikā Mahāsena suffered so severely from the pain of her sores that she was unable to go out, enter, sit, or rise.
Her husband had gone out on some minor business; when he returned and did not see his wife, he asked, "Where has the upāsikā Mahāsena gone?"
The family members said, "He is suffering from illness and pain; he is lying in a single room and is unable to sit up or rise.
Her husband went to his side and asked:
"What suffering do you have?
Is it a disease of wind, heat, or cold?
The upāsikā then related the preceding events in detail.
Upon hearing this, her husband became greatly incensed:
"How can you be so intolerant and faithless? For what reason is this?

The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, lack sense of timing and fail to exercise discretion. If the giver does not know moderation, the receiver ought to know it; yet they have caused my wife such agony that she cannot even sit or rise."
Bearing resentment, he went to the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma. Seeing the upāsaka approaching from afar, the Buddha, through the power of his great compassion, caused the man’s anger to gradually subside and a pure mind to arise; he then prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having thus instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
[The man] then rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Please accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal, as well as that of the community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted through his silence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him, and departed. Throughout the entire night, he prepared many kinds of exquisite foods and drinks.
When the preparations were complete, he spread out seats in the early morning and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time.
The Buddha donned his robe, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the great assembly, went to the house and sat among the multitude.
When the Upāsaka saw that the great assembly was seated, he personally served water for washing.
