*Yi ning ku ti* (Oṃ duḥkha-satya) *Mi ning xi ti* (Mārga-satya) *Duō tā tuó pì jìn ti* (Tad-tathā-prahāṇa-satya) *Tuó luó bì zhī dào ti* (Dharmānvaya-mārga-satya) *Fó shé tuó zhī yě sā pó xiū* (Buddha-jñāna sarva-hetu) *yī qiè xiáng shē mó zhē miè qiú* (sarva-kṣaṇa-śamatha-nirodha-prārthana) *sā pó duō luó yī qiè lí* (sarva-dvāra sarva-virati) *bī lóu lì duō tā yù yuǎn lí* (vīrya-tathā-vivikta-sarva-hetu) *sā pó xiū yī qiè* (sarva-hetu sarva-) *bēi luó dì bù zuò bō bá è yě* (virati akaraṇa pāpa-pāpaka) *tóu qī xiǎng dù kū biān jìn yě* (tuccha-saṃjñā dveṣa-duḥkha-anta-kṣaya) *niè lóu zhē tí rú shì shuō yě* (nirukti-satya evam uktam).
Of these two heavenly kings, one understood and one did not.
The Buddha again spoke in Māgadhī:
*moṣadūṣaṇa śavā sarvadaravi ti iśu ādudhu kṣepa adhipadi*.
The Four Heavenly Kings all understood.
Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
On the bank of the Mandākinī Pond, the Buddha took up his robe and bowl and traveled toward the country of Āmrapālī, where a matted-hair ascetic had formerly resided.
The people of this country deeply revered and placed their faith in the Buddha, and they thought to themselves:
"With what object should we make an offering to the Buddha?
Then they further thought:
"Just as the eight kinds of water-purified juices were received by the sages of old, these should be offered to the Buddha.
He then prepared this great quantity of juice and brought it to present to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Kṣemaka:
"Distribute it among the Saṃgha.
He then gave it to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to drink the eight kinds of gruel.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to drink eight kinds of syrups.
What are the eight?..."
1. Tāla juice, 2. Moca juice, 3. Kola juice, 4. Śelu juice, 5. Śyāmāka juice, 6. Pārūṣaka juice, 7. Āmalaka juice, 8. Grape juice.
"Having purified it with water, you should drink.
The Buddha, having finished his stay in the country of Āmraṇa, took up his robes and bowl and traveled toward the country of Atavaka.
In this country there were father and son bhikṣus who had formerly been barbers.

Their father, Mahāla, heard that the Buddha was traveling from the country of Āmra to the country of Aṭhaka; he thought, "In this place there is no donor to provide for the Saṃgha, nor is there any making of offerings. Who then will provide for the Buddha?"
He then said to his son:
"I have heard that the Buddha is traveling from the kingdom of Āmra and intends to come here; however, there is no donor here to provide for the Saṃgha, nor is there any means of making offerings."
"You may take this bowl and enter the city to seek sesame, non-glutinous rice, small beans, and mung beans to offer to the World-Honored One.
His son was skillful at such tasks; he immediately took the bowl and entered the city, obtaining a great quantity of sesame, non-glutinous rice, small beans, and mung beans.
When the World-Honored One had arrived, the father and son selected a room, prepared excellent seats, and immediately prepared various kinds of gruel:
sesame oil gruel, milk gruel, two kinds of bean gruel, and clear gruel. Having prepared them, they offered them to the Buddha and the Sangha.
The various gruels were so abundant that the leftovers were discarded upon the floor of a single room.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and was walking in meditation, the mahallaka followed the Buddha at a distance; arriving at that spot, he saw the floor strewn with the remains of the gruel.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Mahāla:
"Where did you obtain this much porridge? Did a donor give it to you?
He replied:
"No," [the monk] replied. The Buddha said,
"Is this the property of the Sangha?"
He replied, "No. The Buddha said:
“Where did you get it?
The Mahallaka reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha rebuked the Mahallaka with various reasons and arguments:
"Why is it that one who is called a bhikṣu teaches his son to perform impure acts?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the fivefold assembly shall not teach one another to perform impure acts; if anyone so teaches, they commit a duṣkṛta offense."
From this day forward, craftsmen shall not possess various tools for their work; if they do possess them, they commit an offense.
However, it is not an offense for a former tailor to possess a needle case, for a former scribe to possess a pen case, or for a former copper-smith to possess a drill.
The Buddha, taking his robes and bowl from the country of Āṭhaka, traveled toward the country of Pāvā.
The local nobility of that country had previously made an agreement:
"When the Buddha enters our country, everyone must welcome him for a distance of one yojana."
"If you do not go out to welcome him, you shall be fined five hundred gold coins.
Having heard that the Buddha was coming to meet him, there was among them a member of a prominent clan named Lu Zhi, who was a preeminent athlete and an old acquaintance of Ānanda.
That person had no faith in the Buddha; when Ānanda saw him approaching from afar, he said to him:
"Lu-zhi! It is most excellent that you have come to welcome the Buddha."
Lu Zhi said, “It is not out of faith in the Buddha that I come to welcome you; it is because I am following the customs of my own kin.
Ānanda said:
"What dharma is there?
He replied, "My kinsmen previously established a formal rule: if the Buddha comes, we must all go out to welcome him for one yojana."
"If you do not go out to welcome me, you shall be fined five hundred gold coins. Ānanda!
It is not that I am begrudging these five hundred gold coins; rather, I fear that the kinship will not remain harmonious, and for this reason I have come."
Ānanda took him by the hand and led him to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“This Lu Zhi was an old acquaintance of mine; we were particularly close and friendly, yet he did not believe in the Buddha.”
"I pray that the Buddha will preach the Dharma so that he may attain understanding and liberation.

At that time, the World-Honored One, moved by his compassionate heart, covered him with grace; he immediately attained faith and realization. Thereupon, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, they paid homage to the Buddha and departed, returning to their original seats.
Not long after they had left, the Buddha rose from his seat and proceeded toward his own quarters; Lu-zhi followed the Buddha like a calf follows its mother.

The Buddha entered his room and sat down. Lu Zhi prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Lu Zhi immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
He thought to himself,
"What object should I offer to the Buddha?
He then presented various cakes to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall divide it with the Saṃgha.
He then gave it to the bhikṣus,
but the bhikṣus would not accept it and said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to eat cakes.
He reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I authorize you to eat cakes.
What are these cakes?

Whether they be made of flour, or wheat cakes, or barley cakes, or bean cakes, or carved cakes, or layered-flower cakes—whatever such various kinds of pure cakes there may be, I authorize all of them to be eaten.”
After the Buddha had completed his stay as he traveled through the country of Pāvā, he took up his robes and bowl and journeyed on until he reached Śrāvastī.
While the bhikṣus were begging for alms, they obtained sweet delicacies, milk, curd, ghee, fish, meat, and dried meat; yet the bhikṣus did not accept them, reflecting:
"If we beg for such fine food and drink, we may fall into an offense."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"If you do not beg for it yourself, you should accept what is offered by a donor."
From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to consume four kinds of medicine.
What are these four kinds of medicine?
First, medicine for the proper time; second, medicine for a portion of the day; third, seven-day medicine; and fourth, lifetime medicine.
Regarding "timely medicine," there are five kinds of *khādaniya* (hard foods), five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and five kinds of food-like substances.
What are the five kinds of *khādaniya*?
First, root food; second, stem food; third, leaf food; fourth, ground food; and fifth, fruit food.
What are edible roots?
Taro roots, yam roots, lotus root, radish roots, and turnip roots—various such roots are edible.
What are stalk foods?
Radish stalks, *kharjūra* stalks, basil stalks, and *kolatthi* stalks—various such things as these are stalk *khādaniya*.
What are leaf foods?
Radish leaves, *kharjūra* leaves, coriander leaves, *kālaṃja* leaves, and various other such edible leaves—these leaves constitute *khādaniya*.
What are ground foods?
Rice, barley, wheat, and various others such as these are ground *khaḍaniya* foods.
What are fruit foods?
The *āmra* fruit, the *jambu* fruit, the *pārūṣaka* fruit, the *tinduka* fruit, the *nālikera* fruit, and various others such as these—these fruits constitute *khādaniya*.
What are the five kinds of *pūjānīya* food?
First, rice; second, flour; third, parched grain; fourth, fish; fifth, meat.
These are the five kinds of *pūjānīya* food.
What are the five kinds of food-like substances?
Gruel, millet, coarse wheat, tares, and *kāśa* grass—these various types are called food-like substances.
Unstrained juice is called "timely medicine" (*kālabhaiṣajya*).
As for "medicine for a specific time" (*kālikabhaiṣajya*), if the juice has been properly strained, it is called "medicine for a specific time.
As for "seven-day medicine" (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar are called "seven-day medicine."
Medicines for life-long use are the five kinds of root medicines.

What are the five? First, *śalī*; second, ginger; third, *aśvagandhā* (aconite); fourth, *pāṭhāviṣa*; and fifth, the root of sweet flag. These medicines may be kept in the same room for the remainder of one’s life without fault.
There are five kinds of medicinal fruits:
harītakī, vibhītaka, āmalaka, marica, and pippalī; these may be kept in the same room for as long as one lives.
There are five kinds of salt:
black salt, purple salt, red salt, rock salt, and white salt; these may be kept together with one's bedding and dwelling for as long as life lasts.
There are five kinds of resinous medicinal substances:
Hiṅgu, sājjarasamḍhī, yati, yavāpūṭī, and yavānī—these may be kept in one's room for as long as life lasts.
Five kinds of decoctions:
root-decoction, stem-decoction, leaf-decoction, flower-decoction, and fruit-decoction—these may be kept in one's room for as long as life lasts.
These are the four kinds of medicine:

medicine for the proper time (*kālabhaiṣajya*), medicine for a limited portion of the day (*kālātikrāntabhaiṣajya*), seven-day medicine (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), and lifetime medicine (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*). If one receives these—medicine for the proper time, medicine for a limited portion of the day, seven-day medicine, or lifetime medicine—and combines them into a single place, this medicine should be consumed during the proper time and not outside of it, because of the power of the medicine for the proper time.

If one receives *kālika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāha-bhaiṣajya*, and *yāvajjīva-bhaiṣajya* on the same day, and these medicines are mixed together in one place, they should be taken at their respective times; they should not be taken after their time has passed, because of the power of the *kālika-bhaiṣajya*.

If one receives seven-day medicine and lifetime medicine on the same day, these medicines may be mixed together; they should be consumed for seven days, after which they must not be consumed, because of the potency of the seven-day medicine.
Medicines for life-long use may be taken at will.

However, if on the same day one has received *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the day) that is impure, and subsequently receives *pākṣika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for a fortnight), *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for seven days), or *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for life-long use), and these are mixed together in one place, they should not be consumed.

If on that very day one receives impure *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the specific time) and then receives *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for seven days) or *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for life), and mixes them together in one place, they should not be consumed.
If on that very day one receives impure *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* and then receives *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*, and mixes them together in one place, they should not be consumed.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Regarding these three kinds of medicines—
the timely medicine, the seven-day medicine, and the lifetime medicine— "
"May these three kinds of medicine be kept overnight and then received by mouth?
The Buddha said, "They may not."
“May these three kinds of medicine be received orally when taken improperly?
The Buddha said, “They may not.”
“May these three kinds of medicine be taken by hand and received by mouth, even when one is not ill?
The Buddha said, “They may not.”
“If these three kinds of medicine are received with the hand and received by word of mouth, may one who is ill take them?
The Buddha said,
“One may.”
The Sixth Section on Medicines within the Seven Dharmas is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 26.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 27. The Seventh Part of the Fourth Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
7. The Rules on Robes (Cīvara-vastu), Part One of Seven. The seventh among the seven rules concerning robes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Five bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
"What kind of robes should one wear?
The Buddha said,
"One should wear paṃsukūla robes."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. His body was cold and damp, and he required a purgative medicine. The Buddha told Ānanda, “My body is cold and damp;
you should take note of this matter yourself.”

Ānanda, having received these instructions, went to the physician Jīvaka and said to him, “The Buddha’s body is cold and damp and requires the administration of purgatives; you yourself know how to handle this matter.”
Jīvaka said, "Elder,
please return; I shall follow after you."
Jīva reflected: "The Buddha’s virtue is most venerable;

it is not appropriate to offer him medicinal wood or bitter medicines as one would for others. I shall instead take blue lotuses and fumigate them with inferior medicinal herbs to present to the Buddha."
He then took blue lotuses and, having perfumed them with medicinal herbs, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
“These *utpala* flowers have been perfumed with medicinal herbs and can be used to treat the body; I pray that the Buddha will accept them.”
"If one inhales this medicine once, there will be ten bouts; if twice, twenty bouts; if thrice, thirty bouts.
After the Buddha accepted it, he remained silent.
Jīvaka, wishing to return, gave Ānanda detailed instructions on the regimen for attending to the illness before departing.
The Buddha smelled the medicine once and took ten breaths; he smelled it a second time and took twenty breaths; he smelled it a third time and took twenty-nine breaths.
Jīvaka, clearly aware of the timing, returned and approached the Buddha to pay his respects, asking:
"World-Honored One!"
"I do not know if you have taken [the medicine] twenty-nine times?
The Buddha said,
"Just now I smelled your medicine twenty-nine times."
Jīva, knowing that the Buddha’s physical ailment was not yet fully resolved, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“He must drink a small amount of warm water; after drinking it, he should undergo one more enema, and thus continue accordingly until thirty enemas have been completed.”

Jīva returned home and prepared medicines according to the illness, along with soft rice, gruel, soup, and *tāgara* medicine; he presented these necessities, and [the patient’s] movements became light and easy, and the suffering of the ailment was no more.
The Buddha regained his sight through the power of Jīvaka, and his complexion returned to its original state.
Jīvaka took a *śāṇa* cloth worth hundreds of thousands and wished to offer it to the Buddha; he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said to him:
“I have treated the king and his ministers, and they have all granted me their wishes.”
"Today I have treated the Buddha; I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me one wish.
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already transcended all wishes."
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
“May I be granted this wish?
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"What kind of vow do you seek?
Jīvaka replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"This is a fine mṛgadāra cloth worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. May the Buddha accept it out of compassion.
The Buddha accepted it by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted it by his silence, he immediately offered the fine mṛgadāra cloth worth one hundred thousand to the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"Today Jīvaka has given me a deep-mauñja robe worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. From this day forth, I allow that if there is one who gives such a robe to a bhikṣu, he may accept and wear it as he pleases."
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu wishes to wear a *pāṃśukūla* robe, he is permitted to wear it;
if he wishes to wear a robe offered by a layperson (*gṛhapati*), he is likewise permitted to wear it.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, riding in an elephant carriage, went out from the city of Rājagṛha at dawn desiring to see the Buddha.

The king had faith in and revered the Buddha; then, as he traveled along the road, a certain non-Buddhist brahmin approached from the opposite direction. Seeing him from afar, the king took him for a śramaṇa and commanded his driver to stop the elephant so that he might dismount and pay him homage.
The minister asked the king,
"What do you wish to do?
The king replied:
"I wish to pay homage to the incoming bhikṣu.
The minister said,
"Great King!"
"He is not a disciple of the Buddha, but merely a non-Buddhist brahmin.
The king was ashamed and asked his charioteer,
"If we go now to see the Buddha, how far from here is it by carriage?"
"Where may I alight?
The charioteer answered him fully.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the robes of the Saṃgha may be made distinct from the robes of the non-Buddhists, so that they may be clearly distinguished.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"For what reason do you wish for the robes to be different?

The king reported this matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma to the king, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him; the king then paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, Ānanda was attending upon the Buddha from behind, holding a fan to fan him.
The Buddha looked back and said to Ānanda, "I wish to travel through the lands of the Southern Mountains.
Having received this instruction, Ānanda followed him immediately.

Having arrived in the kingdom of the Southern Mountains, it was time for the alms-round; after finishing his meal, he went beneath a tree, spread out his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and sat down cross-legged. At that time, near the mountain, there were excellent rice fields with their ridges and furrows perfectly aligned.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Do you see those rice fields with their ridges and furrows so perfectly aligned?"
He replied, “I see it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Can this deep-colored *moraṇḍa* cloth be used as a robe for this field?
Ānanda replied, "It can."
He then gave the robe to Ānanda.

Having received it, Ānanda stepped back slightly and immediately cut and pinned the seams along the spine of the garment; he folded the panels on both sides and spread them out, then returned the robe to the Buddha.
The Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
This robe, cut and pieced in this manner, is made in accordance with the Dharma."

The Buddha, taking his robe and bowl from the kingdom of Dakṣiṇāgiri, proceeded toward Rājagṛha. Upon arrival, he assembled the Saṃgha for this reason; having assembled the Saṃgha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the wearing of robes made of cut-and-sewn cloth. One who does not wear cut-and-sewn cloth must not enter a village."
"If one enters [the village], one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to wear robes offered by householders. When faithful householders and brahmins made offerings to the Saṃgha, they gave many robes—*kambala*, *kauśeya*, and multicolored *karpāsa*. Consequently, the bhikṣus came to possess many robes.
The Buddha, knowing that the bhikṣus were keeping many robes and that these many robes hindered their practice of the Path, wished to establish a limit on them. He said to Ānanda:
"I wish to travel toward the kingdom of Vaiśālī."
Ānanda received the command and followed him immediately.
Upon arriving at the assembly, it happened to be the winter solstice; for eight nights, a cold wind had been piercing through the bamboo.
At that time, the Buddha was wearing a single *kaṭhina* robe and was walking in meditation on the open ground during the first watch of the night.
When the first watch of the night had passed and the middle watch had arrived, the Buddha’s body felt cold, so he said to Ānanda,
“Bring me the second saṃghāṭī robe.
Ānanda immediately took the robe and presented it to the Buddha.
The Buddha took the robe and put it on, then walked back and forth in the open air during the middle watch of the night.
After the middle watch had passed and the latter part of the night approached, the Buddha’s body felt cold, so he said to Ānanda:
“Bring me the third saṃghāṭī robe.”
Ānanda immediately handed over the robe.
The Buddha took the robe and walked up and down on the open ground. The Buddha reflected:
"The robes of the bhikṣus are sufficient for their needs."
When that night had passed, the Buddha, for this reason, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the monks, he addressed them:
"From now on, I allow three robes; they should neither be fewer nor more."
"If one keeps [such cloth] in small quantities, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*;
if one keeps it in large quantities, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
There was a bhikṣu who possessed a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe). Having heard that the Buddha had established the precept that one should not enter a village wearing uncut cloth, he reflected:
"I have a rag-robe that is torn; I shall mend it by making hook-and-loop seams as a basis for giving.
He then took his needle and thread to the gateway of the Jeta Grove and mended the rag-robe, intending to use it as a robe made of cut pieces.
After the meal, the Buddha was walking for exercise with his attendant Ānanda when he reached that place and saw him.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked:
"What do you intend to do?"
He replied:

"The World-Honored One has established a precept for us that we should not enter a village wearing uncut robes. I have a rag-robe (*pāṃśukūla*) that is torn; I wish to patch it with strips of cloth, so I must cut the robe."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, bhikṣu!
When patching a paṃsukūla robe, one should use cloth that has been cut into pieces.”
From now on, I permit you to keep four kinds of *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) garments. What are the four?
First, the garment from a cemetery; second, the garment brought forth [from a refuse heap]; third, the garment without an owner; fourth, the garment from the earth.
What is the "cemetery cloth" (*śmāśānika*)?
It is cloth that has wrapped a corpse and been discarded in a cemetery; this is called the cemetery cloth.
What is the "outcaste cloth" (*pāṃśukūla*)?
To wrap a corpse’s garment and bring it forth to offer to a bhikṣu is what constitutes a "garment brought out.
What is a "masterless garment"?
If, within a village or in an open space, a garment does not belong to anyone—whether a man, a woman, a *paṇḍaka*, or one with both sexual organs—that is a masterless garment.
What is meant by "earth-cloth" (pāṃśukūla)?
It refers to discarded and worn-out items found in streets and alleys, or among graves, or in refuse heaps; this is called earth-cloth.

If a bhikṣu obtains a new garment from among the graves, he should make a saṃghāṭī of double thickness, an uttarāsaṅga of single thickness, an antarvāsaka of single thickness, and a niṣīdana of double thickness.
Furthermore, if one intends to make a triple-layered *saṃghāṭī* and a triple-layered *niṣīdana*,

and a bhikṣu obtains an old garment from a cemetery, he should make the *saṃghāṭī* four layers thick, the *uttarāsaṅga* two layers thick, the *antarvāsaka* two layers thick, and the *niṣīdana* four layers thick.
The same applies to robes obtained from others or robes that have no owner; it is permitted to make such earth-colored robes as heavy as one desires.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a mother named Viśākhā, the daughter of Mṛgāra. She went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha taught her the Dharma through various causes and conditions, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her, after which he remained silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had finished teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them with his Dharma discourse, he rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, arranged his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for tomorrow."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by his silence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning home, he prepared various kinds of many and delicious foods throughout the entire night.
During the first watch of the night, the Buddha was walking back and forth in the open air together with Ānanda. Observing the constellations, the Buddha spoke to Ānanda, saying:
"If someone who knows the signs of the stars were to ask you now:
'When will it rain?'"
"He will surely say:
'It shall rain for seven years.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"When the first watch of the night has passed and the middle watch arrives, these stellar signs disappear and other stellar signs appear.
If at that time someone asks a master of signs,
'When will it rain?'"
"He will surely say:
'It shall rain after seven months have passed.
He then spoke again to Ānanda:
"When the middle watch of the night has passed and the latter watch arrives, these stellar signs vanish and other stellar signs appear.
If at that time one asks those who know the signs,
'When will it rain?'"
"He will surely say:
'It shall rain for seven days.

That night passed and the earth was clear; then from the east clouds emerged, shaped like round bowls and filling the entire sky. These clouds were capable of producing a great rain that filled all the hollows and pits.
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Tell the bhikṣus:
'This bowl-cloud rain possesses merit capable of removing illness; if any bhikṣus wish to bathe, they should stand in the open air and wash.'"
Ānanda, having received these instructions, spoke to the bhikṣus:
"This bowl-cloud rain possesses merit that can eliminate illness; any bhikṣus who wish to bathe should stand in the open air and wash."
At that time, the bhikṣus stood about on the open ground at their own convenience to bathe.
Then, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ, having prepared the food and drink, rose early in the morning and arranged the seating.
She sent a maidservant to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come!
The meal is prepared; may the Buddha know the proper time."
The maidservant immediately accepted her instructions and went to the Jeta Grove to invite the bhikṣus. Peering through a hole in the door, she saw them naked and bathing in the open.
Having seen this, her heart was not pleased, and she thought to herself:
"There are no bhikṣus here at all; these are all shameless naked ascetics."
Having had this thought, he immediately returned and said to his master:
"In Jeta’s Grove there is not a single bhikṣu; they are all naked ascetics."

Vishakha’s mother was wise and of sharp faculties; she knew that it would rain today and that the bhikṣus would surely bathe naked in the open air. This maidservant, however, being foolish and ignorant, spoke these words:
"There is not a single bhikṣu in Jeta’s Grove; they are all naked heretics."
She immediately called another maidservant and sent her to the Jeta Grove to knock on the gate and announce:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared.
Having received these instructions, she went to the Jeta Grove, knocked on the gate, and made a sound.
"The time has come; the meal is prepared; the Buddha himself knows the proper time.
Thereupon, the Buddha and the great assembly donned their robes and took up their bowls, and surrounded by the monks, they went together to his house.
The Buddha was seated among the Saṃgha. Viśākhā herself served the water for washing and personally offered him many kinds of delicious food and drink.

When he had finished eating and she had offered the final rinsing water, knowing that he had set aside his bowl, she took a small stool and sat before the Buddha, wishing to hear the Dharma. She addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"Please grant me my wish.
The Buddha said,
"The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have already transcended all wishes."
Viśākhā said, "I wish to receive [this] as a boon.
The Buddha said:
"I shall grant you a wish.
What wish do you desire? Viśākhā said:

"I wish to give rain-bathing robes to the community of bhikṣus, water-bathing robes to the community of bhikṣuṇīs; I shall provide food for visiting bhikṣus, food for bhikṣus traveling from afar, food for sick bhikṣus, and food for those attending to the sick; I shall constantly provide gruel to the community of bhikṣus; and I shall provide medicinal decoctions and necessary supplies for the sake of the illness of both well-known and obscure bhikṣus."
The Buddha said,
"For what reason do you wish to provide the bhikṣu-saṃgha with rain-bathing robes?
He replied:
"Venerable Sir!

This morning, after I had prepared the seats, I sent a messenger to Jetavana to inform the Buddha that it was time. At the gate, I saw various bhikṣus bathing naked in the open air amidst the rain. When my maidservant returned, she said:
'There is not a single bhikṣu in Jetavana; there are only those who follow external paths.'"
"Venerable Sir!

When a bhikṣu stands naked before the Buddha, his preceptor (upādhyāya), his instructor (ācārya), or any of the senior monks (sthavira), he would be without shame. Therefore, I give this rain-bathing robe (varṣāśāṭī) to the community of bhikṣus so that they may freely bathe in the open air during the rains."
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide bathing robes for the community of bhikṣuṇīs?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!
Once, I went with several laywomen to bathe in the river Ajiravatī.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs also entered the river to bathe naked. When the laywomen saw this, they were displeased and rebuked them, saying:”
"These women have meager merit; their bodies are inauspicious, coarse, with large bellies and sagging breasts. Of what use are they as bhikṣuṇīs?
"O Virtuous One!
Women are naked by nature and ugly. For this reason, I wish to provide the nuns with bathing robes."
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide food and drink for the visiting bhikṣus?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!
These visiting bhikṣus do not know where they may go or where they may not go.

They are utterly exhausted from the road and have not yet found rest; therefore, I wish to provide them with food and drink, after which they may learn for themselves where it is permissible or impermissible to proceed.”
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to give food to the bhikṣu who is traveling far?
She replied:
"Venerable Sir!

When a bhikṣu traveling on a long journey waits for the time of the community meal, or goes out to beg for alms, his companions may abandon him; he might enter a dangerous path at night or travel alone through the wilderness."
“Because I give food, they do not lose their companions and do not enter dangerous paths; for this reason, I provide them with food and drink.
“Vaiśākha! For what reason do you wish to provide food and drink to these sick bhikṣus?”
He replied, "Venerable Sir,

if a sick bhikṣu does not receive food and drink suited to his illness, the illness will be difficult to cure; therefore, by providing him with food and drink suited to his illness, the illness is easily cured."
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide food and drink for the monk who is tending to the sick?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!

If the bhikṣu who attends to the sick waits for the meal after the community has eaten, or goes out to beg for alms, the duties of nursing that sick bhikṣu will be neglected—whether it be cooking rice, preparing gruel, making soup, boiling meat, preparing medicinal decoctions, emptying or filling the vessels for excrement and urine, or discarding the spittoon. For this reason, I give food and drink to the bhikṣu who attends to the sick so that his nursing duties are not neglected; thus he may cook rice, prepare gruel, make soup, boil meat, prepare medicinal decoctions, empty and fill the vessels for excrement and urine, and discard the spittoon.”
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to constantly provide gruel for the community of bhikṣus?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!
If a bhikṣu does not eat gruel, he may suffer from hunger and thirst, or wind may arise within his abdomen at times.
Because I constantly provide him with gruel, he is free from these various afflictions.”
“Viśākhā! For what reason do you wish to provide medicinal broths and necessary items for the sick—both for bhikṣus with many acquaintances and those with few?”
He replied, "Venerable sir!
This sick bhikṣu must have various items required for medicinal decoctions; for this reason, I am giving them."
Furthermore, Venerable Sir!

Suppose I hear that a certain bhikṣu has died at such-and-such a residence, and that the Buddha has declared: "That bhikṣu has severed the three fetters and attained the stage of Srotāpanna; he is no longer subject to rebirth in the evil realms and is destined for Nirvāṇa, having at most seven more births among gods and humans, after which he shall reach the end of all suffering."
"Venerable sir!
I shall ask:
'Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?'"
"If I hear that this bhikṣu has previously come to Śrāvastī, I think to myself:

'This elder may have accepted my rain-bath robe, or food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, or food and drink for bhikṣus traveling from afar, or food according to his illness, or food for tending to the sick, or perhaps he regularly received rice gruel, or medicinal decoctions and various requisites for a sick bhikṣu.'"
"Venerable sir!
It is for this reason that my mind of awakening is fulfilled.
Venerable sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikṣu has died at such-and-such a residence, and the Buddha has declared that this bhikṣu has exhausted the three fetters, attenuated the three poisons, and attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, who will return to this world once more to bring an end to the limits of suffering.
I shall ask:
"Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?
If I hear that this bhikṣu has indeed come to Śrāvastī.
"Venerable Sir!
I have reflected thus:

'This elder may accept my rain-bath robe, or accept food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, or food and drink for those traveling from afar, or food and drink for those who are ill, or food and drink for those attending the sick, or the daily rice gruel, or medicinal decoctions and various requisites for a sick bhikṣu.'"
"Venerable sir!
It is for this reason that my awakening-mind (bodhicitta) is fulfilled.
Venerable sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikṣu has died at his dwelling place, and the Buddha has declared that this bhikṣu has attained the stage of Anāgāmin, with the five lower fetters exhausted, and will attain parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms without returning to this world; then [I know he has not fallen].
"Venerable One! I shall ask:
'Has this Elder ever come to Śrāvastī before?'"
"If I hear that this bhikṣu has previously come here, I reflect:

'This elder may have accepted my rain-bathing robe, or food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, or food and drink for those traveling from afar, or food and drink according to his illness, or food and drink for tending to the sick, or perhaps the daily rice-gruel, or medicinal decoctions and various requisites for a sick bhikṣu.'"
"Venerable sir!
It is for this reason that my awakening-mind is fulfilled.
Venerable sir!"

If I hear that a certain bhikkhu has died at a certain residence, and the Buddha has declared that bhikkhu to have attained arhatship—that his births are ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he has realized for himself through direct knowledge—[then I am satisfied].
I shall ask:
"Has this elder ever come to Śrāvastī?
If I hear that this bhikṣu has indeed come, I will reflect:

"This elder has either accepted from me a rain-bathing robe, or food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, food and drink for those traveling afar, food and drink for those suffering from illness, food and drink for those tending to the sick, or he has constantly provided me with gruel, medicinal decoctions, and various requisites for sick bhikṣus."
"Because of these causes and conditions, my awakening-mind is fulfilled.
Venerable Sir!
Thus, through the accomplishment of my wealth and merit, I gather the merit of the Dharma by means of these causes and conditions."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā!"
I have heard these various vows of yours:

that you will provide the *varṣāśāṭī* robes for the community of bhikṣus and the bathing robes for the community of bhikṣuṇīs; food and drink for visiting bhikṣus, food and drink for bhikṣus traveling from afar, food and drink for bhikṣus according to their illnesses, and food and drink for bhikṣus attending to the sick; that you will constantly provide gruel for the community of bhikṣus; and that you will provide medicinal decoctions and various requisites for the sake of illness to those bhikṣus who are well-known and those who are obscure.
“Viśākhā! This is the accomplishment of wealth and merit; by these causes and conditions, one gathers the merit of the Dharma.
Having taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened Viśākhā with various teachings, the Buddha rose from his seat and departed.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha; having assembled the Sangha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to keep rain-bathing robes and to bathe at will in the open air."
When those bhikṣus learned that the Buddha had permitted the keeping of rain-bathing robes, they began to keep them by making them wide and long.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he rebuked them with various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, when the Buddha permits the keeping of rain-bathing robes, they immediately make them wide and long and keep such large ones?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha; having assembled the Sangha and being already aware of the situation, he intentionally questioned the bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that I have permitted the keeping of a rain-bathing robe, nevertheless make it wide and long and keep such a large one?"
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, when making a rain-bath robe, it should be made according to the prescribed measurements. Among these, the measurement is six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width."
"If one makes it exceeding the prescribed measure, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the soil was salty and damp, and many bhikṣus suffered from boils and sores.
There was a bhikṣu whose abscess was discharging pus and blood, which soaked his *antarvāsaka* until it resembled water.
The Buddha saw him from afar; knowing the situation, he intentionally asked that bhikṣu:
"Why is pus and blood flowing from your body, soaking your *antarvāsaka* as if it were water?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“World-Honored One!
Pus and blood have flowed from my abscess and sores, defiling my antaravāsaka.”
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the monks, he addressed them:
"From this day forward, I permit monks who have boils or ulcers to wear a wound-covering garment, even for ten days after the ulcer has healed."
"If one exceeds this, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
When the monks learned that the Buddha had permitted the keeping of wound-covering robes, they began to make them excessively wide and long.
Some monks who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the *dhūta* austerities heard of this matter and were displeased; they rebuked them, saying:
“How is it that a bhikṣu, knowing the Buddha has permitted the keeping of a wound-covering robe, makes one wide and long and keeps it?
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him through various causes and conditions, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha. Having assembled the Sangha, the Buddha, knowing [the facts], asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“How is it that a bhikṣu, knowing that the Buddha has permitted the keeping of a wound-covering cloth (vastraka), nevertheless makes one that is wide and long and keeps it?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“From this day forward, when you wish to make a wound-covering cloth, you must first make it according to the prescribed measurements. The measurement for this is four spans (vitasti) in length and two spans in width.”
"If one exceeds [the prescribed time] in making it, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the bhikṣus washed their bedding that had been soiled by impurities; having risen early, they hung them out to dry near the gate of the vihāra.

At mealtime, the Buddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. He saw that the bedding and mats, soiled by impurities, had been washed early in the morning and were hanging out to dry between the gates of the monastery.
After the meal, the Buddha assembled the Sangha and, having gathered them, addressed the bhikṣus:

"Today at mealtime, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. I saw that the bedding and mats of the bhikṣus, soiled by impurities, had been washed in the early morning and were hanging out to dry between the gates of the monastery."
"O you bhikṣus! This is improper;
it should not be so. You have used the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha without due consideration.

Brahmins and lay devotees, with bodies and minds exhausted by toil and their flesh and blood depleted, give these things as offerings to cultivate merit; therefore, you should exercise careful consideration and use them sparingly."
For a monk with distracted thoughts who sleeps without one-pointed concentration, there are five disadvantages.

What are the five? First, the suffering of difficulty falling asleep; second, the suffering of difficulty waking up; third, seeing evil dreams; fourth, not being protected by benevolent deities while sleeping; and fifth, when awake, the mind finds it difficult to enter into wholesome states of awareness and contemplation.
For a bhikṣu who sleeps with an undistracted mind and single-pointed concentration, there are five beneficial matters.

What are the five? First, he experiences no hardship or suffering in sleep; second, he awakens easily from sleep; third, he has no evil dreams while sleeping; fourth, benevolent deities come to protect him during sleep; and fifth, upon waking, his mind easily enters into wholesome contemplation of the Dharma.

“Bhikṣus, if even one who still possesses lust, anger, and ignorance, and has not yet abandoned desire, can sleep with undistracted mindfulness and single-minded concentration without losing semen, how much more so for one who has abandoned desire?
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I allow you to keep a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), for the purpose of protecting the bedding of the Saṃgha.”
"One should not lie upon a monastic bedding without having spread out a *niṣīdana*.
When the monks learned that the Buddha had permitted them to keep *niṣīdanās*, they began to make them wide and long.
There were some bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, knowing that the Buddha permitted the keeping of a *niṣīdana*, nevertheless keep one that is wide and long and large?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the Saṃgha. Once the Saṃgha was assembled, the Buddha, knowing the situation, asked the bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"Why, being called bhikṣus, do you know that the Buddha permits the keeping of a *niṣīdana*, yet then make it wide and long and keep one so large?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the niṣīdana must be made according to measure; its measure shall be two spans in length and one and a half spans in width."
"If one exceeds this limit, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at mealtime he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Having finished eating, he returned toward the Andhavana forest, where he spread out his sitting mat beneath a tree and sat down cross-legged.
The Elder Kālodāyin also entered the Andhavana forest and, not far from the Buddha, spread out his *niṣīdana* beneath a tree and sat down.
This elder was large of body; his two knees touched the ground, so he held up his robe with both hands and made this aspiration:
"When will the Buddha allow me to make a *niṣīdana* by measuring one span along the edge of the threads? Then my wish would be fulfilled."
In the afternoon, the Buddha arose from meditation. For this reason, he assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Today at mealtime, I put on my robes, took my bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. After eating, I returned to the Andhavana forest, spread out a sitting mat beneath a tree, and sat down."
Kālodayin returned from his almsround and sat beneath a tree, reflecting:
"Where is the Buddha practicing the path today? I shall practice the path in that very place."
I entered the Andhavana forest and spread my *niṣīdana* beneath a tree to sit; Kāḷudāyin did likewise.
This son of good family was large of stature, and his two knees touched the ground while his two hands reached up to grasp his robe. He made this vow, saying:
"When will the Buddha allow me to make a *niṣīdana* measuring one span (*vitasti*) along the edge of the threads, so that it may be thus complete?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit you to make a border of one span (vitasti) of thread for the niṣīdana.
This precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu wishes to make a niṣīdana, he should make it according to the prescribed measure: its length shall be two vitastis and its width one and a half vitastis;
an additional vitasti may be added to the border for the fringe.
"If one exceeds [the prescribed measure] in making it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

The Elder Nanda was the Buddha’s younger brother, born of his maternal aunt; he resembled the Buddha in physical form, yet he was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha in respect to thirty of the marks.

Nanda made robes equal in measure to those of the Buddha. When the bhikṣus gathered for the mealtime or gathered after midday, they saw him coming from afar and rose to greet him, thinking, "Our Great Teacher, the Buddha, has come."
As he drew near, the elder bhikṣu recognized that it was Nanda;
feeling ashamed, he thought to himself, "I am a junior to him, yet he rises to greet me.
Nanda, likewise feeling abashed, said:
"He even commanded the senior elders to rise and welcome me.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, questioned Nanda:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“From this day forward, your robes should be made by tearing them, dyeing them, and purifying them.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should give robes to Nanda to spread out for drying.
If there are others like him, the Saṃgha should likewise act with one mind to spread them out for drying."
From this day forward, if a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to the Buddha’s robe, or exceeds it, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
The Buddha’s robe is nine spans in length and six spans in width.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha:
“Please allow me to wear robes made of *kūrmaka* grass.”
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to wear robes made of *kusa* grass.
For what reason?..."

Wearing robes of *kusa* grass does not hinder one from attaining the Way; likewise, it is through contentment, few desires, knowing the proper time, and knowing the proper measure, through diligent study, taking little, and practicing frugality, that one follows the *dhūta* practices in a quiet place toward *nirvāṇa*.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Please allow me to wear a kauśeya garment.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to wear *kauśeya* garments. Why is this?
Wearing *kauśeya* garments does not hinder the attainment of the Way; it accords with contentment, fewness of desires, and even leads toward *nirvāṇa*."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Please allow me to wear a saṇi robe.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear hemp garments; hemp garments do not hinder the attainment of the Way, and through fewness of desires and contentment, one may even follow toward Nirvana.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"I ask that I be allowed to wear wild-hemp garments."
The Buddha said:

“I permit you to wear garments of wild hemp; wearing garments of wild hemp does not hinder one from attaining the Way, for it accords with fewness of desires and contentment. The same applies to *kappāsika* and *kambala* garments.”
There was a merchant who possessed a *kṣaumī* garment made of *kimpila* wool, which he could not sell for any price.
Having heard that the Elder Subhūti had attained the fruits of this present life through his practice of giving, he immediately took the garment and offered it to Subhūti.
Subhūti did not accept it, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to receive this robe.
The lay devotees became resentful and said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, constantly praise giving, yet now they refuse to accept what is offered.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I authorize you to possess *kambala* robes; for *kambala* robes do not hinder the attainment of the Path, and they lead to fewness of desires, contentment, and even unto Nirvāṇa."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Please allow me to adopt the practice of nakedness.
The Buddha said:
“The practice of nakedness should not be accepted.
If one accepts nakedness, one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense. Why is this?
"To receive the practice of nakedness is the mark of a non-Buddhist.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Please allow me to wear a woolen garment (kambala)."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear hair-cloth (keśa-kaṃbala).
If one wears it, one incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya."
"Why is this? Because these are the characteristics of non-Buddhists.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Please allow me to wear a garment made of the wings of a horn-owl.
The Buddha said,
“One should not wear a garment made of the wings of a horn-owl.”
If one wears them, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Why is this? Because they are the marks of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Please allow me to wear coarse woolen garments.
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear coarse woolen garments.
If one wears them, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“Please allow me to wear a garment made of leather.
The Buddha said,
“I do not allow the wearing of garments made of leather.”
"If you wear them, you will incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Please allow me to wear a single garment."
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit wearing a single garment.
If one wears it, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Please allow me to wear both the upper and lower robes.
The Buddha said:
"I have already permitted the three robes; they should neither be fewer nor more.
If a bhikṣu keeps fewer than required, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*; if he keeps more, he falls into the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If one wears upper or lower robes [in this manner], one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Please allow me to wear clothes made of beaten wood."
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the wearing of garments made from beaten wood.
If one wears them, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“May I be permitted to wear robes made of *aku* grass, *baku* grass, *kūśa* grass, *manya* grass, *babhru* grass, and *śāṇa* grass?”
The Buddha said:
"None are permitted to wear them.
If one wears them, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
The group of six bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“Please allow us to remove the hair from our bodies.
The Buddha said:
"One should not remove the body hair.
To remove body hair, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The group of six bhikṣus addressed the Buddha:
"Listen as I put on this true blue robe.
The Buddha said,
"The group of six bhikṣus seek two kinds [of robes]:..."
"Previously you sought to remove the hair from the body; now you seek genuine blue garments.
The Buddha said:

"Genuine blue, yellow, red, or white garments—including all furs and skins, single-sleeved robes, double-layered robes, all woolen cloaks, all hooded robes, two-sleeved robes, all embroidered robes, all shirts, all trousers, all pleated trousers, all loincloths, all *pāramīḷi* robes, all *saṃkhalikā* robes, and all white robes—a bhikṣu should not wear any of these."
"If you wear it, you will incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
A certain bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
"Please allow me to wear tree-cotton garments (*vṛkṣaja-vastra*)."
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the wearing of tree-grown garments.
If one wears them, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Please allow me to wear a coarse woolen *kambala*.
The Buddha said:
"One must not wear coarse woolen *kambala*.
If one wears it, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
There are five reasons why coarse woolen *kambala* is improper to use."
"What are the five? They are:
being extremely cold in winter, extremely hot in summer, coarse and rough, hard and rigid, and causing the skin to become coarse.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

The Elder Bhikṣu Nanda left his saṃghāṭī robe in the Andhavana grove; having put on his upper and lower robes, he entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. He lost the saṃghāṭī, and after his meal, though he searched for it, he could not find it.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable elders!
I left my saṃghāṭī robe in the Andhavana grove; having put on my upper and lower robes, I entered the city to beg for alms and lost the saṃghāṭī."
"What should I do? The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the situation], asked the bhikṣu Nanda:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
"World-Honored One!

The Buddha praised, through various causes and conditions, the practice of taking all things with one when departing. "If a bhikṣu dwells with few desires—wearing robes merely to cover the body and eating food merely to sustain the frame—this is the sphere of action for such a bhikṣu. Together with his robe and bowl, he has no attachment or lingering concern, just as a bird flies through the air carrying its feathers along with it."

The bhikṣu is also like this: having few desires and being content, his robes serve merely to cover his body and his food serves merely to fill his belly. This is the sphere of action for such a bhikṣu; accompanied by his robe and bowl, he has no lingering attachment, just like a bird in flight.
After the Buddha had praised, through various causes and conditions, the practice of taking all one's belongings with one when traveling, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should not enter the homes of laypeople without your three robes."
"If one enters [the village], one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Ānanda left his saṃghāṭī robe in the Jeta Grove during a rainstorm; he put on his upper and lower robes and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing [the situation], asked Ānanda:
"Is it true that when it was raining in Jeta’s Grove, you left your saṃghāṭī robe behind and entered the city for alms wearing only your upper and lower robes?"
Ānanda said: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason?
Ānanda replied:
“Because of rain from the heavens.

Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions, and having finished praising the precepts and the observance of the precepts, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five reasons for which it is permitted to keep the saṃghāṭī robe.”
What are the five?
First, there is a monastery where a bhikṣu resides;
second, if one has accepted the kaṭhina robe.
Third, if it rains;
fourth, if it is about to rain;
fifth, if there is a distribution of alms outside the village.
These are the five causes and conditions.
Furthermore, there are five causes and conditions for retaining the saṃghāṭī robe.
What are these five?
1. There is a monastery where bhikṣus reside;
2. or if the kaṭhina robe has been spread;
3. or if there is a market stall or a charitable assembly.
Fourth, at market stalls and charitable assemblies;
fifth, at crossroads.
These are the five causes and conditions.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, when the various non-Buddhist renunciants had completed their summer retreat during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the lay disciples of those non-Buddhists offered them robes and clothing.
The upāsakas, their faith in the Buddha-dharma pure, reflected with clear minds:
"These teachers of false doctrines and evil ways even know to offer robes at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the conclusion of the summer retreat."
"When we, the noble Saṃgha, have completed the summer retreat and it is time for the *pravāraṇā*, why should we not give offerings of robes?
Thereupon, he took the bundles of robes and went to the Bamboo Grove to offer them to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive robes for the rainy season retreat when the invitation at the conclusion of the summer retreat (pravāraṇā) takes place.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"It is permitted to receive the robes offered during the *anvāhāra* (the distribution at the conclusion of the rains retreat) once the *varṣā* (rains retreat) is finished and the *pravāraṇā* has been performed.
When the śrāmaṇeras came to claim their share of the robes, the bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to share in the distribution of robes offered during the summer retreat with the śrāmaṇeras.
They reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Listen, and it shall be granted.
The bhikṣus reflected thus:
"The Buddha has said:"
"I have granted it," [the king] said. "I do not know how much was granted," he reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Whether the śrāmaṇera is standing or sitting, if various donors give alms by hand in succession, however much or little it may be, it should belong to the śrāmaṇera.
If the donors do not distinguish [the recipient], then divide it into four parts."
"Give a fourth part to the śrāmaṇeras.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony following the summer retreat, various lay disciples offered gifts of household items:
water jars, cords and necklaces, *lūcaka* mats, covers for fire-hearth lids, fans, leather sandals, and curved walking sticks.
The upāsakas, their faith in the Buddha-dharma pure, reflected:
"Even these teachers of false doctrines know to give various gifts during the time of the summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony."
"When it is time for our noble Saṃgha to perform the *pravāraṇā* at the conclusion of the summer retreat, why should we not give gifts of various items?
Thinking thus, they followed the practice of the bhikṣus and gave various kinds of things:

whether it was an alms bowl (*pātra*), a large bowl (*kuṇḍikā*), a medium bowl (*ardhakuṇḍikā*), a water jar (*kaṭacchu*), a small water jar (*ardhakaṭacchu*), a waist-belt with rings, a meditation cushion (*dhyānapiṇḍaka*), a robe-strap, a bowl-rest, a water pitcher (*kamaṇḍalu*), a bowl bag, a sunshade, a fan, or leather sandals—such various requisites required by bhikṣus—they took them and went to the Bamboo Grove to offer them to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not accept them, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive items as required by individual bhikṣus during the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow that at the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) during the time of the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), one may accept whatever items are required by a bhikṣu.
At that time, the śrāmaṇeras came to request their share of the items required by the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not give them, saying to the śrāmaṇeras:

"The Buddha has permitted that when the summer retreat ends and the invitation for self-criticism (*pravāraṇā*) is held, robes offered as gifts shall be shared with the *śrāmaṇeras*; however, he has not yet permitted that other items required by the monks be shared with the *śrāmaṇeras*."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It should be given."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has said:
'One should give.'"
"I do not know how much was given.
He reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there are śrāmaṇeras standing, sitting, or in line, whatever the donors give with their own hands, whether much or little, belongs to the śrāmaṇeras.
If the donors do not distinguish [the recipients], the gift shall be divided into four parts, and the fourth part is given to the śrāmaṇeras."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Śākya son Upananda observed the rains retreat in two locations for the sake of receiving offerings.
The bhikṣus did not know which location they should receive their share of the robes.
He informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Give it to the place where he is observing the rains retreat."
The bhikṣus said,
“We shall observe the rains retreat in two places.
The Buddha said:
"In which place do you spend more days?
He replied,
"In both places, the days are equal."
The Buddha asked,
"Where will you perform the *pravāraṇā*?
They replied:
"Let there be *pravāraṇā* at both places.
The Buddha asked,
"At which place should the *pravāraṇā* be performed first?"
"In this place, the share of robes is given.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Śākya son Upananda, during the final month of the summer retreat, went on an inspection tour of the various monasteries. He wished to know in which places the monks who had completed their retreat had obtained many articles of clothing; wherever there were many offerings, he would go there.
Seeing him from afar, the bhikṣus rose to greet him, prepared a seat for him, and invited him to sit. They exchanged greetings with one another, asking, "Are you well? Are you at ease?
After remaining silent for a short while, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!"
"In this case, may the Saṃgha residing here receive the offered robe?
The bhikṣus replied, "They may."
"Has it been divided yet?
He replied, "It has not been divided."
He said, "Bring it here!
Divide it right here."
The bhikṣus brought [the portions] and placed them before Baddhananda to be divided. Once they were divided, the elder took his portion and was about to depart.
Baddhananda said, "Venerable sir, wait a moment."
He asked, "What is the matter? He replied:
“Wait but a moment.
Baddhālī was able to preach the Dharma with varied speech, eloquent speech, and inexhaustible speech; as he preached such excellent Dharma, the Elder heard it and rejoiced greatly.
Out of affection for the Dharma, he said to Baddhālinda,
"My share of the robes belongs to you.
A second and a third time the Elder spoke likewise, until all the robes belonging to the Saṃgha were divided and given to Baddhālinda.
In this way, having obtained many robes from one, two, or three places, he carried them in a large bundle and entered the Jeta Grove.
As the bhikṣus were walking up and down in the open space near the gate of the Jeta Grove, they saw him coming from afar and spoke among themselves:
"The Śākya son Upananda is coming; this shameless man has committed many acts that are seen, heard, or suspected as evil, and he has brought back a bundle full of robes."
As they drew near, the bhikṣus asked,
"Where did you obtain these robes?
He replied:
"It was obtained because he extensively preached the Dharma to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus, who were of few desires, contented with little, and practiced the dhūta austerities, rebuked him, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if he observes the rains retreat in one place and receives his share of robes in another?"
After the various bhikṣus had rebuked him with many reasons, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why is it called being a bhikṣu if one observes the rains retreat in one place and receives one's share of robes in another?
At that time, the Buddha merely rebuked him; he had not yet established a formal precept for the bhikṣus.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala at a certain residence, observing the rains retreat together with a great community of bhikṣus.

The lay devotees of that country, seeing that the Sangha was numerous, provided robes for the community of bhikṣus from their various households; they also gave robes for individual rooms and robes for the later period of the retreat.
Later, when the Buddha was observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in the Jeta Grove, there were two elderly bhikṣus staying at that residence who were also observing the retreat.
The lay devotees (*upāsaka*) reflected:
"We shall give to the Saṃgha as we have done in the past so that our duties are not neglected; thus the bhikṣus will receive the offerings, and we shall gain merit."
The laypeople sent many garments, which were to be given to the community of monks residing at that monastery according to the established rule.
These two elderly bhikṣus reflected:
"These garments are many, while we are few; if we divide them, what offense do you think we would incur?"
His mind was filled with doubt and he could not distinguish the truth.

At that time, after the summer retreat, Upāli’s brother, Upananda, went on an inspection tour of the various monasteries, wishing to know in which place the bhikṣus who had spent the rains retreat had received the greatest offerings of robes and other requisites.
Bhadanta thought to himself, "The Buddha spent his previous year's rainy season retreat in that place; there must surely be many robes offered as gifts there.
He then went to that residence.
When the two elder bhikṣus saw him coming from afar, they rose to welcome him and offered him a seat. They exchanged greetings, asking whether he was at ease or not.
After a brief silence, they asked:
"Do the monks residing here receive offerings of clothing and requisites?"
He replied, “I have. He asked:
"Has it been divided yet?
He replied,
"It has not been divided."
He asked, "For what reason do you not divide it?
He replied:
"These robes are many, while we are few. If we were to divide them, what offense would we incur? Thinking thus, they hesitated and did not divide them.
Upāli asked: "What is the fault in this?
Vāṣpa said: [The answer follows].
"You do not know how to divide it; if you were to divide it, what offense would you incur?
The two elder bhikṣus asked, "Are you able to divide it?"
He replied, “I can.
In this matter,
a formal ritual (karmavācanā) should be performed.”
He immediately brought the various garments and placed them before him.
Upāli divided them into three heaps, placing one heap between each of the two monks and standing himself between the other two heaps, saying:
"Listen as the *karmavācanā* is performed."
“If you two are one aggregate, then in this way you have three;
with both aggregates and myself, in this way I have three.”
Question:
"Is this *karmavācanā* valid?
Answer: "It is."
"Very well!
said Baddhālī, and he took up his large bundle of robes and departed.
He then said:
"Venerable Elder, our various robes and articles have not yet been distributed.
Upāli said, "I shall give you a share;
one who knows the Dharma should be given a fine robe."
He replied, "I shall give it.

Then, from among that collection, Upāli took a robe of great value and set it aside; having divided the remainder into two portions, he himself carried a large bundle of robes and entered the Jeta Grove.
The bhikṣus were walking back and forth in the open space between the gates when they saw him coming from afar and spoke among themselves:
"This is the shameless man, Upananda; he has committed many acts of evil that are seen, heard, or suspected, and he has taken many robes and bags."
He then approached them, and the bhikṣus said,
"Upananda! Where did you obtain these robes?"
Bhadanta recounted this matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
There was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; upon hearing this, he felt shame and reproached him, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu and yet intentionally seize the property of an elder bhikṣu?"
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him with various reasons, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, the Buddha, knowing the situation, asked Upāli (Bhadanta):
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why is it that you, who call yourself a bhikṣu, have taken the property of an elder bhikṣu?
After the Buddha had rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Upananda has not only seized [property] in this present life; he did so in previous lives as well."
This matter is permitted.
Long ago, in a bend of a river, there were two otters who caught a large carp; unable to divide it, the two otters remained on opposite sides to guard it.
A jackal came there wishing to drink water, and seeing [the elephant], said:
"Nephew! What are you doing in this place?"
The otter said, "Uncle!
I caught this carp in a bend of the river; I cannot share it."
"Are you able to divide it?
The jackal replied, "I am."
"In this regard, a verse should be spoken.
The jackal divided [the prey] into three portions and asked the otter:
"Who among you prefers to enter shallow water?"
He replied, "It is a otter.
[The king asked,] "Who can enter the deep?"
He replied, "It is a otter.
The jackal said:
"Listen as I recite this verse:
'If one enters shallowly, one should give the tail; if one enters deeply, one should give the head;
as for the flesh of the body in between, it should be given to those who know the Dharma.'"
"A jackal was carrying a fish in its mouth when a female came and spoke this verse to ask:
'From where did you bring this?
You found it full in your mouth in the river;'"
"Thus, it has neither head nor tail; the carp delights in meat.
The male jackal spoke this verse in reply:
"People strike one another with words, Yet they do not know how to discern the Dharma."
"One who is able to discern can obtain what is found in an official's storehouse;
it was a headless and tailless carp, therefore I have obtained food.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"The two otters were those two elder bhikṣus.
The jackal was Upananda. In his previous life, Upananda had robbed them; in this life, he has robbed them again."
After the Buddha had rebuked Baddhananda with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, when you observe the rains retreat at this location, you must not receive a share of robes from any other place."
"If you accept it, you will incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

At a certain residence, a single bhikṣu was observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*). For the sake of the community of monks observing the summer retreat, the people there offered various robes and items intended for distribution.

Even though various people may offer robes and other requisites for the sake of the community of monks observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), a single bhikṣu who has alone observed the summer retreat should receive them.
The same applies to two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or four bhikṣus.
It is the same for having a dwelling place or not having a dwelling place.
It is likewise for being in a village or in an araṇya (wilderness).

Suppose there is a single dwelling where one bhikṣu observes the summer retreat; because of this visiting bhikṣu, the people there make many offerings of robes and other items to the Saṃgha that ought to be distributed.
Although many people may give various robes to the Saṃgha because they are guests of the resident bhikṣus, the robe should be divided among the present members of the Saṃgha.
However, since this one bhikṣu has completed the summer retreat (varṣā), he alone should receive this robe.
The same applies to two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, and four bhikṣus.
It is likewise whether there is a monastery or no monastery.
It is likewise whether there is a village or a forest hermitage.
"If the Saṃgha is split after the *pravāraṇā* has been concluded, should the portion of the summer retreat robes be given [to the members]?
The Buddha said,
"It should be given."
“Should a bhikṣu who has been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (formal act of suspension) after the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticize) be given a share of the robes?
The Buddha said,
“He should not be given one.”
“Once the *pravāraṇā* has concluded, if a bhikṣu arrives at that faction, should he be given a share of the *varṣā-cīvara*?
The Buddha said:
“If he arrives among a community that acts according to the Dharma, he should be given [a share].”
"After the *pravāraṇā* has concluded, if a bhikṣu says of himself,
'I am a layperson,' should he be given a share of the summer retreat robes?"
The Buddha said:
"It should not be given.
After the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was concluded, a bhikṣu spoke of himself, saying:
“I am a śrāmaṇera.
Should I be given my share of the summer retreat robes?
The Buddha said:
"It should be divided with the śrāmaṇeras.
After the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was concluded, a bhikṣu declared of himself: "I am not a bhikṣu."
“Should the portion of the summer retreat robes be given to him?
The Buddha said,
“It should not be given.”
"If one says: 'I am an outsider;

I have not been seen [to commit an offense], I have not been suspended, I am of evil and heterodox views, I have not been removed from suspension, I do not live in communion, and I live in various ways that are not in communion.'"
He said to himself: "I have committed a border offense;

I was originally a layman; I am a eunuch; I have defiled a bhikṣuṇī; I am a person who has crossed over [the boundary]; I have killed my father and mother; I have killed an arhat; I have caused a schism in the Saṃgha; and with an evil mind, I have shed the blood of a Buddha."
"Should such persons as these be given their share of the summer retreat robes?
The Buddha said,
"They should not be given."
“After the *pravāraṇā* has concluded, if a bhikṣu travels to another country, should he be given his share of the summer retreat robes?
The Buddha said:
