“There are cases where it should be given and cases where it should not be given. It should be given if one knows he will return; it should not be given if one knows he will not return.”
If one has entrusted another to take [the robes], all portions of the robes should be given to them;
if one has not entrusted another to take them, they should not be given.
One who has received such an entrustment should perform all duties on behalf of the Saṃgha.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 27 [continued] and Fascicle 28; Chapter 4, Recitation 8,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The Seventh Dharma: The Rules on Robes, Part Seven, Lower.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“There are eight kinds of giving.”
What are the eight?
First, giving according to the realm;
second, giving based on reliance;
3. Restricted giving;
4. Giving obtained through solicitation;
5. Giving obtained by the Saṃgha.
Sixth, receiving gifts in the presence [of the donor];
seventh, receiving gifts during the summer retreat;
eighth, receiving gifts through referral.
"What is meant by 'giving to a specific field' (*kṣetra-dāna*)?
One person said:
"This robe is given to the community of monks residing here."
"In the latter month of summer, the kaṭhina robe is received. Who should receive this robe?
The Buddha said:
"Even if the kaṭhina robe is received in the latter month of summer, if a bhikṣu enters within these boundaries, he should receive it."
This is called giving based on a boundary (*dhātu*).
What is meant by giving based on reliance (*niśraya*)?

For example, many bhikṣus establish an internal boundary (*antarā-sīmā*) at several monasteries; having completed the summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā*, they relinquish their original boundary and then establish an internal boundary by demarcating the walls of the monastery compound.

In this matter, for the sake of the community of monks observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), various people have offered robes and items intended for distribution. To whom should these robes belong?
The Buddha said:

"Even though they have left their original territory, since those bhikṣus spent the majority of their time dwelling within the boundaries of that specific area during the summer retreat, all the bhikṣus should share in the distribution of these garments and articles."
This is what is meant by giving based on reliance.
What is restricted giving?
There is a certain residence where two groups of bhikṣu-saṃghas are observing the summer retreat: one group that accepts the Dharma and one group that does not accept the Dharma.
When this community of monks had completed the summer retreat, they established the following restriction:
"We shall accept the offerings of this clan, and you shall accept the offerings of that clan."
"Accept alms from this family; you accept alms from that family.
Accept alms from the places where we travel; you accept alms from the places where you travel."
"In this village we shall receive the alms given to us; in that village you shall receive the alms given to you.
In this destination-village we shall receive the alms given to us; in that destination-village you shall receive the alms given to you."
"In these streets and lanes where there are many people, we shall receive the offerings; in those streets and lanes where there are many people, you shall receive them.
Then, for the sake of the Sangha observing the summer retreat (varṣā), the people there took the hands of the elders and made offerings of various robes and items to be distributed to the Sangha.
They addressed the Buddha, saying, "Who should receive these garments and articles?"
The Buddha said:
"Whichever school appoints the *upādhyāya* (senior elder), that property should belong to that school. [He continued:
"If a donor takes the hand of the first senior elder or the hand of the second senior elder and says:"
"This object is being given to the Sangha.
To whom, then, should this object belong? He replied:
"If the two elders each belong to one school, they should belong to those respective schools.
If the two elders each belong to one school, they should belong to two schools; how then should [the community] be divided?"
He replied:
"Divide it equally into four parts; the fourth part should be given to the śrāmaṇera.
This is called obtaining a gift through restriction.
What is the gift of providing?
It is when one makes a gift for the sake of another, or makes a gift based on a specific occasion:

on the eighth, twenty-third, fourteenth, twenty-ninth, fifteenth, thirtieth, sixteenth, or the first day of the month, up until the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, giving even a single coin to a certain place; whatever items are given to that designated place, this is called the gift of providing.
What is a gift obtained by the Saṃgha?
It is when a donor at a residence says:
"Give this robe to the Saṃgha of this residence."
At that time, during the last month of the summer retreat, they did not receive the kaṭhina robe at that residence.
They asked the Buddha, "Who should receive this robe?
The Buddha said:
"In the latter month of summer, this is the residence; even though the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, if the bhikṣus dwell within this residence, this robe should belong to them."
This is what constitutes a gift received by the Saṃgha.
What is a gift received in the presence [of the recipient]?
There is a donor who says:
"This dwelling place belongs to the Saṃgha present here.
At that time, during the latter month of the summer retreat, this dwelling place received the kaṭhina robe. They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who should receive this robe?"
The Buddha said:
"Even if it is the last month of the summer retreat and the *kaṭhina* robe has been accepted at this residence, if there are monks currently residing in this place, this robe should belong to them."
This is how one obtains gifts through being present before [the donor].
How does one obtain gifts by means of the summer retreat (*varṣā*)?
There is a donor who says:
"This robe belongs to the community of monks who have completed the summer retreat at this residence.
At that time, it was not yet the final month of the summer retreat, and the *kaṭhina* robe had not been accepted at this residence. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Who should receive this robe?"
The Buddha said:

"If it is not during the latter month of the summer retreat, and the *kaṭhina* robe has not been accepted in this residence, then when the monks residing in this place have completed their summer retreat, these individuals should accept this robe."
This constitutes obtaining offerings during the summer retreat.
How does one demonstrate obtaining offerings?
There is a donor who says:
"This robe is from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, or from Mount Vipula-vatsa, or from Mount Saptaparṇī, or from Mount Satadru."
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Who should receive this robe?
The Buddha said:
"Where was this robe shown?
It should be accepted where it was shown.
This constitutes receiving a gift through indication.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Aśvajit, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, was traveling through various countries with a great community of five hundred bhikṣus.
Because of the Elder Aśvajit, the Saṃgha received abundant offerings, including daily meals of various *tambula* porridges and many gifts of clothing.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Because this elder is our teacher, the Saṃgha has received great offerings; we have been given timely food, *taṭṭaka*, and many robes as gifts."
The bhikṣus went to the teacher Māṭhara and asked him:
"Venerable sir, have you received great offerings? At this time, many *taṭṭaka*-cakes and various articles of clothing were bestowed upon you as gifts."
"Elder! Who should receive these robes?
The Elder Ācariya replied:
"Venerable Elders!
As it is stated in the Buddha’s Vinaya:

'If there is a single bhikṣu who observes the summer retreat at a certain residence, even though people may have made offerings for the sake of visiting bhikṣus, the robes belonging to the Saṃgha should be distributed as property.'"
If this one bhikṣu is alone here observing the summer rains retreat, he should receive these robes alone.
It is the same for two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or four bhikṣus.
"It is the same for those with a fixed residence, those without a fixed residence, and those in forest hermitages where there are no villages.
"Venerable Elders!
You should accept robes in this manner."
"Just as it was with the Elder Ācariya, so it was with the Elder Yasas and the Elder Yasodhara.
Furthermore, on another occasion, a great assembly of elder bhikṣus, headed by Mahākāśyapa, were residing in the Mango Grove at Pāṭaliputra."
At that time, in a certain residence in the kingdom of Magadha, there lived a single bhikṣu alone.
For the sake of the community of monks observing the summer retreat (varṣā), the people there offered various robes and items intended for distribution.
That bhikṣu reflected thus:
"The people of this residence have offered various robes as items to be distributed for the sake of the Saṃgha.
I alone am not the Saṃgha; I should go and ask the elder Kāśyapa and other senior bhikṣus: 'Who should receive these garments and articles?'"
He then related these matters in detail to the elders.
The elders said,
"As the Buddha has taught in the Vinaya:..."

"There was a bhikṣu who observed the summer retreat at a single residence. For the sake of the saṃgha observing the summer retreat, these people offered various robes and items that were to be distributed."
If a single bhikṣu observes the summer retreat alone, he may accept this robe.
It is the same for two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or four bhikṣus.
This also applies whether there is a residence or no residence, whether there is a village or a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
"Robes such as these should be accepted.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a son of Anāthapiṇḍada named Saṃgharakṣita; because he wore his hair tied in a topknot, he went to the Jeta Grove and prepared an abundant offering of food to provide for the Sangha.

There was a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. When the lay devotees saw the large gathering, they made offerings of various robes for the sake of the Saṃgha—items that were to be distributed among the monks present.
The senior bhikṣu said:

"This is the last month of the summer retreat; it is at this time that one may accept a day's worth of robe-cloth. This is the time when the items to be distributed among the saṃgha who have completed the summer rains retreat should be apportioned."
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Even if the kaṭhina robe is received during the final month of the summer retreat, it is called a 'robe due to special circumstances'; the present saṃgha should divide it."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

An arhat bhikṣu entered parinirvāṇa; for the sake of this bhikṣu, [the donor] went to the Jeta Grove and prepared an abundant offering of food for the Saṃgha, and many bhikṣus gathered there, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
When the lay devotees saw the great assembly gathered there for the sake of the Saṃgha, they offered various robes as gifts to be distributed among the monks present.
The resident bhikṣus said:

"It is the final month of the summer retreat, and this is the time for receiving the kaṭhina robe; these robes, being gifts to the Saṃgha that has completed the summer rains retreat, should be divided."
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Even though the kaṭhina robe has been accepted at the residence during the final month of the summer retreat, because of these circumstances, the robe should be divided among the present saṃgha."
The śrāmaṇeras came to claim their share of the robes, but the bhikṣus did not give them.
The bhikṣus said:

"The Buddha has taught that the share of robes from the summer retreat (varṣā) should be given to the śrāmaṇeras; items belonging to the bhikṣus' personal property should be given to the śrāmaṇeras; however, the Buddha did not say that the *niyata* (designated) robes should be given."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to give it."
The bhikṣus did not know how much to give,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"When donors make offerings, if a śrāmaṇera is standing, sitting, or present in the sequence [of the assembly], and the gift is bestowed with their own hands, it should belong to the śrāmaṇera.
If the donor does not specify [the recipient] and the distribution has been completed according to the sequence, one-fourth of the portion is given to the śrāmaṇera."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada died, and consequently the Jetavana grove fell into ruin. The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Monks, if it can be repaired, then repair it according to the Dharma.
The monks attempted to repair it but were unable to do so; as it continued to fall apart, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has a son named Saṃgharakṣita; you should say to him:
'This Jeta Grove was built by your father, but it is now dilapidated. Are you able to repair it?'"
The bhikṣus went to him and said, "Saṃgharakṣa!
This Jeta Grove was built by your father; since it has fallen into ruin today, why do you not repair it?"
He replied: "Venerable sirs!
I previously knew that my father purchased eighteen hundred million pieces of gold for this vacant land to give to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; that it has been broken up today is not my business."
"If the Saṃgha grants me the Jeta Grove, I shall repair it.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You should give it.
There are two people who gain great merit:
one who newly builds and one who repairs what is old; both shall obtain immeasurable merit."
How should it be granted?
Saṃgharakṣita shall remain within the internal boundary, and one bhikṣu should proclaim thus in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This Jeta Grove has no owner, and Saṃgharakṣa wishes to repair it.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent, so that this ownerless Jeta Grove may be given to Saṃgharakṣa for the purpose of repair.
Thus he makes the formal motion:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This Jeta Grove has no owner; Saṃgharakṣa is capable of maintaining it."
This Jeta Grove has no owner; it shall be restored by Saṃgharakṣa.
Those elders who consent to the Jeta Grove being restored by Saṃgharakṣa, let those elders remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak.
"The Sangha has completed the granting; the Jeta Grove is now without an owner and is being administered by Saṃgharakṣita. Since the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."

"In the kingdom of Kośala, there was a certain dwelling where a single bhikṣu resided. When the kaṭhina robes had been dismantled at the end of the spring months, the Saṃgha there received a gift of property that ought to be divided among those present."
That bhikṣu reflects thus:
"The Saṃgha residing here has obtained various robes and articles that should be distributed among those present.
I am but a single person and not the Saṃgha; why have I not gone to the Buddha’s presence to ask: [why this is so]?"
"Who should receive these robes and articles?

That bhikṣu then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and after a short while, reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In the spring month, the *kaṭhina* robe ceremony is concluded.

In a certain monastery within the kingdom of Kośala, there lived a single bhikṣu; therein, the Saṃgha received a gift intended for the *saṃmukha-saṃgha* (the assembly present) which was to be distributed.
“I am alone and not part of a Saṃgha; how should these robes and articles be received?
The Buddha said:

“If there is a single bhikṣu dwelling in a single residence, and people offer various robes for the sake of the Saṃgha, those items intended for distribution among the present Saṃgha [should be treated as follows].”
When this bhikṣu obtains this robe, he should resolve in his mind and speak with his mouth:
"This cloth item was acquired by the Saṃgha; it should be divided, and it shall belong to me. I shall guard it, receive it, and use it."
"Acting in this manner is called obtaining the *karmavācanā*.
If other bhikṣus come, one must not forcibly demand [the robe].
If one does not act in this manner, that bhikṣu should not accept this robe."
If one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, it should likewise be shared with the other bhikṣus.
If one does not act in this manner, even upon leaving the boundary, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, which should likewise be shared with other bhikṣus.
If there are two bhikṣus staying in one residence, how should they divide [the requisites]?
They should divide them by mutual exchange and receive their own shares.
How is it done by mutual exchange?
One bhikṣu should speak thus: "These robes were given by these people for the sake of the Saṃgha;

as for all these robes, the Saṃgha should divide the items. Of this portion, such an amount is my share; I give this share to you, Venerable One. This share belongs to the Venerable One; may you guard it, receive it, and use it."
The second bhikṣu should also do likewise; this is called the "successive distribution.
What is called the "individual receipt"?
One bhikṣu should speak as follows:

"These robes were donated by various people for the sake of the Saṃgha; as for these robes which are to be distributed among the present members of the Saṃgha, such an amount from among these robe-cloths is yours—it belongs to you, it is for your protection, it is received by you, and it is for your use."
The second bhikṣu acts in the same manner; this is called "receiving one's own portion.
If one acts in this way, it is called "attaining the *karmavācanā*.
If other bhikṣus arrive, one must not forcibly demand [the portion].
If one does not act in this manner, that bhikṣu should not accept this robe; if he accepts it, he incurs the offense of duṣkṛta, and he must also share it with another bhikṣu.
If one does not go outside the boundary in this manner, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* (突吉羅), and [the property] should likewise be shared with other bhikṣus.
Suppose there are three bhikṣus at a single residence.
How is it divided?
Three bhikṣus should divide it by passing it around, or receive their own shares, or divide it by means of counting sticks (*śalākā*).
What is division by passing it around?
As explained above,
the same applies to the division by personal allotment (*svabhāga*).
What is the division by counting sticks (*śalākābhāga*)?
This robe shall be divided into two portions; it should be spoken thus:
"This portion belongs to the senior monk (sthavira); this portion belongs to the junior monk (navaka).
Furthermore, this portion belongs to the junior monk; this portion belongs to the senior monk."
When this has been done, one tally should be cast.
If another bhikṣu sees this, he should not cast another tally.
If he does cast one, the bhikṣus commit the offense of *dukkaṭa*, and that [share] should also be divided among the other bhikṣus.
If one does not act in this manner, upon leaving the boundary, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* (突吉羅); the property should be divided equally among the other bhikṣus.
Suppose there are four bhikṣus residing in a single dwelling place.
How should it be divided?
The four bhikṣus should divide it by mutual exchange, or by personal allotment, or by voting with tallies, or by formal monastic decree (*saṃgha-karman*).
Mutual exchange, personal allotment, and voting with tallies are also as explained above.
What is the division by *saṃgha-karman*?
The *saṃgha* should perform the *karman* to give this robe to one bhikṣu. Having assembled the *saṃgha* with a single mind, one bhikṣu within the *saṃgha* should announce:
"Venerable *saṃgha*, listen!"
This robe is an item that the resident monks of this dwelling place have acquired and should divide among themselves in their presence.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let the Sangha perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) regarding this robe and bestow it upon the monk so-and-so.
Thus it is announced.
[The motion for] the second *karmavācanā* is as follows:
"The Sangha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of bestowing this robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
"If a bhikṣu has received a robe through a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakarma), yet takes it and refuses to return it, saying:
'It was truly given as an offering; it was well-bestowed, well-received according to the Dharma, and the matter was properly settled—all this occurred within the Saṃgha. Why must it be reclaimed?'"
The Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu should instruct him thus:
'This giving is practiced for the sake of purity.'"
"If he returns it, that is well.
If he does not return it, one should take it by force.
He must be taught to repent for the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
At that time, the śrāmaṇeras came to claim their share of the robes, but the bhikṣus did not give them any, saying:

"The Buddha has stated that when robes are distributed upon the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (varṣā), a share is given to the śrāmaṇeras; that items required by a bhikṣu are shared with the śrāmaṇeras; and that robes obtained through specific causes and conditions are shared with the śrāmaṇeras. However, it has not been said that robes obtained outside the proper season (akāla-cīvara) are to be shared with the śrāmaṇeras."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It should be given.
The bhikṣus did not know how much should be given,
so they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a śrāmaṇera is either sitting or standing, and a donor gives a gift with his own hand in succession, it should belong to the śrāmaṇera.
If it is not given in this manner, one-fourth of the portion should be given to the śrāmaṇera."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
In a certain residence in the land of Kośala, a bhikṣu died; the bhikṣus did not know what should be done with his robes and bowl.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should grant it to a single bhikṣu through formal ritual action (karmavācanā)."
Regarding the *karmavācanā*: within a harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu proclaims:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

A certain bhikṣu has died. Whatever light personal belongings this bhikṣu possessed—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide these items; the Saṃgha, by means of a formal act (*karmavācanā*), shall give them to [the name of] a certain bhikṣu."

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: this bhikṣu named So-and-so has died; whatever light personal requisites this bhikṣu possessed—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide these items and, through a formal act (kamma), bestow them upon the bhikṣu named So-and-so.
Thus it was announced:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has died. Whatever light personal belongings this bhikṣu possessed—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide these items."

"Venerable Saṃgha, Bhikṣu so-and-so has died. Regarding the light personal belongings belonging to this Bhikṣu: if they are robes, the present Saṃgha should divide them; if they are not robes, the Saṃgha shall, by means of a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), give them to Bhikṣu so-and-so."

"Whichever elders consent that when a certain bhikṣu has died, his light personal requisites—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide these items and, through a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma), bestow them upon a certain bhikṣu."
"Venerable sirs, if you approve, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.

The Saṃgha has finished performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to bestow upon the bhikṣu named so-and-so, who has died, all his light personal belongings—whether robes or non-robes—from among the items to be distributed by the present Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"In a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣu died. After his robes and bowl had been distributed among the Saṃgha, the other bhikṣus asked:
'Who looked after this sick bhikṣu?'"
A certain bhikṣu said,
"I [do]. The Saṃgha said:
"Carry this dead man away.
The bhikṣu said,
"Venerable sir!"
"I am neither a caṇḍāla nor one afflicted with leprosy; my robes and bowl are to be divided among the Saṅgha. Why then would I carry away a dead man?
While this person was alive, he honored and loved me; I have already repaid him."
"Whoever among you desires this dead man may carry him away.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should first give the six items belonging to the monk who tended the sick; as for other light items, the Sangha should divide them, but heavy items should not be divided.
How are the six items of the attendant to be given?"
When the Saṃgha has assembled with a single mind, one bhikṣu among them should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

A certain bhikṣu has died. These six personal items belonging to that bhikṣu are to be divided by the present Saṃgha; the Saṃgha, through formal act (karmavācanā), grants them to the attendant who nursed him."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: a certain bhikṣu has died; the six personal belongings belonging to this bhikṣu should be divided by the present Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha shall, through formal motion (jñapti-karman), bestow them upon the attendant who cared for him.
Thus he makes the formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has died; the six personal effects belonging to this bhikṣu should be divided by the present Saṃgha."

"Venerable sirs, monk so-and-so has died; the six personal effects belonging to this deceased monk should be divided by the assembly of monks present here. The Saṃgha shall, through formal motion (jñapti-karman), bestow them upon the attendant who cared for him.

Which elders consent that, since monk so-and-so has died, his six personal effects should be divided by the assembly of monks present here, and that the Saṃgha shall, through formal motion, bestow them upon the attendant?"
"Venerable sirs, those who approve of this remain silent; those who do not approve may speak.

"The Saṃgha has approved that the six personal effects belonging to the deceased bhikṣu [named] so-and-so shall be divided by the present Saṃgha. The Saṃgha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of bestowing them upon the attendant. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."

"In a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣu died. The personal belongings of this bhikṣu had been deposited in various places. Once the Saṃgha had finished distributing the bhikṣu’s belongings among the monks present, they asked the bhikṣu who had attended to him:
'Who provided for and looked after [the deceased]? "
They replied, "We do. The Saṃgha said:
"You should go to those various places where [the robes] were deposited and request them.
When the attendants went to request them but could not obtain them, they began to quarrel and speak ill of one another. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The six items currently present should first be given to the attendant; the remaining light articles the Saṃgha should divide, but heavy articles should not be divided.
In a certain residence in the Kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣu died. This bhikṣu possessed many robes, many bowls, and much property, yet it was not known what kind of saṃghāṭī this bhikṣu had received.
What is the *uttarāsaṅga*?
What is the *antarvāsaka*?
What is the alms bowl?
"What is a water-strainer?
What is a sitting mat?
They reported these matters to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Who is the primary attendant?
The attendant should first ask the patient: [who is your primary attendant?]"
"What kind of saṃghāṭī do you receive?
What kind of uttarāsaṅga? What kind of antarvāsaka?"
What is the alms bowl?
What is the water-strainer?
What is the sitting mat (niṣīdana)?

If, after such a question has been asked, one gives the six types of requisites for living to the attendant, the remaining light items should be divided by the Saṃgha, while heavy items should not be divided.

If one does not ask in this manner, or if one does not know, or if one does not believe, and one gives the six types of requisites that are neither very good nor very bad, the remaining light items should be divided by the Saṃgha, while heavy items should not be divided.

In a certain monastery in the kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣu died. While the Saṃgha was dividing the robes and bowls of the deceased bhikṣu in front of his corpse, that deceased bhikṣu stirred and spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable elders! Upādhyāyas!"
"Do not divide my robes and bowl.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Do not divide [the belongings] immediately in front of the corpse.
Only when the corpse has been removed, or when the Saṃgha is at another location, should they be divided."
A novice monk studying under the patronage of the land of Kosala died; the bhikṣus did not know what to do with his robes and bowl.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"At the time of death, the robes and bowl should be divided among the monks present.
At a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, a śrāmaṇera died, and the bhikṣus did not know what should be done with his robes and bowl.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The inner and outer robes worn by him should be given to the attendant who nursed him; the remaining light articles should be divided among the Sangha, but heavy articles should not be divided."
How should it be granted?
When the Saṃgha has assembled with a single mind, one bhikṣu within the Saṃgha should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"Such-and-such a śrāmaṇera has died; these are the inner and outer robes belonging to this śrāmaṇera.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, grant that the inner and outer robes of the deceased śrāmaṇera be divided by the present Saṃgha, and that the Saṃgha, through formal motion and resolution (jñapti-karman), bestow them upon the attendant who cared for the sick."
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This śrāmaṇera named So-and-so has died. Whatever inner and outer robes belong to this śrāmaṇera are property to be divided among the present Saṃgha; the Saṃgha shall, by means of a formal act (karmavācanā), grant them to the attendant who cared for him."

"Whichever elders approve that the robes and outer garments of the deceased śrāmaṇera, which are to be distributed by the present Saṃgha as property, be given to the attendant through a formal act (karmavācanā) of the Saṃgha—let those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve should speak."

“The Saṃgha has granted the inner and outer robes belonging to the deceased śrāmaṇera so-and-so to the attendant; this is the property of the present Saṃgha that should be distributed. The Saṃgha has completed the formal act (karmavācanā) by granting it to the attendant. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held thus.”
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"There are items that may be divided and items that may not be divided.
Which are the items that may be divided?"
"What are the items that should not be divided?
The Buddha said:
"All fields and lands, all houses and dwellings, all beds, couches, and bedding, all fine carriages, all coarse carriages, half-decorated carriages, and sedan chairs should not be divided."

"No iron objects should be divided; except for cauldrons and jars with a capacity of two *dou* or less, which may be divided. Excluding bowls, small bowls, half-bowls, *kian-ts'ai*, small *kian-ts'ai*, hair-cutting razors, tongs and tweezers, nail-clippers, needle-shears, door-hooks, curved door-hooks, razor cases, impurity-scraping combs, nasal-irrigation tubes, irons, incense burners, incense bowls, robe-hangers, wall-hooks, ladles, and *chan-zhen* supports—apart from these aforementioned items, all other iron objects shall not be divided."

“None of the copper objects should be divided. With the exception of cauldrons and jars with a capacity of two *dou* or less, which may be divided; and with the exception of water basins, jar lids, knife sheaths, scrapers for removing grime, nasal syringes, irons, incense burners, incense bowls, clothing hooks, wall hooks, meditation weights, and spoons and bowl-rests—apart from these aforementioned items, none of the copper objects should be divided.”
"No stone objects should be divided, except for cauldrons and jars; those with a capacity of two *dou* or less may be divided.
Also included are water jars, basins, lids, scrapers for removing grime from water vessels, nasal syringes, irons, incense burners, incense-stand hooks, and meditation weights."
Excluding the aforementioned items, all stone objects should not be divided;
all crystal objects should not be divided, except for cooking pots, incense-bowl hooks, incense burners, and irons—the rest are as stated above.
“None of the earthenware items should be divided, with the exception of basins with a capacity of two *dou* or less, which may be divided.

These include: water jars, basin lids, bowls for water, small bowls, half-bowls, *kaiji* (small cooking vessels), small *kaiji*, knife sheaths, scrapers, nasal syringes, irons, incense burners, and meditation weights. Excluding these aforementioned items, all other earthenware vessels should not be divided.”

"All items made of shell should not be divided, with the exception of a knife case, a scraper for removing grime, a nasal syringe, an ironing board, a meditation weight, an incense burner, an incense spoon for the bowl, a robe hook, a medicine box, and a ladle-rest; these items made of shell should be divided. All other items should not be divided."
"All items made of ivory are also like this.

All items made of horn should not be divided; however, with the exception of those measuring half a *śu* or less, they may be divided. Excluding knife sheaths, robe hooks, wall hooks, ear-scrapers, nasal syringes, meditation weights, medicine boxes, and ladles for supporting bowls—all such items made of horn may be divided, while the remainder should not be divided."

"None of the leather articles should be divided, with the exception of bags for holding ghee or oil with a capacity of half a *śu* or less; however, the leather straps for binding sandals, the leather for boots, deer leather, tanned leather, and the leather used to wrap the heels and toes should be divided."

"None of the wooden articles should be divided, with the exception of basins holding two *śu* or less; water jars, washbasins, jar lids, knife sheaths, scrapers for removing stains, robe hooks, bowl hooks, wall hooks, bowl supports, and meditation weights—all such wooden articles may be divided, while all others should not be divided."
"None of the bamboo articles should be divided; however, with the exception of sunshades, fans, boxes, chests, mats, and staffs, these should be divided. None of the red ochre should be divided."
“Dyed robes, whether they have been boiled or not yet boiled, should not be divided.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“There is a residence where one bhikṣu who observes the precepts and one bhikṣu who has been expelled live together.”
If a monk who maintains the precepts dies, his robes and requisites belong to the suspended monk.
If a suspended monk dies, his robes and requisites belong to the monk who maintains the precepts.
If other expelled bhikṣus come, they should not be given [these things].
"In a single residence, there lived one bhikṣu who observed the precepts and two expelled bhikṣus together."
If a monk who maintains the precepts dies, his robes and requisites belong to the monk who has been suspended.
If a suspended monk dies, his robes and requisites belong to the monk who maintains the precepts.
If other expelled bhikṣus come, they should not be given [the property].
"In a single residence, one bhikṣu who observes the precepts and three expelled bhikṣus dwell together.
If the bhikṣu who observes the precepts dies, his robes and requisites belong to the expelled bhikṣus."
If a bhikkhu who has been expelled dies, his robes and requisites belong to the bhikkhu who observes the precepts.
If another expelled bhikkhu comes, they should not be given to him.
"In a certain residence, one bhikkhu who observes the precepts and four expelled bhikkhus lived together."
If a monk who maintains the precepts dies, his robes and personal effects belong to the monk who has been suspended.
If a monk who has been suspended dies, his robes and personal effects belong to the monk who maintains the precepts.
If other expelled bhikṣus come, one should not give [the robe] to them.
"In a certain residence, there are two bhikṣus who observe the precepts and one expelled bhikṣu;
or two bhikṣus who observe the precepts and two expelled bhikṣus."
Two monks who maintain the precepts and one monk who has been expelled;
two monks who maintain the precepts and four monks who have been expelled—these cases are also like this.
In a single residence, there are three monks who maintain the precepts and one monk who has been expelled;
Three bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and two bhikṣus who have been expelled;
three bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and three bhikṣus who have been expelled;
three bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and four bhikṣus who have been expelled—the same applies in these cases as well.
“In a single residence: four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and one bhikṣu who has been suspended;
four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and two bhikṣus who have been suspended;
four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and three bhikṣus who have been suspended.”
The same applies to four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts and four bhikṣus who have been expelled.
"In one residence, one expelled bhikṣu and one bhikṣu who maintains the precepts dwell together."
If a monk who has been expelled dies, his robes and personal effects belong to the monk who maintains the precepts.
If the monk who maintains the precepts dies, his robes and personal effects belong to the expelled monk.
If another monk who maintains the precepts arrives, they should be given to him.
One expelled bhikṣu and two bhikṣus who maintain the precepts;
one expelled bhikṣu and three bhikṣus who maintain the precepts;
one expelled bhikṣu and four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts—it is the same for these cases as well.
"In one residence: one expelled bhikṣu and one bhikṣu who guards the precepts;
two expelled bhikṣus and two bhikṣus who guard the precepts;
two expelled bhikṣus and three bhikṣus who guard the precepts."
The same applies when there are two bhikṣus who have been expelled and four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts.
In a single residence, there may be three expelled bhikṣus and one bhikṣu who maintains the precepts;
or three expelled bhikṣus and two bhikṣus who maintain the precepts.
Three bhikṣus who have been suspended and three bhikṣus who maintain the precepts;
three bhikṣus who have been suspended and four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts, are also like this.
In a single residence, there are four bhikṣus who have been suspended and one bhikṣu who maintains the precepts.
Four expelled bhikṣus and two bhikṣus who maintain the precepts;
four expelled bhikṣus and three bhikṣus who maintain the precepts;
four expelled bhikṣus and four bhikṣus who maintain the precepts—it is the same for these cases as well.
In a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, two bhikṣus were dwelling; one bhikṣu died.
This remaining bhikṣu reflected thus:
"The Buddha has taught in the Vinaya:..."
"When a bhikṣu dies, the robes and bowl belonging to him should be divided among the Saṃgha present there.
Since I am but a single person and not the Saṃgha, I shall go to the Buddha and ask:
'To whom should these robes and bowl belong?'"
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. After a short while, he withdrew from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
We two bhikṣus were residing in the kingdom of Kośala; one of us has died.”
I reflected thus:
"In the Buddha's Vinaya it is said:
'When a bhikṣu dies, his robes, bowl, and belongings should be divided among the monks present.'"
"I am but a single person, not the Saṃgha.
Now I ask the World-Honored One:
"To whom should these robes and bowls belong?"
The Buddha said: "There were two bhikṣus living together in one place. When one bhikṣu died, at the very moment of his death, the remaining bhikṣu should reflect in his mind and speak these words:

'Bhikṣu So-and-so has died. This bhikṣu possessed such and such light personal requisites—whether robes or non-robes—which are items to be distributed among the present Saṃgha. These items belong to me; I shall guard them, receive them, and use them.'"
When the *karmavācanā* has been performed in this manner, if another bhikṣu arrives, he may not be forced to surrender [the items].
If it is not performed in this way, the robes and bowl of that bhikṣu should not be accepted;
if they are accepted, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*, and they must also be shared with the other bhikṣus.
If one does not depart from the boundary in this manner, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; furthermore, the [deceased monk's] portion should also be shared with other monks.
Suppose there are three monks at a single residence, and one monk dies.
Regarding these two bhikṣus and their robes and bowls, they may either distribute them by successive transfer or receive them as their own portions.
What is meant by "successive transfer"?
One bhikṣu should reflect and say as follows:
"Elder! A certain bhikṣu has died; this bhikṣu possessed such-and-such light personal requisites, whether robes or non-robes. The present Saṃgha should divide these items."
"This much portion of the goods belongs to me;
this portion is given to you, Venerable One; this portion you shall protect, receive, and use for yourself.
The second bhikṣu also thought in the same way:
"Venerable sirs!
A certain bhikṣu has died; this bhikṣu possessed such-and-such light personal belongings, whether robes or non-robes, which the present Saṃgha should divide."
"This much portion of the goods belongs to me;
this portion is given to you, Venerable One; this portion you shall protect yourself, receive yourself, and use yourself.
This is called "successive distribution."
What is the portion for one's own consumption?
A single bhikṣu should reflect and say:
"Venerable sir!..."
A certain bhikṣu has died; this bhikṣu possessed such light personal effects, whether robes or non-robes, which the present saṃgha should divide.
"This much portion of goods belongs to you; this portion, Elder, is for your own protection, your own acceptance, and your own use.
The second bhikṣu also spoke and thought in the same way: "Elder!"
"A certain bhikṣu has died; this bhikṣu possessed such-and-such light articles of livelihood, whether robes or non-robes; the present community of monks (saṃgha) should divide these items."
"This portion of goods belonging to you is of such an amount; this portion, Elder, is for your own protection, your own acceptance, and your own use.
This is called "accepting one's own portion.
Once it has been thus finalized, if another bhikṣu arrives, he may not forcibly demand it.
If one does not act in this manner, that bhikṣu should not accept the robe;
if he accepts it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense, and it must also be shared with another bhikṣu.
In this way, one who does not participate incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for leaving the boundary; furthermore, [the property] should be divided among the other monks.
"If four monks reside in one place and one monk dies, the remaining three monks may divide it by passing it around, or receive their shares directly, or divide it by casting lots."
The sequential distribution and the individual allotment are as explained above.
What is the distribution by counting sticks (*śalākā*)?
The robes and bowls are to be divided into two portions, and one should speak as follows:
"This portion belongs to the senior monk; this portion belongs to the junior monk.
If it belongs to the junior monk, it belongs to the senior monk.
When he has thus finished, one tally should fall, yet another monk sees that it should not have fallen.
If the second tally is cast, the bhikṣus have committed a duṣkṛta offense; it should likewise be shared among the other bhikṣus.
If they do not act in this manner, they commit a duṣkṛta offense upon leaving the boundary; it should likewise be shared among the other bhikṣus.

If five bhikṣus reside in one dwelling place and one bhikṣu dies, the remaining four bhikṣus shall divide his robes and bowl-articles either by successive distribution, by individual allotment, by voting with tally-sticks, or by formal ritual action (karmavācanā).
The distribution by successive transfer, the distribution for personal use, and the distribution by voting sticks are as explained above.
What is the distribution by formal ritual (*karmavācanā*)?
Regarding these robes and bowls, the Saṃgha should perform a formal ritual to bestow them upon a single bhikṣu.
When the Saṃgha has assembled with a single mind, one bhikṣu among them should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Bhikṣu so-and-so has died, leaving behind such-and-such light personal effects, whether robes or non-robes; the present Saṃgha should divide these items."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: there are such-and-such light articles of livelihood belonging to the bhikṣu so-and-so—whether robes or non-robes—which the present Saṃgha should divide; the Saṃgha shall now perform the *karmavācanā* and grant them to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Thus it is announced. The formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is performed as follows:

"The Saṃgha has already granted the *karman* to the bhikṣu so-and-so; that bhikṣu has died. Whatever light personal requisites this bhikṣu possessed—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide these items. The Saṃgha has completed the *karman* by granting [the items] to the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
“The Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā* to grant this robe, bowl, and property to a bhikṣu. This bhikṣu accepted it himself but refuses to return it, saying:
‘The entire Saṃgha has granted it according to the Dharma, taken it according to the Dharma, sworn according to the Dharma, and concluded the discourse according to the Dharma.’”
"Why do you now seek it back?
The Buddha said,
"One should speak thus:"
"O Bhikṣu! Since this was given out of purity, you should return it to the Saṃgha.
If it is returned, that is well.
"If he does not return it, you should take it by force and instruct him to repent for the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
When the śrāmaṇeras came to claim their share of these robes, the bhikṣus did not give them. The Buddha said: "The share of the *pravāraṇā* robe should be given;

the share of items belonging to the bhikṣus according to the Dharma should be given; the share of robes obtained through special circumstances should be given; and the share of out-of-season robes should be given."
The Buddha had not yet spoken regarding the distribution of the robes of a deceased bhikṣu; therefore, this matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to give them."
The bhikṣus did not know how much to give.
The Buddha said:
"It should be divided into four parts; the fourth part should be given to the śrāmaṇeras."
The Buddha said,
“Monks! There is a monk who upholds the Dharma dwelling among monks who do not uphold the Dharma.”
When a bhikkhu who upholds the Dharma dies, the bhikkhus who do not uphold the Dharma send a messenger to the place where the bhikkhus who uphold the Dharma are, saying:
"A certain bhikkhu among you has died here; take his robes and bowl."
If the bhikṣus who follow the Dharma take it away, that is well.
If they do not take it, it should be used for the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha’s lodgings in the four directions.
If a bhikṣu who does not follow the Dharma stays among the bhikṣus who follow the Dharma...
If one dies, a Dharma-upholding bhikṣu shall send a messenger to where the non-Dharma-upholding bhikṣus reside, saying:
"A certain bhikṣu among you has died here; take his robes and bowl."
"It would be well if those bhikṣus who do not accept the Dharma were to take it away.
If they do not take it with them, it should be used to repair the lodgings and bedding of the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Then, the bhikṣus who accept the Dharma, having expelled one bhikṣu, went to where the bhikṣus who do not accept the Dharma were and said:
"Venerable sirs!
Having removed my offenses and attained purification, I shall practice the 'not-taking-up' dharma.
If he dies before his offenses have been removed, the monks who received the dharma should return his robes and bowl.
If one dies after having had their offense removed, their robes and bowl belong to those bhikṣus who do not accept the Dharma.
"There are certain bhikṣus who do not accept the Dharma who have expelled a bhikṣu; that bhikṣu then goes to where the bhikṣus who do accept the Dharma are and says:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"Having cleared away my offenses and attained purification, I shall receive the Dharma.
If he dies before his offenses have been cleared, his robes and bowl belong to those bhikṣus who do not receive the Dharma.
"If one dies having been cleared of an offense, his robes and bowl should belong to those bhikṣus who have received the legal authorization.
There was a bhikṣu who had robes that ought to be relinquished; this bhikṣu gave them to the group of six bhikṣus.
The group of six bhikṣus took [the requisites] for their own use and refused to return them.
At that time, there were other bhikṣus who were distressed, as they could not find pure and trustworthy bhikṣus.

In the month following the summer retreat, the Buddha was traveling through various countries. While the other bhikṣus were wearing newly dyed robes, this particular bhikṣu was wearing worn-out, tattered clothes.
When the Buddha saw this bhikṣu, he knew the reason but asked him nonetheless:
"Why are you wearing such worn-out and tattered clothes?"
He replied,
"I have a robe that ought to be relinquished, which I gave to the group of six bhikṣus.
The group of six bhikṣus took it for their own use and refused to return it to me."
Furthermore, there were other bhikṣus who suffered from affliction and were unable to obtain a pure and trustworthy bhikṣu to give [the robe] to them.
The Buddha said:
"If it is given as an act of pure generosity, the bhikṣu at that time should immediately take it back."
"If one has taken something that is good, and it is not being returned, one should forcibly seize it back and instruct the person to repent for the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], he rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and returned. That night, he prepared many kinds of pure and exquisite food and drink. At dawn, having arranged the seating places, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time."
The Buddha himself remained in his room to receive his portion of the meal while the entire Saṃgha entered the householder’s residence; Ānanda delivered the Buddha’s portion.
There are five causes and conditions for which the Buddha remains in the vihāra to receive his portion of the meal.
What are the five?
First, when wishing to enter meditative concentration;
second, when wishing to preach the Dharma for the sake of the devas.
Third, wandering to view the various rooms;
fourth, attending to a sick bhikṣu;
fifth, desiring to establish a precept that has not yet been established.
The Buddha knew that the bhikṣus had entered the house of a layperson and, taking the door-latch, were inspecting all the rooms; he saw that at one dwelling the door-panels were open.
A sick bhikṣu, suffering in pain without a companion, was lying in his own excrement and urine.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked the sick bhikṣu:
"What affliction do you suffer that you have no one to attend to you, lying here upon your own excrement and urine?
The bhikṣu, being loyal and upright, truthfully informed the Buddha of his condition:
"Venerable sir!
By nature I am indolent; when others have business, I do not assist them.
Now that I am ill, others likewise do not look after me."
The Buddha thought to himself:
"This faithful son of good family— I shall stroke his body with my hand.
At that moment, the Buddha immediately stroked him with his hand; as he was being stroked, the bhikṣu’s suffering was instantly healed, and his body and mind became peaceful and blissful.

The Buddha gently assisted him in rising, helped him put on his robes, and led him out of the room; he then gently assisted him in sitting down and washed him, handing him a clean robe for him to wear.
As for the soiled items, he washed, wrung, and dried them; returning inside, he gently set aside the impurities of mucus and spittle, removed the grass mats, and sprinkled and swept the floor.
Having further spread out a layer of grass bedding, he gently helped him up, dressed him, and led him into the room; he then assisted him to sit upon the grass bedding.
He addressed the sick bhikṣu:
"If you do not strive diligently for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, reaching what has not yet been reached, and realizing what has not yet been realized..."
"You shall experience suffering for as long as that time, and it shall be even more intense than this.
The bhikṣu also thought to himself:
"Now, by the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, he has rubbed my body with his hand."
"As soon as he applied his hand, my bodily pain was immediately healed, and my body and mind became peaceful and joyful.

This bhikṣu, mindful of the Buddha’s great kindness, gave rise to a wholesome mind; attaining pure faith, he established various vows. Reverencing the Buddha’s merits, he restrained his thoughts and focused his mind one-pointedly upon the Buddha.
The Buddha, in accordance with the monk’s disposition, skillfully expounded the Dharma for him; while seated upon a grass mat, the monk attained arhatship by not grasping at any phenomena.

Having established this bhikṣu as foremost among those who have exhausted their outflows, the Buddha emerged from that room, closed the door, descended from the stairs, returned to his own room, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down cross-legged.

At that time, when the householder saw that the assembly of monks was seated, he rose from his seat, personally provided water for washing, and served various foods and drinks according to their needs.
When the meal was finished, having washed his hands and set aside his bowl, he took a small stool and sat before the Sangha, desiring to listen to the teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu, having finished preaching the Dharma, returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when the bhikṣus have returned from their midday meal, they ask the bhikṣus:
"Was the food delicious? Did the Saṃgha receive its fill?"
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable sir,
the food was delicious and we are fully satiated."
When the bhikṣus returned from their meal, the World-Honored One questioned them as follows:
"Was the food delicious?
Was the Saṃgha satisfied?"
The bhikṣus said,
"Venerable sir,
the food was delicious and we are fully satiated."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Today, as I took my key and went to inspect all the rooms, I saw a sick bhikṣu whose illness was so acute with pain that he lay alone without anyone to look after him, immersed in his own excrement and urine."
"O bhikṣus! This is not right;
why do you not look after one another and provide for one another?
Having entered into my Dharma, you have no parents or brothers; if you do not look after one another, who then shall look after you?"
After the Buddha had rebuked the bhikṣus with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should attend to those who are ill.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
“Who should provide for and attend to the sick?
The Buddha said:
“The upādhyāya and the ācārya;”
The same applies to fellow *upādhyāyas* and fellow *ācāryas*.
If these four types of persons are unavailable, the Saṃgha should provide for them.
If the Saṃgha does not provide for them, the Saṃgha incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If the Saṃgha appoints someone and that person is unwilling to go, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
From this day forward, the rule for bhikṣus who attend to the sick shall be established.

As for the method of attending to the sick: one should act according to whatever the patient requires; from time to time, one should go to the side of the patient and inquire about the causes and conditions of their illness.

Having inquired about the causes and conditions of the illness, one then asks the physician, or the bhikṣu who understands the illness, or the bhikṣu who has seen the illness: "By what medicine will this be cured?"
If the physician instructs that a certain medicine should be taken, one should go to the kitchen the following day to see what food the monks are preparing;
if there is anything suitable for the illness, the attendant should then proceed [to the sick person].
If there is no food provided specifically for the sick, one should take what is supplied by the Saṃgha to provide for that patient.
If such things are not available in that residence, one should request supplies from a virtuous and worthy bhikṣu to provide for the patient.
If these things are not available, one should seek them from a learned and virtuous bhikṣu.

If these are also not available, one should leave behind the six items belonging to the sick bhikṣu; as for his other belongings, they should be exchanged for what is required to provide for the patient.

If such things are not available, one may exchange the heavy object received for a light object and take possession of it; having obtained money, one may seek what is required to provide for the sick.
If such things are not available, one may exchange the iron bowl received for a clay bowl and take possession of it; having obtained money, one may purchase what is required to provide for the sick.
If these things are not available, the caregiver should provide them themselves.
If they do not have them themselves, they should beg from others to supply the patient.
If there are no acquaintances from whom they can obtain them by begging, they should beg for choice food and provide it to the patient.

The monk who attends to the sick should go to the bedside of the patient from time to time and expound the profound Dharma for him, so as to awaken his wisdom regarding what is the path and what is not the path.
In this manner, the sick monk may expound the Dharma according to his inclination.
If it is a case of illness among those in the forest retreat (āraṇyaka), one should praise the qualities of the forest retreat in their presence.
If they are studying the Sūtras, one should praise the study of the Sūtras in their presence.
If one studies the Vinaya, one should praise the Vinaya in their presence.
If one is a master of the Dharma, one should praise the Abhidharma in their presence.
If one assists in communal affairs, one should praise the assistance rendered in communal affairs.

If there is a person of great virtue known to many, one should ask about the characteristics of the first stage, the second, the third, and the fourth stages, as well as the fruits ranging from that of a *srotāpanna* up to that of an *arhat*.

If he has died, after providing for his funeral needs according to his merit, one should wash any robes that require washing, wring them out, dry them in the sun, roll and fold them, and then carry them slowly into the midst of the Saṃgha. One should announce it thus:

"A certain bhikṣu has died; these are that bhikṣu’s saṃghāṭī, these are his uttarāsaṅga, these are his antarvāsaka, this is his bowl, this is his water-strainer, this is his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and these are his other requisites. By means of these, he has attained such a superior rebirth."
The Buddha said:
"There are three kinds of sick people:

there are those who, whether they obtain or do not obtain food and drink appropriate to their illness; whether they obtain or do not obtain medicine appropriate to their illness; or whether they obtain or do not obtain a nurse according to their needs—cannot recover."

“Suppose there is a sick person who, whether they obtain food and drink suited to their illness or not, whether they obtain medicine appropriate for their illness or not, and whether they obtain a nurse who attends to them as desired or not, is still able to recover.”
"Suppose there is a sick person who would recover if they obtain food and drink suitable to their illness, but would die if they do not;
or who would recover if they obtain medicine appropriate to their illness, but would die if they do not;
or who would recover if they obtain a nurse according to their wishes, but would die if they do not."
Because of these illnesses, I permit the tending of the sick. It is also good to provide for and support those of the two aforementioned types of patients.
There are five difficulties in tending to the sick.
What are the five?
First, being of a wicked nature such that one cannot converse with them;
second, instructing a caregiver who does not believe or accept the instructions.
Third, consuming food and drink that is unsuitable for one's illness while failing to know how to moderate one's intake;
fourth, being unwilling to take medicine;
fifth, being unable to exercise self-restraint and moderation.
There are these five qualities by which a patient is difficult to care for.
There are five matters by which a patient is easy to care for.
What are the five?
First, not having a malicious nature;
second, being able to believe and accept the instructions of the caregiver;
third, distinguishing between what should and should not be eaten according to the specific illness.
Fourth, he is able to take medicine himself;
fifth, he is able to exercise self-restraint and moderation in his intake.
A patient who possesses these five qualities is easy to care for.
There are five qualities by which a patient-caregiver is unable to provide care.
What are the five?
First, they have a malicious nature and cannot be spoken with.
Second, when instructed by a patient, they do not follow their words;
third, they do not distinguish between what should and should not be eaten according to the illness;
fourth, they are unable to seek medicine from others for the sake of the patient.
Fifth, being unable to endure.
One who possesses these five qualities is unable to care for a sick person.
There are five qualities by which one is able to care for a sick person:
First, one is not of a malicious nature and is capable of conversing with others;
second, when a patient is instructed, they follow those instructions immediately;
third, one is able to know the appropriate food and drink for a given illness, as well as what should be eaten and what should not be eaten.
Fourth, one is able to seek medicine for the sick person from others;
fifth, one is able to endure.
Possessing these five qualities, one is able to attend to the sick.
“There are five qualities by which a patient is difficult to attend to.
What are the five?
First, he is of evil character and cannot be spoken to.”
Second, they do not understand that all illnesses arise and cease in accordance with impermanence;
third, when illness arises within the body, its bitterness and suffering bring no joy, and because it threatens their life-force, they are unable to endure it;
fourth, they seek all pleasures from others, and though they have the slight capacity to act for themselves, they do not do so.

Within the five aggregates of clinging, one does not contemplate their arising and ceasing, nor does one contemplate: "This is the aggregate of form, this is the origin of the aggregate of form, this is the cessation of the aggregate of form"; "this is the aggregate of feeling, this is the aggregate of perception, this is the aggregate of formations"; "this is the aggregate of consciousness, this is the origin of the aggregate of consciousness, this is the cessation of the aggregate of consciousness."
There are five qualities by which a patient is difficult to care for,
and five qualities by which a patient is easy to care for.
What are these five?
First, one is not of a malicious nature and is capable of engaging in conversation;
second, one knows how all pains arise and cease, contemplating their impermanence;
third, when illness arises within the body—characterized by hardship, acute pain, and distress that threatens life—one is able to endure it with patience.
Fourth, one does not seek even a small thing from others, being able to perform tasks oneself;

fifth, one is able to contemplate the arising and ceasing within the five aggregates of clinging: "This is the aggregate of form, this is the origin of the aggregate of form, this is the cessation of the aggregate of form"; "This is the aggregate of feeling, this is the aggregate of perception, this is the aggregate of formations"; "This is the aggregate of consciousness, this is the origin of the aggregate of consciousness, this is the cessation of the aggregate of consciousness."
"There are these five qualities by which a patient is easy to care for.
Furthermore, there are five qualities by which a caregiver is unable to provide care.
What are these five?"
First, they are of a wicked nature and cannot be spoken to;
second, when there is much excrement and urine from many sick people, or when entering and exiting with earthen bowls and spittoons, or when spitting, they are displeased;
third, they seek wealth, goods, food, and drink for their own sake and not for the sake of the Dharma.

Within the four or five aggregates of clinging, one is unable to contemplate their arising and ceasing, nor [discern]: "This is the aggregate of form; this is the habitual tendency of the aggregate of form; this is the exhaustion of the aggregate of form. Likewise for the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness: "This is the aggregate of consciousness; this is the habitual tendency of the aggregate of consciousness; this is the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness."

Fifth, being unable to go to the bedside of the patient at the appropriate time to expound the profound and wondrous Dharma, to show what is the path and what is not the path, and to generate wisdom in them—
this is the fifth factor by which one is unable to nurse the sick.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If a bhikṣu sends another bhikṣu to give a robe to a third bhikṣu,
and the bhikṣu to whom the robe was sent dies, and the one who takes it from the deceased bhikṣu does so with his consent, this is an improper taking.”
To accept clothing from one who is deceased is an improper acceptance.
If the original owner is still alive and takes it with their consent, it is a proper taking.
To accept long robes is a proper acceptance.
There was a bhikṣu who sent another bhikṣu to give a robe to a third bhikṣu.
The original owner died, and [the recipient] took it with the consent of those present; this is an improper acquisition.
He accepted the robe belonging to the deceased; this is an improper acceptance.
"To take what has been given to a living bhikṣu with his consent is a proper taking.
To receive an extra robe (cīvara) [in this manner] is a proper reception.
This concludes the seventh rule concerning robes within the Seven Rules. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Volume 28.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Twenty-nine, Part One of the Fifth Recitation, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
Section Ten: The Eight Dharmas; Chapter One: The Rules for the Kaṭhina Robe. Among the Eight Dharmas, this is the First: The Rules for the Kaṭhina Robe.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat in the kingdom of Saṃjaya; having finished the three-month period and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and having completed the making of their robes, they took up their robes and bowls and headed toward Śrāvastī, traveling along a road where there was much rain and muddy water.

Because of the heavy rains and muddy water, those bhikṣus were extremely exhausted and distressed by the hot wind; they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with these words of inquiry:
"Are you patient?
Are you well?"
"Was your summer retreat pleasant?
Did you not lack for almsfood, and were you not fatigued by the roads?
Thus did the Buddha inquire after the welfare of the bhikṣus.
"Are you patient?
Are you content?
Is your summer retreat peaceful and happy?"
“Is there no lack of almsfood, and are you not fatigued by the journey?
The bhikṣus replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"You have spent the rains retreat contentedly with few desires, obtained alms-food without lack,
yet you are utterly exhausted from the journey. The Buddha asked the bhikṣus,
"In what way did you spend the rains retreat contentedly with few desires, obtain alms-food without lack, yet remain utterly exhausted from the journey?"
The bhikṣus replied:

"We were in retreat during the summer rains in the kingdom of Saṃkāśya. Having completed the three months and finished the *pravāraṇā*, we made our robes and set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī carrying our bowls and robes. On the way, because of the rain and the abundance of mud and water, we were greatly distressed by hot winds and became utterly exhausted."
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, you have indeed endured the rains retreat with contentment and joy; your alms-seeking has not been lacking, and your exhaustion from the roads is great.
From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to assemble in one place after the rains retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony to receive the *kaṭhina* robe."
For one who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, even their previous robes are not lost, let alone new ones.
As for the method of accepting the *kaṭhina*, the Saṃgha, being united in a single mind, accepts it on the day they obtain the cloth.
What is meant by "the day one obtains the robe"?
If one obtains the robe on the first day of the month, one receives it on that very day.
If one obtains it on the second day, or the third day, and so on up to the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is likewise.
A single bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the Saṃgha, being in harmony, shall accept the kaṭhina robe."
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha receive the kaṭhina robe.
Thus is the motion.
One should first appoint a person to receive the kaṭhina robe and should ask him:
"Who is able to act as the person for the Saṃgha to receive the kaṭhina robe?
If among them a single bhikṣu says,
"I am able."
The Buddha said:
"If there are five qualities, one should not be appointed as the person who receives the kaṭhina robe.
What are these five?
If one follows desire, follows hatred, follows fear, follows delusion, or does not know what has been accepted or not accepted— if one possesses these five qualities,
one should not be appointed as the person who accepts the *kaṭhina* robe.

If one does not follow desire, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, does not follow delusion, and knows what has been accepted or not accepted— if one possesses these [five] qualities, one should be appointed as the person who accepts the *kaṭhina* robe.
In this regard, one bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so is capable of acting as the person for the Saṃgha to receive the kaṭhina robe."
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person to receive the kaṭhina robe.
This is the formal motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The monk so-and-so is capable of acting as the receiver of the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now appoints so-and-so to act as the receiver of the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha.
"Whichever elders among you approve of appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so as the receiver of the kaṭhina cloth for the Saṃgha, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak up.
"The Saṃgha has finished appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so as the receiver of the kaṭhina cloth for the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

"At that time, if the Saṃgha first receives a gift of robes, the monks who have entered the rains retreat (*varṣā*) should divide them; these robes should be bestowed through a formal act of the Saṃgha (*karmavācanā*).
The person receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, acting according to the Dharma, shall, with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, have one bhikṣu in the midst of the assembly proclaim:
'May the venerable Saṃgha listen!'"
The Saṃgha of this residence has obtained these donated robes; they should be distributed among the monks who have completed the rains retreat.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to grant these robes to a certain monk, so that he may use them as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain them without being separated from this residence.
Thus he makes the formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This dwelling-place has received this gift of robes; it shall be distributed among the monks who have observed the rains retreat."

The Saṃgha performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to grant this robe to the bhikṣu [Name], so that the Saṃgha may make it into a *kaṭhina* robe and he may accept and maintain it without being separated from this dwelling place.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s formal act of granting this robe to the bhikṣu [Name] to make it into a *kaṭhina* robe for him to accept and maintain without being separated from this dwelling place, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.

"The Saṃgha has performed the *karmavācanā* by granting this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so to serve as his *kaṭhina* robe; he shall maintain it without being separated from this residence. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"At that time, together with the four capable ones—namely, the bhikṣus who wash, dye, cut, pin, and stitch—he should measure it with care.
When washing, he should give rise to this thought:
'With this robe, I shall make a kaṭhina robe and accept it.'"
When dyeing, cutting, sewing, embroidering, and measuring it for the sake of comfort, he should form this thought:
"I shall accept this robe as a *kaṭhina* robe."
If these six thoughts arise, it is called properly making the kaṭhina robe;
if these six thoughts do not arise, it is not called properly making the kaṭhina robe.
Furthermore, there are three thoughts:
"I shall accept this robe as a *kaṭhina* robe; I am now accepting this robe as a *kaṭhina* robe; I have finished accepting this robe as a *kaṭhina* robe."
"If these three thoughts arise, it is called properly making the kaṭhina robe;
if these three thoughts do not arise, it is not called properly making the kaṭhina robe."
Furthermore, there are two thoughts:
"I shall accept this robe as a kaṭhina robe," and "I have finished accepting this robe as a kaṭhina robe."
If these two thoughts arise, it is called the proper performance of the kaṭhina robe ceremony.
If these two thoughts are absent, the person who performs the kaṭhina ceremony incurs the offense of duṣkṛta.
At that time, the Elder Upāli bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
what is called the procedure for receiving the kaṭhina robe?"
The Buddha said:

"One who acts as the receiver of the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha should wash it with a single-minded focus, dye it with a single-minded focus, cut it with a single-minded focus, pin it with a single-minded focus, stitch it with a single-minded focus, and measure it with a single-minded focus on its secure dimensions."
When the person making the *kaṭhina* robe washes this cloth, they should form this thought:
"With this cloth, I shall make and receive the *kaṭhina*.
At the time of dyeing, at the time of cutting, at the time of pinning, at the time of sewing, and at the time of measuring for the dimensions, they should in all cases form this same thought.
"By means of this robe, I shall perform the formal acceptance of the kaṭhina.
If this bhikṣu gives rise to these six thoughts, it is called the proper performance of the kaṭhina.
If these six states of mind are absent, it is not called the proper performance of the kaṭhina robe.
Furthermore, there are three states of mind:
one forms the thought, "I shall accept this robe as the kaṭhina robe; I am now accepting this robe as the kaṭhina robe; I have finished accepting this robe as the kaṭhina robe."
If this bhikṣu gives rise to these three thoughts, it is called the proper making of the kaṭhina robe;
if he lacks these three thoughts, it is not called the proper making of the kaṭhina robe.
Furthermore, one should give rise to two thoughts, forming this reflection:
"I accept this robe as the kaṭhina robe; I have finished accepting this robe as the kaṭhina robe."
If a bhikṣu gives rise to these two thoughts, he is said to have properly performed the kaṭhina ceremony.
If one performs the kaṭhina ceremony without these two thoughts, one incurs the offense of duṣkṛta.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"It is not merely by measuring that one is said to receive the kaṭhina robe.
