It is not merely by dyeing, nor merely by the border, nor merely by marking the four corners, nor merely by making the leaf-edges, nor merely by pinning it together; therefore, it is called receiving the kaṭhina robe."
If one uses old or worn-out robes to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is not called "acceptance.
If one has already previously accepted [the robe] as a *kaṭhina* robe, and now accepts it again, it is not called "acceptance."
If one uses a robe that is not of the proper season to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is not called "accepted.
If one dyes it with the color of *uragasāra* gold to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is not called "accepted."
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe from cloth that has been kept overnight, it is not called "acceptance.
If one does not accept the *kaṭhina* robe with a resolute mind, it is not called "acceptance."
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe from impure cloth, it is not called "accepted.
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe that is less than the prescribed measure, it is not called "accepted."
If one makes a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, or an *antarvāsaka* that is of reduced measurement as a *kaṭhina* robe, it is not called "accepted."
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe out of an uncut garment, it is not called "acceptance.
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe out of an uncut *saṃghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, or *antarvāsaka*, it is not called "acceptance."
If the making of the *kaṭhina* robe is not yet finished, it is not called "having accepted" (*pratigraha*).

If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe using the robes of another monk, a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*), a male novice (*śrāmaṇera*), or a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*), it is not called "having accepted."
The Buddha said to Upāli:

“If, on the day the Saṃgha formally accepts the kaṭhina robe according to the Dharma, a bhikṣu who has been away from his summer retreat returns and hears that the kaṭhina has already been accepted, yet does not express his approval, this person shall not be considered as having received the kaṭhina.”
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"This is called the formal acceptance of the kaṭhina robe.
If one obtains a robe offered in haste and uses it as a kaṭhina robe, this is called a proper acceptance."
If one uses a used robe to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is called "properly received.
If one uses a new robe to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is called "properly received."
If one uses cloth that has been kept overnight to make the kaṭhina robe, it is called "properly received.
If one uses pure cloth to make the kaṭhina robe, it is called "properly received."
If one uses a purified robe (*pāriśuddhika-cīvara*) to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is called "properly received.
If one uses a cut-and-sewn *saṃghāṭī*, *uttarāsaṅga*, or *antarvāsaka* to make a *kaṭhina* robe, it is called "properly received."
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe using patches of cloth, it is called "properly received.
If one makes a *kaṭhina* robe using the robes of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is called "properly received."
The Buddha said to Upāli:

"If, on the day the Saṃgha formally accepts the kaṭhina robe according to the Dharma, there is a bhikṣu who was in retreat and has gone outside the boundary, but returns that very day; having heard that the kaṭhina has been accepted, he rejoices and complies with it—such a person is said to have properly accepted [the kaṭhina]."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe’?”
The Buddha said:
“There are eight matters that constitute the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe.
What are the eight?
First, when the robe is completed;
second, when the robe is nearly completed;
third, at the time of departure.
Fourth is the time of hearing;
fifth is the time of loss;
sixth is the time of generating the resolve.
Seventh, the lapse of the time limit;
eighth, the relinquishment.
Regarding the first six: suppose there is a person who has received the *kaṭhina* robe and takes his own robes outside the boundary, thinking to himself:
"I shall not return here to make this robe.
When he departs, it is said that he has relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe.
Suppose someone accepts the *kaṭhina* robe and, taking all his robes with him, goes beyond the boundary, thinking:
"I shall not return to this place to make the robe.
After that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I shall not return to that place, nor shall I make the robe there."
"Upon departing, one is said to have relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe.
Suppose there is someone who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe and, taking his robes with him, goes beyond the boundary, thinking:
'I shall not return to this place to make my robes.'"
If one makes a robe outside the boundary while thinking,
"I shall not return to that place," then at the moment the robe is completed, it is said that the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished.
Suppose there is a person who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe and takes his own robes beyond the boundary, thinking:
"I shall not return to this place to make my robes.

This person makes the robes outside the boundary; having finished making them, because he does not guard them well, they are lost. Since he has no other material to work with, at the moment he loses the robes, it is said that he relinquishes the *kaṭhina*.
Suppose there is a person who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe and takes his own robes outside the boundary, thinking:
"I shall return to this place to make my robes.
Having gone outside the boundary, he makes the robes there; whether they are finished or not yet finished, he thinks:
"I shall return to my original place and perform it slowly.
If, after a long time, it is not completed and the person passes the limit of the designated period, it is called "abandoning the kaṭhina robe."
"Suppose there is a person who has accepted the kaṭhina robe and, taking his robes with him, goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall return to this place to make my robes.'"
Having heard outside the boundary that the Saṃgha had already relinquished the kaṭhina robe, he immediately thought:
"The kaṭhina robe has been relinquished; I shall no longer return."
This is called "renouncing the *kaṭhina* robe by hearing [the announcement].
Suppose there is someone who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe and takes his robes with him to go outside the boundary, thinking:
"I shall return to this place to make my robes."
He then makes the robe outside the boundary; whether that robe is finished or not, he thinks:
"I have returned to my original place and have not yet relinquished the kaṭhina."
"Having arrived, he relinquishes the *kaṭhina* robe together with the Saṃgha; this is called 'relinquishment.
This is the first set of six.

"The second set of six is as follows: If a bhikṣu, after having received the *kaṭhina* robe, has finished making a certain number of *vipāla* robes and takes his remaining robes out of the boundary, he forms this thought:"
"I shall not return to this residence to make robes.
When that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes as much *vipula* cloth and the robes for holding [the kaṭhina] and goes out of the boundary, he forms this thought:
"I will not return to this place to make the robe.
After that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I will not return to that place, nor will I make the robe there."
"Upon departing, it is said that one has relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina*, makes such-and-such *vipāla* robes and takes his existing robes out of the boundary, thinking:
'I shall not return to this residence to make robes.'"
If one makes a robe outside the boundary while thinking,
"I shall not return to that place," then at the moment the robe is completed, it is said that the *kaṭhina* has been relinquished.
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, makes a certain number of vipāla robes, takes his existing robes and goes beyond the boundary, thinking:
'I will not return to this place to make robes.'"
If this person makes robes outside the boundary and loses them because they did not properly guard them, and has no other material to make more,
at the moment he loses the robes, it is said that he has relinquished the *kaṭhina*.
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, makes such-and-such a *vipāla* robe, takes his existing robes and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
That person then leaves the boundary and goes away; outside the boundary, he makes a robe—whether it is finished or not yet finished—he forms this thought:
"I shall return to my original place and make it at my leisure."
If, after a long time, it is not completed, and this person passes the fixed limit of time, they are said to have relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe.
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, makes such-and-such *vipāla* robes, takes his existing robes and goes outside the boundary, and thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make the robes.'"
Having heard from outside the boundary that the Sangha had already relinquished the kaṭhina robe, he thought to himself:
"The kaṭhina robe has been relinquished; I shall not return to my original place."
When that bhikṣu hears this, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
If a bhikṣu, having received the kaṭhina robe, makes such a *vipāla* robe and takes his existing robes out of the boundary, thinking:
"I shall return to this place to make the robe."
He then makes a robe outside the boundary; whether that robe has been made or not yet made, he forms this thought:
"I have returned to my original place and have not yet relinquished the kaṭhina."
"Having arrived, one relinquishes the *kaṭhina* cloth together with the Saṃgha; this is called 'relinquishing.
This is the second set of six completed.
Furthermore, there are twenty ways of relinquishing the *kaṭhina* cloth."
If a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his robes and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
"I will not return to this residence to make my robes."
Once that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I will not return to my original residence, nor will I make robes.
At the moment that bhikṣu departs, it is said that he relinquishes the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his robes and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall not return to this residence to make my robes.'"
When that bhikṣu goes outside the boundary to make robes, he forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original residence.
At the moment the robe is completed, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
"Third, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his robes and goes beyond the boundary, thinking:
'I shall not return to this residence to make my robes.'"
If this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, and having finished making them, loses them because he did not guard them well and has no other material with which to make more,
at the moment he loses the robes, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his robes and goes beyond the boundary, thinking:
'I shall not return to this residence to make my robes.'"
This bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary; having made this much and leaving that much unfinished, he works slowly and for a long time without completing them.
Then he thinks:
"I shall return to my original location."
"When this bhikṣu has passed the limit of the period, it is called 'the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe.
This is the first set of four.

"The second set of four is: if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina robe takes his robes and goes outside the boundary, neither managing them, nor saying he will return, nor saying he will not return."
When departing from the boundary, if one forms the thought:
"I shall not return to this residence to make robes," that bhikṣu,
at the moment of departure, is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes his own robes outside the boundary, neither attending to them, nor saying he will return, nor saying he will not return."
If one goes outside the boundary to make robes and forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original place to make the robes," then at the moment the robes are completed, it is said that the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished.

"Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his own robes and goes beyond the boundary, neither attending to them, nor saying he will return, nor saying he will not return, that bhikṣu shall make the robes outside the boundary."

Once the robes have been made, if they are lost because they were not properly guarded and there is no other material to make more, the moment the robes are lost is called the relinquishment of the *kaṭhina*.

"The fourth [case]: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the *kaṭhina* takes his robes and goes outside the boundary, neither managing them nor declaring whether he will return or not, and while outside the boundary he thinks:
'I shall not return to my original place.'"

If he makes robes at that very place, whether they are finished or not, and he works slowly such that they remain unfinished for a long time, once that bhikṣu exceeds the prescribed limit, it is called the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe.
This is called the second set of four.
"The third set of four is: if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, he thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
If that bhikṣu, being outside the boundary, further thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place,
nor shall I make the robe," then at the moment that bhikṣu departs, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
"Second, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, he thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
If that bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary and further thinks,
"I will not return to my original place to make the robe," then at the moment the robe is completed, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
"Third, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, he thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
If that bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary,

and having finished making them, loses them because he did not guard them well, and has no further material with which to make them, at the moment the robes are lost, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, he forms this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
This bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary; having made such a portion and leaving such a portion unmade, he works slowly and for a long time without completing them.
He then thinks:
"I shall return to my original place."
"When this bhikṣu exceeds the limit of time, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
This is called the third set of four.
As for the fourth set of four: if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes the robe and goes outside the boundary, thinking thus:"
"I shall return to this place to make robes.
Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquishes the kaṭhina robe and thinks:
"I will not return to my original place, nor will I make robes."
"When that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes the robe and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
Having heard this outside the boundary, he relinquished the kaṭhina robe; that bhikṣu then began making robes outside the boundary.
He further thought to himself:
"I shall not return to my original location to make the robes."
"When the robe is finished, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robe and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I will not return to this place to make the robe.'"
Having heard this outside the boundary, that person relinquishes the *kaṭhina* robe and immediately begins making a robe outside the boundary.
Once the robe is made, because they do not guard it well, it is lost; having no other material to make another, the moment it is lost is called the relinquishment of the *kaṭhina*.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, he forms this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"

Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquished the kaṭhina robe and began making robes outside the boundary. Having made a certain amount and leaving a certain amount unfinished, he worked slowly and for a long time without completing them, thinking to himself:
"I shall not return to my original location."
"When this bhikṣu exceeds the fixed limit, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
This is called the fourth set of four.
"The fifth set of four is: if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes the robe and goes outside the boundary, thinking thus:"
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While making the robe outside the boundary, that bhikṣu further thinks:
"I will not return to my original place."
"When that bhikṣu has finished making the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robes and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall return to this place to make my robe.'"
This person makes a robe outside the boundary.
Having finished making it, he leaves the *vīrapaṭa* robe nearly completed and sets it aside, thinking to himself:
"I shall not return this *vīrapaṭa* robe to that place."
"When the robe is nearly finished, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robe and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
After that bhikṣu has heard from outside the boundary that the kaṭhina has been relinquished, he thinks:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina, I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes."
"By virtue of hearing [this], it is said that one has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Fourth: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes the robe and goes outside the boundary, thinking:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"

If this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, having already made such-and-such a portion and not yet made such-and-such a portion, and he makes them slowly, then before the kaṭhina has been relinquished, he returns to this residence and relinquishes the kaṭhina together with the Saṃgha; this is called "relinquishment."
This is called the fifth way of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
Furthermore, there are twenty ways of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
If a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe and takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he forms this thought:
"I will not return to this dwelling place to make the robe.
This bhikṣu, being outside the boundary, forms this thought:
"I will not return to my original dwelling place, nor will I make the robe."
"When that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes the robe and goes beyond the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this residence to make a robe.'"
When he goes outside the boundary to make robes, he forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original residence.
At the moment the robe is completed, it is said that he has relinquished the *kaṭhina*.
"Third, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this residence to make the robe.'"

If this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, and having finished making them, loses them because he did not guard them well, and has no further material with which to make them, then at the moment the robes are lost, it is called the relinquishment of the kaṭhina.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this residence to make the robe.'"
This bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary; having made this much and not yet made that much, he works slowly and for a long time without completing it.
He then thinks:
"I shall return to my original location."
"When this bhikṣu exceeds the limit of time, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
This is the first of the four [cases].
The remaining three and four cases—those not attended to, those where it is expected to be returned, and those relinquished upon hearing [the news]—are also as explained above."
"The fifth of the four [cases]: if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his own robes beyond the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make my robes.'"
This bhikṣu makes the robe outside the boundary.
He further thinks:
"I shall not return to my original location."
"When this bhikṣu has finished making the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, and thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
This person makes a robe outside the boundary; having finished making it, he leaves the *vīralla* robe nearly complete and sets it aside, thinking:
"I shall not return this *vīralla* robe to that place."
"When the robe is finished, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he makes this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make my robe.'"
After that bhikṣu has heard from outside the boundary that the kaṭhina robe has been relinquished, he thinks to himself:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina robe, I shall not return to my original location, nor shall I make robes."
“Because of having heard [the announcement], it is said that one has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
‘Fourth: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he forms this thought:
“I shall return to this place to make my robes.”’”

If this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, having already made such a portion and leaving such a portion unfinished, and proceeds to make them slowly, yet returns to this place before the kaṭhina has been relinquished to relinquish the kaṭhina together with the Saṃgha, it is called "relinquishment."
This is called the fifth *catur-varga* relinquishment of the *kaṭhina* robe.
This is called the second set of five *catur-varga* relinquishments of the *kaṭhina* robe.
Furthermore, there are twenty relinquishments of the *kaṭhina* robe.
First, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his own robes beyond the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and forms this thought:
"I shall not return to this place to make my robes."
Failing to obtain what was hoped for and obtaining what was not hoped for, that bhikṣu, while outside the boundary, thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make the robe."
"When that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes the robe and goes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this place to make a robe.'"
Failing to obtain what was expected and obtaining what was not expected, while that bhikṣu is making robes outside the boundary, he forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original location."
"When this robe is completed, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he thinks:
'I shall not return to this place to make the robe.'"
Not obtaining what was hoped for, yet obtaining what was not hoped for, this bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary.
Having finished making the robe, because he does not guard it well, he loses it; he has no further material with which to make another.
If the robe is lost, it is said that the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this place to make [a robe]. "

Not obtaining what was expected, yet obtaining what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary; having made such a portion and leaving such a portion unmade, he works slowly and for a long time without completing it.
Furthermore, he thinks:
"I shall return to my original place.
When that bhikṣu exceeds the fixed limit, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
The remaining cases—three and four—where one does not manage the robe, where there is no expectation of returning, or where one abandons it after hearing [the news], are also like this.
"Regarding the fifth set of four: if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he forms this thought:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Not obtaining what was expected, yet obtaining what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary.
He then thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place."
"When that bhikṣu has finished making the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, and thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make my robe.'"
Failing to obtain what was expected and obtaining what was not expected, this person makes a robe outside the boundary.
Having finished making the robe, he leaves the *vīralla* robe hanging unfinished and thinks:
"This *vīralla* robe shall not be returned to its original place."
"When the robe is finished, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he should form this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make my robe.'"
If he does not obtain what he hoped for, or obtains what he did not hope for, and that bhikṣu hears that the kaṭhina has been relinquished outside the boundary, that bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina, I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes."
"Because of hearing [the announcement], it is said that the kaṭhina robe has been relinquished.
Fourth, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make a robe.'"

If he does not obtain what he expected or obtains what was not expected, and this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary—having already made a certain portion and having yet to make another portion—he makes them slowly; and while the kaṭhina has not yet been relinquished, he returns to this place and relinquishes the kaṭhina together with the Saṃgha, it is then called "relinquished."
This is called the fifth [method] of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
This is called the third set of five and four.
Furthermore, there are twenty ways of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
First, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his existing robes beyond the boundary in the hope of obtaining more robes, and forms this thought:
"I shall not return to this place to make my robes."
Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and having obtained what was not expected, once he has left the boundary, he forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original residence, nor shall I make a robe."
"When that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his robes and goes beyond the boundary, hoping to obtain more robes, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return here to make my robes.'"
Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and instead obtained what was not expected, that bhikṣu, while making robes outside the boundary, forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original location."
"When this robe is completed, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this place to make the robe.'"
"Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and obtained what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary.
Once the robes are made, because he does not guard them well, they are lost; having no further material to make more, at the moment the robes are lost, it is called the relinquishing of the kaṭhina."
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, with the hope of obtaining another robe, he forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this place to make the robe.'"

"Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and instead obtaining what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary; having made such a portion and leaving such a portion unfinished, he works slowly and for a long time without completing it."
Furthermore, he thinks:
"I shall return to my original place.
When that bhikṣu exceeds the fixed time limit, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
The remaining [cases], the third and fourth—those who do not manage the robe, those who expect to return in the future, and those who abandon it upon hearing [the announcement]—are also like this.
"The fifth set of four: if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, with the hope of obtaining [another] robe, he thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
"Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and obtained what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary.
He then further thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place."
“When that bhikṣu has finished making the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robes and goes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he makes this thought:
‘I shall return to this place to make my robe.’”
"Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and instead obtained what was not expected, this person makes a robe outside the boundary.
Once the robe is made, he leaves the *vippala* robe nearly finished and set aside, thinking:
'This *vippala* robe shall not be returned to that place.'"
"When the robe is finished, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina takes the robe outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining [another] robe, he thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"
"Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and having obtained what was not expected, this bhikṣu hears that the kaṭhina has been relinquished outside the boundary. This bhikṣu then thinks:
'If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina, I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes.'"
"Because of having heard [the announcement], he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Fourth: if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe out of the boundary, hoping to obtain another robe, he forms this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"

"Having abandoned what was expected to be obtained and having obtained what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary; having made such a portion and leaving such a portion unmade, he works on them slowly. Before the kaṭhina cloth has been relinquished, he returns to this place and relinquishes the kaṭhina together with the Saṃgha; this is called 'relinquishment'."
This is called the fifth [method] of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe through four ways.
This is called the fourth set of five.
Furthermore, there are twenty ways of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
First, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and forms this thought:
"I shall not return to this residence to make my robes."
Having failed to obtain what was hoped for, having not abandoned what was hoped for, and having obtained what was not hoped for, that bhikṣu, after going outside the boundary, further thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make a robe."
"When that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his robes and goes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this place to make my robes.'"
If he does not obtain what he hoped for, does not abandon what he hoped for, or obtains what was not hoped for, that bhikṣu, while making robes outside the boundary, forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original place."
"When these robes are completed, they are termed 'the relinquishing of the kaṭhina.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this residence to make the robe.'"
If he does not obtain what was expected, does not obtain what was expected, or obtains what was not expected, and that bhikṣu goes outside the boundary to make a robe;

having finished making the robe, if it is lost because he did not guard it well and he has no other material to make another robe, then at the moment the robe is lost, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, and forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this residence to make the robe.'"

Not obtaining what was expected, not abandoning what was expected, or obtaining what was not expected, this bhikṣu makes a robe outside the monastery boundary; having already made such a portion and leaving such a portion unfinished, he works slowly and for a long time without completing it.
Furthermore, he thinks:
"I shall return to my original place.
When that bhikṣu exceeds the fixed limit, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
The remaining cases—three and four—where one does not manage the robe, where one intends to return later, or where one abandons it after hearing [the announcement], are also like this.
"Regarding the fifth set of four: if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his own robe and goes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining another robe, he thinks:
'I shall return to this place to make my robe.'"
Not obtaining what was hoped for, not abandoning what was hoped for, and obtaining what was not hoped for, that bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary and further thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place."
"When this bhikṣu has finished making the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, and forms this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make my robe.'"
If one does not obtain what was hoped for, does not abandon what was hoped for, or obtains what was not hoped for, that person makes a robe outside the boundary.
Having made the robe, while the *vīrāla* robe is nearly finished but remains unfinished, he forms this thought:
"This *vīrāla* robe shall not be returned to that place."
"When the robe is finished, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he should form this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make my robes.'"

If he does not obtain what he hoped for, does not achieve what he hoped for, or obtains what he did not hope for, and this bhikṣu hears that the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished outside the boundary, that bhikṣu thinks:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the *kaṭhina*, I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes."
"By virtue of having heard [the announcement], he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Fourth, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more cloth, he forms this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make my robes.'"

If one does not obtain what was hoped for, does not abandon what was hoped for, or obtains what was not hoped for; if this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, having already made such a portion and leaving such a portion unfinished, making them slowly; and while the kaṭhina has not yet been relinquished, he returns to this place and relinquishes the kaṭhina together with the Saṃgha—this is called "relinquishment."
This is called the fifth [method] of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
This is the fifth set of five.
Furthermore, there are twenty ways of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
First, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes the robe and goes beyond the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, he forms this thought:
"I shall not return to this place to make the robe."

Not obtaining what was hoped for yet not severing what was hoped for; obtaining what was not hoped for while still diligently seeking what was hoped for—this hope is also severed, and what was not hoped for is obtained.
Once that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I will not return to my original place, nor will I make robes.
At the moment that bhikṣu departs, it is said that he relinquishes the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu, having received the kaṭhina robe, takes the robe out of the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and thinks:
'I shall not return to this place to make the robe.'"

Not obtaining what was hoped for, not severing what was hoped for, and obtaining what was not hoped for, one again diligently seeks what is hoped for; yet this hope is also severed, and what was not hoped for is obtained.
When this bhikṣu goes outside the boundary to make robes and thinks,
"I shall not return to my original place," at the moment the robes are finished, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina.
"Third, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, he forms this thought:
'I shall not return to this place to make the robe.'"

Not obtaining what one hopes for, not severing what one hopes for, and obtaining what was not hoped for; yet again, one diligently seeks what one hopes for, whereby that hope is severed and what was not hoped for is obtained.

If a bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, and having finished making them, loses them because he did not guard them well, and has no further material with which to make robes, at the moment they are lost, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and thinks:
'I shall not return to this residence to make a robe.'"

Not obtaining what one hopes for, not severing what one hopes for, and obtaining what was not hoped for—yet again striving to seek what one hopes for, that hope is severed and what was not hoped for is obtained.
This bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary; having made such a portion, he leaves that much unfinished and works slowly, so that it is not completed for a long time.
He then thinks:
"I shall return to my original place."
"When that bhikṣu exceeds the limit of time, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
The same applies to the other three cases: not managing the robe, the expectation of returning it later, and relinquishing it upon hearing [the news], all are likewise."
"The fifth of the four [cases]: if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, takes his own robes beyond the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make my robes.'"

Not obtaining what one hopes for, not severing what one hopes for, and obtaining what was not hoped for; yet again, diligently seeking what one hopes for, that hope is also severed, and what was not hoped for is obtained.
This bhikṣu makes a robe outside the boundary and thinks to himself:
"I shall not return to my original residence."
"When that bhikṣu has finished making the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Second, if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, and forms this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make the robe.'"

Not obtaining what was hoped for, yet not severing what was hoped for; obtaining what was not hoped for, yet still diligently seeking what was hoped for—this hope is also severed, yet what was not hoped for is obtained.
This person makes a robe outside the boundary; having finished making it, he leaves the *vibhāṅga* robe hanging unfinished and thinks:
"I shall not return this *vibhāṅga* robe to that place."
"When the robe is finished, it is said that the *kaṭhina* has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the *kaṭhina* takes his robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, he should form this thought:
'I shall return to this place to make my robes.'"

Not obtaining what one hopes for, not severing what one hopes for, and obtaining what was not hoped for; yet again, diligently seeking what one hopes for, that hope is severed and what was not hoped for is obtained.
After that bhikṣu has heard from outside the boundary that the kaṭhina has been relinquished, he thinks to himself:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina, I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes."
"Because of having heard [the announcement], it is said that the kaṭhina robe has been relinquished.
'Fourth, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his own robes outside the boundary with the hope of obtaining more robes, he forms this thought:
"I shall return to this place to make my robes."'"

Not obtaining what one hopes for, not severing what one hopes for, and obtaining what was not hoped for, yet again diligently seeking what one hopes for—this hope is also severed, and what was not hoped for is obtained.

If this bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, having already completed a certain portion and leaving a certain portion unfinished, and he proceeds to make them slowly while the kaṭhina robe has not yet been relinquished,
and then returns to this place to relinquish the kaṭhina together with the Saṃgha, it is called "relinquishment."
This is called the fifth [method] of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
This is called the sixth [set of] five and four.
Furthermore, there are twelve ways of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
First, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe-material outside the boundary,
but because the material is insufficient, he thinks:
"I shall return to this place to make the robe."
If that bhikṣu is outside the boundary, and another person says to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth here;
I shall make it for you," that bhikṣu, while outside the boundary, forms this thought:
"I shall not return to my original location, nor shall I make robes.
When this bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his robe and goes outside the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While that bhikṣu was outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring your robe; I shall make it for you.
This person goes outside the boundary and has another make the robe, thinking:
"I will not return to my original location; I am having the robe made outside the boundary."
"When the robes are completed, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Third, if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina robe takes the robe and goes outside the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While that bhikṣu was outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the cloth and wealth; I shall make a robe for you.
This bhikṣu then makes the robe outside the boundary.

Once the robe is finished, because he does not guard it well, he loses it. Having no further materials to make another, at the moment this bhikṣu loses the robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and takes the robe-material outside the boundary,
but because the material is insufficient, he thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Outside the boundary, another person says:
"Bring the cloth; I will make it for you.

This bhikṣu, being outside the boundary, has another person make the robe for him. Once it has been made to such an extent and remains unmade to such an extent, he makes it slowly and it is not completed for a long time.
Furthermore, he thinks:
"I shall return to my original place.
When that bhikṣu exceeds the prescribed time limit, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Fifth, if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe-cloth and takes it outside the boundary,
but because the material for the robe is insufficient, he thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Outside the boundary, another person says:
"Bring the robe-cloth here; I will make it for you.
Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquishes the kaṭhina and thinks thus:
"I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes.
When this bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Sixth, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe takes his robe and goes beyond the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While he was outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquished the kaṭhina. He then thought:
"I shall not return to my original location.
If a bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, when the robes are completed, it is termed the relinquishing of the kaṭhina.
Seventh: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robe and goes outside the boundary.
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robes.
While he was outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquished the kaṭhina, and that bhikṣu made the robe outside the boundary.

Once the robe has been made, if it is lost because it was not properly guarded and there is no other material with which to make another robe, the moment the robe is lost is called the relinquishment of the *kaṭhina*.
"Eighth: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the *kaṭhina* takes his robe and goes beyond the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.

This bhikṣu, having heard outside the boundary that the Saṃgha had already relinquished the kaṭhina, began making the robe outside the boundary. Having made such a portion and leaving such a portion unfinished, he worked on the robe slowly and did not complete it for a long time.
If the time limit has passed, it is called the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe.
Ninth: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe goes outside the boundary, and because his materials for robes are insufficient, he thinks:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robes."
Outside the boundary, another person says:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I will make a robe for you.
That bhikṣu, while outside the boundary, thinks to himself:
"I shall not return to my original place.
If a bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, when the robes are completed, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Tenth: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes his robe and goes outside the boundary.
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
This bhikṣu causes another to make the robe outside the boundary. Once the robe has been made, the *vīralla* robe is nearly finished and left behind, and this person thinks:
"This *vīralla* robe shall not be returned to its original place."
"When the robe is completed, it is said that the kaṭhina has been relinquished.
Eleventh: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina takes the robe and goes beyond the boundary."
Lacking sufficient robes or materials, he thinks:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person says to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
This bhikṣu, having heard from outside the boundary that the Saṃgha had already relinquished the kaṭhina, thought to himself:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina, I shall neither return to my original location nor make the robe."
"When that bhikṣu hears this, it is called the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe.
Twelfth: if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina robe takes the robe and goes outside the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robes.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.

That bhikṣu then makes the robe outside the boundary; having made such a portion and leaving such a portion still unfinished, he returns to this residence while the Saṃgha has not yet relinquished the kaṭhina cloth.
When one renounces it together with the Saṃgha, it is called the "renunciation of the kaṭhina robe.
Furthermore, there are twelve ways of renouncing the kaṭhina robe.
First: if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe or the *vibhāva* robe, and having taken the robe out of the boundary, because the material of the robe is not yet complete, he forms this thought:
"I shall return to this dwelling place to make the robe.
While that bhikṣu is outside the boundary, another person says to him:
"Bring the robe here; I will make it for you."
If that bhikṣu, having gone outside the boundary, thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place,
nor shall I make robes," then at the moment that bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu has received a kaṭhina robe or a vipula robe and takes the robe-material outside the boundary,
but because the material is insufficient, he thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Outside the boundary, another person says to that bhikṣu, "Bring the robe-cloth here; I will make it for you.
That bhikṣu, being outside the boundary, causes another to make the robe-cloth, forming this thought:
"If I do not return to my original location, but instead make robes outside the boundary," then at the moment the robes are finished, it is said that the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished.
"Third, if a bhikṣu accepts the *kaṭhina* robe and the *vipula* robe, and then takes the robes out of the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robes.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
This bhikṣu made the robe outside the boundary, but because he did not properly guard it after it was finished, he lost it, and he had no further material with which to make another.
When this bhikṣu loses his robe, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina.
Fourth, if a bhikṣu who has received the kaṭhina or the vipula robe takes the robe and goes outside the boundary.
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.

This bhikṣu, being outside the boundary, has another person make the robe-cloth for him; once some of it has been made while some remains unfinished, he makes it slowly and it is not completed for a long time.
Furthermore, one should think:
"I shall return to my original place.
If this bhikṣu exceeds the prescribed time limit, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Fifth, if a bhikṣu accepts a kaṭhina robe or a vipula robe and takes the robe-cloth outside the boundary,
but because the materials for the robe are insufficient, he thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Outside the boundary, another person says:
"Bring the robe-cloth here; I will make it for you.
Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquishes the kaṭhina, thinking thus:
"I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I make robes.
When this bhikṣu departs, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Sixth: if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe and the vipula robe, and takes the robes out of the boundary.
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robes.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make a robe for you.
Having heard this outside the boundary, that bhikṣu relinquished the kaṭhina privileges and further thought:
"I will not return to my original location."
"If a bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, the moment the robes are finished, it is called the relinquishing of the kaṭhina.
Seventh, if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe or a vipula robe and carries the robe out of the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
Having heard this outside the boundary, the bhikṣu relinquished the kaṭhina, and he made the robe outside the boundary.
Once the robe was finished, because he did not guard it well, he lost it; having no other material to work with, at the moment the robe was lost, it is termed the relinquishment of the kaṭhina.
"Eighth: If a bhikṣu has received a kaṭhina robe or a vipula robe and takes the robe-material outside the boundary, but because the materials are insufficient, he thinks:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Outside the boundary, another person says:
"Bring the robe-cloth here; I will make it for you.
This bhikṣu hears outside the boundary that the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina.
If one makes robes outside the boundary, having made such a portion and leaving such a portion unfinished, making them slowly and taking a long time to complete them,
then once the limit of the period has passed, it is called the relinquishment of the *kaṭhina* robe.
"Ninth, if a bhikṣu has received a *kaṭhina* robe or a *vipula* robe and carries the robe-material outside the boundary,
but because the materials are insufficient, he forms this thought:
'I shall return to this residence to make the robe.'"
Outside the boundary, another person says:
"Bring the robe; I will make it for you.
This bhikṣu, while outside the boundary, thinks to himself:
"I shall not return to my original place.
If a bhikṣu makes robes outside the boundary, at the moment the robes are completed, he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina.
Tenth: if a bhikṣu accepts the kaṭhina robe or a vipula robe and carries the robe out beyond the boundary.
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robes.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
This bhikṣu, being outside the boundary, had another person make the robe for him.
While the robe was being made, Vipula left it unfinished and set it aside. Then this person thought to himself:
"If this *vibhāṣā* robe does not return to its original place," when the robe is finished being made, it is then called "the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina* robe.
"Eleventh: If a bhikṣu has received a *kaṭhina* robe or a *vibhāṣā* robe, and carries the robe out beyond the boundary."
Because his robes and materials were insufficient, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.
Hearing from outside the boundary that the Sangha has already relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe, that bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"If the Sangha has already relinquished the *kaṭhina*, I will not return to my original location, nor will I make the robe."
“When a bhikṣu hears this, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Twelfth: if a bhikṣu, having received a kaṭhina robe or a vipula robe, takes the robe and goes outside the boundary.”
Because he lacked sufficient cloth and wealth, he thought:
"I shall return to this residence to make my robe.
While outside the boundary, another person said to him:
"Bring the robe-cloth; I shall make it for you.

This bhikṣu then makes the robe outside the boundary; having completed a certain portion and leaving a certain portion unfinished, he returns to this residence while the Saṃgha has not yet relinquished the kaṭhina.
When one renounces it together with the Saṃgha, it is called the renunciation of the kaṭhina robe.
This constitutes the twelfth.
Furthermore, there are two other sets of five ways of renouncing the kaṭhina robe.
Regarding the first five cases: if a bhikṣu has received the kaṭhina robe, finished making it, and taken it out of the boundary, he does so with a mind of security, thinking:
"I shall go to such-and-such a residence; that residence is auspicious. If that place is pleasant, I shall stay; if it is not pleasant, I shall return."
Once that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I shall not return to my original place.
At the moment that bhikṣu departs, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu has received the kaṭhina robe, finished making it, and taken it across the boundary, he does so with a mind of security, thinking:
'I shall go to such-and-such a residence; if that residence is pleasant, I shall stay; if it is not pleasant, I shall return.'"
Once that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I shall not go to such-and-such a place, nor shall I return to my original location.
At the moment that bhikṣu departs, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Third, if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe, and having finished making the robe, takes it out of the boundary, he does so with a mind of security, thinking:
'I shall go to such-and-such a residence; if that residence is pleasant, I shall stay; if it is not pleasant, I shall return.'"
If this bhikṣu remains outside the boundary for a long time— neither going to that dwelling place nor returning to his original dwelling place—
he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe because he has exceeded the prescribed limit.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu has received the kaṭhina robe, finished making it, and taken it out of the boundary, he does so with a mind of security, thinking:
'I shall go to such-and-such a residence; if that residence is pleasant, I will stay; if it is not pleasant, I shall return.'"
When that bhikṣu hears from outside the boundary that the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina robe,
he thinks to himself:
"If the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina robe, I shall neither return to my original residence nor go to such-and-such a place."
When that bhikṣu hears this, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Fifth, if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe finishes making his robes and takes them out of the boundary, with a mind of security he thinks:
'I shall go to such-and-such a dwelling; if that dwelling is pleasant, I will stay; if it is not pleasant, I shall return.'"

If that bhikṣu goes outside the boundary—whether he stays at that other residence or not—and returns to this residence before the kaṭhina robe has been relinquished, and then relinquishes the kaṭhina robe together with the Saṃgha, it is called "relinquished."
These are called the first five ways of relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe.
"As for the latter five: if a bhikṣu has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, finished making his robes, and taken them out of the boundary, he forms this thought:
'If I find companions, I shall go to such-and-such a place; if I do not find them, I shall return.'"
If that bhikṣu goes beyond the boundary and thinks,
"I shall not return to my original residence," then at the moment he departs, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Second, if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe, and having finished making the robe, takes it out of the boundary, he thinks:
'If I find companions, I shall go to such-and-such a place; if I do not find them, I shall return.'"
Once that bhikṣu has gone beyond the boundary, he further thinks:
"I shall not go to such-and-such a direction or such-and-such a place, nor shall I return to my original location.
At the moment that bhikṣu departs, it is said that he relinquishes the kaṭhina robe.
"Third, if a bhikṣu has accepted the kaṭhina robe, finished making the robe, and taken it out of the boundary, he forms this thought:
'If I find companions, I shall go to such-and-such a place; if I do not find them, I shall return to this dwelling place.'"
If this bhikṣu goes outside the boundary, neither reaching that destination nor returning to his original place, but remains outside the boundary for a long time;
when he exceeds the prescribed limit, it is said that he has relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
"Fourth, if a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, finishes making it and takes it out of the boundary, he thinks:
'If I find companions, I shall go to such-and-such a place; if I do not find them, I shall return. "
That bhikṣu hears outside the boundary that the Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
That bhikṣu then thinks:
"The Saṃgha has already relinquished the kaṭhina robe; I shall not return to my original place, nor shall I go to such-and-such a region."
"Because that bhikṣu has heard [the proclamation], he is said to have relinquished the kaṭhina robe.
Fifth: if a bhikṣu who has accepted the kaṭhina robe finishes making his robes and takes them out of the boundary, he forms this thought:
'If I find companions, I shall go to such-and-such a place; if I do not find them, I shall return.'"

If that bhikṣu goes outside the boundary, whether he proceeds to that place or not, and returns to this location before the kaṭhina robe has been relinquished, and then relinquishes the kaṭhina robe together with the Saṃgha, it is called "relinquished."
This is called the second set of five [cases] for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe.
Two sixes, six twenties; two twelves and two fives, totaling one hundred and sixty-six.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Twenty-nine;
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll Thirty; Part Two of the Fifth Recitation, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
2. The Kauśāmbī Dharmas: The Second of the Eight Dharmas of Kauśāmbī.
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who committed an offense requiring confession.
Out of compassion and with the desire to bring him benefit, profit, and peace, the bhikṣus spoke of his transgressions and instructed him to repent according to the Dharma.
That bhikṣu said:
"I do not know what I have committed; since I do not know it, how shall I recognize the offense?"
"How shall he perform his confession? The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣu refuses to confess directly; we must carry out a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against him for not acknowledging his offense."
Having formed this thought, he immediately carried out the formal act of suspension for not seeing [the offense] against that bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu delighted in upholding the precepts, possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame, was widely learned and well-known, and had much power and influence to provide assistance.
In the vicinity of his dwelling, many bhikṣus were socializing with one another.
This man sent a messenger with these words:
"I am innocent, yet the bhikṣus have performed an illegal *karmavācanā* to expel me. This expulsion may be overturned; you all should assemble."
The monks from the four quarters immediately assembled together, desiring to settle this matter.
That monk related the full account to the monks, saying:

"Because of such causes and conditions, I am without fault; yet these monks have acted contrary to the Dharma by forcibly imposing upon me the *tajjaniya-kamma* of 'not seeing [the offense],' which is a reversible act."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they could not bear it and said:

"This bhikṣu is truly without fault; the Saṃgha has acted contrary to the Dharma by forcibly imposing a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) upon him for non-confession. This matter is subvertible."
Thus, being resolutely compliant with those who have been suspended, he opposes all the monks who carry out the suspension.

For this reason, disputes and quarrels arise; the Saṃgha is split, there is contention within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha is divided, and the Saṃgha is at variance. He creates the causes and conditions for a schism in the Saṃgha, splitting it into two factions.
One group said,
"This bhikṣu is guilty of an offense.
Another group said:
"This bhikṣu is without fault," said one group;
"He has been expelled in accordance with the Dharma," said another.
One group said,
"He was expelled contrary to the Dharma.
Another group said:
"If the formal act of suspension is contrary to the Dharma, it may be overturned.
One school says:
"If the formal act of suspension is in accordance with the Dharma, it cannot be overturned."
Thus, as their verbal disputes and quarrels did not cease, the Saṃgha was eventually split into two factions.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.

The Buddha immediately had the monks who were compliant and those who had been subject to formal exclusion move to a short distance away, and then addressed the bhikṣus who had carried out the exclusion:
"If you [charge] them with matters that lack a causal basis or foundation, and they do not confess of their own accord, you should not carry out an act of banishment. Why is this?

There may be a bhikṣu who has committed an offense that requires confession; out of compassion and wishing to bring him benefit, profit, peace, and happiness, other bhikṣus speak to him of his offense and instruct him to confess it according to the Dharma."

If there is a bhikṣu who delights in upholding the precepts, possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame, is learned and well-informed, wields great power, and has many supporters— if such a person exists,
the Saṃgha should first reflect that there are five conditions under which he should not be subjected to formal suspension (pravāsanīya-karman).
What are the five?

That we should carry out a formal act of suspension against this bhikṣu for not seeing [his offense], not recite the Prātimokṣa together with him, not perform the saṃgha-karmas together with him, not share the *taṭbhaṇa* (the meal before noon) together with him, and not rise from our seats to greet or see him off as we would an elder.
For these reasons, there arise quarrels, mutual accusations, schisms in the Saṃgha, disputes within the Saṃgha, divisions of the Saṃgha, and dissensions of the Saṃgha.
Monks should also reflect that because these five conditions exist, they must not carry out an act of banishment.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu commits an offense that requires confession, the other bhikṣus, out of compassion and wishing to bring him benefit, profit, and happiness, point out his transgression and instruct him to confess it according to the Dharma.

This bhikṣu delights in upholding the precepts and possesses a sense of shame and dread of blame; he has few acquaintances, lacks great influence, and has no many supporters; in the dwellings on all four sides, there are few people with whom he converses or with whom he conducts affairs.
The Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should first reflect that there are five qualities for which one should be expelled.
What are these five?"

If we were to carry out a formal act of suspension against this bhikṣu for not acknowledging his offense, exclude him from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa and the Saṃgha’s karmavācanā, refuse to share the *taṭṭubhana* meal with him, refuse to share the midday meal with him, and fail to rise from our seats to greet or bid him farewell.
For these reasons, do not give rise to signs of strife, contention, or verbal disputes; let the Saṃgha be harmonious, free from dispute, without division, and without dissension.
Having reflected upon these five dharmas, one should carry out the formal act of banishment.

After the Buddha had spoken thus, he again sent away those bhikṣus who were subject to the formal act of banishment, having them move to a short distance, and called forth those bhikṣus who were in accord with the banishment, saying to them:
"You bhikṣus, do not associate with those who have committed an offense but do not recognize their own transgression."

Why is this? If a bhikṣu commits an offense that requires confession, the other bhikṣus, out of compassion and wishing to bring him benefit, profit, peace, and happiness, point out his transgression and instruct him to confess it according to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu who has committed an offense can contemplate five things, he will see his offense according to the Dharma.
What are these five?

If I view my offense as not being in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha may impose upon me the act of *ajñapti-karma* (formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense); I shall not be permitted to participate in the recitation of the Prātimokṣa or in the *saṃgha-karman*; I shall not be permitted to share the *taṭṭopana* (the meal before noon); I shall not be permitted to share the midday meal; and I shall not be permitted to follow the senior monks by rising from my seat to greet them or to escort them.
Why is this? Because these bhikṣus delight in upholding the precepts and possess a sense of shame and remorse; they cannot act out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion for my sake.
"This offender, by reflecting upon these five dharmas, is able to see his offense according to the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.

Then, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī who had been subject to formal exclusion (pravāsanīya-karman) were reciting the Prātimokṣa within the boundary and performing the formal acts (saṃgha-karman) of the Saṃgha.
Whatever *karmas* were permitted by the Buddha, they all performed in this manner.

Both the monks who were in accord with the decision and those who had been suspended also went outside the boundary to recite the precepts and perform the *saṃgha-karmas*, performing all such *karmas* exactly as permitted by the Buddha.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
At that time, the Buddha immediately had the bhikṣus who were assisting the formal act of suspension and the bhikṣu being suspended move to a short distance away.
He questioned the bhikṣus who had performed the act of banishment:
"Is it true that within the boundary, at the communal residence, you have recited the precepts and performed the saṃgha-karmas exactly as I have authorized them to be performed?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
He further asked those monks who had complied with him and those who had been expelled:
"When performing the *saṃgha-karman* of reciting the *Prātimokṣa* outside the boundary, do you all perform it exactly as I have authorized for such *karman*?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, bhikṣu!”

If you, together with monks who are compliant and monks who have been suspended, perform the recitation of the precepts and carry out monastic *karmavācanā* within the boundary, then all such *karmas* that you perform in accordance with what I have permitted are called "unlawful" (*adharma*).

Why is this? Because you are distinct from them; they do not dwell together with you, nor do you dwell together with them; you do not engage in affairs together with them, nor do they engage in affairs together with you.

If they perform the *saṃgha-karman* of reciting the precepts together with you within the same boundary, and perform the *karman* in accordance with what I have permitted, all such acts are termed illegal. Why is this?

Because he is distinct from you, he does not dwell together with you, nor do you dwell together with him; you do not engage in affairs together with him, nor does he engage in affairs together with you.
The formal acts (karmas) performed by them are likewise all in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this?
Because they are distinct from you; it is not appropriate for them to dwell together or engage in communal affairs with you.
There are two kinds of non-cohabitation.
What are the two?
First, a bhikṣu personally commits an act that constitutes non-cohabitation.
Second, when the Saṃgha is in harmony, they perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of "not living together" (*asaṃvāsika*) against him according to the Dharma.
There are two kinds of living together:
first, living together by one's own physical action; [and second, living together through formal authorization].
Second, when the Sangha is in harmony, they perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of granting him common residence according to the Dharma.
If a monk who has been subjected to censure or banishment abandons that group and enters this group, he should immediately be granted common residence.

If, based on a formal act of reconciliation (*niśraya-karman*), a formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), or a formal act of subordination (*tarjanīya-karman*), a bhikṣu abandons that group and enters this group, they should immediately live together in harmony.

"If a person who has been suspended humbles himself and submits, and if he goes outside the boundary to receive the lifting of his suspension, he may immediately dwell together with the community that has lifted the suspension.

At that time, the Buddha sent the bhikṣus who were performing the suspension to move a short distance away, and addressed the bhikṣus who were following the suspension and those who had performed the suspension, saying:
"Did you truly go outside the boundary to recite the precepts and perform the saṃgha-karmans, carrying out all such actions as I have authorized for karmans?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
He further asked those bhikṣus:
"When performing the *poṣadha* and the formal monastic procedures (*saṃgha-karman*) within the boundaries, do you all carry them out exactly as I have authorized for such procedures?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, bhikṣu!”

If you, together with those bhikṣus who have been subject to the act of banishment, perform the recitation of the precepts and carry out monastic *karmavācanā* outside the boundary, even if you perform these *karmas* in accordance with what I have permitted for communal performance, all such *karmas* are termed illegal (*adharma*).

Why is this? Because you are distinct from them; they do not dwell together with you, nor do you dwell together with them; you do not engage in affairs together with them, nor do they engage in affairs together with you.

If they perform the *saṃgha-karman* of reciting the precepts together with you outside the boundary, according to what I have permitted regarding the performance of *karman*, all such acts are called illegal. Why is this?

Because they are distinct from you, they do not dwell together with you, nor do you dwell together with them; you do not engage in affairs together with them, nor do they engage in affairs together with you.
The *karmavācanā* performed by them is also entirely in accordance with the Dharma. Why is this?
Because they are distinct from you and should not dwell together or engage in communal affairs with you.
There are two kinds of non-cohabitation:
first, non-cohabitation due to one's own actions;
second, non-cohabitation through a formal act of the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma.
They perform the formal act of *asaṃvāsa* (exclusion from communal living).
There are two kinds of communal living:
first, communal living through one's own person; [second, communal living through shared ritual acts].
Second, when the Saṃgha is in harmony, they perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of granting him common residence according to the Dharma.
If a monk who has been subjected to the penalty of censure (*tarjanīya*) abandons that group and enters this group, he should immediately be granted common residence.

If a bhikṣu who has received a *niśraya-karman*, a *pravāsanīya-karman*, or a *tarjanīya-karman* leaves that community and enters this community, he should immediately be allowed to dwell together with them.

"If a bhikṣu who has been suspended humbles himself and, having gone outside the boundary, seeks to be released from that suspension, he may immediately dwell together with the community from whom he was released.
This occurred while the Buddha was at Kauśāmbī.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted through his silence, the householder prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Returning home, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink throughout the entire night. Rising early, he arranged the seating area and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come;
may the Buddha know the proper time."
The bhikṣus went to the house of a lay devotee, while the Buddha remained in his own quarters to await his portion of the meal.
