Once the bhikṣus had entered the layman’s house, a dispute arose; they began to argue and revile one another, committing unwholesome deeds of body that are improper for those who have left the household life.
The householder said to the bhikṣus, “Venerable sirs, please wait a moment.

He had them all take their seats, personally served them water, and personally provided them with abundant and delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied. Once the meal was finished and the water for washing hands had been served, he took a small stool and sat down, wishing to hear the Dharma.

When the Elder had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed. After the meal, the bhikṣus returned to their quarters, put away their robes and bowls, and went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when the bhikṣus have finished their meal, they inquire with these words:
"Was the food delicious?
Was the Saṃgha satisfied?"
The Buddha then greeted them with these words:
"Monks, was the food delicious and were you all satiated?
The monks replied:
“World-Honored One!
The food and drink were most delicious, and the assembly of monks was fully satiated.
He related these matters to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them, saying:

"How can one who is called a bhikṣu enter the homes of laypeople and initiate matters of strife and contention, engaging in mutual recrimination and verbal abuse, thereby giving rise to evil karma of the body—things that those who have left the household life ought not to do?"
The Buddha said:
"From now on, members of separate schools or different assemblies should not sit close together so as to give rise to unwholesome karma.

When such different assemblies gather, it is permitted for a monk who knows the Dharma to ensure they remain at a distance; he shall arrange the seats with a space of one *śayanāsana* (bed-space) left between them, and only then perform the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, carry out various *karmas*, and provide instruction to the *bhikṣuṇīs*."
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī took pleasure in quarreling and engaging in mutual disputes.
The Buddha then taught and transformed these bhikṣus as follows:
"Do not quarrel or speak harshly to one another. Why is this?
One who employs anger and resentment does not extinguish anger and resentment; only the power of forbearance can extinguish them."
Thereupon, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, King of Dharma, let this be for now!
That man has provoked me; why should I not retaliate?”
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew a short distance away and thought to himself:
"I have now distanced myself from the conduct and rules of discipline practiced by the Bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, who are constantly fond of quarreling, disputing, reviling, and abusing one another."
Having finished preaching the *Āyuṣmanta-rāja-sūtra* in detail, he rose from his seat and went to the kingdom of Caitya, traveling by stages until he arrived at Śrāvastī.

At that time, the wise men of Kauśāmbī heard that the Buddha did not delight in the quarreling and contentious speech of the Kauśāmbī bhikṣus, nor in their conduct, deportment, and rules of discipline; therefore, they abandoned them and went to other countries, thinking:
"We should treat these bhikṣus with contempt and show them little respect."

Having had this thought, they immediately spoke to one another and all began to treat him with contempt; they no longer respected, made offerings to, or praised him, and their hearts of reverence grew increasingly diminished.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The laypeople now treat us with contempt; they no longer respect, make offerings to, or praise us, and their hearts of reverence have grown increasingly diminished."
"Why do we not go to Śrāvastī to visit the Buddha?
Having had this thought, they stayed there as long as they pleased, then took up their robes and bowls and went to Śrāvastī to visit the Buddha.

Venerable Śāriputra, having heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were fond of quarreling and disputing with one another, and that those worthy ones no longer respected, made offerings to, or praised him because they had given rise to arrogance, he set out for the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Having heard this, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī delight in quarreling and mutual recrimination. Because those worthy ones no longer respect, make offerings to, or praise me—due to the arising of pride—I have come here.”
“World-Honored One!
What should we do regarding this bhikṣu?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Among these, those who preach what is not the Dharma should not be respected, honored, or praised.
Those who preach the Dharma should be respected, honored, and praised."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should we recognize those who speak what is not the Dharma and those who speak the Dharma?”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“If a bhikṣu speaks of what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaks of Dharma as not Dharma; speaks of what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, speaks of Vinaya as not Vinaya;
speaks of an offense as no offense, speaks of no offense as an offense; speaks of what is light as heavy, speaks of what is heavy as...”
To speak of what is light as being with remainder, or to speak of what has remainder as being without remainder;
to speak of the dharmas that are always practiced as not being always practiced, or to speak of the dharmas that are not always practiced as being always practiced;
to speak what is not speech, or to speak what is not speech as speech—this is called one who speaks what is not the Dharma, and such a person should not be respected or honored.
One should not praise them; one should not teach them to read or recite the sūtras and Dharma, nor answer their questions regarding doubts;
one should not receive from them the instruction to read or recite the sūtras and Dharma, nor ask them about one's doubts;
one should not give them robes, alms bowls, door-keys, *kālika-bhaiṣajya*, *yāmika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, or *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*, nor should one receive robes or alms bowls from them.
...door-bolts, medicines to be taken at the proper time, medicines to be taken during the specific part of the day, medicines for seven days, and medicines for life.
Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu declares what is not Dharma to be Dharma, or declares what is Dharma to be Dharma; or declares what is not Vinaya to be Vinaya, or declares what is Vinaya [to be not Vinaya]...

To speak of the Vinaya as the Vinaya; to speak of an offense as an offense; to speak of what is not an offense as not an offense; to speak of what is light as light; to speak of what is heavy as heavy;
to speak of what is without remainder (anavaśeṣa) as without remainder; to speak of what has remainder (sāvaśeṣa) as having remainder;

to speak of that which is a rule of constant practice as a rule of constant practice; to speak of that which is not a rule of constant practice as not a rule of constant practice—to speak thus is called "speaking."
One who neither speaks nor refrains from speaking is called a "Dharma-preacher. Such a person should be respected, honored, and praised;
one should instruct them to read and recite the sūtras and Dharma, and answer their questions regarding doubts.

Furthermore, one should receive from them the reading and recitation of the sūtras and Dharma, inquire of them regarding doubts, and provide them with robes, alms-bowls, door-keys, food taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*), and food taken during the specific periods of the day (*kālātikrāntabhojana*).
Regarding seven-day medicines and lifetime medicines, one should likewise receive [the permission for] robes, alms bowls, door-keys,
timely medicines, timed medicines, seven-day medicines, and lifetime medicines; in all cases, one should provide bedding and furniture.
The Elder Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila were also questioned in this same manner.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī delighted in quarreling and mutual recrimination; because those venerable ones did not respect or honor them, and had given rise to pride, they had come toward the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Having heard this, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī delight in quarreling and mutual recrimination. Because those venerable ones do not respect, honor, or praise them, and have given rise to arrogance, they have come here.”
“World-Honored One!
Regarding this bhikṣu, what should we do?
The Buddha said:
"Gautamī! Among these, those who speak what is not the Dharma should not be revered, honored, or praised.
Those who speak the Dharma should be revered and honored."
Gautamī asked, “How does one know who speaks what is not the Dharma and who speaks the Dharma?
The Buddha told Gautamī:

"Listen well! If a bhikṣu speaks of what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaks of Dharma as not Dharma; speaks of what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, speaks of Vinaya as not Vinaya; speaks of an offense as no offense, speaks of no offense as an offense; speaks of a grave matter as light, speaks of a light matter as grave; or speaks of a non-remainder offense as a remainder offense."

To speak of what is incomplete as complete, to speak of the dharmas that are always practiced as dharmas not always practiced, to speak of dharmas not always practiced as dharmas always practiced, to speak of what is not speech as speech, and to speak of what is not spoken as speech—this is called one who speaks non-Dharma. Such a person should not be revered, honored, or praised; one should not instruct them in the reading or recitation of the sūtras and dharmas, nor answer their questions or doubts. One should not receive from them the instruction, reading, or recitation of the sūtras and dharmas, nor inquire of them regarding doubts. Furthermore, one should not give them robes, bowls, door-keys, *kālika-bhaiṣajya*, *yāmika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, or *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*.

One should not receive from such a person robes, alms bowls, door-keys, food for the current day, food for a specific part of the day, seven-day medicine, or lifetime medicine; nor should one receive from such a person the fortnightly instruction on the Dharma.

Gautamī! If a bhikṣu speaks of what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma, of Dharma as Dharma; speaks of what is non-Vinaya as non-Vinaya, of Vinaya as Vinaya; speaks of an offense as an offense, of a non-offense as a non-offense; speaks of a light offense as light, of a heavy offense as heavy; speaks of an offense with remainder as having remainder, of an offense without remainder as without remainder; speaks of a practice that is always followed as a practice always followed, and of a practice not always followed as a practice not always followed; and speaks of what has been spoken as spoken, and of what has not been spoken as not spoken—this is called one who speaks the Dharma, and such a person should be respected, honored, and praised.

One should teach the methods for reciting and chanting the sutras and answer the questions regarding doubts; likewise, one should receive from them the methods for reciting and chanting the sutras and inquire about their doubts. One should also provide them with robes and alms bowls, door-keys, food to be taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*), food to be taken during the specific part of the day (*kālātikrāntabhojana*), food to be taken for seven days (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), and medicine to be taken for as long as one lives (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*).

One should also receive from this person the robes and bowl, the door-bolt, the food for the current day, the food for the specific time-period, the seven-day medicine, and the lifetime medicine; one should also receive from this person the instruction on the Dharma every half-month.
The bhikṣuṇī Kisāgotamī, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, the bhikṣuṇī Cūḍapanthaka-Nanda, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā, and the śrāmaṇerikā Śailā also asked in this same manner.

King Prasenajit of Kosala heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were fond of quarreling and disputing with one another; because those worthy ones did not receive respect or offerings, they had come to this country.
Having heard this, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One! What should we do?"
The Buddha said,
“Great King! Among these,
those who preach what is not the Dharma should not be revered or supported with offerings.”
"One who preaches the Dharma should be honored and supported.
"World-Honored One!
How does one know who is preaching the Dharma and who is preaching what is not the Dharma?"
The Buddha said: “Great King! You should listen to the words of two types of people.

If a bhikṣu speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, or speaks Dharma as what is not Dharma, he is called one who speaks non-Dharma. One should not respect, honor, or praise him; one should not instruct him to read or recite the sūtras and Dharma, nor answer his questions on doubts. One should not receive from him instruction in reading or reciting the sūtras and Dharma, nor inquire of him regarding doubts. One should not give him robes, alms bowls, door-keys, *kālika-bhaiṣajya*, *yāmika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, or *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*.
"Great King!

If there is a bhikṣu who declares what is not Dharma as not Dharma and what is Dharma as Dharma, you should respectfully provide for him, make offerings to him, praise him, and instruct him in the recitation of the sūtras and Dharma; you should answer his questions regarding doubts. Furthermore, you should receive from him the instruction on the recitation of the sūtras and Dharma, and inquire of him regarding his doubts. You should also give him robes and bowls, a door-bolt, and the medicines appropriate for the time, the medicines appropriate for a portion of the day, the seven-day medicines, and the medicines for life."
"Great King!
You should provide food and drink for the entire Saṃgha of both divisions.
The great householder Sudatta, Ānanda, and Bhāradvāja Piṇḍola also asked in this same manner.

Lady Mallikā heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were fond of quarreling and disputing with one another; because those worthy ones were not respected, honored, or praised, they had come to this country.
Having heard this, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should we do regarding this bhikṣu?”
The Buddha said:
"Lady Mallikā! If there are those among them who speak what is not the Dharma, they should not be respected, honored, or praised."
"One who preaches the Dharma should be respected, honored, and praised.
"World-Honored One!
How shall we know who is a preacher of the Dharma and who is a preacher of what is not the Dharma?"
The Buddha said, “Lady Mallikā! You should listen to the words of two kinds of people.

If a bhikṣu speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, or speaks Dharma as what is not Dharma, he is called one who speaks non-Dharma; such a person should not be honored, supported, or praised. One should not instruct him to read or recite the sūtras and Dharma, nor answer his questions or doubts. One should not receive from him instruction on reading or reciting the sūtras and Dharma, nor ask him about one’s doubts. One should not give him robes, alms bowls, keys, *kālika* medicine, *yāmika* medicine, *saptāhika* medicine, or *yāvajjīvika* medicine.”

Lady Mallikā! If a bhikkhu speaks of what is not Dhamma as not Dhamma, and speaks of what is Dhamma as Dhamma, he is called a speaker of the Dhamma; he should be respected, honored, praised, and provided with instruction, the recitation of the scriptures, and answers to his doubts. One should also receive from him the instruction and recitation of the scriptures and inquire of him regarding one's doubts. One should provide him with robes, alms bowls, keys, food for the appropriate time (*kālabhojana*), food for the specific part of the day (*khaṇabhojana*), food for seven days (*sattāhakālika*), and life-long medicine (*yāvajīvikabhesajja*); and one should provide all the food and drink for both divisions of the Saṅgha.
Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā, the housewife Puṣpadattā, and the housewife Sujātā asked the same question.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard that the monks of Kauśāmbī were fond of quarreling and engaging in mutual disputes and had consequently entered his territory, went to where the Buddha was staying. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [...]”
The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, fond of quarreling and engaging in mutual disputes, have come into this boundary. How should we allocate the bedding and furniture to them?
The Buddha said:
"I have previously stated that one should provide bedding and furniture; according to the seniority of their respective groups, the bedding and furniture should first be given to them."
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Śāriputra followed the senior elder and first provided him with bedding and requisites.
While the Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī,
at that time a monk who had been subject to formal suspension wandered alone and lived alone, reflecting as follows:
"For my sake, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.
Among them, a bhikṣu says:
'This person is guilty.'"
Some said, "This person is without fault. Others said:
"He has been expelled according to the Dharma. Some said,
"He has been expelled contrary to the Dharma."
Some said: "If one has been expelled in accordance with the Dharma, he cannot be overturned. Others said:
"A formal act of banishment that is contrary to the Dharma may be overturned;
all such acts are for my sake.
However, as I have actually committed an offense, a formal act of banishment in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned."
"What should I do now?
Having reflected thus, he went to the bhikṣu Anurādha and said:
"Alone in my travels and alone in my dwelling, I have been reflecting as follows:"
"For my sake, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.
Among them, a bhikṣu says:
'This person is guilty.'"
Some said, "This person is without fault. Others said:
"He has been expelled according to the Dharma. Some said,
"He has been expelled not according to the Dharma."
Some said: "A formal expulsion according to the Dharma cannot be overturned. Others said:
"An unlawful *pravāsanīya* (banishment) may be subverted; this is all for my sake.
As for me, having actually committed an offense, a lawful *pravāsanīya* cannot be subverted."
"What shall I do now?
Following their instructions, the monks took the suspended monk to where the monks who were performing the suspension were and said:
"This suspended monk has come to me and said:"
"I walked alone and dwelt alone, and this thought occurred to me:
'For my sake, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.'"
Among them, some bhikṣus said,
"This person is guilty," while others said:
"This person is without fault.
Others said: "He has been expelled in accordance with the Dharma."
Some said: "He was expelled contrary to the Dharma. Others said: [He was expelled contrary to the Dharma.]
"One who has been expelled according to the Dharma cannot be overturned.
Some say: "One who has been expelled contrary to the Dharma can be overturned."
"All this is for my sake. I have indeed committed an offense;
I must be expelled according to the Dharma, and that expulsion cannot be overturned.
What should I do now?"

Having carried out the formal act of banishment against those bhikṣus, they took the banished bhikṣu and the bhikṣus who supported him to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This monk, acting in accordance [with the others], brought the monk who was subject to the act of banishment to us and said:
"This monk who is subject to banishment said:
'When I am walking alone and dwelling alone, I have this thought:'"
"For my sake, the Saṃgha has engaged in strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.
Among them, there are bhikṣus who say:

Some said, "This person is without fault. Others said:

Some said: "An expulsion performed in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned. Others said:
"An unlawful suspension may be subverted; this is all for my sake.
As for me, having actually committed an offense, a lawful suspension cannot be subverted."
"What shall I do now?
The Buddha said, "This bhikṣu has indeed committed an offense; he must be expelled according to the Dharma, and this decision is not to be overturned."
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of remorse, submits himself after being subdued, the saṃgha should grant him release from the suspension.

As for the method of granting release: the harmonious saṃgha should assemble with one mind; the suspended bhikṣu should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel on his right knee, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!..."
For my sake, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.
Among them, a bhikṣu says:
"This person has committed an offense."
Some said, "This person is without fault. Others said:

Some said: "An expulsion performed in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned. Others said:

I, bhikṣu so-and-so, have indeed committed an offense; a lawful suspension is not to be revoked."
I now repent with a contrite heart, submit myself, and beg the Saṃgha for release from my suspension.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], repent with a contrite heart, submit myself, and pray that the Saṃgha will grant me release from suspension out of compassion.
A second and a third time he likewise requested.
Thereupon, one bhikṣu proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This expelled bhikṣu, so-and-so, says:
"For my sake, the Saṃgha has quarreled, disputed, and engaged in contention; the Saṃgha has been split, the Saṃgha has been at variance, and the Saṃgha has become divided.
Among them, there are bhikṣus who say:"
"This person is guilty," some say;
"This person is not guilty," others say.
Some said, "He has been expelled in accordance with the Dharma. Others said:
"It was an unlawful expulsion. Some said,
"It was a lawful expulsion that cannot be overturned."
Some said: "An expulsion that is contrary to the Dharma may be overturned.
All of this was for my sake.
"I have indeed committed an offense; I am subject to formal suspension according to the Dharma and cannot be released from it.
This bhikṣu [Name], having felt remorse and been subdued, has now come before the Saṃgha to request release from his suspension.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha revoke the suspension of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is called the *jñapti* (motion).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This expelled bhikṣu, [name], says:

Among them, there are bhikṣus who say:"
"This person is guilty," some say;
"This person is not guilty," others say.
Some said, "He was expelled in accordance with the Dharma. Others said:

Some said: "An expulsion that is contrary to the Dharma may be overturned. [The others replied:
"It is all for my sake; as I have indeed committed an offense, an expulsion that is in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned."

"This bhikṣu so-and-so, having been subject to the act of banishment, has repented with a contrite heart and submitted himself. The Saṃgha now grants the lifting of the banishment for this bhikṣu so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to granting the lifting of the banishment for this bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."
Thus is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
"The Saṃgha has completed the lifting of the suspension for the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying at Kauśāmbī.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu was wandering and dwelling alone, and he reflected thus:
"On my account, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division."
Among them, some bhikṣus said:
"This person is guilty. Others said:
"This person is without fault," some said;
others said, "He has been expelled in accordance with the Dharma."
Some said: "He was expelled contrary to the Dharma. Others said: [He was expelled contrary to the Dharma.]
"It is said: 'An expulsion performed in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned. Others say:
'An expulsion not performed in accordance with the Dharma can be overturned.'"
"All this was for my sake. I have indeed committed an offense, and I am to be expelled according to the Dharma; this cannot be overturned.

My heart is filled with remorse, and having humbled myself and confessed, the Saṃgha has already granted me release from expulsion. I should now enter the midst of the Saṃgha and together bring about harmony."
Having reflected thus, he approached the monks who were compliant with him and said:
"While walking alone and dwelling alone, I had this thought:
'On my account, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.'"
Among them, some bhikṣus said,
"This person is guilty," while others said:
"This person is without fault.
Others said: "He has been expelled in accordance with the Dharma."
Some said, "He was expelled contrary to the Dharma. Others said:
"A formal act of banishment performed according to the Dharma is indestructible.
Some say: "A formal act of banishment not performed according to the Dharma is destructible."
"All this is for my sake. I have indeed committed an offense, and I am to be expelled according to the Dharma; this decision cannot be overturned.

My mind is filled with remorse, and having been subdued, I come forward to confess. The Saṃgha has already granted me release from expulsion; I should now enter the Saṃgha and together practice in harmony."
The compliant bhikṣus then took that bhikṣu to where the bhikṣus who were carrying out the formal act of banishment were and said to them: "This bhikṣu says:
'I travel alone and dwell alone, and I reflect thus:'"
"For my sake, the Saṃgha has fallen into strife, mutual accusation, schism, contention, and division.
Among them, there is a bhikṣu who says:
'This person is guilty.'"
Some said: "There is no offense. Others said: [There is an offense.]
"He has been expelled according to the Dharma. Some said,
"He has been expelled not according to the Dharma."
Some said: "A formal act of banishment carried out according to the Dharma cannot be overturned. Others said:
"A formal suspension that is contrary to the Dharma may be overturned; this is for my sake.
As for me, having actually committed an offense, a formal suspension in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned."

“Because my heart felt remorse and I submitted myself for discipline, the Saṃgha has already granted me release from the suspension; I should now enter the Saṃgha and together perform acts of harmony.

Having been suspended, those bhikṣus immediately took that bhikṣu and the bhikṣus who were in accord with him to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Then those monks, acting in accordance with the Dharma, led that monk to me and said: "This monk says:
'I walked alone and dwelt alone, and I had this thought:'"
"For my sake, the Saṃgha has engaged in strife, mutual recrimination, schism, contention, and division.
Among them, a bhikṣu says:
'This person is guilty.'"
Some said, "There is no offense. Others said:
"He has been expelled according to the Dharma. Some said,
"He has been expelled contrary to the Dharma."
Some said: "A formal act of exclusion performed in accordance with the Dharma cannot be overturned. Others said:
“An unlawful suspension may be overturned; this is all for my sake.
Since I am truly guilty, a lawful suspension cannot be overturned.”
"Because my heart felt remorse and I submitted myself for discipline, the Saṃgha has already granted me release from the suspension; I should now enter among the Saṃgha to bring about harmony.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"

"O bhikṣus, for the sake of harmony, you may investigate this matter as minutely as one would divide a single hair into a hundred parts; do not investigate this matter so minutely for the sake of causing a schism in the Saṃgha."
The Buddha said:
"You should act together in harmony.
If the time for the *poṣadha* has not yet arrived, one should announce within the Saṃgha: "
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now, for the sake of the harmony of the Saṃgha, if it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let us now perform the Poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa, even though it is not the regular Poṣadha day, for the sake of the harmony of the Saṃgha."
"This is called 'white.
Immediately, the *poṣadha* was performed and the *Prātimokṣa* was recited.
This concludes the second section, the Kauśāmbī Rules, among the eight rules. 3. The Campā Rules: Among the eight rules, the third is the Campā Rules. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus performed illegal formal acts (karmavācanā) in various places:

one person would expel another; one person would expel two, three, or four people; two people would expel two people; two people would expel three, four, or one person; three people would expel three people; three people would expel four, one, or two people; and four people would expel four people.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and rebuked, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who performs illegal *karmavācanās* everywhere—expelling one person by means of one, two, three, or four;
expelling two persons by means of two, three, four, or one; expelling three persons by means of three, four, one, or two; and expelling four persons by means of four?"
Having thus rebuked them, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked them, saying:

"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus perform illegal *karmavācanā* proceedings everywhere—such as one person expelling one person, two, three, or four persons; two persons expelling two, three, four, or one person; three persons expelling three, four, one, or two persons; and four persons expelling four persons?"
The Buddha merely rebuked him but did not yet establish a precept.
While the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Campā, there was a village named Rājagṛha in the country of Aśmaka; in it lived an elder bhikṣu named Saṃgharakṣita, who served as the *karmadāna*.
The group of six bhikṣus were traveling through the country of Kāśī toward the country of Campā and arrived at the village of King Śarva.
When those [other] bhikṣus saw them coming from afar, they went out to meet them, took their robes and bowls for them, and showed them the rooms, saying:
"These are the rooms, beds, bedding, covers, and pillows; you may settle yourselves in them according to seniority."
He provided him with bathing requisites, oil, and bath powder; and for those who wished to have their bodies rubbed and massaged, he provided the rubbing and massaging.

This *māmathi* (preceptor) sat in meditation at night, and in the early morning entered the royal city of Śrāvastī. Arriving at the houses of the various nobles, he praised the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"The group of six bhikṣus are disciples of the Buddha; they are learned, skillful in preaching the Dharma, and possess unimpeded eloquence."
"For this reason, you all should provide *taṃpala* food as a midday meal for the Saṅgha.
Immediately, those Brahmins and lay devotees who had faith provided *taṃpala* food as a midday meal for the Saṅgha.
After the group of six bhikṣus had eaten this food, they became robust, attained a fine complexion, gained strength, and their bodies became supple;
they said to one another, "This good man has honored and praised us by preparing such excellent food."
For several days thereafter, [the offerings] were no longer continued. The group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"This good man has become even worse; he no longer respects, makes offerings to, or praises us. We should summon him here."
He immediately summoned them to come; the group of six asked, "Why do you no longer show us respect, make offerings to us, or praise us?
They replied:
"This King, the Brahmins, and the householders of the village of Sarvagrāma who believe my words have been instructed to provide offerings.
My power and influence can rightly extend only this far; I cannot obtain more."
The group of six bhikṣus asked,
"Do you see your transgression?
He replied:
"What fault have I committed?
The group of six replied,
"You no longer look upon us with the same respect, honor, offerings, and praise as you did before."
He said, "I do not see my offense.
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"This man refuses to confess directly; we shall perform an *ajñapti-karman* of suspension for his refusal to acknowledge [the offense] against him.
They then performed the *ajñapti-karman* of suspension against him.
This person thought to himself:

"The group of six bhikṣus has no valid reason; they did not first inform me, yet they forcibly carried out a formal act of suspension against me for refusal to see an offense. Why should I not go to the country of Campā to visit the Buddha?"

Having reflected thus, he stayed as long as he wished in the royal village of Sāvatthī, then took his robe and bowl and went to the land of Campā to visit the Buddha; there he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they inquire of him thus:
"Are you able to endure?
Are you at ease?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not exhausted by the journey?
Thus the Buddha spoke, inquiring after the health of the bhikṣu Sāṃkathyadharin.
"Are you able to endure?
Are you sufficient?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Was it not difficult to beg for alms, and were you not utterly exhausted on the road? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"It is bearable; it is sufficient; there is no difficulty in begging for alms; and I am not fatigued by the journey.
He reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer] already, the Buddha nevertheless asked the bhikṣu Sona:
"For what reason have the group of six bhikṣus expelled you?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Without cause and without reason, they have unjustly expelled me for not seeing [an offense].
The Buddha said, "If the group of six bhikṣus has expelled you without cause and without reason, and you are innocent, do not grieve; I shall be your companion in the Dharma."

When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the bhikṣu who had been subject to the act of banishment was heading toward the country of Campā to visit the Buddha’s dwelling, they thought, “We too shall go to where the Buddha is.

Having reflected thus and stayed as they pleased, they took up their robes and bowls, traveled toward the country of Campā, and arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling. There they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they inquire with these words:
"Are you able to endure?
Are you at ease?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not exhausted by the journey?
The Buddha then used these words to inquire after the six groups of bhikṣus.
"Are you able to endure it?
Are you sufficient?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Was it not difficult to beg for alms? Were you not utterly exhausted on the road?
The group of six bhikṣus replied, "World-Honored One!"
"It is bearable, sufficient, and lived in peace; begging for alms is not difficult, and the journey is not exhausting.
Knowing the answer, the Buddha intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"In the village of Rājagṛha, have you carried out a formal act of suspension against any bhikṣu for refusal to see an offense?"
He replied, “Indeed there are,
World-Honored One!”
Question:
"By what causes and conditions was he expelled?
Answer: "He said:"
"Without cause and without reason, they have forcibly carried out an expulsion against one who is innocent.
For this matter and due to prior circumstances, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various reasons, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can those called bhikṣus, without cause and without reason, forcibly carry out an expulsion against one who is innocent?"
What is meant by saying that a bhikṣu performs illegal *karmavācanā* (formal acts) in various instances?

It refers to one person expelling one person, two persons, three persons, or four persons; two persons expelling two persons, three persons, four persons, or one person; three persons expelling three persons, four persons, one person, or two persons; and four persons expelling four persons.
If a bhikṣu expels one person alone, he commits one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he expels two people alone, he commits two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If he expels three people alone, he commits three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one person expels four people, there are four *dukkaṭa* offenses.
If two people expel two people, there are two *dukkaṭa* offenses.
If two people expel three people, there are three *dukkaṭa* offenses.
If two people expel four people, they commit four *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If three people expel one person, they commit one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If three people expel three people, they commit three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If three persons expel four persons, there are four *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If three persons expel one person, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If three persons expel two persons, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If four persons expel four persons, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense,
because they create the conditions for schism in the Saṃgha.
If one person expels one person, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) and should not be performed.
If one person expels two, three, or four people, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) and should not be performed.
If two people expel two, three, four, or one person, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
If three persons expel three persons, four persons, one person, or two persons, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
If four persons expel four persons, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
If one person expels one person, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
If one person expels two, three, or four persons, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
If two persons expel two, three, four, or one person, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
If three persons expel three persons, four persons, one person, or two persons, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
If four persons expel four persons, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
A formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed by a group of four; in this case, it is accomplished by four bhikṣus.
A formal act may be performed by a group of five; in this case, it is accomplished by five bhikṣus.
A formal act may be performed by a group of ten; in this case, it is accomplished by ten bhikṣus.
A formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed by a group of twenty; herein, it must consist of exactly twenty bhikṣus.
If a formal act is to be performed by a group of four, it must not be carried out with fewer than four bhikṣus; such an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*) should not be performed.
If a layperson acts as the fourth member, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) and should not be performed.

If it is a *śrāmaṇera*, one who is not a bhikṣu, a non-Buddhist, one who has not been suspended for not seeing an offense, one who has not been suspended for not making amends, one who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, one who does not live in communion, one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, one who was originally a layman and defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a eunuch, one who has crossed over [to another sect], one who has killed his father or mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who has shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind—if such a person acts as the fourth member, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
The *karmavācanā* may be performed by a group of five; if it is performed by fewer than five bhikṣus, it is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
If a layperson acts as the fifth member, it is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.

If a śrāmaṇera, a non-bhikṣu, a follower of an external path, one who has not been suspended for not seeing an offense, one who has not been suspended for not making amends, one who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, one who does not live in communion, one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, a former layman who defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a eunuch, one who has crossed over [to another sect], one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Buddha—if such a person acts as the fifth member, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) and should not be performed.
A formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed by a quorum of ten; if it is performed by fewer than ten, it is an illegal formal act and should not be performed.
If a layperson serves as the tenth member, it is an illegal formal act and should not be performed.

If a śrāmaṇera, one who is not a bhikṣu, a follower of an external path, one who has not been seen [to commit an offense], one who has not been formally suspended, one whose evil and false views have not been removed, one who does not live in communion, one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, one who was originally a layperson and defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a eunuch, one who has crossed over [to another sect], one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Buddha—if such a person serves as the tenth member, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) and should not be performed.
A *karmavācanā* may be performed by a group of twenty; if it is performed by fewer than twenty, it is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
If a layperson serves as the twentieth person, it is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.

If the twentieth person is a śrāmaṇera, one who is not a bhikṣu, a follower of an external path, one who has not been suspended for not seeing an offense, one who has not been suspended for not making amends, one who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, one with whom communal residence is not shared, one of various types of those with whom communal residence is not shared, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, one who was originally a layperson and defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a eunuch, one who has crossed over [to another sect], one who has split the internal or external Sangha, one who has killed his father, killed his mother, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Sangha, or shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind—if such a person serves as the twentieth person, this is an illegal *karmavācanā* and should not be performed.
If a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) that requires the fourfold assembly is performed by fewer than four bhikṣus, the *karmavācanā* is not valid.
If a *karmavācanā* that requires the fourfold assembly is performed with a layperson as the fourth member, it is an illegal *karmavācanā*; it is not valid and should not be performed.

If a śrāmaṇera, or even one who has shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind, acts as the fourth member, this is an illegal karman; the karman is not established and should not have been performed.
If a formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed by a group of five, yet it is performed by fewer than five bhikṣus, the formal act is not accomplished.
If a formal act may be performed by a group of five, and a layperson serves as the fifth member, this is contrary to the Dharma; the formal act is not accomplished and should not be performed.

If a śrāmaṇera, one who is not a bhikṣu, a follower of an external path, one who has not been expelled for not seeing [an offense], one who has not performed the formal act of expulsion, one whose evil and false views have not been removed through expulsion, one who does not live in communion, one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, one who was originally a layman and defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Buddha—if such persons serve as the fifth member, it is contrary to the Dharma; the *karmavācanā* is not valid and should not be performed.
If a formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed by a group of ten, yet it is performed by fewer than ten, the formal act is not accomplished and should not be performed.
If a formal act may be performed by a group of ten, and a layperson serves as the tenth member, this is contrary to the Dharma; the formal act is not accomplished and should not be performed.

If a śrāmaṇera, one who is not a bhikṣu, a non-Buddhist, one who has not been seen [as guilty], one for whom no formal act of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman) has been performed, one whose evil and heterodox views have not been removed, one who does not live in communion, one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, one who was originally a layperson and defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who with malicious intent has shed the blood of a Buddha—if such persons serve as the tenth member, this is contrary to the Dharma; the *karman* is not valid and should not be performed.
If a formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be performed by a group of twenty, performing it with fewer than twenty bhikṣus does not constitute a valid formal act; it should not be performed.

If a formal act may be performed by a saṃgha of twenty, and a layperson serves as the twentieth member, this is contrary to the Dharma; it does not constitute a valid formal act and should not be performed.

If the twentieth person is a śrāmaṇera, one who is not a bhikṣu, a follower of an external path, one who has not been suspended for not seeing an offense, one who has not been suspended for not making amends, one who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, one who does not live in communion, one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense, one who was originally a layman and defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a paṇḍaka (impotent man), one who has crossed over [to another sect], one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who with an evil mind has shed the blood of a Buddha—if such persons serve as the twentieth person, it is contrary to the Dharma; the karmavācanā is not accomplished and should not be performed.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, one who is currently undergoing parivāsa (probation) should not serve as the fourth member [of the quorum] when performing the formal act of parivāsa.
Nor should one who has completed parivāsa serve as the fourth member when performing the formal act of parivāsa."
If one who is undergoing *mānatva* constitutes the fourth person, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of separate residence (*parivāsa*) should not be performed.
If one who has completed the *mānatva* constitutes the fourth person, the formal act of separate residence should not be performed.
If one who does not live in communion acts as the fourth member, the formal act of separate residence (pārivāsika-karman) should not be performed.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and of like view may perform the formal act of separate residence.
From now on, if a person under parivāsa (probation) acts as the fourth member, the *mānāpya* (rehabilitation) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If a person whose *parivāsa* has been completed acts as the fourth member, the *mānāpya* *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If one who is undergoing *mānāpya* or one who has completed the *mānāpya* constitutes the fourth member [of the quorum], the *mānāpya* karman should not be performed.
If one who is not in communal residence (*asaṃvāsika*) constitutes the fourth member, the *mānāpya* karman should not be performed.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view may perform the *mānatva* karmavācanā.
From now on, if one who is undergoing separate residence (*pārivāsika*) acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement) karmavācanā should not be performed.
If one who has completed the *parivāsa* (probation) constitutes the fourth member [of the quorum], the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If one who is practicing *mānatva* (penance) constitutes the fourth member, the *mūlāpakarṣa* *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If a person who has completed the *mānatva* penance acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If a person who does not live in communion (*asamvāsika*) acts as the fourth member, the *mūlāpakarṣa* *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
At the very least, when four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view are present, one may perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status) karmavācanā.
From this day forward, if a person in *parivāsa* (probation) serves as the twentieth member [of the quorum], the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation of offenses) karmavācanā should not be performed.

If one who has completed the *parivāsa* (probation), one who is currently undergoing the *mānatva* (penance), or one who has completed the *mānatva* acts as the twentieth person, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the removal of guilt (*āpattivyutthāna*) should not be performed.
If a person who does not live in communion acts as the twentieth member, the *karmavācanā* for absolving from an offense (*āpatti-vinodana*) should not be performed.
At the very minimum, twenty pure bhikṣus of identical views must be present to perform the *karmavācanā* for absolving from an offense.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“Four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view are called the Saṃgha.
If five bhikṣus are pure and share the same view, they are called the Saṃgha.”
If ten bhikṣus are pure and of one view, this is called the Saṃgha.
If twenty bhikṣus are pure and of one view, this is called the Saṃgha.

Within these, when four bhikṣus are pure and of one view, they may perform various *karmas* according to the Dharma, with the exception of the *karma* for the *pravāraṇā*, the *karma* for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the *karma* for the removal of offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*).

Among these, when five bhikṣus are pure and share a common view within the Saṃgha, they may perform various formal acts (karmas) in accordance with the Dharma, except for the formal act of receiving full ordination in the Middle Kingdom and the formal act of expiation from offenses.

Among these, ten bhikṣus who are pure and of one view may perform all formal acts (karmas) according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha, with the exception of the formal act for the removal of guilt (āpattivyutthāna-karman).
Among these, twenty bhikṣus who are pure and of one view may perform all formal acts according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.
At that time, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is there any case where the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) that is not in accordance with the Dharma?”
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"There are five kinds of saṃgha:
first, the shameless and immodest saṃgha;..."
Second, the sheep-like monks;
third, the separate community of monks;
fourth, the pure monks.
Fifth is the Sangha of Reality.
As for the Sangha of the Shameless: those bhikṣus who have broken the precepts are called the Sangha of the Shameless.

As for the Sangha of the Sheep: if bhikṣus are ordinary persons of dull faculties and lack wisdom, like a flock of sheep gathered in one place with nothing to know—these bhikṣus do not know the *poṣadha*, they do not know the *poṣadha-karman*, they do not know the recitation of the precepts, and they do not know the Dharma assemblies; these are called the Sangha of the Sheep.
"To separate from the community of monks" means that if various bhikṣus perform various *karmas* separately in different locations within a single boundary.
"The pure community of monks" refers to ordinary persons who maintain the precepts and ordinary persons who have attained victory; these are called the pure community of monks.
The true Saṃgha consists of those who are in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is called the true Saṃgha.
Among these, the first three types of Saṃgha can perform illegal formal acts (adharma-karman), whereas the latter two types cannot perform illegal formal acts.
The Buddha told Upāli:
“Furthermore, there are four kinds of *karmavācanā*:
illegal *karmavācanā*, legal *karmavācanā*, a *karmavācanā* performed by a separate assembly, and a *karmavācanā* performed by a harmonious assembly.”
Regarding illegal *karmas*: if a *jñapti-karman* is performed without the *jñapti*, it is called an illegal *karman*;
if a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is performed without the *jñapti*, this too is illegal;
furthermore, if one performs the *jñapti* but fails to proclaim the *karman*, this also is illegal.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* (formal motion) without first making the *jñapti* (announcement), this is also contrary to the Dharma;
if one performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one announcement and three motions) while omitting the announcement, this is also contrary to the Dharma;
and if, after the announcement has been made, one does not perform the *karmavācanā* three times, this is also contrary to the Dharma.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* by reciting it three times without first making a formal motion (*jñapti*), it is an illegal *karman*;
if one should grant the *bhūtapratyākhyāna-vinaya* (settlement by presence) but grants the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), it is an illegal *karman*;
if one should grant the *smṛtivinaya* but grants the *bhūtapratyākhyāna-vinaya*, it is an illegal *karman*.
To grant the *smṛti-vinaya* (rehabilitation through recollection) when one should grant the *amūḍha-vinaya* (rehabilitation for those who were not insane) is an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*).
To grant the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (rehabilitation in the presence of the assembly) when one should grant the *amūḍha-vinaya* is an illegal formal act.

To grant the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane) when the *pratijñā-kāraka-vinaya* (the discipline based on confession) should be granted, is an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*).
To grant the *pratijñā-kāraka-vinaya* when the *amūḍha-vinaya* should be granted, is an illegal formal act.
To grant the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya* when the *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya* should be granted, is an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*).
To grant the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya* when the *yadbhūyaiṣīya-vinaya* should be granted, is an illegal formal act.
To grant the *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya* (disciplinary procedure for seeking the truth) when one should grant the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) is an illegal formal act (*adharma-karman*).
To grant the *tarjanīya-karman* when one should grant the *yathābhūta-mṛṣā-vinaya* is an illegal formal act.
To grant the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) and the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) together is an illegal *karman*.
To grant the *niśraya-karman* and the *tarjanīya-karman* together is an illegal *karman*.
To grant the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) when the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) should be granted is an illegal formal act.
To grant the formal act of dependence when the formal act of expulsion should be granted is an illegal formal act.
To perform a *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) when a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) should be performed, is an illegal *karman*.
To perform a *pravāsanīya-karman* when a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya-karman* should be performed, is an illegal *karman*.
To grant the *tāpanīya-karman* (act of subduing) and the *parivāsa-karman* (act of probation) together is an illegal *karman*.
To grant the *parivāsa-karman* and the *tāpanīya-karman* together is an illegal *karman*.
To grant the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* when one should grant the *mānāpya* (rehabilitation) *karmavācanā* is an illegal *karmavācanā*.
To grant the *pārivāsika-mūlāpakarṣa* (return to the beginning of probation) *karmavācanā* when one should grant the *mānāpya* *karmavācanā* is an illegal *karmavācanā*.
To grant the *āpattivyutthāpana-karman* and the *yadbhūyaḥkaraṇīya-karman* is an illegal karman.
To grant the *āpattivyutthāpana-karman* and the *mānāpya-karman* is an illegal karman.

If various matters arise within the Saṃgha that are settled in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, these are all termed "unlawful" (adharma).
This is called an unlawful formal act (adharma-karman).
"Regarding *dharmakarma* (legal formal acts): if a motion (*jñapti*) is performed using a motion, this is a *dharmakarma*.
If a motion-and-one-announcement (*jñaptidvitīyakarman*) is performed by making the motion and then announcing once, this is a *dharmakarma*."
If, after the motion (*jñapti*) has been made, it is proclaimed three times during the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, this is a legal formal act.
If one should grant the *bhūta-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) where the *bhūta-vinaya* is appropriate, this is a legal formal act.

If one should grant *smṛtivinaya* where *smṛtivinaya* is appropriate; grant *amūḍhavinaya* where *amūḍhavinaya* is appropriate; grant *pratijñākāraka* where *pratijñākāraka* is appropriate; grant *tattvānusaraṇa-vinaya* where *tattvānusaraṇa-vinaya* is appropriate; grant the *tarjanīyakarman* where the *tarjanīya* is appropriate; grant the *niśrayakarman* where the *niśraya* is appropriate; grant the *pratisāraṇīyakarman* where the *pratisāraṇīya* is appropriate; grant the *pravāsanīyakarman* where the *pravāsana* is appropriate; grant the *parivāsakarman* where the *parivāsa* is appropriate; grant the *mānatva* where the *mānatva* is appropriate; grant the *mūlāpakarṣa* where the *mūlāpakarṣa* is appropriate; and grant the *āvarhaṇa* where the *āvarhaṇa* is appropriate—this is called a legal (*dharmika*) formal act (*karman*).

If various matters arise within the Saṃgha and they are settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called a *dharmika-karman* (a formal act in accordance with the Dharma).

As for a *pṛthag-jana-karman* (a formal act performed by a separate assembly): when the bhikṣus required for that formal act do not assemble together in one place; when those who may grant their consent (*chanda*) do not grant it; or when a bhikṣu present before the assembly objects and the objection is upheld—this is called a *pṛthag-jana-karman*.

Furthermore, there is the *bhedasaṃgha-karman* (the formal act of a divided assembly). In this formal act, the monks required for the procedure are gathered in one place; those who may give their consent (*chanda*) do not give it, and the monks present obstruct the proceedings even though they are qualified to do so. This is called the *bhedasaṃgha-karman*.

Furthermore, there is the *bhinnasaṃgha-karman* (act of the divided assembly). In this *karman*, the monks required for the procedure must assemble in one place; those who may give their consent (*chanda*) must give their consent, and any monk present who would obstruct must effect the obstruction. This is called the *bhinnasaṃgha-karman*.

"A formal act of concord (saṃghakamma) is that in which the required bhikṣus assemble in one place, those who may give their consent do so, and the bhikṣus present do not obstruct what could be obstructed; this is called a formal act of concord."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Which bhikṣus may prevent the acceptance [of a robe],
and which bhikṣus may not prevent its acceptance?"
The Buddha said:
"If the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* in accordance with the Dharma, and there is a monk therein who objects, it should not be accepted;

likewise if a layperson (*avadātavasana*), a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), one who is not a monk, a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), one who has been suspended for not seeing an offense (*adarśanārhasthāpita*), one who has been suspended for not making amends (*apratinisṛṣṭārhasthāpita*), one who has been suspended for not relinquishing evil views (*apratiniḥsṛṣṭāpāpaka-dṛṣṭisthāpita*), one who does not live in communion (*asaṃvāsika*), one who lives in various forms of non-communion, one who confesses to having committed a grave offense (*guru-apatti*), one who was originally a layperson who defiled a bhikṣuṇī, a paṇḍaka (impotent man), a *vaitulyika* (one who has gone over to another sect), one who has killed his father, one who has killed his mother, one who has killed an Arhat, one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or one who has shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind—if such persons object, it should not be accepted."
If those within the boundary obstruct a formal act (*karmavācanā*) being performed by those outside the boundary, it should not be accepted;
if those outside the boundary obstruct a formal act being performed by those within the boundary, it should not be accepted;
if those at a lower level obstruct a formal act being performed by those at a higher level, it should not be accepted.
If one is at a high place while others obstruct those below from performing the *karmavācanā*, one should not accept it;

if those who would obstruct do not reach the place where the Saṃgha is performing the *karmavācanā*; if they have reached it but do not request permission (*anujñā*); or if a person of broken precepts (*duḥśīla*) obstructs—in all these cases, one should not accept it.
Furthermore, if a person of broken precepts mentally obstructs [the procedure], one should likewise not accept it; this is called "that which should not be accepted."
Regarding those who should accept a prohibition: if the Saṃgha performs an illegal *karmavācanā*, and a bhikṣu therein offers a prohibition, it should be accepted.
If the Saṃgha performs an illegal *karmavācanā* within a boundary (*sīmā*), and a bhikṣu within that boundary offers a prohibition, it should be accepted.
If a monk who has been obstructed arrives at the assembly after having requested permission to speak, his [statement] should be accepted.
If a monk who upholds the precepts obstructs him, it should be accepted.
This is called "that which should be accepted."

There were certain bhikṣus who, through an illegal and schismatic assembly, suspended a bhikṣu. Then a community of bhikṣus came to resolve the matter; there was an illegal and schismatic assembly, an illegal and harmonious assembly, a semblance-of-dharma and schismatic assembly, a semblance-of-dharma and harmonious assembly, a legal and schismatic assembly, and a legal and harmonious assembly.

Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣus who, through an illegal assembly in concord, expelled a bhikṣu. Then a community of bhikṣus arrived to resolve the matter; there were [assemblies that were] an illegal separate assembly, an illegal assembly in concord, an assembly resembling the Dharma but separate, an assembly resembling the Dharma but in concord, a legal separate assembly, and a legal assembly in concord.

Furthermore, there are monks who, through a semblance of the Dharma and a separate assembly, expel a monk. Then a community of monks arrives to resolve the matter; there are cases involving an illegal separate assembly, an illegal united assembly, a semblance of the Dharma with a separate assembly, a semblance of the Dharma with a united assembly, a legal separate assembly, and a legal united assembly.

Furthermore, there are cases where monks, appearing to act in accordance with the Dharma, carry out a formal act of banishment against a monk by a concordant assembly (*saṃgha*). Then, another assembly of monks arrives to resolve the matter; these include: an illegal separate assembly, an illegal concordant assembly, an assembly resembling the Dharma that is separate, an assembly resembling the Dharma that is concordant, a legal separate assembly, and a legal concordant assembly.

Furthermore, there are cases where a community of bhikṣus has, in accordance with the Dharma, performed a formal act of exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against a bhikṣu. Then another community of bhikṣus arrives to revoke that act; these include: an illegal act by a separate assembly, an illegal act by a united assembly, an act resembling the Dharma by a separate assembly, an act resembling the Dharma by a united assembly, a legal act by a separate assembly, and a legal act by a united assembly.

Furthermore, there is a community of monks who, in accordance with the Dharma, perform a formal act of suspension against a monk; then another community of monks comes to revoke that act—whether it be an illegal separate assembly, an illegal united assembly, a semblance-of-Dharma separate assembly, a semblance-of-Dharma united assembly, a legal separate assembly, or a legal united assembly.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"In this context, one assembly is called 'the true formal act of suspension,' namely, a harmonious assembly acting according to the Dharma;
another assembly is called 'the true resolution of suspension,' namely, a harmonious assembly resolving [the matter] according to the Dharma."
The third of the eight rules concerning Campā is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 30.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 31. The Third Recitation, Part Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The *Pratideśanīya-dharma*, the fourth among the eight dharmas; according to the Dan edition, it is the beginning of the fourth section on the *Tajñā-karman* among the eight dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus in the kingdom of Śrāvastī:

one named Pañca and the other Rūka. They delighted in quarreling and disputing with one another; having already engaged in disputes and arguments with various other bhikṣus, they recognized these [other] bhikṣus as quarrelsome and went to them, saying:
"You must resolutely and firmly maintain this matter and not be struck down by others. You shall be victorious, and we will assist you."
He further addressed the second faction, saying:
"You must resolutely and firmly maintain this matter and not allow yourselves to be struck down by others; if you achieve victory, I shall assist you."

For this reason, monks who have not yet been split will be split, and those already split cannot be reconciled; matters that have not yet arisen within the Saṃgha will arise, and those already arisen cannot be extinguished.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu delight in quarreling and mutual recrimination?"
Knowing that these were quarreling bhikṣus, he went to their place and said:
"You must resolutely and firmly maintain this matter and not be struck down by others; if you achieve victory, I shall assist you."
He further addressed the second faction, saying:
"You must resolutely and firmly uphold this matter and not be struck down by others; if you achieve victory, I shall provide assistance."

For these reasons, those who have not yet split the Saṃgha will split it, and those who have already split it cannot be reconciled; matters that have not yet arisen will arise, and matters that have already arisen cannot be extinguished.
Having thus rebuked them, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [what had occurred], he intentionally asked the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked them with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu delight in quarreling and mutual recrimination? Knowing that they are quarreling and recriminating, he goes to their place and says:
'You must resolutely and firmly maintain this matter and do not let others strike at you; you shall achieve victory, and I will assist you.'"
He further addressed the second faction, saying:
"You must resolutely and firmly uphold this matter and not be struck down by others; if you achieve victory, I shall provide assistance."

For these reasons, those who have not yet split the Saṃgha will split it, and those who have already split it cannot be reconciled; matters that have not yet arisen within the Saṃgha will arise, and matters that have already arisen cannot be extinguished.
Having thus rebuked him, he said to the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *kutikaraṇa* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka.
Should there be anyone else who acts in such a manner, you should likewise perform the *kutikaraṇa* against them."
If a bhikṣu commits an offense in any of three matters, a *kaṭhina-karman* (act of censure) should be performed against him:
whether it be breaking the precepts, breaking right view, or breaking proper deportment.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons for whom the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) should be performed:
those who delight in quarreling, those who delight in disputing, and those who delight in mutual recrimination.
There are three ways of performing the *tarjanīya-karman* that are contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya:
A formal act of suspension may be performed in the absence of the person to be suspended, without first announcing the matter, and without causing them to recall it.
There are three types of acts that are in accordance with the Dharma:
those performed in the presence of the person to be suspended, those performed after first announcing the matter, and those performed after causing them to recall it.
There are three kinds that can be subverted:
acting contrary to the Dharma, acting with a divided assembly, and acting without the person being present.
There are three kinds that cannot be subverted:
It is performed according to the Dharma, performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and performed in the presence of the individuals concerned.
There are three ways in which it may be subject to schism:
if it is performed contrary to the Dharma, if it is performed by a factional assembly, or if it is performed without first announcing the matter.
There are three kinds that cannot be split:
those performed according to the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed after first announcing the matter.
There are three kinds that can be split:

There are three types of formal acts that cannot be overturned: those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a non-unified assembly, and those performed without causing [the members] to remember [the offense].
There are three types that can be overturned:
those performed in accordance with the Dharma, those performed by a unified Sangha, and those performed while causing [the members] to remember [the offense].
Furthermore, there are three kinds of illegal and non-disciplinary acts that may be subverted:

performing them against one who has not committed an offense, performing them against one who has committed an offense that cannot be atoned for, and performing them against one who has already atoned for the offense.
There are three kinds of legal acts that cannot be overturned:
those performed for one who has committed an offense, those performed for one who has committed an offense that can be confessed, and those performed for one who has not yet confessed.
There are three kinds that can be overturned:

There are three kinds of actions that cannot be overturned: those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a separate assembly, and those performed for one who has not committed an offense.
There are three kinds that can be overturned:
those performed in accordance with the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed for one who has committed an offense.
There are three kinds that can be invalidated:
those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a separate assembly, and those not performed for the sake of repentance.
There are three kinds that cannot be invalidated:
It is performed according to the Dharma, performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and performed for one who has committed an offense that can be confessed.
There are three types of [actions] that may cause a schism:
those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a divided assembly, and those performed for one who has already confessed their offense.
There are three kinds that cannot be overturned:
those performed according to the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed for one who has not yet atoned for their offense.
Regarding the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu shall announce within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Pañcalaka delights in quarreling and mutual dispute. Knowing that these bhikṣus were quarreling, he went to them and said:
'You must firmly maintain this matter and do not let others strike at you; you shall achieve victory, and I will assist you.'"
He further said to the second group of bhikṣus:
"You must firmly uphold this matter and not allow yourselves to be struck down by others; you shall achieve victory, and I will assist you."

For this reason, monks who have not yet been divided will be divided, and those already divided cannot be reconciled; matters that have not yet arisen within the Saṃgha will arise, and those already arisen cannot be extinguished.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall perform the *kutikarman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Paṇḍaluka. For as long as you, bhikṣu Paṇḍaluka, continue to engage in impure conduct and do not cease your harsh speech, for that duration the Saṃgha shall perform the *kutikarman* against you.
"This is called the motion.
Thus is the formal act of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Saṃgha has completed the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) against the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
Regarding the conduct of a bhikṣu who has received the *kukṛtya-karman* (the act of censure): this bhikṣu should not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others;
he should not accept dependence (*niśraya*) from others;
and he must not maintain a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).
One must not undergo the *karmavācanā* for admonishing a bhikṣuṇī; if one has previously undergone it, one should not admonish her.

One must not commit a second offense of the same nature as the *kaṭhina* (severe) *karmavācanā* offense; one must not commit an offense similar to it; one must not commit an offense exceeding it. One must not criticize various *karmas*, nor criticize those who perform the *karma*. One must not expose the faults or offenses of pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣus.
One must not beg for permission from others, nor say: "I shall bring forth your offense."
"One should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, nor should one oppose pure monks; rather, one should subdue the mind and act with reverence in accordance with the Dharma.
If one does not practice according to this Dharma, one shall not be released from this *kaṭhina-karman* (severe disciplinary measure) for as long as one lives."
Immediately, the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, withdrew to one side and performed the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka.

Once the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka had received the *tarjanīya-karman*, his mind was filled with remorse and he became subdued; being respectful and humble, he petitioned the Saṃgha for the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If Paṇḍuluka repents in his heart and is subdued, the Saṃgha should grant him release."
If there should be others who are likewise such persons, they too should be granted release.
If a bhikṣu does not act in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should not grant him release from the *kaṭhina-karman* (act of censure).
