If one ordains another by conferring the full precepts (upasampadā), acts as a formal mentor (niśraya) for another while keeping a novice (śrāmaṇera), performs the formal ritual (karma) of instructing a bhikṣuṇī, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, commits a grave offense, commits an offense similar [to a pārājika], commits an offense exceeding that, reviles a formal ritual, reviles those who perform the formal ritual, requests from another the permission to clear a bhikṣu of his offense, or says:
"I shall clear your offense."
If one obstructs the recitation of the *poṣadha* and the *pravāraṇā*, opposes pure monks, and does not repent in their heart or submit with humility, they should not be granted release.
If one acts in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should grant them the lifting of the *duṣkṛta* (painful) *karman*.
They shall not confer the full ordination upon others, shall not act as a preceptor for others, shall not keep novices, and shall not receive instructions from bhikṣuṇīs.

If the *karmavācanā* has already been performed, and one does not instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; if one has not committed a repeated offense, nor a similar offense, nor an offense exceeding that; if one does not criticize the *karmavācanā*, nor the person performing the *karmavācanā*; if one does not request permission from others; if one does not bring forth the offenses of pure bhikṣus;
and if one does not say: "I shall bring forth your offense."
He does not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, nor does he oppose pure bhikṣus.
If his mind becomes remorseful, subdued, and softened, one should grant him the lifting of the *kaṭhina-karman*.

Regarding the ritual procedure for the *jñapti-karman* (formal motion): The harmonious Saṃgha, with one mind, [should act as follows]. The bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka rises from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and spoke these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please attend!..."
I, the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka, take delight in quarreling and engaging in mutual disputes. Knowing that these bhikṣus were quarreling and disputing, I went to them and said:
"You must firmly uphold this matter and not let others strike against you; may you achieve victory, and I shall assist you."
He further said to the second group of bhikṣus:
"You must firmly uphold this matter and not allow yourselves to be struck down by others; if you achieve victory, I shall assist you."

"For these reasons, those monks who have not yet been divided are divided, and those already divided cannot be reconciled; matters that have not yet arisen within the Saṃgha arise, and matters already arisen cannot be extinguished. Therefore, the Saṃgha has performed the *kaṭhina-karman* (act of censure) against us."
We have received the *tāpanīya-karman* (act of censure). Our hearts are filled with remorse and we are subdued; we now beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this *tāpanīya-karman*.
We, the Bhikṣus Paṇḍuluka, are now remorseful and subdued; out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant us its release.
A second and third time he likewise requested.
Immediately, one bhikṣu proclaimed among the saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu Pañcāla was fond of quarreling and engaging in mutual disputes. Knowing that these bhikṣus were quarreling, he went to them and said:
"You must firmly maintain this matter and not let others strike against you; if you achieve victory, I shall assist you."
He further said to the monks of the second faction:
"You must firmly uphold this matter and not allow yourselves to be struck down by others; you shall be victorious, and I will assist you."

For these reasons, those monks who have not yet been split are split, and those already split cannot be reconciled; matters that have not yet arisen within the Saṃgha arise, and matters already arisen cannot be extinguished. Therefore, the Saṃgha performs the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against them.
This bhikṣu Pañcāla, having undergone the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), has repented with a humbled mind and now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha lift the *kaṭhina* (severe) *karmavācanā* against the bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka.
This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Sangha has finished lifting the *kutikarman* (act of censure) against the bhikṣu Paṇḍaluka; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Śreṇika repeatedly committed offenses and repeatedly confessed his transgressions without limit.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the formal act of *niśraya-karman* (the rite of dependence) against the bhikṣu Śreṇika."
"If there are other such bhikṣus as well, they too should be granted the formal act of dependence (niśraya-karman).
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu has committed an offense in three matters, he should be granted the formal act of dependence."
Whether it be breaking the precepts, breaking right view, or breaking proper decorum;
furthermore, there are three kinds:
delighting in strife, delighting in contention, and delighting in mutual dispute.
There are three kinds of formal acts of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) that are contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya:
performing them when the person who is to be suspended is not present; performing them without first announcing their offense; and performing them without causing them to remember [the offense].
There are three kinds of formal acts of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) that are in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya:
performing them in the presence of one who cannot be refuted, performing them by first proclaiming his offense, and performing them by causing him to remember [the offense].
There are three kinds that can be subverted:
acting contrary to the Dharma, acting with a divided assembly, and acting in the absence of the person concerned.
There are three kinds that cannot be subverted:
It is performed according to the Dharma, performed by a harmonious assembly, and performed in the presence of the individuals concerned.
There are three ways it may be subject to schism:
if performed contrary to the Dharma, if performed by a divided assembly, or if performed without first proclaiming the offense.
There are three kinds that cannot be split:
those performed according to the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed after first proclaiming the offense.
There are three kinds that can be split:
There are three kinds of invalid acts: those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a non-unified assembly, and those performed without causing [the members] to remember [the offense].
There are three kinds of acts that cannot be overturned:
those performed in accordance with the Dharma, those performed by a unified Sangha, and those performed while causing [the members] to remember [the offense].
There are three types that may be revoked:
those given to one who has not committed an offense, those given to one for whom the offense cannot be atoned for, and those given to one who has already atoned for the offense.
There are three types that may not be revoked:
There are three types of formal acts: those performed for one who has committed an offense, those performed for one who is fit to confess, and those performed for one who has not yet confessed.
There are three ways in which an act may be subject to invalidation:
performing it contrary to the Dharma, performing it with a divided assembly, and performing it for one who has not committed an offense.
There are three kinds that cannot be split:
those performed according to the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed for one who has committed an offense.
There are three kinds that can be split:
It is performed contrary to the Dharma, performed by a divided assembly, and performed for the purpose of an irreparable offense.
There are three kinds that cannot be subverted:
those performed in accordance with the Dharma, performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and performed for the purpose of a reparable offense.
There are three kinds that can be subverted:
those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a separate assembly, and those performed for one who has already confessed their transgression.
There are three kinds that cannot be subverted:
It is performed according to the Dharma, performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and performed for one who has not yet atoned for their offense.
There are two kinds of *niśraya-karman*:
first, "You should be instructed to dwell in dependence upon such-and-such a person."
Second, the *niśraya-karman* (the formal act of dependence) should be explained.
Regarding the *niśraya-karman*: with a single-mindedly harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu should proclaim within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu Śīva has repeatedly committed offenses and repeatedly confessed them, without limit.

If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate and grants its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) upon the bhikṣu Śīva: for as long as you, Śīva, engage in impure conduct and do not conform to the Path, for that duration the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of dependence upon you.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has completed the act of dependence (niśraya-karman) against the bhikṣu Śivaka. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

Regarding the conduct of a bhikṣu who has received the formal act of dependence (niśraya-karman): he should not confer the full ordination (upasampadā) upon others; he should not accept dependence from others; he may not keep a śrāmaṇera; he may not receive the formal act for instructing bhikṣuṇīs; if he previously accepted it, he should not instruct them; he should not commit a grave offense; he should not commit an offense similar [to one already committed]; he should not commit an offense more serious than that; he should not criticize the formal act; he should not criticize the person performing the formal act; he should not expose the faults or offenses of a pure bhikṣu; he should not beg for permission from others; and he should not say: "I shall expose your offense."
"One should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, nor should one oppose a pure bhikṣu.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, withdrew to one side and performed the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) for the bhikṣu Śreṇika.
Because Śreṇika had performed the *karmavācanā*, his mind was repentant, subdued, and softened; he then requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *niśraya-karman*.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If the bhikṣu Śreṇika’s mind is repentant and subdued, the Saṃgha should grant him the lifting [of the penalty]."
If there are others who are likewise, they too should be granted release.

If a bhikṣu does not act in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should not grant him release from the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence). This applies if he ordains others, acts as a preceptor for others, keeps śrāmaṇeras, performs the *karman* of instructing bhikṣuṇīs, or if he has previously accepted [the duty] to instruct bhikṣuṇīs despite being unfit to do so; or if he commits a grave offense, or an offense similar to it, or an offense exceeding it; or if he reviles the *karman*, or reviles those performing the *karman*; or if he begs for permission from others, or exposes the offenses of pure bhikṣus, or says: "I shall expose your offenses."
If one obstructs the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, opposes pure monks, or does not repent with a contrite heart and become humble and pliant, the *saṃgha* should not grant release from the penalty.

If one acts in accordance with the Dharma, the *saṃgha* should grant release from the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence). One should not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, nor provide dependence to others, nor keep *śrāmaṇeras*, nor perform the *karman* for instructing *bhikṣuṇīs*. If one has previously accepted the duty of instructing *bhikṣuṇīs*, one should no longer do so. One must not commit a grave offense again, nor commit an offense similar to the previous one, nor commit an offense exceeding it. One must not criticize the *karman*, nor criticize those performing the *karman*, nor seek permission from others [to act], nor expose the offenses of pure monks, nor say: "I shall expose your offense."
He does not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, nor does he oppose pure bhikṣus.
If his mind has become repentant, subdued, and supple, he should be granted the *niśraya-vimocana-karman*.

Regarding the method for performing the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence): The harmonious Saṃgha, being of one mind, [should act as follows]. The bhikṣu Śreṇika rises from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and spoke these words:

"Venerable Saṃgha, please take heed. I, the bhikṣu Śreṇika, have repeatedly committed offenses and repeatedly repented them without limit; therefore, the Saṃgha has performed the *niśraya-karman* against me."
Because I received the *niśraya-karman*, my mind was filled with remorse and I submitted to discipline; I now beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this *niśraya-karman*.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant me its release.
A second and a third time he likewise requested.
Immediately, one bhikṣu proclaimed among the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu Śreṇika repeatedly committed offenses and repeatedly confessed them without limit; therefore, the Saṃgha performed the *niśraya-karman* against him.
Because this bhikṣu Śreṇika has received the *niśraya-karman*, his mind has been remorseful and subdued, and he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *niśraya-karman*.
"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha grant the revocation of the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) for the bhikṣu Śreṇika.
This is called the *jñapti* (motion).
Thus is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
"The Saṃgha has completed the *niśraya-vimocana-karman* for the bhikṣu Śīva; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the kingdom of Kṛṣṇagiri, there were two bhikṣus, Aśvinī and Pūrṇa, who defiled families and engaged in evil conduct. Their defiling of families was seen by all, heard by all, and known by all; their engagement in evil conduct was likewise seen, heard, and known by all.
This bhikṣu sits on the same bed as a woman; eats from the same dish; drinks alcohol from the same vessel; eats after midday;
eats food that has been stored overnight; eats food that was not formally offered or for which the *khalupaścādbhakti* (refusal of further food) rule has not been performed;
plays musical sounds by beating a drum or pinching the lips; makes music with the teeth; strikes a bronze basin, or plucks a *tāla* lute.
[They] made various kinds of music, song, and dance with tree leaves; they wore garlands and necklaces and anointed their bodies with perfumes;
they wore garments scented with incense and sprinkled themselves with water; they personally gathered flowers or had others gather them for them;
they personally strung flower garlands or had others string them for them; they personally placed flowers upon their heads or had others place them there; they [themselves] wore [them].
He causes earrings to be worn; he takes other women away himself or causes others to take them away;

he causes elephants to fight, horses to fight, chariots to fight, infantry to fight, rams to fight, water buffaloes to fight, dogs to fight, cocks to fight, men to fight, and women to fight; he also fights with his own hands or strikes [others].
They trample with their feet, run in all four directions, change their attire, gallop and leap about,
float and submerge in water, break and cut down trees, strike their arms, slap their thighs, weep, cry out loudly,
or whistle and speak gibberish in the various languages of foreign lands; they bound backward like fish writhing, and hurl objects into the air.
He himself went to receive her, and together with a woman, boarded a large ship to perform music;
he rode upon elephants, horses, and carriages, and led a great multitude blowing conch shells as they entered the groves and gardens—
performing all such various kinds of evil and impure acts.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the formal act of expulsion (pravāsanīya-karman) against the bhikṣus Aśvaka and Punarvasuka."
"If there are further bhikṣus such as these, they too should be subjected to the formal act of expulsion (nāśanīya-karman).
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu commits an offense regarding three matters, the Saṃgha should subject him to the formal act of expulsion."
If one has violated the precepts, violated the views, or violated the decorum,
there are three types for whom the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) should be performed:
those who delight in fighting, those who delight in quarreling, and those who delight in mutual verbal disputes.
There are three kinds of illegal and non-disciplinary *karman* for the act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*):
performing it when the person subject to it is not present, performing it without first declaring their offense, and performing it without causing them to remember [the offense].
There are three ways in which the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) is performed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya:
performing it in the presence of one who cannot be refuted, performing it after first proclaiming their offense, and performing it by causing them to remember [the offense].
There are three kinds that can be subverted:
acting contrary to the Dharma, acting with a divided assembly, and acting in the absence of the person concerned.
There are three kinds that cannot be subverted:
It is performed according to the Dharma, performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and performed in the presence of the individuals concerned.
There are three ways in which it may be subject to disruption:
if it is performed contrary to the Dharma, if it is performed by a separate assembly, or if the offense is not first declared.
There are three kinds that cannot be split:
those performed according to the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed after first proclaiming the offense.
There are three kinds that can be split:

There are three types of actions that cannot be overturned: those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a fragmented assembly, and those performed without causing [the members] to remember.
There are three types that can be overturned:
those performed in accordance with the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed while causing [the members] to remember.
There are three types of acts of *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) that may be annulled:

performing it against one who has not committed an offense, performing it against one whose offense is not subject to confession, and performing it against one who has already confessed their offense.
There are three kinds of acts of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) that cannot be overturned:
those performed for one who has committed an offense, those performed for one whose offense is subject to confession, and those performed for one who has not yet confessed their offense.
There are three kinds that can be overturned:

There are three types of actions that cannot be overturned: those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a dissension of the Saṃgha, and those performed for one who has not committed an offense.
There are three types that can be overturned:
those performed in accordance with the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and those performed for one who has committed an offense.
There are three kinds that can be broken:
those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a separate assembly, and those performed for the sake of an irreproachable offense.
There are three kinds that cannot be broken:
It is performed according to the Dharma, performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and performed for one who is capable of repentance.
There are three types of [actions] that can cause a schism:
those performed contrary to the Dharma, those performed by a divided assembly, and those performed with one who has already repented.
There are three kinds of *anavavāda* (irreversible acts):
those performed according to the Dharma, those performed by a harmonious Saṃgha, and the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) performed against one who has not yet atoned for their offense.
Regarding the procedure for the *pravāsanīya-karman*: with the Saṃgha gathered in harmony and focused on a single mind, one bhikṣu should announce within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These bhikṣus, Maśaka and Pūrṇa, have defiled families and committed evil deeds. That they have defiled families is seen, heard, and known by all; that they have committed evil deeds is likewise seen, heard, and known. The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of expulsion against [Name]."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against the bhikṣus Aśvaka and Punarvasuka; for as long as you, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, do not abandon this impure conduct, for that duration shall the Saṃgha perform the formal act of expulsion against you.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has completed the act of banishment against the bhikṣus Maśuka and Pūrṇa. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."

Regarding the conduct of a monk who has undergone the formal act of *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (expulsion): he should not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; he may not receive dependence (*nissaya*) from another; he may not keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); he may not perform the formal act of instructing nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-ovādaka-kamma*); if he was previously authorized, he should no longer instruct them; he should not commit the same offense for which he was expelled; he should not commit a similar offense; he should not commit an offense more serious than that; he should not criticize the formal act; he should not criticize those who performed the formal act; he should not expose the faults or offenses of pure monks; and he should not request permission from others [to act].
One should not say, "I shall absolve you of your offense.
One should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, nor should one oppose pure bhikṣus; rather, one should subdue the mind and pay respect in accordance with the Dharma.
"If one does not practice according to this Dharma, one shall not be released from the *pravāsanīya-karman* for as long as one lives.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, withdrew to one side and performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* against Aśvaka and Punarvasuka.

Because the bhikṣus Aśvayuj and Pūrṇamāsa had undergone the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment), their minds became remorseful, subdued, and softened; they then requested the Saṃgha to revoke the *pravāsanīya-karman*.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"If the bhikṣus Aśvayuj and Pūrṇamāsa have become subdued in mind, the Saṃgha should grant them revocation."
If there are others who are likewise, the Saṃgha should also grant them release.

If a bhikṣu does not act in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should not grant him release from the *karman* of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), nor should it grant him the full ordination (*upasampadā*) for another, provide him with formal reliance (*niśraya*), allow him to keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), perform the *karman* of instructing a bhikṣuṇī, actually instruct a bhikṣuṇī, commit a grave offense, commit an offense similar to that [grave offense], commit an offense exceeding that [grave offense], criticize the *karman*, criticize the person performing the *karman*, request permission from another, or expose the offenses of a pure bhikṣu.
If one says,
"I shall absolve you of your offense," yet obstructs the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*, or acts in opposition to pure bhikṣus.
If one does not feel remorse in their heart, is subdued, and remains pliant, they should not be granted release.

If they act in accordance with the Dharma, the Saṃgha should grant them release from the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment). They shall not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; they shall not serve as a preceptor for others; they shall not keep novices (*śrāmaṇera*); they shall not receive the *karman* for instructing bhikṣuṇīs; they shall not instruct bhikṣuṇīs; they shall not commit grave offenses again; they shall not commit offenses similar to those already committed; they shall not commit offenses more serious than those; they shall not criticize the *karman*; they shall not criticize those who perform the *karman*; they shall not request permission from others; they shall not expose the offenses of pure bhikṣus; and they shall not say: "I expose your offense."
One should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, nor oppose pure bhikṣus.
If the mind is remorseful, subdued, and softened, one should grant the *an-utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (the act of releasing the suspension).

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for the formal act of expulsion: the harmonious Saṃgha, being of one mind, [should proceed as follows]. The bhikṣus Aśvayuja and Pūrṇamāsa rise from their seats, bare their right shoulders, remove their leather sandals, kneel with their right knees on the ground, join their palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!
"Venerable sirs, the bhikṣus Aśvaka and Punarvasuka have defiled families and committed evil deeds.

That they have defiled families is seen, heard, and known by all; that they have committed evil deeds is also seen, heard, and known by all. Therefore, the Saṃgha has performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against us."

Because we have been subjected to the formal act of expulsion (*nissāraṇīya-karman*), our minds are filled with remorse and we are subdued; we now beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this act of expulsion.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant us its release.
A second and a third time he requested in this same manner.
Immediately, one bhikṣu proclaimed among the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

These monks, Aśvinī and Pūrṇā, have defiled families and engaged in evil conduct; that they have defiled families is seen, heard, and known by all, and that they have engaged in evil conduct is likewise seen, heard, and known by all. The Saṃgha has therefore performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them.

Because these bhikṣus, Aśvinī and Pūrṇā, have undergone the formal act of expulsion (nissāraṇīya-kamma), their minds are filled with remorse and they have been subdued; they now petition the Saṃgha for the lifting of the expulsion.

"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, listen: the Saṃgha grants the bhikṣus Maśuka and Pūrṇamaśuka the lifting of the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Sangha has completed the formal act of *niḥsāraṇīya-karman* (expulsion) against the bhikṣus Ma-su and Man-su; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a village in the kingdom of Kāśi named Makaranda; in it lived a wealthy and noble householder named Citta, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures, as well as fields, houses, people, servants, and attendants.

This person has taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; they do not doubt the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, nor do they doubt suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. Having seen the truths, they have attained the Way.
In the Āmra grove at the village of Maṣakadhāya, he built a monastery for the monks and invited the community of bhikṣus, saying:
"May the Venerable Ones deign to accept!"

Dwelling here in the monastic quarters of this Āmra grove, I shall provide offerings of robes, alms bowls, door-bolts, medicines for the time, medicines for the night, medicines for seven days, and medicines for life; furthermore, I am able to instruct you in the recitation of the Dharma and answer your questions regarding doubts, with the sole exception of the Vinaya.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Uttara who, in the Āmra Grove of the householder Citta, acted as the *māmaka* (steward) for the monastery and the *dattika* (donor).

At that time, there was the bhikṣu Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, who, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus—all of whom were forest-dwellers, wearers of rag-robes, and alms-seekers, delighting in staying, walking, sitting, or standing in open spaces—possessed pure conduct regarding food, drink, robes, and bowls, inspiring reverence in others as they traveled through the country of Kāśī and arrived at the village of Makhiṇḍiya.

When the householder Citta saw these visiting bhikṣus—their coming and going, sitting and standing, eating and drinking, and their robes and bowls—all of whose deportment was pure, he immediately gave rise to a heart of pure reverence.
Because of this visiting bhikṣu, he invited the Saṃgha to his own home for a meal on the following day.
At that time, the master of the monastery heard that the householder Citta had not first informed him, saying:
"I have invited the Saṃgha to my home for a meal because of a visiting bhikṣu."
“I am Māmattī, the mistress of the Tiṭṭhabhūta lodging in the Āmra Grove of the householder Citta.
The householder Citta did not ask me; rather, it was because of a visiting bhikkhu that he invited the Saṅgha for a meal at his residence.”
"After this night has passed, I shall speak with this householder.

Having thought thus, the bhikṣu Uttara rose at dawn, put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the householder's residence. There he saw various kinds of delicious food and drink prepared and various multicolored seats spread out.
He asked, "Why are there no sesame *mōdaka* (joy-pills)?"
The householder replied:
"I would now like to speak a parable; if you will listen, I shall tell it.
Venerable Uttara!..."
In the north there was a group of merchants who carried chickens to the east to trade.

A crow came down and mated with a chicken, producing offspring that, when they cried out, could neither make the sound of a chicken nor the sound of a crow; whenever they wished to cry out, they made the sound of both a chicken and a crow.
"Uttara! You are just like that;
although you speak various kinds of virtuous words concerning the Buddha-dharma, you also speak evil words.
The bhikṣu Uttara said:
“You have reviled me; this Āmra-ārāma of yours I now return to you.
I shall go to the east to visit the Buddha, where I will make offerings and attend upon him.”
The householder said, "Venerable One! Dwell in my monastic quarters,

and I shall provide you throughout your life with robes, alms bowls, door-keys, medicinal food for the daytime, medicinal food for the night-time, medicinal food for seven days, and medicinal food for as long as life lasts."
Furthermore, you should teach him to read and recite the sūtras and dharmas, and answer his questions and doubts, with the sole exception of the Vinaya.
The bhikṣu spoke to the householder a second and a third time:
“You have reviled and abused me; this is your Āmra-vihāra, so I shall return it to you. I am going to the East to visit the Buddha’s dwelling to make offerings and attend upon him personally.”
The householder invited him a second and third time, saying: "Uttara!

Dwell in my monastic quarters, and I shall provide you with robes, alms bowls, door-bolts, and medicines for the appropriate time, for the night, for seven days, and for life-long use as long as you live. Furthermore, I shall instruct you in the recitation of the sūtras and the Dharma, and answer whatever doubts you may have—except for the Vinaya."
At that time, the bhikṣu Uttara wished to travel to the east to visit the Buddha.
A householder said to him, "Regarding the matters you have spoken of and those I have spoken of, report them all to the Buddha exactly as they are, without adding or omitting anything."
"If you do not accept my invitation now, you will surely return later.
The bhikṣu Uttara immediately took up his robes and bowl and traveled toward Śrāvastī to visit the Buddha. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with these words:
"Are you able to endure? Are you content? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Is it not difficult to beg for alms? Are you not exhausted by the journey?
With these words, the Buddha inquired after the bhikṣu Uttara:
"Are you able to endure, are you content, and do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Was it not difficult to beg for alms, and were you not utterly exhausted on the road? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"It is bearable, sufficient, and lived in peace; begging for alms is not difficult, and the journey does not cause exhaustion.
He related these matters to the Buddha in detail.
Having heard this, the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"You should perform a *karmavācanā* of subordination against the bhikṣu Uttara, so that he may humble himself before the householder Citta and repent."
If there are further such persons, the Saṃgha should likewise perform the *avavāda-karman* (act of subordination) for them.
If a bhikṣu has committed an offense in any of three matters— namely, violation of the precepts (*śīla*),
violation of views (*dṛṣṭi*), or violation of conduct (*ācāra*)— the Saṃgha should perform the *avavāda-karman* for him.
Furthermore, there are three types of persons with whom the *avavāda-karman* (act of subordination) should be performed:
those who delight in fighting, those who delight in quarreling, and those who delight in mutual verbal disputes.
If a bhikṣu possesses five qualities, the Saṃgha should perform the *avavāda-karman* against him:
If a bhikṣu reviles the Buddha, or reviles the Dharma, or reviles the Saṃgha, or violates the precepts, or violates the rules of decorum;
furthermore, if there are five conditions, the Saṃgha should grant him the *karmavācanā* of submissiveness (*tāpanīya-karman*):

if he speaks harshly to laypeople, or insults laypeople, or disparages the households of laypeople, or causes separation among the households of laypeople, or employs means to drive laypeople out with the intent to cause them decline and distress.
Furthermore, there are five matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *avakāśaka-karman* (act of reconciliation):
speaking harshly to a bhikṣu, reviling a bhikṣu, disparaging a bhikṣu, destroying a bhikṣu’s gains and offerings, and seeking means to drive a bhikṣu out so as to cause him distress and affliction.
Furthermore, there are five matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of reconciliation):

inciting a layperson to fight with another layperson; inciting a layperson to fight with a bhikṣu; inciting a bhikṣu to fight with another bhikṣu; inciting a bhikṣu to fight with a layperson; and speaking of unpleasant matters concerning a layperson.
When the Saṃgha performs the formal act of "lowering the mind," those performing the act should first reflect upon three matters:
Is what this layperson has said true or not?
"Can this bhikṣu perform such a deed?
Can this bhikṣu be made to humble his mind?
Having reflected thus, he then performs the formal act of humbling the mind (*naimittika-karman*).
The procedure for performing the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of humble intent) is as follows: with a single-minded and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu proclaims:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The householder Citta provides for the Saṃgha as if serving his own master."
This bhikṣu Uttara has, in our presence, reviled us with harsh words.

If the Saṃgha deems it the right time and grants its consent, let the Saṃgha perform an act of reconciliation (*adhyāśaya-karman*) against the bhikṣu Uttara, requiring him to offer an apology to the householder Citta.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

"The Saṃgha has performed the *adhyāśaya-karman* for the bhikṣu Uttara, commanding him to repent before the householder Citta. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
At that time, the Saṃgha should dispatch a capable bhikṣu to take the bhikṣu Uttara to the householder Citta and say to him:
"This bhikṣu has reviled you with harsh words in your presence; the Saṃgha has already dealt with him according to the Dharma. You should now accept his confession."

If the one receiving the confession immediately causes this layperson to move from a place where he can hear to a place where he can be seen, the bhikṣu Uttara should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession toward that bhikṣu.
If the layperson does not accept it, the Saṃgha should then appoint two capable bhikṣus to speak to the layperson, saying:
"The bhikṣu Uttara reviled you with harsh words in your presence; the Saṃgha has already dealt with him according to the Dharma, and you should now accept his confession."
If he accepts it, he should immediately have the layperson move to a place where he can be seen but cannot hear, and the bhikṣu Uttara should perform a *duṣkṛta* confession before the two bhikṣus.
If they still do not accept it, the Saṃgha shall then again grant it to three or four capable bhikṣus, who shall say to the householder:
"This bhikṣu has reviled you with harsh words in your presence; the Saṃgha has already dealt with him according to the Dharma. You should now accept his confession of his transgression."

If he accepts [the confession], he should immediately have the layperson move to a place where he can be seen but cannot hear, and the bhikṣu Uttara should then perform a *duṣkṛta* confession before those bhikṣus.

If, however, he does not accept [the instruction], and if this householder is widely known and well-acquainted, possesses great influence, or has the power of officials or the power of bandits, such that he can personally commit evil deeds to harass and disturb the Saṃgha or cause others to do so, the Saṃgha should say to that bhikṣu:

"This householder is widely known and well-acquainted; he possesses the power of officials and the power of bandits, and is capable of committing evil deeds himself as well as causing others to do so. You should leave this dwelling place."
"If a bhikṣu remains by force, the Saṃgha incurs no offense.
While the Buddha was at Kauśāmbī,
at that time the bhikṣu Chandaka committed an offense requiring confession (deśanā-garhya).
Out of compassion and with the desire to benefit, profit, and bring him peace and happiness, the bhikṣus said to him regarding his offense:
"Instruct him to see his offense according to the Dharma and to repent; do not conceal it."
Chanda said, "I see no fault; why should I repent?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should carry out a formal act of suspension against Canda;
if there are other bhikṣus who act in such a manner, you should likewise carry out this act against them."
If a bhikṣu has committed an offense in any of three matters, he should be subjected to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* for not seeing [the offense]:
namely, violation of the precepts (*śīla*), violation of views (*dṛṣṭi*), and violation of conduct (*ācāra*).
Furthermore, there are three other matters in which the Saṃgha should subject him to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* for not seeing [the offense]:
They delight in fighting and quarreling, and they delight in mutual recrimination.
When the Saṃgha intends to carry out a formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense (*adarśanāya-pratiniḥsarga*), it should first reflect upon five matters:

"If we perform this suspension for refusal to see an offense against this bhikṣu, he will not participate with us in the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts, or the *pravāraṇā*; he will not participate in various *karmas*; he will not share in the midday meal; he will not share in the communal distribution of alms-bowls; and he will not rise to greet or bid farewell to the elders. Because of these causes and conditions, disputes will arise, along with mutual recrimination and abuse; the Saṃgha will be split, the Saṃgha will be contentious, the Saṃgha will be divided, and the Saṃgha will be at variance."
Having reflected upon these five points, one should not carry out an act of banishment.

If we were to carry out an act of banishment for this bhikṣu on the grounds that he does not acknowledge his offense, we would not join him in the uposatha, the recitation of the precepts, the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), or in performing various formal acts (*karmas*); we would not share meals with him, nor share the distribution of alms-bowls; and we would not rise from our seats to greet or see him off as a senior elder. For these reasons, no strife, quarreling, mutual accusation, or mutual abuse would arise; the Saṃgha would remain in harmony, free from dispute, without division, and without dissension.
Having reflected upon these five matters, one should carry out the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense (*adarśana-pratiniḥsarga*) against him.
The bhikṣu who has committed the offense should also reflect upon five matters:

"If the bhikṣus carry out the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense against me, they shall not perform the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), or the *pravāraṇā* with me; they shall not perform various formal acts (*karmas*) together with me; they shall not share a midday meal with me; they shall not share *bhandapāna* with me; and I shall not be permitted to rise from my seat to greet or see them off as they depart."
Why is this? Because these bhikṣus delight in upholding the precepts and possess a sense of shame and remorse; they cannot act out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion for my sake.
Having reflected upon this matter, one should undergo the formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense (*adarśana-bhikṣu-nāśana*).
As for the ritual procedure for performing the formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense: the Saṃgha, being united with a single mind, one bhikṣu shall proclaim within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense and does not see it as such according to the Dharma.

If the Saṃgha’s time has come, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall carry out a formal act of suspension for non-seeing against the bhikṣu Chanda; for as long as you, Chanda, have committed an offense and have not seen it as such according to the Dharma, for that same duration the Saṃgha shall carry out the suspension for non-seeing against you.
"O monks, we shall not perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) together with you, nor shall we dwell together with you in the affairs of the Saṃgha:

whether it be a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*); nor shall we participate in the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*; you shall not be included among the fourteen classes of persons; we shall not engage in joint business or co-residence with you, but shall treat you with loathing as if you were a *caṇḍāla*."
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of suspension for non-appearance against the bhikṣu Canda. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!"

Regarding the conduct for a monk who has been suspended for not seeing an offense: he should not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; he should not accept dependence (*niśraya*) from others; he should not keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); he should not perform the formal act (*karma*) of instructing nuns; if he was previously authorized, he should no longer instruct them; he should not commit a grave offense; he should not commit an offense similar to that which led to his suspension; he should not commit an offense more serious than that; he should not criticize the formal act; he should not criticize those performing the formal act; he should not receive the rising, welcoming, or seeing off of pure monks, nor their offerings of robes, bowls, bedding, washing or wiping of feet, or footstools; unless he is ill, he should not accept massage from others; and he should remain remorseful, subdued, and humble in mind.
The Buddha said,
"If one does not practice according to this Dharma, one shall not be released from this *karman* for as long as one lives.
Thereupon, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus moved a short distance to one side and performed the *ajñapti-karman* of suspension for non-appearance against the bhikṣu Chandaka.
After the formal act of suspension for refusal to see [the offense] had been performed, the bhikṣu Cchanda did not submit his mind and spoke thus:
"What business is it of yours?
I do not count you."
Having spoken these words, he took up his robes and bowl and traveled from one monastery to another through the kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, Kāśī, Kośala, Kuru, Pañcāla, Avanti, and Aparānta.

The bhikṣus of various lands, hearing that Chandaka had been expelled, did not perform formal acts (karmavācanā) with him—whether it be a motion (jñapti), a motion followed by one announcement (jñaptidvitīya), or a motion followed by three announcements (jñapticaturtha)—nor did they participate in the Poṣadha or the Prātimokṣa recitation; they did not include him among the fourteen persons who are excluded from the assembly, nor could they engage in communal affairs with him. They loathed him as if he were a caṇḍāla, neither dwelling with him nor engaging in any joint activities.

He returned to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, where, with a mind filled with remorse and subdued, he requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of his *adarśanāyābhiṣkambha* (suspension for refusal to see an offense).
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should grant the bhikṣu Chanda the lifting of his *adarśanāyābhiṣkambha*."
If there are others who are likewise such persons, they too should be granted release. If a bhikṣu does not act according to the Dharma,
the Saṃgha should not grant him release from the *adarśanāyā-apratikarmāyā-āpattiyā* (formal act for one who does not see his offense),
nor should he confer the full ordination upon others, nor act as a preceptor for others, nor keep śrāmaṇeras, nor receive formal instructions.
The formal legal procedures (*karmavācanā*) for bhikṣuṇīs; or instructing and admonishing bhikṣuṇīs; or committing a grave offense;
or committing an offense similar to that; or committing an offense exceeding that; or censuring a formal procedure or the person conducting the procedure;
or receiving a pure bhikṣu by rising to greet him, seeing him off, making offerings, or providing robes, alms bowls, bedding, and washing or wiping his feet.
Using a foot-stool; if not ill, accepting massage from another; assuming the appearance of a layperson (*avadātavasana*);
assuming the appearance of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*); engaging in affairs with non-Buddhists; doing what one ought not to do;
failing to train in the *bhikṣu* precepts; reviling and scolding *bhikṣus*; speaking harshly to *bhikṣus*; disparaging *bhikṣus*; practicing sorcery.
This will cause the Sangha to lose its dwelling place and its offerings;
it is intended to subdue the bhikṣus both within and outside the boundary who delight in strife, mutual recrimination, lack of self-restraint, and a lack of reverence, gentleness, and humility.
If one acts in this manner, one should not be granted the *ajñapti* (formal resolution) for the *adarśanāyotkṣepaṇīya-karman* (suspension for failure to acknowledge an offense).
If one has received the *adarśanāyotkṣepaṇīya-karman*, one must not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others,

must not act as a preceptor (*niśraya*) for others, must not keep novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*), must not receive the formal procedure (*karman*) for instructing bhikṣuṇīs, and must not provide instruction.
A bhikṣuṇī who has not committed a grave offense, nor committed a similar offense, nor committed an offense exceeding this;
who does not criticize the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), nor criticize those performing the *karmavācanā*;

who does not receive from a pure bhikṣu the rising to greet, the welcoming and seeing off, or the offering of robes, alms-bowls, bedding, and seats; and who does not receive [services such as] washing the feet, wiping the feet, or the footstool—if she does not...
When ill, one should not accept massage from others; one should not assume the appearance of a layperson or the appearance of a non-Buddhist;
one should not engage in affairs with non-Buddhists; one should perform what ought to be performed; one should train in the bhikṣu precepts; one should not revile or scold bhikṣus;
one should not speak harshly to bhikṣus; one should not disparage bhikṣus; and one should not employ means to cause the Saṃgha to lose its residence.
Abiding in the loss of offerings, he does not wish to subdue monks within or outside the boundary;
he takes no pleasure in quarreling or mutual recrimination, but with a mind of remorse, he seeks to subdue himself through reverence and gentleness.
If one acts in such a manner, they should be granted the *abbhāna* (rehabilitation) for *tassapāpiyasikā* (formal act of censure for not seeing an offense).

As for the procedure for the *abbhāna* for *tassapāpiyasikā*: the Saṃgha, being united with a single mind, [the monk] Channa should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please attend to me!"

I, Chanda, have committed an offense that requires confession; because I did not see it as such according to the Dharma, the Saṃgha has performed an act of *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (suspension for refusal to see an offense) against me.

The bhikṣus do not engage in joint work or co-residence with me, nor do they perform the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* with me; they do not include me in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, nor in any other formal acts (*karman*). I am excluded from being counted among the fourteen classes of persons, and they treat me with loathing, as if I were a *caṇḍāla*.
"Now my attendant, Chanda, has repented with a contrite and softened heart; he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *ajñapti-karman* of non-seeing.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant me its lifting."
A second and a third time he likewise requested.
Thereupon, one bhikṣu proclaimed among the saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, Chanda, having committed an offense and not viewing it as such, was subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* for refusal to see his fault. Consequently, the other bhikṣus do not engage in communal affairs with him, nor do they dwell together; they do not perform the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* with him, nor do they participate in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*. He is excluded from the number of the fourteen [categories of] persons, being treated with loathing like a caṇḍāla.
The bhikṣu Cchanda now feels remorse and has been subdued; he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *ajñāna-pratikṣepa-karman* (the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant the lifting of the *ajñāna-pratikṣepa-karman* for the bhikṣu Cchanda.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has finished lifting the *ajñāna-pravāsanīya-karman* from the bhikṣu Canda. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Elder Chandaka had committed an offense that required confession.
Out of compassion and with the desire to bring him benefit and happiness, the bhikṣus pointed out his offense to him and instructed him to confess it according to the Dharma.
He replied,
"I recognize this as a transgression, yet I am unable to repent according to the Dharma.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* against you and Chandaka, whether it has already been performed or not.
If there are others who are like this, they too should be subjected to the same.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"If a bhikṣu commits any one of three offenses, a *ajñapti-karma* of non-expulsion (*akaraṇīya-nāśana*) should be performed against him:
whether he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his conduct, a non-expulsion should be decreed."
Furthermore, there are three cases where the Saṃgha should grant [a formal act] but not carry out the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment):
those who delight in fighting, those who delight in quarreling, and those who delight in mutual recrimination.
When the Saṃgha intends to perform such an act but chooses not to carry it out, it should first reflect upon five matters:

If we were to carry out or fail to carry out the act of formal suspension against this bhikṣu—refusing to perform the *poṣadha* or various *karmas* with him, refusing to share the midday meal, refusing to share the *pātra-bhājana*, and not rising to greet or see him off as for a senior elder—for these reasons, disputes would arise, leading to mutual recrimination and abuse, the schism of the Saṃgha, contention within the Saṃgha, the separation of the Saṃgha, and the division of the Saṃgha.
Having reflected upon these five points, one should not carry out an act of banishment.

Whether we perform or do not perform the act of banishment against this bhikṣu, we shall not participate with him in the poṣadha or in any formal monastic procedures (karmas); we shall not share the midday meal or the *bhandapāna*; and we shall not rise to greet or see him off as he departs from his seat. For these reasons, no strife, contention, mutual accusation, or mutual abuse shall arise; the Saṃgha will remain in harmony, free from dispute, without division, and without dissension.
Having reflected upon these five factors, they should carry out the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against him.
The bhikṣu who has committed the offense should also reflect upon five factors:

"Will these bhikṣus carry out or not carry out my banishment? Will they not join me in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, nor perform various formal acts (*karmas*) with me? Will they not share the midday meal or the *bhatta-paṭṭa* (extra food) with me? Will they not rise to greet and pay homage to me as they would to a senior elder?"
Why is this? Because these bhikṣus delight in upholding the precepts and possess a sense of shame and remorse; they do not act out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion for my sake.
Having reflected upon these five factors, one should undergo the *ajñapti-karman* of non-expulsion.
Regarding the procedure for the *ajñapti-karman* of non-expulsion: the Saṃgha, being harmonious and of one mind, a single bhikṣu should announce within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu, Chanda, has committed an offense and recognized it, yet he is unable to repent according to the Dharma.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and carry out the *ajñapti-karma* of non-association against the bhikṣu Chanda: for as long as you, Chanda, have committed an offense and recognized it but have been unable to repent according to the Dharma, for that duration the Saṃgha shall carry out this *ajñapti-karma* of non-association against you.

The bhikṣus shall not perform any formal acts (*karmas*) with you—whether a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*)—nor shall they participate in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* with you; you shall not be included among the fourteen classes of persons, nor shall they engage in work or dwell together with you, treating you with contempt as if you were a *caṇḍāla*.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of suspension for non-compliance against the bhikṣu Cchanda. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

Regarding the rules of conduct for a monk who has received the *akaraṇīya* (the decree of non-action): he must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; he must not act as a preceptor (*niśraya*) for others; he must not keep a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); he must not perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of instructing nuns; if he had previously accepted such a role, he must no longer instruct them; he must not commit a grave offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*); he must not commit an offense similar to one; he must not commit an offense more serious than that; he must not criticize a formal ritual; he must not criticize those who perform a formal ritual; he must not expose the faults of pure monks; he must not accept the rising to greet, welcoming, seeing off, or offerings of robes, bowls, and bedding from pure monks; he must not accept services such as washing feet, wiping feet, or using a footstool; except when ill, he must not accept massage from others; and he should repent in his heart, remain humble, and maintain a gentle disposition.
The Buddha said:
"If one does not act according to this Dharma, one shall not be released from this *karmavācanā* for as long as one lives.

Thereupon, the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, withdrew to one side and performed the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against the bhikṣu Chandaka. However, the bhikṣu Chandaka did not submit his mind and spoke these words:
"What concern is it of yours?
I do not count you.
Having said this, he took up his robes and bowl and traveled from one dwelling place to another through the kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, Kāśī, Kośala, Kuru, and Avanti-Matsya.

When the bhikṣus of various lands heard that the bhikṣu Chandaka had been expelled, and that the other bhikṣus would no longer perform *karmavācanā* with him, nor live together with him; that in all communal affairs—whether it be a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)—nor in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*; that he was not permitted to join the ranks of the fourteen types of persons, nor to engage in joint affairs or dwell together; and that he was treated with such loathing as if he were a *caṇḍāla*, they likewise ceased to live or work together with him.
The bhikṣu Chandaka returned to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī; with a mind of repentance and self-restraint, he requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *ajñapti-karma* of non-expulsion.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should grant the bhikṣu Chandaka the lifting of the *ajñapti-karma* of non-expulsion."
If there are others such as these, they too should be granted release.
However, if a bhikṣu who has been expelled does not act according to the prescribed rules, the Saṃgha should not grant him release;
nor should he confer full ordination upon others, provide dependence to others, keep śrāmaṇeras, or receive instructions from other bhikṣus.
The *bhikṣuṇī*-karma; or instructing *bhikṣuṇīs*; or committing a grave offense; or committing a similar offense;
or committing an offense exceeding that; or censuring a *karma*; or censuring one who performs a *karma*;
or receiving from a pure *bhikṣu* the rising to greet, the welcoming and seeing off, or the offering of robes, bowls, bedding, washing the feet, or wiping the feet.
If one who is not ill accepts massage from others; or assumes the appearance of a layperson (*avadātavasana*) or the appearance of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*);
or engages in affairs with non-Buddhists; or performs what should not be performed; or fails to train in the *bhikṣu* precepts; or reviles and scolds *bhikṣus*;
or speaks harshly toward *bhikṣus*; or disparages *bhikṣus*; or employs skillful means to cause them... [to do so].

The Saṃgha loses its place of residence and its offerings; it desires to subdue the bhikṣus within and outside the boundary who delight in strife and mutual recrimination, yet their minds do not repent, and they remain unsubdued, lacking respect and gentleness.
If one does not act in this manner, one should not grant the *akaraṇīya* (the status of being exempt from formal acts) nor perform the *pravāsanīya* (act of banishment).
If one has received the *akaraṇīya* status, one must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others,
must not provide dependence (*niśraya*) to others, must not keep novices (*śrāmaṇera*), must not receive the formal motion (*jñapti*) for instructing bhikṣuṇīs, and must not provide instruction.
A bhikṣuṇī must not commit a grave offense, nor commit an offense similar to one, nor commit an offense exceeding it;
she must not criticize the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), nor criticize those performing the *karmavācanā*;

she must not receive from a pure bhikṣu rising to greet her, escorting her, making offerings, or providing robes, bowls, bedding, or a footstool for washing and wiping her feet; and when not ill, she must not accept being massaged.
Māra, do not assume the appearance of a layperson; do not assume the appearance of a non-Buddhist;
do not associate with non-Buddhists; perform what ought to be performed; train in the bhikṣu precepts; do not revile bhikṣus;
do not speak harshly to bhikṣus; do not disparage bhikṣus; and do not employ means to cause the Saṃgha to lose its dwelling place or its stability.
One makes offerings, does not wish to subjugate monks within or outside the boundary, takes no pleasure in quarreling or mutual recrimination,
and with a mind of repentance, practices subjugation, reverence, gentleness, and flexibility.
If one practices in this manner, they should be granted the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) rather than being subjected to *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension).

Regarding the procedure for the *amūḷhavinaya*: the Saṃgha, being united with a single mind, [should act as follows]: the bhikṣu Cchanda should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!..."
"Because I, Chanda, committed an offense and was unable to repent according to the Dharma, the Saṃgha has performed an *ajñapti-karma* of non-action against me.

The bhikṣus do not associate with me in work or residence; they do not perform the *jñapti-karma*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karma*, or the *jñapti-caturtha-karma* with me; they do not include me in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*; I am not permitted to enter or stand among the fourteen classes of persons, and they loathe me as if I were a *caṇḍāla*."
"I, Chanda, now feel regret; my mind is subdued and softened. I beg the Saṃgha to revoke the *ajñapti-karman* of suspension.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant me its revocation."
A second and a third time he likewise requested.
Immediately, one bhikṣu proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, Chanda, having committed an offense and recognized it, was unable to repent according to the Dharma. The Saṃgha performed the *ajñapti-karman* of suspension against him.

The other bhikṣus did not engage in communal affairs with him, nor did they dwell with him; they did not perform the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* together with him, nor did they participate in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*. He was not permitted to join the ranks of the fourteen types of persons, and he was loathed like a *caṇḍāla*.
Because the bhikṣu Chanda has received this *karmavācanā*, his mind is repentant, subdued, and softened; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *akaraṇīya-pratiniḥsarga-karman*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant the bhikṣu Chanda the lifting of the *akaraṇīya-pratiniḥsarga-karman*.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

"The Saṃgha has completed the revocation of the *ajñaptikaraṇīya* (act of not performing the formal act) against the bhikṣu Cchanda. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to a wicked and false view, saying:

"I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma in this way: regarding those things called 'obstructive dharmas' spoken of by the Buddha, practicing these obstructive dharmas cannot obstruct the Path."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should carry out the formal act of suspension against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for not relinquishing his evil and false views."
"If there are others who are likewise such persons, they too should be dealt with in this manner.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu has committed an offense among these three matters, he should be subjected to the formal act of *ukkhilepanā* (expulsion for not abandoning evil views)."
Whether it be breaking the precepts, breaking right view, or breaking proper decorum;
furthermore, there are three things:
delighting in strife, delighting in contention, and delighting in mutual recrimination.
When the Saṃgha performs the *pravāsanīya-karman* of suspension for one who has committed evil and does not abandon it, at that time one should first contemplate five things:

"If we perform this *pravāsanīya-karman* of suspension for this bhikṣu—refusing to participate with him in the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*, refusing to perform various formal acts (*karmas*) together with him, refusing to share the midday meal or the *bhandana* (alms-food) with him, and refusing to rise from our seats to greet or see him off as an elder—then by reason of these causes and conditions, disputes will arise, people will speak ill of and revile one another, and there will be a schism in the Saṃgha, contention within the Saṃgha, division of the Saṃgha, and separation of the Saṃgha."
Having reflected on this matter, one should not carry out a formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

If I were to carry out a formal act of banishment against this bhikṣu for his evil and heterodox views that have not been removed, we would not perform the *poṣadha* or various *karman* rituals together; we would not share the midday meal or the *pātra-bhājana*; and we would not rise to greet or see him off as he approaches or departs from the seat of the elder. For these reasons, there would arise no strife, mutual accusation, or mutual abuse; the Saṃgha would remain in harmony, free from dispute, without division, and without dissension.
Having reflected on this matter, they should carry out the formal act of banishment against him.
The offending bhikṣu should also reflect upon five matters:

"These bhikṣus are performing an evil and heterodox act of non-expulsion against me; they will not participate with me in the poṣadha or various karmavācanas; they will not share with me the midday meal or the *baddhapātra* (the meal brought in a bowl); and they will not rise to greet or see me off as I pass by the elders."
Why is this? Because those bhikṣus possess a sense of shame and dread of blame, and delight in upholding the precepts; they cannot act out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion for my sake.
Having reflected on this matter, one should undergo the *pāpikā-dṛṣṭi-aniḥsaraṇa-aniṣkāsana* (the formal act of not removing and not expelling for holding evil views).
Regarding the procedure for the *pāpikā-dṛṣṭi-aniḥsaraṇa-aniṣkāsana*: the Saṃgha, being harmoniously united with a single mind, one bhikṣu shall proclaim within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to a wicked and heterodox view, saying:
"I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma in this way: regarding the obstructive dharmas taught by the Buddha, practicing these obstructive dharmas cannot obstruct the Path."

"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall carry out the formal act of *pravāsanīya* (banishment) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for his evil and heterodox views that he does not relinquish.

You, Ariṣṭa, for as long as you continue to harbor evil and heterodox views and do not repent in accordance with the Dharma, for that duration the Saṃgha shall carry out the formal act of *pravāsanīya* against you for those very same evil and heterodox views."

The bhikṣus shall not perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) together with you, nor shall they dwell with you in the affairs of the Saṃgha—whether it be a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*)—nor shall they participate in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, nor shall they be included among the fourteen classes of persons; they shall not engage in work or dwell together with you, but shall treat you with aversion as if you were a *caṇḍāla*.
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act of motion and threefold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

The Sangha has completed the formal act of suspension for the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa on account of his evil and false views that he does not relinquish. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld as such!"

Regarding the practice for a bhikṣu who has not abandoned evil and wrong views and is subject to banishment: he must not confer full ordination upon others; he must not act as a preceptor for others; he must not maintain śrāmaṇeras; he must not accept the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for instructing bhikṣuṇīs; if he has previously accepted it, he must not provide instruction; he must not commit a grave offense; he must not commit an offense similar to one already committed; he must not commit an offense more serious than that; he must not criticize a formal ritual; he must not criticize those performing the ritual; he must not receive from pure bhikṣus acts such as rising to greet them, seeing them off, making offerings, or providing robes, bowls, bedding, washing their feet, or wiping their feet and footstools; and unless he is ill, he must not accept massage from others. He should instead cultivate a mind of repentance, remain humble and compliant.
The Buddha said,
"If one who has been subject to the act of banishment does not conduct himself accordingly, he shall not be released from that *karma* for as long as his life lasts.

Thereupon, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus stepped back slightly to one side and performed the formal act of banishment against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for his evil and unrighteous views that had not been relinquished.
With a heart full of regret, subdued and humble, he requested the Sangha to lift the suspension from him.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should grant the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa release from the suspension for not abandoning his evil and heterodox views."
If there are others who are likewise such persons, they too should be granted release.
However, if a bhikṣu has been suspended for not abandoning evil and wrong views, and the formal act of suspension has not been performed, the Saṃgha should not grant him release.
Furthermore, [one who is thus suspended] must not confer full ordination upon others, must not serve as a preceptor for others, and must not keep śrāmaṇeras.
Whether it be receiving the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for instructing bhikṣuṇīs, or instructing bhikṣuṇīs, or committing a grave offense, or committing an offense similar to that,
or committing an offense exceeding that, or censuring the formal act, or censuring the person performing the formal act,
or receiving from a pure bhikṣu rising to greet, welcoming, seeing off, or making offerings of robes, bowls, bedding, and so forth.
One must possess a foot-washing stand and a cloth for wiping the feet; unless one is ill, one should not accept massage from others.

One should not assume the appearance of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), nor the appearance of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*); one should not engage in affairs with non-Buddhists, nor do what ought not to be done.
One should not fail to train in the *bhikṣu* precepts, nor revile or scold a *bhikṣu*, nor speak harsh words toward a *bhikṣu*, nor disparage them.
He reviles monks, devises means to cause the Saṃgha to lose its dwelling place and its gains, and seeks to subdue the monks both within and outside the boundary;
he delights in strife, mutual recrimination, and verbal disputes, and his mind is neither subdued nor characterized by reverence and gentleness.
If one acts in such a manner, one should not be granted absolution.
If a bhikṣu has been expelled, he shall not confer full ordination upon others,
nor act as a preceptor for others, nor keep śrāmaṇeras, nor perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of instructing bhikṣuṇīs, nor provide instruction to bhikṣuṇīs.
One should not commit grave offenses; one should not commit offenses similar [to those already committed]; one should not commit offenses exceeding these; one should not criticize the *karmavācanā*;
one should not criticize the person performing the *karmavācanā*;

one should not accept from a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu the rising to greet, the welcoming and seeing off, or the offerings of robes, bowls, bedding, washing the feet, wiping the feet, or a footstool; and if not ill, one should not accept massage from others.
Not assuming the appearance of a layperson (*avadātavasana*) or the appearance of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), not engaging in affairs with non-Buddhists,
performing what ought to be performed, training in the *bhikṣu* precepts, not reviling *bhikṣus*, not speaking harshly to *bhikṣus*, not disparaging *bhikṣus*,
and not employing means to cause the Saṃgha to lose its dwelling place or its material support.
If one wishes to subdue monks within and outside the boundary who take no pleasure in quarreling or mutual recrimination, and who feel remorse, become subdued,
and show respect and gentleness—
if such a person practices in this way, one should grant them release from the suspension for not abandoning evil views.

Regarding the procedure for resolving one who has abandoned evil and heterodox views without being subject to formal suspension: the Saṃgha, being united with a single mind, [should act as follows]. The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!
I, Ariṣṭa, have given rise to an evil and false view, saying:
"I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma; regarding the obstructive dharmas taught by the Buddha, practicing these obstructive dharmas cannot obstruct the Path."
Therefore, the Saṃgha has performed an act of *pravāsanīya-karman* against me for being evil and holding wrong views that are not relinquished.

The bhikṣus do not perform formal acts with me—neither *jñapti-karman*, nor *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, nor *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; they do not participate in my *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, nor am I included among the fourteen types of persons; they loathe me as if I were a caṇḍāla.
I, Ariṭṭha, now feel remorse; my mind is subdued and softened, and I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of the *kamma* of suspension for not abandoning evil views.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant me its lifting.

The monk Kāḷudāyin intentionally emitted semen and committed this saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; as he did not conceal it, he requests from the Saṃgha the *pārivāsika* (probation) of the original day.

The Saṃgha is that of the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin, who intentionally emitted semen; he has committed one offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa which was not concealed. The Saṃgha grants him the parivāsa of returning to the original status.

"Which elders consent that this bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin, having intentionally emitted semen and committed this saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is a single offense not concealed, now requests from the Saṃgha the *pārivāsika* (probationary) discipline for the original day?"

The bhikṣu Kālodāyin intentionally emitted semen; he has committed this saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which was not concealed. He is granted the *mūlaparivāsa* (initial probation); remain silent if you approve, or speak out if you do not.
