Thus it was said three times.

"The Saṃgha has already granted the *pūrvakalpa* (penance of returning to the beginning) to the bhikṣu Kālodāyin, who intentionally emitted semen and committed one offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* without concealment; the granting of the *pūrvakalpa* is now complete. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld as such."

This bhikṣu Kāḷodāyin, having committed an offense in the interim, underwent the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status). Having completed the *parivāsa* (probation) for his prior offense, and having completed the six-night *mānatva* (penance) within the Saṃgha, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!"
"What shall I do? The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"You should grant the bhikṣu Kāḷodāyin absolution from his offense. Since he committed an offense during that interval, he must undergo *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the beginning). Once he has completed the *parivāsa* (probation) for his prior offense, and has performed the six-night *mānatva* (penance) within the Saṃgha, you shall grant him absolution."
If there are other such bhikṣus, they too should perform the rite of rehabilitation (*āpattivyutthāna*).

As for the method of rehabilitation: with a single-minded assembly of the Saṃgha, this bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!..."

I, the bhikṣu Kālodāyin, intentionally emitted semen and committed one offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa; having concealed it, I request from the Saṃgha the practice of parivāsa for as many days as it was concealed.
During the period of concealment, I underwent the *parivāsa* (probation) separately from the Saṃgha; during that same period of concealment, I performed the *parivāsa* within the midst of the Saṃgha.
Having completed the *parivāsa* within the Saṃgha during that period of concealment, I now request from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānāpya* (penance).

The Saṃgha has already granted me six nights of *mānatva*. While I was practicing the six nights of *mānatva* within the Saṃgha, after so many days and before so many days had elapsed, I intentionally emitted semen during that interval, thereby committing this one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which I did not conceal. I have requested from the Saṃgha the *pārivāsika-mūla-parivāsa*, and the Saṃgha has granted me the *mūla-parivāsa*.

I, the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin, having committed an offense during that interval, have undergone the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning). Having completed the *parivāsa* (probation) for the prior offense and having completed the six-night *mānatva* (penance), I now beg the Saṃgha for absolution from the offense.

Venerable Saṃgha, I, the bhikṣu Kālodāyin, committed an offense during this interval and underwent the *mūlaparivāsa*. Having first performed the *parivāsa* for that offense, I have now completed the six-night *mānatva*. Out of compassion, please grant me absolution from the offense.
Thus he spoke three times.
Immediately, one bhikṣu proclaimed among the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Kālodāyin intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing one offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa; he concealed this offense and requested from the Saṃgha the practice of parivāsa for as many days as it was concealed.
The Saṃgha grants him *parivāsa* according to the number of days he concealed [the offense];

having already performed the *parivāsa* within the Saṃgha for as many days as he concealed it, and having completed the *parivāsa* within the Saṃgha for those days of concealment, he requests from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*.

The Saṃgha granted him six nights of *mānatva*. While he was undergoing the six nights of *mānatva* within the Saṃgha, after such and such days had passed and before others had elapsed, he again emitted semen due to a prior cause; thus he committed one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense which he did not conceal. He requested from the Saṃgha the *pārivāsika-mūla-parivāsa*, and the Saṃgha granted him the *mūla-parivāsa*.

The bhikṣu Kālodāyin committed an offense during the interim and underwent the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the beginning). Having completed the *parivāsa* (probation) for his prior offense, and having completed the six-night *mānatva* (penance), he requested absolution from the Saṃgha.

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent: the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin committed an offense during the period of *mūlāpakarṣa*; having completed the previous period of *parivāsa* and having completed the six-night *mānatva*, the Saṃgha shall now grant him absolution from the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).
Thus he makes his formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing one offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa. Having concealed it, he has requested from the Saṃgha the practice of *parivāsa* (probation) for as many days as it was concealed. The Saṃgha has granted him *parivāsa* for those days of concealment, and he has already performed the *parivāsa* within the Saṃgha for those days of concealment."

Having completed the *parivāsa* (probation) among the Saṃgha for as many days as he had concealed [the offense], he requests from the Saṃgha a six-night *mānatva* (penance). The Saṃgha grants him the six-night *mānatva*.

While he is performing the six-night *mānatva* within the Saṃgha, after such and such days have passed and such and such days remain unexpired, he again intentionally emits semen, committing one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense which he does not conceal. He requests from the Saṃgha the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the original term), and the Saṃgha performs the *mūlāpakarṣa* for him.

This bhikṣu Kāḷodāyin committed an offense during that interval and underwent the *mūlaparivāsa* (initial penance). Having completed the prior *parivāsa* (probation) for the original offense, he then completed the six-night *mānatva* (expiation) within the Saṃgha, and now requests absolution from the Saṃgha.

The bhikṣu Saṃgharudāyin committed an offense during the interim and underwent the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning). Having completed the *parivāsa* (probation) for his prior offense, he has now completed the six-night *mānatva* within the Saṃgha; he should now be granted absolution from the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin—who committed an offense during his period of probation and has now completed the *pārivāsika* (probation), and who has completed the six-night *mānatva* within the Saṃgha—granting him the restoration from the offense, let them remain silent; if you do not consent, then speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said three times.

"The Saṃgha has already granted the purification of the offense to the bhikṣu Kālodāyin; having committed an offense during that interval, he underwent the *mūlāpakarṣa* penance, completed the *parivāsa* for his previous offense, and has now completed the six-night *mānāpya* within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Kālodāyin committed various saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses: first, he intentionally emitted semen and concealed it for one night;

second, he touched the body of a woman and concealed it for two nights; third, he spoke coarse and wicked words to a woman and concealed it for three nights; fourth, he praised himself for receiving offerings and concealed it for four nights; fifth, he committed the offense of acting as a matchmaker and concealed it for five nights. He then said to the bhikṣus:
"What should I do? The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should grant this person the formal act of parivāsa for five nights; once he has completed the parivāsa, grant him six nights of mānāpya."
"When the *mānatva* penance has been completed, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the removal of the offense shall be granted.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who committed various *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and concealed them. Specifically, he committed one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of intentional emission of semen and concealed it for one night.
The second offense was touching a woman, concealed for two nights.
The third offense was engaging in coarse and wicked speech with a woman, concealed for three nights.
The fourth offense was praising oneself for receiving offerings, concealed for four nights.
The fifth offense is acting as a matchmaker for marriage, concealed for five nights.
The sixth offense is building a hut for oneself when no donor has provided the materials, concealed for six nights.
The seventh offense is building a large dwelling for oneself when a donor has provided the materials, concealed for seven nights.
The eighth root pārājika offense: slandering another bhikṣu while concealing it for eight nights.
The ninth offense: committing a minor matter and slandering another bhikṣu as having committed a pārājika offense while concealing it for nine nights.
The tenth is to diligently seek means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha and conceal it for ten nights.
The eleventh is to commit an offense that assists in causing a schism in the Saṃgha and conceal it for eleven nights.
The twelfth [offense]: defiling another's family and committing evil conduct, concealed for twelve nights.
The thirteenth [offense]: committing harsh speech, concealed for thirteen nights.
Having related these matters to the bhikṣus,
he asked, "What should I do?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should grant this person a period of parivāsa (separate residence) for thirteen days; when the parivāsa is completed, grant him six nights of mānatva (probation).
When the six nights of mānatva are completed, perform the karman of rehabilitation from the offense."

The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus committed an offense."

Being identical in similarity, identical in not having been purified, identical in not having been liberated, identical in not having arisen [from the offense], and identical in having gone outside the boundary, one performs the *parivāsa*, *mānatva*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and *āvarhaṇa* for another bhikṣu; being identical in similarity, identical in not having been purified, identical in not having been liberated, identical in not having arisen, and identical in having entered within the boundary, one receives from a pure bhikṣu the rites of rising to meet, prostrating, joining the palms, and making offerings according to seniority.
Among them, there were bhikṣus who possessed few desires, were contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and said:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense similar to others, being equally impure, equally unliberated, equally unarisen [from the offense], and equally outside the boundary, undergoes the separate residence (parivāsa), the six-night mānatva, the re-initiation (mūlāpakarṣa), and the rehabilitation from the offense; yet, when he is similarly guilty of an offense, equally impure, equally unliberated, equally unarisen, and equally inside the boundary, receives from pure bhikṣus rising to greet him, prostrating, joining palms, and making offerings as if he were a senior elder?"
Having thus rebuked them, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, having assembled the community of bhikṣus, knowingly asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"How can one who is called a bhikṣu—being identical in his offense, identical in his lack of purification, identical in his lack of liberation, identical in his lack of emergence, and identical in his departure from the boundary—yet undergo *pārivāsika*, *mānatva* for six nights, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and rehabilitation (*ābṛhaṇa*) alongside other bhikṣus; and how can he, while remaining identical in his offense, identical in his lack of purification, identical in his lack of liberation, identical in his lack of emergence, and identical in his re-entry into the boundary, receive from a bhikṣu observing the *sthiti-śīla* (the precept of abiding) the rising to welcome, prostration, joining of palms, and offerings due to a senior elder?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one who is undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) should not serve as the fourth member [of the quorum] when performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of *parivāsa*."
If one who has completed the *parivāsa* (probation) acts as the fourth person, the *parivāsa* formal act (*karmavācanā*) should not be performed.
If one who is undergoing the *mānatva* (penance) acts as the fourth person, the *parivāsa* formal act should not be performed.
If one who has completed the *mānatva* penance acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If one who does not live in communion (*asamvāsika*) acts as the fourth member, the *parivāsa* *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
When there are at least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view, one may perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment).
From now on, when a person undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) serves as the fourth member [of the quorum], the *mānatva-karman* (act of penance) should not be performed.

If one who has completed the *parivāsa* (probation), one currently undergoing the *mānatva* (penance), one who has completed the *mānatva*, or one who is not in communion (*asamvāsa*) acts as the fourth person, the *mānatva* should not be performed.
When there are at least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view, the *mānatva* karmavācanā may be performed.
From now on, when one who is undergoing *parivāsa* acts as the fourth person, a *pārivāsika-mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status) karmavācanā must not be performed.

One who has completed the parivāsa, one who is undergoing the mānatva, one who has completed the mānatva, and one who does not live in communion—if these constitute the fourth member [of the quorum], the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning) karmavācanā must not be performed.
When there are at least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view, one may perform the *mūlāpakarṣa-karman*.
From now on, a person undergoing *parivāsa* shall serve as the twentieth member [of the quorum]; one must not perform the *āvarhaṇa-karman* (the rite for absolution from offense).

If one who has completed the *parivāsa*, one undergoing the *mānatva* ritual, one who has completed the *mānatva*, or one who is not in communion serves as the twentieth person, the ritual for absolution from the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*) should not be performed.
When there are at least twenty bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view, the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offenses may be performed.
If a bhikṣu himself possesses an offense, he is not permitted to receive the removal of that offense from another.

From now on, the rules for the practice of the *parivāsa* (probation) are being explained. This person undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) should train in the duties of one undergoing probation: he must not accept from a monk who is observing the *upavāsa* precepts the services of welcoming or seeing him off, bowing in greeting, joining his palms in reverence, making offerings of robes, alms-bowls, bedding, or water for washing the hands or feet, nor a footstool for wiping the feet; furthermore, unless he is ill, he must not accept the service of massage or other such offerings from others.
A person undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) shall not sit on the same bed as a monk who maintains the precepts; he shall not sit on a fine bed.
If a monk who maintains the precepts is walking, the person undergoing *parivāsa* should not sit.
If two persons living separately may not sit together on the same bed, how much less so many?

They must not walk in the place where a bhikṣu who observes the precepts walks; they must not walk in the same walking area as a bhikṣu who observes the precepts; they must not walk in a preferred walking area; and they must not walk in front of a pure bhikṣu.
Two persons undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) may not share the same walking path (*caṅkrama*), let alone more than one.
When a visiting bhikṣu arrives, the person undergoing probation should confess to him the offense they have committed.
At the time of the *poṣadha*, one should enter among the Saṃgha and three times confess one's offenses.
If one is ill, one should send a messenger to the Saṃgha and say:
"A certain person in separate residence (*parivāsa*) is ill and cannot come; may the Saṃgha take note."

A person undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) must not accept the confession of others; he must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; he must not act as a preceptor (*niśraya*) for others; he must not keep novices (*śrāmaṇera*); he must not perform the formal ritual (*karma*) of instructing bhikṣuṇīs; if he has previously accepted such a duty, he must not perform the instruction; he must not commit a grave offense again; he must not commit an offense similar to the one for which he was sentenced; he must not commit an offense more serious than that; he must not criticize a formal ritual; he must not criticize those who performed the ritual; he must not request permission from pure bhikṣus; and he must not say: "I shall bring about your expulsion from this offense."

One should not oppose pure bhikṣus; one should not obstruct the poṣadha, the pravāraṇa, or any formal ritual (karmavācanā); one should not proclaim the offenses of pure bhikṣus; one should not cause others to recall their offenses; and one should not engage in mutual verbal disputes.
One should repent in one's mind, subdue oneself, become gentle, and show respect; one should walk behind the pure bhikṣus and sit in a lower position.

If the Saṃgha appoints individuals in succession for communal activities, one should receive [offerings] according to the order of the elders, fill the bowl with water according to the order of the elders, receive the *varṣāśāṭī* robe according to the order of the elders, and sit for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony according to the order of the elders.
One should not say to a bhikṣu of pure speech with such a mind:
"Give me my share of the food; I fear others will know of me or see my transgression.

When those undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) eat together, they should sit according to the order of seniority among the elders. They should be given the lowest rooms, inferior bedding, and lowly seats.

If there are many individuals undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation), the dwellings, bedding, and seating should be assigned to them in order according to seniority. Those undergoing the *parivāsa* should not go before other monks when entering the houses of others; those who follow behind may do as they please.

Second, regarding those undergoing *parivāsa* (probation): a monk who is undergoing *parivāsa* should not reside in a place where there are no other monks, nor should he reside in a place where there are no monks.

Furthermore, a monk undergoing *parivāsa* should not reside with one who has completed his *parivāsa*, nor with one who is undergoing *mānatva* (penance), nor with one who has completed his *mānatva*, nor with one who is subject to *asaṃvāsa* (exclusion from the community). In such cases, he should not reside in a place where there are no other monks, nor should he reside in a place where there are no monks.
A person undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) should not dwell under the same roof as a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu, nor should they dwell under the same roof in a non-residence (*anāvāsa*).

If a person undergoing *parivāsa* dwells with one whose *parivāsa* has been completed, or with one undergoing *mānatva*, or with one whose *mānatva* has been completed, or with one who is not in communion (*asamvāsika*), they should not dwell under the same roof in a residence, nor should they dwell under the same roof in a non-residence.
If a person living apart intends to travel, he should first reflect:
"Will I be able to reach the dwelling place of the resident bhikṣus by traveling today?
If he knows that he can reach it, he should go.
If one does not go, one loses this single night.
If one is unable to practice this Dharma, one should reflect thus:
"I am unable to practice this matter."
One should say: "I ought to perform the *parivāsa* and *mānatva* procedures; I paused for a moment and did not manage to do so.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:

"If a person practicing *parivāsa* or a person practicing *mānatva* has a reason that prevents them from performing these duties, for how many nights should they be permitted to suspend [the practice]?
The Buddha said,
"They should be permitted to suspend it for twenty-five nights."
From now on, when a person undergoing *parivāsa* acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of *parivāsa* should not be performed.
Likewise, if there are two persons undergoing *parivāsa* and two persons who are pure (*viśuddha*), the formal act of *parivāsa* may not be performed either.
If there are three persons undergoing parivāsa (probation) and one person who is pure, none of those undergoing parivāsa may perform the formal act of parivāsa.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure, living together, and of the same view may perform the formal act of parivāsa.
From now on, when a person has completed their *parivāsa* (probation), they may serve as the fourth member [of the quorum], but they must not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of *parivāsa*.

If there are two persons who have completed *parivāsa* and two persons who are pure; or three persons who have completed *parivāsa* and one person who is pure; or if all [members] have completed *parivāsa*, none of these cases may perform the formal act of *parivāsa*.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the formal act (karmavācanā) of separate residence (parivāsa).
From now on, if one who is undergoing the penance of mānatva serves as the fourth member, the formal act of separate residence cannot be performed.

If there are two persons undergoing *mānatva* and two pure persons; or if there are three persons undergoing *mānatva* and one pure person; or if all are persons undergoing *mānatva*, none of them may perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of separate residence (*pṛthagnivāsa*).
At least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment).
From now on, if a person who has completed the *mānatva* penance serves as the fourth member [of the quorum], the *pravāsanīya-karman* should not be performed.

If there are two persons who have completed the *mānatva* penance together with two pure persons; or three persons who have completed the *mānatva* penance together with one pure person; or if all have completed the *mānatva* penance, none of them may undergo the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of separate residence (*pṛthagnivāsa*).
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the formal act (karmavācanā) of separate residence (parivāsa).
From now on, one who does not live in common with others must not be used as the fourth member to perform the formal act of separate residence.

If there are two persons who do not live together and both are pure; or three persons who do not live together and one is pure; or if all do not live together, none of these should perform [the ritual].
When there are at least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view, a *pārivāsika-karman* (formal act of separate residence) should be performed.
From now on, if a person undergoing *parivāsa* serves as the fourth member [of the quorum], a *mānatva-karman* (formal act of penance) should not be performed.

If there are two persons undergoing parivāsa and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing parivāsa and one person who is pure; or if all are persons undergoing parivāsa—in all these cases, the *mānatva* karmavācanā should not be performed.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the *mānāpya* karmavācanā.
From now on, if a person who has completed their separate residence (*parivāsa*) acts as the fourth member, the *mānāpya* karmavācanā should not be performed.

If there are two persons who have completed the *parivāsa* and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons who have completed the *parivāsa* and one person who is pure; or if all [the monks] have completed the *parivāsa*, in all such cases, the *mānatva* karmavācanā should not be performed.
At least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the *mānāpya* karma.
From now on, when one who is undergoing the *mānāpya* penance serves as the fourth member, the *mānāpya* karma should not be performed.

If there are two persons undergoing *mānāpya* and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing *mānāpya* and one person who is pure; or if all [the participants] are persons undergoing *mānāpya*, the *mānāpya-karman* should not be performed.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the *mānāpya* (probation) *karmavācanā*.
From now on, if a person who has already completed their *mānāpya* acts as the fourth member, the *mānāpya* *karmavācanā* must not be performed.

If there are two persons who have completed the *mānatva* penance and two pure persons; or if there are three persons who have completed the *mānatva* penance and one pure person; or if all [of them] have completed the *mānatva* penance—in none of these cases should the *mānatva* formal act (*karmavācanā*) be performed.
At the very least, four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same views may perform the *mānāpya* karmavācanā.
From now on, one who does not live in common with the community shall not be made the fourth person to perform the *mānāpya* karmavācanā.

If there are two persons who do not live together with one another and both are pure; or three persons who do not live together with one another and one is pure; or if all [the participants] do not live together with one another, in no case should the *mānatva* karmavācanā be performed.
At the very least, when four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view are present, the *mānatva* karmavācanā should be performed.
From now on, one who is undergoing *parivāsa* (separate residence) shall serve as the fourth member; the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction of the period of penance) karmavācanā should not be performed.

Whether it be two persons undergoing parivāsa and two pure persons, or three persons undergoing parivāsa and one pure person, or all those undergoing parivāsa, none of them should undergo the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement) *karmavācanā*.

From now on, if a person who has completed the *parivāsa* (probation) acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], one should not perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status) *karmavācanā*.

This applies whether there are two persons who have completed the *parivāsa* and two pure persons; or three persons who have completed the *parivāsa* and one pure person; or if all [members] have completed the *parivāsa*; in all such cases, one must not perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* *karmavācanā*.
From now on, when one who is practicing *mānatva* constitutes the fourth member [of the quorum], the *pārivāsika-mūla-parivāsa* (renewal of the probation) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.

Whether there are two persons practicing *mānatva* with two pure persons, or three persons practicing *mānatva* with one pure person, or if all are persons practicing *mānatva*, in all such cases, the *pārivāsika-mūla-parivāsa* *karmavācanā* must not be performed.
When there are at least four bhikṣus who are pure, living together, and of the same view, one may perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status) karmavācanā.
From now on, when one who has completed the *mānatva* penance serves as the fourth member [of the quorum], one should not perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* karmavācanā.

If there are two persons who have completed the *mānāpya*, and two pure persons; or if there are three persons who have completed the *mānāpya*, and one pure person; or if all [the offenders] have completed the *mānāpya*, in all such cases, the *yadbhūyaḥkaraṇīya* (reinstatement to the original status) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.
If one who does not live in communion serves as the fourth member, the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the original status) *karmavācanā* should not be performed.

Whether it be two persons who do not live in communion with two persons who are pure, or three persons who do not live in communion with one person who is pure, or if all [members] do not live in communion, the *mūlāpakarṣa* *karmavācanā* should in no case be performed.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who share the same view regarding the purification; they should perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reversion to the beginning) *karmavācanā*.
From now on, a person undergoing separate residence (*parivāsa*) may serve as the fourth member [of the quorum], but one who is currently undergoing separate residence within the community may not.

If there are two persons undergoing *parivāsa* and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing *parivāsa* and one person who is pure; or if all are persons undergoing *parivāsa*, none of them should perform the *parivāsa* within the assembly.
If there are at least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view, one should perform the *parivāsa* (probation) among them.
From now on, once the *parivāsa* has been completed, the person shall be the fourth member [of the quorum]; within that assembly, one may not perform the *parivāsa*.

If there are two persons who have completed the *parivāsa* penance and two persons who are pure; or if there is one person who has completed the *parivāsa* penance and one person who is pure; or if all [the persons] have completed the *parivāsa* penance—in none of these cases may they perform the *mānāpya* penance within that assembly.
If there are at least four bhikṣus who share the same view regarding the four purifications, one may perform the *parivāsa* (probation) among them.
From now on, when a person performing the *mānatva* (penance) constitutes the fourth member, one should not perform the *parivāsa* within that assembly.

If there are two persons undergoing *mānāpya* and two pure persons; or if there are three persons undergoing *mānāpya* and one pure person; or if all are persons undergoing *mānāpya*, they should not perform the separate residence (*parivāsa*) within that assembly.
From now on, if a person who has completed the *mānatva* penance acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], he should not undergo the *parivāsa* probation within that assembly.

Likewise, if there are two persons who have completed the *mānatva* and two pure persons; or three persons who have completed the *mānatva* and one pure person; or if all [the members] have completed the *mānatva*, none of them should undergo the *parivāsa* probation within that assembly.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who are pure and of one view; it is such a group that should perform the *parivāsa* (probation) within the assembly.
From now on, one who does not live in communion with the community should not serve as the fourth member of the assembly for the purpose of performing the *parivāsa*.

If there are two persons living apart who are both pure, or three persons living apart with one pure person, or if all are persons living apart, none of them should undergo the *parivāsa* penance within the assembly.
At least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view should be present; such a person should undergo the *parivāsa* (probation) within the community.
From now on, when one undergoing *parivāsa* acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], they should not perform the *mānatva* (penance) within the community.

If there are two persons undergoing parivāsa and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing parivāsa and one person who is pure; or if all are persons undergoing parivāsa—in none of these cases should they perform the mānatva within the assembly.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view; it is in such a group that one should undergo the *mānatva* penance.

From now on, when the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*) is completed, the person [who has finished it] shall serve as the fourth member of the assembly; it is not appropriate to undergo the *mānatva* penance within the general community.

If there are two persons who have completed the parivāsa and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons who have completed the parivāsa and one person who is pure; or if all have completed the parivāsa—in none of these cases should they perform the mānatva within the assembly.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view; it is in such a group that one should perform the *mānatva* penance.
From now on, when a person is performing *mānatva*, they should not be the fourth member of the assembly while performing the *mānatva*.

If there are two persons undergoing *mānāpya* and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing *mānāpya* and one person who is pure; or if all are persons undergoing *mānāpya*—in none of these cases should they perform the *mānāpya* penance within the assembly.
From now on, when one who has completed the *mānatva* penance acts as the fourth person [in the quorum], he should not perform the *mānatva* within that assembly.

Whether it be two persons who have completed the *mānatva* and two pure persons, or three persons who have completed the *mānatva* and one pure person, or even if all [members] have completed the *mānatva*, none of them should perform the *mānatva* within that assembly.
At least four bhikṣus who are pure and of common view should perform the *mānatva* penance within the assembly.
From now on, one who does not live in communion with the community should not serve as the fourth person in performing the *mānatva* within the assembly.

If there are two persons living apart from one another who are both pure, or three persons living apart from one another with one being pure, or if all are living apart from one another, none of them should perform the *mānatva* penance within the assembly.
At least four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view should be present; it is in such a group that one should perform the *mānatva*.
From now on, when a person is performing the *parivāsa*, they should act as the fourth member [of the quorum]; it is not appropriate for them to perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* within the assembly.

If there are two persons undergoing parivāsa and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing parivāsa and one person who is pure; or if all are persons undergoing parivāsa—in none of these cases should they perform the mūlaparivāsa within the assembly.

From now on, when a person has completed the *parivāsa* (probation), they should serve as the fourth member [of the quorum]; one must not perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction of the period of penance) within such a group.

This applies whether there are two persons who have completed the *parivāsa* and two pure persons (*viśuddha*), or three persons who have completed the *parivāsa* and one pure person, or even if all members have completed the *parivāsa*; in none of these cases should the *mūlāpakarṣa* be performed within the assembly.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who share the same views regarding the four purifications; [only then] should one undergo the *mūlaparivāsa* within that assembly.
From now on, when a person is performing the *mānatva*, they should not be the fourth member of the assembly for the purpose of undergoing the *mūlaparivāsa*.

If there are two persons undergoing *mānāpya* and two persons who are pure; or if there are three persons undergoing *mānāpya* and one person who is pure; or if all are persons undergoing *mānāpya*—in none of these cases should they perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* penance within the assembly.
From now on, when one who has completed the *mānatva* penance acts as the fourth member [of the quorum], he should not perform the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction to the beginning) within that assembly.

This applies whether there are two persons who have completed the *mānatva* and two pure persons (*pariśuddha*), or three persons who have completed the *mānatva* and one pure person, or even if all [members] have completed the *mānatva*; in all such cases, the *mūlāpakarṣa* should not be performed within that assembly.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view; they should perform the *mūlaparivāsa* within the assembly.
From now on, one who does not live in communion (*asaṃvāsika*) may not serve as the fourth member [of the quorum] for performing the *mūlaparivāsa* within the assembly.

If there are two persons living apart who are both pure, or three persons living apart with one who is pure, or if all are persons living apart, none of them should undergo the *mūlaparivāsa* penance within the assembly.
At the very least, there must be four bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view; they should perform the *mūlaparivāsa* (initial penance) within the assembly.

From now on, one who is undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) shall serve as the twentieth member [of the quorum], but he should not participate in the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of releasing one from the offense.
If there are two *parivāsa* monks and eighteen pure monks; or three *parivāsa* monks and seventeen pure monks;
or four *parivāsa* monks and sixteen pure monks; or five *parivāsa* monks and fifteen pure monks;
or six *parivāsa* monks and fourteen pure monks; or seven *parivāsa* monks and thirteen [pure monks].
A pure person and eight persons in separate residence (parivāsa) and twelve pure persons; nine persons in separate residence and eleven pure persons;
ten persons in separate residence and ten pure persons; eleven persons in separate residence and nine pure persons;
twelve persons in separate residence and eight pure persons; or thirteen persons in separate residence.

If there are seven persons in the state of complete purification (*parisuddha*), or fourteen persons in the state of separate residence (*pārivāsika*) with six persons in the state of complete purification;

or fifteen persons in the state of separate residence with five persons in the state of complete purification; or sixteen persons in the state of separate residence with four persons in the state of complete purification;

or seventeen persons in the state of separate residence with three persons in the state of complete purification; or eighteen persons in the state of separate residence with two persons in the state of complete purification; or ten...
A single person undergoing parivāsa (probation) or one who is pure— indeed, no one undergoing parivāsa at all—
should perform the *abbhāna-kamma* (ceremony for absolution from offense).
At the very least, twenty bhikṣus who are pure and of like view may perform the *abbhāna-kamma*.

From now on, if one who has completed the separate residence (parivāsa) serves as the twentieth person, or one undergoing the penance of mānatva serves as the twentieth person, or one who has completed the mānatva serves as the twentieth person, or one who is not in communion (asamvāsa) serves as the twentieth person, none of these should perform the formal act of absolution from the offense (āpattivyutthāna-karman).

From now on, this applies equally to those who have completed two periods of separate residence (*pārivāsika*), to eighteen persons of pure conduct (*pariśuddha*), and even to all those who do not live in common (*asamvāsa*).
At the very minimum, twenty bhikṣus of pure conduct and shared views should perform the *karmavācanā* for the removal of guilt (*ābṛhaka-karman*).

The fifth section on the practice of the eight dharmas is concluded. 6. The Prohibitions: The sixth section on the eight dharmas concerning prohibitions. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, on the fifteenth day during the *poṣadha* ceremony, the World-Honored One sat upon a seat prepared before the assembly of monks and observed the minds of the bhikṣus.
Having observed the minds of the bhikṣus, he entered meditative concentration in silence during the first watch of the night.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the first watch of the night had passed and the Buddha and the Saṃgha had sat for a long time, [the bhikṣu] wished, "May the World-Honored One recite the Prātimokṣa.
At that time, the Buddha remained silent.
When the middle watch of the night arrived, this bhikṣu rose from his seat for a second time; he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The first watch of the night has passed, and the middle watch has also passed; the Buddha and the Saṃgha have sat for a long time. We pray that the World-Honored One will recite the Prātimokṣa.”
The Buddha remained silent.
When the latter part of the night arrived, for the third time this bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has also passed, and much of the last watch has passed; the eastern quarter is about to stir.
The Buddha and the Saṅgha have sat for a long time; may the World-Honored One please recite the Prātimokṣa.
At that time, the Buddha said to those bhikṣus,
"My assembly is not pure.
At that moment, the Elder Maudgalyāyana was seated among the assembly, and he thought to himself:
"For whose sake has the Buddha made this statement:
'My assembly is not pure'?
I shall enter meditative concentration and observe for whose sake the Buddha has spoken these words."
He immediately entered meditative concentration to observe the minds of all the assembly.
While observing in this manner, he saw that the Buddha had acted toward an impure bhikṣu.
He then arose from concentration, went to where that bhikṣu was, seized him by the arm, dragged him out, and said:
“Fool! Depart from here! Be extinguished!”
"You have forever departed from the dharma of a bhikṣu; you are now the very last one remaining in common residence within this Saṃgha.

Having thus expelled the bhikṣu, Maudgalyāyana closed the door, lowered the bolt, and went to where the Buddha was staying. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Regarding those monks whom the Buddha has declared to be impure, I have already expelled them, saying:
"Fools! Depart far away and be extinguished; you are forever severed from the dharma of a monk."
"You are now the last one remaining in common residence within this Saṃgha.
"World-Honored One!
The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has also passed, and much of the final watch has elapsed; the eastern quarter is about to stir."
After the Buddha and the Saṃgha had sat for a long time, [the monks] said, "We pray that the World-Honored One will recite the Prātimokṣa.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"This foolish person has committed a grave offense, for he has distressed both the Buddha and the Saṃgha."
"Maudgalyāyana!
If the Buddha were to recite the Prātimokṣa among an impure assembly, the heads of those impure persons would split into seven pieces.
Maudgalyāyana!"
"From this day forward, you yourselves shall recite the Prātimokṣa;
the Buddha will no longer recite it for you,
Maudgalyāyana!"
Just as the great ocean gradually becomes deeper and wider, so too is the Buddha-dharma.
Precepts are established in succession, regulations are instituted in succession, and teachings are imparted in succession.
"Maudgalyāyana!
If within my Dharma there is the sequential establishment of precepts, the sequential formulation of regulations, and the sequential instruction in the teachings, this is rare within my Dharma,
Maudgalyāyana!"
Just as the great ocean does not overstep its constant boundaries, so too is my Dharma.
Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, they shall protect the precepts without deficiency, even at the cost of their own lives.
Maudgalyāyana!

If, within my Dharma, there are precepts that have been established such that monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen do not transgress them even for the sake of losing their lives, this is rare within my Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana!
Just as the great ocean is deep and vast, infinitely deep and vast, so too is the Buddha-dharma; its profound meaning is infinite.
Maudgalyāyana!
If the meaning of the Buddha-dharma is profound and vast, profoundly and vastly immeasurable, this is rare within my Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana!
For example, just as the great ocean has a single uniform salty taste, so too is the Buddha-dharma: it has the single uniform taste of liberation.
"Maudgalyāyana!
If the Dharma of the Buddha were of a single flavor— the flavor of liberation— that would be rare within my teaching,
Maudgalyāyana!"

For example, the great ocean is the dwelling place of many large creatures; the makara, the tortoise, the crocodile, the śiśumāra, the timi, and the timingila—these are not considered extraordinary when found within the ocean.

There are beings with bodies one hundred yojanas in length, and others with bodies two hundred, three hundred, even up to seven hundred yojanas; that such sentient beings dwell within the great ocean is not yet considered extraordinary.
Maudgalyāyana!
The dwelling place of great beings within the ocean of the Buddha-dharma is also like this.

"Great beings" refers to those who are Arhats or those progressing toward Arhatship; those who are Anāgāmins or those progressing toward Anāgāminship; those who are Sakṛdāgāmins or those progressing toward Sakṛdāgāminship; and those who are Srotāpannas or those progressing toward Srotāpannaship.
Maudgalyāyana!

Within the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is the dwelling place of great beings; whether they be Arhats or those still training for the stage of Srotāpanna, such individuals are rare within my Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana!
It is like the great ocean, which is filled with many jewels and immeasurable treasures of various kinds. These treasures are:
gold, silver, pearls, musaragalva, agate, lapis lazuli, maṇi-jewels, shells, coral, and *loutshi* [candana].
Maudgalyāyana!

The ocean of the Buddha-dharma is likewise: it is filled with many and immeasurable jewels of various kinds, namely the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
Maudgalyāyana!

If within my Buddha-dharma there were many treasures, immeasurable treasures, and various kinds of jewels piled up to overflowing—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path—this would be rare within my dharma.
Maudgalyāyana!
It is like the great ocean, which is pure and does not harbor putrid corpses; yet if there were a putrid corpse, it would be blown onto the shore by the wind.
Maudgalyāyana!
The Tathāgata’s ocean of Dharma is likewise pure and does not harbor putrid corpses.
A "putrid corpse" refers to one who has broken the precepts:

their mind delights in evil dharmas, they are rotten within and leaking without, they claim to practice the holy life when they do not, and they call themselves śramaṇas when they are not; these are called putrid corpses.
Such persons, though they constantly follow the assembly, are in truth far removed from it.
The Buddha-dharma is pure and does not harbor putrid corpses; this is a rare occurrence within my teaching.
Maudgalyāyana!

It is like the great ocean of the Jambudvīpa world-system, into which four great rivers flow: namely, the Gaṅgā River, the Yamunā River, the Sarayū River, and the Aciravatī River. Even if there were dragons who emerged from the water and let fall torrential rains as thick as wagon axles, the ocean would neither increase nor decrease because of receiving such water.

It is likewise within the Buddha-dharma: a member of the kṣatriya caste who leaves the household life out of faith, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the three dharma robes, and attains the realization of indestructible liberation of mind—this neither increases nor decreases.

In this same way, whether one is of the Brahmin caste, the Vaiśya caste, or the Śūdra caste, if they go forth out of faith, shaving off hair and beard and donning the three Dharma robes, they will attain the indestructible realization of liberation through the mind, which neither increases nor decreases.
"Maudgalyāyana!

If within my Buddha-dharma there are those of the kṣatriya caste down to the śūdra caste who, having left the home life out of faith, attain the liberation of an unshakable mind—neither increasing nor decreasing—that is rare within my Dharma."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you yourselves shall recite the precepts together; the Tathāgata will no longer recite them for you.

At that time, because the Buddha no longer recited the precepts, when the bhikṣus recited them, some arrived while others did not, and among those seated in the assembly, there were bhikṣus who had committed offenses.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When the poṣadha is observed and the Prātimokṣa is recited, all bhikṣus should come."
"If there is a cause and condition, one should grant the purity of consent (*chanda*), but those who have violated the precepts within the assembly should be excluded.
At that time, among the bhikṣus, some wished to exclude [the offender] while others did not wish to exclude him. The Buddha said:
"Those who wish to exclude should exclude; those who do not wish to exclude should not forcibly exclude."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they wished to prevent [the action] but did not know how to do so.
The Buddha said:
"If you see something with your own eyes, you should prevent it."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who possessed the divine eye, who saw various bhikṣus committing offenses falling like heavy rain. Having seen this, he attempted to restrain them; because of these circumstances, disputes arose, and they were unable to perform the poṣadha ceremony and recite the Prātimokṣa.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not rely on the divine eye; you should use what is seen with the physical eye to prevent [the offense].
When the bhikṣus used the physical eye to prevent it, disputes arose, and they were unable to perform the uposatha and recite the Prātimokṣa. The Buddha said:
"One should refute by means of what has been heard.

When using what has been heard to refute, there is much that is heard: one hears that a certain bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika*, another has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, another has committed a *pāyattika*, another has committed a *pratideśanīya*, and another has committed a *duṣkṛta*. Having heard these, one refutes them all.
For this reason, disputes arose and the *poṣadha* ceremony for the recitation of the precepts could not be performed.
The Buddha said: "One should suspend [the ceremony] due to doubt.

Many bhikṣus had various doubts: whether they had committed an offense with their body or their speech; whether they had committed an offense involving a remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) or one without a remainder (*anavaśeṣa*); whether they were in a village or in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).
Because of these doubts, they obstructed the occurrence of disputes and were unable to perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts. The Buddha said:
"One should use self-accusation to obstruct; those who are pure should remain silent."
There is an illegal obstruction of the *poṣadha* ceremony, and there is a legal obstruction of the *poṣadha* ceremony.
If a bhikṣu obstructs the *poṣadha* ceremony on the basis of one of the five kinds of offenses without foundation, this is called illegal.

Regarding "in accordance with the Dharma": if a bhikṣu, among the five kinds of offenses, raises a fundamental objection that prohibits the recitation of the precepts, this is called "in accordance with the Dharma.

There are two kinds of objections to the recitation of the precepts that are contrary to the Dharma, and two kinds of objections to the recitation of the precepts that are in accordance with the Dharma.

The two types of *adharma* (unlawful) are: among the five kinds of offenses, to suspend the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) based on groundless charges, whether an offense was committed or not; these are called the two types of *adharma*. The two types of *dharma* (lawful) are:
among the five kinds of offenses, to do so based on grounds that exist, whether an offense was committed or not; these are called the two types of *dharma*.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of unlawful obstruction to the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, and three kinds of lawful obstruction to the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

As for the three unlawful ones: if a bhikṣu obstructs the recitation on the grounds of unfounded charges of broken precepts (*śīla*), unfounded charges of broken views (*dṛṣṭi*), or unfounded charges of broken conduct (*ācāra*), these are called the three unlawful obstructions to the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

Regarding the three lawful [grounds for] suspension of the *poṣadha*: there are those who have violated the precepts through their roots, who have violated the views, and who have violated the decorum; these are called the three lawful grounds for suspending the recitation of the *poṣadha*.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of unlawful suspensions of the *poṣadha* and four kinds of lawful suspensions of the *poṣadha*.

Regarding the four types of unlawful obstruction: groundless accusations of broken precepts, broken right view, broken right livelihood, and broken dignified conduct—these are called the four unlawful obstructions to the recitation of the precepts.

Regarding the four cases that accord with the Dharma: there are instances where one's roots of virtue are broken, one's right view is broken, one's right livelihood is broken, or one's dignified conduct is broken; these are called the four cases that accord with the Dharma which prohibit the recitation of the precepts.
Furthermore, there are five unlawful ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha* and five lawful ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.
Regarding the five unlawful obstructions: to obstruct the recitation of the *Poṣadha* on grounds of a groundless *pārājika* offense is called an unlawful obstruction.

To obstruct the recitation of the Prātimokṣa on grounds that are baseless—namely, on charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta* offense—is called the five kinds of illegal obstructions.
Regarding the five kinds of lawful prohibitions: when there is a root offense of *pārājika* that prohibits the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, this is called a lawful prohibition.
When there is a root offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *dukkaṭa* that prohibits the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, these are called the five kinds of lawful prohibitions.
Furthermore, there are six unlawful ways of obstructing the *poṣadha* ceremony and six lawful ways of obstructing it.

As for the six unlawful ways: obstructing on the basis of groundless charges of broken precepts—whether they were committed or not; obstructing on the basis of groundless charges of broken views—whether they were held or not; and obstructing on the basis of groundless charges of broken livelihood—whether it was practiced or not. These are called the six unlawful obstructions.

Regarding the six cases that are in accordance with the Dharma: there are instances where one has the root [of the offense] but does not break the precepts, whether they have been committed or not; there are instances where one has the root but breaks the view, whether it has been committed or not; and there are instances where one has the root but breaks the livelihood, whether it has been committed or not. These are called the six cases in accordance with the Dharma that prohibit the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.
Furthermore, there are seven unlawful ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha* and seven lawful ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

Regarding the seven unlawful ways: obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha* on grounds of an unfounded *pārājika*; on grounds of an unfounded *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* arising from harsh speech; and *duṣkṛta* arising from a *sthūlātyaya*; and [another] *duṣkṛta*. These are called the seven unlawful obstructions.

The seven lawful [grounds for] prohibition are: a root offense of *pārājika*; a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; a *pāyattika* offense; a *pratideśanīya* offense; an *dukkaṭa* offense arising from harsh speech; an *dukkaṭa* offense arising from a *sthūlātyaya*; and an *dukkaṭa* offense that prohibits the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. These are called the seven lawful prohibitions.
Furthermore, there are eight unrighteous ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha* and eight righteous ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

As for the eight unrighteous ways: to obstruct the recitation of the *Poṣadha* on grounds that are baseless—namely, charges of broken precepts, broken views, broken livelihood, or broken decorum, whether such acts were committed or not committed—is called the eight unrighteous ways of obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

The eight lawful grounds for prohibiting the recitation of the *Poṣadha* are: prohibiting the recitation on account of a root offense regarding broken precepts, whether committed or not; on account of a root offense regarding broken views, whether committed or not; on account of a root offense regarding broken livelihood, whether committed or not; and on account of a root offense regarding broken deportment, whether committed or not. These are called the eight lawful grounds for prohibiting the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

Furthermore, there are nine unrighteous ways of obstructing the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) and nine righteous ways of obstructing the *poṣadha*. As for the nine unrighteous ways: obstructing the *poṣadha* on grounds that are baseless yet involve a formal offense;

obstructing it when there is no baseless charge of a formal offense; obstructing it when there is no baseless charge of both a formal offense and its non-occurrence; obstructing it when there is no baseless charge of a formal offense; obstructing it when there is no baseless charge of the non-occurrence of a formal offense; obstructing it when there is no baseless charge of both the occurrence and non-occurrence of a formal offense; obstructing it when there is a baseless charge of both a formal offense and its non-occurrence; obstructing it when there is a baseless charge of both a formal offense and the non-occurrence of one; and obstructing it when there is a baseless charge of both a formal offense and the non-occurrence of another—these are called the nine unrighteous obstructions.

The nine legitimate ways of obstructing the *poṣadha* are as follows: obstructing the *poṣadha* by means of a formal act (*karman*) that has a basis but is incomplete; by one that has a basis but is not performed; by one that has a basis and is both performed and not performed; by one that has a basis and is complete; by one that has a basis but is not complete; by one that has a basis and is both complete and not complete; by one that has a basis and is both incomplete and complete; by one that has a basis and is both incomplete and not complete; and by one that has a basis and is both incomplete and complete. These are called the nine legitimate ways of obstructing the *poṣadha*.
Furthermore, there are ten unrighteous ways of obstructing the *poṣadha* ceremony and ten righteous ways of obstructing the *poṣadha* ceremony.

As for the ten unrighteous ways: if a bhikṣu has not committed a *pārājika* offense; if a bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense but the Saṃgha has not yet expelled him from that offense; if he has not reviled the Saṃgha; if a bhikṣu has reviled the Saṃgha but the Saṃgha does not intend to expel him from that offense; if he has not renounced the precepts; if the Saṃgha does not intend to resolve the matter of his renunciation of the precepts; if he is acting in accordance with the lawful business of the Saṃgha; if he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his conduct, yet the obstruction of the *poṣadha* is based on not seeing, not hearing, or not suspecting [such transgressions]—these are called the ten unrighteous obstructions.

The ten *yathādharma* (legitimate) grounds for suspending the *poṣadha*: if a bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense; or if the Saṃgha intends to bring a *pārājika* matter to a conclusion; or if he reviles the Saṃgha; or if the Saṃgha intends to bring a matter of reviling the Saṃgha to a conclusion; or if he has renounced the precepts (*śīla*); or if the Saṃgha intends to bring a matter of renouncing the precepts to a conclusion; or if a bhikṣu does not comply with a legitimate matter of the Saṃgha; or if he has violated the precepts (*vinaya*); or if he has violated his views (*dṛṣṭi*); or if he has violated his conduct (*ācāra*) or views; or if, due to what has been seen, heard, or suspected, he obstructs the recitation of the *poṣadha*. These are called the ten legitimate grounds for suspending the *poṣadha*.

"If a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense: if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu exhibiting the outward signs of having committed a pārājika offense; or if he hears from another that a certain bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense; or if that person himself says, 'I have committed a pārājika offense'; or if a bhikṣu, though not seeing it with his own eyes, hears it through a succession of reports, whether by way of hearsay or suspicion, that a certain bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense."
If the bhikṣus, based on what they have seen, heard, or suspected, wish to obstruct this bhikṣu from reciting the precepts at this or that dwelling place, they should speak as follows:
"We obstruct such-and-such a bhikṣu from reciting the precepts; since such-and-such a bhikṣu is present in the assembly, the Saṃgha cannot perform the uposatha and recite the precepts."
This is called a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense.

Regarding the case where the Saṃgha intends to deal with a pārājika matter: when the Saṃgha intends to investigate the matter of a bhikṣu who has committed a pārājika offense, if an obstacle arises—whether it be one of the aforementioned obstacles or any one of the eight obstacles—and the matter remains undecided, the Saṃgha rises from their seats and departs.
Immediately, one bhikṣu among the saṃgha shall proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now the Saṃgha intends to investigate a certain bhikṣu regarding an offense of pārājika. However, such difficulties have arisen, or other difficulties have arisen; if any one of the eight difficulties arises, this matter remains unresolved, and the Saṃgha shall rise from their seats and depart."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: at the next time of the Uposatha, the Saṃgha shall first settle the matter of such-and-such a bhikṣu.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
If the bhikṣus are able to settle this bhikṣu's matter at the subsequent Uposatha, it is well.
If they cannot be expelled, and if the bhikṣus wish to prohibit this bhikṣu from reciting the precepts at this or that dwelling place, they should speak as follows:
"We prohibit such-and-such bhikṣu from reciting the precepts; because such-and-such bhikṣu is present within the assembly, the Saṃgha is unable to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts."
This is called "the desire of the Saṃgha to bring forth the matter of a bhikṣu’s offense of pārājika.

Regarding "reviling the Saṃgha": if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu exhibiting the signs of reviling the Saṃgha and, by those very signs, reviles the Saṃgha; or if he hears from another that a certain bhikṣu has reviled the Saṃgha; or if that bhikṣu himself says, "I have reviled the Saṃgha."

If a bhikṣu, though not having seen it with his own eyes, hears through successive reports that a certain bhikṣu has disparaged the Saṃgha—whether out of hearing, doubt, or seeing—if the bhikṣus, relying on what they have seen, heard, or doubted, wish to obstruct this bhikṣu from reciting the Prātimokṣa in either this residence or that residence, they should speak as follows:
"We obstruct such-and-such a bhikṣu from reciting the Prātimokṣa; because such-and-such a bhikṣu is present in the assembly, the Saṃgha may not recite the Prātimokṣa."
This is called "reviling the Saṃgha.

When the Saṃgha intends to resolve a matter concerning the reviling of the Saṃgha—such as when a bhikṣu has reviled the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha wishes to investigate that bhikṣu’s conduct—if one of the eight difficulties arises or other circumstances occur, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises while the matter remains unresolved, the Saṃgha may rise from their seats and depart.
Immediately, one bhikṣu shall announce among the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now the Saṃgha wishes to investigate a certain bhikṣu for slighting the affairs of the Saṃgha. Because of this difficulty, or due to other causes, or because one or another of the eight obstacles has arisen, this matter remains unresolved; therefore, the Saṃgha rises from its seats and departs."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha first settle this matter concerning such-and-such a bhikṣu at the next uposatha.
This is called the formal motion (jñapti).
If the bhikṣus are able to first settle this matter concerning that bhikṣu at the subsequent uposatha, it is well.
If they cannot be expelled, and if the bhikṣus wish to prohibit this bhikṣu from reciting the precepts at this or that dwelling place, they should speak as follows:
"We prohibit such-and-such a bhikṣu from reciting the precepts; since such-and-such a bhikṣu is present within the assembly, the Saṃgha should not perform the uposatha and recite the precepts."
This is called "desiring to leave and disparaging the affairs of the Saṃgha.

Regarding "one who abandons the precepts": if a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu exhibiting the signs of abandoning the precepts and thereby abandons them; or if he hears from another that a certain bhikṣu has abandoned the precepts; or if that bhikṣu himself says, "I abandon the precepts."

If a monk, although not seeing it with his own eyes, hears through hearsay or suspects that a certain monk has renounced the precepts, and if the monks—relying on what they have seen, heard, or suspected—desire to obstruct the recitation of the *Poṣadha* for that monk in this or that residence, they should speak as follows:
"We obstruct the *Poṣadha* of such-and-such a monk; while that monk is present within the assembly, the Saṃgha may not recite the *Poṣadha*."
This is called "renouncing the precepts.

Regarding the matter of wishing to go forth and renounce the precepts: suppose a bhikṣu renounces the precepts, and while the Saṃgha wishes to investigate this bhikṣu’s case, various difficulties arise—whether these specific difficulties or other difficulties, or any one of the eight difficulties—should any such difficulty arise, the Saṃgha rises from their seats and departs.
Immediately, one bhikṣu within the Saṃgha shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

We now wish to investigate the matter of a certain bhikṣu’s renunciation of the precepts. Whether this was due to the arising of difficulties or other causes and conditions—if any one of the eight difficulties has arisen and the matter remains unresolved—the Saṃgha may rise from their seats and depart."
"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: at the next time of the Uposatha, the Saṃgha shall first settle this matter concerning such-and-such a bhikṣu.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
If the bhikṣus are able to settle this bhikṣu's matter at the subsequent Uposatha, it is well.
If they cannot be expelled, and if the bhikṣus wish to prohibit this bhikṣu from reciting the *poṣadha* at this or that residence, they should speak as follows:
"We prohibit such-and-such bhikṣu from reciting the *poṣadha*; since such-and-such bhikṣu is present within the assembly, the Saṃgha should not perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts."
This is called the matter of wishing to leave and relinquish the precepts.

"Not complying with the legal affairs of the Saṃgha" refers to the various actions performed by the Saṃgha, such as the *jñapti-karman* (one motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (one motion and one proclamation), the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations), the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the establishment of the fourteen types of *karman*.

If a bhikṣu sees signs that another bhikṣu is not in accord with the legal procedures of the Saṃgha; or if he hears from another that a certain bhikṣu is not in accord with the legal procedures of the Saṃgha; or if that bhikṣu himself says, "I am not in accord with the legal procedures of the Saṃgha."

If a monk, although not having seen it with his own eyes, hears through successive reports that he has heard or suspected that a certain monk does not comply with the legal procedures of the Saṃgha, the monks—whether based on what they have seen, heard, or suspected—should exclude that monk from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa in this or that residence, saying:
"We exclude such-and-such a monk from the recitation of the Prātimokṣa; as long as that monk is present in the assembly, the Saṃgha should not perform the Uposatha and recite the Prātimokṣa."
This is called not acting in accordance with the affairs of the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
Regarding those who break the precepts: there are bhikṣus who commit a pārājika offense, a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, a pāyattika offense, a pratideśanīya offense, or a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu sees the outward signs of another bhikṣu’s transgression of the precepts; or if he hears from another that a certain bhikṣu has broken the precepts; or if that person speaks of it himself;

or even if the bhikṣu does not see it with his own eyes before him, but hears through a succession of reports that a certain bhikṣu has broken the precepts, whether by way of hearing a conviction or hearing a doubt.
If the bhikṣus, based on what they have seen, heard, or suspected, wish to obstruct this bhikṣu from reciting the Prātimokṣa in this or that dwelling place, they should speak as follows:
"We obstruct such-and-such a bhikṣu from reciting the Prātimokṣa; because such-and-such a bhikṣu is present in the assembly, the Saṃgha may not recite the Prātimokṣa."
This is called the breaking of precepts.
As for "breaking views," this refers to the sixty-two views with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their basis; or if one gives rise to other views, such as:

there is no sin, no merit, no giving, no good, no evil, no retribution for good and evil deeds, no present world and no future world, no father, no mother, and no arhats in the world who have attained right practice and realized it for themselves through direct experience in this life and the next.
"My births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence after this body.
If other bhikṣus see signs that this bhikṣu has fallen away from his view, or if they hear it from another, or if that bhikṣu himself declares it.

If a bhikṣu, although not having seen it with his own eyes, hears through successive reports that a certain bhikṣu has violated the [right] view—whether based on what he has heard, what he has suspected, or what he has seen—if the bhikṣus wish to obstruct the recitation of the Prātimokṣa for that bhikṣu in this or that residence, they should speak as follows:
"We obstruct the recitation of the Prātimokṣa for such-and-such a bhikṣu; because such-and-such a bhikṣu is present in the assembly, the Saṃgha may not recite the Prātimokṣa."
This is called the destruction of views.
As for the destruction of proper conduct: there is a bhikṣu who, in the presence of his upādhyāya, ācārya, and all senior elders, engages in wicked and improper conduct that destroys proper decorum.

If the bhikṣus see that this bhikṣu has violated the marks of dignified demeanor, or if they hear from another that a certain bhikṣu has violated the marks of dignified demeanor, or if he himself declares it.

If a monk, although not seeing it with his own eyes, hears through hearsay or suspects that a certain monk has violated the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*), and if the monks—relying on what they have seen, heard, or suspected—wish to prohibit that monk from reciting the *Prātimokṣa* in this or that residence, they should speak as follows:
"We prohibit such-and-such a monk from reciting the *Prātimokṣa*; while that monk is present among the assembly, the *Prātimokṣa* must not be recited."
"This is called violating the rules of decorum.
(The sixth of the eight dharmas concerning prohibitions is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 33;
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 34; Fifth Recitation, Part Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty. Section 7:
The Rules on Bedding and Requisites. The seventh of the eight rules concerns the rules on bedding and requisites.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus treated one another with contempt and lacked respectful conduct.
Seeing that the bhikṣus were treating one another with contempt and lacking respectful conduct, for this reason the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"What do you think?"
"Who, O Bhikṣus, should act as the senior elder (upādhyāya), receiving water first and receiving food and drink first?
A certain bhikṣu replied:
"World-Honored One!"

If there is a bhikṣu of kṣatriya lineage who has left the household life out of faith, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the dharma robes, this person should be given the seat of honor, the first water, and the first food and drink.
Again, another bhikṣu said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu is of Brahmin lineage and has left the household life out of faith, shaving his hair and beard and donning the dharma robes, this person should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.”
Again, another bhikṣu said:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikṣu of the Vaiśya caste who has left the home life out of faith, shaving his hair and beard and donning the Dharma robes, this person should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.”
Again, another bhikṣu said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu has attained arhatship with the exhaustion of outflows, has accomplished what was to be done, has laid down the heavy burden, has exhausted all fetters of existence, and has attained liberation of mind through perfect wisdom—such a bhikṣu should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.”
Again, another bhikṣu said:
"World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu has attained the stage of Anāgāmin, having severed the five lower fetters and no longer returning to this world, such a bhikṣu should be the first to sit, the first to receive water, and the first to receive food and drink."
Again, another bhikṣu said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu has attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin—having severed the three fetters and attenuated the three poisons—and returns once more to this world to bring an end to suffering, such a bhikṣu should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.”
Again, another bhikṣu said:
“World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu has attained the stage of srotāpanna, having severed the three fetters, will not fall into the three evil realms, and is destined for pure knowledge, returning between humans and devas seven times—dying and being reborn seven times—to reach the end of suffering; such a bhikṣu should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.”
Although the bhikṣus spoke in various ways, they did not accord with the Buddha’s intention.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“You should listen with one mind: which bhikṣu should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke of the causal conditions of his past lives, saying to the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, near the foot of the Snowy Mountains, three birds and beasts lived together:
first, a francolin; second, a monkey; and third, an elephant."
These three kinds of birds and beasts mutually disparage one another and lack respectful conduct; these three kinds of birds and beasts together think to themselves:
"Why do we not show mutual respect?"
"If he had been born before us, he should have honored, respected, and instructed us.
Then the francolin and the monkey asked the elephant,
"What do you remember from the past?"
At that time, there was a large *piṇḍīta* tree at that spot.
The elephant said, "When I was small, I walked through here; this tree passed beneath my belly.
Then the elephant and the francolin asked the monkey:
"What do you remember from the past? He replied, "I remember when I was young;
sitting on the ground, I grasped this tree and pressed its top down until it reached the earth."
The elephant said to the monkey, "Your years are greater than mine; I shall pay you respect and honor, and you should preach the Dharma for me.
The monkey then asked the partridge:
"What do you remember from the past?
He replied, "In that place there was a large bibhītaka tree; at that time I ate its fruit and defecated here, and thus this tree grew to such great size. This is what I remember."
The monkey said to the francolin partridge, "Your age is greater than mine; I shall honor and revere you, and you should preach the Dharma for me.
