At that time, the elephant paid respect to the monkey, listened to him receive the Dharma, and then preached it to the other elephants.
The monkey respectfully attended to the francolin bird, listening to the Dharma and teaching it to other monkeys, while the francolin bird taught the Dharma to other francolin birds.
These three animals had previously delighted in killing living beings, stealing the property of others, sexual misconduct, and false speech.
All these birds and beasts thought to themselves:
"Why should we not abandon the evil karmas of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying?
Having had this thought, they immediately abandoned killing, theft, sexual misconduct, and lying.
"Even among animals, those who fully practice these four dharmas will all be reborn in the heavens upon the end of their lives.
The Buddha said:
"At that time, the Dharma of the partridges was widely practiced and disseminated, manifesting itself to both the devas and the people of the world."
"Why do animals and other such beings practice virtue?
Why do they no longer encroach upon and devour the grain of humans?
He further thought thus:
"Even animals are still able to respect one another; how much more so should we?

At that time, all people in the world respected and honored each other, extensively practiced the *caṭaka* dharma, and observed the five precepts; when their lives ended, they were reborn in the heavens."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"As for that partridge at that time, could it have been anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
"The monkey was Śāriputra, and the elephant was Maudgalyāyana.
The Buddha said, "Even animals, though lacking knowledge, still practice mutual respect and the dharma of honoring one another; thus they obtain great benefit for themselves and also benefit others."
How much more so for you who have left the household life out of faith, having shaved off your hair and beards and donned the dharma robes; you ought to respect one another.
There are three types of persons who are not like this.
What are these three?
All those who have not received the full ordination are inferior to those who have received the full ordination;
all those of lower rank are inferior to those of higher rank;

and all those who perform duties and speak contrary to the Dharma, even if they act as presiding elders (*upādhyāya*), are inferior to those of lower rank who do not perform such duties but speak in accordance with the Dharma.
"One who has received the full precepts is superior to one who has not received them; every elder is superior to those of lower rank; and the Buddha is superior to all the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
Then he spoke in verse:
"If a person does not respect the Buddha, nor the assembly of his disciples;
they will be reviled by people in this present life, and in future lives they will fall into the evil realms."
“If a person knows how to revere the Buddha and the assembly of his disciples,
they will be praised by people in the present life and reborn in the heavens in future lives.
After the Buddha had praised the dharma of reverence through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, from the time one first receives the full ordination (upasampadā) until even a great muhūrta has passed, that person should sit first, receive water first, and receive food and drink first.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal the following day. The Buddha granted his consent by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted the invitation, the householder returned home and prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night. Rising early the next morning, he arranged the seating and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; may the Holy One know it is time."
At that time, the Buddha and the Saṃgha went to the householder’s home. The Śākya son Upananda was one who frequently entered and left the homes of others.
Then, the Śākya son Upananda rose early, dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered and left the house of another.
Then, the bhikṣu who had descended from his seat immediately after Bāṇaṃdā the Śākya son asked Bāṇaṃdā’s disciple Dharma,
"Has your teacher come?
He replied:
"My preceptor has many affairs and many obligations; he enjoys frequenting the homes of others. This morning, rising early, he entered and frequented the homes of others; he may come, or he may not."
That bhikṣu did not leave Vāḍiśa’s seat and sat down.

When the householder saw that the Buddha and the Saṃgha were seated, he personally served water and began to distribute food; before the distribution was complete, the Śākya son Vāḍiśa came forward to take his place in the order of seating, causing the bhikṣu who had been sitting on the lower seat to rise.
That bhikṣu then caused the next bhikṣu below him to rise; in this manner, three or four of those in the lower seats all rose, and for this reason the assembly became distracted and disordered.
The lay devotees rebuked Upananda, saying:
"There was such a great abundance of food that it was distributed equally to all; why did you need to sit in the next seat?
If you were so eager to sit in the next seat, why did you not come earlier?"
"I do not now know who has attained it and who has not,
or who has attained it profoundly and who has not.
When the Buddha heard the householder’s reproach and saw that the bhikṣus were distracted, he remained silent.
After the meal, for these reasons, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the Śākyan son Upananda:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu cause a junior monk to rise when food is being served simply because he is a senior elder?"
Having thus rebuked them, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, when food or drink is being served, or once it has been finished serving, one must not cause a junior monk to rise.
If one causes him to rise, one commits a duṣkṛta offense."

If a bhikṣu has a reason involving his upādhyāya or ācārya and rises out of a mind of reverence, he should not cause a second person of lower rank to rise; if he causes them to rise, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
The Buddha said:

"From now on, I permit bhikṣus to sit together on one bed for a period of three years; I permit three bhikṣus to sit together on a coarse-plank bed; I permit two people to sit together on a fine-plank bed; and I permit only one person to sit on a single bed."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the five bhikṣus addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Where should we dwell?
The Buddha said,
"You should dwell among mountain crags, bamboo groves, and beneath trees."

The bhikṣus stayed overnight in mountain caves, bamboo groves, and beneath trees; they rose early to go to their preceptors and teachers in order to receive and study the scriptures, recite them, resolve their doubts, and receive the Dharma.
At that time, the householder Bhaddiya rose early and departed from the city of Rājagṛha, intending to go to the Bamboo Grove to pay his respects to the World-Honored One.
As he went along, the householder saw several bhikṣus coming down from mountain crags, bamboo groves, and trees, and he asked them:
"Venerable sirs!"
"From where have you come? He replied,
"I have come from beneath the trees of the mountain crags and bamboo groves."
The householder asked,
"For what reason are you here among these mountain crags, bamboo groves, and beneath the trees?
The bhikṣus replied:
“There is no longer any place to stay.
The householder said,
“I shall build various dwellings for you all.”
He replied,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to dwell within the lodgings.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow the bhikṣus to dwell in rooms.

At that time, a lay devotee immediately built various rooms for the bhikṣus; they were high, spacious, magnificent, and adorned with various colored paintings. However, there was no bedding or covering material, so the bhikṣus were unable to lie down. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to spread grass or tree leaves to lie upon, and to separately make garments to cover the body and materials to cover the place [of rest]."
"In this country, there are many insects that breed in the heat within grass and leaves.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make mats, rugs, and screens.
Although they followed these instructions, insects still bred there. The Buddha said:
“Listen; you are permitted to make beds.
The bhikṣus took soft wood to make bed frames and slats, but because it was coarse, it caused them physical distress. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I permit you to make mattresses.”
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what material should a mat be made?
The Buddha said:
"You may use a mattress made from sugarcane residue, bottle-gourd vines, melon vines, *kṣaumaka* grass, cotton, *muñja* grass, *śara* grass, hemp, or even water-moss."
At that time, the bhikṣus lay down with their heads hanging because they had no pillows. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make pillows of grass.
The bhikṣus used soft grass for their pillows, which pricked their heads. The Buddha said:
"Listen and accept this: woolen cloth.
As there were no doors on the various rooms and buildings, dogs, oxen, horses, deer, and monkeys would enter; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit the making of door panels."

Because the door panels were not fitted with locks, thieves entered and stole their robes and bowls. When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said, "I allow you to fasten them with cords.
The bhikṣus did not know how to fasten them.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to use a wooden wedge.
The bhikṣus did not know how to make one.
The Buddha said:
"One should make a hole and pass a rope through it to pull it closed.
After it was closed, they were unable to open it again. The Buddha said:
"One should make a door-bolt hook.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"What material should be used to make it?"
The Buddha said,
"One should make it of iron, or copper, or wood.
Having made it, they did not know how to open it.
The Buddha said:
"Make a hole in the middle of the door leaf and insert a hook to pull it shut.
When the bhikṣus had nothing to grasp when closing the door, the Buddha said:
"One should make a hole in the door-panel and attach a ring.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what material should the ring be made?"
The Buddha said:
"One should use iron, or copper, or wood, or *kūrcama*, or *kārpāsa* cotton, or *muñja* grass, or hemp.
At that time, the various rooms were dark because they lacked windows; the Buddha said:
"Allow me to open the window.

Once the window was opened, geese, wild ducks, peacocks, parrots, śāri birds, kalaviṅka birds, jīvañjīvaka birds, and swallows entered through the opening; because they made such noise, they disturbed the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation and reciting the sūtras.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should install lattice screens.
Although the lattice screens had been installed, the birds still managed to enter; the Buddha said:
"One should give a net.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"What kind of material should be used to make the net?"
The Buddha said:
"One should use wool, cotton, *vija*, *pāṃsukūla*, or hemp to make it.
Once they had been made, they rotted and fell apart. The Buddha said:
"It should be covered.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what should it be covered?"
The Buddha said:
"One should use wood to construct a pulley for the offering.
Once it was made, the interior of the room was dark; the Buddha said:
"One should make it like the eyes of a sparrow.
After it was made, it was still dark, so the Buddha said,
"One should make a window-opening."
At that time, the heat having passed and the cold having arrived, the wind blew through the opening where there was no screen, and the cold entered.
The Buddha said, "A screen should be made.
Once the screen was made, it fell off as soon as it was slightly moved. The Buddha said:
"One should make the covering wider at the top and bottom.
After it was made, the two panels did not meet;
the Buddha said, "One should make it wide enough so that they overlap."
Having made it, it wobbled; the Buddha said, "Fix the bolt so that it points upward.
[The monks] did not know how to close it.
The Buddha said:
"It should be closed by pulling with a rope.
Once it was closed, it could not be opened; the Buddha said:
"One should make holes and provide two ropes: one rope for pulling shut and one rope for pulling open.
At that time, because the various rooms had not been plastered, snakes, centipedes, and venomous insects were born between the bricks and bit the bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"They should be plastered."
When the mud had been applied and the walls were coarse and rough, and the robes were torn, the Buddha said, "One should apply fine plaster.
At that time, because the various rooms and dwellings were covered with mud, they leaked during prolonged rain; the Buddha said:
"One should cover it with grass.
After it was covered, there was still leakage over the ridgepole. The Buddha said:
"Cover the ridgepole thickly."
After it had been covered, it was blown away by the wind. The Buddha said:
"One should tie both sides.
After they were tied, there was still leakage from both ends. The Buddha said:
"One should apply a thick layer of grass and mud and secure it with stakes.
When the mud became soft and fell away during the rain, the Buddha said:
"One should cover it with a basin."
The jar fell to the ground again and was broken;
the Buddha said, "One should bore holes in the jar and fasten it with wooden pegs.
Rain entered through the holes, so the Buddha said:
"One should fashion a basket-like cover to close over the opening.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī, having some minor business, arrived in Rājagṛha and stayed overnight in the house of a lay devotee.

This householder had invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal the following day; therefore, he rose in the late night and called his children, servants, and laborers from both inside and outside the house, saying:
"All of you, rise quickly! Split wood, fetch water, set out the cauldrons and pots, and cook rice and soup."
This householder was personally decorating his hall and arranging seats for many people.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself:
"Does this householder wish to hold a wedding?"
"Are you inviting the king and his ministers?
Or are you preparing for a great assembly of almsgiving?
Having had these thoughts, he asked the householder:
"Do you wish to marry, or do you intend to invite the king and his ministers, or are you preparing for a great assembly of almsgiving?
The householder replied,
"I am not marrying, nor am I inviting the king or his ministers."
"I have invited the Buddha and the Sangha for tomorrow's meal, and am therefore preparing a great assembly for almsgiving.
When Anāthapiṇḍada first heard the name "Buddha," his heart rejoiced and his hair stood on end;
he asked, "Who is this person called the Buddha?"
The householder replied, "There is a prince of the Śākya kings who, having left the household life out of faith, has attained the unsurpassed path; therefore, he is called the Buddha.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'Saṃgha'?
He replied:

"There are various people of various lineages and various different origins who have left the household life, shaved off their hair and beards, donned the Dharma robes, and followed the Buddha to renounce the world; this is called the Saṃgha."
He asked again,
"Where is the Buddha now?
He replied:
"He is nearby at the Śītavana forest; you may come to see him as you please.

The householder Anāthapiṇḍada, desiring to see him with a sincere heart, saw the signs of dawn appear in the night. He immediately departed from his house and reached the gate of the Great Power Deity, where the gate opened spontaneously.
This was the constant custom for this gate: at the first watch of the night, the conch was blown for the arrival of guests;
at the last watch of the night, it was blown for the departure of people.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada saw the gate open and thought, "The night must have ended. He stepped out, but not far away, the light of dawn had not yet appeared; it was so dark that nothing could be seen.
Immediately struck with terror and his hair standing on end, he thought:
"Could it be that non-human spirits are tormenting me?
He then sought to retreat.
At that time, the gate-guardian deity Mahāsthāmaprāpta manifested a brilliant light that illuminated the entire charnel ground and spoke, saying:
"Go! Do not fear further.
In a previous life, I was your spiritual friend, the Brahmin Guṇa-skandha; we were householders who shared a heart of mutual respect."

In the past, when I arrived at Rājagṛha, I saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; I bowed my head to them in salutation and sat before them, whereupon they immediately preached the Dharma for me, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening me.

Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened you, I have taken the three refuges and the five precepts. By virtue of these causes and conditions, I was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and am now stationed at this gate; therefore, I tell you: if you go, you will obtain great benefit, so proceed directly without doubt.
At that time, a celestial deity spoke this verse:
“If a person were to obtain a hundred horses, A hundred sets of ornaments and finery,
And a hundred mule-drawn chariots— These would not equal a single step forward.”
Even if there were a hundred snow-mountain elephants, with vast bodies and tusks,
adorned with pure gold and most exceptionally magnificent,
they would not equal one-sixteenth part of taking a single step forward.
A hundred beautiful women from the north, adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and golden seals—
though they are youthful, handsome, and exquisite—
even compared to you taking a single step forward, they do not equal one-sixteenth part of your merit.
Even the foremost jewel of a woman belonging to a Universal Monarch, compared to your taking a single step forward, does not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
Therefore, proceed straight ahead; do not again harbor doubt or regret and turn back.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada thought to himself, "The Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha must surely be of no small significance, for they have caused a deva to so earnestly deliver this instruction.

He then proceeded from within the light to the Śītavana cemetery. At that moment, the ground became clear, and the Buddha was walking up and down in the open air; he stopped there to wait for the householder.
At that time, the householder, according to the custom of laypeople, inquired after the Buddha’s well-being:
"World-Honored One,
are you resting in peace and comfort?"
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"I have removed all outflows of desire, liberated and departed from the world;
having severed all taints, my mind has extinguished all feverish afflictions."
"Because I have attained the state of tranquility, my sleep is always peaceful and secure.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat down at the place where he had been walking. The householder prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew, and sat to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him. He spoke first of the fruits of giving, morality, and rebirth in heaven; he spoke of the faults of the five desires and the suffering and affliction of the world; and he distinguished between the peace and joy of renunciation and the defilement and purity of worldly life.

The Buddha, knowing that this person’s mind was harmonized, supple, and capable of receiving the supreme Dharma, preached for him the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a pure white cloth easily takes dye, so it was with this person; upon hearing the Dharma, he attained awakening. Immediately on his seat, he saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, and mastered the Dharma. Having severed all doubt and no longer following others, he attained fearlessness within the Buddha-Dharma.
Rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

My heart delights in the Buddha-Dharma; know that I shall serve as an upāsaka for the rest of my life. I pray that the World-Honored One and the Saṃgha will accept my invitation for the summer retreat and dwell in Śrāvastī.”
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha intentionally asked the householder,
"What is your name? He replied:
"My name is Sudatta; because I provide for the orphaned and the solitary, the people of this country call me the Giver of Orphans (Anāthapiṇḍada).
The Buddha asked Sudatta, "Is there a monastery for the Saṃgha in the kingdom of Śrāvastī?"
He replied,
"Not yet, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
"If there is a monastery or dwelling place where monks may come and go, they may do so.
If there is none, the monks must not go there, stay, or lodge."
He further said, "I pray that the World-Honored One will simply accept my invitation; I am able to provide monasteries for the bhikṣus so that they may come and go and find rest therein."
"I pray that the World-Honored One will dispatch Śāriputra to serve as my preceptor for the construction of the monastery.
The Buddha commanded Śāriputra:
"You shall serve as the preceptor for the householder in the construction of the monastery."

The householder then went to the Bamboo Grove and inspected the lecture hall, the warm bathhouse, the dining hall, the kitchen, the bathing area, the gatehouse, the meditation hall, and the latrines; having taken note of their features, the householder finished his business in Rājagṛha and returned toward Śrāvastī.
While traveling, he learned where the Buddha was scheduled to stay for the night. He spoke to his relatives, acquaintances, and all those who owed him debts, saying: "Do you know?

Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, I shall build for the Buddha here such things as a lecture hall, a warm bathhouse, a dining hall, a kitchen, a place for bathing, a gatehouse, a meditation hall, and facilities for the large and small lavatories."

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada established a monastery for half a yojana, commanding his attendants to provide all necessary supplies; in this manner, he issued successive instructions as far as the city of Śrāvastī.
Having arrived, he did not enter the city nor return to his own home; instead, he circled the city searching for a site for a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), reflecting on the road:

"Who possesses a fine garden that is convenient for coming and going, where the groves are lush and the flowing water is pure, free from venomous stings, mosquitoes, and gadflies, and where there is no great wind or heat and little noise day or night? In such a place, I shall erect a monastic dwelling to offer to the Buddha and the Saṃgha."

While traveling in this manner, he saw that Prince Jeta’s park was convenient for coming and going; its groves were lush and flourishing with fine flowing streams, free from venomous insects, mosquitoes, and gadflies, and without great winds or excessive heat. It was tranquil by day and night, with little sound.
Even as he gave rise to the thought,
"I shall build a monastery here to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha," Anāthapiṇḍada returned to the city of Śrāvastī;
without entering his own house, he went directly to Prince Jeta and said to him:
"Purchase my grove; I wish to give it to you.
The prince replied, "This grove of mine is not something that can be purchased; even if gold coins were spread out to fill it entirely, I would still not sell it."
The householder said,
"The price for the garden has already been settled.
The prince replied:
"I will not give up my price.
Because of this cause and condition, they fell into mutual dispute and went together to the chief minister, Puṇyavasu, the arbiter, to recount these matters in detail.
Then the minister, who was capable of deciding legal matters, said to the prince:
"Your garden has already been sold; you ought to pay the price at once.
Why do you say:..."
"Spread out gold coins.

Anāthapiṇḍada immediately returned home and dispatched elephants, horses, and carriages to carry loads of gold coins to the Jeta Grove, spreading them across the ground; however, there was still a small amount remaining that was insufficient.
The householder reflected:
"From which treasury shall I draw gold to fill this ground, so that it is neither too much nor too little?
When Prince Jeta saw him silent, he spoke to the householder, saying:
"If you wish to repent and change your mind, give me back the gold and return the garden land to me.
He replied, "O Prince!..."
"My mind has no regrets; I only reflect upon this:
'Which treasury shall I open so that the gold is neither too much nor too little, but exactly sufficient?
Having heard this, the prince then thought to himself:
"The Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the assembly must be truly great and not insignificant to cause a layman to relinquish such precious goods.
Having thought this, he said to the layman:
"Do not spread out any more coins; I shall build a gatehouse here within this space as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha."
At that time, the householder consented out of compassion, and the prince erected a gatehouse within it as a gift for the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Then, taking Śāriputra as his teacher, the householder constructed sixteen great multi-storied pavilions and sixty cave-dwellings within this park.
The Buddha, knowing that the monasteries in Śrāvastī were already prepared, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"I shall travel to Śrāvastī; you all should go with me."
The bhikṣus accepted the instruction and vowed to follow him all together.
At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, set out for Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing where the Buddha and the Saṃgha were staying for the night, told their disciples:
"Go to the lodging and reserve a fine room for the Buddha; take possession of any other excellent rooms for ourselves."
The disciples received these instructions and went first to their lodgings; they reserved the best rooms for the Buddha and took the next best ones for their teacher.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived behind the Buddha; when they wished to take rooms after the Buddha’s quarters had been assigned, a bhikṣu said:
"Others have already taken them."
In this manner, the second, third, and fourth [monks] all said, "I shall take it first.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana took a room at the edge and stayed there.
Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:
“Where do Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana dwell now?
He replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"He is staying in a peripheral room.
The Buddha said,
"Call him here!"
He immediately arrived and asked Śāriputra,
"For what reason do you dwell in a peripheral room?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
The group of six bhikṣus, knowing where the Buddha would stay for the night, first sent their disciples, saying:
‘Go to the lodging place; reserve a fine room for the Buddha, and take possession of any other good ones for us.’”

"The disciples received our instructions and came here first; they reserved the best rooms for the Buddha and took the next best ones for themselves. We arrived after the Buddha, and now we wish to take the remaining rooms."
A certain bhikṣu said, "Another has already taken it first.
In this way, the second, third, and fourth all said they had taken it first; for this reason, we dwell in the peripheral rooms.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, it is permitted to take up residence in rooms according to the seniority of the *sthaviras*.

Immediately, the group of six bhikṣus expelled a sick bhikṣu from his room. At that time, the attendant bhikṣu, carrying the sick man’s vessels for excrement and urine, as well as his spittoon and straw mat, went from one room to another; he suffered great exhaustion and the patient’s illness grew worse.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not follow an elder monk in driving out a sick bhikṣu from his room; whoever drives him out commits a duṣkṛta offense."
When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha did not permit them to drive out a sick bhikṣu by following the seniority of the elders, they immediately feigned illness.
On another occasion, a visiting bhikṣu arrived at sunset, knocking on the door and seeking lodging. The bhikṣu from the group of six was inside and answered the knock;
the visitor asked, "How many years of seniority do you have?"
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We are sick people; why must we ask about our seniority?
They asked:
"What is your illness? He replied,
"I suffer from a painful ulcer hanging from my mouth, and I am also afflicted by a cracking between my toes."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If such a person feigns illness, he should be expelled in due order; all duties within the Saṃgha must be performed by him."
When the sick bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s words, they all stayed in fine rooms. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Even though one is truly ill, one should not stay in superior or upper rooms.”
The person in charge of bedding and requisites should assess the rooms and assign a medium-sized room to the sick.
A medium-sized room is one that can accommodate the patient, the attendant, and the bedding, allowing them all to sit or lie down.

At that time, the Buddha arrived in succession at Śrāvastī. The bhikṣus wished to enter the rainy season retreat; they first performed the preliminary tasks: they plastered the wall holes and the earthen mounds, and they hurriedly shook out their beds, couches, ropes, bedding, and pillows.
The group of six bhikṣus were by nature indolent; standing at a distance, they watched and thought:
"Once they have finished making it and received the bedsteads, we shall go there and, following the order of seniority, drive them out."

After the monks had finished their preliminary duties, spread out their beds, couches, and bedding, and sat down, the group of six monks knocked on the door, and the monk inside responded to the sound.
The group of six bhikṣus asked,
"How many years of seniority do you have?
They replied:
"How many years [of seniority] do you have?
The group of six bhikṣus said, "Get up and leave; I am the senior elder."
The bhikṣus said,
"Will you come with us?
They replied:
"Come together.
"Will you perform the original rite?
He replied:
“I will not do it. The bhikṣus said, “You came here together with us; if you do not perform your original task, we cannot go.”
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha did not say:
'One who does not perform the *pūrvakalpa* (prior practice) shall not dwell in succession with others.'"
"It was only said:
'Receive the lodgings and bedding according to seniority.
We are the seniors; why do you not go?"
The group of six bhikṣus were robust and possessed great physical strength; without mindfulness of guarding the precepts, they entered the house and forcibly seized [the others], dragging them out.
The other bhikṣus had delicate bodies, so their heads and necks were injured and bruised, and their robes and bowls were torn and shattered.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, one who knows how to distribute bedding and furniture should be appointed.
The procedure for appointing one who knows how to distribute bedding and furniture is as follows: the harmonious Saṃgha, with a single mind, should speak thus:"
"Who can act as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha?
If among them there is a bhikṣu who says, "I can."
The Buddha said:
"If there are five qualities, one should not be appointed as the person in charge of distributing bedding and furniture.
What are these five?

If one follows desire, follows hatred, follows fear, follows delusion, or does not know what has been obtained or not obtained—if these five qualities are present, one should not be appointed as the person in charge of distributing bedding.
If one is endowed with [the opposite] five qualities, one should be appointed as the person in charge of distributing bedding.
What are the five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what has been obtained and what has not been obtained.
At that time, a single bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu [Name] is capable of serving as the distributor of bedding and furniture for the community of monks.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as the distributor of bedding and furniture."
Thus it is announced.
Thus is the motion followed by a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
"The Saṃgha has completed the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of bedding and furniture. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

Having been appointed as the person responsible for distributing bedding, one should inquire among the senior bhikṣus for those who are well-regarded, truthful, and capable of discerning the distribution of bedding; one should ask them what kind of offerings are present in these separate rooms.
"What kind of offerings are there in that separate room?
What kind of offerings are there upon this multi-storied pavilion?
The senior bhikṣu should answer truthfully.

The person in charge of distributing bedding should weigh the quantity of bedding against the number of bhikṣus. Having thus weighed the bedding and the number of bhikṣus, if one bhikṣu should receive one room, he shall be given a separate room.
One should first follow the senior elder (*sthavira*) in performing the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*), speaking as follows:
"Venerable Senior Elder!
In such-and-such a separate room there is such an offering; in such-and-such another separate room there is likewise such an offering."
"Venerable Elder, whichever you wish to take, take it as you please.
Having taken it, he should next speak to the second Elder.
Once he has taken it according to his wish, he should again speak to the third Elder.
If the first senior monk says,
"I wish to take the room of the third senior monk," the Buddha said:
"One should not grant it; rather, one should instruct them to perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
In this manner, all [requisites] should be granted in succession.
If a monk has sufficient housing, a room should be granted; in this manner, if there is a surplus of bedding, bedding should be granted in succession."
In this sequence, if bedding and furniture are sufficient, one should provide the bedding and furniture.

Regarding the distribution of the items according to the Dharma: the person in charge of the bedding should first address the Elder, saying, "Please take whatever you wish at your own discretion," and should say:
"There is such-and-such an offering upon this bed; there is such-and-such an offering upon that bed. Which one does the Elder wish to take?"
Once the first senior monk has taken his portion according to his wish, he next addresses the second senior monk.
After the second senior monk has taken his portion, he next addresses the third senior monk.
After the third senior elder has taken [the bedding], if the first senior elder says:
"I wish to take the bed and bedding of the third senior elder," the Buddha said:
"One should not give it; rather, one should instruct him to perform a *duṣkṛta* confession.
On one occasion, the Śākya son Upananda took bedding from within the Jeta Grove and went to another place. He then said to the bhikṣus there:
"You have taken your portion from this place; for what reason have you also taken it from another?"
He replied,
“I shall not take it again.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu takes bedding and requisites from that place again, it is already considered relinquished at this location.
If he says:..."
"I shall not take it again.
This is also called "renouncing that bedding," as explained in detail in the *Jātaka of the Brahmin Woman Cowherd*.
The Buddha said:
"Formerly, there was the wife of a cowherd Brahmin who instructed a bandit to kill her husband and take his property. On the way, they encountered water.
The bandit said to the woman:
'Stay here on this bank; I will first ferry the goods across and shall return to ferry you.'"
The thief then took the clothing and belongings and crossed to the other shore. The woman called out, saying, "Come across and take me with you!
The thief replied:
"You wretched slave!
Since your own husband does not love you, how could you possibly love me?
Having said this, he immediately abandoned her and departed, leaving the wife standing there naked.
Bhadanta did likewise; having abandoned these bedding materials and taken them elsewhere, they were lost in this place, yet he further said:
"I shall not take them again."
There he lost it again.

Furthermore, in the past, a jackal carried a piece of meat to the edge of a body of water; seeing a fish in the water with its belly turned upward, he immediately abandoned the meat, intending to go and catch the fish.
At that time, a flying bird carried away this meat;
the Śākya son Upananda acted in exactly the same way.
Having rebuked him thus, the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, if a bhikṣu has already taken one portion of bedding, he should not take another.
If he takes another, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, observing the rains retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus at a certain location.
At that time, there were few bhikṣus observing the rains retreat at the Jeta Grove, yet the bedding and furniture were many.

After the bhikṣus had each divided them among themselves, some remained undistributed. Those who had built dwellings for laypeople came and asked, "Are there any bhikṣus residing in the bedding and furniture I have provided?"
He replied:
"No one dwells there. Why is that?"

Currently, there are many bedding requisites at the Jetavana but few monks; the Buddha has permitted one to accept only a single set of bedding and not many sets of bedding, which is why no one remains to reside there.
The laypeople said, "In our rooms there are already bedding, blankets, pillows, and food for the morning meal; it would be well if we were to provide you with rooms, robes, and food for your stay."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should first give one portion to each person; if there are elders, one should give them another portion as well, in order to exhaust the contents of the storehouse."
If it is still not exhausted, one should give it a third time for the sake of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).
If it is still not exhausted, one should give it next until it is finished, for the sake of maintaining and treating it.
At that time, the kingdom of Kośala was in a state of turmoil; out of fear, many bhikṣus gathered in one place to observe the rains retreat.

While they were seated there, visiting bhikṣus arrived and placed their robes and bowls in various locations—the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path (*caṅkrama*), and the head of the walking path—staying there while waiting for bedding.

The Buddha saw that various bhikṣus were at the place for washing feet, in the lecture hall, in the gatehouse, on the walking path, and at the head of the walking path; they were carrying their robes and bowls to these various locations and staying there waiting for bedding.
Knowing [the reason], the Buddha asked Ānanda:

"For what reason have the bhikṣus taken their robes and bowls and placed them in the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, or at the head of the walking path? Where are they staying and waiting?"
He replied:
"Because the kingdom of Kośala is in a state of turmoil and the bhikṣus are afraid, many have gathered in one place for the rains retreat.

When these visiting bhikṣus arrived, they placed their robes and bowls at the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, and at the head of the walking path, waiting for their share of bedding."
The Buddha said:
"From now on, two kinds of *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) are permitted:
first, the early *varṣā*; second, the late *varṣā*."
"One should grant rooms and bedding to those monks who have entered the later retreat.

Upon hearing that the Buddha had permitted granting rooms and bedding to those in the later retreat, he immediately sought to take the rooms and bedding from the senior monk (*sthavira*) who was in the earlier retreat. For this reason, a dispute arose.
The Buddha said:
"An *upadhivārika* (senior monk) who has entered the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*) should not take a dwelling or bedding from a senior monk who has entered the earlier retreat (*pūrvikā varṣā*).
If the senior monk of the earlier retreat possesses two sets of bedding, he should give one set to the other."

Furthermore, the kingdom of Kośala was in a state of turmoil and disorder. Many bhikṣus gathered in one place for the rains retreat (*varṣā*), and after they had finished distributing the rooms and bedding, other bhikṣus arrived from elsewhere.

They stayed in the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path (*caṅkrama*), and at the head of the walking path, placing their robes and bowls in these various locations while waiting for the distribution of bedding.

The Buddha saw various bhikṣus carrying their robes and bowls to these various places to wait for the distribution of bedding and seating materials. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:

"For what reason are the bhikṣus staying at the place for washing feet, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, and the head of the walking path, carrying their robes and bowls to these various places? Where are they staying and waiting?"
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
The kingdom of Kośala is in a state of turmoil and is filled with fear.”

When the bhikṣus had finished distributing the bedding for the rainy season retreat, other bhikṣus arrived from elsewhere. They placed their robes and bowls at the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, and the head of the walking path, waiting there for the distribution of bedding.
The Buddha said:
"If there are those who have not yet been allotted bedding and furniture, they should be given their share; those who have already been allotted theirs should dwell together.
Furthermore, at one time, the kingdom of Kośala was in a state of turmoil, and its ministers were engaged in fighting in various places.

The bhikṣus had already entered the later period of the rainy season retreat when many visiting bhikṣus arrived. They placed their robes and bowls at the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking paths, and the head of the walking paths, waiting for their share of bedding and seats to be assigned.
The Buddha saw visiting bhikṣus carrying their robes and bowls and placing them in various locations while waiting for their share of bedding. Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda:

"For what reason are these visiting bhikṣus staying in the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, and at the head of the walking path, placing their robes and bowls in these various places? Where are they staying and waiting?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
The kingdom of Kośala is in a state of chaos and turmoil; its ministers are engaged in battles everywhere.”

After the monks had finished their retreat, these visiting monks arrived and went to the place for washing feet, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, and the head of the walking path; there they placed their robes and bowls and waited for their share of bedding.
The Buddha said:

"If there is an empty room, it should be given to him; if there is none, he should dwell together with others. He should be provided with a warm chamber to place his robes and bowl, and he should go on almsround following the community of monks."

If there is an elder bhikṣu among those present who is virtuous and delights in meritorious deeds, he should seek out clothing and requisites for the visiting bhikṣu, ensuring that this bhikṣu does not depart empty-handed.
At that time, there was a forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu who requested from an elder bhikṣu that his robes and bowl be carried for him and that a dwelling be provided for him.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to carry the robes and bowls of a forest-dweller or provide a dwelling for him."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit you to provide alms-bowls, robes, and dwellings for bhikṣus who practice in the forest.
At that time, there were visiting bhikṣus who came for a short time and, finding no place to stay, were exhausted and deeply distressed. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should temporarily provide a dwelling and bedding.
Once, after a certain bhikṣu had come to stay overnight, he rose early and departed.
Regarding all the offerings contained within that room—from the morning meal to the clothing for the dwelling—the resident bhikṣu became suspicious:
"A visiting bhikṣu came to this room to stay overnight; having risen early, he departed. There is a portion of offerings here, but we do not know what to do with it.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"Even though the visiting bhikṣu stayed there overnight, the resident should receive the dwelling and its appurtenances."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus neglected the study of the Vinaya, devoting themselves instead to reciting the Sūtras and the Abhidharma, and distancing themselves from the Vinaya.
The Buddha saw that the bhikṣus were not studying the Vinaya, but were instead reciting the Sūtras and the Abhidharma;
because they were far removed from the Vinaya, he observed them and praised those bhikṣus who were proficient in the Vinaya, commending them to their faces: "Venerable Upāli!"
"The most excellent and foremost among all those who uphold the Vinaya.
The bhikṣus then thought:
"The Buddha praises the bhikṣu who is proficient in the Vinaya, praising him in our very presence:"
"The Elder Upāli is the foremost among all those who uphold the Vinaya. Why,
then, should we not study and recite the Vinaya?"
The elder senior bhikṣus received and recited the Vinaya from the elder Upāli.

Because he respected his seniors, the elder Upāli did not instruct them while sitting in a higher position; and because he revered the Dharma, he did not instruct them while sitting in a lower position.
Whether walking or standing, he taught them.

At that time, because the Elder Upāli had been walking and standing for a long duration, he suffered from foot pain and ailments in his calves, knees, thighs, waist, ribs, and back. He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the answer] already, he intentionally asked the Elder Upāli:

"Upāli, is it true that there was a senior bhikṣu from whom you received the Vinaya, and that you did not sit on a high seat to teach him out of respect for the senior bhikṣu, nor did you sit on a low seat to teach him out of reverence for the Dharma?"
"When you were walking or standing, because you practiced those postures for so long, did you not suffer from pain in your feet, calves, knees, thighs, waist, ribs, and back?
Was this not truly the case?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One.”

The Buddha praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having thus praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow a junior bhikṣu who wishes to instruct a senior bhikṣu in the Dharma to sit in a higher position while teaching, for the sake of honoring the Dharma."
If an elder (sthavira) wishes to receive the Dharma from a junior monk (navaka), he should sit in a lower position to receive it, out of respect for the Dharma.
From now on, it is permitted for a junior bhikṣu who teaches the Dharma to an elder to sit on a seat of equal height with him, out of respect for the elder.
The Buddha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala.
The elders Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kapphiṇa all followed along with the Buddha.
What these elders have said is true; they are able to use harsh and cutting words to subdue the assembly and perform various *karmavācanā* (formal acts) for the bhikṣus:
the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), and the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment).

At that time, there was a residence in the kingdom of Kośala where many bhikṣus dwelt. These bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—including Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kapphiṇa—had arrived and was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala. They knew that these elders spoke words of truth and were able to subdue the multitude with piercing admonitions, performing various formal acts (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣus:
the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), the act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), the act of reconciliation (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*), and the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).
"Now they will surely perform various *karmas* for us once they arrive here; why do we not entrust this dwelling place to one bhikṣu by means of a *karman*?
Having thought thus, they immediately entrusted the *karman* for that dwelling place to one bhikṣu.
When the Buddha arrived at that place, the bhikṣu prepared an excellent seat for the Buddha and placed it in a fine room; he then withdrew to a short distance to hide himself, thinking:
"If I remain here, the Buddha will surely have me prepare seats and bedding for the visiting bhikṣus."

After the Buddha had accepted this room, the other visiting bhikṣus placed their robes and bowls in various locations—the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gateway pavilion, the walking path, and the head of the walking path—waiting for their share of bedding.

The Buddha saw that the bhikṣus were placing their robes and bowls in various locations—such as the washing area for feet, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, and the head of the walking path—and waiting for the distribution of bedding. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason have the bhikṣus placed their robes and bowls in these various places and stayed there? What are they waiting for?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
I shall wait until the senior bhikṣus have distributed the bedding and furniture.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and tell the resident bhikṣus:
'Open your rooms and give your bedding and seats to the visiting bhikṣus.'"
Ānanda, having received these instructions, said to the resident bhikṣus:
"Open the room and give the bedding and requisites to the visiting bhikṣu.
The resident bhikṣus replied:
"Do you know? This is not a monastery cell; we have assigned it to a single bhikṣu by means of a formal act (karmavācanā).
Among them was a bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and rebuked them, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a monastery cell to a single bhikṣu?
Having rebuked him, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the elder bhikṣu:
“How can a bhikṣu grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a monastic dwelling to a single bhikṣu?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, it is not permitted to grant the formal act for a monastic dwelling to a single bhikṣu.”
If one gives [a dwelling], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
even if it is a monastic cell (*saṃghārāma*), if it is given, it does not constitute a valid gift.
The Buddha again traveled with a great assembly of bhikṣus through various lands; in places where there were no monastic cells, they would seek lodging in the forests.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to their disciples:
"Go first to the lodgings; select the best trees for the Buddha, and take the next best ones for us to occupy."
The disciples went on ahead, reserving the finest trees for the Buddha and taking the next best ones for themselves.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana followed behind the Buddha and arrived at their turn to choose a tree.
A bhikṣu said,
"Another has already taken it.
Thus, the second, third, and fourth all said, "It has already been taken."
Even as far as staying overnight under a tree outside,
the Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked Ānanda:
"Where are Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana now?"
He replied,
“He is outside, walking beneath a tree.
The Buddha said:
"Call him here!
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went to call him.
Knowing [the situation], the Buddha asked Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"Why have you all gone outside to walk beneath the trees?
They replied,
"World-Honored One!"
The group of six bhikṣus, knowing where the Buddha was staying, told their disciples:
"Go first to the lodging; reserve a fine tree for the Buddha, and take the next best one for us."
"We followed behind the Buddha and arrived; next, we wished to take possession of the tree.
Then a bhikṣu said:
'Another has already claimed it.'"
In this manner, for the second, third, and fourth times, they all said, "We have already taken [a spot]," and therefore we went outside to sit beneath the trees.
The Buddha said, "From now on,
I allow the bhikṣus to occupy places under the trees according to the order of seniority."

When the junior bhikṣus heard this, they took all the grass mats and leaf mats that were beneath the fine trees and carried them away; when the [senior] bhikṣus asked for them back, the juniors would not give them up.
For this reason, disputes arose. The Buddha said:
"One should not take them away.

When the elder bhikṣus heard that taking them away was not permitted, they would not give away the grass mats, leaf mats, or the mats personally laid out by junior bhikṣus that were already present under the trees. The Buddha said:
"Those who were first [arrived] should remain; the rest are permitted to take [their belongings] and depart.
The Buddha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, was traveling through the kingdom of Kāśī, followed by all his great disciples:
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandika, Kapphiṇa, and others.
What these elders have said is true; they are able to use harsh and cutting words to subdue the assembly and perform various *karmavācanā* rites for the bhikṣus:
the rite of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), the rite of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), the rite of humbling oneself (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*), and the rite of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

At that time, there were several bhikṣus on Mount Kāla who did not mindfully guard their precepts. They heard that the Buddha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, Kapphiṇa, and others—was traveling through the kingdom of Kāśī. These elders spoke words of truth, capable of using harsh and urgent speech to subdue the multitude, and they performed acts of censure (kukṛtya-karman), acts of dependence (niśraya-karman), acts of humility (tāpaniya-karman), and acts of expulsion (pravāsanīya-karman) against those bhikṣus.
“Are these people coming here intending to perform various *karmas* against us?

In the Buddha’s Vinaya, it is said that one must not grant the *karman* for a monastery to a single bhikṣu. We shall now divide this monastery into four parts; according to the land of the Saṃgha, the rooms, the gardens, the roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—all shall be divided into four parts.”

Having formed this thought, he immediately divided the monastic quarters, the monastic grounds, the rooms, the groves, and the roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, all of which were formally distributed into four portions by *karmavācanā* and given to the four bhikṣus.
As the Buddha was traveling with the bhikṣus, he arrived at this place. The resident bhikṣus there prepared a fine room for the Buddha and hid themselves at a slight distance, thinking:
"We fear that the Buddha will issue instructions to open up rooms and distribute bedding and furniture among the bhikṣus."

When visiting bhikṣus arrived, they stood at the foot-washing area, the lecture hall, the gatehouse, the walking path, or at the head of the walking path, holding their robes and bowls, waiting for the distribution of bedding.
The Buddha saw that the bhikṣus had placed their robes and bowls in these locations while waiting for their share of bedding. Knowing this, he intentionally asked Ānanda:

"For what reason have the bhikṣus placed their robes and bowls at the place for washing feet, in the lecture hall, in the gatehouse, in the walking path, or at the head of the walking path? Where are they staying while they wait?"
He replied:
"World-Honored One!
These bhikṣus are waiting for the senior bhikṣus to distribute the bedding and furniture."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and instruct the resident bhikṣus to open their rooms and provide bedding for the visiting bhikṣus.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda immediately went and spoke to the resident bhikṣus.
He opened the room and gave the dwelling and bedding to the visiting bhikṣu.
The resident bhikṣu said:

"In this monastery, the dwellings, rooms, groves, roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all divided into four parts; they have been formally assigned by *karmavācanā* to four bhikṣus and are not the property of the Saṃgha."
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu divide a monastery into four parts and, through formal ritual (karmavācanā), grant it to four bhikṣus?"
Having rebuked him, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted to divide a monastery dwelling into four parts.
If one does so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; this does not constitute a valid division."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Āravī.
At that time, the monastic quarters in Āravī had collapsed. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason has this multi-storied monastic hall collapsed?"
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Among those who maintain this monastery, there are those who have died, those who are ill, those who have violated the precepts, and those who have gone to other countries.”
The Buddha said:

"Regarding those who have died or those who have renounced the precepts, the Saṃgha should further perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint someone to oversee these matters. If there is anyone who is ill, one should ask them:
'Are you still able to repair this ruined dwelling?'"
If he says, "I can," one should wait.
If one says,
"I cannot," another person should be appointed in their stead.
If someone has gone to another country and there is doubt that they will return, one should wait for them.
If it is known that they will not return, one should appoint another person to oversee the affairs performed by that individual.
After the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus appointed individuals to serve as administrators (vaiyāvṛtyakara).
Among those administrators, there were some who merely swept a small area of ground, some who plugged a small hole, or some who covered a shed with a few blades of grass.
The Buddha said: "Those who perform such minor tasks should not be appointed as administrators."
"If one is able to accomplish great matters, they should be appointed through *karmavācanā* as an administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*).
The monks then appointed those who were capable of acquiring much wealth and accomplishing tasks as administrators for life. The Buddha said: "This should not be done."
"If a dwelling is old and dilapidated, it should be constructed within six years.
If it is a new dwelling, it should be constructed within twelve years.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"From now on, the person in charge of the lodgings should offer the invitation for self-reproval (*pravāraṇā*) regarding three matters:
the winter quarters, the spring quarters, and the summer quarters.
The Saṃgha asks: "
"You require which room?
A winter room, a spring room, or a summer room?
If he says:
"I require a winter room.
If [a room] for spring or summer is available, it should be assigned according to the order of seniority of the *upādhyāya*.
If [the monk] says:
"I require a summer dwelling.
"Winter dwellings and spring dwellings shall be assigned according to the order of seniority of the *sthaviras*.
[This occurred] while the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the householder Bhaddiya erected a multi-storied monastery building, lofty and magnificent, which drew many men and women to view it.
The people thought to themselves:
"This must be a stūpa of the Buddha, or perhaps a stūpa of an Arhat."

In this monastic dwelling, many people were prostrating and surrounding him, creating much noise from elephants, horses, men, and women, which interfered with his sitting meditation and recitation of the scriptures.
At that time, the Elder Upadhyaya left the multi-storied pavilion and took up residence in a small room.
At that time, whenever visiting bhikṣus arrived, they all thought to themselves:
"There must be a senior elder (sthavira) within this multi-storied hall; why do we not go to stay in a small room at the edge?"
He immediately went to knock on the door; there was a sound from within the room, and the visiting bhikṣu asked, "How many years of seniority do you have?
He replied:
"I have been [a bhikṣu] for so many years.
The visiting bhikṣu thought:
"If the bhikṣus in this small room have been [bhikṣus] for so many years, how much more so those in the large room!"

There were those who had gone to the place for washing feet, the lecture hall, the middle gate, or stayed overnight under the eaves; rising at dawn, they went before the upper story and stood, wishing to pay their respects to the senior monks.
There were some young bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras who, descending from an upper story of a multi-storied pavilion,
asked a visiting bhikṣu,
"What are you doing? He replied:
"Desiring to pay respects to the elder," he said,
"there is no elder here."
He asked, "Who is the one who has been staying here for a long time?
He replied:
"We do," the visiting bhikṣus said.
"Those of us who know [the rules] should stay overnight here."
He asked the visiting bhikṣu,
"Where did you stay overnight?
One who had stayed where there was a place for washing feet replied:
"I am staying at the foot-washing place.
The one in the lecture hall replied,
"I am staying in the lecture hall."
When those under the portico replied,
"We slept in the portico," the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should appoint a person to oversee the distribution of bedding and seats.
This person overseeing the distribution of bedding and seats should assign them according to the order of the senior monks (sthavira), saying:
'This is the dwelling and bedding for the senior monk; you shall occupy it in due order.'"
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kāśī, observing the rains retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
When the lay devotees saw the Buddha and the community of monks, they made a mutual agreement among themselves:
"Today you shall prepare various kinds of food and drink; tomorrow it will be the turn of such-and-such a person."
Thus, various kinds of food were circulated in succession:
food for mutual consumption, food prepared intentionally, food for the fifteenth day, and food for the thirtieth day.

Once this regulation had been established, there were those who prepared it early and those who prepared it late; those who were nearby and those who were far away; those that were delicious and those that were not. Among these, an ignorant bhikṣu was instructed to go to a certain house, where there was food prepared early, food prepared late, and food from nearby, all of which was excellent.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus came to take [the items] from this place repeatedly.
A householder asked them, "Why do you come so often?
Why do the great elders not come?"
He replied, “There is no one who knows how to eat who has instructed us; it is because your house is nearby and you prepare food and drink so excellently that we come frequently.”
The householder said:
"We provide this food for the elders!
It is not for you alone; why do you come so frequently?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who knows the food [distribution] should be appointed."
Regarding the procedure for appointing a person to oversee food: the harmonious Saṃgha, with a single mind, should ask, "Who is able to act as the overseer of food for the Saṃgha?
If among them there is a bhikṣu who says:
"I am able. However, if one possesses five qualities, one should not be appointed as the person in charge of food.
What are these five?
If one acts out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion, and lacks knowledge of what has been obtained and what has not,
then even if one possesses these five qualities, one should not be appointed as the person in charge of food.
What are the five?
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what has been obtained and what has not been obtained.
At that time, one bhikṣu should announce in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so is capable of acting as the distributor of food for the community of monks.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that this bhikṣu so-and-so shall act as the distributor of food."
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus the formal act of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) is performed:
"The Saṃgha has completed the appointment of the monk so-and-so as the distributor of food. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
Regarding the method for assigning those who distribute food, one should assign them in order, saying:
"If you, [Name], go to such-and-such a house.
Among the monks thus assigned, some receive it early and some late; some receive it from nearby and some from afar; some receive fine food and some receive coarse food.
There were some who obtained it late and said,
"He intentionally gave this place to me.
Those who had obtained a distant location also said:
"Therefore, he stays far away from me.
When she receives something unpleasant, she says:
"Therefore, he treats me like this."
In the meantime, he spoke other words.
The Buddha said:
"One should state his name."
“If there is a bhikṣu who has received an unfavorable dwelling place, he may then wipe out his name and change it for a favorable one.
The Buddha said:
“One should write the names on wooden boards, collect them in one place, and when the community gathers, they should be taken in order starting from the senior-most monk.”

Some arrived late, while others were far away; those who reached the gate of the host’s residence early stood waiting at the head of the alley for a long time for food, becoming weary of heart, feeling nauseous, and finding no pleasure.
The laypeople came out, saw him, and said:
"We permit you to enter and sit within our gate at your own pleasure.
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to enter the gates of laypeople's homes and sit waiting for food.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit these bhikṣus to enter the gates of laypeople's homes and sit waiting for food."
At that time, there were the sounds of elephants, horses, and men and women, which interfered with the recitation of scriptures and seated meditation. The Buddha said:
"If they cause interference, go outside the gate."
They waited outside the gate for the right time; when people came and circled around on all four sides to look, they saw [the structure] and all laughed.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should construct a foundation of earth."
Being troubled by wind and rain, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a *tusu* (thatch roof) covering.
Because it was thin, rain leaked through; the Buddha said:
"One should cover it thickly.
After it had been covered thickly, [water] leaked over the ridge; the Buddha said:
"Cover it again."
Furthermore, as there was no place to sit, the Buddha said:
"One should seek out wooden planks to sit upon.
When someone stole the planks and took them away, the Buddha said:
"It should be sunk into the ground.
Again it was lost, so the Buddha said:
"One should make a mound of earth."
Because it was not plastered, there were venomous snakes and centipedes within that caused the bhikṣus to be bitten. The Buddha said:
"It should be plastered.
After it had been plastered, it became coarse and rough, tearing their robes. The Buddha said:
"One should use fine clay.
When the bhikṣus required water, the Buddha said,
"One should construct a well."
After the well had been made, it was extremely difficult to fetch water using a bowl or a small vessel;
the Buddha said, "One should make a jar to fetch water.
When they were unable to keep up with the task of fetching water, the Buddha said:
"It should be tied with a rope.
The bhikṣus' hands were soft; when they pulled the rope, their hands ached.
The Buddha said, "A pulley should be made."
When someone fell into a well, the Buddha said,
"A railing should be constructed.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what material should the well-railing be made?
The Buddha said,
"It should be made of wood, stone, or brick."
After this had been done, women of various ages went to the well to fetch water. At that time, their hands touched one another. The Buddha said:
"One should construct a partition above the well; they should each draw water from one side."
A householder came out from inside his house and said to the bhikṣu, "I am preparing food at such-and-such a monastery;
you and your group of people should go to that monastery to eat."
When he was on his way, there were various dangers such as lions, tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears; he reported these matters to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should tell the donor:
'There are such fears and terrors here; please give me food at that place.'"
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the lay devotees prepared various kinds of gruels:
ghee-gruel, sesame-gruel, oil-gruel, milk-gruel, mung-bean gruel, mocha-bean gruel, hemp-seed gruel, and thin gruel.
Having prepared this porridge, he took it and went to the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were standing by the gate of the monastery; seeing him from afar, they asked, "What object are you carrying?"
He replied,
“It is rice gruel.
He asked again:
"What kind of gruel?
He replied, "Ghee-gruel,
sesame-gruel, oil-gruel, milk-gruel, mung bean-gruel, mocha-bean-gruel, hempseed-gruel, and thin gruel."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said:
"We shall go; first give us ghee porridge, sesame porridge, oil porridge, milk porridge, mung bean porridge, mocha-bean porridge, and hemp-seed porridge."
"You take this thin gruel into the saṃghārāma and give it to the Elder.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they did not know what to do.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, a person shall be appointed by *karmavācanā* to distribute the rice gruel.
The vessel used to hold the gruel shall be the very same vessel used for its distribution.

Among these—butter gruel, sesame gruel, oil gruel, milk gruel, mung bean gruel, mocha-bean gruel, and hemp-seed gruel—the senior monks (*sthavira*) receive the superior, rich, and fatty portions, while the junior monks (*navaka*) receive the dregs from the bottom.
When the thin gruel was being distributed, the senior monks received the broth while the junior monks received the dregs.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow you to keep large helmets and large jars. Pour the gruel into these vessels to mix it together, and then distribute it using large bowls and large ladles."
When it was inconvenient to distribute [the food] in this manner, the Buddha said:
"One should use a ladle to distribute it.
After distributing it with the ladle, some portions remained while others were insufficient; the Buddha said:
"A smaller ladle should be made for the purpose of distributing [the food].
The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

Various householders prepared diverse kinds of *pāyasa* (milk-rice), sesame *modaka*, stone-honey *modaka*, honey *modaka*, *śakulī* cakes, *pupphalī* cakes, *maṇḍitaka* cakes, "elephant-ear" cakes, *māṃsāpūpa* (dumplings) cakes, and *jambūlī* cakes; they took these cakes toward the monastery.
The group of six bhikṣus rose early and stood by the gate; having seen him, they asked, "What object are you carrying?
He replied:
“Various kinds of pūpa cakes, namely: sesame modakas, rock-sugar modakas, honey modakas, śakulī cakes, pāpuraṇa cakes, maṇḍika cakes, hastikarṇa cakes, mantuṇḍaka cakes, and jambuphala cakes.”
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We wish to go on our travels;
first, give us sesame *modakas*, honey *modakas*, śakulī cakes, pāpuraṇa cakes, and maṇḍika cakes."
"You take the elephant ear, the *huántún*, and the *jiānfulí* cake and enter to give them to the Elder.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should perform the *karmavācanā* to appoint a person to distribute the bowls.
The person appointed to distribute the bowls should divide them into equal portions.
If further fine bowls arrive, they should also be distributed in successive order."
"If it is not sufficient for today, there will be more tomorrow; you should continue to give them in succession.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, various lay devotees prepared various medicines—namely, ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, ginger, black pepper, long pepper, black salt, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, *pālinda*, *viñjimantha*, *yavaśūka*, and *mānaka*—and carried them to the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus rose early and stood by the gate;
having seen him, they asked, "What object are you carrying? He replied:
"Various medicines:
namely, ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, ginger and black pepper, *pippalī*, black salt, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, *bhallātaka*, *viḍa-mantha-dhānya*, and *mānaka-tuvarā-harītakī*."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"We wish to go on a journey; give us ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, ginger, pepper, long pepper, and black salt."
Take these—harītakī, vibhītaka, āmalaka, pālāśa, viḍaṅga, and mānaka-tuvaraka—and enter the saṃghārāma to present them to the Elder.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you should appoint a person to distribute the medicine; that person shall divide the medicine into equal portions and distribute them."
If expensive medicine arrives, it should be set aside separately.
If a sick bhikṣu requests it, he should be given medicine worth two and a half coins.
If he requests more than that, he should be made to pay the full price.
The Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Ālavī were constantly asking householders for materials to make utensils.
The householders said:
"How can we constantly provide for you?
Why do you not provide for yourselves by making vessels?
They replied:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep vessels for making [food].
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit you to keep vessels for making [food]."

In a monastery in the kingdom of Ālavi, there was a hired carpenter who worked for half a month, one month, or even a year. This carpenter would work during the day and leave in the evening; however, he would lose the tools he had left behind. The Buddha said:
"A monk should be appointed to oversee the making of the tools."
The bhikṣu appointed as the keeper of utensils finished making them and gathered the collection of utensils in one place, but they were again lost and exhausted.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to designate a single room for the storage of utensils."
Regarding the procedure for establishing a storage room for utensils: with the Saṃgha gathered in harmony and with a single mind, one bhikṣu shall announce within the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This certain dwelling is being established by the Saṃgha as a storage room for utensils."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let this certain room be designated as the place for preparing the utensils.
This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
“‘The Saṃgha has established such-and-such a room as a workshop for making utensils; the Saṃgha consents, as it is silent. Thus this matter is so upheld!
Once this room had been established, the bhikṣu in charge of making utensils took the utensils and placed them in both the upper and lower rooms. The Buddha said:
“They should not be placed in two locations.”
"If one occupies an upper room, a lower room should be given to the Saṃgha;
if one occupies a lower room, an upper room should be given to the Saṃgha.
On another occasion, a group of bhikṣus was traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī, and along the way, they stayed overnight in an empty monastery.
The next day, when the bhikṣus entered the village for alms, the laypeople asked them,
"Where did you stay overnight?
They replied:
"I am staying overnight in a monastery.
"In which room or dwelling are you staying?
He replied:
“In such-and-such a room.
The lay devotee said, “This is my room; why did you not send a messenger to inform us?”
