"You should provide them with medicinal decoctions, oil, lamps, bedding, and all manner of necessities.

The lay devotees then escorted those who had stayed in their respective rooms back to their own homes; they prepared seats for them to sit upon, personally served them water, and personally provided them with abundant and delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied.
Having rinsed his mouth with water, he took a small chair and sat down to listen to the preaching of the Dharma. He said to the bhikṣus:
"In my monastic quarters there are bedding and requisites available both before and after meals; why do you not stay here?"
"Furthermore, you should provide robes and coverlets, wishing that this monastic dwelling may be put to use.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is permitted that if the various bhikṣus first wish to depart from an empty monastery, they should perform a *karmavācanā* to appoint one bhikṣu to remain permanently.
One who knows the rules for establishing the monastery should, with a single mind and in harmony with the Saṃgha, ask:
'Who is able to serve as the permanent resident bhikṣu?'"
"Know that such-and-such an empty monastery exists.
If there is a bhikṣu who says,
"I am able," [he may go].
"There are five qualities by which one should not be appointed as a permanently resident bhikṣu. What are these five?
Following favoritism, following hatred, following fear, following delusion, and lacking the knowledge to distinguish between what should and should not be done."
If one possesses five qualities, they should be established as a permanently residing bhikṣu:
not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what should and should not be done.
Immediately, a monk among the assembly of monks proclaimed:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so is capable of serving as the administrator of the permanent property for the vacant monastery of So-and-so."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the monk so-and-so be appointed as the resident manager of the empty monastery so-and-so.
This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal procedure of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
"The Sangha has appointed the bhikṣu so-and-so as the permanent overseer for the empty monastery of so-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld accordingly!"

The resident bhikṣus of the empty monastery should patrol the monastery grounds; first they should repair the stūpas, next attend to the affairs of the Saṃgha of the four quarters, next oversee the preparation of food and drink for the Saṃgha, next determine what items are to be distributed, and finally attend to the affairs of the senior, middle, and junior bhikṣus.
Whichever virtuous and eminent bhikṣus there may be, one should not employ them for menial tasks.
A bhikṣu who knows the monastery should make this vow:
"May those bhikṣus who have not yet arrived come; and for those who have already arrived, I shall provide robes, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites so that they lack nothing."
If one is able to make such a vow and practice it, the Saṃgha shall grant it according to that person's wish.
If they require food, one should freely provide them with excellent food.
If they require housing or bedding, all should be freely provided.

There were many royal ministers who came repeatedly to visit and inspect the dwellings in the Bamboo Grove. When they arrived, they would request food, firewood, and lamps; [the monks] did not know what to do, fearing transgression if they gave them these things, yet fearing trouble if they did not.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should appoint a person to oversee the distribution.
Once such a person has been appointed, even without informing the community of monks, he may use nineteen coins to provide for guests."
"If you require more, you should inform the Saṃgha, and they shall give it to you.
In a forest hermitage in the kingdom of Kośala, there was a thief who went to the hermitage to beg for food. The person preparing the meal said, "The food does not depend on me;
I cannot give it to you. You must seek it from the śrāmaṇeras yourself."
The bandits immediately demanded it from the śrāmaṇera, who said:
“I cannot give it to you; you must ask the bhikṣu in charge of food.
They then asked the bhikṣu in charge of food, and the bhikṣu in charge of food said:
"This food has been prepared for the sake of the Saṃgha, not for you," [the monks said].
The thieves said to one another,
"How could this bhikṣu be willing to give us food so straightforwardly?"
He then seized a bhikṣu by his hands and feet, cut him at the waist, and severed him. The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If there is such a place of fear, if he begs for a little and you give a little, if he begs for half and you give half, or if he asks for everything and you give everything—do not, on account of these circumstances, suffer great decline and affliction."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the community of monks obtained robes, but there was no one to guard them.
The Buddha said, "One should appoint a person to guard the robes."
Regarding the procedure for appointing a person to guard the robes, the harmonious Saṃgha should, with a single mind, ask:
"Who is able to guard the various robes for the Saṃgha?
If a bhikṣu says:
"I am able. However, if there are five conditions, one should not be ordained.
What are these five?

One does not know from where the robe was obtained, one does not know the value of the robe, or upon obtaining the robe, one does not know how to accept it; one does not know its number of pieces, and one forgets the place where the robe was worn.
If one possesses five qualities, one should be established [in the office].

What are the five? Knowing from where the robe was obtained; knowing the price of that robe; knowing what may be accepted; knowing the number [of robes]; and not forgetting the place where the robe was worn.
Immediately, a monk among the assembly of monks proclaimed:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, is capable of serving as the guardian of the robes for the Sangha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the custodian of robes.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
“‘The Saṃgha has appointed the bhikṣu [Name] as the guardian of robes; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
Once the guardian of robes had been appointed, there was yet no one to distribute the robes. The Buddha said:
“One should appoint a distributor of robes.”
Regarding the establishment of the rule: the harmonious Saṃgha, being of one mind, should ask, "Who is able to act as the distributor of robes for the Saṃgha?
If there is a bhikṣu who says:
"I am able. However, if there are five conditions, one should not take up the position.
What are these five?

If one does not know the material of the robes, does not know the color of the robes, does not know the value of the robes, does not know the number of robes, and does not know whether [the robes] have been given or not,
there are furthermore five qualities for which one should not be appointed as the distributor of robes.
What are the five?
Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and not knowing whether [the robe] has been given or not.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with these five qualities, he should be appointed as the distributor of robes.
One must know the material of the robe, know its color, know its price, know the number of pieces, and know whether it has been given or not.
Furthermore, there are five qualities:
not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing whether it has been given or not.
Immediately, a monk within the Saṃgha shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so is capable of acting as the distributor of robes for the Saṃgha."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of robes.
This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and two proclamations (*jñaptidvitīyakarman*).
"The Sangha has appointed the bhikṣu [Name] as the distributor of robes; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was no one to distribute bathing robes. This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should appoint a distributor of bathing robes."
"It should be known that those who distribute bathing robes must give them according to the order of the senior monks. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the monastic quarters within the Jeta Grove, there was no monk who knew the proper timing to announce the hours; no one struck the *gandī* gong; no one swept, sprinkled water, or plastered the lecture hall and the dining area; no one arranged the beds and mats in successive order; no one instructed on the purification of fruits and vegetables; no one inspected the insects in the fermented grain wine; when it was time for food and drink, no one served water; and when the assembly spoke in disorder, no one snapped their fingers to signal silence.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“A *karmadāna* (steward) should be appointed.
As for the method of appointment, the harmonious Saṃgha, with a single mind, should ask:”
"Who can serve as the *karmadāna* for the Saṃgha?
If among them a bhikṣu says,
"I am able," [he should be appointed].
“There are five qualities for which one should not be appointed as *karmadāna*.
What are the five?
Acting out of favoritism, acting out of malice, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and lacking knowledge of what is pure and what is impure.”
If one accomplishes five qualities, one should be appointed as the *karmadāna*.
These five qualities are: not following favoritism, not following hatred, not following fear, not following delusion, and knowing what is pure and what is impure.
Immediately, a monk among the assembly of monks proclaimed:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so is capable of serving as the karmadāna for the Sangha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as karmadāna.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
"The Sangha has appointed the bhikṣu [Name] as the *karmadāna* (steward). Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!

The bhikṣu serving as *karmadāna* should know the time limits and know when to announce the time; he should know when to strike the *gandi*; he should know how to sweep, sprinkle water, and plaster the lecture hall and the dining area; he should know how to arrange the beds and seats in continuous succession; he should know how to instruct on the purification of fruits and vegetables; he should know how to inspect for insects in the bitter wine; he should know how to distribute water during meals; and he should snap his fingers when the assembly is speaking in a distracted manner.

At that time, the śrāmaṇeras followed their preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya) in their work; they associated with their preceptors and instructors; they conversed and worked together with those who were acquainted with them; and they lived in the same country, the same city, and the same village as them.
When there were no śrāmaṇeras among the bhikṣus, there arose various disturbances.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One person should be appointed as a supervisor to have the śrāmaṇeras perform the work."

First, attend to the affairs of the stūpa; next, perform the affairs of the Saṃgha of the four directions; next, attend to the preparation of food and drink; next, manage the divisible property; and finally, instruct on the distribution [of items] to the senior, middle, and junior monks.
In this manner, the procedure should be carried out for the entire Saṃgha.

A novice (śrāmaṇera) should be appointed as the distributor; once the appointment of the distributor is complete, he should first be instructed to attend to the affairs of the stūpa, then the affairs of the Saṃgha of the four quarters, and the preparation of food and drink. Next, he should distribute the divisible items in order to the elders (sthavira), the middle-ranking monks (madhyama), and the junior monks (navaka). In this way, the procedure should be carried out for the entire Saṃgha.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra went to the Bamboo Grove to visit and observe.
The king asked:
“Where is the Elder Mahākāśyapa now?
The bhikṣu replied,
“Great King!”
"The Elder Mahākāśyapa is currently treading mud on Vulture Peak.
The king immediately went to see him and asked,
"Venerable One!"
"Why did you do this yourself? He replied,
"Great King!"
"Who shall act as my laborer?
The king said,
"I myself shall serve as his laborer."
Having spoken thus, he returned.
On another occasion, King Bimbisāra went again to the Bamboo Grove to visit;
the king asked, "Where is the Elder Mahākāśyapa now?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am treading mud on Vulture Peak.
The king immediately went to see him and asked:
"Venerable sir!
Why did you do this yourself? He replied:
"Great King!
Who shall act as my attendant?
The king replied:
"I shall serve as his laborer.
Mahākāśyapa replied, "Great King!"
"Though I spoke to you repeatedly, you did not grant it.
At that time, the king felt ashamed and withdrew slightly to one side, asking his ministers:
"Did I not speak these words before?"
The minister replied,
"The King previously spoke these words.
The King said:
“When was it? He replied, “At such-and-such a date and month;
calculating from the time of my previous statement, five hundred days have already passed.”
The king immediately descended the mountain; at that time, the local people captured five hundred bands of thieves and presented them to the king.
The king asked, "Who are these people?"
He replied, "They are thieves.
The king asked:
"What crime should he be charged with?
The minister replied,
"The crime merits the death penalty."
The king asked the thief,
"Can you act according to my will?
The thief replied:
“Great King!
What do you wish to do?
The king said:
"Are you able to provide for these good people?
The bandits replied,
"If we have received the great kindness of the King, whom else would we follow if not him?"
The minister said,
"This thief must surely have stolen the property of the bhikṣus.
The king said:
"I can employ skillful means to ensure that he does not steal or plunder.

At that time, the king provided him with many fields, houses, and people, and gave him double the amount of grain and food; not far from the Bamboo Grove, he established a settlement for the *kappiyakāraka* (pure men).

At that time, the attendants provided for those with whom they were acquainted, with whom they shared common affairs, who resided in the same country or city, who were subject to the same fears, or with whom they had some prior connection; they did not provide for the others.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"You should appoint a pure attendant (kappiya-kāraka) to oversee the work. You should instruct him to first perform tasks for the stūpa, next for the Saṃgha of the four directions, next for food and drink, next for items that may be distributed, and finally to assist the senior, middle, and junior monks; in this manner, he shall attend to all the needs of the Saṃgha."
"Regarding the appointment of a steward (*kappiya-kāraka*): one should instead appoint from among the lay followers (*avadātavasana*) those who are diligent and capable of managing affairs.
The tenth section on the rules for bedding and furniture within the eight categories of rules is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 34;
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 35; the seventh part of the fifth recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Rules for Settling Disputes. Among the eight categories of rules, this is the eighth: the rules for settling disputes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus quarreled with one another, speaking harsh words to each other;
the bhikṣuṇīs quarreled with one another;
the śikṣamāṇās quarreled with one another; and the śrāmaṇeras quarreled with one another.
The śrāmaṇerikās were quarreling among themselves, addressing one another with harsh words.
The bhikṣu Kālodāyin, having also quarreled with the bhikṣus and addressed them with harsh words, then sided with and assisted those bhikṣuṇīs.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased in their hearts and rebuked him, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, having already quarreled with other bhikṣus, forcibly side with and assist a bhikṣuṇī?"
Having rebuked him thus, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, knowing the answer already, asked the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
After the Buddha had rebuked the bhikṣu Kālodāyin with various causes and conditions, he said:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu, having engaged in disputes and spoken harsh words to other bhikṣus, then forcibly assist those bhikṣuṇīs?"
Having thus rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, four kinds of legal issues will arise:
first, issues of contention (*adhikaraṇa*);..."
Second, matters lacking a basis;
third, matters concerning the commission of offenses;
fourth, matters of constant practice.

Regarding matters of contention: for example, when monks dispute with one another, speaking harsh words to each other, arguing over whether "this is the Dharma" or "this is not the Dharma," or "this is wholesome" or "this is unwholesome. Because they contend with one another in this way, they assist their own side and alienate others; this is called a matter of contention.

Regarding "matters lacking a basis": for example, when various bhikṣus accuse another bhikṣu of having committed an offense—whether it be an offense with remainder that was committed, an offense with remainder that was not committed, an offense with remainder both committed and not committed;

or an offense without remainder that was committed, an offense without remainder that was not committed, an offense without remainder both committed and not committed; or an offense both with and without remainder that was committed, an offense both with and without remainder that was not committed, or an offense both with and without remainder both committed and not committed—in these cases, they bring forth the accusation of an offense based on no foundation. Because there is no basis, they become mutually entangled; this is called a matter lacking a basis.
Regarding the matter of offenses, there are five kinds of transgressions:
the *pārājika*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *pāyattika*, the *pratideśanīya*, and the *dukkaṭa*.
Whether it be an offense committed, defiled, or not repented—this is called the matter of committing an offense.
"Matters of constant practice" refers to the affairs performed by the Saṃgha:

namely, the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*, and the establishment of the fourteen types of *karman*—these are called matters of constant practice.
What is the root of matters concerning strife?
There are fourteen causes and conditions for schism in the Saṃgha and six roots of strife; these are called the roots of matters concerning strife.
What is the fundamental basis of matters lacking a foundation?
There are three roots:
the root of seeing, the root of hearing, and the root of doubt.
If a bhikṣu engages in quarreling and mutual accusation with another bhikṣu, and having committed an offense himself, causes another to speak of it:

There is: having committed a remainder and not having committed a remainder; having committed a remainder and not having committed [it] again; if there is no remainder, neither having committed nor not having committed a remainder; having committed no remainder and not having committed [it] again; if there is both a remainder and no remainder, neither having committed nor not having committed both; having committed both a remainder and no remainder and not having committed [them] again; and having committed both a remainder and no remainder and not having committed [them] again.
If, by means of speech or mind, one causes another to say: "There was a remainder committed" when there was no remainder committed;

"There was a remainder committed" when it was not committed; "There was a remainder committed" when it was both committed and not committed; "There was no remainder committed" when there was no remainder committed; "There was no remainder committed" when it was not committed; "There was no remainder committed" when it was both committed and not committed; or "There was a remainder and no remainder committed" when it was not committed; or "There was a remainder and no remainder committed" when it was both committed and not committed; and if, from among these, one brings forth a different charge against another, this is called the fundamental basis of groundless matters.
What is the root of disputes arising from offenses?
From what do they originate?
They arise from five kinds of offenses; they take these five kinds of offenses as their root.

There are offenses committed through the body but not through speech or mind; there are offenses committed through speech but not through body or mind; there are offenses committed through both body and mind but not through speech; there are offenses committed through both speech and mind but not through the body; and there are offenses committed through body, speech, and mind. There are no offenses committed by the mind alone.
From what does this transgression arise? This is called the root of the offense.
Regarding the actions one constantly performs, what serves as their basis?
From what matter do they arise?
All matters that are undertaken arise from the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha is their root. This is called the root of the matters of constant practice.
"Are all instances of quarreling termed 'matters of dispute'?"
Are all matters of dispute also called quarrels?

There are matters of dispute that are not quarrels; there are quarrels that are not matters of dispute; there are those that are both quarrels and matters of dispute; and there are those that are neither quarrels nor matters of dispute.
There is that which is a dispute but not a matter of contention: if monks merely speak to one another, a dispute has not yet been formed.
There is that which is a matter of contention but not a dispute: the three kinds of matters of contention.
There are cases where there is both strife and a matter of dispute: if bhikṣus engage in mutual verbal abuse, it constitutes both a matter of strife and a matter of dispute.
There are cases where there is neither strife nor a matter of dispute: these are cases other than the three mentioned above.
Are all instances of dispute without a basis (anuvāda) necessarily called "disputes concerning matters" (adhikaraṇa)?
Are there also cases where what is called a "dispute concerning matters" is also a "dispute without a basis"?

There are disputes without a basis that are not disputes concerning matters; there are disputes concerning matters that are not disputes without a basis; there are disputes without a basis that are also disputes concerning matters; and there are those that are neither disputes without a basis nor disputes concerning matters.
Regarding "disputes concerning non-matters that are not disputes concerning matters": this refers merely to proclaiming the faults of others without yet having initiated a dispute.
Regarding "disputes concerning matters that are not non-matter disputes": these are the three types of disputes.
Regarding "there is a dispute over non-matters that is also a matter of dispute": there is a case where a monk has a dispute over non-matters and also gives rise to a matter of dispute.
Regarding "neither a dispute over non-matters nor a matter of dispute": setting aside the three preceding cases, are all instances of committing an offense called matters of dispute?
Are there matters of dispute that are also called offenses?

There are matters of offense that are not matters of dispute; there are matters of dispute that are not offenses; there are matters that are both offenses and matters of dispute; and there are matters that are neither offenses nor matters of dispute.
There are offenses that are not matters of dispute; these are what are termed "offenses.
There are matters of dispute that are not offenses; these are the three kinds of disputes.
There are those that are both offenses and matters of dispute; these are what are termed "offenses that are also disputes."
Regarding "neither an offense nor a matter of dispute": apart from the three aforementioned cases, are all habitual activities termed "matters of dispute"?
And are there matters of dispute that are also termed "habitual activities"?

There are matters that are habitual practices but not subjects of dispute; there are matters that are subjects of dispute but not habitual practices; there are matters that are both habitual practices and subjects of dispute; and there are matters that are neither habitual practices nor subjects of dispute.
There are matters that are regularly practiced but are not matters of dispute; these are termed formal procedures (*karmavastu*).
There are matters of dispute that are not regularly practiced; these are the three types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).
There are matters that are both regularly practiced and matters of dispute; these are both regularly practiced and matters of dispute.
Regarding matters that are neither of extreme conduct nor of dispute: these exclude the three aforementioned categories.
Are matters of contention wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
They may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is called "virtuous"?
There are bhikṣus who engage in dispute with virtuous minds, saying: "This is the Dharma, this is not the Dharma; this is the Vinaya, this is not the Vinaya. This is called virtuous.
What is unwholesome?
There is a bhikṣu with an unwholesome mind who engages in dispute, claiming, "This is the Dharma, this is not the Dharma; this is the Vinaya, this is not the Vinaya. This is called unwholesome.
What is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*)?

There are certain bhikṣus who do not dispute with one another out of either a wholesome or an unwholesome mind, [arguing] whether this is the Dharma or not the Dharma, or whether this is the Vinaya or not the Vinaya; this is called indeterminate.
Is a dispute concerning groundless matters wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
It may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. As for the wholesome:
if monks, with a wholesome mind, engage in a dispute together and bring forth the offenses of other monks;

There is that which is partially done; there is that which is partially not done; there is that which is both partially done and partially not done; there is that which is entirely done; there is that which is entirely not done; there is that which is neither entirely done nor entirely not done; there is that which is both partially and entirely done; there is that which is both partially and entirely not done; and there is that which is both partially and entirely done and not done. These are called "wholesome."

Regarding what is unwholesome: if various bhikṣus, with unwholesome minds, engage in mutual dispute to expose the offenses of others—whether it be a formal act involving a remainder (sāvaśeṣa), a formal act not involving a remainder, a formal act both involving and not involving a remainder, a formal act without a remainder, a formal act not without a remainder, a formal act neither without nor involving a remainder, a formal act both involving and without a remainder, a formal act not involving and without a remainder, or a formal act both involving and without a remainder—this is called unwholesome.

Regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): if various bhikṣus, with neither a wholesome mind nor an unwholesome mind, together dispute the offenses of others—whether it be a formal offense with remainder (*sāvaśeṣa*) that was committed, one with remainder that was not committed, one with remainder both committed and not committed;

or a formal offense without remainder (*anavaśeṣa*) that was committed, one without remainder that was not committed, one without remainder both committed and not committed; or a formal offense both with and without remainder that was committed, one both with and without remainder that was not committed, or one both with and without remainder both committed and not committed—this is called the indeterminate.
Is the matter of committing an offense wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
The matter of committing an offense is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
As for the unwholesome: if various bhikṣus knowingly violate a precept established by the Buddha, this is called unwholesome.
Regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): when one does not intentionally transgress the precepts established by the Buddha, this is called the indeterminate.
Regarding the actions performed habitually, are they wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
It may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. As for the wholesome:

if bhikṣus perform a *jñapti-karman*, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* with a wholesome mind, or perform the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā*, or establish the *karman* of the fourteen persons, this is called wholesome.

Regarding what is unwholesome: if monks, with an unwholesome mind, perform a *jñapti-karman*, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā*, or establish the *karman* of the fourteen persons, this is called unwholesome.

Regarding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*): if monks perform a formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), as well as the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or the formal acts involving fourteen persons, without either a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind, these are called indeterminate.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"By how many methods for settling disputes are matters of dispute settled?
The Buddha said:
“There are two ways to settle a dispute.
What are the two?
Settling by means of *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and settling by means of *yebhuyyasikā* (settlement by majority decision).”
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
By how many methods for settling disputes are matters concerning groundless charges settled?"
The Buddha said:
"They are settled by means of the four methods for settling disputes.

They are settled by the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (settlement before the assembly) and the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement through recollection); they are settled by the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* and the *amūḷha-vinaya* (settlement for one who is not insane); and they are settled by the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* and the *tatsvabhāva-aiṣīya-vinaya* (settlement by searching for the truth)."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
By how many methods for settling disputes are matters concerning offenses settled?"
The Buddha said:
"The matters of settling disputes are settled by three methods:

through *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) and *pratijñāvinaya* (settlement by confession); and through *saṃmukhavinaya* and *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement by spreading grass)."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
By how many methods for settling disputes are the matters of constant practice settled?"
The Buddha said:
"A dispute is settled by means of a single method of settling disputes: settlement through presence (sammukhā-vinaya).
How is a dispute over contention settled by means of two methods of settling disputes?"
"Monks! In whatever residence there is a dispute involving signs of contention, this matter shall be entrusted to a *talaṭṭha* for adjudication.
The *talaṭṭha* monk should accept this matter and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching."

If a *talaṭṭha* bhikṣu can bring about cessation in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this matter is called "cessation by means of a single method for settling disputes," namely, the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement through presence).
"Presence" means the presence of persons and the presence of the *vinaya*. Regarding the presence of persons:
when those who assist in the formal act of censure and the person against whom the charge is brought are assembled together in one place, this is called the presence of persons.

When the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) is applied, it is when a matter is settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; this is called *saṃmukhavinaya*.

If a *talaṭṭha* (a single elder) is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, he should relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should accept this matter and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Saṃgha is able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the parties).
Regarding *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*. As for the presence of the Saṃgha:

all those monks who are capable of performing the *karmavācanā* together therein must assemble in one place with minds in harmony; those entitled to convey their consent (*chanda*) must bring that consent; and present monks who are capable of obstructing [the proceeding] must not do so. This is called the presence of the Saṃgha.
"Presence of the person" means that the person who initiated the matter and those who assisted in raising it gather together in one place; this is called "presence of the person.
"Presence of the *vinaya*" means resolving the matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the *vinaya*, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; this is called "resolution."

If the Saṃgha is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, then two *uḍāyikulas* should be appointed from within the Saṃgha; they should perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to authorize this person to resolve the matter.
Regarding the *karmavācanā*: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu asks within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as the *āvāsika* (resident monk) to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha's teaching?"
If among the Saṃgha there should be one who says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, he should not be appointed as an avavādaka (instructor).
What are the five?
Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and not knowing whether [a fault] has been abandoned or not.
One who possesses these five qualities should be appointed as an *avakāśika* (a monk who assigns lodgings).
One should not act out of desire, nor act out of hatred, nor act out of fear, nor act out of delusion; one should know what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu should announce in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

"Such-and-such a monk, so-and-so, is capable of acting as an *avakāśaka* (one who provides space), resolving matters according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, in accordance with the affairs of the Saṃgha."

If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the bhikṣus named So-and-so and So-and-so be appointed as *āvāsika-kulika*, capable of adjudicating matters according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*):

'The Saṃgha appoints so-and-so and so-and-so bhikṣus as *āvāsika* (resident) and *karmakāraka* (officiant) to conclude the business of the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.'"
“If these two, the crows and the pigeons, are senior monks (*sthavira*), the junior monks (*navaka*) should give their consent (*chanda*) to these two and then depart to a distance.

If these two, the crows and the pigeons, are junior monks, they should receive the consent from the senior monks and then move a short distance away; then this matter should be settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.”

If the two *kukkutas* and the *kaurava* can settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of a single *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhavinaya*.
Regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

If these two *ubhatovyañjanaka* (eunuchs) are unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, then these two *ubhatovyañjanaka* should be replaced by another two *ubhatovyañjanaka*.
Regarding the establishment of the rules: when the Saṃgha is unified in one mind, a single bhikṣu shall ask within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as the *karmakāraka* (executor of formal acts) to carry out the business of the Saṃgha?"
If he says, "I am able," one bhikṣu shall announce in the midst of the saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These bhikṣus, so-and-so and so-and-so, are capable of acting as the *karmakāraka* (executor of formal acts); they shall adjudicate the matter according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, in accordance with the affairs of the Saṃgha."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so as *āvāsika-kāraka* (stewards), who are able to adjudicate matters according to the Dharma in accordance with the affairs of the Saṃgha.
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act with a motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

"The Saṃgha appoints so-and-so and so-and-so bhikṣus as *āvāsika* (resident) and *karmakāra* (officer) to conclude the business within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld thus!"
"If the two, Kakkaṭa and Kukkula, are the senior monks (*sthavira*), the junior monks (*navaka*) should give their consent (*chanda*) and then move a short distance away.

If the two, Kakkaṭa and Kukkula, are the junior monks, they should take the consent from the senior monks and then move a short distance away; they must settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching."

If the two *kukkuṭa* and *rova* [monks] can settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of others).
Regarding the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"Presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "presence of the person" and "presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.
If the two former *dvāv-āvartaka-kaurava* are unable to settle the matter according to the Dharma, it shall be returned to the original two *dvāv-āvartaka-kaurava*.
Those original two *dvāv-āvartaka-kaurava* should then settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching.
If one is able to settle this matter according to the Dharma, it is called settling through the application of a single *vinaya* method, namely, the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).
As for *sammukhavinaya*, it means the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the individual and the presence of the Vinaya are also as explained above.

If these two previously mentioned *kaukṛtya* (remorseful) monks are unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it should be relinquished and entrusted to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should accept this matter and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the Saṃgha accepts this matter and is able to settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Regarding the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

"If the Saṃgha is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, the Saṃgha should dispatch a messenger to the Saṃgha residing in a nearby location and say these words:

'This matter arose through such and such causes and conditions; the Thera could not settle it, the assembly of monks could not settle it, the two *Uvācīras* could not settle it, the next two *Uvācīras* could not settle it, the previous two *Uvācīras* could not settle it, and the Saṃgha itself could not settle it.'"
"Venerable sirs!
Let us assemble for the sake of resolving this matter.
At that moment, that assembly should assemble.
If the Saṃgha has already entered the rains retreat, one may go away for seven days.
If those seven days are exhausted, one may go away for thirty-nine nights.
If those thirty-nine nights are exhausted, one must break the retreat and assemble at one place; having accepted these matters, they should be brought to an end.
The monks of the local community should accept this matter and settle it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

If the monks of the local community are able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling a dispute through the application of the *ekamūlaka-niḥsaraṇa* (the single-rooted resolution), namely, the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
Regarding *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

If the local community of monks is unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, then at that time one should appoint two *kukkura* (dog-like) *kula* (clansmen) within the community to adjudicate it.
Regarding the ritual procedure for appointing a *kukkuta-kāra* (a mediator): with the Saṃgha gathered in harmony and focused in one mind, one bhikṣu shall ask within the assembly:
"Who is able to act as a *kukkuta-kāra* to settle this matter concerning the community according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha's teaching?"
In this regard, if one says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, one should not be appointed to the office.
What are the five?
Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and not knowing whether [the offense] has been abandoned or not.
If one possesses these five qualities, one should be appointed as an *avavādaka* (instructor).
Not following desire, not following hatred, not following fear, and not following delusion, he knows what has been abandoned and what has not been abandoned.
At that moment, a certain bhikṣu proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

"Such-and-such a monk, such-and-such a bhikṣu, is capable of acting as an *avavādaka* (a mediator), and is able to settle matters within the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching."

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so shall act as *avavādaka* (advisers), resolving matters according to the Dharma in accordance with the affairs of the Saṃgha.
This is called the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

"The Saṃgha has appointed such-and-such and such-and-such bhikṣus as *āvāsika* (resident) and *karmakāraka* (officiant) to conclude the business of the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."

"If these two monks, the Avakulika brothers, are the senior monks (*sthavira*), then the junior monks (*navaka*) should come, convey their consent (*chanda*) to these two Avakulika monks, and then move to a short distance away."

If this second bird, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, is the junior seat-holder, he should receive the *chanda* from the senior bhikṣu, then move a short distance away, and settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching.

If these two, Āvīci and Kuvera, can settle this matter according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of others).
Regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"Presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "presence of the person" and "presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.

If the two *dvau-dhruva-kula* (two-owl-voting groups) are unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, another two *dvau-dhruva-kula* should be established.
The one who establishes the rule shall, with a single mind, ask within the harmonious Saṃgha:
"Who is able to act as the *karmakāra* (executor of duties) to adjudicate matters according to the Dharma in accordance with the affairs of the Saṃgha?"
If he says, "I am able," one monk shall announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so are capable of acting as *avavādaka* (advisers), resolving matters according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so act as *avavādakas* to resolve matters within the Saṃgha."
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

"The Saṃgha appoints such-and-such a person and such-and-such a bhikṣu to act as the *āvāsika* (resident) to conclude the affairs within the Saṃgha. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
“If the two, Kakudha and Kallavāḷa, are the senior monks (sthavira), the junior monks (navaka) should give their consent (*chanda*) and then move a short distance away.

If the two, Kakudha and Kallavāḷa, are the junior monks, they should take the consent from the senior monks and then move a short distance away; they should settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching.”

If the two *kukkutas* and the *āvāsika* are able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya*.
Regarding the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.
If the *āvāsika* *kula* is unable to settle this matter according to the Dharma, it should be returned to the previous *kula*.
The previous *kula* should accept this matter and settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching.

If this Kukkula can resolve this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it is called resolving by means of a single *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the assembly).
Regarding *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
"Presence of the Saṃgha" is as explained above; "presence of the person" and "presence of the *vinaya*" are also as explained above.
If Srona Kūṭadanta is still unable to resolve the matter in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, it should be relinquished to the Saṃgha.

The Saṃgha should accept this matter and resolve it in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching by means of one form of legal procedure (*vinaya*), namely, the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (the presence of the parties).
Regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

"If the monks of the nearby residence are unable to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, and if those monks hear that in such-and-such a place there is a community of monks with excellent elders who know how to recite the Prātimokṣa, and that in this community there are many bhikṣus who are masters of the Sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkā."

The monks residing at this nearby location should dispatch a messenger to the community of monks at that [distant] place; they should first appoint a person to convey the matter, or, if outside the boundary, ensure the number of the assembly of monks is complete.
Regarding the establishment of the rule, the unified Saṃgha should ask with one mind:
"Who is able to act as a messenger to take this matter from this place to that place, or to resolve this matter along the way?"
In this regard, if someone says,
"I am able," yet possesses five qualities, they should not be appointed as a messenger:
One who follows desire, follows hatred, follows fear, follows delusion, and does not know what has been extinguished and what has not been extinguished—such a person should not be appointed.
However, if one possesses five qualities, they should be established as a transmitter of the tradition:
one who does not follow desire, does not follow hatred, does not follow fear, does not follow delusion, and knows what has been extinguished and what has not been extinguished.
At that time, the messenger should take this matter with him.

If, while on the way, he can settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called settling it by means of one *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
Regarding the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.

If the person conveying the matter is unable to settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching while on the way, one should carry the case to the place where that person resides.
Having arrived at that residence, if there are elder bhikṣus there who are senior, learned, and well-known, one should say to those people:

"This matter of dispute arose from such causes and conditions. The *talaṭṭha* could not resolve it; the Saṃgha could not resolve it; the first two *ubhatovyañjanaka* monks could not resolve it; the second two *ubhatovyañjanaka* monks could not resolve it; it was returned to the first two *ubhatovyañjanaka* monks, yet they again could not resolve it; it was returned to the Saṃgha, yet the Saṃgha again could not resolve it; the Saṃgha of the neighboring residence could not resolve it; the two *ubhatovyañjanaka* monks of the neighboring residence could not resolve it; the second two *ubhatovyañjanaka* monks also could not resolve it; it was returned to the first two *ubhatovyañjanaka* monks, yet they again could not resolve it; it was returned to the Saṃgha of the neighboring residence, yet they again could not resolve it; and while being transmitted through the path of human hands, this matter could not be resolved. It has now come here to you, O Elder!"
"Can you endure this matter and renounce it?
If he says, "I can renounce it," [then proceed].
"You should agree upon a time limit.
If no time limit is set, we shall not give it to you.
A time limit may extend up to nine months."
"There are five kinds of matters that are difficult to sever:
first, firmness; second, strength; third, perversity; fourth, coming and going; and fifth, doubt and fear."
"Obstinate" means being attached to this matter.
"Strong" refers to the person undertaking the task or the person possessing the task being vigorous, robust, and powerful.
"Rebellious" refers to the person undertaking the task or the person possessing the task having a wicked and rebellious disposition.
"Coming and going" refers to this matter proceeding from one dwelling place to another.
"Doubt and fear" refers to the bhikṣus' fear that while settling the matter, they might break the harmonious Saṃgha—united as one mind—into two factions.
First, one must appoint a person to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*). They should be appointed in this manner:
the harmonious Saṃgha, being of one mind, should ask:
"Who is able to act as the distributor of the voting sticks?"
Among them, some people said,
"I can. There are five qualities by which one should not be appointed as a person to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*):
One who acts out of affection, out of hatred, out of fear, or out of delusion, and who does not know when it is appropriate to cast a tally or when it is not, [should not be appointed].
If one possesses five qualities, he should be established as the person who casts the tallies:
he does not act out of affection, he does not act out of hatred, he does not act out of fear, he does not act out of delusion, and he knows when it is appropriate to cast a tally and when it is not.
Among them, one bhikṣu shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named So-and-so is able to act as the distributor of voting sticks for the Saṃgha."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience; let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks.
This is called the *jñapti*.
Thus is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement).
"Having completed the appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks, the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter shall be upheld!
If a bhikṣu has been appointed as the distributor of voting sticks, he should, according to the number of monks, prepare two kinds of sticks:
one portion long and one portion short.
One part was white and one part was black.
For those who spoke according to the Dharma, he prepared long tally-sticks;
for those who spoke what was not in accordance with the Dharma, he prepared short tally-sticks.
Those who speak according to the Dharma shall take white counting sticks;
those who speak contrary to the Dharma shall take black counting sticks.
Those speaking in accordance with the Dharma shall hold their sticks with the right hand; those speaking contrary to the Dharma shall hold theirs with the left hand.
It is said that one should hold the tally for the Dharma loosely when announcing it, and hold the tally for what is not the Dharma tightly.
First, one should announce the tally for the Dharma; afterwards, one should announce the tally for what is not the Dharma.
The person distributing the tallies should speak as follows:
"This is the tally for those who speak according to the Dharma; this is the tally for those who speak contrary to the Dharma.

Once the distribution of tallies is completed, if the tally of those who speak according to the Dharma exceeds that of the others by even one, this matter is termed "settlement by means of two *vinayas*," namely: the *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*) and the *vinaya* of majority decision (*yadbhūyaḥ-sammatā-vinaya*).

Regarding *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): if, within this matter, those who assist in the formal accusation and the person being accused are all gathered together in one place in the presence of the assembly, and the issue is settled in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching through their collective presence, this is called *sammukhavinaya*.
Regarding "seeking many *yadbhūyaḥ* (majority) *vinayas*": herein one should seek and inquire through coming and going to resolve [the matter] according to the Dharma.

If those who speak what is not Dharma are even one more than [those who speak what is Dharma], this matter is also called "settled by means of two *vinayas*": the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and the *yadbhūyovinnaya* (settlement by majority).

Regarding the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): if, within this matter, the person who supports the formal accusation, the person against whom the accusation is made, and those involved in the case all come together in one place in the presence of one another, and the issue is resolved in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called *saṃmukha-vinaya*.
Regarding "seeking much within this Vinaya": herein one should seek, investigate, inquire about, and eliminate what is non-Dharma through coming and going.
There are four types of persons who cast voting sticks (*śalākā*):
first, those who cast them in secret; second, those who cast them perversely; third, those who cast them according to a prearranged agreement; and fourth, those who cast them universally.

Regarding "concealing the distribution of voting tickets" (*saṃvṛta-śalākā-cāra*): if one distributes voting tickets while walking in the dark, or if one distributes voting tickets where there are walls or obstructions, this is called concealing the distribution of voting tickets.

Regarding "distributing voting tickets in reverse order" (*viparyasta-śalākā-cāra*): if one distributes voting tickets in reverse order—giving the voting ticket for those who speak according to the Dharma to those who speak contrary to the Dharma, and giving the voting ticket for those who speak contrary to the Dharma to those who speak according to the Dharma—this is called "reverse order."

Regarding "making an agreement": if various bhikṣus make an agreement with their preceptors (upādhyāya) or instructors (ācārya); or with those who share the same preceptor or the same instructor; or with acquaintances; or with those they converse with; or with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); or with those of like mind; or according to country; or according to village; or according to place—making such an agreement as this: "We shall take such and such voting sticks (śalākā);
you must not stay far from me, nor be separate or different, nor fail to speak together; we shall perform one and the same task."
This is called the "appointment.

When the entire Saṃgha takes up the voting sticks (*śalākā*), at that time all members of the Saṃgha should assemble together in one place; they must not take up their consent (*chanda*). Why is this?
Because many bhikṣus speak what is not the Dharma, this is called "the entire Saṃgha taking the voting sticks.

If the assembly of monks, along with the great elders and senior theras, can resolve this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, it is then called "resolving by means of one *vinaya*," namely, the *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*).
Regarding the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence): it is the presence of the Saṃgha, the presence of the person, and the presence of the *vinaya*.
The presence of the Saṃgha is as explained above; the presence of the person and the presence of the *vinaya* are also as explained above.
"If the Saṃgha and the elders, while reciting the Prātimokṣa, are unable to settle this matter, it should be returned to the official who transmits the proceedings.
That official shall take up the matter and resolve it on the path, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching."

If the person conveying the matter is able, while on the way, to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, this is called settling by means of a single *vinaya*.
This refers to the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence). *Saṃmukha-vinaya* is as explained above.

"If the person conveying the matter is unable to resolve it in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, then that bhikṣu, while on his way, may hear that in a certain monastery there are three bhikṣus, or two, or one bhikṣu, who are able to uphold the Sūtras, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkās, and who are honored and respected by the fourfold assembly."
The messenger should go to that dwelling place and say to one bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."

This matter arises from such and such causes and conditions; it cannot be settled by the *talaṭṭha* (the one who has committed the offense), nor can it be settled by the Saṃgha, nor can it be settled by the *pūrva-āvartaka-gaura*, nor can it be settled by the *paścima-āvartaka-gaura*. It cannot be settled by the *pūrva-āvartaka-gaura* returning, nor can it be settled by the Saṃgha returning. It cannot be settled by the Saṃgha of the neighboring residence (*upāśraya*), nor can it be settled by the *pūrva-āvartaka-gaura*, nor can it be settled by the *paścima-āvartaka-gaura*, nor can it be settled by the *pūrva-āvartaka-gaura* returning, nor can it be settled by the Saṃgha of the neighboring residence returning. It cannot be settled during the transmission of the matter through the path of men, nor can it be settled by a great assembly of monks and elders who know how to recite the *Prātimokṣa*, nor can it be settled by the person transmitting the matter while on the road.
Even three or two bhikṣus—those who can uphold the Sūtras, those who uphold the Vinaya, and those who uphold the Mātṛkā, and who are revered by the fourfold assembly—are unable to sever it.
"Venerable sirs, take up this matter; settle it according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha's teaching.
Then that bhikṣu who is honored and respected by the fourfold assembly should speak thus:
"It is not possible for two people to argue with each other and both be victorious; herein, one must necessarily be the winner and the other the loser."
If one speaks in such a manner, they are called one who speaks according to the Dharma; if one does not speak in such a manner, they are called one who speaks what is not the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu, after a matter has been settled according to the Dharma, should initiate it again, it is a pāyattika.
If he merely censures [the settlement], it is a duṣkṛta.
There are ten kinds of legal voting sticks and ten kinds of illegal voting sticks.

The ten ways of casting ballots improperly are: casting a ballot for a trivial matter; casting a ballot for a matter that has already passed; casting a ballot without consulting the elders; casting a ballot in an illegal manner; casting a ballot by a separate assembly; casting a ballot in an illegal manner by a separate assembly; using this ballot-casting with the intent to cause many to act illegally; using this ballot-casting which will result in many acting illegally; using this ballot-casting with the intent to break the harmonious Saṃgha; and using this ballot-casting which will result in breaking the harmonious Saṃgha.
He asked: "What is meant by 'not casting the voting tally for a minor matter'?
He replied:
"One does not cast voting tickets for matters that can be confessed.
As for casting voting tickets for matters already past, such matters proceed from this residence to that residence.

One who casts voting tickets without consulting the elders—does he not go to consult those bhikṣus who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās, asking what is wholesome and what is unwholesome?"
What is blameworthy and what is blameless?
What is white and what is black?
What brings benefit in this life and what brings benefit in future lives?
What constitutes a procedure that guides and benefits people, being wholesome rather than unwholesome?
"Casting ballots contrary to the Dharma" means casting ballots in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma.
"Casting ballots apart from the assembly" means casting ballots in a separate location within the same boundary (*sīmā*).
"Performing a vote by an illegal separate assembly" means performing a vote in a separate location within the same boundary (*sīmā*) in a manner that is not according to the Dharma.
One employs this voting procedure with the intent to cause many to act illegally; that is, the bhikṣu first forms the intention:
"By means of this voting, I shall cause many to speak what is not in accordance with the Dharma."
Thinking that by casting these ballots many bhikṣus will act contrary to the Dharma, that bhikṣu first forms this intention:
"By casting these ballots, many will speak what is contrary to the Dharma."
Regarding one who uses these voting tallies with the intent to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, that bhikṣu first forms the intention:
"I shall use these voting tallies to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha.
Regarding one who uses these voting tallies and is about to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, that bhikṣu first forms the intention:
"I shall cast the voting tally to break the harmonious Saṃgha. These are called the ten kinds of unlawful casting of the voting tally.

"The ten kinds of lawful casting of the voting tally are: casting the tally for a minor matter; casting the tally for a matter that has not yet been settled; casting the tally after consulting with the elders; casting the tally lawfully; casting the tally with a harmonious assembly; casting the tally with a harmonious assembly in accordance with the Dharma; casting the tally with the intention that those acting lawfully shall be numerous; casting the tally with the expectation that those acting lawfully shall be numerous; casting the tally with the intention to bring about harmony in the Saṃgha; and casting the tally with the expectation that the Saṃgha shall be brought into harmony."
Question:
"What is meant by 'casting lots on account of a minor matter'? Answer:
"Regarding the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*) for matters that may be confessed:
as for the distribution of voting sticks for matters not yet concluded, this matter has remained in this residence and has not yet reached that residence.
When asking the elders who distribute the voting sticks, there are bhikṣus who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā; one should go to them frequently to consult them."
What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
What is blameworthy and what is blameless?
What is white and what is black?
What is benefit in this life?
What is benefit in future lives?
What is the conduct that leads people toward benefit—what is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
"Acting according to the Dharma when casting lots" means acting in a manner that does not violate the Dharma when casting lots.
"The assembly acting in harmony when casting lots" means that the monks within the same boundary act together in unison in one place when casting lots.

Regarding the distribution of voting tallies (*śalākā*) by a harmonious assembly in accordance with the Dharma: it means that the assembly within the same boundary gathers in one place to distribute the tallies in accordance with the Dharma.
The purpose of using these tallies is to ensure that many act in accordance with the Dharma; thus, the bhikṣu first forms this intention:
"By means of this distribution of tallies, may many speak in accordance with the Dharma."
Thinking, "By means of this distribution of voting tickets (*śalākā*), there will likely be many monks who act in accordance with the Dharma," that monk first forms the intention:
"By means of this distribution of voting tickets, there will likely be many monks who speak in accordance with the Dharma."
Regarding one who uses this distribution of voting-slips (śalākā) with the intent to bring the Saṃgha into harmony, that bhikṣu first forms the intention:
"I shall use this distribution of voting-slips to cause the Saṃgha to be harmonious.
Regarding one who uses this distribution of voting-slips intending that the Saṃgha shall be brought into harmony, that bhikṣu first forms the intention:
"By using these voting sticks, the Saṃgha shall be brought into harmony;
this is called the tenth method of voting in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding matters of the Saṃgha, they may be entrusted to the Saṃgha, or to three persons, two persons, or one person."
Regarding monastic affairs (*saṃghakaraṇīya*): the Saṃgha should undertake monastic affairs;
three persons, two persons, or even one person may undertake them.
The Saṃgha should terminate monastic affairs; three persons, two persons, or even one person may terminate them.
This is called the settling of a dispute concerning a formal matter by means of two *vinayas*.
"How is a dispute concerning a groundless matter settled by means of four *vinayas*?

Namely: settlement through presence and through recollection; or settlement through presence and through non-delusion; or settlement through presence and through searching for the truth regarding the offense."
What is meant by cessation through presence and cessation through recollection?
For example, the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta was slandered by the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā with groundless charges of a pārājika offense.
For this reason, whether it be the Saṃgha, or three persons, two persons, or one person, they should repeatedly speak of this matter to cause him to remember.
This Bhikṣu Dabba requested from the Saṃgha the *bhiṣaṇīya* (act of recollection) according to the Vinaya.
The Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.

Regarding the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of others): when the person to whom the *smṛtivinaya* is granted and the one who has received the *smṛtivinaya* are brought together in one place, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching—this is called the settlement through both the *sammukhavinaya* and the *smṛtivinaya*.
What is meant by "manifesting before one" and "the cessation of non-delusion"?
For example, the bhikṣu Śreṇika had a deranged and inverted mind; he committed various evils, impure deeds, and acts contrary to the Path—things that a renunciant ought not to do.
This person shall regain their original mind; for this reason, whether it be a Saṃgha, or three people, two people, or one person, they should repeatedly speak to them so that they may remember.

This bhikṣu Śreṇika requested the *amūḍhavinaya* from the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha granted him the *amūḍhavinaya*, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
Among these, what is the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence)?

When one who has been granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for the non-deluded) and those who have attained the *amūḍha-vinaya* come together in one place, acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching—this is called the settlement through the *saṃmukha-vinaya* and the *amūḍha-vinaya*.
What is the *pratyakṣa* (face-to-face) and *yadbhūya-viniścaya* (settling according to what has been found)?

It is as in the case of the Śākya bhikṣu Hastiśīrṣa, who, being without shame or remorse, committed an offense regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected; he first admitted his transgression but later claimed he had not done it.
The Saṃgha truly seeks the *bhikṣuṇī* for this person in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the *vinaya*, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
Among these, what is the *sammukha-vinaya* (the presence of the assembly)?

When those who seek the *yathābhūta-vinaya* (the discipline of seeking the truth) and those who have attained the *yathābhūta-vinaya* are brought together in one place, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, this is called the settlement through *saṃmukha-vinaya* (presence) and *yathābhūta-vinaya*.
This is called settling a groundless matter by means of the four *vinayas*: namely, presence and recollection; presence and non-delusion; and presence and searching for the truth.
Question:
"How is it that the matter of an offense is settled by means of the three methods for settling disputes? Answer:
"What are called *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) and *pratijñākāraka* (by confession), and *sammukhavinaya* and *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass)?
What is *sammukhavinaya* and *pratijñākāraka*?
It is when a bhikṣu, whether another bhikṣu has accused him of an offense or not, or has caused him to remember it or not, confesses of his own accord: [I have committed such-and-such an offense]."
"I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This bhikṣu requests parivāsa from the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, grants him parivāsa.
In this context, what is meant by "in the presence of"?

It means that one who is undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) and those who have completed their *parivāsa* are united in one place, acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
The offender has entered into a separate residence from that person; in this case, how can it be called a confession in accordance with the Dharma?
For example, if a bhikṣu—whether another bhikṣu has accused him of an offense or not, or whether he has been made to remember it or not—declares of himself:
"I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
"He should be granted the *mānāpya* (probation), the re-initiation of the original term (*mūlāpakarṣa*), and the rehabilitation from the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).

That bhikṣu requests from the Saṃgha the formal acts (*karmas*) for the *mānāpya*, the re-initiation of the original term, and the rehabilitation from the offense; the Saṃgha then performs the act of rehabilitation according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Buddha’s teaching."
In what manner is this matter manifested and granted?

It is when the person being cleared of the offense and the one who grants the clearing of the offense come together in one place, acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
When the author of the offense has cleared that bhikṣu of his transgression, how can this further be called a "confession in accordance with the Dharma"?
For example, whether another person accuses him of an offense or does not accuse him, whether he is made to remember it or is not made to remember it, he himself declares:
"I have committed an offense that requires confession."

Regarding those present therein: they shall act together with the person confessing their transgression and the person presiding over the confession in one place, acting in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching.
"The author and the act may be confessed; this is called the settlement through *saṃmukhavinaya* (presence before the assembly) and *pratijñāvinaya* (confession by one's own word).
He asked again:
"What is the settlement through *saṃmukhavinaya* and *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass)?"
“Suppose, in a certain residence, various bhikṣus delight in quarreling and speaking harsh words to one another.
These bhikṣus, having come together in harmony, reflect thus:
‘We have greatly declined and lost our gains; we have gone forth out of faith within the Buddha’s Dharma, yet now we engage in harsh speech and mutual reproach.’”
"If we were to seek the root of this matter, then that which has not yet arisen would arise, and that which has already arisen could not be extinguished.
At this point, one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
