"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent: this matter shall be settled by the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) method.
This is called the formal motion (*jñapti*).

Immediately, these bhikṣus should divide themselves into two groups. Within these, if there is an elder, or one next in seniority, or one who is well-versed in the general meaning of the Prātimokṣa, or one who knows the Prātimokṣa itself, they should say to one of these groups:
"We have suffered a great loss and not gained anything; we have met with great decline and no benefit; it is a great evil and unwholesome.
Out of faith, we left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma, yet now we delight in quarreling and speaking ill of one another."
If we were to seek the root of this matter, there would be matters arising within the Saṃgha that have not yet arisen, and matters already arisen that could not be extinguished.

Now, you must all humble yourselves before us; regarding the offenses we have committed—excluding those of *sthūlātyaya* and those associated with laypeople—you must now confess and repent for these matters in our presence, without concealment.
If not even one bhikṣu among them speaks [in protest], they should go to where the second group of the assembly is; there, an elder or senior monk should say:
"We have suffered a great loss and not a gain, a great decline and not a benefit, a great evil and what is unwholesome."
Out of faith, we have left the household life to seek the Way within the Buddha-dharma, yet now we delight in quarreling and speaking against one another.
If we were to seek the root of this matter, then disputes not yet arisen within the Saṃgha would arise, and those already arisen could not be extinguished.

Now you all should humble yourselves before us; regarding the offenses we have committed—excluding those of *sthūlātyaya* and those associated with laypeople—we shall now, for our own sake and for the sake of others, openly confess and repent before you without concealment.
The bhikṣus said,
"Do you see your own fault?
He replied:
"I see my fault.
"Repent according to the Dharma; do not commit it again.
The second group of the assembly should also speak in this manner.
This is called the *tṛṇastāraka-vinaya*.
In this context, what is meant by "being present"?

It refers to being assembled in one place with the person who spreads the grass and those who receive the spreading of the grass; acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching; and the performer performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of spreading the grass—this is called "presence" and the "extinction through spreading the grass."
This is called the matter of an offense extinguished by three *vinayas*, namely: presence (*sammukha*), confession (*pratijñā*), and the spreading of grass (*tṛṇa-prastāraka*).
Question:
"Regarding the matters of constant practice, why are they extinguished by the single *vinaya* of presence?"

“With those who have been authorized to perform the formal motion (*jñapti*), one should assemble in one place with those authorized to perform the motion, and in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, perform the *jñapti-ekakarma*, the *jñapti-dvitīyakarma*, and the *jñapti-caturthakarma*; as well as the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts, the *pravāraṇā*, the observance of the *varṣā* retreat, and the establishment of the fourteen types of formal acts.”

When one who performs the *kamma* and those who receive the *kamma* assemble in one place to act in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, this is called the "procedure for constant practice" which employs a single *vinaya*, namely, the *sammukhā-vinaya* (the presence of the assembly).
The eighth section on legal matters concerning disputes among the eight categories of dharma is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 35.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 36. First part of the sixth recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
Sixth Recitation, Section 11: Miscellaneous Recitations, Part 1, Story of Devadatta, First in the Miscellaneous Recitations.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, Devadatta had a pure heart of faith and devotion toward the Buddha’s Dharma. He donned ornaments worth three hundred thousand gold coins and went forth into homelessness. He rode upon a well-trained elephant worth one hundred thousand gold coins; this elephant was further adorned with golden nets and other trappings, also worth one hundred thousand gold coins.
The robes worn by Devadatta were also worth one hundred thousand gold coins.

Having left the household life to become a bhikṣu, Devadatta practiced with a virtuous mind for twelve years; he read the scriptures, recited them, inquired about doubts, received the Dharma, and practiced seated meditation, during which time he thoroughly read and recited all the teachings spoken by the Buddha.

At that time, the bhikṣus possessed great supernormal powers and influence. Because of the Jambū tree, the land was named Jambudvīpa; these bhikṣus would take fruit from this Jambū tree and return to eat it.
Not far from the Jambū tree, there were groves of harītakī, āmalaka, and bhallātaka trees; they would take these various fruits and return to their dwellings to eat them.
From Uttarakuru, they would take naturally grown non-glutinous rice and return to eat it.
He took food from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and returned to eat it;
he manifested various supernatural powers in the east, west, south, and north.
Having seen this, Devadatta immediately conceived a greedy mind and thought to himself:
"When shall I be able to possess great supernormal powers?
[I wish that] because it is named Jambū after the Jambū tree, I might take fruit from this Jambū tree and eat it;
or, not far from the Jambū tree, there are groves of harītakī, āmalaka, and vibhītaka trees, from which I might take these various fruits and eat them where I dwell."
He took naturally grown non-glutinous rice from Uttarakuru and returned to eat it;
he took *sudhā* food from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and returned to eat it;
and he manifested various supernormal powers in the east, west, south, and north.
"What if I were now to go to the Buddha's dwelling and inquire about the path of supernatural powers?
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and inquired about the path of supernatural powers.
The Buddha already knew that this person would commit evil deeds within this Dharma; therefore, he did not speak, saying:
"Devadatta, stop!
What use have you for these supernatural powers?"
"You should contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

When Devadatta heard these words, he could not endure them nor did he find them pleasing; instead, his mind was solely intent upon the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*). He thought to himself:

"Śāriputra has been declared by the Buddha to be the foremost among all the wise disciples. I shall go to Śāriputra and inquire about the methods of supernatural faculties; he will surely explain them to me."
Having thought this, he immediately went to inquire about the way of supernatural powers.
Śāriputra also knew beforehand that this man would commit evil deeds within this Dharma; therefore, he did not speak of it, but said:
"Devadatta, stop! Do not do so!"
"What use is this supernatural power?
You should contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
When Devadatta heard these words, he could not endure them nor did he find them pleasing; instead, he focused his mind solely on supernatural powers and thought to himself:

“Maudgalyāyana was declared by the Buddha in his foremost sutra to be the most supreme and preeminent among the disciples in the way of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). I shall go to him and inquire about the way of supernormal powers; he will surely explain it to me.”
Having thought this, he immediately went to inquire about the way of supernatural powers.
Maudgalyāyana already knew that this man would commit evil deeds within this Dharma; therefore, he did not speak of them, but said:
"Devadatta, you must stop!"
"What use is there for the way of supernatural powers?
You should contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Having heard this, Devadatta could not endure it nor did he find joy in it; instead, he focused his mind single-mindedly on the way of supernatural powers.
In this manner, they passed the word down until it reached at least one person; since the assembly of great disciples numbered less than five hundred, he did not preach for them.
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"Ānanda is my younger brother. In the Buddha’s foremost sūtra, it was said that among all the many learned disciples, Ānanda is the most excellent and supreme."
"Why should I not go to him and ask about the way of supernatural powers?
He shall explain it to me.
Having thought thus, he immediately went to him and asked about the way of supernatural powers.

Because Ānanda had not yet abandoned desire, he did not know the matters of the past and future; thus, by means of his wisdom derived from extensive learning, he spoke of the path of supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
Having received the methods for supernatural powers, Devadatta diligently practiced them among mountains, forests, wildernesses, ravines, and valleys.
Through diligent cultivation, he attained the four mundane dhyānas; based on these four dhyānas, he gave rise to supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*).
Having given rise to supernormal powers, because of the Jambu tree, it was named Jambudvīpa; from that Jambu tree, he took fruit and returned to eat it.
Not far from the Jambu tree, there were great groves of harītakī, āmalaka, and vibhītaka; he took fruit from these various trees and returned to his dwelling to eat them.
From Uttarakuru, he took naturally grown non-glutinous rice and ate it;
from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he took the food of the Sudharmā Hall and ate it;
and in the east, west, south, and north, he manifested various supernatural powers.
Devadatta had long harbored an evil mind toward the Buddha, thinking to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama is not superior to me in lineage.
He is of the Gautama clan, born into the Śākya family; I too am of the Gautama clan, born into the Śākya family."
"Those who offer many gifts with pure hearts do so because of the power of my supernormal abilities (*ṛddhibala*).
In which family shall I employ my supernormal abilities to gather them in, so that many people will follow me?"
He thought to himself:
"King Bimbisāra is the most powerful in the kingdom, and he is a disciple of the Buddha who has reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Even if I were to employ my supernatural powers to drag him away, I would ultimately never succeed."
Devadatta had long been proficient in various secular texts concerning the stars and constellations, the physiognomy of men for good or ill fortune, and the anomalous signs of heaven and earth.
Upon seeing the prince of King Bimbisāra, Ajātaśatru, his physical marks were clearly manifest;
Devadatta thought: "I shall win him over through my supernormal powers; he will certainly become my patron."
"For this reason, many people follow him.

Having thought thus, he transformed his body into a precious elephant and, at the house of Prince Ajātaśatru, entered through a gate and exited through a non-gate, or entered through a non-gate and exited through a gate; manifesting such signs, he intended to make it known that this was Devadatta.

He further transformed his body into a precious horse, entering through a non-gate and exiting through a gate, or entering through a gate and exiting through a non-gate, manifesting such signs in order to make it known that this was Devadatta.
Again, a jeweled garland appeared, emerging from the crown prince’s knees.
At that time, the crown prince took the garland and tied it upon his forehead, manifesting this sign in order to make it known that this was Devadatta.
He further manifested as a handsome young child, adorned with necklaces of gold and jewels, rolling back and forth upon the crown prince’s lap.
The prince cooed and embraced him, playing with him and spitting into his mouth; he displayed such signs in order to make it known that this was Devadatta.

By means of this supernatural power, he drew the heart of Prince Ajātaśatru toward himself, causing him to give rise to evil and false views, namely that Devadatta’s supernatural power surpassed that of the Buddha. Consequently, the prince conceived a heart of affection and reverence, making offerings of robes, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; even daily, he sent five hundred cauldrons of food and drink and five hundred chariots surrounding him, coming to Devadatta’s location to personally serve the food with his own hands.

At that time, before midday, the bhikṣus dressed themselves, took their bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. They heard that Prince Ajātaśatru was providing such offerings for Devadatta—robes, bedding, and medicinal requisites—and that every day he sent five hundred cauldrons of food and drink, surrounded by five hundred chariots, going in person to Devadatta’s residence to serve the meal with his own hands, while Devadatta and his five hundred disciples received these offerings.
Having heard this, after his meal he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Today, having put on my robes and taken up my bowl, I entered the city to beg for food. I heard that Prince Ajātaśatru has made such offerings to Devadatta—robes, bedding, and medicinal requisites—and sends five hundred cauldrons of food and drink every day, surrounded by five hundred chariots. He goes in person to Devadatta’s place and serves the food with his own hands; Devadatta, together with five hundred bhikṣus, receives these offerings.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“Do not covet the offerings of Devadatta. Why is this?
This is because Devadatta’s receiving of offerings leads to his own ruin.
It is like the bamboo that dies when it bears fruit, or the plantain tree which likewise perishes upon fruition, or like the mule that dies when it becomes pregnant.
"The same applies to Devadatta’s receiving of offerings; it serves only to bring about his own ruin.
It is like the bamboo or the reed, which dies because of its fruit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke these verses:
“The plantain perishes because of its fruit; the same is true for bamboo and reeds.
The mule dies because of pregnancy;
the petty man is ruined by receiving support.”
"This is likewise so.
You foolish Devadatta!
For as long as you receive such gains and offerings, for that same duration you shall endure various sufferings throughout the long night, because you have been born in an evil realm."
He said to the bhikṣus:
“Suppose a strong man were to break the nose of a vicious dog; what do you think?
Would that dog become even more vicious?”
He replied,
“It is indeed evil,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

"The foolish Devadatta is just like this; for as long as he receives such offerings, for that same length of time he will suffer affliction through the long night, because he will be reborn in evil realms."
At that time, Devadatta’s offerings increased even further; his mind became shrouded by greed for these offerings, and he conceived such an evil thought:
"If the Buddha now abandons the Saṃgha, I shall lead the assembly of monks."
When he gave rise to such a thought, he lost his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was staying in the Kālīṅga Valley in the country of Ceti. There was a bhikṣu named Gavāṃpati-Kauśilya, who was the disciple of the Elder Maudgalyāyana.
This bhikṣu abandoned the five desires and cultivated the four brahma-vihāras; at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

When the Brahmā god Kāpuṭa saw that Devadatta had fallen away from his supernormal powers, having seen this, he vanished from the Brahma world and appeared before Maudgalyāyana in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm.
Rising from his meditative concentration, he addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Do you know? Devadatta has lost his supernatural powers. It was well that you went to the Buddha's presence and spoke of this; you should report this matter to the Buddha."
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Why do I not enter meditative concentration to observe Devadatta’s mind?

He immediately entered concentration and observed Devadatta’s mind; seeing that he had lost his supernormal powers, he rose from concentration and remained silent, accepting the words of the Brahmā God Kāpuṭa.
At that time, Brahmā, knowing that Maudgalyāyana had accepted by remaining silent, prostrated with his head at [Maudgalyāyana’s] feet, circumambulated him to the right, and vanished.

Having accepted the invitation of Brahmā, Maudgalyāyana immediately entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), vanished from the valley of Kālaṅgara in the kingdom of Caitya, and appeared in Rājagṛha, not far from the Buddha.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana arose from his meditative concentration and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"As the Brahmā god Kāmadhara has said, Devadatta has indeed lost his supernatural powers.
The Buddha said,
"Did you not previously know that Devadatta’s mind was as [the Brahmā] Kāmadhara had spoken?"
While the Buddha was speaking these words with Maudgalyāyana, Devadatta immediately arrived together with four disciples.
Seeing Devadatta approaching from afar, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Do not say anything; this foolish man comes here to manifest his own deeds."
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Why do I not enter meditative concentration right here on this seat so that Devadatta cannot see me?
He immediately entered concentration on that very seat, and Devadatta could no longer see him.
Devadatta went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and together with his four disciples, withdrew to sit to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you are now advanced in years and decrepit; you may entrust the community of monks to me, while the Buddha alone enjoys the bliss of the present life."
"Make the Saṃgha belong to me; I shall lead them.

The Buddha said, "Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana possess great wisdom and supernormal powers, yet even the Buddha did not entrust the Saṃgha to them; how much less should he entrust it to you—a fool who eats spittle, a dead man!"
At that time, when Devadatta heard the Buddha call him by such names as "foolish person who eats spittle" and "dead man," he became greatly incensed and sought to destroy the World-Honored One.
With his eyebrows hanging down in sorrow and dejection, he lowered his head and remained silent without speaking; having reflected thus, he immediately rose and departed, thinking to himself:
"The Buddha praises only Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, making them great, while disparaging us and making us seem lowly and insignificant."
This was the first time Devadatta gave rise to a heart of resentment toward the Buddha, as well as toward Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the other great disciples.
At that time, Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him with a fan. The Buddha looked back and said to Ānanda:
"Have all the bhikṣus residing in Rājagṛha assemble in the lecture hall; once they have assembled, inform me."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately ordered all the bhikṣus residing in Rājagṛha to assemble in the lecture hall. Once they had assembled, he went to inform the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! [The assembly has gathered.]”
"The bhikṣus of Rājagṛha have already gathered in the lecture hall; the Buddha himself knows the proper time.
The Buddha then took his attendant Ānanda and went to the lecture hall, where he sat upon a prepared seat in the midst of the assembly of monks and instructed the bhikṣus:
"There are five kinds of teachers in the world."
What are the five?

First, there is a teacher who does not maintain pure precepts, yet claims that his observance of the precepts is pure. Because his disciples live together with him, they know that the teacher does not maintain the precepts and is impure, even though he claims his observance of the precepts is pure.
"If we were to speak of our teacher as being real [in the ultimate sense], he might not be pleased.
If our teacher is not pleased, how could we possibly speak?
It is because we have received the teacher's grace that we have obtained robes, bedding, medicinal requisites, and food and drink."
"If you, Master, would truly look after us, you should know for yourself.

In this way, the teacher protects and upholds the precepts for the sake of the disciples, and the teacher likewise seeks protection and the upholding of the precepts from the disciples; such a person is the first teacher in the world.

As for the second teacher, he maintains an impure livelihood yet claims to have a pure livelihood. Because his disciples live together with him, they know that the teacher maintains an impure livelihood yet claims to have a pure livelihood.
[They think: "If we were to speak of the teacher's reality as it truly is, he might become displeased."
"If the teacher is not pleased, how should we speak?
It is because we rely upon the teacher that we receive robes, bedding, medicine, and food and drink.
If the teacher has good regard for us, he will naturally perceive it himself."

A teacher such as this protects and safeguards the pure livelihood of his disciples, and this teacher also seeks protection and safeguarding of his pure livelihood from his disciples; this is called the second kind of teacher in the world.

Regarding the third teacher: his knowledge and vision are not pure, yet he claims that his knowledge and vision are pure; because his disciples live together with him, they know that the teacher’s knowledge and vision are not pure, even though he claims they are pure.
"If we were to speak of our teacher as being real, he might become displeased.
If our teacher is displeased, how could we possibly speak?
It is because we have relied upon our teacher that we have obtained robes, bedding, medicinal requisites, and food and drink."
"If you, Master, would truly look after us, you should naturally perceive it for yourself.

A teacher such as this provides protection for his disciples' knowledge and vision, and he himself also seeks protection for his knowledge and vision from his disciples; this is called the third kind of teacher in the world.

As for the fourth teacher: he is one who does not know the proper course of action but claims to know it. Because his disciples live together with him, they come to know that the teacher does not know the proper course of action but claims to know it.
"If I were to speak of the Teacher as being real, he might become displeased.
If the Teacher were displeased, how could we speak?

It is because we have received favor from the Teacher that we obtain robes, bedding, medicinal requisites, and food and drink; if the Teacher looks after us with kindness, he will surely perceive it himself."

A teacher such as this provides protection and performs services of benefit for his disciples; likewise, he also seeks protection and services of benefit from his disciples. This is called the fourth kind of teacher in the world.

Regarding the fifth teacher: he does not teach the Dharma of purity, yet claims to teach the Dharma of purity; because his disciples live together with him, they come to know that the teacher does not teach the Dharma of purity, even though he claims to teach the Dharma of purity.
"If we were to speak of our teacher as being real [in the ultimate sense], he might become displeased.
If our teacher becomes displeased, how could we possibly speak?
It is because we have received the teacher's grace that we have obtained robes, bedding, medicinal requisites, and food and drink."
"If you, Master, would look after us, we ourselves shall surely come to realize it.

A teacher such as this provides protection for his disciples by teaching the Dharma of purity, and he himself also seeks protection from his disciples by teaching the Dharma of purity; this is called the fifth kind of teacher in the world.
The Buddha said:
“The Tathāgata maintains pure precepts and also says of himself, ‘I maintain pure precepts.
The disciples do not conceal the Tathāgata’s pure maintenance of precepts, nor does the Tathāgata seek for his disciples to conceal his pure maintenance of precepts.”
The Tathāgata is one of pure livelihood; he himself declares, "I am of pure livelihood.
His disciples do not need to protect the Tathāgata’s purity of livelihood, nor does the Tathāgata seek for his disciples to protect his purity of livelihood.
The Tathāgata possesses pure knowledge and vision, and he himself declares, "My knowledge and vision are pure.
His disciples do not seek to conceal or protect the Tathāgata’s purity of knowledge and vision, nor does the Tathāgata seek for his disciples to conceal or protect his purity of knowledge and vision.
The Tathāgata is one who speaks well; he himself declares, "I am one who speaks well.
His disciples do not conceal the Tathāgata’s skillful speech, nor does the Tathāgata seek for his disciples to conceal his skillful speech.
The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of purity, declaring himself, "I teach the Dharma of purity.
His disciples do not seek to shield the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma of purity, nor does the Tathāgata seek for his disciples to shield his teaching of the Dharma of purity.
The Buddha said, “The Tathāgata truly possesses this Dharma; why do you not speak it according to reality?
A Buddha does not conform to others, nor is he a person of weak speech; for example, when a potter holds a raw clay jar, he does not dare to grasp it too hastily.”
The Tathāgata speaks words of truth, words of clarity, and words of subduing; those who are steadfast shall remain, while those who are not steadfast shall depart.
You all should endure and accept the Tathāgata’s words of Dharma.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta desired to break the harmony of the Saṃgha; he adopted the means for breaking the Saṃgha and, out of a jealous mind and through deliberate artifice, formed this thought:
"I alone cannot succeed in breaking the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroying his turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
Devadatta had four disciples who were his companions:
first, Kokālika; second, Khaṇḍadravya; third, Kaṭamorakatiṣya; and fourth, Samudradatta.
Having approached these four men, he said to them:
"I and you shall together break the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroy his turning of the Wheel of Dharma; thus we shall obtain such fame and renown."
"We can break apart the Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama, destroy his turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and cause its disintegration.
Those four men said to Devadatta:
"The disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama possess great wisdom and great supernormal powers; they have attained the divine eye and the knowledge of others' minds."
"This man knows that we wish to break the harmonious Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroy his turning of the Wheel of Dharma; how then can we succeed in breaking it?
Devadatta said to the four men:

"The śramaṇa Gautama has young disciples who have newly entered his teaching and left the household life not long ago. We should go to them and entice them with five practices, saying to those bhikṣus:"

"For as long as life lasts, you shall accept and wear the patched robe; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of begging for food; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of eating only one meal a day; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of sitting in the open air; for as long as life lasts, you shall accept the practice of abstaining from meat."
"If a bhikṣu receives these five dharmas, he will quickly attain nirvāṇa.
If there are elder or senior bhikṣus who are learned and well-informed, who have long practiced the holy life and attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma, one should say to them:
"The Buddha is now aged and decrepit; he delights in solitude and enjoys the bliss of the present dharma. Whatever you require, I shall provide for you."
"By such means as these, we shall be able to break the Saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama and destroy his turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
The four bhikṣus replied, "So be it."

Devadatta! Later, Devadatta went to where the young bhikṣus were and enticed them with five practices, saying to the bhikṣus: "For as long as life lasts, you shall observe the practice of wearing rag-robes;

for as long as life lasts, you shall observe the practice of begging for food; for as long as life lasts, you shall observe the practice of eating only one meal a day; for as long as life lasts, you shall observe the practice of sitting in the open air; for as long as life lasts, you shall observe the practice of abstaining from meat."
"If you practice these five dharmas, you will swiftly attain nirvāṇa.
He then spoke again to the elder bhikṣus and senior monks:
"The Buddha is now aged and his years are in decline; he delights in solitude and enjoys the happiness of the present dharma. Whatever you require, I shall provide for you."

At that time, Devadatta taught what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma; he taught what is not the Vinaya as the Vinaya, and what is the Vinaya as not the Vinaya; he taught what is not an offense as an offense, and what is an offense as not an offense; he taught what is light as heavy, and what is heavy as light; he taught what has a remainder as having no remainder, and what has no remainder as having a remainder; he taught what is a constant practice as not a constant practice, and what is not a constant practice as a constant practice; he taught what is not a teaching as a teaching, and what is a teaching as not a teaching.

At that time, having seen that Devadatta intended to split the harmonious Saṃgha and destroy the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

This Devadatta now wishes to break the harmonious Saṃgha; he upholds the causes and conditions for breaking the Saṃgha. This person speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, and what is Dharma as not Dharma; he speaks what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, and what is Vinaya as not Vinaya; he speaks what is not an offense as an offense, and what is an offense as not an offense; he speaks what is light as heavy, and what is heavy as light; he speaks what has a remainder as having no remainder, and what has no remainder as having a remainder; he speaks what is a constant practice as not a constant practice, and what is not a constant practice as a constant practice; he speaks what is not a teaching as a teaching, and what is a teaching as not a teaching.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus,
"You should reprove Devadatta and cause him to abandon this matter of creating a schism in the Saṃgha.
Having received the Buddha’s words, those bhikṣus went to where Devadatta was and said to him:
"Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not uphold matters that lead to a schism in the Saṃgha. You should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha.
Those who are in harmony with the Saṃgha live in joy and without contention, with a single mind and a single training, like water and milk mixed together, attaining a state of peaceful dwelling."
"You should abandon this matter of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
At that time, Devadatta did not abandon this matter.
Then Devadatta’s four companions rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"Do not speak of this matter concerning Devadatta. Why is this?
This person teaches the Dharma and teaches the Vinaya; what this person says is our own intention."
"It is known that he speaks what is right, not what is wrong; all that this man says is what we desire, delight in, and accept.

Thus the bhikṣus admonished Devadatta twice and thrice, but they were unable to make him abandon his evil and heterodox views. They then rose from their seats, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We have already issued a command, yet Devadatta has not abandoned his evil and heterodox ways.
His four companions further spoke thus:
'You must not speak of this matter concerning Devadatta.'"
Why is this? Because when these people preach the Dharma and the Vinaya, everything they say accords with our own intentions;
we know that they speak what is correct and not what is incorrect, for everything they say is precisely what we desire, delight in, and accept.
"Although the bhikṣus have admonished him twice and thrice, he does not relinquish this matter.
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:

"If the foolish Devadatta and his four companions were to break my harmonious Saṃgha and destroy the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, I shall personally admonish Devadatta and cause him to relinquish this matter."
Having formed this thought, the Buddha immediately exhorted Devadatta himself:
"Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not take up the causes and conditions for a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead remain in harmony with the Saṃgha."
Those who live in harmony with the Saṃgha rejoice without contention; being of one mind and one training, like water mixed with milk, they dwell in peace and happiness.

You must not declare what is not Dharma to be Dharma, or declare Dharma to be non-Dharma; do not declare what is not Vinaya to be Vinaya, or declare Vinaya to be non-Vinaya; do not declare what is not an offense to be an offense, or declare an offense to be no offense; do not declare what is light to be heavy, or what is heavy to be light; do not declare what is with remainder to be without remainder, or what is without remainder to be with remainder; do not declare what is a customary practice to be a non-customary practice, or what is a non-customary practice to be a customary practice; do not declare what is not a teaching to be a teaching, or a teaching to be what is not a teaching. You should abandon these matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s oral instruction, Devadatta temporarily desisted from this matter.

While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, Prince Ajātaśatru and all his ministers and generals placed their faith and respect in Devadatta; these people assisted the bhikṣu Devadatta by making offerings of food before and after meals, as well as *tambula*.

To those young bhikṣus who had been ordained for not long, Devadatta used large bowls, small bowls, large and small metal canteens, robe-hooks, meditation weights, cords and belts, spoons and ladles, bowl-rests, fans and parasols, leather sandals, and whatever other items the bhikṣus required, all of which he employed to deceive and entice them.

Devadatta, surrounded by a respectful retinue of one hundred, or two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred bhikṣus, entered the city of Rājagṛha and separately received excellent offerings, including meals before and after eating, as well as *tambūla*.

There were certain senior elder bhikṣus who had attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma and long cultivated the holy life. When these bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms, they might receive stale cold rice or receive nothing at all; or they might receive foul-smelling parched grain or receive nothing at all. Thus, with such coarse food, they might be either full or not full.
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and censured it for various reasons:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu if he is surrounded by a respectful retinue of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred bhikṣus, and separately receives offerings of morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambula*?"

Those elder bhikṣus who are senior, who have tasted the flavor of the Buddha-dharma and long practiced the holy life—when these bhikṣus enter the city to beg for food, do they receive stale cold rice, or fail to receive any; or do they receive foul-smelling flour, or fail to receive any; and thus, with such coarse food, are they satisfied or not?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked him intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣu who, surrounded by a respectful retinue of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred bhikṣus, separately accepts offerings of morning meals, afternoon meals, and *tambala*?"

The elder bhikṣus, who have long cultivated the holy life and attained the flavor of the Buddha-dharma—when these bhikṣus enter the city to beg for alms, do they receive cold, stale rice, or fail to receive any; or do they receive foul-smelling parched grain, or fail to receive any; and thus, with such coarse food, are they satisfied or not?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, for the sake of two beneficial reasons, I prohibit eating in a separate group; however, I permit three people to eat together.
One benefit is to protect the donor out of compassion."

"To benefit both [self and others], you must break the power and influence of those bhikṣus who harbor evil desires; do not allow such persons of evil desire to form separate assemblies or perform separate legal acts in opposition to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha was staying at Gṛdhrakūṭa Hill near Rājagṛha, dwelling in the cave of the Kambala Yakṣa. Rising early, he put on his robes, took his alms-bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food.
After his meal, he returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and entered the cave of the yakṣa Kambala to sit in meditation.

At that time, Devadatta, exerting himself with skillful means to harm the Buddha, hired four wicked and powerful men; they went up to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, carrying a large rock together, and waited at the entrance of the cave of the yakṣa Kambala for the time when the Buddha would be walking about.
In the afternoon, the Buddha emerged from the stone cave and walked back and forth in the shade before it.
At that time, four wicked men, together with Devadatta, pushed a rock intending to hurl it at the Buddha.

At that time, the yakṣa Kimpila deeply revered and recollected the Buddha; having seen this, he caught the rock with both hands and threw it elsewhere, but fragments of the stone flew toward the Buddha.

The Buddha, wishing to cause sentient beings to give rise to a mind of revulsion and fear, and to demonstrate that all karmic actions do not fail to yield their retribution, entered a state of meditative concentration for this reason. He vanished from the head of his walking path and appeared in the east; as he walked, the broken stones followed him, and it was likewise so in the south, west, and north.
At that time, when the Buddha submerged himself into the great ocean waters, the shattered stones followed him.
When the Buddha further entered Mount Sumeru, the stones likewise followed after him.
Upon reaching the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings, the stones continued to follow him.

From the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and further to the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha Heavens—the stone followed him everywhere.

At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers and returned to walking meditation while standing upright; the stone fell upon the Buddha’s foot, wounding it so that blood flowed, causing him deep physical pain and distress.
Having warded off this suffering through the power of his diligence, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, Nor by entering among the rocks of the mountains;
Neither in heaven nor within the earth— There is no place where one can evade the retribution of karma.”
"Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea; not by entering the mountain crags, nor in the heavens or the depths of the earth, can one escape the calamities of past evil deeds.
At that time, when Devadatta and the four wicked men had first committed the crime of rebellion, the Buddha looked up at them; the four fled in terror as if being pursued by hunters.
The Buddha called out to the four men:
"Come! I shall preach the Dharma for you."

He then returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha taught him the Dharma in various ways, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, the Buddha said: “Go!
"Do not come this way.
Devadatta immediately became enraged and hired eight more men, instructing them to go and kill those four.
When the Buddha saw the eight men, he spoke to them:
"Come! I shall teach you the Dharma.

The eight men immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha taught them the Dharma in various ways, instructing, inspiring, benefiting, and gladdening them. Having thus instructed, inspired, benefited, and gladdened them, he said:
"Young man, go away!
Do not come by this path.
At that time, Devadatta again dispatched sixteen men with the intent to kill the eight, saying:
"Go and kill these eight people, for they have cut off my speech.
From afar, the Buddha saw sixteen people and said to them:
"Young men, come here!"
"I shall preach the Dharma for you.

He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, preached the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden him.
Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, he said:
"Go! Do not take the path you have come by."
Devadatta again sent thirty-two men, saying to them:
"Go and kill these sixteen people, so as to eliminate their divisive speech.
From afar, the Buddha saw the thirty-two men and said to them:
"Young man, come here!
I shall teach you the Dharma.

He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, taught the Dharma to him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, he said: "Go as you please.
At that time, the bhikṣus surrounded the four sides of the stone cave; some stood and some sat, fearing that Devadatta might harm the Buddha.
The Buddha saw the bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Ānanda: "Bhikṣus!
For what reason are you standing, sitting, or staying around the four sides of this stone cave? What are you waiting for?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
Devadatta wishes to harm the Buddha; for this reason, the bhikṣus stand, sit, and remain encircling the four sides of the stone cave, hoping that Devadatta will not come to harm the Buddha.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"It is impossible that Devadatta could take the life of the Buddha.
It is also impossible that the Buddha should die due to external causes."
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Take with you the bhikṣus who are following you and enter the streets, marketplaces, and public dwellings of Rājagṛha, and proclaim:
'As for the deeds performed by Devadatta—whether performed by body or by speech—do not say they are the deeds of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha.'"
"This is the work of Devadatta and his disciples.

Having received these instructions, Ānanda immediately led the monks who were traveling with him to Rājagṛha. In the streets, marketplaces, and public dwellings where many people resided, he proclaimed:
"The deeds performed by Devadatta in body and speech—do not say they are the deeds of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; these are the deeds performed by Devadatta and his disciples."
After this proclamation was made, the high officials of Prince Ajātaśatru’s inner palace heard these words and thought to themselves:
"The śramaṇa Gautama, out of jealousy and anger toward Devadatta, has caused this proclamation to be made:
'This superior man Devadatta is capable of committing evil and heterodox acts with his body and speech.'"
Devadatta also heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had sent people into the streets, marketplaces, and crowded dwellings of Rājagṛha to proclaim:
"The deeds performed by Devadatta in body and speech are not the deeds of the Buddha, nor the deeds of the Dharma, nor the deeds of the Saṃgha; these are the deeds of Devadatta and his disciples."
Having heard this, his anger and resentment redoubled toward the Buddha, and he went immediately to Prince Ajātaśatru and said:
"You have killed your father; I shall kill the Buddha.
You shall be king in the kingdom of Magadha; I shall become a Buddha."
"In this kingdom of Magadha, there is now both a new king and a new Buddha; is this not a most joyful thing!
Upon hearing these words, Prince Ajātaśatru’s joy penetrated deeply into his heart, and he accepted Devadatta’s counsel.
Once, when King Bimbisāra was driving a carriage drawn by swift horses into the royal park for recreation,
the prince stood at the head of the street holding a sharp sword, waiting for him.

At that time, the king was amusing himself with music and dance in his garden during the day; as evening approached and he was returning to the palace, the king drew near, whereupon [the prince] took a pinḍīra sword and hurled it at him from afar.
Because the chariot was swift, he managed to escape this peril.
Since the Prince had not harmed the King, he immediately fled.
The officials soon surrounded him to capture him and took him to the King’s presence.
The king asked the prince,
"What do you wish to do? He replied:
"I wish to seize the King's life.
He asked, "On whose word do you act?"
He replied,
"I followed the words of the superior man, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
At that time, some ministers spoke as follows:
"All śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, should be beaten to death.
Another said,
"What crimes have all these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, committed?"
"You should kill Devadatta and his disciples.
Another said,
"What crimes have Devadatta's disciples committed?"
"Kill only Devadatta.
Another said,
"Why kill all these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas?"
"Why did you kill the disciples of Devadatta?
Why did you kill Devadatta himself?
Your Majesty is virtuous, noble, and gentle; you would release even those who deserve death—how then could you kill these śramaṇas who have left the household life?"
"Why do we not report this matter to the King? If we act according to the King’s instructions, the case will be settled; why trouble ourselves to exert our own efforts?
After the King had returned to the palace, he sat in his hall of justice for this very matter. The ministers and officials all came to pay their respects and stood to one side.
The king said,
"Regarding the matter that arose yesterday, how should it be resolved?
He replied:
Among the ministers, some said:
"All śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, should be beaten to death. Others said:
"What crimes have all these śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya, committed?
Devadatta and his disciples should be put to death. Some said:
"What crimes have Devadatta’s disciples committed?
Simply kill Devadatta. Some said:
"Why have you killed the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?
Why have you killed the disciples of Devadatta?
Why have you killed Devadatta?"
"Your Majesty is virtuous, noble, and gentle; you have even released those who deserved death. Why then do you kill these śramaṇas who have left the household life?
Why should we not report this matter to the King? Once the King has issued his command for their punishment, the matter will be settled; why trouble ourselves to exert our own strength?"
The King said: "Previously, those śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas sent someone to proclaim:
'Whatever deeds are performed by Devadatta through body and speech, do not say they are the deeds of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha.'"
"This is the work of Devadatta and his disciples.
This matter has already been proclaimed previously.
When the king heard these words from the minister:
"All śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, should be beaten to death.
The King must not accept these words. Some say:
"What crimes have these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, committed that they should be killed?
Devadatta and his disciples.
The king, however, should not accept this statement.
Some said:
"What crimes have the disciples of Devadatta committed?
Devadatta should be put to death."
The king should not accept these words either. Some say:
"Why did you kill all those śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas?"
"Why did you kill the disciples of Devadatta?
Why did you kill Devadatta?

Your Majesty is virtuous, noble, gentle, and kind; you release those who ought to die. Following your Majesty’s instructions, our administrative duties are accomplished; why then trouble ourselves to exert our own strength?"
The king approved this and granted him villages, fields, houses, wealth,
and goods. Then the king asked the prince himself,
"What do you wish to do?"
Immediately casting aside shame and remorse, he replied:
"I wish to seize the King's life. Why is this?"
The king has the royal drum, the royal music, the royal parasol, and when he travels, a golden water-pitcher is carried before him.
I have no royal drum, no royal music, no royal parasol, and no golden water-pitcher carried before me when I travel.
The king then provided the crown prince with the royal drum, the royal musicians, the royal parasol-bearer, and the golden water-pitcher for use while traveling to precede him.
At that time, two kings beat the drums, two kings led the procession, two kings held the parasols, and two kings carried the golden water-pitchers in front.
In the method of governing a kingdom, one must not follow the whims of all people.
When King Bimbisāra had not yet attained the Way, he did things that did not conform to the wishes of others; consequently, the people harbored resentment and thought to themselves:
"When the time comes, we shall take our revenge."
These wicked people approached Ajātaśatru and said,
"In which kingdom are there two rulers?
The king replied:
"What are the two lords? He replied:
"Two kings beat the drums; two kings perform music; two kings hold parasols; when the two kings travel, they carry golden water-pitchers before them; and two kings lead the procession."
“When your father the King later governs the kingdom, he will surely take your life and rule alone; you should employ skillful means to deal with the king.
Upon hearing this, King Ajātaśatru was delighted and acquiesced, immediately ordering his ministers and officials to arrest his father the King and place him in prison.
The minister, having received these instructions, immediately arrested him and cast him into prison.

The Great King was kind, virtuous, gentle, and noble; hundreds of thousands of people brought various delicacies to visit and inquire after the King’s well-being, and the King ate them to sustain his life.
After several days had passed, King Ajātaśatru asked,
"Is the Great King alive?
He replied:
"Is he alive? "How can he be alive? He replied:
"Let those who inquire after his health provide him with food and drink for his sustenance.
The king then issued an edict to the prison official:
"From this day forward, do not allow anyone to enter."
Later, the king’s consort stole food and brought it in; the king ate it and was restored to life.
After several days had passed, the king asked again:
"Great King, are you alive?"
He replied, “I am alive. [The other asked,] “How have you survived?”
He replied,
"It is because the king’s consort has come to provide food and drink.
He then immediately commanded the prison official not to allow the consort to enter.

There was a chief consort who held the Great King in deep reverence; she smeared food upon her garment, put on another upper robe, and went into the prison. She removed the garment and gave it to the King so that he might eat and survive.
After several days had passed, the king asked again:
"Is my father king still alive?
He replied:
"Is he alive? "How can he be alive? He replied:
"The chief consort has come; it is because she obtained food that we have survived.
The king said, "Do not allow the chief consort to enter."

The father king was in prison when he saw Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa from afar. Seeing the Buddha and the Saṅgha—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kapphiṇa—ascending and descending the mountain, the great king was restored to life because of the joy he felt at seeing the Buddha and the Saṅgha from a distance.
After several days had passed, Ajātaśatru asked again:
"Is my father, the king, still alive?
He replied:
"He is alive. "How can he be alive?
the minister replied with a jealous heart:
“Because we saw the Buddha and the Sangha from afar, we have lived.
The king immediately issued an order to erect barriers so that they could not see him.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they enter a city for a great cause, they manifest such supernormal powers as these:
Elephants trumpeted deeply, horses neighed mournfully, and oxen bellowed;
geese, swans, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and gibbons—all these birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds;
great drums, small drums, lutes, zithers, flutes, biwa lutes, pipes, harps, reed organs, and gongs and cymbals resounded spontaneously without being struck.

All the gold, silver, and precious vessels, as well as the various internal and external ornaments within the residences of the nobles, spontaneously produced sounds from within their chests and caskets;
the blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the mute were able to speak, and those with hunchbacks or lameness were able to stretch their limbs;

the lame and crippled regained their hands and feet, the squinting regained their correct vision, and those with goiters were freed from their pain and attained happiness; the effects of poison were neutralized, and the insane were restored to their senses.

Those who kill shall abstain from killing; those who steal shall abstain from stealing; those who engage in sexual misconduct shall not engage in sexual misconduct; those who speak falsehoods shall not speak falsehoods; those who engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous chatter shall not engage in such chatter; those who are covetous shall not be covetous; those who harbor ill will shall not harbor ill will;
and those with wrong views shall abandon wrong views. Those imprisoned and bound in dungeons, shackled and fettered, shall all attain liberation.
Those in places of urgency and turmoil shall all obtain tranquility and solitude.
Those who have not yet planted roots of goodness plant them; those who have already planted them cause them to increase; and those who have already increased them attain liberation.
All treasures hidden as subterranean hoards spontaneously appear.
Such rare events bring benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha entered the city of Rājagṛha; as his right foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate, all manner of such auspicious omens appeared.
King Bimbisāra had previously seen this omen and knew that the Buddha was about to enter the city; the king stood at a window of his palace to watch the Buddha entering.
Because the king attained the Noble Path and rejoiced upon seeing the Buddha and the Saṅgha, he remained alive.
After several days had passed, Ajātaśatru asked again:
"Is the king still alive?
He replied:
"He lives. "How does he live?
The ministers, with jealous hearts, replied:
"The Buddha entered the city and manifested his supernormal powers; because the King, his father, followed him through the hole and beheld the Buddha, he was restored to life.
King Ajātaśatru said, "Shave the soles of the Great King's feet with a sharp blade, then pull back the skin and bind it tightly so that it cannot move to the east or west."
He immediately followed the instruction and scraped the soles of the Great King’s feet, binding them so tightly that he could not move about.
For this reason, the King lay down and grew increasingly emaciated and gravely ill.
On another occasion, King Ajātaśatru was eating together with his mother; the King had a son named Udāyibhadra, who was playing with a puppy at the head of the road.
The king asked,
"Udayabhadda, where is he now? He replied:
"While on the road, he was playing with a dog.
The King said, "Call him here; I will eat with him."
He immediately took the puppy and followed the messenger back; the prince would not eat.
The king asked, "For what reason?"
The prince said,
"If Your Majesty permits me to give food to the puppy, then I shall eat.
The king said:
"As you wish," the prince said;
he ate some himself and took some with him to give to the dog.
The king spoke to his mother, saying:
“I have performed a difficult deed. Why is this?
Out of love for my son, I sprinkled the head of a Kṣatriya king with water and fed him together with a dog.”
The mother said,
"This is not a difficult task. Why is that?"
"If there are people who eat dog meat, what is strange about giving you food?
Have you ever known that your father committed a difficult deed?
The king said:
"What difficult thing did you do?
His mother replied, "When you were young, a carbuncle grew on your finger; you suffered such acute pain that you could not sleep day or night."
Your father held you in his lap and placed a finger from a carbuncle in his mouth; because the Great King’s body was so soft, you were able to sleep peacefully.
Due to the warmth from his mouth, the carbuncle ripened and its pus burst forth.
The Great King thought to himself,
"To point back at the spittle and pus would only increase my son's suffering.
He then immediately swallowed the pus.
"Your father has performed this difficult task; I pray that you will release him at once.
Upon hearing this, the king remained silent.
The mother believed he had already been released.
Once the sound issued from within the palace, it was proclaimed that the Great King had been released; the news reached every street and lane that the Great King had emerged.
Because the King was virtuous and good, hundreds of thousands of people all exclaimed: "Excellent!"
They all went to the place of confinement and each spoke these words:
"Great King, you shall be released.
Having heard this, the Great King thought to himself:
"My son is so wicked and rebellious, lacking any heart of compassion; I do not know what he will do to punish me.
Having thought this, she threw herself beneath the bed and immediately passed away.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru had usurped the life of his father, the king, thereby incurring the grave offense of parricide.
The Buddha was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa at Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One dressed in his upper robe and took his alms bowl before noon, entering the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. Having finished eating, he returned to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and sat cross-legged for seven days, experiencing the bliss of meditative concentration.
After seven days had passed, before midday, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city for the purpose of begging for alms.
At that time, Devadatta heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was in Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

Before midday, Gautama dressed, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food; having finished eating, he returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and sat cross-legged for seven days, experiencing the bliss of meditative concentration.
When seven days had passed, before the midday meal, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city for the purpose of begging for alms.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru had an elephant named Dhanapāla, who was fierce, possessed great strength, and was peerless throughout the four quarters.
At that time, Devadatta took five hundred gold coins and said to the elephant trainer:
"Do you know? The King honors and supports me;
I am now able to cause either harm or benefit to others."
"I now give these five hundred coins to you; once the matter is successfully accomplished, I shall provide you with generous support, including fields, houses, and people.
He asked, "What matter?"
He replied, “The śramaṇa Gautama is with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus on Vulture Peak Mountain.

During the morning, the śramaṇa Gautama put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. Having finished his meal, he returned to Vulture Peak Mountain and, for seven days, sat cross-legged in meditation, experiencing the bliss of dhyāna.”
After seven days have passed, before midday, he will put on his robes and take his bowl to enter the city for the sake of alms.
Can you give wine to the elephant to intoxicate him, loosen his chains and remove his tether, and cause him to take the life of the śramaṇa Gautama?
The elephant trainer replied, “Yes.
This is a minor matter; this elephant belongs to me, so I do not think you will forget to repay me.”
Devadatta said:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama will enter the city in seven days from now.
He immediately counted on his fingers and marked the days with tally-sticks; when the seventh day arrived, he tied up an elephant that was intoxicated with wine and waited for the Buddha.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they enter a city on a great occasion, such auspicious omens appear:
elephants trumpet deeply, horses neigh plaintively, and the lords of the oxen bellow;
geese, swans, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and gibbons—all these birds utter harmonious and elegant sounds.
Great drums, small drums, harps, zithers, flutes, lutes, pipes, lyres, oboes, and gongs and cymbals resounded spontaneously without being struck;
all the golden and silver vessels and various ornamental furnishings within and without the mansions of the nobility naturally produced sounds from within their chests and boxes;

the blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the mute were able to speak, those with hunchbacks and lameness were able to stretch and move, the lame regained their hands and feet, those with squinting eyes had them set straight, those with goiters were freed from their pain and attained joy, the effects of poison were neutralized, and the insane were restored to their senses.

Those who kill shall abstain from killing; those who steal shall abstain from stealing; those who engage in sexual misconduct shall not engage in sexual misconduct; those who speak falsely shall not speak falsely; those who engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech shall not engage in such speech; those who are greedy shall not be greedy; those who are angry shall not be angry; and those with wrong views shall abandon wrong views.
Those imprisoned and bound in jail, shackled and fettered, shall all attain liberation;
those in places of turmoil and haste shall all find solitude and leisure.
Those who have not yet planted roots of goodness plant them; those who have already planted them cause them to grow; and those who have already grown them attain liberation.
All treasures hidden as subterranean hoards spontaneously manifest themselves.
Through such rare and wondrous events, all sentient beings obtained benefit.
When the Buddha reached the city and placed his right foot upon the threshold of the gate, there immediately appeared various kinds of auspicious omens.

The elephant trainer had previously seen these signs and knew that the Buddha was entering the city; he immediately untied the elephant’s tether and let it loose, intending for it to harm the Buddha, yet no one was able to restrain it.
This elephant had three protuberances on its face; intoxicated and frantic, it trampled and kicked about, causing a multitude of hundreds of thousands to be struck with great terror.
Those who had entered their houses and those who were in secluded, covered places left the streets and lanes entirely empty, except for the Buddha and his disciples.
Seeing from afar the elephant Dhana-pālaka approaching, a wise man went toward the Buddha and addressed him, saying: “World-Honored One! [The elephant Dhana-pālaka is coming.]”

This elephant has drunk wine until intoxicated; having been released from its tethering ropes, it is being sent to harm the Buddha, and there is no one able to restrain it. We pray that the Buddha will either enter our house or return out of the city, so as not to let this elephant take the life of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"It is impossible for a wealth-guarding elephant to take the life of the Buddha.
It is also impossible for the Buddha to die due to external causes."
The worthy one’s heart was filled with great joy, and he said:
"It is impossible for a wealth-guarding elephant to take the Buddha's life;
it is also impossible for the Buddha to die due to external causes."
At that time, the crowd stood upon the upper stories and balconies of the houses, making a great clamor.
Then some who lacked faith said,
"This elephant, Guardian of Wealth, might perhaps kill the Buddha."
Those with faith said,
"It is impossible for this wealth-guarding elephant to kill the Buddha. When the elephant saw the Buddha from afar,
it immediately gnashed its teeth, raised its trunk, bristled its tail, and flattened its ears as it strove to charge toward the Buddha's location.
When the bhikṣus saw the elephant approaching from afar, they were all greatly terrified and fled, abandoning the Buddha, with the sole exception of Ānanda.

As the elephant drew near to the Buddha, the Buddha immediately employed the power of the *maitrī-samādhi*; the elephant’s intoxication was instantly sobered, and it prostrated itself before the Buddha, wiping the Buddha’s feet with its trunk. The Buddha stroked its head with his right hand and spoke this verse:
“The World-Honored One, with his long arms, And hands possessing the soft marks of the wheels;”
"Patting the elephant's head, he instructs it as a father instructs his son.
The Buddha said:
"Great elephant, do not give rise to evil karma."
Those who perform evil deeds will not be reborn in a favorable realm.
There is the elephant Tiloca, the elephant Himava, the elephant Khaṇḍaka,
and the elephant Bhadraka.
"The celestial beings worship the Buddha, remaining free from negligence and frivolity;
those who are negligent and frivolous shall not be born in a happy realm.
If you remain diligent, you shall surely be reborn in the heavens."

After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he taught, instructed, inspired, and gladdened Dhanapāla the elephant with the Dharma; having thus taught, instructed, inspired, and gladdened him, he remained silent.

At that time, because Dhanapāla had heard the Dharma from the Buddha, his heart was filled with remorse and tears fell. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
At that time, having heard that the Buddha had subdued the wicked elephant—an event of such rarity—the multitude gathered in immeasurable numbers.
Having seen this vast assembly, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Prepare a seat for me and provide water."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately prepared a seat and water at that spot. Joining his palms, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The seat has been prepared and the water is ready; may the Buddha know the proper time.”
The Buddha then washed his feet, sat upon the prepared seat, and entered meditative concentration.
Vanishing from that place, he appeared in the eastern sky, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
he then entered the fire-light samādhi, manifesting various colored rays of light.
Blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, pale green, purple, and azure;

fire issued from the lower part of his body while water issued from the upper part, and again, fire issued from the upper part of his body while water issued from the lower part; it was likewise so in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Having manifested these various supernormal powers, he returned to his original seat and sat as before.

Those among the multitude who had previously harbored feelings of aversion and fear, upon witnessing the Buddha’s miraculous transformations and his subduing of the intoxicated elephant, immediately conceived deep faith and reverence toward the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing that sentient beings possess deep faith and pliancy, teaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities.

Among this assembly, there are those who have attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), those who have attained the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), those who have attained the stage of "Patience in Accordance with the Path" (*kṣānti*), those whose three poisons are attenuated, those who are free from desire, and those who have attained the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). There are those who have attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, those who have attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and those who have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*. There are those who plant the causal conditions for the Śrāvaka vehicle, those who plant the causal conditions for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and those who plant the causal conditions for the Buddha vehicle. In this way, he benefits immeasurable sentient beings.
On that day, the Buddha took no food; grasping Ānanda by the arm, he returned through the air to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

When the bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had returned, they all went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said to the Buddha:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
"In this way, even during times of urgent peril, Ānanda did not abandon the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"It is not only now that Ānanda did not abandon the Buddha in times of urgent peril; in past lives as well, he did not abandon the Buddha during times of urgent peril. I shall now relate this."
In a past age, there was a king of deer named Māhātmya (威德) who lived near the foot of the Snowy Mountains and served as the leader of five hundred deer.
At that time, a hunter set out grain and laid snares.
As the deer king walked forward, his right foot fell into a snare of hair.
The deer king thought to himself:
"If I manifest my form now, the other deer will not dare to eat the grain; I must wait until the grain is entirely consumed before I reveal myself."
When he manifested his feet, all the deer fled; only one female deer remained and spoke this verse:
"Great King, you should know that this fowler is coming. I pray that you will diligently employ skillful means to escape from this snare."
At that time, the deer king replied in verse:
"I have exerted myself with skillful means, yet my strength is exhausted; the hair-noose has tightened further, and I cannot escape."
At that time, seeing that the hunter was drawing closer, the female deer spoke again in verse:
"Great King, you should know: The fowler is drawing near; I pray you, apply yourself with skillful means To find a way out of this snare."
The Deer King replied:
"I have exerted myself with skillful means, yet my strength is now exhausted;
the hair-noose has tightened further, and I cannot escape."
When the female deer saw that the hunter had arrived, she spoke these verses to him:
"With your sharp blade, first kill my body; then, I pray, you will release the Deer King so that he may depart."
Upon hearing this, the hunter gave rise to a heart of compassion and rare wonder, thinking:
"Because this beast so deeply loves another, it is able to give up its own life.
He replied with a verse:
"I shall never kill you, nor shall I kill the king of deer;
I release both you and the king of deer, so go wherever you please."
The hunter immediately released the deer king.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Was the deer king of old anyone other than this person?"
Do not view this as something else; it was I myself who was that deer king.
Those five hundred deer were none other than you five hundred bhikṣus.
Just as you abandoned me in times of urgent fear in past lives, so too do you abandon me now in a time of urgent fear.
The hunter at that time was none other than this elephant guarding his treasure;
he did not harm me in past lives, nor does he harm me in this life.
The female deer at that time was Ānanda.
"In past lives, when there was urgent fear, he did not abandon me; in this present life, when there is urgent fear, he likewise does not abandon me.
For these reasons, the Buddha then related the second Jātaka tale.
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, there was a city named Vārāṇasī. Beside the city was a pond called Varṣākāra.
In that pond there was abundant water, many fish, many turtles, and many geese, swans, and ducks."
Among them was a king of geese named Rāṣṭrapāla, who served as the leader of five hundred geese.
At that time, there was a hunter who had first set out a snare of hair near some grain. As the goose king walked forward, his right foot became caught in the snare. He thought to himself:
"If I pull my foot out of this snare, the other geese will not dare to eat the grain; I must wait until the grain is completely consumed before I reveal myself."
Having finished eating the grain, he immediately manifested his feet; the flock of geese abandoned the king and flew away.
Only one minister, named Soma, did not abandon the king and depart.
The Goose King, who governed the kingdom, said to his minister, "I appoint you to the office of king; lead the way for all the geese.
The minister replied:
"No. He asked, "For what reason?"
At that time, the great minister replied in verse:
"I vow to follow the King, unchanging through death and life; it would be better to die with the King than to live apart from him."
"Great King, you should know that this fowler has arrived; he merely exerts diligent skillful means to seek our release from these snares.
At that time, the Goose King replied in verse:
"I have exerted diligent skillful means, yet my strength is already exhausted; the hair-snares tighten ever more."
"He cannot escape.
At that time, seeing that the fowler was drawing near, the minister spoke again in verse:
"Great King, you should know: the fowler is about to arrive; pray, exert yourself in skillful means."
"I seek release from this snare.
At that time, the king of geese replied in verse:
"I have exerted myself with skillful means, yet my strength is exhausted; the hair-snare grows ever tighter."
"There is no escape.
'O Great King, my hair, fat, and flesh are equal to yours and no different;
you may kill me with a blade, but I shall release you without harming you.'"
At that time, the fowler thought to himself:
"That an animal, out of such deep affection for another, would even give up its own life is truly most rare.
Having had this thought, he spoke to the minister, saying:
"I shall not kill you; I release both you and the king. Go wherever you please in joy.
The hunter then untied the goose-king and let him go.
When the two geese had traveled a short distance together, they spoke to one another:
"This hunter has performed a rare feat by granting us our lives.
Had he killed one first and the other later, who could have prevented it?
We shall repay him generously with the necessities of life."
Having heard this, the hunter asked,
"What do you mean, that you cannot go?
The two geese replied:
"We can go, provided you explain this:
'You have performed a marvelous feat by granting us our lives.
If you were to kill one first and then kill the other, who could have prevented it?'"
"Our means of livelihood shall be used to repay you generously.
The hunter asked the geese, "You are animals;
what means of livelihood do you have with which to repay me?"
The two geese replied, "The King of Vārāṇasī is named Brahmadatta; give us to him.
Then the hunter said:
"He might harm you; why should I give it to you?
The goose said, "Do not bind me; simply take me away as I fly."

At that time, the hunter placed the two geese upon his two shoulders and walked through the streets and alleys of the city. Because these geese were so handsome, everyone delighted in seeing them and many people cherished them with affection.
Among the crowd, some said:
"I will give you five coins.
Others gave ten coins or twenty coins, all saying:
"Wait a moment; do not kill him.
By the time this man reaches the royal palace, he will have acquired great wealth.
Once the hunter arrived at the gate of the royal palace, he set the goose down upon the ground.
The king of geese said to the gatekeeper,
"Inform King Brahmadatta that the goose-king is now outside the gate.
He went at once to inform the king, who immediately granted him entry and provided him with a golden couch.
The minister Soma exchanged appropriate greetings with him, and then, taking his seat, he inquired after King Brahmadatta’s welfare in verse:
"Is Your Majesty’s person at ease?"
Is the land prosperous?
Do you transform the people according to the Dharma?
Do you govern the kingdom with an impartial mind?
At that time, King Brahmadatta replied in verse:
"I have always been at peace and secure; my kingdom is forever abundant and tranquil.
I transform the people with the Dharma, treating them all with impartiality and without partiality."
Thus he replied with five hundred verses.
When King Brahmadatta heard what was said, he thought to himself:
"The king of geese is so profoundly wise and discerning."
The minister Soma remained silent at that time. King Brahmadatta said, "Why do you remain silent?
The minister replied:
"You are a human king and sovereign of a kingdom; this goose king is the sovereign of a marshland.
When two sovereigns converse together, how dare you interrupt?
The king thought to himself:
"This is a worthy minister," he said,
addressing him as "Soma!"
"I have a fine garden; would you be able to dwell within it?
