I shall further assemble various geese and create a pond for you, providing whatever food you desire."
He replied, "I cannot.
The king asked:
"Why is that? the goose king said.
"Perhaps the King, having woken from sleep, forgot to clear me away and has ordered that geese be prepared as meat."
"If the cook cannot obtain another goose, he may kill us to provide for the King's kitchen.

The Goose King, Rājahaṃsa, entered the royal palace, while the other geese emerged from the rain-formed pond and circled above the palace, crying out piteously; their wings were wet, and water splashed onto and defiled the palace halls.
The king looked up and saw that the water had defiled the palace; wondering at this, he asked, "What is this?
The goose-king replied:
"These are my attendants.
The king said,
"Do you wish to leave?"
He replied,
"I wish to go.
The king said:
"What do you require? they asked.
He replied, "I was captured by hunters; they have performed a marvelous deed for us by granting us our lives."
"If one were killed first and another later, who could prevent it?
The king said,
"How should I repay him?"
The two geese replied,
"We shall give you gold, silver, musāragalva, agate, clothing, and food.
Having spoken these words, they soared up into the void.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Was that Goose King who ruled the country at that time anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
Those five hundred geese were these five hundred bhikṣus; in times of past urgency and fear they abandoned me, and in times of present urgency and fear they have likewise abandoned me.
The hunter who guarded the treasure elephant was none other than myself in a past life; he did not harm me then, nor does he harm me now.
King Brahmadatta was King Śuddhodana, and the minister Soma was Ānanda.
"In times of past urgency and fear, you did not abandon me; now, in this time of urgency and fear, you likewise do not abandon me.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha immediately recounted the third Jātaka:
"In a past age, near the foot of the Snowy Mountains, there lived a lion, king of beasts, who was the leader of five hundred lions."
Later, when this lion king grew old, sick, emaciated, and blind, he went before the other lions and fell into an empty well; all five hundred lions then abandoned him and departed.
At that time, not far from the empty well, there was a jackal who, seeing the lion king, thought to himself:
"The reason I am able to dwell in this forest in peace and security, and obtain meat to my heart's content, is solely because of the lion king."
"The Lion King has now fallen into this place of peril; how shall we repay his kindness?

At that time, there was a channel of flowing water by the side of the well, and the jackal used its mouth and paws to direct the water into the well. As the water filled the well, the lion floated out.
Then the deity of this forest spoke in verse:
"Though one's own body be strong and powerful, One should take the weak as a friend;
A small jackal was able to rescue The lion king from the perilous well."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"As for that Lion King at that time, was he anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
The five hundred lions were these bhikṣus;
in times of urgent peril in the past, they abandoned me and departed, and now, in a time of urgent peril, they have likewise abandoned me and departed.
"The jackal was Ānanda.
In past lives he cherished me, and now too he cherishes me.
For this reason, the Buddha then gave a detailed exposition of five hundred of his previous births (*jātaka*).

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
The second part of the account of Devadatta from the *Saṃyukta-āgama*:
The Buddha was staying at Mount Vaibhāra near Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of seven hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, during the forenoon, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, followed by Ānanda.
After the meal, he went to the lecture hall and sat upon the prepared seat before the assembly of monks.
Devadatta did likewise; before midday, he dressed, took up his bowl, and with Kālodāyin following behind him, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
After the meal, they went to the lecture hall and sat down in order. Once seated, Devadatta proclaimed among the Saṃgha:

"Bhikṣus should, for as long as life lasts, accept and wear the patched robe; should, for as long as life lasts, accept and practice begging for food; should, for as long as life lasts, accept and observe the practice of eating only once a day; should, for as long as life lasts, accept and dwell in the open air; and should, for as long as life lasts, accept and abstain from meat and fish."

These five dharmas accord with having few desires and being content, being easy to support and easy to satisfy, knowing the proper time and the proper measure, maintaining pure precepts through diligence, single-minded seclusion, and turning toward the gate of Nirvana.
"If a bhikṣu practices these five dharmas, he will swiftly attain nirvāṇa. At that time, Devadatta proclaimed what was not Dharma as Dharma, and what was Dharma as not Dharma;

he proclaimed what was wholesome as unwholesome, and what was unwholesome as wholesome; he proclaimed what was an offense as no offense, and what was no offense as an offense; he proclaimed what was light as heavy, and what was heavy as light; he proclaimed what was with remainder as without remainder, and what was without remainder as with remainder; he proclaimed what was the constant practice of the Dharma as not the constant practice of the Dharma, and what was not the constant practice of the Dharma as the constant practice of the Dharma; he proclaimed speech as non-speech, and non-speech as speech.
At that time, the Buddha personally admonished Devadatta:
"Do not employ means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha; do not uphold matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha.

You should live in harmonious union with the Saṃgha; for those who are in harmony, there is joy and no contention. With one mind and one training, like water and milk blending together, you shall practice in peace and happiness."

Do not speak what is contrary to the Dharma as the Dharma, or the Dharma as contrary to the Dharma; do not speak what is unwholesome as wholesome, or the wholesome as unwholesome; do not speak of a transgression as non-transgression, or a non-transgression as a transgression; do not speak of what is light as heavy, or what is heavy as light; do not speak of what entails a remainder as being without remainder, or what is without remainder as entailing a remainder; do not speak of a practice that is always to be followed as not always to be followed, or a practice that is not always to be followed as always to be followed; do not speak what is speech as non-speech, or what is non-speech as speech.
When Devadatta heard the Buddha’s such exhortation, he did not abandon the causes and conditions for causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
While the Buddha was thus exhorting Devadatta and he still refused to relinquish this matter, at that time the bhikṣu Kālodāyin stood behind Devadatta and fanned him with a fan.
The bhikṣu Kālatiṣya immediately bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just as the Buddha praises the merits of dhūta practices, so too does the venerable Devadatta praise the merits of dhūta practices."
"Why would a Buddha give rise to a mind of jealousy?
The Buddha said,
"Foolish man!"
What jealousy could I possibly have?
The Buddhas of the past praised the patched robe and permitted the wearing of the patched robe;
I too now praise the patched robe and permit the wearing of the patched robe, as well as the wearing of the robes of laypeople.
Foolish man!
The Buddhas of the past praised begging for food and permitted begging for food.
I now likewise praise begging for food and permit begging for food, as well as accepting invitations to eat.
"You foolish man!
The Buddhas of the past praised eating once a day and permitted eating once a day.
I now praise eating once a day and permit eating once a day, and I also permit eating a second time."
"O foolish man!
The Buddhas of the past praised dwelling in the open air and permitted dwelling in the open air.
I now praise dwelling in the open air and permit dwelling in the open air, and I also permit dwelling in a dwelling-place."
"You fool!
I do not permit the eating of three kinds of impure meat:
that which is seen, that which is heard, and that which is suspected."
"Seeing" means seeing with one's own eyes that this animal was killed for one's sake.
"Hearing" means hearing from a trustworthy person that this animal was killed for one's sake.

As for those who doubt: in this place there are no butchers or sellers of meat, nor are there any animals that die of their own accord; yet these people are so wicked that they can intentionally deprive the lives of animals.
You fools!
"These three kinds of meat I do not permit you to eat.
You foolish people!
I have permitted the eating of the three kinds of pure meat."
What are the three?
Not seeing, not hearing, and not doubting.
"Not seeing" means not having seen with one's own eyes that one killed this animal for the sake of oneself.
"Not having heard" means not having heard from a trustworthy person that this animal was killed specifically for one's sake.
"Not doubting" means that among those present there is a butcher who possesses a compassionate heart and is unable to take the life of the animal.
"I have heard that one may eat these three kinds of pure meat. Fool!

In the case of great sacrifices—namely, the elephant sacrifice, the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the *aja-vipya* sacrifice, the *tri-yajña-pāta* sacrifice, the *yathākāmam* sacrifice, or any sacrifice at a worldly assembly where living beings are killed—in such great sacrifices and worldly assemblies, I do not permit the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya to eat meat."
"Why is this? Because this great sacrificial assembly is composed entirely of guests.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha rose from his seat and entered a room to sit in meditation.
At that time, Devadatta spoke these words: "I, Devadatta, shall proclaim within the Saṃgha:

'A bhikṣu should wear the patched robe for as long as life lasts; he should beg for food for as long as life lasts; he should eat only one meal a day for as long as life lasts; he should dwell in the open air for as long as life lasts; and he should not eat meat or fish for as long as life lasts.'"
"Whichever bhikṣu delights in these five points shall arise and take a tally.
Having spoken thus, Devadatta and his four companions immediately rose and took the tallies.
A second time, Devadatta spoke thus: "I, Devadatta, have proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
'Monks should wear patched robes for as long as life lasts;

they should beg for food for as long as life lasts; they should eat only one meal a day for as long as life lasts; they should dwell in the open air for as long as life lasts; and they should not eat meat or fish for as long as life lasts.'"
"Whichever bhikṣu delights in these five dharmas shall arise and take up a tally-stick.
After the second statement had been proclaimed, two hundred and fifty bhikṣus rose from their seats and took up the tally-sticks.
Devadatta spoke again for the third time: "I, Devadatta, have proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
'Monks should wear the patched robe (pāṃsukūla) for as long as life lasts;

they should beg for food for as long as life lasts; they should eat only one meal a day for as long as life lasts; they should dwell in the open air for as long as life lasts; and they should not consume meat or fish for as long as life lasts.'"
"Whichever bhikṣu delights in these five dharmas shall arise and take a tally.
After the third proclamation, another two hundred and fifty bhikṣus rose from their seats and took tallies.
At that time, Devadatta led this assembly back to his own residence and established further rules and regulations.
Devadatta spoke thus: "One should wear the patched robe (nāṃgali) for as long as one lives;

one should beg for food for as long as one lives; one should eat only one meal a day for as long as one lives; one should dwell in the open air for as long as one lives; and one should not consume meat or fish for as long as one lives. Any bhikṣu who does not delight in or tolerate these five dharmas is far removed from us; he is distinct from me and shall not speak with me."
In the late afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from his meditation chamber and sat among the community of monks, addressing them:
"Devadatta has obscured his mind with the eightfold wrong dharma and does not realize he is causing a schism in the Saṃgha."
"What are the eight?
They are gain and loss, defamation and praise, honor and disparagement, suffering and pleasure, evil friends, and evil associates.
When Devadatta heard the Buddha say that he had split the Saṃgha and destroyed the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, he was delighted and thought to himself:
“The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal powers and majesty; I can break his Saṃgha of harmony. My good reputation shall spread in the four directions:
‘The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal powers and majesty, yet Devadatta was able to break his Saṃgha of harmony.’”
Just as when the Buddha sat in the midst of the Saṃgha with Śāriputra on his right and Maudgalyāyana on his left,
so it was for Devadatta, with Kokālika on his right and Kāḷudāyin on his left.
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!
We shall now go among the followers of Devadatta; if there are those who can be transformed, we shall instruct and lead them back.”
The Buddha said,
"As you wish.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana then went at once to Devadatta’s lecture hall.
There was a bhikṣu who saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana go to the assembly of Devadatta, where they were wallowing on the ground and weeping like logs being turned around; he thought to himself:
"In such an evil age as this, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have abandoned the World-Honored One and instead gone over to Devadatta."
The Buddha, seeing the bhikṣu, knew the answer yet asked him on purpose:
"Why are you now writhing and weeping like a block of wood?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
In such an evil age, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana will abandon the Tathāgata and instead go over to Devadatta.
The Buddha said:
“Monks! It is impossible that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana would abandon me and seek wisdom elsewhere.
When the monks heard the Buddha’s words, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they exclaimed:
“Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!
It is impossible for anyone to abandon the Tathāgata and seek wisdom elsewhere.
At that time, Devadatta saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana approaching from afar; his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:
"The two foremost great disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama now belong to me.
Just as when the Buddha saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana approaching, he raised his right hand and said, "Welcome! Welcome!"
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!
Devadatta was just the same; seeing Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana approaching, he also raised his right hand and said:
'Welcome!'"
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!
He then dispatched Kūṭadanta to attend Śāriputra on the right, and Kālodāyin to attend Maudgalyāyana on the left.
Just as the Buddha, while among the assembly, said to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
"Preach the Dharma to the assembly for me; my backache has subsided for a moment," so too did Devadatta,
while among the assembly, say to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"Preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus; my back pains have subsided for a moment.
Then the Buddha spread out his four-layered *uttarāsaṅga* robe, used his *saṃghāṭī* as a pillow, and lay down on his right side.
Devadatta was likewise; he spread out his four pieces of undergarment and *uttarāsaṅga*, used his *saṃghāṭī* as a pillow, and lay on his right side.

At that time, there was a deva who, out of deep affection for the Buddha’s Dharma, caused Devadatta to fall asleep, turning him onto his left side so that he snored, muttered in his sleep, groaned and tossed about, and ground his teeth with a sound.

At that time, Śāriputra preached the Dharma for the bhikṣus, praising the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts through various causes and conditions; he also censured Devadatta in various ways, speaking of his transgressions and the path of evil, saying that he was destined to fall into the Avīci Hell for a lifespan of one kalpa, from which there would be no salvation.

Maudgalyāyana immediately entered such a meditative concentration; by the power of this samādhi, he vanished from that place and appeared in the empty space of the eastern quarter, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;
he then entered the fire-light samādhi and manifested various colored rays:
blue, yellow, red, white, purple, azure, pale green, and emerald.

Water issued from the upper part of his body and fire from the lower part; or fire issued from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part. It was likewise so in the south, west, and north.
Having manifested these miraculous transformations, he returned to his original seat.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus within the assembly, having witnessed the supernatural powers and heard the teaching of the Dharma, thought to themselves:
"We may have erred and fallen into a wrong path."

A second time, Śāriputra again preached the Dharma to the bhikṣus, praising the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts through various causes and conditions; he also censured Devadatta in various ways, speaking of his transgressions and evil deeds, and how he was destined for the Avīci Hell for a lifespan of one kalpa, from which there would be no salvation.

Maudgalyāyana immediately entered such a meditative concentration; by the power of this samādhi, he vanished from that place and appeared in the empty space of the eastern direction, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
he entered the fire-light samādhi and manifested various colored lights:
blue, yellow, red, white, purple, azure, pale green, and emerald.
Water issued from his upper body and fire from his lower body; alternatively, fire issued from his upper body and water from his lower body. It was likewise so in the south, west, and north.
Having manifested these supernatural transformations, he returned to his original seat.
Secondly, the bhikṣus became doubtful and thought to themselves:
"Are we on the wrong path?

Thirdly, Śāriputra again preached the Dharma for them, using various causes and conditions to praise the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts; he used various rebukes to speak of Devadatta’s transgressions and his descent into the evil path, stating that he shall fall into the Avīci Hell for the duration of one kalpa, where he cannot be saved.

Maudgalyāyana immediately entered such a meditative concentration; by the power of this samādhi, he vanished from that place and appeared in the empty space to the east, manifesting the four dignified postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;
he then entered the fire-light samādhi and manifested various colored lights:
blue, yellow, red, white, purple, azure, pale green, and emerald.
Water flowed from his upper body and fire from his lower body; or fire flowed from his upper body and water from his lower body. It was likewise so in the south, west, and north.
Having manifested these supernatural transformations, he returned to his original seat.
Third, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"We have indeed erred and are certain to fall into a wrong path.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana immediately rose from their seats and departed, and five hundred bhikṣus likewise rose from their seats and departed.

At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and five hundred bhikṣus together went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that moment, Devadatta’s lecture hall was empty and devoid of the great assembly, with only his four companions remaining.
Kāḷudāyī was previously standing to the left of Devadatta. When Devadatta saw Maudgalyāyana approaching, he pushed Kāḷudāyī aside to make way for Maudgalyāyana.
At that moment, for this reason, Kāḷudāyī kicked Devadatta with his right foot to wake him, saying:
"O Devadatta, you who delight in the assembly!"
“Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have seized your assembly and departed.
Once Devadatta had awakened and saw that the lecture hall was empty, he fell from his bed in a state of confusion and distress.
At that time, his four companions sprinkled him with cold water, and he regained consciousness, thinking to himself:
"I am the Great Man of the Śākya clan, Gautama; I cannot be humbled or made to submit to another.
He said to the bhikṣus:
"Previously, the teachings of the non-Buddhists had become obscured and were not clearly understood; I shall now bring them forth, clarify them, and abide within these teachings."
"You should all know that from this day forward, I no longer belong to the śramaṇa Gautama.
When these words were spoken, it was termed "abandoning the precepts.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have sought an opportunity against Devadatta and quickly found it.
The Buddha said:
"Not only has Devadatta found an opportunity against me in this present life, but he has also found such an opportunity in past lives.
Listen well now!
The Buddha then related the causes and conditions of his previous births in detail, saying to the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a master archer who had many disciples.
The master thought to himself:
'Among my disciples, the one most skilled shall be given my daughter as a wife, along with a chariot drawn by four horses, a thousand arrows in a case, and a thousand pieces of gold.'"

Subsequently, knowing that one disciple was most skillful at archery, he immediately gave his daughter to him in marriage, along with a chariot drawn by four horses, a thousand arrows attached to hairpins, and a thousand pieces of gold.

The disciple returned to his residence with the girl in a single carriage. On the road, there were a thousand bandits; seeing them, the other people said to the disciple, "There are a thousand bandits here;
do not take this path, lest you be harassed by the bandits."
This disciple, having given rise to a mind of arrogance and relying on his own skills, departed along that road.

At that time, a thousand bandits had descended by the side of the road to eat; the disciple stopped his carriage in the middle of the path and sent his wife to speak to the leader of the bandits, saying:
"Give me my share of the food."
The wife immediately went to him and said to the leader of the bandits,
"A certain master archer sent me here specifically to request my share of the food.
The leader of the bandits then thought to himself:
"Since such a messenger was sent on this road, he must certainly be fearless; we should give him his share of food.
All the bandits, filled with anxiety, thought to themselves:
"What is the use of us living?"
"Why not kill this man, take this woman as your wife, and use the four-horse chariot, the thousand arrows, and the thousand pieces of gold?
He said to the woman, "Go back; you shall receive no share of the food."
The woman replied,
"He is unwilling to give us our share of the food.
He sent another messenger to speak with her again, saying:
"If you are unwilling to give me my share of food, each of you must rise, arm yourselves, and come together to fight.
He went back and spoke these words again.

Then, one hundred men from among those bandits armed themselves and came to fight; the disciple killed those hundred with a hundred arrows. In this manner, he dealt with two hundred, three hundred, and so on, up to nine hundred and ninety-nine men, leaving only one arrow remaining to confront the leader of the bandits.
The leader of the bandits thought to himself:
"What use is this life to me?
A single man has slaughtered a thousand people."
He immediately rose, took up his staff, grasped his bow, and nocked an arrow.
Both men were skilled archers and each sought an opportunity against the other.
The disciple thought to himself:
"How might I find an opportunity?
he thought. He then said to his wife:
"Move away from him for a short while and dance, shaking your body so that your ornaments make a sound and you reveal your form by lifting your garment."
The woman immediately began to sing and dance to one side, moving her body so that her ornaments made a sound and she raised her garment to reveal herself.
Upon seeing and hearing this, the leader of the bandits was moved by desire; his disciple, seizing the opportunity, shot an arrow and killed him.
The Buddha said:
"As for that archery master at that time, could he have been anyone else?
It was none other than myself."
The disciple was Śāriputra;
the woman was Maudgalyāyana;
and the leader of the bandits at that time was Devadatta.
"At that time, those two sought an opportunity and found it; now, they have again sought an opportunity and found it.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively related this Jātaka tale.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘schism in the Saṃgha,’ what constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha?
To what extent does one reach the designation of ‘schism in the Saṃgha’?”
The Buddha said to Upāli: “There are fourteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
one may employ whichever among these is appropriate. The fourteen are: teaching what is not Dharma as Dharma, teaching Dharma as not Dharma;

teaching what is not virtuous as virtuous, teaching what is virtuous as not virtuous; teaching an offense as no offense, teaching no offense as an offense; teaching a light matter as heavy, teaching a heavy matter as light; teaching what has a remainder as being without remainder, teaching what is without remainder as having a remainder; teaching a practice that is always followed as not a practice always followed, teaching a practice that is not always followed as a practice always followed; and teaching what is not a formal statement as a formal statement, teaching a formal statement as not a formal statement.”
In this regard, to speak what is not Dharma as Dharma is a sthūlātyaya;
to speak Dharma as non-Dharma is a sthūlātyaya;
to speak what is not wholesome as wholesome is a sthūlātyaya.
To speak of what is wholesome as unwholesome is a sthūlātyaya.
To speak of what is not an offense as an offense is a sthūlātyaya.
To speak of what is an offense as not an offense is a sthūlātyaya.
To say there is a remainder when there is no remainder is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To say there is no remainder when there is a remainder is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak of what is light as being heavy is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak of a light offense as grave constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak of a practice that is regularly performed as a practice not regularly performed constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak of a practice not regularly performed as a practice regularly performed constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak what is not the teaching as the teaching is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
To speak the teaching as what is not the teaching is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a bhikṣu teaches what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and by means of this non-Dharma instructs the assembly to subdue it and break the harmony of the Saṃgha—having broken the harmony of the Saṃgha, he incurs a great sin; having incurred that great sin, for the duration of one kalpa he shall fall into the Avīci Hell.

If a bhikṣu speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaks Dharma as not Dharma; speaks what is not wholesome as wholesome, speaks what is wholesome as not wholesome; speaks what is an offense as no offense, speaks what is no offense as an offense; speaks what has a remainder as having no remainder, speaks what has no remainder as having a remainder; speaks what is light as heavy, speaks what is heavy as light; speaks what is a customary practice as not a customary practice, speaks what is not a customary practice as a customary practice; speaks what is not a formal teaching as a formal teaching, speaks what is a formal teaching as not a formal teaching.

If a bhikṣu, by means of these fourteen unlawful matters, instructs the assembly to suppress it and causes the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, having caused the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha, he incurs a great offense; having incurred that great offense, for the duration of one kalpa he shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
Upāli! These fourteen matters are called "schism in the Saṃgha.
If any one of these fourteen matters is employed, it is likewise called "schism in the Saṃgha."

If a bhikṣu perceives what is contrary to the Dharma as contrary to the Dharma, conceives a view contrary to the Dharma regarding the schism of the Saṃgha, and knowing that the schism of the Saṃgha is contrary to the Dharma, causes a schism with such a mind, he incurs an ānantarya offense.

If a bhikṣu perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and while causing a schism in the Saṃgha harbors doubt, yet proceeds to cause the schism with that very mind, he incurs the immediate offense (ānantarya).
If a bhikṣu perceives what is not Dharma as not Dharma, but while causing a schism in the Saṃgha holds the view that it is Dharma, this person does not incur the immediate offense.
If a bhikṣu perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma and, while causing a schism in the Saṃgha, holds the view that it is Dharma, this bhikṣu does not incur the ānantarya offense.
If a bhikṣu perceives what is not Dharma as Dharma and, regarding the causes and conditions for the schism of the Saṃgha, harbors doubt, this bhikṣu does not incur the ānantarya offense.
Upāli again asked the Buddha,
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘a harmonious Saṃgha’?”
The Buddha said to Upāli:
“There are fourteen matters that are called ‘schism in the Saṃgha’;
if these matters are extinguished, it is called ‘harmony in the Saṃgha.’”

Fourteenth: To declare what is not Dharma as not Dharma, and what is Dharma as Dharma; to declare what is wholesome as wholesome, and what is unwholesome as unwholesome; to declare an offense as an offense, and a non-offense as a non-offense; to declare what involves a remainder as involving a remainder, and what is without remainder as without remainder; to declare a light offense as light, and a heavy offense as heavy; to declare a practice that is always to be followed as a practice always to be followed, and a practice not always to be followed as a practice not always to be followed; and to declare what has been spoken as having been spoken, and what has not been spoken as not having been spoken.

If a bhikṣu speaks of what is not Dharma as being not Dharma, and by this teaching he disciplines the assembly, reconciles the divided assembly, and restores the broken assembly, he will eternally enjoy the bliss of the heavens.

If a bhikṣu speaks of what is Dharma as being Dharma, and by this teaching he disciplines the assembly, reconciles the divided assembly, and restores the broken assembly, he will eternally enjoy the bliss of the heavens.

If a bhikṣu speaks well of what is well-spoken, and speaks not well of what is not well-spoken; speaks of an offense as an offense, and speaks of what is not an offense as not an offense; speaks of what entails a remainder as having a remainder, and speaks of what is without a remainder as being without a remainder; speaks of what is light as light, and speaks of what is heavy as heavy; speaks of a rule that is always to be practiced as a rule always to be practiced, and speaks of a rule not always to be practiced as not always to be practiced; and speaks of what is spoken as spoken, and speaks of what is not spoken as not spoken.
If one uses these fourteen methods to instruct the assembly, subdue the assembly, reconcile a divided assembly, and cause them to eternally enjoy the bliss of the heavens—
this is called the "harmonization of the Saṃgha through fourteen matters."
"If a bhikṣu, from among these fourteen matters, employs whichever matter is appropriate to bring the Saṃgha into harmony, he will eternally enjoy the bliss of the heavens.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"A single bhikṣu cannot break a harmonious Saṃgha; nor can two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [bhikṣus] break a harmonious Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha of bhikṣus can be split by as few as nine bhikṣus who are pure and share the same view. Upāli!
A single bhikṣuṇī cannot split a harmonious Saṃgha; nor can two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine bhikṣuṇīs who are pure and share the same view split a harmonious Saṃgha.

Upāli! A single śikṣamāṇā, a single śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, or a single male or female renunciant cannot cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha. Nor can two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine who are pure and hold the same view cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha.
Upāli! There are two causes and conditions by which a schism in the Saṃgha is defined:
first, the formal proclamation; second, the taking of voting sticks.
"Proclaiming" refers to, for example, when Devadatta, within the Saṃgha, proclaims up to a second and third time:
"I, Devadatta, speak these words.
"Taking the voting sticks" refers to, for example, when Devadatta, having finished his initial proclamation, takes the voting sticks together with his four companions.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
Can a bhikṣu who has been expelled cause a schism in the Saṃgha?”

Furthermore, can those who follow and comply with the monk under suspension, those who assist those who follow and comply with him; or those who carry out the suspension, those who follow and comply with those who carry it out, and those who assist those who follow and comply with them; or the Great Elder and the monks who follow and comply with the Great Elder, and those who assist those who follow and comply with the Great Elder—all of these cause a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
"All bhikṣus are capable of causing a schism in the Saṃgha, with the sole exception of one who has been expelled, who cannot cause a schism.
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were beating their own bodies with wooden clubs.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent! You are virtuous. [The Buddha said:
"One should discipline oneself with a wooden staff, like a king or a great minister.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not treat the body with wooden sticks.
To do so is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The bhikṣus then treated their bodies with wooden balls, whereupon the Buddha said:
“From now on, it is not permitted to treat the body with wooden balls.
Whoever treats it thus commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus bathed and used a razor to scrape off the hair from their bodies. The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
Yet they bathe and shave their body hair and remove it, just like kings or great ministers."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, when bathing, you are not permitted to use a razor to scrape off body hair.
To do so is a *duṣkṛta* offense."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Caṅgī who had much body hair. After bathing, the water remaining in his hair made his clothes damp and ruined, and his body became foul-smelling. He reported this matter to the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will permit the use of a razor to scrape away the water while bathing."
The Buddha said,
"It is permitted.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus smeared their bodies with incense, and the lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
“Various bhikṣus say of themselves:
‘We are virtuous and excellent.
They smear their bodies with fragrant perfumes, like kings or high ministers.”
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you are not permitted to smear fragrances upon your bodies.
To do so is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The group of six bhikṣus massaged their bodies with their palms, and the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
"Using the palms to massage the body, as a king or a high minister does.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit using the palms to massage the body."
To massage one's own body constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are two types of palms:
the palm of the hand and the sole of the foot.
To treat with the palms of the hands is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
to treat with the soles of the feet is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To treat with any other part of the body, excluding the palms and soles, is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were massaging their bodies against a pillar. When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, you are not permitted to massage your bodies against a pillar."
If one uses a wall for this purpose, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus used a wall to groom their bodies and used a stone to groom their bodies. The Buddha said:
“From now on, you should not use a wall or a stone to groom your bodies.”
"If one treats [the patient] in this manner, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Śreṇika Mānamantṛputra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Having understood that the Buddha had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, Śreṇika Māṇava prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night. Rising early in the morning, he arranged the seating and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; may the Holy One know the proper time."

At that time, the bhikṣus anointed their feet with oil; because this country was full of dust, it settled upon the bhikṣus' feet. When the laywomen (gṛhapatnī) wished to pay homage, they would take the bhikṣus' feet in both hands, and only after washing their hands would they take up their bowls and serve the food.
A bhikṣu said to a householder’s wife,
“First wash your hands and then take hold of the bowl.
She replied:
"It has been washed.
If you had not come up with your feet smeared with oil, what fault would there have been?
The Buddha saw that the householder’s wife was reproaching the bhikṣu for doing such a thing.
After the Buddha had finished his meal, he returned to the monastery and, having assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should not enter the homes of laypeople with oil smeared on your feet."
"To enter the house of a layperson with oil applied to one's feet is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, if there is mud or a wound, applying it and entering is not an offense.
The group of six bhikṣus then smeared oil on their heads, and the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent,' yet they smear their heads with oil just like white-robed laymen."
The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to smear oil on his head.
To do so is a duṣkṛta offense."
"If one has newly shaved one's hair, or has a headache, or has applied ointment inside the dwelling, there is no offense.
The group of six bhikṣus adorned their faces and bodies, whereupon the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus themselves claim:"
"Excellent and virtuous!
Your countenance is adorned like that of a king or a high minister.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not adorn your faces.
To adorn them is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Because of this prohibition against adornment, the group of six bhikṣus painted their eyes.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
“They painted eyes like those of a king or a high minister.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
“From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣus to paint eyes for the sake of adornment.”
To paint [an image] is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
There are five kinds of painting eyes: first, painting with ink;
second, painting with *āñjana* (ultra-blue); third, painting with various pigments; fourth, painting with flowers; and fifth, painting with tree resin.
"If one draws eyes for the purpose of treating a disease, there is no offense.
The group of six bhikṣus tied threads around their wrists, and the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus say of themselves:..."
"Excellent and virtuous!
Having said this, he tied multicolored threads around his wrists, just as a king or a high minister does.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted to tie threads of various colors around the wrist.
To do so is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus draped threads across their armpits, and the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
“Some bhikṣus say of themselves:
‘We are virtuous and excellent,’ yet they wear their robes over one shoulder with a cord under the arm, like brahmins.”
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to wear a thread around his armpit.
To wear a thread around the armpit is a duṣkṛta offense."
The group of six bhikṣus kept articles for adorning the body, and the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"He keeps ornaments for adorning the body and adorns himself with them, like a king or a high minister.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣus to keep ornaments for adorning the body."
"To possess [such items] is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus adorned themselves with armlets;
the Buddha said, "One should not possess armlets to adorn oneself."
"To keep [such items] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus wore finger rings like kings or high ministers.
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear finger rings.
To wear them is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus wore necklaces; the Buddha said:
“A bhikṣu should not wear ornaments.
To wear them is a duṣkṛta offense.
The group of six bhikṣus wore thread bracelets on their arms, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not wear thread bracelets on his arms.
To wear them is a duṣkṛta offense.
The group of six bhikṣus pierced their ears with gold and silver earrings; the Buddha said:
"One must not pierce the ears with a lock-shaped earpick.
To pierce the ears [with such a tool] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Elder Bāḍhi, while formerly a layman, used a grape-leaf-shaped earpick; even after becoming a bhikṣu, he continued to use it due to his former habitual tendencies.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying, "These bhikṣus wear grape-leaf tongs; they look like kings or high ministers.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not wear them.
To wear them is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Because the Buddha had prohibited all ornaments, the group of six bhikṣus then made ear-rings from silk, cloth-cord, tree leaves, tree bark, wood, pewter, lead, and tin, and wore them. The laypeople said:
"You do not wear earrings made of gold or silver leaves; what need have you for ear-rings?
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣus to wear ear-rings made of silk, cloth-cord, tree leaves, tree bark, wood, white tin, lead, or pewter."
"To wear [ornaments], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Even to pierce the earlobes with a blade of grass, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore earrings; the Buddha said:
"One should not wear earrings;
to wear them is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus kept precious items for binding their hair.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"Keeping hair-binding jeweled objects, such as those used by kings or high ministers.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, you should not keep hair-binding jeweled objects."
"To keep [such items] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus wore golden garlands.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
‘We are virtuous and excellent,’ yet they wear golden garlands like kings or great ministers.”
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not wear a golden garland.
One who wears one commits a duṣkṛta offense."
Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus polished their nails until they were white. The Buddha said:
"One should not polish the nails until they are white.
To do so is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the bhikṣus entered Rājagṛha to beg for food and obtained āmra fruits and āmra fruit soup.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not permitted us to accept āmra fruits or āmra fruit soup."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit bhikṣus to accept *āmra* fruits and *āmra* fruit soups.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra had an *āmra* tree that always bore fruit. Because the king had faith and reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma, he asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you eat the mango fruit? He replied, "I did."
The king said, "Eat these mango fruits from my tree.

This fruit-guardian did not have faith or reverence for the Buddha-dharma; although there were fine, yellow, ripe fruits, he had reserved them as the king’s portion, as well as the portions for the queen, the prince, and the high ministers and officials.
Among these fruits, there were those that were unripe, green, bruised, or damaged by insects and birds; [the keeper] brought these to give to the bhikṣus.
When the group of six bhikṣus arrived at that place, they took the ripe, yellow, and excellent fruits and said to the fruit-keeper:
"Give them to us."
The person replied, "You have already taken [it]; why must you receive it again?
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community of bhikṣus, he asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu who first touches a mango fruit himself and then receives it from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) to eat?"
From now on, monks, if one touches an āmra fruit with one's own hand and subsequently receives it from a *kappiya-kāraka*, one should not eat it.
To eat it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
"Just as with the mango fruit, so it is with all other fruits.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala sent a messenger to King Bimbisāra, praising King Prasenajit by saying:

"Our King is virtuous and possesses great merit; four jars spontaneously become filled with milk to provide for the King’s drink, and non-glutinous rice spontaneously fills eight pecks daily to provide for the King’s food."
King Bimbisāra also praised his own country, saying:
"In this land of mine, mangoes grow perennially; and from the trees of the householder Jotika, exquisite garments are produced."
King Bimbisāra immediately dispatched a messenger with orders for the park keeper to deliver some mangoes.
The park keeper thought to himself:
"Because of this incident of the śramaṇa taking the fruit, the World-Honored One will surely prohibit the bhikṣus from eating mangoes."
The park keeper then said to the king’s messenger, “There are no mangoes in this garden;
all the fruit has already been eaten by the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.”
The messenger returned and reported to the king:
"The park keeper said:
'All the mangoes have already been eaten by the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.'"
The King said:
"I myself know that this is not the time for fruit.
If there were even a small amount, it could be shown to that messenger so that he might recognize its appearance."
After the park keeper had obtained a small amount of fruit, he went to present it to the king.
A bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this matter and was displeased; he rebuked him, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣu if, while eating mangoes that are always in season, he causes the consecrated king to send his own messenger and yet fail to obtain them?"
Having rebuked him, he reported this matter to the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community, the Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu eat the mango fruit while it is still growing on the tree, such that when the consecrated king sent his own messenger to seek it, he could not obtain it?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, one must not eat the *āmra* fruit that bears fruit constantly.
Whoever eats it commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, some bhikṣus entered Śrāvastī to beg for food and received āmra soup.
The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not accept it, thinking to themselves:
"We fear we shall fall into the fault of begging for choice food.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"If others give it of their own accord without being asked, you may accept it."
In a certain monastery in the kingdom of Kosala, the Saṃgha received a gift of fruit. The bhikṣus did not know what to do about it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be consumed after being prepared as five kinds of *kalpya* (permissible) food."
"What are the five?
Purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by claw, purification by parrot, and purification by non-production of offspring.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Kṛmīla.
At that time, Aniruddha’s fellow disciple suffered from dry mouth; the physician instructed him to hold an *āmalaka* fruit in his mouth, saying that his condition would thus be cured.
The disciple replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted me to hold an *āmalaka* fruit in my mouth."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow a bhikṣu whose mouth is diseased to hold an āmalaka fruit in his mouth.
For what reason? Because it is beneficial for the mouth."
"It is because it is suitable for the condition of dry mouth.

There was a monastery in the kingdom of Kośala where monks received a gift of fruit; they accepted it from a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) before it had been formally purified (anupasampanna). The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should eat the outer skin; do not eat the seeds.
[This occurred] while the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the householder Jyotiṣka was away on business when a traveler returned from the ocean carrying a piece of sandalwood as a gift for him.
The householder was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable quantities of gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, coral, and other such treasures.
Having obtained this sandalwood, he did not take it to heart; instead, he had it fashioned into a sandalwood bowl, placed it inside a netted bag, and suspended it from a high ivory peg.
He then spoke these words:
"If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa can obtain it by means of a ladder or a staff, let them take it."
At that time, Pūrṇa Kāśyapa, hearing that the householder Jyotiṣka had made a sandalwood bowl for him, went at once to ask:
"Did you make a sandalwood bowl for me?"
The householder replied, "I have made a sandalwood bowl and hung it high upon an ivory peg; I shall give it to any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can obtain it without using a ladder or a staff."
Pūrṇa thought to himself,
"This householder wishes to see my supernormal powers," and he immediately tore off his head and departed.

Māgandiya-putta, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Ajita Keśakambalin, hearing that the householder Jotika was making sandalwood bowls for me, went to his place and asked:
"Are you making sandalwood bowls for us?"

The householder said, "I have made a sandalwood bowl and hung it high upon an ivory peg; I will give it to any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can obtain it without using a ladder or a staff—it is not that I would not give it."
They all thought to themselves,
"This householder wishes to see the power of supernatural transformations," and they gouged out their own eyes and departed.

At that time, the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja heard that the householder Jyotiṣka had made a sandalwood bowl-case and hung it on a high ivory peg, saying that he would give it to any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who could obtain it without using a ladder or a staff, and would not give it otherwise.
Having heard this, he went to where Maudgalyāyana was and said:
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
Do you know?"
The householder Jyotiṣka made a sandalwood bowl and placed it inside a net-bag, hanging it high upon a peg made of ivory, saying:
"I shall give this to any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can take it without using a ladder or a staff; otherwise, I shall not give it."
Maudgalyāyana said, "Among those who give the lion's roar, you are the foremost; you may go and fetch it.

Then, at dawn, the Elder Piṇḍola Bharadvāja put on his robes, took up his bowl, and with excellent deportment in walking, standing, sitting, and standing, went to the house of the householder Jyotiṣka.
The householder Jyotiṣka saw from afar that Piṇḍola was walking, standing, sitting, and standing with pure deportment, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl; he thought to himself:
"A bhikṣu who walks, stands, sits, and stands with such pure deportment, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl, will certainly be able to take the bowl."
The householder immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward Piṇḍola, and said:
"Welcome, Bhāradvāja!
It has been a long time since you last came here."
He was commanded to take a seat and sat down. The householder Jotika bowed his head at the feet of Pāṭikāputra; once Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja was seated, he asked the householder:
"Is it true that you made a sandalwood bowl, placed it inside a net-bag, and hung it on a high ivory peg, saying:
'I shall give it to any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can take it without using a ladder or a staff; otherwise, I will not give it'?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
Piṇḍola then entered such a state of meditative concentration that he reached out his hand from his seat, took the bowl, and showed it to the lay devotee.
The householder said,
"As I previously stated, it now belongs to you.
The householder spoke again:
"Come here for a moment.
He immediately took the bowl and went inside, filled it to the brim with cooked rice, and presented it to Piṇḍola.
After Piṇḍola had finished eating, he took the bowl and showed it to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Look at this bowl; its fragrance is excellent and delightful.
The bhikṣus said, "It is indeed so!"
"From where did you obtain it?
Piṇḍola then recounted the aforementioned events in detail.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing these matters, he was displeased and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked him, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, for the sake of the property of naked ascetics, manifest superhuman noble dharmas before one who has not received the full ordination?
Having rebuked him, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, "Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One!
The Buddha rebuked Piṇḍola in various ways and by many causes and conditions:
“How can it be that a bhikṣu, for the sake of a wooden bowl belonging to a naked ascetic, manifests superhuman noble dharmas before one who has not received full ordination?”
Having rebuked him, he said to Pāṭala:
"I banish you for as long as your life lasts; you must not remain here in Jambudvīpa.

Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Piṇḍola bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and returned to his own quarters. He then returned all the bedding, mats, beds, and couches belonging to the Saṃgha that he had been using to the Saṃgha.

Carrying his robe and bowl, he entered such a meditative concentration that he vanished from Jambudvīpa and appeared in Aparagoyānī. Having arrived, he extensively taught and transformed many upāsakas and upāsikās; he took on many disciples, established monasteries and dwellings, maintained co-practitioners and resident disciples, and widely proclaimed the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the Buddha dispatched Piṇḍola and, before long, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the monks, he addressed them:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to keep the eight kinds of bowls."
What are the eight?
A golden bowl, a silver bowl, a lapis lazuli bowl, a maṇi-jewel bowl, a copper bowl, a white tin bowl, a wooden bowl, and a stone bowl.
To keep [an extra bowl] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
I allow you all to keep two kinds of bowls:
iron bowls and clay bowls.
The earthen bowl was easily broken, so the Buddha said,
"Repair it. Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what should it be sewn?
The Buddha said,
"It should be made with wool, kusa grass, cotton, hemp, muñja grass, or vāra grass."
Because that country was very hot, insects grew within the seams.
The Buddha said:
"The seams should be undone; after they have been aired in the sun, they may be re-sewn."
The bhikṣus were exhausted from untying, drying, and reassembling their bowls day after day.
There was a bhikṣu who was skilled at forging copper, and he said to the Buddha:
"I pray that you will permit us to repair bowls using two kinds of materials."
"Whether it be iron or copper.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to use either iron or copper."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu, having given rise to lustful thoughts, cut off his own male organ, suffering such agony that he was on the verge of death.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Look at this foolish person!
He should abandon what is different, yet he abandons what is different.
That which should be abandoned is greed, hatred, and delusion.”
Having rebuked them in this way, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I do not permit the cutting off of the male organ.
Whoever cuts it off commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, while splitting wood for bathing purposes, was bitten on a finger by a venomous snake emerging from a rotten log.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This poison will surely enter my body."
He immediately cut off his own finger; it was because of this that his finger remained stumped.
When the lay devotees entered the monastery and saw the bhikṣu with a stumped finger, they said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, also have stumped fingers."
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it to the Buddha.
For various reasons, the Buddha rebuked him:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu cut off his own fingers?"
Having thus rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not cut off your own fingers.
Whoever cuts off their own fingers commits a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha said:
"From now on, in such circumstances, I allow you to wrap your fingers with a cord and use a knife to lance out the poison.
There were six groups of bhikṣus who went to watch performances of music, song, and dance; the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
Yet they go to watch and listen to music, song, and dance, like kings or great ministers."
Among them were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it to the Buddha.
Knowing [the situation], the Buddha asked the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu go of his own accord to watch or listen to music, singing, and dancing?
Having thus rebuked him, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, bhikṣus should not go to watch or listen to music, singing, or dancing.
To go and watch is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, when the group of six bhikṣus sang themselves, the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent,' yet they sing like laypeople."
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, they were displeased and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should not sing."
To sing is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are five faults in singing:
attachment of one's own mind; [and so forth].
Causing others to become greedily attached;
frequently giving rise to discursive thought and investigation when dwelling alone;
and having one's mind constantly shrouded by sensual desire.
When the laypeople heard this, they said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, also sing; they are no different from us.
Furthermore, there were five faults:
One is personally attached through craving;
one causes others to give rise to attachment;
and one frequently gives rise to discursive thought and investigation while dwelling alone.
"His mind is constantly shrouded by greed;
when other young bhikṣus hear him, they likewise follow his example, and having so followed, they constantly give rise to greedy thoughts and thus violate the precepts.
There was a bhikṣu named Baddhi, who was foremost in chanting; as this bhikṣu had a beautiful voice, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will permit me to perform vocal chanting.
The Buddha said:
“Listen, you may perform the melodic recitation (*bhāṣya*).
There are five benefits to such recitation:
the body does not grow weary, what has been memorized is not forgotten, the mind does not become fatigued, the voice is not impaired, and the speech is easily understood.”
Furthermore, there are five benefits:

the body does not become exhausted; one does not forget what has been remembered; the mind does not grow weary; the voice does not deteriorate; and when the gods hear the sound of the chanting, their hearts are filled with joy.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had eaten from their iron bowls, they placed the bowls on the ground; moisture arose and caused them to spoil. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow you to place a piece of worn-out cloth beneath the bowl."
"In this country it is very hot, and insects breed within the inner robe.
The Buddha said, "You should make an item for holding the bowl.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what material should the bowl-rest be made?
The Buddha said,
"It should be made of white tin, lead, or pewter."
Because insects were born after it was made, the Buddha said:
"One should construct a stand for the bowl.
After it was made, the earthenware bowl fell to the ground from the stand and broke; the Buddha said:
"It should be placed inside a box.
When the alms bowl was placed in the box, it made a clattering sound as it touched other items.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to wrap it in a piece of coarse cloth before placing it in the box."

The Elder Cūḍapanthaka washed a clay bowl and set it out in the sun; as the heat caused moisture to exude, he said to the bhikṣus, "This clay bowl is impure and greasy; bhikṣus should not use it for food."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked Udāyin:
“You indeed washed the earthenware bowl and placed it in the sun during the day until moisture exuded from it, and then said to the bhikṣus:
‘The earthenware bowl has become greasy and impure; bhikṣus should not use it for food.’”
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"From now on, after washing an earthenware bowl, you must not place it in the sun to dry.
To place it in the sun is an *dukkaṭa* offense."

At that time, a bhikṣu had a costly robe which he wished to wash clean in water and then cut and sew into a garment. As he was biting the edges with his teeth or pulling them apart, the robe became torn and shredded here and there in every direction. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit you to keep a small knife at the beginning of each month for the purpose of cutting garments."
At that time, they sewed their robes using chicken feathers and bird feathers; once sewn, the robes were easily damaged, frayed, and shrank. The Buddha said:
"I allow the use of two kinds of needles:
iron needles and copper needles, with pointed noses, round noses, or square noses."
At that time, the bhikṣus sewed their robes while holding them on their laps; as they sewed, the fabric became wrinkled.
The Buddha said, "Spread [the robe] on the ground and sew.
When the bhikṣus spread it on the ground to sew, soil adhered to it. The Buddha said:
"One should smear the ground with cow dung.
At times, it might not be level; the Buddha said:
"I allow you to bind the four edges with cords."
After it had been sewn, some parts were not straight;
the Buddha said, "Smooth it out in every place.
At times, some parts were uneven; the Buddha said:
"Carve wood to serve as a gauge.
When sewing, the needle would not reach the front, and his fingertips were wounded and broken. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use a finger-stick."
At that time, needles, knives, tweezers, and wooden probes were each kept in different places and were difficult to find when needed. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to place them in a single location using a container."
When sewing the patchwork robe, they were fond of damaging the borders;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to attach a simulated border.
When this robe was spread out on the outside, it was easily lost; the Buddha said:
"Listen to the folding.
When he was about to roll it up, he joyfully unrolled it.
The Buddha said, "Bind it with a cord."
At another time, when wind and rain soiled their robes, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear them while in a sheltered place.
While wearing them in a sheltered place on the ground, insects began to eat them; the Buddha said:
"Listen to the driving of a peg against the wall.
At that time, the head of the peg was slippery and his robe fell to the ground.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a curved-headed peg."
The bhikṣus varied in height; some were short and had to cut and sew their robes and beds to fit their bodies, while others were tall and had to search elsewhere for longer beds. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to bore holes at both ends so that they may protrude, enabling them to be used in common."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used mirrors to reflect their faces. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit reflecting one's face.
To reflect one's face is a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus either reflected their faces in their alms bowls or reflected them in water. The Buddha said:
"If one reflects one's face in an alms bowl or in water, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"If one is tending to a facial sore, there is no offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus combed their hair with a comb. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu must not comb his hair with a comb."
"If one combs the hair, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus also used a brush to brush their heads; the Buddha said:
"If one brushes [the head], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus left a small amount of hair on the crown of their heads. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit leaving [hair] behind."
"If one leaves it [the hair] [in that manner], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus left their hair curled; the Buddha said:
"One should not leave the hair curled."
"If one leaves it [the hair] [to grow], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus left their hair to grow long. The Buddha said:
"One should not leave the hair to grow long."
If one leaves it [longer than that], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, for a forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu, there is no offense if it grows to two inches in length.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from leprosy and scabies who said to the physician Jīvaka,
"Cure my illness.
Jīvaka replied:
"One may enter the bathhouse to wash and thus recover.
The bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted entering the bathhouse to wash."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to enter the bathhouse to wash.
There are five merits to washing: [text continues]"

First, the removal of impurities; second, the purification of the body; third, the elimination of cold-related ailments within the body; fourth, the alleviation of wind disorders; and fifth, the attainment of peace and security.
At that time, there was no seating in the bathhouse, and the bhikṣus had nowhere to sit while bathing. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to install seats within the bathhouse."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what material should it be made?
The Buddha said:
"It was made using wood, stone, and bricks.
At that time, mud came out from the floor of the bathhouse, and the bhikṣus washed with muddy water.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to install a wooden bench in the bathhouse."
Upāli asked the Buddha,
"What material should be used to make a bench?
The Buddha said:
"It was made with wood, stone, and bricks.
At that time, a fire-pit was placed inside the bathhouse, and the bhikṣus felt uneasy while bathing. The Buddha said:
"It should be fixed securely against the wall."
At that time, they did not construct a hearth, and the flames rose directly upward to the roof.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to install a hearth.
When firewood was placed into the hearth all at once, the intensity of the fire had already subsided by the time a later bhikṣu came to wash it; the Buddha said:
"Use a pair of tongs.
At that time, when he was placing long firewood, it tended to fall; if he tried to lift it with his hands, his hands would be burned.
The Buddha said, "Lift it with a fork."
When he was about to lift the fork, the bhikṣu’s head, being hairless, became hot and painful. The Buddha said:
"Cover the head with a moist object.
At that time, [the bhikṣu] required earth to smear upon his body; the Buddha said:
"One should keep a vessel for holding soil.
At that time, when water was needed, the Buddha said:
"One should keep a vessel for holding water."
At that time, the water vessel was too small.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep a jar.
When the jar was filled with water, it was placed upon the hearth; then a piece of firewood fell onto it, breaking the jar. The Buddha said:
"Drill a hole in the wall, fix a wooden frame, and place a water jar within it.
At that time, the jar was so high that some bhikṣus could not reach it to fetch water.
The Buddha said, "It should not be placed so high."
At that time, when [the bowl] was placed in a low position, a bhikṣu bumped it with his shoulder. The Buddha said:
"It must not be too low or too high; it should be placed level with the shoulder or level with the head."
At that time, wind entered the bathhouse because it had no door.
The Buddha said, "A door and panels should be installed.
At that time, when the bhikṣus entered the bathhouse, they were unable to close the door. The Buddha said:
"Let one bhikṣu look after the door.
At that time, because the bathhouse had no windows, it was dark; the Buddha said, "Install windows."
At that time, because the bathhouse had no place for smoke to exit, it became blackened by soot.
The Buddha said, "Provide a place for the smoke to exit.
At that time, some bhikṣus used soap powder while others used earth; because of the damp heat, insects bred in the bathhouse. The Buddha said:
"One should wash it away until it is clean.
At that time, there was a great deal of water in the bathhouse, so the Buddha said:
"One should drain the water."
When the bhikṣus emerged from the water, some were nauseated or fell ill.
The Buddha said, "One should install a drainage pipe.
Inside the drainage pipe there were snakes, scorpions, and centipedes, which crawled in and stung the bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"One should cover the openings of the water drains with woven cloth.
At that time, after finishing his bath, a monk left the bathhouse without taking anything; later, the bathhouse was consumed by fire. The Buddha said:
"The last monk to leave should collect all the articles, remove the jars and pots, extinguish the fire, close the door, and lower the bolt before departing."
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī. There was a householder there named Mahānāman, who was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and treasures, and possessed great estates, lands, and power.
There was a bhikṣu named Kālodāyin who was an old acquaintance of this elder, with whom he had long been familiar and who came and went between them.
At the time for the meal, Kālodāyin put on his robes, took up his bowl and sitting mat, and went to where Mahānāman Licchavi was.
Seeing the bhikṣu approaching from afar, Li Chang praised him, saying: "Welcome!
Please sit here."
He immediately spread out his sitting mat.
Then Mahānāman Licchavi bowed his head at the [monk’s] feet and sat to one side.
The bhikṣu said to Mahānāman Licchavi:
"You should now go to the Blessed One and speak to him thus:
'How can a bhikṣu engage in unchaste conduct?
This son of the Malla Dhānañjaya has engaged in unchaste conduct with my wife.'"
The mahānāman Licchavi said to Kālodayin,
“How can you baselessly slander a pure bhikṣu?
The bhikṣu Kālodayin replied to the mahānāman Licchavi:
"If I do not speak these words to the Buddha, I shall no longer converse with you, nor shall I enter your house.
Because Mahānāman Licchavi deeply loved and respected this bhikṣu, he immediately thought:
"If I do not say these words, the bhikṣu Kālopa-tiśya will certainly not speak with me, nor will he enter my house."
He then said to the bhikṣu,
"I shall speak these words to the Buddha.
At that time, Mahānāma Licchavi went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bhikṣu engage in unchaste conduct?
This son of the Malla, Dabba Mallaputta, has engaged in unchaste conduct with my wife.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you, turn over your alms bowls and do not go to the house of the great official Li Chang.
Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs must not go to the house of the great official Li Chang to receive food with their own hands."
Furthermore, there are such persons who should also have their *pātra* (alms bowl) overturned.
The procedure for overturning the *pātra* is as follows: the Saṃgha should assemble with one mind, and one bhikṣu should proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This Mahānāman Licchavi has slandered the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta, who is pure in his holy life, by charging him with a groundless *pārājika* offense.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and listening, grant in unison this Mahānāman Licchavi the *pātra-ovaddha* (the overturning of the alms-bowl).
"O bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, you must not go to this household to receive food with your own hands; thus it is announced."
"A formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* [is performed]:
'The Saṃgha has completed the overturning of the bowl; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
“The Saṃgha has already performed the *pātrāvavartana* (turning down of the bowl) against the great man Licchavi.
No bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs shall go to the house of the great man Licchavi to receive food with their own hands.”
The bhikṣus again had this thought:
"Who could go to the house of the elder and speak these words:
'The Saṃgha has overturned its bowl'?"
No bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs shall go to your house to receive food with their own hands.
He further thought:
"The Elder Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant; among all the bhikṣus, he praises pure brahmacarya. Ānanda is capable of going to this great and famous house of Licchavi and speaking these words:

'The Saṃgha has already performed the *pātra-nyāma* (the overturning of the bowl); no bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī shall henceforth receive food with their own hands at your home.'"
The bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us go to Ānanda and say this:

'The Saṃgha has already performed the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa* (the overturning of the bowl) against Mahānāman Licchavi; therefore, no bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī shall go to Mahānāman Licchavi’s house to receive food with their own hands.'"
After the bhikṣus had spoken these words, they went to where Ānanda was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable Ānanda!"

"The Sangha has already performed the *pātra-nyubja* (turning-over of the bowl) against Mahānāman Licchavi; none of the five classes of monastics may go to Mahānāman Licchavi’s house to receive food with their own hands.
We thought to ourselves:
'Who is able to go to the house of the elder and speak these words?'"
"The Sangha has performed the *pātrāvakṣepa* (turning over the alms-bowl) against you; none of the five classes of monastics shall go to your house to receive food with their own hands.
The bhikṣus then thought further:
