"Only the Elder Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant; the Buddha has always praised his pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) among the assembly of bhikṣus, and he is capable of going there and speaking these words:"
"The Saṃgha has now performed the ritual of overturning the bowl for the elder; none of the five classes of monastics shall go to your house to receive food with their own hands.
Thus spoke the Elder Ānanda.
Now you may go to the house of Mahānāman Licchavi and say these words:
"The Saṃgha has already turned its bowl upside down for you; none of the five classes of monastics shall again go to your house to receive food with their own hands."
At that time, Ānanda accepted [the invitation] in silence.
When the bhikṣus saw that Ānanda had accepted, they rose from their seats, paid homage, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Then, when the night had passed, Ānanda dressed in his robes and took his bowl before midday and went to the house of Mahānāman Licchavi.
The Great Name Lichang saw Ānanda coming from afar; he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, stood to one side, and with palms joined, said:
"Welcome, Ānanda!"
"Sit here. Ānanda replied, "I may not sit."
Mahānāman Licchavi asked,
"For what reason may it not be obtained?
Ānanda replied:

"The Sangha has already performed the *pātrabhedana* (the overturning of the bowl) against Mahānāma Licchavi; none of the five classes of monastics shall go to your house to receive food with their own hands.
Mahānāma Licchavi said to Ānanda:
"I am now truly bringing harm upon myself; no merit shall arise."
Ānanda replied, “You have indeed harmed yourself; no merit will arise.
He then asked Ānanda:
"May I now go to the Buddha's presence and look up at his alms bowl?
Ānanda replied, "You may not."
Having heard these words, Mahānāman Licchavi was overcome with grief and confusion, and he fell to the ground.
Mahānāman Licchavi’s wife supported his head and raised him up;
she sprinkled water on his face, and after a long time, he regained consciousness.
The wife said to Mahānāman Licchavi:
"Is there truly such suffering as this? Or is there even greater suffering than this?
She spoke thus to herself:
“I am without fault, yet he faces the Buddha and speaks of my transgressions, slandering me in this assembly of pure bhikṣus by claiming that I have engaged in unchaste conduct.
At that time, Mahānāman Licchavi went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I pray that you will turn your bowl upward for me.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"For this reason, he is called Li-chang, 'Upright Bowl'."

Regarding the method for looking up at the alms bowl: with a single mind, the harmonious Saṃgha—this being the great name Lichang—exposes the right shoulder, joins the palms, and kneels on the ground, saying:
"May the Saṃgha take note!

I, Mahānāman Licchavi, spoke with harsh words and slandered the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta, a practitioner of pure brahmacarya, by falsely accusing him of unchaste conduct despite there being no basis for such a charge. Consequently, the Saṅgha has performed the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa* (the overturning of the bowl) against me; none of the five classes of monastics shall come to my house to receive food from my hand.
"I now pray that the Sangha will turn their bowls upward again, so that all five groups of monastics may come and go to my house as before and receive food directly from my hands out of compassion!
Thus he begged three times.
A single bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This man named Mahānāman Li-chang reviled and slandered the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā, son of the Malla, a pure practitioner of the holy life, by falsely accusing him with a groundless *pārājika* offense. Therefore, the Saṃgha has performed the *pātra-parivartana* (turning over of the bowl) against him; none of the five classes of followers shall go to the house of Mahānāman Li-chang to receive food directly from his hand."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha allow Mahānāma Licchavi, who holds his bowl aloft, to come and go as before and receive food with his own hands.
This is the motion. [Then follows] the formal act of fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Sangha has finished looking up at the bowl; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 37, Miscellaneous Recitation 20;
*Vinaya*, Scroll 38, Third Recitation of the Sixth [Section].
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty. Section 2:
Miscellaneous Dharmas, Part 3: Clarifying Miscellaneous Dharmas.
While the Buddha was traveling among the people of the country of Pāṅgā to teach and transform them, there was a place named Śiśumāra, where there was a monastery called Vaiśālī-migāramātu-ārāma.
This was the site where the Śiśumāra had been lost; in the house of Prince Puṣya, a new hall had been completed named Kumāra, into which no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa had yet entered to sit.

At that time, the prince heard that the Buddha was traveling among the people of the country of Pāka, teaching and transforming them, and was staying at the Veṇuvana (Bamboo Grove) monastery in the village of Ambalaṭṭhikā, teaching and transforming them:

"I now have a new hall named Kumāra; it has not been long since its completion, and it has not been long since its decoration and painting were finished. No śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have yet entered to sit within it."
"If the World-Honored One and the community of monks enter my house first, I shall gain great benefit. Why is this?
Because the Buddha has entered my house; once the Buddha has entered, I shall enter afterwards."
Prince Puṣya immediately summoned Sāñjayī Gāutami and said to him:

"I have heard that the World-Honored One is traveling among the people of the country of the Pākas, teaching and transforming them, and is currently staying at the Veṇugrāmaka monastery in the village of Vairambhya, traveling about and teaching."

"I now have a new hall named Kumāra, recently completed and not yet entered by any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas to sit within. If the Buddha enters first, I shall obtain great benefit; once the Buddha has entered, I shall enter afterwards."
"O Sarvagupta Dārumāla!
Go to where the Blessed One is and, in my name, address the Buddha, saying:
'Blessed One!'"
Prince Puṣya bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being, and spoke these words:
“Prince Puṣya has a newly constructed hall named Kumāra, which no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have yet entered; Prince Puṣya now invites the Buddha and the Saṃgha.”
Then, having received the words of Prince Sarvārthasiddha, Satyaka Kauṇḍinyaputra went to where the Blessed One was and spoke these words:
"Blessed One!"
Prince Puṇya bowed his head at the feet of the World-Honored One to pay his respects and inquired:
"Are you free from illness and affliction, and do you dwell in peace and comfort?

I have a newly constructed hall named Kumāra; it has not been long since its completion, nor has it been long since its decoration and painting were finished. I invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal tomorrow."
The Buddha said,
"May this prince always attain peace and happiness.
The Buddha then addressed Sāṇa Kokālika:
“Devas and humans constantly seek happiness; likewise, all nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other sentient beings also seek happiness.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking, he remained silent.
Then Sāṇa Kokālika, seeing that the Buddha was silent, circumambulated him to the right and departed. He went to the place where Prince Puṣya was and spoke these words:
“The śramaṇa Gautama has already accepted the prince’s invitation; it shall be according to the prince’s wish.”

At that time, Prince Puṣya prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink throughout the entire night. Having finished the preparations, early in the morning he arranged seats, spread garments upon the ground, and adorned the Kumāra Hall and its steps.
When the palace had been fully adorned, he immediately said to Sāṇa Kokanada Malla:
"Go to the place where the World-Honored One is and announce that the time has come.
Having received these instructions, Sāṇa Kokanada Malla went at once to the place where the World-Honored One was and announced:
"The time has come.
At that time, the World-Honored One dressed in his upper robe before midday, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by the great assembly, proceeded to the residence of Prince Puṣya.
Thereupon, the prince issued instructions to his household, commanding everyone, both great and small, to go outside the door.
At that time, the prince saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar; he immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, stood to one side, and spoke these words:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
The prince went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and welcomed the World-Honored One to the Kumāra Hall.
The prince stood by the side of the steps, and the Buddha and the Saṃgha proceeded to the top of the steps and stood there.
At that time, Prince Pukkusa joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that from the place where the cotton cloth was spread upon the hall above, you will grant us peace and security for a long night."
At that time, the Elder Ānanda was fanning the Buddha with a fan from behind him.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Exhort the prince in accordance with the Dharma. Then Ānanda spoke to Prince Puṣya:
"Please set aside the robes and coverlets spread upon the ground; those on the bed may remain.
The prince was unwilling to do so, whereupon Ānanda said to the prince:
"The Buddha, out of compassion for future sentient beings, requests that you set them aside for now."
Then Prince Puṅgala immediately withdrew the robes and coverings spread upon the ground. At that time, the prince joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The ground-covering has been withdrawn; I pray that the Buddha will ascend to the hall, so that we may always obtain peace and security."
The Buddha immediately ascended the hall, spread out his sitting mat, and sat before the bhikṣus.
At that time, the prince personally served water and set out various kinds of food and drink, until the Saṃgha was fully satisfied.

Having finished eating, he withdrew his bowl and offered water for washing. While the water was being offered, the prince held a basin to receive it; once the task was completed, he listened to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
The Buddha taught him various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden him. Having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, the Buddha rose from his seat and departed.
Then, after the meal, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"If a cloth is spread upon the ground, one must not walk upon it.
To walk upon it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."

When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin who was extremely wealthy, possessing abundant riches, treasures, fields, houses, cattle, and sheep; he lacked only one thing: he had no children.
She sought out all the celestial deities, namely the water spirits and tree spirits; for the sake of obtaining a son, she exhausted every means but could not succeed.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who frequently came and went from her house.
When she returned on a later day, the Brahmin woman’s menses appeared. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī said to the woman:
“You are not pure. I have heard it said:
‘If one takes the water used to wash the robes of an Arhat and bathes with that liquid, one will immediately obtain a son.’”
"In this world, there is no one else besides the Buddha and his assembly of disciples.
If the World-Honored One comes to enter your house, you shall be able to have a son.
When the Brahmin’s wife heard this, she said:
"How can we use skillful means to cause the Buddha to enter our home?
He then spoke to the brāhmaṇa with skillful words:
"I have heard this:"
"Take the water used for washing the robes of an Arhat, and by bathing with that liquid, you shall obtain a son.
Apart from the Buddha and his assembly of disciples, there is no other source for this.
"If the Buddha enters our home, we shall be able to have a son.
At that time, the Brahmin did not believe these words; however, for the sake of obtaining a son, he replied, "As you wish."
The wife said,
"Go and invite the Buddha. Thereupon,
the brahmin went to where the World-Honored One was, sat to one side, and exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One.
After the Buddha had taught the Dharma to him in various ways, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, he remained silent.
The brahmin said:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for tomorrow."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, he rose from his seat, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Arriving at his own residence, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night.
Having completed the preparations, he arranged seats in the early morning and spread various materials upon the ground, extending even to the outer gate. He then went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared. May the Buddha know that it is time."
The bhikṣus went to the brahmin’s house, while the Buddha stayed in his own quarters to receive his portion of the food.
At that time, the bhikṣus stepped aside from the ground-covering and entered the house first. Then the brahmin thought to himself:
“They did not walk upon the ground-covering when entering; they shall walk upon it when departing.”

When the bhikṣus were seated, [the host] personally provided water for washing and served the food. Once the Saṃgha had eaten their fill and finished the meal, they put away their bowls, washed their hands, and offered verses of blessing.
Having offered the blessings, they withdrew from the seat of the elder in order, removed their mats from the ground, and departed.
At that time, the brahmin was displeased in his heart, thinking:
"This śramaṇa is one who cuts off the lineage; he has ruined my brahmanical conduct. Whatever I have done to perform this offering, it never bears fruit."
After the meal, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when bhikṣus come after a meal, they greet them with these words:
"Was the food delicious? Were the monks well-satisfied?"
The Buddha then greeted the bhikṣus with these words:
"Was the food delicious and were you all satiated?
The bhikṣus replied:
"The food and drink were most excellent, and the community of monks was fully satisfied.
He related these circumstances to the Buddha in detail.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, out of compassion for sentient beings, I permit you to walk upon mats spread on the ground.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the Buddha had permitted walking upon mats spread on the ground, they went first to the Brahmin’s house because of their prior connection with him. The bhikṣuṇīs then spoke to the Brahmin’s wife, saying:

“The Buddha previously established a precept not permitting bhikṣus to walk upon mats spread on the ground; however, due to these circumstances, he has now granted permission. You should invite him again to step upon them and pass over.”
Then the Brahmin’s wife spoke to her husband with skillful means:
“The Buddha previously established a precept that does not permit bhikṣus to walk upon ground-coverings; for this reason, he has now granted permission. You may invite him once again.”
The Brahmin’s heart was also not pleased; however, for the sake of his son, he replied, "As you wish.
His wife said to her husband:
"You may go and invite the Buddha.
The brahmin went to where the World-Honored One was, sat to one side, and exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One.
The Buddha taught the brahmin various Dharmas, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having thus instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, he remained silent.
The brāhmaṇa said to the Buddha,
“I pray that you accept my invitation for tomorrow.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], the brahmin rose from his seat and departed.
Throughout the night, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink. At dawn, having spread various items upon the ground as far as the outer gate, he went to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared."

At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes and took up his bowl; surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, he went to the house and sat down. Having seated himself, he personally washed his hands and feet and partook of the food.

Having finished eating, he withdrew his bowl and performed the ritual washing of the hands; the brahmin remained before the Buddha to listen to the teaching of the Dharma. Having listened to the teaching of the Dharma, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“Will a son be born to my family? The Buddha said, “A son will be born;

having been born, he shall go forth into homelessness. His second-born son shall also go forth into homelessness, and his third-born son shall also go forth into homelessness; the one born after that shall remain at home.”

After the Buddha had finished his *pravāraṇā*, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings. There was a bhikṣu who walked along carrying a bowl, medicinal herbs, and leather sandals in his hands.
When the Buddha saw this bhikṣu, knowing the reason yet asking for the sake of instruction, he said:
"Why are you walking about carrying a bowl, medicinal herbs, and leather sandals?"
He replied,
"I have nowhere else to which I can cling.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to keep three kinds of bags:
a bag for the bowl, a bag for medicinal herbs, and a bag for leather sandals.
[The Buddha was staying] in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus placed their sitting mats in one location and stayed overnight elsewhere. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not stay overnight separated from the sitting mat you have received."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
In the kingdom of Kośala, there was a forest hermitage where two bhikṣus were residing.
One bhikṣu had violated the precepts, while the other maintained them purely.
These two bhikṣus had never before seen the Buddha and desired to go together to see him; on their way, they encountered water containing insects.
The one who has broken the precepts says to the one who maintains the precepts:
"Let us drink this water together.
The one who maintains the precepts says:
"There are insects in the water; how can it be drunk?
The one who has violated the precepts replied, "If I do not drink, I shall die, and I will not be able to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, or [meet] the Sangha."
The one who observed the precepts said, "I will not drink until death.

At that time, the one who had violated the precepts drank, while the one who observed the precepts died from not drinking. He was immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, endowed with a celestial body, and went first to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating at his feet and standing to one side.
Having stood to one side, the Buddha taught him the Dharma in various ways, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
He immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Sangha; for as long as I live, I shall be a lay follower (upāsaka).”
After the Buddha had further preached the Dharma for him, he remained silent; the deva, having prostrated before the Buddha, suddenly vanished.

Later, the water-drinker arrived at the Buddha’s location, where the Buddha was preaching the Dharma surrounded by an immeasurable multitude. Seeing this bhikṣu arrive at his presence, the Buddha then opened his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) to reveal his golden-hued body, saying:
"You foolish man!
"If you wish to see my physical body,
it is not as good as those who uphold the precepts seeing my Dharma-body first.
The Buddha spoke these verses:
"With a mind that does not observe well, you see without discernment;
like a moth rushing into a flame, you foolishly crave to gaze upon my body.
This physical form is nothing but impure—what is it that you wish to see?"
Within is fat, blood, and flesh, covered on the outside by thin skin.
Though scorched by thirst, they still practice respectful discipline;
guarding my teaching until death, they see me, not you.
After the Buddha had spoken this verse, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, it is not permitted to travel without carrying a water-strainer.
If one travels without carrying one, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
There is no offense if there is clear flowing water, or a large river, or a spring; within a distance of twenty *li* from this monastery to that monastery, there is no offense.

At that time, there was a matter requiring the monks' presence in a village; however, because they lacked water filters (*parisrāvaṇa*), they did not go. Since they could not accomplish their business if they did not go, they informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said:
"If a single bhikṣu possesses a water-strainer, he may go together with you.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had some business in a village and went to inform a bhikṣu they knew:
"I have a matter for which we may go together to the village.
That bhikṣu said,
"I do not have a water-strainer."
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We have it; we shall go together.
They replied:

"So be it. While traveling, they fell into a dispute on the road. Upon encountering water containing insects, the group of six bhikṣus used their water-strainers to filter the water for themselves to drink, but they refused the request of that bhikṣu and would not give him any. That bhikṣu was so parched with thirst that he was on the verge of death.
Because of these reasons, they informed the Buddha, who said:
"If a bhikṣu has not previously quarreled with another and harbors no feelings of resentment, he should travel together with him; if he harbors feelings of resentment, he should not go together."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate from wooden vessels. The Buddha said:
"From now on, eating from wooden vessels is not permitted."
"If one uses food [in such a manner], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept wooden stools to eat from, or kept small wooden beds to eat from, or kept wooden platters to eat from. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit keeping wooden stools, wooden beds, or wooden platters for eating."
"If one uses it for food, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus ate from a single bowl together. The Buddha said:
"One must not eat from the same bowl.
If one eats from the same bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if, having finished eating, one passes the food over [to another]."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
The group of six bhikṣus ate without wearing their saṃghāṭī robes. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit eating without wearing the saṃghāṭī robe."
"To eat food while remaining unclad is an *dukkaṭa* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus rubbed their bodies while naked. The Buddha said:
"One must not scrub while naked.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, when the group of six bhikṣus scrubbed while naked, the Buddha said:
"If one does not permit rubbing against those who are naked, the offender commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There were two bhikṣus who, both being naked, rubbed against each other; the Buddha said:
"If one rubs against another while both are naked, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu named Kaṅkila who found a living mung bean within a pot of mung bean soup; he took it out and placed it on the ground.
This bean was capable of producing sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruit. This bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"This soup is impure and should not be eaten.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. Knowing the reason, the Buddha questioned Udāyin:
"Is it true that you found a living mung bean in the soup, which, if taken out and placed on the ground, would produce sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruit? And did you say to the bhikṣus:"
"Is this soup impure and thus unfit to be eaten?
He replied, "Indeed it is."
“World-Honored One!

The Buddha praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts through various causes and conditions. Having finished praising the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“If this soup is not yet cooked, it should be cooked further.”
"If it has already been produced, one should purify it and then cook it.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for designating a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*). The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I do not permit the designation of ‘pure ground.
Should anyone do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu named Gomaya who, having finished eating, would chew again.
When the bhikṣus saw him chewing food at an improper time, they said to one another,
"This bhikṣu is eating past midday. Having heard this,
their hearts were filled with sorrow and displeasure, and they reported the matter to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"Do not say that this bhikṣu ate past the proper time. Why is that?
"This bhikṣu was constantly born among cattle for five hundred previous lifetimes; although he has now obtained a human body, the residual habits remain.
The Buddha said, "If there are others who likewise ruminate, they should do so in a secluded and covered place, and not ruminate before a crowd."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Pāka.
At that time, Prince Pāka invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the prince rose from his seat and departed. Returning home, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night. In the early morning, having arranged the seating area, he went to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared. May the Noble One know the time.
Then the Buddha, surrounded by the bhikṣus before and behind him, went to the house of Prince Puṅgala and sat down upon the seat.

In that household, many members, both young and old, did not believe in the Buddha; they were either Brahmins or people from the borderlands. Their manner of serving food was improper: they placed half in the bowl and half on the ground. The bhikṣus did not know how they should receive the food.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That which falls onto the grass or leaves upon which one is sitting may be eaten.
If there is soil adhering to it, blow the soil away and then eat."
"Or there are some indigenous people who obtain food by washing it with water.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then the group of six bhikṣus ate from copper basins.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"Eating from a copper basin is like the practice of the Brahmins.
The Buddha said,
"Eating from a copper basin is not permitted."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus washed their feet at the foot-washing place; while washing their feet, they conversed with one another.
Other bhikṣus saw him vomiting and feeling faint; the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not converse with others while washing your feet.
One who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."

After the Buddha had finished the *pravāraṇā*, he was traveling about to teach and transform others. He saw a bhikṣu walking while holding a leather sandal in his hand; knowing the reason, the Buddha asked him intentionally:
"Why are you walking while holding a leather sandal in your hand?"
He replied,
"My leather sandals bite my feet.
My feet are itchy and numb, yet I have nothing with which to rub them."
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep wooden foot-rubbers for use, in order to relieve itching of the feet.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a donor offered fans to the Sangha, but the bhikṣus would not accept them, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep fans.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to keep them.
The Sangha may keep them, and an individual may also keep them.
Again, someone offered a whisk to the Sangha, but the bhikṣus would not accept it.
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep whisks.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to keep them."
"The Sangha may possess it; even a single person may possess it.
At that time, someone offered a yak-tail whisk to the Sangha, but the bhikṣus would not accept it, not knowing what it was for.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept and use it to sweep the stūpas of the Buddha and those of the Arhats.
At that time, someone offered a fly-whisk with a handle made of maṇi jewels to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus would not accept it, not knowing how they should use it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to use it to sweep the stūpas of the Buddha and the stūpas of the Arhats.
At that time, a donor offered tāla leaves to the Saṃgha, and the bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep tala leaves.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Sangha may accept them, and an individual may also accept them."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of others carrying parasols themselves.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"What is it called for a bhikṣu to enter another's house carrying a parasol, like a king or a great minister?
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit entering another's house while carrying a parasol."
One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one understands [the situation] or places it outside the gate.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

There were two brahmins, one named Gopa and the other named Yava, who left the household life out of firm faith in the Buddha’s Dharma. Having originally recited the four Vedas of the non-Buddhists, after their ordination they continued to recite the Buddhist scriptures with those same vocal tones.

At that time, one person died and another remained alone; he forgot the Buddhist scriptures he was reciting and could not master them fluently. Seeking a companion, he found none, and his heart became sorrowful and unhappy. He reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, those who recite Buddhist scriptures using the phonetics of non-Buddhist texts commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

There were bhikṣus who abandoned the Sūtras, the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya, and instead recited secular books, literary compositions, and military treatises, distancing themselves from the Buddhist scriptures. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if any bhikṣus study or recite secular books, literary compositions, or military treatises, it shall be a duṣkṛta offense."

Before the Buddha had yet laid down this precept, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were seated upon high thrones, preaching the Dharma to the newly ordained bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras and instructing them in the recitation of non-Buddhist texts for the purpose of refuting the arguments of the heretics.
Once this precept had been established, the elders Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana no longer occupied high seats to preach the Dharma or teach secular texts to newly ordained bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras.

At that time, the various non-Buddhists heard that the śramaṇa Gautama did not permit his disciples to study or recite non-Buddhist texts; consequently, these brahmins went to the Buddhist lay followers (upāsakas) who had faith and said to them:
"We should go together to where the bhikṣus are."
He replied, “As you wish.
When the non-Buddhists arrived, they engaged in debate with the newly ordained bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras.
None of the newly ordained bhikṣus or śrāmaṇeras were able to answer, for two reasons:
first, because they had recently entered the Path; second, because the Buddha had established a precept prohibiting their study [of such matters].
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners mocked the lay followers, saying:
"Is it truly as you say—that this is your great teacher, the one whom you honor, the one you revere, and the one who eats before all others?"
When the upāsakas heard of this matter, their hearts were filled with grief and they were not at ease; they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From now on, I permit you to recite and study the books of non-Buddhists for the purpose of refuting them."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin set fire to various grasses and trees; because of this burning, he killed many kinds of insects.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, bhikṣus must not set fire to anything.
If one sets fire to something, they shall incur the offense corresponding to whatever is killed."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

There was a nurse who had not yet completed five years of seniority; he went out on behalf of a patient, leaving his formal dependence (niśraya) behind to enter a village, but failed to obtain medicine.
At that time, he thought to himself of the Buddha’s established precept: "One must not stay apart from one's preceptor for even a single night. He immediately sought a preceptor there.
However, his new preceptor also fell ill, and he thought to himself:
"That preceptor is ill, and this preceptor is also ill."
"What should I do now?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is permitted for you to remain without a formal preceptor (niśraya) for five nights or six nights without committing an offense."
Once this precept had been established, the group of six bhikṣus, having heard that the Buddha had permitted it, did not seek formal dependence for five nights.
Why was this? They thought, "If we obtain formal dependence, we will have to provide for them."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, if one has a qualified preceptor (niśrayācārya) yet fails to rely upon him for even a single night, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
"If a bhikṣu has no preceptor (niśraya), he must not even take the water used by the Saṃgha for washing feet.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin wore his upper robe (saṃkakṣikā) backwards; when the bhikṣus saw this, they were terrified.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not wear the *kūṭa* robe inverted.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"There is no offense in covering one's body with what was originally inside a garment.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
at that time there was a person who offered to the Elder Subhūti a double-layered garment, holding both the outer and inner layers together.
Subhūti said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted the simultaneous grasping of both the inner and outer robes.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is permitted to keep a pair of robes, both inner and outer, for communal use; they may be kept by the community as a whole, and also by an individual.
Furthermore, someone offered Elder Subhūti a pair of robes where one half was made of dyed cloth and the other half was not dyed.
At that time, Subhūti did not accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept robes that are half-dyed and half-undyed.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit you to possess and wear garments that are half-finished and half-unfinished.
The Sangha may accept them, and a single individual may also accept them.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there were five bhikṣus who obtained a robe five cubits long and three cubits wide; they put on this robe and entered a village to beg for alms.
The robes were so long that they trailed on the ground and became soiled by the earth; when stepped upon by the feet, the hems fell to the ground and could not be worn properly.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to provide fasteners and ties for long robes, and to attach them near the edges."
Because his old robes dragged on the ground and were soiled with dust, and because he stepped on them as they fell, causing them to be worn unevenly, the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow you to fold them up and wear them.

At that time, the Buddha himself provided fastenings and ties: he placed a fastening four finger-widths from the front edge and a tie eight finger-widths from the back edge, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"It should be done in this manner.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who entered a village without fastening his inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī). Inside the village, it fell to the ground, and that bhikṣu felt great shame and remorse.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for one who enters a village without fastening their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*.
A certain bhikṣu fastened his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with a single loop; while entering the village, he sneezed, causing the cord to break and fall to the ground."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted to tie the nivāsana (undergarment) with a single loop when entering a village.
One who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, someone offered Elder Subhūti a fine thread to tie into a waistband, but Subhūti did not accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to accept fine thread for a waistband."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep three kinds of belts:
first, those made of fine thread; second, those made of rope; and third, those made of woven strips."
When they wore the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) with the waistband too tight, it tore. The Buddha said, "One should apply a ring [to the waistband].

The group of six bhikṣus wore the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* like two ears; they wore the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with fine pleats; they wore the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with a saw-toothed edge; they wore the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* unevenly; and they wore a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* made of fine, coarse [fabric]. The Buddha said:

"One must not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) with both ears hanging down; one must not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with fine pleats; one must not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with a saw-toothed hem; one must not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* unevenly; and one must not wear a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* made of thin, coarse cloth."
"To wear [it] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha,
at that time the group of six bhikṣus stroked their beards and hair with their hands, like oxen licking with their tongues.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit the manual rubbing of the beard and hair.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, two members of the group of six bhikṣus lay together on one bed.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“From now on, it is not permitted for two people to lie down together on one bed.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta*.
If one person sits and one person lies down, there is no offense.”
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus lay down together on a single mat upon the ground. The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for two people to lie down together on one mat."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if each person has their own separate bedding.
At that time, two members of the group of six bhikṣus lay down together under one covering cloth. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not lie down together under the same covering cloth.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if each person has their own separate undergarment."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore the garments of laypeople, and the householders rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and of good character.'"
“If one wears secular clothing, how is this different from being a layperson?
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not wear secular clothing.”
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha,
at that time the group of six bhikṣus folded their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robes in a manner resembling wrestlers or performers.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not fold or crease your robes.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There is no offense for those who climb ladders to roof houses or plaster over them.
When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the group of six bhikṣus were walking along carrying loads, appearing just like donkeys or oxen laden with burdens.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit traveling while carrying a burden.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a border village in the kingdom of Kośala that was constantly threatened by bandits.
Because the people of the village feared the bandits, they abandoned their homes and departed from that place.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī. This bhikṣu carried an earthen bowl and a staff; as he passed through the villages, the people saw him from afar and thought to themselves:
"This is a bandit coming, carrying a spear and a shield."
Having seen him, she was struck with fear and retreated back into the pavilion.
As the bhikṣu gradually drew near, she recognized him as a śramaṇa and asked,
"What kind of śramaṇa are you?"
He replied,
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas. He said:
"You have lost the dharma of a śramaṇa and destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa, causing us to be filled with fear.
Not knowing what to do, that bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From now on, when traveling, it is not permitted to carry a staff or a water-strainer bag.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
After the *pravāraṇā*, the Buddha was wandering among the people, and there was a certain emaciated bhikṣu who walked along carrying his bowl in his hand.
The Buddha, knowing the reason, asked:
"Why are you walking with a bowl held in your hand?
He replied:
"There is nothing to hold [the bowl].
The Buddha said:
"From now on, for bhikṣus who are emaciated, aged, or ill, the Saṃgha shall grant formal authorization (karmavācanā) to carry a bowl placed within a staff-case."
It should be performed in this manner:

With a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, that aged and infirm bhikṣu shall rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, [Name], an elderly and sick bhikṣu, beg the Saṃgha for permission to carry a staff and a net-bag containing my bowl while walking.
Out of compassion, may the Saṃgha grant me, this elderly and sick bhikṣu, permission to carry a staff and a net-bag containing my bowl while walking.
Thus he requests three times.
The Saṃgha should listen to his truth.
If that bhikṣu says:
"Old and sick.
[If] he is not actually old and sick, one should not grant permission.
If he says:
"Old and sick. If one is truly old and sick, they should be permitted [to leave].
A single bhikṣu shall announce within the saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named [Name] is aged and infirm; he requests from the Saṃgha permission to carry a staff and a bag containing his bowl while walking.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this aged and infirm bhikṣu permission to carry a staff and a bag containing his bowl while walking."
Thus it is announced.
[The motion for] the second *karmavācanā* is as follows:

"The Saṃgha has granted this aged and infirm bhikṣu permission to carry a staff and to travel with his bowl placed in a carrying net. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld accordingly."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, surrounded by the great assembly as he taught the Dharma.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala was seated in the gathering. There was a bhikṣu who, having eaten garlic, walked away from the assembly; this bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I must not cause the Buddha or the king to smell this stench."
The Buddha saw this bhikṣu from afar; for the king’s sake, he taught various dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden him. Having heard the Dharma, the king’s heart was filled with great joy.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, he remained silent, and the king circumambulated the Buddha to the right before departing.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda was fanning the Buddha with a fan behind him.
Not long after the king had departed, the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked Ānanda:
"Why is this bhikṣu walking far away from the great assembly?"
He replied, "This bhikṣu has eaten garlic; fearing that the Buddha and the king might smell it, he does not dare to approach the Buddha.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
“Does a bhikṣu eat such food as this? He replied, “I do.”
“If one eats such things as these, one loses the benefit of the Dharma.
The Buddha said,
“If this bhikṣu enters among the assembly and hears my Dharma, he shall attain right view.”
He said to the bhikṣus,
"This matter should not have been done.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus must not eat garlic.
If they do, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra suffered from a wind disorder.
The physician instructed him, saying, "Boil garlic in milk and eat it. Śāriputra said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted the eating of garlic boiled in milk.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"I permit the eating of garlic boiled in milk; one should proceed according to the rules for eating garlic."
What is the practice in accordance with the Dharma?

One who eats garlic should not approach the Buddha, nor even the preceptor (upādhyāya), the ācārya, any senior monks (sthavira), a stūpa of the Buddha, a stūpa of a śrāvaka, a heated bathhouse, a lecture hall, or the kitchen where the Sangha eats. One must not stand near the outer gate of the monastery; one must not enter the monastic latrines to defecate or urinate; one must not enter the monastic bathhouse; and one must not enter places where the multitude sits. One should instead reside in a secluded room.
If one is urgently pressed by the need for defecation or urination, one should have someone dig a place in the ground for these purposes.
If no *karmadāna* (attendant) is available, one should go to a remote and secluded spot to relieve oneself.

Once the illness has been cured, one should sweep and sprinkle the dwelling area and smear the floor; bedding, mattresses, and mats should be shaken out, and anything that has become foul-smelling should be washed.
That bhikṣu emerged from his room, closed the door, lowered the bolt, and having lowered the bolt, departed.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took harītakī fruits themselves, gave them to a pure person, and then accepted them from him to eat.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One should not take harītakī fruit with one's own hands and then give it to a lay attendant to receive and eat from.
One who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
"All other fruits are likewise.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu named Nandi. This bhikṣu acted as a preceptor for a śrāmaṇera in training, as previously described.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the Elder Piṅgalavatsa suffered from eye pain. A physician instructed him, saying:
"Prepare a medicinal compound into pills, place them over a fire, and inhale the smoke."
Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what materials should medicine be prepared?
The Buddha said:
"Except for the medicinal incense of *śyāmāka* wood, one should take all other perfumes, place them in the fire, and catch the smoke with the hand to swallow it.
At that time, they were unable to catch the smoke with their hands;
the Buddha said, "Make a tube."
At that time, because the tube was too long, no smoke could be drawn.
The Buddha said, "Do not make it too long.
Again, when they made it too short, it burned their hands. The Buddha said:
"Do not make them too short.
Furthermore, at times the medicinal pills were kept in one place and the tube in another, making them difficult to retrieve when needed. The Buddha said:
"You should keep a bag to contain them."
When the bamboo tube was broken while being filled with medicinal pills, the Buddha said:
"A partition should be placed inside.
After the partition had been applied, the head of the tube was not tied and it fell to the ground; the Buddha said:
"One should tie it around the head.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
there was a sick bhikṣu who, having smeared his body with ghee and oil, did not wash it and suffered from itching and distress.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should use soap powder to wash.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what materials is the bath-powder (*snāna-kaṣāya*) made?
The Buddha said:
"It is made with large beans (*māṣa*), small beans (*mudga*), *mo-she* beans, peas, *kātīparā* grass, and *lipiṇḍa* seeds."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Śāriputra suffered from a feverish blood disorder. At that time, a physician instructed him, saying:
"Wash with *sāmāni* water."
Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what material should a *sāmaṇerī* (novice nun) be made?
The Buddha said:
"Excluding poisonous trees, one should take the flowers and leaves of all other trees to make [the remedy].
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Piṅgiyāni suffered from eye pain; at that time, a physician instructed him, saying:
"One should administer an oily enema through the nose.

At that time, a bhikṣu used his finger to drip it into the nostrils, or took some with a tuft of wool to drip it in; as he was dripping it, it did not flow in easily, and the pain in his eye increased even more, becoming extremely severe.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Make a tube for irrigation.
When they made the tube too large, the nozzle would not fit.
Again, he made it too small; it overflowed and was lost, rendering it unusable.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Make it neither too large nor too small; it should be the size of one *pātra* or half a *pātra*. If you wish to spit, catch it with your hand."
Because he caught it with his hand, he wished to vomit;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to use a worn-out rag to catch it.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Pilindavatsa suffered from eye pain. When a relative sent a vehicle to summon him, he replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted the use of vehicles."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Those who are ill are permitted to ride in carriages.
At that time, the Buddha had not yet permitted riding in palanquins; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen to the rules for riding in a carriage.
When that bhikṣu rode in a carriage with his feet dangling down, the Buddha said:
"One should keep the feet tucked up onto the floorboard."
When he tucked his feet away, his body became unstable.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to hold onto a wooden rack.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was fond of comfort; when he held onto the wooden rack, his hands were pained. The Buddha said:
“They wrapped the wood with cloth.
When sitting, the sun shone upon his face;
the Buddha said, “One should provide a canopy.”
"If all items required for the adornment of any vehicle [or assembly] are needed, they are all permitted to be made.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were defecating everywhere within the Jetavana Grove. The yakṣa Vajrapāṇi and various non-human beings all became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"Should one perform the act of impurity here?
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One should not defecate in various places; it should be done in a single location."
After they had done this in one place, a great heap of dung was formed. The Buddha said:
"Clear it away.
As they were clearing it away, the bhikṣus felt nauseated and faint. The Buddha said:
"Dig the ground to make a pit.
After the pit was made, there was excrement by the side of the pit which soiled the bhikṣus' feet. The Buddha said:
"One should provide a place for resting the feet."
Upāli asked the Buddha,
“With what material should the footrest be made?
The Buddha said:
[He replied,] "I made it of wood, stone, and bricks.
When he was defecating in the open air without a screen, people saw him.
The Buddha said, "One should construct a screen."
When the two saw each other at that time, the Buddha said:
"You should give a partition.
After they had given the partition, they happened to see each other again as they were entering and leaving; the Buddha said:
"One should provide separate mats for the doors.
At that time, there was an elderly bhikṣu who liked to fall backward when going to the latrine and would instead lie prone as he tried to stand up. The Buddha said:
"One should provide a footrest so that he may stand upright."
When rising, he required water to wash the place where he had defecated;
the Buddha said, "You should keep a water vessel.
Furthermore, as he had no soil for washing his hands, the Buddha said:
"One should place it on the ground.
When the ground was too small, the Buddha said:
"Place it in a large vessel."
At that time, when a vessel was placed on level ground, domestic animals—such as oxen, horses, deer, monkeys, or dogs—would come and trample it and break it. The Buddha said:
"One should dig into the ground and place the vessel there."
Furthermore, when the top was not covered, venomous snakes, maggots, centipedes, and millipedes would enter and bite the bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"The top should be covered."
Furthermore, when washing his hands, the ground became so muddy that it defiled his feet.
The Buddha said, "One should provide a place for setting the feet down.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"What materials should be used to make a footrest?
The Buddha said,
"Use wood, stone, or brick."
When the bhikṣus washed, their private parts were exposed. The Buddha said, "A screen should be provided.
Or, when two or three people washed together and saw one another, the Buddha said:
"One should provide a partitioned room.
Furthermore, when they encountered one another while entering or exiting, the Buddha said:
"One should provide separate doors."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
The various bhikṣus urinated here and there, and the Vajra-devas and other non-human beings all became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"Should one perform such impure acts in this place?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not urinate here and there; one should do so in a single place.
Once it had become like a flowing stream in that spot, the Buddha said:
"One should place a jar.
When the jar was full, the Buddha said:
"It should be discarded."
When the bhikṣu vomited while discarding it, the Buddha said:
"Make a hole beneath the jar so that [the waste] may exit.
After a long time, the jar became foul-smelling; the Buddha said:
"One should cover it.
When the bhikṣu removed the cover, the smell of his urine became even more intense. The Buddha said:
"Cover it, but leave a small hole to allow the foul odor to escape."
At that time, urine flowed from the four sides of the jar and soiled his feet.
The Buddha said, "One should provide a place for the feet to rest.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what should it be made?
The Buddha said,
"It should be made from wood, stone, or brick."
When the bhikṣus were urinating and their private parts were exposed, the Buddha said:
"One should provide a screen.
When they were urinating and could see one another, the Buddha said:
"One should provide a partition.
After providing the partition, they happened to see one another as they were entering and exiting;
the Buddha said, "One should provide a door."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, someone offered clay jars to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus would not accept them, not knowing what they were to be used for.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be used for bathing; fill it with water and use it within the bathhouse.

While the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kṛmīla, he taught the Dharma of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to a great assembly of bhikṣus—namely, form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
At that time, when the Buddha sneezed, five hundred bhikṣus all spoke with one voice at once,
saying, "Long life!
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“Is it because you say ‘old age and longevity’ that one actually attains old age and longevity? “No,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not address someone as 'venerable elder.
To address someone as 'venerable elder' constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
When the bhikṣus entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, various donors offered them many kinds of excellent foods:
milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, honey, fish, and dried meat. The bhikṣus did not accept them, thinking, "Could it be that we are begging for fine delicacies?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one obtains something without having asked for it, it should be accepted.
(The first twenty rules are concluded.)
[From the Twenty Dharmas, Part Two] The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the householder Bāḍhī had constructed a great monastery (saṃghārāma) adorned with various ornaments, yet he had not roofed over the upper chambers, so they were leaking.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should be covered.
After it was covered, [the water] still leaked from his back; the Buddha said:
"Cover it more thickly.
After it had been covered thickly, the wind blew it away. The Buddha said:
"You should drive in stakes."
After the peg had been driven in, the top of the hole leaked;
the Buddha said, "One should provide a basin to cover it.
After it was covered, the basin easily fell to the ground; the Buddha said:
"One should pierce holes in the bottom and drive in nails.
After the nails were driven in, water leaked inside;
the Buddha said, "One should drive in nails and place a lid over the pot."
After he had placed the lid on the cauldron, the wind blew against the stakes, causing them to shake and make a noise. The Buddha said:
"One should wrap the head [of the stake] with grass, leaves, or tree bark; having wrapped it, one may place the lid on the cauldron."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a bhikṣu possessed an expensive fire-cleansed garment (*agniśodhana-vastra*). When two or three bhikṣus shook it together, the garment became shriveled and misshapen during the shaking. The Buddha said:
"One should strike it with a thin stick to remove the dust."
When he struck it, the soil entered the long strip.
The Buddha said, "Strike it again with a small stick.
When he struck it, the soil entered the short strip. The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, strike it with a small stick.
The Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a bhikṣu had newly dyed his robe; he used a broom to sweep away the dye-sediment, and as the color faded from the cloth, the path to awakening appeared upon it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should use a new hand-towel to remove the dregs.
[This occurred] when the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the householder Bhadrika constructed a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma) that was exceedingly vast and adorned with various ornaments; many people came to see it.
Because there was no ground covering, much dust and soil rose up and fouled the interior of the monastery.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"It would be well if the Buddha were to permit the covering of the ground.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should place a ground-covering over it.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus had no pestle for preparing medicines. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should grind it upon a stone.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra had constructed five hundred monasteries within the Bamboo Grove; some were completed, while others were unfinished.
At that time, when the king passed away, King Ajātaśatru went to the Bamboo Grove to visit and saw these dwellings;
he immediately asked, "For whom were these built?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Great King! This was undertaken by your father, the King.
While some parts were completed and others remained unfinished, the King passed away.”
The king asked the bhikṣu,
"Why was it not brought to completion?
He replied:
"There is no payment," the king said.
"I shall give you payment."
When the dwelling was completed, because there were no stairs or walkways, no one was staying inside.
The King asked the bhikṣus,
"Is there anyone in this room?"
He replied, "No. [The other asked,] "For what reason?"
He replied, "Because there are no steps.
The king said:
"I shall do it. The bhikṣu replied,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted its performance."
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said,
"I allow you to do so.
At that time, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what material should the steps be made?
The Buddha said,
"They should be made of wood, stone, or brick."
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the monastic quarters were extremely large, and many visiting bhikṣus arrived at all times.

Those who arrived during the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night would take away large beds, some taking away rope-cots, some taking away large mattresses, and some taking away seat-mats; they would then stay overnight in those very places and depart the next morning, leaving them behind.

At that time, Dharmaruci was in charge of the monastic bedding. On subsequent days, when he had to carry beds and mattresses from place to place, it became extremely difficult for him. He thought to himself:
"It would be well if the Buddha were to permit beds and mattresses to be sewn together with needles."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to sew it; however, when sewing, do not sew at the center of the bedding.
When they were carrying the bed from east to west, the wool gathered together in one place, and they immediately had this thought:
"It would be well if the Buddha would allow me to sew the center.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said,
"I allow you to sew it with a needle."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what material should a needle be made?
The Buddha said:
“[It may be] made of iron, made of copper, or made of wood.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra suffered from a disease of hot blood; a physician instructed him, saying:
"He heated stones and placed them in milk to drink.
He replied,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted heating stones and placing them in milk to drink."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I allow you to heat stones and place them in the milk to drink.
When heating the stones, some bhikṣus used grass, wood leaves, or pieces of broken pottery to hold the stones over the milk, and the ashes and soil defiled the milk.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From now on, I permit you to make supports and locks out of copper or iron; place stones inside them and heat them, then lift the locks and shake them to remove the ash before adding it to the milk."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A certain person offered a brazier to the Elder Subhūti, but Subhūti said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted its acceptance."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is permitted to receive it.
At that time, as he was burning wood, embers fell to the ground; the bhikṣu picked them up with his hand and burned his hand. The Buddha said:
"Listen to the instruction on making fire-stirring tools.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra suffered from a wind disorder, and his physician instructed him as follows:
"I shall wash with warm water.
He replied,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted washing with warm water."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to warm water. When warming it,
they used either a bowl or a *kaṇḍolaka* (a small vessel), but the water was insufficient.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to warm [the water] in a cauldron.
The bhikṣus filled a cauldron with water and placed it in the open air; when they placed firewood around the sides and lit it, the cauldron broke.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should provide three hearths.
At that time, they placed the cauldron upon the hearths and lit fires beneath them, but the firewood was difficult to ignite.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should split the firewood with an axe and then burn it.
This was when the Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī.
At that time, the lintel of the temple gate was broken. The Buddha, having already perceived this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Why is the lintel of this temple gate broken?
He replied:
"The carpenter is in such a hurry that he cannot work.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Go and fetch some wood for making tools."
Ānanda received the Buddha’s instruction, sought out wood and tools, and brought them to the Buddha.
The Buddha took them and personally repaired the lintel of the stūpa gate. Having finished the repair, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, I permit you to keep all kinds of wooden tools; any bhikṣu who is capable of performing repairs may do so.”
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Āravī.
At that time, the monastic quarters were covered over; the bhikṣus stood on the ground and could not reach to hand out the grass. The Buddha said:
"One should provide stools."
Because the oranges had already been distributed and [the time] had passed, the Buddha said:
"One should provide a ladder.
Because the ladder had already been provided and it was not universal, the Buddha said:
"One should provide shelves.
Having provided the shelves, [the monks] did not know how to provide [the food].
The Buddha said:
"One should drive stakes into the rafters and tie ropes to the stakes to move the platform as desired.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who suffered from an inflamed male organ; pus and blood defiled his robes.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"It should be wrapped with cloth.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

There was a bhikṣu who was ill, and his attendant was young in years; standing up to support the sick bhikṣu, he became exhausted from standing for so long, fell to the ground, and was on the verge of death.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"A young bhikṣu acting as an attendant may sit together with the patient, out of compassion for the patient."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Some bhikṣus, wearing newly dyed robes, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms and encountered rain.
At that time, the bhikṣus folded their robes and placed them in one spot; because they were damp, the color appeared different.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be dried in the sun; when drying it, spread it out on the ground to dry.
After it had been dried, dust adhered to it, and the Buddha said:
"It should be smeared with cow dung and dried in the sun.
After it had been dried, the robes did not dry in a timely manner. The Buddha said:
"Dry them on a rope."
Because it did not dry in a timely manner, the Buddha said, "One should apply curved pegs.
Even after applying the curved pegs, it still did not dry in a timely manner; the Buddha said:
"One should spread it out on a bed.
Because it did not dry in a timely manner after being spread out, the Buddha said:
"One should provide a rack."
When setting up the shelves, they obstructed the walking path. The Buddha said:
"They should be placed together in one location.
Once they were placed together, they were close to the wall and became soiled with dust. The Buddha said:
"One should keep it away from the wall.
Because it was not drying at the proper time once it was moved away from the wall, the Buddha said:
"One should hang it high up to dry."
The Buddha was staying in the country of Āravī.

At that time, the bhikṣus prepared bathing requisites. When a bhikṣu was bathing, he took off his clothes and placed them on bare ground before entering the bathhouse to wash. A venomous snake, a maggot, and a centipede entered the clothes; when the bhikṣu put them back on, he was stung by the insects. The Buddha said:
"One should hang clothes on a rack, and having placed the clothes there, enter the bathhouse to wash."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Lady Mallikā entered the Jetavana to listen to the Dharma, while the bhikṣus were preaching the Dharma in the darkness.
Lady Mallikā said to the bhikṣus:
"Why do you not light a lamp?
He replied, "There is no lamp."
The lady said,
"I shall give you a lamp.
He replied:
"We have not yet been permitted by the Buddha to light lamps.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Queen Mallikā offered high seats to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept them."
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to receive it.
Then, Queen Mallikā thought to herself:
“May the Buddha permit me to paint this high seat; it would be well.
The Buddha said, “With the exception of images depicting the sexual union of men and women, all others are permitted to be painted.”
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus chewed long willow twigs. When the lay devotees saw this, they rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent and virtuous!
But why do you chew long willow twigs?
A bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard this matter and was displeased; he reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the truth] yet asking deliberately, he said to the group of six bhikṣus: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus in various ways:
"What is it called for a bhikṣu to chew long willow twigs?
The Buddha said,
"From now on, you must not chew long willow twigs."
"One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At that time, some bhikṣus were chewing short tooth-sticks. The Buddha was walking up and down (caṅkrama) in that place. When the bhikṣus saw the Buddha approaching from afar, out of reverence they immediately swallowed the tooth-sticks; they became choked and could not swallow them, nearly dying. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I permit the use of three kinds of tooth-sticks:
superior, middling, and inferior."
"The longest is twelve finger-breadths; the shortest is six finger-breadths; that which is between these two is called medium.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who ordained a young boy as his attendant disciple (*sārdha-vihārin*). This disciple did not act in accordance with the Dharma, and other bhikṣus said:
"This disciple is not acting in accordance with the Dharma;
why do you not expel him? He replied, "This is my son's disciple; how could I expel him?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a son or a disciple does not act in accordance with the Dharma, they should be expelled."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the novice Rāhula disobeyed his preceptor Kālodāyin, who then expelled him from the monastery.
At that time, the novice Rāhula was weeping outside the gate of the Jetavana.
When the Buddha came from outside and entered the Jetavana, he saw Rāhula weeping and, knowing the reason, asked:
"Why are you weeping?"
Rāhula reported this matter in detail to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you must not expel a śrāmaṇera from the saṃghārāma; rather, he should be expelled from his room."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus spat on clean ground, and the ground became damaged.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not spit upon clean ground.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know where they should spit.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should catch the spittle with one's hand.
When catching the spittle, they felt nauseous and faint; the Buddha said:
"One should keep a spittoon.
When the spittoon became full, the Buddha said,
"It should be discarded."
When he discarded it, he wished to spit again.
The Buddha said, "Place ash, sand, or charred material into the spitting vessel to cause the saliva to dissolve.

While the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, the Elder Kāśyapa came down from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; as he descended, he was scorched by the sun, and his face became soiled, entering into his eyes and causing them to ache.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep hand towels for wiping.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Bāḍhi practiced the dhūta ascetic virtues; when entering the bathhouse to wash, he did not allow others to rub his body, thinking to himself:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to rub my own body with a cord."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow the use of braided cords.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"With what materials is it made?
The Buddha said,
"With wool, kusa grass, cotton, muñja grass, and śāṇa grass."
Śāriputra, suffering from a back ailment, thought to himself:
"It would be well if the Buddha would allow me to sit using a meditation belt.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Sit with the meditation belt on.
Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what material is the meditation belt made?"
The Buddha said:
"They are made from wool, kusa grass, cotton, muñja grass, and the bark of vāsa grass.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One suffered from a wind-related ailment causing back pain. Then the physician instructed him, saying:
"Anoint your body with ghee; once you have anointed your body, lie down inside a trough filled with warm water."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Bring some warm water in a trough.
Ānanda received the instruction and brought the warm water, having filled a trough with it.
At that time, the Buddha anointed his body with ghee and entered [the bath] to lie down; having lain down, his illness was cured.
Because of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"From now on, it is permitted that if one has a wind-related illness, one may anoint the body with ghee and lie down in warm water."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.
The bhikṣus were preparing bedding and furniture when many visiting bhikṣus arrived at dusk; as the monastic provisions for bedding were insufficient, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it should be given according to the order of seniority. To those who have no bedding or mats, give grass or leaves, and let each person spread their own bedding and lie down."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, in a forest retreat in the kingdom of Kośala. There lived a certain bhikṣu who produced fire using a crystal gem.
At that time, a thief staying in that place saw fire emerge from within the jewel of the bhikṣu and thought to himself,
"This must certainly be a Vaiḍūrya jewel.
The thief then said to the bhikṣu:
"Give me this lapis lazuli bead.
The bhikṣu replied,
"O good man!"
"I do not have a lapis lazuli bead.
At that time, the thief thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu refuses to give it to me directly; I shall kill this bhikṣu."
Having killed the bhikṣu, he searched for the jewel and found a crystal bead inside a needle-case;
the thief then said to his companions, "It was for the sake of this crystal bead that I killed this bhikṣu."
Then the robbers laid the deceased bhikṣu on his back, placed the crystal bead back into his navel, and departed. Later,
after their meal, the bhikṣus were walking for exercise when they saw the deceased bhikṣu and said to one another,
"It was because of this bead that he was killed by someone."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus for this purpose, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you must not possess moon-jewels or sun-jewels.
