If anyone possesses them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus washed expensive fire-rubbed garments on a stone; having washed them, they were ruined.
The Buddha said:
"One should wash them by rubbing them with the hands upon a wooden board."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Queen Mallikā constructed a lecture hall, adorned it with various ornaments, and offered it to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept a lecture hall adorned with various ornaments and enter or exit within it."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This hall is pure; you may enter and exit within it."

At that time, there were geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, *kuśala* birds, *kukila* birds, *jīvamjīvaka* birds, and various swift-flying swallows entering and exiting and making sounds, which disturbed the bhikṣus as they sat in meditation and recited the sūtras.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should provide a railing.
After the railing had been provided, they entered [the monastery] as before; the Buddha said:
"One should provide a net.
At that time, Upāli asked the Buddha,
"With what material should the net be made?"
The Buddha said:
"Make them from wool, kusa grass, cotton, muñja grass, hemp, or dragon-hair hide.
Once they were made, they quickly rotted; the Buddha said:
"One should provide a net for the eyes of the sparrows.
Because the birds still continued to come, the Buddha said:
"One should hang a curtain."
When hanging the curtain, it was dark;
the Buddha said, "One should provide a cord to pull it up.
While the Buddha was in the country of Ālavī, a newly constructed monastery lacked tools for sweeping the ground, and the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should make a broom.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Piṅgiyānī suffered from eye pain and thought to himself:
"If it would be well for me to sit in a high place, may I be permitted to do so.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to sit in a high place."
While at a high place, fearing he might fall to the ground, he thought:
"It would be well if the Buddha would allow me to install a railing at a high place.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen: a railing should be constructed at a high place.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the monastic quarters had no gate, and oxen, horses, monkeys, dogs, and other animals would enter.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"A gate should be constructed.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know where to place their needles.
The Buddha said:
"You should make needle cases."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus did not know where to place medicinal herbs.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep a container for storing medicinal substances.
When the bhikṣus had no place to dry their medicinal substances, they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should make a rack for drying medicinal substances."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered mats to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept mats."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to keep them, and individuals may also keep them.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not keep mats or covers for themselves, and thus they damaged the bedding of the Saṃgha; sitting on it bare-bodied, the hair would stick to their bodies when they stood up.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep one's own mat and spread it over the communal mat.
If one does not spread it oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.
A bhikṣu was washing with one foot raised in the open air when he fell to the ground and nearly died.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep items for washing the feet.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"What materials should be used to make these items for washing the feet?"
The Buddha said, "Construct it using wood, stone, and bricks.

While the Buddha was in the kingdom of Ālavī, he was building a new saṃghārāma; at that time, there had been a long drought and the ground was parched and withered, but subsequently it rained heavily and the earth everywhere broke apart.
When the bhikṣus were walking in and out, their feet damaged the ground. The Buddha said:
"One should provide a place for the feet to tread upon.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"What materials should be used to make the stepping-stones?
The Buddha said,
"They should be made of wood, stone, or brick."
That monastery had many rooms, and at that time the bhikṣus each made a place for stepping down in front of their own rooms. The Buddha said:
"It is best to make a continuous line of stepping-down places all around."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

A group of bhikṣus were traveling from Kośala toward Śrāvastī; along the way, there was a flowing irrigation channel. Upon reaching the bank of the channel, the bhikṣus stopped and, having removed their leather sandals, struck them together.
When they clapped their hands together, dust flew up, and all the devas became angry.
They rebuked the bhikṣus, saying, "One should not do such a thing here. The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, one must not beat leather sandals while walking on the road.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"If leather sandals become dusty while walking on the road, one should wipe them with soft sheepskin.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a son of the nāgas, having developed faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, came to Jetavana in order to hear the Dharma.
There was a bhikṣu who tied a rope around his neck and abandoned him in a desolate place.
At that time, the nāga boy wept toward his mother, and his mother said:
"Why are you weeping?"
He replied,
“I entered the Jeta Grove to listen to the Dharma, and a certain bhikṣu tied a rope around my neck and cast me away in a desolate place.
The dragon mother became greatly incensed and went to where the Buddha was, speaking to the Buddha about the bhikṣus.

At that time, the Buddha was preaching the Dharma surrounded by a great assembly. Seeing the nāga approaching from afar, the Buddha, through the power of the samādhi of loving-kindness, extinguished its poisonous intent. When the mother nāga reached the place where the Buddha was, she stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These bhikṣus are wicked and unwholesome; yet because my son has faith, he came to enter Jetavana to listen to the Dharma."
The bhikṣus tied a rope around the dragon’s neck and cast it far away to a desolate place. For the young dragon to be thus bound by a rope was most distressing, like being cast out and abandoned.

At that time, the Buddha, through various causes and conditions, taught the Dharma to the mother of the nāgas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her; having done so, he remained silent.
Then, having heard the Dharma, the mother of the nāgas prostrated to the Buddha, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after the mother of the dragon had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus on this matter and said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you must not catch snakes with nets and discard them.
Whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
"One may listen [to the sound] by placing a vessel over one's head and going to a secluded place far away; however, one must not keep a snake-trap.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This was spoken when the Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a groom had some business and came to Śrāvastī; he prepared various kinds of *tambala* for the Saṃgha and offered them by filling vessels to present to the monks.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept *tambala*."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "This pure food should be accepted.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus had no substance with which to soak their robes. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep troughs, basins, and tubs for soaking clothes.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus had no items with which to wash their robes. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep troughs, basins, and tubs for washing clothes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the elder Bhadrika constructed a great monastery, adorned it with various colors—blue, red, white, and black—and offered it to the Saṃgha, thinking thus:
"If the Buddha would permit me to adorn a dwelling with blue, red, white, and black colors and offer it to the Saṃgha,
that would be well. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to adorn a dwelling with blue, red, white, and black colors and offer it to the Saṃgha."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The householder Ugga, carrying a vessel of ox-head sandalwood worth one hundred thousand taels of gold and a seat from Jambudvīpa, went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!...”
"This vessel of ox-head sandalwood is worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, as is this Jambū river cloth; may the Buddha accept them.
If the Buddha should suffer from a wind disorder, he may use this sandalwood vessel to hold oil for anointing his body."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

When the elder saw that the Buddha had accepted by his silence, he immediately presented the bull-head sandalwood vessel to the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after the householder had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus on this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:

"The householder Ugga has offered a vessel of ox-head sandalwood worth one hundred thousand measures of gold, as well as bedding from Jambudvīpa. From now on, if there is a bhikṣu with such an illness, it should be used by him even if he does not request it."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Someone offered the Saṃgha various blended incenses, but the bhikṣus did not accept them, not knowing what they were to be used for.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be accepted and used to plaster the dwellings.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were plastering the exterior of the dwellings, many people came to view the stūpa and monastery; seeing this fragrant plaster on the outside of the dwellings, the people thought they were the Buddha’s stūpa or the stūpas of the śrāvakas.

At that time, there were many crowds of people, elephants, horses, oxen, and carriages, along with the sounds of men and women, which disturbed the bhikṣus’ sitting meditation and recitation of the sūtras; thus, the bhikṣus were displeased in their hearts.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From now on, if you obtain fragrant paste, you should apply it inside the dwelling, and to the bed, the bed-legs, the bed-feet, the bed-boards, the bed-sides, the clothing pegs, the clothing racks, and the four walls of the floor."
"One who anoints in this manner causes the monastery to obtain fragrance, and the donor obtains merit.
*Śāriputra-vinaya*, Volume 38; *Saṃyukta-uddāna*, Volume 3;
*Śāriputra-vinaya*, Volume 39, Part 4 of the Sixth Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Part Four of the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* on Miscellaneous Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Krumu, where he was assembled together with a great assembly of five hundred [monks].
At that time, the World-Honored One was teaching the Dharma of the five aggregates—namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—to five hundred bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus placed their alms bowls on the open ground, whereupon a celestial Māra transformed himself into the body of a great ox and approached the bowls.
A certain bhikṣu saw from afar a cow approaching his alms-bowl and said to the bhikṣu sitting beside him:
"Look at this large cow coming toward my bowl; will it not break my bowl?"
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"This is not a cow; it is a creation of Māra, intended to destroy your minds.
The Buddha spoke thus.
"From now on, a place for placing the alms bowl should be made within the dwellings.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī,
there was a bhikṣu who, traveling together with merchants from the kingdom of Kośala, arrived at Śrāvastī.

At that time, a merchant had his cart fully loaded with oil and was traveling along a dangerous and difficult stretch of road. There was another merchant whose cart was broken and whose oxen were lame;
this man said to his companions, "Take as much oil as you can according to your strength, and do not abandon it here."
The companions said, "Our own carts are already fully laden; if you take [the goods], we shall both suffer loss together.
The companions then abandoned him and departed.
This merchant was guarding the oil alone, feeling sorrowful and unhappy in his heart.
The bhikṣus followed behind him; they stayed behind for two reasons:
first, they feared dust would soil it, and second, they disliked the noise of the cart.
When the oil-keeper saw the bhikṣus approaching, he was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"This oil does not belong to me; I shall now offer it to the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus arrived, he spoke to them:
"Gather in one place; I shall give oil to the Saṃgha.
At that time, the bhikṣus each took portions of the oil, placing it in bowls, half-bowls, and small jars. Having filled them, they departed, passing through the marketplace on their way.
When the merchant saw the bhikṣus carrying oil, he immediately conceived a jealous mind and said to the bhikṣus:
"Where did you buy this oil?
Where will you sell it?"
"In what place shall we unload the pack-animals?
In what place shall we take up our profits?
When the bhikṣus heard these words, their hearts were not pleased, and they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not carry oil on a pole while walking along the road.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
After the *pravāraṇā*, the Buddha traveled about, teaching and transforming beings.
There was a bhikṣu walking while holding a leather sandal in his hand. When the Buddha saw him, he knew the reason but asked nonetheless:
"Why are you walking while holding a leather sandal in your hand?
He replied:
“I have a wound between my toes and there is nothing to apply to it.
The Buddha said, “From now on,
I permit you to keep a bag for holding ghee or oil, with a capacity of one *śu* or half a *śu*, and furthermore, you should also keep a covering for the bag.”
The Buddha traveled from the kingdom of Kāśī with the bhikṣus toward Śrāvastī.
As the bhikṣus proceeded, various devas followed them, thinking:
"If these bhikṣus should preach the Dharma, we shall listen and obtain great benefit."
While the bhikṣus were traveling, they engaged in playful and frivolous conversation. All the devas became indignant and rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"When the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas travel along the road, why do they not preach the Dharma and offer prayers of blessing so that the devas may find joy and benefit?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, when bhikṣus are traveling on a road, they should preach the Dharma and recite prayers of benediction; thus the devas will rejoice and bring about benefit."
When a bhikṣu dwells in a grove, beneath a tree, by the water’s edge, at a spring, or in a place frequented by many people, many devas often gather there and all think:
"Perhaps these bhikṣus will preach the Dharma; we shall listen and receive great benefit."

"When the bhikṣus dwell in gardens, beneath trees, by the water's edge, at the springs, or in places frequented by many people, they preach the Dharma and offer prayers of benediction; thus the various devas obtain joy and benefit."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“From now on, when you dwell in gardens, dwell under trees, dwell by the water’s edge, dwell by springs, or dwell in crowded places, you should recite dhāraṇīs and offer prayers for blessings; thus the devas will rejoice and bring about benefit.”
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A bhikṣu was traveling toward dusk through a place infested with bandits.
Upon seeing the bandits, that bhikṣu lost his robe out of fear of them.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:

"From now on, a bhikṣu must not travel toward a place where there are bandits at dusk. If there is a necessary reason to travel at dusk, he should place his robes over both shoulders, fasten them with a cord around his waist, and pass quickly through the path where the bandits are."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.
At that time, there was no water in Ālavī, so the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "A well should be dug."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.
In that country there was a newly constructed monastery where the bhikṣus swept the ground without discarding any waste.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep a dustpan.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu suffering from diarrhea; because he had to rise repeatedly, he became extremely exhausted.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should bore holes in the bed and place a vessel beneath it.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
For example, the brahmin King Puṣkarasādi requested three forms of salutation from the Buddha, saying:

"If the śramaṇa Gautama sees me riding an elephant, whether I am holding the reins, wearing leather sandals, drawing up my legs, or removing the turban from my head—upon seeing these, he should know that I have already paid homage to the śramaṇa Gautama."

When I am traveling on the road, whether I stand on one foot, remove my celestial crown, or set aside my parasol—having seen these signs, you should know that I have already paid homage to the World-Honored One.

If the śramaṇa Gautama sees me in the midst of the great assembly when I speak in a loud voice, when I laugh, or when I flick the corner of my robe, upon seeing this, he should know that I have paid homage to the World-Honored One.
"Should a bhikṣu perform these three kinds of salutations?
The Buddha said, "He may not."
The Buddha said to Upāli:
“To utter ‘Vandana’ (homage) is verbal expression;
to bow the body is called purity of mind.”

Upāli! When a bhikṣu pays homage, he should rise from his seat, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, and receive the feet of the senior monk with both hands.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, various bhikṣus shaved their hair here and there throughout the Jetavana. At that time, the devas and the vajra-deities all became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"One should not do this in this place."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you should not shave your hair in various places."
At that time, hair accumulated in great quantities. The Buddha said, "It should be discarded.
When it was being discarded, the bhikṣus felt nauseated and vomited. The Buddha said:
"One should dig a pit in one place.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, someone offered flower garlands to the Saṃgha; the bhikṣus did not accept them, not knowing what to do with the flower garlands.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept it; you should nail it to the wall with a pin. The monastery shall obtain incense, and the donor shall obtain merit."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the hair of the community of monks had grown long, and the barbers were extremely busy. There was then a barber who became a bhikṣu, and this bhikṣu thought to himself:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to keep a barber’s razor to shave the hair of the monks."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep a razor to shave the hair for the Saṃgha.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the monks' fingernails were long, and the hair-cutters were afraid.
There was then a hair-cutter who had become a bhikṣu, and this bhikṣu thought to himself:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to keep a nail-clipping knife to cut the nails for the Saṃgha."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to keep a knife for the Sangha to trim the nails.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃkha’s nose hair grew long, and the barber was distressed by it.
There was then a barber who had become a bhikṣu, and this bhikṣu thought to himself:
“It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to keep tweezers to pluck out the nose hair from Saṃkha’s nose.”
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to keep tweezers for plucking the hair from within the noses of the Saṃgha.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus had spread out rope beds in the open air and sat cross-legged in meditation. When they fell asleep due to the heat of the day, their heads moved.
A venomous snake crawled along the front of the rope beds; seeing the bhikṣus' heads moving, the snake thought to itself:
"Perhaps they wish to harm me."

He immediately leaped up and stung the bhikṣu on the forehead; however, the bhikṣu was still fast asleep and did not wake. He stung him on the forehead a second time, yet still did not wake. When he stung him on the forehead a third time, the bhikṣu died instantly.
After the meal, the bhikṣus were walking up and down in that place when they saw that this bhikṣu had died;
not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community of bhikṣus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, supports shall be provided beneath the legs of rope-beds, measuring eight finger-widths.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Elder Pilindavatsa suffered from eye pain. When he entered the bathhouse to wash, sweat entered his eyes and his pain increased. The Buddha said:
"One should apply mud to the forehead.
At that time, the smell of the mud entered his eyes, causing the pain to increase even further.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should mix incense with clay and smear it upon the forehead.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
the Elder Upāli questioned the Buddha:
As the Buddha said:
"O Maudgalyāyana!
From this day forth, let the Saṃgha recite the precepts by themselves; I shall not enter among the monks."
The bhikṣus did not know who should recite the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"The senior monk (sthavira) should recite them."
"If the Elder is unable, the next Elder in seniority [should speak];
in this manner, whoever is capable shall speak.
At that time, there was a reciter of the precepts who forgot various parts; when he forgot, he remained silent. The Buddha said:
"One should bestow it.
The bhikṣus then bestowed it in successive order. The Buddha said:
"One should not bestow it in successive order; one should only bestow it at the place where it was forgotten."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
“The brahmin Aṅgada offered the Buddha eight kinds of beverages:”
Regarding *cūṭapāna*, *mūlapāna*, *kolapāna*, *lakuca-pāna*, *śrīparṇī-pāna*, *pāriśat-pāna*, peach juice, grape juice, and so forth: having received them today, may they be drunk tomorrow?
The Buddha said:
"If it is free of dregs, the sick person may drink it;
if it contains dregs, drinking is not permitted."
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

There was a large monastic residence (vihāra) there, in which a visiting bhikṣu would come during each of the three watches—early night, midnight, and late night—and upon seeing a junior bhikṣu, he would strip off his own robes, sit down, and order him to rise.
The junior monk replied, "I am staying, Venerable; you do not know the proper time.
The monks did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“From now on, whether it be when the time is announced or when the *gandī* is struck, one should first take a portion of the bedding and then spread out one’s own bedding and light a lamp. When the stars appear, place a meditation cushion upon your head; from this point forward, you should not require a junior monk to rise.”
"To send [someone] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī.

The senior monk (*sthavira*) of Ālavī practiced meditation during the first watch of the night and returned to his cell during the middle watch; on his way back to the cell, he feared lions, tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should construct walls on all four sides of the dwelling, or else encircle the four sides with a fence and erect stakes.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Ālavī.
There was a new dwelling where there had been no rain for a long time due to a drought; later, it finally rained heavily, and the great floodwaters soaked the walls until they rotted and collapsed.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should construct drainage channels around it, and a trench should be dug on all four sides."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the hair of the bhikṣuṇīs had grown long, and because the barbers were busy, they were unable to shave them.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Tiṣyā who had previously been a barber; she thought to herself:
"If the Buddha would permit me to keep a razor to shave the hair of bhikṣuṇīs, it would be well.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep a razor to shave the hair of bhikṣuṇīs."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the nuns’ monks had long nails, and the barber was afraid.
There was a nun named Tiṣyā who had previously been a barber; she thought to herself:
"If the Buddha would permit me to keep a nail-cutter to trim the nails of the bhikṣuṇīs, it would be well.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep a nail-cutter to trim the nails for the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the nuns of the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha had long nose hairs, and the barbers were afraid.
There was a nun named Tiṣyā who had previously been a barber; she thought to herself:
"If the Buddha would permit me to keep tweezers to pluck the nose hairs of the bhikṣuṇīs, that would be well.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep tweezers to pluck the nose hairs of the bhikṣuṇīs."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore lower garments made of cowrie shells and pearls.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
Yet they wear garments adorned with shells and pearls, like kings or high ministers."
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did such a thing?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus wear garments adorned with cowrie shells and pearls?
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not wear garments made of cowrie shells or pearls.
Whoever wears them commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
The brahmin Ajita took a robe and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha said to Ajita, "Divide this robe and give it to the Saṃgha.
When he then divided it and gave it to the monks, the bhikṣus would not accept it, saying:
"I already possess the three robes; what use have I for this robe?
That brahmin returned to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The bhikṣus will not accept my robes.
At that time, the Buddha took a knife and gave it to Ajātaśatru, instructing him:
"Use this knife to cut one piece of fine cotton cloth into strips for robe borders, giving one segment to each person."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Bāṭi was wearing a patchwork robe that was torn and tattered in pieces.
When the Buddha saw Bāṭi, he knew the situation but asked him intentionally:
"Why is your patched robe so torn?
He replied,
"Because it is a *pāṃsukūla*, World-Honored One."
"For this reason, it is torn apart.
The Buddha said to Bāḍhi:
"Whether it be a paṃsukūla (rag-robe) or a householder's robe, one should skillfully cut, treat, and sew them so that they are perfectly regular, with separate borders applied."

After the Buddha had completed the *pravāraṇā*, he traveled through the human world to teach and transform beings. There was a bhikṣu walking along while holding a leather sandal in his hand; the Buddha saw this bhikṣu and, though he already knew the reason, asked him on purpose:
"For what reason are you walking while holding a leather sandal in your hand?"
He replied,
"My leather sandals have torn and broken.
At that time, the cobbler was too terrified to repair them, so the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit you to keep awls and knives, and to keep leather; if you are able to sew, you may sew and repair as you wish.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha was not proficient in reciting the Prātimokṣa. The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha is not proficient in reciting the Prātimokṣa. We pray that the World-Honored One will instruct them so that they may recite it proficiently."
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted. Why is this?"
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī who can receive and uphold my words after hearing them only once, bring her here.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī returned to her dwelling place, and the bhikṣuṇīs asked her,
"Were you able to receive the instruction on the recitation of the precepts?"
He replied, “I cannot. “Why can you not?”
The Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī who can receive and uphold my words upon hearing them but once, bring her here.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī, who had gone forth from a Brahmin family and possessed great power of mindfulness, said to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"I am able to receive and uphold [the precepts].
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, taking with her the bhikṣuṇī Śaikṣā, went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the World-Honored One intended to travel for two months to teach and transform beings; at that moment, many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the two bhikṣuṇīs were unable to hear the recitation of the precepts, so they returned to their residence.
The other bhikṣuṇīs asked them,
"Were you able to receive the instruction for reciting the precepts?"
He replied, “I cannot. “Why can you not?”
He replied:

"The Buddha intends to go on a journey for two months. Many devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans will all come to where the Buddha is, and [the monks] will not be able to hear the precepts."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had completed his two-month journey, he returned to Śrāvastī.

Immediately, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī took the bhikṣuṇī Cūḍāpanthaka and went to the place where the Buddha was; having prostrated with her head at his feet and stood to one side, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The bhikṣuṇīs were not proficient in reciting the precepts and requested, "May the World-Honored One instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha said, "It shall not be so."
"Why is this? If there be a bhikṣuṇī who, upon hearing my words but once, is able to receive and uphold them, she shall come here. Gopamā said:
“May the Blessed One speak it, so that the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī may be able to receive and uphold it.
The Buddha then spoke it for her, and the bhikṣuṇī Śrīmatī immediately received and upheld it.
At that time, the World-Honored One further taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā with various discourses on the Dharma.
When the Buddha had finished teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā, he remained silent.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Not long after the bhikṣuṇīs Gautamī and Śuklā had departed by circumambulating to the right, the Buddha, having observed this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, bhikṣus should recite the bhikṣuṇī precepts so that they are not forgotten or lost."

Why is this? Because women are prone to forgetfulness and their wisdom is easily distracted; after my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣuṇīs shall inquire about the rules of the precepts from the great assembly of monks.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma. Then an elder bhikṣu arrived late and rose from his second seat; the one in the second seat then rose for the third. As the elders arrived in succession, they rose in turn, causing disorder among the assembly and obstructing their listening to the Dharma.
The householders thought to themselves:
"In this place there is neither a first meal nor a subsequent meal; what is the use of sitting in order?
It will hinder our listening to the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the elders reproaching the bhikṣus, gathered the community of bhikṣus for this matter and said to them:
"From now on, when the Dharma is being taught, if a senior elder (sthavira) arrives, you must not ask a junior monk (navaka) to rise."
If one rises [when not required], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or the teacher (*ācārya*) comes, one may rise of one's own accord out of respect, but one must not cause others to rise.
If one causes others to rise, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, three bhikṣus who have been separated by an interval of three years may sit together on a large bed.
Two persons may sit together on a single rope-couch, but three may not."
"One should sit alone upon the bed; two people should not sit together.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was an elder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], they rose from their seats, prostrated with their heads at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Upon returning home, they prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink throughout the entire night.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were previously in dispute; it was the turn of the group of seventeen to guard the monastery, while it was the turn of the group of six to go out to receive the meal. They did not return at the proper time, as described in the account of the incident involving the tree-climbing.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There were two bhikṣus:
one named Caṇḍa and the other named Suda; these two bhikṣus were close friends.
These two bhikṣus tried on each other’s robes, as described in the *Sūtra on Skillful Recitation*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A pig-herder lost his pigs, and a wicked man by the moat of the Jetavana killed a pig, cut the meat into portions, and carried them away.
At that time, before midday, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Seeing pig intestines on the ground, they said to one another:
"You take these and cook them; I shall enter the city to beg for food."
There were some who were cooking and some who were begging for alms.
At that time, the man who had lost his pig entered the Jetavana Grove searching for it; seeing smoke rising, he went to the side of the bhikṣus and asked, “Venerable Sirs! Why is there smoke?”
"What is being done here? he asked. He replied, "Pig intestines are being boiled."
The man said, "I have now lost my pig; you are boiling its entrails, so you must have killed my pig.
They replied:
"I do not kill.
He asked, "Where did you get it?"
He replied, "It may be obtained from the ground along the moat.
They then said to one another:
"This bhikṣu refuses to confess his fault; let us take him before the authorities for judgment.
They then took him to the authorities.
At that time, the judge said:
"Venerable sir!
Did you truly kill the pig?
He replied:
"We did not kill it!
We obtained these intestines from the edge of the moat surrounding our Jeta Grove.
At that time, the adjudicator—who was a great believer in the Buddha’s Dharma and capable of making correct judgments—spoke as follows:
"A bhikṣu must certainly not kill pigs; let the bhikṣus depart, and from now on do not again take pig intestines from the open ground.
The bhikṣu told this to the other bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, one must not take pig intestines from the open ground."
"To take [it] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies equally to sugarcane and *tāla* fruit within a garden.
At that time, there was a man whose relative had died; he wrapped the deceased in white cotton cloth and abandoned him.
As Ānanda was walking along the road, he saw a corpse with a cotton cloth upon it and went to take it.
At that moment, the corpse moved its shoulder and said,
"Do not take my cloth."
Ānanda immediately left the cotton cloth and went away.
Upon arriving at the Jeta Grove, he said to the bhikṣus:
"While traveling on the road, I saw a dead person with a white cotton cloth upon them."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Kṛṣṇa Ānanda, who was physically robust.
He asked, "Where is the dead person?
Ānanda replied:
"In such-and-such a place.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu went to the corpse and took the white cotton cloth; the corpse moved its shoulder and said, "Venerable Kālānanda!"
"Do not take my white cotton cloth.
Then Kṛṣṇa Ānanda spat upon this dead person and said: "Preta!"
"From where have you come to be so greedily attached to this robe?
Because of your stinginess and greed in previous lives, you have fallen among the hungry ghosts.
Black Ānanda immediately took up the robe and walked away, while the ghost followed behind, wailing as it pursued him.

Kṛṣṇa Ānanda took this white cotton cloth and entered the Jeta Grove; at that time, a powerful benevolent deity guarding the gate of the Jeta Grove would not allow this ghost to enter, and he immediately fell into the moat.
Then Kṛṣṇa Ānanda showed the cotton cloth to the bhikṣus and said,
"I took this cotton cloth from that dead man.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Where is the dead man?
He replied,
"He has now fallen into the moat of the Jeta Grove."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, one must not take items from a corpse that has not yet decomposed."
"To take [it] constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used needles to draw upon the bodies of corpses to cause them to decay so as to take the clothing. Someone saw this and rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:"
"How excellent and virtuous! [he thought].
"How can one be like a *caṇḍāla*, piercing a corpse with a needle to take its clothing?
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was not pleased. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not pierce a corpse with a needle.
To do so is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the Buddha said to Kṛṣṇa Ānanda:

“Return the corpse to its original place and cover it again with white cotton cloth. You should walk behind the hungry ghosts and not ahead of them; you should stay on their left side and not their right; you should remain near the head and not near the feet, lest you be seized by the ghosts.”
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Someone offered wooden buckets to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, but the bhikṣuṇīs would not accept them, not knowing what they were to be used for.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should take it and use it to hold bath powder.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Cūḍānandā, whose features were upright and whose complexion was pure. She used a coarse waist-cord to bind her *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī* (undergarment), folding both sides so that her hips appeared broad and her waist appeared slender.
A merchant saw this and said to his companions, "Look at the crotch of this bhikṣuṇī!
When the bhikṣuṇī heard this, she was displeased and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs must not wear their nivāsana robes with both sides pleated together at the hips.
Any who violate this shall be guilty of a duṣkṛta offense.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who, not wearing an undergarment, leaned against a newly painted wall, causing the colors and plaster to flake off.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, if a bhikṣu leans against a painted wall without wearing an undergarment, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus were lighting fires in various places throughout the Jetavana, as if they were in a smithy.
All the Vajrapāṇi spirits became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"What is it called for a bhikṣu to defile this ground?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not kindle fires in various places.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You should kindle them in only one place."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus bathed in various places within the Jeta Grove, using either soap powder or earth; because of the moisture and heat, worms were produced.
All the Vajra deities angrily rebuked them, saying:
"How can you be called bhikṣus and yet defile this ground?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not bathe in various places; you should bathe at one location using a water drain.
This occurred while the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śākya.
Śreṇika Mahānāman invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Upon arriving at his residence, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink throughout the entire night. In the early morning, having arranged the seating area, he went to where the Buddha was and said, "The time has come;
may the Buddha know the time."

The Buddha and the community of bhikṣus entered his house; as it happened there was meat, and after the Buddha and the Saṃgha had taken their seats in order, Mahānāma the Śākya personally served the rice and distributed the meat.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept dogs; having finished eating quickly, they picked up the bones until their bowls were full, placed them before them, and raised their eyes to look haughtily.
Then Śreṇika Mahānāman, while making his rounds to inspect the monks' meal, observed who was receiving it.
"Who has not received it?
Who has received it repeatedly?
Seeing that this bowl was filled to the brim with items, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable One!
This bowl is the insignia of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; why do you treat this bowl with such contempt?
I am not concerned that you yourself hold the bowl in low esteem, but I fear that later you might carry this impure bowl and receive my food."
At that time, after the Buddha had seen Śreṇika Mahānāman’s reproach, he rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can you place impure things in your alms bowls?"
"From now on, you must not place impure things in your alms bowl.
Whoever does so commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus supported their bowls with their feet while receiving food.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not support your bowl with your feet while receiving food."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used the tips of their leather sandals to support their bowls while receiving food.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not accept food with sandals on and supporting the bowl with your head.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the group of six bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon those who did not possess bowls.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were fond of quarreling with one another.
It happened that the turn for the group of six to guard the monastery came first, while it was the turn of the group of seventeen to go out and receive food.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus came from the bhikṣu who was guarding the monastery quarters and asked for their alms bowls.
When asked, "What are you doing with them? they replied:
"I will give you some food.
That bhikṣu said,
"I have no bowl."
He asked, "Did you go forth without an alms bowl?
He replied:
"So be it," said the seventeen groups of bhikṣus, and they spoke thus:
"You are a person of great wisdom and virtue; even without a bowl, you may receive full ordination."
That bhikṣu, hearing these words, was displeased in heart and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, one who does not possess a bowl shall not be permitted to go forth or receive full ordination."
"If one gives it to a recipient, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, at that time the Śākya son Upananda ordained a leader of bandits as a monk; later, he entered Rājagṛha to beg for food.
When the women at the house where he arrived saw this bhikṣu coming, they hid their clothes and belongings, saying:
"This man is a hypocrite who pretends to beg for food; he surely wishes to come and take our clothes."
When that bhikṣu heard these words, his heart was not pleased, and he spoke of it to the other bhikṣus. The bhikṣus then related this matter in detail to the Buddha.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter, the Buddha, though already aware of it, asked Upāli (Bhadanta) intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked Upananda with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu ordain a leader of bandits as a renunciant?
Having rebuked him with these various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you must not ordain the leaders of thieves as renunciants.
If you do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, due to special circumstances, you wish to ordain one, once ordained, you must cause them to depart from their original location for a distance of five or six *yojanas*."
"If you know someone who is virtuous and of good character, you may bring him back here.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a famine and food was scarce. A certain bhikṣu, whose years since ordination had not yet reached five and who was thus required to receive formal dependence (*niśraya*), went to the home of his relatives. After staying for four or five days, he took his leave and wished to depart.
Relatives asked,
"For what reason are you leaving?
He replied:
"I must rely upon [him]," [the relative] said.
The Venerable One replied, "Noble one!"
"In this age of famine, some may even die of starvation; what use is there in relying [on such things]?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, during times of famine, you may come daily to the place where your preceptor resides to listen and stay;
you may come every day. If you cannot come every day, you may come every five days."
If one cannot come within five days, one should come at the time of the *poṣadha*.
If one cannot come even at the time of the *poṣadha*, then up to two and a half *yojanas* away, one must come to see the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) by the time of the *pravāraṇā*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a border village in the kingdom of Kośala; at that time, King Prasenajit levied taxes on this border village, and the people of the village all abandoned it and departed.
There was a monk residing in that place who, because he could not obtain food and clothing, abandoned his dwelling and departed.
Later, the king issued an edict that they were no longer to be taxed or seized; when the people heard this, they immediately returned to their original locations, but the monks had not yet returned.

At that time, various non-Buddhist practitioners came from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī. Passing through the monastery grounds, they saw that the monastery was pure and magnificently adorned, yet it was filled with cooking pots, cauldrons, jars, vessels, basins, seats, and bedding. They said to the lay devotees:
"This monastery of yours is empty; it would be well if we were permitted to dwell here."
He replied, "As you wish.
The non-Buddhists then remained there.

There were certain bhikṣus traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī who arrived at this monastery; there they saw that the rooms were pure and magnificently adorned, with cooking pots, cauldrons, jars, vessels, basins, seats, and bedding filling the entire complex.
The bhikṣus said to one another, "This naked ascetic has no fields, houses, or households; by what means could he have prepared such an offering?
This must surely have been the former residence of a bhikṣu."
The bhikṣus said to him, "Go. He replied:
"Why have you left?
They replied,
"This was formerly our dwelling place."
The non-Buddhists replied, "Venerable Sir! This was not obtained from you;
nor did you settle us here. We obtained it from the householder, and if the householder dismisses us, we shall depart."
The bhikṣus went and said to the householder:
"This was originally our dwelling place as śramaṇas; it would be well if you would allow us to reside here once again."
The laypeople asked the bhikṣus,
"How many years has it been since you abandoned this monastery and left?
They replied:
"Ten years.
The laypeople asked the non-Buddhist practitioners,
"How many years have you been living here?"
He replied, "Ten years.
The laypeople then said this:
"This cannot be obtained. Why is this?
The bhikṣu has already been gone for ten years, and the non-Buddhists have also resided here for ten years; therefore, he may not be sent away."
The bhikṣus remained silent.
They reported this matter to the king, who said:
"Who said that one must leave after ten years, or stay for ten years, before being permitted to depart?"
At that time, the king immediately sent a man who struck the heterodox practitioner with his fist, breaking his teeth, and then sent him away.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From now on, for those two monasteries that are situated near one another, they should perform the *karmavācanā* together and receive offerings in one place, while holding the *poṣadha* in both places; this is how it should be done.
As for the ritual procedure: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu shall announce:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
"In such-and-such places and such-and-such places, there should be one place for receiving offerings and two places for the *poṣadha*.

If the Saṃgha deems it timely, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that there shall be one place for receiving offerings and two places for the *poṣadha* in such-and-such places and such-and-such places."
Thus he announces:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
At such-and-such a place and such-and-such a place, there is one location for receiving offerings and two locations for the *poṣadha*."
"Whichever elders among you consent to receiving alms at one place while performing the *poṣadha* at two places—those who consent remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
"The Saṃgha has finished performing the *poṣadha* at two places while receiving alms at one place. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

If one of these two locations is vacant, all the robes, bedding, and various articles therein should be gathered together in that one place; when other monks arrive later, they shall then be divided and distributed among them.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus either carried items upon their heads or wore items around their waists.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not walk with objects carried upon your head or objects girded at your waist.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda ordained a general of King Bimbisāra’s army.
At that time, the people of a frontier region rebelled, and when the king investigated this general, someone replied:
"He has gone forth as a monk."
“Under whom did you go forth?
He replied, “Under a śramaṇa.”
“Who is a śramaṇa? He replied,
“The son of the Śākyas is a śramaṇa.”
The king spoke with anger:
"This bhikṣu will surely lead away all my attendants.
Among them was a bhikṣu of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was not pleased, and he reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus;
knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Upananda: "Did you truly do this? He replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
“What is it called when a bhikṣu arbitrarily ordains someone known to the king?
The Buddha said:
“From now on, one must not ordain those known to the king.”
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
the Śākya son Bāṇaṃdita quarreled with a merchant's son.
The merchant’s son became angry and struck Baddhālaka with his fist.
At that time, Baddhālaka went to the place where legal cases were being adjudicated and said,
"This merchant’s son has beaten me."
Question: "On account of what did they dispute?
He replied with the aforementioned matter.
Then the judge summoned the merchant’s son; once he had arrived, he asked him, "Did you strike the bhikṣu?
He replied:
"Hit him! At that moment, the judge asked about the legal code:
"What offense does one incur for hitting a bhikṣu?"
He replied,
"According to the regulation, whichever part of the body was used to strike him, that very part should be severed.
He then asked the merchant’s son:
"With which part of the body did you strike?
He replied,
"With my right hand."
Then the judge cut off his right hand.

When the people of the city heard that the śramaṇa Śākyaputra had had a man’s hand cut off, one person told it to two, and two told it to three; thus the ill repute spread until it filled the entire city of Śrāvastī.
Among them was a bhikṣu who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, he was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Baddhananda intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the Śākya son Upananda with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu say that a person has had their hand cut off?
The Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not say that someone’s hand has been cut off.
Whoever violates this commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This was while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a non-Buddhist who, with a mind of faith and longing, desired to go forth from the household life. He went to the bhikṣus and said, "I wish to go forth.
What difficult matters are there within the dharma of going forth?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"There are four reliances:
first, relying on wearing rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) one may go forth and receive full ordination."
He replied,
"I cannot wear the tattered clothes of a dead person. He asked:
"What further difficulty is there besides this?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have always relied on alms-gathering to leave the household life and receive full ordination."
He replied, "My dharma is to beg for food; what further difficulty could there be?
He answered:
"One who dwells under a tree is permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.
He replied, "In my Dharma, one dwells under a tree; what further difficulty could there be?"
He replied,
"I have left home and received full ordination by relying on the discarded medicine of the dust.
He answered:
"I cannot take this medicine.
Having heard these words, he refused to go forth and receive full ordination.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"One should not first explain the four reliances; rather, one should first complete the bestowal of full ordination, and only then explain the four reliances."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who had lost his robe and bowl. A bhikṣu who was an acquaintance saw these robes and bowl in another place;
he immediately seized them and said, "These are such-and-such a person's robes and bowl; I now take them from your hands."
He said, "I bought it. He asked:
"Who saw you when you bought it?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One who buys it is not a thief; one who steals it is a thief.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"How much was this robe purchased for?"
"If one has actually purchased it, one should return the original price and take [the robe].

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣus were traveling for two months. At that time, the bhikṣus of the group of six had acquaintances who entrusted their robes to the bhikṣus of the group of six before departing, as previously described.
The Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, five bhikṣus asked the Buddha:
"With what substance are robes dyed?"
The Buddha said:
"It should be dyed with the juice of roots, stems, leaves, flowers, or fruits, or dyed with the dung of a newborn calf.

While the Buddha was in the kingdom of Ālavī, a newly constructed monastery had no place for the bhikṣus to practice walking meditation (caṅkrama). They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should construct a place for walking meditation (caṅkrama).
Because that land was hot, sweat flowed while they were walking;
the Buddha said, "One should plant trees at the place for walking meditation."

[End of the first twenty dharmas. Regarding the second twenty dharmas: When the Buddha had first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, some merchants offered him ghee and milk-gruel. After the Buddha had eaten it, wind arose within his abdomen.

At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra saw that the Buddha was suffering from a wind-related ailment. Because of the Jambu tree—after which the continent is named Jambudvīpa—and not far from that tree, there was a grove of harītakī trees.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra took some excellent harītakī fruits and presented them to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Not far from the Jambu tree, there is a grove of harītakī trees. I have taken these fine harītakī fruits here; I pray that the Buddha will accept and eat them, so that your wind-related ailment may be cured and you may move about and rest with ease."
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, seeing that the Buddha had accepted, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after Śakra had gone, the Buddha immediately consumed this harītakī; his wind-disorder was instantly cured, and when he threw the seed upon the ground, a harītakī tree grew forth.
The tree grew large and produced *harītakī* fruits; when they ripened to a yellow color, they fell to the ground and covered it entirely.
Seeing this, the Buddha knew the reason already, yet he intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason do the bhikṣus not eat these *harītakī* fruits?"
Ānanda said,
"It is because the World-Honored One has established the rule that one must not consume food received overnight.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Since the previously received *harītakī* has already been consumed, there is no offense in eating this now.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus had no containers for their clothing;
the Buddha said, "You should make boxes."
Because that land was hot, insects were born there. The Buddha said:
"One should place *nāgakesara* wood and the roots of the *navilā* grass inside the robe chest; because of the fragrance, insects will not be born."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered blankets to the community of monks, but the bhikṣus would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept blankets."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Sangha may accept it, and a single individual may also accept it.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore robes with loose threads, robes with knotted threads, robes with interlaced threads, robes with brushed threads, and robes that had not been purified.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not wear robes with loose threads at the head, knotted threads at the head, interlaced threads at the head, or brushed threads at the head."
"If one wears [such a garment], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one wears a garment that has not been consecrated (*apariśuddha*), it is a *pāyattika*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not wear robes with frayed edges left by monks or laypeople—whether those with frayed edges, those with knotted frayed edges, those with interlaced frayed edges, or those with brushed frayed edges—and they did not treat them as purified garments.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If the Saṃgha or a layperson has a robe with frayed edges, a robe with knotted frayed edges, a robe with interlaced frayed edges, a brushed frayed-edge robe, or a robe that has not been formally purified (akalpiya), one may wear it."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
When an Arhat entered parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"As the Buddha has said:"
"There are eighty thousand families of worms within the body.
If one burns the body, one would kill these worms.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"When a person dies, the various worms within them also die.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha permits me to cremate the body of an arhat, it would be well.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said,
"I permit you to cremate the body of an arhat."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to erect stūpas for arhats.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The Buddha has permitted us to pay homage to the stūpas of arhats.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
“It would be well if the Buddha would permit us to make offerings at the stūpas of arhats.”
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make offerings at the stūpas of arhats.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Kātyāyana had a merchant disciple who, returning from the sea, offered him a conch-shell waistband as a gift.
Kātyāyana did not accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to accept gifts of conch-shell waistbands."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"It may be accepted.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A certain sick bhikṣu said to his attendant:
"If you can care for me well and cherish me, then when my life comes to an end, all my possessions shall be given entirely to you."
Having spoken thus, he passed away. The *gandī* was struck to assemble the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha said to the attendant:
"Bring all the belongings belonging to the deceased monk; they should be divided among the Saṃgha present here."
The caregiver said:
"This is not the property of the Saṃgha.
For what reason?"
When I visited a patient, the patient said to me:
"If you can look after me well and cherish me with affection, then when my life comes to an end, all my possessions shall be given entirely to you."
"Because of this matter, it is not the property of the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no such death that [the property] shall be given according to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu passes away, his belongings should be divided by the *saṃgha* present there.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.

There was a bhikṣu who had performed a formal act of pure giving (*viśuddha-dāna*) to another bhikṣu. When the owner of the goods passed away, the community immediately struck the *gaṇḍī* to assemble the monks.
When the monks sent someone to fetch the robes and belongings of the deceased bhikṣu, the bhikṣu who had received the pure gift replied:
"These are not the property of the Saṃgha."
"Why is this? Because that deceased bhikṣu previously made a pure gift to me.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"It was given for the sake of purification.
After he has passed away, the present Saṃgha should divide it."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A bhikṣu had made a formal gift (*pariṣkāra-dāna*) of his robes to another bhikṣu, but the recipient died.
At that time, the *gaṇḍī* was struck to assemble the Saṃgha; that bhikṣu came personally with the robes and gave them to the Saṃgha, saying:
"This is the property of the Saṃgha.
The monks asked:
"For what reason?"
He replied,
"I previously made a pure gift to a deceased bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the person who received the pure gift dies, it should again be offered as a pure gift to another person.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a certain bhikṣu made a pure gift to another bhikṣu; however, the recipient of the gift violated his precepts, and the other bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one returns the *pariṣkāra-dāna* (gift of requisites), it may be purifiedly given again to another person.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who had made a *pariṣkāra-dāna* of his requisites to a co-practitioner disciple. When the disciple committed an improper act, the teacher rebuked him, saying:
"Do not stay near me.
Thus, the disciple went and stayed near the group of six bhikṣus.
Although the disciple initially intended to repent, because he remained close to the group of six bhikṣus, he had no heart for repentance.
The teacher went and said to his disciple,
"Why do you not repent before me? He replied:
"I cannot," [the disciple] replied. The Master said,
"I have previously made a pure gift of this robe to you."
The disciple said,
"I shall now give it to the Buddha.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a disciple is reprimanded by his teacher and not permitted to perform manual labor, he should perform a formal act of relinquishment (*naiḥsargika*) to another person.
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the ground was damp, so the bhikṣus stayed in cloth tents they had made.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Will we not be guilty of the offense of keeping an extra robe for more than ten nights?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If these robes are used for the purpose of making a hut, there is no offense."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ālavī.
At that time, there were insects in the well water, and the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be strained.
When straining it, two or three people held it together; while holding it, it was not steady. The Buddha said:
"One should make a water-strainer ring. After straining the water, pour the insects into a well."
The insects in the well became increasingly numerous, so the Buddha said:
"Take a vessel filled with water.
After straining the water, pour the insects into it; having poured them into it, then carry them and pour them into flowing water."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Is it possible that while monks are receiving the *kaṭhina* robe within the Saṃgha, there might be some who do not receive it?
He replied:
“There is. If a bhikṣu observes the rains retreat in one place but receives the *kaṭhina* robe in this [other] place, it is said that he has not obtained it.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu, without having received the kaṭhina robe, can nevertheless be said to have received it?
He replied, "There is."

If a bhikṣu has completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony after observing the rains retreat at this location, and having gone outside the boundary returns within it, hears that the Saṃgha is today receiving the *guṇavatī-cīvara*,
and upon hearing this rejoices, it is termed "receiving."
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Is it possible that when some bhikṣus relinquish their *kaṭhina* robe, others do not relinquish theirs?
The Buddha said:

“There is. If a bhikṣu has received a kaṭhina cloth in another location, and the Saṃgha there relinquishes the cloth, even though that bhikṣu is present [in the original location], it is not considered a relinquishment.”
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Is it possible that if the Saṃgha relinquishes the *kaṭhina* robe while a certain bhikṣu is absent, the relinquishment is still considered valid?"
He replied: "There is.

If a bhikṣu who has accepted the *kaṭhina* robe goes outside the boundary and hears that the *kaṭhina* robe is being relinquished, and he rejoices in it, this is called 'attaining the relinquishment'."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
In a residence in the kingdom of Kośala, someone offered property to the Saṃgha; the gaṇḍī was struck to assemble the monks, and once they had gathered and divided the goods, they rose.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus came from outside the boundary and said to the bhikṣus:
"We shall divide among ourselves whatever property belongs to this saṃgha; you bhikṣus may then divide it again."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If the ghaṇṭā has been struck, the Saṃgha has reached consensus, and the distribution of goods has already commenced, and a bhikṣu arrives from outside the boundary, one may give him a share if he so desires, but one must not forcibly divide the remainder."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a man from the kingdom of Kośala offered robes to the Saṃgha. Then, the group of six bhikṣus went to the monastery and spoke to one another in pairs:
"Let us stand in a secluded place when we see the bhikṣus about to divide the robes."
“Once they have finished dividing the property, we shall go out to the outskirts and cause them to divide it again.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus saw that the other bhikṣus were already staying in a secluded place; they then struck the *ghanṭī* to assemble the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus said to one another, “Summon these six bhikṣus! We seek their whereabouts but cannot find them.”
Someone said, "This bhikṣu has many affairs; he will surely go out.
They then divided the goods together and rose.
Then the group of six bhikṣus came within the boundary and said,
"This should be shared by us together.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spoke these words:
"If you do not believe that I am within the boundary, there are bhikṣus here who have seen me; let the bhikṣus share it with us again.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If the *ghaṇṭā* has been struck and the Sangha has already risen after distributing the items, if a bhikṣu from within the boundary arrives, one may give [the remaining portion] to him if one wishes; one must not force a redistribution."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a bhikṣu spread out expensive fire-cleansed cloth and deep-mo-gan cloth upon his bed to sit; when he rose, he nearly tore them.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That which should be spread out, you should spread out; that which should be placed, you should place; act according to what is appropriate."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
For the purpose of the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣus struck the *gandi*; the one reciting the precepts said:
"If you do not come, let those who have made a formal entrustment (*anuśrāvaṇa*) speak."
A certain bhikṣu spoke thus:
"A certain bhikṣu is pure and has given his consent (chanda).
He was asked:
"Where has that bhikṣu gone?
He replied,
"He has gone beyond the boundary."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, one who has given his consent (chanda) must not go beyond the boundary."
"One who commits [this offense] incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
For the sake of the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣus struck the *gandi*; the one reciting the precepts said:
"Let the one who conveys the consent speak.
A certain bhikṣu announced:
"The bhikṣu so-and-so is pure and conveys his consent."
He asked, "Where is this bhikṣu? He replied:
"Outside the boundary.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not receive the formal consent (*chanda*) of those outside the boundary.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
For the sake of the poṣadha, he struck the ghaṇṭī to assemble the Saṃgha, and the one who recited the precepts said:
"Who will instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?
They replied:
“Kāḷudāyin,” he asked, “where are you?”
He replied,
"I am traveling outside the boundary.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, those who receive instructions from a bhikṣuṇī must not travel beyond the boundary.
One who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus successively gave their consent, their proxy-votes, their invitations for the *pravāraṇā*, and their absolution of offenses to one another.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not pass on [the transmission of] purity, the formal consent (chanda), the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā), or the removal of offenses."
"One who commits [this] offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) not far from the monastery in the kingdom of Kośala. At the time of the *poṣadha*, it rained, and the monks within the monastery thought to themselves:
"The forest-dwelling bhikṣus shall come.
Then the community at the forest hermitage further thought:
"The bhikṣus from the monastery shall come."
At that time, as neither side would yield, the *poṣadha* could not be performed.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should perform the *poṣadha* in a single location through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*); it should be conducted in this manner.
As for the procedure: with the Saṃgha gathered in harmony and with one mind, one bhikṣu should announce within the assembly:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
"This particular hall shall be made the place for the *poṣadha*.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent that this particular hall be made the place for the *poṣadha*.
Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion with one proclamation) is as follows:
"The Sangha has heard that the construction of such-and-such a hall as a place for the *poṣadha* is completed. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Lady Mallikā, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, went to the Jeta Grove and asked the bhikṣus,
"How many monks are there here?"
He replied, “I do not know.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “You should count.
At that time, the bhikṣus counted by calling out names; while counting by calling out names, they became confused and lost count. The Buddha said:
"One should cast the voting sticks.
The lady asked again:
"How many śrāmaṇeras are there?"
He replied, "I do not know.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
