"Śrāmaṇeras should also cast lots. At that time,
the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
During the time of the Saṃgha’s Poṣadha ceremony, Queen Mallikā offered money to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus would not accept it,
saying, "The Buddha has not yet permitted the acceptance of Poṣadha funds.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to receive it.

At that time, before the monks had reached the *poṣadha* assembly, they recited the precepts and performed the *poṣadha* on the second or third day. Monks who came for the sake of the *poṣadha* did not receive the offerings of the *poṣadha*.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not recite the precepts two or three days in advance."
"One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha said:
"One should perform the *poṣadha* at the time for the *poṣadha*, so that when monks come for the *poṣadha*, they may receive offerings."
At that time, the śrāmaṇeras requested their shares.
He replied:
"Because you did not participate in the poṣadha, did not perform the karmavācanā, did not recite the precepts, and did not enter into the poṣadha assembly, I shall not give you a share."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Because the śrāmaṇeras have received voting tallies, they should be given their share."
Although the Buddha permitted [the giving], it was not known how much should be given.
The Buddha said:
"If a śrāmaṇera is in the order of the procession and a dānapati gives with their own hands, they should give an equal portion."
"If one gives only to the Saṃgha, the great bhikṣus shall receive three parts, and the śrāmaṇeras shall receive one part.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then the group of six bhikṣus sat on a single bed together with a layperson.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not sit on the same seat as a layperson."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat on a single bed with a śrāmaṇera.
The other bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not sit on the same bed as a śrāmaṇera.
One who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, monks stayed together with a śrāmaṇera for two nights; on the third night, they sent him out.
As he was leaving, the śrāmaṇera had previously smeared oil on his feet, and as he stepped onto the floor covering, the oil stained the floor covering.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, when oil has been applied to the feet, one must not walk upon a floor-covering."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the monks of the group of six (*ṣaḍvargika*) were mutually enticing one another's disciples. Then an elder rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣus do not know how they may keep disciples and instruct them in accordance with the Dharma;
thus these group-of-six bhikṣus entice my disciples.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not entice the disciples of others.
One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus each made a solemn oath, saying:
"If we were to entice your disciples, may we be under the curse of the Buddha, the curse of the Dharma, and the curse of the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, a bhikṣu must not recite incantations for himself, nor must he recite incantations for others."
"If one curses oneself or curses another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made a vow with an object, saying:
"If I entice away your disciples, I shall forfeit this object."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not make vows for yourselves or for others by means of material objects."
"If one makes a vow regarding an object for oneself or for another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus lost their robes and bowls and said to the other bhikṣus:
"We have lost our robes and bowls; we should flee together.
At that time, each of the bhikṣus reflected on this, not knowing what to do.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, bhikṣus shall not hide themselves away, nor shall they cause others to hide themselves away.
If one does so oneself or causes another to do so, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"Why is this? Because incantation and fleeing are of one kind.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus borrowed white garments and said to the person from whom they had taken them,
"If you do not return them when the time comes, we shall demand double.
The person who had given the items was filled with fear.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not demand a double payment from others."
"One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, tigers and wolves had killed a deer and were selecting choice pieces of meat to eat. A bhikṣu passed along this path after midday and saw the dead deer; they spoke to one another, saying:
"Take this back; eat it tomorrow.
He then took the remains of the deer and returned home.
At that time, the tiger, driven by hunger, rose up to search for the remains of the deer and roared as he circled around the Jeta Grove.
The Buddha saw the tiger roar; knowing the reason, he intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason is this tiger roaring?
He replied:
“World-Honored One,
it is because a bhikṣu has brought meat left over from a tiger.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not take the remains left by tigers.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Why is this?
Because the tiger has not yet ceased its expectation [of food].
If one takes what remains from a lion, there is no offense. Why is this?
"Because the lion has severed all hope.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
there was a bhikṣu who, without first seeking permission from another bhikṣu, proceeded to expose the offense of another.
When that bhikṣu heard of this matter, his heart was not pleased, and he reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From now on, if another person does not permit it, one must not speak of their offenses, nor cause them to remember their offenses, nor obstruct their recitation of the precepts or their *pravāraṇā*, nor obstruct their instruction of bhikṣuṇīs."
"To obstruct [a superior] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a junior bhikṣu who called upon a senior bhikṣu without showing respect; when the senior bhikṣu heard this, his mind was displeased.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not address an elder without showing him respect."
"If one calls an elder without showing respect, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know how to address an elder.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, when a junior bhikṣu addresses a senior bhikṣu,
he shall call him 'Venerable One (āyuṣmat). At that time, merely calling him 'Venerable One' was still considered inadequate, so the Buddha said:"
"From now on, you shall be called Elder [Name],
just as one calls Elder Śāriputra, Elder Maudgalyāyana, Elder Ānanda, Elder Nandiya, and Elder Kapphiṇa."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There were the bhikṣu Nāla and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā; these two would engage in playful chatter together, causing disturbance and vexation to the other bhikṣus.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The actions of the bhikṣu Nala and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā were unwholesome; what they consumed was like that of a thief."
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *akalpa-karman* (act of non-purity) against these two individuals.
With a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu shall proclaim as follows:"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus, Nala and Śilā bhikṣuṇī, have been harassing the bhikṣus with playful and joking speech.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its ear, then these bhikṣus, Nala and Śilā bhikṣuṇī, who have harassed the bhikṣus with playful and joking speech, shall be treated as those who have consumed food through theft."
Thus it is announced. The motion and one subsequent proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) are as follows:
“The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of impurity against the bhikṣu Nala and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!”

After the Saṃgha had finished performing the *akalpa-karman* (impure ritual act) against these two individuals, the two of them felt remorse in their hearts; recognizing their own transgressions, they confessed and repented in all four directions, saying:
"We previously disturbed the Saṃgha, but now we have given rise to a pure mind. We beg you to revoke the *akalpa-karman*."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Since the bhikṣu Nala and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā have repented and given rise to a pure mind, you should grant them the *karma* of relinquishing the state of impurity."
It should be performed in this manner:

with a single-mindedly harmonious Saṃgha, the bhikṣu Nanda and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā rise from their seats, bare their right shoulders, remove their leather sandals, place their right knees on the ground, join their palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Because the bhikṣu Mānava and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā engaged in playful chatter and disturbed the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha has performed an impure *karmavācanā* against us; whatever we have consumed is like stolen property.
We now repent our transgressions and give rise to a pure mind; we beg that you relinquish this impure *karmavācanā*.
May the food received by us, the bhikṣu Nanda and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā, not be like stolen property, out of compassion!
A second and a third time he likewise requested.
Then, one bhikṣu among the Saṃgha proclaimed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Because the bhikṣu Nala and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā engaged in playful chatter and disturbed the Saṃgha, they were subjected to an impure *karmavācanā*; whatever they consumed was as if it were stolen.

These two individuals now repent their transgressions and give rise to a pure mind; they beg the Sangha to revoke the formal act of impurity (*aśuddha-karman*), so that what they have consumed shall not be considered as theft.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall perform the *jñapti-karman* of revoking the formal act of impurity against the bhikṣu Nāla and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā, so that what they consume shall not be considered as theft.
Thus it is announced. This is the motion followed by the threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*):

"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act of revoking the *akalpa-karman* (the act of declaring one impure) against the bhikṣu Nala and the bhikṣuṇī Śilā. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, a bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
"With what kind of hide should leather sandals be made?
The Buddha said:
"Except for five kinds of skins:
the skin of a lion, the skin of a tiger, the skin of a leopard, the skin of a otter, and the skin of a cat.
Furthermore, except for five other kinds of skins:"
"Elephant hide, horse hide, dog hide, jackal hide, and black antelope hide—these are prohibited; for all others, making them is permitted.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, someone offered the Saṃgha leather sandals made from the skin of a large fish (*ānanda*). The bhikṣus did not accept them.
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to wear sandals made of sturgeon leather.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should accept sandals made of sturgeon leather."
"Because it is coarse, cover it with oxhide.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, a certain person offered the Saṃgha sandals made of fish skin and leather; the bhikṣus would not accept them.
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to accept sandals made of fish-skin leather.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to accept sandals made of fish-skin leather."
"Because my eyes ache, I have covered them with an ox-hide.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Someone offered sinews to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus would not accept them, not knowing what they were to be used for.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to use it to make door-bolts and door-ropes.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, [this occurred].
Someone offered bear skins to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus did not accept them, not knowing what to do with them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should accept them; you should wear them inside the doors of the monastic quarters to wipe your feet before entering the rooms."

After the Buddha had finished his *pravāraṇā*, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings. He saw a bhikṣu walking while holding a leather sandal in his hand; knowing the reason already, he asked him:
"For what reason are you walking while holding a leather sandal in your hand?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is because these leather sandals have injured my feet."
The Buddha said, "One should cover it with soft leather.
After he had covered it, while walking he brushed against the ground; the Buddha said:
"The Net of Subsequent Giving should be established.
While the Buddha was in the kingdom of Āravī,
there was a monk in charge of administrative affairs who went into the mountains every day for timber and bamboo.
When entering the mountains, he was afraid of lions, tigers, wolves, bears, brown bears, and *tāla-kṣa* trees on the path; fearing these, he did not follow the proper route.

As he walked, thorns and the spines of soapberry plants pierced his feet. This bhikṣu made sandals from *nāga-vāla* grass, but because there was much mud and water on the path, his feet were damaged. The Buddha said:
"You should make shoes that allow you to pass through mud and water."

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove. There was a kinsman of the Buddha who, hearing that someone of his own clan had left the household life and attained Buddhahood, said to his parents:
"I wish to go and see the Buddha."
The parents thought to themselves:
"If he goes to the Buddha's presence, he may well renounce the household life.
At that time, the parents spoke to him regarding various obstacles, saying:
“There are terrors of lions on the road, as well as terrors of tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears.
He further addressed his parents,
saying, “I must certainly go.”
Knowing that he was determined to depart, his parents said to him:
"We now part from you; if you do go forth into the religious life, you must come back here.
He replied:

"So be it. He immediately went to where the Buddha was, and upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side. The Buddha granted him the going-forth and conferred the precepts upon him.
Later, he took his leave and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to return and see my parents and kinsmen.
The Buddha said:
"Go; do not stay long.
He then returned home, and many of his kinsmen each detained him for one day; in this manner, much time passed.
At that time, fresh snow fell, so the bhikṣu took leave of his kinsmen and desired to return to the presence of the Buddha.
He replied, "It has just snowed; how can you go?
Can you wear white leather boots?"
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted me to wear white leather boots.

He immediately returned; on the way, his hands grew cold, his feet ached, and his eyes pained him. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with these words of inquiry:
"Are you patient?
Are you well?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is your alms-seeking not lacking, and are you not fatigued by the road?
The Buddha then addressed this monk with these words of inquiry.
"Are you patient?
Are you dwelling in comfort and ease?
Do you lack nothing for alms, and are you not weary from the road?"
The bhikṣu said, "I dwell in contentment and ease;
my alms-seeking has not been lacking, and I am not fatigued by the roads.
He then related these matters in detail to the Buddha. Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked him intentionally:
"What is that land like?
He replied,
"It has much snow."
The Buddha said,
"From now on, in countries with heavy snowfall, I permit the wearing of white leather boots in order to protect against the snow.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada painted the legs of five hundred rope-seated couches with vermilion lacquer and offered them to the Saṃgha at Jetavana.
The bhikṣus would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to paint the legs of rope-seated couches with vermilion."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"This bed is pure and should be accepted.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the householder Bāḍhī offered a monastery adorned with various ornaments to the Saṅgha, but the bhikṣus would not accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept monasteries adorned with various ornaments."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "This dwelling is pure; it should be accepted.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

The householder Ugga Suvāna went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. Having taught, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with various discourses on the Dharma, the Buddha remained silent.
At that time, after the householder Ugga had observed the Buddha’s various discourses on the Dharma in silence, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I invite the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal tomorrow.”
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by his silence, he returned home and spent the entire night preparing various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink. He also adorned five hundred couches made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, thinking to himself:
"He will not accept one; he shall surely accept the other."
He further prepared five hundred gold plates, silver plates, lapis lazuli plates, and crystal plates, thinking to himself:
"If he does not accept one, he shall accept another."
He also prepared five hundred bowls made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, thinking:
"I shall not accept one [type], but shall instead accept one [from each]."
When morning came, he went to inform the Buddha that it was time.

The Buddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the house together with the community of bhikṣus. He offered a couch made of five hundred pieces of gold to the Buddha, but at that time the Buddha did not accept it.
Furthermore, he offered silver beds, lapis lazuli beds, and crystal beds, but the Buddha did not accept them.
At that time, the elder removed these precious beds and spread other beds instead, covering them with thick cushions; the Buddha then sat down upon them.
At that time, the elder offered five hundred golden plates to the Buddha, but the Buddha did not accept them.
He further offered silver plates, lapis lazuli plates, and crystal plates as gifts to the Buddha, yet the Buddha still did not accept them.
At that time, the elder offered five hundred golden bowls to the Buddha, but the Buddha did not accept them.
He further offered silver bowls, lapis lazuli bowls, and crystal bowls, yet the Buddha did not accept these either.
The Buddha said:
"I have previously permitted two kinds of bowls:
iron bowls and clay bowls; one should not possess eight kinds of bowls."

The householder then served water and food of various excellent flavors; when the Buddha and the Saṃgha had finished eating and withdrawn their bowls, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha, desiring to listen to the Dharma.
The Buddha, having preached the Dharma to them in various ways—teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them—arose from his seat and departed.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 39.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 40, Part 5 of the Sixth Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Part Five of the Clarification of Miscellaneous Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a brahmin who had a daughter born to him; her features were upright and her complexion pure. Because her complexion was so pure, she was named Wondrous Light (Prabhāvatī).
When this girl was born, a physiognomist divined:
"This girl shall later share herself with five hundred men."
When the people heard this, the girl was twelve years old and there was no one who sought her hand.
At that time, a certain Brahmin had a neighboring merchant who frequently went to sea to gather treasures.
From atop the tower, the merchant saw the woman from afar; immediately a lustful mind arose within him, and he asked the others, "Whose daughter is she?
They replied:
"This is a certain Brahmin girl. "Is she married?
He replied:
"No. "Is there anyone who seeks it? He replied:
"Not yet. He asked again,
"For what reason is there no one who seeks [it]?"
He replied,
“This girl has one fault.
[The other asked], “What is her fault?”
He replied:
"When this girl was born, a physiognomist divined:
'This girl shall later share herself with five hundred men.'"
When the people heard this, no one sought her hand as she reached the age of twelve.
At that time, a merchant thought to himself:
"Except for the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, there is no one capable of entering my house by force; furthermore, the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no such faults. I shall take her as my wife."
He immediately went to seek her hand in marriage.
Not long after he had arrived at her home, a group of merchants formed a caravan intending to enter the ocean.

According to the custom of that country for entering the sea, one must have someone who has previously entered the ocean; if such a person was unwilling to go himself, they would insist on taking him along by force.
Then the merchant called to the gatekeeper and spoke these words:
"I wish to go out to sea; do not allow any man to enter my house by force, with the exception of the Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas."
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya are likewise free from this fault.
He replied, "So it is."
Having spoken these words, she departed.
Later, when śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas came to her house to beg for alms, the woman saw them and said:
"Come and satisfy my lust with me."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one should not go to such a house if one has never gone there before; if one does go, one should not sit down."
"Why is this? Because this house must certainly have the fault of unchaste conduct.
Later, that woman fell ill and passed away during the night; her family members placed her in a decorated coffin and cast her away at the place for the dead.
At that time, five hundred bandits were traveling through this place; seeing this dead woman, they immediately conceived lustful thoughts and engaged in sexual intercourse.
Having finished their act, the five hundred men departed.
Because this woman previously told śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas,
"Come and engage in sexual desire with me," due to those causes and conditions,
she fell into an evil realm; in the northern part of that country, she was born as a lustful nāga named Vidhata.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a bhikṣu suffering from an abscess who went to Jīvaka and said,
"Please treat this illness of mine."
Jīvaka replied,
"I shall let it ripen.
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted [the use of] fermented [liquids].
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to ferment them until they are mature."
Jīvaka spoke again:
"It should be broken. He replied:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted the lancing of an abscess.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit its lancing."
Jīvaka spoke again:
"One should press out the pus.
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted pressing.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit pressing."
Jīvaka spoke again:
"One should eat food mixed with pus.
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted its use.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"I permit the application of various medicinal treatments for pus."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, in Rājagṛha, there was a great month-long sacrifice for the nāga Kṛīla.
Then, people took goods from the royal storehouses and prepared various kinds of food and drink to distribute to all.

At that time, many people gathered from various places; some had concave chests, while others had convex chests; some had feet like those of elephants, while others had feet like those of horses; furthermore, some had ears like those of elephants or horses, while others had ears shaped like winnowing baskets.
In this way, there were many people resembling elephants, horses, men, and women—both large and small—all filling the space with great joy.
At that time, many merchants from the four quarters came to the guesthouse.
Because the king did not collect taxes when he performed this sacrifice, there were no prohibitions or restrictions; those crossing were not taxed, and travelers did not have to pay transit fees.
As the sacrifice drew to a close, the merchants each thought to themselves:
"Will this king not tax us all at once?"
Before the sacrifice was completed, they departed.

Later, when the sacrifice had concluded and everyone had returned to their respective places, those with sunken chests, protruding chests, elephant feet, horse feet, elephant ears, horse ears, and ears like winnowing baskets all remained.
On a later day, they went to wander among many people, at celestial shrines, and among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
At that time, because the group of six bhikṣus were wicked, their fine śrāmaṇeras and disciples did not stay near them for two reasons:
first, because [the teachers] violated the precepts; second, because [the disciples] feared that they would cause us to violate the precepts.
At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus saw such a person, they thought to themselves:
"If we were to ordain other people, they would surely abandon us and leave;
but if we ordain this one now, there will be no one to instruct them to leave."
The group of six bhikṣus went to those people and said,
"Why do you not go forth [into the religious life]?
They replied:
"We are in such a state; who will deliver us?
If there is one capable of delivering us, we shall go forth into homelessness.
Then the group of six bhikṣus said:
"If you can guard my dwelling for me, go out to meet food for me, and carry my bowl, I shall ordain you.
The group of six bhikṣus immediately ordained this man; whenever there was a place where the Buddha and the Saṃgha were invited, they would first send him off with the bowl for two reasons:
first, because he walked slowly, and second, because he was ashamed to walk together with them.
Having seen this, the various non-Buddhists rebuked the donors, saying:
"Is that which you venerate truly as you claim? Is it your stūpa, your foremost one, your first to eat, and your leader who goes before you—the very object of your offerings?"
When the lay followers (upāsakas) heard this, they were displeased and reported the matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha, having assembled the community of monks (bhikṣusaṃgha), knowingly asked the group of six monks (ṣaḍvargika bhikṣus):
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied, "I truly did,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus ordain people with sunken chests, protruding chests, elephant feet, horse feet, elephant ears, horse ears, or winnowing-basket ears?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not ordain those with sunken chests, protruding chests, elephant feet, horse feet, elephant ears, horse ears, or ears like winnowing baskets."
"If one ordains them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
the Elder Upāli had two *śrāmaṇeras*:
One was named Dasa and the other was named Pāla.
At the time of receiving the precepts, the novice Dasa said to Pāla:
"You receive the precepts first; I shall provide for all your needs."
Pāla said to Udāyī, “You were the first to receive the precepts; I shall provide you with whatever you require.
At that time, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Is it permissible for two śrāmaṇeras to receive the full precepts through a simultaneous *karmavācanā*?
The Buddha said,
"It is permissible."
It should be performed in this manner:
with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣu therein shall proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
To this Daśabala and Pāla, Upāli granted full ordination; they requested full ordination from the Saṃgha, with the Elder Upāli acting as their preceptor.
If the Sangha’s time has come, may the Sangha listen with patience: the Sangha shall confer full ordination upon Dharmadāsa and Pāra, with the Elder Upāli acting as preceptor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The formal motion and threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) were performed:
"The Sangha has already conferred full ordination upon Datta and Pāla, with the Elder Upāli acting as preceptor. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
"We do not know where the Buddha is teaching the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma;
we do not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
“In the six great cities:
Campā, Śrāvastī, Vaiśālī, Rājagṛha, Vārāṇasī, and Kapilavastu.”
Why is this? It is because I dwell there most often, and all manner of transformations occur in that place.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Yaśas, together with five hundred bhikṣus, came from Kośala to Śrāvastī intending to enter the rains retreat.
Then the resident bhikṣus and the visiting bhikṣus exchanged greetings, and the residents carried the robes and bowls for the visitors.

When he was carrying his robes and bowl, there arose a great clamor and the voices of many people. Hearing this great clamor and the voices of many people, the Buddha, knowing the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Within this monastery, for what reason is there such a great clamor and the voices of so many people?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Elder Yaśas, together with five hundred bhikṣus, has come from the kingdom of Kośala to Śrāvastī, wishing to enter the rains retreat.”

At that time, the resident bhikṣus and the visiting bhikṣus greeted one another; they took up the robes and bowls for the visiting bhikṣus, and for this reason there was such a great clamor and the sound of many voices.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Go and tell Yaśas and the other five hundred people:
'Because you made such a loud noise, you have been driven out; you shall not be permitted to dwell in Śrāvastī for the summer retreat.'"
Ānanda, having received these instructions, went and said to Yaśas:
“Because you all made such a loud noise, the World-Honored One has expelled you; you shall not spend the rains retreat in Śrāvastī.”
At that time, Yaśas and the other five hundred men went to a village on the banks of the Bhagīrathī River to enter the rains retreat.
Then the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has sent us because of the great noise; it would be well if we remained silent."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit silence.
At that time, the bhikṣus fell asleep; having fallen asleep, they said to one another:
"It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to dwell in individual rooms.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to dwell in individual rooms; you may also sleep in individual rooms."
They further said to one another,
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit us who are staying here as a community.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The assembly is settled; even as they sit, they fall asleep.
They then said to one another, "It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to wash our heads with water."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to wash your heads with water.
At that time, the bhikṣus found it inconvenient when taking up water with their hands; the Buddha said:
"One should make a vessel.
When the water in the vessel was large and soaked the robe, he made it small; but when it was small, there was not enough water.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not make it too large, nor too small; one should accept only one *pātra* or one and a half *pātras*.
At that time, the vessels were made without handles; when pouring, they fell onto the heads of others, causing such pain and distress that they nearly died.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should provide a handle.
There was a bhikṣu who fell asleep while sitting; another bhikṣu poured water over him, whereupon he said:
"I was not sleeping; why did you pour water on me?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who is asleep cannot be trusted, but one who pours [water] can be trusted."
There are five instances where one may sprinkle water upon another:

first, out of compassion; second, when not intending to cause the other distress; third, when the other is asleep; fourth, when the other’s head is leaning against a wall; and fifth, when the other has their legs extended.
The bhikṣus continued to sleep and said to one another,
"It would be well if we could listen for the sound of hand-clapping.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; strike with your hand.
A certain bhikṣu was dozing while seated, and another bhikṣu struck him with his hand. He then said:
"I am not sleeping; why are you pushing me?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who is asleep is untrustworthy; one who strikes [the gong] is trustworthy."
There are five circumstances under which one may strike another with the hand:
first, out of compassion; second, to prevent him from disturbing others; third, when he is asleep; fourth, when his head is leaning against a wall; and fifth, when his legs are stretched out.
The bhikṣus continued to sleep and said to one another,
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to throw balls.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen: throw the ball, and on the following day, return.
On the following day, the bhikṣus did not know with whom they should return.
The Buddha said:
"Return it to its original owner.
If the owner is not present, give it to the one who lit the lamp.
If the one who lit the lamp is not present, give it to the one who performed the labor."
"The one who holds it is not here; you should place it on the ground in the center of the hall and cover it.
Having placed it on the ground in the center of the hall and covered it, he returned to his seat. While seated, seeing another bhikṣu sleeping, he took the ball and threw it at him.
The other said, "I am not sleeping; why did you throw it at me?"
The Buddha said:
“One who sleeps cannot be trusted; one who throws can be trusted.
There are five ways of throwing a ball at another:”
"First, compassion; second, not troubling others; third, sleep; fourth, leaning one's head against a wall; fifth, stretching out one's legs.
Because the bhikṣus continued to sleep, they said to one another, "It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to use meditation staffs (dhyāna-daṇḍa)."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow the use of a meditation staff.
At that time, the head of the meditation staff was pointed; when he struck with it, he damaged his *antarvāsaka*.
They said to one another,
"It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to wrap our staffs with materials at the tips.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should wrap the head of the meditation staff with cloth.
At that time, the meditation staff struck the ground and made a noise;
the Buddha said, "The bottom end should also be wrapped."
The bhikṣus did not know how to take up the meditation staff (dhyāna-daṇḍa).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When taking up the meditation staff, you should give rise to a mind of reverence."
The bhikṣus did not know how to generate a mind of reverence.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should hold the staff with both hands and carry it upon the crown of one's head."

There was a bhikṣu who was sitting and dozing. Another bhikṣu seized his meditation staff and struck the dozing one. The dozing one started up in alarm and stood looking about; the other bhikṣus remained silent and made no sound, whereupon he immediately fell to the ground in a faint.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu falls asleep while sitting, he should rise; he should look after those who are sleeping and strike them with a meditation staff (dhyāna-yaṣṭi). Having struck them, he should return to his seat."
If there is no one sleeping, he should go out the door, wander about, and then re-enter to check again.
If he sees someone sleeping, he should strike them with the meditation staff; having struck them, he returns to his seat.
"If there is no one sleeping, place the staff back in its original spot and sit.
A certain bhikṣu was sitting and dozing; another bhikṣu struck him with a meditation staff, whereupon he said:
"I am not sleeping! Why are you striking me?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who is sleepy is not to be trusted; one who strikes with a staff is to be trusted.
There are five conditions for striking another with a meditation staff: [list follows]"
First, compassion;
second, not harming others;
third, sleep.
"Fourth, leaning the head against a wall;
fifth, stretching out the legs.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to sleep and said to one another:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to wear meditation weights.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said,
"I permit you to wear meditation weights."
At that time, the meditation cushions had no holes; when they were worn, they fell to the ground.
They said to one another, "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to make holes in them."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a hole.
Once the hole is made, pass a cord through it; attach a knot to the end of the cord and hang a meditation weight from it four finger-widths above the forehead."
The bhikṣus then tied ropes around their heads and placed the meditation weights behind them. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not tie ropes around your heads and place meditation weights behind them."
"To cross over [the legs] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, because the meditation bolster fell and he was thus asleep, this matter was reported to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If the meditation bolster falls once, you may stretch out one leg; if it falls twice, you may stretch out two legs; if it falls three times, you should rise and walk."
While walking, they became confused as they came and went; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should walk in succession according to the manner of a goose.
While walking, a junior monk touched the shoulder of a senior monk; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When walking, a junior monk must not touch the shoulder of a senior monk.
A junior monk should walk behind a senior monk and must not stay close to him.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to sleep and said to one another:
"It would be well if the Buddha were to establish a time for us.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to establish a time."
The bhikṣus said to one another,
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted [the use of footwear] during two seasons.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Let us agree to work during two periods," they said to one another.
"It would be well to work during the night as well."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to work at night during the appropriate times.
They then spoke to one another, saying:
"It would be well if you were to listen to me regarding the schedule for daytime work.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said,
"I allow the schedule for daytime work."
They further said to one another,
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit us to sit for seven days.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, we are permitted to sit for seven days.
They further said to one another,
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to remain in constant seated meditation."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to practice constant sitting meditation.

At that time, he authorized specific periods for it: the two periods [of the day], the night period, the daytime period, the seven-day period, and the period of constant sitting. Because they did not chew tooth-sticks, their mouths became foul-smelling, and they began to speak to one another as follows:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit us to chew tooth-sticks.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"I permit the chewing of tooth-sticks; there are five benefits to it:"
First, the mouth does not become bitter; second, the mouth does not become foul-smelling; third, it eliminates wind disorders; fourth, it eliminates feverish illnesses;
fifth, it eliminates phlegm and mucus. Furthermore, there are five additional benefits:
first, it eliminates wind; second, it eliminates heat; third, the mouth gains a savory flavor; fourth, one has an appetite for food; fifth, the eyes become clear.

At that time, they established specific periods: the two watches of the night, the daytime, the seven-day period, and the period of constant sitting meditation. During these times, they did not bathe and remained foul-smelling with dirt;
the bhikṣus said to one another, "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to bathe."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to wash.
At that time, those who entered where the stream flowed swiftly were carried away by the water. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should install pillars in the water to create an obstruction for holding onto while washing.

At that time, he permitted the following periods: the two times [of day and night], the night-time, the daytime, the seven-day period, and the time of constant seated meditation. During these times, the bhikṣus attained immeasurable knowledge and vision, and realized the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat.
Knowing that the bhikṣus had already attained realization, the Buddha, for this reason, assembled the Saṃgha and said to the bhikṣus:
"There is light in that place.
It is the law of the Buddhas dwelling in the world to hold two great assemblies each year:
The last month of spring and the last month of summer.
Regarding the last month of spring: monks from various regions and countries arrive everywhere, thinking:
"When we enter the rains retreat, we shall practice the Dharma taught by the Buddha and dwell in peace and happiness."
This is called the first great assembly.

Regarding the final month of the summer retreat: when the bhikṣus had completed their three-month summer *varṣā* retreat and finished making their robes, they took their robes and bowls and went to where the Buddha was, thinking:
"We have not seen the Buddha for a long time; we have not seen the World-Honored One for a long time."
This was the second great assembly.

At that time, the bhikṣus along the banks of the Bhagīrathī River, having completed their three-month summer retreat and finished making their robes, took up their bowls and robes and came to where the Buddha was.
When the Buddha saw from afar that the bhikṣu of the Bhagurā River was approaching, he entered the first dhyāna, and the bhikṣu of the Bhagurā River also entered the first dhyāna.
The Buddha arose from the first dhyāna and entered the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the spheres of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The bhikṣu Bhāguma also arose from the first dhyāna and entered the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness [samādhis].
At that time, the Elder Ānanda saw from afar the bhikṣu Bhadrika approaching; he immediately joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May the World-Honored One converse with the bhikṣu Bhadrika, so that the bhikṣu Bhadrika may enjoy peace and happiness for a long night.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Do not speak such words, Ānanda!
"As I know it, can you also know it? Ānanda!
When I saw the bhikṣu Bhārgava approaching from afar, I had entered the first dhyāna, and the bhikṣu Bhārgava had also entered the first dhyāna."

When I first entered the first dhyāna, and subsequently entered the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the realms of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the bhikṣu Bhagu also entered the first dhyāna, and subsequently entered the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the realms of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus named Aśvaka and Punarvasuka living on the Black Mountain (Kāla-parvata).
They resided there defiling the families of others; this was seen by all, heard by all, and known by all, as these bhikṣus were [engaged] with women.
Sitting on the same bed as another person; eating from the same dish; drinking alcohol from the same vessel;

eating after midday; eating food kept overnight; eating leftover food kept overnight; eating without having received it; eating food that has not been formally offered according to the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rule;
playing the lute; making musical sounds by pursing the lips; making music by gnashing the teeth; and striking copper [cymbals].
Using a basin, *tāla* leaves, or performing various other kinds of music, song, and dance;
wearing garlands and necklaces; smearing the body with perfumes; wearing garments scented with incense; sprinkling water upon one another;
personally plucking flowers or causing others to pluck them; personally stringing flower garlands or causing others to string them; and placing flowers upon the head...
To cause others to wear [ornaments], to wear earrings oneself, or to cause others to wear them;
to take another’s wife away oneself, or to cause others to take her away;

or to cause elephants to fight, chariots to fight, infantry to fight, rams to fight, water buffaloes to fight, dogs to fight, cocks to fight, men and women to fight, adult males to fight, adult females to fight, young males to fight, or young females to fight—and likewise to engage in fighting oneself.

Clapping hands and keeping time with the rhythm, they ran about in all four directions; they changed their attire and ornaments, galloping and leaping about; they floated and submerged themselves in water; they cut down trees; they shook their arms and struck their thighs while wailing and crying out loudly; they whistled and spoke gibberish in the various languages of different countries; they skipped, turned back, and moved like writhing fish; they threw objects into the air and caught them again; they rode upon women on boats, making them perform as musicians; or they rode elephants and horses, traveled in carriages and litters, and led great crowds of people, blowing conches and chanting as they entered the groves—performing such various kinds of evil and impure acts.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda was traveling from the kingdom of Kāśī toward Śrāvastī; having arrived at the village of Kālapura, he stayed there for the night. When morning came, he put on his robes, took his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Ānanda entered the city with an empty bowl and returned to the city with an empty bowl.
Not far from the city, a great multitude of people had gathered; Ānanda went to them and asked, "This land of yours is prosperous and joyful, and teeming with many people."
"Now, as I go for alms, I enter with an empty bowl and return with an empty bowl.
Is there no śramaṇa son of the Śākyas here who has committed even a small amount of evil?"
At that time, there was a wise man named Uruvilvā who was among that assembly; rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and said to Ānanda:
"Does the Venerable One not know?
"Venerable Ānanda! These two bhikṣus, Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, have committed various evil deeds, as described at length above.
These two bhikṣus have committed such evils that they have defiled all households, which has been seen, heard, and known by all."

Then the venerable Uruvelakassapa invited Ānanda to enter his own dwelling, prepared a seat for him to sit upon, personally offered him water, and served him abundant and delicious food until he was fully satisfied.
Having finished his meal, he washed his hands and took up his bowl; the Venerable Ānanda took a small seat, desiring to hear the Dharma.

After Ānanda had taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened him with various causes and conditions, he rose from his seat and departed for his own quarters. There, he returned the bedding he had received to the resident bhikṣu, took up his robes and bowl, and set out on his journey toward Śrāvastī.
Gradually approaching the Buddha's presence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with these words of inquiry: "Are you well?
Are you enduring?"
Are your feet sound?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of almsfood, and are you not weary from the road?
The Buddha greeted him with these words: "Ānanda,
are you well?"
Are your feet sound?
Do you dwell in peace and comfort?
Is alms-seeking not difficult for you, and are you not weary from the road?
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
He dwells in contentment and ease; he has not lacked for almsfood; and he is not fatigued by the journey.”
For these reasons, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked Aśvalāyana and Pūrṇamāsa:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣus sit upon the same bed as a woman, even to the point of engaging in mistaken speech?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not sit on the same bed as a woman.
To sit together [in such a manner] constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
One must not eat together with a woman.
To eat together with one is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not drink alcohol from the same vessel as a woman.
To drink [it] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not eat at improper times.
To eat [at such a time] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
One must not consume leftover food kept overnight;
whoever does so commits a *pāyattika* offense.
One must not handle food improperly.
To eat [it] constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
One must not eat without having received it;
to eat [it] thus constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If one eats food that has not been formally offered according to the rules for leftover food, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats food that has been stored overnight inside [the monastery], it is a *dukkaṭa*.

One must not play the lute or drum the reed-pipe; one must not gnaw on teeth to keep time; one must not blow on objects to keep time; one must not strike a copper basin to keep time; one must not beat palm leaves to keep time; one must not sing; one must not clap hands to keep time; and one must not dance.
Those who violate these rules commit *duṣkṛta* offenses.
One must not wear flower garlands, nor wear incense garlands; one must not smear fragrant oils on the body, nor wear garments perfumed with incense.
Those who violate this rule all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not sprinkle water upon one another;
those who do so incur an offense according to the circumstances.
One must not pluck flowers oneself nor cause another to pluck them.
Whether one takes them oneself or instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
One must not string flower garlands nor cause another to string flower necklaces.
If one strings [the flowers] oneself or causes another to string them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not make flower garlands oneself, nor should one instruct others to do so.
If one makes them oneself or instructs another to make them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not string flowers oneself, nor should one instruct another to string them.
If one strings them oneself or causes another to do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not personally go to the homes of boys or girls to serve them, nor should one instruct another to go to the homes of boys or girls to serve them.
Whether one goes there oneself or instructs another to go, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense accordingly.
One must not engage in elephant fights, horse fights, or chariot fights.

One must not join in human games; one must not fight rams, nor fight water buffaloes, nor fight cocks, nor fight dogs, nor fight women, nor fight men, nor fight boys or girls; one must not fight oneself, nor instruct others to fight.
One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not swing one's arms, must not stomp one's feet, must not throw objects into the air, must not adorn the face, must not run, and must not jump.
To commit these offenses constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
One must not cut down or clear away grasses and trees;
to do so constitutes a *pāyattika*.
One must not walk aimlessly;
one who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not weep, one must not cry out loudly, and one must not whistle.
Those who violate these rules all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not stand on one's head, must not throw [the robe] away, and must not wriggle like a fish.
Those who violate these rules all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not play with bells;
whoever violates this incurs an offense according to the gravity of the act.
One must not sing or engage in musical entertainment with women on a boat.
Those who violate this rule all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not ride elephants, horses, or carriages; one must not ride on people; and one must not enter gardens or parks in a ceremonial procession.
Those who violate these rules all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One must not offer sacrifices to fire, nor must one speak falsely.
Those who violate these rules incur offenses according to their specific transgressions.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

The bhikṣu Kālika went to watch elephant fights, horse fights, chariot fights, wrestling, ram fights, buffalo fights, cockfights, dogfights, fights between men and women, and fights between boys and girls, going there to watch them himself.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not go to watch fights involving elephants, horses, or even young boys and girls.
Any who violate this shall be guilty of a duṣkṛta offense."
(The twenty dharmas for nuns are concluded. Next, the rules for bhikṣuṇīs are explained.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has received the eight weighty rules, she has thereby left the household life, received full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī;
what, then, should be done for the other bhikṣuṇīs?”
The Buddha said:
"It should be performed through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in the presence [of the assembly].
This was when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus performed formal legal acts (karmavācanā) for the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs were displeased.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, the bhikṣus should not perform formal legal acts for the bhikṣuṇīs."

A bhikṣuṇī may perform a formal act (karmavācanā) for another bhikṣuṇī, with the exception of the formal act for receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā), the formal act for the penance of mānāpya, and the formal act for rehabilitation from an offense (āpattivyutthāna).
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs performed a formal ritual (karmavācanā) against the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus were displeased.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“Bhikṣuṇīs should not perform formal acts (karmas) for bhikṣus; rather, bhikṣus shall perform formal acts for bhikṣus, with the exception of the formal acts concerning not prostrating, not conversing, and not making offerings.”
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, because they were oppressed by their husbands, fathers-in-law, and mothers-in-law, several women left the household life to become bhikṣuṇīs.
Later, because they were oppressed by the bhikṣuṇīs with whom they lived—namely their preceptors (upādhyāyinī) and instructors (ācāryinī)—they returned to being laywomen (avadātavastra).
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:

"These ill-omened and wretched women! We were their masters at first; in the interim, they became bhikṣuṇīs and received our respect; now we have returned to receiving their respect—there is no constancy in this."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"If a bhikṣuṇī violates the precepts even once, she shall no longer be permitted to leave the household life or receive full ordination.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl before midday, was entering the city of Rājagṛha from Vulture Peak Mountain to beg for food.
At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was walking hurriedly ahead of Mahākāśyapa.
Mahākāśyapa said: "Sister!
If you would hurry, or if you would step aside from my path."
He immediately reviled him, saying:
"You were originally a non-Buddhist; what urgent business do you have that you do not walk at a leisurely pace?
Mahākāśyapa replied:
“Evil woman!
I do not reproach you; I reproach Ānanda.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to walk in front of bhikṣus; if they walk in front, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having dressed before midday and taken her bowl, went out to beg for food.
After her meal, she placed her *niṣīdana* on her left shoulder and entered the Andhavana forest, where she sat cross-legged beneath a tree. At that moment, a snake came and entered her female organ.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to sit in a large [haughty] manner.
If one sits in such a manner, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"If one sits with one leg extended, there is no offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Upāli asked the Buddha:
“The Blessed One has not permitted bhikṣuṇīs to bring forth the charges of a bhikṣu regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected.
Is there perhaps any circumstance by which a bhikṣuṇī might bring forth the charges of a bhikṣu regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected without committing an offense?”
The Buddha said:
"There is none!
With the exception of speech:”
"Do not associate with evil friends or evil companions.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who instructed another bhikṣu to violate the precepts; [the instructor] incurred an offense accordingly.
If one instructs a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to renounce the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a bhikṣuṇī to renounce the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta offense;
if a bhikṣuṇī instructs a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, śrāmaṇerī, or bhikṣu to renounce the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a śikṣamāṇā instructs another śikṣamāṇā to violate the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she instructs a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī to violate the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇera teaches another śrāmaṇera to violate the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he teaches a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or a śikṣamāṇā to violate the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇerī teaches another śrāmaṇerī to transgress the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she teaches a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇera to transgress the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu entices another bhikṣu with various objects, he commits an offense;
if he entices a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī entices another bhikṣuṇī with various objects, she commits an offense;
if she entices a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā entices another śikṣamāṇā with various objects, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she entices a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇera entices another śrāmaṇera with various objects, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he entices a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or a śikṣamāṇā, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇerikā entices another śrāmaṇerikā with various objects, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she entices a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu makes a sound of reproach toward another bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he makes a sound of reproach toward a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a threatening sound toward another bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she makes a threatening sound toward a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta;
if a bhikṣuṇī makes a threatening sound toward a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If a śikṣamāṇā utters a harsh word toward another śikṣamāṇā, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she utters a harsh word toward a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇera utters a harsh word toward another śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he utters a harsh word toward a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇerī makes a sound of contempt toward another śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she makes a sound of contempt toward a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, or śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu treats another bhikṣu with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu treats a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī treats another bhikṣuṇī with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī treats a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a śikṣamāṇā treats another śikṣamāṇā with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she treats a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇera treats another śrāmaṇera with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he treats a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or a śikṣamāṇā with contempt, it is likewise a duṣkṛta in all cases.
If a śrāmaṇerī treats another śrāmaṇerī with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she treats a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇera with contempt, it is in all cases a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu speaks harshly to another bhikṣu, he commits an offense;
if he speaks harshly to a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks harshly to another bhikṣuṇī, she commits an offense;
if she speaks harshly to a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā speaks harsh words to another śikṣamāṇā, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she speaks them to a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise a duṣkṛta in all cases.
If a śrāmaṇera speaks harsh words to another śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he speaks harsh words to a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or a śikṣamāṇā, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śrāmaṇerī [speaks] to another śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she speaks to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went to Jetavana to listen to the Dharma; after the bhikṣus had finished spreading out their bedding and requisites, there were many left over.

The bhikṣuṇīs, distressed because they were seeking bedding and seats, said to the bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, you have already spread out your bedding and seats; please lend us some of the remainder to sit upon."
The bhikṣus said,
“The Buddha has not yet permitted us to distribute the bedding and mats once they are finished and then give the remainder to the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to spread out their bedding and seating materials, and then give what remains for the bhikṣuṇīs to sit upon.
This was while the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, having dressed in his upper robe and taken up his alms bowl before midday, entered the city of Rājagṛha from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to beg for food.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā followed behind him and nudged Mahākāśyapa’s back with her elbow.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"Evil woman!
I do not reproach you; I reproach Ānanda."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to hide behind a bhikṣu’s back.
If one hides there, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, certain bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta wore multi-colored vests. The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves:"
"Excellent! You possess virtue.
She then donned garments of variegated colors, like those of a royal consort or the wife of a high minister.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, bhikṣuṇīs should not wear garments of variegated colors.
If they do so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs bound their bodies with ropes of various colors, belts made of pig intestines, and threads of variegated silk.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to bind their bodies with ropes of various colors, belts made of pig intestines, or threads of variegated silk."
"If one ties them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha,
at that time certain bhikṣuṇīs who assisted Devadatta wore garments with fine pleats, garments with fringes, garments made of raw silk, and garments of fine, thin fabric.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to wear four kinds of robes.
If they wear them, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā intentionally yawned, and the other bhikṣuṇīs asked her, "What are you doing?"
He replied,
"I experienced the pleasure of touch.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“A bhikṣuṇī should not grimace.
If she deliberately grimaces, it is a duṣkṛta.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a certain bhikṣu who, while begging for alms, requested two portions at once:
he ate the first portion himself and returned the second portion to his dwelling to give to a bhikṣuṇī.

Because it was raining when this bhikṣu begged for the two portions of food, the bhikṣuṇī did not come; as there was no one to eat this portion, he discarded it within the monastery grounds, whereupon flocks of birds gathered and made a great clamor.
After the meal, the Buddha took Ānanda with him to that place. Having already perceived the situation through his supernormal knowledge, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Why have these birds gathered here and made such a great clamor?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
there was a certain bhikṣu who begged for two portions of food:”
The alms-gatherer ate for himself first and later divided the remainder to give to the bhikṣuṇīs.
When he went out to gather two portions of food, because it was raining, the bhikṣuṇīs did not come; as there was no one to eat this portion, he discarded it within the monastery grounds.
"For this reason, the various birds have gathered in great numbers and are making a loud noise.
Knowing the cause, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Have the bhikṣus given food to bhikṣuṇīs who are not their relatives?"
Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One,
I shall give it.”
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community, he censured the bhikṣus in various ways:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣu give food to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From now on, a bhikṣu must not give food to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
To do so constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a famine in the world and alms were difficult to obtain; the bhikṣus received food on festival days and had much left over.
The bhikṣuṇīs, unable to find food, became distressed and said to the bhikṣus:
“Give us your leftover food.
The bhikṣus said,
“The Buddha has not yet permitted us to give leftover food to the bhikṣuṇīs.”
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "During such times of famine and scarcity, I allow you to give leftover food to bhikṣuṇīs.

When the era of famine had passed and the time of abundance and prosperity arrived, the bhikṣus continued to give leftover food to the bhikṣuṇīs as they had done during the famine; however, the bhikṣuṇīs did not accept it, saying:
"You who have kept food overnight, I too have kept food overnight.
You who are impure, I too am impure.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, what has been stored overnight by a bhikṣu is pure for a bhikṣuṇī; what has been stored overnight by a bhikṣuṇī is pure for a bhikṣu."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus questioned the bhikṣuṇīs regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path, and the bhikṣuṇīs felt ashamed and displeased.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣus to question bhikṣuṇīs regarding the obstructing dharmas; bhikṣuṇīs should question bhikṣuṇīs regarding the obstructing dharmas.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs questioned the bhikṣus regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path; the bhikṣus were ashamed and displeased.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:

"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to question bhikṣus regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path; rather, bhikṣus should question bhikṣus regarding the dharmas that obstruct the path."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon a śikṣamāṇā who was unable to speak properly.
This śikṣamāṇā addressed the Buddha, saying:
He said, "Deliver me.
Because his speech was incorrect, he then said,
"Anoint me."
The young bhikṣuṇīs laughed at her, and because of this, the śikṣamāṇā felt ashamed and departed.
Due to this incident, she ultimately did not receive full ordination.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, if there is a formal proposal that is not properly made by a *śikṣamāṇā*, other bhikṣuṇīs should request it on her behalf.

As for the procedure for requesting on her behalf: the community of bhikṣuṇīs should be harmoniously assembled with a single mind; the bhikṣuṇī who requests on her behalf should rise from her seat, bare her right shoulder, kneel with her right knee on the ground, join her palms, and speak as follows:"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This śikṣamāṇā [Name], whose speech was incorrect, has requested from the Saṃgha the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] as her preceptor-nun."
"The Sangha should grant deliverance and confer full ordination upon the śikṣamāṇā [Name] out of compassion!
The second [monk] should also say:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!..."
This śikṣamāṇā [Name], whose speech is not correct, requests from the Saṃgha the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] as her preceptor-nun (upādhyāyikā).
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant deliverance and confer full ordination upon this śikṣamāṇā [Name], with [Name] as her preceptor-nun!
The third [motion] should also be stated as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This śikṣamāṇā so-and-so has spoken improperly; she requests from the Saṃgha the full ordination, with so-and-so as her preceptress."
“The Saṃgha should grant ordination and confer the full precepts upon the śikṣamāṇā [named] So-and-so, out of compassion!
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, during the period before the rains, dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā followed after him and smelled Mahākāśyapa.
Mahākāśyapa said,
“Sister!...”
"If you go ahead, do not smell me.
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"Venerable sir, please go first."
She smelled it again and again without ceasing.
Mahākāśyapa said:
"Wicked woman!"
"I do not reproach you; I reproach Ānanda.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to smell a bhikṣu."
"If she smells it, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a merchant’s wife in the city whose husband was away on a journey; she had been having an illicit affair with another man, and her belly gradually grew large.
Out of fear of her husband, the woman induced a miscarriage herself, thinking:
"There is no one with a like mind who will take this dead child away.
She remained there in grief, guarding the child.

There was a bhikṣuṇī who frequently entered and left this household. Before midday, she put on her robes, took her bowl, and went to that house; seeing the wife there filled with sorrow and anxiety, she asked, "For what reason?"
She replied, "My husband is away, and I have become pregnant through an illicit affair with another man.
Fearing my husband's wrath, I aborted the fetus myself; however, there is no one with whom I can abandon it."
"Can you take this for me? He replied, "I can."
"If I take him away, who would know?
He then placed the dead child in one jar, covered it with another jar, and carried them away to a secluded place to discard them.
At that time, there were some young people who enjoyed joking and laughing; seeing the bhikṣuṇī discard the jar, they said to one another, "What is there inside this discarded jar?"
He immediately went to look and saw the dead infant, whereupon he said:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas engage in sexual misconduct, causing bhikṣuṇīs to conceive children whom they then kill and discard."
One person told two people, and two people told three; in this manner, the evil reputation spread by word of mouth until it filled the city of Śrāvastī.
Those bhikṣus who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this matter and were displeased. They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, a bhikṣuṇī must not cause another to discard a dead fetus."
"If you abandon him, you will commit an offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
at that time Gopa gave birth to a son and had this thought:
"The Buddha has established a precept forbidding contact with men.
Now that I have given birth to a son, I do not know what to do.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is permitted for the mother herself to touch the infant until it is able to leave her; other bhikṣuṇīs should not touch it.
Should any touch it, they commit an offense."
"If one can avoid the mother's touch, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
at that time Gopā gave birth to a son and had this thought:
“The Buddha has established the precepts, stating that one must not even spend a single night sleeping with a man.
Now that I have given birth to this child, what should I do?
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From now on, it is permitted for [a mother] to stay overnight with [her daughter] until she is able to wean her; however, if she stays overnight once she has been weaned, the mother commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
For any other bhikṣuṇī to stay overnight [with such a girl], it is a *pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Kūṭadanta had a son born to him, and he thought:
"The Buddha has said that a bhikṣuṇī must not stay alone in a room for even a single night; she must stay in a room together with another bhikṣuṇī."
"What should I do now?
She reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:

"You should perform the *karman* of solitary confinement for the bhikṣuṇī Guḍata; should there be any other bhikṣuṇīs like her, you should likewise perform the *karman* of solitary confinement for them."

Regarding the *karmavācanā* for a solitary cell: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, the Bhikṣuṇī Gūḍha rises from her seat, removes her leather sandals, bares her right shoulder, places her right knee on the ground, and speaks these words:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, please take note!"
