"I, Gopā, have given birth to a son; I request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a separate dwelling.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the formal act for a separate dwelling!
He requested thus a second and a third time.
Among them, one bhikṣuṇī should announce in the midst of the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Gopā has given birth to a son and requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a private room."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of assigning a separate dwelling to the bhikṣuṇī Kukkuṭā.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). [The second *karmavācanā* follows. This is called the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
"Since the Saṃgha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the nun Gopikā regarding her solitary dwelling, and since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus entered and left the families of householders and became their acquaintances.
The wives of those householders said to the bhikṣus, "Please ordain our daughters and cause them to become upāsikās."
The bhikṣus replied,
“We do not touch women with our hands. How,
then, can they be ordained?”
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Out of a heart of compassion, you should grant her the going-forth and ordain her as an upāsikā."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs frequented the homes of other families and became their acquaintances.
The laypeople said, "Ordain our sons and make them upāsakas."
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "Our hands do not touch boys; how then can we be ordained?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Out of a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, you should ordain them as upāsikās.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇīs entered and left the families of householders and became their close acquaintances. The wives of the laymen then spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
“Give us a small amount of worn-out clothing for the sake of guarding this young child.
The bhikṣuṇīs said, “You speak perversely;
you, who are laypeople (*avadātavasana*), should provide offerings to us. Why do you instead demand [clothing] from us?”
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Out of a heart of compassion, you should give it to her."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were many noble women of the Śākya clan who had left the household life to become bhikṣuṇīs; they went about begging for alms with their breasts exposed.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"Exposing their breasts while going on alms-round, like the wives of kings or ministers.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to wear a side-covering robe (*kakṣāśāṭī*) when they go out to beg for alms.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who entered the Rāmagrāma Garden alone; she encountered bandits who stripped her of her clothes until she was naked.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the Rāmagrāma Garden, nor may they enter any other gardens."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha,
a bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta entered a pond to bathe in front of a man.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.'"
"Bathing in front of men is no different from being a prostitute.
A bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities heard of this matter and was displeased; she reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha. Having assembled the Saṃgha, he rebuked her with various reasons, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī bathe in the presence of a man?"
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs should not bathe in front of men.
To bathe [in such a manner], it is a pāyattika.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, who deeply protected the Buddha’s Dharma, performed formal acts (*karmavācanā*) against the bhikṣuṇīs using words of censure, namely:

the formal act of reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*), the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), and the formal act of submissiveness (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*).
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke with contempt:
"So-and-so is my preceptor (upādhyāyī), so-and-so is my instructor (ācāryā), and I received full ordination from such-and-such a community of monks."
"This aged and decrepit bhikṣuṇī does not know who her preceptress (upādhyāyinī) or teacher (ācāryinī) was,
nor from which Saṃgha she received full ordination.
When Gopikā heard this, her heart was displeased, and she reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha and said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Do not trouble Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī!
When Gautamī accepted the eight weighty rules, she immediately went forth and obtained full ordination, becoming a bhikṣuṇī."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, having dressed in her robes and taken up her bowl before midday, entered the city to beg for food.
After her meal, she placed her *niṣadana* (sitting mat) upon her shoulder and entered the Andhavana forest, where she spread out the *niṣadana* and sat in half-lotus posture beneath a tree.
At that time, there was a Brahmin boy who conceived a lustful attachment toward a bhikṣuṇī;
he went to where the bhikṣuṇī was and said, "Come, let us engage in unchaste acts together."
The bhikṣuṇī Puṣpā thought to herself,
"If I resist him, he might forcibly seize me.
She spoke, saying:
"Wait a moment!
he asked. "For what reason should you wait a moment?"
The bhikṣuṇī immediately used her supernormal powers to transform her inner body into an outer body, whereupon the brahmin boy said in anger:
"I loathe you!"
She immediately struck her head with her fist, and both eyes popped out.
The other bhikṣuṇīs caught the eyes in a water vessel and went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇīs:

"One should speak words of truth: 'The bhikṣuṇī Puṣpavarṇā has deep faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma; there is no pure thing within the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha that she has not given as an offering. By virtue of this truth, may her two eyes be restored to their former state.'"
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these truthful words, their eyes were restored as they were before.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs must not reside in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka)."
"If one remains [in such a place], one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time some bhikṣuṇīs were living near herdsmen; because of the sounds of elephants, horses, men and women, and boys and girls, their sitting in meditation and reciting the sūtras were hindered.
These bhikṣuṇīs rose early, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the homes of their relatives, acquaintances, and donors;
there the laypeople asked them, "Are you well?"
He replied: "It is not at peace! Why is that?"
"We live near the herdsmen, and because of the sounds of elephants, horses, men, women, boys, and girls, they disturb our sitting in meditation, reciting the sūtras, and practicing the Path."
The laypeople said,
"We shall build lodgings for you.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to reside in dwellings.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to construct monasteries (saṃghārāma)."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta lived together with several virtuous bhikṣuṇīs and harassed those virtuous bhikṣuṇīs.
Before noon, several virtuous bhikṣuṇīs put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the homes of their relatives, acquaintances, and donors.
There, the laypeople asked them: "Are you all well?"
He replied, "It is not peaceful!
[The other asked,] "For what reason?"
She replied,
"She lives together with the bhikṣuṇī who assists Devadatta, and she harasses us.
The householder said to her:
"I shall build separate dwellings for you.
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to reside in separate dwellings."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to build separate dwellings.
While the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, at that time the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta took pleasure in standing in high places outside the gates to look about. The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
“Those bhikṣuṇīs said of themselves,
‘We are virtuous and excellent,’ yet they stood on high places outside the gate looking about like courtesans.”
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to stand in high places outside the gate to look out.
If they so stand and look, it is a pāyattika offense."
Since the Buddha did not permit standing at a high place outside the door to look in, they instead looked through the lattice windows.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs themselves claim:..."
"Excellent! She is virtuous.
Looking through the lattice window, [he saw her] as if she were the king’s consort or the wife of a high minister.
A bhikṣuṇī of few desires and contentment heard of this matter and was displeased; she reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī look through the lattice of a window?
From now on, you must not look through the lattice of a window."
"To look [at it] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
at that time the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon *śikṣamāṇās* and asked them:
"Are you a woman? She replied,
"I possess both sexual organs."
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This person with dual sexual organs is incapable of being a woman; because they are incapable of being a woman, I do not permit their going forth or receiving full ordination."
If one who has already left the household life and received full ordination possesses both sexual organs, they shall be subject to expulsion. Why is this?
Because a person with both organs cannot fulfill the role of a woman; within my Dharma, such a person does not give rise to the wholesome *bhikṣuṇī* discipline.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon śikṣamāṇās and asked them: "Are you women?"
She replied, "When I urinate, feces come out; when I defecate, urine comes out.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If the two paths have joined and she cannot become a woman, she should not be granted ordination or receive the full precepts."
If one who has already left the household life and received full ordination [is found to be] a hermaphrodite, they should be expelled. Why is this?
Because a person with two sexual organs is incapable of practicing as a woman; within my Dharma, such a person cannot give rise to the *vinaya* of wholesome dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon śikṣamāṇās and asked them:
"Do you have the monthly courses?"
She replied,
“It is always there.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one is constantly subject to menstrual taboos and cannot engage in sexual intercourse, she should not be granted ordination or the full precepts.
If she has already been ordained and received the full precepts, she should be expelled."
"Why is this? Because one who is constantly menstruating cannot give rise to the wholesome *dharma-vinaya* within my teaching.
Thus spoke the Buddha while residing in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon a śikṣamāṇā and asked her:
"Do you have menstruation?
She replied:
"I always observe the monthly fast.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do about this matter and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One who is perpetually menstruating may not become a nun; she is not permitted to leave the household life or receive full ordination.
If she has already left the household life and received full ordination, she should be expelled."
"Why is this? Because one who constantly observes the lunar taboos (*māsa-parihāra*) cannot give rise to the *bhikṣuṇī* who produces wholesome dharmas within my teaching.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon a śikṣamāṇā and asked her:
"Are you a woman? She replied:
"I have very few female characteristics.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there are few female characteristics and she cannot function as a woman, she shall not be permitted to go forth and receive full ordination.
If she has already gone forth and received full ordination, she should be subject to expulsion."

"Why is this? Because there are few who, while possessing the marks of a woman, cannot act as a woman; for within my Dharma, they do not give rise to the wholesome qualities that lead to discipline (*vinaya*).
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, who walked through the streets while her menstrual period had not yet ceased, causing blood to fall and defile the ground.
The lay devotees rebuked her, saying:
"O ill-omened, wretched woman!"
"If one has a disease that is taboo on this particular day of the month, how can one go out into the streets?
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣuṇī goes abroad while her menstrual period has not yet ceased, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There were some bhikṣuṇīs who were poor; while their menstrual periods had not yet ceased, they begged from others for rice, soup, vegetables, firewood, grass, lamps, and candles, thereby undergoing various sufferings.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should wrap oneself in a robe when going out to beg for alms.
[This occurred] while the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, having dressed in his robes and taken up his alms bowl before midday, was walking from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain toward Rājagṛha city to beg for food.
At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had risen early and was standing at the city gate, observing which men entering or leaving were handsome and which were ugly.
As Mahākāśyapa entered, he spat and said:
"Inauspicious!
I saw a heretic this morning as I was rising."
Mahākāśyapa said:
"Evil woman!
I do not reproach you; I reproach Ānanda."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs must not spit upon a bhikṣu.
If they do so, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs confessed and disclosed their grave offenses (sthūlātyaya) in the presence of the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣuṇīs felt ashamed and did not know what to do.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, a bhikṣuṇī should not confess a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) before a bhikṣu; she should confess it before a bhikṣuṇī."
When the bhikṣuṇīs confessed their offenses, they did not know what offense it was or to which category it belonged.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should question the bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir!'"
"What offense is committed by doing this?
What is the name of this offense?
The bhikṣu should reply:
"Whoever commits such an act shall incur such a transgression; they are subsumed under a certain category, and this offense is named so-and-so.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī, though her menstrual period had not yet ceased, went to the Jetavana to listen to the Dharma. She sat upon a monk’s bedding and stained it with blood.
Dabba Mallaputta, being in charge of the bedding and furniture for the Saṅgha, on another day while it was being washed, spoke with reproach:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have such illnesses; why do they sit upon the Saṅgha's bedding and furniture?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, if a bhikṣuṇī’s menstrual period has not yet ceased, she must not sit upon the bedding and mats belonging to the Saṃgha."
"To sit [there] constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
While the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, there was a nun who assisted Devadatta; she stood at a tavern selling liquor and experienced great suffering when being asked for the price.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"Why do you renunciants set up a tavern?
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs should not establish wine shops.
If they do so, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a maidservant as her attendant.
The lay devotees rebuked her, saying:
“Various bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
‘We are virtuous and excellent,’ yet they keep female slaves as their attendants, just like the wives of kings or ministers.”
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted to keep female slaves as attendants."
"If one keeps [her] as a follower, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā ordained a courtesan as her disciple.
When morning arrived, she dressed, took her bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. She spoke to the householders with whom she had previously engaged in unchaste conduct, saying:
"I previously engaged in unchaste acts with this bhikṣuṇī."
That bhikṣuṇī was distressed and troubled by this matter, and she reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you are not permitted to ordain female prostitutes."
"If one crosses [the threshold], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Elder Kālodāyin, having dressed before midday and taken his bowl, entered the city to beg for food. The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā followed behind him and, with her hand, touched Kālodāyin. Kālodāyin immediately kicked and struck her with his hands and feet until she fell to the ground, saying:
"You wretched woman!
You spat upon Mahākāśyapa; do you think I am like him?
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs must not touch the bodies of bhikṣus.
One who touches them commits an offense."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kāloratīśa passed away. This man had seven sister bhikṣuṇīs:
Thullanandā, Cūlanandā, Tiṣyā, Upatiṣyā, Kṣemā, Haliddikā, and Lekhatā. They possessed great power and influence, and they performed sacrifices for his cremated corpse.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying, "You have left the household life to enter the Path; why are you providing food and drink for the dead?
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, no bhikṣuṇīs shall perform sacrifices for the dead.
Should any perform such a sacrifice, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who lost his male organ and developed female organs. The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"She shall enter among the community of bhikṣuṇīs using the number of years she had previously spent as a renunciant and having received full ordination.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who lost her female organs and acquired male organs.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do,
so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should immediately have them enter the community of bhikṣus according to their age since they first left home and received full ordination.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who lost his male organ and acquired a female organ.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"He should be subjected to the penalty of parivāsa (banishment).
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who lost her female organ and acquired a male organ.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do about this matter and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"He should be subjected to the penalty of parivāsa (banishment).
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a brahmin who had a daughter born to him who was so beautiful and exquisite that her value was equal to half the kingdom of Kāśī.

This girl was married into a brahmin family, but before long her husband died. Many people came to seek her hand in marriage, namely great ministers, high officials, householders, and caravan leaders.
This woman’s heart delighted in leaving the household life, and she said:
"I wish to leave the household life and become a bhikṣuṇī; I do not delight in remaining in the secular world.
She then went to the Royal Garden and became a bhikṣuṇī.
When various wicked people heard that the woman of the Vaṅkāśika clan had gone forth, they thought:
"We must now plunder her away.
They further reflected thus:
“The bhikṣuṇīs are protected by the King; if one were to forcibly seize them, one would incur punishment from the authorities.
However, when they have gone forth and received full ordination, we shall plunder and take them by the road.”
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this matter, they did not know what to do and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, it is permitted for a half-Kāśī woman to receive full ordination by sending a messenger.
If there is anyone else who is similarly beautiful, it is likewise permitted for them to receive full ordination by sending a messenger."

Regarding the method for one who is to receive the precepts: the harmonious Saṃgha should be of one mind. This person should rise from their seat, bare the right shoulder, remove their leather sandals, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join their palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The nun So-and-so from Vaṅkāśī, with the nun So-and-so as her preceptor,
has sent me to request full ordination from the Saṃgha. May the Saṃgha,
out of compassion, grant her full ordination with the nun So-and-so as her preceptor.
The second one also says:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Such-and-such a Bhikṣuṇī of the Upagaśi clan has [the Bhikṣuṇī] So-and-so as her preceptress."
This Upāsikā Vaṅkāśī has sent me to request full ordination from the Saṃgha.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me full ordination with such-and-such as my Preceptor Nun (upādhyāyī).
The third [monk] also says:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Such-and-such a woman from the region of Upagaśi has such-and-such a nun as her preceptor."
This Upāsikā Vaṅkāśī has sent me to request full ordination from the Saṃgha.
May the Saṃgha grant me deliverance and confer full ordination upon me, with the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my preceptor, out of compassion for me.
At that time, one bhikṣu should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Such-and-such a Half-Kāśī woman has [the nun] So-and-so as her preceptor-nun."
This Upāsikā Vaṅkāśī has sent a messenger to the Saṃgha to request full ordination with such-and-such a Bhikṣuṇī as her preceptor.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I shall now question the messenger of Vaṅkāśī regarding the six matters within the Saṃgha.
"This is called 'white. One should say:
"Listen, you, Bhaginī of the Kāśi clan; now is the time for truthful speech. Now the Saṃgha questions you: what is true, you should say is true; what is not true, you should say is not true."
He asked the messenger,
"Has Bhaṅgakāśīnī previously been pure?
Has she studied the six rules for two years?"
Has she been ordained by a bhikṣuṇī through the proper formal procedure?
Has the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, being united and in harmony, performed the *karmavācanā* for her affiliation with a preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*)?
Are her five robes and alms bowl complete?
"What is the name of the Upādhyāyinī?
What is the name of the Bhikṣuṇī Kaśika? [She replies:
"The name of the Upādhyāyinī is So-and-so; the name of the Bhikṣuṇī Kaśika is So-and-so."
If there is a matter that has not yet been asked about, it should be asked; once the questioning is finished, one should say:
"Be silent. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Bhikṣuṇī Upārdhakāśī, named [Name], has [Name] as her preceptor-ni.
This Bhikṣuṇī Upārdhakāśī has sent a messenger to the Saṃgha to request the full ordination, with [Name] as her preceptor-ni.
The messenger said:

"Upālinī of the Kāśis was previously pure; she has studied the six rules for two years, and the bhikṣuṇīs have already performed the preliminary rites. With a single-minded and harmonious community of bhikṣuṇīs, the formal act (karmavācanā) of assigning her to a preceptress has been performed, and she is fully equipped with the five robes and the alms bowl."

The nun from the region of Ardha-kāśī, whose name is [so-and-so], with the preceptor-nun named [so-and-so] as her preceptor—if it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
the Saṃgha shall employ this messenger to confer full ordination upon the nun from the region of Ardha-kāśī, with the preceptor-nun [so-and-so] as her preceptor.
"This is called 'white.
Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The half-Kāśī woman named [Name], with the precept-mother named [Name] as her upādhyāyī."
This woman, Upārdhakāśī, has sent a messenger to the Saṃgha to request full ordination (*upasampadā*), with such-and-such a nun as her preceptor (*upādhyāyī*).
The messenger says:

"Upārdhakāśī was previously pure; she has studied the six rules for two years, and the bhikṣuṇīs have already performed the preliminary rites. With a single-minded and harmonious bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, they shall perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of appointing a preceptor; she possesses the five robes and the alms bowl."
The Saṅgha grants full ordination to the half-Kāśī woman [Name], with the preceptor nun [Name].
Which elders who consent to granting full ordination to the half-Kāśī woman remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak.
"This is called the completion of the first *karmavācanā*.
A second time, one should say:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
The nun So-and-so from the region of Ardha-kāśī, with the nun So-and-so as her preceptor,
is this nun from Ardha-kāśī who has sent a messenger to the Saṃgha to request the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The messenger says:

“Bhaginī Upakaśinī has previously been pure; she has studied the six rules for two years, and the bhikṣuṇīs have already performed the preliminary rites. With a unified and harmonious saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, the formal act (karmavācanā) of affiliation with a preceptress (upādhyāyinī) is performed, and she is fully equipped with the five robes and the alms bowl.”
"Such-and-such a Bhikṣuṇī from the region of Ardha-kāśi, with such-and-such a Bhikṣuṇī as her preceptor.
The Saṃgha grants full ordination to this Bhikṣuṇī from the region of Ardha-kāśi, with such-and-such a Bhikṣuṇī as her preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha granting full ordination to the half-Kāśī woman so-and-so, with such-and-such as her preceptor-ni, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak."
"This is called the completion of the second *karmavācanā*.
The third [motion] should further be recited:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
The nun [Name], a native of Upakaśi, with the nun [Name] as her preceptor,
has sent a messenger to the Sangha to request the full ordination, with the nun [Name] as her preceptor.
The messenger said:

"Bhaginī Aḍakāśikā has previously been pure; she has studied the six rules for two years, and the bhikṣuṇīs have already performed the preliminary rites. With a unified and harmonious community of bhikṣuṇīs, the formal act (karmavācanā) of assigning her a preceptress (upādhyāyinī) has been performed, and she is complete with the five robes and bowl."
"Such-and-such a woman from the region of Upakaśi, with such-and-such a nun as her preceptor.
The Sangha grants full ordination to this woman from Upakaśi, with such-and-such a nun as her preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to granting full ordination to the half-Kāśī woman named [Name],
with [Name] as her preceptress (upādhyāyikā), should remain silent;
those who do not consent should speak."
"This third *karmavācanā* is concluded.
The Saṃgha has granted full ordination to the half-Kāśī woman, [Name], with [Name] as her preceptor nun.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"

That messenger should then return to the nuns' quarters and announce the *karmavācanā* to the nun Bhadrakāśī; it should neither be too much nor too little, and he should also explain to her the three refuges and the eight *pārājika* rules.
"As for the remaining rules of training, the Upādhyāya and Ācārya shall gradually explain them to you in detail.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had committed an offense against Kālodāyin; Kālodāyin then barred this bhikṣuṇī from entering the monastery.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to this bhikṣuṇī:
"Why do you not repent before Kāḷudāyin?
She replied:
"If you have been barred from entering the monastery, how can I repent?
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not prevent a bhikṣuṇī from entering a monastery; however, he should prevent her from entering his own quarters.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs committed transgressions against the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus were displeased in their hearts.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense against a bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should prohibit that bhikṣuṇī from participating in the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), the invitation for criticism (pravāraṇā), and the receiving of instructions."

After the Buddha had thus given these instructions, that bhikṣu obstructed the bhikṣuṇīs from reciting the precepts, performing the *pravāraṇā*, and receiving the teaching and admonition; yet the other bhikṣus permitted it. Because of this matter, a dispute arose.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This obstructed bhikṣu should be permitted to listen; others should not be permitted."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus pointed out the faults of the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs were displeased in their hearts and spoke as follows:
“Regarding the transgressions we have committed, O bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣus have obstructed us from reciting the Prātimokṣa, from performing the Pravāraṇā, and from receiving instructions.
As for the transgressions the bhikṣus have committed against us, who is able to speak with them?”
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu commits an offense against a bhikṣuṇī, that bhikṣu should go back to that bhikṣuṇī and repent for his transgression."
After the Buddha had thus instructed them, the bhikṣu apologized to the bhikṣuṇī, but the bhikṣuṇī would not accept it.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When a bhikṣu apologizes to a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī should accept it."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a bhikṣuṇī committed an offense against Kālodāyin; Kālodāyin then prevented her from receiving instruction and admonition, and having finished his business, he departed beyond the boundary.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Why do you not repent before Kāḷudāyin?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"Having been censured for my instruction, I have gone beyond the boundary; to whom shall I confess my transgression?
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, a bhikṣu shall not obstruct a bhikṣuṇī from leaving the boundary.
If she leaves the boundary, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, at the Jetavana Monastery, there was a barber who shaved the nuns' heads. He enticed and deceived one śikṣamāṇā, causing her to ruin her resolve for the renunciant life; he likewise enticed and deceived a second and a third person. Because of these matters, the community of nuns diminished.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When shaving the hair, one should have a virtuous bhikṣuṇī stand by the side and watch."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta rented a dwelling; later, when it came time to pay the rent, she experienced great distress.
The laypeople rebuked her, saying:
"You who have left the household life, why do you rent houses?
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, no bhikṣuṇīs shall rent houses."
"If one hires [another] to do so, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha,
at that time a bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta used bodily ornaments to adorn her person.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and possessed of merit.'"
"Using body-care items to groom the body, as the wives of kings or ministers do.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs should not use body-care items to groom their bodies."
"If she treats it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who then treated her own body with tiles, stones, or her fists.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not treat the body with tiles, stones, or the fist.
If one treats the body with such objects oneself, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"In brief, a bhikṣuṇī should not adorn her body with any material objects.
If she does so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the two assemblies of monks were in harmony.
At that moment, the *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs* were expelled, and they said to one another: "Do you know?"
"Why have you driven us out?
Tonight we shall all gather in one place, each according to our own preference, to dwell together in harmony.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were displeased and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs should not perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at night.
All bhikṣuṇīs should rise early and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony before the bhikṣus."
At that time, there were many bhikṣuṇīs—more than five hundred—and as each of them performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony one by one, the time for the meal had already passed.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, the bhikṣuṇīs should not perform the *pravāraṇā* with the community of bhikṣus one by one."
A single bhikṣuṇī should represent the entire saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs and perform the *pravāraṇā* before the saṃgha of bhikṣus.

As for the procedure for representing the *pravāraṇā*: the person representing the *pravāraṇā* rises from her seat, removes her leather sandals, kneels with her right knee on the ground, joins her palms, and speaks as follows:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is harmonious; they pay homage at the feet of the venerable saṃgha and inquire whether you are free from illness and affliction, and whether your daily life is peaceful."
Having exchanged greetings, he spoke thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, take heed!
We have completed our three-month rains retreat; we now request the Venerable Saṃgha to speak of any offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."
"Out of compassion for us, may the venerable Saṃgha declare our offenses; this will cause the increase of wholesome dharmas.
The second [monk] should also say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!"

"The community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, bows its head at the feet of the venerable Saṃgha and inquires after his health: Are you free from illness and affliction, and are you dwelling in peace?
Having thus inquired, they speak these words:
'We have completed our three-month rains retreat; we now request the Saṃgha to grant us the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā) regarding any offenses seen, heard, or suspected.'"
"Out of compassion for us, may the Venerable Saṃgha declare our offenses; this will cause our wholesome dharmas to increase.
A third time, one should likewise say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take note!"

"The community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, bows its head at the feet of the venerable Saṃgha and inquires after his health: Are you free from illness and affliction, and are you dwelling in peace?
Having made this inquiry, they speak thus:
'We have completed our three-month rains retreat; we now request that the Saṃgha grant us the invitation for self-examination (pravāraṇā) regarding any faults seen, heard, or suspected.'"
"Out of compassion for us, O Venerable Saṃgha, may you explain our offenses; this will cause our wholesome dharmas to increase.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha of both divisions for a meal the following day, and the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], the householder prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he prepared various kinds of many delicious foods throughout the entire night.
Rising early in the morning, he arranged the seats and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; the food is ready. May the Holy One know the proper time."
The Buddha and the Saṃgha of the two divisions entered her house; the bhikṣuṇīs sat down according to their seniority of wisdom.

When the lay devotee saw that the Buddha and the Saṃgha of the two divisions were seated, he personally offered water for washing and prepared to serve food and drink. However, a bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta addressed the lay devotee, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī is the foremost elder; this is the second elder; this one is a master of the Vinaya; this one is a master of the Abhidharma."
The householder said,
"We do not know and are not familiar with who is the first elder, the second elder, the upholder of the Vinaya, or the upholder of the Abhidharma."
"There is plenty of food to satisfy everyone; do not engage in idle chatter.
If you do not cease, you all may rise and eat while we remain seated."
The Buddha saw the bhikṣuṇī from afar making these remarks and heard the householder’s reproach. After the meal, on account of this matter, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and said to them:
"From now on, it is permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to sit according to the order of seniority."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the two assemblies of monks for a meal the following day. The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the householder prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. He returned to his own home and prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food throughout the entire night.
Rising early, he spread out the seats and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared. May the Holy One know the proper time.
The Buddha and the two assemblies of monks entered his residence.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who asked another bhikṣuṇī,
"How many years old are you?
She replied:
“Wait a moment; I shall ask my preceptress (upādhyāyī), my teacher (ācāryā), and my co-resident (sahavāsinī).
She then went to ask her preceptress, her teacher, and her co-resident, saying:
“How many years of age am I?”
The preceptor-ni and the others replied,
“We are doubtful and have forgotten.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Two or three senior monks should ask those seated in order; the others who do not remember [the sequence] may simply sit.
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who went up a mountain to an āraṇya dwelling in order to receive instruction. She encountered bandits who stripped her of her clothes, leaving her naked.
The other bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The bhikṣuṇīs should stay within the village to wait for the bhikṣus. The bhikṣuṇīs stayed in the village waiting;

meanwhile, a bhikṣu entered the village to beg for food and returned by another path to his mountain hermitage (āraṇya). By then, the sun was already high in the sky, and the bhikṣuṇīs were on the verge of having to go without food.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"Two people should go together.
Thereupon, the two went together.
The two of them, not knowing the Dharma, went to look at a painted hall.
A bhikṣu asked them,
"Do you wish to receive instruction?"
He replied, “It is so.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Two bhikṣuṇīs who are learned in the Dharma and possess clear understanding should be sent to receive the instruction.
Thereupon, two bhikṣuṇīs who were learned in the Dharma and possessed clear understanding were dispatched.
These two bhikṣuṇīs intended to bring about harmony among the entire Saṃgha of bhikṣus, saying, "We shall receive the instruction."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not necessary for the entire Saṃgha to assemble; rather, whichever bhikṣu they see should receive the instruction.

At other times, when they went to the place of a bhikṣu, some wished to receive the instruction while others did not. Those who did not wish to do so would leave and depart, and the bhikṣuṇīs would then follow after them.
The laypeople who were in the monastery said this:
"The bhikṣuṇī desired to engage in sexual intercourse, but because the bhikṣu did not wish for it, he abandoned her and departed."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not rise and leave."
"If you do not wish to do so, you should say:
'I am unable to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had received the instruction and returned to complete the recitation of the precepts, they went to the monastery the following day but did not know whom to inform.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should return and inform the bhikṣu who provided the instruction."
At that time, that bhikṣuṇī stood at the door and asked,
"Is there such a person here? He replied:
“Who is it? The bhikṣuṇī replied,
“It is such-and-such a person.”
"This matter should not be done in this way.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“A bhikṣuṇī should inquire about the name and clan of the bhikṣu who is to instruct her, and she should remember them well.
She should ask:
‘Such-and-such a bhikṣu is my upādhyāya; such-and-such a bhikṣu is my ācārya; such-and-such a bhikṣu is my disciple.’”
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs received an offering of waistbands, but the bhikṣuṇīs would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep waistbands."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, I permit the community of bhikṣuṇīs to accept gifts of bundles, and individuals may also accept them.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, while going through the streets for alms with her bowl of food in hand, encountered a venomous snake on the roof above; its excrement fell into her food.
The bhikṣuṇī ate this food, and when the poison took effect, she was on the verge of death. She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should make a lid to cover the top of one's food vessel."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta was carrying a load on her back, appearing like a beast of burden.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall carry anything on their backs.
If any carry anything on their backs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who assisted Devadatta were making flower garlands for hire and suffered distress when being paid.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"You have left the household life; what use have you for making flower garlands for hire?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to work as flower-garland makers for hire.
To work as a hired laborer is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who assisted Devadatta kept vessels for holding excrement, namely bronze basins, wash-basins, and bronze ladles.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.'"
“Keep such vessels as those used by the wives of kings or ministers.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to keep copper helmets used as receptacles for excrement, nor copper basins, washing basins, or copper ladles.”
If one keeps [such items], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense for keeping a copper water jar, a copper washbasin, or a copper lid.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who brewed alcohol, and a layperson said to her, "You are renunciants; why do you brew alcohol?
A bhikṣuṇī of few desires and contentment heard of this matter and was displeased in her heart. She reported this affair to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having assembled the community, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs shall not produce intoxicants.
Should any produce intoxicants, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were several women who had recently arrived; their husbands went abroad and died, and these women abandoned their homes and market stalls to leave the household life and become bhikṣuṇīs.
Having become bhikṣuṇīs, they rented houses to others; later, when the time came to pay the rent, they suffered various afflictions.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"You have left the household life; what use is it for you to rent houses?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to lease houses or market stalls.
If one leases them to others, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, wearing a new, coarse garment, walked through a busy market street with her body exposed.
The laypeople asked,
"Virtuous lady, what is the name of this garment?
She replied:
“This is what is called a new coarse garment.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
“The bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:”
"How excellent and virtuous!
Why are you wearing these new, coarse garments, like the wives of kings or the wives of high ministers?
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to wear thin or coarse clothing.
To wear such is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta bathing at a place where women bathe.
The laypeople rebuked her, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs themselves claim:..."
"Excellent and virtuous!
she said, as she bathed at the women's bathing place, like the wife of a king or the wife of a high minister.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to bathe in places where women wash.
If they do so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā used soap powder to bathe her body and inserted it into her female organ.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to use soap powder to bathe."
"To use it [thus] is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā swam upstream in the water. The other bhikṣuṇīs asked her:
"Why are you traveling against the current?
He replied,
"I wish to experience the pleasure of touch."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to swim against the current in water.
If one swims against the current, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta possessed alms-bowl rests decorated with various colors. The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves:..."
"It is well and virtuous.
[She] kept a bowl of variegated colors, like the wives of kings or ministers.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I do not permit bhikṣuṇīs to keep bowls with variegated rims.
Should they keep one, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This was said by the Buddha while he was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs received a crystal vessel as an offering, but the bhikṣuṇīs would not accept it,
asking, "What use have we for this?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit bhikṣuṇīs to accept crystal vessels to be used as water containers for the Saṃgha.
This was the twentieth rule; later, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who went for alms; having dressed in his robes and taken up his bowl before midday, he entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Upon reaching the house where he sought alms, he entered the outer gate but did not take note of the middle gate, nor did he take note of the inner gate.
On his way back, he mistakenly entered another door, thinking it was the exit.
Having entered, he saw a woman lying on her back; she had discharged impurity in a dream. Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu felt ashamed and went back out.
After he had left, the husband of this woman arrived; seeing his wife lying with her body exposed and impurity flowing, he immediately thought:
"This bhikṣu must have engaged in unchaste conduct with my wife."
He then went and seized the bhikṣu, saying:
"Bhikṣu, are you well?
You have committed an act of impurity with my wife."
The bhikṣu replied, "I did not.
The husband said:
"Why have you entered my house?
He replied, "I thought this was the exit."
He immediately reviled the bhikṣu,
saying, "How is it that you enter my room and claim this door is for exiting?
That man then struck the bhikṣu violently with his hands and feet before releasing him.
Because of the sound of striking the bhikṣu, the woman immediately woke up and said to her husband,
"What are you doing? He replied:
“Strike the bhikṣu!
“Why strike him? “I strike him because of you.”
The wife said to her husband, "This bhikṣu has done me no wrong; it was I who discharged impurity in a dream.
The husband then reviled his wife:
"You committed an act of impurity with me; why did you not subdue yourself?
Having said this, he struck the bhikṣu with his hands and feet until the man was exhausted, then left him.
After the bhikṣu had endured great suffering, he returned and reported the matter to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus for this reason, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of alms-seeking: [alms from house to house and alms by invitation]."
First, those who have accepted an invitation; second, those who have not accepted an invitation.

If one who has accepted an invitation wishes to receive a portion of the Sangha's property, they must first relinquish the practice of begging for food before receiving that portion of the Sangha's property.
If one does not relinquish the practice of begging for alms but accepts a portion of the Sangha's property, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, after having accepted a portion of the Sangha's property, one deliberately says,
"I am a beggar for alms," [one also incurs an offense].
One who says this commits the *pāyattika* offense of lying.

If a person who has not accepted an invitation wishes to accept an invitation, or wishes to accept a portion of the Sangha’s property, they should first relinquish the practice of alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*) before accepting the invitation or the portion of the Sangha’s property.
If one does not relinquish the practice of begging for food yet accepts an invitation or receives a portion of the Sangha's property, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. If,
after having accepted an invitation or received a portion of the Sangha's property, one intentionally says,
"I am a beggar for alms," [one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense].
Whoever says this commits the offense of *pāyattika* for false speech.
The Buddha said:
“From now on, I shall teach you the method for begging for food; when a bhikṣu begs for food, he should train himself to practice this method.”
When wishing to descend from the bed, one should lower one foot slowly, then lower the second foot, and rise up slowly and steadily.
One should then go slowly to the rack to take the *antarvāsa*, not pulling it, and put it on slowly and steadily.
Having put it on, one should look to the left and right to see if it is level and straight.
If it is not level and straight, one should put it on again; if it is level and straight, one should stop.
Slowly take the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* from the rack without pulling it, and put it on calmly and slowly.
Having put it on, look to the left and right: is it even and straight?
If it is not even and straight, you should put it on again; if it is even and straight, stop.
Slowly take the *uttarāsaṅga* from the rack; do not pull it, but put it on calmly and steadily.
Having put it on, look to the left and right to see if it is level and straight.
If it is not level and straight, you should adjust it; if it is level and straight, stop.
Slowly take the saṃghāṭī from the rack without pulling it, and place it calmly over the left shoulder.
Take up the alms bowl slowly; do not let it drop to the ground.
Take up the mendicant’s staff slowly; you should not drag it along the floor.
When approaching the door, push the bolt open calmly and exit slowly.
When exiting the door, do not let your robe touch either side.
Having exited, you should pull the door leaf with your left hand and the bolt with your right hand.
If the door leaf is on the right and the bolt is on the left, pull the leaf with your right hand and lower the bolt with your left hand.
Having descended from the ladder, one should inspect whether it is secure;
if it is not secure, close it again, but if it is secure, stop.
If walking with the Buddha, one should remain behind him.

One should inform the preceptor and, having circumambulated the Buddha stūpa and the śrāvaka stūpa clockwise, slowly pour the water into the bowl, taking care not to let the pitcher and the bowl strike one another.
One should wash the bowl slowly and calmly, ensuring it makes no sound.
One must not scoop water to pour over the bottom of the bowl.
If the gate of the monastic quarters is closed, one should gently withdraw the bolt to open the door and exit slowly and calmly.
When leaving the door, do not let your robes touch either side.
You should slowly set your bowl and staff in one place, then slowly put on a single layer of leather sandals.
You should slowly take up your bowl and staff, and proceed along the path with steady composure.
When walking, do not drag your leather sandals.
Once you have approached the village, set aside your bowl and staff gently in one place; you should then gently take up your saṃghāṭī robe and put it on.
Having put it on, you should check whether it is properly aligned and straight.
If it is not level and upright, one should adjust it; if it is level and upright, one should stop.
When slowly taking up the bowl and staff to enter an alleyway, one must not look upward or downward, but should proceed straight ahead.
If one sees from afar a mad elephant, a mad horse, a mad ox, a mad dog, or a mad naked ascetic, one should yield the path.

When arriving at the house where one is to beg for food, one should clearly recognize the characteristics of the outer gate, the middle gate, and the inner gate; having entered the courtyard, one should stand still and snap the fingers.
If nothing is obtained, one should snap the fingers a second time.
If still nothing is obtained, one should snap the fingers a third time.
After snapping the fingers three times, if something is obtained, one should hold the bowl with both hands, bend the body, and receive the food.
When going on almsround at other locations, one should observe the time and season.
If it is still early in the day, one may go again for alms; once the proper time has arrived, one should stop.
One should not look up or down, but gaze straight ahead as one walks.
If one sees from afar a mad elephant, a mad horse, a mad ox, a mad dog, or a mad naked ascetic, one should avoid them.
When leaving a village, one should slowly set aside the bowl and staff in one place.
He should slowly take up his saṃghāṭī robe, fold it in the middle, shake it out, and place it over his left shoulder; he should then slowly take up his bowl and staff.

If he arrives at the place where the meal is being served first, he should arrange the seats and beds, take up the foot-rubbing materials, the foot-wiping materials, and set out the water jars and water vessels; he should also sweep the dining area and smear the floor with plaster.
If one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) is at the place where food is being consumed, if one obtains excellent food, one should first give it to the preceptor or teacher.
When giving them a drink, do not allow their fingers to enter the vessel.

If one arrives later, one should lift up the bed and seat, put away the foot-rubbing materials and foot-wiping cloths, set out the water jars and water vessels, sweep and sprinkle the floor to remove filth, and then return to the room.

Upon entering the room, one should pull the bolt, close the door, and approach the seat; then, slowly drawing up one leg and then the other, one should sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) and contemplate the practice of the Dharma.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a certain householder had some excellent radishes. For the sake of these radishes, he invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for *tambula* (refreshments), and the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], he returned home and spent the entire night preparing various kinds of exquisite food and drink. At dawn, he arranged the seats and went to inform him:
"The time has come; may the Buddha know the proper moment himself."

When the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus had entered the house and were seated, the elder personally served water and personally offered radish roots. As the bhikṣus chewed the radish roots, they made a noise.
There was a bhikṣu who had previously been a performer; whenever he saw food that made a sound, he would immediately break into dance.
At that time, another bhikṣu laughed, and turnips emerged from his mouth and nose.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "
"How can you cause others to laugh like a performer?
Seeing that this bhikṣu had acted in such a manner and was being rebuked by the lay devotees, the Buddha returned after his meal.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he said to that bhikṣu:
"With what intention did you do this?
He replied:
"It is for two reasons:
first, to look at others; second, with the desire to cause laughter.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense if it is for the purpose of looking at others.
If it is for the purpose of laughing, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if one has not yet eaten cooked food, one must not eat vegetables or fruit.
If one eats them beforehand, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
When the new Jetavana had been completed, the lay devotees prepared offerings. A great many bhikṣus arrived, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
The bhikṣus entered in disorder, sat in disorder, ate in disorder, rose in disorder, and departed in disorder. The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who enter in order, sit in order, eat in order, rise in order, and depart in order."
These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
"We are virtuous and of good character.
Yet they enter in disorder, sit in disorder, eat in disorder, rise in disorder, and depart in disorder; one does not know who has received [the offerings].
"Who does not obtain [it]?
Who obtains it repeatedly?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should enter in order, sit in order, eat in order, rise in order, and depart in order."

At that time, the bhikṣus entered in order, sat down in order, ate in order, rose in order, and departed in order; they entered in silence, sat down in silence, ate in silence, rose in silence, and departed in silence.
The lay devotees rebuked them, saying:
"There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who offer hymns of praise and prayers of benediction.
Yet these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent, virtuous one!
Having said this, he entered in silence, sat down in silence, ate in silence, rose in silence, and departed in silence; we did not know whether the food was good or not.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, during mealtime, you should chant verses of praise and offer blessings."
The bhikṣus did not know who should perform it. The Buddha said:
"The senior monk (sthavira) shall do it.
At that time, Steyanandā had little learning and meager knowledge, yet she was the senior monk; the Buddha said:
"If the Elder is unable, the next in order should act.
If the second is unable, the third should act.
In this manner, whoever is capable should act."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, various women took turns inviting the Buddha and the Saṃgha, preparing diverse kinds of food and drink.
After the bhikṣus had finished eating, they departed without reciting verses or offering prayers of blessing.
The women said, "We women are of little merit;
who will chant verses, offer blessings, and praise us?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you should also perform *bhāṣya*, incantations, vows, and praises for women.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) present, four senior monks (*sthavira*) shall remain behind."
While they were staying there, the elder monks became faint and distressed;
they questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should tell the women to depart.
This occurred while the Buddha was in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu named Mantuḷa, born of the Brahmin caste, who had gone forth as a monk. Suffering from a chronic diarrhea, he thought to himself:
"Why must I wash with water so frequently?"
The Buddha said, "One should wipe it with an object.
When wiping, he used a single leaf; after wiping, it was still not clean. The Buddha said:
"One should use two layers.
When using two layers for wiping, one layer becomes soiled by the hand. The Buddha said:
"One should cut off the folded portion."
At that time, the anus was injured by cutting it. The Buddha said:
"One should not cut it; one should instead use a single piece of clean cloth for wiping.
When wiping, he threw the used cloth away into the latrine. Once the latrine became full after this practice, the Buddha said:
“They should be placed in one location.
At that time, clean leaves and unclean leaves were placed together in one spot; when they were being taken up, the hands became soiled. The Buddha said:
“Place the clean leaves on the right side, and discard the unclean leaves on the left side.”
When it formed a large mass in one place, the Buddha said, "Remove it.
When he was removing it, he vomited; the Buddha said:
"One should place the vessel;
if it becomes full, discard the remainder in another location.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus chewed tooth-sticks in the place where they washed their feet; later, when other bhikṣus arrived, they saw the filth and were nauseated.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with various causes and conditions:
"How can those who are called bhikṣus chew tooth-sticks in the place where the Saṃgha washes its feet?
Having rebuked them, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one must not chew tooth-sticks in the presence of the Buddha;
nor before one's preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), before any senior monks (sthavira), before a Buddha stūpa, or before a stūpa of a śrāvaka."

One must not chew tooth-sticks in a greenhouse, a lecture hall, the kitchen, before the main gate, near the latrines, at places where water is kept, in the urinal, within the bathhouse, or in any place where many people pass.
To chew [it] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if it is in the presence of a bhikṣu of the same seniority.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a naked ascetic suffering from scabies who went to Jīvaka and said,
"Cure this disease of mine.
He replied:
"One can only recover by bathing in a bathhouse.
The non-Buddhist practitioners said this:
"We are non-Buddhists; we go naked and possess no attachments. By what means could we obtain a bathhouse to bathe?"
Jīvaka said, "Is there any bhikṣu who is a relative or an acquaintance?
He replied:
"No," Jīvaka replied,
"only by bathing in a heated bathhouse can he be cured."
The non-Buddhist practitioner then went to the Bamboo Grove and asked the newly ordained bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras:
"When do you bathe in the bathhouse?"
He replied, "On such-and-such a day.

Then the non-Buddhists counted the days on their fingers, or counted the days by throwing stones, or counted the days by using tally-sticks, noting how many days had already passed and how many days remained.

When the time for bathing arrived, he came to the Bamboo Grove and stood to one side, observing how the bhikṣus entered the bathhouse to wash: some bhikṣus entered wearing their robes, while others entered with their bodies smeared with mud.
The non-Buddhist practitioner immediately entered with his body smeared with mud, appearing like an elderly senior monk (*sthavira*).
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"From where has this senior monk come?"
They said to one another, "The Elder is coming; let us give the Elder a bed.
They immediately provided a bed and placed a vessel full of water before him.
After he had sweated, the bhikṣus also rubbed his feet, thighs, arms, chest, and back.
Having rubbed his entire body, the scabies was immediately removed, and his body attained purity.
Once they had been purified, he called for the robes to be brought to give them to the elder;
the non-Buddhists said, "You are not well-favored; what use have you for these robes?
The bhikṣus replied:
"It is unwholesome.
"Are you not washing it for the non-Buddhists?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one must not rub oneself while naked; nor may another rub someone who is naked; furthermore, two people who are both naked must not rub each other."

A bhikṣu must not perform a prostration in the dark; he must not prostrate to one whose face is covered; he must not prostrate to one who is sleeping; he must not prostrate to one who has entered samādhi; he must not prostrate to one who is chewing a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha), nor may he himself perform a prostration while chewing a tooth-stick.
When washing one's face, one must not perform a prostration, nor should one prostrate toward someone who is washing their face.
When eating, one must not perform a prostration, nor should one prostrate toward someone who is eating.
While one is sewing one's own clothes, one must not perform a prostration, nor should one perform a prostration toward the person who is sewing them.
While one is shaving one's own head, one must not perform a prostration, nor should one perform a prostration toward the person who is shaving one's head.
One who occupies a superior position must not pay homage to one in an inferior position, nor shall one in an inferior position pay homage to one in a superior position.
One must not pay homage to another person in the presence of the Buddha, nor in the presence of a stūpa of the Buddha, nor in the presence of a stūpa of a śrāvaka.
One must not pay respects at places for defecation or urination, at places for drawing water, in the bathhouse, or even in any place that is not secure.
While traveling on a road, one must not pay respects; however, if one wishes to pay respects with a sincere heart, one should say:
"Venerable Elder, please stop; I wish to pay you respects."
"If one who remains should be saluted, but one who does not remain should not be saluted.
While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī,
there was a visiting bhikṣu who arrived at dusk and was assigned an empty room.
At that time, there was a snake sleeping on a tray atop the bed; the bhikṣu sat down upon it without looking and was bitten by the snake, dying together with it.
After five or six days, blue flies emerged. Seeing the flies entering and exiting, the bhikṣus said to one another, "Blue flies are emerging from this room; we should go in and look."
Having entered, he saw it and said:
"This bhikṣu must have been sitting upon this snake; he will be bitten by the snake and both will surely die.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
This matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, the rules of etiquette for guest bhikṣus shall be taught."

If a visiting bhikṣu arrives at a monastic dwelling, he should bare one shoulder and put on his robes; he should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with its upper edge lowered, and having carried his robe-bag on his right shoulder, he should shift it to his left shoulder.
If a staff, an oil-sack, leather sandals, or a needle-case are held in the right hand, they should be moved to the left hand.
If one wishes to defecate or urinate, one should first withdraw outside before entering the monastery; if water is available, one should enter after washing the feet;
if water is not available, one should enter after wiping the feet with grass or tree leaves.
If the door is closed, one should request it be opened; if it is open, one should enter.

If it is not open, and there is a wall, moat, or thorny hedge outside the monastery, one should stand where one can be seen, maintaining pure deportment with a single mind, manifesting the bearing of a great man to inspire wholesome thoughts in others.
If one sees an elder bhikṣu, one should ask:
"In this monastery, are there rooms for bhikṣus of such-and-such seniority? If he says:
"There is. He then said,
"Open the door."
Having entered, he asks again:
"Is there anyone in this room?
If [someone] says:
If [he says] "Empty," one should ask:
"With what water?"
If he says, "Well water," one should request a basin for rinsing,
as well as a rope and a broom; one should then open the door of the room and snap one's fingers.
If there is a venomous snake, one should snap one's fingers to drive it away, then slowly go out and remove the pillows, bedding, mattresses, and floor coverings.

Having removed them, one should sweep and sprinkle the ground and apply plaster; shake out the beds, mats, bedding, pillows, and floor coverings; and once the insects have been sought out and removed, one should spread everything back as it was before.
The foot-washing basin and the regular water flask were both filled with water; he took his leather sandals to the water’s edge to wash them.
Having wiped the sandals, wrung out the cloth, and spread it out to dry, he took the sandals and first wiped the front part, then the back, and finally the straps in the middle.
If the water vessel is on the left side, one should take water with the left hand and wash the feet with the right hand;
if it is on the right side, one should take water with the right hand and wash the feet with the left hand.
Having washed his feet and put on his leather sandals, he entered the room, closed the door, lowered the bolt, and sat back down upon the rope-couch. First he drew up one leg, then the other;
having drawn them up, he sat firmly and contemplated all phenomena with right observation.
When the site has been finalized, one should ask the resident bhikṣus:
"In this monastery, is there food before the midday meal or no food before the midday meal?
Is there food at the proper time or no food at the proper time?"
Where are there households with vicious dogs, vicious oxen, unmarried girls, or widows?
Where are there households subject to the *saṃgha-karman* of "learning the household" (*śikṣamāṇa-kuṭumbaka*) or the *karman* of overturning the bowl (*pātra-nikubjana*)?
"Where may one go? Where may one not go?
Having asked these things, one should proceed to beg for food.

When a visiting bhikṣu wishes to depart, he should return the water pitcher, the rope, and the broom to their original owners; having put away his bedding and closed the door and lowered the bolt, he may leave.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Abhirati.

At that time, a newly constructed monastery had a bhikṣu serving as its master builder; he carried the saṃghāṭī robe while transporting stones, bricks, grass, and mud, and plastered the walls with his hands.
They smeared the walls with black mud, bran mud, and soiled plaster; they coated the walls with red-colored mud and white-colored mud.
Having swept and plastered the monastic quarters, their robes became soiled by the ground; wearing these soiled robes, they entered the village to beg for alms.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who put on clean robes when entering a village to beg for food.
Yet these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, claim for themselves:"
"Excellent! You possess virtue.
Wearing these soiled robes, he entered the village to beg for alms like an oil-presser.
Among them was a bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, his heart was displeased, and he reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"From now on, you must not wear the saṃghāṭī while carrying stones, carrying mud, carrying grass, or plastering walls; nor may you smear walls with your hands, or apply husk-mud to the walls, or sprinkle and plaster the ground of the monastery cells."

One must not tread upon the *saṃghāṭī* with one's feet; one must not spread the *saṃghāṭī* out to sit on; one must not lie down upon the *saṃghāṭī*; and one must not wear the *saṃghāṭī* as an undergarment against the body.
He put on the saṃghāṭī robe according to the rules for putting on the saṃghāṭī;
he put on the uttarāsaṅga robe according to the rules for putting on the uttarāsaṅga;
he put on the antaravāsaka robe according to the rules for putting on the antaravāsaka.
One should purify [the robes] by means of three kinds of dyed colors; one must not wear robes of five kinds of pure colors, except for the patched robe (*nāṃgala*).
If a bhikṣu is poor and has few robes, and is unable to obtain a robe made of cut pieces, he may attach patches to his robe—whether five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, or more than fifteen.
"If one is able to obtain [cloth], it should be cut and made into a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, and an antarvāsaka; this is the rule for robes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a large monastic complex where, during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, many guest bhikṣus would come to stay at all times and depart at dawn.
The senior monk asked the junior monk,
"Why are there no visiting bhikṣus?
He replied:
“Yes. “Why did he not come to see the Elder?
We do not know whether that person came or went.”
The bhikṣus did not know what to do regarding this matter, so they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When visiting bhikṣus arrive, they should first pay homage to the senior monks."

At that time, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus in that monastery; as each visiting bhikṣu performed his prostrations, the first watch of the night passed, and because they were utterly exhausted from their journey, they were unable to complete them all.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should inquire after the health of the four senior elders."
A visiting bhikṣu arrived in the evening and asked,
"Where is the foremost elder?
He replied:
"He is at Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata.
He asked again,
"Where is the second elder?"
He replied,
"In the district of Vyākaraṇa.
He asked again:
"Where is the third Elder?
He replied,
"He is in the Kosthaka Ward."
He asked again,
"Where is the fourth elder?
He replied:
"In the Sādhukāra-vihāra.
When he went there to pay his respects, he encountered fears along the way of lions, tigers, and wolves; fears of leopards, bears, brown bears, and many rākṣasas.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
