"Whenever he entered a monastery cell, he would immediately pay homage to those four senior elders.
While prostrating, he stood outside the gate of the large hall for a long time, becoming faint and distressed, vomiting, and feeling ill at ease."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do;
they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one is able to see the elder at that time, one should pay homage; if one is unable to see him at that time, then one should desist."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
In a forest retreat in the kingdom of Kośala, there was a bhikṣu dwelling therein.
At that time, bandits entered the monastery and saw the bhikṣu on the upper story; they immediately sent someone to bring the bhikṣu down.
At that time, the leader of those bandits had faith and reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma, and he said:
"Do not take the bhikṣu down; let us first see whether there is fire or not. He said:
"No. "Is there food? He replied:
"No. "Is there water? He replied:
"No," they said to one another,
"these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are pure."
"Look, is there water at the place for washing feet? He replied, "No."
"Look at the water-pitcher for purification and the pitcher for daily use; is there any water?
He replied, "There is none."
Having said this, he commanded:
"Bring that bhikṣu here.
They immediately brought him down and questioned him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Is there fire? He replied:
“No. “Do you have fire-drills? I wish to kindle a fire.”
He replied, "No, Venerable Sir. "Venerable Sir! [he continued].
"We are hungry; is there any food?
They replied, "There is none."
He asked, "Do you have any eating vessels?
I wish to prepare some food."
He replied, "No, Venerable Sir. "Venerable Sir! [he continued].
"We are thirsty; is there water? They replied, "No."
“Do you have a water vessel? He replied, “No.”
“Venerable Sir!
Are these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, pure? Is there water for washing the feet?
Are there a vessel for pure water and a vessel for constant use?”
He replied, “No. He asked again:
“Venerable sir!
I wish to go to that village; please show me the way.
He replied:
"I do not know.
He asked again:
"What time of day is it?"
He replied, “I do not know.
He asked again:
"What day is it today?
He replied, "I do not know."
He asked again,
"Do you chant gāthās?
He replied:
"No," he replied. He spoke again:
"Is it a prayer for blessings?"
He replied, “I cannot.
He spoke again:
“Praise the Dharma?
He replied, “I cannot.”
The thieves said to one another:
"This forest-dwelling bhikṣu possesses not a single quality of a forest-dweller; this bhikṣu has surely gone forth because he cannot support himself. We must beat him severely."
Having struck that bhikṣu with his hands and feet, he departed.
That bhikṣu suffered great pain and distress, and reported this matter to the other bhikṣus. The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha of these events.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, you must instruct forest-dwelling bhikṣus in the proper rules of conduct.

You should train yourselves in these dharmas: from now on, when a person approaches a forest-dwelling bhikṣu, he should first engage them in conversation; he should maintain right mindfulness with a pleasant and serene countenance, and must not hang his head. He should say:”

“Welcome. One should maintain fire and a fire-drill; one should maintain food and eating utensils; one should maintain water and water vessels; one should maintain water for washing the feet and a foot-washing vessel; one should keep the *śikya* (pure-water flask) and the *dhāraṇī-ghaṭa* (constant-use flask) filled with water. One should know the directions, know the days, know the seasons, know the nights, and know the divisions of the night; one should know the constellations and study the methods of the constellations; one should recite the *Sūtras*, the *Vinaya*, and the *Abhidharma*; one should study and understand the *Sūtras*, the *Vinaya*, and the *Abhidharma*; and one should know the first, second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*, as well as the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*.

If one has not yet attained [this], one should know that one ought to recite and study it; one should not keep the "sun-jewel" or "moon-jewel," and such matters of the Dharma should be understood extensively.
One should keep a meditation staff (*dhyāna-daṇḍa*), as explained in detail in the *Ghoṣila-sūtra*, and one should practice it accordingly.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The brahmin Ajita carried cakes made of śreṣṭha-kulī flour and went to where the Buddha was;
he gave them to the Buddha, who said, "Distribute them among the Saṃgha."
Having thus distributed [the food] to the Saṃgha, he stood before the Buddha to hear the benediction, and the Buddha preached the Dharma to him in various ways.
As the bhikṣus were eating the cakes, they made a noise; Ajātaśatru joined his palms and said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!”
“Does the śramaṇa Gautama teach all his disciples so that they are all able to accept it?
The Buddha said,
“There are those who accept it and those who do not.”
The brahmin said, “It is so,
Gautama! There are conditioned phenomena,
and there is nutriment for conditioned phenomena.”
The Buddha taught the Dharma to Ajātaśatru in various ways, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he remained silent.

When Ajātaśatru had heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, which instructed, benefited, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you must not eat at the time of preaching the Dharma, at the time of offering prayers of blessing, or at the time of praising the Dharma."
"To eat [it], it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
While the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
he dressed in the forenoon, took his bowl, and entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food.
There was a newly ordained bhikṣu who, before the midday meal, dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city first to beg for food.
The Buddha saw this bhikṣu from afar standing before another’s gate; the bhikṣu also saw the Buddha, and upon seeing him, he felt shame and lowered his head.
When the Buddha had returned from his almsround and finished putting away his robe and bowl, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"Today, before noon, I put on my robes and took up my bowl to enter the city for alms. There I saw a newly ordained bhikṣu who had also put on his robes and taken up his bowl, entering the city ahead of me to beg for food."
"Because I saw this bhikṣu, and this bhikṣu saw me, he felt shame and lowered his head.
He then said to the bhikṣus:
"Who went into the city before midday, having dressed and taken up their bowls to beg for food?"
That bhikṣu, filled with shame and remorse, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and said to the Buddha,
"It was I. The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is because you have seen me that you feel shame and remorse, and thus restrain your emotions.”

If you see bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of other paths, you should likewise restrain your emotions and lower your head; thus you shall attain peace and happiness for a long night.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The elder Udāyin had a co-practitioner disciple who lacked a mind of respect; he entered the saṃghārāma without a mind of respect.
Then the Elder Udayin went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and having sat to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My fellow-practicing disciples lack a heart of reverence; even when entering the monastery, they likewise lack a heart of reverence.”
“World-Honored One!
How can one cause disciples to have a heart of reverence toward their preceptors?
The Buddha said:
“Wait a moment, Udāyin! You shall speak when I question you.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter, the Buddha spoke to Udāyin:
“Speak what you wish to say.
Utpada replied:
“World-Honored One!
My fellow practitioners and disciples lack a mind of reverence, and even when entering the monastic quarters, they likewise lack a mind of reverence.
How can I cause my disciples to have a mind of reverence toward their preceptors?
The Buddha said to Udāyin:
"A co-practitioner disciple should give rise to a mind of reverence toward his preceptor; he should also give rise to a mind of reverence when entering the monastic quarters.

He should provide the preceptor with his bowl and robes, the door-bolt, and medicines for the time, medicines for a portion of the day, medicines for seven days, and medicines for as long as life lasts."

If the preceptor is making robes, one should assist him; whether it is when washing the robes, dyeing them, cutting the patches, pinning them, sewing them, or stretching them out, one should assist in all such tasks.
If one is unable to do it oneself, one should hire others to do it.
If one is unable to complete the work oneself, one should also borrow help from others.
If one is able to complete it oneself, one should do so and must not remain idle.
The Buddha said to Udāyin:
"When your preceptor wishes to bathe in the bathhouse, the disciple should first prepare the bathing requisites, such as fuel, oil, and bathing powder."
When the preceptor enters the bathhouse, the disciple should provide him with a bathing robe, take away his undergarments, offer him a bench, provide a water flask, and hand him a staff.
If the preceptor lacks strength, the disciple should support him with his hands.
If he is severely frail, the disciple should carry him into the bathhouse on his back. He should arrange the robes to one side, seat him upon a bed, and place a water basin before him.
"If a disciple wishes to wash, he should inform his preceptor and wash facing a wall, maintaining the perception of illness and the perception of medicine.
The Buddha said:
"When the preceptor perspires, the disciple should first rub his feet, followed by his shoulders, thighs, waist, spine, chest, and back."
When the preceptor has finished bathing, one should hand him his robe, take up the bed, fetch the water vessel, and take up the staff; one should also place firewood into the stove.

If the preceptor is weak, one should support him with one's hands; if he is very frail, one should carry him back to the room and seat him upon the bed. One should take up the bathing robe, offer him the bedding robe, set out the chamber pot and urinal, and provide a spittoon.
If a disciple wishes to bathe again, he should inform his preceptor before bathing.

If he is the last one to bathe in the bathhouse, he should lift the rope-beds and place them in one spot, lift the water jars and water pots, cover the fire with ash, exit the bathhouse, close the door, lower the bolt, and then depart.

When you wish to recite it, if you are able to master it after three inquiries, you should receive it from your preceptor according to your capacity; having received it, you should dwell in a solitary place, recollecting and contemplating it.
If you obtain it, recite [the verses]; if you do not obtain it, ask again.
On the following day, you should collect the vessels for excrement, urine, and spittle; having discarded them, you should ask the Upādhyāya:
"Do you require rice gruel? Do you require solid food?"
If he says, "I need gruel," one should prepare the cauldron and vessel, and provide a ladle and a spoon.
If they say,
"We need food," one should prepare the food and prepare the food vessels.

If the preceptor is ill, the disciple should attend to him, whether he recovers or passes away; he should seek food appropriate for the illness and medicine appropriate for the illness, and he should take the preceptor’s belongings to make offerings.

If the preceptor has nothing, one should provide for it oneself; if one has nothing oneself, one should seek it from others; if there are no acquaintances and it cannot be obtained, then if one obtains something excellent while begging for alms, one should give it to the preceptor.
Uttiya! When the Saṃgha grants the *smṛti-karman* (act of recollection) or the *amūḍha-karman* (act for one not insane) to the upādhyāya, you should go in his stead and speak these words:
"The Saṃgha has granted the *smṛti-karman* or the *amūḍha-karman* to my upādhyāya."

When the Saṃgha is performing the *tatsvabhāva* (severe) karmavācanā, the *niśraya* (dependence) karmavācanā, the *pravāsanīya* (expulsion) karmavācanā, or the *pratisāraṇīya* (reconciliation) karmavācanā against his upādhyāya, the disciple shall assist the upādhyāya by speaking according to the Dharma:
"May the Saṃgha not perform the *tatsvabhāva* karmavācanā, the *niśraya* karmavācanā, the *pravāsanīya* karmavācanā, or the *pratisāraṇīya* karmavācanā against my upādhyāya."
If the Sangha has already performed these acts of *kaṭhina-karman*, *niśraya-karman*, *pravāsanīya-karman*, and *pratisāraṇīya-karman* against the upādhyāya, the disciple should say:
"The Sangha has performed light *karman* against my upādhyāya; do not perform it heavily."
"Uttiya! If the Saṃgha grants the *mānāpya* (probation) rite of 'seeking the offense' (*mārgitavyāpatti*) to the upādhyāya, the disciple should go and say:
'The Saṃgha should not grant the *mānāpya* rite of seeking the offense to my upādhyāya in accordance with the Dharma.'"
If the Sangha has completed the *jñapti-karman* for the preceptor’s search for his offense (*paryeṣaṇā-āpatti*), the disciple should request of the Sangha:
"Act with leniency; do not act with severity.

If the Sangha has performed the *ajñāna-pravāsanīya-karman* against the preceptor, or the *apravāsanīya-karman*, or the *akuśala-dṛṣṭy-apratinihsarga-pravāsanīya-karman*, the disciple should go and inform the Sangha, saying:
"Do not teach what is not to be seen; do not teach what is not to be done; do not teach what is not to be removed.
Utpali! If the preceptor commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and the formal acts of *parivāsa*, *mānatva*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and *āvarhaṇa* are to be performed for him, the disciple should go and say:

“The Saṃgha has, in accordance with the Dharma, performed for me the formal acts of separate residence (pārivāsika), penance (mānatva), reintegration into the original status (āvarhaṇa), and absolution from offenses (ābṛhaṇa). Udāyin!

Such a disciple, if he does not inform his preceptor, must not instruct others in the recitation of the sūtras; he must not recite the sūtras so as to cause others to memorize them; nor may he recite alongside them.
Without having informed one's preceptor, one must not receive the Dharma from another, nor may one bestow the Dharma upon another.
One must not receive the *smṛti* (recollection) from another, nor may one recite it simultaneously with them.

One must not give another one's robes or alms bowl, door-hooks, medicines to be taken at the proper time (*kālabhaiṣajya*), medicines to be taken at specific intervals (*yāmika-bhaiṣajya*), seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), or lifetime medicines (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*).
One must not make robes for others, nor cause others to make robes.
One must not shave others' hair, nor cause others to shave one's hair.

One may not perform any action whatsoever without informing the Upādhyāya, except for the acts of answering the calls of nature, chewing the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha), and prostrating before the Buddha.
Uttiya! If the preceptor wishes to enter a village, the disciple should offer him the robe for entering a village, and should fold and lift up the bedding robe.

If the disciple follows the preceptor into the village, he should take hold of his bowl, staff, and saṃghāṭī; he should not walk ahead, nor should he stand too close, nor should they walk side by side.
If the teacher speaks what is not the Dharma, one should admonish him to desist; if he speaks the Dharma, one should rejoice in it.
If he receives offerings while preaching the Dharma, the disciple should accept them.
When he arrives at a village, the disciple should present him with his bowl, staff, and saṃghāṭī robe.
If the disciple goes out from the village before his preceptor, he should not stay far away; he should take up the preceptor’s bowl, staff, and saṃghāṭī robe.
If the preceptor travels along the same road, the disciple should take up the staff, the oil-skin bag, the leather sandals, and the needle-and-thread bag.
Uttiya! A disciple should go to the presence of the preceptor three times each day:
at dawn, after the meal, and at sunset.

At the time of rising, one should remove the vessels for excrement, urine, and spittle; after eating, one should sweep, sprinkle water, and smear the ground; at sunset, one should take the vessels for excrement, urine, and spittle and place them by the side.
Uttiya said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
If a disciple practices this Dharma toward his preceptor, how should the preceptor act toward the disciple?”
The Buddha said to Udāyin:

"When a disciple practices in this manner, the preceptor should instruct him to recite the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma; he should provide him with robes, a bowl, a staff, and a door-knob, as well as medicinal substances for immediate use, for a portion of the day, for seven days, and for life."
When a disciple is making a robe, the preceptor should assist him in its making.
Whether it be washing the cloth, dyeing it, cutting it into pieces, pinning and stitching it, or stretching it out, he should assist in all such tasks.
If one is unable to do it oneself, one should hire another;
if one cannot complete the work by oneself, one should also have others assist;
and one should provide full assistance according to one's ability, never remaining idle.

If the preceptor sees that a disciple is ill, he should attend to them to see whether they live or die; he should provide and seek out food appropriate for the illness and medicine appropriate for the illness.

He should take the disciple’s belongings to use for this purpose; if the disciple has no belongings, the preceptor should give him his own property, or if he has no property of his own, he should seek it from others to give. If he has no acquaintances, he may not be able to obtain it through seeking.
If, while begging for alms, one obtains good food, one should give it [to the teacher].
If the Saṃgha grants a disciple the *smṛti-kaṛman* (act of mindfulness) or the *amūḍha-kaṛman* (act of non-delusion), one should say:
"The Saṃgha has granted my disciple the *smṛti-kaṛman* and the *amūḍha-kaṛman* in accordance with the Dharma."

If the Saṃgha intends to perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), or the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against a disciple, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should assist him by speaking according to the Dharma:
"Do not perform the *tarjanīya-karman*, the *niśraya-karman*, the *pravāsanīya-karman*, or the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* against my disciple."
If the Saṃgha has already completed the *tarjanīya-karman*, the *niśraya-karman*, the *pravāsanīya-karman*, or the *pratisāraṇīya-karman*, one should say:
"Perform it lightly; do not perform it heavily."
If the Saṃgha intends to perform the *mānāpya* (act of seeking atonement) against a disciple,
the preceptor should assist by saying,
"Do not do it. Once the Saṃgha has completed the *mānāpya*, the preceptor should assist by saying:
"Act lightly; do not act heavily. Utpali!
If the Saṃgha grants a disciple the *ajñapti-karman* of non-seeing, the *karman* of non-expulsion, or the *karman* of non-removal for stubborn wrong views, the preceptor should say:
"Do not instruct to see what is not seen; do not instruct to do what is not done; do not instruct to remove what is not to be removed. Udāyin!
If a disciple commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one should perform for him the formal acts of *parivāsa*, *mānatva*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and *āvarhaṇa*. The preceptor (*upādhyāya*) speaks as follows:
“The Saṃgha shall perform for my disciple the formal acts of separate residence (pārivāsika), penance (mānatva), reintegration (āvarhaṇa), and rehabilitation from offense (ābṛhaṇa). O Utpala!
You should instruct your disciple three times each day:
At dawn, after meals, and at sunset.
Regarding the instruction for dawn:
"Do not associate with evil friends, evil companions, or wicked people."
After the meal, he instructs him, saying:
"Do not associate with evil friends, evil companions, or wicked people.
At sunset, he instructs him, saying:
"Do not associate with evil friends, evil companions, or wicked people.
If they act contrary to the Dharma, you should rebuke and stop them, O Uttiya!
There are three kinds of rebukes:
first, not addressing someone by name; second, not speaking with them; third, not permitting them to do what they wish to do.
*Śāriputra Vinaya*, Scroll 41.

*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 42, Part One of the Seventh Recitation, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India together with Kumārajīva during the Later Qin dynasty. Seventh Recitation, 12:
Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, 1: The Eight Pārājika Dharmas; Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya, First: The Unshared Precepts, The Eight Pārājika Dharmas.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the Rājaka Garden Monastery within Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Cūḍānandā, who was young and beautiful.
There was a son of the householder Mṛgāra who was also young and handsome.
This man conceived a lustful mind toward the bhikṣuṇī Cūḍapanthaka’s sister, and that bhikṣuṇī likewise conceived a lustful mind toward this man.
The son of Mṛgāra reflected thus:

"If I tell this bhikṣuṇī to do such a thing, I shall incur sin myself; the king will punish me, my ill repute will spread in all four directions, and when my body breaks up at the end of life, I shall fall into hell."
The bhikṣuṇī also reflected in this way:

"If I tell this man that he committed this act, I shall incur guilt myself and cause him to incur guilt as well; my ill repute will spread in all four directions, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs will punish me according to the Dharma, the devas and benevolent spirits will no longer protect me, and when my body perishes at the end of my life, I shall fall into hell."

This bhikṣuṇī constantly dwelt upon that man; because she could not have her way, she became ill and emaciated, lying within her cell, having lost her dignified deportment and being unable to come or go.
When that man heard that this bhikṣuṇī was ill and suffering, lying in her room unable to move about, he thought to himself: "This bhikṣuṇī has no other ailment;

she has become so emaciated and is undergoing such suffering solely because she thinks of me. Why should I not go to where this bhikṣuṇī is? Even without speaking of this matter, I shall be able to cure her illness."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the Bhikkhunī Saṅghārāma in Rājagaha;
having arrived, he asked the bhikkhunīs, "Where is the bhikkhunī Cūḷa-Nandā?"
He replied, "I am lying ill in such-and-such a room, suffering from affliction; my physical composure is broken and I am unable to move about.
That man then went to the bhikṣuṇīs' quarters, where he touched, embraced, and seized her, saying these words:
"Is your illness slightly abated?
Can you endure it?
Is your suffering not increasing?"
She replied, "The illness does not abate; it is unbearable, and my suffering and affliction increase.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī uttered foul and impure words from her mouth, speaking thus:
"This is my portion; he does not love me, so I shall love him.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing this matter, she was displeased in her heart and rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, with a mind full of outflows, she allows a man with a mind full of outflows to touch, embrace, or seize her?"
Having rebuked her with various reasons and causes, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing the facts, the Buddha asked the bhikṣuṇī Cūḍānandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: "I have indeed done so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī listen, with a mind full of outflows, to a man whose mind is also full of outflows as he touches, embraces, or seizes her?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus: "For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs:

for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha; for the sake of the Saṃgha being perfectly gathered; for the sake of the Saṃgha dwelling in peace and happiness; for the sake of subduing those with arrogant minds; so that those with a sense of shame may obtain peace and happiness; so that those without faith may attain pure faith; so that those who already have faith may increase it; to prevent afflictions and outflows in this present life; to sever the evil destinies in future lives; and so that the Brahma-faring may endure for a long time."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows a man with a lustful mind to pull back her robe from below the hairline to above the wrists and knees, and to rub her body up or down, pull or push her, press or pinch her, or embrace her from above or below, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
"One with a defiled mind" refers to one who develops a deep-seated bond of craving toward such a person; the same applies to a man with a defiled mind.
"Male" refers to a human male capable of performing sexual acts.
*Pārājika*: This offense is blameworthy, evil, deep, and heavy; it causes one to fall back and fail to reach [the goal], and for this reason it is called *pārājika*.

"Not to dwell together" means that the other bhikṣuṇīs do not perform formal monastic acts with this bhikṣuṇī, namely: the motion (*jñapti-karman*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), and the thirteen formal acts pertaining to bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the offenses within this, there are eight types:
if a bhikṣuṇī gives rise to a lustful mind and allows a man with a lustful mind to pull back her robe and stroke her face, she commits a pārājika offense.

Whether it be the neck, the chest and ribs, the spine, the abdomen and navel, the areas of the anus and genitals, or the thighs down to the knees—if one rubs them in the direction of the hair, or rubs against it, or pulls, pushes, presses, or pinches, it is likewise [an offense].
If one lifts the robe and touches [the body] above the hairline, below the wrists, or below the knees, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, allows a man with a defiled mind to lift her robe so that he may embrace her from the ground onto a table, it is a *pārājika*.

If one moves from a small table onto a single-seat bed, from a single-seat bed onto a large bed, from a large bed onto a palanquin, from a palanquin onto a carriage, from a carriage onto a horse, from a horse onto an elephant, or from an elephant onto a hall, in all such cases it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī with a mind of leakage allows a man with a mind of leakage to pull back her robe, and she is carried from atop the hall onto an elephant, from the elephant onto a horse, from the horse onto a chariot, from the chariot onto a palanquin, from the palanquin onto a large bed, from the large bed onto a single-seated couch, from the single-seated couch onto a desk, and from the desk onto the ground—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense in every instance.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows a man with a lustful mind to lift her up or down by removing her robe and embracing her above the hairline, below the wrists, or below the knees, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣuṇī has a lustful mind, and allows a man with a lustful mind to stroke her face while their robes remain on, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If [the hand] reaches the throat, the chest or ribs, the spine, the abdomen, the navel, the openings for the large and small intestines, or the thighs and knees, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
As it is with stroking in the direction of the hair, so it is likewise for stroking against the hair, pulling, pushing, pressing, or pinching.
To touch another with the body while wearing clothes above the hairline, below the wrists, or below the knees constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, if a nun with impure thoughts allows a man with impure thoughts to embrace her while they are both clothed, from the ground up to a table, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If one moves from a small table to a single-seated bed, from a single-seated bed to a large bed, from a large bed to a palanquin, from a palanquin to a carriage, from a carriage to a horse, from a horse to an elephant, or from an elephant to a hall, in each case it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī with a defiled mind allows a man with a defiled mind to embrace her while clad in their robes—carrying her from the hall onto an elephant, from the elephant onto a horse, from the horse onto a chariot, from the chariot onto a palanquin, from the palanquin onto a large couch, from the large couch onto a single-seated couch, from the single-seated couch onto a table, and from the table onto the ground—it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense in every instance.
If one carries another person up or down while holding them by their clothing above the hairline, below the wrists, or below the knees, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

There is no offense if one perceives the person as a father, a brother, or a son; or if there is danger from being swept away by water, fire, swords, spears, bows, or staffs; or if one is about to fall into a pit; or if one encounters the peril of wild beasts or evil spirits. There is no offense in these cases.
All those with unattached minds do not commit offenses.
The five matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.

Then, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta permitted the group of six bhikṣus to take their hands, take their robes, stand together, speak together, and make appointments together; they entered secluded places to wait for men to arrive, behaving with their entire bodies like women of the white-robed laity.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, her heart was displeased, and she censured it with various reasons, saying:

"How can one called a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind full of outflows, allow a man with a mind full of outflows to take her hand, take hold of her robe, stand together with him, converse with him, make appointments with him, or enter a secluded place to wait for the man to come, with her whole body acting like a laywoman?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked the bhikṣuṇī who had supported Devadatta:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:

"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind full of outflows, allow a man with a mind full of outflows to take her hand, take hold of her robe, stand together, converse together, make appointments together, or enter a secluded place to wait for the man to come, with her whole body acting like that of a laywoman?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, allows a man with a defiled mind to take her hand, take hold of her robe, stand together, converse together, make an appointment together, enter a secluded place, wait for the man to arrive, and expose her entire body as a laywoman does—performing these eight acts to manifest signs of lustful attachment—that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.
"One with a defiled mind" refers to one who develops deep-seated bonds of attachment toward such a person; the same applies to a man with a defiled mind.
"Man" refers to a male human being capable of engaging in sexual acts.
"Grasping the hand" refers to that which is from the wrist forward; this is called the hand.
"Grasping the garment" refers to grasping the undergarment worn next to the body.
"Standing together" refers to a place where impure speech may be spoken.
"Engaging in conversation" refers to speaking impure words.
"Making an appointment together" refers to going to a place where evil acts may be committed.
"Entering a secluded or concealed place" refers to a location shielded by a wall, shielded by a grass mat, or shielded by a cloth curtain.
Regarding "waiting for a man to come," this refers to engaging in unwholesome acts.
"With her whole body like that of a woman in white robes" means that whether he seizes her or embraces her, she does not oppose the man's intentions, just as a woman in white robes would not.
By employing these eight matters, one manifests the signs of greedy attachment and commits a *pārājika* offense.
A *pārājika* is a transgression that is wicked, evil, deep, and heavy; it results in falling back and being rendered inferior.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits this offense, she is no longer called a śramaṇī nor a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.

Regarding "not living together," it means that the other bhikṣuṇīs do not perform formal acts with her, namely: the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), and the establishment of the thirteen formal acts for bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī with lustful intent allows a man with lustful intent to take her hand, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she allows him to take hold of her robe, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one stands together with them, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one speaks together with them, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one makes an appointment together with them, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she enters a secluded place, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If she waits for a man to come, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If her body is like that of a laywoman (*avadātavastrā*) in relation to the man, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one performs all eight actions, one commits a *pārājika* offense.
[The sixth section is concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There were two bhikṣuṇīs who were sisters:
The elder sister was named Mitrā and the younger sister was named Metrī.
The bhikṣuṇī Mitrā engaged in impure conduct and committed sexual misconduct;
the bhikṣuṇī Metrī was virtuous and did not commit sexual misconduct.
Later, the bhikṣuṇī Mitrā reverted from the precepts and became a laywoman.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to speak to the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyī, saying,
"Is it not well for your sister to have reverted from the precepts and become a laywoman?"
He replied, "I also previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had committed such and such impure conduct; however, I simply did not wish to report it myself, nor did I wish to speak of it to the Saṃgha."
Some people asked:
"What is meant by 'a bhikṣuṇī who defiles her own elder sister'?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī who, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it?
Having rebuked her with various reasons, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī Maitreyī:
"Did you truly do such a thing?
She replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī who, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it?
After rebuking her for various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it for even a single night;
and if that [first] bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the other bhikṣuṇī has either left the order, remained [in the order], ceased [her status], or departed, subsequently says:
"I also previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had committed such and such impure conduct; however, she did not wish to confess it herself, nor did she wish to report it to the Saṃgha."
Or someone might say:
"What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī who defiles her own sister?
Such a bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense; she should not live in community with the others.
"Knows" means: either she knows it herself, or she has heard it from another, or the nun who committed the offense has confessed it herself.
"Gross offense" means: either a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, all transgressions are termed "coarse" (*sthūla*); however, because five types of transgressions are specifically distinguished, two types are designated as coarse.
Regarding "one night": from sunset until the earth has not yet risen [at dawn], this is called night.
That bhikṣuṇī who has "fallen away" has fallen away from the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
One who "remains" remains within the dharma of a layperson.
One who is "expelled" is subject to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching.
Having departed, he enters among the followers of external paths and then speaks thus:
"I previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had committed such and such impure conduct; I did not wish to report it myself, nor did I wish to speak of it to the Saṃgha."
Or suppose someone were to say:
"How can this sister defile her own elder sister?
Such a bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and should not live in community with the others.
"Pārājika" refers to a transgression that is wicked, evil, and profoundly grave, resulting in a fall from one's status.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits such an offense, she is no longer a śramaṇī nor a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.

"Those who do not live together" means that the bhikṣuṇīs do not perform formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*) with them, namely: the motion (*jñapti*), the motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya-karman*), the motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), and the establishment of the thirteen formal acts for bhikṣuṇīs.

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense at the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and that bhikṣuṇī conceals it throughout the entire day while maintaining the perception that it is a pārājika offense, she commits a pārājika offense upon the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

If it is a bhikṣuṇī who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not seeing [an offense], to the act of suspension for not making amends, or to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views; or if she is insane, deranged, or her mind is impaired by illness—at such times, concealing [the offense] does not constitute an offense.

If she has been suspended from the community, or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, and at that time she conceals another's offense until the end of the day, she commits a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī [concealing an offense] when the day has ended, at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, or in the afternoon; [she must report it].
In the afternoon; at the time of sunset; after sunset;
during the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night;
during the first watch of the middle watch, the middle watch of the middle watch, and the last watch of the middle watch.

During the first watch of the latter part of the night, the middle watch of the latter part of the night, or the last watch of the latter part of the night, if one conceals [the offense] until the end of the day, one commits a *pārājika*.
If, within this context of a *pārājika*, one perceives it as a *pārājika* and conceals it until the end of the day, one commits a *pārājika*.

If it is a bhikṣuṇī who has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense, or to the act of non-suspension, or to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views, or whose mind is deranged, distracted, or impaired by illness, then at that time, she incurs no offense even if she conceals [the matter].

If she is released from the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then at the time when the concealment of another's offense reaches the end of the [rain] retreat (*āvāsa*), she commits a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī [concealing an offense], and it reaches the end of the retreat, she commits a *pārājika* offense.

Regarding the *pārājika* offenses—whether they are called *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta*—if a bhikṣuṇī conceals an offense that she perceives as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* when it is actually a *pārājika*, until the end of the rainy season retreat, she commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣuṇī: at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, in the afternoon;
in the late afternoon, at sunset, or after sunset.
During the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night;
during the first watch of the middle watch, the middle watch of the middle watch, and the last watch of the middle watch;

during the first watch of the last watch, the middle watch of the last watch, and the last watch of the last watch—if one sees a bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense, and within that pārājika offense, [one perceives it] as a saṃghāvaśeṣa, as a pāyattika, as a pratideśanīya, or as a duṣkṛta.

If, regarding an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), one perceives it as an offense requiring formal meeting of the Sangha (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) and conceals it until the end of the day, one commits an offense of defeat.
The same applies if one perceives it as an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*), an offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*), or an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

If the Sangha has performed an *adarśana-pravāsanīya* (exclusion for not seeing an offense), an *aprati-karman-pravāsanīya* (exclusion for not making amends), or an *apratinihsṛṣṭa-pāpaka-dṛṣṭi-pravāsanīya* (exclusion for not relinquishing evil views) against this bhikṣuṇī, or if she is insane, deranged, or mentally impaired by illness, then concealing [the offense] at that time does not constitute an offense.

If she has been suspended, or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then at the time when the concealment of another's offense reaches the end of the [rainy season] retreat, she commits a *pārājika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a *pārājika* offense at the conclusion of the retreat, and she harbors doubt regarding that *pārājika*, wondering whether it is a *pārājika* or not a *pārājika*?
Later, having severed his doubts, he perceives what is a *pārājika* offense as being a *pārājika* offense; if he conceals it until the end of the night, he commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣuṇī: at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, or in the afternoon;
In the afternoon; at sunset; having set;
during the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night;
during the first watch of the midnight, the middle watch of the midnight, and the last watch of the midnight.

During the first watch of the latter part of the night, the middle watch, and the final watch, he saw a bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense; regarding that pārājika, he conceived doubt as to whether it was indeed a pārājika or not a pārājika.
Later, having severed his doubts, he perceives a *pārājika* offense as such; if he conceals it until the end of the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), he commits a *pārājika*.

However, if the Saṃgha has performed an act of suspension for not seeing an offense, or has failed to perform an act of suspension, or has performed an act of suspension for not relinquishing wicked views, or if the bhikṣuṇī is deranged, distracted, or her mind is impaired by illness, then there is no offense in concealing it at that time.

If the Sangha grants this bhikṣuṇī release from her suspension, or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then, having concealed another's offense until the end of the rainy season retreat, she commits a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense when the ground is clearly visible, yet she harbors doubt regarding that pārājika—wondering whether it is a pārājika or a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
whether it is a pārājika or a pāyattika;
or whether it is a pārājika or a prātideśanika;
Is it a *pārājika* or a *dukkaṭa*?
Later, when his doubts are severed, he forms the perception that it was a *pārājika* offense; if he conceals it until the end of the night, he commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣuṇī: at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, or in the afternoon;
in the late afternoon, at sunset, or after sunset; [if she enters a village, she commits an offense.]
During the first watch of the night—its initial, middle, and final portions;
the middle watch of the night—its initial, middle, and final portions;

and the last watch of the night—its initial, middle, and final portions—he sees a bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense, yet he conceives doubt regarding that pārājika: "Is this a pārājika or a saṃghāvaśeṣa?"
Is it a *pārājika* or a *pāyattika*;
is it a *pārājika* or a *pratideśanīya*;
or is it a *pārājika* or a *dukkaṭa*?
At a later time, having severed her doubts, she perceives a *pārājika* offense as such; if she conceals it until the end of the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), she commits a *pārājika*.

However, if the Saṃgha has performed an act of suspension for non-confession (*adarśana-pratikarman*) against this bhikṣuṇī, or an act of suspension for not confessing, or an act of suspension for not abandoning evil views, or if she is at that time deranged, distracted, or mentally impaired by illness, then concealing it during those times does not constitute a *pārājika* offense.

If the Sangha grants this bhikṣuṇī release from her suspension, or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then, having concealed [the offense] until the end of the rainy season retreat, she commits a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense when the ground is clearly visible, but harbors doubt regarding that pārājika—wondering whether it is a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?
Later, having severed his doubt, he perceives what was a *pārājika* offense as a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if he conceals it until the end of the day, he commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣuṇī: at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, or in the afternoon;
in the late afternoon, at sunset, or after sunset.
During the first watch of the night—its initial, middle, and final portions;
the middle watch of the night—its initial, middle, and final portions;

and the last watch of the night—its initial, middle, and final portions—he sees another bhikṣuṇī who has committed a pārājika offense, yet he entertains doubt regarding that pārājika: "Is this a pārājika or a saṃghāvaśeṣa?"
Is it a *pārājika* or a *pāyattika*;
is it a *pārājika* or a *pratideśanīya*;
or is it a *pārājika* or a *duṣkṛta*?

At a later time, having severed his doubt, he conceives the notion that it was a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense within the category of *pārājika*; by concealing it until the end of the night, he commits a *pārājika*.

If the Saṃgha has performed an *adarśana-pravāsanīya* (exclusion for not seeing an offense), an *apratinisṛṣṭa-pravāsanīya* (exclusion for not renouncing a wrong view), or an *apratiniḥsṛṣṭa-pāpaka-dṛṣṭi-pravāsanīya* (exclusion for not abandoning evil views) against this bhikṣuṇī, and she conceals it while her mind is deranged, distracted, or impaired by illness, she commits no offense.

If the Sangha grants this bhikṣuṇī release from her suspension, or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then, having concealed another's offense until the end of the [rainy season] retreat, she commits a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense when the ground is cleared, yet she harbors doubt regarding that pārājika—wondering whether it is a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?

Later, having severed her doubt, she conceived the notion that what was a *pārājika* offense was actually a *pāyattika* offense; yet, by concealing it until the end of the day, she commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣuṇī: at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, or in the afternoon;
In the afternoon; at sunset; having set;
during the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night;
during the first watch of the midnight, the middle watch of the midnight, and the last watch of the midnight.

During the first watch of the latter part of the night, the middle watch, or the last watch, he sees a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a pārājika offense; he then develops doubt regarding that pārājika, wondering: "Is it a pārājika, or a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika, or a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?"

Later, having severed her doubt, she conceives the notion that what was a *pārājika* offense was actually a *pāyattika* offense. If she conceals it until the end of the rainy season retreat (*vassa*), she commits a *pārājika*.

If the Saṃgha has performed an act of suspension against this bhikṣuṇī for not acknowledging an offense, for not undergoing suspension, or for not relinquishing evil views; or if she is at that time insane, deranged, or mentally impaired by illness—then concealing it during those times does not constitute a *pārājika*.

If the Sangha grants this bhikṣuṇī release from her suspension, or if her suffering ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then, having concealed another's offense until the end of the rainy season retreat, she commits a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī, at the conclusion of the day, sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense, but harbors doubt regarding that pārājika—wondering whether it is a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?

At a later time, having severed his doubts, he perceives what is a *pārājika* offense as a *pratideśanīya* offense; yet, by concealing another's offense until the end of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī [may not go] at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, or in the afternoon;
in the late afternoon, at sunset, or after sunset.
During the first watch of the night, the middle watch of the night, and the last watch of the night;
during the first watch of the middle watch, the middle watch of the middle watch, and the last watch of the middle watch;

and during the first watch of the last watch, the middle watch of the last watch, and the last watch of the last watch—if he sees a bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense, yet conceives doubt regarding that pārājika, wondering: "Is this a pārājika, or a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika, or a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?"

Later, having severed his doubts, he conceives the notion that what constitutes a *pārājika* offense is actually a *pratideśanīya* offense; yet, by concealing another's offense until the end of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he commits a *pārājika*.

If the Saṃgha has carried out an act of suspension against this bhikṣuṇī for not seeing [an offense], for not making amends, or for not relinquishing evil views, and at that time the bhikṣuṇī is deranged in mind, distracted in mind, or her mind is impaired by illness, then concealing [the offense] does not constitute a pārājika offense.

If the Saṃgha grants this bhikṣuṇī release from her suspension, or if her suffering ceases and she regains her original mind, then, having concealed another's offense until the end of the [rain] retreat, she commits a pārājika offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī, at the conclusion of the day’s observance, sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense, but regarding that pārājika she harbors doubt—wondering whether it is a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?

Later, having severed his doubts, he perceives what constitutes a *pārājika* offense as a *duṣkṛta*; if he conceals another's offense until the end of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he commits a *pārājika*.
Furthermore, regarding a bhikṣuṇī: at sunrise, after sunrise;
before noon, at midday, in the afternoon;
in the late afternoon, at sunset, or after sunset; [if she acts as described, it constitutes an offense].
During the first watch of the night, its middle portion, and its last portion;
during the middle watch of the night, its first portion, its middle portion, and its last portion;

and during the last watch of the night, its first portion, its middle portion, and its last portion—having seen a bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense, he conceives doubt regarding that pārājika: "Is it a pārājika, or a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika, or a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta?"

At a later time, having severed his doubts, he conceives the notion that [the offense] among the *pārājika* offenses is merely a *duṣkṛta*; yet, by concealing another’s offense until the end of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), he commits a *pārājika*.

If the Saṃgha has performed against this bhikṣuṇī the formal act of suspension for not seeing [an offense], the formal act of suspension for not confessing [an offense], or the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views, and if at that time the bhikṣuṇī is deranged in mind, distracted in mind, or her mind is impaired by illness, then she does not commit a pārājika offense by concealing it.

If the Sangha grants this bhikṣuṇī release from her suspension, or if her suffering ceases and she regains her original state of mind, then, having concealed another's offense until the end of the rainy season retreat, she commits a pārājika offense.
The seven matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Then the Saṃgha, being of one mind and in harmony, performed an act of suspension for the bhikṣu Kāloratīśa on the ground of his failure to acknowledge an offense.
This bhikṣu Kālopa-tiṣya had seven sister bhikṣuṇīs:
first, Stūlanandā; second, Cūḍanandā; third, Tiṣyā; fourth, Upatiṣyā; fifth, Tiṣyāvatī; sixth, Tiṣyapālā.
7. Tiṣyarakṣitā. These bhikṣuṇīs, hearing that the saṃgha of Kālo-tiṣya had performed an *ajñapti-karma* (act of suspension) against him for not acknowledging his offense, went to ask Kālo-tiṣya:
"Did the saṃgha truly perform an *ajñapti-karma* against you?"
She replied,
"I truly did this. The bhikṣuṇīs said:

"Do not humble yourself with soft words to subdue us; we shall provide you with wealth, robes, bowls, door-bolts, medicines for the time, medicines for the night, medicines for seven days, and medicines for life. If you have questions regarding the recitation or study of the scriptures, we shall instruct you. Why do you seek to subdue us?"
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, she rebuked them, saying:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, knowing that the bhikṣu-saṃgha is united and in harmony when it carries out a formal act of suspension for refusal to see an offense (*adarśanāya-pratiniḥsarga*), she alone—without a second, without companion or partner, neither ceasing nor resting—continues to comply with his conduct?"
After the bhikṣuṇīs had thus rebuked them, they reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of the two divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned those bhikṣuṇīs:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:

"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī knowingly follow a bhikṣu who has been lawfully expelled by a unified and harmonious Saṃgha for not acknowledging an offense—remaining alone without a second, without companion or partner, neither resting nor ceasing?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been lawfully subjected to the formal act of *ajñapti* (suspension for not seeing an offense) by a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, yet she follows him alone, without a second, without companion or partner, continuing in compliance without ceasing or resting; [she commits an offense].
O bhikṣuṇīs, you should admonish that bhikṣuṇī in this way:

"This bhikṣu has been suspended by the united Saṃgha through a formal act for not seeing [his offense]; he is alone without a second, without companion or partner, and persists without ceasing or resting. You must not follow his conduct."

When these bhikṣuṇīs are thus admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, if they persist in this matter and do not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish them a second and a third time to cause them to relinquish this matter.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes this matter, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
"Knowing" means knowing it by oneself, hearing it from another, or having the offending bhikṣu confess it himself.
"In accordance with the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, [and thus] carrying out the formal act of banishment.
"Solitary, peerless, without companion or partner" means that all the bhikṣuṇīs have been expelled, leaving her solitary, peerless, without companion or partner.
"Without ceasing" means she does not humble herself nor submit.
"Non-ceasing" means not abandoning evil and false views.
"Conforming" has two kinds:
giving material wealth and giving the Dharma.
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to this expelled bhikṣu:

"You must humble yourself and show deference toward the Great Saṃgha; if you do not humble yourself and show deference, the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha shall perform the formal act (karman) of not prostrating to you, not speaking with you, and not making offerings to you."

"If this bhikṣu humbles himself and submits, that is well; if he does not humble himself and repent his fault, the bhikṣuṇīs should, with one mind and in harmony, perform for this bhikṣu the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not prostrating, not speaking together, and not making offerings."
Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal procedure): The community of bhikṣuṇīs, being unified with one mind, shall have one bhikṣuṇī proclaim:
"Venerable bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been subjected by the unified saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging [an offense]; he is solitary and alone, without a second, without companion or partner, neither ceasing nor resting."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this formal act (*karmavācanā*) to the bhikṣu so-and-so: that he shall not prostrate, shall not converse, and shall not receive offerings.
This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

"The Saṃgha has completed the *karman* for the monk so-and-so, decreeing that he shall not prostrate, shall not converse, and shall not receive offerings. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
The community of bhikṣuṇīs should also speak thus to those who assist that bhikṣu:

"This bhikṣu has been suspended by the harmonious Saṃgha for his refusal to see [his offense]; he is alone, without a second, without companion or partner, neither ceasing nor resting. You must not follow or assist him in his conduct."

When these bhikṣuṇīs are thus admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, if they persist in this matter and do not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish them a second and a third time to relinquish that matter.
If she relinquishes this matter upon the second and third admonitions, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
A pārājika is a fault that is corrupt, evil, deep, and heavy; one who falls into it is inferior [to the saṃgha].
If a bhikṣuṇī commits this offense, she is no longer called a śramaṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan; she has lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.

Regarding "not living together," it means that the other bhikṣuṇīs do not perform formal acts with her, namely: the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* (Uposatha), the *pravāraṇā*, and the establishment of the thirteen *bhikṣuṇī*-karman procedures.

Regarding the offenses herein: if the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal act (kamma) of "not prostrating," "not conversing with," or "not making offerings" [to that monk], and at that time a Bhikṣuṇī teaches this monk a discourse (sūtra), if it is taught in verse (gāthā), there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for each verse;
if it is taught in prose (varga), there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for each prose section.
If it is explained as separate sentences, for each sentence there is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If a bhikṣu who has been expelled teaches a bhikṣuṇī to recite the sūtras, and the bhikṣuṇī receives the teaching in verses, for each verse there is a *dukkaṭa*;
if she receives the teaching in chapters, for each chapter there is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one receives the teaching by reciting it phrase by phrase, for each phrase there is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If a bhikṣuṇī provides material offerings or gives a bowl, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If she gives robes, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
To give door-hooks, food for the current day, food for the night, food for seven days, or medicine for life—all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one expels a bhikṣu and gives material offerings to a bhikṣuṇī, or gives her robes and bowls, and the bhikṣuṇī accepts them, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a door-bolt, or food to be taken at the proper time, food for a night, food for seven days, or food for life, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense in all cases.

If a community of bhikṣuṇīs has completed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not bowing, not conversing, and not making offerings [to a certain bhikṣu], and at that time a bhikṣuṇī instructs that bhikṣu in the recitation of the scriptures: if it is taught in verse form, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each verse;
if it is taught in prose sections, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each section;
if it is taught phrase by phrase, there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense for each phrase.
If a monk who has been expelled instructs a bhikṣuṇī in the recitation of the sūtras: if he teaches it in verse form, for each verse there is a sthūlātyaya;
if he teaches it in prose sections, for each section there is a sthūlātyaya;
if he teaches it by individual phrases, for each phrase there is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣuṇī provides material offerings to a bhikṣu who has been expelled, or gives him an alms bowl, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she gives him a robe, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she gives him a door-bolt or a medicinal drug to be taken at the proper time, it is in all cases a sthūlātyaya.
Regarding medicines for a night, for seven days, or for life, [taking them] in all such cases constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one expels a bhikṣu and gives wealth as an offering to a bhikṣuṇī, or gives her a bowl, and the bhikṣuṇī accepts it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts robes, door-hooks, food for the time, food for the night, seven-day medicine, or lifetime medicine, it is all a sthūlātyaya offense.
The bhikṣuṇīs should first instruct that assisting bhikṣuṇī with gentle words, saying:
"Do not assist the bhikṣu who has been expelled; do not follow his conduct."

If they relinquish [the offense] when spoken to gently, one should instruct them to perform repentance for numerous *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) and numerous *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) to emerge from the transgression.
If they do not relinquish it despite gentle speech, one should administer a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to issue a reprimand.
Regarding the formal injunction (*yokcheda-dharma*): the community of bhikṣuṇīs shall assemble with one mind, and one bhikṣuṇī shall proclaim:
"Venerable bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so has been subjected by the unified saṃgha to the act of suspension for not acknowledging [an offense]; he remains solitary, without a second, without companion, and without associate, neither ceasing nor resting."
The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has assisted [him], and although she has been admonished with gentle words, she does not desist.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now admonish the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so:

"This bhikṣu is being dealt with by the harmonious Saṃgha through the formal act of suspension for refusal to see [an offense]; he is solitary, without a second, without companion, and without partner, neither ceasing nor resting."
"You bhikṣuṇīs, do not follow and comply with this.
This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
“The Saṃgha has finished exhorting the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!

As the Buddha previously taught, these bhikṣuṇīs should exhort her, even up to three times, to cause her to abandon this matter; this is called “exhortation,” this is called “instruction,” and this is called “exhortation and instruction.”
If one does not relinquish [the position] despite being exhorted with gentle words, there is no offense.

If, after the first statement has been made but not yet finished, or after the second statement has been made but not yet finished, or while the third statement is being made but not yet finished; or if it is an illegal separate assembly, an illegal united assembly, a semblance of a legal separate assembly, or a semblance of a legal united assembly; or if it is a legal separate assembly that is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching—if one does not relinquish [the position] despite being exhorted in these cases, there is no offense.
If, after being admonished three times in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, she still does not relinquish [the offense], that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika.

The eight pārājikas are concluded. Regarding the seventeen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas, among the ten rules not shared [with bhikṣus], this is the first. This first matter is the fourth of the seventeen; it was when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Śyāmāvatī, who was young and beautiful.
A certain merchant, having seen her, conceived lustful thoughts and thought to himself:
"The bhikṣuṇīs are protected by the King; I cannot forcibly commit an impure act with her. I shall instead invite her to provide for her needs through offerings."
Having formed this thought, he went to that bhikṣuṇī and said:
"Whatever things you require—whether food and drink, clothing, bedding, or medicinal requisites—I shall provide them for you."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"I shall accept your invitation. Later,
that bhikṣuṇī requested from him all the food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicinal decoctions, firewood, grass, lamps, and candles she required.
Knowing that the bhikṣuṇī’s mind had become softened, the merchant said to her,
"Come and engage in sexual intercourse.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Do not speak such words; I am one who upholds the precepts and has severed lust.
The merchant replied angrily, "You little slave!"
"If you maintain the precepts and have severed lustful desire, why do you accept my offerings of clothing and food?
He then forcibly seized the bhikṣuṇī, who cried out in a loud voice.
Immediately, many people gathered and asked,
"Why are you crying out so loudly?
The merchant replied:
"This bhikṣuṇī accepts my food and clothing, yet she does not follow my wishes.
The laypeople said to the bhikṣuṇī,
"Since you accept goods from others, why do you not follow their wishes?"
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I did not accept those goods for the sake of sexual desire; rather, this merchant came to me of his own accord and invited me, saying:
'Whatever you require—clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, firewood, grass, lamps, or candles—I shall provide them to you as you wish.'"
"I do not know with what intention he gave it to me.
The householders said,
"Is this merchant from your father's side or your mother's side?"
The bhikṣuṇī said, "It was not.
The laypeople said:
"If they were not your parents, and if they were not virtuous people seeking merit, why would they not know to give you wealth?
When they gave you wealth and clothing, it was surely for the sake of sexual desire."
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"How can these bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
'We are virtuous and meritorious'?"
“Is this like the way a courtesan takes the wealth of others?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the bhikṣuṇī Śivika: "Did you truly do this? She replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī taking food with her own hand from a man whose mind is subject to outflows?
Having rebuked them for various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
‘For ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:’”

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind affected by taints, takes food with her own hand from a man whose mind is affected by taints, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa that must be confessed; it is an offense committed at its first instance.
"One with a defiled mind" refers to one who has deep-seated fetters of craving toward such a person; the same applies to a man with a defiled mind.
"Man" refers to a male human being capable of engaging in sexual acts.
Regarding "food," there are five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods), five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods), and five kinds of similar foods.
The five *khādaniya* are: root food, stem food, leaf food, flower food, and fruit food.
The five *pūjāni* (solid foods) are: boiled rice, parched grain flour, parched grain, fish, and meat.
The five similar foods (*bhojanakalpa*) are: congee, millet, wild barley, *yava* grass seeds, and *kāśī* food.

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means that this offense belongs to the *saṃgha*; within the *saṃgha*, there remains a remnant [of the transgression], and because it can be extinguished through repentance before the *saṃgha*, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, takes solid food from the hand of a man who has a lustful mind using her own hand, she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one takes stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, cooked rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, meat, porridge, millet, wild barley, weeds, or *kāśī* food, it is all a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If there is a layperson who, because of a certain bhikṣuṇī, provides food for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, yet gives a greater portion of food specifically to that bhikṣuṇī whom they favor.
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts [the gift], it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
The fourth precept is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who went and said to the bhikṣuṇī Śivaka:
"If you possess an untainted mind while the man possesses a tainted mind, what power do you have over him if he simply takes food from his own hand to eat or uses it as he pleases?"
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she says to another bhikṣuṇī:

'Your mind is free of outflows, while the man’s mind is with outflows; what power do you have over me that he should take food from his own hand and give it to you to eat, or let you use it as you please?'"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked that bhikṣuṇī: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who encourages another bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'You have a mind free from outflows; what can a man with a mind possessed by outflows do for you? Take food with your own hands and eat it, or use it as you please—what power does he have over you?'"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If a bhikṣuṇī says:
"If you have a mind free from outflows, what can a man with a mind possessed of outflows do to you by taking food from his own hand and giving it to you to eat, or using it as you please?"
"This dharma is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which may be confessed. Regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa*:
this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; within the Saṃgha there remains a residue [of the transgression], which is extinguished through confession before the Saṃgha. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī, "What can you possibly do?
You have a mind of outflows; take food with your own hands from a man who has a mind of outflows, eat it, or use it as you please."
Saṃghāvaśeṣa. If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
"If you have a mind free from outflows, and a man with a mind possessed of outflows gives you food, simply take it, eat it, and use it as you please; what can he possibly do to you?"
Saṃghāvaśeṣa. If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
“If you have a mind of passion, what can a man with a mind of passion do to you?”
"You must not take food with your own hands from them to eat, nor use it as you please.
This constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
"If you possess an untainted mind while the man possesses a tainted mind, what power do you have over him?
You must simply not take food with your own hands to eat, nor use it as you please; [if you do so], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
The fifth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Bhadrā, who was the daughter of a Kāpiśī brahmin.
The bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā had a sister who had died; she went to visit her brother-in-law and, while preaching the Dharma for him, remained until sunset.
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If I return to the vihāra now, I fear there may be bandits on the road."
She then remained at the householder’s residence.
The householder thought to himself:
“If this bhikṣuṇī does not leave, she must intend to renounce her precepts; I shall seek someone to take her elder sister’s place.”
Having had this thought, he said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"In my house there is much wealth and precious treasure; all the ornaments for the hands, feet, head, and face that your sister possessed are still there."
"If I were to take another woman as my wife, I would not be able to look after my son well, nor would he find joy in her.
If you wish to return to the life of a householder, become the mother of my son; you shall look upon my son as your own child, and my son shall likewise look upon you as his mother."
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If I oppose these words, they might even force me [to comply].
Why not remain silent!"
He then sat in silence.

The householder thought to himself that he wished to revert to his lay life, but remained silent only because his sister had recently died; at midnight he spoke these words again, and in the latter part of the night he spoke them once more.
When the ground was cleared, that bhikṣuṇī was freed from her state of urgent distress; she returned to the vihāra and related this matter in detail to the bhikṣuṇīs.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she sleeps alone by herself?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked Bhaddā Bhikkhunī: "Is it true that you have done this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who sleeps alone by herself?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stays alone by herself, even for a single night, this offense is a saṃghāvaśeṣa, which must be confessed.'"
