"Night" refers to the period from sunset until the earth has not yet awakened; the interval between these is called night.

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means that this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; within the Saṃgha there remains a remnant [of the fault], which is extinguished through repentance before the Saṃgha—this is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī sleeps alone by herself after sunset until the end of the night, she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

After the sun has set, it is likewise during the first watch of the first part of the night, the middle watch of the first part of the night, and the last watch of the first part of the night; during the first watch of the middle part of the night, the middle watch of the middle part of the night, and the last watch of the middle part of the night; and during the first watch of the last part of the night, the middle watch of the last part of the night, and the last watch of the last part of the night.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī stays alone by herself until dawn, and continues so until dawn the following day, she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
There is no offense if she is accompanied by another bhikṣuṇī, or if that companion renounces the precepts, dies, joins a non-Buddhist sect, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises.
The sixth precept consists of four matters; the first matter is concluded.
When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, there was at that time a bhikṣuṇī named Thullanandā, who was well-informed and widely known, and who delighted in frequenting various households.
This bhikṣuṇī rose early and put on her robes; she entered one house and left another, leaving one house and entering yet another.
At the hour of *bhuḥ* (late afternoon), she returned, utterly exhausted, and lay down in the monastic quarters, saying:
"My feet ache, my calves ache, my ribs ache, and my back aches."
She said to the bhikṣuṇīs, "Massage me.
The bhikṣuṇīs replied:
“Noble daughter!
From where have you come?
She replied:
"He enters such-and-such a house and leaves such-and-such a house; he leaves such-and-such a house and re-enters such-and-such a house.
They asked him, "Are you performing services for the Buddha or services for the Sangha?"
She replied, "I did not! The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"If she were not going for the sake of the Buddha’s affairs or the Sangha’s affairs, why would she undertake such a journey and become so utterly exhausted?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, her heart was displeased, and through various reasons she rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she travels alone by herself during the day?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who, during the day, travels alone to the home of a layperson?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If a bhikṣuṇī, whether by night or by day, goes alone to the house of a layperson, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa that must be confessed, committed upon the first transgression.
"During the day" means from when the earth is bright until the sun has not yet set; the interval between these two points is called "during the day.
Regarding the offense therein: if a bhikṣuṇī travels alone by herself, departing at the time the earth is bright and returning at the time the sun has set, she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

At the time of sunrise, after sunrise, during the forenoon, at midday, in the afternoon, at the time of sunset, when departing after sunset, and when returning after sunset—on all these occasions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the bhikṣuṇī traveling with him renounces the precepts, dies, joins a non-Buddhist sect, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises, there is no offense.
The two matters concluded.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, out of a fondness for seeing men, went to the city gate early in the morning and stood there watching the men as they entered and exited, observing who was handsome and who was ugly.
He saw a man emerge who was handsome; a mind of attachment arose within him, and he asked, "Where do you wish to go?
The man replied:
"Let us go to such-and-such a village.
Thullanandā said, "I will go with you."
The householder said,
"As you wish. Thereupon,
on the road, that bhikṣuṇī engaged in playful conversation with the householder, laughing and shouting loudly.
On account of certain business, the layperson entered a village; the bhikṣuṇī, having no business of her own, stood waiting for the layperson outside the village.
When the layperson entered a second village, the bhikṣuṇī likewise stood waiting outside.
The householder entered a third village. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī returned to the monastic quarters at the hour of *pradoṣa* and lay down. She said to the other bhikṣuṇīs: "I am utterly exhausted;
my feet ache, my calves ache, my knees ache, my ribs ache, and my back aches. Massage me."
The bhikṣuṇīs asked,
"Where have you come from?
She replied:
"I have come from one village to another.
He asked,
"Did you perform services for the Buddha or for the Sangha?"
She replied, "No! The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"If she had not gone for the sake of the Buddha's affairs or the Sangha's affairs, why would she have undergone such conduct and become so utterly exhausted?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, her heart was displeased, and she rebuked her with various reasons, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who goes alone to another village?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, asked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī go alone to another village?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, whether by night or by day, travels alone to another village, it is an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that must be confessed.'"
Regarding "traveling," there are two kinds:
traveling by waterway and traveling by landway.
As for the offense therein: if a bhikṣuṇī travels alone on a land route to another village, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If he returns halfway, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If there is no inhabited village but an open space even as small as one *krośa*, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If he returns halfway, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to traveling by waterway.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is traveling together with him renounces the precepts, dies, joins a non-Buddhist sect, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises, there is no offense.
The fifth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through the country of Kośala toward Śrāvastī; on the way, they reached the bank of a river and stayed there, saying:
"Who can enter the water first to see how deep it is?"
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī named Śuklā, who was agile and possessed great strength; having been born into a brahmin family, she spoke these words:
"I shall enter first."
He immediately entered the water and crossed to the other shore; however, the water suddenly surged like a torrent, and he was unable to return.
He stayed alone on that shore for the night, when a bandit came and stripped him of his clothes, leaving him naked.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content with little, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she stays overnight alone on the other shore?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Xiūmùqiā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied: "I did indeed do so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī stay overnight alone on the other shore?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣuṇī, whether by night or by day, in another village or in another boundary, should cross to the other side of a river and sleep alone, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa, which is to be confessed at its first commission.’”
"As for 'rivers,' there are two kinds:
first, those that can be crossed by taking off one's clothes; second, those that can be crossed without taking off one's clothes."
A river is that which has two banks with a flow of water coming and going between them, following the current of the stream.
Regarding the offense therein: if a bhikṣuṇī, being alone, undresses to cross the river, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if she turns back midway, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If two bhikṣuṇīs cross a river together, and one crosses while the other returns, the one who crosses commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and the one who returns commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī takes off her robes to cross a pool of water, the one who crosses commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if she returns midway, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If two bhikṣuṇīs cross a pond together, one crossing while the other returns: the one who crosses commits a sthūlātyaya, and the one who returns commits a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī crosses a river with her robes lifted up, the one who crosses commits a sthūlātyaya; if she turns back midway, she commits a duṣkṛta.
If two bhikṣuṇīs lift their robes to cross a river, and one crosses while the other returns, the one who crosses commits a sthūlātyaya, and the one who returns commits a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī lifts her robe to cross a pond alone, the one who crosses commits a duṣkṛta, and the one who returns midway also commits a duṣkṛta.

If two bhikṣuṇīs lift their robes to cross a pool of water, and one crosses while the other returns, the one who crosses commits a duṣkṛta offense, and the one who returns likewise commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If they cross by means of a bridge, a causeway, or a boat, there is no offense.
If one crosses with a bhikṣuṇī together, there is no offense if she renounces the precepts, dies, joins a non-Buddhist sect, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises.
The sixth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus built monasteries near the city of Vāgīśatā, and they gradually became numerous there.

There was a layperson’s residence surrounded by elephants trumpeting, horses neighing, and the voices of men and women, both young and old; because of these sounds, it hindered the bhikṣus from reciting the sūtras, practicing meditation, and walking the path.

In that place there was a householder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who possessed majestic power and abundant wealth and treasures, including people, fields, houses, lapis lazuli, and agate; he was fully endowed with all the marks of various forms of prosperity.

The monks instructed them to build a monastery elsewhere, so the householder immediately built a monastery in the Añjana Grove. The monks then abandoned their monastery near the city and entered the monastery in the Añjana Grove to dwell there.
A group of bhikṣuṇīs was traveling through the country of Kośala toward Śrāvastī. Upon arriving at the city of Vajrī, they stayed overnight in an old monastery.

Seeing that it was fully equipped with beds, couches, bedding, basins, vessels, cauldrons, and various other utensils, all of which were clean and fit for habitation, the bhikṣuṇīs went to the bhikṣus and said:
"Venerable sirs, since you have already abandoned this monastery, we shall dwell within it."
The bhikṣus said,
"As you wish. Later,
when the master of that monastery died, his sons divided the property, and the monastery was included among the items to be divided.
One boy who had obtained this monastery went and said to the bhikṣuṇīs,
"You all must leave!
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Why have you made us leave?
They replied,
"We have been assigned this monastery as our portion."
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I did not receive it from you; I received it from the bhikṣus.
If the bhikṣus cause me to leave, I shall leave, but I will not follow your words."
In that assembly, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Sūmukhā, who had gone forth from among the Brahmin caste; she was agile and possessed great strength, and she spoke forcefully while engaging in disputes.
Because the householder’s son could not bear the anger, he struck the bhikṣuṇī; the bhikṣuṇī immediately went to the local officials and said, “This man, so-and-so’s son, has beaten me.”
The officials asked,
"For what reason did you strike her?
The bhikṣuṇī then explained the preceding events in detail.
The officials said:
"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, should not lose this monastery. Why is that?
"The master wrestles with the child, and the child wrestles with the master;
such is the nature of things. The officials sent someone to summon the child and asked him, "Did you strike the bhikṣuṇī?"
He replied,
"I truly struck him.
The officials examined the case according to the laws and regulations:
"What offense should one who strikes a renunciant incur?
The Vinaya states:
"The specific body part used [in the striking] shall be immediately amputated."
The officials asked,
"With what object did you strike?
He replied:
"Strike with the hand.
He asked again,
"With which hand?"
He replied,
"The right hand. Thereupon,
the right hand was severed.
At that time, an ill repute spread abroad:
"The Śākya nuns say that people cut off others' hands.
One person told it to two, and two told it to three; thus it was passed along until it filled the entire city of Vṛji.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her for various reasons, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī say that another's hand should be cut off?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Śuddhikā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī say that another person's hand should be cut off?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the presence of a king, a government official, a brāhmaṇa, or a householder, and relying upon her influence speaks on behalf of others, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa that must be confessed; it is an offense committed at the first instance.'"
A "king" refers to one of the Kṣatriya caste who has received the royal consecration by the sprinkling of water upon his head; he is called a "Kṣatriya king consecrated by water.
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or even a woman who receives the office of king, they are likewise called "kings consecrated by water."
An official is one who consumes the grain rations, fields, and houses provided by the state.
A brahmin is one born into the brahmin caste.
A householder is anyone other than a king, an official, or a brahmin, who is not a renunciant; such a person is called a householder.
"Relying on power to speak against others" means that, depending on the influence of others, one delights in engaging in quarrels and mutual accusations.
"Saṃghāvaśeṣa" means that this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; there remains a residue within the Saṃgha, which is extinguished through repentance before the Saṃgha. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī approaches a king, a group of officials, a brāhmaṇa, or a householder, and speaks on behalf of someone by relying on her power and influence, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If, while a legal matter is being adjudicated, one stands before the adjudicators and out of anger reviles the person originally struck, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one reviles the person originally struck in the presence of others [not involved in the adjudication], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one scolds another in a secluded place and the other does not speak [in response], there is no offense.
The seventh precept is concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 40;
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 43; Part Two of the Seventh Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra from North India together with Kumārajīva during the Later Qin dynasty.
The twenty-seventh section of the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya, concerning the Saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, contains ten "non-common" precepts; this is the remainder [of that section].
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a thousand generals; half were of the Kṣatriya caste and half were of the Brāhmaṇa caste. One division was named Aiśvara, and the other was named Dattamaṇa.
King Prasenajit had a small vassal state in rebellion; he issued orders to a thousand generals to go and subdue it.
They went forth to wage war, returned having defeated the enemy, and addressed the king, saying:
"We have achieved victory; we pray that Your Majesty may always be victorious."
Upon hearing this, the king’s heart was filled with joy and delight, and he said:
“What wish do you desire?
I shall grant it to you.”
The general said:
"My wife has committed a crime by not following my will; I grant her six days to drink the potion of death, and on the seventh day, I shall split her body with a cow-tongue blade."
The king said, "I grant you this boon.

At that time, there was a Kṣatriya who would not follow his wife's wishes; he intended to give her a lethal drink on the sixth day, and on the seventh day, he would tear her body apart with an ox-tongue blade.
This woman had many relatives with great influence who came to intervene and would not allow her to drink the lethal potion.

However, according to the law of warriors, when one person has a matter at hand, all others must assist; once the assembly of Kṣatriyas had gathered, they forcibly compelled her to drink the lethal potion.
When the seven days had passed, he used an ox-tongue blade to tear his body apart into two parts.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Senā, the daughter of the householder Maṇa, who frequently came and went from that household.

Rising early and putting on his robes, he entered this house and saw that while all the other Kṣatriya women were bathing, adorning themselves, and wearing fine garments and necklaces, this particular Kṣatriya woman was alone wearing soiled clothes, her body unadorned, sitting there in sorrowful distress.
The bhikṣuṇī asked, “Other women all wear fine, adorned garments; why do you alone wear soiled clothes, and why do you sit here unadorned and sorrowful?”
He replied, "Have you not heard?
The other asked:
"What is it? she asked. He replied, "I did not follow my husband's will;
now I am undergoing the 'death-drink' for six days, and on the seventh day, they shall split my body into two parts with a cow-tongue blade."
"Can you take me away?
If I go, who will be there to awaken me?
He replied:
"Yes. The bhikṣuṇī immediately covered the woman with her kāṣāya robe, led her away, and ordained her within the nunnery.
Later, when a multitude of kṣatriyas gathered and intended to kill her with ox-tongue knives, the people said:
"Call this woman here!
He entered the house to search for her but did not see her; he sought her everywhere but could not find her.
The assembly of Kṣatriyas said:
"Who regularly enters and leaves this house?
He replied, "There is a bhikṣuṇī named Sīnā who constantly comes and goes to my home; perhaps she has taken her away."
The assembly of kṣatriyas immediately went to surround the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma at Rājaka.
Not long after the kṣatriya women had gone forth, the bhikṣuṇīs wished to prevent the kṣatriya assembly from entering.
In that assembly, there was a young kṣatriya who, being ignorant of sin and merit, spoke these words:
"All bhikṣuṇīs should be split into two parts with an ox-tongue knife."
Among them, an elder kṣatriya said:
"The bhikṣuṇīs are protected by the king; it would be improper for us to commit such an evil deed rashly, or perhaps it might not even be possible."
"Wait a moment; I shall first inform the King. Whatever the King commands, you must follow his instructions.
The bhikṣuṇīs then went to Lady Mallikā and explained the matter in detail. The lady immediately reported it to the King.
Because the king knew this beforehand, he sat upon the throne in the palace; the kṣatriyas went to the king’s presence, prostrated themselves, and said:
“May Your Majesty always be victorious.
The king said:
"I previously granted you a boon; you should now grant me one.
The assembly of Kṣatriyas said, "We shall grant it according to the Great King's wish."
The king said, "This Kṣatriya woman has now gone forth into homelessness; she is reborn and is no longer a Kṣatriya woman.
The assembly of Kṣatriyas said:
"Now, in accordance with Your Majesty's wish, she shall be released.
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to tell the bhikṣuṇī:
"O virtuous daughters!..."

"This matter is not right. You know that this thief-woman deserves death; you know that the King will not permit it and the Kṣatriyas will not permit it. Such a woman should not be granted ordination. If the Kṣatriyas were to divide you into two factions, what would I do?"

When the Buddha hears of this matter, he will surely establish a precept for you all: "If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a woman is a thief who has been executed and killed, and this is known to all people, and the king and the kṣatriyas do not permit it, she must not be ordained as a disciple."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, because of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] already, he nevertheless asked the bhikṣuṇī Sīna: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who, knowing that a female thief has been sentenced to death, ordains her as a disciple?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is a thief who has been executed and killed, and that this is known to all people and is not permitted by the king and the kṣatriya assembly, yet ordains her as a disciple, this is an offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa, the first transgression, which requires confession.
"Knows" means: either she knows it herself, or she hears it from another, or the female thief tells her herself.
There are two kinds of thieves:
first, those who steal and plunder material wealth; second, those who steal one's person.
"Condemned to death" means that one has committed a crime for which the penalty is death.
"Known by many people" means known, seen, and heard by a great number of people.
"Not permitted" means that the king does not permit his life to continue.
Regarding "the Kṣatriya assembly does not permit": it means that the two assemblies do not permit one's livelihood.
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; there is a remnant within the Saṃgha, which is extinguished through repentance before the Saṃgha; thus it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offenses herein: if the preceptor nun knows, the instructor nun knows, or the community of bhikṣuṇīs knows, the preceptor nun commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
the instructor nun commits a sthūlātyaya;
and the community commits a duṣkṛta.
If the preceptor nun knows, the instructor nun knows, and the Saṃgha does not know, the preceptor nun commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
the instructor nun commits a sthūlātyaya offense;
the Saṃgha commits no offense.
If the preceptor nun knows [of the offense] while the instructor nun and the Sangha do not know, the preceptor nun commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
the instructor nun and the Sangha do not commit an offense.
If one is entirely unaware of it, there is no offense.
The eighth matter concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Then, the elder Chanda’s mother became a bhikṣuṇī, named Upavāhā.
The sister became a bhikṣuṇī named Chāndatī.
Chāndatī was of an evil disposition and committed unwholesome deeds, constantly harassing the other bhikṣuṇīs.

When the bhikṣuṇīs wished to perform a *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against Chāndatī, this Upavāha, who was a judge for the Saṃgha, obstructed the assembly within the Saṃgha so that the *karman* could not be carried out.
At one time, when Upāli was away on other business, the bhikṣuṇīs said:
"We shall now perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against the bhikṣuṇī Chándikā."
A bhikṣuṇī said, “Upavāha might perhaps obstruct it midway.
Another bhikṣuṇī said:
“Upasāḍhā has gone elsewhere; she has many acquaintances and will not return for some time.
The bhikṣuṇīs immediately struck the ghaṇṭā to assemble the community of nuns and performed the *pravāsanīyakarman* (act of banishment) against Chándikā.
The next day, when the crowd heard that the bhikṣuṇī Chánditā had been expelled, the bhikṣuṇī Upasamā returned to her sister’s place, and they exchanged greetings with one another.
The icchantika said,
"Do not speak with me. He asked:
"Why? She replied, "The bhikṣuṇīs have performed a formal act (karmavācanā) to expel me."
Upavāha thought to himself: "This matter is improper;

while I was acting as the adjudicator for the Saṃgha, they forcibly carried out the act of banishment in my absence. Now I cannot question the bhikṣuṇīs without having received their formal consent (chanda); I must go outside the boundary and grant them release from the banishment."
At that time, Upavāha did not consult the bhikṣuṇīs nor take their formal consent (*chanda*), but immediately went outside the boundary to revoke the suspension of Chandra.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked him with various reasons:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, knowing that the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha had performed a legal and harmonious *karmavācanā* to suspend a bhikṣuṇī, she does not consult the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha, does not take the consent of the bhikṣuṇīs, and goes outside the boundary to revoke the suspension for another?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Upavāhā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who, knowing that the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha has performed a formal act of banishment according to the Dharma, neither consults the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha nor takes their consent (kṣānti), yet goes outside the boundary to lift the banishment for a bhikṣuṇī?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has been suspended by a united and harmonious Saṃgha for not acknowledging an offense, neither consults the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha nor obtains their consent (kṣānti), yet goes outside the boundary to effect the lifting of that suspension for another, this constitutes an initial offense of saṃghāvaśeṣa that must be confessed.
"Knowing" means knowing it oneself, hearing it from another, or hearing it spoken by the person themselves.
"In accordance with the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching for formal suspension.
"Not consulting the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha" means not reporting this matter to the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha.
"Not taking the *chanda* (consent)" means not even taking the *chanda* of four persons.
"To go outside the boundary" means to go beyond the boundary of the community's fence, wall, or enclosure.
"To resolve the suspension" means either to resolve it oneself or to cause another to resolve it.

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means that this offense belongs to the *saṃgha*; within the *saṃgha* there remains a remnant [of the transgression], which is extinguished through repentance before the *saṃgha*. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Regarding the offenses herein: if the preceptor nun knows, the person performing the *karmavācanā* knows, and the Saṃgha knows, then the preceptor nun commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the person performing the *karmavācanā* commits a *sthūlātyaya*, and the Saṃgha commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If the preceptor nun knows, the person performing the *karmavācanā* knows, but the Saṃgha does not know, the preceptor nun commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the person performing the *karmavācanā* commits a *sthūlātyaya*, and the Saṃgha commits no offense.

If the preceptor nun knows [the offense], while the person performing the *karmavācanā* and the Saṃgha do not know, the preceptor nun commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, whereas the person performing the *karmavācanā* and the Saṃgha do not commit an offense.
If one does not know anything [of the offense], there is no transgression.
The ninth matter is concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was then a bhikṣuṇī named Kālā, who had originally been a follower of non-Buddhist paths; she delighted in quarreling and engaging in mutual verbal disputes.
When this bhikṣuṇī quarrels with other bhikṣuṇīs, she says:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha, I renounce the precepts."

"It is not only the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, who know this; there are other śramaṇas and brahmins who possess a sense of shame and propriety, who are virtuous and delight in upholding the precepts—I shall practice the holy life under them."

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased in her heart and, through various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, during a time of strife, they say such things as:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the precepts'?"

"It is not only the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who know this; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and propriety, who are virtuous, and who delight in upholding the precepts—I shall practice the holy life under them."
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the bhikṣuṇī Kālā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī, while engaged in quarreling and disputing, speak thus:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the precepts'?"

Not only do the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, know this, but there are also other śramaṇas and brahmins who possess a sense of shame and propriety, who are virtuous, and who delight in upholding the precepts; from them I shall practice the holy life.
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣuṇī, while quarreling with another bhikṣuṇī, should say:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, I renounce the precepts."

"It is not only the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who know this; there are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and propriety and delight in upholding the precepts, from whom I shall practice the holy life."
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Do not, when quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs, speak these words:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha, I renounce the precepts.'"

"It is not only the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who know this; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and propriety and delight in upholding the precepts—toward them I shall practice the holy life."
"You should delight in practicing the holy life within the Buddha’s Dharma and abandon this mind of personal aversion.

If that bhikṣuṇī, when admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs in this manner, persists in her position and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time to make her relinquish that matter.
If a bhikṣuṇī relinquishes [the matter] when admonished for a second and third time, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, then this rule, having been formally admonished up to three times, constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that must be confessed.

Regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; within the Saṃgha there remains a remnant [of the offense], which is extinguished through repentance before the Saṃgha. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī says,
"I renounce the Buddha," it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one says,
"I renounce the Dharma," it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says,
"I renounce the Saṃgha," it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one says,
"I renounce the precepts," in all such cases it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one should say:

"It is not only the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, who know the Way; there are other śramaṇas and brahmins who possess a sense of shame and propriety and delight in upholding the precepts; I shall practice the holy life under them."
Because she reviled the Sangha, she incurs a *pāyattika*.

The bhikṣuṇīs should first admonish her with gentle words; if she then desists, they should instruct her to confess four *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *pāyattika* offense to purify herself from the transgression.
If she does not relinquish [her position] despite gentle words, she should be admonished through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
As for the method of admonition: the Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs should assemble in harmony with a single mind, and one bhikṣuṇī should announce:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs!..."
This bhikṣuṇī Kālā was formerly a follower of external paths; now, while quarreling with the other bhikṣuṇīs, she spoke these words:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, and I renounce the precepts."

"It is not only the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who know this; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and propriety, who are virtuous, and who delight in upholding the precepts. I shall practice the holy life under them."
"Having already been exhorted with gentle words, she does not abandon her evil and heterodox views.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:
the Saṃgha now exhorts the bhikṣuṇī Kālā: 'Do not, when quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs, speak as follows:'"
“I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha, and I renounce the precepts.

It is not only the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who know the Path; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess a sense of shame and propriety and delight in upholding the precepts. I shall practice the holy life under them.”
"This is called the motion (jñapti).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"The Saṃgha has finished its exhortation to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such!"

As the Buddha previously stated, regarding this bhikṣuṇī, the other bhikṣuṇīs should issue a formal admonition, even up to three exhortations, to make her relinquish this matter; this is called an admonition, this is called an instruction, and this is called an admonition-instruction.
If one does not desist when exhorted with gentle words, there is no offense.

This applies if, during the first admonition, it is not yet finished or has been finished; during the second admonition, it is not yet finished or has been finished; or during the third admonition, it is not yet finished. It also applies if the assembly is unrighteous and divided, unrighteous and united, similar to the Dharma and divided, or similar to the Dharma and united; or if the assembly follows what is according to the Dharma but is divided, or follows what is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching—if one does not desist when exhorted in such cases, there is no offense.
If, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, she is admonished three times and yet does not relinquish [the offense], that bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The fourteenth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī delighted in quarreling and mutual recrimination, saying at such times:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs acts out of favoritism, acts out of hatred, acts out of fear, and acts out of delusion."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, during a time of mutual strife and contention, she speaks thus:
'The community of bhikṣuṇīs acts out of favoritism, acts out of hatred, acts out of fear, and acts out of delusion'?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions; knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī Kālā, saying: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī, when engaged in mutual strife and contention, speak thus:
'The community of bhikṣuṇīs'?"
"Acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, and acting out of delusion.
Having thus rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while quarreling with another bhikṣuṇī, should say:
'The community of bhikṣuṇīs acts out of favoritism, acts out of hatred, acts out of fear, and acts out of delusion.'"
The other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī in this way:
"Do not speak thus when you are quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs:
'The Saṅgha of bhikṣuṇīs acts out of favoritism, acts out of hatred, acts out of fear, and acts out of delusion.'"
Why is this? Because the community of bhikṣuṇīs does not act out of attachment, does not act out of aversion, does not act out of fear, and does not act out of delusion.
"You, bhikṣuṇī, must abandon these words of compliance born of attachment, words of compliance born of hatred, words of compliance born of fear, and words of compliance born of delusion.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner and she persists in her position and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time to make her relinquish that matter.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she abandons this matter, it is well.
If she does not abandon it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished up to three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that must be confessed.
Regarding *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; there remains a residue within the Saṃgha, which is extinguished through confession before the Saṃgha. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī says,
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs acts according to favoritism," it is a sthūlātyaya.
"Acting in accordance with anger" constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
"Acting in accordance with fear" constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
"Acting in accordance with delusion" constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The bhikṣuṇīs should first admonish her with gentle words; if she then relinquishes [the offense], they should instruct her to perform the confession and purification for four sthūlātyaya offenses.
If she does not relinquish it despite the gentle words, they should admonish her through a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
Regarding the formal injunction: with the Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs in concord, one bhikṣuṇī should announce within the assembly:
"Venerable bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣuṇī Kālā was formerly a follower of external paths; now, while disputing with the bhikṣuṇīs, she has spoken as follows:"
"O bhikṣuṇīs, you act out of favoritism, act out of malice, act out of fear, and act out of delusion.
Although she had been admonished with gentle words, they did not desist.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience:
the Saṃgha now issues this injunction to the bhikṣuṇī Kālā: "Do not, when quarreling with the bhikṣuṇīs, speak these words:
'The bhikṣuṇīs act out of favoritism, act out of hatred, act out of fear, and act out of delusion.'"
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Saṃgha has finished its exhortation to the bhikṣuṇī Kālā. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such!"

As the Buddha previously stated, regarding this bhikṣuṇī, the other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her, even up to three times of formal exhortation, to make her abandon this matter. This is called "admonition" (saṃvāsanā), this is called "instruction" (anuśāsana), and this is called "admonition and instruction" (saṃvāsanā-anuśāsana).
If, after being exhorted with gentle words, one does not relinquish [the position], there is no offense.

If, during the first formal proclamation, it is not yet finished when the proclamation is completed; or during the second proclamation, it is not yet finished when the proclamation is completed; or during the third proclamation, it is not yet finished; or if it is an illegal separate assembly, an illegal united assembly, a semblance-of-dharma separate assembly, a semblance-of-dharma united assembly, a legal separate assembly, or something different from the Dharma, different from the Vinaya, and different from the Buddha’s teaching—if, after being exhorted, one does not relinquish [the position], there is no offense.

If, after being formally admonished three times in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, she does not relinquish [the offense], that bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The fifteenth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣuṇīs:

one named Dharmā and the other named Dhammā. They conspired together to commit evil deeds, acquired a bad reputation, constantly troubled the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and concealed their offenses from one another.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, her heart was displeased, and for various reasons she rebuked them, saying:
"How can you call yourselves bhikṣuṇīs if you act together in unwholesome deeds, incur an evil reputation, constantly harass the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and cover one another's offenses?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked them with various causes and conditions:
"How can you be called bhikṣuṇīs who, with one mind, collectively commit evil deeds, incur an evil reputation, constantly harass the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and cover for one another's offenses?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If two bhikṣuṇīs, being of one mind, together commit evil deeds, acquire an evil reputation, constantly harass the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and conceal their offenses from one another.
The other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish these two bhikṣuṇīs in this way:

"You two must not act with one mind, nor commit evil deeds together, thereby bringing a bad reputation upon yourselves and constantly harassing the community of bhikṣuṇīs while covering for each other's offenses."
Each of you should practice seclusion; if you practice seclusion, the Buddha-dharma will flourish, whereas you are now abandoning it for the sake of conforming to unwholesome conduct.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have thus admonished them, if these two bhikṣuṇīs persist in this matter and do not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish them a second and a third time to make them relinquish it.
If he relinquishes it upon the second or third admonition, it is well.
If he does not relinquish it, then this matter, having been admonished up to three times, constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that must be confessed.
"The two bhikṣuṇīs who committed evil deeds" refers to those who performed evil and heterodox acts through the misconduct of body and speech.
"Having an evil reputation" means that it was heard and known throughout the four quarters.
"To harass the community of bhikṣuṇīs" refers to harassing as few as four bhikṣuṇīs.
"To conceal each other's offenses" means that having together committed impure acts, they each hide one another's transgressions so that others do not know of them.

*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means that this offense belongs to the *saṃgha*; there remains a residue within the *saṃgha*, which is extinguished through repentance before the *saṃgha*. This is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offenses herein: if two bhikṣuṇīs, with a common intent, together create unwholesome conditions, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If there is an evil reputation [resulting from their actions], it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she causes discord within the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If they mutually conceal each other’s offenses, it is a sthūlātyaya.
The bhikṣuṇīs should first attempt to instruct her with gentle words to abandon this matter.
If he relinquishes it, one should instruct him to perform the confession and purification for four *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If he does not relinquish it despite gentle words, one should issue a formal command through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Regarding the *karmavācanā* procedure: with a unified and harmonious Saṃgha, one bhikṣuṇī shall proclaim within the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs:
"Venerable bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

These two bhikṣuṇīs, Dharmadinnā and [the other], have acted together in evil deeds, have acquired an evil reputation, and have constantly troubled the community of monks. They have mutually concealed their offenses, and though they have been admonished with gentle words, they do not relinquish them."
If the time for the Saṃgha has come, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now issues this injunction to these two bhikṣuṇīs:
"You must not join together in committing evil deeds, nor bring forth an evil reputation, nor constantly harass the community of bhikṣuṇīs, nor conceal one another's offenses."
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Sangha has completed its exhortation; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be upheld in this manner!"

As the Buddha previously stated, regarding this bhikṣuṇī, the other bhikṣuṇīs should issue a formal admonition (saṃvaraṇa), even up to three times of exhortation, to cause her to abandon this matter; this is called an admonition, this is called an instruction, and this is called an admonitory instruction (saṃvaranānuśāsana).
If, after being exhorted with gentle words, one does not relinquish [the position], there is no offense.

If, during the first formal proclamation, it is not yet finished when it is finished; or during the second proclamation, it is not yet finished when it is finished; or during the third proclamation, it is not yet finished; or if it is an illegal separate assembly, an illegal united assembly, a semblance-of-dharma separate assembly, a semblance-of-dharma united assembly, a lawful separate assembly, or something different from the Dharma, different from the Vinaya, and different from the Buddha’s teaching—if, after being exhorted, one does not relinquish it, there is no offense.
If, after being admonished three times in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, she does not relinquish [the offense], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for that bhikṣuṇī.
The sixteenth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta went to the two bhikṣuṇīs Dharmā and Dhammadinnā and spoke to them as follows:
"You two should not live apart; you ought to practice with one mind."
If you practitioners who live apart do not attain growth, those who practice with a unified mind will indeed attain growth.
Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are likewise those such as yourselves; it was out of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to live apart.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing this matter, she was displeased in her heart and, for various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she goes and says to the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā:
'You should not practice separately; you should practice with a single mind'?"
If those who practice separately do not attain growth, then those who practice with a unified mind shall attain growth.
Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are likewise those such as yourselves; it was out of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to practice separately.
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, asked the bhikṣuṇī who had supported Devadatta:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who goes and says to the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā:
'You should not act separately; you should act with a single mind'?"
If those who practice separately do not attain growth, those who practice with a unified mind will indeed attain growth.
Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are likewise those such as yourselves; it was because of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to practice separately.
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs two bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"You two should not practice separately; you should practice with one mind.
Those who practice separately will not achieve growth, whereas those who practice with one mind will attain growth."
"Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are others just like you; it was because of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to live separately.
The bhikṣuṇīs should thus admonish that bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not instruct those two bhikṣuṇīs to speak as follows:"
"Do not act with divisiveness; you should act with unity.
Those who act with divisiveness do not achieve growth, whereas those who act with unity do achieve growth."
"Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are others just like you; it was because of anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to practice separation.
You should abandon this encouragement of improper conduct.

When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner, if that bhikṣuṇī persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time to cause her to relinquish it.
If he relinquishes it upon the second or third admonition, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, then for this offense, having been admonished up to three times, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
he must confess his transgression.

Regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: this offense belongs to the Saṃgha; there remains a residue within the Saṃgha, which is extinguished through repentance before the Saṃgha; thus it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī exhorts two other bhikṣuṇīs, saying,
"You two should not travel separately," it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one says, "One should practice with a unified mind," it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one says,
"Those who practice separately cannot achieve growth," it is a sthūlātyaya.
"If you practice with a like-minded person, you will surely attain growth," constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says:
"Among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are also those such as yourselves; it is because the Saṃgha is angry that they have instructed you to practice separately."
Because she has reviled the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika offense.

The bhikṣuṇīs should first instruct her with gentle words to relinquish [her position]; they should instruct her to perform four sthūlātyaya offenses and one pāyattika offense as confession to purify the guilt.
If she does not relinquish [the offense] despite gentle words, she should be admonished through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
As for the method of the *karman*, the Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs, being harmonious and of one mind, shall have one bhikṣuṇī announce within the assembly:
"May the venerable Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs listen!..."
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, instructed two bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"You two should not live apart; you should act with one mind."
Those who practice separation cannot achieve growth, whereas those who practice with a unified mind do attain growth.
Within the community of bhikṣuṇīs, there are others just like you; however, because the Saṃgha was displeased, they instructed you to practice separation.
"Having been thus admonished with gentle words, she does not desist.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now admonish the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so:
'Do not instruct the two bhikṣuṇīs so-and-so to speak as follows:'"
"Do not practice in separation; you should practice with a unified mind.
Those who practice in separation do not attain growth, while those who practice with a unified mind do indeed attain growth."
"There are also those within the Saṃgha who are just like you; it was because of their anger that the Saṃgha instructed you to practice separately.
You should abandon this encouragement of improper conduct.
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"The Saṃgha has finished its exhortation to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!"

As the Buddha previously stated: "If these bhikṣuṇīs, after being admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs up to three times to relinquish this matter, do so, this is called an injunction, this is called an instruction, and this is called an injunction-instruction."

If one does not relinquish [the offense] despite being exhorted with gentle words, there is no offense. If, when the first admonition has been spoken but not yet finished, or when it has been finished;

or when the second admonition has been spoken but not yet finished, or when it has been finished; or when the third admonition has been spoken but not yet finished; or if the assembly is undisciplined and divided, or the assembly is disciplined and united but acts unlawfully; or if it is an assembly that resembles the Dharma but is divided, or resembles the Dharma and is united; or if it is an assembly that is lawful but divided, or follows a different Dharma, a different Vinaya, and a different teaching of the Buddha—if one does not relinquish [the offense] despite being exhorted in these ways, there is no offense.

If, after being formally admonished three times in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teachings, she does not relinquish [the offense], that bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

The seventeenth matter is concluded. 3. The Thirty Niḥsargika-Pāyattika Dharmas for Bhikṣuṇīs. Regarding these, nineteen are identical [to those for bhikṣus] and thus are not set forth here; the remaining ones that differ are fully set forth. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta; she possessed many alms bowls, which she broke and left unused.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she possesses many alms bowls, breaks them, and leaves them unused?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he questioned the bhikṣuṇī who had assisted Devadatta: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps many alms bowls and lets them break and go unused?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms-bowl for even one night, and keeps it beyond that limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.’”
"One night" refers to the period from sunset until the earth has not yet risen; the interval between these is called one night.
As for the bowl, there are three types:
superior, middling, and inferior.
Regarding the "superior bowl" (uttara-pātra): receiving three *pātra* of rice, one *pātra* of soup, and half a *pātra* of other edible food—this is called the superior bowl.
Regarding the "inferior bowl" (adhama-pātra): receiving one *pātra* of rice, half a *pātra* of soup, and half a *pātra* of other edible food—this is called the inferior bowl.
If it is of medium size between the upper and lower limits, it is called a "medium bowl.
If it exceeds the upper limit or falls short of the lower limit, it is not called a bowl.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: this bowl must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms-bowl for more than one night, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The nineteenth matter is concluded.
Since the previous commentary already stated they were identical and thus not recorded separately, why is this case of a bhikṣu recorded again?
This instance involves only a single night, whereas that involved more than ten days.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a senior bhikṣuṇī who was a resident, and a bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta who was a visitor; they obtained cloth offerings at this residence, which the Saṃgha of those who had entered the rains retreat should divide.
The senior bhikṣuṇīs said:
"This is the last month of the summer retreat; this is the dwelling where the kaṭhina robe was accepted. This is seasonal clothing, and the saṃgha who observed the rains retreat should divide it."
The nun who supported Devadatta said:
"You do not understand well; although you received the kaṭhina robe during the final month of the summer retreat, this is an out-of-season robe, and the present saṃgha should divide it."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta divided seasonal robes into non-seasonal robe portions.

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta-austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if they divide seasonal robes into non-seasonal robe portions?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī treat seasonal robes as non-seasonal robe allotments?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī distributes seasonal robes as non-seasonal robes, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed. As for the transgression herein:

if a bhikṣuṇī treats a robe for the proper season as a robe for the improper season, according to the portion [treated] and according to what she obtains, she incurs that many *niḥsargika-pāyattikas*.
The twentieth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was an established bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta, and a visiting bhikṣuṇī who was virtuous.
In this matter, when the Saṃgha receives a gift of robes, they should be distributed among the resident monks present.
A visiting bhikṣuṇī said:
"This is not the final month of the summer retreat, and this residence has not accepted the kaṭhina robe; therefore, these robes should be distributed among the Saṃgha present."
The nun who supported Devadatta said:

"Although it is not the end of the summer retreat and the *kaṭhina* robe has not been received, this is nevertheless seasonal clothing; it should be divided among the monks who have completed the *vassa* retreat."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta divided out-of-season robes as if they were in-season robes.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who divides out-of-season robes as if they were in-season robes?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the facts] yet asking for the sake of formality, he asked the bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī treat out-of-season robes as in-season robes and distribute them?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī treats out-of-season robes as in-season robes and distributes them, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
Regarding the *niḥsargika-pāyattika*: this robe must be relinquished, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣuṇī treats a non-seasonal robe as a seasonal robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
According to the circumstances and the time, she incurs as many *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* as were obtained.
The twenty-first matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Thullanandā who had a disciple named Śreṣṭhā, who was virtuous and possessed of merit.
Thullanandā gave this disciple a single piece of cut-and-sewn robe-cloth and went to the Jeta Grove wearing it.
This bhikṣuṇī was an old acquaintance of Baddhananda; when Baddhananda saw the bhikṣuṇī approaching, a greedy attachment arose in his heart toward that robe-cloth.
The bhikṣuṇī bowed her head at his feet in salutation and sat to one side.
Baddhananda said, "Good woman!
Your robe is beautiful and lovely."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
“It is indeed excellent.
Upāli, the son of Bānaṃdā, said:
"You may give it to me.
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"I cannot give it."
Bhadanta said, "I shall give you my robe in exchange for yours.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"No," [she replied].

"Bhadananda is a great Dharma master; his eloquence enables him to preach the Dharma skillfully. She then preached various subtle and wonderful Dharmas for him, causing the bhikṣuṇī to give rise to a heart of joy. She took a piece of cut-and-sewn robe-cloth and gave it to Bhadananda, who immediately gave her a garment that was quite acceptable.
A bhikṣuṇī, wearing this robe, entered the bhikṣuṇī saṃghārāma. Her preceptress asked her, "Where is your robe?
She replied:
"I am trading with another.
"With whom are you trading?
He replied:
"Give it to Upananda.
The preceptress said,
"Upananda has deceived and enticed you."
The disciple said,
"Whether by deception or by inducement, the trade has already been completed.
The preceptor nun said:
