A merchant saw this bhikṣuṇī and went to speak to the generals, saying:
"That you have obtained wealth and pleasure is entirely due to the karmic conditions of the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinna; why can you not each provide her with a set of fine robes?"

"This bhikṣuṇī is now, during the eight nights of this winter when the cold wind splits the bamboo, wearing a single-layered robe while going on almsround. If you are unable to each make one robe for her, you should all work together to make one robe and give it to her."
In order to incite pride in her, the merchants all said,
"We shall provide it together.
They then called out to the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"What kind of robe do you require?
I shall give it to you according to your wish. The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I require a robe worth five hundred coins.
At that time, the various military commanders purchased and gave it to her as she wished.
When this bhikṣuṇī went out to beg for alms wearing an expensive robe, the laypeople rebuked her, saying:
“Various bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
‘We are virtuous and meritorious,’ yet they wear expensive garments while going on almsround, like the wives of kings or ministers.”
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she wears expensive clothing while going on almsround?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed, I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī wear expensive clothing while going on almsround?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to beg for a heavy robe, she may beg for one worth up to four kārṣāpaṇas.'"
"If one begs for more than this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "money," this refers to large coins up to those worth sixteen small coins.
A *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense means that the robe must be relinquished and the *pāyattika* guilt must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī begs for a heavy robe exceeding the value of four *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
For every portion begged and for every portion obtained, there is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The twenty-ninth matter concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the cold winter had passed and it was the heat of summer; the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā was wearing heavy robes, and with sweat flowing from her head and face and her vision blurred, she went out to beg for alms.
A certain merchant, having seen this, immediately went to speak to the generals, saying:
"O village chiefs, that you have obtained wealth and happiness is entirely due to the connection with the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinna; could you not each provide her with a light robe?"

"This bhikṣuṇī is now wearing heavy robes during the heat; her head and face are dripping with sweat, and her vision is blurred as she goes on alms-round. If you cannot each provide her with a light robe, you should all work together to make one robe and give it to her."
The merchants incited their warriors to give rise to arrogance, and they all said,
"We shall provide it together.
They immediately summoned the bhikṣuṇī and asked her:
"What kind of robe do you require?
I shall give it to you according to your wish. He replied:
"I require a robe worth two hundred and fifty coins.
At that time, the various military commanders purchased and gave it to her according to her wish.
When this bhikṣuṇī wore this robe while going on alms-round, the laypeople rebuked her, saying:
“Some bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
‘We are virtuous and meritorious.
Yet they wear expensive, fine garments while going on almsround, like the wives of kings or ministers.”
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who wears expensive, fine garments while going on almsround?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked that bhikṣuṇī: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī wear expensive, light clothing while going on almsround?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to beg for light clothing, it should not exceed a value of two and a half coins.'"
"To solicit more than this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Money" refers to large coins, up to those worth sixteen small coins.
A *niḥsargika-pāyattika* means that the robe must be relinquished and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī begs for light clothing exceeding two and a half coins, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
For every coin begged and obtained, there is a corresponding *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The thirty matters are concluded. 4. One hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* rules for individuals. Regarding these one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* rules, the first seventy-one are not set forth here because they are identical to those of the great community (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). From the seventy-second rule onwards, the remaining one hundred and seven rules differ from those of the *bhikṣus*, and are therefore explained separately.
Regarding the first precept on eating garlic: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a keeper of a garlic garden named Ajita; his garlic and vegetables were flourishing, so he invited the bhikṣuṇīs, saying, "Those who need garlic may come and take it."

At that time, the śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs plucked garlic for one year; when it reached the second or third year, the garlic garden failed to grow, so they abandoned the garden and departed, unable to plant it again.
Furthermore, there was a lay devotee who planted garlic in its former location; because of their original intention, various śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs came back again to pull out the garlic.
The owner of the garden thought to himself, "Who is stealing my garlic? I shall lie in wait to catch them.
The householder then hid in a secluded spot to observe, and seeing the śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs pulling up the garlic, the householder said:
"Do not take my garlic.
He replied, "The householder Ajita of Śrāvastī has invited me to take garlic; why should this concern you?"
The householder said:
"The original landowner abandoned his fields because of you;
now I am planting garlic there, so do not take it."
The śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs felt ashamed and said:
"We did not know this; from now on, we dare not take [them] again."
The laypeople scolded them in anger, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and meritorious.'"
"Eating garlic like a laywoman.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī and yet eat garlic like a laywoman?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked that bhikṣuṇī:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī eat garlic like a woman of the white-robed laity?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī eats raw garlic or cooked garlic, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the term *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī eats raw garlic, it is a *pāyattika*.
To eat cooked garlic, it is a *pāyattika*.
To eat garlic seeds, it is a *pāyattika*.
To eat the stalks or leaves, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one eats garlic skins or garlic stalks, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is for the purpose of treating a disease or applying it to a wound, there is no offense.
The seventy-two matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had someone shave the hair from her private parts.
The other bhikṣuṇīs asked her, "What are you doing?"
She replied, "I shaved the hair in the areas for urination and defecation for the sake of beauty.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
“How can a bhikṣuṇī have someone shave the hair of her private parts?
Having rebuked her with various reasons, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions;
knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this? She replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“How can a bhikṣuṇī have another person shave the hair of her private parts?
Having rebuked her with various reasons and circumstances, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.”
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair of the private parts [the anus or the vulva], it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair of the anus, it is a pāyattika.
If she shaves the hair of the vulva, it is a pāyattika.
Apart from these two places, if she shaves the hair of other areas, it is a duṣkṛta.
The seventy-third matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā inserted her finger into the female organ.
The other bhikṣuṇīs asked her:
"What are you doing? He replied,
"I am experiencing smoothness."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she inserts a finger into the female organ for the sake of experiencing its smoothness?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī insert her finger into the female organ for the sake of its smoothness?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī inserts a finger into the female organ, it is a pāyattika. Regarding "pāyattika":
it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent this offense, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī inserts her finger into the female organ, it is a pāyattika.
For every insertion, she incurs a corresponding number of pāyattikas.
At one time, there was a bhikṣuṇī whose female organ had become foul-smelling and putrid because she had not washed it for a long time. The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the two divisions of the Saṃgha. He praised the precepts and praised those who uphold the precepts; having praised the precepts and those who uphold them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī inserts her finger into the female organ, except when washing, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, without washing, inserts her finger into the female organ, it is a pāyattika.
Furthermore, for every instance [of this], she incurs a *pāyattika*.
Again, because of the occasion of bathing, a bhikṣuṇī inserted her finger deeply into the female organ; the other bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, while washing herself, inserts her finger into the female organ beyond two finger-joints, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī inserts her finger into the female organ, it is a pāyattika when it exceeds two finger-joints during washing.
For every insertion, she incurs as many pāyattikas as there were insertions.
Seventy-fourth [Case] concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā struck her female organ with her palm.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked her:
"What are you doing? he asked. She replied, "I wish to make her plump and beautiful."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she slaps her female organ with her palm in order to make it plump and attractive?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī strike her female organ with the palm of her hand in order to make it plump and attractive?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī slaps her female organ with her palm, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Palms" refers to two kinds:
the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
"Pāyattika" means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī slaps the female organ with the palm of her hand, it is a pāyattika;
if she slaps it with the sole of her foot, it is likewise a pāyattika.
If one strikes with anything other than the palms of the hands or feet, it is a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
[The seventy-fifth rule concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣuṇīs:
One was named Rāṭhā and the other was named Parāṭhā; both originally came from noble families.

These two bhikṣuṇīs rose early in the morning and went to the homes of their relatives, acquaintances, and donors, where they received fine food and drink to eat, yet they all said, "It is not delicious."
He asked, "Who prepared this food?
The host replied:
"It was prepared by the cook.
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"Why have you prepared food that has no flavor?"
The host asked, "Can you do it? The bhikṣuṇī replied:
“I can! If there is a favorable day when you wish to hold a festival, or if you wish to go to the water’s edge, come and tell me, and I shall prepare food and drink for you.”
Later, when the master of the house arrived on a fine day and wished to enter the garden, he called for the bhikṣuṇī.

The bhikṣuṇī came and prepared food and drink for him. In that household, there was a hired cook who, guarding the kitchen, stood at the gate; seeing cooked food, he came out and asked, "Who cooked this food?"
The host replied, "There are two bhikṣuṇīs:
one named Rāṭhā and the other named Parāṭhā; they cooked this food."
The hired laborer who provided her food spoke with anger:
"This has ruined the way of a bhikṣuṇī and burned away the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī; it has robbed me of my livelihood.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī of few desires and contentment who practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the two divisions of the Saṃgha and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the two bhikṣuṇīs: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī boiling raw food to make a meal?
Having rebuked her with various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī cooks raw food to make a meal, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī cooks raw food to make a meal, it is a pāyattika.
For every portion she cooks, she incurs that many pāyattikas.
There is no offense if one cooks it again, or if there is an urgent cause and one cooks it after purifying it with fire;
these are the seventy-six matters concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a householder who, due to the conditions of impermanence, lost his wealth, property, and fields; his family members all died, leaving only the husband and wife remaining.
The householder thought to himself:

"Among all those who possess the joy of merit and are free from decline and affliction, none surpass the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; why should I not go to them and seek to leave the household life?"
The husband immediately went to the Jetavana and became a bhikṣu, while the wife went to the Rājakārāma monastery and became a bhikṣuṇī.

When it was time for the bhikṣu to receive food, he took his meal and went to the bhikṣuṇī’s monastery; the bhikṣuṇī had already prepared a tray with sauces, vegetables, fruits, and melons, waiting for the bhikṣu to arrive.

At that time, this bhikṣu took his food and went to the bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra to sit and eat; the bhikṣuṇī rose to give him sauce and vegetables, and they spoke together of matters from their former lives as householders.
Because the bhikṣu was angry and could not endure it, he immediately threw the rice from his hand onto the face of the bhikṣuṇī.
Because the bhikṣuṇī was also angry, she poured hot soup over the bhikṣu’s head; this was impure and shameful.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and rebuked him, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she stands before a bhikṣu to wait upon him during his meal?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, questioned that bhikṣuṇī intentionally:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī stand before a bhikṣu while he is eating to wait upon him?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stands before a bhikṣu while he is eating to wait upon him, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the term *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī stands before a bhikṣu while he is eating to wait upon him, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of standing up and sitting down again, one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were times.
If, after giving food to a bhikṣu, one sits back down or goes elsewhere, there is no offense.
The seventy-seventh matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā threw excrement and urine outside the wall.
This monastery was near a main street; at that moment, a minister of King Prasenajit named Maṇi, dressed in clean garments, was passing along this street when the filth fell upon his head.
At that time, when the minister was being rebuked by the king, there was a Brahmin skilled in physiognomy who followed behind him.
The Brahmin said:
"Wash your head quickly and return to the presence of the king; this is an auspicious sign, and you will surely obtain great benefit."
The minister immediately washed his head and went to the king’s presence; the king was delighted and restored him to his original office.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had thrown excrement and urine over a wall, which fell upon the head of King Prasenajit’s minister and defiled his head, and that the king consequently restored him to his original office, [they were scandalized].
"This minister Maṇi is cruel and devoid of compassion; what kind of suffering will he inflict upon us?
Thinking thus, out of fear, all departed except for those bhikṣuṇīs who were old or ill.
At that time, the minister Maṇi had this thought:
"That I have regained my former office is entirely due to the circumstances involving the nuns' quarters; I shall go to comfort the bhikṣuṇīs."
The minister Maṇi then went to the nuns’ quarters and, seeing that there were few bhikṣuṇīs there, asked the elderly and infirm bhikṣuṇīs:
“Why is it that the community of bhikṣuṇīs here is so small?”
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Do you not know? He replied:
"I do not know," the bhikṣuṇī said.
"The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā threw excrement and urine outside the wall."
As King Prasenajit’s minister Maṇi was passing through this alley, [the fruit] fell upon his head.
The king restored him to his original post; however, this man was cruel and lacked compassion. The bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"We know what kind of torment he will inflict upon us."
Reflecting thus out of fear, all the bhikṣuṇīs fled;
we, however, being old and sickly and lacking strength, were unable to go.
The great minister said:
"I am that very Maṇi, the minister of King Prasenajit. Do not be afraid;
I shall provide you with food and drink, firewood and grass, lamps and candles, clothing, and the gift of fearlessness."

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she throws excrement and urine outside the wall?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī throw excrement and urine outside the wall?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī throws excrement or urine outside a wall, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī throws feces or urine outside a wall, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of throwing, one incurs as many *pāyattikas* as there were [instances].
If two bhikṣuṇīs together discharge excrement or urine into a single vessel, and one person lifts it up while the other throws it outside the wall.
To lift it is a *duṣkṛta*;
to throw it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī throws it with her hand, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one wraps [the grass] in straw or soil and throws it outside the wall, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The seventy-eighth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in front of the entrance to the nuns’ quarters at the Royal Park Monastery (*Rājakārāma*), there was lush, growing grass where many miscellaneous people gathered and sat, observing the physical appearances of the bhikṣuṇīs as they entered and exited, and mocked them with laughter, saying: [text continues]
"Look at this bhikṣuṇī: her eyes are squinting, these eyes are decayed, her nose is short, she has a goiter, she is pale, she is dark, she is beautiful, she is ugly."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard these words, they were displeased and thought to themselves:
"All those who have gathered here are solely because of the lush and beautiful growth of the living grass."
"If there is no grass, one should not dwell therein.
The bhikṣuṇīs gathered various excrement and urine and discarded them upon the grass; the grass immediately became putrid and rotted, withering and dying.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are ill-fated and wretched women! Is there no other secluded latrine?
Why do you void excrement and urine here in this place of pure and lush grass?"

[The eighty-third case ends. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

"For what reason?
The śikṣamāṇā replied:
"Light the lamp.
He asked, "For what reason?"
“Just bring a lamp. When the lamp was brought, she saw the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā sitting with a man in the dark.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her for various reasons:

Then the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā made a male organ out of tree resin, tied it to her heel, and later inserted it into her female organ.
At that time, a fire broke out and burned the bhikṣuṇīs’ quarters.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, forgetting to extinguish it, ran out of the room and said to the laypeople:
"A fire has broken out here; douse it with water to extinguish it."
A certain merchant, seeing that Sthūlanandā was in such a state, said to others:
"Look at this bhikṣuṇī; she possesses such fine ornaments."

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, after rebuking [the offender] with various reasons, reported it in detail to the Buddha.

If one inserts it into the female organ (*bhaga*) of another bhikṣuṇī, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The eighty-five matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was of an evil nature and prone to anger; she did not enjoy living together with virtuous bhikṣuṇīs. She deceived an ignorant bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Come and live with me, and I shall provide you with all the things you require."
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "So be it.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā delighted in frequenting the homes of others, being well-known and widely recognized there.
When the rain falls, he rises early and goes from one house to another.
By the time the sun sets, his robes are all soaked; like an *āraḍa* bird, he returns to his dwelling and says:
"My feet ache, my calves ache, my sides ache, and my back aches."
The ignorant bhikṣuṇī asked,
"From where have you come? He replied:
“I have come from such-and-such a house and am now going to such-and-such a house.

Why do you instruct me?
When I called for you previously, did I wish for you to instruct me?”

“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
“How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī address another bhikṣuṇī as follows:”
"Come, virtuous woman, dwell with me; I shall provide you with all that you require.
Having rebuked her with various such reasons for her later anger and dragging her out, he addressed the bhikṣus:

From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger or displeasure, drags herself out or causes another to drag her out, it is a pāyattika.
If she is unable to drag herself out, it is a duṣkṛta.
Whether one drags it out oneself or causes another to drag it out, for each instance this occurs, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If it cannot be removed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The eighty-sixth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, two bhikṣuṇīs who were supporters of Devadatta lay together on a single bed and engaged in various kinds of impure acts.

Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, asked the bhikṣuṇīs who had supported Devadatta:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,

The Buddha rebuked them with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can those who call themselves bhikṣuṇīs lie together on one bed and engage in all manner of impure acts?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

Regarding "pāyattika": it burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.

For every instance of lying together, one incurs that many pāyattikas.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta entered the house of a donor and stood together with the group of six bhikṣus, conversing and whispering in secret, while she sent away the bhikṣuṇīs who were traveling with them.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,

The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who enters the house of a layperson and stands together, speaks together, or converses in secret with a single bhikṣu?"

"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and stands or converses with a single bhikṣu, or engages in private conversation with him, and then dismisses another bhikṣuṇī who was accompanying her for the sake of seeking a secluded opportunity, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.

To engage in secret conversation [with a nun] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Because one seeks a secluded opportunity, to send a fellow traveling bhikṣuṇī away from a place where she can hear is a *pāyattika* offense.
If she does not leave the place where she can hear, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The ninety matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”

If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and stands together with, speaks with, or converses in secret with a single layman, and having sent away another bhikṣuṇī who was accompanying her, does so for the purpose of speaking alone, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can create an obstacle to the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and stands alone with a single man, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if she converses with him, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To engage in secret conversation [with a nun] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Because one seeks to speak in private, if one sends an accompanying bhikṣuṇī away from the range of hearing, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If she does not leave the range of hearing, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The ninety-one cases are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was then a bhikṣuṇī named Kālā who had originally been a follower of external paths; she quarreled with other bhikṣuṇīs, became angry with them, and beat her own body while weeping.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she quarrels with another bhikṣuṇī, becomes angry with her, beats herself, and weeps?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Kālā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī quarrel with another bhikṣuṇī, harbor mutual anger, and beat her own body while weeping?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, quarreling and becoming angry with another bhikṣuṇī, strikes her own body and weeps, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it burns, boils, and obstructs; if one does not repent of the transgression, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, having quarreled with other bhikṣuṇīs and become angry with them, strikes her own body and weeps, it is a pāyattika.
If she strikes her own body but does not weep, she incurs a duṣkṛta.
For every blow struck against the body, she cried out, and for each instance, she incurred a *pāyattika* offense.
The ninety-two matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālī, who had formerly been a non-Buddhist, while engaged in a dispute with other bhikṣuṇīs, performed incantations of her own making and incantations of *niraya* (hell).

"If you slander me regarding this matter, it shall cause you to fail to attain the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path; it shall cause you to fall into the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts in every successive life."

If I were to possess such things, may I be prevented from attaining the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold path; and may I fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts in every lifetime.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī when, during a dispute with another bhikṣuṇī, she performs incantations for ritual magic or incantations for hell?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Kālā: “Did you truly do this?”
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī, when quarreling with another bhikṣuṇī, employ spells for ritual rites or spells for the hells?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while quarreling with another bhikṣuṇī, performs incantations for ritual magic or incantations for hell, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it burns, boils, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, while quarreling with another bhikṣuṇī, performs incantations for ritual action or incantations for hell, saying:
"If you slander me on account of this matter, may you not attain the four foundations of mindfulness."

"Pāyattika. 'One does not attain the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold path'—all such instances constitute a pāyattika offense."
If one says,
"You shall fall into hell in every successive lifetime," it is a pāyattika.
"To fall among animals or hungry ghosts" constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If one says:

"If I possess this [fault], may it prevent me from attaining the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path."
In all such cases, it is a pāyattika.
If one says:
"In birth after birth, I have fallen into the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts," [it is likewise a pāyattika].
"In each case, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every such statement made, one incurs that many *pāyattikas*.
The ninety-three matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī."

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Thullanandā who had a co-practitioner disciple named Siyavasa; he was well-disposed and delighted in upholding the precepts, yet he was prone to forgetting his teacher’s instructions.

When she was asked to hand over her belongings, she placed them in one spot and went elsewhere to search for them; when the items were required, they could not be found. Furthermore, on another occasion, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā returned from a village, and her disciple Sīvaka went out to meet her, wishing to take her robe and bowl from her; however, she drew back and would not give them to him.
Śroṇa immediately became angry and said to the bhikṣuṇīs, "I did not steal it;
my preceptor-ni does not believe me.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"What is lack of faith?
"When my teacher was walking back and forth, I went out onto the path to meet him, wishing to take his bowl for him; he withdrew his body and would not let me have it.
I wished to take his robe for him; again, he withdrew his body and would not let me have it."
The bhikṣuṇīs went and said to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, "Your disciple maintains the precepts well; why do you not believe her?"
She replied, "How could I not believe?
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Your disciple wishes to take your alms bowl for you, yet you withdraw your body and do not give it;
she wishes to take your robe for you, yet again you withdraw your body and do not give it.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said:

"It is not that I do not trust him; rather, this man is prone to forgetfulness. Whenever he moves an object to another place, he searches for it elsewhere. When he needs an item, he cannot find it despite searching; for this reason, I do not give it to him."

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased in her heart and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī fail to examine an object with careful scrutiny and instead harbor resentment?"
Having rebuked her with various reasons, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Śivakattherī: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī fail to examine an object carefully and then harbor resentment?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, without having carefully examined an object, becomes resentful or harbors ill will toward it, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, without examining an object carefully, harbors resentment, it is a *pāyattika*.
According to the degree of resentment, one incurs as many *pāyattis* as there were instances.
The ninety-four matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, where he observed the rains retreat together with a large community of bhikṣus in Rājagṛha.
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, Kumbhīra, and other such great disciples all observed the rains retreat together with the Buddha.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through other lands during the summer retreat; while on their journey, they killed various living plants and small insects.
The laypeople became angry and rebuked them, saying:
"The Buddha, together with the great assembly—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandiya, Kapphiṇa, and others—is observing the rains retreat in Rājagṛha."
These bhikṣuṇīs said of themselves:
"We are virtuous and meritorious.
During the summer retreat, they traveled through various countries, killing all manner of living plants and small insects.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she wanders through various countries during the summer retreat, killing living plants and small insects?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who wanders through various countries during the summer retreat, killing living plants and small insects?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī wanders through other countries during the summer retreat without a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī wanders to another country during the summer retreat without a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.
For every distance she travels, she incurs as many pāyattikas as there are units of distance traversed.

The ninety-five matters are concluded. While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, having finished the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, he traveled through other countries for two months. Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandiya, Kapphiṇa, and other great disciples all followed the Buddha on his travels to other countries, yet these bhikṣuṇīs remained behind and did not go.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:

"When the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony had concluded, he traveled through other countries for two months accompanied by his great disciples—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandiya, Kapphiṇa, and others—as they traveled about, yet the bhikṣuṇīs did not go."
"You wicked little girl, you do not wish to leave this room.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“What is meant by saying that a bhikṣuṇī, having finished the *pravāraṇā*, does not travel to another place for even one night?
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, he said to the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.”
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the *pravāraṇā*, does not travel to another place for even one night, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding *pāyattika*: it burns, boils, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the *pravāraṇā*, does not travel to another place for even one night, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every day she does not go, she incurs that many *pāyattikas*.
The ninety-six matters concluded. *Sarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, Fascicle 44.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 45. Section 7, Part 4.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India together with Kumārajīva during the Later Qin dynasty.
Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya, Chapter Four Hundred Seventy-Eight, Second Part of the *Pācittika*:
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit, the ruler of Kośala, had a small kingdom in rebellion.
The king assembled his fourfold army— elephant troops,
cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry— and having assembled these four divisions, he went forth in person to wage war. Meanwhile,
the bhikṣuṇīs were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī, and on the road they encountered this army.
Within that assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, an elder bhikṣuṇī who knew the Dharma said,
"Let us move aside a little.
The junior bhikṣuṇīs then said:
"Why have you fled?
King Prasenajit believes in the Buddha-dharma; Prince Jeta, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, Niśṛtadhara, Pūrṇa, and others—all believe in the Buddha-dharma."
"Who can stop us? We shall simply go straight ahead.
Having spoken thus, they went straight on and were stripped of their clothes by the vanguard, leaving them naked.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the king:
"The vanguard soldiers have stripped us of our clothes.
The King said, "I provided all these troops with gold, silver, and grain rewards from the villages so that they might fight; now that you have been robbed of your garments, they cannot be recovered."
"Now there are military forces within this kingdom; why do you wander about?
If the Buddha hears of this, he will surely establish a precept for you:
'One should not wander through suspicious or dangerous places within the kingdom.'"
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the two communities of monks and, though he already knew the facts, deliberately asked the bhikṣuṇīs: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who wanders through suspicious and dangerous places within the country?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wanders through a suspicious or dangerous place within the country, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī wanders through suspicious or fearful places within the country, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every step he travels, he incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are steps.
The ninety-seven matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then, on the borders of King Ajātaśatru’s realm, a small kingdom rebelled and assembled the fourfold army:
Having assembled the fourfold army—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—the king set out in person to wage war.
Meanwhile, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling from the Vṛji country toward Rājagṛha and encountered the royal army on the road.
Among them was an elder bhikṣuṇī who knew the Dharma; seeing the army approaching from afar, she said, "Let us flee.
The young bhikṣuṇīs, who did not know the Dharma, said:
"What is the cause for this distress?
King Ajātaśatru believes in the Buddha-dharma; the youth Ābābadha, the youth Jīvaka, and Āluka all believe in and revere the Buddha-dharma. We should simply go straight ahead."
Having spoken thus, she went straight away, where she was stripped naked by the soldiers marching in front.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the king,
"The soldiers marching in front have stripped us."
The king said,
"I provided all these troops with villages, gold, silver, and rewards for their sustenance before they fought.
Now that I have seized your garments, they cannot be returned."
"Now, you are traveling abroad in places of doubt and fear; why do you wander about?
If the Buddha hears of this matter, he will surely establish a precept for you:
'No bhikṣuṇīs shall wander abroad in places of doubt or fear.'"
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇīs: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who wanders through places outside the monastery that are suspicious or dangerous?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wanders outside the monastery grounds in a place that is suspicious or dangerous, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī wanders outside the monastery grounds in a place of uncertainty or fear, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of traveling [with a monk], one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were instances.
The ninety-eight matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then there was the bhikṣuṇī Kālī, who had originally been a follower of external paths and took pleasure in wandering about for sightseeing.
These bhikṣuṇīs rose early and went to temples, music halls, debating halls for the Dharma, monasteries for renunciants, and halls for viewing paintings; the laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and meritorious. "
"Therefore, she went to look at the painting hall, appearing like a woman of the non-Buddhist sects.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, her heart was displeased, and she related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī Kālā: “Did you truly do this? She replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"What is it to call a bhikṣuṇī one who intentionally goes to look at a painted house?
Having rebuked her with various reasons and circumstances, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally goes to look at a painted house, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī intentionally goes to look at a painted house, if she is able to see it, it is a pāyattika; if she does not see it, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one goes from a lower place to a higher place and is able to see [the object], it is a *pāyattika*; if unable to see it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one goes from a higher place to a lower place and is able to see it, it is a *pāyattika*; if unable to see it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one does not go intentionally, but the path passes through the center, there is no offense.
The ninety-nine matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who had assisted Devadatta and was a long-time resident; she had a virtuous and excellent bhikṣuṇī friend who was a visitor.

At that time, the resident bhikṣuṇīs went out to welcome her; they exchanged greetings with her as she held her robes and bowl, provided hot water for her to wash her feet, applied oil to her feet, and offered her a fine bed and couch.
The visiting bhikṣuṇī said, "Light the lamp."
The resident bhikṣuṇī asked,
"What do you wish to do?
The visiting bhikṣuṇī replied:
"In the first watch of the night, you should practice seated meditation, recite the scriptures, chant hymns, and offer prayers.
The senior bhikṣuṇīs said, "You have been exhausted from traveling; you should simply lie down to rest."
Having spoken these words, she immediately lay down to sleep.
The visiting bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"How can we lie down at the first watch of the night without practicing dhyāna, reciting the sūtras or hymns, or offering prayers?"
Thereupon, Jyotiṣkā sat in meditation, recited the sūtras and chants, and finished her prayers; she then wished to lie down.
Having heard the sound, the bhikṣuṇī who assisted Devadatta woke up and asked, "Virtuous woman!..."
"What are you doing? They replied, "We have finished sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, chanting, and offering prayers; we now wish to lie down."
The senior bhikṣuṇīs said: "O virtuous daughters!
Sleep yields no fruit and brings no reward;
the Buddha praises wakefulness and censures sleep. Now we shall remain awake, neither lying down nor sleeping."
She then sat down with one leg extended.
The virtuous bhikṣuṇīs reflected:
"How can we lie down in the light of a lamp?"
The resident bhikṣuṇīs sat in meditation, recited the sūtras, and chanted prayers during the middle watch of the night; by the final watch, they lay down to sleep.
The visiting bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"How can we lie down to sleep during the final watch?"
The visiting bhikṣuṇīs were utterly exhausted from the journey; because they could not lie down all night, their bodies were ill at ease.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased in heart and rebuked them, saying:
"How can one call herself a bhikṣuṇī if those who arrived first cause distress to those who arrived later?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, asked that bhikṣuṇī intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī disturb those who have already settled there?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī who has already been residing there causes distress to one who arrives later, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī who has already been residing there causes distress to one who arrives later, it is a *pāyattika*.
According to the degree of provocation, one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were instances.
The hundred matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the virtuous bhikṣuṇīs were residents, while the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta were guests.

At that time, when the resident bhikṣuṇīs saw the visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrive, they went out to welcome them, inquired after their well-being, took up their robes and bowls for them, provided water for washing their feet, anointed their feet with oil, and gave them beds and bedding.
The senior bhikṣuṇī said:
"Virtuous daughter!
Light the lamp."
The visiting bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Do not light the lamp; we are utterly exhausted from the road and have been unable to practice meditation, recite the sūtras, chant, or offer prayers. We wish to lie down."
The senior bhikṣuṇīs reflected:
"Why is it that we do not practice dhyāna, recite the sūtras or chants, or offer prayers during the first watch of the night, but instead lie down to sleep?"
She immediately arose, lit a lamp, sat in meditation, recited the scriptures, chanted hymns, and offered prayers; having finished, she wished to lie down.
A visiting bhikṣuṇī heard this sound and woke up, saying:
"Virtuous woman, what do you intend to do?"
They replied,
"We have finished our meditation and wish to lie down.
The visiting bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Sleep is fruitless and brings no reward; the Buddha praises the practice of not sleeping and censures sleep. We shall remain awake and not sleep now.
Having said this, they lit lamps and sat in meditation.
The resident bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves,
"How can we lie down while there is still light?
When the visiting bhikṣuṇīs had finished sitting in meditation during the middle watch of the night, they lay down during the latter watch.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reflected:
"How can we lie down during the latter part of the night?
For this reason, they did not lie down throughout the entire night, and their bodies were not at ease.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī disturb those who have already taken up residence?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions. Knowing the situation, he intentionally asked the visiting bhikṣuṇī: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī disturb a bhikṣuṇī who has already taken up residence?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī who is a later resident causes distress to a former resident, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī who is staying later causes distress to one who is staying earlier, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each instance of causing distress, one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were instances.
This concludes the one hundred and one rules. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had a co-resident bhikṣuṇī who was suffering from illness. Fearing that she would have to provide for the patient’s needs, Thullanandā abandoned her and went to another village.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to where the sick bhikṣuṇī was and said to her:
"You performed all the tasks for Thullanandā.
Now that you are suffering from illness, how can we look after you?"
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Will the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā be able to provide for me?
I fear that out of concern for my appearance, she will abandon me."

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased in her heart and, through various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, when a co-resident bhikṣuṇī is suffering from illness, she abandons her and goes to another village?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked Thullanandā intentionally: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī abandon a bhikṣuṇī who is living together with her and suffering from illness, and go to another village?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not provide for the medical needs of a fellow bhikṣuṇī who is suffering from illness, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it is burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī does not provide for the medical needs of a fellow bhikṣuṇī who is suffering from illness, it is a pāyattika.
For every instance of failing to provide such support, she incurs a corresponding number of pāyattikas.
The one hundred and second matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, having dressed in his upper robe and taken up his alms bowl before midday, entered the house of a lay devotee for the purpose of begging for food.
At that time, there was a householder’s wife at the place where [Mahākāśyapa] was stationed; seeing Mahākāśyapa from afar, she immediately rose and went out to welcome him.
Stūlananda, who had previously been in that house, saw Mahākāśyapa from afar but did not rise to go and welcome him.

The householder’s wife took hold of his feet with her hands, bowed her head to the ground in salutation to the Elder Mahākāśyapa, washed her hands, took the bowl, filled it with rice, poured soup over it, and gave it to him; Mahākāśyapa then took it and departed.

The householder’s wife went to where Thullanandā was and said, "Do you know that this Elder Mahākāśyapa is a great disciple of the Buddha, honored by gods and humans as a field of merit? What evil would there be in rising to greet him?"
Thullanandā said, "Mahākāśyapa was originally an outsider, a brāhmaṇa; he is someone you hold in high esteem and respect, but he is not one whom I revere.
The householder’s wife, filled with anger, rebuked her, saying:
“Various bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
‘We are virtuous and meritorious.
Yet when they see a bhikṣu approaching, they do not rise, acting like women of the non-Buddhist sects.”
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, said: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī fail to rise when seeing a bhikṣu approaching?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu approaching and does not rise, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu coming and does not rise, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance one sees [a woman] and fails to rise, one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were instances.
The one hundred and three matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the Elder Kālodāyin frequently visited a certain family; before midday, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to their house.

There was a bhikṣuṇī named Śrī-Gautamī who was previously staying in this house; seeing Kālodāyin coming from afar, she immediately rose to meet him, led him inside, showed him a seat, exchanged greetings with him, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood before him with palms joined.

Kāḷudāyin had been preaching the Dharma for a long time; the bhikṣuṇī became dazed and confused, her vision darkened, and she fell to the ground. The householder’s wife then sprinkled water on her face, and she regained her composure.
The householder’s wife said:
“What affliction do you suffer?
What sorrow do you grieve over?”
She replied, “I have no illness and no sorrow; it is only because I stood for so long that I became dazed and fell to the ground.

The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions. Through various causes and conditions, he praised the precepts and praised the upholding of the precepts. Having praised the precepts and the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sits down without first asking permission from a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī sits down without first asking permission from a bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of sitting without being asked permission, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The one hundred and fourth section concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs wished to travel to other countries and addressed the king, saying:
“We wish to travel through other countries; Your Majesty should issue a decree to all nations that the people must not block our path or harass us.
The King immediately dispatched messengers to command the four quarters:
“Do not harass the bhikṣuṇīs; provide them with whatever they require, such as food, drink, lamps, and candles.”

As the bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on their journey, they arrived at a village where there was no monastery. They went to the house of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) wishing to stay the night, and said to the layperson:
"Please leave the house; we wish to stay overnight within it."
The householder said, "Noble lady!
I am in my own home; where would you have me go?"
The bhikṣuṇī spoke again:
"Just get out! Do you wish to harass me or deceive me?
If you do not leave, I have the power of the authorities to cause you distress."
The householder thought to himself:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are protected by the king and possess official power and influence; they might perhaps trouble me.
Having had this thought, he became fearful and immediately departed.
This lay devotee was old, emaciated, and weak; during the cold winter season, he went out from his house and was on the verge of death.
The other lay devotees rebuked him, saying:
"How can these bhikṣuṇīs claim for themselves:..."
"Excellent! This is meritorious.
Without asking the host, she spread out her bedding as if she were the wife of a king or the wife of a high minister.
Among those present was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said: "Did you truly do this? They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“What is it to call a bhikṣuṇī one who spreads out bedding without first asking the owner?
Having rebuked her with various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī spreads out bedding or causes someone else to spread it without first asking the owner's permission, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī spreads out bedding without asking the owner, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one causes another to spread [a seat], it is a *pāyattika*.
Whether one spreads it oneself without asking permission or causes another to spread it, for each instance, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
The one hundred and five matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs wished to say to the bhikṣus:
"Just as you have not relied upon another for five years, we likewise shall do so."
"You have been keeping disciples for ten years; we are the same—what difference is there?

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing this matter, she was displeased and, rebuking her through various reasons, reported it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the truth] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Did you truly do such a thing?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“What is it called for a bhikṣuṇī to ‘disregard the great assembly’?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“From this day forward, it is permitted that bhikṣuṇīs who have completed six years since receiving full ordination need not rely upon another; those who have not completed six years must rely upon another. At twelve years, one may maintain a group of disciples.”
For ten reasons, the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs: from this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has not reached twelve years of seniority should take on disciples, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī who has not reached twelve years of seniority keeps a following of disciples, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each person she keeps, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense for that many individuals.
The one hundred and sixth matter is concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having reached twelve years of standing and wishing to take on a group of followers, said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"I have completed twelve years since receiving full ordination; now wishing to take on disciples, what should I do?
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā to take on disciples."
If there are other bhikṣuṇīs such as these, they too should be granted the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a group of followers (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

As for the ritual procedure for the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a group of followers: the community of bhikṣuṇīs should assemble with a single mind; the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā should rise from her seat, bare her right shoulder, remove her leather sandals, kneel with her right knee on the ground, join her palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!"
I, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having fulfilled twelve years since receiving the full precepts, wish to maintain a group of disciples.

I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for maintaining disciples; may the Saṃgha perform for me, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, the formal act for maintaining disciples out of compassion.
A second and third time, she should likewise request.
At that time, one bhikṣuṇī should announce within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having completed twelve years since her full ordination, desired to take on disciples.
This bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā then requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for taking on disciples.

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of authorizing the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā to maintain a following of disciples.
This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

"The Saṃgha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for authorizing the nun Thullanandā to maintain a retinue of disciples. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!"
For ten reasons, he established this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs: from now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve years of seniority has not yet performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being authorized to have followers, yet she takes followers, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve years of seniority has not yet performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being authorized to maintain a following, yet maintains a following, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each one she keeps, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense for that many instances.
The one hundred and seventh matter is concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept unmarried girls who were less than twelve years of age as members of her group.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who maintains a group consisting of unmarried girls who have not yet reached twelve years of age?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī maintain a group consisting of unmarried girls who have not yet reached twelve years of age?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī maintains a group consisting of unmarried girls who have not yet reached twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika.
A pāyattika is that which burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī gathers a group consisting of unmarried girls who have not yet reached twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika.
For every girl she keeps, she incurs that many pāyattikas.
The one hundred and eighth matter is concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having reached the age of twelve, took in as a disciple a married woman who had not yet undergone the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of being assigned to a preceptor (*upādhyāyinī*), and she maintained her as part of the community.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, regarding a girl who has reached twelve years of age and is already married, she keeps her as a member of the community without first performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of assigning her to a preceptor-ni?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though already aware of it, asked him: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I did."
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who, having received a girl of eleven years who has already been married, keeps her as part of the community without first performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for her to belong to a preceptor (*upādhyāyinī*)?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī, having taken as her followers a group of girls who are at least twelve years old and have been married, yet has not performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of assigning them to a preceptor-ni (upādhyāyinī), it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps as a member of the community a girl who is already twelve years old and has been married, without having performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of assigning her to a preceptor (upādhyāyinī), it is a *pāyattika*.
For every person she keeps, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each one acquired.
This concludes the one hundred and nine matters. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
