Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a group of followers but failed to instruct or admonish them, nor did she preach the Dharma to them.
The disciple said:
"Preceptor Nun!
Why do you not instruct me, and why do you not preach the Dharma for me?"
She replied,
“I have not instructed you, nor have I taught the Dharma to you.
The disciple reported this matter to the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs recounted it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"Did you truly do this? She replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"What is it to be called a bhikṣuṇī who maintains a group of followers but does not instruct them, nor preach the Dharma to them?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You must perform the *tshig-pa'i las* (niyasa-karman) against Steun-lan-na-da."
If there are others who act in this manner, they too should be subjected to the *jñapti-karman* of suspension (*pravāsanīya*).
As for the procedure for the *karman* of suspension: with the Saṃgha of nuns gathered in harmony and with one mind, one bhikṣuṇī shall announce within the assembly:
"Venerable nuns of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept disciples but did not instruct them nor preach the Dharma to them.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and listening, perform the *niyata-karman* (act of restraint) against Thullanandā:
"You, Thullanandā, must no longer keep a following."
"This is called the motion (*jñapti*).
Thus is the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
'The Saṃgha has completed the *karman* for Sthūlanandā to cease keeping a retinue. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!'"
For ten reasons, he established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has been granted the formal act of suspension (niḥsargika-karman) by the Saṃgha maintains a following of disciples, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī who has been subjected to the *niyata-karman* (act of suspension) by the Saṃgha continues to maintain a following of disciples, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each member of the assembly he keeps, he incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are members.
The section on the one hundred and ten matters is concluded. The Text of the Six Dharmas for the Ordination Platform: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a householder’s wife named Halāhalā, who was very wealthy, possessed great riches, and was endowed with all manner of prosperous signs, including fields and houses.
Due to the conditions of impermanence, this householder’s wife had lost all her wealth and property and her family members were scattered, leaving her alone.
The householder’s wife was pregnant; because of her grief over the loss of her kin, her wealth, and her husband, her body became emaciated and the fetus shrank, whereupon she thought:
"The child in my womb will either die or rot."
She further thought:
"Among all those who enjoy the bliss of merit, none surpass the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas; I shall go forth among them and become a bhikṣuṇī."
She then went to the Rājakārāma monastery and became a bhikṣuṇī.
This woman took delight in her renunciation; because she was stout, her belly gradually grew large.
The other bhikṣuṇīs drove her out of the monastic compound.
"You are a person who has committed sexual misconduct; do not stay here.
He replied, "Since I went forth from home, I have not engaged in sexual desire; however, while I was still living as a householder, I became pregnant."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Do not say that this bhikṣuṇī has broken her brahmacarya; before she was a white-robed laywoman, she was already pregnant."
From now on, it is permitted for a śrāmaṇerikā to train in the six dharmas for two years so that it may be known whether she is pregnant or not.

Regarding the reception of the six dharmas: if a śrāmaṇerikā first arrives, she should be instructed to prostrate herself at the feet of the saṃgha one by one in due order; having finished the prostrations, she should next request a preceptor (upādhyāyinī).
The Preceptor should instruct her, saying:
"I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], request the Venerable One to act as my upādhyāyinī.
Because the Venerable One acts as my upādhyāyinī, the Saṃgha shall grant me the two-year training in the precepts."
The second [candidate] should also say:
"I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], request the Venerable One to be my upādhyāyī-nī.
Because the Venerable One acts as my upādhyāyī-nī, the Saṃgha should grant me the two-year training in the precepts."
The third time, one should likewise say:
"I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], request the Venerable One to be my upādhyāyinī.
Because the Venerable One acts as my upādhyāyinī, the Saṃgha shall grant me two years of training in the precepts."
One bhikṣuṇī should ask the preceptor bhikṣuṇī:
"Are you able to act as the preceptor for [Name]?
If she says:
"Yes. He should then be led into the boundary area and placed where he can see but cannot hear.
At that time, one should ask:
"Is the Saṃgha in harmony? "The Saṃgha is in harmonious unity;
we shall perform the business of the Saṃgha. This preceptor-ni, [Name], and this śrāmaṇerī, [Name], the Saṃgha shall grant them two years of training in the precepts."
The second [monk] should also say:

"The Saṃgha is united in one mind; it shall perform the business of the Saṃgha. This preceptor-ni, so-and-so, and this śrāmaṇerī, so-and-so—the Saṃgha shall grant them the two-year training in the precepts."
The third [monk] should also say:

"The Sangha is united in one mind; we shall perform the business of the Sangha. This preceptor nun, [name], and this śrāmaṇerī, [name], the Sangha shall grant them two years of training in the precepts."
If the Saṃgha is united in harmony, they should summon the śrāmaṇerī and instruct her to prostrate at the feet of each member of the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha one by one.
Once she has prostrated with her head and face at their feet, they should next instruct her to request the two-year training in the precepts from the Saṃgha, speaking as follows:
"I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my preceptor, request the two-year training in the precepts from the Saṃgha."
‘With the nun [Name] as my preceptor, may the Saṃgha grant me the two-year training in the precepts, out of compassion, O Preceptor [Name]!
The second [request] should also be spoken thus:
‘I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with the nun [Name] as my preceptor, beg the Saṃgha for the two-year training in the precepts.’
"Because of the preceptor-ni [Name], the Sangha should grant me two years of training in the precepts; out of compassion, Preceptor-ni [Name]!
The third time, one should also say:
"I, the śrāmaṇerī [Name], because of the preceptor-ni [Name], request from the Sangha two years of training in the precepts."
"Due to the presence of the preceptor-ni [Name], the Saṃgha shall grant me two years of training in the precepts; may the preceptor-ni [Name] have compassion for me!
At that moment, the Preceptor should announce within the Saṃgha:
"May the venerable bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha listen!..."
This śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name] as her preceptor, requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts. The name of the bhikṣuṇī preceptor is [Name].

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent; let the Saṃgha grant the two-year training in the precepts to this śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī preceptor [Name] as her preceptor.
Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as her preceptor (upādhyāyinī), requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts."
The Saṃgha now grants two years of training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as her precept-upādhyāyī.
Those of you, venerable nuns of the Saṃgha, who consent to granting two years of training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as her precept-upādhyāyī, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
This is called the first *karmavācanā*.
A second time, he says:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā, [name], requests from the Saṃgha two years of training in the precepts, with [name] as her precept-upādhyāyī.
The Saṃgha now grants two years of training in the precepts to this śrāmaṇerikā, [name], with [name] as her precept-upādhyāyī.
Whichever bhikṣuṇīs consent to grant the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī [Name] as preceptor, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, speak.
"This is called the second *karmavācanā*.
The third is further stated:
'Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!'"
This śrāmaṇerī [Name], with [Name] as her preceptress (upādhyāyikā), requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts.
The Saṃgha now grants the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with [Name] as her preceptress, the two-year training in the precepts.
Whichever bhikṣuṇīs consent to grant the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with the bhikṣuṇī [Name] as preceptor, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, please speak.
"This is called the third *karmavācanā*.
The Saṃgha has already granted the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerī [Name], with [Name] as the precept-mother; the Saṃgha consents, for it is silent. Thus this matter is so upheld!"
"Immediately, he taught her the six rules for a śikṣamāṇā:
'Listen, you śikṣamāṇā!
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the one who knows and the one who sees—has proclaimed these six rules for a śikṣamāṇā.'"
"You, Śikṣamāṇā, shall receive and practice this for as long as you live.

For various reasons, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has censured desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; the Buddha has taught the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire."

If a śikṣamāṇā enters into the practice of a śikṣamāṇā, yet does not relinquish the precepts or emerge from them despite their weakness, and consents to sexual intercourse through mutual mental intention—even with an animal—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śrāmaṇerī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the status of a śikṣamāṇā. This act must never be committed for as long as one lives.
If one is able to uphold this, one should say:
"I am able.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has used various causes and conditions to rebuke theft and plunder while praising non-theft; even a single thread, a single inch of cloth, or a single drop of oil—if not given, it should not be taken.
In this regard, the Buddha has prescribed that the minimum amount constitutes five *kārsāpaṇas*, or what is equivalent to five *kārsāpaṇas*.
If a *śikṣamāṇā* commits such an act of theft, whether the king seizes her, beats her, binds her, or banishes her, or if he says to her: "You are a thief!
[she is no longer a *śikṣamāṇā*].
"You childish one! You fool!
You have fallen into official punishment."

"If a śikṣamāṇā steals in such a manner, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śrāmaṇerī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā, and this act must never be committed for as long as life lasts."
If one is able to uphold it, they should say:
"I am able.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has through various causes and conditions rebuked the taking of life and praised abstaining from killing; one should not intentionally deprive even an ant of its life, let alone a human being!
If a śikṣamāṇā intentionally takes the life of a human being with her own hand, or provides a weapon, or instructs them to die, or praises death, saying: "Ho!..."
"What use is living a life of evil? Death is better than life.

Following this person's inclination, he teaches death and praises death through various causes and conditions: by using traps for catching many animals, snares for many animals, nets, pitfalls, or nooses; by means of *vīṭarāga* (mechanical) killing or pseudo-*vīṭarāga* killing; by suffocating to death; by causing an abortion; by pressing on the womb to kill; by throwing into fire or water; by pushing down from a height; by sending someone to kill along the road; or by conceiving an evil intention toward the *kalala*—the embryo at the initial stage of conception within the mother’s womb—which possesses both faculties, the body-faculty and the life-faculty, and thereby employing the means to take its life.

If one dies by such means, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śrāmaṇerī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā, and this act must never be committed for as long as life lasts.
If one is able to uphold it, they should say:
"I am able.
The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked false speech and praised non-false speech; he taught that one should not even speak falsely in jest, let alone intentionally speak falsely!
If a śikṣamāṇā, not knowing and not seeing any superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), says of herself:
"I know thus, I see thus; I am one who is progressing toward arhatship, I am an arhat;
I am one who is progressing toward anāgāminship, I am an anāgāmin; or I am one who is progressing toward sakṛdāgāminship, I am a sakṛdāgāmin; or I am a srotaāpanna... [and so forth].
Whether one is a candidate for stream-entry or a stream-enterer; or has attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna;
or has attained the immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
or has attained the formless attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
If I have attained the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-smṛti),
then the devas come to me, as do the nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas;
they question me and I answer them, and I question them and they answer me.

If a śikṣamāṇā speaks such a falsehood, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śrāmaṇerī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā, and this act must never be committed for as long as life lasts.
If one is able to uphold it, one should say:
"I am able.

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, the thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; the Buddha taught the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

If a śikṣamāṇā, with a mind affected by leakage, listens to a man whose mind is likewise affected, while he is naked from the hairline to the wrists and above the knees, and she experiences his smoothness and softness.
Whether stroking the body with the grain or against the grain, whether pushing or pulling, whether holding from below to lift up or holding from above to press down, or pressing upon a sore.
She is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śrāmaṇerī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the status of a śikṣamāṇā.
If she has committed [an offense], she may receive it again.
Within this, you must not commit [these acts] for as long as life lasts.
Are you able to uphold them?
If you are able to uphold them, you should say:
“Yes, [I can].

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire; he praised the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinction of the fever of desire.

If a śikṣamāṇā, with a lustful mind, listens to a man with a lustful mind—whether by taking his hand, or taking hold of his garment, or standing together, or conversing together, or making an appointment together, or entering a secluded place, or waiting for the man, or giving herself [to him]—it is according to the rules for a laywoman.
If she gives these eight things away herself, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, no longer a śrāmaṇerī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost the dharma of a śikṣamāṇā.
If you should commit an offense, it may be received again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not act [in such a way].
Are you able to uphold this?
If one can say,
"I can," [the preceptor says]: "Listen, [Name]!
The Saṃgha has already conferred upon you the training rules; as a śikṣamāṇā who upholds the six dharmas, you are named a śikṣamāṇā.

You have obtained a complete assembly of upādhyāyī nuns, a complete assembly of ācāryā nuns, and the full Saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs; you have obtained a complete place of practice, a complete territory, and the aspiration of a wheel-turning monarch.

Now that you have completed [the training], you should revere the Three Jewels—the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel—as well as your preceptress and your ācāryā; you should also revere those of the superior, middle, and junior seats.
One should diligently practice the three trainings:
the training in virtuous ethical discipline, the training in virtuous concentration, and the training in virtuous wisdom.
One should cultivate the three gates of liberation:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
You should diligently apply yourself to the three activities:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and exhorting others to perform meritorious deeds.

These dharmas open the gate to Nirvana, leading to the attainment of the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat. Just as a lotus flower in the water grows and blossoms day by day, you too shall likewise grow in the dharmas of the Path; thereafter, you shall receive full ordination.
“Within the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, you have already attained the precepts so difficult to obtain;
since they are hard to find even in times of no calamity, do not let what you have gained be in vain.”
"Prostrating with his head at the feet of the Saṃgha, he circumambulated them to the right and departed with joy.
For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps as a disciple one who has not studied the six dharmas for two years, it is a pāyattika.
A pāyattika is that which burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī takes a disciple into her following after less than two years of training in the six rules, it is a pāyattika.
For every such case of taking [a disciple], she incurs that many pāyattikas. This concludes the one hundred and eleven matters. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had a disciple who had studied the six dharmas for two years; although she had not yet performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of affiliation with her preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*), Thullanandā nevertheless kept her as part of the community.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if her disciple has studied the six rules for two years, yet before the formal *karmavācanā* of belonging to the preceptor-ni has been performed, she already keeps her as part of the community?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, addressed the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who, when a disciple has studied the six dharmas for two years, yet before the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for belonging to a preceptor-ni (upādhyāyinī) has been performed, keeps her as part of the community?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a disciple as part of her community after two years of training in the six rules, without having performed the formal act of *karmavācanā* to assign her to a preceptor-ni, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps as her own a disciple who has studied the six rules for two years, yet has not yet performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of belonging to a preceptor-ni (*upādhyāyinī*), it is a *pāyattika*.
For every person she keeps as a follower, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each one.
The one hundred and twelve matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇīs, for the sake of keeping followers, underwent great hardship; they washed clothes, dyed clothes, cut them, and sewed them together.
After the disciple had received the full ordination, she abandoned her preceptress and departed.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this matter, they rebuked her, saying:
"This inauspicious and wretched woman!"

I have undergone great hardship for you—making your robes, washing them, dyeing them, cutting them, and sewing them—and yet, as soon as you have received the Great Precepts, you abandon me and depart?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to follow an upādhyāyinī for two years."
For ten reasons, he established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having received full ordination, does not attend upon her preceptor nun (upādhyāyinī) for two years, it is a pāyattika offense."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, having received the full ordination, does not attend upon her preceptor (upādhyāyinī) for two years, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each nun who follows or does not follow her preceptor (upādhyāyinī), she incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are followers.
The one hundred and thirteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā maintained a group of disciples but did not provide them with material goods or the Dharma.
The disciples said,
"Preceptor Nun, why do you not give us wealth and the Dharma?
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā replied:
"I will not give you wealth or the Dharma.
The disciples said,
"If you do not give us wealth or the Dharma, we shall go elsewhere."
Thullanandā said, "The Buddha has established a precept:
you must follow me for two years; if you go elsewhere, you will incur a pāyattika offense."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she keeps a disciple yet does not provide her with wealth or the Dharma?"
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked him: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī keep a disciple yet fail to provide her with wealth and the Dharma?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a disciple but does not provide her with material goods or the Dharma, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī maintains a group of followers but does not provide them with material goods or the Dharma, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of not giving [the robe], one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were [instances].
This concludes the one hundred and fourteen matters. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a courtesan for the sake of the community.
This nun, who was formerly a courtesan, dressed herself before midday, took her bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Among them, a householder spoke these words:
"I once engaged in such-and-such acts with this nun."
When this bhikṣuṇī heard of these matters, her heart was not pleased, and she spoke of them to the other bhikṣuṇīs; the bhikṣuṇīs then reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"Did you truly do this? She replied:
"It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
“What is it to call a bhikṣuṇī one who keeps a courtesan for the sake of the community?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he said to the bhikṣus:
“From now on, you should not keep a courtesan for the sake of the community.”
To keep [such items] is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there is a valid reason for keeping them, they should be taken far from their original location, at least five or six *yojanas*.
For ten reasons, the Buddha established this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a courtesan for the sake of the community, within a distance of five or six yojanas from her original location, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps a courtesan for the sake of the community, within a distance of five or six *yojanas* from her original location, it is a *pāyattika*.
If she follows her [the girl] without going far away, she incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are steps taken.
The one hundred and fifteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a girl who was not yet twenty years of age as a member of the community.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, through various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps a girl less than twenty years of age as a member of the community?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps a girl less than twenty years of age as a member of the community?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī maintains a girl who is less than twenty years of age as a member of the community, it is a pāyattika.’”
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, boils, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps a girl who is less than twenty years of age as a member of the community, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each instance of keeping [a girl], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each such case.
The one hundred and sixteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, without having performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of appointing a preceptor (*upādhyāyinī*), kept a twenty-year-old girl as a member of the community.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who possessed few desires, was contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if, without having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of belonging to a preceptress (upādhyāyinī), she keeps a twenty-year-old girl as part of the community?"
Having rebuked her with various reasons and causes, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Sangha of both divisions; knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who,
without having performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for affiliation with a preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*), keeps a girl of twenty years of age as a member of the community?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a girl who has reached twenty years of age as a member of the community without having performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of assigning her to a preceptor-ni (*upādhyāyinī*), it is a *pāyattika* offense.
A *pāyattika* offense is one that burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, without having performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of affiliation with a preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*), keeps a girl who has reached twenty years of age for the sake of the community, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For each instance of keeping [a woman], one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are instances.
This concludes the one hundred and seventeen matters. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a devoted woman as a member of the community.
This bhikṣuṇī, Filial Daughter, did not recite the sūtras, engage in question-and-answer sessions,
or practice dhyāna. The other bhikṣuṇīs asked her,
“For what reason do you not read and recite the sūtras, engage in question-and-answer sessions, or practice dhyāna?”
She replied, "O virtuous women!
I am sorrowful because my father has died,
or my mother has died, or my brothers have died, or my sisters, sons, and daughters have died, or my husband has died."
"How can one recite and chant the sūtras, engage in question-and-answer sessions, and practice seated meditation?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her for various reasons:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps a filial daughter as a member of the community?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī maintain a devoted woman for the sake of the community?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a female devotee for the sake of the community, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps a female devotee (*upāsikā*) for the sake of the community, it is a *pāyattika*.
For each one kept, she incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are.
This concludes the one hundred and eighteen matters. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a group of women who followed her, both male and female.
Before midday, this bhikṣuṇī put on her robes and took up her bowl, walking for alms while surrounded by men and women before and behind her.
The laypeople said to one another: "Do you know?"
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are people who engage in sexual desire; they have fathered sons and daughters together with the community of bhikṣuṇīs within the monastic quarters.

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, she was displeased and, through various causes and conditions, rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she keeps men and women with her, acting as a mother to a crowd?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally asked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī keep men and women about her and treat them as a retinue?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a woman with male and female children in her retinue, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps a woman with male and female children as her own attendant, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every woman she keeps, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense accordingly.
The one hundred and nineteen matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a woman of ill character as a member of the community.

Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased in her heart and, through various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps a woman of evil character as a member of the community?"
Having rebuked her with various reasons and causes, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions; knowing the situation, he intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī keep a woman of ill character as a member of the community?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a woman of bad character as a member of the community, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps a woman of evil character as a member of the community, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every such person kept, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each one acquired.
The one hundred and twenty matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept as a member of the community a girl who was twenty years of age, yet had not studied the six rules for two years.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, her heart was displeased, and for various reasons she rebuked them, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she keeps a girl who is twenty years old as a member of the community without having had her train in the six rules for two years?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed, I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps as a member of the community a girl of twenty years who has not studied the six rules for two years?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a girl who has reached twenty years of age as a member of the community without having her train in the six rules for two years, it is a pāyattika.
A *pāyattika* is that which burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī keeps a girl who has reached twenty years of age as a member of the community without having her train in the six rules for two years, it is a pāyattika.
For each instance of keeping [the animals], one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there were [animals] acquired.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs did not know what constituted the six dharmas;
the Buddha said:
"Together with the four *pārājikas*, and from the hairline down to the wrists and knees, receiving the eight matters as signs of manifesting attachment—this is called the six dharmas.
The one hundred and twenty-one items are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā kept a girl who was twenty years old, who had studied the six rules for two years, as a member of the community without performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of affiliation with a preceptor-nun.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who, having few desires and being content, practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and censured it for various reasons:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps as a member of the community a girl of twenty years of age who has studied the six rules for two years, yet has not performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) of affiliation with a preceptor-ni?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied, “Indeed, I did,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who, when a girl has reached twenty years of age and has studied the six dharmas for two years, fails to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of assigning her to a preceptor-nun (*upādhyāyinī*), yet instead keeps her as part of the community?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī, having received a girl who has reached twenty years of age and has trained in the six rules for two years, should admit her into the community without performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of affiliation with a preceptor-ni (upādhyāyinī), it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.

As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī takes into her community a girl who is twenty years of age and has studied the six rules for two years, yet has not performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of becoming affiliated with a preceptor-ni (*upādhyāyinī*), it is a *pāyattika*.
For every animal kept, one incurs as many *pāyattika* offenses as there are animals acquired.
One hundred and twenty-two matters are concluded. *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), Volume 45.

The 178th section of the *Prātimokṣa* rules, Part Three.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī who supported Devadatta frequently entered and left the homes of lay families.
A certain householder’s wife said to her,
“Please ordain me so that I may leave the household life.”
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Give me your bowl and I shall ordain you;

give me your robe, your door-knob, your medicinal food for the day, your medicinal food for the half-month, your medicinal food for seven days, and your medicinal food for life, and I shall ordain you into the homeless life."
The householder’s wife said,
“Do you take people as laborers?
The bhikṣuṇīs replied:
"Yes. On another day, some virtuous bhikṣuṇīs went to the house of this layman, and the laywoman asked them:
"Is it true that you are wandering about as hired laborers to ordain people?"
The virtuous bhikṣuṇī asked: “Who said this?
The householder’s wife replied:
"I said to the bhikṣuṇī Cāudā:
'You should ordain me and let me go forth.
She then said to me:"
"Bring me your bowl and I shall deliver you;
bring me your robe, your door-latch, your *kālika* medicine, your *yāmika* medicine, your *saptāhika* medicine, and your *yāvajjīvika* medicine, and I shall deliver you."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, she was displeased and rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī to speak thus:

'If you give me a bowl, give me robes, a door-bolt, medicinal food for the day, medicinal food for a portion of the day, medicinal food for seven days, or medicinal food for as long as life lasts, I shall ordain you'?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked the bhikṣuṇī who had supported Devadatta: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
"Indeed, World-Honored One, I did."
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī speak thus:
'Bring me a bowl and robes, a door-bolt, *tatkṣaṇika-bhaiṣajya*, *yāmika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*, and *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*, and I shall ordain you'?"
After the Buddha had rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
If a bhikṣuṇī should say this:
"If you give me a bowl, robes, a door-bolt, *kālāgra-bhaiṣajya*, *kālika-bhaiṣajya*, *saptāha-bhaiṣajya*, and *yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*, I shall ordain you."
"An *pāyattika*. An *pāyattika* is that which burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī speaks these words:
“Give me your bowl and robes, your door-latch, and your medicines for the time, for the specific time, for seven days, and for life-long use; I shall deliver you.”
"In all such cases, it is a *pāyattika*.
For every instance of making such a statement, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
This constitutes the one hundred twenty-third matter. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī."
At that time in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a householder whose wife did not follow her husband’s instructions; he beat her with his hands and feet and drove her out of the house.
A bhikṣuṇī who frequently entered and left this household went to where the wife was.
When this householder arrived at another village, he thought to himself:
"Has my wife perhaps run away?
Upon returning home and searching for her, he could not find her; the householder then thought:
"My wife must go to the bhikṣuṇī vihāra.
The householder further thought:
"Let her remain there so that she may be well-disciplined; afterwards, I shall take her back."
After the woman had stayed for five or six days, she said to a bhikṣuṇī she knew:
"Virtuous lady!
Why do you not ordain me?"
He replied, "Your husband is still alive; how could you have crossed over?
The wife said:
"If he does not employ me, yet requires my services, he ought to come himself or send a messenger.
The bhikṣuṇī then ordained her and caused her to leave the household life.
When the householder heard that his wife had left the household life, he spoke with anger to her preceptor, saying:
"You wicked bhikṣuṇī, you thieving bhikṣuṇī! You have ruined my family."
"Why have you ruined my family?
He replied,
"You took my wife and made her a bhikṣuṇī."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "She is your wife; you may take her away.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
“Some bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves,
‘She is virtuous and possesses merit,’ yet when the husband does not give his permission,
they nonetheless ordain other women, such as the wives of kings or the wives of great ministers.”
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she ordains another woman's wife without the master’s permission?"
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and, though he already knew the facts, asked that bhikṣuṇī:
"Did you truly do such a thing?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī who keeps a slave for the community without the master's permission?
Having rebuked her with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a woman as a member of the community without the permission of her female guardian, it is a pāyattika.'"
There are three types of cases where the master does not grant permission:
if she is an unmarried daughter;
or if her parents do not grant permission.

If she has already been married but has not yet arrived at her husband's home, neither side is permitted to grant permission; if she has already arrived at her husband's home, the husband is not permitted to grant permission—this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
*Pāyattika* means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī ordains someone whose husband has not given permission, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one permits ordination [in violation of the rule], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense accordingly.
The one hundred twenty-four matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a mahā-śikṣamāṇā who assisted the bhikṣuṇī Cūḍapanthaka and was eligible to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The bhikṣuṇī Śroṇā, seeing this great śikṣamāṇā, immediately said to her:
"Why do you not receive the full precepts?
She replied:
“The nun Cūḍāpanthaka is violent and fond of quarreling; I do not wish to receive the full ordination from her.
If you will serve as my preceptress (upādhyāyī), I shall receive the full ordination.”
She said to Śikṣādattā,
"Since you have studied the six rules for two years, I shall maintain you as a member of the community.
After this *śikṣamāṇā* had completed her two-year study of the six rules, she spoke to Śikṣādattā, saying:
"You said to me:
'If you study the six dharmas for two years, I shall maintain you as a member of the community.
I have already studied the six dharmas for two years; you should now maintain me."
Śreṣṭha said, "I do not keep you. Why is that?"
"You assist the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā, who is fierce, violent, and fond of quarreling; she can harm others herself and can also incite others to do so. For this reason, I do not keep you."
He further said:
"If you cannot support me, why did you tell me to study the six dharmas for two years?
Had you not told me beforehand, I would not have studied the six dharmas for two years."
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she censured her for various reasons, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī and say to another:
'Study the six rules for two years, and I shall accept you as my disciple'?"
"Later, you then ceased to keep [the requisites]?
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported this matter extensively to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions; knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he addressed that bhikṣuṇī:
“Did you truly do this? He replied,
“I truly did.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
“How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī say to another:”
"Having said, 'I will take you into my care once you have studied the six dharmas for two years,' he subsequently failed to do so.
Having rebuked him with various such reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another: "
"If you study the six dharmas for two years, I shall keep you as a disciple hereafter.
If he does not keep her, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Pāyattika" means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī says to another,
"You shall train in the six rules for two years,
and I shall accept you as a disciple," but later does not accept her, it is a pāyattika.
If one follows [the rule] of not keeping [a disciple], one incurs a *pāyattika* upon each instance of acquisition.
The one hundred twenty-five matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā ordained disciples year after year and said to them:
“Wherever I enter, you all should follow me in.
Whatever I obtain, you too shall obtain.
Once, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā put on her robes, took up her bowl, and went out to beg for alms; having entered a certain house, she departed with her bowl full.
Next, a disciple entered and likewise received a full bowl to take away.
A second and a third disciple also entered in succession.
The householder was unable to give any more, so he immediately closed the door and spoke these words:
"Who can provide food for these inauspicious bhikṣuṇīs?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, regarding this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, said: "Did you truly do this?
They replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
For various reasons, the Buddha rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
“What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī ordaining a disciple year after year?
Having rebuked her with various reasons, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a disciple every year, it is a pāyattika. Regarding "pāyattika":
it means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī ordains a disciple year after year, it is a pāyattika.
For each successive year she ordains one, she incurs a pāyattika for each instance.
There is no offense if one ordains one person after an interval of a year, or if one ordains two persons [after such an interval].
The one hundred twenty-six matters are concluded. The text concerning the *bhikṣuṇī* ordination platform: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a Kāpilī woman who had become a bhikṣuṇī named Bhadrā; she had a śikṣamāṇā who was ready to receive full ordination.
At that time, Ānanda regularly acted as the representative for the bhikṣuṇīs to select a group of ten bhikṣus to confer the full ordination upon her.

At that time, Ānanda, having dressed in his robes and taken up his bowl before midday, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. The bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā saw Ānanda begging for food in Śrāvastī from afar; she went to where he was, prostrated with her head at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
"Venerable Ānanda!"
"I have a śikṣamāṇā who is ready to receive the full precepts; I pray that you will appoint a group of ten bhikṣus.
Ānanda asked, "Has the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha yet performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for her to seek affiliation with a preceptress (upādhyāyinī)?"
He replied, "I have done so.
[The other asked,] "When did you do it?"
He replied,
"I made it yesterday.
Ānanda then accepted it in silence.
Knowing that Ānanda had accepted [the food], the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā prostrated herself at his feet and departed.
Having finished eating the alms-food he had begged for, Ānanda arrived at the Jetavana and wandered about with his door-knob, going from one cell to another.
The Buddha saw from afar Ānanda wandering from room to room carrying a door-bolt;
knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda, "For what purpose do you carry a door-bolt as you wander from room to room?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā has a śikṣamāṇā who is to receive the full ordination; she has told me to dispatch a group of ten bhikṣus.”
"I now wish to appoint one; for this reason, I am carrying the door-bolt as I wander through the various rooms.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Have the bhikṣuṇīs yet performed the *karmavācanā* for requesting the precept-entrustment (*śrāmaṇerī-upasampadā*) from their preceptor-ni?"
He replied, “It has been made.
[The other asked,] “When was it made?”
He replied, "I did it yesterday.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda:

“Do the bhikṣuṇīs perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of begging for disciples belonging to their preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*) using a previously prepared formula, wishing to maintain a group of followers?
They replied,
“We do use a previously prepared formula.”
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions. Knowing [the facts] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā: “Did you truly do this?”
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions:
"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī use the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) of begging for a preceptor (*upādhyāyī*) from the previous day to maintain a group of disciples?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having previously performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of requesting [permission] from her preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*) to maintain a group of disciples, does so [without authorization], it is an *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*: it burns, cooks, and obstructs; if one does not repent, it can hinder the Path.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, having performed the formal act (karmavācanā) of begging for [permission] from her preceptor (upādhyāyī), uses [the authority] to keep a following of disciples, it is a pāyattika.
For every disciple she keeps, she incurs a pāyattika for each one.
Although the Buddha had thus permitted the reception of the full precepts (upasampadā), the bhikṣuṇīs did not know how it should be received.
The Buddha said:

"Regarding the method for receiving full ordination: when a bhikṣuṇī first arrives, she shall lead the śikṣamāṇā into the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs and instruct her to bow her head at the feet of each member of the Saṃgha until the ceremony is complete."
The *ni-karmācārya* (nun officiant) should instruct her on receiving the robe and bowl, asking: "Is this robe yours?
She should reply:
"Yes. He should be instructed to repeat my words:
"I, [Name], accept this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips; I shall maintain it as a robe of cut-and-sewn cloth."
The second:
"I accept this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of so many strips; I shall maintain it as a robe made of cut pieces. The third:
"I accept this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of so many strips;
it is a robe made of cut pieces and shall be worn. Next, he asks: "Is this robe yours?"
He replies: "It is.
[The preceptor says:
"I, [Name], receive this *uttarāsaṅga* robe of seven strips, with two pieces long and one short, as a cut-and-sewn robe to be maintained."

The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī who possesses five qualities should not be appointed as a teacher.
What are these five?"

Teaching according to desire, teaching according to hatred, teaching according to fear, teaching according to delusion, or teaching without knowing what should be taught and what should not be taught—
if one possesses these five qualities, one should act as a teacher.
What are the five dharmas?

Not following instructions out of attachment, not following instructions out of aversion, not following instructions out of fear, not following instructions out of delusion, and knowing which instructions are to be followed and which are not.

So-and-so, with So-and-so as her preceptor-nun (upādhyāyinī), desires to receive full ordination (upasampadā). She now requests the Saṃgha for the conferral of full ordination, with So-and-so as her preceptor-nun."

So-and-so has declared herself pure and has practiced the dharma of renunciation accordingly; she has already studied the six rules for two years. The community of bhikṣuṇīs has completed the preliminary formal act (*pūrvakarma*), and having reached consensus, they have performed the *karmavācanā* for her affiliation with a preceptor-ni. She is fully equipped with the five robes and the alms bowl.
I, [Name], with the preceptor nun named [Name],
request that the Sangha grant me full ordination, with the preceptor nun named [Name] acting as my preceptor.
"Whichever elders approve of [the name of] so-and-so receiving full ordination with so-and-so as preceptor-ni, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This second *karmavācanā* is concluded."
The third [motion]:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so, with So-and-so as her preceptor-ni, desires to receive full ordination; she now requests the Saṃgha for full ordination, with So-and-so as her preceptor-ni."

So-and-so has declared herself pure and has practiced the dharma of going forth accordingly; she has already studied the six rules for two years. The community of bhikṣuṇīs has completed the preliminary formal act (*pūrvakarma*). The community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, has performed the *karmavācanā* for her affiliation with a preceptor-ni. She is fully equipped with the five robes and the alms bowl.
I, named [Name], have a preceptor nun named [Name].
The Sangha should confer the full ordination upon me, with the preceptor nun named [Name] as my preceptor.
"Whichever elders approve that so-and-so receive full ordination with so-and-so as her preceptor-ni, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*."
"The Sangha has already conferred the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor nun. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus!"
One should instruct them to say:
"If someone asks,
'How old are you?'"
One should answer:
"There is no year.
[He asks: "What season is it?"
One should answer according to the time:
"Whether it be spring, summer, winter, or whether there is an intercalary month or not.
One should always answer this matter in accordance with the truth, and you should keep this in mind for as long as you live.
One should then explain the Three Dependences as follows: "Listen, [Name]!
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the Knower and the Seer—has proclaimed the three dependences for a bhikṣuṇī receiving the full precepts."
A bhikṣuṇī relies on these dharmas to leave the household life, receive the precepts, and practice the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
What are the three?
First, she relies on rag-robes (pāṃśukūla).
A bhikṣuṇī, relying on these [robes], may go forth, receive the precepts, and practice the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.

If she further obtains surplus robes—namely, robes of red hemp, white hemp, *śāṇa* hemp, *kṣaumika* silk, *kauśeya* silk, *kambala* wool, or *kārpāsa* cotton—such pure robes as these are all considered surplus robes that may be obtained.
"In this regard, for as long as you live, will you be able to rely upon rag-robes? If you can, you should say: 'I can.'"
"Second, regarding reliance on alms-gathering:

when a bhikṣuṇī has left the household life, received the precepts, and practices the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī, if she further obtains surplus offerings of food—whether it be communal meals, specially prepared meals, meals on festival days, meals on the first day of the month, meals on the sixteenth day, meals for the Saṃgha as a whole, meals for a specific residence, or invited meals, whether from the Saṃgha collectively or individually—all such pure foods are termed 'surplus acquisitions.'"
Within this, can you maintain the practice of relying on almsfood for as long as life lasts?
If you can, you should say: "I can."
Third is reliance on discarded medicinal substances.
A bhikṣuṇī who has left the household life and received the precepts practices the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
If she further receives an abundance of offerings, such as ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar;
The four kinds of purified fats:
bear fat, donkey fat, pig fat, and sturgeon fat;
the five kinds of root medicines:
Ginger, galangal, red aconite, *pāṭhā*, *viśā*, and sweet flag root;
the five kinds of medicinal fruits:
*harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *bibhītaka*, black pepper, and *pippalī*.
The five kinds of salt:
purple salt, red salt, white salt, black salt, and rock salt;
the five kinds of broth:
Flower decoctions, leaf decoctions, root decoctions, stem decoctions, and fruit decoctions;
and five kinds of tree resins:
asafoetida resin, sājjarasa resin, dhyāyaka resin, dhyāyakahati resin, and dhyāyakanada resin.
These and other such pure medicines are obtained in abundance.
You shall rely upon discarded medicines; are you able to maintain this for as long as you live?
If you can, you should say: "I can."
“Yes. Next, one should recite the eight *pārājika* rules:
“Listen, [Name]!

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the Knower and the Seer—has declared that these bhikṣuṇīs who have received full ordination must observe the three dependencies and the eight rules involving defeat.

If a bhikṣuṇī, among these eight rules involving defeat, commits any one of them, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī, just as when the head of a tāla tree is cut off, it never grows again and can never increase further.

It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī: regarding any offense among the eight *pārājika* rules, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, by means of various causes and conditions, rebuked sensual desire, the perception of sensual desire, the longing for sensual desire, sensual thoughts, and the fever of sensual desire.
The Buddha praised the severing of sensual desire, the removal of the perception of sensual desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of sensual desire.

If a bhikṣuṇī, having entered the bhikṣuṇī precepts together [with others], does not relinquish the precepts, nor does she perceive her vows as weakened, yet follows her own will to engage in sexual desire even with an animal, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These things must not be done for as long as one lives.
If you can uphold them, you should say: "I can."

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the practice of stealing and seizing the Dharma, and praised the practice of not stealing or seizing it; he taught that one should not steal even a single thread, a single inch of cloth, or a single drop of oil.
In this regard, the Buddha established a rule: it is at least five *māṣakas*, or the equivalent value of five *māṣakas*.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits such an act of theft, whether the king seizes her, beats her, binds her, or banishes her, he shall say:
"You are a thief! You are a child! You are a fool! You have fallen into official punishment!"

If a bhikṣuṇī steals or seizes in this manner, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and destroyed the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These matters must not be committed for as long as one lives.
If you can uphold them, you should say: "I can."
The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked the taking of life and praised the abstention from killing.
He taught that one should not intentionally deprive even an ant of its life, let alone a human being!
If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hand, intentionally takes a human life; or provides a weapon; or instructs another to die; or praises death, saying:
"Alas!..."
"What is the use of living a life of evil? Death is better than life; let him follow his heart’s desire for death!

Thus, through various causes and conditions, they teach death and praise death. Whether by means of *ūmāra* (poisoned food), *tōmara* (a lethal weapon), setting snares, nets, or traps; whether by means of a *vidala* (a wooden puppet) or something resembling a *vidala*; whether by suffocating, causing an abortion, pressing upon the belly, throwing into fire or water, pushing from a height, causing death on the road, or by conceiving an evil intention toward a fetus—just as it first receives the two faculties of body and life within the mother's womb—and employing the skillful means to take its life.
If one dies by such causes and conditions, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These matters must not be committed for as long as one lives.
If you are able to uphold them, you should say:
"I am able."

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked false speech and, through various causes and conditions, praised truthful speech; therein, one should not even speak falsely in jest, let alone intentionally speak falsely!
If a bhikṣuṇī, without knowing or seeing the state beyond the human (uttarimanussadhamma), says of herself:
"I know thus, I see thus; I am one who is progressing toward Arhatship, or an Arhat;
or one who is progressing toward Anāgāminship, or an Anāgāmin; or one who is progressing toward Sakṛdāgāminship, or a Sakṛdāgāmin; or one who is [progressing toward] Srotāpanna..."
A candidate for stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka) or a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), whether they have attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, or the fourth dhyāna;
or have attained the immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
or have attained the formless attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Established in meditative concentration, if one attains the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) or mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the devas come to my presence;
the nāgas, yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and rākṣasas come to my presence.
They question me and I answer them; I question them and they answer me.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks such a falsehood, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These matters must not be committed for as long as one lives.
If you are able to uphold them, you should say:
"I am able."

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; the Buddha taught the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, allows a man with a lustful mind to expose his clothing from the hairline down to the wrists or knees and above the knees, and he then rubs her body upward or downward, embraces, pulls, pushes, lifts up, lowers down, or presses upon her private parts, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These matters must not be done for as long as one lives.
If you are able [to observe them], you should say:
"I am able."

The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked desire, the perception of desire, the longing for desire, the thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire; the Buddha taught the severing of desire, the removal of the perception of desire, and the extinguishing of the fever of desire.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of lust, listens to a man with a lustful mind, takes his hand, takes hold of his robe, stands together with him, converses with him, makes an appointment with him, enters a secluded place with him, waits for the man to come, or goes there herself—just as a laywoman would do.
By these eight matters, the signs of greedy attachment are revealed; she is not a bhikṣuṇī, not a śramaṇī, and not a daughter of the Śākya; she has lost and extinguished the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These matters must not be committed for as long as one lives.
If you are able to uphold them, you should say:
"I am able."
The Buddha, by means of various causes and conditions, rebuked evil associates and evil companions, and praised virtuous associates and virtuous companions.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, conceals it for even a single night, and subsequently—whether that bhikṣuṇī has fallen away, remained, been expelled, or departed far away—should say:

"I previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had such and such matters, but I did not wish to speak of them to others, nor did I wish to speak of them to the Saṃgha, nor did I wish for others to know. [She commits an offense.]
Having spoken thus, he said:
"How can you, sister, defile your elder sister?
You are no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, no longer a daughter of the Śākya; you have fallen away from and destroyed the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī."
These matters must not be committed for as long as one lives.
If you are able to uphold them, you should say:
"I am able."
The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, rebuked evil associates and evil companions, while praising virtuous companions and virtuous friends.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣu has been suspended by a unified and harmonious Saṃgha for not acknowledging an offense, yet follows, assists, and supports him alone and without a second—without companion or partner—and does not cease or desist from doing so.
The bhikṣuṇīs should say this to that bhikṣuṇī:

"The Saṃgha, with one mind and in harmony, has performed an act of suspension for not seeing [the offense]. This bhikṣu is solitary, without a second, without companion or partner, and he does not cease or desist; you must not follow him."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the other bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner, persists in this matter and does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her a second and a third time so that she may relinquish this matter."
If she relinquishes [the offense] upon the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a śramaṇī, and no longer a daughter of the Śākya; she has fallen away from and lost the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
These matters must not be committed for as long as one lives.
If you are able to uphold them, you should say:
"I am able."
One should say to her:
"From this day forth, you should maintain a mind that is gentle and pliant, being easy to instruct and compliant with the teacher’s guidance.

You, [Name], have now completed the reception of the full ordination. You have obtained an excellent Upādhyāyinī, an excellent Ācāryinī, an excellent Saṃgha, an excellent monastery, excellent donors, an excellent place for practicing the Way, and an excellent land; even the wishes of a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King could not be fulfilled, yet you have now attained fulfillment."
You should reverently honor the Three Jewels:
the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel.
You should train in the three trainings:
The training in virtuous ethics, the training in virtuous mind, and the training in virtuous wisdom.
One cultivates the three gates of liberation:
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Diligently practice the three types of action:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and assisting in communal affairs.

If you diligently practice these dharmas, you shall open the gates to the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the gate to the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the gate to the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the gate to the fruit of *arhat*. Just as blue, red, and white lotuses grow day by day in the water, so too shall all your roots of goodness increase day by day.
"The remaining rules of the precepts, the Upādhyāya and Ācārya will gradually explain in detail for you.
He then spoke in verse:
"You have received the full ordination, And you now deeply understand the Buddha-dharma;
Universally virtuous, truly subtle and wondrous, a vast accumulation of precious jewels;
the aspirations of Śakra, Lord of Devas, the aspirations of the Cakravartin King,
and the aspirations of Yama, King of the Dead— all these you have now fulfilled.
One should always be diligent and energetic, cultivating all wholesome dharmas;
by diligently practicing the three karmas, one shall open the gate of the Deathless.
Amidst all phenomena, one attains unobstructed wisdom.
Just as a flower grows day by day, so too shall your roots of goodness increase.
As for the remaining precepts and dharmas taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
your preceptor and ācārya shall explain them to you in detail.
"Prostrating with his head at the feet of the Saṅgha, he circumambulated them to the right and departed in joy.
The one hundred twenty-seventh matter is concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the wives of the householders in the city of Śrāvastī went to bathe in the river Ajiravatī.
Previously, there was a bhikṣuṇī who bathed naked in a river. Several housewives rebuked her, saying:
"Inauspicious and wretched woman! With such a coarse body, a large belly, and sagging breasts, what use is there in being a bhikṣuṇī?"
"Why do you not instead renounce the precepts and become a slave?
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing this matter, she was displeased and reported it to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions.
Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to that bhikṣuṇī, "Did you truly do this? She replied:
“It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"What is this that is called a bhikṣuṇī washing in the open while naked?
Having rebuked her with various reasons, he said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, it is permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to keep a bathing robe to wear when washing in the open air."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs, knowing that the Buddha had permitted the keeping of bathing robes, made them wide and long.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities; hearing of this matter, she was displeased and rebuked them for various reasons:
"How can one called a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Buddha has permitted the keeping of bathing robes, make them so wide, long, and large?"
Having rebuked her with various reasons and causes, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇīs: "Did you truly do this?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can one who calls herself a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that I have permitted the keeping of a bathing robe, make it so wide and long?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to make a bathing robe, she should make it according to the prescribed measurement.
The measurement is five Sugata-spans in length and two and a half spans in width.
"To do more than this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
A *pāyattika* is that which burns, cooks, covers, and obstructs; if one does not repent the offense, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī wishes to make a bathing robe, if it exceeds the prescribed length but does not exceed the prescribed width, it is a pāyattika.
If it exceeds the prescribed width but does not exceed the prescribed length, it is a pāyattika.
If one exceeds the prescribed length and width, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
The one hundred twenty-eight matters are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
