"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī rubs her body with scented ointments, sesame powder, or sesame dregs, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "pāyattika": it means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī rubs her body with incense, it is a pāyattika.
If she rubs her body with scented ointments, sesame powder, or sesame dregs, it is likewise a pāyattika in all such cases.
For every instance of using it to rub the body, one incurs as many *pāyattis* as there were applications.
The one hundred and sixty-four matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta did not anoint their bodies with perfume themselves, nor did they rub their bodies with perfume themselves; instead, they rubbed their bodies with sesame powder and sesame dregs, and had *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇerīs*, and laywomen rub their bodies.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked them, saying:

"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she causes śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, or laywomen to smear their bodies with perfume, rub their bodies with incense, or rub their bodies with sesame powder and sesame dregs?"
After rebuking her with various causes and conditions, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the facts] yet asking as a formal inquiry, he asked the bhikṣuṇī who had supported Devadatta:
"Did you truly do these things?"
He replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One, I did.”
The Buddha rebuked her with various causes and conditions, saying:

"How can one who is called a bhikṣuṇī have a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇerī, or a laywoman anoint their bodies with perfume, rub their bodies with incense, or rub their bodies with sesame powder and sesame dregs?"
Having rebuked them with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣuṇī causes another person to smear her body with perfume and then rub her body with it, or to rub her body with sesame powder or sesame dregs, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the term *pāyattika*: it means burning, boiling, and obscuring; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī causes another person to rub her body with perfume, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one causes another to smear fragrant substances on one's body, it is a pāyattika.
To rub the body with sesame powder or sesame dregs is also a pāyattika.
For every instance of causing another to rub [the body], one incurs as many pāyattikas as there were instances.
The one hundred and sixty-fifth case concludes. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā stood at the door of a courtesan wearing a head-ornament.
When various brahmins and householders came near him, he immediately kicked them with his feet and said:
"Do you wish to engage in sexual misconduct with me?"
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs say of themselves:
'We are excellent and possess merit.'"
Wearing her head-ornament, she stood at the gate of a courtesan’s house; when she saw people approaching, she kicked them with her feet.
Among those present was a bhikṣuṇī who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Upon hearing this matter, she was displeased and related it in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions. Knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"Did you truly do this? She replied:
"It was indeed done,
Blessed One.
The Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī wear a head-ornament and stand at the door of a courtesan?
Having rebuked her in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī wears a head-covering, it is a pāyattika. Regarding "pāyattika":
it means burning, boiling, covering, and obstructing; if one does not repent, it can obstruct the Path.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī wears a head-ornament, it is a pāyattika.
If she makes one, it is a duṣkṛta.
If she repairs an old ornament, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one gives it to another to wear, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
One hundred and sixty-six matters are concluded. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a young, beautiful, and lovely *śikṣamāṇā* who assisted the bhikṣuṇī Cīrṇavatī and wished to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
A wicked person, seeing her, conceived a mind of greedy attachment and thought:
"This bhikṣuṇī is protected by the king; she cannot be forcibly abducted.
Furthermore, according to the rule for bhikṣuṇīs, they must receive the full ordination from a bhikṣu."
"If this śikṣamāṇā goes out to receive the precepts, I shall seize her and take her away.
When that śikṣamāṇā went out to receive the full ordination (mahā-śīla), that wicked man forcibly seized her and took her away.
Among them was a bhikṣuṇī who had few desires, was content, and practiced the dhūta austerities. Hearing of this matter, she was displeased and, for various reasons, rebuked her, saying:
"How can one be called a bhikṣuṇī if she does not inform the bhikṣuṇīs in the monastery before departing on a distant journey?"
Having rebuked her with various reasons, she reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and, after rebuking her with various reasons, said:

This is called the first *pāṭidesanīya* dharma.

The Eight Respectful Rules for Bhikṣuṇīs. When the day for the Bhikṣuṇī Poṣadha arrives, she should go to the monastery and, according to her preference, invite a Bhikṣu to receive the instructions of the Dharma.
The community of bhikṣuṇīs must first achieve internal harmony; they shall then appoint one bhikṣuṇī to come and receive the instruction and admonition, and she must come accompanied by a companion.
Having arrived, she shall prostrate with her head at the feet of the bhikṣu who is giving the instruction, inquire after his well-being, and speak as follows:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is in harmony; we prostrate with our heads at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus and request the dharma of fortnightly instruction."
"I shall receive and uphold the Dharma as commanded and instructed.
The bhikṣu should say to the bhikṣuṇī:
"The Buddha Śākyamuni—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Knower, the Seer—has proclaimed the Eight Rules of Respect for bhikṣuṇīs every half-month."
What are the eight?
First, a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received full ordination, should with single-minded humility pay homage at his feet.
Second, a bhikṣuṇī must request the bhikṣu-saṃgha for the conferral of full ordination.
Third, if a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must request from both assemblies the *mānatva* rite for half a month.
Fourth, where there are no bhikṣus residing, a bhikṣuṇī may not observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

Fifth, when the bhikṣuṇīs have completed their rainy-season retreat (varṣā), they should seek [the confession of] offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected from within both divisions of the Saṃgha.
Sixth, every half-month, the bhikṣuṇīs must receive the eight rules of respect (gurudharma) from the bhikṣus.
Seventh, if a bhikṣuṇī says to a bhikṣu,
"Please allow me to ask questions concerning the Sūtra, the Vinaya,
and the Abhidharma," the bhikṣu should answer her if he grants permission; if he does not grant permission, she must not ask.
"Eight: A bhikṣuṇī must not speak of a bhikṣu’s offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
These are the eight.
When a bhikṣuṇī receives these eight rules of respect, she should announce them within the community of bhikṣuṇīs during the poṣadha ceremony.

When the *poṣadha* has concluded and the following day arrives, the bhikṣuṇīs who previously received the Eight Rules of Respect (*gurudharma*) should return to pay homage at the feet of the bhikṣu who provides the instruction.

The community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, shall prostrate with their heads at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus; thus the *poṣadha* of the harmonious community of bhikṣuṇīs is concluded.

Next, the rules for bhikṣus are explained: when the Saṃgha is in harmony and reciting the Prātimokṣa, the bhikṣu who is instructing the bhikṣuṇīs, upon hearing the bhikṣu reciting the Prātimokṣa, asks:
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall we do first?"
The bhikṣu who is to provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs should go to the place of the elder, bare his right shoulder, kneel with his right knee on the ground, and join his palms, saying:

"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is in harmony; they prostrate themselves at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus and request the dharma of fortnightly instruction as commanded by the dharma of instruction. I shall receive it all."
The senior monk should say:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs is in harmony; there is no need to perform the formal act of instruction.
That bhikṣu then returns and tells the bhikṣuṇīs:
“The community of monks says to you:
‘The Buddha has already relinquished the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for instructing bhikṣuṇīs by means of a harmonious community of bhikṣuṇīs.
A bhikṣu who instructs bhikṣuṇīs must not go outside the boundary.”
If one goes outside the boundary, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Fascicle 48; Part One of the Eighth Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra from North India together with Kumārajīva during the Later Qin dynasty.
Section 13: One Dharma Increasing by One (Ekottarika-dharma). Part 1: The First of the One Dharmas Increasing by One.
The Buddha, the Bhagavat, was dwelling in Śrāvastī.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"If a man assumes the deportment, the physical characteristics, the clothing, and the form of a woman, and then receives the precepts according to the rules for men, does he obtain the precepts?"
The Buddha said:
"He obtains the precepts, but the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
He asked again:

"If a woman assumes the deportment of a man, the male characteristics, male attire, and male physical form, and then receives the precepts according to the female method, does she obtain the precepts?"
The Buddha said,
"He obtains the precepts, but the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
He asked again:
“If one has not yet been ordained as a renunciant, and one then confers full ordination upon them, does he obtain the precepts?
The Buddha said,
“He obtains the precepts, but the Saṃgha incurs an offense.”
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus enticed the disciples of others by providing them with the Dharma and food. The elder monks rebuked them, saying:
"How can you teach and transform disciples in accordance with the Dharma, only for the group of six bhikṣus to entice them away and provide them with the Dharma and food?"
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not entice the disciples of others by means of either the Dharma or food."
"If one entices [another], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
He asked again:
"If a bhikṣu does not wish to revert his precepts, but speaks to another, saying:"
"Are you acting as my preceptor?
By accepting [me] as your preceptor, have you not then reverted from the precepts?
The Buddha said:
"No, it was merely a joke.
Knowing the answer, the Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Was the boy able to eat the food that drove away the crows?"
He replied, “I can.
The World-Honored One, the Buddha, said:
“From now on, it is permitted for a śrāmaṇera who can drive away crows, even one as young as seven years old, to be ordained as a śrāmaṇera.
At that time, King Bimbisāra [instituted] a leap month every six years; the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should follow the laws of the king.
At that time, King Bimbisāra observed a six-month short year; the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should follow the laws of the kingdom.
The first month of spring is large [thirty days] and the second month is small [twenty-nine days]; the third month is large and the fourth month is small."
The first month of summer is large and the second month is small; the third month is large and the fourth month is small.
The first month of winter is large and the second month is small; the third month is large and the fourth month is small.
He asked again:
"If the *poṣadha* is recited at a place that is not a bhikṣu’s residence, is this considered a valid *poṣadha*?
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī recites the precepts, is this the recitation of the precepts?
He asked again:
"If a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts recites the precepts, is this the recitation of the precepts?"
The Buddha said:

"This is not called 'reciting the precepts. One may listen to the recitation of the precepts and perform the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), but one cannot count toward the quorum for the recitation of the precepts, the *varṣā*, or other formal acts (*karmavācanā*)."
“Is there any bhikṣu who is pure while on the ground and pure while in the air?
The Buddha said, “No.”
“Are the sky and the earth pure?
The Buddha said, “They are not.”
“Can both [of them] attain purification while remaining in mid-air?
The Buddha said,
“They cannot.”
“Is it permissible to receive the purity-attestation of one who is outside the boundary while remaining within the boundary?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permissible.”
“May one who is outside the boundary receive the purity [confession] from someone inside the boundary?
The Buddha said:
“One may not.”
"One who combines the boundaries may receive it;
one who is within the common boundary may also receive it.
He asked again:
“Can those who are on the ground receive the pure recitation of the precepts together with those in the air?
The Buddha said, “They cannot.”
“Can the precepts be recited for one who has attained purity while in mid-air?
The Buddha said,
“They cannot.”
He asked again:
"If both are in mid-air, may they recite the *Poṣadha* together with those on pure ground?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Is it permissible to recite the precepts with one who is pure while inside the boundary for someone who is outside the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Is it permissible to recite the *Poṣadha* with those who are pure within the boundary when one is outside the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"No. However, it is permissible if the boundaries have been joined;
it is also permissible if they are together within the same boundary."
He asked again:
"May those on the ground join with those in the air?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Can one obtain [it] in space as one does on the ground?
The Buddha said:
"No. "If both are in mid-air, can one give their consent (*chanda*)?
The Buddha said:
"No. "May one receive the consent (*chanda*) from within the boundary for those outside the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"No. [The questioner asked:
"May one who is outside the boundary give their consent (chanda) to those within the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
If the boundaries are joined, it is permitted.
If they are together within the boundary, it is permitted."
He asked again:
"May one perform the *karmavācanā* for a formal act of will while on the ground and [the candidate] is in the air?
The Buddha said:
"No. [The questioner asked:
"May one perform the *karma* of desire with those in mid-air and those on the ground?
The Buddha said:
"No. "If both are in mid-air, may the *karma* of granting consent (*yadṛcchā*) be performed?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Is it permissible to grant the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a *chanda* (consent) within the boundary (*sīmā*) to one who is outside the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"No. "Is it permissible to grant the formal act (*karma*) of consent (*chanda*) from outside the boundary to those within the boundary?
The Buddha said:
"No. However, for those who have united the boundaries, it is permissible; for those who are together within the boundary, it is permissible.
He asked again:
"Can one obtain [the fruit] on the ground as well as in mid-air?
The Buddha said:
"One cannot."
“Can one who is in the air obtain the desire for the earth?
The Buddha said,
“One cannot.”
“If both are suspended in mid-air, can one give their consent?
The Buddha said,
“It cannot be done.”
“Is it permissible to grant the *chanda* (consent) of those outside the boundary to those within the boundary?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permissible.”
“May one who is outside the boundary give their consent (*chanda*) to those within the boundary?
The Buddha said:
“One may not.”
"One who has joined the boundary may receive it;
one who is together within the boundary may receive it.
He asked again:
"Is it possible to establish a boundary between what is on the ground and what is in the air?
The Buddha said,
"It is not possible."
“Can one establish a boundary for the desire-realm within the air?
The Buddha said,
“One cannot.”
“Can those two, while both remaining in mid-air, establish a boundary by means of the *chanda* (consent)?
The Buddha said, “They cannot.”
“Is it permissible to establish a boundary by receiving the consent (*chanda*) of those outside the boundary?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permissible.”
“Can one who is outside the boundary confer the formal consent (*chanda*) of those within the boundary to establish a new boundary?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permitted.”
"One who joins the boundary may obtain it;
one who is already within the boundary together with others may also obtain it.
He asked again:
"If one does not relinquish the previous boundary, can one obtain a broad boundary or a narrow boundary?
The Buddha said,
"One cannot."
He asked again:
"Is it permissible to establish boundary markers simultaneously?
The Buddha said:
"It is permissible for one who explains the internal and external characteristics in their entirety.
He asked again:
"Is there any case where a boundary is not relinquished by means of a formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*)?"
The Buddha said, "There is;
for example, within a wall or a moat.
He asked again:
“May a bhikṣu establish a boundary while standing upon a tree?
The Buddha said,
“If the quorum of the assembly is complete at the time of the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it may be done.”
He asked again:
“If the Saṃgha is split, can a boundary be established?
The Buddha said:
"It is permissible to establish a boundary according to the Dharma.
He asked again:
"For how long will the Buddha-dharma of the past remain in the world?"
The Buddha said:
"When pure bhikṣus who do not violate the Dharma recite the precepts, it is called the Dharma abiding in the world.
He asked again:
“How long will the Buddha-dharma remain in the world in the future?
The Buddha said,
“As long as pure bhikṣus recite the precepts without violating the Dharma, it is called the period when the Dharma remains in the world.”
He asked again:
"How long will the World-Honored One’s Dharma remain in the world?
The Buddha said:
"When the pure bhikṣus who do not violate the Dharma recite the precepts, it is called 'the Dharma abiding in the world.
He asked again:
"If bhikṣus first construct a monastery within a village, to what extent should the boundary (sīmā) be established?"
The Buddha said:
"It follows the village; it follows the boundary of the village, extending as far as the place where people come and go.
He asked again:
“If a bhikṣu is constructing a monastery for the first time at a forest dwelling (āraṇyaka-śayanāsana), how large should the boundary (sīmā) be made?
The Buddha said:
“Each side shall be one krośa.”
Within one *krośa*, all the bhikṣus therein must gather together in a single place to perform the *poṣadha* and carry out formal legal acts (*karmavācanā*).
They must not separately recite the precepts or perform formal legal acts apart from the assembly.
"One who performs it separately incurs an offense.
He asked again:
"When the Dharma is about to perish, is a boundary established at that time called 'establishing a boundary'?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not called 'binding the boundary.
At the time when the Dharma perishes, all boundaries, all receiving of precepts, all precepts, and all *karmavācanā* rituals perish."
He asked again:
"If a bhikṣu who has performed the *karmavācanā* dies, and the remaining bhikṣus do not know the boundaries of the precinct, may they relinquish the boundary?
The Buddha said:
“[He] attains [the robe], but relinquishes it.
He asked again:
“If a bhikṣu constructs a monastery on a mountain, may he observe the rains retreat at a location ten *krośas* below the mountain?”
The Buddha said,
“It is obtained.
He asked again:
"Where should the items for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) be given?
The Buddha said,
"They should be given at the place where the *varṣā* was observed."
He asked again:
“If a bhikṣu builds a monastery at the foot of a mountain and observes the rains retreat ten *krośas* up on the mountain, is this permissible?
The Buddha said: “It is permissible.”
“Where should the items for the rainy-season retreat be given?
The Buddha said,
“They should be given according to the place where one has stayed during the retreat.”
He asked again:

"If the Sangha is split into two factions, and one faction has a bhikṣu go beyond the boundary, such that the time for the end of the retreat arrives, is this called a breach of the *anvāsaṃvāsana* (the rainy season retreat)?"
"Does one who loses his robe incur the offense of breaking one's own word?
The Buddha said:
"He does not break the rains retreat nor lose the robe, but he incurs only the offense of breaking one's own word."
He asked again:
"Where does one receive the seven-day rite?
The Buddha said:
"Receive it within the boundary.
"From whom shall I receive it?
The Buddha said:
"Receiving [the precepts] from the five assemblies:
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
He asked again:
“May one receive the seven-day rule by means of a mental intimation?
The Buddha said,
“One may not.”
Five types of persons are exempted:
namely, forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), those who live alone, those traveling on a long journey, those who have been ill for a long time, and those living among their kinsmen during a time of famine.
He asked again:
"Suppose there are non-Buddhist relatives who send a messenger to summon a bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable sir, please come; we are now performing a sacrifice to Maheśvara, Gandharva, and Maṇibhadra.'"
"Is it permissible to break the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) and depart?
The Buddha said,
"It is permissible to depart, for the sake of their purity."
He asked again:

"If a bhikṣu has not mastered the recitation of the Āgamas and wishes to recite them more fluently, or wishes to inquire about them, or wishes to receive further instruction from another, may he break the rains retreat and depart?"
The Buddha said, “It is so.
He asked again:

"If one has not yet attained what is to be attained, has not yet understood what is to be understood, or has not yet realized what is to be realized, may one break the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) to go [in search of it]?
The Buddha said,
"One may go."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“With what kind of hide are the leather sandals made?
[The Buddha replied] as previously stated.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'sitting upon a hide'?
The Buddha said:
"To have one's body clothed is called 'sitting.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'lying upon a hide'?"
The Buddha said:
"To have one's side touch [the ground] is called lying down.
[The monk asked: "What is meant by 'being attached'?"
The Buddha said,
"From the feet to the navel— this is called attachment.
He asked again:
"Can one eat the skin, flesh, blood, and sinews of a lion?
The Buddha said,
"None of these may be eaten."
He asked again:
"May one eat the flesh, blood, and sinews of a black deer skin?"
The Buddha said,
"With the exception of the skin, the remainder may be eaten.
He asked again:
"The Buddha previously stated that one must not eat raw meat or blood. If one is ill and other medicines cannot cure it, is it permissible to eat them?
The Buddha said, "It is permissible to eat them."
"If there is another medicine that can cure the illness, one must not eat [the meat].
To eat it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
A certain bhikṣu suffering from hemorrhoids went to Jīvaka and said:
“Cure this illness of mine,” [the king said]. Jīvaka replied,
“It must be treated by surgical incision.”
The bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha does not permit cutting with a blade.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He pinched it with his fingernails.
When he could not break it even while pinching, the Buddha said:
"Use a splinter of bamboo or a bamboo skewer to cut it."
When they cut it but could not sever it, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One should cut it with a knife in a secluded place.
When King Bimbisāra was dying, the bhikṣus said to one another:
“King Bimbisāra has died; shall we not henceforth stay overnight within [the monastery]?
The Buddha said, “Monks!”
"Do you mean that because King Bimbisāra has died, it is considered 'staying overnight within' [the monastery]?
Because King Ajātaśatru has taken his place, it is not called 'staying overnight within.
There was a bhikṣu who traveled along the same road with a śrāmaṇera and a lay attendant carrying food. At mealtime, the lay attendant brought the food to the bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu would not eat it.
"Could this not be leftover food from the previous night?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“There is no offense for one who carries [the burden] for another.
He asked again:
“Is it permissible to receive and maintain an uncut robe?”
The Buddha said,
"You may receive it.
He asked again:
“Is it permissible to enter a village while wearing them?
The Buddha said, “It is not.”
"How should it be cut?
The Buddha said:
"Five cubits in length and three cubits in width."
There was a robe that was less than five cubits in length;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to keep three kinds of robes:
superior, middling, and inferior."
"The superior [robe] is five cubits long and three cubits wide; the inferior is four cubits long and two and a half cubits wide; that which is between these two is called the middling.
Because the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* was torn while being tied with a cord, the Buddha said:
"One should wear it as a *kuśūla*."
There was a monk with soft skin who, while rubbing his upper arm, wounded it. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Allow a space of about five inches below [the shoulder].
They asked again:
“Should a bhikṣu accept a *kaurava*?
The Buddha said,
“He should not accept it.”
"One who obtains a robe that has been damaged may have it made into a *kuśūla*.
In the kingdom of Kośala, someone offered robes to the Saṃgha; the bhikṣus did not know how to divide them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Divide it into four parts.
Give three parts to the bhikṣus and one part to the śrāmaṇeras."
In the kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣu died, and it was not known how his robes and bowl should be divided.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"Divide them into four parts."
"Give three parts to the bhikṣus and one part to the śrāmaṇeras.
When the newly built Jetavana was completed, many bhikṣus gathered there, numbering twelve hundred and fifty.
When the lay devotees saw the great assembly gathered, they offered robes to the community of bhikṣus;
however, the bhikṣus did not accept them, saying, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept robes as a gift for the Saṃgha."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permissible to accept robes offered to the community of monks.
When someone offered robes to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣuṇīs did not accept them.
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept robes offered by the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to accept robes offered by the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
Someone offered robes to the Saṃgha of both divisions, but the members of the two divisions would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept robes from the Saṃgha of both divisions.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I have received the robes of the two assemblies of monks.
Not knowing how to divide them,
he reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Divide it into four parts.
Give three parts to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and one part to the śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs."
A householder, seeing the great assembly gathered, offered robes to the community of bhikṣus.
The householder thought to himself:
"It would be well if one bhikṣu were to announce and explain this to us."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to announce it.
When announcing, one should not stand so far away that it cannot be heard; the Buddha said: [this is permitted].
"Listen from atop the earthen mound.
Yet, even atop the mound, it could not be heard from afar. The Buddha said:
"One should stand at a high place so that one may both be seen and heard from a distance."
There were some lay devotees who, seeing the great assembly gathered to receive robes, thought to themselves:
"It would be well if I were permitted to place my robes on the robe-rack and enter the Saṃgha.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen. There was a householder who, seeing the great assembly gathered to offer robes to the Saṃgha, thought to himself:
"It would be well if one person were to praise the Saṃgha."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to offer praise.
One who praises the Saṃgha should speak as follows:

“The Saṃgha is endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of mindfulness, the perfection of samādhi, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of liberation, and the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation; it consists of those in training and those beyond training, those liberated in both ways, and those who are progressing toward or have attained the fruits.”
Among them, those who had not yet attained the Path harbored doubts and did not accept their shares, thinking:

"Since I am neither a learner (śaikṣa) nor one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), neither one liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) nor one progressing toward or having attained the fruit, I ought not to receive a share."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should accept it.

If one upholds the precepts, remains in harmony with the Saṃgha, seeks liberation and detachment from birth-and-death, and turns toward Nirvāṇa without seeking rebirth, one practices the three types of action:”
"By practicing seated meditation, reciting the sūtras, and assisting with communal affairs, such a practitioner shall obtain a pure portion of the offerings.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Śobhavatī with five hundred arhats. Having arrived at the house of the elder Cūḍapanthaka to receive food, they proceeded to the Anavatapta Lake to eat.

When Mṛgāramātṛ heard that today the World-Honored One, together with five hundred arhats, had entered the city of Śobhavatī, gone to the house of the elder Cūḍapanthaka to receive food, and then proceeded to the Anavatapta Lake to eat; she heard this.
Having heard this, he conceived faith and with a pure mind went to where the Buddha was staying. Prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet and sitting to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Today you entered the city of Śobhavatī with five hundred arhats; after receiving food at the house of the elder Jīvika, you proceeded to the Anavatapta Lake to eat.”
“World-Honored One!
I now invite the Buddha and separately invite five hundred arhats for tomorrow’s meal.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Upon arriving home, he prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink throughout the entire night. At dawn, he spread out seats; Ānanda and the Buddha then went to receive their portions of the meal.
Then Mṛgāramātṛ first called Ānanda into her house and closed the door; she then went to inform him:
"The time has come; the food and drink are prepared. The Buddha himself knows the proper time."

At that time, the five hundred arhats each used their supernormal powers: some entered through the lattice windows, some descended from the air, some emerged from the ground, and some appeared from within their seats.
Having seen that the Saṃgha was seated, Mṛgāramātṛ opened the door and personally served the food.
At that time, Ānanda, having first finished his own meal, delivered the Buddha’s portion of food; he went to where the Buddha was, poured water for him, and presented the food.
When the Buddha had finished eating, he performed the ritual washing of his hands, and having set aside his bowl, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Today, Mṛgāramātṛ has separately invited five hundred arhats for a meal."
The Buddha, knowing the answer, asked Ānanda:
"Has one bhikṣu been requested from among the Saṃgha?
He replied:
"No," the Buddha said,
"this Mṛgāramātṛ was ignorant and unskillful; she did not invite even a single person from the Saṃgha."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“If Mṛgāramātṛ were to invite even one person from among the Saṃgha, because of this she would, in a future life, obtain great merit, obtain a great reward, and obtain great benefit.”
The Buddha’s words were heard everywhere, both far and near:
"Inviting one person from within the Saṃgha brings great merit; it is superior to separately inviting five hundred arhats.
Faithful brahmins and householders, providing the Saṃgha with morning meals, midday meals, and *tambula*, had this thought:
"The Buddha has permitted it to be well for one person to be requested to offer praise to the Saṃgha.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"I permit such praise."
The one who offers praise says:

"They are fully endowed with ethical discipline, fully endowed with mindfulness, fully endowed with samādhi, fully endowed with wisdom, fully endowed with liberation, and fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; they are fully endowed with the states of those in training and those beyond training; they are both liberated, and they have attained the fruits directed toward the goal."
Among them were those who had not yet attained the Path; with minds full of doubt, they did not accept [the food], thinking:
"I am neither a learner nor one beyond learning; I am neither liberated in both ways nor one progressing toward or having attained the fruit, and therefore I shall not eat."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to eat.

If one upholds the precepts, lives in harmony with the Sangha, seeks liberation and detachment from birth and death, and turns toward Nirvana without seeking rebirth, they practice the three karmas: [body, speech, and mind]."
"By practicing seated meditation, reciting the sutras, and assisting with the affairs of the community—
in this way, a practitioner may receive food in a state of purity.
He asked again:
“If there is a bhikṣu present when the Saṃgha receives the kaṭhina robe, does it not count as receiving it?
The Buddha said, “It does.”
As it is said in the *Saṃyukta-ekottara-khaṇḍa*:
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu, at the time of receiving the kaṭhina robe, is not present among the assembly, yet it is still considered that he has received it?
The Buddha said:
"There is. As it is said in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*:
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu, while in the process of relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe, is not considered to have relinquished it?"
The Buddha said: "There is.
As it is explained in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
“Is there a case where a bhikṣu, without having relinquished the kaṭhina robe, can be said to have relinquished it?
The Buddha said, “There is.”
As stated in the *Saṃyukta-ekottara-khaṇḍa*.
Furthermore, it was asked:
"Does a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts have the power to obstruct others?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
He asked again:
"Is it permissible to receive an entrustment and then obstruct another?
The Buddha said,
"It is not permissible."
He asked again:
"May one receive the *jñapti-karman*?
The Buddha said:
"No," he replied.
He asked again,
"May a layperson (avadātavasana) stop him?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
He asked again:
"May a śrāmaṇera prevent [the ordination]?
The Buddha said, "He may not."
He asked again:

"Are those who are not bhikṣus, non-Buddhists, those who have not been seen [committing an offense], those who have not been subjected to formal suspension (pravāsanīya), those whose evil views have not been removed, those who do not live in communion, those who live in various forms of non-communion, those who have themselves claimed to have committed a grave offense (pārājika), those who were originally laymen, those who have defiled a bhikṣuṇī, eunuchs, those who have crossed over [to another sect], those who have killed their father or mother, those who have killed an arhat, those who have caused a schism in the Saṃgha, and those who have shed the blood of a Buddha with malicious intent—are such persons subject to the prohibition?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
He asked again:

"If one is on the ground while another is in the air, or in the air while another is on the ground, or both are in the air; or if they are inside the boundary while the other is outside, or outside the boundary while the other is inside; or if they have not reached the midst of the Saṃgha, or have not informed the assembly, or are persons of broken precepts—can one who intends to object by mental resolve succeed in obstructing?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
He asked again:
"May a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts recite the *karmavācanā*?
The Buddha said, "He may not."

"As previously stated, regarding those who have committed a grave offense, those who are thieves falsely claiming to be bhikṣus, or those who were originally laypeople and broke the precepts—if they first say, 'I have broken the precepts,' and a karmavācanā is subsequently performed for them, does it count as a valid karmavācanā?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
[The monk asked: "If one first performs the *karmavācanā* and later says, 'I have broken the precepts,' does this count as a valid *karman*?"
The Buddha said, “Yes.
He asked again:
"Is there a case where one performs the *karmavācanā* at the time of receiving the precepts, yet discards the *karmavācanā* after having received them?
The Buddha said, "There is."
“What *karmavācanā* is it that is being relinquished? He replied,
“It is the *karmavācanā* for the full ordination (*upasampadā*).”
“Is there a case where a person who has received the precepts performs a *karmavācanā*, yet a person who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) abandons [the procedure]?
The Buddha said, “There is.”
“What is meant by ‘existing’? He replied,
“I am a layperson (avadātavasana), and thus I immediately relinquish all formal monastic acts (karmavācanā).”
“Is it possible that a bhikṣu who has been suspended, having repented in his heart and humbled himself, might be granted the lifting of the suspension outside the boundary?
Would he obtain the lifting? The Buddha said, “He would obtain the lifting, but the bhikṣus [who performed the act] incur an offense.”
He asked again:
"For what offense is the *kukṛtya-karman* (act of censure) performed?
The Buddha said:
"Quarreling.
He asked again:
"For what offense is the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) performed?"
The Buddha said,
"He repeatedly violates the precepts.
He asked again:
"For what offense was the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) performed?
The Buddha said:
"For defiling families."
He asked again:
"For what offense is the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of reconciliation) performed?
The Buddha said:
"He reviled a layperson.
He asked again:
"If a bhikṣu reviles another bhikṣu, can the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of reconciliation) be performed?"
The Buddha said, "It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
"If one reviles a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of subduing the mind) be performed?"
The Buddha said, "It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
"If a bhikṣuṇī reviles another bhikṣuṇī, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of humbling) be performed against her?"
The Buddha said, "One may perform it. [The questioner asked:
"If one reviles a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or a bhikṣu, may one perform the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of humbling the mind) against them?"
The Buddha said, "It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
"If a śikṣamāṇā reviles another śikṣamāṇā, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of humbling) be performed against her?"
The Buddha said, "It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
"If one reviles a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, or a bhikṣuṇī, may the *karmavācanā* for subduing the mind (*adhyāśaya-karman*) be performed?"
The Buddha said, "It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
"If a śrāmaṇera reviles another śrāmaṇera, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of reconciliation) be performed against him?"
The Buddha said, "It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
"If one reviles a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or a śikṣamāṇā, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of humble submission) be performed?"
The Buddha said, “It may be performed. [The questioner asked:
“If a śrāmaṇerikā reviles another śrāmaṇerikā, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of subduing the mind) be performed against her?”
The Buddha said, “It may be performed. [He asked again:
“If one reviles a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇera, may the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of subduing) be performed?”
The Buddha said, "It may be done.
He asked again:
"If a śrāmaṇera confesses that he has committed sexual misconduct, should he be expelled?
The Buddha said,
"He should be expelled."
He asked again:
"Is there any bhikṣu who, having less than five years of seniority, may live his entire life without relying on another for formal dependence (niśraya) and yet incur no offense?
The Buddha said:
“There is. If a bhikṣu dies before five years have passed, or if he dwells under a preceptor for as long as his life lasts.
He asked again:

"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to commit various dissimilar saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses—such as intentionally emitting semen and concealing it for one night; intentionally touching a woman's body and concealing it for two nights; using harsh speech and concealing it for three nights; praising oneself by offering physical service and concealing it for four nights;

and acting as a matchmaker and concealing it for five nights—and yet, after performing the *parivāsa* (probation) for five nights and the *mānatva* (penance) for six nights, be granted the *karma* for the removal of the offense?"
The Buddha said, "Yes.
He asked again:
“As the Buddha has taught, there are offenses that are similar and offenses that are dissimilar.
What is meant by ‘similar’?
The Buddha said:

"Pārājika and that which resembles pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa and that which resembles saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika and that which resembles pāyattika, pratideśanīya and that which resembles pratideśanīya, duṣkṛta and that which resembles duṣkṛta—this is called resemblance in offense."
"What does 'not similar' mean?
"Pārājika is not similar to Saṃghāvaśeṣa, Pāyattika, Pratideśanīya, or Duṣkṛta; Saṃghāvaśeṣa is not similar to Pāyattika, Pratideśanīya, Duṣkṛta, or Pārājika."
The *pāyattika* is dissimilar to the *pratideśanīya*, the *dukkaṭa*, the *pārājika*, and the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The *pratideśanīya* is dissimilar to the *dukkaṭa*, the *pārājika*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and the *pāyattika*. The *dukkaṭa* is dissimilar to the *pārājika*, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the *pāyattika*, and the *pratideśanīya*.
He asked again:
"As the Buddha has taught that there are offenses that can be measured and offenses that cannot be measured,
what is an offense that can be measured?"
The Buddha said:
"It can be stated as a number.
[The monk asked: "What is an immeasurable offense?"
The Buddha said,
"Their number cannot be told.
He asked again:
“As the Buddha has taught, there are offenses that are concealed and offenses that are not concealed.
What constitutes an offense that is concealed?
The Buddha said:
"To fail to confess for even a brief moment.
"What is meant by 'not concealing'?
"To not conceal for even a brief moment."
The Buddha said to Upāli: "There is one kind of offense whose natures are each distinct:

the nature of *pārājika* offenses is each distinct; the nature of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses is each distinct; the nature of *pāyattika* offenses is each distinct; the nature of *pratideśanīya* offenses is each distinct; and the nature of *duṣkṛta* offenses is each distinct."
After the bhikṣus had performed the formal act of separate residence with another, they sent a messenger to sweep other rooms; as they entered and exited these various places, many people saw them.
The Buddha said:

"Once you have performed the formal act of separate residence with another, you should have the messenger sweep only the interior of the room where you reside; you must not send a messenger to sweep other rooms."
At that time, he was staying in a secluded place and did not see the visiting bhikṣu when he arrived.
The Buddha said:
"One should not stay in a secluded place; one should be visible when a visiting bhikṣu arrives."
At that time, he called out to the visiting bhikṣu by name; having done so, he caused a disturbance.
The Buddha said:
"One must not call out to others; one should simply speak to them so that they may know."
When a visiting bhikṣu departed, [another] ran after him. The Buddha said:
"One should not run while following the standard rules of conduct.
At that time, he pursued him beyond the boundary. The Buddha said:
"You must not go beyond the boundary.
If the person ahead of you goes beyond the boundary, you should remain within your own boundary.

From now on, I shall instruct you in the rules for living apart: you should sweep and sprinkle the Buddha-stūpa and smear its floor; you should also sweep, sprinkle, and smear the floor of the place where the Poṣadha is held, as well as the place where food is taken."
One should arrange the beds and seats in sequence and prepare water for washing the feet, a vessel for rinsing water, and a vessel for regular use filled with water.

One should inform the visiting bhikṣu so that he may be aware of these things; one should wipe his *puṭa* sandals and his feet. All the rules regarding separate residence (*pārivāsika*) must be observed: one should not stay in a secluded place, nor should one stay in a public place.
He asked again:

"Once one has undergone the *parivāsa* (probation), may one perform for another the *parivāsa*, the *mānatva* (penance), the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning), or the *āvarhaṇa* (expiation)?
The Buddha said:
"No," he replied.
He asked again:

"May a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts perform the acts of separate residence (pārivāsika), penance (mānatva), reversion to the beginning of the probationary period (mūlāpakarṣa), or rehabilitation from an offense (ābṛhaṇa) for another?"
The Buddha said,
“It is not permitted.
He asked again:
"May one perform the *parivāsa* penance in the presence of another who is already undergoing *parivāsa*?
The Buddha said:
"One may not."
He asked again:
"If one who has received the full ordination acts as a śrāmaṇera undergoing *parivāsa* or *mānatva*, is that permissible?
The Buddha said:

"No. He asked again: "Is it permissible to give the *chanda* (consent), the *pārisuddhi* (purification), the *varṣa* (formal retreat), or the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation of offenses) to one who is living apart?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not permitted.
He asked again:
“Is it permissible to grant the attainment of precepts, purification for a śrāmaṇera, the formal expression of desire, the observance of the *varṣa*, or the removal of offenses?
The Buddha said, “It is not permissible.”
He asked again:

"May one who has received the *parivāsa* (probation) receive the purity (*śuddhi*), the consent (*chanda*), the observance of the *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat), and the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*)?
The Buddha said:
"No. He asked again: "Is it permissible to receive the precepts from a śrāmaṇera who is pure, to receive his consent, to perform the *varṣā* ceremony, or to undergo the removal of offenses?"
The Buddha said,
"This great bhikṣu may indeed receive it.
He asked again:
"With what materials is the door-bolt made?
The Buddha said:
"It is made of copper, iron, wood, wool, kusha grass, cotton, hemp, or the bark of the śiṃśapā tree."
He asked again,
"What material is used to make the net?
The Buddha said:
"It is made from wool, kusa grass, cotton, hemp, or the bark of the śiṃśapā tree.
He asked again:
"What material is used to make the meditation belt?"
The Buddha said:
"It is made from wool, kusa grass, cotton, hemp, śāṇa grass, bark, and so forth.
He asked again:
"With what material are the sparrow-eyes made?
The Buddha said,
"They are made of wood or bamboo."

At that time, King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a hundred-year period of offerings. However, the people assigned to provide the offerings had little faith and prepared the food improperly; when the bhikṣus went out to seek alms, they were seen to cause distress and confusion among many people.
With a mind of pure faith, the king asked,
"Have the bhikṣus been disturbed?
They replied:
"Troublesome," [the king said].
The King replied, "I also know that you, Great Virtue, are troublesome; I shall provide you with fields and houses in full abundance, according to your wishes."
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept fields and houses.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I shall listen and receive it.
Furthermore, after the householder had constructed dwellings within the Jeta Grove, he provided them with robes, food, bedding, and medicine.
Later, the bhikṣu who was the master of those dwellings went to the householder’s residence to request what he required.

Having arrived and taken their seats, when the time came for the exchange of greetings, the householder’s wife prostrated herself at his feet and sat before him. He then preached the Dharma to her in various ways: with gentle words, with eloquence, and with skillful discourse.
Having heard this teaching of the sublime Dharma, the householder’s wife attained pure faith and said:
"Venerable Sir, this robe is for your sake;
I give it to the monks residing in the monastery. These sons, daughters, and wives of mine also give to the monks residing in the monastery."
That bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I require only one robe; these robes are now too many, and I do not know what to do.
He related this matter in detail to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a layperson builds a monastery cell for the Sangha, and if they offer that cell within the monastery to a single bhikṣu, the monks residing in that cell should share it together.
At that time, a monastery cell at Ālavī had fallen into ruin; the Buddha, seeing this, knew the reason but asked Ānanda deliberately:
"Why has this cell fallen into ruin?"
Ānanda replied,
"Because they are protected by the group of six bhikṣus, no one dares to discipline them.
The Buddha said:
Regarding those six groups of bhikṣus whose dwellings were dilapidated and whom they were unable to repair, it was said that they should have them repaired by others.

Having received [the task], the other people did only a little work and then stopped—such as applying a single lump of mud, a handful of grass, smearing a small patch of ground, slightly filling a hole in the wall, or slightly repairing a mound of earth.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be given to one who has treated few [patients], but it should be given to one who has treated many.
He also gave it for as long as one lived; the Buddha said:
"One should not give it for as long as one lives, nor should one give it for a short time.
If the dwelling has been damaged, one should give it for six years; if it is a new dwelling, one should give it for twelve years."
The bhikṣu Ālavī, being a skilled craftsman, daily requested tools from others.
The laypeople said, "Venerable sir, why do you not make them yourself?"
He replied,
“The Buddha has not yet permitted its possession.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should keep tools for work.

When the Āravī monks were building a new monastery, there were laborers who worked for half a month, or for a month, or for a year; when it rained, they would request food, firewood, grass, and lamps.
When it was time for the bhikṣus to give [the robes], they hesitated in their minds and, fearing transgression, did not give them.
If they did not give them, they would not perform the ritual; the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you know that [the time] has come, call him here and he shall do it; you should give it to him.
There was a bhikṣu wearing newly dyed robes who, while washing his feet on open ground during a rainstorm, soiled the robes that they lost their color and became mottled like white leprosy.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should build a house.
After it was built, because it was not roofed over, it leaked during the rain; the Buddha said:
"It should be covered.
After it was covered, water leaked from the back;
the Buddha said, "The back should be covered thickly."
In the great monastic complex of Rājagṛha, there were often many visiting bhikṣus who arrived during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night.
At such times, the senior bhikṣus would drive the junior bhikṣus away, causing them disturbance.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"When the ghaṇṭā is struck and the announcement is made, one should light lamps, divide the sitting mats, and spread out the bedding. When the stars appear, one should place a meditation weight upon the head. If an elder (sthavira) arrives, one should not drive him away or make him rise."
"If you drive him away, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Furthermore, when a junior monk sat in the place of a senior monk, the senior monk rebuked him, saying:
"How can a junior monk sit in the place of a senior monk?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A junior monk must not sit in the place of a senior monk.
If he does so, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"A junior bhikṣu should inspect his seat and count his seniority; he should sit only where it is appropriate for him to sit.

When the Elder Ārāḍa sat in meditation during the first watch of the night and returned to his room during the middle watch, his disciples escorted him away. Thereafter, junior bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras rose from the floor or from the wooden planks and lay down upon their beds.
The Elder returned and attempted to drive them out in order, but they refused to leave and engaged in quarreling and strife.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If, having finished spreading out bedding during the middle watch of the night, one does not rise from their place in the proper sequence, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one does rise from their place, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The group of six bhikṣus, at the places for defecation and urination and at the places for drawing water, drove others away in turn according to seniority, causing disturbance and vexation; thus some bhikṣus were troubled.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, at places for defecating and urinating, or at places for drawing water, you must not drive others away in succession."
"To drive someone away [from their place] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The group of six bhikṣus drove others away from their places in the foot-washing area, causing them distress and agitation.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, at the place for washing feet, if another has already applied water there, you must not drive them away in turn to make them rise.

Regarding the items used by the Saṃgha for wiping the feet, there was a bhikṣu who first took a foot-cloth (*pādukā*) to wash, wring out, and spread it to dry; at that time, the group of six bhikṣus (the Ṣaḍvargika) took it from him in succession, yet he did not quarrel with them when they would not give it back.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Those who took it first may use it; those who arrive later should wait until its use is finished."

The Sangha was boiling rice porridge; the ladle and spoon had already been taken and washed by a certain bhikṣu, when the group of six bhikṣus successively seized them. He did not fight with them over it.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Those who arrived first may use it; those who arrive later should wait until it is finished."

The Sangha possessed wooden bowls and wooden basins. A certain bhikṣu took one to wash it for use, but the group of six bhikṣus successively seized them from him; he did not fight with them when they would not give them back.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"Those who arrived first may use it; those who arrive later should wait until it is finished."

The Sangha had small bowls, basins, and ladles. A certain bhikṣu had already taken some soap powder to wash them with, but the group of six bhikṣus took them from him in succession; he did not fight with them when they refused to give them back.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who arrived first may use it; those who arrive later should wait until it is finished."

The Sangha possessed razors, tweezers, and nail clippers. A certain bhikṣu took them first and used them for sharpening; the group of six bhikṣus then seized them in succession, yet he did not quarrel with them when they would not give them back.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Those who arrived first may use it; those who arrive later should wait until it is finished."

The Sangha possessed robes, beds, clothespins, ropes, needles, knives, wooden sprinklers, and thimbles; there was a bhikṣu who first took them to spread out the robes, patch the robes, and sew the robes.
The group of six bhikṣus successively seized and tore apart worn-out robes, yet the other monks did not fight with them.
Not knowing what to do, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not give it away.
Those who have already begun using it may continue; those who arrive later must wait until it is finished.
From now on, in such various matters, one must not take another's property by displacing them from their sequence."
"If one takes it by force, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyānī suffered from eye pain and went to a physician; the physician said, "You should have an enema administered to the nose (*nasya*)."
He replied,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted nasal irrigation.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen for the pouring.
At that time, [the practitioner] would sometimes apply it with a finger or with an object, causing the fluid to enter the eye and increasing the pain even further.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should make a nose-cleansing tube.
"If it is made too large, it is not usable; if it is made too small, it is also not usable. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Do not make it large, and do not make it small; it should be the size of one *pāla* and a half *pāla*."

The Saṃgha possessed incense burners, incense boxes, and needle cases; when a bhikṣu first took them for use, the group of six bhikṣus successively seized them from him, yet he did not quarrel with them when they would not give them back.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That which was taken first shall be used."
"Those who come later shall wait until it is finished.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were speaking to one another in the bathhouse, saying:
"This one is scrubbing so-and-so; this one is scrubbing so-and-so."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In the bathhouse, one must not say, 'Rub me! or 'Rub so-and-so!'"
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
There was a monk who was bathing in a bathhouse together with a layperson; a junior monk or a *śrāmaṇera* was rubbing the senior monk's body.
The layperson said to him, "Is this all you do?"
"Furthermore, perform such and such deeds.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were displeased and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not bathe together with laypeople in the same bathhouse.
Any who violate this shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
There was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who was ill and wished to enter the bathhouse to bathe; the Buddha said:
"One should inform a bhikṣu before entering to bathe.
When they informed a bhikṣu and the bhikṣu did not grant permission, the Buddha said:
"If the bhikṣus know that this upāsaka is virtuous and free from verbal faults, they should allow him to enter."
There was a bhikṣu who scrubbed a layperson in the bathhouse. The Buddha said:
"One must not scrub a layperson in the bathhouse.
One who violates this incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
In the country of Ālavī, bedding and seats were being distributed, and many visiting bhikṣus arrived at evening.
Since the bedding was insufficient, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Distribute [the bedding] according to seniority; if there is none, give them grass or leaves.
Each person shall spread out their own bedding and each put on their own undergarment.
The group of six bhikṣus used pumice stones to rub their bodies until their body hair fell out. The Buddha said:
"One must not scrub the body with pumice stones.
One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī, there were fine yellow fruits lying on the ground; having seen this, the Buddha, knowing the answer, intentionally asked Ānanda:
“Monks, why do you not eat these fruits?
Ānanda said,
“World-Honored One!”
The Buddha previously established a precept: there are four kinds of things that the Saṃgha should not divide;
the same applies to three people, two people, or a single person.
One should not divide the grounds of the monastery, the buildings of the monastery, the monastic groves, or the bedding and utensils of the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said, "The fruit should indeed be divided.

When they divided it, one person would take [the portion] while two or three people shared [the remainder]; thus some obtained much while others obtained nothing, and at that time they fought and quarreled together.
The Buddha said:
"Fruits should not be divided; rather, have a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) perform the five kinds of purification, after which they may be accepted and eaten.
There was a bhikṣu who fought with another bhikṣu; later, that bhikṣu fought with yet another bhikṣu, whereupon he seized the latter by the ear as a witness, causing him to cry out loudly.
Many bhikṣus came and asked,
"Why are you crying out so loudly?
He replied:
"This bhikṣu struck me.
He was asked,
"Did you actually strike him?"
He replied, "I did not strike him; I merely seized his ear as witness.
This bhikṣu previously fought with me and cried out loudly because he wished to slander me."
The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not seize another's ear as evidence.
One who violates this incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
"If such a thing occurs, you should say to those nearby:
'This bhikṣu reviled me and struck me.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus enticed the disciples of others, and the elders rebuked them, saying:
"How can we teach our disciples in accordance with the Dharma when these six groups of bhikṣus entice them away?
The Buddha said,
"From now on, you must not entice the disciples of others."
"One who violates this incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
There were some bhikṣus who abandoned their monastery and departed, saying:
'I shall never return to that place. Is this called 'abandoning the boundary' (*sīmā*)?"
The Buddha said,
“Renounce it.
He asked again:
"With what material is the awl made?
The Buddha said,
"It is made of copper or iron."
He asked again,
"With what material was the knife made?
The Buddha said:
“Make it of copper or iron.
He asked again:
“What material shall be used to make the iron?”
The Buddha said:
"Make it using copper, iron, or clay.
He asked again:
"With what materials are jars made?
The Buddha said,
"They are made of copper, iron, clay, or wood."
He asked again,
"What did you use to make the cauldron?
The Buddha said:
"Use copper, iron, or clay to make it.
He asked again:
"What substance is used to make the bathing powder?"
As previously stated, a father and son from the kingdom of Kośala both went forth into homelessness. The father said to the son:
"Why do you not provide me with food and clothing?"
He replied, "We have both gone forth together; there is nothing available to give.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one has it, one should give it; if one does not have it, one must not forcibly demand it.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had a śrāmaṇera who had hair growing in his private parts.
If one slightly opposes the teacher’s wishes, the teacher immediately strips them of their clothes.
To be naked is shameful and something people do not like; this matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not reprimand a śrāmaṇera for a minor offense.
When reprimanding him, one should leave him with a single robe.
The bhikṣus were unable to obtain a sieve for medicinal substances; the Buddha said:
"One should make a medicine-strainer.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered bedding to the Saṃgha, the bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept it."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha may receive it, and a single person may also receive it.
They asked again:
“The Buddha previously stated that a support eight finger-widths high should be placed beneath the legs of a bed.
Why, then, are supports eight finger-widths high being placed beneath the legs of this bed?
The Buddha said:
"If the legs of a bed are less than eight finger-breadths [in height], one should place wooden supports beneath them.
There was a bhikṣu who first took money from another to provide medicine for emesis and purgation; that person subsequently died, and another bhikṣu said to him:
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
"Why is that? He replied,
"I first took the price and gave it to another, then administered the medicine."
That bhikṣu felt doubt in his mind:
"Could this not constitute an offense of pārājika?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what intention did you give it?
He replied, "I gave it out of compassion."
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
The Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not first take payment and then give medicine to others.
One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There was a bhikṣu who, together with some merchants, was traveling from Kośala toward Śrāvastī.
At that time, bandits came to plunder, and the merchants barely managed to save their lives; the merchants had been stripped by the bandits.
Once they had barely saved their lives, the bhikṣus picked up the others' clothes. They felt doubt, wondering: "Will we not commit a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense.

In the kingdom of Kośala there was a temple and a burial mound that had been sprinkled with blood. As some bhikṣus were traveling from Kośala toward Śrāvastī, they circumambulated the burial mound to the right and the temple to the left.
Then the master of the deva-temple said,
"Venerable sir!
Why do you circumambulate the cemetery to the right and the temple to the left?"
He replied,
"I thought these were stupas for the Buddha and stupas for the śrāvakas.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Whether it be a cemetery or a shrine to the gods, one need not circumambulate to the right, nor need one circumambulate to the left; simply proceed along the path."
There was a bhikṣu who, when the time for hunger arrived, went to the home of a relative and stayed for four or five days.
Having stayed there, he said, "I wish to return.
[The relative asked: "For what reason are you leaving?"

As previously stated, the group of six bhikṣus conferred the precepts upon one who did not possess an alms-bowl. This group of six was constantly at variance with the group of seventeen; it was the turn of the group of six to guard the monastic quarters.
The group of seventeen approached next to receive food; they went and said to the group of six disciples, "Bring your bowls here; we shall give you food.
They replied:
"I have no bowl.
He said to him,
"Do you receive the precepts without a bowl?"
He replied, “Yes. Again he said:
"You are a person of great power and influence, yet you have received the precepts without a bowl.
When that bhikṣu heard this, his heart was not pleased, and he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, one must not confer the precepts upon a person who does not possess a bowl."
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
There were two bhikṣus who fought; one bhikṣu wrote characters on another's bowl and placed it before the door of a courtesan.
At that time, a Brahmin householder who was literate entered this house; seeing the inscription on the bowl, he said, "A bhikṣu has also entered this house.
When the bhikṣu heard these words, his heart was not pleased, and he reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, one must not write characters upon an alms-bowl.
If one writes characters upon an alms-bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
As with the bowl, so it is with all other objects."
There is no offense if one makes a mark.
A non-Buddhist with faith who wished to go forth approached a bhikṣu and said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Allow me to go forth.
He asked, "Do you have an almsbowl?"
He replied, "I have no bowl.
[The monks said,] "We cannot grant the going-forth to one who has no bowl."
Having heard these words, he departed and severed the conditions for his renunciation.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what to do, reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One must not ask for an alms bowl beforehand; one may seek a bowl only after having been ordained and entered the monastic life.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered robes to the Saṅgha, the bhikṣus did not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive these."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Sangha may accept it, and a single person may also accept it.
There was a son of a lay devotee who had gone forth as a monk; that lay devotee fell ill and spoke to his relatives:
"I shall give my wealth and property to my son after my death.
Having said this, he passed away.
Later, when the son returned home to visit, they sat together and exchanged greetings; then his kinsmen said:
"Your father, when he was on the verge of death, spoke these words:
'After my passing, I give my wealth and property to my son.
The bhikṣu replied:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to accept offerings made after death.
Not knowing what to do, that bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I previously spoke for the sake of bhikṣus, not for laypeople;
you may take it as you please.
There was a bhikṣu who traveled abroad for two months and was acquainted with the group of six bhikṣus (ṣaḍvargika); he then entrusted his robe to the group of six.
The group of six asked,
"Where are you going? He replied:
"I wish to go on a journey for two months," as previously stated.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who supported Devadatta spoke to the laypeople, saying:
“I wish to enter into marriage with you.
The householders said, “You are a renunciant; how can you enter into marriage with us?”
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, bhikṣuṇīs must not speak of arranging marriages with laypeople."
"If one speaks [of it], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There was a bhikṣu who had previously given the price for a robe to a householder; later, that bhikṣu passed away.
The other bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should seek the goods and take them to be distributed among the Saṃgha.
There was a bhikṣu who had previously taken another's robe without having paid its price; later, that bhikṣu passed away, and the lay devotee went to the bhikṣu’s place and said:
“Venerable sir, this bhikṣu previously took my robe but has not yet given me its price.
The bhikṣus replied,
“Why did you not come to ask for it while that bhikṣu was still alive?”
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If that robe is still there, it should be returned."
"If there is none, you should sell your robes and bowl to repay it.
The group of six bhikṣus acted as brokers for laypeople, taking their hair and taking their flowers.
The laypeople rebuked them, saying:
“You who have left the household life, what use is this *yishong*? Why do you take hair and gather flowers?
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“From now on, you must not act as a *yishong* to cut hair or gather flowers.”
"One who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
A group of six bhikṣus formed a spiritual friendship with another bhikṣu. This bhikṣu entrusted his bowl to one of the six, but on the way, the bowl broke."
When that bhikṣu saw the group of six, he thought to himself:
"If I do not speak quickly, they may ask for a high price. He then said:
"A certain bhikṣu entrusted his bowl to me to give to you; this bowl broke along the way.
The group of six said, "This is not your bowl that broke; it was my bowl that broke."
"Come and repay me!
The bhikṣu did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If one picks up a broken [bowl] with a good intention, one should not be held liable for its replacement.
A certain bhikṣu used an unbaked bowl for food; when he set it on the ground, it chipped and became stained.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should be fumigated.
At that time, a bhikṣu took his bowl and placed it on the ground; when he applied cow dung around its four sides and set it to burn, the bowl broke.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should construct an incense burner for bowls.
After they had made one and placed it on the ground to burn incense, it melted and broke apart during the burning.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"First, pour down some ash.
After they had poured the ash, it soiled their bowls.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One should support it with stones.
When they supported it, the stones did not encircle it completely; because the wind from the brazier entered, the cloth began to wrinkle.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be well-enclosed all around.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and having sat to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

When the World-Honored One travels among people to teach and transform them, I am always filled with longing and desire to see the Buddha. I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me a small portion [of his belongings] so that I may make an offering.”
The Buddha then gave him his hair, nails, and fingernails,
saying, "You shall make offerings to these.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Please allow me to erect a stūpa with my hair and nails.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, sir.
He spoke again:
"Does the Buddha permit me to paint the walls with red, black, and white colors?"
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to paint the walls with red, black, and white colors.
He further said:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to paint stupas.
The Buddha said,
"With the exception of images depicting the union of men and women, all others are permitted to be painted."
Someone made a canopy for offering, but there was no place to secure it.
The Buddha said:
"It should be fixed by driving in a stake."
At that time, the stupa door had no panels, so cattle, deer, monkeys, dogs, and other animals entered it.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should install door panels."
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to install a railing in front of my door.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so."
“It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to install railings all around.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
“I permit you to do so.”
"In this matter, there was no place to set the flowers. He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to make a vessel for holding flowers.
Once the vessel was full after the flowers were placed, the Buddha said:
"One should provide curved pegs.
When the provision of curved pegs was also completed, the Buddha said:
"One should suspend cords all around."
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
