"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to make garlands of mani jewels and fresh flower garlands.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, I shall do it. He further said:
"It would be well if the Buddha permits me to build a cave-dwelling."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
He spoke again:
"If the Buddha permits me to build a stūpa within my cave, it would be well.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to erect a stūpa within the cave."
“It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to provide a door for the cave.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said,
“I permit you to do so.”
“‘May the Buddha permit me to cover the stūpa within my cave,’ [he requested].
The Buddha said,
‘I permit you to cover it.’”
“‘It would be well if the Buddha would allow me to go out from the top of the rafters.
The Buddha said,
‘I allow you to go out.’”
“I would like the Buddha’s permission to install the rafters and arches.
The Buddha said,
“I permit you to do so.”
“If the Buddha permits me to give pillars for the construction of a stūpa, it would be well.
The Buddha said,
“I permit you to do so.”
“‘May the Buddha permit me to adorn the pillars of the stūpa with colored pigments, red ochre, and white lime.
The Buddha said:
‘I permit you to adorn the pillars.’”
“I request permission from the Buddha to paint [images] upon the pillars of the stūpa.
The Buddha said,
“With the exception of images depicting the union of a man and a woman, all others are permitted.”

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with a mind of pure faith, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and having sat to one side, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Since it is not appropriate to fashion an image of the Buddha’s body, I pray that the Buddha will permit me to fashion an image of a bodhisattva attendant; this would be well.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to do so."
He further said:
"When the Buddha was formerly at home, he had a ceremonial banner led before him.
I pray that the Buddha will permit me to act as the one who leads the banner before him; this would be well."
The Buddha said,
“I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] “It would be well if the Buddha would permit us to construct high pedestals before our stūpas to place lions upon them.”
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[He continued,] "It is well if the lion is made with a railing on all four sides, as the Buddha has permitted."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to make them.
[The monk said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to make the lions out of copper."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to do so.
[The monks asked,] "Does the Buddha permit one to attach a banner to a copper lion? The Buddha said, "It is good to attach a banner to a copper lion."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to tie it [to the neck]. It is well that you should offer me incense, flowers, lamps, and music."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to smear the ground of the stūpa with fragrant flowers and oil."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow the use of incense, flowers, and oil to smear upon the ground of the stūpa.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to construct flower-stands."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to construct a place for placing lamps."
The Buddha said,
“I permit you to build.
[The monks said,] “It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to construct a circular hall.”
The Buddha said, "I permit you to do so.
[The monks asked,] "Does the Buddha permit the installation of wooden frames on the hall to hang banners? [The Buddha replied,] "It is good to install wooden frames on the hall to hang banners."
The Buddha said, "I permit you to do so.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada sent his kinsmen, acquaintances, and those who had borrowed items from him— adorned with men and women, and carrying trays and tables laden with flowers, incense, and necklaces— to the householder’s residence.
Having seen this, the lay devotee thought:
"It would be well if these items were placed at the front.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen. “It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to carry an incense burner while walking in front.
The Buddha said:
"Let those who are listening go ahead.
Some non-Buddhists, giving rise to a mind of jealousy, saw this and rebuked them, saying:
"It is like escorting a corpse."
The householder thought to himself,
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to perform music before the image.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, you may do so.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with pure faith, thought to himself:
"By what means can I assemble a great multitude and provide them with food and clothing?"
He went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will permit me to assemble the great assembly for a meal; it would be well.
The Buddha said:
"May it be permitted for the great assembly to eat.
He spoke these words:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to provide food for the great assembly when making offerings to the stūpa."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permits us to hold the Pañcavārṣika festival."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to hold a *pañcavārṣika* assembly.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to hold a six-year assembly."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permits us to hold the assembly from the sixteenth day of the first month until the fifteenth day of the second month."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to hold a festival within our monastery."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to do so. At that time,
the bhikṣus did not enter in order, did not sit in order, did not eat in order, did not rise in order, and did not depart in order.
There were those who entered before [the meal had begun], those who entered while food was being served, those who entered while eating, and those who entered after the meal was finished.
The Buddha said:
"One should announce that the time has arrived."
When the time for the proclamation arrived, the sound was not heard from afar. This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"You should strike the *gandī*.
After striking the *gandī*, it was still not heard from afar. This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"One should beat the drum.
When they beat the drum while on the ground, it could not be heard from afar. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Beat it upon a raised platform."
When he struck it upon the platform, the sound was not heard from afar.
The Buddha said, "You should strike it from a high place so that those at a distance may hear it.
Seeing a great assembly gathered, many people came to look on, and they offered items for the stūpa, items for the Saṃgha of the four quarters, food, and items to be distributed.
The bhikṣus did not know which items belonged to the stūpa,
which items belonged to the Saṃgha of the four quarters,
and which items were for food.
"What items should be divided?
[The monks] reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When distributing the items, have one bhikṣu stand there and observe so that he may know how to distinguish them."
"These are items belonging to the stupa, items belonging to the Saṃgha from the four quarters, food items,
and items that ought to be distributed. The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"Regarding these four kinds of property—
the property of a stūpa, the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters, food, and property that should be distributed— is it permissible to use them interchangeably?
The Buddha said:
"No," the Buddha said to Upāli. "Regarding items belonging to a stūpa:
they must not be given to the Saṃgha of the four directions, they must not be used for food, and they must not be distributed."
Regarding the property of the Sangha of the four directions: it must not be used for food, it must not be distributed, and it must not be used for stūpas.
Regarding food: it must not be distributed, it must not be used for stūpas, and it must not be given to the Sangha of the four directions.
"Those items that should be distributed shall be used by the Saṃgha according to its needs.
When the first rule has been proclaimed and the first phrase completed, it is called "abandoning the precepts.
What is meant by "proclaiming one phrase" being called "abandoning the precepts"?
It means to say:
"I renounce the Buddha.
Uttering these words is called the abandonment of the precepts.
In this way, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the upādhyāya, the ācārya, the co-resident upādhyāya and ācārya, the bhikṣus, the bhikṣuṇīs, the śikṣamāṇās, the śrāmaṇeras, and the śrāmaṇerīs shall know:
"I am a layperson; I am a śrāmaṇera; I am not a bhikṣu; I am a follower of external paths; I am neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya; I do not accept your Dharma."
To speak these words is called "abandoning the precepts.

If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances and great influence such that what he says is trusted and believed by all, and is well-known to the community and able to provide for the Saṃgha, yet he speaks what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaks what is Dharma as not Dharma; speaks what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, speaks what is Vinaya as not Vinaya; speaks an offense as no offense, speaks no offense as an offense; speaks a grave matter as light, speaks a light matter as grave; speaks a non-residual offense as residual, speaks a residual offense as non-residual; speaks what is not a constant practice as a constant practice, speaks what is a constant practice as not a constant practice; speaks what is not a formal teaching as a formal teaching, speaks a formal teaching as not a formal teaching—such a person incurs a great offense.

If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances and great influence, such that all people trust and accept what he says; if he is well-known to the community and able to provide for the Saṃgha; if he speaks of what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma, of Dharma as Dharma, of what is non-Vinaya as non-Vinaya, of Vinaya as Vinaya, of an offense as an offense, of no offense as no offense, of a grave offense as grave, of a light offense as light, of an offense without remainder as without remainder, of an offense with remainder as with remainder, of what is not a standard practice as not a standard practice, of what is a standard practice as a standard practice, and of what is not a formal teaching as not a formal teaching, and of what is a formal teaching as a formal teaching—such a person attains great merit.

If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances and great influence such that all people trust and believe what he says, and is well-known to the assembly and able to provide for the Saṅgha, yet he speaks of what is not Dharma as Dharma and of Dharma as not Dharma—down to speaking of what is not spoken as spoken and of what is spoken as not spoken—such a person cannot benefit himself nor others; he cannot be of benefit to many people, cannot have compassion for sentient beings, and cannot bring benefit, peace, and happiness to devas and humans.

If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances and great influence, such that all people trust and accept what he says; if he is well-known to the community and able to provide for the Saṅgha; if he speaks of the non-Dharma as non-Dharma and the Dharma as Dharma, and even speaks of the non-speech as non-speech and speech as speech—such a person can benefit himself and also benefit others, can be of help to many, and out of compassion for sentient beings, can bring benefit, peace, and security to devas and humans.

If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances and great influence such that all people trust and accept what he says, and is well-known among the community so as to be able to provide for the Saṃgha; yet he speaks of what is not Dharma as Dharma, and of Dharma as not Dharma, even speaking of what is not a teaching as a teaching, and of a teaching as not a teaching—this person is guilty, transgressing, and subject to remorse. His mind is distressed and what he has done gives rise to regret; it is neither pure nor liberated, it is a diminution rather than an increase, and he is ashamed of himself, falls away, and is despised by others, having created various karmas of evil.

If a bhikṣu is widely known, possesses great influence, and his words are trusted and accepted by all; if he is well-known to the community and able to provide for the Saṅgha; and if he declares what is non-Dharma to be non-Dharma and what is Dharma to be Dharma—down to declaring what is not spoken to be not spoken and what is spoken to be spoken—then this person incurs no fault, no transgression, no remorse, and no affliction. His actions bring no regret; he attains purity and liberation, neither diminishes nor declines, but increases in virtue. His own deeds are praised by others, and he performs various wholesome karmas.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world and manifests the Dharma of Vinaya, he does not proclaim the precepts all at once, but teaches them gradually.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world and manifests the Dharma of Vinaya, it is not destroyed all at once, but is destroyed gradually.

There was a bhikṣu who had many acquaintances and possessed great influence; whatever he spoke, people all believed and accepted. Being well-known to the assembly, he was able to provide for the Saṅgha, yet within the Vinaya teachings manifested by the Tathāgata, he gave rise to divergent views.

Within the words, they further compose similar phrases that obstruct the Dharma, conceal the Dharma, do not accord with the Dharma, and fail to clarify what is spoken; such people are border-dwellers and low-born individuals, who are of no benefit to the world and lack the conduct of a true man.

If a bhikṣu has many acquaintances and possesses great influence, such that all people trust and accept what he says; if he is well-known to the community and able to provide for the Saṅgha; if, within the Vinaya teachings manifested by the Tathāgata, he does not give rise to divergent views; if, regarding the wording, he does not compose spurious phrases; if he does not obstruct the Dharma nor conceal the Dharma, but follows the Dharma and explains what is taught with clarity; and if he is not a person from the borderlands, not a person of low birth, and not one who is without benefit, but is a man of proper conduct—[then he is qualified].
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śākya.
Mahāprajāpatī went to where the Buddha was, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"I pray that you may remain in the world for the duration of one kalpa.
For this reason, the Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"One should not praise the Tathāgata in such a manner."
That which you have praised is not a good praise.
One should not praise the Tathāgata in this way; this is not a praise of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
There is one thing that causes the Dharma to perish and disappear: namely, the schism of the Saṃgha.
“There is one dharma that does not perish, does not vanish, and does not disappear: it is because of the harmony of the Saṃgha.

There is one dharma that perishes, vanishes, and disappears: it is because of strife that the Dharma perishes, vanishes, and disappears; likewise, because of mutual contention, mutual abuse, and mutual recrimination, the Dharma perishes, vanishes, and disappears.”

There is one dharma that does not perish, does not vanish, and does not disappear. Because it is without contention, this dharma does not perish, vanish, or disappear. Likewise, because it is without dispute, without mutual abuse, and without mutual recrimination, this dharma does not perish, vanish, or disappear.
“There is one factor by which the Dharma perishes and disappears: it is because of greed that the Dharma perishes and disappears.
Likewise, through lack of contentment, excessive desire, lack of知足 (satisfaction), and through evil desires and evil views, the Dharma perishes and disappears.”
There is one dharma that does not perish, does not vanish, and does not disappear: because of non-greed, the dharma does not perish, vanish, or disappear.
Likewise, because of weariness with the world, fewness of desires, contentment, absence of evil desire, and absence of evil views, the dharma does not perish, vanish, or disappear.

"In whichever direction there are bhikṣus who quarrel, dispute, revile one another, or engage in verbal contention, one should not even hear of such things from that direction, much less dwell upon them."

Because there are such instances of quarreling, mutual abuse, and verbal disputes, one should not even think of whichever direction a monk may be quarreling, abusing, or disputing with another; how much less should one go there?
Because there is much strife, mutual abuse, and mutual recrimination.

In whichever direction there are bhikṣus who do not fight, do not quarrel, do not abuse one another, and do not recriminate, it is in such a direction that one should listen; how much more so when one does not even harbor such thoughts?

Because there is no such thing as quarreling, disputing, reviling, or speaking abusively, one should further keep in mind whichever direction there may be monks who do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not revile, and do not speak abusively; how much more so should one go there?
Because there is no such occurrence of quarreling, mutual abuse, or mutual recrimination.

"In whichever direction there are bhikṣus who quarrel, mutually abuse, and mutually recriminate, one should truly know that in that place three dharmas have been abandoned and three dharmas have been accepted."

Regarding the abandonment of three things: abandoning the obstruction of sensual thoughts, abandoning the obstruction of thoughts of ill will, and abandoning the obstruction of thoughts of envy—this is called the abandonment of the three things.
Regarding the undertaking of three things: undertaking sensual thoughts, undertaking thoughts of ill will, and undertaking thoughts of envy—this is called the undertaking of the three things.
Because there is much such strife, mutual abuse, and mutual accusation of faults.

In whichever direction there are bhikṣus who do not fight, do not quarrel, do not abuse one another, and do not accuse one another, one should truly know that in that place they have abandoned three things and accepted three things.
As for the three things to be abandoned: one abandons thoughts of sensual desire, abandons thoughts of ill will, and abandons thoughts of envy.

As for the three things to be undertaken: one undertakes the restraint of thoughts of sensual desire, undertakes the restraint of thoughts of ill will, and undertakes the restraint of thoughts of envy.
Because there is no such thing as quarreling, reviling one another, or speaking of each other's faults.

"In whichever direction there are bhikṣus who quarrel, revile one another, or speak of each other's faults, know for certain that in that place they have abandoned three qualities and accepted three qualities."

As for the abandonment of the three dharmas: it is the abandonment of the thought of desire, the abandonment of the thought of hatred, and the abandonment of the thought of jealousy; these are called the abandonment of the three dharmas. As for the undertaking of the three dharmas:
it is the undertaking of the thought of desire, the undertaking of the thought of hatred, and the undertaking of the thought of jealousy; these are called the undertaking of the three dharmas.
Because these various faults exist— namely, quarreling, mutual abuse, and mutual disparagement—

in whichever direction there are bhikṣus who do not quarrel, do not dispute, do not abuse one another, and do not disparage one another, one should truly know that in that place they have abandoned three things and adopted three things.

As for abandoning the three dharmas: abandoning the perception of desire, abandoning the perception of hatred, and abandoning the perception of envy—these are called the three dharmas to be abandoned.

As for undertaking the three dharmas: undertaking the restraint of the perception of desire, undertaking the restraint of the perception of hatred, and undertaking the restraint of the perception of envy—these are called the three dharmas to be undertaken.
Because there is no such thing as quarreling, reviling, or speaking of one another's faults.
"In whatever direction monks are quarreling, reviling, or speaking of one another's faults, you should truly know that in that place they have abandoned three qualities and accepted three qualities."

To abandon three things means to abandon the obstruction of the realm of desire, to abandon the obstruction of the realm of hatred, and to abandon the obstruction of the realm of envy; this is called abandoning the three things.
To accept three things means to accept the realm of desire, to accept the realm of hatred, and to accept the realm of envy; this is called accepting the three things.
Because there is this quarreling, mutual reviling, and mutual accusation of faults,

wherever there are bhikṣus who do not quarrel, do not revile one another, and do not accuse one another, one truly knows that in such a place they have abandoned three things and accepted three things.
Regarding the three things to be abandoned: abandoning the realm of desire, abandoning the realm of hatred, and abandoning the realm of envy—these are called the three things to be abandoned.

Regarding the three things to be undertaken: undertaking the restraint of the realm of desire, undertaking the restraint of the realm of hatred, and undertaking the restraint of the realm of envy—these are called the three things to be undertaken.
"Because there is no such thing as quarreling, mutual abuse, or speaking of one another's faults.
[End of Section on One Dharma] **Section Two: The First of the Two Dharmas** "There are two dharmas by which the ignorant commit offenses:
not seeing one's own faults and not repenting for those offenses."
There are two factors by which one who possesses wisdom commits an offense:
seeing the transgression, and having seen the transgression, being able to repent of that offense.
There are two types of offenses:
There are light offenses and heavy offenses.
Furthermore, there are two types of offenses:
those with remainder and those without remainder.
Furthermore, there are two types of offenses:
those that may be confessed to another, and those that may be confessed within one's own mind.
"There are two assemblies: [the assembly of monks and the assembly of nuns]."
The assembly of the Dharma and the assembly of non-Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two assemblies:
the turbid assembly and the pure assembly.
“There are two things because of which the Saṃgha is said to dwell in suffering:
dwelling without joy due to repeated transgressions, and not following the teaching but instead following unwholesome dharmas.
There are two kinds of lack of wisdom:”
One should repent where one ought to repent, and yet does not; one repents where one ought not to repent.
There are two kinds of wisdom:
that which leads one to repent where one ought to repent.
One should not regret what is not to be regretted.
There are two kinds of ignorance:
that which involves transgression and that which involves concealment.
There are two kinds of knowledge:
not transgressing and not concealing.
Regarding those who lack knowledge and conceal [their faults], there are two results:
Hell and hungry ghosts;
for one with wisdom who does not conceal [their faults], there are two fruits:
human and celestial.
The Buddha said:
"Because they do not believe and accept what I have taught, they conceal it.
Those who conceal it shall not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress."
Those who are able to believe and accept what I have taught are said to be without concealment.
Those without concealment shall attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"There are two kinds of goodness:
knowing one's transgressions and knowing how to repent them.
There are two kinds of purity:"
Purity of precepts and purity of view.
There are two kinds of unrighteous views:
viewing what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and viewing the Dharma as not the Dharma.
There are two kinds of views:
the view of what is not Dharma as being non-Dharma, and the view of what is Dharma as being Dharma.
There are two kinds of Vinaya:
There is the discipline for covetousness and the discipline for anger.
There are two types of discipline:
the discipline for bhikṣus and the discipline for bhikṣuṇīs.
There are two types of Vinaya:
the universal Vinaya and the non-universal Vinaya.
"There are two things by which a person of great renown incurs fault: [the first is]..."
To perform what is contrary to the Dharma as the Dharma, or to perform what is the Dharma as contrary to the Dharma—this is called having faults.
There are two things by which one who is well-known does not have faults:
performing what is contrary to the Dharma as contrary to the Dharma, and performing what is the Dharma as the Dharma; this is called being without faults.
“There are two ways of deciding cases that involve fault:
deciding what is contrary to the Dharma as being according to the Dharma, and deciding what is according to the Dharma as being contrary to the Dharma; these are called faulty.
There are two ways of deciding cases that are without fault:”
To declare what is non-Dhamma as non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma as Dhamma is called being without fault.
There are two kinds of speech that are faulty:
to speak of what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and to speak of what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma; this is called being faulty.
There are two types of speech that are faultless:
speaking what is not the Dharma as not the Dharma, and speaking what is the Dharma as the Dharma.
These are called faultless.
“There are two kinds of teachings for instructing people that involve error:
teaching what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and teaching the Dharma as what is not the Dharma; these are called errors.
There are two teachings for instructing people that are without error:”
To teach what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma and Dharma as Dharma is called being without fault.
"There are two things by which the Dharma perishes and disappears:
there is a bhikṣu who doubts the Dharma and doubts the Vinaya; these are called the two things by which the Dharma perishes and disappears."
There are two dharmas by which the Dharma is not extinguished, not lost, and not destroyed:
not doubting the Dharma and not doubting the Vinaya. These are called the two dharmas by which the Dharma is not extinguished, not lost, and not destroyed.
“There are two factors that cause the Dharma to perish and disappear:
there is a bhikṣu who teaches what is not the Dharma and teaches what is not the Vinaya; these are called the two factors that cause the Dharma to perish and disappear.”
There are two dharmas that do not perish, do not vanish, and do not disappear:
the teaching according to the Dharma and the teaching according to the Vinaya; these are called the two dharmas that do not perish, do not vanish, and do not disappear.
"For two reasons the Buddha prohibits separate meals for a group, thereby benefiting the donors:
to prevent wicked bhikṣus from gaining power, and to ensure that the pure community attains peace and happiness."
For two reasons, the World-Honored One performs the *karman* of reprimand (*khara-karman*):
to prevent evil persons from gaining strength and to enable pure persons to gain strength.

Likewise, the *karman* of dependence, the *karman* of expulsion, the *karman* of humbling oneself, the *karman* of suspension for not seeing [an offense], the *karman* of suspension for not making amends, the *karman* of suspension for not relinquishing evil views, the *parivāsa* (probation), the *mānatva* (penance), and the *āvarhaṇa* (restoration) that leads to purification—all these serve to prevent evil persons from gaining strength and to enable pure persons to gain strength.
“There are two things that lead to contention:

declaring what is not Dharma to be Dharma, and declaring what is Dharma to be non-Dharma. These are called the two things that lead to contention. They revile one another and engage in disputes without ceasing;
they engage in various kinds of verbal abuse, do not employ the Vinaya rules, and cause the Sangha to be split, troubled, and divided.”
There are two things that prevent strife:
declaring what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma, and declaring what is Dharma as Dharma.

In this way, there is no strife, no mutual reviling, and no mutual accusation; one refrains from various forms of verbal dispute, employing the Vinaya so that the Saṃgha is not split, the Saṃgha is not troubled, the Saṃgha is not divided, and the Saṃgha does not become discordant.
“For two reasons, the Blessed One has taught that one should act as an upādhyāya:
to attain purity and uphold the precepts in the present, and to ensure that the holy life remains long-lasting and secure in the future.

It is the same for an ācārya, a co-resident disciple, a resident disciple, a śrāmaṇera, one who instructs in the Vinaya and the Prātimokṣa, one who recites the Prātimokṣa, one who suspends the Prātimokṣa, one who suspends the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā), one who suspends the invitation ceremony, one who accuses another of an offense or causes another to remember an offense, and those who perform the *jñapti-karman*, the *sāmagrī-karman*, the *anuśrāvaṇā-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*—in all these cases, there is the attainment of purity and the upholding of the precepts in the present, and the holy life is ensured to remain long-lasting and secure in the future.”
“For two reasons, the Blessed One taught the *saṃmukhavinaya*:
to attain purity and maintain the precepts in the present, and to obtain peace and happiness so that the holy life may endure for a long time.

Likewise, the *smṛtivinaya*, *amūḍhavinaya*, *pratijñāvinaya*, *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*, *yadbhūyaiṣīya*, and *tṛṇaprastāraka*—these also result in attaining purity and maintaining the precepts in the present, and obtaining peace and happiness so that the holy life may endure for a long time.”
“For two reasons, the Blessed One has prescribed the *kukkuṭaka-kamma* (harsh disciplinary action):
to achieve purity in the present through the observance of the precepts,
and to ensure the long-term endurance of the blissful holy life (*brahmacarya*) in the future.”

Likewise, by means of the formal acts of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*), subordination (*tarjanīya-karman*), suspension for not seeing an offense (*adarśana-sthāpanīya*), suspension for not making amends (*apratikarmāraha-sthāpanīya*), suspension for not relinquishing evil views (*āpattiyā apratiniḥsargāraha-sthāpanīya*), separate residence (*parivāsa*), penance (*mānatva*), reversion to the original status (*mūlāpakarṣa*), and the formal act of rehabilitation (*ābṛhaṇīya-karman*), one likewise attains pure observance of the precepts in the present and will subsequently attain the long-lasting abiding of the blissful holy life (*brahmacarya*).
"There are two ways of slandering the Buddha:
speaking of what is not Dharma as Dharma, and speaking of Dharma as not Dharma.
There are two ways of not slandering the Buddha:"
To call what is not Dharma "Dharma," and to call what is Dharma "not Dharma.
There are two ways of transgressing against the Buddha:
to call what is not Dharma "Dharma," and to call what is Dharma "not Dharma."
There are two things that do not constitute a fault in the Buddha:
declaring what is non-Dharma to be non-Dharma, and declaring what is Dharma to be Dharma.
There are two things that do not follow the Buddha’s word:
To call what is not Dharma "Dharma" and to call what is Dharma "not Dharma.
There are two ways of following the Buddha's words:
to call what is not Dharma "not Dharma" and to call what is Dharma "Dharma."
"There are two ways that do not accord with the Vinaya:
declaring what is non-Dharma to be Dharma, and declaring what is Dharma to be non-Dharma.
There are two ways that accord with the Vinaya:"
"To call what is non-Dharma 'Dharma' and what is Dharma 'non-Dharma.
There are two offenses:
to call what is non-Dharma 'Dharma' and to call what is Dharma 'non-Dharma.'"
There are two things that are blameless:
declaring what is non-Dharma as non-Dharma, and declaring what is Dharma as Dharma.
There are two things that entail expulsion:
One discards what is required by oneself; the Saṃgha in concord discards what is required according to the Dharma.
There are two ways in which it is not discarded:
one does not discard what is required by oneself; the Saṃgha in concord does not discard what is required according to the Dharma.
“There are two kinds of non-residence:
self-inflicted non-residence and that which is granted by the harmonious Saṃgha according to the Dharma.
There are two kinds of residence:”
"One may undergo suspension from communal residence (*asāṃvāsika*) either by one's own action or by the Saṃgha in concord acting according to the Dharma.
There are two types of suspension from communal residence involving fault:
that which is self-inflicted and that which is imposed by the Saṃgha in concord according to the Dharma."
There are two ways of living together that are without fault:
living together by one's own action, and being granted permission to live together by the harmonious Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma.
There are two types of harm:
There is causing harm by oneself and the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, inflicting harm upon one.
There are two instances of not causing harm:
not causing harm by oneself and the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, not inflicting harm upon one.
"There are two types of madness and deluded karmas:
those with mindfulness and those without mindfulness.

There are two kinds of innate madness, two kinds of madness caused by incantations, two kinds of madness caused by medicine, two kinds of madness of the mind, and two kinds of madness caused by physical pain."
“There are two pure dharmas that protect the world: a sense of shame (*hrī*) and a sense of dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).

If these two pure dharmas, shame and dread of blame, did not protect the world, then one would not distinguish between father and mother, elder and younger brothers, sisters, sons and daughters, or kinsmen; human dharma would be destroyed, and people would be like oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, jackals, birds, and beasts.”

If these two pure qualities—shame and dread of blame—are present in the world, then one distinguishes between father, mother, brother, sister, son, daughter, and kinsmen; one does not violate the laws of humanity, unlike oxen, sheep, chickens, dogs, jackals, birds, or beasts.
It is impossible for one who lacks this sense of shame and remorse to possess pure dharmas;
if the mind is devoid of pure dharmas, there is only birth and death, and no liberation.

When one possesses this sense of shame and remorse, pure dharmas reside in the mind and it immediately attains purity; thus, one does not undergo further birth and death but crosses to the shore beyond birth and death, never again receiving existence.

The two rules concluded. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 48: The householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Whenever the World-Honored One travels among people to teach and transform them, I am always filled with longing and desire to see the Buddha; I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me a small portion [of his belongings] so that I may make an offering.
The Buddha then gave him his hair and fingernails, saying,
"You shall make offerings to these.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Please allow me to erect a stupa with my hair and nails.
The Buddha said:
“Listen, I shall speak.
He spoke again:
“The Buddha has permitted me to coat the walls with red, black, and white colors.”
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to coat the walls with red, black, and white colors.
He further said:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to paint stupas.
The Buddha said,
"With the exception of images depicting the union of a man and a woman, all others are permitted to be painted."
Furthermore, when someone made an offering of a parasol but there was no place to secure it, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to drive in a stake to fix it.
At that time, the stupa door had no panels, so cattle, deer, monkeys, dogs, and other animals would enter.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should install door panels.
[The monks asked,] "It would be well if the Buddha would permit us to provide railings before the doors."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to construct a railing.
[The monk replied,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to construct a railing all around."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a railing all around.
There was no place there for attaching flowers; he reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make vessels for holding flowers.
Once the vessels were filled with flowers, the Buddha said:
"One should provide curved pegs [to secure them]."
It was still not full. The Buddha said, "A cord should be suspended all around.
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
“If the Buddha permits me to make garlands of mani-jewels and new flower garlands, it would be well.
The Buddha said,
“I permit you to make garlands of mani-jewels and new flower garlands.”
He spoke these words:
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to construct a cave-dwelling.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, you may construct a cave-dwelling.
He further said,
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to build a stūpa within my cave-dwelling."
The Buddha said,
"I permit the construction of a stūpa within the cave.
[The donor] said, "It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to provide the door for the cave."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to provide a door for the cave. [They further requested:
"It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to cover the stūpa within the cave."
The Buddha said,
“I allow you to cover the stūpa within the cave.
[The monk said,] “It would be well if the Buddha would allow me to remove the headpiece from the roof.”
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to go out from the house and prostrate yourself.
[The builder] said, "It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to install the rafters and brackets."
The Buddha said,
"I permit the construction of bracket-capitals and corbels.
[The donor said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to provide pillars for the construction of the stūpa."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to give pillars for the construction of a stūpa.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to adorn the stūpa pillars with colors, red ocher, and white lime."
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to adorn pillars with colors, red ochre, and white lime. [The monks said:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to paint stupas upon the pillars."
The Buddha said,
"With the exception of images depicting the union of a man and a woman,

all others are permitted to be painted. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with pure faith, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and having sat to one side, addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Just as one should not make vows regarding the physical image of the Buddha, it would be well if the Buddha would permit me to serve as an attendant to this image.
The Buddha said:
"Please permit me to make an image of a bodhisattva. He further said:
"When the Buddha was formerly at home, he led the ceremonial banner before him; I pray that the Buddha will permit me to lead the banner before him—this would be well."
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to place a trailing banner in front. [The monks said:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to construct high pedestals before our stūpas to install lion figures."
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to construct a high pedestal to install the lion.
"It would be well," [the monks said], "if the Buddha allows a railing to be made around the four sides of the lion."
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to install railings around the four sides of the lion.
[The king said,] "It would be well if the Buddha would allow me to have the lions made of copper."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to fashion a lion out of copper.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha allowed us to attach a banner to the copper lion."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to attach a banner to the copper lion.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to make offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and music."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to make offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and music.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to smear the ground of the stūpa with fragrant flowers and oil."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
“I permit the use of incense, flowers, and oil to smear upon the ground of the stūpa.
[The monks said,] “It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to construct flower-stands.”
The Buddha said,
“I permit you to construct a flower-stand.
[He added,] “It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to construct a place for lamps.”
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to construct a place for lighting lamps.
[The monk said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to build a circular hall."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to construct a circular hall. [The builder] said,
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to install wooden beams on the ceiling of the hall to hang banners."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to place wooden frames upon your hall and suspend banners from them.

At that time, the kinsmen, acquaintances, and those who had brought offerings for the householder Anāthapiṇḍada decorated young men and women, placing flowers, incense, and necklaces upon their trays and tables, and sent them to the householder’s residence.
Having seen this, the householder thought:
"It would be well if these items were placed in front.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to place flowers, incense, and necklaces upon your tray and go at the front.
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to carry an incense burner and go at the front," [he said].
The Buddha said:
"Listen, let your incense burner go ahead.
Some non-Buddhists, conceiving feelings of jealousy, saw this and rebuked them, saying:
"It is like escorting a corpse."
The householder thought to himself,
"It would be well if the Buddha would permit me to perform music before the image.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Allow the performance of music.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with pure faith, thought to himself:
"By what means can I assemble a great multitude and provide them with food and clothing?"
He went to inform the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will permit me to assemble the great assembly for a meal; it would be well.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, let the great assembly eat.
He spoke these words:
"It would be well if the Buddha permitted me to provide food for the great assembly when making offerings to the stūpa."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow that when making offerings to the stūpa, food be given to the great assembly.
[The monks thought,] "It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to hold the Pañcavārṣika festival."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to hold a *pañcavārṣika* assembly.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted the holding of a six-year assembly."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to hold a six-year assembly.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha would allow us to hold the assembly from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the second month."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
[The monks said,] "It would be well if the Buddha permitted us to hold a festival within our monastery."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to hold a gathering within your monastery.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not enter in order, did not sit in order, did not eat in order, did not rise in order, and did not depart in order; some entered before [others], some entered while food was being distributed, some entered while eating, and some entered after the meal was finished. The Buddha said:
"The time for the proclamation has arrived.
When the sound of the proclamation "the time has arrived" could not be heard from afar, they informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said, "You should strike the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong)."
After the *ghaṇṭā* had been struck, it was not heard from afar. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should strike a drum.
When they struck it while standing on the ground, it was still not heard from afar. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Strike against a target.
When striking against a target, it was still not heard from afar. The Buddha said:
“One should strike from a high place so that it may be both seen and heard from a distance.”
At that time, a great assembly gathered, and many people came to look on, offering items for the stūpa, items for the Saṃgha from the four quarters, food, and items intended for distribution.
The bhikṣus did not know which items belonged to the stūpa,
which items belonged to the Saṃgha of the four quarters,
and which items were for food.
"What items should be divided?
[The monks] reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When distributing the items, have one bhikṣu stand there and observe so that he may know how to distinguish them."
"These are items belonging to the stupa, items belonging to the Saṃgha from the four quarters, food items, and items that ought to be distributed.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"These four kinds of property—
property belonging to a stūpa, property belonging to the Saṃgha from the four quarters, food, and property to be distributed— may they be used interchangeably?
The Buddha said:
"No," the Buddha said to Upāli. "Regarding items belonging to a stūpa,
they must not be given to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, they must not be used for food, and they must not be divided."
Regarding the property of the Sangha of the four quarters: it must not be used for food, it must not be distributed, and it must not be used for stūpas.
If it is used for food, it must not be distributed, it must not be used for stūpas, and it must not be given to the Sangha of the four quarters.
"Those items that ought to be distributed shall be used by the Saṃgha according to its needs.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 49, Part 2 of the Eighth Recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra from North India together with Kumārajīva during the Later Qin Dynasty. 3.
The Second Part of the Ekottarika on the Three Dharmas of the Vinaya. Regarding the Three Dharmas:
"There are three *karmans* that encompass all *karmans*: [the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*]."
That is to say: the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
"There are three kinds of persons who will inevitably fall into the evil destinies and the hells.
What are these three?"
If a person slanders a bhikṣu of pure brahmacarya with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, this is called the first person who will certainly fall into hell.
There is another person who gives rise to evil and false views and says:
"Among all sensual desires, there is no fault."
For this reason, such a person deeply indulges in negligence and gives rein to the five desires; this second person will certainly fall into hell.

There may be someone who has left the household life to become a bhikṣu, yet violates the precepts so that internal corruption flows outward; he is not a śramaṇa but claims to be a śramaṇa, and does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) but claims to practice the holy life.
"This third person will certainly fall into hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to clarify this matter, spoke in verse:
"Lying leads to hell, as do other grave offenses;
such evil and unwholesome people will later receive their retribution together.
When a person is born into this world, an axe is born within their mouth."
By this, one cuts oneself down; this arises from speaking evil words.

Praising those who should be rebuked, and rebuking those who should be praised—through such verbal transgressions one meets with decline, and because of that decline, one does not experience happiness.
To suddenly lose one's wealth and possessions is a minor misfortune;
but to speak evil of virtuous people is a misfortune far more grave than that.
In the Nirarbuda hell, its duration lasts for a hundred thousand years.
In the Avīci hell, for thirty-six plus five [kalpas],
because one spoke evil words with a wicked mind and disparaged the noble ones,
at the end of one’s life one will surely fall into such a hell.
“There are three ways of establishing an offense:
establishing through what was seen, establishing through what was heard, and establishing through what was suspected.
There are three qualities:”

In the Vinaya, singing is like the manner of wailing; in the Vinaya, laughing with bared teeth is like the manner of madness; in the Vinaya, swinging the arms while dancing is like the manner of a child.
“The Tathāgata has three kinds of non-guarding that cannot be known and cannot be seen:
the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is pure and there is nothing impure; this is the Tathāgata’s non-guarding that cannot be known and cannot be seen.”
The Tathāgata’s verbal and mental actions are pure; there is nothing impure about them. Thus, the Tathāgata has no need for protection, as none can know him and none can see him.
"In the world there are three great thieves whom none can match; long-lived beings who commit great crimes, whom none can seize."
What are the three?
There are those who dwell in the wilderness, those who dwell in rugged places, and those who dwell by force.
What is dwelling in the wilderness?
That is to say, within a thicket of grass and trees.
What is dwelling in a rugged place?
It refers to being amidst mountain crags and river bends.
What is meant by "abiding in great strength"?
It refers to the strength of the hands and the strength of the feet.
These are called the three dharmas that are great thieves in the world; though they commit great crimes over a long period of life, no one is able to seize them.
Regarding these three matters, there are wicked bhikṣus who, having committed great offenses, live for a long time and remain for a long duration, such that the Saṃgha is unable to expel them.
They dwell in the wilderness, dwell in mountain fastnesses, and dwell by force.

Those who dwell like wild beasts are those whose precepts are broken and who are internally rotten, leaking impurity; though not śramaṇas, they claim to be śramaṇas, and though not practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya), they claim to be practitioners of the holy life. This is called dwelling like a wild beast.

To dwell in the precipice means to hold wrong views and speak untruthfully, seeing things thus and speaking thus: that there is no giving and no fruit thereof; no retribution for good or evil; no father or mother; no world beyond; no arhat; no stream-enterer (srotāpanna); no once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin); no non-returner (anāgāmin); no present life and no future life; and no dharma to be realized. This is called dwelling in the precipice.
"Abiding with power" means relying on the power of speech and relying on the power of extensive understanding; this is called abiding with power.
These are the three factors by which an evil bhikṣu may live for a long time and commit great offenses, such that the Saṃgha is unable to swiftly expel him.
“There are three things called great thieves that, though long-lived and having committed great offenses, people cannot quickly capture:
those who dwell in the wilderness, those who dwell in rugged places, and those who possess much wealth.”
What is meant by "dwelling in the wilderness"?
It is as previously explained.
What is meant by "dwelling in a rugged place"?
As previously stated,
what is meant by "having abundant wealth"?
It refers to one who possesses extensive fields, houses, dependents, and treasures, and this person thinks to themselves:
"If there is anyone who tells me [the way], I shall give them wealth.
This is called having much wealth.
These are the three qualities by which a great thief lives long and commits great evils, such that people cannot quickly apprehend him.
Regarding these three dharmas, there may be wicked bhikṣus who, having lived for a long time and committed great offenses, cannot be swiftly expelled by the Saṃgha:
namely, those who dwell in the wilderness, those who dwell in dangerous places, and those who dwell in dependence on material things.
What is dwelling in the wilderness?
It is as previously explained.
What is dwelling in a rugged place?
As previously stated:
how does one dwell in dependence on material things?
If one receives a great abundance of offerings:
Regarding various items such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, he forms this thought:
"If there is anyone who asks me for these things, I shall give them to them."
This is called "dwelling by means of material things.
These are the three dharmas whereby a wicked bhikṣu may live for a long time and commit great offenses, yet the Saṃgha is unable to swiftly expel him.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas called "great thieves," whereby one may live for a long time and commit great offenses, yet people are unable to swiftly seize them:
He dwells in dependence on wilderness, he dwells in dependence on rugged places, and he dwells in dependence on strength.
What is dwelling in dependence on wilderness?
It is as previously explained.
What is dwelling in dependence on rugged terrain?
It is as previously explained.
What is dwelling in dependence on strength?
If, relying on a king or those equal to a king, one thinks:
"There is someone who is my ally; this person will assist me," this is called abiding by reliance on power.
These are the three things that are great thieves which, having long life, commit great offenses and cannot be seized by people.
Likewise, there are these three things whereby an evil bhikṣu, having long life, commits great offenses and the Saṃgha cannot quickly expel him:
dwelling in the wilderness, dwelling in the mountains, and dwelling by force.
What is dwelling in the wilderness?
It is as previously explained.
What is dwelling in the rugged mountains?
As previously stated:
How does one dwell in reliance upon the powers?
If a bhikṣu relies on those who recite the Sūtras, those who recite the Vinaya, or those who recite the Abhidharma, he forms this thought:
"If there is someone who speaks in my defense, that person supports me.
These are called the three factors; when an evil bhikṣu has lived for a long time and commits great offenses, the Saṃgha is unable to swiftly expel him.
“In the world there are three great thieves.
What are the three?

First, because he is the leader of a hundred people, he is respectfully surrounded by a hundred; because he is the leader of two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred people, he is respectfully surrounded by five hundred.”
Entering cities and villages, breaking through walls, blocking roads to plunder, destroying cities, and killing people—this is called the first great thief.

Second, there is the bhikṣu who uses the bamboo, wood, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, wealth, or food and drink belonging to the monasteries of the four quarters for his own livelihood, or gives them to lay acquaintances; this is called the second great thief.

Third, there is a bhikṣu who, for the sake of offerings of food and drink, falsely claims to have attained supramundane noble dharmas when he actually possesses none. Thus, surrounded by the respectful attention of a hundred or even five hundred people, he enters cities and villages to receive from others offerings of morning and midday meals; this is called the third great thief.

Among these, there are bandit leaders of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred men who, surrounded by their followers with reverence, enter cities and villages, breach walls, block roads, plunder, destroy cities, and kill people; these are called minor thieves.

If there is a bhikṣu who uses the bamboo, wood, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, property, or food and drink belonging to the saṃgha’s grove in the four directions to sell for his own livelihood, or gives them to lay acquaintances, he is also called a minor thief.
The Buddha said:

"This is the third thief; among the world of devas and humans, the realm of Māra, the Brahma-world, and within the assembly of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans, he is the greatest thief of all."
That is to say, for the sake of food and drink, though they are empty and devoid of the noble dharmas that transcend the human, they deliberately speak falsehoods, claiming to have attained them.
If they enter cities or villages surrounded by a hundred or even five hundred people who pay them respect, receiving from others offerings of morning and midday meals, these are called great thieves.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"A bhikṣu who has not attained the Path yet claims to have attained it is a great thief among gods and humans,
an extremely evil person who violates the precepts."
“When this deluded person’s body perishes, they shall fall into hell.
Section Three on the Three Dharmas concludes. Section Four on the Four Dharmas: “There are four kinds of preceptors (*upādhyāya*): there is the preceptor who gives the Dharma but not food;
there is the preceptor who gives food but not the Dharma; there is the preceptor who gives both the Dharma and food; and there is the preceptor who gives neither the Dharma nor food.”
Among these, one who provides the Dharma but does not provide food should be resided with as an upādhyāya;
one who provides food but does not provide the Dharma should not be resided with.
One who provides both the Dharma and food—such a person should be resided with for as long as life lasts.
One should not remain with those who do not provide the Dharma or food; one should depart even during the dark of night.
It is the same regarding an *ācārya*.
"There are four kinds of persons who repeatedly commit offenses and repeatedly repent for them:..."
First is shamelessness; second is disregard for the precepts; third is a lack of fear; and fourth is delusion.
These are called the four types of persons who repeatedly violate the precepts and repeatedly repent their transgressions.
“In the world there are four kinds of people who feel fear upon seeing a transgression.
What are these four?
Suppose there is a person dressed in black garments, running with his head bowed, who goes before a great multitude and says:”
"I have committed evil deeds, unwholesome and shameful; I shall do whatever pleases the people.
At that time, the crowd rebuked him and drove him out.
A wise person, having seen this, thinks:
"This man, dressed in black garments, runs toward a great multitude and says:
'I have committed evil and unwholesome deeds that are shameful; I shall now do whatever is pleasing to the people.'"
"Because of having committed evil karma, one is rebuked, driven away, and abandoned by the assembly.
I shall admonish myself and also instruct others not to commit such evil karma.
In this way, a bhikṣu should give rise to a sense of dread regarding the *prāyaścittika* offenses; he should understand thus: that which has not been committed shall not be committed.
If one has already committed an offense, they should quickly repent according to the Dharma;
this is called the first person who perceives their fault with dread.
Suppose there were a man dressed in black clothing, running with a club gripped over his shoulder, who went among a great multitude and spoke these words:
"I have committed evil deeds, unwholesome and shameful; I shall do whatever this assembly delights in.
Thereupon, the crowd seized him with clubs, beat him, and drove him out.
A wise person, seeing this, says:
"Because this person committed evil and unwholesome deeds, they have incurred great retribution; I shall admonish myself and instruct others not to commit such evil karma."
"In this way, a bhikṣu should give rise to a sense of dread regarding a *pāyattika* offense; he should understand it thus:
one who has not yet committed it shall not commit it, and if one has already committed it, he should quickly repent."
This is called the second fear regarding the recognition of one's transgressions.
Suppose there is a person dressed in black clothing, running with an iron trident gripped over his shoulder, who goes before a great multitude and says:
"I have committed evil and unwholesome deeds; whatever the assembly desires, that I shall do."
Then the crowd immediately took iron pikes and struck him, seized sharp knives to threaten him, and drove him out through the western city gate, casting him into a ditch.
When a person of wisdom sees this, they say:
"This person has committed evil deeds and thus incurs great retribution; I shall admonish myself and instruct others not to commit such evils."
"In this way, a bhikṣu should give rise to a sense of dread regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; he should understand thus:
those not yet committed shall not be committed, and those already committed shall be swiftly confessed."
This is called the third fear regarding the recognition of one's offenses.

It is like a master thief-catcher who has captured an actual thief, bound his two hands behind his back, beaten a drum while parading him through the streets, led him out through the southern city gate, seated him beneath a stake, and then severed his head.
Upon seeing this, a wise person says:
"Because this person committed evil deeds, they have incurred great retribution; I shall admonish myself and instruct others not to commit such evil deeds."
"In this way, a bhikṣu gives rise to a sense of dread regarding the pārājika offenses; he should understand it thus: 'One who has not yet committed them shall never dare to commit them.
This is called the fourth [aspect of] seeing the offense with dread."
“There are four kinds of *karmas*:
an illegal *karman* performed by a divided assembly; an illegal *karman* performed by a united assembly; a legal *karman* performed by a divided assembly;
and a legal *karman* performed by a united assembly. Among these, that which is an illegal *karman* performed by a divided assembly is not called a valid *karman*.”
If a community that is improperly constituted performs a *karmavācanā*, it is not called performing a *karmavācanā*.
If a community that is properly constituted but divided performs a *karmavācanā*, it is also not called performing a *karmavācanā*.
When a legal matter (*dharma*) is performed by a harmonious assembly through a formal act (*karmavācanā*), this is called a valid formal act.
When an illegal matter is performed by a divided assembly through a formal act, that formal act is illegal and performed by a divided assembly; it should be obstructed and set aside.

When a formal act (*kamma*) is performed by an assembly that is both unlawful and incomplete, that formal act—being unlawful and performed by an incomplete assembly—should be obstructed and set aside.
When a formal act is performed by an assembly that is lawful but incomplete, that formal act—being lawful but performed by an incomplete assembly—should be obstructed and set aside.

When a legal act (*kamma*) is performed by a harmonious assembly in accordance with the Dharma, that legal act is one performed by a harmonious assembly in accordance with the Dharma; it should not be obstructed and should not be set aside.

When a legal act is performed by a schismatic assembly in contravention of the Dharma, that legal act of a schismatic assembly in contravention of the Dharma should not be performed; it is not considered performed, it is not good, and it is not called good; it should be obstructed and should be set aside.

When a community that is improperly united performs a formal act (kamma), that kamma is performed by an improperly united community; it is not called a "performed" act, it is not good, it is not called "good," and it should be obstructed and set aside.

Regarding a legal act (*dharmakarma*) performed by a separate assembly (*vyagrakarma*): such a legal act performed by a separate assembly should not be performed; it is not called "performed," it is not good, it is not called "good," and it should be obstructed and set aside.

When a legal act (*kamma*) is performed by a harmonious assembly in accordance with the Dharma, that legal act is one that should be performed by a harmonious assembly in accordance with the Dharma; it is called "performed," it is excellent, and it is called "excellent. It should not be obstructed and should not be set aside.
“There are four kinds of persons:
first, coarse persons; second, turbid persons; third, intermediate persons; and fourth, superior-superior persons.
Likewise, within the Saṃgha there are four kinds of adjudicators of legal matters:”
There are members of the Saṃgha who adjudicate legal cases and are shameless, lacking skill in meaning and lacking skill in phrasing.
There are members of the Saṃgha who adjudicate legal cases and are shameless, yet skilled in meaning and skilled in phrasing.
There are those who adjudicate monastic affairs who possess a sense of shame, yet lack proficiency in meaning and phrasing.
There are also those who adjudicate monastic affairs who possess a sense of shame, as well as proficiency in both meaning and phrasing.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha lack a sense of shame, are unskilled in meaning, and unskilled in phrasing, they are called coarse persons (*puruṣa*).
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha lack a sense of shame, yet are skilled in meaning and skilled in phrasing, they are called turbid persons (*kaluṣa*).
If those who adjudicate matters for the Sangha possess a sense of shame but lack skill in meaning and phrasing, they are called intermediate persons.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Sangha possess a sense of shame and are skilled in both meaning and phrasing, they are called superior persons.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha are shameless, unskilled in meaning, and unskilled in phrasing, no one will draw near them.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha are shameless, yet skilled in meaning and skilled in phrasing, people will draw near them.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha possess a sense of shame but lack skill in meaning and skill in phrasing, no one will approach them.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha possess a sense of shame and are skilled in both meaning and phrasing, people will approach them.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha are shameless, lack proficiency in meaning, and lack proficiency in phrasing, they are said to be "unfit for conversation.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha are shameless, yet possess proficiency in meaning and proficiency in phrasing, they are "fit for conversation."
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha possess a sense of shame but lack skill in meaning or skill in phrasing, they are not fit to converse with.
If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha possess a sense of shame and are skilled in both meaning and phrasing, they are fit to converse with.

If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha are shameless, unskilled in meaning, and unskilled in phrasing, such adjudicators may be censured, rebuked, and expelled; they are bad people who cause confusion, distress, and give rise to a mind of regret.
Why is this? Such adjudicators cause disputes to arise within the Saṃgha where none existed before, and they are unable to extinguish those that have already arisen.

If these adjudicators of the Saṃgha lack a sense of shame, and are not skilled in meaning or phrasing, such adjudicators are to be censured, rebuked, and expelled; they are bad people who cause confusion, distress, and give rise to a mind of regret and remorse.
Why is this? Such adjudicators cause disputes that have not yet arisen within the Saṃgha to arise, and they are unable to extinguish those that have already arisen.
If an adjudicator of the Saṃgha lacks a sense of shame, is unskilled in meaning, or unskilled in phrasing, such an adjudicator should be taught the meaning and should be taught the phrasing.

If those who adjudicate matters for the Saṃgha possess a sense of shame, are skilled in meaning, and are skilled in phrasing, these adjudicators should be praised and commended as excellent. Why is this?
Because when such persons come into the midst of the Saṃgha to adjudicate matters, disputes that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those already arisen are extinguished.
“There are four kinds of meanings:

there is a meaning that is contrary to the Dharma, which one does not analyze, and even when others examine it, one does not accept it; there is a meaning that is contrary to the Dharma, which one does not analyze, but when others examine it, one accepts it; there is a meaning that is in accordance with the Dharma, which one analyzes, and even when others do not examine it, one does not accept it; and there is a meaning that is in accordance with the Dharma, which one does not analyze, but when others examine it, one accepts it.”
The meaning herein is that when one discriminates what is not the Dharma, does not investigate it thoroughly, and yet accepts it after investigation, these are called the three faults.
Just as with what is not the Dharma, such is the fault.
To discriminate against others is a fault.
To fail to investigate, or to accept what has not been investigated, is a fault.
Within this, there is a principle: it is not the Dharma to discriminate against others, nor to accept what has been investigated without investigation; this constitutes one fault.
To act contrary to the Dharma is a fault.
Not to discriminate others is not a fault.
To investigate and examine that which is received is not a fault.
Regarding the meaning herein: to analyze according to the Dharma yet not investigate others, or to investigate them but not accept [the truth], these are two faults.
That which is according to the Dharma is without fault;
that which analyzes others [in a biased manner] is a fault.
If one does not investigate, or investigates but does not accept [the teaching], this is a fault.
Regarding the meaning herein: if one does not discriminate against others according to the Dharma when investigating, and accepts [the teaching] upon investigation, these are all not faults.
That which is in accordance with the Dharma is not an error.
That which does not discriminate against others is not an error.
That which thoroughly investigates the recipient is not an error.
“There are four ways in which a *talaṭṭha* bhikkhu is unable to settle a dispute:
through attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.
These are called the four ways in which a *talaṭṭha* bhikkhu is unable to settle a dispute.”
There are four qualities by which a *talaṭṭha* bhikṣu can extinguish disputes:
he is without attachment, without hatred, without fear, and without delusion.
These are called the four qualities by which a *talaṭṭha* bhikṣu can extinguish disputes.
“There are four types of *taṇhāruha* bhikkhus:
those who do not skillfully examine the meaning and do not skillfully grasp the meaning;
those who praise what should not be praised and fail to praise what should be praised.”
One should not purify that which requires purification, nor fail to purify that which requires purification;
one should not revere that which does not merit reverence, nor fail to revere that which merits reverence.
There are four types of *tāla-ta* bhikṣus:
They skillfully contemplate the meaning and skillfully grasp the meaning;
they do not praise those who should not be praised, yet they praise those who should be praised;
they do not grant purification to those who should not be purified, yet they bring about purification for those who should be purified.
"One should not show respect where respect is inappropriate, but one should show respect where respect is appropriate.
These are called the four practices by which a *talaṭṭha* bhikṣu can extinguish disputes.
There are four practices of a *talaṭṭha* bhikṣu:"
Not skillfully examining the meaning, not skillfully grasping the meaning;
using forceful speech, not seeking permission from others but proceeding to expose their faults;
having previously harbored a mind of resentment or regret, and holding views of resentment or views of regret.
Acting according to one's own will—
these are called the four modes of conduct that cannot extinguish disputes.
There are four modes of conduct by which a *tālaṭṭha* bhikṣu can extinguish disputes:
One should skillfully contemplate the meaning and skillfully grasp the meaning;
one should not, by means of force or power, beg for or listen to [the teaching] from others;
and one should first be free from a mind of resentment or regret, and free from views that lead to resentment or regret.
Not applying one's own will—these are called the four practices that can extinguish disputes.
"There are four practices by which a *talaṭṭha* bhikṣu incurs guilt: [the list follows]."
Because of attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, there is fault.
There are four types of *talaṭṭha* bhikṣus who are without fault:
because they are without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion, they have no fault.
“There are four ways in which a *tala-tāla* bhikṣu commits an offense:
he does not properly examine the meaning and does not properly grasp the meaning;
he praises what should not be praised and fails to praise what should be praised.”
To purify that which should not be purified, or to fail to purify that which should be purified—these are called the four types of conduct involving transgression.
There are four types of conduct by which a *tālaṭa* bhikṣu is without transgression:
skillfully examining the meaning and skillfully grasping the meaning.
Not praising those who should not be praised while praising those who should be praised;
not granting purification to those who are impure while granting purification to those who should be purified—
these are called the four practices free from fault.
“There are four ways in which a *tala-tāla* bhikṣu commits an offense:
he does not skillfully examine the meaning; he does not skillfully grasp the meaning;
he uses forceful power rather than requesting permission; [and he acts without proper reflection].”
First, there is the mind of resentment and the mind of regret; second, there is the view of resentment and the view of regret;
third, there is self-will.
These are called the four practices that involve faults.
There are four practices by which a *raṭṭhapāla* bhikṣu remains without fault:
he skillfully contemplates the meaning and skillfully grasps the meaning;
he does not use force or power to solicit teachings from others.
First, there was no mind of resentment or remorse; second, there was no view of resentment or view of remorse;
third, one did not harbor intentional thoughts.
These four are without fault.

The Four Dharmas are concluded. 5. The Five Dharmas. First, when the Buddha, the Bhagavān, was dwelling in the kingdom of Śākya, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
"I pray that you will briefly explain what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya, so that I may know what is Dharma, what is Vinaya,
and what is the Buddha’s Dharma. The Buddha said, "Gotamī!"

If one knows that these phenomena follow desire and not non-desire, follow transgression and not non-transgression, follow increase and not non-increase, and turn exclusively toward afflictions without ever departing from them.
Mahāprajāpatī!
You certainly know that this is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the Buddha’s teaching. Gautamī!
If one knows that these dharmas do not follow desire or non-desire, do not follow fault or faultlessness, follow non-increase rather than increase, and do not follow affliction.
“Mahāprajāpatī!
You certainly know that this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, and this is the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

We pray that you will briefly explain what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya, so that we may know what is Dharma, what is Vinaya, and what is the Buddha’s teaching.”
The Buddha said, “Gautamī!

If you know that this teaching follows after greed and does not follow after non-greed; follows after lack of contentment and does not follow after contentment; follows after great desire and does not follow after fewness of desires; follows after being difficult to satisfy and does not follow after being easy to satisfy; follows after being difficult to support and does not follow after being easy to support.”
Gautamī! You certainly know that this is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the Buddha’s teaching. Gautamī!
