[He] reviled [him] with regard to his physical form, his birth, his actions, his many afflictions, and his engagement in worldly dharmas.
"There are five kinds of skins that should not be kept:
the skin of a lion, the skin of a tiger, the skin of a leopard, the skin of an otter, and the skin of a wildcat."
"There are five kinds of hides that should not be kept:
elephant hide, horse hide, dog hide, jackal hide, and black deer hide.
There are five kinds of refuse rags that should not be kept:"
There are garments burnt by fire, garments gnawed by oxen, garments chewed by rats, garments from a first marriage, and garments from childbirth.
There are five kinds of speech that an elderly bhikṣu should not accept when spoken:
speech that is meaningless, speech that is contrary to the Dharma, speech that is contrary to the Vinaya, speech lacking compassion, and speech that is not an instruction.
“There are five self-proclaimed arhats, as previously explained.
The Buddha said to Upāli:
“A bhikṣu who wishes to enter the Saṃgha should abide in five dharmas.”
As previously stated:
"There are five matters that constitute an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, as previously stated.
There are five formal procedures (*vyavasthāna*):
The classification of realms and bases, the classification of giving, the classification of paths and walking places, the classification of precepts, and the classification of views.
"There are five pure colors that should not be kept:
pure red, pure blue, pure golden-yellow, pure yellow-blue, and pure maṇḍitaka color."
“There are five kinds of great colors that should not be kept:
the color of *koṅka*, the color of a black snake, the color of *lūyana*, the color of *caurita*, and the color of *hari-tāla*.”
“There are five matters, Ānanda, by which a bhikkhu who is obstinate cannot settle a dispute:

claiming to have seen what was not seen, claiming to have heard what was not heard, claiming to have remembered what was not remembered, claiming to have known what was not known, and claiming that what is not Dhamma is Dhamma. These are the five matters, Ānanda, by which a bhikkhu who is obstinate cannot settle a dispute.”
Furthermore, there are five things by which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa is able to settle disputes:

stating what was seen as seen, stating what was heard as heard, stating what was remembered as remembered, stating what was known as known, and stating what is Dharma as Dharma. These are the five things by which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa is able to settle disputes.
"Furthermore, there are five things because of which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa cannot extinguish a dispute:
acting out of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion; and declaring what is not Dharma to be Dharma."
These are called the five matters by which the bhikṣu Dāruka is unable to settle a dispute.
Furthermore, there are five other matters by which the bhikṣu Dāruka is able to settle a dispute:
he does not follow favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion; he speaks of the Dharma as being the Dharma. These are called the five matters by which the bhikṣu Dāruka is able to settle a dispute.
"Furthermore, there are five matters in which the bhikṣu Dārittha commits an offense:

to say he has seen what he has not seen; to say he has heard what he has not heard; to say he has remembered what he has not remembered; to say he knows what he does not know; and to say it is the Dharma when it is not the Dharma. These are the five matters in which the bhikṣu Dārittha commits an offense."
There are five matters in which the bhikṣu Dārittha is not at fault:

saying he has seen what he has seen, saying he has heard what he has heard, saying he has sensed what he has sensed, saying he knows what he knows, and saying it is the Dharma what is the Dharma. These are called the five matters in which the bhikṣu Dārittha is not at fault.
"Furthermore, there are five matters concerning which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa has committed an offense:

acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of delusion, and declaring what is not Dharma to be Dharma. These are called the five matters concerning which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa has committed an offense."
Furthermore, there are five circumstances in which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa is not at fault:
he does not act out of favoritism, hatred, fear, or delusion; and he speaks of the Dharma as being the Dharma. These are the five circumstances in which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa is not at fault.
“There are five things, Ānanda, by which a bhikkhu cannot settle a dispute:

he does not understand the dispute well; he does not understand the basis of the dispute well; he does not distinguish the dispute well; he does not know the causes and conditions for settling the dispute; and he does not understand the causes and conditions for a dispute arising again after it has been settled. These are the five things, Ānanda, by which a bhikkhu cannot settle a dispute.”
Furthermore, there are five qualities by which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa is able to settle disputes:

he well understands the dispute; he well understands the basis of the dispute; he well distinguishes the dispute; he well understands the causes and conditions for settling the dispute; and he well understands how, once the dispute has been settled, the causes and conditions for it will not arise again. These are the five qualities by which the bhikṣu Tāliṭa is able to settle disputes.
"Furthermore, there are five matters by which a bhikṣu Tāliṭa cannot extinguish a dispute:

he does not well understand the Sūtras, he does not well understand the Vinaya, he does not well understand the dispute, he does not well understand the basis of the dispute, and he does not well discern the dispute. These are the five matters by which a bhikṣu Tāliṭa cannot extinguish a dispute."
There are five qualities by which a bhikṣu Tāliṭa can extinguish disputes:

he is well-versed in the Sūtras, well-versed in the Vinaya, well-acquainted with disputes, well-acquainted with the grounds for disputes, and skilled in the analysis of disputes. These are the five qualities by which a bhikṣu Tāliṭa can extinguish disputes.
"There are five things by which a bhikṣu of five years' standing need not rely upon another:

knowing what is an offense, knowing what is not an offense, knowing what is light, knowing what is heavy, and being extensively proficient in the beneficial precepts. These are the five things by which a bhikṣu of five years' standing need not rely upon another."
"There are five ways of taking with consent:

if one is a close friend, if the person is living, if the person is present, if after taking it one will speak of it so that they know, and if after taking it the other will certainly rejoice—these are called the five ways of taking with consent."
“There are five reasons why the Tathāgata inspects the various dwellings: to eliminate worldly talk among the bhikṣus;

to have those bedding and furniture that are not properly maintained put in order; to ensure that what has already been maintained remains well-kept and secure; for the sake of the bhikṣus who attend to the sick; and to establish precepts that have not yet been established. These are the five reasons why the Tathāgata inspects the dwellings.”
“There are five matters for which the Tathāgata, though already knowing them, asks questions intentionally:

to provide a causal basis, to establish a precept, to distinguish the meaning and the phrasing, because it resembles the wording of a sūtra, and to enable future sentient beings to understand it for themselves. These are called the five matters for which the Tathāgata, though knowing them, asks questions intentionally.”
“There are five benefits of walking meditation (caṅkramaṇa):
it makes one vigorous, powerful, free from illness, it digests food, and the mind attains firmness; these are called the five benefits of walking meditation.”
"Furthermore, there are five benefits of walking meditation (caṅkramaṇa):

because it enables movement, because it relieves fatigue, because it dispels wind, because it eliminates diseases of cold and heat, and because the mind attains firmness; these are called the five benefits of walking meditation."
"There are five kinds of illegitimate confession:

confessing before one who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), one who does not live in communion (*asamvāsa*), a group that has not received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), one for whom there is no remaining offense (*anavaśeṣa*), or confessing while not having seen the matter; these are called the five kinds of illegitimate confession."
There are five ways of confessing in accordance with the Dharma:

not confessing before one who is undergoing *parivāsa* (probation), not confessing before one who does not live in common residence, not confessing before a group that has not received full ordination (*upasampadā*), confessing while having a remainder of the offense, and confessing upon seeing the nature of the offense. These are called the five matters of confessing in accordance with the Dharma.
"There are five matters by which an *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (act of censure) is performed contrary to the Dharma:

it is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; it is subject to obstruction and should be set aside; it is performed without a basis and without the accused being present; it is performed without a formal charge and without causing the accused to remember [the offense]; and it is performed without the threefold interrogation. These are called the five matters by which an *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* is performed contrary to the Dharma."
There are five ways in which the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) is performed according to the Dharma:

it is in accordance with the Dharma; it is in accordance with the Vinaya; it should not be obstructed nor set aside; the matter is present before one; there is a formal accusation that causes others to remember [the offense]; and it is carried out after three inquiries. These are called the five ways of performing the *tarjanīya-karman* according to the Dharma.
“There are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a ‘good ṭhita’:

one who says they have seen what was seen, heard what was heard, remembered what was remembered, known what was known, and states what is Dharma as being Dharma. These are called the five qualities of a bhikṣu who is a good ṭhita.”
"There are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a good *tāliṭa*:
he does not follow desire, hatred, fear, or delusion; he speaks of the Dharma as being the Dharma. These are called the five qualities of a bhikṣu who is a good *tāliṭa*."
“There are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a good *tāla-tāḍaka*:

he discerns and grasps matters well; he does not speak of faults where there are none; he speaks of faults where they exist; he produces impurity from what is impure and purity from what is pure; and he speaks of the Dharma as the Dharma. These are called the five qualities of a bhikṣu who is a good *tāla-tāḍaka*.”
"There are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a good *tāla*:
he is skilled in discerning matters;
he does not rely on force when adjudicating matters within the Saṃgha."
Having obtained permission, one may raise the matter of another;
one may accept a confession of fault without partiality, perceive the faults of others without partiality, and speak of the faults of others without partiality;
speaking of the Dharma as the Dharma.
These are called the five qualities of a *tāla* monk.
There are five things that constitute a *tāla* monk:

he skillfully grasps the dispute, skillfully knows the basis of the dispute, skillfully distinguishes the dispute, skillfully knows that once the dispute has been extinguished it will not arise again, and he speaks of the Dharma as Dharma. These are called the five qualities of a *tāla* monk.
“There are five qualities that define a bhikṣu who is a good *tāla* (a *talapatta*):

he is skilled in knowing the Sūtras, skilled in knowing the Vinaya, skilled in knowing disputes, skilled in knowing the grounds for disputes, and he speaks of the Dharma as the Dharma. These are called the five qualities of a bhikṣu who is a good *tāla*.”
"Furthermore, there are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a good *tāliṭa*:

having received full ordination for ten years or more; being observant of the precepts; being learned; being skilled in resolving one's own doubts and the doubts of others in accordance with the Dharma; and being well able to sever one's own and others' evil and false views. These are called the five qualities of a good *tāliṭa* bhikṣu."
“There are five qualities that define a *kalyāṇa-tāliṭṭha* bhikṣu:

he is skilled at establishing others in the precepts; he is skilled in teaching the Vinaya and Abhidharma; if a disciple enters another region and becomes unhappy there, he is able to bring them back; and he is able to tend to the sick and instruct others in how to do so. These are called the five qualities of a *kalyāṇa-tāliṭṭha* bhikṣu.”
"There are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a 'good Tāla':
he can cause others to have faith, to observe the precepts, to be learned, to practice generosity, and to possess wisdom; these are called the five qualities of a good Tāla bhikṣu."
"Furthermore, there are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like):

if he himself abides in the precepts of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-śīla*), the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samādhi*), the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-prajñā*), the liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñānadarśana*), and is also able to cause others to abide in the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training—these are called the five qualities of a *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* bhikṣu."
"Furthermore, there are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is an excellent *tāli-ta*:

he knows what constitutes an offense, he knows what does not constitute an offense, he knows what is light, he knows what is heavy, and he is extensively proficient in the beneficial precepts. These are called the five qualities of an excellent *tāli-ta* bhikṣu."
“There are five qualities that characterize a bhikṣu who is a good *tāliṭa*:

he knows the going forth, he knows the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), he knows how to instruct, he knows the rules of dependence (*niśraya*), and he knows what obstructs and what does not obstruct the path; these are called the five qualities of a bhikṣu who is a good *tāliṭa*.”

The Five Dharmas are concluded. 16. The Six Dharmas (as previously explained). 17. The Seven Dharmas (as previously explained). 18. The Eight Dharmas. Regarding the first eight dharmas: one should not keep eight kinds of bowls:
gold bowls, silver bowls, lapis lazuli bowls, crystal bowls, copper bowls, pewter bowls, wooden bowls, and stone bowls; these are called the eight kinds of bowls that should not be kept.
The remainder is as previously stated.
19. Regarding the nine dharmas: First, the Buddha’s words to Upāli:
"A single bhikṣu cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha; two, three, four, or even up to nine bhikṣus who are pure and of like view can cause a schism."

One bhikṣuṇī, one śikṣamāṇā, one śrāmaṇera, one śrāmaṇerī, one male renunciant, or one female renunciant cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha; likewise, two, three, four, or even up to nine such individuals cannot do so either.
Upāli! If there are nine bhikṣus who are pure and of like views, they are able to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
There are nine offenses:

Offenses involving a *pārājika*, offenses involving a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, offenses involving a *pāyattika*, offenses involving a *pratideśanīya*, offenses involving a *duṣkṛta*, offenses involving a *duṣkṛta* for harsh speech, offenses involving a *sthūlātyaya-duṣkṛta*, offenses involving a *vinaya-duṣkṛta*, and offenses involving a *airyāpathika-duṣkṛta*; these are called the nine offenses.
“There are nine types of decline:

decline in precepts, decline in views, decline in livelihood, decline in deportment, decline through one’s own actions, decline through others’ actions, decline in spiritual friends, decline in material requisites, and decline in birth and death; these are called the nine declines.”
There are nine kinds of non-retrogression:

non-retrogression in precepts, non-retrogression in view, non-retrogression in livelihood, non-retrogression in dignified conduct, non-retrogression by oneself, non-retrogression through others, non-retrogression in spiritual friends, non-retrogression in material requisites, and non-retrogression regarding birth and death; these are called the nine non-retrogressions.
The Buddha said to Upāli: “When the bhikṣu Tālaṭa is resolving a dispute, he should examine the speaker by means of nine matters:

examining the disputant; examining his deportment; examining his place of origin and travels; examining his kinsmen; examining his acquaintances; examining his conduct of body and speech; examining his antecedents; examining how they speak to one another; and whether he should listen to others' words and hear them from others. These are called the nine matters by which one should examine the speaker.”
Regarding "disputes," what are the nine matters for examining the speaker?

Examining whether there is fighting or no fighting; examining whether there is disputing or no disputing; examining whether there is mutual support or no mutual support; examining whether there is mutual accusation or no mutual accusation; examining violations of the precepts; examining violations of views; examining violations of livelihood; examining speech; and examining what has been heard from others. These are called the nine matters for which one should examine the speaker.
At that time, the Elder Upāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will briefly teach the Dharma, so that I may know what is the Dharma, what is the Vinaya, and what is the Buddha’s teaching.”
The Buddha said to Upāli: “If a teaching follows desire and not the absence of desire;

follows hatred and not the absence of hatred; follows envy and not the absence of envy; follows coming and going and not the absence of coming and going; follows increase and not the absence of increase; follows strife and not the absence of strife; follows contention and not the absence of contention; follows mutual grasping and not the absence of mutual grasping; and follows mutual verbal dispute and not the absence of mutual verbal dispute—[such a teaching is not the Dharma].”
Upāli! You certainly know that this is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha. Upāli!

If a teaching accords with freedom from desire and does not accord with desire; accords with freedom from hatred and does not accord with hatred; accords with freedom from envy and does not accord with envy; accords with non-coming-and-going and does not accord with coming-and-going; accords with non-increase and does not accord with increase; accords with non-contention and does not accord with contention; accords with non-dispute and does not accord with dispute; accords with non-opposing and does not accord with opposing; accords with non-quarreling and does not accord with quarreling—you should certainly know that this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Buddha’s teaching.
At that time, the Elder Aniruddha went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
"I pray that you will briefly explain the Dharma so that I may know what is the Dharma, what is the Vinaya, and what is the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddha said to Anuruddha: "If a teaching follows greed rather than non-greed;

follows lack of contentment rather than contentment; follows great desire rather than few desires; follows lack of satisfaction rather than satisfaction; follows being difficult to satisfy rather than easy to satisfy; follows negligence rather than diligence; follows what is contrary to the Dharma rather than the Dharma; follows what opposes the Dharma rather than what does not oppose it; and follows worldly speech rather than the language of the Vinaya—[then it is not my teaching]."
The Buddha said to Aniruddha:
"You know with certainty that this is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha. Aniruddha!"

If a teaching accords with non-attachment rather than attachment, with disenchantment rather than lack of disenchantment, with few desires rather than many desires, with contentment rather than discontent, with being easily satisfied rather than being difficult to satisfy, with heedfulness rather than heedlessness, with the Dharma rather than what is contrary to the Dharma, with conformity to the Dharma rather than opposition to the Dharma, and with the language of the Vinaya rather than worldly speech, you may know with certainty that this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, and this is the Buddha’s teaching.
As the Elder Upāli asked, so did Mahāprajāpatī ask;
as the Elder Ānanda asked, so did Gaṅgā Mātā ask.
“There are nine bases of reliance:
if a son of good family relies upon faith and abandons the unwholesome while adopting the wholesome, this is called ‘abandoning the unwholesome and adopting the wholesome.
The same applies to morality, learning, generosity, and wisdom; thus, it is said that a son of good family relies upon faith to abandon the unwholesome and adopt the wholesome.”
Once this person has established themselves in these five dharmas, they should further realize four dharmas:

the patience of the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), the patience of conformity (*anulomikī kṣānti*), the patience of delight (*ratisaṃkhyā kṣānti*), and the patience of relinquishment (*tyāgakṣānti*). These are called the nine bases.
There was a non-Buddhist named Bahudhīti who went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat to one side. Having done so, he addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gautama!
Previously, not long after he had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* beneath a *kaśmarī* tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River in the kingdom of Uruvilvā, I heard from Gautama at that place:
"An Arhat who has exhausted the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) and does not return to birth and death does not perform five things:
he does not intentionally kill living beings, he does not steal, he does not engage in sexual misconduct, he does not intentionally speak falsehoods, and he does not drink intoxicants."
"I have heard these words from Gautama and immediately accepted them with faith.
The Buddha said:
"I have already spoken of this before, and I speak it again now: an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted does not return to birth and death, and does not perform nine things:"

Not intentionally killing living beings, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not intentionally speaking falsehoods, not drinking intoxicants, and not acting out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—these are called the nine matters.
There was a non-Buddhist named Śāṭa who went to where the Buddha was staying to pay his respects; having sat to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Gautama! Previously, while you were in the kingdom of Uruvilvā by the banks of the Nairañjanā River, beneath a single *kaḍali* tree, not long after attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I heard from you there, Gautama:”
The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted does not return to birth and death and does not perform five things:
he does not intentionally kill living beings, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not intentionally speak falsehoods, and does not drink intoxicants.
"Having heard these words from Gautama, I immediately accepted them with faith.
The Buddha said:
"I have already spoken of this before, and I speak it again now: an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted does not return to birth and death and does not perform nine things:"

Not intentionally killing living beings, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not intentionally speaking falsehoods, not drinking intoxicants, not being dishonest, not giving rise to wrong views, seeing the eternal Dharma, and contemplating the impermanence of birth and death—these are called the nine matters that involve nine afflictions:
they bring no profit, no benefit, they afflict me, and they do not bring me peace and security.
The remainder is as previously stated. The Nine Dharmas are concluded. **20. The Ten Dharmas** First, regarding the Ten Dharmas:

there are ten benefits: for the sake of unifying the Saṃgha; for the sake of the Saṃgha being of one mind; for the sake of the Saṃgha practicing in peace and happiness; for the sake of subduing those with arrogant minds; for the sake of causing those without faith to gain faith; for the sake of causing those who already have faith to increase it; for the sake of causing those with a sense of shame and remorse to attain peace and happiness; for the sake of warding off the afflictions and outflows of this present life; for the sake of severing the outflows of future lives; and for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma. These are called the ten benefits.
“There are ten types of speech:

speech concerning the Sūtras, speech concerning the Vinaya, speech concerning the Abhidharma, speech concerning the Upādhyāya, speech concerning the Ācārya, speech concerning the precepts, speech concerning robes, speech concerning the alms-bowl, speech concerning food, and speech concerning medicine; these are called the ten types of speech.”
“There are ten vows:

the vow for the Sūtras, the vow for the Vinaya, the vow for the Abhidharma, the vow for the Upādhyāya, the vow for the Ācārya, the vow for the precepts, the vow for robes, the vow for the bowl, the vow for food, and the vow for medicine; these are called the ten vows.”
“There are ten types of formal acts (*karmas*):

the formal act consisting of a motion (*jñapti-karman*), the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the formal act of the Saṃgha, the formal act of a *tala-tāla* bhikṣu, the formal act concerning the precepts, the formal act that is contrary to the Dharma, the formal act that is in accordance with the Dharma, the formal act performed by a divided assembly, and the formal act performed by a harmonious assembly. These are called the ten formal acts.”
“There are ten forms of discipline:

*duṣkṛta* (reprimand), *niśraya* (dependence), *pravāsanīya* (banishment), *tarjanīya* (humiliation), *adarśanāyotkṣepaṇīya* (suspension for not seeing an offense), *apratikarmāyotkṣepaṇīya* (suspension for not making amends), *apratiniḥsṛṣṭe pāpake dṛṣṭigate utkṣepaṇīya* (suspension for not relinquishing an evil view), *parivāsa* (probation), *mānatva* (penance), and *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement after returning to the beginning); these are called the ten disciplines.”
“There are ten forms of punishment:

censure, dependence, banishment, reconciliation, suspension for not seeing [an offense], suspension for not making amends, suspension for not relinquishing a wrong view, separate residence, *mānāpya*, and the restoration of the original status; these are called the ten punishments.”
“There are ten obstructing conditions for receiving the precepts:

killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, having previously committed a grave offense, being a bhikṣu who dwells as a thief, being a former layperson, being a eunuch, defiling a bhikṣuṇī, and being a person who has crossed over [to another sect]. These are called the ten obstructing conditions for receiving the precepts.”
“There are ten perils:

the peril of kings, the peril of thieves, the peril of fire, the peril of water, the peril of wild beasts, the peril of dragons, the peril of humans, the peril of non-humans, the peril to life, and the peril to the holy life; these are called the ten perils.”
“There are ten that are non-vinaya, namely the ten unwholesome courses of action.
There are ten vinayas, namely the ten wholesome courses of action.
Furthermore, there are ten that are non-vinaya, namely the ten wrong paths.”
There are ten *vinayas*, namely the ten true [stages] of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
There are ten who are without resolve:

one undergoing separate residence (*parivāsa*), one whose separate residence is completed, one practicing *mānatva*, one whose *mānatva* practice is completed, one subject to censure, one dependent on another for support, one who has been expelled, one who must perform an act of submission, one suspended for not seeing [an offense], and one suspended for not making amends; these are called the ten who are without resolve.
“There are ten unrighteous ways of obstructing the recitation of the *pātimokkha*:

not being guilty of a *pārājika* offense, not having committed an act that constitutes a *pārājika*, not having reviled the Saṅgha, not having committed an act that constitutes reviling the Saṅgha, not having renounced the precepts, not having committed an act that constitutes renouncing the precepts, acting in accordance with the lawful affairs of the Saṅgha, not having broken the precepts, not having broken one’s views, and not having broken one’s conduct; furthermore, not having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense]. These are called the ten unrighteous ways of obstructing the recitation of the *pātimokkha*.”
What are the ten lawful grounds for obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*?

They are: having committed a *pārājika* offense; having engaged in the matter of a *pārājika*; having reviled the Saṃgha; having engaged in the matter of reviling the Saṃgha; having renounced the precepts; having engaged in the matter of renouncing the precepts; not conforming to the lawful affairs of the Saṃgha; breaking the precepts; breaking right view; breaking proper conduct; and having seen, heard, or suspected [an offense]. These are called the ten lawful grounds for obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vākaṇālipana. Therein was a lay follower (upāsaka) who possessed faith and devotion; he constructed a dwelling and offered it specifically to the Elder Rāhula, as previously described.
“For ten benefits, the Tathāgata establishes the precepts: for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha; for the sake of the Saṃgha’s unity of mind;

for the sake of the Saṃgha’s dwelling in peace and happiness; for the sake of subduing those with arrogant hearts; for the sake of inspiring faith in those who lack it; for the sake of increasing the faith of those who already have it; for the sake of allowing those with a sense of shame and remorse to dwell in security; for the sake of warding off the afflictions and outflows of the present life; for the sake of severing the outflows of future lives; and for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the Buddha-dharma.”

“The Tathāgata has established the precepts, established the Sūtras, established the Vinaya, and established the Abhidharma; he has recited the Sūtras, recited the Vinaya, and recited the Abhidharma; he has upheld the Sūtras, upheld the Vinaya, and upheld the Abhidharma.”
Those who uphold the Sūtras, those who uphold the Vinaya, and those who uphold the Abhidharma;
they collect the Sūtras, collect the Vinaya, and collect the Abhidharma.
The upādhyāya and ācārya, along with the co-practicing disciples, the resident disciples, and the śrāmaṇeras, teach them the vinaya of dignified conduct.
That which is called the vinaya is the prātimokṣa.
To speak of the *prātimokṣa* is to obstruct the *prātimokṣa*.
To obstruct the *prātimokṣa* is to accept the invitation (*pravāraṇā*).
To accept the invitation is to obstruct the acceptance of the invitation.
One who prevents another from receiving the invitation to self-examination (pravāraṇā) gives their consent (chanda).
One who gives consent receives the consent.
One who receives the consent maintains the consent.
One who holds the desire speaks of the desire;
one who speaks of the desire takes up the desire;
one who takes up the desire bestows purity.
Those who are pure receive purity;
those who receive purity maintain purity;
those who maintain purity proclaim purity.
One who speaks of purity takes up purity;
one who takes up purity grants the purity of consent;
one who grants the purity of consent receives the purity of consent.
One who experiences the purity of desire maintains the purity of desire;
one who maintains the purity of desire proclaims the purity of desire;
one who proclaims the purity of desire takes up the purity of desire.
Those who wish for purity should grant the *pravāraṇā*;
those who grant the *pravāraṇā* should receive the *pravāraṇā*;
those who receive the *pravāraṇā* should maintain the *pravāraṇā*.
One who maintains the invitation (pravāraṇā) speaks the invitation;
one who speaks the invitation takes up the invitation;
one who takes up the invitation relies [upon it].
One who provides dependence;
one to whom dependence is provided; one who receives dependence;
and one who relinquishes dependence.
Regarding the one who relinquishes the reliance [upon another]: it involves subduing and expelling them, as well as agreeing to repentance. Regarding the one who receives the repentance:

there are the *jñapti-karman* (motion), the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion and one proclamation), the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (motion and three proclamations), the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of expulsion), the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), the *adarśana-utkṣepa* (suspension for not seeing an offense), the *aprati-karmatā-utkṣepa* (suspension for not making amends), the *apratinihsṛṣṭe pāpake dṛṣṭigate utkṣepa* (suspension for not renouncing evil views), the *parivāsa* (probation), the *mānatva* (penance), the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction of the probation period), the *āvarhaṇa* (restoration from the beginning), the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation of offenses), the *mārgitavya-pāpaka-lakṣaṇa* (seeking the characteristics of an offense), the *smṛti-vinaya-sammuti-karman* (formal act of agreement to remind another), the *bandhana-karman* (act of confinement), the *anujñā-prārthanā-karman* (formal act of requesting permission), and the *anujñā-jñapti-karman* (formal act of granting permission).
"Those who are not disciplined shall be brought to discipline; all this is for the sake of the ten benefits.

The Ten Dharmas are concluded. 21. Increase Eleven: The First Increase of the Eleven Characteristics. "Regarding a matter that has been transgressed, should one say it was announced (*ārocita*) or should one say it was not announced?"
He replied, "When an offense occurs, one should say 'it must be announced.
Furthermore, when an offense occurs, should one say it is 'form' (rūpa) or should one say it is 'non-form' (arūpa)?"
He replied, "Regarding an offense, one should say 'visible' (rūpa).
Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is 'visible' or 'invisible'?"
He replied, “One should say it is visible. [The Buddha asked:
“Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is counted by its roots or not counted by its roots?”
He replied, "One should say 'the number of faculties.
Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is 'with outflows' (sāsrava) or 'without outflows' (anāsrava)?"
He replied, "One should say they are 'with outflows' (sāsrava).
[The other asked,] "Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?"
He replied: "One should say it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, regarding its transgression, one should say it is mundane (*laukika*) or supramundane (*lokottara*)."
He replied: "One should say 'the world.
Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is included within the aggregates (*skandha*) or not included within the aggregates?"
He replied: "One should say it is included within the aggregates (skandha).
Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is included within the realms (dhātu) or not included within the realms?"
He replied: "One should say it is included within the elements (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is 'accepted' or 'not accepted'?"
He replied, "One should say 'accepted.
Furthermore, regarding the offense, should one say it is composed of the four great elements, or not composed of the four great elements?"
He replied, "It is composed of the four great elements.
[The Buddha asked again: "Furthermore, when committing an offense, should one say 'perception' or 'non-perception'?"
He replied, “One should say ‘perception.
Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it was committed with a distracted mind or with an undistracted mind?”
He replied: "One should say 'with a distracted mind.
Furthermore, when an offense is committed, should one say it was 'defiled' or 'undefiled'?"
He replied, "There are those who are stained and those who are unstained; one who is stained commits an intentional offense.
The Buddha has established the precepts such that one who is unstained does not commit an intentional offense against the rules."
“Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is ‘mixed’ or ‘unmixed’?
He replied, “One should say it is mixed.”
"Furthermore, when one commits an offense, should one say 'with desire' or 'without desire'?
He replied, "With desire."
"Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say there is attachment or no attachment?
He replied, "There is attachment."
"Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is 'with resistance' (sapratigha) or 'without resistance' (apratigha)? He replied:
"With resistance."
"Furthermore, regarding the offense, should one say it was intentional or unintentional?
He replied, "It was intentional."
“Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it has retribution or no retribution?
He replied: “It has retribution.”
"Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is 'karma' or 'non-karma'? He replied,
"It is karma."
“Furthermore, when committing an offense, should one say ‘external sense-base’ or ‘internal sense-base’? He replied,
“Internal sense-base.”
“Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it belongs to the past, the future, or the present?
He replied:
“There are offenses belonging to the past, the future, and the present.”
Regarding the past: if the offense committed has already been confessed and repented before others, this is called the past.
Regarding the future: that which has not yet been committed but is certain to be committed, this is called the future.
"As for 'the present,' it refers to that which is currently being transgressed; this is called the present.
[Question: "Furthermore, regarding a transgression, should one say it is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral?
[Answer: He replied:
“Unwholesome and indeterminate.
‘Unwholesome’ refers to intentional transgressions; because the Buddha has established the precepts, these are called unwholesome.
‘Indeterminate’ refers to non-intentional transgressions of the precepts; these are called indeterminate.”
"Furthermore, when committing an offense, should one say it belongs to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
He replied: "When committing an offense, one should say it belongs to the desire realm."
"Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it pertains to those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa)? He replied:
"It pertains to neither those in training nor those beyond training."
"Furthermore, regarding an offense, should one say it is abandoned by seeing the truths (darśana-heya) or abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?
He replied, "It is abandoned by cultivation."
“Is there an instance where performing such an act constitutes an offense, yet performing that very same act does not constitute an offense?
The Buddha said, “There is.”

If a bhikṣu, while the kaṭhina robe has not been formally accepted, keeps extra robes, eats repeatedly, eats apart from the community, enters a village without having announced his intention, or enters a village without wearing his saṃghāṭī robe, this is called an offense.

If a bhikṣu, having accepted the kaṭhina robe, keeps extra robes, eats frequently, eats apart from the community, enters a village without announcing his presence, or enters a village without wearing his saṃghāṭī, this is called non-offense.
This is called: "committing an offense by performing this act," versus "not committing an offense by performing this act";
and "committing an offense by performing a formal ritual (karmavācanā)," versus "not committing an offense by performing a formal ritual."
"What constitutes an offense for those performing the *karmavācanā*, while those performing the *karmavācanā* themselves remain without offense?

If a monk has been subjected to a formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense (*adarśana-pratiniḥsarga*), for not making amends for an offense (*apratinisṛṣṭa-āpatti*), or for not relinquishing wrong views (*adharma-dṛṣṭi-apratiniḥsarga*), yet that monk himself acknowledges his fault and declares it to others, and they then perform a formal act of release (*pratisaṃharaṇa-karman*) for him outside the boundary (*sīmā*), and subsequently engage in communal affairs, dwell together, and provide instruction with him."
Other bhikṣus spoke thus:

"The Saṃgha has not expelled this bhikṣu for failure to see [his fault], nor has it performed an expulsion against him, nor has it carried out an expulsion for not relinquishing evil views; do not engage in communal affairs with this bhikṣu, do not dwell together with him, and do not instruct him."
He replied,
"This person has recognized their offense and has already been granted the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (the rite of reconciliation). He asked:
"Where is it relinquished? He replied,
"Outside the boundary."
Furthermore, it is said:
"This is an improper relinquishment.

If a bhikṣu—toward one who has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], not been suspended for not making amends, or not been suspended for not abandoning evil views—confesses his own fault to others and, within the boundary, relinquishes [the formal act] while performing communal duties, living together, and receiving instruction.
There was a bhikṣu who said:

"The Saṃgha has not performed an *adarśana-pravāsanīya-karman* against this bhikṣu, nor an *apratinisṛṣṭe-pāpake-dharme-pravāsanīya-karman*; do not engage in communal affairs with this bhikṣu, nor dwell together with him, nor provide him instruction."
He replied,
"I have already relinquished this offense. He asked:
"Where is it relinquished? He replied,
"Within the boundary."
Furthermore, it is said:
"It is well relinquished.
Thus, performing the *karmavācanā* in this manner constitutes an offense; performing the *karmavācanā* in this manner does not constitute an offense.
"There is transgression through knowledge and transgression through ignorance.
One who knows the transgression is one who knows the essential nature of the five kinds of transgressions; this is called 'knowing the transgression.
One who does not know the transgression is one who does not know the essential nature of the five kinds of transgressions; this is called 'not knowing the transgression.'"
Although this person does not know it, they are still said to have committed an offense.
There are those who know for themselves that they have committed an offense and are guilty, and there are those who are known by others to have committed an offense and are guilty.

One who knows for themselves that they have committed an offense and are guilty is so called because they recognize the nature of the five kinds of offenses; this is what is meant by "knowing for oneself that one has committed an offense and is guilty."
"Knowing through another that one has committed an offense" means that if a trustworthy upāsaka attests to it, this is called "knowing through another that one has committed an offense.
There is also "recollection of an offense" and "non-recollection of an offense."
"Recalling an offense" means to recall the substance of the five kinds of offenses; this is called "recalling an offense.
"Not recalling an offense" means not to recall the substance of the five kinds of offenses; this is called "not recalling an offense."
There are offenses committed in the presence [of others] and those not committed in their presence.
Regarding an offense committed in the presence: when there is an actual transgression occurring before one's eyes, this is called "committed in the presence.
Regarding an offense not committed in the presence: if one has not yet committed an offense but is certain to do so, this is called "not committed in the presence."
There are cases of being excluded from communal residence due to an offense, and cases of being excluded from communal residence for various reasons.

There are cases of being excluded from communal residence for various reasons that do not constitute formal exclusion: namely, one who has not been suspended for refusal to see an offense, one who has not been suspended for refusal to make amends, one who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, one who is insane, one whose mind is deranged, and one who is suffering from acute pain—these are called being excluded from communal residence due to an offense.

There are those who commit offenses and are subject to various forms of non-cohabitation (*asaṃvāsa*); there are various forms of non-cohabitation, as well as cases that do not constitute non-cohabitation.

There are those for whom a formal act (*karmavācanā*) has been performed resulting in non-cohabitation; there are those for whom a formal act has been performed resulting in various forms of non-cohabitation; and there are various forms of non-cohabitation that do not constitute [formal] non-cohabitation. If one has not been suspended for refusal to see an offense, has not been suspended, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is insane, deranged, or in pain, this is called being subject to non-cohabitation through a formal act, being subject to various forms of non-cohabitation through a formal act, and having various forms of non-cohabitation that do not constitute [formal] non-cohabitation.

There is that which is known as "not living together," there is that which is known as "various forms of not living together," and there is "various forms of not living together" that is not "not living together. If one has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is insane, deranged, or in pain, this is called "that which is known as not living together," "that which is known as various forms of not living together," and "various forms of not living together" that is not "not living together."

Not knowing about non-residence, not knowing various forms of non-residence, the existence of various forms of non-residence, and what is not non-residence; if one has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is insane, mentally deranged, or in pain—these are called not knowing non-residence, not knowing various forms of non-residence, the existence of various forms of non-residence, and what is not non-residence.
There is that which is called "self-declared non-residence," and there is that which is called "self-declared various non-residences.

There are various non-residences that are not [simply] non-residences: namely, one who has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], one who has not been suspended for not making amends, one who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, one with a deranged mind, one with a distracted mind, and one with a mind of intense suffering. These are termed self-declared non-residence, self-declared various non-residences, and various non-residences that are not [simply] non-residences.

Some say "not living together" (*asaṃvāsa*); some say "various forms of not living together"; there are various forms of not living together, yet it is not a case of not living together. If one has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is insane, deranged, or in pain—this is called "others say not living together," "others say various forms of not living together," "there are various forms of not living together," and "it is not a case of not living together."

There is "recollection with non-cohabitation," there is "recollection with various forms of non-cohabitation," there is "various forms of non-cohabitation" that is not "non-cohabitation. If one has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is insane, deranged, or in pain, this is called "recollection with non-cohabitation," "recollection with various forms of non-cohabitation," and "various forms of non-cohabitation" that is not "non-cohabitation."

There is non-remembrance and non-residence; there is non-remembrance of various forms of non-residence; there is various non-residence that is not non-residence. If one has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is of deranged mind, distracted mind, or afflicted mind—these are called non-remembrance and non-residence, non-remembrance of various forms of non-residence, various non-residences, and that which is not non-residence.

There is face-to-face non-cohabitation; there is face-to-face manifold non-cohabitation; there is manifold non-cohabitation that is not non-cohabitation. If one has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or if one is insane, deranged, or in pain, this is called face-to-face non-cohabitation, face-to-face manifold non-cohabitation, and manifold non-cohabitation that is not non-cohabitation.

There is non-cohabitation in the absence [of the accused], there is various non-cohabitation in the absence [of the accused], there is various non-cohabitation, and there is non-cohabitation that is not [in the absence]. If one has not been seen [committing an offense], has not been subjected to the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*), has not been suspended for not abandoning evil views, or if one is insane, deranged, or in excruciating pain—these are called non-cohabitation in the absence, various non-cohabitation in the absence, various non-cohabitation, and non-cohabitation that is not [in the absence].
“There are those who have committed an offense for whom the Saṃgha performs a formal act (kamma)—namely, three persons, two persons, or one person.
What is meant by ‘there are those who have committed an offense for whom the Saṃgha performs a formal act—namely, three persons, two persons, or one person’?”

If a bhikṣu has been subjected by other bhikṣus to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, for not making amends for an offense, or for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is suspended for being insane, distracted, or in pain; and if that bhikṣu commits such an offense, and the Saṃgha performs a formal ritual (karmavācanā) against him for that very matter—whether it involves three persons, two persons, or one person.
There are those who know that the Saṃgha has performed a *karmavācanā* against them—whether by three, two, or one person.
What is meant by knowing that the Saṃgha has performed a *karmavācanā* against them by three, two, or one person?

If a bhikṣu has been subjected by the Saṃgha to a formal act (*karmavācanā*) while knowing that he is one who has been suspended for not seeing an offense, for not making amends for an offense, for not relinquishing evil views, or for being of deranged mind, distracted mind, or afflicted mind—this is called "the Saṃgha performing a formal act against one who knows," which refers to three persons, two persons, or one person.
There are those who are unaware; the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* (formal act) for them—whether it be three persons, two persons, or one person.
What is meant by "the Saṃgha performing a *karmavācanā* for those who are unaware, whether it be three persons, two persons, or one person"?

If a monk performs a formal act (*kamma*) against a monk who has not been suspended for refusal to see an offense, who has not been suspended for refusal to make amends, who has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or who is insane, deranged, or afflicted by pain—this is called a formal act performed by a Saṃgha that is "not known," which involves three persons, two persons, or one person.
There is a self-assertion regarding the Saṃgha performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against three persons, two persons, or one person.
What is this self-assertion concerning the Saṃgha performing a formal act against three persons, two persons, or one person?

If a monk performs an act of suspension against another monk for not seeing [an offense], for not making amends, for not relinquishing evil views, or for being insane, deranged, or afflicted by pain, this is called "the Saṃgha performing a formal act (kamma) upon oneself," which refers to three persons, two persons, or one person.
There are cases where one does not confess oneself, yet the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against them—whether it be three persons, two persons, or one person.
What is meant by "one does not confess oneself, yet the Saṃgha performs a formal act against them—whether it be three persons, two persons, or one person"?

If a monk has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, or has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is insane, deranged, or in pain—the Sangha may perform a formal act (*kamma*) against him even if he does not state it himself. This applies to cases involving three persons, two persons, or one person.
Regarding those who remember [the offense], the Saṃgha performs the formal act (karmavācanā) for them—whether there be three, two, or one person.
What is meant by "those who remember," for whom the Saṃgha performs the formal act, whether there be three, two, or one person?

If a monk has been subjected by other monks to the act of suspension for not seeing an offense, to the act of suspension for not confessing an offense, to the act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views, or if he is insane, deranged, or suffering from physical pain, and he is considered one who remembers [the offense], the Saṃgha may perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against him; this refers to cases involving three persons, two persons, or a single person.
There are those who do not remember; the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for them in groups of three, two, or one.
What does it mean that the Saṃgha performs a formal act for those who do not remember, in groups of three, two, or one?

If a monk has been suspended for not seeing [an offense], for not making amends, or for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is insane, mentally deranged, or in excruciating pain—these are called those who do not remember. If the Saṃgha performs a formal ritual (karmavācanā) against such a person, it constitutes a case involving three people, two people, or one person.
There is "presence" (sammukhatā) when the Saṃgha performs a formal act (kamma) for three persons, two persons, or one person.
What is meant by "presence," such that the Saṃgha performs a formal act for three persons, two persons, or one person?

If a monk—whether he has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views, or is insane, deranged, or afflicted by pain—the Sangha performs a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) against him in his presence; this refers to cases involving three persons, two persons, or one person.
There are cases where the Saṃgha performs a formal act (karmavācanā) against someone who is not present—namely, against three people, two people, or one person.
What constitutes performing a formal act against three, two, or one person when they are not present?

If a monk has not been suspended for not seeing [an offense], has not been suspended for not making amends, or has not been suspended for not relinquishing evil views; or if he is insane, deranged, or in pain—these are called "not being present. If the Saṃgha performs a formal ritual (karmavācanā) against such a person, it constitutes a case involving three persons, two persons, or one person.
“There are four disciplinary acts (*karmavācanā*):
censure, dependence, banishment, and reconciliation.

“Is it possible that regarding this same matter of claiming to have caused a schism in the Saṃgha, one who has not yet received ordination should not receive it, and one who has already received it should be expelled; yet regarding that very same matter of claiming to have caused a schism in the Saṃgha, one who has not yet received ordination should be granted ordination, and one who has already received it should not be expelled?”
The Buddha said: “There is.

If one perceives what is not Dharma as non-Dharma, yet performs an act that constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha, those who have not yet received the precepts should not receive them, and those who have already received them should be expelled.”
"If the perception of a dharma causes a schism in the Saṃgha, those who have not yet received the precepts should receive them, and those who have already received them should not be expelled.

Is it possible that regarding this same matter, one who declares himself a 'thief-dwelling' bhikṣu—whereby those who have not yet received the precepts should not receive them and those who have already received them should be expelled—is the very same as the case where one who declares himself a 'thief-dwelling' bhikṣu—whereby those who have not yet received the precepts should receive them and those who have already received them should not be expelled?"
The Buddha said: "There are!
If one has attended the poṣadha two or three times, that person—if they have not yet received the precepts—should not receive them; if they have already received them, they should be expelled."

“If, during a single *poṣadha*, whether it is permitted or not permitted, those who have not yet received [the precepts] should receive them, and those who have already received them should not cease [their practice].

Is there such a case where, having defiled a bhikṣuṇī, those who have not yet received [the precepts] should not receive them, while those who have already received them should cease [their practice]; that is to say, in the case of defiling a bhikṣuṇī, those who have not yet received the precepts should receive them, while those who have already received them should not cease?”
The Buddha said: “There is!
If one defiles a bhikṣuṇī through sexual misconduct, one who has not yet received the precepts should not receive them, and one who has already received them should be expelled.”
"If one touches a bhikṣuṇī with bodily contact and defiles her, those who have not yet received [the precepts] should receive them, and those who have already received them should not be expelled.

Is it possible that there is such a case where one says of oneself, 'I have killed my parents,' such that those who have not yet received [the precepts] should not receive them, while those who have already received them should be expelled; yet in this very same matter, one says of oneself, 'I have killed my parents,' such that those who have not yet received [the precepts] should receive them, while those who have already received them should not be expelled?"
The Buddha said: "There is.

If one knows them to be one's parents, and kills them without any other thought or error, that which has not yet been received should not be received, and that which has already been received should be extinguished."

"If one kills one's father or mother out of ignorance or through a mistaken perception, one who has not yet received the precepts should receive them, and one who has already received them need not forfeit them.
At that time, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
Is it possible for one who kills his parents with a virtuous mind to incur both a *pārājika* offense and a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
Or is it when one kills his parents with a non-virtuous mind or an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind?
The Buddha said to Upāli:

"If one kills one's father or mother with a wholesome mind, one incurs both a pārājika offense and a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya); the same applies to killing them with an unwholesome mind or with a neutral (avyākṛta) mind."
What is killing with a wholesome mind?

If a mother is suffering from illness and one kills her to relieve her of that suffering, this is called killing a mother with a wholesome mind; one incurs the *pārājika* offense as well as the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
What is killing one’s mother with an unwholesome mind?
If one kills for the sake of profit, this is called killing one’s mother with an unwholesome mind; one incurs a *pārājika* offense as well as the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
What is killing one’s mother with a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind?

"If, after having made the preparations, the mother dies while he himself is asleep, this is called killing one's mother with an indeterminate mind; he incurs both a *pārājika* offense and a transgression against the root precepts (*ānantarya*).
He asked again:
"Is it possible to kill one's mother with a wholesome mind and yet incur a *pārājika* offense and a transgression against the root precepts?"
"If one kills one's mother with a wholesome mind, does this not constitute a pārājika offense but not a pācittiya of immediate retribution (ānantarya)?
The Buddha said,
"If one kills one's mother with a wholesome mind, it constitutes both a pārājika offense and a pācittiya of immediate retribution."
There is the case where one kills one’s mother with a wholesome mind; this is neither a *pārājika* offense nor a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
How is it that killing one’s mother with a wholesome mind constitutes a *pārājika* offense and a crime of immediate retribution?
And how is it that killing one’s mother with a wholesome mind is neither a *pārājika* offense nor a crime of immediate retribution?
If one ends the life of a mother who is suffering from illness, this is called an offense of *pārājika* and a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).

If a mother is ill and one gives her rice, gruel, or soup, and she passes away after eating it, this is called killing with a wholesome mind; it is neither an offense of *pārājika* nor a crime of immediate retribution.
Upāli! Thus, if one kills one’s mother with a virtuous mind, one incurs both a pārājika offense and a heinous crime (ānantarya);
likewise, there may be neither pārājika nor heinous crime.
He asked again:
"Is it possible that one who kills his mother with an unwholesome mind commits a *pārājika* offense and an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*),
while another who kills his mother with an unwholesome mind commits neither a *pārājika* nor an act of immediate retribution?"
The Buddha said:
"If one kills one's mother with an unwholesome mind, it constitutes a pārājika offense and a transgression against the natural order (ānantarya).
If one kills one's mother with an unwholesome mind, it is neither a pārājika offense nor a transgression against the natural order."
What constitutes killing one’s mother with an unwholesome mind such that one commits a *pārājika* offense and a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
What constitutes killing one’s mother with an unwholesome mind such that it is neither a *pārājika* nor a crime of immediate retribution?
If one takes the life of one’s mother for the sake of profit, this is called killing one’s mother with an unwholesome mind; one commits both a *pārājika* offense and a crime of immediate retribution.
If one sets a trap for the purpose of killing a beast, and the mother falls into it and dies, it is neither a pārājika offense nor a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya). Upāli!
This is called killing one's mother with an unwholesome mind, which constitutes both a pārājika offense and a crime of immediate retribution.
"In this way, if one kills one's mother with an unwholesome mind, it is neither a pārājika offense nor a heinous crime (ānantarya).
He asked again:
"Is it possible that if one kills one's mother with an indeterminate mind, one commits a pārājika offense and a heinous crime?"
"If one kills one's mother with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), is it not a *pārājika* offense nor a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
The Buddha said,
"There are cases where one kills one's mother with an indeterminate mind, yet commits both a *pārājika* offense and a crime of immediate retribution."
If one kills one's mother with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), one does not commit a *pārājika* offense nor incur the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
How is it that killing one's mother with an indeterminate mind constitutes both a *pārājika* offense and a crime of immediate retribution?
How can one kill one's mother with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) and yet not commit a *pārājika* offense nor an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?
If one employs the means to kill one's mother and the mother dies while one is asleep, this is called committing both a *pārājika* offense and an act of immediate retribution.
If one shoots at a tree against a wall and mistakenly kills one's mother, one does not commit a *pārājika* offense nor is it a crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
Upāli! Likewise, if one kills one's mother with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), one commits a *pārājika* offense and it is a crime of immediate retribution.
If one kills one's mother with such an indeterminate mind, one does not commit a pārājika offense, nor is it a pāyattika (heinous) crime. Upāli!
It is the same for killing one's father or killing an arhat.

“Is there any case where a bhikṣu who shares communal duties does not enter the saṃgha nor grant his consent (*chanda*), yet performs all formal acts (*karmas*) within the boundary without committing an offense?”
The Buddha said: "There is!
It is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
I previously told Maudgalyāyana:
"From this day forward, you yourselves shall recite the Prātimokṣa; I shall no longer recite the Prātimokṣa for you."
“Is there any bhikṣu who, without having heard the fivefold recitation of the precepts, may perform the uposatha?
The Buddha said, “There is.”
"If a bhikṣu performs the poṣadha while alone, that is [the case].
As the Buddha said:
"One should not recite the precepts in the presence of a person who has not received full ordination."
"Is it possible that one may recite the precepts before a person who has not yet received full ordination (upasampadā) without committing an offense?
The Buddha said, "There is."
"I previously stated that, setting aside King Prasenajit’s retinue, I spoke to the king alone in order to purify his mind.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Is it an offense committed with a virtuous mind?"
"Is it an offense committed with an unwholesome mind,
or is it an offense committed with a neutral mind?
The Buddha said:
"There are offenses committed with a wholesome mind, offenses committed with an unwholesome mind, and offenses committed with a neutral mind. An offense committed with a wholesome mind is as follows:

if a newly ordained bhikṣu, being unaware of the characteristics of the precepts, personally pulls up grass before a stūpa, personally weeds the grass from a walking path, or personally gathers flowers—this is called an offense committed with a wholesome mind."
An offense committed with an unwholesome mind refers to intentionally violating the precepts established by the Buddha; this is called an offense committed with an unwholesome mind.
An offense committed with a neutral mind refers to unintentionally violating the precepts.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"Does an Arhat commit an offense with a wholesome mind,
or does he commit an offense with an unwholesome mind?"
"Is it an offense committed with an indeterminate mind?
The Buddha said, "Upāli!"
“If an Arhat commits an offense, it is always with an indeterminate mind.
“World-Honored One,
how is it that when an Arhat commits an offense, it is with an indeterminate mind?”
The Buddha said:

"If an Arhat does not recall having kept extra robes, or having eaten repeatedly, or having eaten apart from the community, or having entered a village without announcing his presence, or having entered a village without wearing his saṃghāṭī; or if while sleeping another placed him upon a high or wide bed, or if while sleeping another placed him upon a woman’s bed; or if while he was not yet asleep a person who had not received full ordination left the room, or if while he was sleeping a person who had not received full ordination entered the room—having awakened, he immediately confesses his transgression."
"Upāli! These are called the offenses of an Arhat, all of which are committed with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).
If the Saṃgha is split, is the Saṃgha thereby afflicted? If the Saṃgha is afflicted, is the Saṃgha thereby split?"

“There is a schism in the Saṃgha that is not a disturbance of the Saṃgha; there is a disturbance of the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha; there is a schism in the Saṃgha that is also a disturbance of the Saṃgha; and there is neither a schism in the Saṃgha nor a disturbance of the Saṃgha.”

"Schism in the Saṃgha that is not an affliction of the Saṃgha" refers to when there is a schism in the Saṃgha, yet one does not grasp at or contemplate the fourteen matters that cause a schism; this is called a schism in the Saṃgha that is not an affliction of the Saṃgha.

"Affliction of the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha" refers to when one grasps at and contemplates the fourteen matters that cause a schism, yet the Saṃgha does not actually split; this is called an affliction of the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha.

Regarding "causing a schism in the Saṃgha and causing affliction to the Saṃgha": if one causes a schism in the Saṃgha by taking up and adhering to the fourteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha, this is called "causing a schism in the Saṃgha and causing affliction to the Saṃgha.
Regarding "neither causing a schism in the Saṃgha nor causing affliction to the Saṃgha": this refers to cases other than those mentioned above.

There is a schism in the Saṃgha that is not a dispute of the Saṃgha; there is a dispute of the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha; there is both a schism in the Saṃgha and a dispute of the Saṃgha; and there is neither a schism in the Saṃgha nor a dispute of the Saṃgha.

Regarding what is a schism in the Saṃgha but not a dispute of the Saṃgha: if there is a schism in the Saṃgha, yet the matter is not different, the receiving of offerings is not different, and the boundary is not different, this is called a schism in the Saṃgha that is not a dispute of the Saṃgha.

Regarding "a dispute among the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha": if there are differences regarding monastic affairs, differences regarding the receipt of offerings, and differences regarding boundaries, yet no schism occurs, this is called a dispute among the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha.

Regarding "a schism in the Saṃgha that constitutes a dispute over the schism": if the Saṃgha is split such that there are differences in matters, differences in the receiving of offerings, and differences in boundaries, this is called a schism in the Saṃgha that constitutes a dispute over the schism.
Regarding "neither a schism in the Saṃgha nor a dispute over the schism": this refers to cases other than those mentioned above.

There is a schism in the Saṃgha that is not a separation of the Saṃgha; there is a separation of the Saṃgha that is not a schism in the Saṃgha; there is both a schism in the Saṃgha and a separation of the Saṃgha; and there is neither a schism in the Saṃgha nor a separation of the Saṃgha.

Regarding "a schism in the Saṃgha that is not a separation of the Saṃgha": if there is a schism in the Saṃgha, but the matter is not different, the boundary is not different, and the receiving of offerings is not different, this is called a schism in the Saṃgha that is not a separation of the Saṃgha.

As for "the separation of the Saṃgha without the schism of the Saṃgha": if there are differences regarding the affairs of the Saṃgha, differences regarding the boundary (*sīmā*), and differences regarding the receiving of offerings, yet no schism occurs, this is called "the separation of the Saṃgha without the schism of the Saṃgha."

Regarding "the Sangha is split and the Sangha is divided": if the Sangha is split such that there are differences in matters, differences in boundaries, and differences in receiving offerings, this is called "the Sangha is split and the Sangha is divided.
Regarding "neither the Sangha is split nor the Sangha is divided": this excludes the aforementioned circumstances.

“If the schism of the Saṃgha is a lifespan of one kalpa, is a lifespan of one kalpa the schism of the Saṃgha? “There are cases where there is a schism of the Saṃgha but it is not a lifespan of one kalpa;

there are cases where there is a lifespan of one kalpa but it is not a schism of the Saṃgha; there are cases where there is both a schism of the Saṃgha and it is a lifespan of one kalpa; and there are cases where there is neither a schism of the Saṃgha nor a lifespan of one kalpa.”

Regarding "schism in the Sangha that does not last for an eon": if one causes a schism in the Sangha while perceiving it as the Dharma, this is called a schism in the Sangha that does not last for an eon.

Regarding "those who live for an eon but do not cause a schism": the dragon kings Elāpattra, Maṇasvin, Kālika, Nanda, Upananda, Kapila, and Āśvapala; King Yama; and the Brahmakāyika devas—these are called those who live for an eon but do not cause a schism.
"One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha has a lifespan of one kalpa," as in the case of Devadatta; this is what is meant by "one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha has a lifespan of one kalpa.
"Neither causing a schism in the Saṃgha nor having a lifespan of one kalpa" refers to cases other than those mentioned above.
“If the schism of the Saṃgha results in retribution for one kalpa, does that which results in retribution for one kalpa constitute a schism of the Saṃgha?

“There are cases where there is a schism of the Saṃgha but no retribution for one kalpa; there are cases where there is retribution for one kalpa but no schism of the Saṃgha; there are cases where there is both a schism of the Saṃgha and retribution for one kalpa; and there are cases where there is neither a schism of the Saṃgha nor retribution for one kalpa.”

Regarding "causing a schism in the Sangha that does not entail retribution for one kalpa": if one causes a schism in the Sangha while perceiving it as a mere phenomenon (dharma-saṃjñā), this is called causing a schism in the Sangha that does not entail retribution for one kalpa.

Regarding "retribution for one kalpa that is not causing a schism in the Sangha": such as the dragon kings Elāpattra, Maṇasvin, Kālika, Nanda, Upananda, Kapila, Āśvapala, and King Yama—these are called retribution for one kalpa that is not causing a schism in the Sangha.
Regarding "causing a schism in the Sangha results in a retribution of one kalpa": this refers to Devadatta; such cases are called causing a schism with a retribution of one kalpa.
Regarding "neither causing a schism nor a retribution of one kalpa": this excludes the aforementioned cases.
“If the schism of the Saṃgha is wrong view, is wrong view the schism of the Saṃgha? “There are cases where there is a schism of the Saṃgha that is not wrong view;

there are cases where there is wrong view that is not a schism of the Saṃgha; there are cases where the schism of the Saṃgha is wrong view; and there are cases where there is neither a schism of the Saṃgha nor wrong view.”
To split the Saṃgha without holding wrong views means to split the Saṃgha while perceiving the [false] teaching as the true Dharma; this is called splitting the Saṃgha without wrong views.
To hold wrong views without splitting the Saṃgha refers to the six heretical teachers; this is called wrong views without splitting the Saṃgha.
"One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha is one with wrong view; Devadatta is such a person.
One who neither causes a schism nor holds wrong views is anyone other than those mentioned above.
"If causing a schism in the Saṃgha is ignorance, is ignorance then causing a schism in the Saṃgha?"

“There is schism in the Saṃgha that is not ignorance; there is ignorance that is not schism in the Saṃgha; there is schism in the Saṃgha that is ignorance; and there is neither schism in the Saṃgha nor ignorance.”
Schism in the Saṃgha that is not ignorance refers to schism in the Saṃgha committed with the perception of [the opponent as] a Dharma-teacher; this is schism in the Saṃgha that is not ignorance.

Ignorance that is not schism in the Saṃgha refers to killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an Arhat, or maliciously drawing blood from the body of a Buddha; these are called ignorance that is not schism in the Saṃgha.
Regarding "the schism of the Saṃgha is ignorance," this refers to Devadatta; this is called "the schism of the Saṃgha is ignorance.
Regarding "neither the schism of the Saṃgha nor ignorance," this excludes the aforementioned matters.
At that time, the Elder Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
can a bhikṣu initiate the act of schism in the Saṃgha?”
"Can bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs initiate an act that causes a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu can initiate an act that causes a schism in the Saṃgha; it is not bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs who can initiate an act that causes a schism in the Saṃgha."
He asked again:
"What offense does one commit by causing a schism in the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
