"To cause all bhikṣus to dwell securely within wholesome dharmas and abandon unwholesome ones, so that by being free from unwholesome dharmas they may attain purity"—
this is called the *poṣadha* rite.
Regarding the granting of purity (*pārisuddhi*): when it is time for the *poṣadha*, if a sick bhikṣu is unable to come, one should grant him purity.
If he is able to come but does not, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu, fearing loss of life, violation of the precepts, or the arising of any one of the eight difficulties, is compelled to grant *pārisuddhi*, this is called the method of granting *pārisuddhi*.
Regarding the receiving of the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity): if a bhikṣu receives the *pārisuddhi* from another bhikṣu, it should be received within the boundary (*sīmā*).
If that bhikṣu fears for his life, fears the breaking of the precepts, or if any one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭau durgatayaḥ*) should arise, at that time he should go outside the boundary.
This is called the purification of the confession.
Regarding the declaration of purity: if a bhikṣu receives a confession from another and goes before the Saṃgha to declare it, it is well; if he does not declare it, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.

If one receives [the precepts] from a person who is pure, or while one is asleep, or while one has entered meditative absorption, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises, it is not said that there is no offense.
This is called the teaching on the dharma of purity.

Regarding the *yadharma* (the act of giving consent): "consent" (*yad*) refers to the arousal of the intention; when, in matters concerning the Dharma or the Saṃgha, one accords with the Saṃgha’s rules by granting consent, this is called the *yadharma*.
As for the procedure for granting consent: if a bhikṣu is ill and unable to come, he should grant his consent.
If one who is not ill is able to come but does not do so, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu fears for his life, fears breaking the precepts, or if any one of the eight calamities arises such that he cannot remain, he may grant his consent (*chanda*).
If one has arrived but does not actually come, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
One who gives their consent (*chanda*) should say:
"The bhikṣu has given his consent and has come."
If one says,
"I give," this is called obtaining consent.
If it is given through bodily action, this is called "obtaining consent.
If it is given through verbal action, this is called "obtaining consent.
If it is not given through either bodily or verbal action, it is not called "obtaining consent," and that bhikṣu should be brought before the Saṃgha.
If he does not come, the entire Saṃgha should treat him as a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣus should not perform a separate *karmavācanā*.
If they perform a separate *karmavācanā*, the bhikṣus commit an offense.
This is called receiving the consent (*chanda*) for the *dharmas* of desire.
Regarding the *dharmas* of desire: if a bhikṣu receives consent from another bhikṣu, it should be received within the boundary (*sīmā*).
If that bhikṣu fears for his life, fears breaking the precepts, or if any one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭau āpattayaḥ*) arises, he should go outside the boundary.
This is called the method for receiving the *chanda* (consent).
Regarding the one who proclaims the *chanda*: when a monk who has received the *chanda* arrives among the Saṃgha, he should proclaim that monk’s *chanda*.
If he proclaims it, it is well; if he does not proclaim it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu is asleep, or in meditative absorption, or if one of the eight difficulties arises, he is not guilty of an offense.
This is called the teaching on the dharma of desire.
Regarding the *pārisuddhi-dharma* (the practice of purity): when a bhikṣu says to another,
"I am pure and without offense," this is called the *pārisuddhi-dharma*.
Regarding the granting of *pārisuddhi* (purity): if a bhikṣu is ill and unable to come, he should grant his *pārisuddhi*.
If he is not ill and is able to come but does not do so, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu fears for his life, fears breaking the precepts, or if any one of the eight difficulties arises such that he is unable to remain [in retreat], he should be granted the purity of the *pārivāsika*.
Regarding the one who bestows purity, he says to the bhikṣu:
"Come and bestow purity. If he says:
"To give"—
this is called attaining purity.
If one gives through bodily action, this is also called attaining purity.
If it is given through verbal action, this is called attaining purity.
If it is not given through bodily or verbal action, it is not called attaining purity; that bhikṣu should be brought before the Saṃgha.
If he does not come, the entire Saṃgha should perform the uposatha with that bhikṣu; the bhikṣus should not perform the uposatha separately.
If they perform it separately, the bhikṣus incur an offense.
This is called the *chanda-śuddhi* (consent and purity) procedure.

Regarding the *chanda-śuddhi* procedure: when it is time for the *poṣadha*, if the Saṃgha intends to perform various formal acts (*karmas*), at that time one should collectively grant consent and purity; this is called the *chanda-śuddhi* procedure.
Regarding the dharma of granting consent for purity (*chanda-pārisuddhi*): if a bhikṣu is ill and unable to come, he should grant consent for purity.
If he is not ill and is able to come, he should go to the place where the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha* ceremony.
If one is not ill and is able to come but does not do so, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

However, if a bhikṣu fears for his life, fears breaking the precepts, or if any one of the eight calamities arises such that he is unable to go out, he should grant his consent and purity (*chanda-śuddhi*).
A bhikṣu should say to another bhikṣu:
"Come with the transmission of consent and purity. If he says:
"To give. This is called the purification of desire through speech.
If one gives through bodily action, this is also called the purification of desire through bodily action.
If it is given through verbal action, this is called obtaining purity of consent.
If it is not given through bodily or verbal action, it is not called obtaining purity of consent; that bhikṣu should be brought before the Saṃgha.
If they are unable to come, the entire Saṃgha should perform the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā* with that bhikṣu present; the other bhikṣus should not perform the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā* separately.
If they do so separately, those bhikṣus incur an offense.
This is called the *chanda-viśuddhi-dharma* (the dharma of purification through consent).
Regarding the one who receives the *chanda-viśuddhi-dharma*: if a bhikṣu wishes to receive the consent of another for purification, he should do so within the boundary (*sīmā*).
If he fears for his life, fears breaking the precepts, or if any one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv āpattayaḥ*) arises, he should go outside the boundary.
This is called the method for receiving the purification of desire (*chanda*).
Regarding the explanation of the method for purifying desire: one who receives the purification of desire from another should go before the Saṃgha and declare that bhikṣu’s purification of desire.
If he speaks, it is well; if he does not speak, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, if that bhikṣu is asleep, or has entered meditative concentration, or if one of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) arises, there is no offense in his failure to speak.
This is called the teaching on the purification of desire.

Regarding the method for erecting a stūpa: the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, with deep faith in the Buddha, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"When the World-Honored One was traveling through various lands, I felt a profound thirst and longing because I could not see him. I pray that you will grant me some object so that I may make an offering.
The Buddha gave him his hair and nails, saying, "Householder!"
"You should make offerings to these fingernails and hair.
The householder immediately addressed the Buddha, saying,
"May the World-Honored One grant this wish!"
"Listen to me as I authorize the construction of hair stupas and nail stupas.
The Buddha said,
"I authorize the construction of hair stupas and nail stupas."
This is called the method for erecting a stūpa.
Regarding the site of a stūpa: the land belonging to a stūpa includes gardens, fields, and grain fields; that upon which a stūpa is first erected is called the site of a stūpa.

Regarding the rules for shrines and stupas (*khaṇḍa-stūpa-dharma*): the Buddha permitted the construction of shrine-stupas and pillar-stupas; the Buddha further permitted the construction of all types of stupas—this is called the rule for stupas.

Regarding the inexhaustibility of stupa property: the merchants of Vaiśālī used stupa property to engage in trade for profit to support the stupa. Desiring to travel to a distant place for the sake of seeking profit, they gave these goods to a bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable One!"
"This is property belonging to the stūpa; you should lend it out to earn interest for the purpose of making offerings to the stūpa.
The bhikṣu said, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to lend out stūpa property to earn interest for the purpose of making offerings to the stūpa."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow monastery attendants or lay devotees (upāsaka) to lend out temple property at interest so that the proceeds may be used for the供养 (pūjā) of the stupa."
This is called "stūpa property.

Regarding the method for making inexhaustible offerings to a stūpa: whatever is to be offered to a stūpa—whether white, red, blue, yellow, or other such colors—it is permitted to offer these to the stūpa as well as various decorative ornaments; this is called the method for offering to a stūpa.

Regarding the method for adorning a stūpa: that which should adorn a stūpa includes the vajrāsana, high halls, lofty towers, and multi-storied pavilions; the hanging of various precious bells, radiant images, necklaces, silk banners, flower canopies, and various treasures such as gold, silver, pearls, musāragalva, aśmagarbha, vaidūrya, and crystal. Such exquisite articles of adornment are what should be used to make offerings to the stūpa; this is called the method for adorning a stūpa.

Regarding the method of flowers, incense, and garlands: one should offer these to the stūpa—namely, flowers, powdered incense, unguents, flower garlands, and jewel garlands; one should arrange rows of lamps and perform various musical performances; one should smear the walls with incense and distribute incense caskets; one should spread flowers and incense and sprinkle the ground with fragrant oil. This is called the method of flowers, incense, and garlands.

Regarding the "firm rule" (*dhruva-dharma*): when a bhikṣu dwells in a certain residence, he should accept offerings according to the portion assigned by the donor therein; this is called the firm rule.

Regarding the "firm-firm rule" (*dhruva-dhruva-dharma*): if a donor provides a bhikṣu with food, drink, and clothing, for that reason he abandons two matters—eating at improper times and eating in a separate group; this is called the firm-firm rule.

Regarding the rules for rice gruel: the Buddha permitted the consumption of eight kinds of gruel—ghee gruel, oil gruel, sesame gruel, milk gruel, mung bean gruel, mocha bean gruel, hempseed gruel, and clear gruel. When drinking it, one should not make a sound; this is called the rule for rice gruel.
Regarding the rules for eating: the Buddha permitted nine kinds of food to be eaten:
roots, stalks, leaves, flour-based foods, fruits, sesame seeds, rock honey, and white honey. When eating, one must not make loud noises; this is called the rule for eating.
Regarding the practice of holding and consuming food: the Buddha permitted four kinds of substances to be held and consumed:
ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
When a bhikṣu holds and consumes these four substances, he should form this thought:
"I eat for the purpose of treating illness; it is not for the sake of delicious flavors.
This is called the practice of eating with moderation.
Regarding the rules for eating, the Buddha permitted the consumption of five kinds of food:
Rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, and meat— when a bhikṣu eats such food,

he should give rise to a sense of revulsion, maintaining it only for the sake of preserving his life, and he should be mindful not to fall into the faults of eating at improper times or eating in a separate group.
Furthermore, one should think:
"I perceive this as leftover food.
This is called the method for eating.
Regarding the rules for the alms bowl (*pātra*): the Buddha permitted the possession of two kinds of bowls—ceramic bowls and iron bowls.
One should not possess eight kinds of bowls:
Gold bowls, silver bowls, lapis lazuli bowls, maṇi bowls, copper bowls, pewter bowls, wooden bowls, and stone bowls—these are called the types of bowls.
Regarding the rules for robes (*cīvara-dharma*): there are seven types of robes that need not be formally purified (*pariśuddha*) before being kept by oneself:

the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *antarvāsaka*, the rain-bathing robe, the wound-covering robe, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and other articles used in accordance with the Dharma; these are called the rules for robes.

Regarding the rules for the *niṣīdana*: the Buddha permitted the keeping of a *niṣīdana* for the purpose of protecting bedding. One should not sit upon the bedding of the Saṃgha without a *niṣīdana*. This is called the rule for the *niṣīdana*.

Regarding the method of needles: the Buddha permitted the keeping of two kinds of needles—copper needles and iron needles—with nostrils shaped like broken grain, mung beans, or circles; this is called the method of needles.

Regarding the method for the needle case: the Buddha permitted the keeping of a needle case in order to protect needles so that they would not be lost frequently and have to be sought again, which would hinder one's practice of the Path; this is called the method for the needle case.
Regarding the rule for the water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*): the Buddha permitted the keeping of a water flask; one should keep it well-cleaned and pure—this is called the rule for the water flask.

Regarding the rule for the water flask used daily: one should likewise keep the water in the flask clean and pure, and the lid should be treated in the same way—this is called the rule for the water flask used daily.

Regarding the rule concerning the preceptor (*upādhyāya*): if monks have no preceptor, they will commit various evil deeds; furthermore, when they are ill, there will be no one to attend to them. For this reason, the Buddha permitted the existence of a preceptor, who shall instruct, care for, and preach the Dharma to you.

Although the Buddha permitted the role of preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the bhikṣus were initially reluctant to serve as preceptors; the Buddha then instructed them to do so—this is called the "Dharma of the Preceptor.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Co-resident Disciple" (*sārdhavihārin*): when intending to go abroad, one should inform the preceptor; while traveling, one should follow behind the preceptor and provide for his necessities; one should always attend upon him without distance, never acting contrary to his will in matters of the Dharma; and all actions should be reported to the preceptor, with the exception of defecating or urinating, chewing tooth-sticks, and performing prostrations to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—this is called the "Dharma of the Co-resident Disciple."

Regarding the dharma of the *ācārya*: since there were monks who, lacking an *ācārya*, committed various evils, and because when ill they had no one to attend to them, the Buddha therefore permitted the existence of an *ācārya*. An *ācārya* shall constantly instruct, care for, and preach the Dharma to you.
Although the Buddha permitted the practice of serving as an ācārya, the bhikṣus were unwilling to do so; the Buddha then instructed them to serve as ācāryas—this is called the dharma of the ācārya.

Regarding the rules for a resident disciple (*antevāsin*): when intending to go out, one should inform the *ācārya*; while traveling, one should follow behind the *ācārya* and provide whatever is required; one should follow him closely without being separated, and in all matters according to the Dharma, one must not act contrary to his wishes; everything that is done should be reported to the *ācārya*, with the exception of answering the call of nature, chewing the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), and paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. These are called the rules for a resident disciple.

Regarding the rules for the upādhyāya and ācārya toward their co-resident (sahacara) and near-resident (upasaṃvāsaka) disciples: the upādhyāya and ācārya should regard their co-resident and near-resident disciples as their own sons.
A co-practitioner or close attendant disciple should regard their preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya) as a father.

If you are able to do so, you will cause wholesome qualities to increase within my Dharma; this is called the rule for co-practitioners and close attendant disciples regarding their preceptors and teachers.
Regarding the rules for śrāmaṇeras: the Buddha permitted that a śrāmaṇera may be as young as seven years old, provided he is capable of driving away crows from the food offerings;

this is called the rule for śrāmaṇeras. Regarding the rule for dependence (niśraya): there was once a visiting bhikṣu who had not yet completed five years of seniority. At sunset, he came to the monastery seeking dependence, but after a long time he did not obtain it; he became bewildered and distressed, fell to the ground, and was on the verge of death.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not seek dependence on that very same day; rather, you are permitted to rest for one night before seeking dependence."
At that time, the bhikṣus sought out a place of dependence (niśraya) without inquiring into its merits or defects, and were thus unable to increase wholesome dharmas. The Buddha said:
"Do not seek out a place of dependence; you should instead examine whether this bhikṣu is able to instruct and transform his disciples so as to bring them to goodness."
Observing in this manner, one who possesses complete merit should seek to rely upon them;
if there is no one possessing complete merit, one should further seek another upon whom to rely.
This is called the Dharma of Reliance.
Regarding the granting of dependence: if a bhikṣu has completed ten years [of seniority], he should grant dependence to others.
If one who has completed ten years is dull-witted and lacks understanding, he should not grant dependence to others; this is called the granting of dependence.

Regarding the one who receives dependence (*niśraya*): the bhikṣu should rise from his seat, adjust his robe by exposing one shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, bend his body forward, and grasp the feet of the senior monk (*upādhyāya*) with both hands; he should then request dependence by reciting the formula three times.
This is called the dharma of relying upon [a preceptor].
Regarding the dharma of relinquishing reliance, there are five causes and conditions for relinquishing reliance:
first, the preceptor dies; [the other four follow].
2. Departing from one's own residence;
3. Renouncing the precepts;
4. Abandoning this school to join another school.
Fifth, seeing one's original preceptor (upādhyāya) is called the method for relinquishing formal reliance (*niśraya*). Regarding the method of the site:

whichever ground one intends to build a stūpa or a monastic dwelling upon, one should first inspect that site to ensure that the construction will not obstruct the paths of passage, and that it is fully endowed with groves of trees and water, and is tranquil by day and night, with few mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, heat, and venomous scorpions. In this manner, one should observe the site before building a stūpa or a monastic dwelling.
If one constructs a stūpa or a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma) on ground that has not been inspected, the bhikṣu who builds the stūpa or the monastic dwelling commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the rule regarding the ground (*bhūmi-dharma*).

Regarding the rules for monastic dwellings (*saṃghārāma-dharma*): the Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to maintain various monastic dwellings, including heated rooms (*jantāghara*), lecture halls (*kathina-śālā*), multi-storied pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*), single-story houses, pointed-roofed houses, and *kaṇḍa-śālās*. The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha as a whole to maintain these various dwellings, and also permitted a single individual to maintain them. This is called the rule regarding monastic dwellings.

Regarding the rules for bedding: the bedding permitted by the Buddha for the bhikṣus consists of coarse-woven rope beds, fine-woven rope beds, woolen rugs, mattresses, bedding, and various types of coverings.
The Buddha permitted the community of monks to possess them, and also permitted a single person to possess them; this is called the rule for bedding and furniture (*śayanāsana-vidhi*).
Regarding the rule for repairing stūpas and monasteries: in the kingdom of Ārāvi, various stūpas and monasteries were falling into ruin.
Having known this, the Buddha intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason are these stūpas and monasteries in such a state of ruin?"
Ānanda said,
“Because the group of six bhikṣus wished to have it repaired, the other bhikṣus were afraid and did not dare to do so.
The Buddha said:
"When these six groups of bhikṣus wish to repair a stūpa or a monastery, the Saṃgha should perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) to assign the work to others.

Yet, those bhikṣus who have received the assignment perform only a small amount of manual labor—perhaps placing a single brick, or a bundle of grass, or blocking a single hole, or smearing the floor or wall with mud, or coating the floor and walls with cow dung—and having done such a small amount, they say:
'I no longer wish to work.'"
The Buddha said:

"Such a person should not be granted the formal ritual (karmavācanā). However, if this bhikṣu is capable of performing great meritorious deeds and practicing cultivation, he should be granted the ritual for the maintenance of stūpas and monastic dwellings."
This is called the rule for the restoration of stūpas and monasteries.
Regarding the rule for those who restore stūpas and monasteries: if a bhikṣu wishes to newly construct a stūpa, a monastery, or new bedding and furniture, the Buddha said:

"For this purpose, the Saṃgha should order that all other affairs be abandoned for twelve years. Depending on the scale of the project, they may be ordered to abandon other affairs for eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or one year. They should only be permitted to pile up walls, erect frameworks, and apply timber, plaster, and decorative coatings."
This is called the method for those who maintain the stūpas and monastic dwellings.

Regarding the method of reverence: following the order of seniority, one pays homage, welcomes them upon arrival, and sees them off upon departure; one joins the palms, bows the body, and stands beside the seat of the elder. This is called the method of reverence.

Regarding the method for cleansing powder (*śauca-cūrṇa*): the Buddha permitted the use of the powders of small beans, large beans, masha beans, peas, and wild beans, as well as the powders of various dry grasses such as *ekalīlīvidha*. One must not mix these with fragrant substances.
Except for those who are ill, its use is not permitted for others.
If it was not specifically requested but the donor gave it of their own accord, one may use it as desired.
This is called the rule regarding soap powder (snāna-kaṣāya).
Regarding the rules for fermented drinks (*pāna*): the Buddha permitted eight kinds of fermented drinks which bhikṣus may drink:
*śāli-pāna*, *mora-pāna*, *kola-pāna*, *śīrīṣa-pāna*, *śyāmāka-pāna*, grape juice (*drākṣā-pāna*), *phalūṣa-pāna*, and *dāḍima-pāna*. These are the eight kinds of fermented drinks.
If one purifies it with water, it may be drunk; this is called the rule for fermented drinks (*mantha*). Regarding the rule for medicines:

root medicine, stem medicine, leaf medicine, flower medicine, and fruit medicine—these medicinal herbs were permitted by the Buddha. He permitted the Sangha to store them, and he also permitted an individual to store them; this is called the rule for medicines.

Regarding the method for *suvīra* juice: the Buddha permitted the drinking of *suvīra* juice for the sake of monks suffering from cold-related illnesses; just as he permitted its consumption for the sake of Śāriputra, this is called the method for *suvīra* juice.

Regarding the rules for skins and hides: if there are various skins or hides, a bhikṣu should not keep, wear, or sit upon them, except for boots, leather sandals, the straps of boots, the straps of leather sandals, mats made of *māñjiṣṭha* hide, deer hides, and the lacing and ties of leather sandals; these are called the rules for skins and hides.
Regarding the rules for leather sandals: the Buddha permitted two kinds of leather sandals—the single-layered leather sandal and the worn-out, plain leather sandal.
One should not possess leather sandals that are decorated with various colors; this is called the rule for leather sandals.
Regarding the rule for bed-leg supports: the Buddha permitted two kinds of items for supporting a bed—first, a stool for the latrine, and second, an item for supporting the legs of a bed.
He did not permit the use of eight kinds of bed-leg supports; this is called the rule for bed-leg supports.
Regarding the rule for stools (*mañca*): whether they are movable, have legs, or are ornate—such stools should not be kept; this is called the rule for stools.
Regarding the rule for staffs (*daṇḍa*): the Buddha permitted staffs made of iron or copper for the sake of durability, with a ring at the top.
Furthermore, regarding the rule on the staff: while the Buddha was staying in the Śītavana grove, many venomous crawling insects bit the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said, "One should make a sounding staff to drive away the venomous insects."
This is called the rule concerning the staff (*daṇḍa-dharma*).

Regarding the rule concerning the staff-sack (*daṇḍakośaka-dharma*): the Buddha permitted the use of a net-bag to carry the staff for the sake of protecting it, so that it might not be broken or lost and one would have to seek another, thereby obstructing the practice of the Path. This is called the rule concerning the staff-sack.

Regarding the method for eating garlic: the Buddha permitted bhikṣus with cold-natured illnesses to eat garlic, provided it was eaten mixed with medicine. Those such as Śāriputra followed this method of eating garlic accordingly; this is called the method for eating garlic.

Regarding the rule on razors: the Buddha permitted the community of monks to keep razors, and individuals may also keep them for the purpose of shaving hair and beards; this is called the rule on razors.

Regarding the method for the razor sheath: the Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to keep razor sheaths for the purpose of protection, so that they would not lose them and have to search for them again, which would obstruct their practice of the Path.

Regarding the rule on door-bolts: the Buddha permitted the keeping of door-bolts for the purpose of guarding dwellings. Because one guards the dwelling, one guards oneself; because one guards oneself, one guards one's bedding and requisites. The same applies to locks, door-latches, bolts, keys, and so forth; this is called the rule on door-bolts.
Regarding the rule on vehicles: the Buddha permitted monks with eye ailments to ride in vehicles, such as Piṅgalavatsa; this is called the rule on vehicles. Regarding the rule on umbrellas:
one should not carry an umbrella while entering the house of a layperson, except when carrying it for the purpose of receiving a gift; this is called the rule on umbrellas.
Regarding the rule for fans: the Buddha permitted the community of monks to possess fans, and individuals may also possess them; this is called the rule for fans. Regarding the rule for fly-whisks:
the Buddha permitted the community of monks to possess fly-whisks, and individuals may also possess them; this is called the rule for fly-whisks.

Regarding the rule concerning mirrors: a bhikṣu should not examine his face in a mirror, nor should he look at his own face in a bowl or in water, except when there is a sore on his face; this is called the rule concerning mirrors.
Regarding the method for treating the eyes, there are five kinds of substances used for eye treatment:
black substances, powders of blue-white substances, grass powders, flower powders, and fruit juices. The Buddha said:
"Do not treat the eyes for the sake of physical beauty."
"For the purpose of treating eye diseases, this is called the method for treating the eyes.

Regarding the method for the eye-treatment probe: the Buddha permitted the use of an eye-treatment probe made of iron, copper, conch shell, ivory, horn, wood, or earthenware; this is called the method for the eye-treatment probe."

Regarding the method for storing eye-medicine applicators: these items should be well cared for and protected so that they are not lost and have to be sought again, which would hinder one's practice of the Path. This is called the method for storing eye-medicine applicators.
Regarding the practice concerning flowers, incense, and necklaces: a bhikṣu must not wear them himself, nor should he instruct others to wear them.

If he obtains them without having requested them, he should accept them as he pleases and then use them to make offerings at the stūpas of the Buddha and the stūpas of the Arhats; this is called the practice concerning flowers, incense, and necklaces.

Regarding the rule on singing, dancing, and music: as for singing, dancing, and music, a bhikṣu should not go to witness them himself, nor should he instruct others to go and witness them; all such matters are forbidden. This is called the rule on singing, dancing, and music.
Regarding the method of reclining: a healthy bhikṣu should not lie down during the day; at night, if a lamp is lit, he should likewise not lie down.
If he is prone to snoring while sleeping, he should rise and practice walking meditation (caṅkrama).
If one is unable to rise, one should go to a secluded place; do not disturb others on account of this cause.
This is called the rule for lying down.
As for the rule for sitting: during the day, whether a bhikṣu is sitting or walking in meditation, he should employ the methods for warding off afflictions and hindrances.

During the day, whether sitting or walking, one should eliminate the hindrances; likewise during the first watch of the night, whether sitting or walking, one should also employ the method for eliminating the hindrances.

During the first watch of the night, whether sitting or walking in meditation, having suppressed the hindrances and afflictions, one reaches the middle watch; then, for the sake of rest, one enters the dwelling, spreads the *uttarāsaṅga* folded fourfold as a pillow beneath the head of the *saṃghāṭī*, lies on the bed on the right side with the feet stacked, and brings to mind the perception of the arising of the dawn light.
Rising early in the latter part of the night, whether sitting or walking in meditation, to ward off the hindrances and afflictions—this is called the method of sitting.

Regarding the method of the meditation staff (*dhyāna-yaṣṭi*): the Buddha permitted the use of a dharma-staff and the establishment of a place for it so that it might serve as a support and protection, ensuring it is not lost or required to be sought again, which would obstruct one's practice of the Path; this is called the method of the meditation staff.

Regarding the method for the meditation belt (*dhyāna-bandhana*): the Buddha permitted a monk suffering from waist ailments to possess a meditation belt; as it was permitted for the sake of Śāriputra, this is called the method for the meditation belt.
Regarding the method for wearing the waistband (*kaṭisūtra*):

the Buddha permitted three kinds of waistbands—the woven cord band, the braided band, and the woolen cord band; this is called the method for the waistband. Regarding the method for the robe-belt (*kāyabandhana*):

the Buddha permitted the keeping of a robe-belt in order to gather the robes so they do not fall. One should maintain it well and guard it carefully, lest one lose it and have to seek it again, which would hinder the practice of the Path; this is called the method for the robe-belt.

Regarding the method of gathering and tying the robe: except when working at a high elevation, one should not gather and tie it at other times; this is called the method of gathering and tying the robe. Regarding the method of tossing and striking:

the Buddha permitted tossing and striking to produce sound for the sake of deterring enemies and thieves so that they do not attach themselves [to the robes]; it must not be done at other times; this is called the method of tossing and striking.
Regarding the rule on land: the Buddha permitted the acceptance of land for the purpose of establishing a *saṃghārāma*, and permitted the monks to construct courtyards and dwellings thereon.
As for "grove," a grove is defined as a collection of trees.
"Matters" refers to quarreling, strife, mutual accusation, slander, exposing faults and transgressions, mutual hatred, and mutual alienation.

Since such things are evil for oneself and cause others to be evil as well—being evil in both respects—one should not engage in these various kinds of ruinous and afflictive matters; one should not do any of them at all.
There are two kinds of schism in the Saṃgha:
schism of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and schism of the wheel (*cakra*).
Regarding schism of the *karmavācanā*: if various bhikṣus perform separate *poṣadha* rituals within a single boundary (*sīmā*), this is called schism of the *karmavācanā*.

Regarding "one who breaks the wheel": the "wheel" refers to the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path. To cause people to abandon the Noble Eightfold Path and enter onto a false path is called "breaking the wheel"; this is called the second type of schism in the Saṃgha.

In this way, one should attend upon one’s preceptor (upādhyāya) and ācārya, as well as the senior, middle, and junior monks; one should train according to the teachings as they have been explained above, and one should also thoroughly understand those teachings as they have been explained above.
The section on the Dharma is concluded. Regarding the initial practice of the ritual for formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*):
how should it be performed? The monks should instruct the monk subject to exclusion to abandon such evil conduct.

The monk subject to exclusion must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, must not provide dependence (*niśraya*) to others, and must not maintain a novice (*śrāmaṇera*). The Saṃgha...
One should not perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) to appoint this person to instruct bhikṣuṇīs;
nor should one accept this person if the Saṃgha has performed a *karmavācanā* to appoint them as an instructor of bhikṣuṇīs.

One should not commit the offense for which they were expelled again, nor should one commit an offense similar to it, nor should one commit an offense exceeding the original offense. One should not criticize the *karmavācanā*. Nor...
One should not accept the prostrations of a monk who has been subjected to a formal act of censure (*karmavācanā*) or one who has not been expelled;
nor should one accept his rising to greet him, nor accept his joining of palms, bowing of the body, or acts of reverence;
nor should one accept offerings of robes or alms bowls, nor accept offerings of bedding or sitting mats spread out for him, nor accept water for washing his feet.
One should not accept offerings; one should not accept the service of having one's feet wiped; one should not accept a footstool for supporting the feet;
one should not accept massage of the hands or feet; one should not fail to expose the transgressions of a bhikṣu who has not been expelled; one should not speak to a bhikṣu who has not been expelled;
and one should not engage in communal affairs with him.
One should constantly practice self-restraint, comply with the other bhikṣus, and perform various acts of worship, such as bowing, welcoming, seeing off, and making offerings.
If one does not act according to this dharma, one shall not be released from the suspension for as long as one lives.
This is called the procedure for the banishment of a bhikṣu.
Regarding the various procedures for not living together:
what are these various ways of not living together?
There are two kinds:
first, self-inflicted non-residence;
second, non-residence imposed by the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of the Saṃgha.

A bhikṣu who has committed various types of *asaṃvāsa* offenses should not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, should not provide dependence (*niśraya*) to others, and should not keep novices (*śrāmaṇera*).
The Saṃgha should not perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to appoint him as a teacher of bhikṣuṇīs;
if the Saṃgha has performed such a formal act, he should not accept it, nor should he rise [to acknowledge it].
One should not commit various offenses of non-cohabitation that one has previously committed; nor should one commit similar offenses; nor should one commit offenses exceeding the original ones.
One should not criticize a formal act (*karmavācanā*); nor should one criticize the person performing the formal act.
One should not accept the prostrations of a monk who is undergoing probation (*parivāsa*); nor should one rise to greet him, join one's palms, or bow to him.
One may provide various kinds of physical offerings, but one should not accept offerings of robes or alms bowls; one should not accept offerings of mats for sitting or bedding for lying down;
one should not accept offerings such as water for washing the feet, footstools, or the massaging of hands and feet.
One should not disclose the offenses or transgressions of a bhikṣu who is living apart, nor should one say that he is not living apart.
A bhikṣu should not perform communal duties; he should not accept an appointment as a distributor of bedding and furniture if the Saṃgha performs the formal act (karmavācanā) to appoint him;
he should not accept an appointment as a supervisor of śrāmaṇeras if the Saṃgha performs the formal act to appoint him;
he should not accept an appointment as a superintendent of the monastery grounds if the Saṃgha performs the formal act to appoint him.
If the Saṃgha performs an improper *karmavācanā*, or if the person who has received an invitation from a place where the Saṃgha performs an improper *karmavācanā* should not accept it;
or if the Saṃgha performs an improper *karmavācanā*, the official who oversees the communal affairs (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) for all such *karmas* should not accept [the invitation];
or if the Saṃgha performs an improper *karmavācanā*.
You should subdue your mental conduct and not offend the bhikṣus.
If you offend the bhikṣus, it will further increase various forms of non-residence [with the community].
The bhikṣus should say this to that bhikṣu:
"Elder! You must subdue your evil mind, humble yourself, and eliminate your resentment and pride.

Do not allow the Saṃgha to impose upon you various offenses involving non-cohabitation that would drive you away and cause you to be excluded everywhere. You should repent of this offense here within this Saṃgha; this Saṃgha is able to resolve this offense of yours, whereas the Saṃghas of other places cannot."
If such a person hears these words and their mind is not subdued, they should be expelled, like a wild horse that breaks its tether and bolts away.
This is called the method for bhikṣus who do not dwell together in various ways.
What is the practice of the Bhikṣu Tāla?
There are twenty-two qualities by which one should know him to be of sharp faculties and of great learning.
What are these twenty-two?
He skillfully knows the root from which things arise;
he skillfully discriminates the characteristics of things;
and he skillfully knows the distinctions among things.
He is skilled in knowing the beginning and end of matters;
he is skilled in knowing the lightness and heaviness of matters;
he is skilled in knowing how to eliminate and extinguish matters.
He skillfully knows that once cessation has occurred, it does not arise again;
he skillfully knows the agent of action and the person who possesses the action;
he possesses the power of instruction, being able to cause others to receive and accept his teachings.
Possessing the power of skillful means and gentle speech, one is also able to cause others to accept [the teaching];
possessing the power of self-subjugation, one is also able to cause others to accept it;
knowing shame and remorse, with a mind free from arrogance and no arrogant speech, one’s actions of body, speech, and mind are without partial attachment.
He does not act out of desire, he does not act out of hatred, he does not act out of fear, and he does not act out of delusion.

By accomplishing these twenty-two qualities, he is able to suppress disputes; he does not rely on either of two factions in seeking the Dharma or seeking wealth. This is called the practice of a *tālaṭṭha* bhikṣu.
Regarding the practice of searching for the actual nature of an offense: if a bhikṣu himself says,
"I have this offense," and later says again that he does not.

This bhikṣu shall undergo the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the "searching for a real offense" (*bhūtaparyeṣaṇā-āpattilakṣaṇa*) by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, just as was done for the bhikṣu Hastiśīrṣa.

If a bhikṣu has received this formal procedure for searching for a real offense, that bhikṣu must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, must not provide dependence (*niśraya*) to others, and must not keep novices (*śrāmaṇera*); [this applies to] the Saṃgha.

One should not undergo a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to become a teacher of bhikṣuṇīs; nor should one accept such a position if the Saṃgha has performed the formal act to appoint one as a teacher of bhikṣuṇīs.
One should not give rise to the original offense committed, nor should one commit a similar offense, nor should one commit an offense exceeding the original one.
One should not criticize the formal act, nor should one criticize its performance.
The *karmadāna* (officiant) should not accept prostrations from a bhikṣu who has received the pure precepts;
he should not accept various offerings such as rising to greet him, joining his palms, or bowing his body; he should not accept offerings of robes or alms bowls;
he should not accept offerings of mats for sitting or bedding; and he should not accept water for washing the feet, a footstool, or a foot-massager.

One should perform offerings such as massaging the waist, back, hands, and feet; one must not expose the faults or transgressions of a bhikṣu of pure precepts, nor should one speak ill of a bhikṣu of pure precepts.
One should constantly practice self-restraint of the mind, accord with all bhikṣus, and offer various forms of veneration, including bowing, welcoming, and seeing them off.
If one does not practice according to these rules, one shall not attain liberation from this *karmavācanā* as long as one lives.
This is called the rule for a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) and is subject to the formal search for his fault.

Regarding the rule for a śrāmaṇera undergoing training after a *pārājika* offense: if a bhikṣu has committed sexual misconduct, even for as brief a moment as the snap of a finger, he does not give rise to a mind of concealment.

The community of monks, by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), restores the training rules to this bhikṣu; the detailed explanation is as in the case of Nandiya. This is called "granting training to a śrāmaṇera."

One must observe all the precepts of a great bhikṣu; one should sit on a seat lower than that of a great bhikṣu; one should offer food and drink to a great bhikṣu, while receiving food and drink from those who have not yet received full ordination; one may stay overnight twice in the same room as a great bhikṣu, but one must not stay more than two nights with someone who has not received the great precepts.
A śikṣamāṇa śrāmaṇera may perform two types of *karmavācanā*:
the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā* and the *pravāraṇā* *karmavācanā*.

However, a śikṣamāṇa śrāmaṇera may not serve as a quorum for the Saṃgha to perform the *poṣadha* or other *karmas*. This is called the rule of conduct regarding a śikṣamāṇa śrāmaṇera who has committed a *pārājika* offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 56 and Scroll 57; Part Two of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatāra of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
Regarding the remaining rules for the conduct of senior monks (*sthavira*) as recited in the *Vinaya*:
as for the conduct of senior monks, whether it be when the Saṃgha chants [the invitation] or when the *gandī* gong is struck, they should arrive quickly and take their seats.
Once seated, one should observe the seating order of superior, middling, and inferior, ensuring no one is out of place and instructing them to sit close together.
One should provide visual cues; if they do not notice, one should point with a finger.
If [a fellow monk] does not notice when one snaps one's fingers, one should speak to the person sitting beside them, using gentle and slow words.
When eating or drinking, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should instruct that everything be distributed equally and wait for the announcement of the *saṃghabhadra*.
All members of the Saṃgha should follow the senior monk; this is called the rule for the senior monk of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the rule for the senior monk of a monastery: if the monastery is in a state of decay, the senior monk should repair it himself or employ others to do so.
If you do not see a bhikṣu, you should seek him out.
If there is a sick bhikṣu, you should nurse him and inquire after his well-being.
If there is no one to nurse him, you should provide someone to act as his caregiver.
If the Sangha appoints someone to care for a sick person and that person refuses, the monks should take turns caring for them in order of seniority.

If the sick person is a monk residing within the monastery, he is entitled to receive beneficial offerings; the *upādhyāya* (senior elder) should single-mindedly and diligently employ skillful means to ensure these are not lost.
If one receives such gifts or offerings, they should be set aside and entrusted to a capable bhikṣu to distribute them.
If there is any work to be done within the monastery, the senior monk (sthavira) should first perform it with his own hands.
This is called the rule for the senior monk (*sthavira*) regarding the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma*).

Regarding the rule for the senior monk regarding a separate dwelling (*pṛthag-kuṭī*): if that separate dwelling is dilapidated or destroyed, the senior monk should repair it himself or have someone else repair it.
If one does not see a bhikṣu in the room, one should search for him.
If there is a sick bhikṣu,
one should attend to him and inquire after his well-being.
If there is no one to attend to the patient, one should provide an attendant.
If the attendant is unwilling, those in other rooms should take turns attending in order.
If the monks in other rooms are entitled to receive offerings of profit, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should single-mindedly and diligently employ skillful means to ensure that these are not lost.
If one receives such gifts or offerings, they should be placed with a monk capable of doing so, and he should be instructed to distribute them.
If there is any task to be done within a separate room, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should first perform it with his own hands.
This is called the rule for the senior monk of a separate dwelling.
Regarding "ārāma," it refers to a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).
Among the various regulations within a monastery, if a regulation conforms to the Dharma, and one neither afflicts oneself nor afflicts others, it should be accepted.
If one knows that a restrictive rule will lead to loss of benefit, causing distress to oneself and others, it should not be accepted; one should depart for another place.
If a bhikṣu knows that he possesses the power of shared views to extinguish such an improper restriction in accordance with the Dharma, he should inform the Saṃgha to have it abolished.
This is called the rule for *āraṇyaka* (forest-dwellers).
Regarding the rule for the forest (*vana-dharma*): "forest" refers to a grove of trees.
When the branches and leaves of these trees touch one another within a distance of one *krośa*, one may remain there at will without losing one's robe; this is called the rule for the forest.
"Ārāma" means a monastery (*saṃghārāma*).

Within a monastery there are many separate dwellings, and within these separate dwellings there are various regulations. If these regulations accord with the Dharma, and do not lead to one's own harm nor to the harm of others, they should be accepted.
If one knows that this restriction will cause loss and bring harm to both oneself and others, one should not accept it and should depart for another place.
If a bhikṣu knows that he possesses the power of like views and is able to eliminate this evil restriction in accordance with the Dharma, he should announce it to the assembly to have it eliminated.
This is called the rule for individual rooms.
Regarding the rule for dwellings: whatever dwelling a bhikṣu occupies, he should sweep it, sprinkle water on the floor, apply plaster, and dry and repair his bedding.
If it is soiled, it should be washed.
If one intends to go abroad, one should return the bedding to the Sangha, close the door, and secure the lock.
This is called the rule for dwellings.
Regarding the rules for bedding: if a bhikṣu uses the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha, he may go outside the monastery gate for up to forty-nine *krośas*, but not beyond that.
If he goes further and remains until the time when the ground has become dry, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Regarding the rules for doors: "door" refers to the place of entry and exit. When knocking on a door, one should not knock loudly; when opening a door, one must not push it wide open; and when closing a door, one should do so slowly.
When entering or leaving a room, one should do so calmly and with single-minded attention, ensuring that the robes do not brush against either side of the doorframe;
this is called the "Dharma of the Door.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Window," one should provide a screen; when departing, it should be closed, both for the sake of protecting the monastic quarters and for protecting oneself; this is called the "Dharma of the Window."

Regarding the method for an empty monastery: if a bhikṣu enters an empty monastery, he should sweep and sprinkle it to make it clean. If there are utensils therein that require washing, he should wash them thoroughly and place them in a covered location.
If there is a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant), one should have them clear away the grass from within the monastery grounds.
If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, the bhikṣu should perform whatever tasks are appropriate according to the Dharma.
One should not enter or exit the monastic quarters empty-handed.
This is called the rule for empty monastic cells. Regarding the rule for the alms-bowl (*pātra*): a bhikṣu should regard his bowl as he does his own eyes.

He should not place it on the ground; he should not place it on a stone; he should not place it in a high location; he should not place it under the eaves of a roof; he should not place it on top of a wall; he should not place it in a place for excrement or urine, nor in a place for washing after excrement or urine; he should not carry it into the bathhouse; he should not wash it with sand or cow dung; if it is not yet dry, he should not put it away, nor should he let it become too dry.

One should not intentionally break it nor use it carelessly; rather, one should protect and cherish it well so as not to let it be broken or lost, for to seek a replacement would obstruct one's progress on the Path.
This is called the rule for the bowl.

Regarding the rule for robes: one should protect the robe as one would one's own skin. When wearing the saṃghāṭī, one must not carry tiles, stones, mud, soil, grass, wood, or the like; nor should it be stained with colors such as blue or yellow.

If one is wearing the saṃghāṭī, one should not sweep or smear the ground; one should not tread upon it with the feet, nor spread it out as a seat, nor spread it out for lying down, nor wear it as an undergarment against the body. One should employ the saṃghāṭī according to its proper rules.
The *uttarāsaṅga* should be used according to the rules for the *uttarāsaṅga*;
the *antarvāsaka* should be used according to the rules for the *antarvāsaka*.

These three robes should be kept after having been purified by dyeing them into a "discolored" (mudita) hue; one should not wear them in five kinds of pure colors, nor in other distinct colors, nor as a *nakula-cīvara* (patchwork robe).

If a bhikṣu is poor and has few robes such that he cannot obtain a robe made of cut-and-sewn patches, he should apply patches to his robe—whether five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, or more than fifteen.
If he is able to obtain [the required materials], he should have them cut and sewn into a saṃghāṭī, an uttarāsaṅga, and an antarvāsaka.
This is called the rule for robes.
Regarding the rule for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*): a bhikṣu should not accept a single-layered sitting mat, and once he has accepted a sitting mat, he should not be separated from it.
If one discards it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the rule regarding the *niṣīdana*.
As for the rule regarding the needle, it is as explained above.
Regarding the method for the needle case: the Buddha permitted monks to keep a needle case for the purpose of storing needles.
A bhikṣu should carefully guard it so as not to lose it; otherwise, the trouble of searching for it again will hinder his practice of the Path.
A śrāmaṇera who has broken the precepts and lacks shame or remorse should not be appointed to hold [the needle case].
This is called the rule for the needle case.
The rules for the pure water flask and the regular water flask are also as explained above.
Regarding the method for rice gruel: because it provides five benefits, the consumption of rice gruel is permitted.

These are: to remove hunger, to remove thirst, to relieve flatulence, to eliminate coldness below the navel, and to digest what has been produced in the matured stomach. This is called the method for rice gruel.
Regarding the method of eating: when a bhikṣu eats the five kinds of food, he should contemplate that this food is difficult to obtain and difficult to prepare;
he should contemplate it as it enters the mouth and reaches the stomach and the large intestine;
and he should contemplate that upon its exit, due to the causes and conditions of this food, various afflictions, sinful karmas, and the retribution of suffering arise.
This is called the rule for eating.

Regarding the rule for the place of eating: when a bhikṣu arrives at the place of eating, he should remain silent, with a single-minded focus, maintaining pure deportment that can inspire purity in others; he should enter slowly and sit down slowly. This is called the rule for the place of eating.
Regarding the method for giving food: a bhikṣu should not give food to another before he has received it himself.
Only after having first received it should he then give it to another.
To whom should it be given?

If one's father, mother, a person under confinement, a person in urgent need of food, or a pregnant woman should come, one should observe the situation correctly and give them a small or large amount accordingly;
to an animal, one should give a single mouthful.
This is called the method for receiving food. Regarding the method for begging for alms:

a bhikṣu should receive food from a donor with a single-minded focus; he must not have a distracted mind, nor should he observe whether the food is good or bad. He should instead give rise to the perception of impurity. This is called the method for begging for alms.
Regarding the rules for begging for food, they are explained in detail in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
Regarding the rules for carrying back the alms-food: one should carry the food with a single-minded focus so as not to let it be lost or scattered, and one must not look at whether it is good or bad.
One should observe the timing—whether early or late—and bring back food;
this is called the method for bringing back almsfood. Regarding the *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller) practice:

an *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu should always maintain a single-minded focus and first greet others with a joyful heart, looking upon them with a pleasant countenance as he converses. He should abandon frowning and welcome others with the words, "Welcome. He should maintain fire and a hearth, prepare some food and utensils, and always keep water and water vessels. He should ensure that the water vessel for washing his feet always contains water, and he should likewise ensure that the pure water jar and the latrine water jar also contain water.

He should be well-versed in the paths, well-versed in the calculation of days, well-versed in nights, well-versed in the divisions of the night, and well-versed in the constellations; he should recite the *Nakṣatra-sūtra* and be well-versed in the *Sūtras*, the *Vinaya*, and the *Abhidharma*.
If one thoroughly understands the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, one should thoroughly understand the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.
If one is unable to practice and study, one should inquire about it and recite it; one should not keep a sun-love jewel or a moon-love jewel, but should instead keep the staff of the Dharma.
All possessions one maintains must be in accordance with the Path, as explained in detail in the *Kuṇisā Sutta*.
This is called the Dharma of the araṇya.

Regarding the Dharma of the Araṇya Elder: if the bhikṣus go outside the boundary, the Araṇya Elder should skillfully instruct the junior bhikṣus; he should explain the Dharma of the araṇya to them, teaching, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, while the junior bhikṣus should act in accordance with the Elder’s instructions.
If laypeople come to the forest hermitage (āraṇya), you should preach the profound Dharma for them, point out the right path and the wrong path, and speak of knowledge and vision.
If the laypeople depart, it is well; if they do not depart, give them a small or large amount of food and say these words:
"I have only this much food."
This is called the Dharma of the Aranya Elder.

Regarding the Dharma of dwelling near a village: a bhikṣu dwelling near a village should always maintain a single-minded focus, first greeting others with a joyful heart, looking upon them with a friendly gaze, speaking with them, abandoning frowning expressions, and welcoming them with the words, "Welcome."

One should maintain a fire and a hearth; one should prepare food and utensils, whether in small or large quantities. One should always maintain water and water vessels; the water vessel for washing the feet should always contain water, and the rinsing pitcher and the latrine pitcher should likewise always contain water.

One should be well-versed in the paths, well-versed in the calculation of days, well-versed in nights, well-versed in the divisions of the night, and well-versed in the lunar mansions; one should recite the *nakṣatra-sūtras*, be well-versed in reciting the *sūtras*, *vinaya*, and *abhidharma*, be well-versed in the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, and be well-versed in the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*.
If one is unable to practice and study, one should inquire about it and recite it from memory.
One should not possess sun-crystals (*sūryakānta*) or moon-crystals (*candrakānta*); all items that one possesses must be conducive to the Path, as explained at length in the *Kuṇisya Sūtra*.
This is called the method for dwelling near a village.

Regarding the method for an elder (*sthavira*) who dwells near a village: if an elder *bhikṣu* dwells near a village and the other *bhikṣus* go beyond the boundary, the elder should instruct the junior *bhikṣus*, teaching them the method for dwelling near a village so that they may see, understand, benefit from, and rejoice in it; the junior *bhikṣus* should then act in accordance with the elder’s instructions.

If laypeople come, you should preach the profound Dharma for them, showing them the right path and the wrong path; you should speak of knowledge and vision, and instruct them in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, performing good deeds, and observing the eight precepts.
This is called the method for an elder monk residing near a village.

Regarding the method for the foot-washing basin: when a bhikṣu sees that the foot-washing basin is empty, he should himself pour water into it or have someone else do so; this is called the method for the foot-washing basin.

Regarding the protocol for the senior monk (*sthavira*) during the washing of feet: if the junior monks have already washed their feet, the senior monk should not drive them away; if he does so, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the protocol for the senior monk during the washing of feet.

Regarding the rules for guests: when a visiting bhikṣu first arrives at the monastic quarters, he should bare one shoulder and adjust his robes; if his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is too high, he should lower it;
if his robe-bag is on his right shoulder, he should move it to his left shoulder;
and if his staff, oil-bag, leather sandals, or needle-case are in his right hand, he should shift them to his left hand.
If one has discharged urine or feces, one should first go outside to clean oneself before entering the monastic quarters.
If water is available, one should enter after washing the feet;
if water is not available, one should enter after wiping the feet with grass, wood, or tree leaves.
If the door is closed, one should seek to have it opened; if it is open, one should enter.

If it is not open, and there is a wall, moat, or thorny hedge outside the monastic quarters, one should stand where one can be seen, maintaining pure deportment with single-minded concentration, so as to be able to inspire wholesome thoughts in others.
If one sees an elder bhikṣu, one should ask:
"In this monastic dwelling, are there any rooms belonging to bhikṣus of such-and-such seniority? If he says:
"There is one.
He then told him to open the door.
After the door was opened and he had entered, he asked again:
"Is there someone in this room, or is it empty?
If he says, "It is empty."
One should ask:
"What kind of water do you use? If he says:
"Regarding well water":
one should request a jar, a rope, and a broom.
One should open the door of the room and snap one's fingers; if there are venomous insects, they will depart upon hearing the sound.
One should proceed slowly and calmly to remove the pillows, bedding, mattresses, and floor coverings.

Having removed them, one should sweep and sprinkle the ground with mud. One should shake out the mats, bedding, pillows, and floor coverings to search for insects; having searched for insects, one should spread them back as they were before.
He places water in the foot-washing basin, the pure rinsing pitcher, and the toilet-rinsing pitcher. Taking his leather sandals to the edge of the water, he washes and wipes the items.

Having washed them, he wrings them out; having wrung them out, he spreads them apart. Then, taking the leather sandals, he first wipes the front part, then the back, then the middle, and finally the straps.
If the water jar is on the right side, one should take water with the right hand and wash the feet with the left hand;
if it is on the left side, one should take water with the left hand and wash the feet with the right hand.

Having washed his feet, he put on his leather sandals and entered the room; closing the door and lowering the bolt, he sat upon the rope bed. First, he slowly drew in one foot, and then he drew in the second.
Having drawn them in, he sat upright and correctly contemplated all phenomena (*dharmas*). Once he had thoroughly understood the ground, he should ask the resident bhikṣus:
"Is there food before the meal or after the meal in this monastic cell?"
One should ask:
"Where in the alms-round are there vicious dogs, vicious oxen, young maidens, or widows?
Where are there households that have undergone the formal act of *saṃgha-kuṭi-karman* or the formal act of *pātra-nikubjana*?"
"Where may one go? Where may one not go?
Having asked such matters as these, one should proceed to beg for food.

If a visiting bhikṣu wishes to depart, he shall return the water jar, its rope, and the broom to their original owners; having put away his bedding and closed the door and lowered the bolt, he may leave.
This is called the rule for a visiting bhikṣu.

Regarding the protocol for visiting senior monks (*upadhivārika*): the visiting senior monk should estimate the number of visiting monks and say to the resident monks, "So many visiting monks have arrived;
you should know that so much bedding and seating must be prepared."
This is called the protocol for a visiting senior monk (*upādhyāya*).

Regarding the protocol for a monk who wishes to travel: if a monk intends to travel tomorrow, he should today take leave of his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and teacher (*ācārya*). If they grant permission, he may depart;
if they do not grant permission, he must not depart by force.

If, while staying therein, he realizes that he cannot increase wholesome dharmas, he should leave this monastic dwelling, observe the various directions, and deliberate upon his companions: "Is this person genuine?"
"Are we of one mind?
If you encounter illness or hardship on the road, will you not abandon me and leave?
Having deliberated thus, one should depart.
If one departs without deliberating in this manner, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the rule for those intending to travel.

Regarding the procedure for a senior monk (*sthavira*) who intends to travel: when intending to travel, the senior monk should be the last to depart and must entrust the bedding and furniture to the Saṃgha.
Having emerged from the monastery quarters, he says to his companions, "Do not forget anything.

If any companion has forgotten an object, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should wait for them along the road at no great distance. He should instruct and exhort his companions so that they do not engage in unrighteous conduct, distraction, or frivolous play.
This is called the procedure for an elder who intends to travel.
Regarding the improper time: if a bhikṣu wishes to travel at an improper time, he should inform his upādhyāya or ācārya, saying:
"I shall go to such-and-such a city, such-and-such a village, or to the house of such-and-such a person."
"If permission is granted, one may depart;
if permission is not granted, one should not depart by force.
This is called the rule regarding improper times."

Regarding the rule for untimely assemblies: except for the six days of the fast (upoṣadha), on other untimely occasions, for untimely matters, or sitting at untimely hours—if one hears the announcement of the time or the striking of the *gandī* bell, one should go quickly and take one’s seat in the proper order.
One should act in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings; do not disparage those of higher or lower seniority.
This is called the procedure for an untimely assembly.
Regarding the procedure for the elder in an untimely assembly, it is as explained above.
Regarding the method for the assembly of the Sangha’s senior elders (*sthavira*):

there are six monthly fast days—namely, the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth. On these days, monks who are free from illness should gather together in one place to preach the Dharma.

In this regard, if non-Buddhist teachers come with a mind of jealousy, desiring to refute the Dharma being taught, the bhikṣu should challenge and subdue them in accordance with the Dharma, without resorting to anger or harsh speech.
This is called the method for sitting in an assembly.
Regarding the method for the senior monk (upādhyāya) sitting in an assembly: if a junior monk is already seated and the senior monk arrives, one should not require him to rise.
If one drives him to rise, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the Dharma for those seated in the assembly. Regarding the Dharma for those who preach the Dharma:

one should preach the Dharma with a single-minded focus, giving rise to a mind of compassion and the intent to benefit others. One’s speech should be pure, clear, and dignified; it should proceed in orderly succession with inexhaustible eloquence. Thus preaching the Dharma in accordance with the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, one speaks for the sake of the Dharma and not for the sake of gain or sustenance. This is called the Dharma for those who preach the Dharma.

Regarding the statement "the elder Dharma-preacher": if a junior Dharma-preacher is preaching the Dharma, the elder Dharma-preacher should examine what is being said—whether it is taught in proper sequence or not in sequence;
whether it is the teaching of the Dharma or the teaching of what is not the Dharma.
If the Dharma is taught in proper sequence, one should follow along and praise it as good;
if it is not in sequence or if it teaches what is not the Dharma, one should reprimand and stop it.
This is called the dharma for an elder who expounds the Dharma.
The various non-Buddhist brahmins used to assemble in one place on the six fast days to preach the Dharma, thereby gaining great offerings and increasing their followers.
Because King Bimbisāra deeply cherished the Buddha-Dharma, he thought to himself:

"I wish that the bhikṣus would also assemble in one place on the six fast days to preach the Dharma; I shall lead the great multitude to go and listen to the Dharma myself, so that the bhikṣus may, through these causes and conditions, receive great offerings and increase their followers."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit all monks who are not ill to gather together on the six fast days to preach the Dharma."
The bhikṣus followed the Buddha’s instruction and permitted the preaching of the Dharma together on the six fast days; consequently, kings and their ministers all came to hear the Dharma.
The bhikṣus received great offerings, and their assembly increased.
Some bhikṣus were sitting on the ground preaching the Dharma, but their voices could not be heard from afar; they thought to themselves:
"It would be good if the Buddha would permit us to stand while preaching the Dharma."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to stand while preaching the Dharma.

At that time, the bhikṣus were expounding extensive sūtras; the speaker became weary and distressed, and the listeners grew utterly exhausted. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it is appropriate to stop, the time has come; you may stop.

At that time, the bhikṣus took the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras and, applying them to their own minds, explained them extensively with detailed analysis. The bhikṣus then became suspicious, wondering, "Will this not lead to the destruction of the Dharma?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit you to take the meaning of the Buddhist scriptures to adorn your speech and explain them in sequence; however, the Buddhist scriptures themselves should be read and recited directly, without mixing them with discursive commentary."
At that time, the bhikṣus were chanting chaotically in various places. The Buddha said, "You should not chant chaotically in various places.
At that time, two bhikṣus were chanting together in one place. The Buddha said:
"Two bhikṣus shall not chant together; if they chant together, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, various bhikṣus used this teaching of chanting to obtain material gain. The Buddha said:
"One should not seek material gain through the Dharma; if one obtains it, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
At that time, those who preached and chanted the Dharma took the great assembly to another location to preach and chant. The Buddha said:
"One should not take the great assembly to another location to preach and chant, except for one's own circle of disciples."

At that time, the bhikṣus had those with one eye, those without eyes, those with goiters, those without hands, those with hunched backs, and those who were lame preach the Dharma and perform hymns of praise.
At that time, there was a wise man who deeply cherished the Buddha-dharma, and the various non-Buddhists mocked him, saying:

"Is it truly as you say—that this is the one whom you praise as your teacher, your stupa, and the one you revere; that he is the first to receive offerings, the first to eat, and the one who walks before you?"
All the virtuous ones were deeply ashamed and reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, those who are one-eyed, blind, suffering from ophthalmia or goiters, or those who are handless, lame, or hunchbacked, should not be invited to preach the Dharma or perform chants. If they are invited, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."

At that time, there were those who had broken their precepts and corrupted their right views who were made to preach the Dharma. By virtue of these people preaching the Dharma, they received great offerings and gained power over a multitude of followers; thus, they committed unlawful acts that could not be restrained.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should not invite those who have broken the precepts or hold wrong views to preach the Dharma; if you invite them to preach, you commit a duṣkṛta offense."
Not knowing whom to appoint to preach the Dharma and perform the chanting, the Buddha said:

"If there are those who have previously practiced preaching the Dharma and chanting, have them do so; if there are none who have previously practiced preaching the Dharma and chanting, you should address them in order and instruct them to preach and chant."
"If among the bhikṣus there is no one who has previously practiced preaching and chanting, and they preach and chant without following the proper sequence, the bhikṣus commit a duṣkṛta offense.
This is called the rule for preaching the Dharma.
Regarding the non-exposition of the dharmas of dharmas, it is explained in detail within the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
As for the rules for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), if a bhikṣu wishes to enter the retreat, he should first deliberate upon his place of residence.

If a dwelling place is secure for coming and going, possesses fine groves and excellent water, has little noise day or night, few mosquitoes, gadflies, centipedes, and venomous snakes, and little wind and heat; and if within it there are authentic bhikṣus who can find like-minded bhikṣus with whom to sit in meditation in peace, preach the Dharma, and listen to the Dharma; and if in case of illness one may obtain medicine appropriate to the ailment, food and drink appropriate to the ailment, and attendants to care for the sick—having deliberated upon such matters, one should enter the rains retreat.
If one does not deliberate in this manner regarding the *vassa* (rainy season retreat), one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
As for the rules during the *vassa*: during the *vassa*, unless there is a cause permitted by the Buddha, a bhikṣu must not stay overnight outside the boundary, even for a single night.
For example, when the prince of Kāśi left the household life to become a bhikṣu, his father the king wished to erect a Buddhist stūpa and sent a messenger to summon him, saying:
"Come, let us together build the stūpa."
That bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to break the rainy-season retreat for the sake of constructing a stūpa for the Buddha.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted to depart for the purpose of building a stūpa.
This is called the rule for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
Regarding the rule for the senior monk (*sthavira*) during the *varṣā*: the senior monk of the *varṣā* should inspect the various dwellings to see who is maintaining them and who is not.
If the monastery is well-maintained, one should praise it, saying, "Excellent! If it is not well-maintained, one should instruct that it be repaired.
This is called the procedure for the senior monk (*sthavira*) during the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

Regarding the procedure at the conclusion of the rains retreat: once a bhikṣu has completed the retreat, he should perform three things, including the re-announcement of the boundary divisions (*sīmā*).
If one has received the kaṭhina robe, whatever alms-material is obtained shall be included within the scope of that kaṭhina.
In whichever dwelling one resides, one should sprinkle it with water, sweep it, and apply a coating of mud.

If bedding or seating possesses dust, dirt, or grease, one should shake it out and wash it; having washed and treated it, one should return it to its original place, leave the door, and lower the bolt before departing as one pleases.
This is called the procedure for concluding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).
Regarding the procedure for receiving the community (*saṃgha*), a bhikṣu should deliberate upon the assembly: do they delight in the preaching of the Dharma, or do they delight in silence?
If they delight in the preaching of the Dharma, he should preach as appropriate to the occasion.
If one prefers silence, then one should remain so;
this is called the method for receiving the assembly.

Regarding the method for approaching an assembly: a bhikṣu should first exercise discernment—approaching an assembly of kṣatriyas should be done in such a manner, approaching an assembly of brāhmaṇas should be done in such a manner, approaching an assembly of householders should be done in such a manner, and approaching an assembly of bhikṣus should be done in such a manner.
