Upon arriving among that assembly, he should enter, depart, walk, and sit in such a manner; he should inquire after their welfare and speak in such a manner, or at times remain silent.
This is called the method for attending an assembly.
Regarding the method for receiving an assembly, a bhikṣu who is to receive an assembly should observe: "In this assembly, who practices well and who does not practice well?"

If one is a practitioner of good conduct, one should carefully look after them and provide them with robes, alms bowls, medicinal decoctions, and whatever else they require; if they have committed an offense, one should assist them so that they may emerge from it.
If one is not a practitioner of good conduct, one should reprimand them according to the Dharma to bring their mind into subjection.
This is called the dharma of presiding over an assembly.

Regarding the dharma of the senior monk presiding over an assembly: the senior monk presiding over an assembly should instruct and transform the assembly in accordance with the Dharma; he must not allow them to engage in unrighteousness, frivolity, or distraction. This is called the senior monk presiding over an assembly.
Regarding the exposition of the *Prātimokṣa* method, there are five ways of expounding the *Prātimokṣa*:

first, one recites the introduction to the precepts, while the remainder is as the Saṃgha usually hears it, until the Saṃgha has finished the *Poṣadha* recitation of the precepts; this is called the first.

Furthermore, reciting the introduction to the precepts and the four *pārājika* rules, while the remainder is as heard regularly by the Saṃgha, until the Saṃgha has finished the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts—this is called the second [method].

Furthermore, the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* introduction, the recitation of the four *pārājika* rules, and the recitation of the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules; the remainder is as is customarily heard by the Saṃgha.
Up until the Saṃgha has finished the *Poṣadha* recitation of the precepts—this is called the third.

Furthermore, reciting the introduction to the precepts, reciting the four *pārājika* rules, reciting the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, and reciting the two *aniyata* rules; the remainder is as is customarily heard by the Saṃgha, until the Saṃgha has finished the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts—this is called the fourth.
The fifth is the detailed exposition;
this is called the Dharma of the Prātimokṣa.

Regarding the method for one who recites the Prātimokṣa: the monk who recites the Prātimokṣa should first recite it from memory until he is proficient, so that he does not err when reciting it in the midst of the Saṃgha. This is called the method for one who recites the Prātimokṣa.

Regarding the rules for the *saṃgha* assembly: except on the six monthly fast days (*upoṣadha*), at all other times for the *saṃgha* assembly, *saṃgha* affairs, or sitting in the *saṃgha* seating area—whether when the time is announced or when the *gandī* gong is struck—all *bhikṣus* should depart promptly and sit in the proper sequence according to the Dharma. They should act in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings, and must not treat the superior, middle, or inferior seats with contempt.
This is called the method for the assembly of the Saṃgha.
Regarding the method for the *upādhyāya* (senior monk): it is as explained above concerning the *upādhyāya* at an untimely assembly.

Regarding the method for the *madhyama-bhikṣu* (middle-ranking monk): when a *madhyama-bhikṣu* or a junior monk (*navaka-bhikṣu*) wishes to enter the house of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), they should yield the way for the senior monk to go first and should show reverence toward the senior monk.
If the senior monk goes to relieve himself, the middle-ranking and junior monks should wait for him and not go far away.
If a layperson comes and says,
"Venerable sirs, please enter," [they should respond accordingly].
One should reply:
"Wait a moment; we must wait for the Elder to arrive.
If the donor urgently calls one to enter, one should leave the seat occupied by the Elder and then sit down.
The donor says,
"I offer water.
One should then say:
"Wait a moment; the Elder must enter first.
This is called the procedure for the middle-ranking seat (*madhyama-pīṭha*).

As for the procedure for the junior-ranking seat (*avara-pīṭha*), the junior-ranking bhikṣu should sweep and sprinkle the monastery grounds, the lecture hall, the *poṣadha* hall, and the ground where the community of monks assembles at the gate of the monastery. He should arrange the seating mats in order, prepare the fire and the hearth, prepare the lamps and lamp-stands, fill the foot-washing basins with water, and place water in both the clean water jars and the toilet water jars. In this manner, the junior-ranking monk should perform all such tasks belonging to the Saṃgha.
This is called the Dharma for junior monks.

Regarding the Dharma for senior, middle, and junior monks: senior, middle, and junior bhikṣus should all receive and uphold the precepts as taught by the Buddha; this is called the Dharma for senior, middle, and junior monks.

Regarding the rules for the bathhouse: when a bhikṣu enters the bathhouse, he should maintain a single mind, speak softly, properly maintain his dignified demeanor, and restrain all his sense faculties; this is called the rule for the bathhouse.
Regarding the method of washing in the bathhouse: there are five benefits gained from washing in the bathhouse:
first, the removal of dust and grime;
second, the treatment of the skin to make it uniform in color.
Third, it dispels cold and heat;
fourth, it eliminates wind-disorders;
fifth, it reduces illness and pain.
This is called the method for washing in the bathhouse.

Regarding the procedure for the senior monk (upādhyāya) of the bathhouse: if the senior monk in the bathhouse sees that a junior monk has already finished washing, he should not drive him out; if he drives him out, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called the procedure for the Elder in the bathhouse.

Regarding the procedure for the Preceptor: the Preceptor should instruct and guide his co-practicing disciples, preventing them from associating with evil associates and causing them to draw near to virtuous associates.
One should assist the preceptor with robes, alms bowls, and medicinal requisites; if the preceptor has committed an offense, one should assist him in ensuring he is cleared of it.
This is called the dharma of the preceptor. Regarding the dharma of the co-practitioner disciple:

the co-practitioner disciple must not treat the preceptor with disrespect or arrogance. Whatever tasks are to be performed, they should all be reported to the preceptor. When traveling, one should follow behind the preceptor; one should constantly provide for all his needs and always act in accordance with the preceptor’s intentions without contravening them.

If there is anything to be done, one must not do it without informing the preceptor, except for paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, using a tooth-stick, or attending to defecation and urination.
If a co-practitioner disciple perceives that the preceptor is unable to increase his wholesome qualities, he should inform the preceptor, saying: "Please entrust me to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
The preceptor should deliberate: "What is this bhikṣu’s manner of teaching and transforming others like?
And what is his assembly of disciples like?
If he knows that this bhikṣu is endowed with wholesome qualities, he should entrust him to the care of the disciple.
If one knows that [the preceptor] is incomplete [in his qualities], one should further entrust oneself to another bhikṣu.
If one knows that the upādhyāya is not good, one should depart.
This is called the dharma for a co-practitioner disciple.

Regarding the Dharma of the Ācārya: the Ācārya should instruct and transform his resident disciples, warding them off from evil associates and causing them to draw near to virtuous friends; he should assist them with robes, alms bowls, and medicinal requisites; and if they commit an offense, he should assist them so that they may be released from it. This is called the Dharma of the Ācārya.
Regarding the practice for a resident disciple: a resident disciple should not treat the ācārya with contempt; whatever he undertakes, he should report it all to the ācārya.
When traveling, one should follow behind the ācārya; one should always provide all that is required and always act in accordance with the ācārya’s intentions, never going against them.
If one has not informed the ācārya, one must not perform any activity, except for paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, using a tooth-stick, or attending to defecation and urination.
If a disciple living nearby realizes that he cannot increase wholesome qualities under the ācārya, he should inform the ācārya, saying: "Please entrust me to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
The ācārya should deliberate: "What is the nature of this bhikṣu’s method of teaching and transforming others?
And what is the character of his assembly of disciples?
If he knows that the bhikṣu is fully endowed with wholesome qualities, he should entrust him [with the teachings].
If one knows that [the preceptor] is incomplete [in his qualities], he should entrust himself to another bhikṣu.
If the ācārya is not good, he should depart.
This is called the dharma for a disciple who dwells nearby.
Regarding the rules for a śrāmaṇera: a śrāmaṇera must not treat his upādhyāya with disrespect; whatever he does, he should inform the upādhyāya.
When traveling, he should follow behind the upādhyāya, constantly providing all that is required and acting in accordance with the upādhyāya’s intentions without any opposition.

If one has any task to perform, it must not be done without informing the preceptor, except for paying homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, or using a tooth-stick, or attending to defecation and urination.
If a śrāmaṇera stays by the side of his preceptor and realizes that he cannot increase wholesome qualities, he should inform the preceptor, saying: "Please entrust me to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
The preceptor should deliberate: "What is this bhikṣu’s manner of teaching and transforming others like?
And what is his assembly of disciples like?
If he knows that this bhikṣu is endowed with wholesome qualities, he should entrust him [to another].
If one knows that [the preceptor] is incomplete [in his duties], one should further entrust him to another bhikṣu.
If the upādhyāya is not good, one should leave him.

One should be made to take grass and tree leaves, take fruit and tooth-sticks, remove the grass from within the saṃghārāma, sweep and sprinkle water, and provide food, drink, and medicinal decoctions.
This is called the Dharma for śrāmaṇeras.

Regarding the method of exerting power: if a layperson within the monastery intends to commit an evil act or cause harassment to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus at that time should speak to him with stern and urgent words to subdue him.
If he cannot be subdued, one should not speak directly to the king; first, one should speak to that evil person's associates, and next to the king’s consort, the princes, the ministers, and so forth.
If a person abandons unwholesome actions and stops, not allowing them to occur again, this is called the method of exerting effort (*vīrya*).
Regarding the method for a monk who follows behind: the monk following behind should not be ahead, nor should he be too far behind.
One must not walk shoulder-to-shoulder; one must not speak first, nor should one speak excessively; one should not speak unless questioned, and if questioned, one should answer at that time.
If a bhikṣu walking ahead speaks what is contrary to the Dharma, the bhikṣu behind should reprove and stop him; if he speaks according to the Dharma, one should express approval.
If one receives alms in accordance with the Dharma, it is called the "subsequent bhikṣu-dharma. Regarding the practice of constantly entering the dharma of a renunciant bhikṣu:

when entering for renunciation, one should always restrain the sense faculties and not engage in frivolous play; maintaining pure deportment in accordance with the Dharma, one is able to inspire wholesome thoughts in the donor—this is called the practice of constantly entering the dharma of a renunciant bhikṣu.
Regarding the rules for visiting households: if a bhikṣu enters the home of a donor with a distracted mind and without a sense of renunciation, he constantly incurs five offenses:
first, entering uninvited;
second, sitting in a secluded place; [and so forth].
Third, sitting with authority;
fourth, eating repeatedly;
fifth, a man and a woman not speaking more than five or six words in private: these are called the rules for visiting a household.

Regarding the dharma for those living at home: a householder bhikṣu should be well-acquainted with the distinctions between seating places and the rules for sitting; he should explain the profound Dharma to laypeople, point out the wrong path and the right path, and speak of knowledge and vision.
One should constantly teach [others] to practice giving, uphold the precepts, exercise patience, and perform wholesome deeds, and should grant them the eight precepts.
This is called the Dharma for householders.

Regarding the Dharma for a senior householder: a senior householder should carefully observe his own followers, ensuring that their faculties do not become distracted or frivolous; he should always maintain pure deportment and inspire in the donors a mind of generosity. This is called the Dharma for a senior householder.

Regarding the method of conversing: when a visiting bhikṣu first arrives, the resident bhikṣus should not hastily provide him with bedding and seating. First, they should engage him in conversation; next, they should inquire whether he intends to use the communal bedding and seating. Then, according to whether that bhikṣu is of superior, middling, or inferior status, they should provide him with bedding and seating. This is called the method of conversing together.

Regarding the method of settling (*śayanāsana-vastu*): when a visiting bhikṣu first arrives, he should not hastily demand a room or bedding from the resident bhikṣus. Upon first entering the monastery, he should first stand in a visible place, maintaining pure deportment and restraining his sense faculties. Only then should he speak to the resident bhikṣus regarding the rooms and bedding; this is called the method of settling.
Regarding the method for the water-strainer: a bhikṣu who does not possess a water-strainer should not travel a long distance.

However, if there is pure water, such as river water or flowing stream water, and furthermore, if there is a place of residence within twenty *li*, he need not have a water-strainer; this is called the method for the water-strainer.
Regarding the method of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*): a bhikṣu should walk straight, neither too slowly nor too quickly.
If he cannot walk straight, he should draw lines on the ground to create markers and walk straight along those markers; this is called the method of walking meditation.

Regarding the dharma of open space: in all open space there are no boundaries; those on the ground may face toward those in the air, and those in the air may face toward those on the ground; they cannot obstruct a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) nor perform one themselves—this is called the dharma of open space.
Regarding the method of convenience: if a bhikṣu wishes to enter the latrine, he should first snap his fingers.
If someone has already entered, he should wait for them to come out.
Once they have exited, he should remove his robes and place them in one spot, then enter the latrine and squat.
If defecation or urination has not yet occurred, one should not wait; once it has occurred, one should not linger. This is called the rule for defecation and urination.

Regarding the rule concerning the vicinity of the latrine: a bhikṣu should not recite, study, discuss, or preach the Dharma near the latrine; he should not wash, dye, cut, or sew robes near the latrine. One should not perform any such activities near the latrine, except for the act of defecating or urinating. This is called the rule concerning the vicinity of the latrine.

Regarding the rule for the toilet board: a bhikṣu should relieve himself slowly and calmly so as not to soil the board; this is called the rule for the toilet board. Regarding the rule for sitting on the toilet:

if a junior monk has already entered the toilet and lifted his robe, a senior monk who arrives later should not drive him out; if he drives him out, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is called the rule for the senior monk at the toilet.
Regarding the method of wiping: one should not use sharp instruments to wipe, nor should one use grass; one should use smooth stones or soft wood. This is called the method of wiping.
Regarding the method for washing the anus: if one does not wash the anus, one must not sit or lie upon the bedding used by the Sangha; if one sits or lies there, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there is no water, if one is occupied with laypeople's affairs, or if one is applying medicine and cannot wash, then not washing in such circumstances incurs no offense.
This is called the rule regarding places for washing.

Regarding the rules concerning proximity to a washing place: if one is near a washing place, one should not recite or chant the sūtras or treatises, nor should one preach the Dharma; one should not wash, dye, cut, or sew robes. One should not perform any such activities while near a washing place, with the sole exception of washing itself.
This is called the rule for the washing area.
Regarding the rule for the washing board: a bhikṣu should wash slowly and carefully so as not to wet the board; this is called the rule for the washing board.

Regarding the rule for the senior monk (*sthavira*) at the washing place: if a junior monk is already seated at the washing place when a senior monk arrives later, the senior monk should not drive him away; if he drives him away, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is called the rule for the senior monk at the washing place.
Regarding the rule for the urination area: one must not urinate here and there; it should be done in a designated place.

This is called the rule for the urination area. Regarding the rule concerning proximity to the urination area: a bhikṣu should not recite, study, discuss, or preach the Dharma near the urination area; nor should he wash, dye, cut, or sew his robes near the urination area.
One should not perform any other actions near the place for urination, except for the act of urinating itself.
This is called the rule regarding the place for urination.

Regarding the rule for the wooden board at the urination place: a bhikṣu should urinate with a focused mind and in a calm, steady manner so as not to wet the board. This is called the rule for the wooden board at the urination place.

Regarding the protocol for the senior monk (*sthavira*) at the place for urination: if a junior monk has already entered first, the senior monk should not drive him out upon arrival; if he drives him out, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. This is called the protocol for the senior monk at the place for urination.
Regarding the rules for spitting: a bhikṣu should not spit loudly, nor should he spit upon clean, well-treated ground; this is called the rule for spitting.
Regarding the rules for spitting vessels: the Buddha permitted two kinds of spitting vessels:
those made of earthenware or those made of copper.
One should guard it well so as not to lose it, for seeking it again would obstruct one's practice of the Path.
This is called the rule regarding the spittoon.

As for the rule regarding the bowl-rest (*pātrasthāpana*), the Buddha permitted its use made of brass, copper, iron, lead, tin, pewter, or clay; one should guard it well so as not to lose it, for seeking it again would obstruct one's practice of the Path. This is called the rule regarding the bowl-rest.
Regarding the method for tooth-sticks: the Buddha permitted three types of branches—superior, medium, and inferior.
The superior is twelve *cun* long; the inferior is six *cun*; those between these two are the medium.
This is called the method for using the twig of a tooth-stick.

As for the method for cleaning the teeth: one should not use a sharp object to clean the teeth, one should not force the cleaning, and one should not damage the gums; this is called the method for cleaning the teeth.

Regarding the method for scraping the tongue: one should not use a sharp instrument to scrape it so as to injure the tongue; this is called the method for scraping the tongue. Regarding the method for removing earwax:

one should not use a sharp instrument to remove the wax from the ears, nor should one attempt to remove it by force. One should remove it gradually and gently, taking care not to injure the skin of the ear; this is called the method for removing earwax.
Such rules of the bhikṣus as these should be received, studied, and practiced; that which is contrary to the aforementioned rules is called "unlawful" (adharma).

The practice of the Dharma is complete. 16. The Two Kinds of Vinaya and the Recitation of the Miscellany. The Two Kinds of Vinaya and the Recitation of the Miscellany: Three matters for definitively knowing the characteristics of the Vinaya:
first, the original occasion (nidāna); [second, the rule; third, the application].
Second, the formal enactment of the precepts;
third, the subsequent application of the precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of *vinaya*:
There are the *vinaya* of dispute and the *vinaya* of offense.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of *vinaya*:
the *vinaya* of purity and the *vinaya* of affliction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of *vinaya*:
the *vinaya* for bhikṣus and the *vinaya* for bhikṣuṇīs.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of *vinaya*:
There are two types of *vinaya*: the universal *vinaya* and the non-universal *vinaya*.
Regarding the *vinaya* for disputes: when there is mutual verbal contention, fighting, litigation, reviling, or striking, resulting in a division into two factions, the bhikṣus should investigate:
"By what causes and conditions did this matter arise?"
How can it be extinguished?

As for the causes and conditions that give rise to strife and disorder, they consist of the fourteen matters that cause schism in the Saṃgha and the six roots of contention; these are the causes and conditions that give rise to strife and disorder.
Regarding the matter of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa-vastu*), it is settled by two *vinayas*:
the *vinaya* of presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*) and the *vinaya* of searching for many (*yadbhūyaśo-vinaya*). This is called the *vinaya* of cessation.
What is the *vinaya* of transgression (*āpatti-vinaya*)?
The five classes of offenses that are determinate offenses comprise the Vinaya offenses.
What are the five types?
They are: *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, and *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding these five classes of offenses, one should seek their origin and find their cessation.

As for the "origin," this refers to the causal conditions from which the five classes of offenses arise: there are offenses committed by body alone, not by speech or mind; offenses committed by speech alone, not by body or mind; offenses committed by body and mind, not by speech; offenses committed by speech and mind, not by body; and offenses committed by body, speech, and mind. There are no offenses committed by mind alone; these are called the causal conditions for the arising of offenses.
If one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*), it is extinguished through mental reflection.
If one commits a middling offense, it is extinguished by means of another person.
If one commits an offense requiring the formal act of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is extinguished through that rite. There are also offenses which cannot be extinguished.
There are two types of formal acts for the expiation of an offense:
first, concealment; second, non-concealment.
Regarding concealment, one is granted the period of separate residence (parivāsa) in accordance with the number of days the offense was concealed.
If one does not conceal their offense, they shall only be granted the *mānatva* penance for six days and six nights.
An offense that is incurable cannot be extinguished.
Regarding the *vinaya* of the afflictions (*kleśa*), one should seek out the causes and conditions for their arising and the causes and conditions for their cessation.

Regarding the causal conditions for arising: within the phenomena subject to fetters, the mind clings with greed, and various afflictions arise through perceiving their gratifying flavor; this is called the causal condition for arising. Regarding the causal conditions for cessation:

within the phenomena subject to fetters, one contemplates impermanence, arising and ceasing, and develops weary detachment and relinquishment. With a virtuous mind abiding in the stages of dhyāna and samādhi, one harmonizes all conditioned formations within the focal objects of the mind and enters the three gates of liberation, thereby being able to sever the fetters and latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of the truths and those abandoned through cultivation.

Because of the abandonment of two kinds of fetters, one realizes the fruits of śrāmaṇya; according to the attainment of these fruits, there are distinctions among noble ones (ārya). This is called "the inclusion of the abandonment of fetters.
Regarding the bhikṣu and bhikṣuṇī, they are either pure or impure.
Regarding the term "bhikkhunī-vinaya": it is pure, it is impure; it is pervasive, it is non-pervasive, and it is universally pervasive.
That which is pure when universally pervasive is the acceptance of fermented drinks during the first watch of the night.
Regarding purification during two periods: during the first watch and the last watch of the night, one should either practice seated meditation or recite the scriptures.
Regarding purification for one night: a bhikṣuṇī may keep an extra bowl for one night.
Regarding the purity for two nights: one may stay together with a person who has not yet received full ordination for two nights.
Regarding the purity for three nights: on the third night, the person who has not yet received full ordination must move elsewhere to stay.
Regarding purification after five nights: the Buddha permitted that, at most, one may remain without receiving formal dependence (*niśraya*) for five nights.
Regarding purification after six nights: in a place of fear, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu is permitted to stay apart from his robe for six nights.
Regarding the "purification after seven nights": for one who is ill, it is permitted to keep surplus medicine for up to seven nights before consuming it.
Regarding the "purification after ten nights": a bhikṣu may keep extra robes or alms bowls for up to ten nights at most.
Regarding purification every half-month: one should assemble at a single location every half-month to recite the precepts and perform the *poṣadha*.
Regarding purification every month: if one obtains out-of-season robes, one may keep such robes for a maximum duration of one month.
Regarding the "purity of two months": a bhikṣu is permitted to remain without formal reliance for two months.
Regarding the "purity of three months": a bhikṣu should observe the three-month *varṣā* retreat.

Regarding the "purity of four months": a bhikṣu who has undertaken the practice of sitting in the open air in a land of heavy rains should dwell in an open space for four months, remaining under cover during the eight months [of the dry season].
Regarding the "purity of the fifth month," it refers to a bhikṣu receiving the kaṭhina robe in the fifth month.

Regarding the "purity of the eighth month," it refers to a bhikṣu who practices sitting in the open air; in a land with little rain, he should reside in the open for eight months and remain under cover for four months.
The "purity of nine months" means that if a bhikṣu has unfinished business, he may remain for as long as it takes, but at most until the ninth month.
The "purity of one year" means that after one year, a bhikṣu is permitted to receive the kaṭhina robe.
Regarding "purity after two years": a bhikṣuṇī who has been ordained for two years should always follow her preceptor.

Regarding "purity after three years": when a bhikṣu’s seniority is reduced by three years, he may sit together with [a bhikṣuṇī] on a large rope bed; on a small rope bed, two persons may sit together; on a single-person bed, only one person may sit.
Regarding the "five-year purity": a bhikṣu who has completed five years must rely upon another; once he has fulfilled those five years, he is permitted to dwell apart from his preceptor.
Regarding the "six-year purity": a bhikṣuṇī who has completed six years must rely upon another; once she has fulfilled those six years, she is permitted to dwell apart from her preceptor.
Regarding "pure at seven years of age," the Buddha permitted śrāmaṇeras as young as seven years old.
Regarding "pure at nine years of age," a bhikṣu of nine years of age should perform services for the Saṃgha.
Regarding "ten years of purity," a bhikṣu who has ten years of seniority should maintain a disciple.
Furthermore, even a śrāmaṇerī who is as young as ten years old, provided she has previously been married, may receive the six rules.
Regarding "pure for twelve years": a *śikṣamāṇā* who was previously married and has reached the age of twelve should receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
One who is pure for twelve years is a bhikṣuṇī who should maintain a disciple.
Regarding those purified at eighteen years of age: a girl novice (śrāmaṇerī) who is eighteen years old should receive the six rules (ṣaḍ-dharma).
Regarding those purified at twenty years of age: a male novice (śrāmaṇera) who is twenty years old should receive full ordination (upasampadā);
a female probationer (śikṣamāṇā) who is twenty years old should receive full ordination.
A community of monks numbering twenty should be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Regarding the single pure one: a single bhikṣu should perform the *adhiṣṭhāna-poṣadha*.
The second purity is that two bhikṣus should share the offered requisites by distributing them to one another.
The third purity is the threefold recitation of the *poṣadha*.
The fourth purity is that four bhikṣus should recite the *prātimokṣa*.
Regarding the fivefold purity: five bhikṣus should appoint a person to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
Regarding the eightfold purity: eight bhikṣus should receive the formal procedure for a large assembly.
Regarding the tenfold purity: ten bhikṣus should confer full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Regarding the twenty purifications: twenty bhikṣus should perform the *karmavācanā* for the removal of an offense.
Regarding the purification of the alms bowl: the Buddha permitted two kinds of bowls—clay bowls and iron bowls.
One should not keep eight kinds of bowls.
Regarding the purification of robes (*cīvara*), one may keep seven kinds of robes without performing the formal act of *pariśuddhi* (purification):
the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *antarvāsaka*, the rain-bathing robe, the wound-covering robe, the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and other items among the "one hundred and one things."
Regarding the purity of the knife: the Buddha permitted the keeping of a "moon-head" knife for the purpose of cutting and tailoring robes.
Regarding the purity of the needle: the Buddha permitted the keeping of two kinds of needles—copper needles and iron needles.
There are three kinds of noses:
the flaxen nose, the round nose, and the mung-bean nose; a bhikṣu who lacks a needle should not go [on almsround].
Regarding the purification of defilement, the five bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
With what materials shall we dye our robes?
The Buddha said:
"One should dye it with the juice of roots, the juice of stems, the juice of leaves, the juice of flowers, the juice of fruits, or the juice of the dung of a newborn calf.
Regarding the purification by discoloring: when a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he should apply one of three types of discoloration—either blue, mud-colored, or madder.
Regarding the purity of measurement: one should not make robes equal in size to the Buddha’s robes, but should instead follow the measurements of one's own body.
All such purities should be thoroughly contemplated and examined, as well as the two divisions of the *Prātimokṣa*, along with the *Vinaya-artha-vibhāṣā* and the *Ekottara-vinaya*.

Regarding the causes and conditions that lack an original basis, there are those common to the Vinaya and those not common to it; in such matters, some are pure and not obstructed, while others are impure and obstructed.
For example, colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white are [cases of] impurity and obstruction.
That which is not blue, yellow, red, or white is pure and unobstructed.
For example, the color, fragrance, taste, and power of wine are impure and obstructive;
that which lacks the color of wine, the fragrance of wine, the taste of wine, and the power of wine is pure and unobstructed.

Furthermore, just as the various bhikṣus may use things after they have been purified, so too with the five kinds of seeds: once the bhikṣus have performed the purification of these five kinds of seeds, they may eat them.
Likewise, the eight kinds of fermented liquors may be drunk once they have been purified with water.
The ten kinds of robes, when purified by three methods of discoloration, may be used.
Such things are pure; monks and nuns should use them.
Such things are impure; monks and nuns should not use them.
In such-and-such a place and at such-and-such a time, this thing is pure and may be used by bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
in such-and-such a place and at such-and-such a time, this thing is impure and must not be used by bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

This matter should be used by a certain person at a certain time; for example, it should be used by a bhikṣu who is hungry or by one who is old or ill, but it should not be used by a young or healthy bhikṣu during times of abundance and prosperity.
In such matters, one should deliberate upon the gravity of the offense, its origin and its conclusion, and then apply the rule.

[End of] Section 17 on the Two Offenses. *Pārājika* Dharma 1: The First Precept (The Precept Against Sexual Intercourse). Regarding the *Pārājika* Dharma of the First Precept: When the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, the bhikṣu Sudinna Kalandaputra had this thought: "The Buddha has established the precept to sever sexual desire;
what was done before [the precept was established] is not an offense. I have engaged in much sexual intercourse; I do not know which of these acts constitutes the 'first' [offense]."
"Which place is not prior?
Thus, doubt and regret arose in his mind.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu, Sudinna Kalandaputra, did not commit any sexual misconduct prior to the formulation of the precepts.
Question:
"The Buddha stated that a madman does not commit an offense; to what extent is one considered 'mad'?"
The Buddha said: "There are five characteristics that define a madman: one who goes mad because all his kinsmen have died;

one who goes mad because his wealth has been completely lost; one who goes mad because his lands, enterprises, and people have been completely lost; one who goes mad because the four great elements are in disorder; or one who goes mad due to the retribution of past karma."
Although a bhikṣu may possess these five signs of insanity, if he knows for himself, "I am a bhikṣu," and commits sexual intercourse, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If he does not know this for himself, he does not commit an offense.
Question:
"The Vinaya states that one does not commit an offense with a distracted mind.
What is meant by a 'distracted mind'?"
The Buddha said: "There are five causes and conditions that cause the mind to become distracted:

the mind becomes distracted because one is struck by a non-human being; or the mind becomes distracted because a non-human being causes it to be distracted; or the mind becomes distracted because a non-human being consumes the mind's vital essence; or the mind becomes distracted because of a disorder of the four great elements; or the mind becomes distracted because of the retribution of past karma."
If a bhikṣu possesses these five kinds of distracted mind and is self-aware of it, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense;
if he is not self-aware of it, he does not commit an offense.
Question: "The Buddha said:
'One whose mind is impaired by illness does not commit an offense.'"
"What is meant by a person whose mind is impaired by illness?
There are five kinds of illnesses that impair the mind:
either the mind is impaired by the arising of wind, or by the arising of heat, or by the arising of cold, or by the simultaneous arising of all three, or by the arising of seasonal changes."
If a bhikṣu has these five kinds of mental afflictions that corrupt the mind, and if he recognizes them as such, he incurs a pārājika offense;
if he does not recognize them, he does not commit an offense.

There was a bhikṣu named Vatsiputra. This bhikṣu did not return his precepts, nor did he leave while his precepts were weak; having committed sexual misconduct in his own home, he later regained faith and desired to go forth, thinking:
"I shall ask the bhikṣus."
"I must still receive full ordination and go forth as a bhikṣu;
if I cannot do so, I shall stop.
This person questioned the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

“If a bhikṣu does not return his precepts and does not leave while his precepts are weakened, yet goes to a householder’s home and engages in sexual intercourse, this person shall not receive full ordination.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu who has entered the dharma of the bhikṣus does not return his precepts and does not leave while his precepts are weakened, and commits sexual intercourse—even with an animal—he incurs a pārājika offense.’”
There was a bhikṣu who, perceiving a path as not being a path, engaged in sexual intercourse. Doubt arose in his mind:
"Have I not incurred a pārājika offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one engages in sexual intercourse with the perception that it is a path while it is indeed a path, one commits a pārājika offense.
If one engages in sexual intercourse with the perception that it is not a path while it is indeed a path, one likewise commits a pārājika offense."
If one has doubt while on the road, one also incurs a *pārājika*.
If it is not the road but one perceives it as such, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is not the road but one perceives it as not the road, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Doubting whether it is a non-path also constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
"Path" refers to the urinary tract, the anal tract, and the oral tract.
If one causes [the organ] to enter the anal tract, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one enters the urinary tract, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one enters the oral cavity, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse with an elephant, even if he merely touches its skin, he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If there is no contact, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If there is no contact and semen is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The same applies to cows, horses, camels, donkeys, mules, pigs, sheep, dogs, monkeys, deer, geese, wild geese, peacocks, chickens, and so forth.
If there is physical contact, it is a *pārājika*.
If there is no physical contact, it is a *thullaccaya*.
If there is no physical contact and semen is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
There was a bhikṣu who constantly experienced the arousal of lustful desire.

He said to a spiritual friend, "I am constantly afflicted by the arousal of lustful desire and cannot stop it myself; I could find a woman and engage in sexual intercourse with her, and thus be at peace."
The acquaintance said,
"You may go ahead and do it.
He then followed the acquaintance's words and engaged in sexual intercourse.
The learned bhikṣu felt doubt and remorse, thinking:
"Shall I not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not commit a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"How should one repent for and eliminate a *sthūlātyaya*?
The Buddha said, "There are four kinds of *sthūlātyayas*: [text continues]"

There are *sthūlātyaya* offenses that arise from a *pārājika* and are grave; there are *sthūlātyaya* offenses that arise from a *pārājika* and are light; there are *sthūlātyaya* offenses that arise from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and are grave; and there are *sthūlātyaya* offenses that arise from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and are light.
Upāli! A grave sthūlātyaya arising from a pārājika must be confessed and extinguished before the entire Saṃgha.
A light sthūlātyaya arising from a pārājika must be confessed and extinguished by a community of four bhikṣus outside the boundary.
A grave *sthūlātyaya* arising from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is also expiated by four monks outside the boundary through confession;
a light *sthūlātyaya* arising from a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is expiated by one monk through confession.

The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. There was a bhikṣu named Nandi who, before midday, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Having finished his meal, he took his sitting mat (niṣīdana), placed it upon his left shoulder, and entered the Andhavana forest, where he spread the sitting mat beneath a tree and sat down cross-legged.
A māra deity came, wishing to shatter this bhikṣu’s samādhi, and manifested as an exquisite woman, standing before the bhikṣu.
When the bhikṣu arose from samādhi and opened his eyes, he saw this woman and immediately gave rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
Worldly meditative concentration is not firm; by giving rise to a lustful mind, one loses that concentration and desires to touch the woman's body.
The woman then gradually retreats and moves further away, whereupon the bhikṣu immediately rises and follows after her.

At that time, there was a dead horse in the forest; when he went to the side of the dead horse, his female body disappeared. Because this bhikṣu’s body was consumed by lustful desire, he engaged in sexual intercourse with the dead horse.
Having committed the act of sexual misconduct, when his feverish passion had slightly subsided, he immediately felt remorse and said:

"I have fallen; I am no longer a bhikṣu, nor am I a son of the Śākya. The other bhikṣus will surely reject me and will no longer dwell with me. I ought not to wear the saffron robe with this impure body."
He immediately folded his *kāṣāya* robe, placed it in a bag, and carried it upon his shoulder as he proceeded to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by a great assembly of hundreds of thousands of millions of followers who paid him respectful homage as he preached the Dharma.
When the Buddha saw this bhikṣu coming from afar, he thought to himself:
"If I do not greet him with gentle words and inquire after his well-being, this man will surely break his heart and liver, and hot blood will gush from his mouth."
The bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha said:
“Welcome, Nandi!
Are you able to return to training in that which is studied by bhikṣus?”
When that bhikṣu heard the Buddha say,
“Welcome, Nandi! his heart was filled with great joy, and he thought to himself:
"I shall surely be able to dwell together with the bhikṣus; they will certainly not expel me.
Having reflected thus, he replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
"I am able to return to training in the training of a bhikṣu.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should all return to training the Dharma with the bhikṣu Nandiya; if there are others like the bhikṣu Nandiya, you should likewise train them in the Dharma."
The Saṃgha should be united with one mind; the bhikṣu Nandiya should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel on his right knee, join his palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please take heed!"
I, the bhikṣu Nandiya, having neither returned the precepts nor become weak in them, committed sexual misconduct.
I, Nandiya, have requested from the Saṃgha the restoration of the training; out of compassion for me, Nandiya, the Saṃgha has granted me the restoration of the training.
A second and a third time he should likewise request.
Then, one bhikṣu among the assembly should announce it to the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

The bhikṣu Nandi did not return his precepts, yet he engaged in sexual intercourse while his precepts were not yet weakened. Nandi now requests from the Saṃgha the restoration of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Out of compassion, the Saṃgha now restores the training rules to him.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let us restore the training rules to the bhikṣu Nandiya.
This is the motion.
Thus one performs the formal act with a motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).

"Having finished bestowing the training rules upon the bhikṣu Nandiya, the Saṃgha consents by its silence; thus this matter shall be maintained! Regarding the training rules for a śrāmaṇera under training: one must practice all the precepts established by the Buddha.

He should sit in the lowest seat among the bhikṣus and should serve food, drink, and medicine to the mahābhikṣus, while receiving food and drink from other śrāmaṇeras or laypeople himself. He must not stay in the same room as a mahābhikṣu for more than two nights, nor may he stay with a layperson or a śrāmaṇera for more than two nights. He may participate in the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the two types of *karmavācanā* with the mahābhikṣus; however, when a śrāmaṇera under training is present, he does not count toward the quorum for performing the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or the *karmavācanā*.
In the kingdom of Kośala, there was a bhikṣu dwelling alone in a deep forest. A non-human woman came and said to the bhikṣu, “Come;
let us engage in sexual intercourse.”
The bhikṣu said, "Do not speak such words; I am one who has severed lustful desire.
The woman said:
"If you do not come, I shall ruin your prosperity and bring you misfortune and distress.
The bhikṣu said, "Do as you wish;
I will not engage in sexual misconduct with you."

Having spoken these words, at midnight the bhikṣu lay down to sleep; the female spirit folded his inner robe, took the bhikṣu, and placed him beside a lady in the royal palace, where they both lay down to sleep.
When the king awoke and saw him, he asked, "Who are you?
The bhikṣu replied:
“I am a śramaṇa. “What kind of śramaṇa are you?
He replied:
"I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
The king said,
"Why have you come here?"
The bhikṣu related this matter in detail to the king.
The king said,
"Why do you dwell in the deep mountain forests, being harassed by evil spirits?"
"Go away!
Because I know the Buddha's Dharma, I will not attend to your business.
That bhikṣu was thus freed from a serious matter and reported the full account to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should not dwell in such places as deep mountain forests that are fearsome and devoid of people."
In the kingdom of Kośala, there was a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya. A female piśāca demoness came to him and said to the bhikṣu, "Come and engage in sexual intercourse."
The bhikṣu said, "Do not speak such words; I am one who has severed lust.
The female ghost said:
"If you do not comply, I shall ruin you and bring you suffering and distress.
The bhikṣu said, "Do as you wish;
I will never engage in sexual misconduct with you."
While the bhikṣu was lying down at night, a female ghost wrapped him in a hempen garment and placed him inside a wine jar in a tavern.
The next morning, when the innkeeper saw the bhikṣu inside the wine jar, he asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa. [The other asked,] "What kind of śramaṇa are you?"
He replied,
“A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas. He asked:
"Why are you here? The bhikṣu related the matter in detail.
The keeper of the tavern said:
"Go! Because the bhikṣu had been delivered from this grave matter, he spoke of it to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, monks should not dwell in deep forests, empty places, or terrifying, uninhabited regions.
There was a monk traveling among a herd of fierce oxen; a fierce ox chased him, intending to gore the monk, and the monk fell upon a woman as he fled.
A woman embraced a bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu pushed her away with his hand; this bhikṣu felt doubt, thinking:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should walk calmly and slowly in the midst of the herd of oxen."
There was a bhikṣu who was looking down a well when he fell into it. A woman was already inside the well, and the bhikṣu fell upon her.
The woman grasped the bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu pushed her away.
A householder entered a monastic dwelling and, seeing this bhikṣu at the well, immediately pulled him out.
As he was being pulled out, he emerged together with a woman. The householder asked, "What were you doing in there with that woman?"
The bhikṣu said, “This woman fell first; I fell later.
This bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt.
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, you should watch the well with single-minded attention so that no one falls into it.
There was a bhikṣu who went for alms; before noon, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, arriving at a small gate and wishing to enter.
There was a woman who wished to exit, and the shoulders of the two men touched one another.
This bhikṣu became suspicious, thinking, "Will I not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“If there is no intention, there is no offense.
From this day forward, you should practice alms-gathering slowly.
There was a bhikṣu who was crossing a river by boat together with a woman; when the boat sank into the water, the woman clung to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu pushed her away.
Later, the bhikṣu felt doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, you must board the boat slowly.
There was a man named Kapilakandu who had the appearance of a woman and took pleasure in feminine matters.
She went to the bhikṣuṇīs and said to them, "Ordain me so that I may leave the household life.
Without reflecting, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained her. This woman then began to touch and fondle the bhikṣuṇīs, who drove her away.
Again, she touched a śikṣamāṇā, and the śikṣamāṇā drove her away;
again, she touched a śrāmaṇerī, and the śrāmaṇerī drove her away.
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, you must contemplate well before you should cross over.

There was a merchant who had traveled far away; his wife committed adultery with another man and became pregnant. As her pregnancy grew large, she induced an abortion out of fear. Having aborted the fetus, she saw that the child was dead and was filled with great sorrow and distress. She had no one of like mind whom she could send to discard this dead child.
In that family there was a bhikṣuṇī who frequently entered and left their home. One day, before midday, the bhikṣuṇī put on her robes, took her bowl, and came into the house.
The bhikṣuṇī asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?"

She replied, "My husband has traveled far away; while he was gone, I committed adultery with another and became pregnant. Hearing that my husband was about to return, I was overcome with fear and aborted the fetus myself."
"I am now without a companion who will take this dead child away for me; therefore, I am sorrowful.
She said to the bhikṣuṇī, "O virtuous woman!"
"Can you, for my sake, discard this dead child?
She replied, "I can take it away; who would know?"
She then filled a jar with it, covered the opening with an object, and discarded it far away in a place where no one was walking.
There were some gamblers there who saw this bhikṣuṇī coming with the jar and said to one another,
"Let us go see what the bhikṣuṇī is discarding."
They immediately went together to look.
Seeing the dead child, they said to one another:
"The Śākya bhikṣus have not severed their lust; they have committed sexual intercourse with bhikṣuṇīs, and having become pregnant and given birth, they have abandoned the child."
One person told it to two, and the two told it to three; in this way, the evil reputation spread from one to another until it pervaded the entire city of Śrāvastī.
A certain bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities, heard of this matter and became deeply distressed. He reported the matter to the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha brought the Saṃgha together; knowing the matter, the Buddha asked that bhikṣuṇī:
"Is it true that you did this?
She replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked this bhikṣuṇī with various causes and conditions, saying:
"What is meant by a bhikṣuṇī discarding another's dead fetus?
From this day forward, no bhikṣuṇīs shall discard a dead fetus.
If one discards it, she commits an offense."

When King Prasenajit of Kosala heard that Bhadragavila had gone forth as a renunciant, he immediately invited him to enter the palace and stayed together with him in one place for the four months of the summer retreat.
Later, when the king wished to go to the garden, he said to the gatekeeper:
"Guard the gate well; do not allow this bhikṣuṇī to leave.
The gatekeeper replied:
"Yes. After the king had departed, the gatekeeper thought to himself:
"This bhikṣuṇī wishes to remain here and will not flee."
At that time, due to certain other circumstances, a gatekeeper allowed a bhikṣuṇī, dressed in the finery of a queen, to pass through the gate and proceed directly to the Jetavana.
At that moment, the Buddha was surrounded by a respectful assembly of hundreds of thousands who were listening to his teaching. When the Buddha saw her approaching from afar, he said:
"Welcome, Bhadrakapilā!"

When the Buddha spoke these words, the lady immediately lost her fine garments and ornaments; her hair fell away of its own accord, and the *kāṣāya* robe was upon her body, and she became a *bhikṣuṇī*.

Having become a bhikṣuṇī, she went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. The Buddha then taught her the path of the supernormal powers of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*); immediately, the bhikṣuṇī attained the power of supernormal faculties.
At that time, when the king heard that the maiden Bhadrakapilā had fled, he led his troops to surround the nunnery, whereupon the bhikṣuṇī flew up into the air.
Upon looking up and seeing her, the king felt remorse,
thinking, "How have I defiled this arhat bhikṣuṇī?
Overwhelmed by distress, he fell to the ground.
At that time, the ministers sprinkled him with cold water, whereupon he regained consciousness and apologized to the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs drove him out, saying:
"You are a man who has committed sexual misconduct."
"Go away!
The bhikṣuṇī said, "I have no intention of receiving sexual desire."
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "You were together with the king in the palace for the four months of the summer retreat; why did you not receive [the precepts]?
This bhikṣuṇī did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the situation], the Buddha nevertheless asked that bhikṣuṇī:
"Did you truly receive fine and smooth sensations?"
He replied,
“World-Honored One!
How should I receive it?”
"I perceive this smoothness as if a red-hot iron were entering my body.
The Buddha said,
"If you have no mind that experiences the smoothness, there is no offense."
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇīs:

"Do not speak again of this matter concerning Bhadrakapilā. It is due to the karmic retribution and conditions of a woman's own actions that she has obtained these female organs and was subjected to another's forced sexual assault."
"If a bhikṣuṇī is forcibly seized by another and commits sexual intercourse against her will, she is without fault, as she lacks the intention to consent.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Sujātā, who was beautiful and lovely, capable of stirring the hearts of men.
Kāpilavastuka first approached without speaking and directly touched this bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇī drove him away; having driven him away, she felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "If there is no intention of lust, there is no offense.

There was a bhikṣuṇī named Dhani who was beautiful and lovely, capable of stirring the hearts of men; before midday, she put on her robes, took her bowl, and intended to enter the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
On the road, there were some gamblers who, intending to enter a deep forest, forcibly attempted to commit sexual misconduct with the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs drove them out of the monastery, saying:
"You are people who commit sexual misconduct; you should not stay here."
That bhikṣuṇī said,
"I had no intention to receive the sensation of smoothness.
The other bhikṣuṇīs said:
"A gambler has taken you to a deep forest to commit sexual misconduct; why did you not refuse?
The bhikṣuṇī did not know what to do, so she reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked:
"Did you truly experience fine and smooth sensations?
He replied:
“World-Honored One, how shall I receive it?
I have pushed with my hands, kicked with my feet, and turned my body about, yet I cannot free myself.
The Buddha said:
"If she had no intention and did not consent, there is no offense.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇīs:

"Do not speak again of this matter concerning that bhikṣuṇī. That bhikṣuṇī pushed him with her hands, kicked him with her feet, and turned away without consenting; since she was forcibly seized by another, there is no offense."

There was a bhikṣuṇī named Ārāmikā who, before noon, dressed in her robes and took up her bowl to go begging for food. Several gamblers dragged her into a deep forest and forcibly committed sexual misconduct with her.
The bhikṣuṇīs drove her out of the nunnery, and that bhikṣuṇī said:
"O virtuous ladies!
I have no intention of receiving [the sensation of] smoothness."
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Gamblers have dragged you into a deep forest to commit sexual misconduct.
Why did you not refuse?"
At that time, Ānanda was in the nunnery, and the bhikṣuṇīs said to him,
"Ānanda is here. When Ānanda questioned these bhikṣuṇīs, they were unable to answer because they stood in awe of him.
Ānanda was displeased that she did not answer, and the bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have driven me out of the monastery, and now the Elder Ānanda is also dissatisfied with me; what is the use of my living on?"
"Now I shall go to the Ajiravatī River and throw myself into it to die.
This bhikṣuṇī filled a jar with sand, tied it to her neck, and submerged herself in the water; as the rope broke, her body floated up and sank down again.
At that time, some gamblers playing on the riverbank saw her and said to one another:
"Look at this bhikṣuṇī being carried away by the current; go and fetch her here."
They immediately went out together, supported him to the riverbank, and he regained consciousness once the water had drained from him.
They led him into a deep forest to engage in sexual intercourse, after which they returned to the monastery quarters.
The bhikṣuṇīs drove her out again, saying:
"Previously you said that you had no intention of receiving the touch of smoothness; yet now, a gambler has brought you into a deep forest, committed sexual intercourse with you, and released you."
Not knowing what to do, those bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the situation], the Buddha asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Do you have a mental sensation of smoothness?
He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"How shall I endure this?
I weep and cry out loudly, saying, 'Do not do it! yet I cannot escape.
The Buddha said:
“If you have no intentional mind when experiencing smoothness and softness, there is no offense.
The Buddha spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
“Do not speak of this matter concerning that bhikṣuṇī again. Because of the karmic conditions of their previous lives, women obtain these female organs and do not possess self-mastery over them.”
Even though she weeps and cries, he forcibly seizes her; even though she says "do not do it," he forcibly does it; even though she shouts loudly, he forcibly does it.
If a bhikṣuṇī is forcibly seized by another, there is no offense provided she has no intention of consenting.

The first *pārājika* concludes. Second Precept (The Precept on Theft). Regarding the beginning of the second precept on theft: When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, he established the precept against stealing because of the bhikṣu Daṇḍakī Kumbhakāraputra, saying:
"What was done previously does not constitute an offense."
That bhikṣu felt doubt and regret in his mind, saying:
"I have taken many pieces of timber by theft; I do not know which ones were taken first and which ones were not."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
“Before the precepts were established, the bhikṣu Daṇḍaka took timber at all times without committing an offense; this is called ‘not having committed an offense due to prior action.’”
There was a bhikṣu who took an unowned object from a deserted place and carried it away; doubt arose in his mind:
"Could I not have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one knows that an object belongs to another and takes it, one commits a *pārājika*.
If an object belongs to another and one takes it while perceiving it as not belonging to anyone, one commits a *pārājika*."
If one takes an object belonging to another while harboring doubt, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If an object has no owner, yet one perceives it as having an owner and takes it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one takes an object that has no owner while harboring doubt, one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
"If there is no object belonging to another, and one forms the perception that it does not belong to another, there is no offense.
A bhikṣu took food that had not been given to him and carried it away; doubt arose in his mind:
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should calculate the value of this meal."
"Rice, parched grain, roasted grain, fish, and meat cakes should also have their value calculated.
There was a bhikṣu who came to eat on his own without being invited; he felt doubt in his mind:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should not go to eat unless you have been invited."
"If you go to eat [the food], you will incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There was a resident monk who went to a village, and a monk he knew there took a portion of food for him. When that monk returned from the village, the monk he knew said, "I have taken a portion of food for you."
That bhikṣu said,
"For what reason did you take it?
He replied:
"I took it for your sake.
That bhikṣu said:
"I did not tell you; why did you take it?"
The learned bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“No offense.
From this day forward, if another person has not spoken [to give permission], a bhikṣu should not take a portion of food.
If he takes it without such instruction, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.”
A certain bhikṣu went to a village.
The community of monks was distributing rice, and this bhikṣu had two co-practicing disciples. Because these disciples were unaware of one another, they both took portions of food for him.
Later, the two disciples said to one another:
"Between the portion you have taken and the portion I have taken, who has fully committed the *pārājika* offense?"
Doubt arose in his mind, so he reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should speak among yourselves and have one person take [the requisites]."
"When taking [the food], you should say:
'I am taking a portion of food for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill; when the Saṃgha was distributing rice, the attendant who had taken the rice for him died. The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the patient dies first and the rice is taken afterward, it shall be returned to its original place.
If the rice is taken first and the patient dies afterward, it should be divided as part of the remaining property of the deceased bhikṣu."
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 57 and Scroll 58; Part 3 of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.
During the recitation of the remainder of the precept on stealing in the Vinaya,
the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us go together and commit robbery."
He replied, “As you wish.
The bhikṣu set out, but on the way, remorse arose in his mind and he felt shame.
"How can we, having gone forth out of faith in the sublime Dharma of the Buddha, act as thieves?
Having had this thought, they no longer went [to steal], but their minds were filled with doubt:
"Could it be that we have incurred a *pārājika* offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The bhikṣus then spoke to one another, saying:
"Let us go together to commit robbery.
He replied, "As you wish."
As they were setting out on their way, one person among them felt regret and gave rise to a sense of shame, thinking:
"How can I have left the home life out of faith in the sublime Dharma of the Buddha only to become a thief?"
He further thought:
"If I do not go, others might kill me; we should go together.
I have no need for goods, nor will I take a share."
Having reflected thus, he drove [the person] away; having driven him away, he did not seize another's property therein, nor did he take a share.
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "He has not committed a pārājika offense; he has committed a sthūlātyaya.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus spoke among themselves, saying:
"Let us go together as thieves.
He replied, "Depart as you intend."
Having gone everywhere, they found nothing at all.
These bhikṣus became doubtful:
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Then the bhikṣus spoke to one another, saying:
"Let us go together to commit a robbery.
He replied,
"Depart as you intend."
Among them, half of the bhikṣus acted as guards on the road, while the other half took the goods. Those who were guarding the road said:
"We did not take another's property; we are without fault."
Later, they felt doubt, thinking:
"We have committed such an act; will we not incur a *pārājika* offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us go together as thieves."
He replied, "As you wish.
Having set out, they obtained goods for half [of them] and did not obtain goods for the other half. Those who had not obtained goods said:
"I did not obtain another's property nor take a share; there is no offense.
Yet, he again gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus spoke among themselves:
"Let us go together to commit a robbery.
He replied, "As you wish."
The associates said to him, "You should take only a small amount; do not let it be complete.
Having taken it, when the property of the community was about to be divided and the items amounted to five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, the bhikṣus became doubtful.
"We fear that we have committed a *pārājika* offense.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The gravity of the offense depends on the person taking the object, its removal from its original place, and its value."
The watchmen gave a robe to the bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu did not accept it, thinking:
"Who here is the donor?
Who is the owner?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Accept it according to the donor's gift.
A thief seized a disciple and took him away; the preceptor recovered him by force, and the preceptor felt doubt.
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"If she is definitely under the control of the bandits, she incurs a *pārājika* offense."
"If it was not certain, there is no offense.
It is the same for a disciple who follows closely after an ācārya.
A thief seized a bhikṣu and took him away; later, having stolen himself back from the thief, he returned running and became suspicious:
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense in stealing one's own body."
A bhikṣu carrying taxable goods arrives at a customs gate and thinks:
"If I pass through this gate with these goods, I will commit a pārājika offense.
He then thinks again:
"Regarding this tax, I would rather give it to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; or to my preceptor (upādhyāya) and teacher (ācārya); or to my father and mother.
Having reflected thus, he spoke gentle words to the toll-collector:
"I shall offer these goods as an offering to you for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; or to my preceptor and teacher; or to my father and mother."
"If one gives these items to another, whether to act as a messenger or for one's own necessary provisions, such matters may be carried out through the power of gentle speech without fault."
"Passing over [the boundary] is not an offense.
A bhikṣu, having borrowed a single-seated chair from another bhikṣu, thought to himself:
"I shall not return it later."
The owner sought him out, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Return my bed to me."
Having spoken these words,
"I will not give it to you," he immediately gave rise to a mind of doubt and regret.
"I fear I shall incur a *pārājika* offense.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You do not incur a *pārājika*; you incur a *sthūlātyaya*."
After a bhikṣu has borrowed a scripture from another, he thinks to himself:
"I will not return it.
When the owner comes to demand it back, he says:
"Venerable sir!
Return my sutra to me! he said.
"I will not give it to you.
Immediately, a mind of doubt and regret arose:
"Will I not incur a *pārājika* offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who stole a worn-out garment bag; inside the bag was a garment of great value. Having seen it, he conceived a thought:
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the value of the bag containing the robes is calculated at five coins, one incurs a *pārājika* offense."
"If it is not straight [in its course], one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The thieves took the wine to a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) and drank half of the stored amount. While the bhikṣus were wandering through the woods, they saw the wine and said to their disciples:
"Take this back to our residence and use it to make *kaṭuka-śīta* (sour vinegar)."
The disciple followed the instruction and took it back.
When the bandits returned and could not find the wine, they went to where the bhikṣus were and asked,
"Elders!..."
“Did you bring the liquor from that place?
The bhikṣu replied,
“I brought it.”
The bandits said in anger,
"You are thieves, you are thieves!
The bhikṣu said:
"Why do you call me a thief, thief?
The thief replied, "I am a thief, yet you have stolen from me; therefore, I say 'thief, thief.'"
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what state of mind did you take it?
The bhikṣu said,
"World-Honored One!"
"I thought this was wine and took it because there was no owner," he said.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, if you see any object, you should examine it well before taking it.
The thieves took the meat into the mountain forest, where they ate half and hid the other half.
As the bhikṣus were wandering through the forest, they saw the meat and said to their disciples:
"Take this home to provide for tomorrow.
The disciple followed these instructions and carried it back.
When the bandit returned seeking the meat and could not find it, he went to the bhikṣu and asked:
“Elder! Did you bring that meat from there?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I brought it here.
The robber said angrily,
"You are a thief, a thief!"
The bhikṣu asked,
"Why do you call yourself a 'thief,
a thief'? The thief replied:
"I am a thief, and you have stolen from me; therefore I say, 'Thief! Thief!
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I have incurred a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha. Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied:
“World-Honored One!
I took this meat because I thought it had no owner.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, if you see any object, you should take it only after careful consideration.

It happened that some thieves, having plundered cities and villages, carried money and goods as far as an *āraṇyaka* (forest hermitage). Later, royal forces surrounded that place. Out of fear and in desperation, those thieves gave the goods to the bhikṣus; having given them, they departed.
When laypeople came and saw that the items were in the possession of the bhikṣus, they said:
"Venerable sirs!
These are our belongings; they are now in your hands."
The bhikṣu said,
"A thief gave me this as an offering.
The laypeople said:
"Who would believe your words?
You have either committed the theft yourself, or you obtained it from a thief.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Do not take property from bandits; however, if the leader of the bandits gives it to you, you may take it.
Once you have taken it, you must dye it a ruined color before wearing it."
"If the color has been altered and the owner subsequently seeks it, it should be returned.
A householder removed his garment and placed it by the roadside to relieve himself; a monk wearing patched robes saw it, looked in all four directions and seeing no one, took it and departed.
The layperson said, "Bhikṣu, do not take my robe and leave.
Because the bhikṣu did not hear him, he continued on without stopping; the layperson ran after him, seized the robe, and said:
“Is it not the rule for a bhikṣu that one should not take by force what is not given?
The bhikṣu replied,
“I considered this robe to belong to no one.”
The householder said, "This is my robe;
it does not belong to no one.
The bhikṣu said:
"If you take this robe with you," [the other said].
That bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha. Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I took it because I had no one to belong to," he said.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, when you see an object, you should examine it well before taking it; the object may actually belong to someone, yet appear as if it belongs to no one.
When people have relatives who have died, they discard them at the place for the dead.
The people of this country were by custom fond of cleanliness; they would strip their clothes off and leave them outside where the dead were placed, and only then enter the cremation ground.
When a monk wearing rag-robes (pāṃsukūlika) saw these garments and looked around but saw no one, he took them away.
Having seen this, the layperson said to the bhikṣu, "Do not take my robe away.
Because the bhikṣu did not hear his words, he continued on without stopping; the layperson ran after him, seized and took back the robe, and said:
“Is it not the duty of a bhikṣu to take what is not given?
The bhikṣu replied,
“I thought this robe belonged to no one.”
The layperson said, "This is my robe;
it does not belong to no one.
The bhikṣu said:
"If he takes it away," that bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha. Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I took it because I had no one to whom it belonged," he said.
The Buddha replied,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, if you see any object, you should examine it thoroughly before taking it.
There may be objects that actually belong to someone, yet appear as if they belong to no one.
A laundryman took various garments, soaked them in water, and forgot them as he departed for another village.
He recalled his thoughts, wondering, "Have I not lost this robe?
At that time, a monk who wore rag-robes arrived at that place in search of worn-out rags; seeing the robe and observing that no one was around, he took it and departed.
A washerman came and saw a bhikṣu taking away his clothes, saying to him, "Do not take my clothes!
Because the bhikṣu did not hear him, he continued on without stopping; the washerman ran after him, seized and took back the clothes, and said:
“Is it not the duty of a bhikṣu to refrain from taking what is not given?
The bhikṣu replied,
“I considered this robe to have no owner.”
The laundryman said, "This is my garment;
it does not belong to no one.
The bhikṣu said:
"If he takes it away," that bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
