This matter was reported to the Buddha. Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I thought that because it belonged to no one, I would take it.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, if you see an object, you should examine it well before taking it.
There may be objects that actually belong to someone, yet appear as if they belong to no one.
Furthermore, there was a washerman who took his clothes to the water's edge; having washed them, he wrung them out, and after drying them, sat down in one place to watch over them.
There was a monk wearing patched robes who sought out worn-out rags. Seeing a garment in that place, he looked around and, seeing no one, took it away.
A washerman came by, saw the monk taking the garment, and said to him, "Do not take my garment away!"
Because the bhikṣu did not hear [the warning], he continued on his way without stopping; the washerman ran after him, seized him, and took back the garment, saying:
"Is it the dharma of a bhikṣu to take what is not given?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I thought this robe belonged to no one.
The laundryman said:
"This is my robe; it does not belong to anyone else.
The bhikṣu said, "If this is your robe, take it with you."
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I took it because I thought it belonged to no one."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, if you see an object, you should examine it thoroughly before taking it."
"There is an object that truly belongs to someone, yet appears to belong to no one.
There was a young boy who, carrying a *śāṭaka* (a cloth), spent the whole day playing in the middle of the road; he forgot the cloth and went home.
A *pāṃsukūlika* bhikṣu, seeking a rag-robe, arrived at that place; having seen it, he looked around but saw no one and took it away.
A girl came out from the child’s house and saw him, saying to the bhikṣu:
"Do not take my *śāṭaka* away!"
The bhikṣu said,
"I obtained it on the road.
The woman said:
"My young child was playing all day long in the road with this *śāṭaka* (robe), and he forgot to bring it back home;
do not take it away. The bhikṣu said, "If it is yours, then I shall take it."
The bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I took it because I thought it belonged to no one."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, if you see a robe, take it only after careful consideration."
The bhikṣus who wear patched robes (pāṃsukūlika) wore impure and soiled robes; the devas and vajra-deities were displeased with this, and their own majesty and virtue were diminished.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wear impure and soiled patched robes; to wear them constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."

A certain householder, having heard that the Śākya bhikṣus were able to wear robes made of rags from dust heaps, took eight coins wrapped in expensive cotton cloth, placed them in the refuse so that the threads would be visible, and stood at a distance to watch.
There was a monk wearing robes of discarded rags who, seeking out worn-out cloth, came to this place; having seen the threads, he took them.
Once he had taken them, he saw that they were a highly valuable fine cotton cloth, and so he carried it away.
The householder called out, saying: "Elder!
This is my cotton cloth; do not carry it away."
The bhikṣu said, "I found it myself in the refuse heap; what business is that of yours?
The householder said:
"I have heard that the bhikṣus, the sons of the Śākyas, are able to wear tattered rag-robes. Desiring to test them, I took a high-priced cotton cloth and wrapped eight coins inside it.
There are eight coins within this cloth; if you do not believe me, you may count them."
Having counted them several times, he found that there were indeed eight coins.
The bhikṣu said,
"If these are permitted by you, then take them."
The bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I took it because I thought it belonged to no one."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, if you see an object..."
"You should take it only after careful consideration.
Now, there was a monk wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūlika*) who, having hidden his robes in a certain place, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Another monk wearing rag-robes, seeking out worn-out rags, came to the side of those robes; seeing them and looking around until he saw no one, he took them away, washed them with water, and spread them out to dry by the gate of the Jetavana.

The monk who was the owner of the robe returned from begging for alms; after searching for a long time without success, he wished to enter the Jetavana Grove and saw [the other] by the gate. He said to the monk who had taken the robe:
"Venerable sir!"
"Have you committed a *pārājika* offense?
The monk who took the robe said,
"For what reason?"
The owner of the robe said,
"I entrusted my patched robe to you, yet you have brought it here on your own authority.
The bhikṣu who had taken the robe felt doubt.
“I fear I shall incur a *pārājika* offense.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked:
“With what intention did you take it?”
The bhikṣu said,
“I took it because I thought there was no owner.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, if you see an object, you should take it only after careful consideration; objects left by the deceased are one thing, and objects belonging to no one are another.

In the kingdom of Kośala, near a place where the dead were disposed of, there were various deva shrines. A man who guarded these shrines was washing clothes, wringing them out, and hanging them to dry, but he did not gather them up once they were dry; the wind blew them down into the place where the dead were disposed of.

There was a bhikṣu who lived in a place where people died; while observing corpses there, he saw these robes. Looking around and seeing no one, he took them away. A shrine-keeper saw him and said, "Elder!..."
"Do not take my robe away!
The bhikṣu said, "I obtained it in a place where people are dead; what concern is that of yours?"
The temple guardian said, "This is my robe;
I washed it, wrung it out, and hung it up to dry. Due to some minor circumstance, I did not collect it at the proper time, and the wind blew it down into the place where the dead are kept."
The bhikṣu said,
"If this is your robe, then take it.
The bhikṣu felt doubt.
“I fear I shall incur a *pārājika* offense.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked:
“With what intention did you take it?”
The bhikṣu said,
"I took it because I thought it belonged to no one.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, if you see an object, you should examine it thoroughly before taking it.
The bhikṣus took a middle-sized robe belonging to a deceased person, whereupon the caṇḍālas said:
"Elder! Do not take it.
This is my merchandise for which I am paying customs duties."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if there is clothing belonging to one who has died, a bhikṣu should not take it."
"If you take it, you will incur an offense.
At that time, outside the area where the dead were kept, he searched for and took a small piece of tattered rag; even the caṇḍālas did not permit him to take it.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In this case, do not take it even if it is offered.
If you take it, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal on the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the householder prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Returning to his own home, he prepared many kinds of delicious food and drink during that night.
Having prepared the food, he spread out the seats in the early morning; when the time arrived, he sent a messenger to the Buddha’s dwelling and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, the meal is ready; may the Holy One know that it is time."
When the Buddha and the assembly of monks entered the householder’s residence, the Elder Yaśas remained in the monastery quarters to receive his portion of the meal.
Two young children of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada were playing in the courtyard of the Jetavana monastery when some bandits sought to harass and rob them.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu Yaśas thought:
"This child is pitiable; because he has no knowledge, he will surely be harmed, robbed, and plundered by these thieves."

He immediately entered meditative absorption and, through his supernormal powers, manifested the fourfold army. When the bandits saw this, their hearts were filled with great terror; they thought, "We are surrounded by the power of the king or the power of the local community; we shall surely perish."
Reflecting thus, he quickly departed.
The bhikṣus came and said to Yaśas,
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
Yaśas asked, "For what reason?
The bhikṣus replied:
“Because a thief intended to harm him and seize this child’s belongings, you took them away for his sake.
Yaśas felt doubt about this matter and reported it to the Buddha.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked:
"How did you take it? Yaśas replied,
"I manifested supernatural powers."
The Buddha said, "It is without fault to exercise supernormal powers to take [the food].
There was a householder who invited the Buddha and the community of monks for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, the householder prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Upon arriving at his own residence, he prepared many kinds of exquisite food and drink during that night. Having finished the preparations, he arranged seats in the morning; when the time arrived, he sent a messenger to the Buddha’s location and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The meal is prepared; may the Blessed One know the time.
The Buddha and the community of monks entered the householder’s residence. One bhikṣu remained behind in the monastery to receive his portion of the food, having newly learned a mantra-ritual.
The two young sons of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to play at Jetavana, where some bandits intended to harass, plunder, and rob them.
Upon seeing this, the bhikṣus thought:
"These children are pitiable; because they have no knowledge, they are being harmed and robbed by these bandits."
"I have recently mastered a mantra; let us test it by reciting it to save this child—will it be effective?
He then recited the mantra, whereupon four types of troops emerged. When the bandits saw them, their hearts were filled with great terror, and they thought:
"This must be the power of the government or the force of the local community surrounding us; we may well perish."
Having reflected thus, he fled quickly.
The bhikṣus came and said to the bhikṣu who was guarding the monastery:
"Venerable sir!..."
"You have committed a pārājika offense.
The bhikṣu guarding the monastery said,
"For what reason?"
The bhikṣus said,
“Because people were about to harm and rob this child of his belongings, you took them away.
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt.
"I fear I shall incur a *pārājika* offense.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked:
"With what intention did you take it?"
The bhikṣu said, "I shall recite a new incantation to save this child; I will go out with the fourfold army to seize him.
The Buddha said:
"If one recites new spells, there is no offense.
When the elder bhikṣus arrived at another village, the Saṃgha divided the robes; this bhikṣu had a virtuous friend who took a share of the robes for him.
When that bhikṣu returned from the village, the bhikṣu who was his virtuous friend said to him:
"Venerable sir!
I have taken a portion of robe-cloth for you."
The bhikṣu said,
"For what reason did you take it?
The bhikṣu who was his spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) then gave rise to doubt.
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu does not speak up, he should not have a share of the robes taken for him;
if he should take them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It happened that some elder bhikṣus went to another village while the Saṃgha was dividing the robes, and those bhikṣus had two co-practicing disciples.
Because these two disciples did not know of one another, each took a portion of the robes for their respective preceptors.
Later, the two disciples said to each other:
"You have taken a portion of the robes, and I too have taken a portion of the robes; who among us has fully committed a *pārājika* offense?"
Doubt arose in his mind, so he reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should speak among yourselves and have one person take [it]."
"When receiving it, you should say:
'I am taking this portion of robe-cloth for the sake of such-and-such a bhikṣu.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill; when the Saṃgha divided the robes, the bhikṣu who was tending to him took the portion of robe-cloth on his behalf.
When this sick bhikṣu died, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one takes a share of the robes after the person has already died, it should be returned to its original place."
"If one who has previously taken a share of the robes dies later, they should be divided among the other items of the deceased bhikṣu.
There was a lay devotee who repeatedly used the monastic fields but did not pay the monks their tax dues.
Later, when that householder wished to sow [the field], the former bhikṣu came and said to the householder:
"You have repeatedly used the Saṃgha’s field without paying the price; do not sow now."
"If you wish to plant it, you must pay the price to the Sangha.

When the householder heard these words, he insisted on planting it; however, at that time, an elder bhikṣu lay on the ground to block the plow. The householder felt ashamed and immediately desisted from planting.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forth, do not commit acts that are shameful with your own body.
A certain bhikṣu stole property belonging to the Buddha’s monastery and became filled with doubt.
“I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“If there is a guardian, one should calculate its value.”
"If these conditions are fulfilled, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
A senior monk had a person plow the field belonging to the Saṃgha; this Saṃgha field was adjacent to a householder’s field, and the monk also had a person plow the householder’s field.
The householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Do not sow my field.
The bhikṣu replied:
"I myself have cultivated the field of the Sangha; what business is that of yours?
The householder replied, "This field is mine; no human being serves as its witness."
"In this country, among the various fields, wooden stakes or the bones of the feet or heads of dead people are placed in the soil as markers.
When the householder showed him these signs, the bhikṣu, having seen them, felt ashamed and abandoned his ox and departed.
Later, when that bhikṣu returned and sent someone across to mark the boundary again, the householder saw him and said to the bhikṣu:
"When I was previously disputing with you, did you not already set out the markers for the ground?"
"What shall I do today to sow again?
That bhikṣu immediately abandoned the plow and the ox and departed, his mind filled with doubt:
"Will I not have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should calculate its value.
If it is complete, one incurs a pārājika offense."
If one does not obtain [the flower] in its entirety, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
A certain bhikṣu took a flowering tree without it being given to him and became doubtful:
"Will I not incur a *pārājika* offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should calculate the value of these flowering trees.
If the full amount is reached, one commits a *pārājika* offense."
"Fruit trees are also like this.
Once, a bhikṣu destroyed a stork's nest; consequently, the storks would frequently come to surround the vihāra, crying out piteously in the air.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Why does this woodpecker cry out so piteously?
Ānanda replied, "A bhikṣu destroyed its nest; for that reason, it cries out in grief."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not destroy the nests of woodpeckers.
If you do so, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who took a vulture’s nest to boil it for dyeing. At that time, the vultures constantly came to surround the vihāra, crying out piteously in the air.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, “For what reason are these vultures crying out so piteously?”
Ānanda said, "There was a bhikṣu who took the nest and boiled it for dyeing; that is why it cried out in distress.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not take peacock nests to boil for dyeing;
if you do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There was a householder who possessed a garden of excellent radishes. A certain bhikṣu went to the householder's place and said:
"Give me some radishes," [the monk] said.
The householder asked,
"Do you have the price for them?"
"You should simply ask for it.
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have no price."
The householder said,
"If anyone requires radishes, they should bring the price for them.
If I were to give them away for free, how would I survive?"
The bhikṣu said:
"Is it certain that you will not give it to me?
The householder replied:
"I certainly will not give it to you.
At that time, the bhikṣu used the power of incantations to curse [the tree] so that it withered and dried up.
Having done this, the bhikṣu felt doubt arise in his mind.
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The value of this radish should be calculated."
If it is complete, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if it is incomplete, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same calculation of value should be applied to vegetable gardens, flower gardens, leaf gardens, and fruit gardens.
There was a horse being fed while on the move; a bhikṣu showed it a bundle of grass, and the horse followed the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu pointed toward other grass, intending in his mind that the horse should eat that other grass instead.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
While the bhikṣus were traveling through the country of Kośala toward Śrāvastī, they joined company with some merchants; on their way, there was a dangerous path.
The merchants, riding fine horses, said to the bhikṣus,
"You too should ride such fine horses so that you may quickly traverse this perilous path.
Among them was a bhikṣu who, riding a fine horse, gave rise to a thought and devised this expedient means:
"This horse can be obtained.
His body moved slightly, and he immediately gave rise to doubt:
"Will I not incur a *pārājika* offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not commit a *pārājika* offense; he commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a merchant who had a boat full of treasures; a bhikṣu boarded it for transport across a river, and conceived a thought, employing such a stratagem as follows:
"The treasure can be obtained.
His body moved slightly, and he immediately gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I have committed a *pārājika* offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not commit a *pārājika* offense; he commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

There was a merchant who had loaded a boat full of treasures to cross a river. When the boat sank, the treasures were submerged, and a chest of clothes drifted away with the current; the boat owner was terrified and unable to go retrieve it.
There was a bhikṣu who was washing downstream; having seen [the merchant], he took and carried it away.
When the merchant saw this, he said to the bhikṣu, "Do not seize my clothing chest! The bhikṣu replied:
"I obtained this from within the water; what business is it of yours?
The merchant said, "My ship sank in the water and my treasures were lost; the clothing chest drifted downstream, and because I was terrified, I could not retrieve it in time."
The bhikṣu said,
"If it is so, then take it away.
This bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt.
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
There was a bhikṣu who took property belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions and moved it to another monastery; he felt doubt in his mind:
"I fear I have committed a pārājika offense."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "He does not incur a pārājika offense; he incurs a duṣkṛta.
The thieves led the ox up to the āraṇya, tied it to a tree, and departed.
After the meal, some bhikṣus were walking in meditation in the forest when they saw someone tethering a horse by its halter around a tree.
Feeling compassion for it, the bhikṣus released it; immediately thereafter, they became doubtful:
"Have we not committed a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *duṣkṛta* (or *āpatti-dukkaṭa*) offense.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a celestial deity who could grant people's wishes.
There was a lay devotee who, having obtained his heart's desire through the fulfillment of his wishes, wrapped the body of a celestial image in white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*).
Among them was a bhikṣu named Kālānanda, who possessed great strength and had no fear of divine images; he seized the cloth from the deity and carried it away.
Later, he became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There is a divine image capable of protecting a person's body; a certain lay devotee requested a boon from it and obtained his wish according to his heart's desire."
Because this lay devotee was filled with joy, she tied a golden garland upon her head. The great and valiant Ānanda, the Black One, desired to go and seize the golden garland.
As he approached, the deity terrified him; the bhikṣu’s heart leaped and his hair stood on end, yet he remained undaunted. He subdued the deity, seized the golden garland, and departed with it.
Later, he became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was the wife of a householder who went to the banks of the Ajiravatī River to bathe.
These wives of the householders removed their ornaments and clothing, went onto the bank to enter the water for bathing.
A monkey from a tree on the bank came down, took the pearl necklaces, and climbed back up the tree to depart.

When the householder’s wife had finished her bath at her own pleasure and ascended the bank to put on her clothes, she searched for the pearl necklace for a long time but could not find it, so she left.
Having seen her depart, the monkey returned, placed the necklace back in its original spot, and climbed back up the tree.
After his meal, a bhikṣu was wandering through the forest when he saw these necklaces. Recognizing their owner, he took them back to the householder’s wife.
The householder’s wife said, "Bhikṣu, you are a thief! You stole my necklaces and only returned them to me after feeling remorse."
The bhikṣu said, "I did not do so.
The householder’s wife said:
"How did you obtain it?
The bhikṣu explained the matter in detail.
The bhikṣu’s mind gave rise to doubt.
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."

At the head of the walking path above a cave, a *kang-lang* bird had built a nest; it would constantly bring bones and worn-out rag-robes to discard them on the ground. The bhikṣu who practiced walking meditation there would then destroy this nest, whereupon the bird would frequently come to circle the vihāra in the air, wailing piteously.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"For what reason does this bird cry out so piteously?
Ānanda replied:
"A certain bhikṣu destroyed a nest, and for that reason it cried out piteously.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, you must not destroy the nests of these *kāraṇḍava* birds."
"If one destroys it, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Once, the bhikṣus had a storehouse in a certain place where they kept food, drink, money, and goods. A rat emerged from its hole, stole the money and goods, as well as tattered clothes and food, and carried them back into its hole.
The bhikṣus were doubtful,
asking, "Who has stolen these items? At that time,
there was one bhikṣu who placed his alms-food by the side of the storehouse, waiting for the proper time to eat.
A mouse emerges from its storehouse, carrying food into its hole.
Seeing this, the bhikṣu recognizes that the mouse has stolen the goods; he destroys the hole, takes the mouse's goods, and also takes his own remaining goods entirely for himself.
The bhikṣus said,
"You have committed a pārājika offense.
That bhikṣu said:
"Why is that? the bhikṣus asked.
"Because you took the mouse's belongings," they replied.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not an offense of defeat (pārājika).
From this day forward, one should take what belongs to oneself; one should not take the property of mice.
A certain bhikṣu was lying down in his room when, at night, a mouse brought food and placed it beneath his bed.
The bhikṣu rose early, washed his hands, received [the food] from a lay attendant, and then ate.
The other bhikṣus did not see this bhikṣu begging for alms, yet his hands and feet were always clean and pure;
they therefore asked him, “Venerable sir!...”
"I have not seen you begging for alms; are your hands and feet always so clean?
The bhikṣu replied, "Venerable elders!"

"There was a mouse that would come at night carrying food and place it beneath my bed. After I had risen early and washed my hands, I would receive the food from a *karmadāna* and eat it; for this reason, I have never begged for alms, and my hands and feet remain pure and clean."
The bhikṣus said:
“Venerable sir!
You have committed a pārājika offense.”
That bhikṣu asked,
"For what reason?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Because the mouse did not give it to you, but you took it for yourself to eat.
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of this bhikṣu’s affairs.
For what reason?

This mouse was, in a previous life, the father of this bhikṣu; because he loved his son and felt affection upon seeing him, he constantly placed food beneath the bed for him, and thus this bhikṣu is without fault.
There were some hunters who, pursuing a deer, ran into a monastic dwelling. When these hunters came seeking the deer, the bhikṣus did not give it to them.
After searching for a long time without success, the hunters then departed.
The bhikṣus became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is blameless.
Furthermore, there was another hunter who shot a deer with a non-poisoned arrow; it fled and entered a monastic dwelling.
When the hunter came seeking it, the bhikṣu would not give it up, and after waiting a long time without success, he returned home.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
Once, a hunter shot a deer with a poisoned arrow, and the deer fled into a monastery.
When the hunter came seeking it, the bhikṣus would not give it back to him, whereupon the hunter said:
"This deer, having been struck by a poisoned arrow, will surely die.
The bhikṣu said, "Let it die; I cannot give [the meat] to you."
The hunter did not find an opportunity for a long time and then departed; not long after he had left, the deer died.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should return to the hunter.
If there are hunters who have set deer-traps and a bhikṣu destroys them out of a sense of pleasure, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if he destroys them out of a heart of compassion, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If there is a bird-catcher who has set a snare, and a bhikṣu destroys it out of a sense of pleasure, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he destroys it out of a compassionate heart, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
When various bird-catchers have set snares, if a bhikṣu destroys them out of a sense of pleasure, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one destroys [the net] out of a mind of compassion, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there is a bird-catcher who has spread a fine net, and a bhikṣu destroys it out of a sense of pleasure, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one destroys [the cage] out of a compassionate mind, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a monk, for his own pleasure, destroys a bird-catcher’s cage or cart, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if he destroys it out of a compassionate mind, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
A monk who was buying clothes saw a garment being sold and took it away.
The seller said, "Do not take my garment!
The monk replied:
"I will take this robe, show it to him, and then return it to you.
Later, he conceived the thought that he would not return it after all, and immediately felt doubt:
"Will I not incur a *pārājika* offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who had a carpenter work for him but did not pay the carpenter; the carpenter then demanded his wages.
A bhikṣu gave rise to the thought of not giving, and immediately felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

There was a bhikṣu who took a ceramic vessel from a potter without paying for it. The potter demanded, "Give me the price! The bhikṣu resolved not to give it, and immediately felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"I fear I shall incur a *pārājika* offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a pārājika offense, but incurs a sthūlātyaya.
A bhikṣu purchased goods from a shop without paying the price; when the shopkeeper demanded payment, the bhikṣu resolved in his mind not to give it, and immediately felt doubt and regret.
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "He does not incur a pārājika offense; he incurs a sthūlātyaya."
A sick bhikṣu spoke to the bhikṣus who were nursing him, saying:
"Take this money and prepare three kinds of fresh porridge; I shall drink this porridge and also give it to the Saṃgha."
The monks who were nursing the patient said this:
"Why should we use this price to make porridge for the community of monks? We shall simply make a small amount of porridge for the patient; as for this money, we shall divide it among ourselves."
Having deliberated thus together, they prepared gruel for the sick monk and divided the money among themselves.
At that moment, those monks who were tending to the patient became suspicious, thinking:
"Could it be that we have committed a *pārājika* offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅).
There was a bhikṣu who was ill and desired cakes; he spoke with the bhikṣus attending to him regarding their price.
"Take this price and make cakes; I shall eat them myself and also give them to the community of monks.
The monks who were tending to the sick spoke thus:
"Why should we use this price to make cakes for the community of monks?"
"We shall simply make cakes for the sick bhikṣu; as for this money, we shall divide it among ourselves.
Having deliberated thus together, they made the cakes and gave them to the patient, and then divided the money between them.
The bhikṣus who were tending to the sick immediately became suspicious, thinking:
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
There was a certain bhikṣu who was ill and possessed much money. He thought to himself:
"After my death, the Saṃgha will surely divide up my money; I must now ensure that the Saṃgha is unable to divide it."
Having thought this, he said to the attendant:
"Prepare some mung bean soup and bring it to me.
The attendant prepared the soup and gave it to him; on account of this minor matter, the attendant went out.
The patient placed money into his soup and drank it all at once; because the food was difficult to digest, he died.
The caregiver carried him to a place where dead bodies were discarded, whereupon various birds came and tore open his belly, pulling out his intestines, and the money fell to the ground.
At that time, the assembly of monks immediately struck the *ghanṭā* and called the attendant who looked after the sick man, saying:
"This deceased monk possesses much money; you must bring it here so that the assembly of monks may divide it."
The monks who were tending to the sick could not obtain any money.

There was a monk dwelling in a cemetery who, having gone to the place of the dead to contemplate impermanence, saw this money and brought it to give to the community of monks. He immediately felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"Have I not committed a *pārājika* offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
There was a sick bhikṣu who possessed many fields and spoke to his attendants, saying:
"Summon the bhikṣus; I shall assign this land, whether to the Buddha, to the Saṃgha, or to an individual.
The nurses thought to themselves:
"If this sick bhikṣu gives this land to the Buddha, to the Saṃgha, or to an individual, we shall have nothing left to receive."
Consequently, he did not summon the bhikṣus.
When the sick bhikṣu died, the nursing bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Do not, on account of minor causes, go against the words of a sick person; you should follow the sick person's instructions and do everything for them.
There was a sick bhikṣu who possessed many robes, bowls, and articles of daily life.
The sick bhikṣu said to the bhikṣus who were attending him:
"Summon the bhikṣus; I shall distribute these items to the Buddha, to the Saṃgha, and to individuals."
The attendants of the sick monk thought:
"If this sick monk gives these items to the Buddha, to the Saṃgha, or to other people, we shall have nothing to receive."
Consequently, he did not summon the bhikṣus.
When the sick bhikṣu died, the attendant bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Do not disregard the words of a sick bhikṣu because of minor circumstances; you should follow his instructions and do everything as he directs.
There was a bhikṣuṇī from the East who was traveling along a road with a bhikṣuṇī from Pāṭaliputra; the bhikṣuṇī from Pāṭaliputra was in front, while the bhikṣuṇī from the East was behind her.
The bhikṣuṇī Pāri lost her robe, and a bhikṣuṇī from the East found it.
When they were together in one place, the bhikṣuṇī from the East proclaimed:
"Who has lost this robe? I found it on my territory."
The bhikṣuṇī Pāli said,
"Will you take this robe?
She replied:
"I am taking the robe.
The owner said:
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
He asked, "For what reason? He replied:
"You took it with a thieving mind.
This bhikṣuṇī felt doubt in her heart:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Śivika who delighted in receiving offerings and obtained large quantities of ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
There was a merchant who, seeing this bhikṣuṇī, felt joy in his heart and said:
"Noble lady!
If you require ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar, take as much as you wish from my house."
The bhikṣuṇī replied, “So be it.
While this request was being made, another bhikṣuṇī heard of it; after several days had passed, she went to the merchants’ quarters and spoke falsely, saying:
“Give five sheng of oil to the bhikṣuṇī Śyāmāvatī.
The merchant asked,
“What will you use it for?”
He replied,
"I shall take it to the nunnery.
The merchant then gave it to him.
The bhikṣuṇī took it to the monastery and put it on.
After several days had passed, a merchant saw the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīvatī and said to her:
"Noble lady!..."
"Why do you seek only oil, and not rice, meat, or soup?
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "What are you saying?"
The merchant said,
"Previously, a bhikṣuṇī came and said:
'You requested five measures of oil.'"
“I shall give it to you. Śreṣṭhin said,
“Very well.”
"If you ask for anything else, I shall give it to you as well.
Then Śīlavatī went to that bhikṣuṇī and said:
"You are a base bhikṣuṇī, a wicked bhikṣuṇī, a thief-like bhikṣuṇī; you have committed a pārājika offense."
That bhikṣuṇī asked:
"For what reason? Śreṣṭhī replied:
"The merchant did not give it to you; you took the oil by deceiving him.
She replied, "It was not that I took it without being given; I took it in your name."
That bhikṣuṇī became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
She reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked her:
"With what intention did you take it?
He replied,
"I took it because of the name 'Śyāma'."
The Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense.
Because he spoke a deliberate falsehood, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense."
"From this day forward, you must not take [goods] by falsely assuming another's name; if you do so, you shall be guilty of an offense.
In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a merchant who, having adorned his ship, entered the great ocean. Once he had entered, a nāga came and seized the ship.
The merchants each sought their own tutelary deities, worshipping and making petitions, yet they received no grace and were not granted deliverance.
Among them was one merchant who was a disciple of Maudgalyāyana; since Maudgalyāyana frequently visited his house, the man thought to himself:
"If Maudgalyāyana takes pity on me, I shall surely obtain liberation."
Having reflected thus, he single-mindedly prostrated before Maudgalyāyana.

At that time, the Elder Maudgalyāyana perceived this with his divine eye; he immediately entered meditative concentration and, through his supernormal powers, transformed himself into a king of golden-winged garuḍas and stood at the prow of the ship.
When the nāgas saw this king of the garuḍas, they were struck with great terror; they abandoned their ship and sank into the great ocean, while all the merchants attained safety.
Upon returning to Śrāvastī, they praised Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"He has truly accomplished great supernormal powers; that we were delivered from the sea is entirely due to the power of Maudgalyāyana’s grace."
The bhikṣus went to where Maudgalyāyana was and said to him,
"You have committed a pārājika offense.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"Why is that? the bhikṣus asked.
[The man] replied, "This boat belongs to a nāga; you have simply seized it."
Maudgalyāyana became suspicious and reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked him:
"How did you rescue them?"
Maudgalyāyana said,
“I did so by means of my supernormal powers.
The Buddha said:
"If one uses the power of supernormal faculties, there will be no transgression.

There were merchants from Śrāvastī who had gone out from the city to travel through towns and villages for trade; on a perilous road, they were surrounded by bandits and were unable to advance or retreat.
The merchants each sought their own tutelary deities; though they performed prostrations and offered prayers, they received no grace and could not escape their plight.
Among them was one merchant whose teacher was Maudgalyāyana, who frequently visited his house. This man then thought to himself:
"If Maudgalyāyana takes pity on me, I shall surely be delivered and saved."
Having reflected thus, he single-mindedly paid homage to Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, the Elder Maudgalyāyana perceived this with his divine eye; he immediately entered meditative concentration and, through his supernormal powers, manifested the fourfold army.
When the bandits saw this, they immediately thought to themselves:
"Whether it be the power of the king or the strength of the local village that has come to surround us, we shall certainly not be able to escape."
Thus, terrified, they abandoned [the path] and departed from afar.
The merchants emerged safely from the perilous road;
upon returning to Śrāvastī, they praised Maudgalyāyana:
"Truly, you have accomplished great supernormal powers! That we have been delivered from this perilous path is entirely due to the power of Maudgalyāyana's grace.
The bhikṣus went to Maudgalyāyana and said, "You have committed a pārājika offense."
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"For what reason?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Those merchants were under the control of bandits; that is why you seized them.
Maudgalyāyana became doubtful about this matter and reported it to the Buddha. Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked him:
"How did you rescue them?"
Maudgalyāyana said,
"I did so by means of my supernormal powers.
The Buddha said:
"If one possesses supernatural powers, there is no fault in saving them.

The Elder Pilindavatsa frequently visited the home of a certain lay devotee. There was a young child there; whenever the bhikṣu arrived at the house, the child would grasp his feet to pay homage, and as he rose, he would still hold onto his feet.
A young boy was standing and playing on the bank of a river when a bandit in a boat gradually lured him onto it.

The Elder Piṅgiyānī, seeing this with his divine eye, immediately entered meditative concentration and, through his supernormal powers, stood at the prow of the boat. When the boy saw him, he prostrated at his feet according to the customary rite, grasping one foot with each of his two hands. At that moment, the Elder flew away, and the boy followed him until they reached his home.
The bhikṣus went to where Piṅgalavatsa was and said to him,
"You have committed a pārājika offense. Piṅgalavatsa replied:
"Why is that? the bhikṣus asked.
"Because this child belonged to bandits, and you have seized him."
Pilindavatsa became suspicious; he reported this matter to the Buddha. Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked him:
"How did you rescue him? He replied:
"I shall do so by means of my supernormal powers.
The Buddha said:
"If you were to save them through supernormal powers, they would be without fault."

King Bimbisāra [entrusted] five hundred park-keepers from among the monks in the Bamboo Grove with this task; these five hundred people established a large settlement not far from the Bamboo Grove and resided there, where bandits would frequently come to plunder them.
When the Elder Piṅgiyānī saw this, he thought to himself, "How could I allow this man to be harmed by bandits?

He immediately entered meditative concentration and, through his supernormal powers, created a high wall. The bandits came at night and constructed a high ladder; before they had finished the base, they became terrified and fled.
The bhikṣus went to where Piṅgalavatsa was and said,
"You have committed a pārājika offense. Piṅgalavatsa replied:
"Why is that? the bhikṣus replied,
"Because bandits came and destroyed the village, you then seized [the property]."
Pilindavatsa became doubtful about this matter and reported it to the Buddha. Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked him:
"How did you rescue her? Pilindavatsa replied:
"I shall do so by means of my supernormal powers.
The Buddha said:
"If one were to save others through supernormal powers, there would be no offense."

At the end of the summer retreat, the Śākya son Bānaṃda traveled from place to place, visiting various monasteries, wishing to ascertain the number of monks who had spent the rains retreat there as well as the quantity of their goods.
When they arrived at a certain place, the bhikṣus saw them from afar, rose from their seats, and immediately offered them places to sit.
After exchanging greetings and sitting for a short while in silence, [the visitors] asked the bhikṣus:
"Has the saṃgha of this residence received the offerings for the rainy season retreat?"
The bhikṣus said,
“It is permitted. He asked:
"Has it been divided yet?
He replied, "Not yet."
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa said, "Bring it here; I shall give you your share.
The bhikṣus brought the items and had them divided; Pūraṇa Kāśyapa gave him his portion, and once the elder had received his share, he wished to take it up and depart.
Bhadanta said, "Elder, please stay a moment; do not depart yet.
The Elder replied:
"What shall we do while staying here?
Vāḍananda replied, "You have already received material gifts; I shall now provide you with the gift of the Dharma."
Bhadanta Nanda possessed eloquence and keen faculties; he was able to adorn his speech and expound various sublime dharmas for him.
Because the Elder’s heart was filled with joy, he gave all of his own portion to Bhadanta Nanda, saying:
"I give my entire share to you."
The second and third elders did likewise.
In this manner, the process was repeated throughout the entire assembly of monks.
Thus, by successive transmission, they arrived at monasteries in various locations, obtaining much property in each case, and brought bags of robes back to Jetavana.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were walking up and down near the gate of the Jetavana, they saw Baddhananda coming from afar and said to one another:

"This Śākyaputra Baddhananda is shameless and lacks a sense of remorse; having committed offenses involving what has been seen, heard, or suspected, he is full of desire and never satisfied, yet here he comes carrying this cloth bundle."
As they gradually drew near, the bhikṣus asked Bhaṇḍana,
"From where have you obtained these many articles?
Bhaṇḍana then related the matter at length as described above.
Among them were monks who had few desires, were content, and practiced the dhūtas; hearing this matter, they felt resentment and said:
"How can a monk observe the rains retreat in one place and receive offerings in another?"
After the bhikṣus had rebuked Upananda in various ways, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of these causes and conditions, convened the Saṃgha; knowing [the answer] already, he asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha reproached Baddhālī in various ways and by many causes and conditions:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu dwell in one place during the rains retreat and receive offerings in another?
Although the Buddha reproached him, he did not yet establish a formal precept.
The Buddha was again staying at a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, observing the rains retreat together with a large assembly of bhikṣus.
Many lay devotees, seeing the great multitude of monks, prepared for them dwellings, robes from their own households, and robes for the retreat.
In the following year, the Buddha returned to Jeta’s Grove for the rains retreat. At that place, there were two elder bhikṣus observing the retreat, and these lay devotees thought to themselves:
"We should also provide the Dharma-gift as we did last year, so that the bhikṣus may obtain robes."
"I shall obtain the merit of giving such that it is never severed.
These householders, as they had previously given, brought many garments and articles to this dwelling place and offered them as alms to these two elders.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"These robes and requisites are many; if we were to divide them, what offense do you know we would incur?
Ultimately, they did not dare to divide them.

During the final month of the summer retreat, the Śākya son Upananda traveled from one monastery to another, surveying all the monasteries to see how much alms were received by the monks who had completed their rains retreat. He then thought to himself:
"The Buddha spent last year’s retreat at that place; there must certainly be many offerings there now. I shall go there."
Having thought this, he departed. When the two elders saw him from afar, they rose from their seats to meet him, offered him a seat, and exchanged greetings.
After Upāli (Baddhānanda) was seated, he remained silent for a short while and then asked: "Elders!..."
"In this place where the Saṃgha is observing the rains retreat, is there any gift to be given?
He replied, "There is!"
He asked, "Has it been divided yet?
He replied:
"Not yet distinguished.
"For what reason?
The Elder replied:
"These robes and articles are many, while we are few; if we divide them, how shall we know what offense we have committed?
Vaddhananda said, "It would be well for you not to divide them; if you do divide them, how shall you know what offense you have committed?"
The two elders said to Upananda,
"Are you able to divide it?
He replied:
"Yes," said Baddhananda,
"a formal ritual (karmavācanā) must be performed for this; it cannot be divided directly."
Then the two elders took all their robes and went out, placing them before Baddhālī.
Baddhālī divided these robes into three portions and said,
"You two sit at the edge of one heap."
Sitting between the two groups, he spoke, saying:
"Venerable sirs, listen with single-minded attention to these words of the *karmavācanā*:
'The robes of you two people in one group count as three; the robes of me, one person, in two groups count as three.'"
"Is this *karmavācanā* well performed?
They replied,
"It is excellent."
He wrapped these robes together and intended to carry them away.
The two elders said, “We have not yet divided this collection of robes; how can you depart so abruptly?”
Bhadanta said, "If I am to share it with you, there is one fine robe among these that should be given to one who knows the Dharma; only then shall we divide the rest."
He replied, "I shall give it.
He then took a garment of the highest quality, set it aside, and divided the remaining garments into two portions to give to the two elders.
Bhadrananda immediately wrapped up many articles of clothing and carried them on his back to the Jetavana.
As the bhikṣus were walking up and down by the gate of the Jetavana, they saw Bhadrananda coming from afar and said to one another:
"This man is shameless and lacks remorse; he has committed offenses for which he has been seen, heard of, or suspected. He is a person of excessive desire who knows no satiety."
Having gradually approached him, he asked,
"Bhadanta Nanda! From where have you obtained these many articles of clothing?"
Bhadananda related the preceding events in detail to the bhikṣus.
Among them was a bhikṣu who was of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities; upon hearing this matter, he felt resentment and reproached Bhadananda in various ways:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu intentionally seize the property of two elders?"
Having rebuked him, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
On account of this cause and condition, the Buddha brought the Saṃgha together; knowing the reason, he asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked Baddhala in various ways:
"How can you deceive and intentionally seize the property of this elder bhikṣu?
Having rebuked him with various causes and conditions, he continued:
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Baṇanda has not only seized the property of these two elder bhikṣus in this present life. This Baṇanda!"
"In a previous life, these two elder bhikṣus deceived me and seized my property.
Listen now to what occurred in the interim.
In the past, there were two otters living in a bend of a river; they caught a carp by the riverbank, and as neither could divide it, they both kept hold of it."
A jackal came to drink water; having seen him, [the elephant] asked:
"Uncle! What are you doing?"
The otters said, "Nephew!
We have caught this great fish but cannot divide it among ourselves; can you divide it for us?"
He replied, "I can.
In this case, one must divide according to the phrasing of the scriptures; it may not be divided arbitrarily."
Then the jackal divided the fish into three portions:
the head was one portion, the tail was one portion, and the fleshy middle part was one portion.
Having made these three portions, he asked:
"Who delights in walking near the shore?
He replied, "It is this one."
"Who would like to enter deep water and walk?
He replied, "It is I."
Then the jackal said:
"Listen with a single mind to what the scriptures say:
'To one who walks near the bank, give the tail; to one who enters deep water, give the head; to the knower of the Dharma, give the middle part of the body.'"
At that time, the jackal took the body of the great fish in its mouth and departed.
When his wife saw him returning carrying the great fish, she spoke a verse, asking:
"Excellent, O wise one!"
"From where could one obtain such a carp that fills the mouth yet has neither head nor tail?
He replied, "There are those who are foolish, ignorant of how to settle affairs, and fond of quarreling; because of them, the wise are able to become kings and increase their treasuries."
"This headless and tailless fish was obtained by me through the severing of a matter.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you think these two otters were anyone else?"
These two elder bhikṣus are precisely those very ones.
As for the jackal at that time, could he have been anyone else?
He is none other than the present-day Upananda.
At that time, because Upananda had seized the property of a otter, he now seizes it once again in this life.
After the Buddha had rebuked Upananda with various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one must not observe the rains retreat in one place and take property from another; if one does so, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
Ānanda had a co-practitioner disciple named Ajita, who was gentle, kind, and virtuous, and who frequently entered and left the house of a certain lay devotee.
That lay devotee had two sons; when the lay devotee fell gravely ill, the bhikṣu Ajita went to inquire after him.
The householder provided a seat for him, and they exchanged greetings.
After remaining silent for a short while, the householder said to the monk Ujjaya:
"After my death, look after my two sons; whichever one is more worthy, to him you shall give the keys to the house."
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
That bhikṣu of upright faith then looked upon his virtuous son and gave him the house key.
When the second son asked for his share of the property, the one who possessed the key would not give it to him.
At that time, the young boy went to Ānanda and said, "Venerable Ānanda, please reinstate the bhikṣu Ṛjukaśraddha. Ānanda then reinstated the bhikṣu Ṛjukaśraddha.
This bhikṣu Ṛjukaśraddha was a son of the Śākyas, and he spoke to the five hundred Śākya youths, saying, "Please petition our Upādhyāya on my behalf to grant me absolution for my repentance."
He replied, "How can you cause me to attain repentance? Zhixìn said:

"All of you, take my sons and daughters, even the small children, to the presence of the Upādhyāya; bow your heads at his feet and sit before him. The Upādhyāya will surely preach the Dharma for you."
Once the Upādhyāya has finished preaching the Dharma in silence, you should all take the young children with you and depart.
The Upādhyāya will surely say:
"You must take these young children away."
"When you speak these words, you should say:
'If you will allow this upright and faithful bhikṣu to repent, we shall take him with us.
The Śākyas replied:

"So be it. At that time, five hundred Śākyan youths, following the instructions of the bhikṣu Ajñātakauṇḍinya, took their young sons and daughters to Ānanda’s dwelling. They prostrated themselves at his feet and sat before him. After Ānanda had preached the Dharma for them, he remained silent.
The Śākyas left the young children behind and departed.
At that time, the children cried out, and Ānanda said to them,
"Take these children with you."
He said, "If you permit a bhikṣu of upright faith to perform repentance, I shall take him with me.
Having reflected, Ānanda spoke to the Śākyas:
"I shall hear your confession," Ānanda said, and later he told his disciple:
"You have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There were two bhikṣus who were friends:
one named Caṇḍāla and the other named Sūdaya.
The bhikṣu Caṇḍāla had a saṃghāṭī that he wished to trade, and the bhikṣu Sūdaya required a saṃghāṭī.

The candāla placed the saṃghāṭī inside the room; Sūdayin thought the candāla intended to trade for this robe and said, "I need it now, so let me try it on to see if it fits my body; if it suits me, I shall take it."
When the caṇḍāla entered and saw that he was wearing his own clothes,
he said to him, "You have committed a pārājika offense. Sūdayin replied:
"Why is that? He replied,
"Because you took my robe with a mind of theft."
Sudāyin said: "Not so.
You wish to trade for the saṃghāṭī; I have need of it."
"After you have gone out, I shall take it up and try it to see.
At that time, Sūdayin felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a *pārājika* offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha.
Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?"
He replied,
"I took it with consent.
The Buddha said:
"If one takes with consent, there is no offense.
From this day forward, one should not take property without consent;
if one takes it, there is an offense."
There are five kinds of taking by consent:
first, a trustworthy spiritual friend;
second, a person who is present.
Third, the object is present;
fourth, one informs others at the time of taking;
fifth, the other will certainly be pleased by the taking—these are called the five kinds.
There were two bhikṣus who were friends:
one was named Susīma and the other was named Vāsula.
Susīma was skilled at cutting and sewing robes, while Vāsula required a robe to be cut and sewn. Carrying the materials for the robe, he went to Susīma’s place and asked:
"Whoever can cut this robe, to that person I shall give my alms-bowl.
Suśīma said, "I can cut this robe for you; will you give me the bowl?"
He replied, "I can. Susīma said:
"If you can give me your bowl, leave your robe and wealth with me and go.
He then left his robe and departed.
Later, Susīma cut and sewed it, making two-way openings for leaf-folds and scrolls, and having finished, he returned it to the owner, saying:
"I have finished making a robe for myself using your clothing and wealth; now give me your earthen bowl.
Upasena said, "Are you a hired laborer, a pauper, one who cannot support himself?"
He replied, "Do you not know? It is I."
Immediately, Upasena washed his bowl clean, set it aside, and departed without giving it back.
At that time, Susīma took it away, thinking it was his own property.
When Upāli did not see the bowl, he said to Susīma:
"Good friend! You have committed a pārājika offense."
"Why is this? You took my bowl with a thieving mind.
Susīma was filled with doubt and remorse.
"I fear I shall incur a *pārājika* offense.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you take it? He replied,
"I took it with the thought that it was my own property."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should not work for others for the sake of obtaining goods; if one works for others for the sake of obtaining goods, one incurs a duṣkṛta."
There is no offense if the other person says:
"If you have business, I shall do it for you; if I am guarding the monastery quarters, you shall receive the food portion for me."
"In this way, there is no offense.
There were two visiting bhikṣus:
one named Ajita and the other named Śamathadatta.
When these two guest bhikṣus arrived toward evening, the bhikṣu Śamathadatta was wearing newly dyed, fine robes; upon seeing these robes, Ajita immediately conceived a mind of covetousness.

These two people stayed together in the same room; each rolled up their own documents and wrapped them in these robes, placing them in one spot. Due to a minor circumstance, these robes were moved from their original location.

The bhikṣu Ajita, while the night was not yet over, mistook his own robe for that of Śamathadatta; with a thieving mind, he took it away, but upon examining it on the ground, he realized it was indeed his own. A doubt arose in his mind:
"Could it be that by stealing my own robe, I shall incur a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha. Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it?
He replied:
"I took it with the intention of stealing.
The Buddha said,
"Since you did it previously, there is no offense."
"From this day forward, you must not take your own clothes with a thieving mind; if you take them with a thieving mind, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
A pig-herder lost his pigs, and some thieves, while in the moat surrounding Jetavana, killed the pigs, took the choice meat, and departed, leaving the entrails behind in the moat.
The bhikṣus rose early to beg for alms and saw this intestine;
they said to their disciple, "Take this intestine and boil it; we shall go begging for rice.
The pork-butcher did not see them, so he went searching for them and, seeing smoke from afar, approached to look and found the pork intestines being boiled.
He asked,
"Monks, what are you cooking here?
They replied:
"I am cooking pig intestines," they said.
The pork-butcher replied, "I have lost my pigs;
since you are cooking pig intestines, you must have stolen my pigs."
The bhikṣus replied, "We did not steal your pigs;
we merely found these entrails in the ditch.
The pig-herder said:
"The bhikṣus must speak the truth to me; if the bhikṣus are unwilling to speak the truth to me, I shall report this to the authorities.
Having said this, the official questioned the bhikṣu, saying:
"Did you truly steal the pig?"
The bhikṣu said: "No!
I obtained it myself from within the moat of Jetavana."
The official said,
"These bhikṣus will never be able to kill pigs.
He then released the bhikṣus and let them depart.
"At other times, if you see pig intestines on an open space, do not take them again.
Thus, that bhikṣu was cleared of the dispute; when the other bhikṣus heard of this matter, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, such impure discarded items must not be taken; if one takes them, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This also applies to a person guarding a sugarcane grove who loses sugarcane, or a person guarding a *tāla* grove who loses *tāla* fruit.
There were certain people whose relatives had died; they wrapped them in white cotton cloth and discarded them at the place for the dead.
At that time, Ānanda was wandering through that area, and upon seeing [the body], he took it away.
The dead man immediately moved and said to Ānanda,
"Do not take away my robe.
Ānanda then covered the dead man again with the cotton cloth and departed.
Ānanda went to the Jeta Grove and said to the bhikṣus, "A corpse at such-and-such a place is covered with cotton cloth.
There was a bhikṣu named Kālānanda, who was fierce, robust, and strong; he asked Ānanda:
"Where is it? He replied, "It is there."
He immediately went to take it.
At that moment, the dead man stirred and said to Kṛṣṇa Ānanda,
"Do not snatch my robe!"
Kālānanda reviled him, saying:
"Little ghost!
Wretched ghost!"
"Where did you have such a robe? It is because of your greedy attachment to this robe that you have been born among the hungry ghosts.
Kṛṣṇa Ānanda held the robe and walked ahead, while the corpse followed behind, wailing and weeping.

Kālānanda took this cotton cloth and entered the Jeta Grove. Within the Jeta Grove there were devas and spirits of great majesty and power who would not allow such a minor spirit to enter; consequently, the corpse fell into the moat surrounding the Jeta Grove.
At that time, Kālānanda showed a cotton cloth to the bhikṣus and said, "This is the clothing of a dead person;
I have brought it here. The bhikṣus asked:
"Where is the dead man now?
He replied,
"He is in the moat of Jetavana."
The bhikṣus became doubtful as to what this matter meant,
and they immediately informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Kṛṣṇa Ānanda:
"Return the corpse to its original place and cover it again with the white cotton cloth.
When you travel, you should stay behind and not in front;
walk on the left side and not on the right."
"Stay near the head, not near the feet;
do not let it strike you.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, one must not take clothing from a corpse that has not yet decomposed;
if one takes it, it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
There was a certain monk of great merit who delighted in obtaining butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
A certain merchant saw this bhikṣu and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
If you require ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar, please come to my house and I shall give them to you."
The bhikṣu replied, “So be it.
A co-practicing disciple of that bhikṣu heard this and thought to himself:
"This merchant constantly invites my Upādhyāya and freely provides him with ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
I shall now go there to test whether he truly can provide these things or not."

Having reflected thus, after several days had passed, he went to request five *śīrṣa* of ghee; the merchant gave it to him immediately, and the disciple took it and placed it in his food to give to his preceptor.
After a short time had passed, a merchant saw the bhikṣu and said to him:
"Venerable sir,
why do you not ask for rice, meat, soup, and so forth, but instead ask only for five measures of ghee?"
The bhikṣu asked,
"What do you mean by that? He replied:
“The Great Virtuous One’s disciple has come; he requests five *śīrṣa* of ghee and nothing else.
The bhikṣu said, “Very well.”
"If you seek further, I shall give it to you.
That bhikṣu went to his disciple's place and said,
"You have committed a pārājika offense."
The disciple said,
"For what reason?
[The teacher replied,] "Because you took five measures of ghee from the merchants without their giving it to you."
The disciple said:
"It was not that I took what was not given; this merchant always says to me:
'Please, Upādhyāya, take some ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.'"
"I shall go and try to ask for it, to see whether he can truly give it or not.
If I obtain some ghee, I will return it and put it into my preceptor's food; I will not use it myself.
This disciple then gave rise to doubt:
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You do not incur a *pārājika* offense."
Therefore, because of speaking falsely, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for oil, honey, and rock sugar.
At a certain residence, a tiger in the forest killed a deer and ate its flesh; the remaining bones and meat were left behind.
After their meal, the bhikṣus were walking for exercise in the grove when they saw this leftover deer. Having seen it, they said to one another:
"Let us take this leftover deer and place it in our quarters; we shall eat it tomorrow."
After the bhikṣus had taken [the meat] back and placed it in their quarters, the tiger, hungry, returned to its original location; finding no deer, it roared around the Jetavana monastery.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked Ānanda,
"For what reason does the tiger roar?
Ānanda replied:
"The bhikṣus placed the leftover bones and flesh of a tiger in their rooms; that is why it roars.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, one should not take the leftover bones and flesh of a tiger."
If it is taken, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Why?
Because the tiger has not yet severed its desire for the meat.
If it is the leftover meat of a lion that may be taken, why is this?
Because all hope has been severed.

The second *pārājika* is concluded. 3. The Three Precepts (The Precept Against Killing). Tenth Recitation: The Precept Against Killing. The Buddha was staying at the village of Vajjī on the banks of the river Vaggumudā. Together with the bhikṣus of Vaggumudā, the Buddha established the precept against killing and said:
"What was done previously is without fault."
These bhikṣus gave rise to doubt and regret, thinking:
"I have frequently praised death to these bhikṣus, inciting them to form the resolve for death and kill themselves; I do not know which of these acts shall come first."
The Buddha said, “Before the precepts were established, the bhikṣus of Pāpamada did not commit any offense at any time; therefore, it is said that what was done previously is without fault.
There was a certain bhikṣu who killed a human being while perceiving him as a non-human; this bhikṣu became doubtful.
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one kills a human being while perceiving them as a human being, one incurs a *pārājika* offense."
If one kills a human being while perceiving them as a non-human, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one kills a human being while harboring doubt as to their identity, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one kills a non-human being while perceiving them as a non-human, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
"If one kills one who is not a human being while perceiving them as a human being, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one kills one who is not a human being while harboring doubt about their status, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time; a bhikṣu who was an acquaintance came to visit him, and the sick man said:
"Look for a knife and give it to me.
The bhikṣu asked, "What shall you do with it?"
The sick person said,
"Just bring it to me," and immediately took the knife and gave it to him.
The sick man obtained a knife, took it into his room, sat upon his bed, and used it to cut his own throat.
A bhikṣu who was acquainted with him, after five or six days had passed, began to suspect:
"This sick man took a knife into his room and has not come out for five or six days; he has not returned my knife—what could he possibly be doing?"
He immediately entered the room to look and saw that the sick bhikṣu was dead and the knife lay on the ground.
This bhikṣu thought to himself:
"That the patient has died is due to my causal conditions."
"If I do not give him the knife when he asks for it, then I shall not die.
This bhikṣu gave rise to doubt:
"Will I not incur a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you must not allow a sick person to obtain a knife; if you allow them to obtain a knife, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left the house of a certain lay follower. One morning, the bhikṣu rose early, put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the lay follower’s house; however, the lay follower had gone out and was not there.
His wife prepared a seat for him; once he was seated, they exchanged greetings, and after a brief silence, she said to the bhikṣu, "Come, let us engage in sexual intercourse."
The bhikṣu said, "Do not speak such words; your husband is extremely wicked.
The wife said:
"I can make him well.
After the bhikṣu had departed, she immediately gave the poison to her husband; as soon as the householder ate it, he died.

Later, at another time, the bhikṣu put on his robes, took his bowl, and went again to the householder's home. The woman provided a seat for him, and after he was seated, they exchanged greetings. After a short silence, she said to the bhikṣu:
"Come, let us engage in sexual intercourse.
The bhikṣu said, "Sister, do not speak such words; I am one who has severed all sexual desire."

She said: "Why did you not tell me beforehand that you were one who has severed lustful desire? For your sake, I killed my husband; only now do you say that you are one who has severed lustful desire?"
The bhikṣu said,
"I did not instruct you to kill your husband. He replied:
“You previously said:
‘My husband is very wicked.
The bhikṣu replied:
"I only said: 'Your husband is of a wicked nature.
I did not instruct you to kill him."
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
There was a certain bhikṣu who frequently entered and left the house of a lay devotee. This bhikṣu, before midday, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the house of that lay devotee.
The householder was ill, and his wife said to the bhikṣu,
"Come and engage in sexual intercourse together.
The bhikṣu said:
“Your husband is ill; why do you speak such words?
She replied, “I am able to make him free from illness.”
After the bhikṣu had departed, the wife immediately killed her husband with poison.
At a later time, the bhikṣu again put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to her house.
The wife said, "Come for sexual intercourse."
The bhikṣu said, "I am one who has severed lustful desire;
do not speak such words. His wife said:
"I killed your husband for your sake; why do you now say that I am one who has severed lust?
The bhikṣu said, "I did not instruct you to kill your husband."
I said, "Your husband is ill; why do you speak these words?
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, if a bhikṣu strikes another person with the intent to kill and that person dies, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If the person does not die, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu strikes another with the intent to kill, and while that person has not yet died, the bhikṣu becomes insane or renounces the precepts, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu, out of anger, causes a mother to miscarry: if the mother dies, he incurs a pārājika offense;
if the child dies, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if both die, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If neither dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If, out of anger toward the child, one causes the mother’s womb to miscarry and the child dies, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the mother dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If both die together, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If neither dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣu causes an embryo to fall or move it, and that person dies after being born, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the fetus is a ghost and it dies after being delivered, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If the fetus is an animal and it dies after being delivered, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
There was a certain bhikṣu who was ill and said to his attendant:
"I wish to have some *suvīra* juice."
The attendant gave it to him, and he died immediately after drinking it.
That bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
There was a brahmin suffering from scabies who went to where the bhikṣus were and said:
"If I obtain *suvīra* gruel, I shall recover.
The bhikṣu said, "You are a poor beggar whose belly is always empty; for what reason have you developed this ulcer?"
He replied, "I once had such a sore; by drinking this gruel, I recovered.
The bhikṣu gave him the gruel, and having drunk it, he died immediately.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Without fault.
There was a man impaled upon a wooden stake, suffering extreme agony. A forest-dwelling bhikṣu came to the place of the dead; observing impermanence, he saw this man, who said to the bhikṣu:
“If I obtain *suvīra* juice, I shall live.”
The bhikṣu gave it to him immediately; having drunk it, the man died.
The bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense.

There was a man whose hands and feet had been severed who lay in the moat surrounding Jetavana. Several bhikṣuṇīs came to Jetavana to hear the Dharma; hearing the sound of this man’s weeping, the women, being fickle by nature, went to see him and spoke to one another:
"If there were someone who could give this person medicine so that they die at once, then they would not have to suffer for long.
Among them was a simple-minded bhikṣuṇī who gave him *sūvīra* juice; the man died immediately.
The other bhikṣuṇīs said to her,
"You have committed a pārājika offense.
That bhikṣuṇī replied:
"Why is that? He replied,
"If you had not given this person the drink, he would not have died."
That bhikṣuṇī became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
She reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked her:
"With what intention did you give it?
The bhikṣuṇī replied,
"I gave it because I wished for her to die soon and not have to suffer for long."
The Buddha said, "When that person dies, you shall incur a *pārājika* offense.
In a monastery cell in the kingdom of Āravī, a new dwelling was being constructed; while a bhikṣu was working upon it, a chisel fell from his hand onto the head of a carpenter, who died instantly.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
