He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, when working, you should observe the area below with single-minded attention.
Furthermore, in a monastery cell at Ālavī, a new dwelling was being constructed; while a bhikṣu was working upon it, an axe fell and killed a carpenter.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, when performing this task, you should observe it with single-minded attention.
Furthermore, in a monastic dwelling in the kingdom of Ālavi, a bathhouse was being constructed, and timber was being hoisted up.
A bhikṣu was small in stature but heavy in build; unable to support himself, he fell and killed a carpenter.
The bhikṣus became doubtful, thinking, "Have we not committed a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha. Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you do this?
The bhikṣu replied:
"The people are few, yet the materials are heavy; because their strength cannot sustain them, they lose the materials.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense."
"From this day forward, you should single-mindedly observe the following.

Furthermore, in the kingdom of Āravī, while a bathhouse was being constructed, a beam was being hoisted onto the rafters. Because there were few monks and the beam was heavy, they could not hold it steady; consequently, the beam fell and killed a carpenter.
The bhikṣus became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who, knowing the reason, asked them:
"With what state of mind [did you do this]?
The bhikṣu replied, "There were few bhikṣus and the timber was heavy; because I could not hold it, I lost it."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, when performing [this act], you must contemplate with single-minded focus so as not to cause anyone to be killed."
"If a person is weak, they should not pull heavy timber.
Because the bathhouse was being covered at the city of Āloka, mud was carried up in a sack; when the rope snapped, it killed the carpenter.
The bhikṣus became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, you must apply yourself with proper mindfulness and ensure that you do not kill anyone.
There was a bhikṣu who sat in meditation on a mountain.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who, while on top [of the mountain], pushed a stone that fell onto the head of a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna, and he died immediately.
The bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, when you wish to push a stone, you should announce: "
"Stone! Stone!
A certain bhikṣu was walking through a herd of cattle when a wicked cow chased after him, intending to gore him. The bhikṣu fled and fell upon a small child, who died instantly.
A bhikṣu gave rise to doubt,
thinking, "Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should walk among the cattle with composure.
A certain bhikṣu, having been ill for a long time, was emaciated and hunched-backed; he thought to himself:
"What use is this life to me? I shall now throw myself into a deep pit and die.
He immediately threw himself into the pit.
In the pit there was previously a jackal devouring a corpse; when the bhikṣu fell upon it, the jackal died, and the bhikṣu’s spine became straightened.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I have incurred a pāyattika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, do not commit suicide on account of a minor cause.
A certain bhikṣu sat upon a warm seat and covered himself with his robe; another bhikṣu called out to him, saying:
"Arise! Arise! said that bhikṣu:
"Do not call me up; if I rise, I shall die.
The other bhikṣus called out to him again, saying, "Rise!"
"Get up!
and he died immediately.
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt:
"I shall not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "He does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*."
“If a bhikṣu, though insane, strikes another with the intent to kill, if that person dies, he incurs a pārājika offense;
if he does not die, he incurs a sthūlātyaya.
There was a bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time; because the attendant bhikṣu had been nursing him, he thought to himself:
"I have observed him for a long time; it appears the patient will neither die nor recover.
Since I can no longer attend to him, I shall leave him to his fate.
Because the attendant ceased to provide care, the patient died.
The monk who was tending to the sick became doubtful, thinking:
"Will I not incur a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill and possessed many robes, bowls, and wealth. His attendant, having nursed him for a long time, thought to himself:
"I can no longer continue nursing him. If I leave him to die, his property will be distributed among the Saṃgha."
Because he did not look again, the patient died.
The bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It does not constitute a *pārājika* offense; it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who, because his food did not digest, sat in one place wrapped in thick garments and blankets.
Another bhikṣu came and called out,
"Arise! He replied:
"Do not call me up; if I rise, I shall die.
Another bhikṣu called out to him again, saying, "Rise!"
"Get up!
and he died immediately.
This bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt:
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "He does not incur a pārājika offense; he incurs a sthūlātyaya."
There was a bhikṣu whose abscess had not yet ripened; another bhikṣu came and lanced it, whereupon that bhikṣu died immediately.
This bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a person dies from lancing an abscess before it has ripened, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a person dies after lancing a ripened abscess, there is no offense."
There was a certain bhikṣu who was ill. A caregiver, having long been seeking suitable food and drink for him according to his illness, was unable to obtain it. He said to the patient:
"I have long sought suitable food and drink for you according to your illness but have been unable to find any; now, whenever I happen to get some food, I simply eat it."
That sick man approached for food, and because of eating it, he died.
That bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Will I not have committed a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *pārājika* offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill, and the attendant seeking medicine for him on his behalf could not obtain it.
The attendant went to the patient and said:
"For your sake, I have sought medicine suitable for your illness but could not obtain it; you should now take whatever medicine you can find."
The patient took it as soon as he obtained it and died immediately.
This bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"If one intentionally gives medicine that causes death, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
"If one dies from medicine administered according to the illness, there is no offense.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill and said to his attendant:

"Support me as I rise; support me as I sit; give me my robes to wear; support me as I go out of the room and sit; provide me with a bath; give me my robes to wear; take me to the shade during the day; take me to the sun; take me back to my room; have me sit; have me lie down."
The bhikṣu then died. The bhikṣu who had been attending to him became suspicious:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense.
A bhikṣu who was practicing dhyāna fell asleep; a bhikṣu who was practicing walking meditation touched him with his staff to wake him, and he died immediately.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This bhikṣu had an onset of the 'sword-wind' (śastravāta); whether he was touched or not, he would have died inevitably. Therefore, there is no offense.
A bhikṣu who was sitting in meditation fell asleep; a bhikṣu who was practicing walking meditation threw a cotton ball at him to wake him, and he died immediately.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In this case, because the bhikṣu was afflicted by the 'sword-wind' (śastra-vāyu) and would certainly have died whether [the water] was thrown at him or not, there is no offense.
A bhikṣu practicing meditation fell asleep; another bhikṣu poured water on his head to wake him, and he died immediately.
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This bhikṣu died because the 'wind-sword' (kṣurapra-vāyu) had arisen within him; whether he was given an emetic or not, he would have inevitably died, so there is no offense.

Among the group of seventeen monks, there was a young boy who enjoyed laughing. The bhikṣus seized him and tickled him until he laughed so hard that he died. [The Buddha declared: "There is no offense."
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing [the answer], asked:
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"Because he tickled him in jest, and [the other] laughed so hard that he died.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, you must not tickle others; if you do tickle them, you shall incur a pāyattika offense.
A certain householder obtained fresh grain and fresh vegetables; he first gave them to the community of monks and subsequently ate them himself.
There was an araṇya bhikṣu who frequently entered and left this householder’s residence.
One morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, he entered the householder’s residence, went to his seat, sat down, and exchanged greetings with him.
When this layperson sees an araṇya-dweller, he thinks:
"This fresh grain and fresh vegetables should be given to this araṇya-dweller, and not to the community of monks."
He then took them and gave them to the forest-dwelling bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus thought:
"This layperson always obtains fresh grain and fresh vegetables; he first gives them to the Saṃgha and only then eats them himself."
"Why has this year's [share] not been given to the community of monks?
The bhikṣus asked one another,
"Who is that bhikṣu who enters and leaves that house?"
A certain bhikṣu said:
"There is an araṇyaka bhikṣu who constantly enters and leaves this house; it must have been he who barred the way.
The other bhikṣus said:
"Call that aranyaka bhikṣu here.
When the bhikṣu had arrived, the bhikṣus said to him:
"A certain lay devotee, year after year, always provides fresh grain and fresh vegetables; he first gives them to the Saṃgha and only then eats himself."
"If this year's [crop] is not granted, it must surely be because you are obstructing it.
He replied, "Why would I obstruct it?"
The bhikṣus said, "This bhikṣu refuses to confess directly; we shall press him with two wooden boards to extract his confession.
While being pressed, he died.
The bhikṣus became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a lay devotee who regularly provided the rainy-season retreat robes for the community of monks.
A certain forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu frequently entered and left his house.
Before midday, this bhikṣu put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the house of a lay devotee; having reached his seat, he sat down and exchanged greetings with him.
Upon seeing him, the lay devotee thought:
"I shall give these robes to this forest-dweller (āraṇyaka), not to the Saṃgha."
Having thought this, he immediately took his robe and gave it to that bhikṣu.
The other bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"This certain lay devotee always provides robes for the community during the rainy season retreat; why does he not provide them this year?"
They asked one another,
"Who is that bhikṣu who constantly enters and leaves that house?
Then a certain bhikṣu said:
“There is an aranyaka bhikṣu who constantly enters and leaves this house;
it must have been obstructed by that aranyaka. The bhikṣus said, “Call that bhikṣu here.”
When he had arrived, the bhikṣus asked him, "The lay devotee so-and-so used to provide robes annually for the community of monks during the rainy season retreat.
He has not provided them this year; it must be that you have obstructed him."
He replied, "Why should I have prevented you?
The bhikṣus said:
"This bhikṣu will certainly not confess; we must throw him into the pond.
As soon as he was thrown in, he died.
The bhikṣus became doubtful:
"I shall not incur a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You do not incur a pārājika offense; you incur a sthūlātyaya."

There was a certain bhikṣu who, before midday, dressed in his robes and took up his bowl to enter Śrāvastī for alms. While walking about, he arrived at a gate crowded with many people; casting down his robe, its corner struck a wooden pestle, which fell over and crushed a small child to death.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, when begging for alms, you should maintain single-minded mindfulness of what lies before and behind you.

A certain bhikṣu who was begging for alms put on his robes and took up his bowl before midday, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, and while wandering through various places, arrived at the house of a brāhmaṇa.
The master of the house, having washed his head and body early in the morning and put on new white robes, was seated at the middle gate.
An elder bhikṣu stood beneath the gate and snapped his fingers; hearing the sound of the snap, the brāhmaṇa immediately came out to look.
Upon seeing the bhikṣu, he immediately conceived an evil thought and thought to himself:

"I have not yet performed sacrifices for the gods, nor have I made offerings for my deceased parents and kinsmen; yet this shaven-headed renunciant, wearing dyed and tattered robes—a man who cuts off the lineage—has come before me to beg for food."
With a mind of anger, he pushed against his chest to make himself go, and in doing so, he fell upon a small child, who died immediately.
The bhikṣu became suspicious, thinking:
"Have I not incurred a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, when begging for alms, you must observe what is before and behind with single-minded attention."
There was a bhikṣu who possessed a sorcery for slapping that caused a person’s cheek to be struck and die instantly.
This bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, when you wish to strike [the drum], you must do so gently; do not cause it to die."
There was a bhikṣu who choked while eating; another bhikṣu struck him on the neck with a mallet, causing the food he had choked on, along with blood, to come out, and he died immediately.
This bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
From this day forward, you should strike the gong slowly and gently, merely to cause the food to come out, and not to cause death."
Kālodāyin frequently entered and left a certain household; before midday, he dressed, took his bowl, and went to that house.
In that house was a woman nursing her child; having risen early, she had placed the child on the bed and covered it with a white woolen blanket before departing.
Kāḷodāyin stood at the door and snapped his fingers; the woman came out to look and, seeing Kāḷodāyin, said, "Venerable sir, sit upon this bed.
Without looking, Kāḷodāyin sat down upon the child, who cried out loudly. The woman said:
"There is a child here! There is a child!
Kāḷudāyin was heavy-bodied; as he sat down, the child immediately died and its intestines protruded.
After Kālodāyin had done this, he returned to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"Today I did such a thing.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you do this? [He replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"I sat upon this bed without first inspecting it.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"From this day forward, one must carefully inspect one's bed, couch, or seat before sitting upon it.
If one sits without inspection, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This also applies to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.
Furthermore, there were two bhikṣus, father and son, who were traveling together through the country of Kośala, intending to go to Śrāvastī.
When evening fell, they had not yet crossed a perilous road among them. The son said to his father, "There is a perilous road here;
we must travel quickly across it."
He immediately followed the boy's words and ran swiftly, whereupon he died of exhaustion.
The bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Have I not incurred a pārājika offense as well as the crime of parricide?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
Knowing the situation, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you speak?"
The young bhikṣu said:
"As evening was falling, I feared we would not pass through the perilous path; therefore, out of affectionate concern, I spoke these words to urge him to hurry.
While hurrying, he grew exhausted and died."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.

From this day forth, do not travel on dangerous paths at twilight for the sake of minor causes. If you have already entered a dangerous path, a junior bhikṣu should carry the belongings that an elder bhikṣu is carrying, and he should say to him:"
"If I go on ahead, you should follow after me.
At that time, the bhikṣus became doubtful:
"How is it that a bhikṣu who kills his father does not incur a pārājika offense or the crime of heinousness?"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus, recounted for them a story of his past life, saying to the bhikṣus:

"In a past age, there was a bald man wearing dyed robes who, together with his son, took some cloth to the edge of a body of water. After washing the clothes, he wrung them out, spread them out to dry, folded them, placed them in a bag, and carried them back along the same path."
At that time, it was extremely hot and his vision was blurred; seeing a tree by the roadside, he used his robe-bag as a pillow and fell asleep.
A mosquito came to suck the blood from his head, and when the son saw this, he became angry and thought:
"My father is lying here, utterly exhausted; why has this wretched, evil slave-girl's son, a mosquito, come to drink my father's blood?"
He immediately took up a large club, intending to strike the mosquito; the mosquito flew away, but the club struck his father’s head, and he died instantly.
Then this tree spirit spoke a verse:
“Better to be an enemy of the wise than to be a friend of the ignorant.”
"The fool, in order to harm the mosquito for his father's sake, killed his father when he struck it away.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do you think that the shaven-headed man wearing dyed robes at that time was someone else?"
Do not hold such a view; it was this very same elder bhikṣu.
He who was the son at that time is this bhikṣu today.

Although that son killed his father at that time, he did not incur the crime of parricide; likewise, although he kills his father now, he does not incur the pārājika offense nor the crime of parricide.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 58 and Scroll 59; Part 4 of the *Daśabhāṇavāra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Puṇyatara of North India during the Later Qin dynasty.

In the remainder of the recitation of the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa* concerning the precept against killing, there was a father and son who were both bhikṣus. While traveling through the kingdom of Kośala, they intended to reach Śrāvastī.
Upon arriving at a village that had no monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), the son said to his father:
“Where will you stay tonight?
His father replied,
“I shall stay in this village.”
The boy said, "This is a dwelling place for laypeople within this village; if I were to stay there overnight, how would it differ from this?
His father said:
"Where shall we stay for the night?
The son replied,
"We shall stay for the night on this empty ground."
The father said, "There is the fear of tigers here; when I sleep, you must not sleep.
He replied:
"Yes," [the son] replied.
His father immediately lay down to sleep; as he snored, the tiger heard him and came to bite his head. The father cried out loudly.
The son saw that his father’s head was split open, and because of this, the father died.
The young bhikṣu felt doubt, thinking:
"My father died because of me. My father wished to stay overnight in the village; had I followed my father's instruction, my father would not have died."
"I intended to lie on empty ground and thereby caused my father's death; will I not incur both a *pārājika* offense and the crime of patricide?
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense."
"One should shout loudly and kindle a fire to frighten the tiger away.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, sends a messenger to kill a certain person, and that person dies, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If it does not die, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a bhikṣu who killed a macaque; the other bhikṣus said to him, "You have committed a *pārājika* offense."
That bhikṣu asked:
"For what reason?
The bhikṣus replied:
"A monkey resembles a human; if one kills it, how is this different from killing a person?
This bhikṣu gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"He does not commit a pārājika offense; he commits a pāyattika offense."

While traveling through the kingdom of Kośala toward Śrāvastī, some bhikṣus saw an empty monastery and entered it to look around. They saw bedding, couches, cauldrons, basins, measures, jars, and pots—all the requisites for the community’s livelihood, lacking nothing.
They said to one another, "Why should we not observe the rains retreat here?"
The other bhikṣus said,
"As you wish. Thereupon,
a regulation was established for those who had completed the rains retreat therein:
"We shall not perform the *pravāraṇā* for three months; we shall perform the *pravāraṇā* when the eighth month arrives.
We shall then receive the offerings given at the end of the summer retreat.
When the eighth month of the summer's end arrived and bandits rose up, the bandits thought to themselves:
"Where can one obtain wealth and goods without the need for weapons or battle?
Having had this thought, they said to one another,
"We shall seize the property of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas."
The bandits immediately arrived and surrounded the monastery.

Among the monks was one who had attained supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), as well as some who had originally been great wrestlers and others who had originally been sons of master archers. These monks thought to themselves:
"We have left the household life out of a sincere heart; we ought not to engage in combat with these bandits."
Having formed this thought, he remained silent.
Then bandits came and plundered his robes and garments, leaving him completely naked.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas to assemble their disciples for two great assemblies at fixed times:
The first is the final month of spring, and the second is the final month of summer.

Regarding the final month of spring: monks from various regions and lands come to where the Buddha resides; the Buddha teaches the Dharma to us, and we shall reflect upon and practice it during the three-month *varṣā* retreat. This is the first great assembly.

For the sake of hearing the Dharma, at the end of the summer retreat, after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was concluded and their robes were finished, they took up their robes and bowls and went to where the Buddha was, thinking:
"We have not seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for a long time!"
This was the second great assembly, held for the purpose of seeing the Buddha.

Those bhikṣus who had been robbed, having completed their *pravāraṇā* ceremony and finished making their robes, took up their robes and bowls and set out for Śrāvastī. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated at his feet and sat to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas that when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, they greet him with gentle words of inquiry, saying:
"Are you enduring?
Are you satisfied?"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Is there no lack of alms-food, and are you not weary from the road?
At that time, the Buddha greeted the bhikṣus with these words of inquiry.
"Are you patient?
Are you satisfied?
Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
"Is there no lack of almsfood? Are you not weary from the road?
The bhikṣus replied, "World-Honored One!"
"We have lived with patience, dwelt in peace and happiness, have not lacked for almsfood, and were not weary on the road.
He related all these matters to the Buddha in detail.

On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the Sangha. Having assembled the Sangha, he praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts through various means. Having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"When bandits arrive, you should strike the bells and ring the chimes with a loud voice to terrify them.

When the bhikṣus heard this from the Buddha and perceived the fault in it, they returned to their original location for the rains retreat the following year. Having completed the retreat, they established a new regulation:
"We should not hold the *pravāraṇā* ceremony after three months; we shall instead hold it in the eighth month."
"It is for the purpose of using the offerings received during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) at the end of summer.
When the original bandits rose up in the eighth month at the end of summer, they thought:
"Where might there be money and goods to be obtained without the need for weapons or combat?"
He thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not engage in combat with others; I shall go and plunder their property.
Having thought this, he immediately went and surrounded the monastic quarters.

The bhikṣus had previously prepared defensive equipment against thieves; when the thieves arrived, they immediately entered their dwellings, closed the doors, lowered the shutters, and ascended to the upper stories, making a great clamor to terrify the thieves, striking bells and shaking gongs.
There were two bhikṣus who, in the darkness, threw stones to terrify [a thief]; a stone fell and killed the thief.
The two bhikṣus said to one another, "We both threw stones together; we do not know whose stone killed the thief."
He immediately gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a *pārājika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
When releasing the stone, one should cry out:
‘Stone, fall!’”
"Under the stone!

Thus ends the third *pārājika*. **The Fourth Precept: The Prohibition Against Grave Falsehood** The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī on the banks of the Vākuṇḍā River. The Buddha established this precept for the monks there by the Vākuṇḍā River, saying:
"What was done previously is without fault."
Those bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"For a long time we have falsely claimed superhuman states that we did not possess; we do not know which of these claims came first, nor which did not."
Doubt and regret arose in his mind.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Before the precepts were established, the bhikṣus of Pāpamada did not commit any offense at any time; therefore, what was done previously is without fault."
A bhikṣu, perceiving a human being as a non-human, claims for himself a superhuman attainment (*uttarimanussadhamma*). This bhikṣu then gives rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I have committed a *pārājika* offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one perceives a human being as a human being, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one perceives a human being as a non-human being, one incurs a *pārājika* offense."
If one gives rise to doubt regarding a human being, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If one perceives a non-human as a non-human, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one perceives a non-human as a human, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
"If one gives rise to doubt among non-humans, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There was a bhikṣu who, in the presence of a layperson (*gṛhapati*), claimed to have attained superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
This layperson did not understand; the layperson said:
"What did the Venerable One say?
The bhikṣu replied, "Let it be;
there is no need to ask."
That bhikṣu gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *pārājika* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Someone asked a bhikṣu, "Are you an arhat?"
"Should you accept this offering of the seat of honor and the water of honor?
If he accepts by remaining silent, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a person asks a bhikṣu:
“Are you a brāhmaṇa who has eliminated evil dharmas?
If he accepts by remaining silent, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
When people ask a bhikṣu:
"Do you well guard the gates of the six sense faculties?
If he accepts by remaining silent, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a person asks a bhikṣu:
"If you are an Arhat, then accept these robes.
If he accepts them in silence, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
The same applies to food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and other requisites for livelihood.

A certain bhikṣu frequently entered and left the house of a lay devotee. One day, before midday, that bhikṣu dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to the lay devotee’s residence. The lay devotee came out and stood at the gate, saying:

"If you are an arhat, enter my house, sit in the designated place, receive water with your hand, receive food and drink; having received them, offer a blessing, and once the blessing is finished, depart."
If a bhikṣu enters silently and sits down, and after the meal and the offering of blessings have been completed, he departs, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

There was a certain bhikṣu who frequently entered and left the house of a lay devotee. Before midday, this bhikṣu put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to that house. As the lay devotee came out and stood at the gate, he said:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"If you are an arhat, then enter.
The bhikṣu said, "I am not an arhat; if you permit me to enter, I shall enter."
"If a householder permits it, there is no offense.
This applies likewise to sitting in his seat, receiving water, food, and drink, and offering blessings before departing.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
“From the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, I am able to go everywhere within them, coming and going with mastery over my body.
The bhikṣus said,
“Maudgalyāyana!...”
"How can you have such a thing?
Among the śrāvaka disciples, those with supernormal powers can reach as far as the Brahma world.
Since you possess no superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) and yet speak falsely, you, Maudgalyāyana, shall be expelled and cast out."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s fault regarding this matter. Why is that?

If a person relies on the first dhyāna and, through skillful cultivation of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), attains supernormal powers (abhijñā), that person is then able to travel freely with their body from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If a bhikṣu relies on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it is likewise so.

The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana, relying on the four dhyānas and having well-cultivated the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). If he wished to go from the Avīci Hell upward to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, his body could travel back and forth within them with complete mastery; thus, there is no fault in Maudgalyāyana speaking the truth.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"From the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, I am able to hear with my divine ear every sound produced by sentient beings therein."
The bhikṣus said,
"Maudgalyāyana, how could you have such a thing?
As for the divine ear of a śrāvaka disciple, it can hear at the furthest distance up to the Brahma world."
"You, Maudgalyāyana, have falsely claimed superhuman qualities when you were empty of them; you, Maudgalyāyana, are to be expelled and cast out.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of this transgression as a fault against Maudgalyāyana."
Why is this? If one attains the divine ear by relying on the first dhyāna, that person is able to hear sounds freely throughout the entire range from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If a bhikṣu relies on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it is likewise so.

If the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana, relying on the four dhyānas, has well-cultivated the supernormal power of the divine ear, and if he wishes to hear all the sounds of sentient beings from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, he is able to hear them all; Maudgalyāyana’s truthful speech is without fault.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"From the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, I am able to know all the mental thoughts of the sentient beings therein."
The bhikṣus said:
"Maudgalyāyana!
How could you have done such a thing?"
"The śrāvaka disciples can perceive as far as the Brahma world.
Since you, Maudgalyāyana, falsely claim to possess superhuman qualities that you do not have, you are empty of such attainments; therefore, you are expelled and cast out."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgressions or faults. Why is that?

If a bhikṣu, relying on the first dhyāna, skillfully cultivates the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, he is then able to know all the mental thoughts of sentient beings from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If a bhikṣu relies on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it is also like this.

The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana, having well-cultivated the supernormal power of knowing others' minds based on the four dhyānas, can know all the mental thoughts of sentient beings from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven whenever he wishes to know them; there is no fault in Maudgalyāyana speaking the truth.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"From the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, I am able to know the past lives of all sentient beings therein."
The bhikṣus said:
"Maudgalyāyana!
How could you have done such a thing?"
"The śrāvaka disciples possess the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), capable of knowing as far back as from the Avīci Hell up to the Brahma World.

Since you, [O Maudgalyāyana], falsely claim to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) when you actually have none, you are empty of such attainments; therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you are expelled and cast out!"
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression regarding this matter. Why is that?

If a bhikṣu, relying on the first dhyāna, skillfully cultivates the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, that person will be able to know all the past lives of sentient beings from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If a bhikṣu relies on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it is likewise so.

The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana, having well-cultivated the supernormal power of recollecting past lives based on the four dhyānas, was able to know the past lives of all sentient beings from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; thus, what Maudgalyāyana said is true and without fault.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"From the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, whatever beings there are who die here and are born there, I am able to see them all with my divine eye."
The bhikṣus said: "O Maudgalyāyana!
How could such a thing be?"
"The śrāvaka disciples possess the divine eye, which can see as far as the Avīci Hell up to the Brahma-world.
Since you, Maudgalyāyana, falsely claimed to possess superhuman qualities that you do not have, you are hereby expelled and banished."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression regarding this matter. Why is that?

If a bhikṣu, relying on the first dhyāna, skillfully cultivates the supernormal power of the divine eye, that person will then be able to see, from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, all beings dying here and being reborn there within those realms.
If a person relies on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it is likewise so.

The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana, having well-cultivated the supernormal power of the divine eye based on the four dhyānas, is able to see all beings from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven as they die here and are reborn there; thus, what Maudgalyāyana said is true and without fault.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:

"If anyone says that he seeks the state of an Arhat with outflows exhausted, whose holy life is established, who has accomplished what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, exhausted all fetters of existence, and attained liberation through right knowledge—it is I myself."
"Why is that? Because I am an arhat whose taints are exhausted, and who has attained liberation through right knowledge.
The bhikṣus said:
"How can you have such a thing?
You have attained arhatship with the exhaustion of outflows, and having attained right knowledge, you have reached liberation. Why is this so?"
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana has many affairs and many desires.
Maudgalyāyana!
Since you falsely claimed superhuman attainments when you were actually empty of them, you are hereby expelled and driven out."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression in this matter. Why is that?

If there is one who seeks the true Arhatship of the exhaustion of outflows, in whom the holy life is established and what was to be done has been accomplished, who has laid down the heavy burden and attained his own benefit, who has exhausted all fetters of existence and attained liberation through right knowledge—it is Maudgalyāyana.
Why is this? Maudgalyāyana is indeed an arhat whose outflows are exhausted, and who has attained liberation through right knowledge; therefore, there is no fault in Maudgalyāyana’s truthful speech.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:

"I saw a sentient being, five hundred yojanas in size, whose body was being burned by a great mass of flames. Coming through the air, he cried out and wailed, undergoing extreme and agonizing suffering."
The bhikṣus said:
"Where is there such a sentient being, where is there such a great mass of flames?
Because you falsely claimed superhuman qualities that do not exist, you are empty of them; Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and cast out."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgressions in this matter. Why is that?

I also see these sentient beings, their bodies scorched by flames five hundred yojanas high, coming through the air crying out and weeping in extreme agony; yet they do not wish to speak of it to others.
Why is this? It is because I fear people will not believe me; if people do not believe the Tathāgata’s words, they will suffer great ruin and affliction for a long night.
Maudgalyāyana’s speech was truthful and without fault.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"I saw a sentient being whose single rib was being hewn by five hundred yakṣas with five hundred axes for five hundred days and nights."
"When this rib fell into the seawater, the sea immediately became turbulent and turbid.
The bhikṣus said,
"Maudgalyāyana!..."
"Where is there such a being, where are there such ribs?
You, Maudgalyāyana, have spoken falsely because you claim superhuman states that do not exist. You, Maudgalyāyana, are expelled and cast out!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression regarding this matter."

Why is this? I have also seen these beings, five hundred yakṣas and ghosts, wielding five hundred axes for five hundred days and nights to hack off a single rib; it falls into the seawater, which immediately becomes turbulent and turbid, yet they do not wish to speak of it to others.
Why is this? For fear that people will not believe.
If a person does not believe the words of the Tathāgata, they will undergo great ruin and affliction for a long night.
Maudgalyāyana said, "In truth, there is no offense.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:

"I saw a sentient being whose body was like a great wooden ship, its head like a wine jar, its breathing like the sound of thunder, its eyes like large bronze bowls from Kośala, and its tongue protruding from its mouth like lightning flashing amidst black clouds."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Where is this sentient being?
You, Maudgalyāyana!"
"Because you falsely claimed superhuman qualities that you do not possess, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of this fault or transgression of Maudgalyāyana."

Why is this? I also see these sentient beings whose bodies are like great wooden ships, their heads like wine jars, their panting like the sound of thunder, their eyes like large bronze basins from Kośala, and their tongues protruding from their mouths like flashes of lightning amidst black clouds.
The Tathāgata does not wish to speak of this to others.
Why? Because he fears that people will not believe it.
"If anyone does not believe the words of the Tathāgata, they will suffer great decline and affliction for a long night.
Maudgalyāyana’s speech was truthful and without fault.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:

"To the north there is a lake named Mandākinī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of two hundred yojanas. Its bottom is strewn with golden sand, and it is always filled with water of eight qualities; it is as sweet as pure honey. Various lotuses of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple cover the surface of the lake. Various birds warble in harmony with one another, making it exceedingly delightful. Around the four sides of the lake are various flowering trees and fruit trees."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"How could there be such a pond?
You, Maudgalyāyana, have spoken falsely because you lack any superhuman qualities; therefore, you shall be expelled and driven out."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression regarding this matter. Why is that?

To the north lies this Lake Mandākinī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of two hundred yojanas. Its bottom is strewn with golden sand, and it is perpetually filled with water of eight virtues, as sweet as pure honey. Various lotuses of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple cover the surface of the lake. Diverse birds warble their plaintive songs in harmony, making it exceedingly delightful. Around the four sides of the lake stand various flowering trees and fruit trees; Maudgalyāyana, what he said was indeed without fault.

On another occasion, while Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless concentration of space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*). He had correctly grasped the signs for entering concentration but had not correctly grasped the signs for emerging from it. Upon arising from that samādhi, he heard the sound of a great elephant on the bank of the Sappini Pond.
Having heard it, he immediately re-entered samādhi and thought:
"While I was in samādhi, I heard this sound of an elephant.
Rising from samādhi, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
“I once was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, having entered the formless concentration of space, when I heard the sound of an elephant on the bank of Lake Sābhini.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
“How can such a thing be possible?”
If one were to see or hear anything while entering the meditative absorption of the formless realm (*ārūpya-samādhi*), such a thing is impossible. Why is this?
Because when a person enters the formless absorption, they destroy the characteristics of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) and abandon the characteristics of sound (*śabda-nimitta*).
"Because you falsely claimed superhuman attainments when you were actually empty of them, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You must not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression regarding this matter."
Why is this? Maudgalyāyana perceives past events but does not perceive future events, whereas the Tathāgata perceives both the past and the future.

While Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless concentration of space; he skillfully grasped the signs for entering concentration, but did not skillfully grasp the signs for emerging from concentration.

When this person arose from samādhi, having heard the sound of elephants on the bank of Lake Sābhini, he quickly re-entered the formless concentration of space and then claimed, "I heard the sound while remaining in meditative absorption."
If a person enters the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) and yet sees forms or hears sounds, such a thing is impossible.
Why is this? Because that person has destroyed the characteristics of form and abandoned the characteristics of sound.
"If it were the case, Maudgalyāyana, that you spoke falsely because you lacked superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*), such a thing could not be.
Since Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his mental perception, there is no offense.

On another occasion, while Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless attainment of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samāpatti*); he had correctly grasped the signs for entering meditative absorption but had not correctly grasped the signs for emerging from it.
Emerging from samādhi, he heard the songs of the devas within the celestial city; having heard them, he quickly re-entered meditative concentration and thought:
"While in samādhi, I heard the songs of the devas."
Emerging from that samādhi, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Once, while I was on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered the meditative absorption of the sphere of consciousness, I heard the singing of the devas within the celestial city."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"How can such a principle exist?
Having entered the formless attainments, could one still see forms and hear sounds?"
Why is this? If a person enters the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they destroy the marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) and abandon the marks of sound (*śabda-nimitta*).
You, Maudgalyāyana, falsely claimed to possess superhuman qualities (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*) which you do not have; therefore, you shall be expelled and cast out."
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus,
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana's transgression in this matter. Why is that?
Maudgalyāyana saw what preceded but did not see what followed; the Tathāgata sees both what precedes and what follows.

While Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless concentration of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*); he skillfully grasped the signs for entering concentration, but was not skilled in grasping the signs for emerging from concentration.

Emerging from samādhi, he heard the songs of the devas within the celestial city; having heard them, he quickly re-entered meditative absorption and then claimed, "While in samādhi, I heard these sounds.
It is impossible for one who has entered a formless absorption to see forms or hear sounds.
Why is this? Because such a person has destroyed the perception of form and abandoned the perception of sound.
If, Maudgalyāyana, one who is empty of the superhuman states were to speak falsely, that too would be impossible.
"Maudgalyāyana may speak according to his thoughts without fault.

On another occasion, while Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless concentration of the sphere of nothingness; he skillfully grasped the signs for entering concentration, but did not skillfully grasp the signs for emerging from concentration.
Emerging from samādhi, he heard the sounds of the musical performances of the asuras within the city of the asuras; having heard them, he quickly re-entered meditative concentration and thought:
"While in samādhi, I heard the sounds of the musical performances within the city of the asuras."
Having arisen from that concentration, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Once, while I was on Vulture Peak Mountain, having entered the formless absorption of the sphere of nothingness, I heard the sounds of musical performances by asuras within the city of the asuras."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"How can such a principle exist?
How could one who has entered the formless attainments see forms or hear sounds?"
Why is this? If a person enters the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), they destroy the marks of form (*rūpanimitta*) and abandon the marks of sound (*śabdanimitta*).
You, however, falsely claim to possess superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*) which you do not have; therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and cast out.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s transgression in this matter. Why is that?
Maudgalyāyana saw what preceded but did not see what followed; the Tathāgata sees both what precedes and what follows.

While Maudgalyāyana was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he entered the formless concentration of the sphere of nothingness; he was skilled in perceiving the signs for entering concentration, but unskilled in perceiving the signs for emerging from concentration.

Upon arising from concentration, he hears the sounds of music and instruments within the city of the asuras; having heard them, he quickly re-enters concentration and then claims, "While I was in concentration, I heard these sounds.
It is impossible for one who has entered a formless absorption to see forms or hear sounds.
Why is this? Because such a person has destroyed the perception of form and abandoned the perception of sound.
If, Maudgalyāyana, one who is empty of the superhuman states should speak falsely, that too is impossible.
"Maudgalyāyana may speak according to his thoughts without fault. On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:

"In the north there is Lake Anavatapta, fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty yojanas. Its bottom is covered with golden sand, and it is constantly filled with water of eight virtues. It is as sweet as genuine honey. Blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated lotuses cover the surface of the water everywhere. Various birds warble in harmony with one another; their voices are like the sound of music and are most delightful. Surrounding the four sides of the lake are various flowering trees and fruit trees. There is the dwelling place of the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, who has eight thousand elephants as his retinue."
"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, even the smallest among the eight thousand elephants emerges as the Elephant Treasure to serve as a mount for the Sage King.
The bhikṣus asked, "Where is this pond?"
"How can there be such an elephant?
You have spoken falsely because you are empty and devoid of superhuman qualities; Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of this transgression or fault of Maudgalyāyana. Why is this?

To the north there is Lake Anavatapta, fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty yojanas. Its bottom is covered in golden sand, and it is constantly filled with water of eight virtues, as sweet as pure honey. Blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated lotuses cover the surface of the water everywhere, while various birds warble in harmony like the sound of music, most delightful to hear. Surrounding the four sides of the lake are various flowering trees and fruit trees."
In the palace residence of the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, there are eight thousand elephants as his retinue.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, even the smallest and lowest among these eight thousand elephants emerges as the "Elephant Treasure" to provide a mount for the Sage King.
Maudgalyāyana said, "In truth, there is no offense.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"Within the great outer ocean, on an island, there is Mount Candraprabha, the dwelling place of the palace of the horse-king Brahme. There, he has eight thousand horses as his retinue."
"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, even the smallest among his eight thousand horses emerges as the Horse-Jewel to serve as the Sage King’s mount.
The bhikṣus asked, "How can such a thing exist? Where is there such a horse?"
"You have spoken falsely by claiming superhuman attainments that you do not possess; therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of this fault or transgression regarding Maudgalyāyana."
Why is this? Within the great outer ocean, on an island, there is Mount Candraprabha, the dwelling place of the palace of the horse-king Brahme; there, he has eight thousand horses as his retinue.
"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, even the smallest among his eight thousand horses emerges as the Horse-Jewel to serve as the Sage King's mount.
Maudgalyāyana, what he said was true and without fault."
On another occasion, the bhikṣus asked Maudgalyāyana,
"From where does this water of the Mahī River come?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"This water comes from Lake Anavatapta.
The bhikṣus said, "The water of Lake Anavatapta is sweet and possesses the eight meritorious qualities; how can this water be boiling hot, salty, and bitter? How could such a thing be?"
“Maudgalyāyana!
You have spoken falsely, having no superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*). Maudgalyāyana, you are expelled and cast out!
[Maudgalyāyana] reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak of Maudgalyāyana's faults. Why is this?

The abode of the dragon Anavatapta is extremely far from here; this water was originally endowed with the eight meritorious qualities and was sweet, but having passed through five hundred minor hells on its way up, it has therefore become salty and hot."
If you were to ask Maudgalyāyana,
"For what reason is this water salty and hot?
Maudgalyāyana would be able to answer you accordingly.
“Maudgalyāyana speaks the truth; he is without fault. On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:

“At the base of Vulture Peak Mountain there is a lake five hundred yojanas in extent. At the bottom of the lake is golden sand, and it is filled with water of the eight meritorious qualities, as sweet as pure honey. Blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated lotuses cover the surface of the water everywhere. Various birds warble in harmony like the sound of music. Surrounding the four sides of the lake are various flowering and fruit-bearing trees; this is the palace of the Naga King Manasvin.”
The bhikṣus said,
“Where is such a pond?
Where is such a nāga?”
"You have spoken falsely by claiming superhuman attainments that you do not possess; Maudgalyāyana, you are expelled and driven out.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of such faults or transgressions regarding Maudgalyāyana."

Why is this? At the base of this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, there is a lake five hundred yojanas in extent, its bed strewn with golden sand and filled with water of eight virtues. It is as sweet as pure honey, and blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated lotuses cover its surface. Various birds warble in harmony like the sound of music, and around the four sides of the lake stand various flowering and fruit-bearing trees; this is the palace of the Nāga King Mānasa.
Maudgalyāyana said, "In truth, there is no offense.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is the Hall of Good Dharma; the hall has five hundred pillars."
There was a jeweled pillar, as fine as a single hair, that did not touch the top of the pedestal.
There was a jeweled pavilion, the seat of Śakra Devānām Indra, adorned with various flowers.
"On all its sides there are seats for the various devas, likewise adorned with flowers.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"How can such a thing exist?"
"You have falsely claimed superhuman attainments which you do not possess; therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of such faults or transgressions regarding Maudgalyāyana."
Why is this? In the Sudharma Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are five hundred pillars; among them is a single precious pillar that does not touch the floor by even as much as a hair’s breadth.
There is a jeweled pavilion, the seat of Śakra Devānām Indra, adorned with various flowers.
On all sides of it are the seats of the various devas, likewise adorned with flowers.
Maudgalyāyana said, "In truth, there is no offense.
On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana entered into meditative concentration and saw that the Yakṣa of Vajrī and the Yakṣa of Magadha were fighting; the Yakṣa of Vajrī defeated the Yakṣa of Magadha.
Maudgalyāyana arose from samādhi and said to the bhikṣus,
"The people of Vṛji shall defeat the people of Magadha.
Later, King Ajātaśatru, leading his troops skillfully, defeated the people of Vṛji.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Previously you said:
'The people of Vṛji shall defeat the people of Magadha.'"
"Now the people of Magadha have defeated the Vajjis.
Since you falsely claim to possess superhuman qualities that you do not actually have, you, Maudgalyāyana, shall be expelled and cast out."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of such faults or transgressions regarding Maudgalyāyana. Why is this?"
Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind; the Tathāgata sees both what is before him and what is behind.
When the yakṣas of Vaṅga fought with the yakṣas of Magadha, the yakṣas of Vaṅga defeated the yakṣas of Magadha, and at that time, the people of Vaṅga also defeated the people of Magadha.
"Later, King Ajātaśatru again assembled his troops and won the battle.
Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his thoughts, and there is no fault in this.
Maudgalyāyana then entered meditative concentration once more and saw that the yakṣas of Magadha were fighting with the yakṣas of Vṛji; the yakṣas of Magadha defeated the yakṣas of Vṛji.
Maudgalyāyana arose from samādhi and said to the bhikṣus,
"The people of Magadha shall defeat the people of Vṛji.
Later, during the battle, the people of Vṛji defeated the people of Magadha.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Previously you said:
'The people of Magadha shall defeat the people of Vaṅga.'"
"Now the people of Vṛji have defeated the people of Magadha.
Since you falsely claimed to possess superhuman qualities that you actually lack, Maudgalyāyana, you shall be expelled and cast out."
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"You must not speak of Maudgalyāyana’s faults regarding this matter. Why is that?
Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind; the Tathāgata sees both what is before him and what is behind.
This yakṣa of Magadha fought with the yakṣas of the Vṛji and was victorious, defeating the yakṣas of the Vṛji; at that time, the people of Magadha also defeated the people of the Vṛji.
"Later, the Vṛjis gathered their troops again and fought together, achieving victory.
Since Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his perception of the situation, he is without fault.

On another occasion, Maudgalyāyana entered and departed from a householder’s home as usual; at that time, he dressed in his upper robe and took his bowl before midday to enter the house. The householder prepared a seat for him, and they exchanged greetings.
In this household there was a pregnant woman, and the donor asked Maudgalyāyana,
"Venerable Sir!
Will this woman give birth to a boy?"
"Is it a girl?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"It is a boy."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Then another brahmin came into his house, and the host asked him:
"Has this woman given birth to a son?"
"Did you give birth to a girl?
The brahmin replied,
"I gave birth to a girl."
That woman then gave birth to a daughter.
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:
"You previously stated that the wife of such-and-such a householder would give birth to a son, yet now she has given birth to a daughter."
"Because you falsely claimed superhuman attainments when you were empty of them, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of such faults or transgressions regarding Maudgalyāyana."
Why is this? Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind; the Tathāgata sees both what is before and what is behind.
At that time, this child was male, but later his faculties were transformed into those of a female; since Maudgalyāyana spoke according to his perception of the mind, he is without fault.
Maudgalyāyana’s subsequent conception of a daughter was likewise.

On another occasion, there was a great drought with no rain; Maudgalyāyana entered meditative concentration and saw that seven days hence the heavens would send down a heavy rain, filling all the ditches and pits.
The cities and villages all heard these words and were filled with great joy.

The people of the country all set aside their various affairs, closing up their screens and stores; each person counted on their fingers and marked days with tally-sticks, waiting for the seventh day, wondering how there could still be neither wind nor rain, let alone rain?
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana, "You said that in seven days the heavens would send a great rain to fill all the ditches and pits; yet now there is not even wind, let alone rain."
"Because you falsely claimed superhuman attainments when you were empty of them, Maudgalyāyana, you are to be expelled and driven out.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of Maudgalyāyana’s faults or transgressions regarding this matter."
Why is this? Maudgalyāyana sees what is before him but not what is behind; the Tathāgata sees both what is before him and what is behind.
When a great rain falls for seven days, the Asura King Rāhu receives it with his hands and places it within the great ocean.
"Maudgalyāyana may speak according to his thoughts;
he is without fault. The Elder Śāgata said to the bhikṣus:
"When I enter meditative concentration, I can cause fire to fill everything from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven."
The bhikṣus said:
"How could such a thing be possible?
A śrāvaka disciple can produce a great fire that extends from the Avīci Hell all the way up to the Brahma Heaven."
"Because you falsely claimed superhuman attainments that you did not possess, you are empty of virtue; Śākyamuni, you shall be expelled and driven out!
When the Buddha heard this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"None of you should speak of such faults or transgressions regarding Śākyamuni."

Why is this? If a bhikṣu, relying on the first dhyāna, cultivates the bases of psychic power and attains supernormal powers, that bhikṣu can travel from the Avīci Hell up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, and he can freely fill the space between them with fire.
If a bhikṣu relies on the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it is also like this.

Based upon the four dhyānas, Śāgata has well cultivated the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) and attained great supernormal powers (abhijñā); were he to think of filling everything from the Avīci hell up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven with fire, he could do so at will.
"Śāgata spoke the truth; he is indeed without fault.
The Elder Śubhita said to the bhikṣus:
"I am able, within a single thought-moment, to know the events of five hundred kalpas of my past lives."
The bhikṣus said to Śubhavyūha:
"How can such a thing be?
Among the śrāvaka disciples, at most one can know a single world-system within a single moment of thought."
"Because you falsely claimed superhuman qualities that you do not possess, you are guilty of lying; therefore, Subhadda, you are expelled and driven out.
When the Buddha heard of this matter, he said to the bhikṣus:
"You must not speak of Subhadda’s transgression as a grave offense."
Why is this? This Śubhavyūha was previously reborn here from the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
The lifespan in the Heaven of No-Thought is five hundred kalpas; for this reason, it is said that he knows five hundred kalpas within a single thought-moment.
"In the case of the *śūbdha*, there is no offense if one speaks according to one's own perception.
Thus ends the four *pārājika* rules.
The brief inquiry into the five categories—*saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *aniyata*, *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, *pāyattika*, and *pratideśanīya*—is concluded.
This does not include the rules for training (śaikṣa-dharma) or the seven methods for settling disputes (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
18. The First Saṃghāvaśeṣa: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, he established this precept because of Kālodāyin; prior to this, there was no offense.
The Elder Kāḷudāyin thought to himself and became doubtful:
"I have emitted semen many times; I do not know which of these instances was the first and which were not."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Before the precepts were established, the noble son Kāḷudāyin did not commit an offense when he emitted semen at any time; therefore, it is said that what was done previously is without fault."
A certain bhikṣu, while his body remained motionless, emitted semen; he felt doubt, thinking:
"Have I not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He asked the Buddha about this matter, and the Buddha said:
"It is no offense.

Visākhā Mṛgāramātā, having faith in the Saṃgha, received his feet with both hands and prostrated herself with her head at them. Next she went to Kālodāyin to receive his feet and pay her respects; as soon as she did so, Kālodāyin emitted semen, which fell upon her head.
The upāsikā withdrew her hands slightly to wipe away the semen and joyfully exclaimed:
"I have gained a great benefit!
Among my fellow students, there are those with such great lust who are nevertheless able to sever desire and practice the holy life."
Kāḷudāyin became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
If there is a bhikṣu with such great desire, he should wrap and tie [his member].
A certain bhikṣu, while bathing, emitted semen and felt doubt in his mind.
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
While bathing, a certain bhikṣu had his body massaged by another bhikṣu, whereupon he immediately emitted semen. He felt doubt, thinking:
"Have I not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
A certain bhikṣu, while touching his male organ, emitted semen and felt doubt arise in his mind.
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
The Buddha said,
"If one emits semen by stroking against [the body], one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
"If one emits semen while stroking [the body] for the purpose of concealment, there is no offense.
A certain bhikṣu, having emitted semen due to improper mental attention, felt doubt in his mind:
"Have I not incurred a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
A certain bhikṣu, upon seeing the beautiful form of a woman, emitted semen and felt doubt in his mind.
"Will I not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
If a bhikṣu, because he has taken a woman by the hand, taken her by the foot, taken her by the knee, or taken her by the calf, emits semen and feels doubt, thinking:
"Have I not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
The Buddha said, "There is no offense.
A certain bhikṣu, while being held and embraced by his mother as she spoke improper words to him, emitted semen; he then felt doubt in his mind.
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
The Buddha said, "You do not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; you incur a *duṣkṛta*."
"The same applies to sisters, female companions, and wives with whom one has previously had illicit relations.

If a bhikṣu emits semen upon the body of a recently deceased woman, a bloated woman, a livid woman, a festering woman, a woman being devoured by scavengers, a blood-stained woman, a withered woman, a decomposing woman, or a skeleton, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule was concluded. The Buddha established this precept because of Kālodayin; prior to this, there was no offense.
Kālodayin then had this thought and gave rise to doubt:
"I have for a long time touched the bodies of women; I do not know when it was before [the rule] and when it was after."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
“Before the precepts were established, Kāḷudāyin’s touching of a woman’s body at any time was not an offense; therefore, it is called ‘prior conduct without fault.’”
There was a bhikṣu who, with respect to a human woman, conceived the notion that she was a non-human woman and touched her; later, he became doubtful:
"Have I not perhaps committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"If one perceives a human female as a human female and makes physical contact with her, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one perceives a human female as a non-human female and makes physical contact with her, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
If one touches a human woman while harboring doubt [as to her identity], one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one touches a non-human female while perceiving her as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one touches a non-human female while perceiving her to be a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one touches a non-human female while harboring doubt as to whether she is one, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu touches a woman’s body by treading upon it with his foot, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
If a woman touches a bhikṣu’s body with her foot, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu grasps a woman’s garment, he incurs a duṣkṛta.
If a woman grasps a bhikṣu’s garment, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu grasps a woman by her hairline, her flowers in the hair, her pearls, her ear-ornaments, her earrings, or any such articles of feminine adornment, it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
A woman poured water for a bhikṣu, and as the stream of water flowed without ceasing, the bhikṣu conceived an improper thought toward that woman and immediately felt doubt:
"Will I not incur a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
A bhikṣu embraced his mother, kissed her, and spoke improper words, and he felt doubt in his mind.
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; one incurs a *duṣkṛta*."
"It is the same for sisters, female companions, and wives with whom one previously had illicit relations.

If a bhikṣu touches a recently deceased woman, a bloated woman, a livid woman, a festering woman, a woman being devoured by scavengers, a blood-stained woman, a withered woman, a decomposed woman, or a skeleton, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
The second *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule was concluded. The Buddha, because of the bhikṣu Kāla, the son of Mṛgāra, established this precept; prior to this, there was no offense.
This bhikṣu became doubtful:
"I have acted as a matchmaker for a long time; I do not know which instances were prior to the rule and which were not."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Before the precepts were established, the bhikṣu Kāla acted as a matchmaker at all times without committing an offense; therefore, what he previously did is considered blameless."

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left a certain household. On one occasion, the bhikṣu dressed himself in the morning, took his bowl, and went to the house of a lay devotee; having taken a seat, they exchanged greetings with one another.
After the householder had remained silent for a short while, he said to the bhikṣu:
"Can you go to such-and-such a woman and speak to her on my behalf?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I can speak to him, but I cannot provide an answer for you.
The householder asked,
"How do you know whether this matter will succeed or not?"
The bhikṣu said,
"I shall have a bhikṣu stand at such-and-such a place.
Having spoken these words, that bhikṣu left the householder's residence and saw another bhikṣu, to whom he spoke:
"Stay here for a moment.
That bhikṣu said,
"What is the purpose of staying here?"
He replied, "You need only stay; do not ask.
That bhikṣu, having detained the other bhikṣu, departed. When the householder came out, he saw that bhikṣu staying at the appointed place and said to him:
"Excellent, excellent!
My task has been accomplished.
That bhikṣu said:
"What have you accomplished?
The householder replied,
"What is the use of asking?"
“This is the designated place.
The first bhikṣu felt doubt:
“Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?”
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left a certain household. On one occasion, before the morning meal, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the house of a layperson (*gṛhapati*). The layperson offered him a seat, and once he was seated, they exchanged greetings with one another.
After remaining silent for a short while, the householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Can you tell such-and-such a girl to come?
He replied:
"I can. The bhikṣu went and spoke to the woman, and the woman said,
"I have no need for this thing."
The bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

There was a husband and wife who were angry with one another and lived in discord. A certain bhikṣu frequently entered and left their home; one day, before midday, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to their house. Having taken a seat and exchanged greetings, the bhikṣu caused the two of them to perform repentance.
After these two persons had confessed their transgressions and engaged in sexual intercourse together, the bhikṣu became suspicious, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A man has three kinds of wives:
first, those obtained through wealth;
second, those obtained through ritual propriety."
Third, acquisition through subversion.
Regarding these three kinds of wives, if one were to execute a legal document stating:
"She is not my wife."
If the marital rites have not yet been terminated and she still enters and exits [the house], and he has not yet declared,
"She is not my wife," and the bhikṣu unites with this woman, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Regarding these three kinds of wives, if one were to draw up a contract stating,
"She is not my wife," and the rites of marriage have already been severed so that she no longer enters or leaves the household, yet he has not yet proclaimed [her status]:
"She is not my wife.
At that time, if the bhikṣu reconciles them, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Regarding these three kinds of wives, if she has already executed a contract stating:
"She is not my wife.
Having severed all social ties according to the rites, she no longer enters or exits [the household]; he has already declared:
"She is not my wife."
"At that time, if a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker, he commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

A certain bhikṣu frequently entered and left a particular household. Before midday, this bhikṣu put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*). Having taken a seat and sat down, they exchanged greetings with one another.
After remaining silent for a short while, the lay devotee said to the bhikṣu,
"Can you tell such-and-such a courtesan to come?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I shall speak to her.
