He immediately went to speak to that courtesan, who had come toward the lay devotee, but was taken away by another person along the way.
That bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt:
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*."

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left the house of a certain lay devotee. Before noon, this bhikṣu put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the lay devotee’s house; having taken a seat, they exchanged greetings with one another.
After the layman had remained silent for a short while, he said to the bhikṣu,
"Are you able to tell such-and-such a woman to come?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I can. She immediately went to tell him; the woman had adorned herself and was about to depart when her husband entered, and for this reason she was unable to go.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

There was a bhikṣu who entered and left a certain household; having dressed and taken his bowl before midday, he went to the house of that lay devotee (*gṛhapati*), sat in the seat provided for him, and exchanged greetings with him.
After remaining silent for a short while, the layman said to the bhikṣu:
"Can you tell such-and-such a woman to come?
The bhikṣu replied:
“I can. He went immediately and spoke to her, and the woman consented.
Then this woman had this thought:
"I shall certainly not be able to sleep once I arrive there; I will go only after sleeping now.
When the woman had fallen asleep on the ground, he was ultimately unable to depart.
The bhikṣu felt doubt:
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*."
There was a householder who was infatuated with a certain woman;
he went to her and said, "Grant me permission to engage in sexual intercourse.
The woman replied:
"I am busy now," [the monk] said.
The householder replied,
"How could I know when you would have leisure?"
The woman said, "There is a bhikṣu who frequently enters and leaves my house; I have sent this bhikṣu to strike your back, so you should know that I am free."
The bhikṣu dressed in his robes and took up his bowl before midday, went to her house, and after taking a seat, exchanged greetings with her.
The woman said to the bhikṣu,
"Go and strike that certain householder on the back."
The bhikṣu asked,
"For what reason?
The woman replied:
"Just go and strike him; do not ask questions.
The bhikṣu immediately went there and struck the layman on the back with his fist.
The layman said, "The matter is settled."
The bhikṣu asked,
"What is accomplished?
The householder replied:
"This was a formal agreement.
The bhikṣu became doubtful:
"Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left a certain household. Before midday, this bhikṣu put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*). Having taken a seat, he exchanged greetings with them.
After remaining silent for a short while, the householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir,
could you ask such-and-such a woman to come here?"
The bhikṣus said:
"We ought not to perform menial service for you; however, if you are in urgent need of seeing her, you should organize a gathering for the Saṃgha, and we shall invite this woman to come."

The layperson immediately paid the monk the price for the feast; the monk used that money to prepare a feast for the community of monks and invited this woman. While at the gathering, the layperson engaged in sexual intercourse with the woman.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a merchant’s wife who possessed great beauty.
A certain layman desired to have illicit relations with her, but the woman would not consent.
When her husband passed away, there was a minor matter for which the householder would not allow anyone else to enter or leave his residence.
His mother asked his daughter,
"Is there any expedient means by which one might be allowed to enter or leave?"
The daughter said, "There is.
Her mother asked:
"Who is it? He replied,
"That householder has repeatedly sent messengers on my behalf, desiring to have intercourse with me, but I did not comply."
The mother said, "You may comply with his wish; for your sake, let many people obtain happiness.
The daughter said:
"Who should be sent to speak?
The mother said,
"The bhikṣu who constantly enters and exits may be sent to speak."

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left that household; having put on his robes and taken up his bowl before midday, he entered the house, sat down in the place prepared for him, and after exchanging greetings, asked:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Can you tell such-and-such a matter to the householder [Name]?
He replied, "I can."
He went and told him, and the householder then went.
The bhikṣu felt doubt:
"Will I not incur a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It does not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
There was a lay devotee who built a monastery and constantly provided for that place all necessary requisites for life, such as clothing, bedding, food, drink, and medicinal decoctions.
Not long after, that layman died, and there was no one left to provide the community at that place with the requisites of life—robes, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions.
A certain bhikṣu went to the layman’s wife and said to her:
"Why do you not provide the community of monks at this place with the requisites of life—robes, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions?"
The householder’s wife said, “Venerable sir!
This householder is possessed of merit and prowess; everything that has been provided here is due to his strength.”
"Venerable sir!
If you can cause such-and-such a lay devotee to assign him tasks here, then he may provide for your needs.
The bhikṣu then went to that lay devotee and said:
"Can you go outside my house with the wife of such-and-such a layman to manage the household affairs?
That layman replied, "My own household has many matters to attend to; I cannot manage them all myself."
The bhikṣu said:
“It is for the sake of receiving [offerings] and making offerings to the stūpa and the Saṃgha.
Because this lay devotee had faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, he then said:
"Yes. This householder frequently entered and left [the dwelling] and consorted with the householder's wife.
A bhikṣu became suspicious:
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense."

There was a householder who built a monastery for the Saṃgha and constantly provided it with clothing, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and all other necessities of life. When this householder’s wife died, there was no one left to provide the monastery with clothing, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and all other necessities of life.
A certain bhikṣu went to the layperson’s residence and said to him:
“Why do you no longer provide the bhikṣus in the monastic quarters with robes, food and drink, medicinal requisites, and other necessities for their livelihood?”
The householder said, "Venerable sir!
This wife possesses great merit; all that has been provided originally was through her power."
"If you can manage the household affairs within my home for such-and-such a laywoman, she may provide for you.
The bhikṣu then went to the laywoman's side and said,
"Would you be able to manage the household affairs within [the house] for such-and-such a layman?"
The householder’s wife said, “Venerable sir!
My household has many affairs of its own; I have not been able to manage everything.”
The bhikṣu said,
“It is for the sake of receiving offerings from those who support the stūpa and the Saṃgha.
Because this householder’s wife had faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, she then said:
“Yes. Because this woman frequently came and went, she consorted with the layman.
The bhikṣu gave rise to doubt:
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left a certain household. Before midday, this bhikṣu put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of a lay devotee, where he sat down in the seat provided and exchanged greetings with him.
After remaining silent for a short while, the householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir,
can you tell such-and-such a woman to come here?"
He replied, "I can.
He then went and spoke to that woman; however, both the householder and the woman fell ill at the same time, so they were unable to unite.
A bhikṣu became doubtful, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, but incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left a certain household. One day, before midday, this bhikṣu dressed, took his bowl, and entered that house. The mistress of the house gave him a seat, and they sat together; after exchanging greetings and remaining silent for a short while, the woman said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Can you go and tell the householder so-and-so to come?
He replied, "I can."
He went and told them immediately.
Both the woman and the householder fell ill and were unable to unite.
The bhikṣu became suspicious:
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*."

There was a bhikṣu who frequently entered and left a certain household. Before midday, this bhikṣu dressed, took his bowl, and entered that house. The householder gave him a seat, and after they had exchanged greetings and remained silent for a short while, he said to the bhikṣu:
“Venerable sir!...”
“Can you, for the sake of my son, speak to a certain householder and ask him to give my son a sister, a brother,
or a daughter? He replied, “I can.”
He then went and told them.
At that very moment, the householder’s son and his daughter both fell ill; their spines became hunched, they were struck by madness, and each took another person as a husband.
The bhikṣu then gave rise to doubt.
"I shall not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He does not incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*."
The bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
“If there are lay followers (upāsaka) whose words may be trusted, should there also be non-humans [whose words may be trusted]?
The Buddha said:
“There is! It is the devas who have attained the Path.
He asked again:
“Is there a female human lay follower (*upāsikā*) whose word can be trusted? Might there also be such a non-human female?
The Buddha said, “There is!”
"This is the goddess who attained the Way.
The bhikṣu said to the others,
"I am able to sit cross-legged in mid-air."
"This bhikṣu is empty and devoid of such things; he has committed a pārājika offense.
He further said:
"I can transform one body into many bodies, and many bodies back into one body."

By means of my wisdom, I am able to penetrate all things, whether manifest or unmanifest; I pass through walls, mountains, and trees without obstruction; I emerge from and enter the earth as if entering or exiting clouds; I walk upon water as if on land and traverse the void like a bird; even though the sun and moon possess great majesty and power, I can reach out and touch them with my hand without moving, and I travel freely to and fro even unto the Brahma-world.
"If this matter is empty and lacks reality, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha:
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu makes and wears an impure robe and yet does not incur a *pāyattika* offense?"
The Buddha said: "There are.
For instance, if the warp of a robe is purified while the woof is not, or if the woof is purified while the warp is not, or if both are unpurified."
Regarding "impure [clothing]": it refers to camel hair, cow hair, or the wool of a black sheep, or if they are woven together.
To wear such impure clothing constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Question: "The Vinaya states:
'A bhikṣu should not keep long hair.'"
"If there is a sore on one's head, what should be done?
The Buddha said,
"One should cut it away with scissors."
Question:
"A bhikṣu obtains pure food and eats it with a mind of doubt, thinking:
'Is this food pure or impure?'"
"What offense does one incur?
The Buddha said,
"One incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."
Question:
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu might preach the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences without incurring a pāyattika offense?
The Buddha said:

“There is! If one writes a letter, makes gestures with the hands, or sends a messenger, and speaks more than five or six words of Dharma to a female deva, a female nāga, a female yakṣa, a female preta, a female piśāca, a female kumbhāṇḍa, or a female rākṣasa, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.”
Question:
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu, by constructing more than three layers of roofing, incurs a pāyattika offense?
The Buddha said:
“There is! If one first constructs a house and then covers it with wooden planks as desired.
Question:
"Is there a case where a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel together on a road, yet does not incur a pāyattika offense?
The Buddha said: "There is."

If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a celestial maiden to travel together on a road, or makes an appointment with a nāga maiden, a yakṣī, a preta woman, a piśācī, a kumbhāṇḍī, or a rākṣasī to travel together on a road, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
Question:
"How does one rinse the mouth?
The Buddha said:
"Place water in the mouth and rotate it three times; this is called rinsing the mouth.
Question:
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu eats separately from the community and does not incur a pāyattika offense?"
The Buddha said: "There is!
It is those who eat from the midst of empty space."
Question:
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to commit a pārājika offense by eating?
The Buddha said:
"There is! If one eats it with the intent to steal.
Question:
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu, while sitting in a house for a meal, does not incur a pāyattika offense?
The Buddha said, "There is."
If a woman receives the one-day precepts (upavāsa) but the man does not, and they sit together in the house, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the man receives the one-day precepts but the woman does not, and they sit together in the house, he likewise incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"If both have received the one-day precepts (upavāsa), there is no offense for sitting together in that house.
Question:
"Is it possible for a bhikṣu to eat in a house while sitting alone with a woman without incurring a pāyattika offense?"
The Buddha said: "There is!
If a woman receives the one-day precepts while a man does not receive them, and she sits together with him, she commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If a man receives the one-day precepts but a woman does not, sitting [together] in that situation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If both have received them, there is no offense.
Question:
“Is there a case where a bhikṣu goes to view an army on its march and yet does not incur a pāyattika offense?
The Buddha said, “There is.”
"If one goes to observe the yakṣa army, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
Question:
"Is there any case where a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:"
"Come with me to various households; I shall give you much delicious food and drink.
Later, that bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣu:
"I do not delight in sitting or speaking with you; I find joy in sitting alone and speaking alone."
“Is there not an offense of *pāyattika*?
The Buddha said, “There is.”
If one speaks in the streets or alleys before the person has reached another's house, instructing them to return, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one speaks within the monastery (*saṃghārāma*), there is no offense. Question:

"Is there a case where a bhikṣu, being free from illness, enters the house of a layperson and receives food or drink directly with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, yet does not incur a *pratideśanīya* offense?"
He replied: "There is!
If a bhikṣuṇī carries food or drink herself to a layperson's house and gives it to a bhikṣu, and he receives it with his own hand, there is no offense."
Question:
"Is there a case where a bhikṣuṇī instructs a layperson to give such rice and such soup for a bhikṣu to eat, yet she does not incur a *pāṭidesanīya* offense?"
He replied: "There is.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative of this bhikṣu encourages him to eat, and the bhikṣu eats it without rebuking her, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
The five sections concluded. *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 59.
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, Scroll 60.
Continued Translation by the Tripiṭaka Master Vimalākṣa of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty: *Vinayamātṛkā-pūrvabhāga*.

The Preface to the *Vinaya-sūtra*, Scroll 1: The Chapter on the Five Hundred Bhikṣus Compiling the Tripiṭaka (Upper Volume of the Preface). Chapter One: The Chapter on the Five Hundred Bhikṣus Compiling the Tripiṭaka.

The Buddha, the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*), attained parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at the dwelling place of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara. Thereupon, the Mallas of Kuśinagara made offerings to the body of the Buddha.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa was leading five hundred bhikṣus from the city of Pāvā toward the city of Kuśinagara.
Between these two cities, there was at that moment a brahmin carrying celestial māndārava flowers who had set out from the city of Kuśinagara, intending to go to the city of Pāvā.
The Elder Mahākāśyapa asked,
"Do you know my Great Teacher?
He replied:
"O Consciousness!
Seven days have now passed since your Great Teacher entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees at the abode of the Mallas.
The devas and people of the world have been making offerings to the Buddha’s body; it was from there that I obtained these celestial māndārava flowers."
Mahākāśyapa was displeased; among the disciples, some were filled with great sorrow, some raised their hands and wept, and some fell prostrate on the ground, all saying:
"How swift is the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa!"

"The Eye of the World has been extinguished. Among the bhikṣus, some rolled about on the ground; some were filled with grief and sorrow in their hearts; and some practiced the contemplation of equanimity regarding the characteristics of all phenomena—namely, that all things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. [They reflected: "Regarding this phenomenon of the characteristic of impermanence, how could it ever be permanent?"
When the Buddha was in the world, he often said:
"All things upon which sentient beings delight and cling cannot be maintained for long; they must all eventually be parted from, dispersed, destroyed, and worn away.
At that time, there was a foolish, unwholesome, and incompetent elderly bhikṣu who uttered these evil words:
"That elder always says:
'One should practice this; one should not practice that.
Now I have gained complete freedom; I shall do whatever I desire and stop whenever I wish."
These harsh words were heard only by Kāśyapa; no one else knew of them, for they had been concealed by the supernatural power of the devas.

At that time, in Jambudvīpa, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first senior elder (sthavira); the Elder Kundadhāna was the second senior elder; the Elder Daśabalakāśyapa, the preceptor of Ānanda, was the third senior elder; and the Elder Mahākāśyapa was the fourth senior elder.
Mahākāśyapa was widely learned and possessed great renown; the fourfold assembly all revered him and accepted his words with faith.
When the fourfold assembly heard that Mahākāśyapa was coming from the city of Pāvā, intending to go to the city of Kuśinagara, they all went out halfway along the road to welcome Mahākāśyapa.
When Mahākāśyapa saw the fourfold assembly approaching, he spread out his *niṣīdana* under a tree by the roadside and sat down cross-legged.
Once the fourfold assembly had arrived, they paid homage with their heads at his feet and stood to one side to listen to his teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa had finished teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening the fourfold assembly with various Dharmas. He then dismissed them and returned to the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara.
Mahākāśyapa said: "I am about to arrive;
do not ignite the Buddha's funeral pyre, for I wish to pay homage to the Buddha’s entire body."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, together with the great assembly, arrived at Kuśinagara; having arrived, the devas opened the golden coffin and removed the wrappings.
Then Mahākāśyapa prostrated himself in reverent salutation to the Buddha’s body, and the fourfold assembly likewise performed their obeisance. He then addressed the people, saying:
"Furthermore, wrap the Buddha’s body well with fine new cotton and silk; fill the golden coffin with fresh fragrant oil, place the Buddha’s body therein, and close the lid."
"Furthermore, pile up all kinds of fragrant wood as miscellaneous fuel to form a great pyre.
Mahākāśyapa said to the Mallas:
"You yourselves know the proper time."
The leaders of the Mallas immediately lit the great pyre of fragrant wood.
At that time, seeing the pyre ablaze, the Elder Ānanda was choked with grief and distress, and he spoke this verse:
“The body of the World-Honored One, Reaches even unto the Brahma Heaven;”
"Now he lies within a golden coffin, wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton;
it is drenched with fragrant oil and will be cremated with scented wood.
At that time, as the Buddha’s funeral pyre burned until it was spent, Mahākāśyapa reflected and said:
"How should this fire be extinguished?
He then thought that it should be extinguished with cow's milk.
At that moment, as Mahākāśyapa had this thought, pools of cow's milk—pure, clean, fragrant, and excellent—spontaneously appeared on all four sides.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa took this milk to extinguish the fire and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha’s body was wrapped in a thousand layers of cotton, And cremated with fire;
Yet by the power of the Buddha’s divine majesty, A single inner garment remains.”
"The outermost shall not burn, yet those within shall all be consumed by flame.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, using prepared cotton cloth, took the Buddha’s relics and gave them to the Mallas.

The Mallas followed the Elder Mahākāśyapa as they took the Buddha’s relics, placed them in a golden urn, and set it upon a carriage; burning various incenses and carrying banners and canopies while performing music, they entered the city of Kuśinagara.

At that time, in the city of Kuśinagara, there was a new hall for doctrinal discussion, swept clean and fragrant beyond measure. Silken banners and canopies were suspended, various flowers were scattered about, and ivory couches were spread; upon them were placed golden vases containing the Buddha’s relics.
Ānanda first made various offerings of flowers, incense, music, and other articles; he also instructed the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās to offer worship and pay homage.
At that time, when the Mallas of the city of Pāvā heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa in the city of Kuśinagara, they thought to themselves:
"The Buddha was also our teacher; he is one whom we revere."

He came to the various people and requested a portion of the relics, wishing to erect a stūpa within the city of Pāvā, where he would offer incense, hang silken banners and canopies, and provide offerings throughout his entire life.
The Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara replied:
"The Buddha attained parinirvāṇa within our kingdom; we ourselves have erected a stūpa and made offerings of incense and flowers. You shall not obtain a portion of the śarīra."

At that time, the Kṣatriyas of the Vatsa clan from the kingdom of Cedi; the Kauṇḍinya lineage from the village of Rāmagrāma; the brāhmaṇas of the Vaiśālī kingdom; the Licchavis of the Vaiśālī kingdom; the Śākyas of the Kapilavastu kingdom; and King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, ruler of the Magadha kingdom, heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara, and that people were now making offerings to his relics with incense, flowers, and music.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru commanded his minister, the Brahmin Bāliśakāra, saying:
"Go to the place of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara and, conveying my words, inquire after them extensively: 'Are you vigorous and at ease? Is your body and mind happy?'"
He further addressed the people, saying:

"The Buddha was also my teacher and the one I revere; he has now entered parinirvāṇa in your kingdom. I request a portion of his relics, for I wish to erect a stūpa in the city of Rājagṛha to offer them worship."
"It would be well if you grant it to me; if you do not grant it, I shall raise my armies and seize it from you by force.
Having received these instructions, he immediately arrayed his fourfold army and proceeded directly to the city of Kuśinagara, where he addressed the Mallas, saying:
"O Lord of the Magadha Kingdom!..."
King Ajātaśatru sent boundless inquiries, asking:
"Are your physical strength and well-being secure? Is your body and mind at ease?
He further said:

"The Buddha was also my teacher and the one I revere; he has entered parinirvāṇa here. I come to request a portion of his relics; you should grant them to me, so that I may erect a stūpa in the city of Rājagṛha to offer worship."
The Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara replied to the brahmin minister:
"The Buddha attained parinirvāṇa upon the soil of our country; we ourselves shall erect a stūpa here in Kuśinagara to make offerings to him, and we will not give you a share of the śarīra."
The brahmin minister said:
"The King Ajātaśatru, Lord of Magadha, says to you:
'It would be well if you were to give me the relics.'"
"If you do not grant it to us, we shall mobilize the fourfold army to seize it from you by force.
The Mallas replied, "We ourselves provide for our own worship; we will not give it to you."
The Mallas of the city of Pāvā also assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side.
Kuvera of the village of Rāva likewise assembled his fourfold army and stood to one side.
The kṣatriyas of the country of Cālikā also assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side.
The brahmins of the country of Venu also assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side.
The Licchavis of the kingdom of Vaiśālī also assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side.
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu likewise assembled their fourfold army and stood to one side.
The Brahmin Bhaṇḍagāra increased his fourfold army and stationed himself on one side of the city of Kuśinagara.
At that time, the city of Kuśinagara was surrounded on all sides by the eight armies; for the sake of the śarīras, each wished to seize them for themselves.
At that time, within the great assembly, there was a Brahmin of the Dhūma clan who was among the eight armies and cried out in a loud voice:

"Listen, O leaders of the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara! The Buddha accumulated goodness and cultivated patience for immeasurable kalpas; you all have also constantly heard the praises of the Dharma of patience. Why, today, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, would you raise armies to contend with one another for the sake of his relics?"
"Gentlemen, you should know that this is not an act of reverence.
While Śāriputra is still present, we should simply divide [the relics] into eight portions.
The Mallas said:
"Let us respectfully deliberate on the matter of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the brahmin named Dhūma divided the śarīra into eight portions.
Having finished the division, he again proclaimed in a loud voice:

“O leaders of the Mallas, please listen: we entreat you to grant us the urn containing the śarīras, so that we may return to the village of Pāṭaligrāma to erect a stūpa for the urn and offer worship with flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and music.”
The Mallas replied,
"We respectfully accept your invitation.
At that time, the Brahmin and householder Pippalāyana again shouted out in a loud voice:

"Listen, O leaders of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara! Give me the charcoal from the place where the Buddha was cremated; I wish to return to my own country and erect a charcoal stūpa there, to be honored with flowers, incense, music, and dance."
The Mallas replied to the brahmin:
"We respectfully accept your invitation.

At that time, the Mallas of the city of Kuśinagara obtained the first portion of the relics; they immediately erected a stūpa within their country and made various offerings of flowers, incense, music, and other such things.
The kingdom of Pāvā obtained the second portion of the relics; they returned home and erected a stūpa, making various offerings to it.
The Kauravas of the village of Rāmagrāma obtained the third portion of the relics; they returned home and erected a stūpa, making various offerings to it.
The Kṣatriyas of the country of Cedi obtained the fourth portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made various offerings.
The Brahmins of Vaiśālī obtained the fifth portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made various offerings.
The Licchavis of the kingdom of Vaiśālī obtained the sixth portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made various offerings.
The Śākyas of the kingdom of Kapilavastu obtained the seventh portion of the relics; they returned to their country, erected a stūpa, and made offerings of flowers and incense.

King Ajātaśatru, the ruler of the kingdom of Magadha, obtained the eighth portion of the relics; he returned to the city of Rājagṛha and erected a stūpa there, making offerings of flowers and incense.
A brahmin of the Vatsa clan obtained the urn containing the relics; he returned to the village of Thūna and erected a stūpa there, making offerings of flowers and incense.
The brahmin and householder Pāriyātra will surely obtain the charcoal and return to his country to erect a stūpa in its honor.

At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there will be eight śarīra-stūpas, the ninth being the vase-stūpa, and the tenth the charcoal-stūpa. Thus, after the Buddha’s initial parinirvāṇa, ten stūpas were erected, and from then on, immeasurable stūpas were built.

At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, knowing that the Buddha’s relics had been distributed throughout the ten directions and that laypeople had erected stūpas for them, gathered the Saṃgha for this reason.
When the assembly of monks had gathered, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, I was traveling from the city of Pāvā toward the city of Kuśinagara with five hundred bhikṣus. Between these two cities, I saw a brahmin carrying celestial māndārava flowers, coming from the city of Kuśinagara and intending to go to the city of Pāvā."
I asked the brahmin,
"Upaga, from where have you come?
Where do you intend to go?"
The brahmin replied,
"I have come from the city of Kuśinagara and wish to go to the city of Pāvā.
He asked:
"Do you know my great teacher?
The brahmin replied, "I do."

"Your Great Teacher attained parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees seven days ago; gods and humans have now been making offerings to his relics, and it was from there that I obtained these celestial māndārava flowers."
At that time, my heart was not at ease, and I spoke these words:
"How swift is the Buddha’s entry into nirvana!
The Eye of the World has been extinguished."
Among the bhikṣus, some were filled with great sorrow, some raised their hands and wept, and some collapsed to the ground, all saying:
"How swift is the Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa!"
"The Eye of the World has been extinguished.

Some monks rolled upon the ground; some were filled with grief and sorrow; some practiced the contemplation of equanimity, observing the characteristics of all phenomena: "All things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Since these are the characteristics of impermanence, how could they ever attain permanence?"
While the Buddha was still in the world, he himself declared:
"All things in which sentient beings take pleasure and attachment are difficult to maintain for long; they must all eventually be parted from, dispersed, destroyed, and worn away.
At that time, there was a stubborn, foolish, and unwholesome elderly bhikṣu who spoke these harsh words:
"That elder always says:
'One should practice this; one should not practice that.
Now that I have attained mastery, I shall do whatever I desire and cease from whatever I do not desire."
When this foolish bhikṣu spoke these words, I alone heard them while no one else did; they were concealed by the power of the devas.

Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who spoke before me, declaring what is Dharma to be non-Dharma, what is non-Dharma to be Dharma, what is wholesome to be unwholesome, and what is unwholesome to be wholesome.
"We should now collect all the Sūtras, all the Vinayas, and all the Abhidharmas.
Mahākāśyapa thought to himself:
"I shall collect all the Sūtras, all the Vinayas, and all the Abhidharmas within the Saṃgha."
There may be some ignorant bhikṣus who speak thus:
"One should not compile all the sūtras, all the vinayas, and all the abhidharmas in this manner."
"We should now select from within the Saṃgha those who are intelligent and capable of compiling the Dharma; let us perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to appoint them.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa selected five hundred bhikṣus—excluding one—from within the Saṃgha, calling out each of their names one by one.
These bhikṣus had all studied the Tripiṭaka, attained the three vidyās, extinguished the three poisons, and had all achieved liberation through shared realization.
Among the saṃgha, Mahākāśyapa proclaimed:
"May the venerable saṃgha listen!

These five hundred bhikṣus, with one exception, have had their names recited; they have all studied the Tripiṭaka, attained the three insights (trividyā), extinguished the three poisons, and have all attained liberation through shared realization.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, these five hundred bhikṣus, with one exception, are all those who have mastered the Dharma.
Thus is the formal motion.
At that time, while the Elder Ānanda was among the Saṃgha, the Elder Mahākāśyapa reflected:
"This Ānanda is a person who delights in wholesome study;
the Buddha has said, 'Among those who have heard much, Ānanda is the foremost.
We should now cause Ānanda to act as the compiler of the Dharma."
After the Elder Mahākāśyapa had reflected, he proclaimed before the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Ānanda is a disciple who has trained well; the Buddha said:"
"Ānanda is the foremost among men of great learning.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; we shall now appoint Ānanda as the compiler of the Dharma.
Thus he announced.
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This Ānanda is a person who trains well; the Buddha has said:
"Ānanda is the foremost among those who have heard much.
We should now appoint Ānanda as the compiler of the Dharma.
Which elders approve of Ānanda being appointed as the compiler of the Dharma? Those who approve, remain silent; those who do not approve, let them speak."
“The Saṃgha has already granted its consent for the Venerable Ānanda to complete the compilation of the Dharma; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
The Elder Mahākāśyapa then reflected:
“The compilation of all the Sūtras, all the Vinayas, and all the Abhidharmas is a vast undertaking; it cannot be completed in one day, two days, or even seven days.”
Now, within the Sangha, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) shall be performed: those who can perform the act of assembling the community must observe the rains retreat together in one place;
those who do not perform the act may not observe the rains retreat together in one place.
Having reflected thus, the Elder Mahākāśyapa proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The collection of the Dharma is now extensive; it cannot be completed in one day, two days, or even seven days."
Now, within the Sangha, those who perform the *karmavācanā* may dwell together in one place for the rains retreat;
those who do not perform the *karmavācanā* shall not dwell together in one place for the rains retreat.
"Thus it was announced.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa again had this thought:
"In which land is there peace and security, where there are excellent vihāras, where the four requisites and offerings of food and drink are never lacking, and where there are no bandits?"
He then thought:

"In the city of Rājagṛha, the four requisites for support are fully provided without lack; the realm is peaceful and secure, free from bandits and marauders. We should now go to Rājagṛha to enter the rains retreat."

Having reflected thus, Mahākāśyapa went alone ahead to the vihāra to repair it; he plastered the holes in the walls, leveled the earthen mounds, spread out the beds, swept the floors, shook out the bedding, and prepared medicines, food, drink, clothing, and coverlets.
Knowing that the time for the summer retreat had arrived, Mahākāśyapa entered the summer retreat at Rājagṛha together with five hundred bhikṣus.

At dawn, Mahākāśyapa dressed, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to teach and transform the people. Having gathered offerings of food and drink and completed his instruction on the Dharma, Mahākāśyapa went out to beg for alms himself; having finished eating, he left the city and returned to the monastery.
For this reason, he assembled the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, he reflected:
"Which bhikṣu is able to recite the Vinaya with clarity, so that when we pose difficult questions, he can respond accordingly?"
"We should collect the Vinaya from this person.
He then thought:
"The bhikṣu Upāli is one whom the Buddha constantly praises for reciting the Vinaya; he is the foremost among the bhikṣus in its clear understanding."
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Saṃgha:
"The Buddha has always praised the bhikṣu Upāli as the foremost among those who recite the Vinaya, being most clear and proficient. Bhikṣu Upāli!"
"We shall ask difficult questions and be able to answer them accordingly.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa prepared the Dharma seat.
Once the Bhikṣu Upāli had ascended the high seat and was seated, Mahākāśyapa questioned Upāli:
“From where did the first pārājika originate? Upāli replied,
“The first pārājika originated from the bhikṣu Sudinna, son of Kalandaka, in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.”
"In this regard, what constitutes an offense and what does not?
At that time, Upāli explained at length the characteristics of what constitutes an offense and what does not.
Mahākāśyapa asked Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
"Is it not so? He replied:
"It is so! It is as Upāli has said.
After Mahākāśyapa had finished questioning Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he next questioned the Elder Cunda, then Daśabala-Kāśyapa, and successively questioned the five hundred arhats, down to Ānanda.
Ānanda replied, “I have heard it thus as well; this matter, this Dharma, is wholesome, just as the Elder Upāli has spoken.
Ānanda then asked Mahākāśyapa:
“Is it so? He replied, “It is.”
In this assembly, the Elder Mahākāśyapa proclaimed in a loud voice before the Saṃgha: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The compilation of the first Pārājika rules is now complete.

These are the Dharma, these are the Vinaya, these are the Buddha’s teachings. There is no bhikṣu who would say that what is Dharma is not Dharma, or that what is not Dharma is Dharma; nor would he say that what is Vinaya is not Vinaya, or that what is not Vinaya is Vinaya."
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, let this matter be held thus!
Mahākāśyapa again asked the Elder Upāli:
"From where did the second pārājika offense originate?"
Upāli replied:
“In the city of Rājagṛha, it was concerning the bhikṣu Daṇḍakī, the potter’s son.
“Where did the third pārājika offense originate?”
Upāli replied:
“In the country of the Vṛjis, it was for the bhikṣus dwelling on the banks of the river Bhagīrathī.
Where did the fourth pārājika offense originate?”
He replied,
"In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, for the bhikṣus dwelling on the banks of the river Vāgumātī.
"Where did the first saṃghāvaśeṣa offense originate?"
He replied, “In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, for the bhikṣu Kālodāyin.
A second, third, and fourth time, he replied, “In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, for the bhikṣu Kālodāyin.”
"Where did the fifth Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense originate? Answer:
"In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, concerning the bhikṣu Kāla, son of Mṛḍika."
Mahākāśyapa asked again:
"What constitutes an offense?
What does not constitute an offense?"
Upāli explained at length the characteristics of what constitutes an offense and what does not.
When Mahākāśyapa had finished questioning Upāli, he next questioned Ājñātakauṇḍinya: "Is it so?"
Ājñātakauṇḍinya replied:
"Elder Mahākāśyapa!
I also know it in this way, just as Upāli has said."
Next he questioned the Elder Kunda, then the Ten-Powered Kāśyapa, and in succession questioned the five hundred arhats, down to Ānanda.
Ānanda replied:
"Elder Mahākāśyapa!"
"I also know it to be thus, just as the Elder Upāli has spoken.
Ānanda asked Mahākāśyapa:
"Is it as Upāli has said?"
He replied, "Ānanda!
I also know it to be just as Upāli has said."
Thus, the compilation of the entire Vinaya was completed in successive order.
At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa raised his voice and proclaimed loudly before the Saṃgha:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!

When this entire collection of the Vinaya rules has been completed—this being the Dharma, this being the Vinaya, and this being the Buddha’s teaching—there shall be no bhikṣu who says that what is the Dharma is not the Dharma, or that what is not the Dharma is the Dharma; nor shall there be one who says that what is the Vinaya is not the Vinaya, or that what is not the Vinaya is the Vinaya.
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Buddha's teaching; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, let this matter be thus upheld!
The Elder Mahākāśyapa reflected:
"Which bhikṣu is proficient in reciting the Sūtras and Abhidharma, such that when we pose difficult questions, he can respond accordingly?"
"We should collect the Sūtras and Abhidharma from this person.
At that moment, they had this thought:
"The Buddha has praised the bhikṣu Ānanda as the foremost among all bhikṣus of great learning, for he upholds all the Sūtras and all the Abhidharma."
After Kāśyapa had finished his reflections, he made an announcement before the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Ānanda is a person who trains well; the Buddha has always praised the bhikṣu Ānanda as the foremost among those of great learning."
"We shall question this person clearly on the *sūtras* and the compendium of the *abhidharma*.
Thus we announce.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa prepared a fine, high seat, and Ānanda ascended the high seat and sat down.
Mahākāśyapa asked Ānanda:
"From where did the Buddha first preach the Sūtras?
Ānanda replied:
“Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at the Abode of the Sages.
When Ānanda spoke these words, five hundred bhikṣus knelt upon the ground with their right knees touching it, weeping as they said:
“We received the Dharma directly from the Buddha’s presence and beheld it face-to-face; now we have heard it once again.”
Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"From this day forward, all sūtras, all vinayas, and all abhidharmas shall begin with the words: 'Thus have I heard at one time.'"
Ānanda said: "It is so!
At that time, the Buddha addressed the five bhikṣus:"
"This is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
When I correctly contemplated this Dharma without having previously heard it from another, vision arose, knowledge arose, clarity arose, and awakening arose regarding all phenomena.

This is the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering], this is the Noble Truth of Cessation, and this is the Noble Truth of the Path. When I correctly contemplated these without having previously heard them from another, vision arose, knowledge arose, clarity arose, and awakening arose regarding all phenomena."

"Monks! This noble truth of suffering is to be known because it has been known; when I, having not heard this from another, reflected correctly upon the Dharma, there arose in me regarding these phenomena the eye, the knowledge, the clarity, and the awakening."

"This noble truth of the origin of suffering should be abandoned once it is known; this noble truth of the cessation of suffering should be realized once it is known; this noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering should be cultivated once it is known. When I reflected correctly upon these things, having heard them from no one else, vision arose, knowledge arose, clarity arose, and awakening arose regarding all phenomena."

"O monks! Because this Noble Truth of Suffering has been known and fully understood, as I correctly reflected upon the Dharma not having heard it from another, there arose in me regarding all phenomena the eye, the knowledge, the clarity, and the awakening."

Having known the noble truth of the origin of suffering and abandoned it; having known the noble truth of the cessation of suffering and realized it; and having known the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering and cultivated it—at that time, when I was reflecting with right mindfulness upon the Dharma as I had never heard it from another, there arose in me regarding these phenomena the eye, the knowledge, the clarity, and the awakening.
"O Bhikṣus!

If, for as long as it took me to practice the turning of the Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects within the Four Noble Truths, the eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening did not arise, then among all the world—including its Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans—I would not have attained liberation, detachment, or relinquishment, nor would I have attained the non-perverted mind. At that time, I would also not have had this thought:
'I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

"During this time, through the practice of the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects within the Four Noble Truths, vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening arose in me. Among all the world—with its Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, among this assembly of gods and humans—I have attained liberation, detachment, and relinquishment; I have attained a mind free from inversion."
At that time, I had this thought:
"I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When this Dharma was being taught, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and eighty thousand devas attained the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena, free from dust and removed from defilement.
At that time, the Buddha asked Kauṇḍinya,
"Have you attained the Dharma?
Kauṇḍinya replied:
"I have attained it,
World-Honored One!
"Has Kauṇḍinya attained the Dharma?"
Kauṇḍinya said, “I have attained it,
World-Honored One!”
“Kauṇḍinya, have you attained the Dharma? Kauṇḍinya replied, “I have.”
“World-Honored One!
Because Kauṇḍinya was the first to attain it, he was named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Once Ājñātakauṇḍinya had attained the Dharma, at that moment the earth deities raised their voices and proclaimed in a loud voice:
"O sentient beings!

At Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at the Abode of the Sages, the Buddha has turned the Wheel of Dharma in its three phases and twelve aspects. Among all others—whether śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, or Brahmās—none in this entire world can turn it in accordance with the Dharma. For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the sake of the benefit, peace, and happiness of gods and humans, to increase the host of devas and diminish the hosts of asuras."
When the deities in the sky heard the cry of the earth-deities, they also cried out in loud and resonant voices:
"The Buddha turns the Wheel of Dharma!
When the Four Heavenly Kings heard the cry of the deities in the sky, they too cried out in loud and resonant voices.

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven immediately raised their voices, and reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven, they all cried out in loud and resonant tones:
"O sentient beings!"

The Buddha was staying at the Deer Park, the Abode of Seers, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects—a wheel that no other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, nor anyone else in this entire world, can turn in accordance with the Dharma. He did so for the benefit of many beings, for the happiness of many beings; out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans, to increase the ranks of the devas and diminish the hosts of asuras.

The Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in the Abode of Sages near Vārāṇasī; having turned the Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects, this sutra is therefore titled "The Sutra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma."
Mahākāśyapa asked Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
"Is it as Ānanda has said? He replied:
"Indeed, Elder Mahākāśyapa!
I also know it to be exactly as Ānanda has said."
Next he questioned the Elder Kunda, then the Ten-Powered Kāśyapa, and so on, questioning the five hundred arhats in succession, until finally he asked Upāli:
"Is it as Ānanda has said?"
He replied, “So it is.
Then the Elder Upāli questioned Mahākāśyapa:
“Is it as Ānanda has said? He replied, “It is so!”
"Elder Upāli! I also know it to be exactly as Ānanda has said.
After they had thus questioned one another in turn, the compilation of the entire Sūtra Piṭaka was completed.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa proclaimed among the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The collection of all the Sūtras is complete; these are the Dharma, these are the Vinaya, and these are the Buddha’s teachings. There is no bhikṣu who would say that what is Dharma is not Dharma, or that what is not Dharma is Dharma; nor would he say that what is Vinaya is not Vinaya, or that what is not Vinaya is Vinaya."
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Buddha's teaching; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, let this matter be held thus!
Elder Mahākāśyapa again asked Ānanda:
"Where did the Buddha first teach the Abhidharma?"
Ānanda replied: "Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

'If a person possesses five fears, five transgressions, five enmities, and five extinctions, then because of these five fears, transgressions, and enmities, after death—just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm—they will fall into hell.'"
What are the five?
First, killing;
second, stealing;
Third is sexual misconduct;
fourth is false speech;
fifth is the drinking of intoxicants.

If a person eliminates the five fears, the five sins, the five enmities, and the five extinctions, then because those five fears, sins, enmities, and extinctions have been eliminated, after death—just as a strong man might extend or contract his arm—they will be reborn in the heavens.
What are the five?
First, one does not kill; fearing the retribution of sin, enmity is extinguished.
Not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, and not drinking intoxicants are likewise practiced out of fear that the retribution of sin will extinguish enmity.
The Elder Mahākāśyapa asked Ājñātakauṇḍinya:
"Is it as Ānanda has said? He replied:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
I also know it to be exactly as Ānanda has said.
He then questioned the Venerable Kunda, then the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa, and so on, questioning the five hundred arhats in succession, until finally he questioned Upāli:
“Is it as Ānanda has said? He replied,
“Elder Mahākāśyapa!”
"I also know it to be thus, just as Ānanda has said.
The Elder Upāli asked Mahākāśyapa: "Is it not so?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
When this entire Abhidharma had been compiled, at that time Mahākāśyapa proclaimed loudly before the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The compilation of all the Abhidharma is now complete; this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha. There shall be no bhikṣu who says that what is Dharma is not Dharma, or that what is not Dharma is Dharma, or that what is Vinaya is not Vinaya, or that what is not Vinaya is Vinaya."
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, let this matter be thus upheld!

At that time, when all the Sūtras, all the Abhidharmas, and all the Vinayas had been compiled, the Elder Ānanda bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"I have personally heard and received these words from the Buddha; the Buddha said:"
‘After my parinirvāṇa, if the Saṃgha is united with one mind, they may deliberate upon and relinquish the minor precepts.
Mahākāśyapa replied: “Ānanda!
“Have you asked the Buddha about this?
What is meant by ‘the subtle precepts,’ and how does one ‘unify the mind in harmony and relinquish them’?
Ānanda replied:
“Venerable One,
I did not ask. Kāśyapa said:
"You should ask clearly:
'What is called the subtle precept that the Saṃgha, being of one mind and in harmony, has now relinquished?
Elder Ānanda!"
"If you do not ask the Buddha, you will incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
You must confess this offense according to the Dharma;
do not conceal it. Ānanda replied:
"I did not ask because I did not hold the precepts lightly;
at that time, as the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, my heart was filled with grief and distress, and so I did not ask.
Mahākāśyapa then said to Ānanda:
"The Buddha has spoken to you three times:
'Regarding the various matters of the land of Jambudvīpa, there is no joy greater than that of life.
If a person cultivates the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), they can remain for a kalpa, or even slightly less than a kalpa.'"
Ānanda! The Buddha has well cultivated the four bases of psychic power;
if he so desires, he can remain for a kalpa, or for less than a kalpa, remaining at his own will.
"Why did you not request that the Buddha remain for a long time?
Because of this matter, you have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You must now repent for this offense according to the Dharma; do not conceal it."
Ānanda replied, “It is not that I hold the precepts lightly, nor is it because I lack reverence for the Buddha that I did not request him to remain longer.
At that time, Māra obscured my mind; I was unaware of it myself, and for this reason, I did not immediately request the Buddha to remain for a long time.”
Mahākāśyapa spoke again to Ānanda:
"You have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense by treading upon the Buddha's robe with your foot.
You must confess this transgression according to the Dharma."
Ānanda replied, "I do not hold the precepts lightly, nor do I fail to revere the Buddha.
At that time, a great wind suddenly arose and there was no one else present; I folded the Buddha’s robe, and for this reason I stepped upon it."
Mahākāśyapa spoke again to Ānanda:
"The Buddha said to you:
'Take a bowl of water from the Kakutthā River.'"
You said: "The water of the Kakutthā River is turbid and not yet clear," and you did not immediately take some water.
"Because of this matter, you have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You must confess this transgression according to the Dharma.
Ānanda replied:
"I do not hold the precepts lightly, nor do I fail to revere the Buddha.
However, not long after five hundred chariots had forded the river, the water remained turbid and had not yet cleared; for this reason, I did not immediately take water to offer to the Buddha."
Mahākāśyapa spoke again to Ānanda:
"The Buddha did not permit women to go forth; yet you, having requested as many as three times, have caused women to go forth."
"Because of this matter, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This offense must be confessed according to the Dharma.
Ānanda replied:
"I do not disparage the precepts, nor do I fail to revere the Buddha.
However, all Buddhas of the past had the fourfold assembly; why then does our World-Honored One alone lack them?"
"Therefore, you have made this request up to three times.
Mahākāśyapa spoke again to Ānanda:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, why did you display the Buddha’s mark of the concealed organ to women?"
"Because of this matter, you have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You must confess this transgression according to the Dharma.
Ānanda replied:
"This woman’s merit is shallow; she wishes to behold the marks of a Buddha.
Having seen them, she will become weary of and detached from her female body and subsequently obtain a male form. For this reason, he reveals them to her."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa caused the Elder Ānanda to confess six *duṣkṛta* offenses before the Saṃgha.
Then the Elder Mahākāśyapa assembled the Saṃgha and said:
"We do not permit the abandonment of even the minor precepts."
Why is this? If the non-Buddhist heterodox teachers were to hear of these matters, they would say their disciples are clever. Why is that?
The teacher binds the precepts, while the disciples abandon them.
For this reason, we have gathered with one mind to deliberate and resolve not to permit the relinquishing of even the most minor precepts.
The heterodox teachers and followers of other paths speak as follows:

"While the Great Teacher was present, the Śākya śramaṇas all fully maintained the precepts; after the Teacher’s parinirvāṇa, they were unable to fully maintain the precepts and consequently abandoned them.
The Dharma of the Śākya sons will not long endure; it is like a burning fire that emits smoke—the fire is extinguished and the smoke ceases."
"For this reason, we have gathered with one mind to deliberate and resolve not to permit the relinquishing of even minor precepts.
If we were to permit the abandonment of minor precepts, the bhikṣus would not know which ones are minor precepts."
Or someone might say:
"Subtle precepts are not only the *duṣkṛta*; there are also four *pratideśanīya* offenses, which are likewise called subtle precepts."
"For this reason, we do not permit the relinquishing of minor precepts.
If we were to assemble with one mind and permit the relinquishing of minor precepts, there might be some bhikṣus who would not know which ones are minor precepts."
He spoke these words:
"It is not only the *duṣkṛta* offenses; the four *pratideśanīya*, the ninety *pāyattika*, and others are also called subtle precepts."
"For this reason, we have gathered together with one mind so that no minor precept may be neglected or abandoned.
If we were to gather with one mind and permit the abandonment of minor precepts, there might be some bhikṣus who would not know which ones are minor precepts."
He spoke thus:
"It is not only the *dukkaṭa*; the four *pāyattika-dharmas* and the ninety *pāyattikas* are also subtle precepts."
"The thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattikas* are also called the 'subtle precepts.
For this reason, we do not permit the relinquishing of these subtle precepts.
If we were to assemble with one mind and permit the relinquishing of the subtle precepts, there might be some bhikṣus who would not know which ones are the subtle precepts."
He spoke as follows:

"It is not only the *duṣkṛta* [offenses] that are so; the four *pratideśanīya*, the ninety *pāyattika*, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, and the two *aniyata* dharmas are also called the subtle precepts."
"For this reason, we do not permit the relinquishing of minor precepts.
If we were to assemble with one mind to deliberate and permit the relinquishing of minor precepts, there might be some bhikṣus who would not know which ones are minor precepts."
He spoke as follows:

"The 'subtle precepts' do not refer solely to *dukkaṭa* (offenses of wrong-doing); the four *pāṭidesanīya*, the ninety *pācittiya*, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pācittiya*, the two *aniyata* dharmas, and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are also called subtle precepts."
"For this reason, we do not permit the relinquishing of even minor precepts.
If we were to assemble with one mind to deliberate and permit the relinquishing of minor precepts, there might be a bhikṣu who would say:
'I shall uphold four precepts, while I relinquish the remaining precepts.'"
"For this reason, we have gathered with one mind to deliberate and resolve that we shall not permit the abandonment of even the most minor precepts.
We shall follow the Buddha in establishing the precepts; whatever precepts the Buddha establishes, we shall all receive and uphold them."
In the Buddhist scriptures, regarding the account of the Brahmin Bārasakappa, a high minister in the kingdom of Magadha, it is said among the Seven Principles of Non-extinction: "If, O Bhikṣus!"

“The Buddha does not establish precepts that were not previously established, nor does he abandon precepts that have already been established. As for the precepts as they have been taught and undertaken, the virtuous qualities of the bhikṣus increase and do not diminish.
For this reason, we should all uphold them and never let them go.

The Section on the Compilation of the Dharma by the Tripiṭaka is concluded. 2. The Section on the Seven Hundred Bhikṣus Compiling the Extinction of Evil Dharmas (Preface, Vol. Upper–Middle). The Second Part, Upper Section, of the Section on the Seven Hundred Bhikṣus Compiling the Extinction of Evil Dharmas: One hundred and ten years after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the ten matters arose in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

These ten matters are contrary to the Dharma and not virtuous; they distance one from the Buddha’s teachings, do not accord with the Sūtras, do not accord with the Vinaya, and furthermore, they subvert the characteristics of the Dharma.
Yet these ten matters, the bhikṣus of the kingdom of Vaiśālī employ as the practice of the Dharma, the words of the Dharma, and the purity of the Dharma, and thus they uphold them.
What are the ten matters?
First, purification by salt;
second, purification by the finger.
Third is purity through proximity to a village;
fourth is purity through the arising of harmony;
fifth is purity in such a manner.
Sixth is purity through realization;
seventh is purity of dwelling in poverty;
eighth is purity of practicing the Dharma.
Ninth, the purification of the *niṣīdana* by adding borders;
tenth, the purification of gold, silver, and precious objects.

Furthermore, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī took a large golden bowl from the kingdom of Kośala, departed from the kingdom of Kośala, and entered the kingdom of Vaiśālī. They went on their alms-round in succession, placing whatever they received, whether much or little, into the bowl.
At that time, some people placed ten thousand coins, others a thousand, five hundred, fifty, or even as little as one coin into the bowl.

At that moment, there was the Elder Yaśoda Kālandakaputra, who resided in Vaiśālī; he had attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*) and upheld the Tripitaka—namely, the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
Yaśoda was a disciple of the Elder Ānanda.

Having heard that ten matters had emerged in the kingdom of Vaiśālī—which were neither in accordance with the Dharma nor virtuous, which distanced them from the Buddha’s teachings, which did not enter into the Sūtras nor the Vinaya, and which also violated the characteristics of the Dharma—[Yaśoda investigated].
These ten matters, the bhikṣus of the country of Vaiśālī practice as the Dharma, speak as the Dharma, and purify themselves through the Dharma; thus they uphold them.
What are the ten?
First is purification by salt, up to purification by gold and silver treasures.

The bhikṣus of the kingdom of Vaiśālī also took large golden bowls from the Kośala country; they left the Kośala country and entered the kingdom of Vaiśālī, begging for money in succession, placing whatever was given, regardless of the amount, into their golden bowls.
At that time, some people placed ten thousand coins, or five hundred, one thousand, five hundred, fifty, or even one coin into his bowl.
Having heard of this matter, the Elder Yasada knew that such an act was contrary to the Dharma. He sent a messenger to the lay followers in Vaiśālī, saying:
"The Śramaṇa sons of the Śākya lineage should not beg for gold, silver, or precious objects to store. For various reasons, the Buddha taught the Dharma to the village headman of Maṇicūḍā, saying:"

"From this day forward, monks, if you require firewood, you must beg for firewood; if you require grass, you must beg for grass; if you require a vehicle, you must borrow a vehicle; if you require laborers, you must borrow laborers.
O śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!"
"In this matter, the Buddha did not permit begging for gold, silver, or precious objects, nor their possession.
When the bhikṣus of the kingdom of Vaiśālī heard that Yaśoda had sent a messenger to the lay followers of Vaiśālī saying,

"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya should not beg for gold, silver, or precious objects, nor possess them," [they reflected on] how the Buddha, through various causes and conditions, had preached the Dharma for the headman of the Maṇicūḍaka village:

"From this day forth, monks, when you require firewood, you may beg for firewood; when you require grass, you may beg for grass; when you require a vehicle, you may borrow a vehicle; when you require laborers, you may borrow laborers."
“O Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas! Even until now, the Buddha has not permitted you to beg for gold, silver, or precious objects, nor to store them.

Having heard this, they assembled and divided all the gold, silver, and precious objects among themselves. Among them, some monks took their own shares and carried them out; some had śrāmaṇeras or laypeople carry them away; some placed them on beds and carried them out; some placed them inside boots and carried them out; some wrapped them in clothes and carried them out; or they sent messengers to deliver their shares to Yaśoda.
Yaśoda immediately sent a messenger back, saying:
"Why do you instruct me to accept these impure things?
The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, should not accept such impure things."
The Buddha taught the Dharma through various causes and conditions, saying:

"From this day forward, bhikṣus must beg for firewood and grass when needed; they may borrow vehicles and laborers when necessary; however, I do not permit them to accept or store gold, silver, or precious objects."
The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī reflected and said:
"Yaśoda has exposed our offenses before the lay followers. We should perform a *vinayakarma* of subordination against Yaśoda, compelling him to repent before the lay followers of Vaiśālī."
Having reflected thus, he assembled the Saṃgha and performed the *adhyāśaya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against Yaśoda, ordering him to confess before the lay followers of Vaiśālī.
When Yaśoda heard that the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī had performed the *adhyāśaya-karman* against him, ordering him to confess before the lay followers of Vaiśālī, he thought to himself:
"When I confess before the lay followers, I shall be able to preach the Dharma on every occasion so as to inspire faith in them, saying:"

"The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, taught the Dharma of dependent origination to the village head of Maṇicūḍa, and so forth, up to: 'A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not beg for gold, silver, or precious objects, nor should he store them.'"

Then, on the following day at mealtime, Yaśoda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for food. Having finished eating, he went to the lay followers in Vaiśālī during their time of repentance; there he taught the Dharma on various matters, causing the lay followers to gain faith, saying:
"The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, spoke to Maṇicūḍa:
'A bhikṣu who requires firewood or grass should beg for it; vehicles and laborers should be borrowed.'"
"One should not beg for gold, silver, or precious objects to store.

Thus did the Elder Yaśoda preach the Dharma on each matter; the laypeople immediately attained faith and understanding, realizing that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ought not to beg for gold, silver, or precious objects to store.

When the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī heard that the Elder Yaśoda was confessing before the laypeople of Vaiśālī, explaining the Dharma in detail for each matter so as to inspire faith and understanding in them, they learned that the Buddha had taught through various causes and conditions:
"A bhikṣu may beg for firewood and grass; he may borrow vehicles and laborers; however, he must not beg for gold, silver, or precious objects, nor should he store them."
Having heard this, they reflected thus:
"We must not allow Yaśodharā to remain here; we shall now perform a formal act of exclusion (karmavācanā), decreeing that you must not reside in Vaiśālī."
Having reflected thus, he assembled the Saṃgha and performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against Yaśoda, decreeing that he was not permitted to reside in Vaiśālī.
When the Elder Yaśoda heard that the monks of Vaiśālī had performed a formal act against him, prohibiting his residence in Vaiśālī, [he departed].
Having heard this, he returned to his room and handed over his bedding; then, taking up his robes and bowl, he departed from Vaiśālī. Not long after he had set out, he thought to himself:

"I have escaped from the company of the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī; those bhikṣus possess gold, silver, and precious objects, and they are full of desire and seeking, having perfected in themselves unwholesome dharmas."
Yaśoda was observing the summer rains retreat in the kingdom of Kośala.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti was staying at the Saṃghāṭa Monastery in the city of Mathurā, beneath an Udumbara tree in the Āpātala grove.
This Venerable Subhūti was a master of the Tripitaka, possessed of the three types of supernormal knowledge, and was renowned as a great Arhat.

The Elder Yaśoda, a disciple of the Elder Ānanda, heard that the Elder Subhūti was residing at the Saṃghārāma in the country of Mathurā, beneath an Udumbara tree in the Āpātala grove, as a master of the Tripitaka, possessed of the three types of supernormal knowledge, and renowned as a great Arhat.
Having heard this, he dispatched a messenger to Tripuṭaka, saying:
"Venerable sir, do you know?

Ten matters have arisen in the kingdom of Vaiśālī that are neither legal nor wholesome, which distance one from the Buddha-dharma; they do not accord with the Sūtras, they do not accord with the Vinaya, and they also subvert the characteristics of the Dharma."
The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī practiced this Dharma, declared this Dharma to be pure, and maintained it accordingly.
What are the ten?
The first is purification by means of salt.
Second is purity by pointing out;
third is purity by proximity to a village;
fourth is purity by birth through union.
Fifth is purity in this manner;
sixth is purity through realization;
seventh is purity regarding a dwelling place free from poverty.
Eighth, purity through the practice of the Dharma;
ninth, purity through not adding fringes to the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat);
tenth, purity regarding gold, silver, and precious objects.

The bhikṣus of the kingdom of Vaiśālī also took great golden bowls from Kośala and, departing from the kingdom of Kośala, entered the kingdom of Vaiśālī to beg for money. They went on their rounds begging, placing whatever they received—whether ten thousand coins, a thousand, five hundred, fifty, or even a single coin—into their bowls.
"The elder bhikṣus should assemble and extinguish this evil dharma; if it is not extinguished now, it will surely become great later.

Having heard these words, the Elder Subhūti immediately dispatched messengers to the kingdom of Dakkhiṇāpatha and the kingdom of Aparantaka. In this manner, he sent messengers to all those kingdoms, saying:
"Do you know?"
Ten matters emerged from the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
What are the ten?
First, the purification of salt, up to the purification of gold, silver, and precious objects.
"If these evil dharmas are not extinguished now, they will surely become great in the future.
At that time, the bhikṣus from the countries of Dakṣiṇāpatha, Avanti, and other regions all assembled in Vaiśālī.

At that time, the Elder Revata was residing in the kingdom of Sāṃkāśya; he was a great Arhat of renown who had mastered the Tripitaka and attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). He was fond of practicing the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa) and was a disciple of the Elder Ānanda.

The Elder Subhūti heard that the Elder Revata was residing in the kingdom of Sāṃkāśya; that he was a Tripitaka-master who had attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā), was a renowned Great Arhat, and delighted in practicing the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa).
Having heard this, the elder Subhūti thought to himself:
"Which elder among us should be designated as the senior (*sthavira*)?
We should seek out such an elder to serve as the senior and take charge of these bhikṣus."
Having reflected thus, [they thought], "We should seek out the Elder Revata to explain the true Dharma to the bhikṣus.

At that time, the Elder Subhūti gathered the bhikṣus and requested from laypeople the four types of requisites for their support; having obtained these, he traveled by boat to the kingdom of Sāhañjani and arrived at the place where the Elder Revata was.
The Elder Revata saw Suppabuddha approaching from afar; with a virtuous mind, he rose to greet him and inquired after his well-being:
"Are you not weary from the road?
He took up Suppabuddha’s robes and bowl for him, showed him to his quarters, and spoke to Suppabuddha and the other bhikṣus:
"This is your bed, bedding, and sleeping gear.
If the Elder has prepared bathing requisites— such as bath powder, ash, sesame oil, and firewood—
and after the bath, until nightfall, at that time Revata stays in the same room with Tripuṭaka, sitting much in meditation until dawn.
Then the Elder Revata said to Tripuṭaka, "I have finished performing the rites for honoring guests; you may now proceed with the practices of one who has gone forth.
Having heard these words, the Elder Tripuṭaka dressed in his robes and took up his bowl at mealtime, entering the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having finished his almsround after the meal, he returned to where Revata was and prostrated himself at his feet.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti thought to himself:
"This great Dharma-master Revata might perhaps pose difficult questions regarding my Abhidharma, and I may not be able to explain them quickly."
"I shall now first question the Vṛji monk Revata of Vaiśālī on ten matters.
He then joined his palms and asked:
"Is it permissible to accept salt that has been purified?"
Revata asked Tripuṭaka in return:
"What is meant by 'purity through salt'?
[Tripuṭaka replied: "Venerable Revata!"
The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī took leftover salt that had been kept overnight and placed it into pure food to eat, claiming that this practice was pure.
I asked the Elder whether this was truly pure.
Līlāvaḍa replied: "It is impure; it should not be eaten. [The other asked:
"If one eats it, what offense is incurred?"
He replied,
“One incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Tripuṭa asked again:
“Where did the Buddha establish the precept that this matter should not be eaten? Answer:
“It is stated in the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* of the *Vinaya* concerning Śrāvastī.”
Tripuṭa asked: "Venerable Revata!
Is it permissible to accept [food] purified by two fingers?"
He asked again,
"What is meant by 'purification with two fingers'?
He replied:

“The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, having finished their meal, rose from their seats; without performing the ritual for accepting leftover food, they took morsels between two fingers and ate them, saying that this practice was pure.”
"I ask the Elder: Is it truly pure?
Revata replied, "It is not pure."
"What offense is incurred for [using] impure [substances]?
He replied:
"One incurs a *pāyattika* offense."
He asked again:
"Where did the Buddha establish the precept that this matter should not be practiced?
He replied:
"The country of Vaiśālī, because they did not accept the practice regarding leftover food (*vighasa*), established this precept.
Tripuṭa said: "Venerable Revata!..."
"Is that which is pure by proximity to a village truly pure?
He asked in return:
"What is meant by purity through proximity to a village?"
He replied,
"The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, having obtained food near the edge of a village, eat it without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (refusal of further food) ritual, saying that this matter is pure."
"I ask the Elder: Is it pure? Līlavat replied, "It is not pure."
"What offense is incurred for [using] impure [substances]?
He replied:
"One incurs a *pāyattika* offense."
He asked again:
“In what place did the Buddha say that these matters should not be practiced?
He replied:
"In the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the Buddha established a precept prohibiting the consumption of leftover food.
Tripuṭa said, "Venerable Revata!"
"Is the purity of the conjunction of birth truly pure?
He asked in return:
"What is meant by the purity of the conjunction of birth?"
He replied, “The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī,
having finished their meal and risen from their seats, consumed a mixture of milk, curd, and ghee without having performed the ritual for accepting leftover food, claiming that such an act was pure.”
I asked the Elder, "Is it truly pure?
He replied,
"It is not pure."
“What offense is incurred for [using] impure [substances]?
He replied:
“One incurs a *pāyattika* offense.”
He asked again:
"In what place did the Buddha establish the precept that this matter should not be practiced?
He replied:
"In Vaiśālī, the Buddha established a precept prohibiting the practice of consuming leftover food.
Tripuṭa said, "Venerable Revata!..."
"Is such purity truly pure?
Revata asked in return:
"What is meant by 'such purity'?"
He replied:
"The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, having completed a formal act (karmavācanā) separately within their own internal boundary and common residence, entered the midst of the Saṃgha and proclaimed:
'That formal act was performed at that residence; this matter is pure for the Elder.'"
"Now, when I ask whether this matter is truly pure or not?
He replied:
"It is not pure."
