We do not know where we should move and place it.
The king said:
"Take this and offer it to the community of monks at Zhuyuan.
The minister immediately took it and gave it to the monks of Zhuyuan, who placed it between the doors of the lecture hall in an open space.
When the various generals and officials arrived at Zhuyuan and saw it, they said:
"I have never before seen such a fine object; for what reason should I discard it?
If the King were to hear of this, his mind might become impure.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they did not know what to do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit large beds and high beds in the homes of laypeople; however, bhikṣus must not possess them, nor sit upon them, nor lie down upon them."
"If a person donates high beds or large couches, one may accept them provided they are protected, concealed, and stored away; one must not sit upon them, nor lie down upon them.
When King Prasenajit’s mother died, he took all her belongings from her lifetime and went to the Jetavana to offer them to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus obtained these precious robes: those from the country of Ayojjhā and those from the country of Vatsa-Abhayagiri.
With these fine and precious robes, they spread them upon the ground and walked back and forth upon them.
When the various generals and officials arrived at the Jetavana to inspect it, having seen it, they said:
"We could not even bear to place our hands upon its top; how can it be spread upon the ground and trodden underfoot?"
"If King Prasenajit were to hear of this, his mind might become impure.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what they should do, reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"Listen: whatever among these precious garments is suitable to be made into bedding, make it into bedding; whatever is suitable to be made into robes, make it into robes; whatever of these items may be used as you see fit, make it so.
These most precious garments come from the country of Ayojjhā; the *kūṭāgāra* cloth comes from the country of Vatsa-Avanta.
Expensive robes were used by the bhikṣus as bedding for the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Once, during a great thunderstorm, various flying birds died of fright.

When the lay devotees learned of this, they went out and selected the fine birds; however, they did not take large crows, vultures, owls, horned owls, or *āra* birds, as these were not fit for consumption.

When the time arrived, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for food. Seeing that these birds were all dead and no one was taking them, the bhikṣus said to the other bhikṣus:
"You take these away to boil or roast; we shall return from our alms-round and eat them together with you."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who brought some meat that had been boiled and roasted.
Some bhikṣus asked him, "What kind of meat is this?
He replied:
“Crow meat.
The bhikṣus rebuked him with various reasons:
“How can one called a bhikṣu eat crow meat?”
"This was not permitted by the Buddha.
After the monks had finished censuring him with various reasons, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One must not eat crow meat.
If one eats it, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* (duṣkṛta).
The bhikṣus asked:
“What kind of meat is this?
He replied:
“The meat of small crows, vultures, geese, *vāsa-tul-khyab* (a type of owl), horned owls, *arā* birds, and so forth.”
The bhikṣus rebuked him with various reasons:
"How can one who calls himself a bhikṣu eat the flesh of large crows, vultures, geese, *vāsa-tul-khyo* (a type of owl), horned owls, *ara* birds, and so forth?"
"This is not permitted by the Buddha.
Having finished his reproach, he informed the Buddha, who said:
"One must not eat such meats; the meat of any bird that eats corpses must not be eaten at all."
"If one eats it, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
After the monks had finished their meal, they went to the river Ajiravatī to practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and saw a jackal being carried along by the current in the water.
The monks said to one monk, "Bring this jackal here; we shall eat it tomorrow.
That monk immediately brought it. The next day, some boiled the jackal's meat, while others went out for alms.
The bhikṣus asked:
"Householder!
What kind of meat is this?"
He replied,
"Jackal meat.
The bhikṣus rebuked him for various reasons:
“How can one be called a bhikṣu who eats jackal meat when the Buddha has not yet permitted it?
Having finished his reproach, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“How can one be called a bhikṣu who eats jackal meat? Jackal meat and dog meat are no different.”
"From this day forward, you must not eat the flesh of jackals;
if you do, you shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
As for the people, when their mules died, they were discarded in the moat."
When it was time for the meal, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Seeing a dead mule in a moat, they said to the other bhikṣus:
"Take it away and cook it; when we return from begging for food, we shall eat it together."
The bhikṣus asked,
"What kind of meat is this?
He replied:
“Donkey meat.
The bhikṣus rebuked him with various reasons:
“How can one be called a bhikṣu who eats donkey meat when the Buddha has not yet permitted its consumption?”
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"What difference is there between a mule and a horse?
From this day forward, you must not eat mule meat."
"If you eat it, you will incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
After the meal, the bhikṣus entered the Andhavana forest for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Seeing a dead macaque, they said to the other bhikṣus:
"Take it away; we shall eat it tomorrow."
That bhikṣu then took it.
The next day, there were some who were boiling [food] and some who were going out for alms.
The bhikṣus asked:
“Venerable sir!
What kind of meat is this?
He replied:
“Makaka meat. The bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways:
“How can one be called a bhikṣu who eats makaka meat when the Buddha has not yet permitted its consumption?”
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The flesh of a monkey resembles human flesh; how does it differ from human flesh?
If one eats it, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*."

(The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* section concludes. *Vinaya-nidāna*, Volume Lower, Part 4: Chapter on Causes and Conditions (*Nidāna-varga*), Part 4 of the Introduction. Chapter Four: Causes and Conditions. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Various noble sons of the Śākya clan went forth into homelessness and contracted chronic illnesses.
When these sick men rose early in the morning and went to the homes of their relatives, patrons, or acquaintances, the hosts asked them:
"Are you well?"
He replied,
"I have been ill for a long time and find no joy.
The host asked:
"What kind of illness have you contracted?
He replied,
"I have contracted such-and-such an illness."
The host asked,
"When you were a layperson, how did you treat illness?
He replied:
"Place the medicine inside a cow's bladder and irrigate [the wound].
The host said,
"I shall give you this medicine for treatment."
The bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to apply this medicine.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“[The Buddha said: ‘I allow the use of [oil] for pouring; however, thin-skinned [animals] are not suitable for pouring. The Buddha said:
‘I allow thick-skinned [animals] to be used for pouring in a secluded place; I allow that if a physician instructs it, one may have a relative pour [the oil].’”
"Several noble sons of the Śākyas have gone forth and contracted chronic illnesses.
When these patients rise early in the morning and go to the homes of their relatives, patrons, or acquaintances, the hosts ask them:
'Are you well?'"
He replied,
"I have been ill for a long time and find no joy.
The host asked:
"What kind of illness?
He replied,
"Such-and-such an illness."
The host asked,
"When you were a layman, how did you treat illness?
He replied:
"Treat him with a knife," the host said.
"I will give you a knife."
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to treat [the wound] with a knife.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen to the cutting of the lotus stalk.
The bhikṣu said:
"It is not fit for use."
The Buddha said:
"I allow the use of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, copper, lead, tin, and pearls, [cut] with a knife.
The bhikṣu said:
"Such knives as these are not suitable for treatment.
The Buddha said,
"In a private place, it is permitted to use an iron knife for treatment."
There was a bhikṣu who was ill and said to his attendant:
"Bring me fresh and processed ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
The attendant said:
"No. If these items belonging to the Buddha or the Sangha are impure, have been kept overnight, have been improperly handled, have not been formally received, or have been stored indoors.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"Listen: regarding items belonging to the Buddha, items belonging to the Saṃgha, impure items, items kept overnight, items improperly handled, items not formally received, and items stored indoors—if a sick person obtains such superior items, they should be given to them once they have recovered."
The Elder Pilindavatsa suffered from eye pain; a physician instructed him to apply *rasanāñjana* to his eyes, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted the application of *rasanāñjana* to the eyes."
The Buddha said, "I permit you to use it for treating the eyes.

Later, Piṅgala-bhāradvāja had *rasañjana* in his bowl; he kept small bowls, half-bowls, large *kañcika* containers, and small *kañcika* containers in a net bag suspended from an ivory peg. When he took them out, they dripped and soiled the walls, the bedding, and the dwellings, making them foul-smelling.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to store the *raṃsana* meditation cushions in a box.
The bhikṣus made boxes but did not provide lids; the bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to make a canopy."
The bhikṣus simply made a lid, which caused [the medicine] to fall out. The Buddha said:
"Make a lid for the opening using the wing of a crow, a chicken, or a *śuśuka* (a type of small bird).
When it was applied to the eye, the pain increased further. The Buddha said:
"Let us prepare the voting sticks (*śalākā*). The Elder Upāli asked:
"What material shall be used to make the voting sticks?"
The Buddha said:
"They may be made of iron, copper, shell, ivory, horn, wood, or clay.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forth, one must not establish a *sīmā* (boundary) within the interior of a monastery;
if one does so, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
The Brahmin Ajita prepared eight kinds of gruel for the Buddha:
ghee-gruel, sesame-gruel, oil-gruel, milk-gruel, mung-bean gruel, mocha-bean gruel, hemp-seed gruel, and clear gruel.
"May these eight kinds of gruel— those mixed with root medicines, stem medicines, leaf medicines, flower medicines, and fruit medicines—
be drunk? The Buddha said, "A sick bhikṣu may drink them, but one who is not ill must not drink them."

The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Soma. At that time, a disciple of the elder bhikṣu Aniruddha fell ill; after taking a purgative medicine in the afternoon, he felt a sense of mental distress. The Buddha said:
"Give him boiled rice-pollen juice."
After he was given [the juice], his stupor did not cease.
The Buddha said, "Give him bamboo shoot juice.
After it was given, he was still not cured. The Buddha said:
“Place the rice gruel in a bag, wring out the liquid, and give it to him.
After he had given it, [the patient] was not cured. The Buddha said:
“Take him to a secluded place and give him the rice gruel.”
Upāli asked the Buddha:
“The Buddha has permitted the matted-hair ascetic Kaniya, the brahmin, to offer eight kinds of juices:
śāli juice, mūla juice, kulīra juice, śālī juice, aśvattha juice, prāluṣa juice, kapittha juice, and grape juice.”
"Regarding these eight kinds of syrups— those made from roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits— is it permissible to drink them? The Buddha said,
"If they have no taste of alcohol, are not mixed with food, and are clear rather than turbid, I allow you to drink them."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the lay devotees of the kingdom of Kośala provided water and rock honey as offerings at places along the road where there was no water.
The group of six bhikṣus traveled from the kingdom of Kośala to Śrāvastī, proceeding by stages until they reached a place for distributing water.
The group of six bhikṣus ate only rock honey and did not drink water.
A householder asked, "Why do you eat only rock honey and not drink water?"
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We delight in rock honey; we do not enjoy drinking water.
The donor said:
“I gave you rock honey for the sake of providing drinking water; why do you now eat only the rock honey and not drink the water?
The group of six bhikṣus replied, “We take pleasure in rock honey; we do not enjoy drinking water.”
"These six groups of bhikṣus possess great strength and do not fear violating the precepts.
This lay devotee was unable to rebuke them face-to-face; however, after they had departed, he became angry in his heart and reviled them, saying:
'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:'"
"It is excellent and virtuous," [he said],
"but I wish only to eat rock honey and do not desire to drink water.
When the bhikṣus— who were of few desires, contented, and practiced the dhūta austerities— heard of this matter, they felt shame and remorse, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the consumption of rock honey at five times:
first, upon returning from a long journey;..."
2. If one is ill;
3. if one has eaten little;
4. if one has not obtained food;
5. Regarding those who give water:
in these five circumstances, the consumption of rock sugar (śarkarā) was permitted.
From this day forward, if one does not drink water, the consumption of rock sugar is not permitted.
"If one eats it, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"May honey-melodious syrup that has been kept overnight be drunk?"
The Buddha said:
"A sick bhikṣu may drink it, but one who is not sick may not.
If a bhikṣu receives two kinds of invitations:
First, one requests it from another; second, a bhikṣu receives it.
He asks:
"Will you give it?"
He replied,
"I will give it.
He asked again:
"When will it be given?
He replied,
"When King Bimbisāra invites the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a hundred years of fourfold offerings, at that time it shall be given."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu has two kinds of invitations:
first, an invitation for today; [second, an invitation for another day]."
2. Cold Invitations.
If one receives two invitations on a single day:
one invitation should be given to another, and the other invitation should be accepted by oneself.
There are two kinds of cold invitations:
those that are pure according to what is received, and those that are impure according to what is received.
How is it that an invitation is pure according to what is received?
One partakes of the five *khādaniya* (solid foods), the five *bhojana* (soft foods), and the five *bhojanakalpa* (substitutes for soft foods).
What are the five *khādaniya*?
Roots, stalks, leaves, fruits, and flour-based preparations.
What are the five kinds of food?
Rice, parched grain, flour, fish, and meat.
What are the five kinds of similar food?
Millet, broomcorn millet, barley, *kāśa*, and foxtail millet.
What are the impure things received?
The five kinds of jewels and the five kinds of counterfeit jewels.
The five precious gems are gold, silver, maṇi-jewels, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
What are the five counterfeit gems?
They are red copper, iron, brass, quartz, and lead-tin alloy.
“If pure items are received directly, and impure items are received after being purified.
The bhikṣus of the country of Āloka borrowed tools every day, and a householder said:
“Why do you not make these tools yourselves, instead of borrowing them every day?”
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep tools for making things.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Sangha is permitted to keep all kinds of implements.
There was a householder who built a dwelling at Jetavana, and within it were some articles of offering.
A visiting bhikṣu stayed overnight in that dwelling and asked:
"Who built this dwelling?
He replied,
"It was built by a certain lay devotee."
After staying there for one night, that bhikṣu rose early, put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the householder’s place, saying:
“Why are the provisions for offerings in your dwelling so few?”
The householder said,
"Previously, I gave you a great deal.
The bhikṣu said:
"I have stayed here for only one night, and I see that the provisions for offerings are slightly insufficient.
The householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Let us go together to where the bhikṣu who built this dwelling is."
The householder went to the bhikṣu who was in his original quarters and said,
"The requisites for worship that I originally provided for this elder— where are they now?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“The requisites for offerings that were originally given have been used by a bhikṣu from another room.
The lay devotee said:
"I originally did not intend for this to be used by a bhikṣu from another room; I intended it for use by the bhikṣu who dwells in the dwelling I built for myself.
Since my dwelling is now empty, these articles of offering have been placed elsewhere; this was not appropriate."
The bhikṣu did not know what he should do regarding this matter and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize that whatever dwelling a donor provides, those who reside therein shall share it.
In Śrāvastī, there was a man whose kinsman had been killed by another and left in an open space within the moat of the Jetavana.
A bhikṣu, seeking discarded robes (pāṃśukūla), went to the side of a corpse and took a garment away.
His relatives, searching for him, arrived at the Jetavana and saw this bhikṣu, asking him:
"Venerable One!..."
"Have you seen or heard of such a person?
The bhikṣu replied, "This man died and was discarded in the moat of the Jeta Grove; I took a garment from his side and brought it here."
The relative said, "Lead me to that place.
The bhikṣu then led him there. Upon seeing the corpse, the relative wailed with grief, saying:
"You might even kill my people for the sake of a robe.
The bhikṣu said,
"I truly did not kill them."
"If he has killed him, why did he not take the remaining clothes?
His relatives thought to themselves:
"We spoke to him with gentle words, yet this bhikṣu speaks untruthfully; we shall take him away and present him before the authorities."
He then took him away to the authorities.
The official questioned the bhikṣu:
"Did you truly kill him?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am a bhikṣu; how could I kill a person?
Had I killed him, I would have had to take away his remaining clothing."
The official was intelligent and believed in the Buddha-dharma; knowing that the Śākya bhikṣu would not do such a thing, he released this bhikṣu and let him go.
"If it should happen again like this, a bhikṣu must not take anything without asking another."
That bhikṣu was freed from his fear and told the other bhikṣus about this matter.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one must not take the robes of a person who has been killed without first questioning others."
If one takes it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When the bhikṣus took a rug from the ground where a dead person with an owner lay, the caṇḍālas said:
“Do not take the rug from the ground where the dead lie; we must pay such and such things to the king.”
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"One should not take a cloth from the ground where a person with an owner has died;
if one takes it, one incurs an offense.

When the bhikṣus took a cloth from the ground where a person with an owner had died, and there were discarded rags at its four corners, the caṇḍālas there also forbade it. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you refuse to take it, that is fine;
if you do take it, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a great epidemic in Śrāvastī and many people were dying. The bhikṣus took firewood from the places where the dead were burned to prepare a heated bathhouse for the Saṃgha.
A ghost of burning firewood pursued them, causing all the monks to fall ill. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit you to take firewood from among the dead; if you take it, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
The bhikṣus took woolen cloth, cotton, and fine white linen from a deva temple. The temple guardians said, "Venerable sirs!
These garments belong to the temple; do not take them."
The bhikṣu said,
"What use have these clay and wooden deities for clothing and offerings?
The shrine-keeper replied:
"I shall also take the property from the stūpas of the Buddhas and Arhats.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, one must not take clothing made of wool, cotton, or fine white linen from within a deva temple."
If one takes [them], one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There was a bhikṣu who was ill and possessed many bowls, many robes, and many belongings.
The attendant thought to himself:
"If you hand over all your belongings to me, or instruct that six items be given to the Saṃgha and the remainder to me," he thought.
Having finished his deliberation, he said to the sick bhikṣu:
"Your illness has been long-lasting and shows no sign of improvement; after your death, the Saṃgha shall divide all the property currently present."
"You shall not obtain great merit, nor shall you receive a share of the grace.
While you are still alive, divide the six items among the Sangha, and give the remaining goods to me."
The sick bhikṣu reflected:
"If I do not give [these things] away, I fear they will not look after me well.
Having finished his reflection, he immediately gave the six items to the Saṃgha and gave the remaining belongings to the attendant.
Later, when that bhikṣu’s illness had been cured, the Buddha and the Saṃgha were traveling through various lands during the month following the summer retreat.
While the other bhikṣus wore newly dyed robes, this bhikṣu alone wore tattered clothing.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“Why are you alone wearing these worn-out, tattered robes?
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha rebuked him with various causes and conditions:
"Why is he called a bhikṣu? These six items should not be given to the Saṃgha, nor should they be divided and given to others, nor should one instruct others to give them.
After the Buddha had finished his reprimand through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, these six items should not be given away by oneself, nor should one instruct others to give them."
"If one gives it oneself or instructs another to give it, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"If the dwellings in a monastic residence (*saṃghārāma*) are dilapidated, is it permissible to take the bedding or coverings used therein and trade them for materials to repair them?"
The Buddha said, “It may be done. [The questioner asked:
“If there are two rooms in the Saṃgha’s dwelling that both require repair, is it permissible to sell one room to fund the repairs of the other?”
The Buddha said, "It is permitted.
In a remote village of the kingdom of Kośala, there were bandits at that time; consequently, the lay devotees, fearing the bandits, abandoned the village and departed.
At that time, as almsfood became difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain, they abandoned the property of the stūpa and the property of the Saṃgha and departed with their own robes and bowls.

When the world had become peaceful again after the cessation of those thieves, the lay devotees returned to their original residences, and the bhikṣus began to beg for money and goods for the sake of the stūpa property and the Saṃgha property.
The layperson asked,
"Where are the former items belonging to the stūpa and the items belonging to the Saṃgha?
The bhikṣu replied:
"It has been lost amidst the bandits.
The householder asked,
"Are your own robes and bowl still with you?"
The bhikṣu said,
"I am carrying it with me.
The householder said:
"You yourselves cherish your own robes and bowls, yet you do not cherish the property of the Buddha or the property of the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In times of fear due to bandits, it is permitted to carry [the items] away and later return them to their original place.
Furthermore, during times of banditry, the bhikṣus took their own robes and bowls, as well as the property of the Buddha and the property of the Saṃgha, and carried them out.
While on the road, the group of six bhikṣus encountered them and said,
"We shall use these monastic bedding items.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not give them up, and so they fell into quarreling and contention.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Those who carry it away should use it; the rest should not seek it.

The bhikṣus placed items belonging to the stūpa or the Saṃgha on open ground, then put on their robes and took up their bowls to beg for food. Upon returning, they found that these items had been lost.
The Buddha said:
"When going out to beg for food, one may carry items belonging to the Buddha or the Sangha.
It is improper to carry one's own robes and bowl while bearing such heavy loads. The Buddha said: [This was the case.]
"It is permitted to wrap items in one's robe when going for alms.
A certain bhikṣu placed the property of the Buddha and the property of the Saṃgha in an open space; upon leaving the latrine, he lost those articles.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you wish to protect these items so that they are not lost, you should entrust them to someone or place them in a secluded spot.
At a certain monastery in the kingdom of Kośala, a donor offered robes to the community of bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus were not present there.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be divided among three bhikṣus present; it may also be divided between two bhikṣus, provided that one bhikṣu receives it by means of a mental resolve and verbal declaration."
"If there are three or two śrāmaṇeras, they should divide [the property]; if there is only one person, he should accept it by means of both mental intention and verbal declaration.
At a certain residence in the Kingdom of Kośala, a donor offered various robes and articles to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, but the community of bhikṣuṇīs was not present there.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The three bhikṣuṇīs present here should divide it; the two bhikṣuṇīs should also divide it; and one bhikṣuṇī should receive it by means of a mental resolve expressed in words."
Three śikṣamāṇās and two śikṣamāṇās should divide [the portion]; one śikṣamāṇā may accept it if she forms the intention in her mind and speaks it with her words.
Three śrāmaṇerīs and two śrāmaṇerīs should divide [the portion]; one śrāmaṇerī may accept it if she forms the intention in her mind and speaks it with her words.
In a certain monastery in the kingdom of Kośala, a donor offered robes and requisites to the community of bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus were not present.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Three bhikṣus currently present or two bhikṣus should divide them; one bhikṣu should mentally resolve and verbally declare that he accepts [the portion]."
"Three *śrāmaṇeras* and two *śrāmaṇeras* should divide [the portion]; one *śrāmaṇera* should receive it by means of a mental resolve and verbal declaration.
When at that time there were neither monks nor *śrāmaṇeras*, this matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This property should be divided by the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
If at that time there is also no community of bhikṣuṇīs, three bhikṣuṇīs or two bhikṣuṇīs should divide it; one bhikṣuṇī may receive it by making a formal declaration with her mind and speech."
Three śikṣamāṇās and two śikṣamāṇās should divide [the portion]; one śikṣamāṇā should receive it through mental resolve and verbal expression.
Three śrāmaṇerīs and two śrāmaṇerīs should divide [the portion]; one śrāmaṇerī should receive it through mental resolve and verbal expression.
In a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, a donor offered robes and requisites to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, but there was no community of bhikṣuṇīs present there.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If three bhikṣuṇīs are currently present, two bhikṣuṇīs should divide [the items], and one bhikṣuṇī should accept them by making a formal verbal declaration."
Three śikṣamāṇās and two śikṣamāṇās should divide [the property]; one śikṣamāṇā should receive it through mental intention and verbal expression.
Three śrāmaṇerīs and two śrāmaṇerīs should divide [the property]; one śrāmaṇerī should receive it through mental intention and verbal expression.
If at that time there are no bhikṣuṇīs at all, nor śikṣamāṇās, nor śrāmaṇerīs, then the bhikṣu-saṃgha should divide [the property]; this applies even to the śrāmaṇeras in the same way.
In a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, a donor offered robes and articles to the community of both divisions of the Saṃgha, but the Bhikṣu-saṃgha was not present.
The Buddha said:
"The Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha should divide [the offerings]."
The community of bhikṣuṇīs was also not present. The Buddha said:
"Three bhikṣus or two bhikṣus should divide it; if there is one bhikṣu, he should accept it with a mental intention and verbal expression."
Three bhikṣuṇīs or two bhikṣuṇīs shall divide [the portion], and one bhikṣuṇī, having formed the intention and spoken the words, shall receive it.
Three śikṣamāṇās or two śikṣamāṇās shall divide [the portion], and one śikṣamāṇā, whether having formed the intention or spoken the words, shall receive it.
Three śrāmaṇeras and two śrāmaṇeras should divide [the portion]; one śrāmaṇera, having formed the thought and spoken the words, should receive it.
Three śrāmaṇerīs and two śrāmaṇerīs should divide [the portion]; one śrāmaṇerī, if she has formed the thought and spoken the words, should receive it.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted by his silence, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and returned home. That night he prepared various kinds of food and drink, rose early the next morning, arranged the seats, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is prepared; may the Noble One know the time.
The Saṃgha donned their robes and took up their bowls and entered the householder's residence, while the Buddha remained at the monastery to receive his portion of food.
When the householder saw that the assembly was seated, he personally provided water for washing and served excellent, delicious food and drink to the senior and middle-ranking monks;
however, to those of lower rank and the novices, he gave rice from the sixty-day harvest mixed with sesame dregs and boiled vegetables.

After the various lay devotees had finished offering many kinds of delicious food and drink to the community of monks, they personally provided water for washing their hands and took small seats to sit before the Sangha to listen to the preaching of the Dharma.
When the Elder Śāriputra had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, Rāhula was a śrāmaṇera; after his meal, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas to inquire of the bhikṣus after their meal:
“Was the food delicious? Were you satisfied?”
At that time, the Buddha asked Rāhula,
"Has the Saṃgha eaten its fill?
Rāhula replied:
"One who obtains is satisfied; one who does not obtain is unsatisfied.
The Buddha asked, "Why do you speak these words?"
Rāhula said, “World-Honored One!

The lay devotees provide the most delicious food and drink in abundance for the senior and middle-ranking monks, but they give the junior monks and śrāmaṇeras boiled sixty-day rice mixed with sesame dregs and vegetables.”
At that time, Rāhula was emaciated and lacked physical strength; knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Rāhula, "Why are you so emaciated and lacking in strength?"
Rāhula then spoke in verse:
"Eating sesame oil brings great strength; those who eat ghee obtain a pure complexion.
Sesame dregs and vegetables lack both color and vigor— the Buddha, the God among Gods, knows this for himself."
The Buddha, knowing the answer, asked Rāhula:
"Who among this Saṃgha acts as the elder?
He replied:
“Upādhyāya Śāriputra,” the Buddha said,
“the bhikṣu Śāriputra has eaten impure food.”
When the Elder Śāriputra heard the World-Honored One’s reproach today, saying,
“The bhikṣu Śāriputra eats impure food,” he immediately spat out his food upon hearing these words.
For the rest of his life, he renounced all invitations to meals and offerings from the Saṃgha, constantly adhering to the practice of begging for alms.
The various great and noble lay devotees (upāsakas), wishing to prepare a meal for the Saṃgha and desiring that Śāriputra enter their home, addressed the Buddha:
"We pray that the Buddha will command Śāriputra to accept our invitation."
The Buddha told the people:
"Do not seek to have Śāriputra accept your invitation.
It is the nature of Śāriputra that if he is to receive, he will certainly receive; if he is to reject, he will certainly reject."
Śāriputra, this nature did not arise only in the present life; it existed in past lives as well. If one receives it, one must receive it; if one abandons it, one must abandon it.
"Listen now, all of you!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke at length on the causes and conditions of this past life:
"In a past age, there was a king who was bitten by a venomous snake."
A master of poisons who knows the śāgara-spells brings a venomous snake and first creates a great fire, then says to the snake:
"Would you rather enter this fire?"
"Would you rather go back and swallow the poison?
The venomous snake reflected:
"Once I have spat it out, why would I swallow it again for the sake of my life?"
"Once it has been vomited up, it cannot be eaten again.
I would rather enter the fire and die.
Having reflected thus, he threw himself into the fire.
The Buddha said to the people:
"The snake is now Śāriputra; in past lives, this person must have received what was to be received and must have abandoned what was to be abandoned."
"Now it is likewise so.
At that time, after the Buddha had finished reproaching Śāriputra through various causes and conditions, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should practice the dharma of the senior elder (upādhyāya)."
How should one conduct oneself?

Upon hearing the sound of the gong or the announcement that the time has arrived, one should quickly go to the seating area and take one's seat. One should observe the monks seated in the central positions and those in the lower positions; if there are any who sit improperly, one should point it out to them if they are sitting improperly.
If this bhikṣu does not wake [the others], he should snap his fingers.
If they do not wake upon hearing the snap of his fingers, he should speak to the neighboring seat with calm and gentle words.
When a donor offers food to the Saṃgha, an elder bhikṣu must not eat first.
"When it is time for the meal, one should eat only after hearing the sound of the equal offering; all monks should follow the rules of conduct of the senior monk.
While the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, there was a householder in Rājagṛha named Śrīkūṭa, who was immensely wealthy with vast riches and great power, and was a disciple of the non-Buddhist Brahmins.
This man wondered whether the śramaṇa Gautama possessed omniscience.
He proceeded to where the Buddha was, and after having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat down to one side.
The Buddha then taught the Dharma to Śrīkumāra, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
"This should be practiced; this should not be practiced.
Having taught the Dharma through various causes and conditions, he remained silent.
After the householder Śrīgupta had heard the Dharma, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
Please accept my meal at my home tomorrow out of compassion!
Because he was one who should be delivered, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
At that time, Śreṇika, seeing that the Buddha had accepted by remaining silent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and returned to his house.
Outside the gate, he prepared a great fire pit, causing the fire to be without smoke or flame, and covered it with sand. Then, with such a thought, he spoke these words:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama is an omniscient person, he shall know this matter."
"If the Śramaṇa Gautama and his disciples were not omniscient, they would surely fall into this pit.
He then entered the house, spread out an un-woven sitting mat, and covered it with a white cotton cloth, saying these words with his mind and voice:
"If he is an omniscient one, he should know this matter."
"If he were not an omniscient person, together with his disciples, he would surely fall [into error].
Śrīgupta mixed poison into food and drink, thinking in his heart and speaking with his mouth:
"If he is an omniscient person, he shall know this matter."
"One who is not an omniscient person will die from poisoning within this.
Rising early, he dispatched a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The food and drink are prepared; may the Buddha know the proper time."
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Let none of the monks of the Saṃgha walk ahead of the Buddha; all must remain behind him.
Ānanda received these instructions and ensured that none of the monks walked ahead of the Buddha, and that they all remained behind him.
When the assembly of monks had finished their meal, the Buddha put on his robe, took up his bowl, and walked in front, while the bhikṣus followed behind him.

The Buddha entered the house of Śrīgupta and transformed a pit of fire into a lotus pond filled with pure water—both sweet and cool. Within the water were various lotuses of red and white colors, covering the surface entirely.
At that time, the Buddha and the Sangha all walked upon broad-leaved lotuses and addressed Śrīgupta:
"You, householder, should dispel the doubt in your heart; I am indeed an omniscient one."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, he entered Śreṇika’s house and ascended an uncanopied bed, which he then transformed into one that was canopied.
He addressed Śreṇika: "O Householder!"
"You should dispel the doubts in your mind; I am indeed an omniscient one.
When Śreṇika saw these two miraculous powers, faith was born within him with complete purity, and he came to revere and honor the Buddha.
At that time, Śrīgupta, filled with joy, joined his palms and said to the Buddha:
"There is poison in the food; the Sangha might fall ill. I pray that the Buddha will wait a moment while I prepare further food and drink."
The Buddha said, "Householder!
Simply give this food; the Sangha will not fall ill."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the Saṃgha, no one shall eat until the announcement of equal alms has been made.
Ānanda received these instructions and immediately issued the order within the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Saṃgha!
The Buddha has issued a command: 'None shall eat until the equal distribution of food has been announced.
At that time, the Buddha offered this blessing:"
“Lust, hatred, and delusion are the poisons of this world; the Buddha possesses the true Dharma that removes all poisons.
Once these have been dispelled and relinquished, all Buddhas are free from poison.”
"By virtue of these true words, all poison shall be removed.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the food immediately became pure and free of poison.

At that time, the householder Śrīgupta rose from his seat, offered water for washing, and with his own hands served and presented many kinds of delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied.

Having finished eating and washed his hands, he gathered his bowl. Śrīgupta took a small seat and sat before the Buddha, desiring to hear the Dharma. The Buddha, according to his inclination, preached the profound, pure, and sublime Dharma.
At that very seat, Śrīgupta attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

Thus, Śrīgupta attained the Dharma, saw the Dharma, and knew the Dharma; his mind was purified by wholesome and pure dharmas, his doubts and regrets were removed, he no longer relied on other teachings, he did not follow the words of others, and he attained the power of fearlessness within the Buddha-dharma.
Rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“Venerable One!
From this day forth, I take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha; I shall observe the five precepts as an upāsaka.”
The Buddha further expounded the Dharma for Śrīgupta, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening him.
The Buddha rose from his seat and departed. On account of these causes and conditions, he convened the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not walk in front of the Buddha, nor before your upādhyāyas, ācāryas, or any of the senior elders."
"From this day forward, you shall not eat until the *saṃghabhedaka* (the call for the distribution of food) has been made; if you eat, you shall incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
At a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, the two divisions of the Saṃgha obtained clothing and requisites; the bhikṣus were numerous, while the bhikṣuṇīs were few.
The bhikṣu said, "I shall take two parts; you take one part.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"It is half of the middle portion.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs shall receive an equal share.
Śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs shall receive one-fourth, and the fourth part [shall go to the Saṃgha].

While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, there was a householder named Bhadrika who built a dwelling for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, adorning it most excellently and providing an abundance of food and drink.
There was a gathering of many bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
A householder then made an offering of clothing and requisites to the great assembly.
That householder said:
"The Buddha permitted one to raise one's voice loudly in the midst of the assembly.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to raise your voice loudly in the midst of the assembly when giving alms."
The bhikṣus stood on level ground and called out, but the multitude could not hear them. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to stand and call out from atop a seat.
Although they called out while standing there, they still could not be heard. [The Buddha said: "Stand and call out from a high place so that you may both be seen and heard."
Furthermore, there was a householder who, seeing the great assembly gathered for the distribution of robes and clothing, spoke these words:
"If the Buddha would permit me to offer *āmra* and *bīhara* garments."
The Buddha said,
"I permit Māra and Vihāraśī.
The assembly said:

"If the Buddha would permit me to take the corner of his robe and go," [he thought], "lest I drag it through the dust or tread upon it with my feet. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to tie it to a rope, with one person holding each end."
Because it was dragged through the mud in the center [of the road], this matter was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a wooden carrying-pole (*mokkhaka*).

At that time, young boys and girls were carrying the wooden poles; seeing people along the way performing music, eating, drinking, and playing, they set their ropes aside on one side and ran off to watch, thereby losing their belongings. The Buddha said:
"If those under six years of age, down to infants, as well as śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs— these five groups—
carry robes for [the monks]," the householder spoke again:
"The Buddha permits one to hold an incense burner before them."
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
At that time, as the assembly proceeded in silence, the various non-Buddhist practitioners spoke out of jealousy:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are no different from those carrying out a corpse.
The householder said,
"If the Buddha would allow me to go with the singing and music of worldly custom."
The Buddha said,
“I permit it.
A certain lay devotee, seeing that the great assembly had gathered, offered many robes and articles.
The lay devotee said,
"If the Buddha would permit us to proclaim praises everywhere.
The Buddha said:
“I permit it.
No one accepted these robes and garments. The Buddha said:
“I permit that a *karmavācanā* be performed first, and that one person be authorized to accept them.”
When there was no one to guard it, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to perform a *karmavācanā* to appoint one person to guard it.
A bhikṣu who lacks five qualities should not perform a *karmavācanā* to receive clothing and requisites."
What are the five?

Not knowing whether one has received [an item] or not; not knowing the object received; not knowing its value; not knowing its quantity; or being attached to that which is not a locus for mindfulness.
A bhikṣu who possesses five qualities should perform the formal act (karmavācanā) to receive a robe:
he knows what has been obtained, he knows the object received, he knows its value, he knows its quantity, and he wears it with mindfulness.
In a certain monastery in the kingdom of Kosala, the two divisions of the Saṃgha obtained some cloth and requisites.
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "The Buddha has permitted us to place the items we have been given as offerings in separate locations."
The Buddha said, “I permit it.

However, there were some bhikṣuṇīs to whom no one gave clothing, food and drink, bedding, or medicine for illness; or there were those to whom others gave only a small amount, whereupon they laughed derisively, saying:
"Because I love my wife, I give it to her.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the Buddha,
"Please allow us to place our donated items back in one location."
The Buddha said,
"It is permitted.
When no one was there to divide these robes and articles, the Buddha said:
"One who knows how to divide the goods should perform the *karmavācanā*.
There are five qualities that a monk must not possess to be appointed by *karmavācanā* as a distributor of robes.
What are these five?
If one does not know the characteristics of the robe, does not know its color, does not know its value, does not know the number, or does not remember whether it was given or not, [one is unfit].
A bhikṣu who possesses five qualities should serve as the distributor of robes:
he must know the characteristics of the robe, know its color, know its value, know the number, and remember whether it was given or not.
When the bhikṣuṇīs were distributing the robes, they praised them, saying, "This is good; that is not good," thereby disturbing the assembly. The Buddha said:
"When distributing robes, one should not offer praise, as it disturbs the assembly;
one should accept one's share of the robes in silence."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were people in the Jeta Grove who, for the purpose of preparing a new dwelling, had prepared food and drink; a great assembly of bhikṣus gathered, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.

The bhikṣus entered in disorder, sat down in disorder, and ate in disorder, lacking any proper sequence; some bhikṣus entered before the meal had begun, some entered while the meal was in progress, and some entered after the meal was finished.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should announce that the time has arrived.
Although they announced that the time had arrived, those in the distance could not hear it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should strike the ghaṇṭā.
Although they struck it, those at a distance could not hear it.
The Buddha said,
"You should beat the drum.
When they beat the drum on level ground, it could not be heard from afar.
The Buddha said:
"One should strike while standing upon the mound.
Still they did not hear it, so the Buddha said:
"One should stand at a high place to strike, so as to both see and hear.
At times there may be no one to oversee the food; the food is not yet prepared or cooked, and though the time has arrived, the food is poor.
At other times there is someone to oversee the food; the food is prepared and cooked, and when the time arrives, the food is excellent.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The person who supervises the distribution of food should perform the *karmavācanā* within the Saṃgha.
At a certain residence in the Kingdom of Kośala, the two divisions of the Saṃgha obtained clothing and requisites; as there were few bhikṣus and many bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣus said:
"This clothing and property shall be divided into two halves; one half is for the community of bhikṣus, and the other half is for the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Originally our community was small, so the bhikṣus took two shares while we took only one."
"Today there is much; why should we give only half?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should divide it equally."
For *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs*, four parts are allotted, with one part of the fourth [part] remaining.
At times, when a donor provides food for the Saṃgha in an open, unsheltered place, there may be leftover cakes on the trays, leftover rice in the baskets, and soup in wooden bowls.
The various non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners were jealous; they placed dregs of wine into the rice and soups, thinking thus:
"This food is impure, so that the renunciants will not be able to eat it."
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do, so they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it can be set aside, set it aside; the remainder may be eaten."

If monks pass a bowl of food back and forth with a śrāmaṇera—where a monk turns his food over to the śrāmaṇera, and the śrāmaṇera turns his food over to the monk—and the monk washes his hands and receives it again from the śrāmaṇera, he may have a doubt in his mind:
"This might be impure food."
He then informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one single-mindedly and truly gives a bowl of food to a śrāmaṇera, this is considered pure.
When the śrāmaṇeras were walking about carrying vessels, jars, baskets, helmets, and ladles to distribute the food, the bhikṣus received their portions of food from the śrāmaṇeras.
If a śrāmaṇera serves food and a bhikṣu receives it,
the bhikṣu may have a doubt:
"Could this not be considered 'touched food'?"
Not knowing what to do,
they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu who receives food by touch commits no offense.

After the bhikṣus had finished eating, they gave the bowls containing leftover food to śrāmaṇeras and laypeople; once the śrāmaṇeras and laypeople had finished washing the bowls, they returned them to the various jars, baskets, and vessels.
The bhikṣus reflected:
"This may be impure.
The Buddha said:
"One should give the bowl to a lay attendant with a single mind; this is called purification.
There were some bhikṣus who had donors provide food for them in an open space.
When the bhikṣus had finished eating, they left their food vessels there and departed; wind and rain made them muddy, dirty, and impure.
The Buddha said,
"Utensils should be thoroughly washed and placed in a covered location.

When the bhikṣus used soap powder two or three times and it did not completely remove the grease because of its stickiness, they scraped off the grease with wood and then washed the utensils with soap powder.
The water was extremely far away, yet laypeople offered it as a gift.
The laypeople said, "We know the water is very far away; why do you use so much of it?
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
The Buddha said:
"If one rinses with pure water once, twice, or three times, and then washes thoroughly with soap powder (kṣāra), this matter shall be considered purified.

At that time, there was a stagnant pool which the monks took for use; elephants, horses, donkeys, oxen, sheep, pigs, and dogs all entered it to drink, leaving behind impurities such as excrement and urine.
Leaves, flowers, and fruits all fell into the water, becoming putrid, foul-smelling, and impure.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"That which is impure in the water may be removed; the remaining water should be drunk."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying, “The water is turbid and salty; may it be drunk?
The Buddha said:
"If one previously suspected it was impure, one should not drink; if one did not previously suspect it, one may drink.
There was a monastery in the kingdom of Kośala where the Saṃgha received a gift of clothing and requisites, but it was not located in every place.
The *karmakāra* bhikṣu did not know what he should do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"These robes and articles should be divided into two portions, and one should speak as follows:"
"This portion belongs to the senior monk; this portion belongs to the junior monk.
He spoke thus:
"This portion belongs to the junior monk; this portion belongs to the senior monk."
Once the formal act (kamma) has been completed, it should immediately be concluded.
If another bhikkhu arrives, one who does not wish to participate should not be granted [the status].
If the aforementioned procedure is not performed, [the status] should not be accepted.
If one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense by not acting in this manner when leaving the boundary,
one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense and should likewise share [the property] with other bhikṣus.
Regarding these garments and belongings, one should calculate their value:
"I shall take this portion; the remainder belongs to you.
I shall accept this division."
If one performs the aforementioned procedure, it should be completed through *karmavācanā*.
When another bhikṣu arrives, if he does not wish to share [the property], it should not be given to him.
If the procedure is not performed in this manner, the portion should be shared with other bhikṣus.
If it is not according to the method described above, one should not accept the distribution outside the boundary; otherwise, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If a single bhikṣu says:
"Take one garment from among these robes and declare it my portion; the remainder shall belong to you all."
When the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for this has been completed, the remaining rules are as above.
These robes and requisites should be formally assigned to one bhikṣu.
How should they be assigned?
When the assembly of monks has gathered with one mind, a single bhikṣu should announce among the community:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These robes and articles are to be divided by the present Saṃgha residing at this location."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the monk so-and-so be granted [the robe] by the Saṃgha through formal act (karmavācanā).
Thus is the motion. This is the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
"Monks, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for giving the robe-cloth to monk so-and-so is finished. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld!
After that monk has received the robe-cloth, he refuses to return home and says:
"Where are there good dharmas, good words, or good methods of giving? All of these are within the Sangha; why should I return home?"
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do, so they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Give it because you are pure."
If he speaks thus, it is well for that bhikṣu to return; if he does not return, he should be forcibly taken back.
That bhikṣu should be instructed to confess his *duṣkṛta* offense.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
“The Buddha has permitted the bhikṣus to wear these garments:
the body-covering robe, the body-wiping cloth, the foot-wiping cloth, the face-wiping cloth, the saṃkakṣikā, and the antarvāsaka. What are the names of these garments?”
The Buddha said:
“It is called *pāṅkara*; in the Jin language, it means ‘an auxiliary robe for the body. Upāli asked:
"How is this robe to be accepted?
He replied: "This robe is to be addressed with these words:"
"This pāṅkara robe is for my own use. [The Buddha asked:
"From what kind of person should it be accepted?
The Buddha said:
"One should receive [the precepts] from within the five groups.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"If a senior bhikṣu is not intelligent and performs an illegal obstruction, does such an act constitute a valid obstruction?"
The Buddha said,
"It is not accomplished.
He asked again:
“If one maintains the precepts while performing what is unrighteous and non-virtuous, does this constitute a valid restraint?
The Buddha said: “It does not.”
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"As the Buddha has said:
'If one obstructs a formal act (karmavācanā) that is in accordance with the Dharma, that obstruction of the formal act is not established.'"
“Is it not the case that everything is negated? The Buddha said, “No.”
Upāli! There may be a śrāmaṇera who, at the time of receiving full ordination, feels regret in his heart and does not wish to receive it, saying:
"I do not wish to receive full ordination."
These words constitute a denial.
When a śrāmaṇerī receives the six rules and becomes a śikṣamāṇā, she says these words:
"I do not wish to receive the six rules."
These words constitute a formal refusal.
When a śikṣamāṇā receives full ordination, she says:
"I do not wish to receive full ordination."
These words constitute a denial.
If a bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and the saṃgha performs for him the parivāsa, mānāpya, mūlāpakarṣa, and āvarhaṇa karmas, that bhikṣu says:
"Do not do it; I do not need it."
These words constitute a refusal.
If fourteen bhikṣus ought to perform a formal act (karmavācanā) within the Saṃgha, yet they say:
"We do not need it."
"These words constitute a prohibition. Upāli asked:

"If there is a bhikṣu who has been expelled and wishes to perform repentance, and at the time of repentance he humbles his mind and follows the Dharma of the Saṃgha, may a *karmavācanā* be performed outside the boundary to lift the expulsion?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted.
One who performs an act of formal dismissal commits an offense."
Upāli asked the Buddha:
“In another place, the Buddha said:
‘There are two causes and conditions by which one knows that the Saṃgha has been split:’”
"First, one proclaims within the Saṃgha; second, one receives the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
If there is a person living as a thief (*caura-vāsika*) who proclaims the distribution of the voting sticks within the Saṃgha, is this called 'schism of the Saṃgha'?
The Buddha said: [It is not.]
"Not broken.
"If one distributes voting tickets (*śalākā*) among the Saṃgha for a *śikṣamāṇa* śrāmaṇera, is this called 'breaking the Saṃgha'?
The Buddha said:
"Not broken. Upāli asked:
"If four people who were originally laypeople cast voting sticks within the assembly, does this constitute a schism in the Saṃgha?"
The Buddha said, “It is not broken. [The questioner asked:
“If the number is complete, but one bhikṣu’s male organ transforms into a female organ, does this constitute a schism of the Saṃgha?”
The Buddha said,
"It is not broken. Upāli asked:
"If one is sitting on a seat spread with grass or a long bed, may one sit together with a person who has not yet received full ordination?
The Buddha said,
"One may sit."
“May one sit together with a eunuch?
The Buddha said,
“It is not permitted.”
"May one sit together with a śrāmaṇera who is under training?
The Buddha said,
"One may sit."
"May one sit together with a śrāmaṇera who is still in training?
The Buddha said, "No."
Upāli asked the Buddha,
"What is the measurement for the length of a bed or seat?
The Buddha said:
"A bed that is extremely small, sufficient for four people to sit upon, is called a 'long bed'.

A lay devotee built a dwelling within the Jetavana; while a bhikṣu was staying in this dwelling, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Seeing him, the lay devotee asked:
"Why are you begging for food?"
The bhikṣu said,
“Because I am unable to obtain food.
The householder said:
"Venerable sir, you may return; I shall send food for you.
Having said this, he sent it.
The bhikṣu asked:
"To whom is this food to be given?
The messenger replied,
"This food is for the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣu immediately sent a messenger to place the food at the location where the Sangha’s meal was kept.
On the following day, that bhikṣu again dressed in his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
The layperson saw him again and asked,
"Venerable sir, why do you beg for food?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I beg because I have no food.
The householder said, "I sent you food yesterday; why did you not eat it?"
The bhikṣu said:
"Regarding the food you have sent, I asked the messenger:
'To whom is this food given?'"
The messenger said, "Give it to the Saṃgha.
I then took it and placed it in the place where the food for the Saṃgha is kept; that is why I did not eat it.
The householder said, "I am not sending food for the entire Saṃgha; I am sending food for the monk who stays in my room.
The bhikṣu did not know what he should do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a donor provides offerings for the monks residing in a dwelling, the monks residing in that dwelling should accept them.
There was a lay devotee who built a dwelling within the Jeta Grove. After several days had passed, this lay devotee went to the Jeta Grove, wishing to listen to the Dharma.

Entering the quarters where duties were performed, at sunset he struck the *gandī* to invite them to hear the Dharma. As the bhikṣus sat in the darkness preaching the Dharma, the lay devotee said, "Venerable sirs, please light a lamp."
The bhikṣu said,
"There is no ghee or oil.
The householder said:
"I shall send someone to deliver it for you, Venerable Sir.
He then sent it.
The bhikṣu said:
"To whom? The messenger replied,
"To the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣu immediately sent a person to take ghee and oil and place them where the saṃgha lights its lamps.

On another occasion, a lay devotee went to the Jetavana and entered his own cell to listen to the Dharma. As was the custom, the ghaṇṭā was struck at dusk; the saṃgha sat in the darkness while the Dharma was being preached.
The lay devotee said, "Venerable sirs, light the lamps."
The bhikṣu said,
"There is no ghee or oil.
The householder said:
"I previously gave it to you for delivery; why do you not light it?
The bhikṣu replied, "You delivered it to the Saṃgha, so I had an attendant take the ghee and oil and place them where all the lamps of the Saṃgha are lit."
The householder said, "I am not sending ghee and oil for the entire Saṃgha; I am sending it for the bhikṣu residing here.
The bhikṣu did not know what he should do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If these offerings are for the bhikṣus residing in the dwelling, those items should be used by the bhikṣus residing in the dwelling; they should divide them among themselves, including the clarified butter and oil for anointing the feet, as well as leather sandals, robes, bowls, fruits, and medicines—all are likewise."
The Buddha said:
"If a donor says, 'Venerable One, for how long will you stay here? Whatever the Venerable One requires, you may use it as you please.'"
If he says, "This object belongs to you; take it and go," one may carry it away.

The monks took up the bedding and furniture belonging to the Saṃgha without first putting on their robes; consequently, the Saṃgha’s bedding became worn out, faded in color, and unpleasant, becoming soiled, foul-smelling, and infested with lice.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, regarding the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha, it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to take them for use without wearing a body-covering robe.
If he uses them, he commits a duṣkṛta offense."
The bhikṣus did not know how long the saṃkakṣikā (body-covering robe) should be made.
The Buddha said:
"At the very least, it must cover three parts of the body."
"What are the three?
The chest, the waist, and the knees.
The bhikṣus did not take care of or protect the monastic bedding, and other bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One must not fail to protect and cherish the use of the Sangha’s bedding and requisites; if one uses them without protecting and cherishing them, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
There are five matters regarding which one does not protect and cherish."
"What are the five?
Water, sun, dust, dirt, and physical abrasion—these are the five things for which one need not guard or cherish [the bedding].
The bhikṣus used the monastic bedding while standing in the rain; consequently, the bedding lost its color and the dye ran out.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not stand in the rain wearing monastic property; if you do so, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

A bhikṣu used the monastic bedding to warm his body over a fire; as a result, the cloth became smoky and foul-smelling, its color faded and diminished, and it became brittle, torn, and wrinkled. The Buddha said:
"One who wears monastic bedding must not warm their body over a fire; if they do so, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, if it is worn upon the back while warming the body over a fire, there is no offense."

When a bhikṣu uses the monastic bedding and furniture, enters places for defecation or urination, enters places for washing after defecating or urinating, or enters the bathhouse, that bedding loses its color, becomes soiled and foul-smelling, and develops lice.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not wear monastic bedding or robes when entering places for defecation or urination, nor when washing those areas, nor when entering the bathhouse."
"If you enter while wearing it, you will incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

When the group of six bhikṣus wished to have their hair shaved, one junior bhikṣu had not yet finished shaving and was not yet wearing his kāṣāya; the group of six bhikṣus drove the junior bhikṣu away, saying:
"You are too small!"
The Buddha said:
"When shaving the hair, if a young bhikṣu has a small amount of hair remaining, one should not drive him away.
If one drives him away, one incurs the offense of duṣkṛta."
The Saṃgha’s razor, tweezers, nail-clippers, and knives had been sharpened by the bhikṣus who wished to use them, but the group of six bhikṣus came and drove them away, saying:
“We are the elders!”
"You are small; give it to me.
The bhikṣus did not give it to him, and they quarreled and reviled one another.
The Buddha said:
"One should not give it; if there is someone who has previously received it for polishing, one should give it to another after they have finished using it.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw junior bhikṣus entering the latrine or urinal, or entering the place for washing after defecation or urination, they drove them away, saying:
"I am a senior elder!"
"You are too small.
This caused those who were not ill to fall ill, and those who were already ill to become more severely afflicted.
The Buddha said:
"In the places for defecation and urination, or the washing areas for defecation and urination, one who enters later should not drive out those who entered first.
If one drives them out, it constitutes the offense of *dukkaṭa*."
The group of six bhikṣus said to other bhikṣus in the bathhouse:
"Arise and leave!
We are the senior monks; you are junior."
The Buddha said:
"In the bathhouse, a senior monk (upādhyāya) should not drive a junior monk away; he should wait for him to leave.
If he drives him away, he commits the offense of duṣkṛta."

The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī. At that time, the Elder Ānanda was preaching the Dharma among a great assembly. When the foremost elder arrived, Ānanda instructed him to rise; when the second and third elders arrived, he likewise instructed them to rise. Consequently, the assembly dispersed, none remaining with a single-minded focus.
The laypeople said, "Venerable Sir!
There is no morning meal nor midday meal here; why did you rise upon the arrival of the Elder, causing the assembly to disperse and breaking the congregation listening to the Dharma?"
"If the Elder wishes to sit in the place of the Elder, why did he not enter first?
This Ānanda preaches the Dharma without knowing the beginning, without knowing the end, without knowing the sequence, and without knowing the causal conditions—for whose sake does he preach?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, when the Dharma is being taught or when it is being heard, one should not rise upon the arrival of a senior monk (sthavira), nor should a senior monk compel a junior monk (navaka) to rise."
Whether one rises on one's own initiative or urges another to rise, both incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The Buddha said:
"If the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* comes, one should rise out of respect; one should not tell others to rise."
If one speaks to another person while rising, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
From this day forward, it is permitted for three people to sit together on a bed with a coarse frame and a long rope.
They may sit together if they have been [ordained] for three years or less; if four years have passed, they may not sit together.
"On a bed with thin crossbars and ropes, two people may sit together; on a single bed, only one person may sit. There was a monk who possessed cauldrons, pots, and jars.
After the various bhikṣus had used them to boil dye, they were placed elsewhere. When the monk took his robe and placed it into the dye, the group of six bhikṣus came and said to the other bhikṣus:
"Give us the cauldrons, pots, and jars. I am a senior elder and you are junior; I wish to use them."
Having poured the dye into one object and then poured it into another, the dye gradually diminished and the color of the cloth turned black.
The bhikṣus did not give [the robe] to him; they quarreled and reviled him.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not give it.
If a bhikṣu has already taken and used it, he should later give it to the senior monk."
When only a small amount of dye remained, the Elder came and asked for it but was unwilling to give it. The Buddha said:
"If only a small amount remains and can be moved to another place, you should give it."
The bhikṣus took trees from the monastery grounds to boil rice, soup, meat, broth, medicine, and dye. The resident bhikṣus were displeased and spoke thus:
"We have labored with great hardship to cultivate these trees; yet you guest bhikṣus, without speaking to us, have taken them in silence and burned them."
The Buddha said:
"You should speak to the senior bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, the flowers of the trees within the monastic park should be gathered for use in making offerings to the stūpas of the Buddha and the stūpas of the Arhats.

If there are lay attendants (karmadāna), they should be instructed to gather the fruit for consumption. As for the large timber on the trees, the Saṃgha of the four quarters should use it to make beams and rafters.”
"The bark, branches, and leaves of the trees may be used at will by the bhikṣus.

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, Anāthapiṇḍada completed the construction of the Jetavana; having adorned it with various ornaments, he provided the four requisites as offerings to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not accept [the offer], saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive such decorated dwellings.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen and receive [the teaching] in a pure dwelling.
The group of six bhikṣus then drove away a bhikṣu who was practicing meditation, saying: "Arise!"
"I am the senior elder; you are junior.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, who said:
"When practicing meditation, one should not calculate seniority or juniority; one should not drive [the other] away."
"If you drive them away, you commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
When the monks used the monastery water to wash their feet, the group of six monks (Ṣaḍvargika) drove them away, saying:
"You are junior; we are the senior monks (*sthavira*)."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When washing one's feet, one should not drive others away by calculating their seniority.
If one drives them away, it constitutes the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
The bhikṣus hurriedly washed, wrung out, and spread out the monks' foot-wiping cloths, intending to wipe their double-layered leather sandals. The group of six bhikṣus said, "Get up and leave!
I am the senior; you are junior. Bring the foot-wiping cloth here so that I may use it."
The bhikṣus did not give it to him, and they quarreled and reviled him.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not give it; however, if the former person has finished using it, one should give it."
At a certain residence, an elder bhikṣu borrowed and used property belonging to a stūpa for his own purposes.
When that bhikṣu died, the other bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The value of the robes and bowls shall be calculated and offered to the stupa; the remainder should be divided among the monks."
In a certain monastery, a monk had dedicated his robes and bowl to the use of the stūpa.
When that monk died, the other monks did not know what should be done.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding property belonging to a stūpa, its value should be calculated and returned; the property [of the community] present there should be divided among the monks.
A single bhikṣu residing at one location borrowed property belonging to the Saṃgha from the four quarters and used it for his own private purposes.
When that bhikṣu died, the bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"The value of the goods shall be calculated and delivered to the Saṃgha of the four directions; the remainder shall be divided among the monks present.
If a single bhikṣu residing at one location has lent his robes and bowl for the use of the Saṃgha of the four directions..."
When that bhikṣu died, the other bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Regarding the value of robes, alms bowls, and items belonging to the Sangha of the four directions, they should be returned;
those belonging to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the local community) should be divided among them. This applies equally to visiting monks and resident monks.
A monk entrusted his robes and bowl to a layperson, but the layperson lost them. The monk went to the layperson's place to demand them back, and the layperson said:
"Lost. The bhikṣu said:
"You have lost it yourself; I have not lost it."
"If it is lost, you must compensate for it yourself.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it was well-guarded and yet lost, one should not have to compensate."
"If it is not found, you must compensate for the loss.
A merchant entrusted clothing and goods to a bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu lost them.
When the merchant went to the bhikṣu to demand restitution, the bhikṣu said:
"Lost," said the merchant.
"You have lost it yourself; I have not lost it."
"If it is lost, you must compensate for it yourself.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one has obtained [the object] through one's own free will, one should not be required to compensate."
"If you do not have the autonomy [to decide], you should repay it.
There was a householder who, having finished building a dwelling within the Jeta Grove, prepared a meal for a great multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, people from the lands of the four directions who were not practitioners of the Dharma all came to the assembly. Some made offerings to the bhikṣus, and when the bhikṣus recited their blessings, they praised the Buddha, saying:
"O Buddha of great power and great virtue!"
"Praise be to the Dharma, of great virtue and great power!
Praise be to the Sangha, of great virtue and great power!
Praise be to the Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kambala—thus to the Three Jewels, infinite, immeasurable, and incalculable!"

Among them, some may hold the name of the Buddha, some the name of the Dharma, some the name of the Saṃgha; some may hold the names of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, or Kambala; or some may hold the names of countless, immeasurable, and asaṃkhyeya beings. This great assembly will before long disperse, and these individuals will each return to their own fields, houses, and villages.
On other occasions, when various bhikṣus went out to the fields and villages of the various countries to beg for alms, some who held the name of the Buddha would say:
"The Buddha has come; give him an offering.
Those who held the name of the Dharma would say:
“Dharma has come; give alms.
The one holding the names of the Saṃgha says:
“The Saṃgha has come; give alms.”
The one bearing the name Śāriputra said, “Śāriputra has come; give him alms.
Those bearing such names as Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nanda, Kambila, and countless, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya others spoke likewise.
“For incalculable, immeasurable, and asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he has practiced giving incalculably, immeasurably, and asaṃkhyeyly.
Yet the bhikṣus did not accept this food.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
