"These people from the borderlands did not know that they were giving food for the sake of these bhikṣus; rather, they gave it under the name of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and to Śāriputra, and to countless, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya offerings of food and drink. You may accept them as you please."
There was a bhikṣu who was ill, and he had relatives residing at another monastery.
When those visiting bhikṣus came to inquire after his health, the sick bhikṣu asked them to sit.
Once they were seated and had inquired after him, the visiting bhikṣus stayed for only a short while and then rose to depart.
The sick bhikṣu asked,
"Why are you leaving?
They replied:
"I have not brought my robes and bowl.
The sick bhikṣu said,
"I shall give you my robe."
He gave it to him immediately.
The visiting bhikṣu stayed there for one night and departed the next day carrying this robe. Seeing this, the sick bhikṣu said:
"Do not carry away my robe."
The visiting bhikṣu said,
"This robe is truly yours to give me.
The sick bhikṣu said:
"I am giving it to you because it is impermanent; I am giving it to you because you have received it.
The visiting bhikṣu said, "It is indeed given permanently."
The sick bhikṣu did not know what he should do and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This was not given as a true gift, but was given for the sake of purification; this bhikṣu should return the robe."
"Use gentle speech to return [the goods] to the owner; do not take them back by force. Teach him to undergo repentance for the *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the Buddha was residing at the Jeta Grove Monastery, a fire gradually approached and began to burn the Jeta Grove. At that time, the Buddha made this prayer:
"I have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and am a true Arhat who has attained the Way of the Buddha. By virtue of this truthful word, may the fire be extinguished immediately. And so it was.
The bhikṣus took the monastic bedding and placed it in one location; after the fire was extinguished, they did not know which rooms the various pieces of bedding originally belonged to.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should make a mark.
Because the mark cannot distinguish them, one should further create a different sign."
Because they were made with distinct shapes, they could not be recognized; [the monks] thought, "One should make wheels, one should make contract marks, and one should make auspicious characters.
Because they acted in this way, they still could not identify them. The Buddha said, "One should make letters."
"This item was given as a gift by the householder So-and-so; it belongs to the room of So-and-so.
Although one knows that this bedding and furniture belong to someone, one still does not know to which specific storied pavilion this item belongs.
Which belongs to the upper pavilion?
Which belongs to the middle pavilion?
Which belongs to the lower pavilion?
The Buddha said:
"One should write the characters clearly at the top, indicating whether they belong to the upper, middle, or lower sections.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada constructed a multi-storied building to offer to the Saṃgha, the monks would not accept it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept the storied pavilion.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada offered mats to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha did not accept them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to accept the mat.
The householder then informed the Buddha:
"I wish to offer this intricately patterned woolen carpet to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said,
"Except for those made with female figures, all others are permitted."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada prepared five hundred single-seated lacquered-painted couches along with cushions and offered them to the Saṃgha; however, the monks did not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep such high-quality single-seated couches."
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to accept such pure, high-quality beds for solitary sitting.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada died; consequently, the Jeta Grove fell into ruin as no one remained to maintain it.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A formal ritual (karmavācanā) should be performed, as explained in the section on the seven dharma-robes.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
When the kinsmen of these people die, they wrap them in white cotton cloth and discard them in the place for the dead, thinking thus:
"This person is dead; what use is this cloth?"
"If you offer this to the Sangha, you shall obtain merit.
Having finished his reflections, he immediately took the white cotton cloth and went to the Jetavana to give it as an offering to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus would not accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept clothing discarded at places where the dead are left.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to accept them."
There was a poor man who died; his body was wrapped in a garment and discarded at a burial ground, whereupon he thought to himself:
"What use has this dead man for this garment?"
"If one gives to the Saṃgha, one may obtain merit.
Having finished these reflections, he immediately took [the offerings] and went to the Jetavana to give them to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not accept them, saying:
"This robe has no owner; from whom should it be received?
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"There is no other person [from whom it may be received]; it should be received according to the Dharma."
When that person’s kinsman dies, they think to themselves:
"I shall wrap [the body] in different clothes.
Having wrapped the impure body in different clothes, they then seek out their original robes from the bhikṣus to wrap the body for transport to the place where dead persons are discarded.
The relatives went to where the bhikṣus were and asked for their original robes back.
The bhikṣus did not give them to them.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be given.
Relatives wrapped the deceased in this way, thinking:
"This garment is inauspicious; who would accept it when it has already wrapped two corpses?"
They cast it out together with the corpse; once they had finished casting it out and returned, that robe was lost.
The bhikṣus went back to ask the man for it, and he replied, "It has already been lost."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is well to come forth and seek [what is owed] with gentle words; one should not seek it by force unless the dharma permits.
There was a bhikṣu who sold wine on credit and died before the debt had been repaid.
The wine merchant demanded payment for the wine from the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus replied,
"Why did you not demand it while this bhikṣu was still alive?
The wine merchant said:
"Reimburse me for the price of the wine; if you do not, I shall spread your ill repute, saying: 'The Śākya śramaṇa drank wine and refused to pay for it.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has robes and bowl items that should be used to repay [the debt]; if the owner has no property, one should take items from the Saṃgha to provide the repayment. Why is this?..."
"I fear it will bring ill repute upon the bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
A group of merchants from Śrāvastī were about to set out on their journey; along the road, through a desolate wilderness and a place of dread, there was an exceptionally fine vihāra.
A merchant entered the vihāra and saw the bhikṣus sitting in silence, neither sleeping nor dozing, but practicing dhyāna and entering deep meditative absorption.
Upon seeing the bhikṣus, the merchant conceived a profound and pure faith, and said to his sons and grandsons:
"Look for some food and drink, however little there may be, and bring it here to offer as alms to these excellent bhikṣus."
The young man replied,
"There is no other food remaining, but there is a small amount of grapes.
The merchant said:
"Give as much as you can, for if one does not practice giving, there will be no merit.
He then gave the grapes to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus divided them among themselves, each receiving five pieces.
The bhikṣus each sought a pure attendant (kappiyakāraka), but some found them while others did not; not knowing what they should do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Collect all the grapes in one place and purify them by fire; then you may eat them."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Āravī.

During the first watch of the night, the elder bhikṣus sat in meditation; during the middle watch, they each returned to their respective rooms to sleep. Along the way, they were terrified by various malevolent insects, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and brown bears.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit walking with a lit torch.
When Lady Mallikā went to the Jetavana wishing to hear the Dharma, the bhikṣus were preaching the Dharma in the darkness, and Lady Mallikā said:
“Venerable One, please light the lamp.
The bhikṣus replied,
“There is no ghee or oil.”
The lady said,
"I shall send it," and on the following day she sent it immediately.
The bhikṣus immediately lit lamps and placed them on the ground, but they were not very bright.
Queen Mallikā then provided lamp-stands for them, but the bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept lamp-stands."
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the use of lamp-stands.
While the Buddha was in Rājagṛha,

the group of six bhikṣus smeared their feet with impure fats— the fats of lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, and bears— and then went into the stables of others' elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and donkeys.
When these animals smelled the stench of the fat, they all pulled against their yokes and traces and fled in terror.
The people asked,
"Why are the animals running away in such fear?"
The group of six bhikṣus said, "We possess great majesty and supernormal powers; that is why we fled in alarm.
The lay devotees, filled with anger, rebuked and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent.
They are like hunters who smear their feet with the fat of wild beasts to cause the animals to flee in terror, yet they say:"
"I possess great supernormal power and majestic virtue.
When the bhikṣus, who were of few desires and easily contented, heard this, they were displeased in their hearts and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the fat of various evil beasts must not be used to anoint the feet.
If one uses it, they commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

King Prasenajit went to the Jetavana intending to listen to the Dharma; on that day, however, it was the *poṣadha* ceremony for the recitation of the precepts, and the bhikṣus said to him, "Great King!"
"Come forth!
We wish to perform a religious rite.
The king said:
"I wish to listen to the ritual of the Dharma.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to recite the precepts in the presence of those who have not received full ordination."
"The king certainly wishes to hear [the teaching], yet the bhikṣus do not know what they should do.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize you to recite the precepts in the presence of King Prasenajit and other kings.
When the ministers, soldiers, and officials have been dismissed, at that time King Prasenajit will attain purity of mind."
There was a man who offered vast lands to the bhikṣus as gifts, but the bhikṣus would not accept them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the Saṃgha to accept and utilize them for the construction of groves, separate rooms, dwellings, and walking paths."

The five bhikṣus wore robes of three and a half cubits and entered the village to beg for food; these robes trailed on the ground, their feet stepped on the soil and dirtied them, and the wind blew, exposing their bodies. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to receive the nivāsana (undergarment) and wear it when entering the village; the nivāsana shall be four cubits in length and two cubits in width."

The bhikṣus of the kingdom of Ālavī daily carried stones, earth, bricks, tiles, mud, and clay to repair the Buddha’s stūpas and vihāras; their robes were soiled with impurities and dirt as they went on their almsrounds.
The laypeople became angry and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
'We are virtuous and excellent. "

"Even the various non-Buddhist Brahmins come to beg for alms wearing clean robes; yet now these sons of the Śākyas come to beg for alms wearing soiled garments, like sesame oil pressers or like figures made of clay."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, when performing manual labor, I allow you to wear an inner *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment).
This was while the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
When various noble sons of the Śākyas went forth as renunciants, they wandered for alms laughing and joking with their chests bared.
A brāhmaṇa said:
"The sons of the Śākyas say of themselves:"
"How excellent and virtuous! [he said].
"Now, while joking and laughing, he begs for alms with his chest exposed, causing all the people to see him.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to wear the saṃghāṭī robe over the chest when entering a village for alms.
The bhikṣus rose early and entered the village for alms; having obtained food, they set it aside to one side, waiting for the proper time to eat.
At that time, there was a great wind and rain, and dust entered the food in the bowls.
The bhikṣus felt regretful and said:
"We would have to receive this food again, yet the time for the meal has arrived and we cannot find a *kappiya-kāraka*."
The bhikṣus were unable to obtain a *kappiyakāraka* (a person who prepares allowable food), and as the time for the meal was about to pass, they informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to eat five kinds of impure things provided they have not been formally accepted (*an-aṅgīkṛta*):"
"Rice dust, grain dust, water dust, cloth dust, and wind dust—these are the five kinds of dust.

At that time, the bhikṣus of the kingdom of Kośala received a portion of sugarcane; the elder monks received much, yet they had few teeth, while those of middle and lower rank, as well as the śrāmaṇeras, received little, which they consumed entirely with their sharp teeth.
Seeing that the Elder wished to obtain more, they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, during meal times, [the food] should be divided equally.
Many bhikṣus from the kingdom of Kośala were observing the summer retreat; when the lay devotees saw the many bhikṣus, they wished to invite them to a meal in successive order.
If one reduces one's own food and distributes it as alms to the bhikṣus— whether for half-monthly meals or monthly meals—

and after the bhikṣus have finished receiving the food and the invitation (pravāraṇā) has been performed during the month following the summer retreat, and the distribution of robes and the distribution of food have been completed, each person departs on their own.
Other bhikṣus were traveling through Kosala when they reached their destination near Śrāvastī; there, a heavy rain fell out of season.
The bhikṣus asked, "Is there any donor here who can provide us with food?"
A bhikṣu said: "No. He asked:
"Is there food for the Saṃgha?
He replied:
"There was originally food for the Saṃgha; however, after the last month of the summer retreat, once the distribution of robes and the distribution of food were completed, everyone has departed."
The bhikṣus, being of few desires and contented, were displeased when they heard this matter and rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you be called bhikṣus if, after the summer retreat is over, you divide up the food provided by the Saṃgha among yourselves and depart?"
After the monks had finished censuring him with various reasons, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the food of the Saṃgha should not be divided."

If one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* by dividing [the space], from this day forward, when observing the rains retreat under a tree, if there is a fine tree, one should yield it to a senior elder; as it is with a tree, so it is with an open space under a tree.
"There are matters that require a formal act (*karmavācanā*) involving fourteen persons.

While the Buddha was in the country of Varga, there was a son of a nobleman named Pūrṇa who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal at his residence the following day; the Buddha and the Saṃgha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Māṭhara, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and returned home. That night, he prepared various kinds of food and drink, arranged the seating, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know the proper time."
The Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks in front and behind, entered Mantiśā together with them; the Buddha sat upon the prepared seat in the midst of the assembly.
The sons and grandsons of Mantiśā did not have faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha; they were all Brahmins.

When people from the borderlands were serving food, they did not give it quickly, nor did they give much, nor did they give with a single-minded intention; while giving, they touched the bhikṣu’s hand.
The bhikṣu said to them, "Lift your hands high and do not touch my hand."
The youth said, "I am neither a leper nor a caṇḍāla; why do you treat me with such hostility?
The bhikṣus did not know what they should say.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it is not given with contempt, one may accept it."
"If one touches [an object] out of negligence, it should not be accepted by hand.
In a certain monastery in the Kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣu died.
This deceased bhikṣu had entrusted his robes, bowl, and belongings to the nunnery.
The bhikṣus said:
"We should divide it.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"We should divide it.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu, before his death, entrusts his robes, bowl, or other belongings to a bhikṣuṇī, the present community of bhikṣus should divide them.
At a certain residence in the kingdom of Kośala, a bhikṣuṇī died.
This deceased bhikṣuṇī had entrusted her robes, bowl, and belongings to the bhikṣus’ monastery.
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
“We should divide them.”
The bhikṣus said,
"We should divide it.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, before her death, entrusts her robes, bowl, or other belongings to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha present there should divide them.
This was when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
The Śākya son Upananda died; his robes and bowl were worth three hundred thousand taels of gold.
King Prasenajit of Kośala said:
"Since this man has no sons, these goods should belong to me."
The Buddha sent a messenger to speak to King Prasenajit, saying:
"Great King!
When you grant the provisions for people from cities and villages, do you perhaps give a greater share of those provisions to Upananda?"
The king said,
"I will not give it.
The Buddha said:
"By whose power have we been enabled to live? That is what should be shared.
It is by the power of the Saṃgha that we now take [this].
Upon hearing these excellent instructions, the king desisted.
The kṣatriyas said:
"This bhikṣu is of the same lineage and birth as we; he is likewise of the kṣatriya caste. Therefore, these robes and bowl should belong to us."
The Buddha sent a messenger to speak to the kṣatriyas, saying:
"When you attend to matters of state, great affairs, or official business, do you ever consult Bhaṇḍana?"
He replied, "I did not ask.
[The Buddha asked again:
"While Upananda was away, when you were attending to official business, did you wait for Upananda?"
He replied, "I do not wait.
The Buddha said:
“Bhadrananda performed the *karmavācanā* together with the Saṃgha; since the Saṃgha did not perform the *karmavācanā* while Bhadrananda was absent, these robes and bowls should belong to the Saṃgha.
Upon hearing this excellent instruction, the Kṣatriyas desisted.
Among the various kinsmen, both on the paternal and maternal sides, as well as those related by marriage, all said:
"This is Baddhananda; he is our uncle, our father’s brother, our maternal uncle, our nephew, or our cousin. These robes and bowl should rightfully belong to us."
The Buddha sent a messenger to say to them:
"When you give your daughters in marriage, take wives, hold gatherings, or exchange money and goods, do you ever wait for Baddhālita to share in them?"
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:
“Those who share food and clothing with Bāṇa-datta should receive their portion of these garments.
Since the Saṃgha gave food to Bāṇa-datta, these items—garments and bowls—should belong to the Saṃgha.”
Upon hearing these excellent instructions, the kinsmen desisted.

However, the robes, bowl, and personal effects of Upananda were deposited elsewhere; when Upananda died in that other location, the bhikṣus where the items were kept said, "We should divide these robes, bowl, and belongings."
The bhikṣus at the place of death said,
"We should divide these robes and bowls.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"These robes, alms bowls, and other belongings shall be divided among the *saṃgha* present within the boundary.

As for the robes, alms bowls, and belongings of Upananda, he had lent them out for interest in various places; he died in one place, while others in different places owed him debts. After his death, the monks in those places where the debts were owed said:
"This property we should divide among ourselves.
The bhikṣus at the place of death said,
"This property we should divide among ourselves."
The Buddha said:
"Within the boundary where the debt was incurred, that bhikṣu should divide [the property].
Regarding the robes and bowl of Upananda, he acted as guarantor for interest in one place while dying in another; he provided security in one place while receiving the interest in another.
The bhikṣus at the place of death said,
"These robes and bowl should belong to us.
The bhikṣus at the place where the breath departed said:
"These robes and bowl should belong to us," said the bhikṣus who had acted as guarantors.
"These robes and bowl should belong to us."
The Buddha said:
"The Sangha present within the boundaries of the monastery where the guarantee was made should divide it.

As for the robes and bowl of Upananda that had been lent out as collateral, Upananda died in one place, the collateral remained in another place, and the person who had taken the money was also in yet another place.
The bhikṣus at the place where he died said,
"These goods and wealth should belong to us.
The bhikṣus at the place where the pledge was held said:
"This property should belong to us.
The bhikṣus at the place where the money was taken said,
"This property should belong to us."
The Buddha said:
"The physical objects within the boundary of the monastery shall be divided among the bhikṣus present there.

Regarding the robes, bowls, and property of Upananda, he had given them as collateral for a loan and received a promissory note; Upananda died in one place, the person who took the money was in another place, and the person who drew up the note was also in another place.
The bhikṣus at the place where [the donor] died said,
"This property should belong to us.
The bhikṣus at the place where the money was collected said:
"This property should belong to us.
Those bhikṣus who held the documents in their hands said,
"This property should belong to us."
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The bhikṣus present within the boundary where the hand holding the document is located should divide it."
"Whether one holds a promissory note or pledges an object, these two are no different.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Mūlaparṇaka died; his robes and bowl were originally entrusted to the Elder Ānanda.
Mūlaparagaṇa died in one place, the Elder Ānanda was in another place, and the robes, bowl, and belongings he had entrusted were in yet another place.
The bhikṣus at the place of death said,
"These robes, bowl, and belongings should belong to us."
The bhikṣus residing at the place where the Elder Ānanda stayed said,
"These robes and bowl items should belong to us.
The bhikṣus who had entrusted their robes and bowl items there also said:
"This robe and bowl should belong to us.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Wherever Ānanda may be within the boundaries of the community, the bhikṣus present there should divide [the property].
*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, fascicle 61.
